summary: Newell and Simon present an information processing theory of human problem solving, built from task analyses and protocol evidence in cryptarithmetic, logic and chess, and stated in full in the final theory chapter.

unitSummaries.Introduction: States the book's aim and scope, the character of the information processing theory, and the plan of the five parts.
unitSummaries.Chapter 2: Defines an information processing system and the notations, symbol structures, programs and production systems used throughout the book.
unitSummaries.Chapter 3: Asks whether problem solving theory describes the person or the task environment, and how environments and problems are represented as problem spaces.
unitSummaries.Chapter 4: Describes how an information processing system solves problems: generate and test, selective search and heuristics, with the Logic Theorist as a worked example.
unitSummaries.Chapter 5: Analyses the cryptarithmetic task and its problem spaces (basic, augmented, algebraic and others) before any human data are examined.
unitSummaries.Chapter 6: Analyses one subject's protocol with a problem behavior graph and a production system, and measures how much of the behavior the system explains.
unitSummaries.Chapter 7: Tests whether the S3 theory covers other cryptarithmetic subjects, using problem spaces, strategies and episodes, plus eye-movement data.
unitSummaries.Chapter 8: Analyses the symbolic logic task and its problem space, and introduces the General Problem Solver and the sources of problem difficulty.
unitSummaries.Chapter 9: Compares GPS simulations with fragments of human protocols on logic problems, examining behavior on Problem D1 in detail.
unitSummaries.Chapter 10: Broadens the logic analysis to many subjects and problems: plans, episodes, a difficult problem, working-backward episodes and sources of difficulty.
unitSummaries.Chapter 11: Analyses the chess task environment and reviews the major chess-playing programs, from Turing's to Greenblatt's.
unitSummaries.Chapter 12: Analyses one chess subject's search behavior, episodes and move generation, and assesses a set of productions against the protocol.
unitSummaries.Chapter 13: Extends the chess analysis with de Groot's data, progressive deepening, means-ends analysis, checkmating combinations and perceptual aspects.
unitSummaries.Chapter 14: States the theory in full: the information processing system, problem space, methods and programs, how individual spaces and programs are determined, and task structures.
unitSummaries.Epilogue: Looks back on the trip through the data and what information processing explanations say about problem solving behavior.
unitSummaries.Historical Addendum: Traces the antecedents of the work: pre-history, the post-war setting, the critical years 1954-1958 and the road ahead.
unitSummaries.Reading the book as a whole: Ties the introduction, the three task areas and the theory together: the problems, the evidence and where the theory ends.

concepts.title: One work cannot do everything
concepts.question: Why do the authors say that no single work can advance understanding very far?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The book aims to advance understanding of how humans think, by setting out a theory of human problem solving and a body of evidence for judging it. Any single work, though, is limited in what it can cover.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The authors treat science as a series of successive approximations: not everything can be done at once, so one must start somewhere. A work that tries to cover all human thinking becomes superficial; a work that probes in depth leaves many important aspects untouched.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Here the support is the authors' reasoning about a trade-off, not data. The data come later: the book pairs its theory with a body of empirical evidence so that readers can assess the theory.

card.rule: According to the authors, one work must trade breadth for depth, and this book chooses depth.
card.limits: Limiting the scope is a place to start, not a claim that the neglected parts do not matter. The theory may also speak beyond its first base.

concepts.title: A map of how the human system varies
concepts.question: Along which three dimensions does the book mark out the part of human behavior it studies?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A human being varies in many ways, and a single book cannot study them all. The authors use one diagram, Figure 1.1, to mark out which portions of the total human system this work includes.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The diagram centers on the individual, a system with parts such as sensory subsystems, memory, effectors and arousal subsystems. It varies along three dimensions: the task dimension (the class of situation), the performance-learning-development dimension, and the individual-difference dimension.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The figure is a map, not a finding. The authors illustrate the task dimension with a whole geography of activities: a human does mathematics, walks, argues, drives and buys food. Performing, learning and developing are told apart, roughly by time scale.

blocks.label: Assumed
blocks.text: The authors say it makes little difference that the best list of subsystems is unsure, because a study can be limited to one or a few parts. They admit the distinctions are imperfect.

card.rule: Locate a study by its task, by whether people perform, learn or develop, and by which people are compared.
card.limits: The three dimensions are a rough guide: for example, learning and maturation often cannot be told apart with confidence.

concepts.title: Adults, short symbolic problems
concepts.question: Which people, tasks and activities does the book concentrate on?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Every region of the map of human variation leaves out most human phenomena. The authors must say which region this book studies, as others might study intelligence across species or social roles among students.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The book studies the performance of intelligent adults in our own culture on short problems of about half an hour, moderately difficult and symbolic. Its three main tasks are chess, symbolic logic and cryptarithmetic puzzles, and it studies the integrated activities that make up problem solving.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors say what is left out. Perception, motor skill and personality variables are not central. They study performance primarily, learning only a little, and development or age differences not at all.

blocks.label: Limit
blocks.text: Very quick reactions (half a second or less) and activity over days or years are left out too. These restrictions describe a central focus, not a set of boundaries.

card.rule: The central focus is adult performance on short symbolic problems, studied as integrated activity.
card.limits: A focus is not a fence: the authors do not claim the excluded matters are irrelevant to problem solving.

concepts.title: The shift of outlook around 1956
concepts.question: What change in scientific outlook, dated around 1956, does the book say its approach belongs to?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: For several decades psychology focused on learning, on lower organisms and on tasks simple from an adult human viewpoint. The authors say their own choices were largely opportunistic, although an opportunism lasting twenty years.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Within the last dozen years the authors saw a general change in outlook, dated roughly from 1956. The common new emphasis was not problem solving as such. It was exploring complex processes and accepting the need to be explicit about internal, symbolic mechanisms.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors date the change by four works from three fields: Bruner, Goodnow and Austin on thinking, and Miller's paper on the number seven in psychology; Chomsky's paper on models of language; and their own paper on the Logic Theory Machine in computer science.

card.rule: Around 1956 several fields began to treat complex processes and explicit internal symbolic mechanisms as the thing to study.
card.limits: The four works do not share one specific lineage; the authors trace them only loosely to technology and applied mathematics.

concepts.title: More than a metaphor
concepts.question: When does calling a human an information processor stop being a metaphor?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The theory views a human as a processor of information. But information and processing are old, general concepts, so the label could be vacuous. Saying a computer is an instance of an information processor makes it a metaphor: man as a digital computer.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Something ceases to be metaphor when detailed calculations can be made from it. The authors use an abstract concept of an information processing system, which makes it possible to represent a particular man at work on a particular task in a precise symbolic model, so that aspects of his behavior can be calculated.

blocks.label: Assumed
blocks.text: The model hypothesizes, in extreme form, discrete symbols and a small set of elementary processes, each precisely defined and limited. This is an approximation, possibly a severe one, but it gives a grip on symbolic behavior. It steers away from physiological models of continuous mechanisms.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The support offered here is the argument itself: the model allows calculation, which a metaphor does not. The evidence that the calculations match human behavior comes later in the book.

card.rule: According to the authors, a precise symbolic model from which specific behavior can be calculated is no metaphor.
card.limits: The model is still an approximation that assumes neat discrete symbols; it does not claim that man is a digital computer.

concepts.title: Why chess, logic and puzzles
concepts.question: Why did the authors pick tasks such as chess and logic, and not language or pattern recognition?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Once the authors chose to study symbolic systems precisely, many tasks stayed open. They needed to explain why chess, symbolic logic and puzzles were chosen, and why other kinds of thinking were not.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: A theory of problem solving needs good task analyses and an inventory of possible problem solving mechanisms, from which one can surmise what humans actually use. So the authors work where artificial intelligence, the part of computer science that gets machines to do tasks requiring intelligence, has supplied plausible mechanisms: game players, theorem provers and puzzle solvers.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors give reasons against other areas. Language work has mostly analyzed grammar (competence) and not use of language (performance), and programs for meaning and use are fewer, newer and less developed. Pattern recognition machines are built around the single act of recognition, not sequential integrated behavior.

blocks.label: Assumed
blocks.text: The authors add that artificial intelligence does not move independently of psychology: much of it started from psychological concerns.

card.rule: Choose task environments in which artificial intelligence has already supplied an array of plausible mechanisms.
card.limits: The tasks are not the only worthwhile ones. Many other kinds of thinking, such as designing a house, are beyond the current state of the art, not unimportant.

concepts.title: Performance before learning
concepts.question: Why do the authors study performance before learning and development?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Humans learn continuously and develop from a complex starting point. A reader may ask why the book does not begin with learning or development, and the authors call their emphasis on performance a scientific bet.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Learning is a second-order effect: it transforms a system capable of certain performances into one capable of additional ones. A precise study of learning must therefore start from a model of a performing organism, so that learning can be represented as changes in the model. If performance is not well understood, studying learning is premature.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The mathematization of learning theory in the last decade shows the point: it needs a model of the organism first. As for development, the authors say they have too imperfect a view of the final system to predict from the developmental process to the structures it produces.

blocks.label: Limit
blocks.text: The strategy is not costless. Without learning, one cannot draw inferences about the performance system from the fact that it must be capable of modification through learning.

card.rule: Understand the performing system first; learning, as a second-order change to it, comes later.
card.limits: The authors admit a cost and expect learning and development to be built into a later, more complete theory.

concepts.title: What is left out, and why
concepts.question: Why do the authors set aside perception, motor skills, motivation and personality?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Sensory and motor skills, many aspects of perception, and motivation and personality are real parts of behavior. The authors must say why a book on thinking leaves them out.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: For perception and motor skills, the concern is central symbolic activity and sequential behavior; the authors say motor skills lack a mechanistic representation as powerful as the information processing one, and seem partly nonsymbolic. Motivation and personality are left out because of a view about the order in which theory should develop, not about their importance.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Many motivational and emotional phenomena operate through the lens of the cognitive system, as work by Schachter and Singer indicates. So a plausible strategy is to put cognitive models in order before moving on. The authors made one exploratory foray into motivation and emotion.

blocks.label: Alternative
blocks.text: Other thinkers took a different route: Bartlett made motor skills the key metaphor for thinking, and the Gestalt school used perception as the touchstone of central activity.

card.rule: Leaving a topic out can be a claim about the order of theory building, not about the topic's importance.
card.limits: The authors do not claim the excluded topics are unimportant. They present the order of development as a conviction, not as something proved.

concepts.title: Giving a theory its shape
concepts.question: What does it mean to state the "shape" of a theory, and why do the authors do it first?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Before the details of a theory arrive, a reader needs a framework. The authors say a theory of man as an information processing system, at least when he solves problems, has a gross shape that can be characterized briefly.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Examples of shape: Newtonian mechanics is axiomatic and deductive; classical astronomy is empirical but not experimental; biochemistry consists in part of a large catalog of mechanisms; intelligence testing deals with the human as a static collection of traits or factors.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors offer these four labels as illustrations. Each places a theory in an overall framework in which the pieces fit as the theory is assembled step by step.

card.rule: A theory's shape is its overall framework, not its detailed content.
card.limits: A shape label is a thumbnail. It does not give the full content of a theory.

concepts.title: Mechanisms that explain, not just describe
concepts.question: What does it mean that the theory is reductionistic, and what does it refuse to say about the brain?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A theory of behavior can give relations or laws from which one concludes what behavior must be, or it can posit the processes that produce the behavior. The authors take the second route.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The theory posits a set of processes or mechanisms that produce the behavior of the thinking human. It is therefore reductionistic, and it purports to explain behavior, not just describe it, however parsimoniously.

blocks.label: Assumed
blocks.text: The processes presumably exist in the central nervous system, as internal parts of the organism. Nothing in the theory says so, but massive physiological evidence points there.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors decline to speculate about physiological correspondences. No plausible localizations exist yet for immediate memory, for the symbol (the engram), or for the act of adding two plus two, so nothing physiological can be said of this material.

card.rule: Posit the internal mechanisms that produce behavior, and do not assign them to places in the brain.
card.limits: Reduction is relative: the elementary processes and their organization are not explained by the theory.

concepts.title: Model one person, then ask what is common
concepts.question: Why does the theory model one person at a time, and what problem does that create?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The technique for building information processing systems leads to particular programs for particular tasks. In psychology it leads to a model of a single individual on a single task, so full particularity is the rule. The hard part is getting back to what is general to all humans.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: This reverses earlier psychology, which drew a line between clinical efforts on the individual in all his uniqueness (idiographic) and experimental efforts treating an individual only as an intersection of statistically defined populations (nomothetic). Here individual differences are not tacked on; grouped data are not used to test the theory if it can be helped.

blocks.label: Assumed
blocks.text: The authors take as natural Freud's dictum that all behavior is caused, and do not assume behavior is fundamentally stochastic with regularities showing only in averages.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors say this is a consequence of viewing the human as a complex mechanism whose parts and connections can ultimately be deciphered, a view accepted in most science outside psychology.

card.rule: Model the individual first, then ask what is common to all human information processors.
card.limits: The cost is generalization: getting from one person's model to what all humans share is the hard part.

concepts.title: A theory that does the task it explains
concepts.question: What does it mean that the theory is content-oriented, and what limit do the authors admit?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: In 1955 McClelland criticized psychology for abstracting from content: by describing only basic universal processes, such as in learning, it ignored a major part of its domain. He set content against process.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The present theory is strongly oriented to content, and this shows in a peculiarity: the theory performs the tasks it explains. A good theory of a good chess player can play good chess. The theory describes the manipulation of information down to a level where a simple interpreter, such as a digital computer, can turn it into an effective process. Not all versions of the theory are carried so far, of course; in general the theory can deal with the full content of a task.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors do not contrast content with process. It is of the nature of information processes to deal with content: something counts as content only if processes exist that treat it as information, discriminating on the basis of it.

blocks.label: Limit
blocks.text: No system yet understands a poem, that is, fully assimilates its content. Faith that it might goes beyond the evidence in the book, and each reader must make his own extrapolation.

card.rule: A content-oriented theory is one that can carry out the task it explains, though not all versions of the theory are carried that far.
card.limits: There is no compelling evidence that the content handled so far is typical of all the content that humans handle.

concepts.title: The program as the theory's equations
concepts.question: What does "dynamic" mean for this theory, and what plays the role of differential equations?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A theory can describe a system at one moment or describe how it changes through time. The authors want the second: a dynamic theory, but not in the sense in which the term is used in depth psychology.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The theory describes the time course of behavior. Its natural formalism is the program, which plays a role directly analogous to systems of differential equations in theories with continuous state spaces, such as classical physics. The state of a thinking system is a collection of symbolic structures in a memory.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors contrast the two formalisms. A program generally specifies a discrete change in a single component of the state, one symbol structure, at a moment in time. A differential equation system specifies infinitesimal changes in all coordinates at once. They call these details dictated by the nature of the system.

card.rule: In this theory a program does what differential equations do in classical physics: it says how the state changes.
card.limits: The analogy is one of role: programs change one symbol structure at a moment, not all coordinates at once.

concepts.title: Strategies for analyzing a dynamic system
concepts.question: What strategies do theorists of dynamic systems use, and which does this book rely on most?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A dynamic theorist wants to infer the behavior of a system over long periods, given only laws that say what happens in the next instant of time.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Three strategies are used. First, trace the time course from a completely specific initial state by applying the laws again and again. This is often called simulation and is a mainstay of the present work. Second, solve the laws to express the state at each time as a function of the initial state. This is rarely successful for complex systems and cannot yet be used with theories like these.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The third strategy avoids solving the system. The theorist explores steady states (where nothing changes), asymptotic behavior (what happens in the long run) or invariants (properties that hold despite variation elsewhere). All of these show up in the study of information processing systems, but limits on mathematical technique keep most analyses informal and empirical.

card.rule: When a dynamic system cannot be solved, simulate it step by step, or look for steady states, long-run behavior and invariants.
card.limits: Analytic solution is rarely possible for complex systems, so the authors' analyses stay informal and heavily empirical.

concepts.title: Rich data on each individual
concepts.question: Why does the theory rely on verbal protocols rather than control-group experiments?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The theory is not short of data, yet it uses little experimental design with control groups. The authors give three reasons: the phenomena depend strongly on history, the focus is the individual, and much happens within a single problem solving encounter.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Instead it becomes essential to get enough data about each subject to identify what information he has and how he is processing it. Combined with the content orientation, this leads to emphasizing verbal behavior as data, because of its high output rate.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The analysis of verbal protocols is a typical technique for verifying the theory and has become something of a hallmark of the information processing approach.

card.rule: Use rich data on each individual, especially verbal protocols, since classical control-group experiments rarely fit.
card.limits: "Not experimental" does not mean data are ignored. It means classical designs are only rarely useful here.

concepts.title: Why the book uses little statistics
concepts.question: Why does the book make little use of the standard statistical apparatus?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Theories of dynamic, history-dependent systems are hard to test, and saturation with content, meaning diverse meaningful symbolic structures, makes matters worse.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: So the book makes very little use of the standard statistical apparatus. Theory and data are still compared, and some attempts are made to measure and tabulate such comparisons.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors say their data analysis techniques resemble those of the biochemist or the archaeologist more than those of the agricultural experimenter.

card.rule: Compare theory and data directly, in the manner of the biochemist or archaeologist, and use standard statistics sparingly.
card.limits: Little statistics is not none: comparisons are still measured and tabulated.

concepts.title: Can the mechanisms do the task?
concepts.question: What does the sufficiency requirement ask of a theory first?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Almost never has it been asked of a psychological theory whether it could explain why man was capable of performing the behaviors in question. The emphasis on sufficiency is still rather foreign to psychology.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The theory puts a high premium on discovering systems of mechanisms sufficient to perform the cognitive task. A system able to perform is a first approximation, taking into account gross limits on human information processing such as processing rate and immediate memory. Then one develops a revised system with higher fidelity to specific data on human processing.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The concern arises not just in this theory but in the whole development of which it is a part. In taking sufficiency first, the authors adopt a particular approximating sequence in science, a choice they say is not without consequences.

card.rule: First show a system, within human limits, that can do the task; then refine it toward fit with specific data.
card.limits: A sufficient system is only a first approximation: that it can do the task does not show humans do it that way.

concepts.title: Five parts of the book
concepts.question: How is the book divided into five parts, and what does each do?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Before the theory is developed, the reader needs a plan. The authors give a short one, so that the features of the theory do not come as a surprise.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The book has five parts. Part I lays technical groundwork. Parts II, III and IV each take up a different task environment: cryptarithmetic, then elementary symbolic logic, then chess. Part V, Chapter 14 alone, states the theory in comprehensive form.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors say Parts III and IV deal with their task in the same manner as Part II. The investigations are limited to three areas, yet they say the theory has a more substantial scope.

card.rule: First the groundwork, then three task environments, and last the theory stated as a whole.
card.limits: The empirical work is limited to three areas, even though the theory is meant to reach further.

concepts.title: Part I: the groundwork chapters
concepts.question: What do Chapters 2, 3 and 4 set up for the rest of the book?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The later parts need three things in place: a definition of the system that solves problems, a clear view of the setting in which it works, and an account of how such a system goes about solving them.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Chapter 2 defines an information processing system (IPS) in a somewhat axiomatic way, to make clear what concepts are involved. Chapter 3 considers the task environment and its role in a psychological theory, including whether a theory of problem solving is about human beings or about the task environment, and how environments and problems are represented.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Chapter 4 discusses the species of information processing system that solves problems: generate-and-test, selective search and heuristics (devices that aid discovery), the assessment of task difficulty, and a detailed look at the Logic Theorist, which consolidates the lessons of Part I.

card.rule: Part I defines the system, the environment it works in, and the kind of system that solves problems.
card.limits: Part I is preparation; the human data begin with the later parts.

concepts.title: Parts II to IV: the empirical chapters
concepts.question: What does each empirical chapter, 5 to 13, do?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Each of the three task environments is studied in the same manner: first an analysis of the task, then the empirical analysis of individual protocols, then a broader look at human behavior.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Part II covers cryptarithmetic. Chapter 5 analyzes the task. Chapter 6 gives the first analysis of human behavior: subject S3 on a single puzzle, with a verbal protocol, a way of plotting his search (the Problem Behavior Graph) and his program as a production system. Chapter 7 adds four more subjects, a new tool called the episode, and one subject with eye movement data.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Part III covers elementary symbolic logic: Chapter 8 the task environment and the General Problem Solver (GPS), and Chapter 9 attempts to simulate two protocol fragments with GPS. Part IV covers chess: Chapter 11 the task analysis, Chapter 12 an individual protocol, and Chapter 13 a broader view.

card.rule: Each empirical part moves from task analysis to an individual's protocol to a broader view.
card.limits: The pattern is approximate: cryptarithmetic adds the Problem Behavior Graph and episodes, while logic adds GPS simulation.

concepts.title: What the chapter sets out to do
concepts.question: What two jobs does this chapter do, and what job does it leave to later chapters?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors' theory says humans think and solve problems as information processing systems (IPS's). Before that claim can be tested, a reader has to know what it means.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The chapter does two linked jobs. It describes the organization and functions of an IPS, and it introduces the notations used for the structure and behavior of IPS's throughout the book.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: None is offered here for the postulate itself. The authors say explaining its meaning does not justify it; empirical verification is the task of later chapters.

card.rule: This chapter explains what the IPS claim means and fixes the notation; it does not try to prove the claim.
card.limits: Our reading: a clear statement of a claim is not support for it, so nothing in this chapter should be cited as evidence that people really work this way.

concepts.title: Why plausibility is a poor test
concepts.question: Why do the authors refuse to judge the IPS postulate by how plausible it sounds?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Many readers will find the claim that humans are IPS's highly implausible, and others quite plausible. Can how it sounds decide whether it is right?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: According to the authors, the plausibility of a fundamental hypothesis is almost always time-dependent. New hypotheses are seldom thought plausible. Empirical support, and success in explaining a significant range of phenomena, make a hypothesis more plausible.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors give a general observation about how hypotheses are received, not a particular case from this chapter. Their conclusion is to wait for the empirical evidence.

card.rule: Do not judge a fundamental hypothesis by how plausible it sounds now; judge it after the empirical evidence is in.
card.limits: The point is about fundamental hypotheses. Our reading: it does not say first impressions are worthless, only that they are a poor test of a new idea.

concepts.title: The four parts of an IPS
concepts.question: What four components make up an IPS, and what must the memory be able to do?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The theory needs a precise description of the kind of system it says a thinking human is.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: An IPS is a system consisting of a memory containing symbol structures, a processor, effectors and receptors. A memory is a component capable of storing and retaining symbol structures.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors show the general structure in Figure 2.1 and lay down a set of interrelated definitions and postulates. Figure 2.1 is a diagram of boxes; the parts are named in the text.

card.rule: An IPS is a memory holding symbol structures, a processor, receptors and effectors.
card.limits: Our reading: the definition names the parts but does not yet say how any one of them works; the next ideas fill that in.

concepts.title: Symbols, structures and information processes
concepts.question: How do the definitions build from symbols to symbol structures to information processes?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The theory must say what the memory holds and what the processor works on.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: There is a set of elements called symbols. A symbol structure is a set of tokens (instances or occurrences) of symbols connected by a set of relations. An information process is a process that has symbol structures for some of its inputs or outputs.

blocks.label: Term
blocks.text: Token: one instance or occurrence of a symbol, as against the symbol as a kind.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: These are definitions and postulates 1, 2 and 4 of the chapter's list, so they are stipulated, not argued.

card.rule: Symbols are elements; a symbol structure is tokens linked by relations; an information process takes or gives symbol structures.
card.limits: A process that handles no symbol structure at all, for example, is not an information process in this sense.

concepts.title: What a processor consists of
concepts.question: What three components make up the processor of an IPS?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The IPS needs a part that does the actual work on symbol structures and settles what happens next.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: A processor consists of (a) a fixed set of elementary information processes (eip's), (b) a short-term memory (STM) that holds the input and output symbol structures of the eip's, and (c) an interpreter that determines the sequence of eip's to be executed, as a function of the symbol structures in STM.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: This is postulate 5 in the chapter's list, so it is a stipulated definition. The Morse example later shows all three parts at work.

card.rule: A processor is a fixed set of eip's, a short-term memory for their inputs and outputs, and an interpreter that picks the sequence.
card.limits: The interpreter is a part of the processor, separate from the eip's it sequences; what it can see is limited to what is in STM.

concepts.title: When a symbol structure designates an object
concepts.question: What has to be true for a symbol structure to designate an object?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: What makes a symbol structure stand for something, rather than be a mere pattern?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: A symbol structure designates (equivalently, references or points to) an object if there exist information processes that admit the symbol structure as input and either (a) affect the object or (b) produce, as output, symbol structures that depend on the object.

blocks.label: Term
blocks.text: Object: whatever is designated. The next idea lists what the authors include under this word.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: This is postulate 6, stated as a definition. The authors do not argue for it; they use it and illustrate it with examples.

card.rule: A structure designates an object when some information process, given the structure, affects the object or produces outputs that depend on it.
card.limits: Designation is defined through what processes can do with a structure, so a structure no process can use to reach an object does not designate it in this sense.

concepts.title: Programs and primitive symbols
concepts.question: What makes a symbol structure a program, and what makes a symbol primitive?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The theory needs to say how a symbol structure can direct behavior, and which symbols the system takes as given.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: A symbol structure is a program if (a) the object it designates is an information process and (b) the interpreter, given the program, can execute that process. A symbol is primitive if its designation, or its creation, is fixed by the elementary information processes or by the external environment.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: These are postulates 7 and 8, stated as definitions. The Primitive Symbols section later gives examples of what the authors take as primitive.

card.rule: A program is a symbol structure that designates a process the interpreter can execute; a primitive symbol has its designation fixed from outside the symbol structures.
card.limits: A list of process names that no interpreter can run is not a program in this sense.

concepts.title: The three sorts of object
concepts.question: Which three sorts of thing can a symbol structure designate?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The definitions use the word object loosely. What does it cover?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The authors use object for at least three sorts of things: (1) symbol structures stored in the IPS's memories, which they classify as data structures and programs; (2) processes the IPS is capable of executing; (3) an external environment of sensible, readable stimuli.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors give the list as a statement of how the word is used, not as an argument.

card.rule: An object may be a stored symbol structure, a process the IPS can execute, or something in the external environment.
card.limits: The list is open: the authors say object covers at least these three sorts.

concepts.title: Direct and indirect designation
concepts.question: How indirect can designation be, and which designations does the book mostly deal with?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A designating symbol might point straight at its object or reach it by several steps. How much indirection do the authors allow?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The relation between a designating symbol and its object can have any degree of directness or indirectness. A structure can point to a program, or to a structure that points to a structure that points onward to a program.

blocks.label: Assumed
blocks.text: Because the book focuses on central processes, the authors expect to deal often with structures that designate other structures in memory and with structures that designate programs.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors offer this as a stipulation about how symbols designate, not as data: they say they expect to meet structures that designate structures and programs often in the chapters ahead.

card.rule: Designation can be as indirect as needed: a structure may point to a structure that points to a program.
card.limits: Indirection costs nothing in principle here, but each link needs processes that can follow it.

concepts.title: A worked IPS: Morse symbols
concepts.question: How would a Morse-code IPS represent what it perceives?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors want a concrete system to make the postulates easier to follow. They choose an IPS that sends and receives Morse code.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The system perceives short (dot) and long (dash) signals and short (letter space) and long (word space) intervals. These evoke tokens of four primitive symbol types in STM. Sequences are represented as lists composed with the relation next.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: An illustration, not a test: the authors use it to make the assumptions concrete. There would also be symbol types designating the letters of the Roman alphabet, which are external objects.

card.rule: A Morse IPS maps four kinds of external signal onto four primitive symbol types and strings them into lists using next.
card.limits: The example is a simple teaching case. It shows how the pieces fit but does not show that people work this way.

concepts.title: Reading, writing, encoding and decoding
concepts.question: What do reading, writing, encoding and decoding processes do in the Morse IPS?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The Morse IPS has to take signals in, put signals out, and move between letters and their signal patterns.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: A reading program designates a process that, given a symbol structure for an external stimulus location, creates in STM the structure designating the stimulus there. A writing program designates the inverse process. Encoding and decoding processes convert between a letter token and its list of signal tokens.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors describe these processes as possibilities in an illustrative system; no data are involved.

card.rule: Reading puts a designation of the outside into STM, writing does the reverse, and encoding and decoding convert letters and signal lists.
card.limits: These are processes the example imagines. The authors do not claim that people have exactly these.

concepts.title: Building a bigger process from small ones
concepts.question: How can elementary processes combine to test whether two lists are identical?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The Morse example needs a way to tell whether two lists are the same, using only simple operations.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: One elementary process finds the member of a list that is next to a given member. Another tests whether two tokens are identical, that is, instances of the same symbol type. Combined step by step they test list identity: take the next token of each list, compare them, and stop with not identical on any difference or when one list ends first.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Figure 2.2 gives the four numbered steps. The authors leave out the added steps for finding the first token of each list.

card.rule: Larger processes are composed from elementary ones; two lists are identical only if every token matches and both end together.
card.limits: Figure 2.2 is a sketch that omits the steps for finding the first token on each list.

concepts.title: Abstract postulates and computer realizations
concepts.question: What do the IPS postulates leave open, and what does a computer realization show or fail to show?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Do the postulates say what the system is made of, and does the existence of computers that fit them show that people are IPS's?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The postulates characterize memory, elementary processes, symbol structures and the interpretive process abstractly. They assert nothing about physical or biological realization. Digital computers, which can be programmed to fit them, show that such systems can be realized by a determinate mechanism and can simulate the system defined.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The existence and behavior of digital computers. The authors say plainly that this does not prove humans are well modeled by such a system; that question comes later.

card.rule: The postulates are abstract; a computer shows an IPS can be built, not that humans are one.
card.limits: The argument shows only that the postulates can be realized, which is weaker than showing that humans realize them.

concepts.title: Symbol tokens and symbol types
concepts.question: What is the difference between a symbol token and a symbol type, and why does it matter?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The same symbol can appear several times in one structure, so counting symbols is ambiguous.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Symbol tokens are patterns that the IPS can compare and judge equal or different. A class of all tokens judged identical is a symbol type. Tokens of one type differ only in being distinct occurrences.

blocks.label: Term
blocks.text: Symbol: the word is used for either a token or a type, and context makes clear which is meant.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors point to a list with repeated tokens and note that the question how many symbols appear is ambiguous until it is known whether types or tokens are meant.

card.rule: A token is one occurrence; a type is the class of tokens the system judges identical; say which you are counting.
card.limits: Whether two tokens are of the same type is a judgment made by the system, so it can depend on the system's own discriminations.

concepts.title: Structures built from relations
concepts.question: How do relations turn symbol tokens into structures, and is one relation always enough?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A set of tokens becomes a structure only if relations connect them.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Symbol structures are built up from symbol tokens and relations. There may be only a single relation, such as next, which builds sequences. There may instead be several relations.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The Morse lists use only next. The authors point to another example where one relation is not enough.

card.rule: A structure is tokens plus relations; a single relation such as next gives sequences, and several relations give richer structures.
card.limits: A structure with several relations can sometimes be recoded with fewer, but the recoding may bury the original relations.

concepts.title: What makes symbols symbolic
concepts.question: What does a process need to be able to do with a symbol for the symbol to designate?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: What turns a pattern into a symbol rather than a mark?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: According to the authors, symbols are symbolic by their ability to designate, that is, to have a referent. An information process can take a symbol token as input and gain access to the referenced object, to affect it or be affected by it: to read it, modify it, build a new structure with it, and so on.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors illustrate with a pair, color and house, that a process turns into the symbol white; they give no data.

card.rule: A symbol is symbolic because processes can use a token of it to reach its referent and read it, change it or build with it.
card.limits: Our reading: a pattern no process could use to reach anything would not be symbolic in this sense.

concepts.title: The prototype of designation
concepts.question: Which relation do linguists take as the model case of designation, and which do the authors take?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Linguists start from simple cases of naming and struggle to extend them. The authors want a model case that fits an IPS.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: In discussing language, the model case of designation is a proper name and the object named, extended with difficulty to words like house, running, truth, beauty and justice. In the authors' theory the prototypic relationship is between a symbol and a symbol structure: X2 names the list (A, B, C), so a token of X2 gives access to the list and, for example, its first element, A.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors give X2 as an example. They do not argue the choice beyond saying that almost all other designation follows from this ability.

card.rule: Linguists model designation on name to person; the authors model it on a symbol naming a symbol structure.
card.limits: The authors' claim is about their own theory; it is a choice of prototype, not a finding about language.

concepts.title: Concepts apply at every level
concepts.question: Do notions like designation apply only to elementary processes?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The definitions are given for elementary processes, yet the book will use them for large composite ones.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: According to the authors, many concepts they introduce apply to arbitrary information processes, not just elementary ones. The processes that interpret indirect designations need not be elementary but can be built up out of other processes.

blocks.label: Assumed
blocks.text: The authors will not always repeat the qualification that a notion applies at all levels, and they leave the reader to supply it.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors offer no data here, only a statement of how the book will proceed: they say the notions apply to arbitrary processes and that interpreting indirect designations can be built from other processes.

card.rule: Notions such as designation hold at every level of processing, and processes that follow indirect designations can be composed.
card.limits: Because the authors leave the qualification implicit, a reader should check which level of process a statement is about.

concepts.title: Two kinds of primitive symbol
concepts.question: Which symbols have their meaning fixed from outside the symbol structures?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Any theory has to start from symbols whose meaning is given, not built from other symbols.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Some symbols have their meaning fixed by elementary information processes that treat them in fixed ways. There are two main kinds: (1) symbols designating specific events or structures in the external environment, evoked by a receptor process or causing an effector process to create them; (2) symbols designating elementary information processes, so that those processes can be executed through the symbols.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: This elaborates postulate 8. The authors give examples of choices in the next ideas.

card.rule: Primitive symbols are those whose designation is fixed by elementary processes: symbols for external events or structures, and symbols for elementary processes.
card.limits: Which collection is primitive for a given IPS varies with the application.

concepts.title: Letters as primitive symbols
concepts.question: Why does the book treat letters as primitive symbols, and what does that assume about the subject?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Problem solving research should not have to model how the eye recognizes a letter.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The authors take the letters of the English alphabet, the digits, punctuation marks and a few special symbols, such as the implication sign, as primitive symbols designating external stimuli. All instances of the letter c are then of one type, which assumes the subject does not discriminate between two tokens of c under the experiment's conditions.

blocks.label: Assumed
blocks.text: This is an assumption about the subject, to be settled empirically. If it is wrong in a particular application, the error will show in the theory's inability to account for observed behavior.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Offered as a modeling choice, not a finding.

card.rule: The book takes letters and similar marks as primitive, assuming the subject treats all tokens of a letter alike under the experiment's conditions.
card.limits: The assumption can fail: under some conditions the subject does discriminate between tokens of the same letter.

concepts.title: Primitives have no degrees of similarity
concepts.question: What can the theory not say about primitive letters, and how could it say more?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: If letters are primitive, can the theory say that s looks more like z than like t?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: No. Primitive symbols can only be tokens of the same type or of different types; there is no notion of degree of difference. The alphabet's ordering is itself primitively defined. To get degrees of similarity, represent letters not as primitives but as organizations of simpler elementary characteristics, such as a description of loops, intersections and curves.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The argument rests on the definition of primitive: nothing is analyzed beneath it, so nothing is available to compare.

card.rule: Primitive letters are the same or different, never more or less alike; similarity needs descriptions built from simpler features.
card.limits: The limit is chosen: treating letters as primitive gives up similarity effects where they matter for behavior.

concepts.title: Describing chessmen with attribute-value pairs
concepts.question: How can a symbol for a chessman carry information about the man?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A chess-playing program must store facts about each piece.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: A described symbol has a description, a set of attribute-value pairs associated with it, as with the Morse list (W, A, S) described by part-of-speech: verb and tense: past. A chessman is a symbol whose attributes are type (king, queen, rook, bishop, knight, pawn), color (White, Black) and position (a square).

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors use chess as one of the problem-solving situations considered later; this is a representation example, not a result.

card.rule: A described symbol carries attribute-value pairs; a chessman has type, color and position.
card.limits: Our reading: the same piece must be re-described when it moves, since position is one of its attributes.

concepts.title: Logic expressions as lists
concepts.question: How can a logic expression with brackets be stored as a list?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Subjects in a logic task work with expressions like (P or Q) and (Q implies R). How can one be held in memory?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: One way is a flat list of its primitive symbols, with each bracket as a token. Another treats the brackets as delimiters of subgroups and omits them: the expression becomes a list of connective, left part and right part, such as (and, A, B) where A designates the list (or, P, Q) and B the list (implies, Q, R).

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors show these as alternative representations of one expression; they do not claim a subject stores either.

card.rule: A bracketed expression can be a flat list of tokens or a nested list whose positions encode connective, left part and right part.
card.limits: The nested list leans on a convention about positions; the flat list leaves the grouping to be read from the brackets.

concepts.title: Logic expressions as associations
concepts.question: How can an expression be stored with nothing but attribute-value associations?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Can an expression's structure and content both be stored with no list or tree at all?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Yes. Take attributes term, connective, left and right, and base symbols for nodes x1, x2, and so on. Each node is described by its attributes. The scheme encodes structure and content uniformly: it uses no symbol structure, only a pattern of namings.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors show the associations for (P or Q) and (Q implies R) and a graph of them in Figure 2.4. They add that other schemes exist, such as Polish prefix notation.

card.rule: Attribute-value associations can carry an expression's structure and content with no list or tree.
card.limits: The scheme works only if processes can look up an attribute of a node.
card.example: connective(x1) = and; connective(x2) = or; connective(x3) = implies; term(x4) = P; term(x5) = Q; term(x6) = Q; term(x7) = R; left(x1) = x2; left(x2) = x4; left(x3) = x6; right(x1) = x3; right(x2) = x5; right(x3) = x7.

concepts.title: Many equivalent representations
concepts.question: What do the different representations have in common, and when does the choice show in behavior?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The same expression can be stored in several ways. Does it matter which?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: All these representations are closely related. The bracketed form uses brackets to encode structure; the list and tree use the organization of symbol structures; the association scheme uses namings. All a representation needs is some scheme of associations plus information processes that can extract the connections.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors compare the schemes side by side for one expression. They note that one cannot always tell from output which internal representation an IPS uses, especially when they are as isomorphic as these.

card.rule: Many representations can carry the same information; what matters is a scheme of associations and processes that can read the connections.
card.limits: Where representations differ in what is easy to extract, the choice can change observable behavior.

concepts.title: Lists and associations as core structures
concepts.question: Which two kinds of symbol structure do the authors treat as their core?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The postulates say nothing about which structures and designations are available.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The authors take two structures as the core: (1) list structures, built from the single relation next, sometimes with its inverse prior, in which symbols can name other lists to give hierarchies; (2) attribute-value associations, sets of attributes and values, both symbols, in which each attribute designates a unique value.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Both structures have been illustrated several times in the chapter. Others are introduced later only as representations for special purposes.

card.rule: The book's core symbol structures are lists, built with next, and attribute-value associations.
card.limits: The two are a working choice; the authors allow other structures for special purposes.

concepts.title: What an elementary process must be like
concepts.question: What two requirements must elementary processes meet, and why is solve-problem not an acceptable one?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The entire behavior of an IPS is compounded out of sequences of elementary processes. What may count as one?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Elementary means not further analyzed in the theory. Which processes are elementary depends on the application, but there must be a collection general and powerful enough to compose all the macroscopic performances of the IPS, and each must be well defined, realizable by known mechanisms.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors argue by example: taking solve-problem as an eip would tell us nothing about how problem solving is actually accomplished, so there would be no point.

card.rule: Elementary processes must be well defined and realizable, and together powerful enough to compose all the system's behavior.
card.limits: Elementary does not mean the same set for every purpose; it depends on the application.

concepts.title: A small set of elementary processes suffices
concepts.question: How many elementary processes are needed, and is the set unique?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Might the set of elementary processes depend entirely on the task the IPS is meant to perform?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: No. A relatively small set of elementary processes suffices to produce the full generality of information processing. There is no unique basis: many adequate sets exist, with corresponding schemes of composition. All include certain fundamental types of operations, though not in a single form.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors call this a major foundation stone of computer science. They say a proof of sufficiency, and what such a proof could mean, is more involved.

card.rule: A small set of elementary processes is enough for general information processing, but many different sets will do.
card.limits: The authors list the fundamental types but do not prove sufficiency here.

concepts.title: Discrimination, tests and comparisons
concepts.question: What do the discrimination and test-and-compare processes let an IPS do?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: An IPS has to behave differently depending on what it finds.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Discrimination: the system behaves in alternative ways depending on the symbol structures in STM, and the behavior is arbitrarily alterable, so control can be transferred to an independent program. Tests and comparisons: the system can determine whether two symbol tokens do or do not belong to the same symbol type. Comparisons often couple with conditional behavior.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: These are the first two of the fundamental types of elementary process the authors list as a sufficient basic set.

card.rule: Discrimination lets behavior depend on STM contents; tests and comparisons decide whether two tokens are of one type.
card.limits: The list is of types of operation, not a fixed set of named processes.

concepts.title: Creating symbols and writing structures
concepts.question: What must the symbol-creating and structure-writing processes be able to do?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The IPS must be able to make new symbols and build and change structures.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Symbol creation: new symbols can be created at will and set to designate specified symbol structures, carrying no meaning other than that designation. Writing symbol structures: it must be possible to create, copy and modify structures, by changing or deleting tokens or appending new tokens with specified relations. Many variations are possible if they allow building arbitrary structures.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: These are the third and fourth types in the authors' list of fundamental elementary processes.

card.rule: Symbols can be created arbitrarily and set to designate structures; structures can be created, copied and modified.
card.limits: The authors do not require one particular set of writing operations.

concepts.title: External reading and writing, access and storage
concepts.question: What do the last three kinds of elementary process require?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The IPS has to deal with the outside world, reach parts of structures, and keep structures for later.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Reading and writing externally: stimuli are designated by internal symbols, and responses are produced from internal structures. Designating symbol structures: any part of a structure can be designated, and other parts reached from given parts and relations, so no part is in principle inaccessible. Storing: a structure can be remembered and retrieved at any time via a structure that designates it.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: These are the last three types in the authors' list. The amount of memory conditions how complex the stored whole can be.

card.rule: An IPS must be able to read and write externally, reach every part of a structure, and store and retrieve structures by designation.
card.limits: Our reading: these are requirements on the kind of operation, not claims about how people do it.

concepts.title: The interpreter looks only at STM
concepts.question: What may the interpreter consult to decide what to do next, and why is that no real limit?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The behavior of an IPS is sequences of elementary processes; more macroscopic processes are composed of them until the behavior called problem solving emerges. What decides the order?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The authors make a final assumption: the interpreter bases its determination of sequential behavior solely on the information stored in STM. Since STM contents change with almost every eip executed, this is no essential limit on behavior in the long run, though it localizes the immediate stimulus for behavior in the short run.

blocks.label: Assumed
blocks.text: The first of two problems about the interpreter: as observers we must hypothesize a set of rules, a program, that describes the sequence of eip's an IPS executes as a function of its informational context. As inductive scientists we must discover this program to describe a human solving a problem.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors give an argument, not an experiment: because STM contents change with almost every elementary process executed, basing the next step solely on STM places no essential limit on behavior.

card.rule: The interpreter chooses what to do next from STM contents alone, and since STM keeps changing this limits nothing in the long run.
card.limits: In the short run the immediate stimulus for behavior is whatever is in STM, so anything not in STM cannot yet affect the next step.

concepts.title: A program in programming-language form
concepts.question: How does a programming-language description handle choices and repeated cycles?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: How can the behavior of a house thermostat be written down as a program?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The program is a structure of processes: each list component designates an elementary process or a subprogram, and a program is executed recursively, component by component. Discriminations test and branch to a numbered step; if no control statement is satisfied, execution continues in written order. Programs contain loops, and each loop needs at least one conditional branch so that it can finally be left.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The thermostat program in Figure 2.5 observes the temperature, tests whether the furnace is on, and turns it on or off, with a single loop that is never left.

card.rule: A program is a structure of processes with numbered steps, branching on tests, and loops that need a conditional exit.
card.limits: The thermostat's one loop runs forever by design; a loop without a conditional branch could never end.
card.example: Observe the temperature: if low go to the furnace-on step, if high go to the furnace-off step, otherwise repeat. Furnace-on: test if the furnace is on; if not, turn it on; go back to the start.

concepts.title: Flow diagrams and production systems
concepts.question: How does a production system describe behavior, and what happens when several conditions are true?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The same sort of behavior can be described in different notations. Which notation fits a man crossing a street?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: A flow diagram shows elementary processes with arrows for the execution sequence. A production system is a list of conditional statements: the process to the right of an arrow is performed if the condition to its left becomes true. When several conditions are true, the one higher in the list takes priority. Each statement is a production.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Figure 2.7 describes a walker: red light means stop, green means move, and two lower productions alternate the feet. With a red light there is no movement even though the lower conditions also hold.

card.rule: In a production system each condition-action pair is a production, and the topmost true condition wins.
card.limits: Priority by list order is a convention of this scheme, not a feature every rule system must share.
card.example: traffic-light red, then stop. traffic-light green, then move. move and left-foot-on-pavement, then step-with-right-foot. move and right-foot-on-pavement, then step-with-left-foot.

concepts.title: A program is an observer's description
concepts.question: When is a program just our description of a system, and when is it inside the system?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Does a thermostat follow a program the way a person follows a recipe?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: As described so far, a program is external to the IPS: it is the outside observer's way of describing the system, and the use of different schemes for the three examples emphasizes that. A bimetallic strip can open and close a circuit and so behave as the thermostat program says, yet the system does not follow a program; it behaves according to physical laws and its geometry.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors' contrast: sometimes the IPS holds an internal representation of the program that controls its behavior, as in a player piano, so that the system executes processes under the control of the program.

card.rule: A program may merely describe a system from outside; only some systems hold and follow a program internally.
card.limits: A description that fits behavior does not show that the system contains the description.

concepts.title: Mechanism or interpreted program?
concepts.question: Can we always tell whether a process is a built-in mechanism or an interpreted program?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Take a find operation that locates the first occurrence of a symbol S in a list L. Is it a mechanism or a program run by an interpreter?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The system might possess a mechanism that directly carries out the find. Or it might execute the program of Figure 2.8 under an interpreter. Unless there is some means of examining the system's microstructure, it would be impossible to distinguish the two.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors say it is not always possible to draw a sharp boundary between the part of a system regarded as a mechanism and the part governed by an interpreted program.

card.rule: Outer behavior alone often cannot show whether a process is a mechanism or an interpreted program.
card.limits: Our reading: telling the two apart needs evidence about internal structure, which behavior may not supply.

concepts.title: What recognition means
concepts.question: What does a recognition process produce, and why does it make a word into a symbol?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Recognition will matter in the book's psychological theories, so the authors work through one example in detail.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: By recognizing a word the authors mean: when a word is input, the process outputs to STM the designation of a symbol structure containing aspects of its meaning, such as spelling, pronunciation, synonyms and visual representations of the referent. A recognition process makes the word into a symbol by providing a way to gain access to an appropriate structure, given the word.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors say it could be done by a unitary process or by an interpretive system, and they describe the second as an illustration of interpretation.

card.rule: Recognition gives access to a symbol structure for a word, and that access is what makes the word a symbol.
card.limits: Recognition here is not the same as selecting different behaviors; it identifies the structure on which later behavior is based.

concepts.title: A discrimination net
concepts.question: How does a net of test nodes lead from an input word to its meaning?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: How can recognition be done by an interpreter that follows a stored structure?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Memory holds nodes of two types: test nodes and terminal nodes. A test node has a test and a set of other nodes, one for each outcome. A terminal node holds the structure giving the meaning of words sorted to it. The net-interpreter applies the first node's test to the word, follows the outcome to the next node, and repeats until a terminal node is reached.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In the authors' fragment the first test is test-first-letter. For the word DOG the result is D, which leads to a node with test-last-letter, whose result G leads onward until the terminal for DOG is found.

card.rule: A discrimination net sorts a word through tests until a terminal node, which holds the meaning structure.
card.limits: A net recognizes only through the tests it has: words that agree on every tested feature reach the same terminal.

concepts.title: Why an interpreter is worth having
concepts.question: What does an interpreter trade away, and where do the limits on an IPS's behavior lie?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Why describe recognition, or anything else, as an interpreter running over stored structure rather than as one big mechanism?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: An interpreter replaces a large amount of mechanism by a small interpreter plus a large amount of symbolic structure. Despite a simple interpreter, the behavior of an IPS is limited only by the complexity of the symbol structures that can be built, because the eip's are tools to construct and read such structures. The limits therefore lie in the content of the stored programs, not in the IPS itself.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors argue from the design: a small fixed interpreter plus tools for building structure leaves complexity unlimited in principle.

card.rule: A small interpreter plus large stored structure gives unlimited complexity: the limits lie in the programs, not the IPS.
card.limits: Speed is a separate limit that no stored program can remove.

concepts.title: When a true interpreter is needed
concepts.question: When does it matter whether an IPS really interprets a program rather than merely behaves as one describes?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Programs are how the authors present every IPS. Does the IPS itself need to interpret them?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Often it makes no difference whether the interpreter is a complete mechanism producing the behavior or a true interpreter that follows a program. It matters only if the IPS wishes to do something with a program other than execute it: analyze, construct or modify it. Then it must deal with the program as a symbol structure and operate in a truly interpretive mode.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors point out that if the interpreter is only a mechanism, nothing can be said about its internal structure in information processing terms.

card.rule: A true interpreter is needed only when the IPS must treat a program as data: to analyze, construct or modify it.
card.limits: For merely executing a program, a mechanism that behaves as described is enough.

concepts.title: An interpreter with a stack
concepts.question: How does an interpreter run programs whose steps are themselves programs?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A program list may contain names of other program lists. The interpreter must run each sub-list and then resume where it left off.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: In the simplified language each symbol on a program list is either an eip or the name of another list. The interpreter must tell whether a symbol designates an eip and execute it, read a program as a structure, and keep its place with a stack: a list with a symbol added to or removed from its front, called pushing and popping. A subprogram's name is pushed when it is to run, and popping returns the prior symbol when it finishes.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: For P1 = (eip1, eip2, P2, P3, eip3), P2 = (eip4, eip5), P3 = (eip6, P4, eip7), P4 = (P2, P2, eip8) the interpreter executes eip1, eip2, eip4, eip5, eip6, eip4, eip5, eip4, eip5, eip8, eip7, eip3.

card.rule: A stack keeps the interpreter's place so that sub-programs run in full and then control returns to the calling list.
card.limits: A stack is convenient and powerful but not the only possible place-keeping device if hierarchies are shallow.

concepts.section: The Relation of an IPS to Language
concepts.title: An IPS as a language processor
concepts.question: How do the concepts of linguistics line up with those of an IPS?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: What is the relation between language and the concept of an information processing system?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The authors say an IPS is in a fundamental sense a language processor, and its basic concepts have almost the same origins as those behind transformational grammars. In linguistics a language has elements (like symbols) arranged in strings (like lists), and a grammar says which strings are well formed. The IPS's stored symbol structures are not strings and play the role of deep structures: representations of meanings with which the IPS represents and solves problems.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: This is an argument from correspondence of concepts. The authors conclude that their theory of problem solving can be viewed as a partial theory of linguistics, of the deep structures used in problem solving.

card.rule: IPS symbols and lists correspond to linguistic elements and strings, and stored structures play the role of deep structures.
card.limits: The authors say they will have little to say explicitly about linguistics; the parallel is partial.

concepts.title: Why the book needs a notation
concepts.question: What four jobs does the book's notation do, and why is it informal?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The book will define many IPS's. It needs a systematic way to write them that readers can follow.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The notation has four related uses: to define programs (the theories of an individual's behavior), to define task environments (the external situations that set tasks, stated in symbolic terms), to describe traces (step-by-step accounts of a program run in a task environment) and to encode protocols (records of subjects' behavior, including their verbalizations).

blocks.label: Alternative
blocks.text: A completely formal language, needed to simulate an IPS on a computer, would be unreadable and could not preserve the programs' original formulations. The authors adopt informal conventions that could be formalized, and give the formal definition in Appendix 2.1.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors offer a design argument: a fully formal language would be unreadable and could not keep the programs' original formulations, so informal conventions that could be formalized are used instead.

card.rule: The notation defines programs, task environments, traces and protocols, and is informal so that it can be read.
card.limits: Because the book is to be read rather than written, the syntactic details are of secondary importance.

concepts.title: General notational conventions
concepts.question: How are names, lists, assignments and operands written in the book's notation?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Figure 2.12 shows the top level of the Logic Theorist as a sequential process. How are its names and lines to be read?

blocks.label: Model
