blocks.text: Identifiers are ordinary English words, hyphenated into one name so that a simple identifier is unambiguous, for example untried-problems. Lists are parenthesized sequences without commas, such as (theorem1 theorem2 theorem3). A colon assigns an identifier to a process or structure. Operands can be given in functional notation or with prepositions as separators.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Figure 2.12 uses these conventions: the top line names the process Logic Theorist and follows it with a colon, and line 1 uses prepositions: insert problem on untried-problems at end.

card.rule: Hyphenated words name things, lists are parenthesized without commas, a colon assigns a name, and operands may follow prepositions.
card.limits: Identifiers are arbitrary labels; xyz would work as well, but English words help the reader remember.

concepts.title: The process first, then naming and control
concepts.question: In a line of a sequential process, what comes first and what is subordinate?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Each bit of processing does something, may give its result a name, and passes control on. Which of these should the notation put first?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Common languages such as FORTRAN and ALGOL give name assignment priority and treat control as separate actions. The authors put the process first, then add subordinately whether a name is assigned and where control goes. The double arrow reads and produces. Control clauses follow the name.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In line 7 of Figure 2.12 the main process is applying the method, then a new identifier is noted, then control: if the method fails, return to the generator. The authors say the usual forms hide some of what is going on from an IPS point of view.

card.rule: Write the process first; the name given to its result and the control that follows are subordinate clauses.
card.limits: Control actions can sense only the nature of the result just produced, so they are limited to simple discriminations.

concepts.title: Avoiding embedding and temporary names
concepts.question: What conventions replace nested function calls and temporary names?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Programs refer to earlier results by assignment to a fresh name or by embedding one expression in another.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Embedding, as in F(a + b), cuts the need for temporary identifiers but obscures the sequential control flow, so the authors avoid it. To limit temporary names they use three conventions: put control actions in the context of the processing they depend on; use a process's name to stand for its result; and use the special term result for the most recently obtained result.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors give an example with the term result and say its three occurrences are all different. See the example below.

card.rule: Avoid nested calls; refer to results by the process's name or by the word result.
card.limits: The term result always means the most recent result, so each use must be read in its place.
card.example: sum(3, 5); divide result by 2; subtract 1 from result, if result = 3 stop and report ok. The three occurrences of result have the values 8, 4 and 3.

concepts.title: Generate, test, find and report
concepts.question: What do the basic processes generate, test, find, apply and report do?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Figure 2.12 uses basic processes with special forms. What do they do?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Generate takes a set and produces its elements in sequence, giving each to a subprocess; it is used for all repetitive operations. Test or test if is followed by a condition built from Boolean connectives and basic relations. Find tries to find the value of a relation, such as next or first, or the structure designated by an association. Apply runs a process on operands, and report outputs the text that follows it.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Figure 2.12 has two generates, nested, at lines 2 and 6. At line 2 each element is named current-problem; at line 6 the set of methods gives the element name method.

card.rule: Generate repeats a subprocess over each element of a set; test, find, apply and report do the single steps.
card.limits: The authors say deep nesting of conditions will never occur in their examples, even though the conventions permit it.

concepts.title: Writing a production system
concepts.question: How is a production system written, and how does control move through it?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Figure 2.13 rewrites a slightly elaborated thermostat as a production system. How are its parts written and run?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The identifier assigned to the whole system covers all its productions. Each production has a condition and an action sequence. An action is an operator, which may be parameterized, such as turn-on[furnace]. A condition is a single discrimination or a conjunction of them, using only matching and detection. Control starts at the top of the list, takes the first true condition, executes its action sequence and starts over at the top.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The only other control action is stop, which ends the entire execution. No directed control, such as a go to, is possible in a production system.

card.rule: A production system runs from the top: the first true condition fires, then control starts again at the top.
card.limits: Conditions can make only simple discriminations, just as control actions in sequential processes can.
card.example: Thermostat: the first production has the action stop, one production has the action call-repair-man and turn-on[electric-heater], and two more switch the furnace on and off depending on temperature and furnace state.

concepts.title: Backus Normal Form: classes and alternatives
concepts.question: How does BNF name classes of expressions, concatenate them and offer alternatives?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The conditions of productions are patterns of symbol structures. A language is needed to talk about whole classes of expressions.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Backus Normal Form (BNF) is a standard metanotation for describing the grammars of programming languages. Class names are written in angular brackets. Classes and characters are concatenated to form patterns. A bar means either-or. The meta-assignment symbol gives a new name to a class built from these.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors give examples.

blocks.label: Notation
blocks.text: Each line below defines a class.
blocks.code:
<letter> A <letter> D   covers WARD, BARD, BAAD, ZAPD
<letter> | <letter><letter>   is one or two letters
<small-word> ::= <letter> | <letter><letter>
<bigger-word> ::= <small-word> | <letter><small-word>

card.rule: BNF names classes in angular brackets, builds patterns by concatenation, offers alternatives with a bar and names classes with ::=.
card.limits: BNF fixes class membership only; it does not by itself label the parts of a matched expression.

concepts.title: Recursion in BNF
concepts.question: How can a short BNF definition describe an unlimited class of expressions?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Alternatives and concatenation give only finite classes. How can a class like all whole numbers be defined?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: BNF admits recursive definition: a class may be defined in terms of itself, which gives infinite classes of simple but useful structure. A digit is an integer, and a digit followed by an integer is an integer. Lists and well-formed logic expressions are defined the same way.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors build 334 step by step: 4 is a digit and so an integer, 34 is a digit followed by an integer, and so on. Their grammar defines every well-formed logic expression over P, Q, R and S.

blocks.label: Notation
blocks.text: The four definitions below give integer, list, symbol-sequence and logic expression, each defined partly in terms of itself.

card.rule: A recursive definition uses its own class name, so a finite rule describes an unlimited class.
card.limits: Recursion here is limited to simple structures; BNF admits only a restricted set of patterns.

concepts.title: Designating the parts of a matched pattern
concepts.question: How can an action refer to the particular parts a pattern matched?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A production such as the distributive law needs its action to copy the very expression its condition matched. BNF alone gives only class membership.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: If there is only one class of a given type in the pattern, the class name can designate the matched member. The authors extend this by indexing distinct occurrences, so that expression.1, expression.2 and expression.3 name the matched parts, which obtain their values from the pattern in the condition.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors write the expanding side of the distributive law as one production, with the indexed names on both sides of the arrow. See the example below.

card.rule: Index the class names so each occurrence in the condition can be named in the action.
card.limits: The authors keep patterns restricted to what can be recognized directly by match and detection.
card.example: Expression.1 or (expression.2 and expression.3) gives (expression.1 or expression.2) and (expression.1 or expression.3). This is the expanding side of the distributive law, written as a production.

concepts.title: What Chapter 2 has accomplished
concepts.question: What has Chapter 2 done toward the basic hypothesis, and what comes next?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The chapter began with the claim that humans operate as information processing systems. What has it achieved?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: It has taken the first steps toward specifying that hypothesis: eight postulates describe the hypothesized system, the first four sections spell out their meaning, and the last section sets the notation for defining programs, task environments, traces and protocols.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The chapter provides no empirical test. The authors present its work as preparation for the later chapters.

card.rule: Chapter 2 specifies the hypothesis and the notation; testing it is for later chapters.
card.limits: Specifying a hypothesis and testing it are separate tasks; this chapter does the first only.

concepts.title: Reading a BNF definition with quotation marks
concepts.question: How are alternatives, recursion and a quoted bar read in the appendix's sample definition?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Appendix 2.1 formally defines the notation using standard BNF with quotation marks added. How is its sample class read?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The class X has five alternatives: the letter A; B followed by C; D followed by any member of E; F followed by any member of X followed by G; and H followed by a quoted bar and G. The fourth is recursive and includes infinitely many expressions. The quotes show that the bar there is a character, not the metasymbol.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors list FAG, FFAGG and FFFAGGG as members of the fourth subclass. If E is K or KK, then D followed by E has the two expressions DK and DKK.

blocks.label: Notation
blocks.code:
<X> ::= A | B C | D <E> | F <X> G | H "|" G
<E> ::= K | K K

card.rule: In a BNF definition, alternatives are separated by bars, recursion makes infinite classes, and quotes turn a bar into a plain character.
card.limits: The appendix gives only the syntax; it leaves the semantics of the language to the discussion in the chapter.

concepts.title: The structure of the formal language
concepts.question: How is the formal language of the appendix organized, and how are production conditions limited?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The appendix defines the notation completely in syntax. How is it organized?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The language has three parts. The first introduces symbols, symbol structures and ways of naming processes, and underlies every definition. The rest split into two groups, one defining sequential processes and the other production systems. Definitions go from the bottom up, in clumps headed by a class of conceptual importance.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The appendix gives syntax only and not semantics, since the chapter has discussed the concepts. A reader of the book need not master it: the notation is to be read, not written.

card.rule: A common first part serves two languages: sequential processes with control statements, and production systems with restricted conditions.
card.limits: Our reading: the appendix is reference material for the syntax; the chapter's examples carry the meaning.

concepts.title: Demanded behavior tells about the task
concepts.question: When a motivated person does what the situation demands, what does the behavior reveal more about?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: People and animals placed in a problem situation with a goal usually show adaptive, or rational, behavior: behavior that suits the goal given the problem environment.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: According to the authors, if a situation demands certain behavior and the subject shows it, the behavior tells more about the task environment than about the subject. All we learn about the subject is that he is motivated and able to find and carry out what the situation calls for.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors argue by implication: put the same subject in a different situation and he would behave differently, so the behavior cannot be a fixed trait of his.

card.rule: Behavior demanded by the situation reveals the task environment, not the person.
card.limits: This holds only while the person is motivated and able. Where behavior departs from what the situation demands, the person's own makeup becomes visible.

concepts.title: Economics skips the psychology
concepts.question: How can economics predict behavior while avoiding the psychology of decision making?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Economics predicts certain human behavior, yet has built an impressive structure on a single psychological postulate.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The postulate: economic man is motivated to maximize his utility, or in some uses his profit, and is able to find and carry out the maximizing behavior. Given this, his actions can be inferred from the structure of the choices he faces.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors cite the way economics finesses questions of value and preference: the utility function is placed among the given data of the problem, not among the behavior to be explained.

card.rule: Assume motivation and ability, then infer behavior from the structure of the choices.
card.limits: The shortcut explains nothing about why the person wants what he wants or why he fails to find the best choice.

concepts.title: Where rational prediction fails
concepts.question: What does a gap between predicted rational behavior and actual behavior tell us about the subject?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: In concept attainment, a subject classifies stimuli as instances of an unknown concept and is told right or wrong after each reply. If the subject is motivated, there presumably exists an optimal strategy that discloses the concept in the fewest expected trials.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The authors say laboratory subjects often depart from the rational model, and the explanation must lie inside the subject: limits on determining the best behavior or on carrying it out.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Departures are often large and tend to vanish only when the rational behavior is transparently obvious. In simple concept experiments, the key limit is how many symbols can be held in short-term memory.

card.rule: When a motivated subject falls short of the rational model, look for limits inside the subject.
card.limits: The shortfall only points to the subject if motivation and perception were adequate; an unmotivated or unseeing subject changes what the experiment is.

concepts.title: A two-bladed theory
concepts.question: Why does a theory of problem solving need both an analysis of the task environment and of the subject?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Observing a properly motivated subject on an intellective task shows intendedly rational behavior, or behavior of limited rationality. What can such behavior teach us?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Two kinds of knowledge result. Behavior that is precisely what the situation calls for informs us about the task environment. Behavior that departs from perfect rationality informs us about the psychology of the subject and the mechanisms limiting performance.

blocks.label: Term
blocks.text: Task environment: an environment coupled with a goal, problem, or task, the one for which the subject's motivation is assumed. The task defines a point of view that delimits the environment.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors liken the theory to scissors, which cannot cut paper without two blades: one blade is the task environment, the other the limits of the subject.

card.rule: A theory of problem solving needs two blades: demands of the task environment and the psychology of the subject.
card.limits: A complete theory of task environments would cover all of human knowledge, so the authors bound it, while still giving the task environment more attention than usual.

concepts.title: Three things to keep apart
concepts.question: Which three things must be kept distinct when talking about a task environment?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Psychology has long faced the problem of defining the effective stimulus: what exactly is the subject responding to?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The authors keep three things apart: the environment itself, the subject's internal representation of it (the problem space), and the theorist's objective description of it.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In the Necker cube demonstration, a flat drawing is shown and the subject builds a three-dimensional reading. For almost all subjects two readings are possible, and neither is veridical, because the drawing is two-dimensional.

card.rule: Keep apart the environment, the subject's representation of it, and the theorist's description.
card.limits: Where the stimulus is simple, as with the Necker cube, describing it is not hard; the distinction matters more as situations get complex.

concepts.title: When a description is veridical
concepts.question: When can a stimulus be described in words so that the description is true to what the subject meets?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Some stimuli, like the Necker cube, can be described verbally; others, like a van Gogh painting or even a reproduction of it, cannot. Why the difference?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: A description is veridical if a stimulus built from it, by one skilled in the art, produces the same behavior as the original. A stimulus is describable only if every subject encodes it in highly simplified form, and if subjects encode in different languages no one description fits all.

blocks.label: Assumed
blocks.text: A description also postulates the vocabulary of elements and relations the subject will use in his initial encoding. The Necker cube is assumed to be handled as line segments and plane figures.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Experience with human subjects gives assurance about line drawings. With a frog, describing the stimulus in terms of lines would be rash, and the difficulty of building pattern-recognizing devices shows that line encoding is not trivial.

card.rule: A description is veridical only if it matches the vocabulary in which subjects first encode the stimulus.
card.limits: Assurance comes from experience with the subjects' own kind; with other species or perhaps cultures, it weakens.

concepts.title: The problem space
concepts.question: What is a subject's problem space, and what does it contain?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Describing the subject's behavior objectively is harder than describing the stimulus. We must describe not only actual behaviors but the set of possible behaviors, and the behaviors he considers in thought that never become overt.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The space in which his problem solving activities take place is called the problem space. It represents the initial situation, the desired goal situation, intermediate states imagined or experienced, and the concepts he uses to describe them.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors argue from what any account must cover: the actual behaviors, the set of possible behaviors they are drawn from, and thinking responses that never become overt. A list of actual moves alone would leave these out.

blocks.label: Limit
blocks.text: The problem space cannot yet be pointed to as an objective fact for a human subject. Describing it is itself constructing a representation of the task environment: the subject's.

card.rule: A problem space is the subject's internal representation of initial, goal and intermediate states and of the changes possible among them.
card.limits: It is not an objective fact one can point to. The authors' description of behavior is molar, not molecular.

concepts.title: The game tree for number scrabble
concepts.question: How can all possible plays of a game be laid out, and how does minimax use that layout?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Number scrabble: nine cards bear the digits 1 to 9. Two players draw alternately; the first to hold exactly three of his cards summing to 15 wins, and if all are drawn without that, the game is a draw. How can the possibilities for playing be represented objectively?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Every possible play is a permutation of the nine digits, so the plays form a tree arranged by first digit chosen, then second, and so on.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The game has perfect information and a finite tree, so an optimal strategy follows by minimax: assign win, draw or lose to each terminal, then work backward, taking the best outcome at the player's own turn and the worst at the opponent's.

card.rule: A finite game of perfect information has a game tree, and minimax works backward through it.
card.limits: The game tree is one representation among others, and it is not the subject's own.

concepts.title: Considered moves outside the tree
concepts.question: Why must a theory of the subject's thinking include moves that are not legal?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Is the game tree enough to describe what a number scrabble player considers? Suppose the moves so far are 3, 5; 9, 7. The first player holds 3 and 9, which total 12.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The player may reason that the digit needed is 15 minus 12, which is 3, and so consider the sequence 3, 5; 9, 7; 3. But a 3 has already been drawn, so the move is illegal and lies outside the game tree. A theory of the subject's thoughts must include such considered but infeasible behaviors.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors say we must represent the subject's wishes and dreams as well as his realistic thoughts. If the player said aloud that there is no 3, that would be concrete evidence of his having gone outside the game tree.

card.rule: Represent the moves a subject considers, even those that are illegal or impossible.
card.limits: Such considerations may stay covert. Only overt remarks or actions give direct evidence of them.

concepts.title: Two games, one structure
concepts.question: In what sense are tic-tac-toe and number scrabble the same game, and does knowing one help with the other?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The subject may recode a situation completely. Tic-tac-toe, where players mark squares of a three-by-three array alternately and win by completing a line, looks different from number scrabble.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: They are formally equivalent. Place the digits 1 to 9 in a magic square whose rows, columns and diagonals each sum to 15: a line of three squares is then exactly a triple of digits summing to 15. Equivalence does not mean a good strategy transfers immediately.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The converse, that any three digits summing to 15 lie in a row, column or diagonal, can be checked by enumeration. A player can use the magic square by visualizing it, or translate the strategy into number terms.

card.rule: Formally equivalent games can be played with different internal representations, and strategy does not transfer automatically.
card.limits: Equivalence is formal. A person who knows one game well may not see, or be able to use, the other.

concepts.title: No description has a monopoly
concepts.question: Why can the experimenter not simply pick the true representation of a task?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Number scrabble and tic-tac-toe are formally equivalent, and subjects can occasionally represent a task internally in quite different ways. Which description should the experimenter use for the problem space?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Any player could use either representation, a combination, or one that permits illegal moves. The experimenter's description would be no less subjective than the player's, and no particular description has a claim to complete or exclusive veridicality.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Since the two games are formally equivalent, it is not clear which description should represent the problem space. The authors, instead of untying this knot, ask whether the experimenter need use an explicit representation of the task environment at all.

card.rule: No single representation of a task environment is the true one, so a theory cannot assume it.
card.limits: The authors do not say description is hopeless; they look for ways around the problem in the next pages.

concepts.title: Predict from the stimulus
concepts.question: If no true problem exists, what can enter a theory as the independent variable?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: If the experimenter does not know the real problem, what can the theory use to predict the subject's representation?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The subject's behavior cannot depend on what the problem really is, since neither he nor we know that, but only on what the stimulus is, including the feedback he receives as a result of his behavior. So the stimulus, not the real problem, is what should enter as the independent variable.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Even when predicting how differences in problem statements affect solving, the authors say we need not describe the external task environment, only the stimulus and feedback rules.

card.rule: Use the stimulus and feedback rules as the independent variables, not an unknowable real problem.
card.limits: This avoids the objective description by hypothesizing the subject's representation; it does not supply the representation itself.

concepts.title: Equate the environment with all representations
concepts.question: How can an experimenter treat the real environment as the whole set of representations people find for it?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A second way out of the problem of describing the task environment is pragmatic: build a hypothetical problem space that is objective only in that every representation human subjects actually use can be embedded in it as a specialization.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Let many subjects study the environment over a long time. They devise representations and change them. The authors equate the real environment with the whole set of representations generated by then, together with the mappings relating each representation to the others.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The pattern they rely on: as subjects keep studying, the rate at which they generate new representations gradually falls toward an asymptote, and later additions appear rarely if at all.

blocks.label: Assumed
blocks.text: The requirement matters where subjects employ several representations and the theory is concerned with which they use or how they acquire them. It can be met approximately where the situation is complex relative to the time subjects have.

card.rule: Equate the real environment with the set of representations people generate until new ones stop appearing, plus the mappings among them.
card.limits: No formal theory of all representations of an interesting task yet exists, and the equation is only as good as the study that produced the set.

concepts.title: Testing a hypothesized representation
concepts.question: How can a claim about a subject's internal representation be checked against behavior?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors' theories state the central processes and memory contents of the subject, and so assert which representation the subject uses. Can such assertions be tested?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Yes, to the extent that different problem spaces would lead to different behavior in the task. Suppose a subject is hypothesized to use the magic square for number scrabble. If he holds two digits that share no line, reasons arithmetically about the third, and searches for it, the hypothesis is contradicted.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Our own example: a subject holding 1 and 2 says that makes 3, so he needs 12. On the magic square those digits lie on no common line, so a magic-square thinker would not treat them as a basis for a winning triple.

card.rule: A hypothesis about a subject's problem space is testable when rival spaces predict different behavior.
card.limits: Where two representations would lead to the same moves, behavior cannot choose between them.

concepts.title: Language and thought
concepts.question: In what sense, according to the authors, is language needed for thinking?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Psychology has long debated how language and thought relate. Dewey listed three views: they are identical; words are clothing of thought, needed only to convey it; or language is not thought but is needed for thinking.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The authors trace the dispute to ambiguity in the word language. Their position: processing symbol structures that mirror natural language strings, the surface structure, is inessential to problem solving. The internal symbol structures that represent problems are the linguist's deep structure, so if language means deep structure it is essential.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: If the problem representations explain behavior, the claim gains support. The alternative needs a second set of deep structures running in parallel with the problem representations, which the authors call unparsimonious and unsupported by evidence.

card.rule: Surface language is clothing for conveying thought; deep structure, the internal symbol structures, is necessary for thinking.
card.limits: Linguists' sketches tie deep structures to single sentences, whereas the authors' structures are large contexts reaching beyond sentences.

concepts.title: Encoding a game in an IPS
concepts.question: How can an information processing system store and operate on a game's objects, sets, relations and moves?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The tic-tac-toe and number scrabble examples assumed the subject behaves like the information processing system (IPS) of Chapter 2. How could such a system actually store and process a problem space? Number scrabble gives a concrete case.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Objects become symbols, sets of objects become lists, relations become associations, and moves become processes that change the internal structures as the move would change the external objects or relations. Other processes test features and embody strategies.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In number scrabble the objects are two players and nine pieces, with three sets: unmoved-pieces and each player's pieces. Each player has an own-pieces association; each piece has an integer association. A move takes a piece from unmoved-pieces to the mover's list.

card.rule: Objects are symbols, sets are lists, relations are associations, and moves are processes that edit those structures.
card.limits: The authors' purpose is to show what such an encoding involves, not to claim how human subjects really represent number scrabble.

concepts.title: A program that finds a winning move
concepts.question: How does an IPS discover whether it has an immediately winning move in number scrabble?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Given the number scrabble representation, how could a player find out whether he has an immediate winning move?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Generate pairs from his own pieces. For each pair, sum the integers, then take the complement, the amount needed to reach 15. Then look through the unmoved pieces for one carrying that integer. If found, move it; if none works, report no move.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors comment on cost: the repeated subprocess seems expensive, but a more efficient process would consider only pairs containing the most recently moved piece, since others were considered earlier.

card.rule: Generate own pairs, compute the 15's complement of each sum, and search the unmoved pieces for it.
card.limits: The program works for the representation shown; other representations may need other programs and costs.

concepts.title: Representation decides the cost
concepts.question: Why can finding a forking move be costly in one representation of a game and cheap in an equivalent one?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A forking move sets up two possible winning moves for the next round, so the opponent cannot counter both. How costly is it to find one in the number scrabble representation, compared with tic-tac-toe?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: In number scrabble, three generators are nested: one for pairs of the player's pieces and two over unmoved pieces. In the tic-tac-toe representation, each piece is linked to the triads (rows, columns, diagonals) it belongs to, and a piece that lies on two triads each holding one remaining unmoved piece and one of the player's gives a fork. That is much simpler.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The number scrabble player could store the triad lists too, but whether this information is readily accessible is the crux of the difference in representations. In tic-tac-toe the lists are directly available in the diagram, which can be scanned rapidly; in number scrabble a human has them only if he writes or memorizes them.

card.rule: Equivalent representations differ in which information is readily accessible, and that decides how costly a process is.
card.limits: The cost belongs to representation plus processor: a player who memorizes the triads gets the simple process in number scrabble too.

concepts.title: How much detail to specify
concepts.question: How much detail about encodings and programs must a description of information processing give?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: How explicitly must a theory state the encodings and programs behind its information processing?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: As long as the processes are quite definite and elementary, it can be assumed that some encoding and some straightforward programs exist that do the job, so neither need be specified. The authors give explicit specifications only where the encoding or operations matter, and generally float above that level of detail.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors point to running computer programs for various tasks as a continuing guarantee that the lower, more detailed levels have been made explicit in many cases and could be in others.

card.rule: For definite, elementary processes, assume an encoding and programs exist and describe at a higher level.
card.limits: Detail must be given where the specific encoding of objects or operations becomes important for the argument.

concepts.title: Only what the goal makes relevant
concepts.question: Why does a problem space leave out most properties of the environment?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: So far, problem spaces have been defined in relation to task goals and restricted to task-relevant parts of the environment, but the relation between goal and environment was left implicit.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The interdependence of task environment and goal separates what is task-relevant from what is irrelevant, so only the relevant parts need enter the problem space. It also lets the processes available to the system be applied to specific task environments.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In the number scrabble example the physical size and color of the pieces were never specified.

blocks.label: Assumed
blocks.text: Reader and authors automatically assumed that such properties were irrelevant to the goal.

card.rule: Include in the problem space only what the goal makes relevant.
card.limits: The relevant set depends on the goal; a task with a different goal would make different properties relevant.

concepts.title: What it means to have a problem
concepts.question: When is a person confronted with a problem, and what kinds of objects and actions can be involved?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors need a definition of having a problem that covers eating an apple and proving a theorem.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: A person has a problem when he wants something and does not know immediately what series of actions will get it. The desired object may be tangible or abstract, specific or general, physical or symbolic. The actions may be physical, perceptual or purely mental.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The book concentrates on symbol systems, such as proofs, and on manipulating symbol structures. The authors say this does not severely limit the analysis except at its physiological boundaries, because the crucial activities in complex problem solving take place centrally, even when the object is physical.

card.rule: A problem exists when something is wanted and the way to get it is not immediately known.
card.limits: The restriction to symbols leaves out physiological aspects of sensory and motor skill, especially real-time coordination.

concepts.title: A problem as given information
concepts.question: What information must a solver have for something to count as a problem for it?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors prefer not to define having a problem directly. They try to say what a problem is by saying what information is given to the solver.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: To have a problem implies the solver is given information about what is desired, under what conditions, by what tools and operations, from what initial information, and with what resources. The solver interprets it as goal, side conditions and so on. Represent the information as symbol structures, assume the interpretation lies in the IPS's program, and a problem is defined.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: A textbook statement of Given a triangle ABC, Prove that its angle bisectors meet in one point is a problem only if the solver interprets triangle, bisecting, Given and Prove, and is motivated.

card.rule: A problem is information about goal, conditions, tools, start and resources, plus the solver's interpretation of it.
card.limits: No guarantee exists that every problem fits the two general representations the authors define; other classes may remain.

concepts.title: Well-defined problems
concepts.question: When is a problem well defined for a system?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Some problems give the solver a way to know a proposed answer is right; others do not. The authors want to mark the difference.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: A problem is well defined if a test exists, performable by the system, that determines whether a proposed object is a solution. Performable means with a relatively small amount of processing effort.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: If the task is to construct a symbolic expression with characteristics p1 to pn, and the system has relatively simple tests for whether an expression has each characteristic, the problem is well defined. The notion goes back to McCarthy.

card.rule: A problem is well defined if candidate solutions can be tested with small effort.
card.limits: Well defined does not mean easy: finding a candidate that passes the test can be hard.

concepts.title: Find a member of the goal set
concepts.question: How can a problem be stated in terms of a set of candidates and a goal subset?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors want a general way to state problems so that general methods can be tied to them.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Given a set U, find a member of a subset of U having specified properties, called the goal-set G. They call this the set representation (set-theoretic or set-predicate would be equally apt).

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In most cases a set of possible solutions can be defined. For a crossword puzzle, U is all arrays of letters for the white squares, and G the arrays in which every horizontal and vertical run forms a word satisfying its definition.

card.rule: State the problem as: given U, find a member of the goal subset G.
card.limits: The problem solver is not really handed U; he is given a process for generating elements of it.

concepts.title: Why problems are problems
concepts.question: What makes a problem hard, when a test of any answer is cheap?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Why are problems problems, if solutions can be recognized by a test?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Three reasons, not the only ones: the set U given to the solver can be very large, often immense; the actual solutions G can be spread widely and rarely through it; and the cost of obtaining and testing each new element can be very high.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The solver is not really given U but a process for generating its elements in some order. This generator has properties of its own, such as a cost per element, which problem statements usually do not specify. The search for the Northwest Passage is the authors' example of high cost.

card.rule: A problem is hard when U is huge, G is sparse, or generating and testing candidates is costly.
card.limits: The three reasons are examples, not a complete list.

concepts.title: Factoring a problem into subproblems
concepts.question: How can a set problem be split into subproblems, and why do they stay linked?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A set-theoretic problem can sometimes be decomposed into subproblems, each characterized the same way. A crossword puzzle shows how.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: A problem characterized by U and G can be split into subproblems that are each characterized the same way, though the subproblems may stay linked.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Crossword: take n subproblems, one per word. For each, U_i is the set of English words and G_i holds the words that fit the definition d_i, have length k_i, and match the crossing word's letter at each intersection.

blocks.label: Limit
blocks.text: The intersection condition makes the solution sets depend on one another: the subproblems are linked.

card.rule: Split a set problem into subproblems of the same kind, but expect their solution sets to be interdependent.
card.limits: Interdependence means a choice in one subproblem changes what counts as a solution in another.

concepts.title: A proof as a set problem
concepts.question: What two properties make a sequence of expressions a proof of a theorem?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: As a step toward a search representation, the authors restate the discovery of a proof in Euclidean geometry or elementary logic in set terms.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: A proof of theorem t is a sequence of subexpressions. U is the set of such sequences, and a sequence belongs to G if it has two properties: p1, each subexpression is an axiom or follows from previous ones by the rules of inference; p2, the final subexpression is t.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The tests factor into parts. The test for p2 concerns only the last subexpression. The test for p1 splits into one test per step, each relating a step to the one or two earlier steps it is directly derived from.

card.rule: A proof is a sequence whose every step is an axiom or follows from earlier steps, and whose last step is the theorem.
card.limits: The factoring works because each step is checked against a few earlier steps, not the whole sequence.

concepts.title: State language and process language
concepts.question: How can a proof be described by both what expressions are and what operations produce them?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The same theorem can be reached in several ways of speaking: as an expression, or as the end of a chain of operations.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The sequence u_t results from applying operators Q_1 to Q_t in turn, starting from u_0, the axioms and theorems given at the start. Symbols for expressions, parts of expressions, characteristics and differences form the state language. Symbols for operators, sequences of operators and their characteristics form the process language.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: A proof is most simply described with both languages: u_t is a proof of t if its last expression equals t, if it can be written as that chain of operator applications, if all Q_i are admissible rules of inference, and if u_0 holds axioms and proved theorems.

card.rule: State language names expressions and their features; process language names operators and their sequences; a proof needs both.
card.limits: The same object can be designated through either language: as an expression or as the result of operators.

concepts.title: State space and action space
concepts.question: What four things define a solution in most domains, and what does the state-process distinction explain about a goal-seeking organism?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The two aspects seen in theorem proving are not peculiar to it. Problem solutions in most domains share a structure.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: A solution is defined by characteristics of a terminal state, an initial state, conditions on admissible transformations of one state into another, and sometimes characteristics of intermediate states.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: For an organism seeking a goal object, the goal is symbolized in state language, while the process language supplies the series of signals that tells the effectors how to change the state. The authors tie state language to the afferent system and process language to the efferent system.

card.rule: Solutions are defined by start, end, admissible transformations and sometimes intermediate states; the state-process split is basic.
card.limits: The link to afferent and efferent systems is the authors' way of grounding the distinction in an organism.

concepts.title: Three meanings of solution
concepts.question: In what three senses is the word solution used, and what does the book call each?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: In everyday speech, solution is used in several ways. Which thing is meant depends on the problem.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: In theorem proving the solution is the sequence of expressions u_t, called the solution-path. For an organism reaching a goal object it is the sequence of operators, called the solution-action-sequence. In a crossword it is the terminal state, called the solution-object.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Used without qualification, the context shows which of the three is meant. Where it must be distinguished, the authors use the three terms.

card.rule: Solution can mean the path, the action sequence, or the object reached; say which when it matters.
card.limits: The word is left unqualified when context settles which of the three is meant.

concepts.title: The search tree
concepts.question: How does working forward from the start produce a branching tree of candidate paths?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: During a solution attempt, more than one path may be possible.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Working forward, several admissible operators may apply at the start, giving paths u_01, u_02; each of these can be extended by several operators, giving u_011, u_012, u_021 and so on. The result is a branching tree of paths, called a search tree or discovery tree.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The terminal branches are compared with the conditions on the last expression until one satisfies them; the path leading to it is a solution path.

card.rule: Applying every admissible operator at each state yields a search tree; a branch whose end meets the goal conditions is a solution path.
card.limits: A tree grows quickly when many operators apply at each state.

concepts.title: Searching in other spaces
concepts.question: Why does a solver's search often not take place in the external environment?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The search representation treats nodes as realizable states and links as actions. But actual search usually does not take place in the external environment.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Nodes can be imaginable states internal to the solver, generated by operators that need not satisfy every admissibility condition; unsuitable sequences can be modified or rejected later. A solver may work backward from the desired state, using roughly inverse operators.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: A chess player may conceive, by search, a mating configuration, then start a new search for moves that reach it. The search tree of moves she explores is not part of the solution, only a structure for predicting consequences and evaluating the next move.

blocks.label: Limit
blocks.text: The structure of the search space depends on the problem space and program the solver uses, not only on the task environment.

card.rule: Search can occur among imagined states, conjectured goals or plans, so the search space belongs to the solver as well as to the task.
card.limits: Many problems still fit the plain form: a solution object plus a path of admissible operators.

concepts.title: Everyday problems as U and G
concepts.question: How do the authors cast a safe, a machine design, a program and a translation as set problems?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Can ordinary problems be written as a set U and a goal set G?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Safe: U is all dial settings and G the settings that open it, usually one. Machine design: U is all parameter values and G those that meet the specifications at minimum cost. Matrix inversion program: U is all instruction sequences and G a sequence that does the inversion. Translation: U is all word sequences in English and G those with acceptable syntax and style and the original's meaning.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The set formulation is more general than the search form, because a problem stated with U and G can often be represented as a maze in several different ways.

card.rule: Name the set of candidates and the subset that qualifies, and many problems fit the set form.
card.limits: Different techniques can define vastly different search spaces for the same U and G.

concepts.title: Two ways to explain behavior
concepts.question: How do a process explanation and a demands explanation of the same behavior relate?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A theory can explain behavior in two ways. Do they conflict?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: In the process explanation, a problem space is given, an IPS with a goal is specified, and the system set in the environment produces a stream of behavior to compare with the person's. In the demands explanation, the problem solver is an adaptive system and acted as he did because the task environment demanded it.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors see no necessary conflict, provided the IPS did solve the problem: its symbol manipulations were then an effective way of meeting the task's demands. The second kind of explanation assumes the goal was held, motivation adequate, and the goal attainable.

blocks.label: Limit
blocks.text: The inferred programs may be idiosyncratic and ephemeral, just what the task demanded. The authors use both explanations.

card.rule: A program that matches behavior and a demand that explains the behavior can both hold; the first may show only adaptation.
card.limits: The demands explanation assumes a motivated, capable solver, though it can still predict the obvious moves of a solver who fails.

concepts.title: What counts as a demand
concepts.question: What is a demand of the task environment, and who makes it?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The demands explanation needs a definition of a demand that does not depend on the particular solver.

blocks.label: Term
blocks.text: A demand of the task environment is a constraint on the behavior of the problem solver that must be satisfied for the goal to be attained.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The environment itself makes no demands; the problem or goal does, through the solver's commitment to attaining it. The features of the environment that give rise to demands form its relevant structure, or texture.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The concept is conditioned on the goal being held and the solver being adequately motivated. The authors ensure this in their experiments, and people in our culture often declare their goals openly, so it is easy to check.

card.rule: A demand is a constraint that behavior must satisfy to reach the goal, and it arises from the goal, not from the environment alone.
card.limits: If a demand turned out to depend on the solver's own program, the split into task environment and solver would be a mirage.

concepts.title: Task invariants
concepts.question: What is a task invariant, and why is it a demand independent of the solver?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: When can we say behavior is necessary for a goal, without reference to the particular solver?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Take an environment, a problem solver and a goal. If every path in the environment that leads to the goal has a certain property, the behavior corresponding to it is a demand of the task environment. Winning tic-tac-toe, for instance, involves having three in a row.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Such demands are invariants of the situation, so they cannot depend on the nature of the solver. Their invariance holds however much analysis is needed to reveal it.

blocks.label: Limit
blocks.text: An invariant can be obvious, as in tic-tac-toe, or can need a hard proof to establish.

card.rule: A property shared by every path to the goal is a demand, whoever the solver is.
card.limits: A property true of all successful paths only counts as an invariant once shown; showing it can take enormous effort.

concepts.title: Where the solver ends
concepts.question: Where should the line between the environment and the problem solver be drawn?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Can the admissible operators always be regarded as part of the environment? Take a deep chasm with a single bridge: crossing the bridge seems a demand of the environment.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: But a solver with a chartered airplane, wings or teleportation need not use the bridge, so the original statement smuggled in assumptions about the solver. Pragmatically, draw the boundary closer to the center of the IPS, so capabilities for physically altering the external environment count as properties of the environment.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In mathematical proof the problem does not arise, since admissible operators are defined formally and accepted by both experimenter and subject. In actions on the real world, possibility and admissibility are empirical, not definitional.

blocks.label: Limit
blocks.text: If we move too many capabilities, such as arithmetic, to the environment, nothing is left of the solver and no room for a theory of him.

card.rule: Treat possibilities of physical action as environment, but keep the solver's own processing to describe him.
card.limits: Shifting the boundary too far leaves no solver to theorize about.

concepts.title: Measuring adaptivity
concepts.question: What can a measure built from success on one kind of problem predict, and how widely?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The success a system has with problems of a certain kind can be used to construct a measure of its adaptivity, or intelligence, in environments resembling those the test problems were set in.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Such a measure is highly predictive of performance in a very similar environment and less predictive in environments with different characteristics. Only to the extent it predicts across diverse environments might it be called general intelligence, which the authors do not need.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Measures specific to classes of environments are enough. The authors compare this to common practice in psychometrics.

card.rule: An adaptivity measure predicts well in similar environments and less well in different ones.
card.limits: The authors do not claim a general intelligence; a class-specific measure is enough for their purposes.

concepts.title: Demands depend on intelligence
concepts.question: Why can what the environment demands differ for solvers of different intelligence?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Crossing a chasm by its bridge may be a demand on a solver of ordinary intelligence. A far more inventive solver might invent the airplane, or think of chartering one, and for him crossing the bridge is no demand.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: If all external action possibilities belong to the environment, crossing is a demand on neither. If only thinkable external actions are included, the two solvers face different environments. The pragmatic remedy is to study solvers from a reasonably narrow range of intelligence, and to describe the environment differently for populations of widely differing intelligence.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In the search representation, the task environment is the space of search paths accessible to solvers of a specified intelligence. If intelligence is scalable, the space of the more intelligent solver includes, as a subpart, the smaller and sparser space of the less intelligent one. Demands are then properties invariant over all paths to a solution.

card.rule: Describe the environment for a given level of intelligence; demands are the invariants of the paths that level can reach.
card.limits: This works for a homogeneous group; it does not hold one description for solvers of widely different intelligence.

concepts.title: Skill, knowledge and chess ratings
concepts.question: What do ability measures in a domain reflect, and how do chess ratings show the idea?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: What does a domain ability measure reflect: general aptitude, or knowledge? Chess serves as the authors' example.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The relevant ability measures reflect the solver's knowledge of the problem domain in addition to any problem solving aptitude. According to the authors there is probably some correlation between chess skill and standard intelligence measures, though no hard data exist, and undoubtedly a much higher correlation with chess knowledge.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Chess skill is unidimensional enough for official scalar ratings. In the American system class A runs from 1800 to 2000, expert 2000 to 2200, master 2200 to 2400 and senior master over 2400. A 300-point gap makes the outcome predictable: the stronger player would probably lose no more than one game in twenty, nor draw more than one in five.

card.rule: Domain ability reflects domain knowledge as well as aptitude, and players of similar strength see similar things.
card.limits: The authors give the claimed correlations without hard data.

concepts.title: Collapsing the obvious
concepts.question: Why does a description of a task leave out the easy steps?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Describing every link of every search path would be unwieldy. Is there a way to simplify the description of search paths?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The difficulty of search for a solver of given intelligence is measured by the expected size of his search tree, and this can be applied to any segment of a path. Nodes whose attainment is obvious from one another can be merged into one node, keeping detail only for the hard passageways between clusters.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors use the image of a landscape: the detailed topography of flat or gently rolling plains has little import, while the location and shape of the mountain passes are what matter.

card.rule: Merge nodes that are obviously reachable from one another and describe in detail only the hard passages.
card.limits: What counts as obvious depends on the solver; for beginners many steps are not obvious.

concepts.title: Behavior as a sequence of episodes
concepts.question: What is an episode, and what should a theory attend to once behavior is described in episodes?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Once obvious detail is dropped, how should behavior be described?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Behavior is often described as a sequence of episodes, each a succinctly describable segment of behavior associated with attaining a goal.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: If a goal is easy to attain, or easy to identify as unattainable, the detailed behavior in getting to it need not concern us. Each episode can be treated as a unit, attending mainly to what determines which episodes start and how they end.

card.rule: Treat behavior as a sequence of goal-directed episodes and study what starts and ends each.
card.limits: Treating an episode as a unit is only justified when its goal is easy for the solver.

concepts.title: Narrowing the domain and the subjects
concepts.question: How do the authors avoid committing to the assumption that intelligence generalizes across task domains?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The approach commits the authors to specifying the intelligence of the solver. Does it commit them to a general intelligence across domains?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: No. Generality across task domains remains an empirical question, settled by evidence, not definition. So they restrict the domains, choosing problems from a definite class, such as chess, cryptarithmetic or elementary logic, and assume only a unidimensional ability within each.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Here the support is the authors' reasoning about their chosen domains, not data. They call chess, cryptarithmetic and elementary logic extremely homogeneous compared with intelligence test batteries, and even all three together a relatively homogeneous area, so they need not postulate that the ordering of solvers in chess agrees with that in logic. They also use a restricted class of subjects, intelligent enough to understand and accept the tasks yet not so smart or knowledgeable that the tasks are trivial.

card.rule: Restrict to a homogeneous class of tasks and to subjects for whom the tasks are neither impossible nor trivial.
card.limits: The restrictions buy tenability, not generality; whether intelligence generalizes across domains is left to evidence.

concepts.title: Same space, shared resources
concepts.question: What two further restrictions reduce variation between subjects in a task analysis?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Much of the variation in response to a task, especially the extreme variation, comes from differences in the representations subjects use.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Second restriction: assume the solvers use a problem space of a specific character. If two subjects use radically different spaces, analyze the task twice, possibly reaching different difficulty measures and invariants. Third restriction: treat some informational resources as aspects of the task environment rather than of the solver.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In cryptarithmetic, for example, all subjects may be assumed to know that a number of the form B = A + A is even, so this fact is placed in the task environment. The main technique is to choose subjects who are naive about the particular problems or the kind of task.

card.rule: Fix the problem space assumed, put shared knowledge in the environment, and pick naive subjects to cut variance.
card.limits: In chess the authors relax naivete about the kind of task, since subjects must be chess players.

concepts.title: The chapter's four questions
concepts.question: What four questions does the chapter raise, and what answer does it give to each?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The chapter asks how to define a task environment for a human problem solver viewed as an IPS.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Question one: how to represent the external environment. We have no privileged access to the real world of another human, so our representation amounts to a set of hypotheses about the subject's encoding. Question two: how the subject represents it internally, the problem space. Question three: how to represent problems and goals, with the set and search representations. Question four: how task environment and solver relate, answered through invariants and demands.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The chapter's own work supports each answer: the Necker cube and number scrabble for the first two issues, the set and search representations for the third, and task invariants for the fourth.

blocks.label: Limit
blocks.text: The authors leave open that some problems fit neither representation, and that the subject's space may lie outside the legal space the experimenter sees.

card.rule: Four issues structure the chapter: the environment, the problem space, the representation of problems, and the demands of the task.
card.limits: The chapter raises issues and illustrates them with simple examples rather than settling them.

concepts.title: Setting the stage for what follows
concepts.question: What does the chapter leave for later, and what links the task environment to the solver?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The chapter aims to raise issues and introduce concepts, not to work out a real task environment in detail.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The goal, accepted by the problem solver and to be attained in the task environment, provides the interface between the two components of the theory: the IPS (Chapter 2) and the task environment (this chapter).

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors chose simple examples and metaphors because a real task environment would bury the broad issues in technical particulars. Three later parts deal with cryptarithmetic, elementary logic and chess, using the concepts introduced here.

card.rule: The accepted goal is the interface between the IPS and the task environment; later parts apply the concepts to real tasks.
card.limits: General concepts such as problem space and task invariants become operational only through detailed analysis of a particular environment.

concepts.title: Two questions for a theory of problem solving
concepts.question: Which two questions must the theory answer, and which kinds of system should it cover?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The first chapters supplied a task environment and an information processing system (IPS). Still missing is an account of how an IPS can actually solve problems in a given task environment.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The chapter answers two questions: how can a problem be solved, and what makes a problem difficult? The authors say the answers form a theory that should apply to man, beast and machine alike, so long as each can be represented as an IPS of the Chapter 2 type.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors do not try to show the theory's full breadth here. They give an overview with a few simple examples, then study one program, the Logic Theorist, in depth.

card.rule: A theory of problem solving must say how problems can be solved and what makes them difficult, for any system that can be treated as an IPS.
card.limits: This chapter supplies tools for the later analyses of human behavior; it is not a full demonstration of the theory's breadth.

concepts.title: Input translation and the internal representation
concepts.question: What does the first process do before the solver chooses any method?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A problem arrives from an external environment, but the solver can work on it only inside itself. Something must turn the outside situation into material the solver can use.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: An initial process, the input translation, produces inside the solver an internal representation of the external environment and selects a problem space. All later problem solving happens within that representation, which may make solutions obvious, obscure or unattainable.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: This is the first of five parts of the organization the authors sketch for any problem solver in their Figure 4.1: environment, input translation, method selection, method application, and the options after a method ends.

card.rule: Problem solving begins when an input translation builds an internal representation and selects the problem space in which the rest of the work happens.
card.limits: The representation can hide or block the solution; the chapter mostly takes it as given and studies what happens inside it.

concepts.title: Selecting, applying and halting a method
concepts.question: Once the problem is represented, what does the solver select, and what can stop it?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: With a representation in place, the solver needs something to direct its behavior toward the goal, and a way to stop when that direction fails.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The system selects a method: a process bearing a rational relation to attaining a solution as formulated and seen in the internal representation. The selected method comes to control the solver's behavior, internal and external. Its execution may be halted by processes in the method itself or by more general processes that monitor it.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: These are steps 2 and 3 of the authors' five-part organization of a problem solver, set out in their Figure 4.1.

card.rule: A solver selects a method that fits its representation, lets it control behavior, and stands ready to halt it from inside or outside.
card.limits: The method is rational relative to the internal representation, which can be a poor picture of the real problem.

concepts.title: Three options when a method ends
concepts.question: What can the solver do when a method has been terminated?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Methods do not always reach the goal. The solver needs a repertoire of responses for the moment a method stops without a solution.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: When a method is terminated, three options are open: (a) another method may be attempted, (b) a different internal representation may be selected and the problem reformulated, or (c) the attempt to solve the problem may be abandoned.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: These are options (a), (b) and (c) in step 4 of the authors' five-part organization of a problem solver (Figure 4.1).

card.rule: After a method ends, the solver tries another method, switches representation, or gives up.
card.limits: The list is the authors' scheme for any solver; it does not say which option a given solver will choose.

concepts.title: Subgoals produced by a method
concepts.question: What may a method create while it runs, and what may the solver do with it?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A method pursuing a goal may reach a point where it cannot continue without first settling something else.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: During its operation, a method may produce new problems, called subgoals. The solver may elect to attempt one of them, or it may set the new subgoal aside and continue with another branch of the original method.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: This is part 5 of the authors' five-part organization of a problem solver (Figure 4.1).

card.rule: A running method can raise subgoals, and the solver may pursue one or leave it for another branch.
card.limits: Whether subgoals are worth creating depends on the method; the card says only that the option exists.

concepts.title: A serial solver that sees in parallel
concepts.question: How many methods can the solver run at once, and how much can it perceive at once?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A system that selects methods, switches representations and manages subgoals needs a way of doing so without chaos.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The IPS is fundamentally serial: it evokes and activates one method at a time. At a more detailed perceptual level, such as scanning the task environment or the internal representation, it may have some parallel processing capability. In the authors' words, the solver may see many things at once but does only one thing at a time about them.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors state this as a property of the IPS described in Chapter 2, and it frames the analysis of methods that follows.

card.rule: The problem solver runs one method at a time, even though its perception may take in many things at once.
card.limits: The parallelism the authors allow is perceptual and detailed; it does not mean several methods run together.

concepts.title: The goal-method-evaluate loop and its stack
concepts.question: What cycle does the solver's behavior follow, and why must it store goals?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A solver that shifts from method to method, and raises subgoals along the way, shows behavior that is hard to follow unless its overall pattern is described.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Behavior is segmented under the control of one method after another and iterative: select a goal, select a method, evaluate the results, select a goal again. Because methods can raise subgoals, behavior is also recursive: pending goals are held in abeyance, then re-evoked when new goals are reached.

blocks.label: Term
blocks.text: Recursion makes behaviors remote in time depend on each other, so the solver needs an apparatus for goal control and storage. In computer terms, goals are pushed down and later popped up, like a pushdown list or stack.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors support this structure from the logic of the scheme itself and a footnote adds a link to the interpreter of Chapter 2.

card.rule: The solver loops through goal, method and evaluation, and stores pending goals on a stack so that earlier goals return after later ones.
card.limits: The stack is a computer term for the storage needed, not a claim about how the human brain stores goals.
card.example: While writing a report you realise you need a figure; making the figure needs a data table; the table needs a file you must find. You find the file, build the table, draw the figure, and return to the report: goals pushed in that order and popped in reverse.

concepts.title: Two parts of the theory: representation and methods
concepts.question: How does the theory divide, and which part gets most attention in this book?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The solver's behavior implies how a theory of it must be organized. Some of the work concerns how a problem is represented and some concerns solving within a representation.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: One part of the theory deals with possible representations, their selection and installation. The other principal part deals with problem solving within a given representation: it defines a set of methods together with executive organizations for selecting and evaluating them.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors observe that most past progress has concerned the second part, and that this book has more to say about methods and executive organizations than about creating or switching representations.

card.rule: The theory has a representation part and a within-representation part; the book mostly develops the second.
card.limits: The weaker half is the representation part, which the authors say has received little attention so far.

concepts.title: Why representation gets less attention
concepts.question: What do the authors say about how much is known about representations?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A theory of problem solving would ideally explain how representations are created, selected and modified, but little is known about that.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Most progress so far has concerned the second component, methods. Much less is known about the nature of representations or about selecting and modifying them. The authors say their theory has much more to say about methods and executive organizations.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: They argue the limit may not be too damaging because some studied representations have very wide applicability and because their human subjects do not change representation appreciably in the problems studied.

card.rule: The authors admit that representation is the less developed part of the theory and justify their focus on methods by the tasks they study.
card.limits: The justification covers the tasks in this book; it does not claim representations never matter.

concepts.title: The Nine Dot Problem
concepts.question: Why is the Nine Dot Problem hard, and where does the difficulty lie?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A subject sees a square array of nine dots and must draw four straight lines, without raising the pencil, that pass through all nine dots.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Most subjects adopt a representation that assumes the lines must end on the dots and cannot go outside the square. That restriction comes from the representation and not from the problem statement; with it the problem is unsolvable. If the subject considers lines extending outside the square, a solution comes quickly.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors use it as a familiar example of a problem whose whole difficulty lies in finding the right representation.
