card.rule: In the Nine Dot Problem the obstacle is a restriction the representation adds, not one the problem states; drop it and the problem is solved quickly.
card.limits: The problem shows that representation alone can decide difficulty; it is not a model of problems whose difficulty lies in search.
card.example: Nine dots in a 3-by-3 square. Starting outside the square, a first line passes through three dots, a second turns outside the square and passes through two or three more, and so on. Lines that end on the dots cannot cover all nine; lines that extend outside can.

concepts.title: What a method is and what it needs
concepts.question: What is a method, and what two things determine its means and its ends?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The theory has to say what the units of problem solving are. The authors choose the method as the unit.

blocks.label: Term
blocks.text: A method is a collection of information processes that combine a series of means to attain an end, or at least to attempt to. It can be understood only in reference to its goal.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The usable means are dictated by the internal representation, because specifying a problem space determines the ways the initial situation can change toward the goal situation. Ends arise from the formulation of goals or subgoals.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors note that the theory falls into parts, each concerned with the methods tied to one problem formulation, and that usually a single method goes with each basic formulation.

card.rule: A method is a set of processes combining means to reach an end, and it is defined by its goal and by the means its representation allows.
card.limits: A method attempts the end; it does not guarantee it.

concepts.title: One method for each basic formulation
concepts.question: Which method goes with the set-predicate formulation, and which with the search formulation?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Several methods can exist for one problem formulation, so the theory needs to know which methods to expect for each basic formulation.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: In general there is a single method associated with each of the more basic types of problem formulation. With the set-predicate formulation of Chapter 3 goes the generate-and-test method; with the search formulation goes a heuristic search method.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Chapter 3 introduced the two formulations; this chapter gives each formulation its method.

card.rule: Set-predicate goes with generate-and-test; search goes with heuristic search.
card.limits: Several methods can exist for one formulation; the pairing names the single basic method, not the only possible one.

concepts.title: Interpretation: fitting a method to a problem
concepts.question: How does a general method come to deal with one particular problem?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A method exists in the solver before it meets any particular task, so it was fashioned without knowledge of the specific problems it will face.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The solver needs mechanisms to bring the method into correspondence with each problem. Fitting a particular situation to the method is a process of interpretation, in the logicians' sense. One general scheme embeds in the method symbol structures that stand for abstract potential situations; interpretation matches their variables with elements of the internally symbolized problem.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: A footnote compares this to parameter passing in a subroutine for sin(x): the routine is written with a variable x, and a special process stores the value 30 in the cell called x when sin(30) is wanted.

card.rule: A method contains abstract symbol structures; interpretation fills their variables with the particulars of the current problem.
card.limits: The authors say they have no reason to suppose this is the only possible scheme for interpretation.

concepts.title: Information-rich and information-poor problem spaces
concepts.question: How does the amount of information in a problem space affect the methods that can be used?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A method needs givens from the problem formulation, and the problem space must be able to supply them. The question is what happens when a space holds more or less information than a method needs.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The formulation must be coupled with the problem space as well as with the method. A space can hold more information than a method and formulation minimally require, since information need not be used just because it is there. In an information-rich space many methods become applicable as less of the information is used. In an information-poor space only one or two weak methods are usable, still able to proceed but inefficiently.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors cite Newell (1969a) for the weak-methods point.

card.rule: A richer problem space allows more methods; a poor one leaves only a few weak methods.
card.limits: Having information does not mean the solver can use it; the later difficulty section takes up that gap.

concepts.title: Measuring difficulty and where it comes from
concepts.question: How can difficulty be measured, and what two things determine it?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The chapter's second question asks what makes a problem difficult. Difficulty can be judged in several ways, none perfect.

blocks.label: Term
blocks.text: Measures include whether a solution is attained, the time needed to find one, and the quality of the solution. They are related, but imperfectly; none applies uniformly or is free of conceptual difficulty.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Whatever measure is used, difficulty is determined by the interaction between the task environment and the program of the IPS, meaning a set of methods plus an executive structure for selecting and applying them.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors want to dissect a global measure such as total solution time into parts: the time of each method, or of each component process. Each part of the program adds an increment of time.

card.rule: Difficulty is the product of the task environment meeting the solver's methods and executive, and it should be traced to components, not left as one global number.
card.limits: The authors do not expect to isolate all determinants of difficulty unless the whole program and problem structure are examined in full detail.

concepts.title: A solver that tries methods one after another
concepts.question: What do the two formulae say about chance of success and time as methods are tried?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A solver does not run all methods at once. It picks one, tries it, and moves on if it fails. How does that shape the chance of success and the time taken?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The basic structure is disjunctive: select a method; if it succeeds, done; if not, select another. With N methods tried, probability-of-solution = 1 - (1 - p)^N, where p is the chance a method succeeds. time-to-solution = setup-time + N x (selection-time + execution-time).

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors say these formulae, though very approximate, express the essence of problem solving: the solver keeps trying one method after another until it succeeds or quits, and pays a price in time for each.

card.rule: Each method gives another chance of success and costs another round of selecting and executing.
card.limits: The formulae are very approximate and assume constant time and success chance per method.
card.example: If a method succeeds with chance 0.3 each time, one try gives 0.3, two give 0.51 and three give about 0.66.

concepts.title: The limits of the success-and-time formulae
concepts.question: Which assumptions behind the formulae are shaky?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The two formulae are tidy but rest on strong simplifications.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The two formulae treat problem solving as trying methods one after another, each costing time and having some chance of success.

blocks.label: Assumed
blocks.text: Each method is assumed to have a constant execution time and a constant chance of success; the chance of success of different methods is assumed mutually independent.

blocks.label: Limit
blocks.text: It is not clear what probability of a solution can mean when a method either solves the problem or does not. Methods need not be independent: a failure may give diagnostic information about which method to try next. The formulae also reflect no qualitative differences among solutions.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors still say the formulae express the essence of what is going on in problem solving.

card.rule: The formulae are a rough guide: they assume constant times, constant and independent success chances, and they ignore the quality of solutions.
card.limits: Use them for the essence, trying methods one after another at a cost, not for exact predictions.

concepts.title: Problem space size as a key to difficulty
concepts.question: How does the size of the problem space relate to difficulty for elementary and for sophisticated methods?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Per-method formulae need a method-level view. The authors look for a quick guide to difficulty before studying each method in detail.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The problem space defines the set of possibilities for the solution as the solver sees it. Methods consider elements of the space one by one. For the most elementary methods, which search the entire space, time to solution is roughly proportional to the size of the space. The effect of more sophisticated methods can often be described as cutting down the part of the space that must be explored in order to find a solution.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The size of the problem space is one key to estimating difficulty.

card.rule: For elementary methods that search the whole space, solving time grows roughly in proportion to the size of the space.
card.limits: Sophisticated methods that use information cut down the part of the space explored, so size alone may overstate difficulty for them.

concepts.title: Information shrinks the space to a subspace
concepts.question: How does relevant information change the space a solver has to search?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The solver begins in the space in which it first encodes the problem, which already gives a measure of how big a world it must consider. That space can also be a mistaken one, as in the Nine Dot Problem.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: With each piece of relevant information applied, whether from the problem statement or from memory, the solver cuts down the problem space by limiting itself to a more relevant subspace. When no more relevant information is left, it must adopt a method that examines all elements of the remaining subspace.

blocks.label: Assumed
blocks.text: The authors call this view olympian because it assumes that having information is sufficient for using it to make the reduction.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors offer the view as an argument and a contrast, calling it olympian because it assumes that having information is enough to use it; they cite the Nine Dot Problem as a case where the starting space can be mistaken.

card.rule: Each usable piece of information shrinks the space to a more relevant subspace; what remains is searched exhaustively.
card.limits: The solver may hold information and not know how to use it, so the real reduction can be smaller than the olympian picture.

concepts.title: Similar solvers reach the same subspace
concepts.question: When should we expect two solvers to behave alike, and how can behavior be predicted?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: If problem solving depends on the subspace a solver reaches, differences between solvers may show up as differences in that subspace.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Two solvers of about the same intelligence and ability will detect and use about the same information in going from the initial space to the subspace where their methods apply.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Solvers of widely different ability may achieve quite different reductions and face different demands, so separate analyses may be needed. If the problem space a subject operates in can be found by observation, it can be used to predict later behavior.

card.rule: Equal-ability solvers reach about the same subspace; the subspace a subject works in helps predict what the subject does next.
card.limits: With widely different ability, the subspaces differ and each solver needs its own analysis.

concepts.title: The recognition method
concepts.question: What is the one universal method, and why does the usual difficulty measure not apply to it?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Asked the value of pi, a person may answer 3.1416 at once. Is that a case of problem solving?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Yes, in the set-predicate sense: given the real numbers, find the one that equals pi. The answer is solved by recognition: it was already in memory and was evoked by understanding the question. Recognition is the one universal method; it applies to every problem formulation because it is not sensitive to the details of the formulation.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The triviality owes to the solver's repertoire of methods. The authors note that the pi example fits the set-predicate definition of a problem.

blocks.label: Limit
blocks.text: When a problem is solved by recognition the usual measures of problem difficulty do not apply, since the result is immediate.

card.rule: Recognition solves a problem by evoking an answer already in memory, and it applies to every formulation.
card.limits: Recognition is not easy for every solver: whether it applies depends on what the solver already holds.

concepts.title: Why recognition matters: the last step of reduction
concepts.question: If recognition rarely solves hard problems directly, why is it important?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Recognition seldom solves hard problems directly, though occasionally a subject has seen the problem before. So why does the chapter stress it?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Problem solving often proceeds by reduction: a hard problem is replaced with ostensibly easier ones. If reduction is to succeed, some subproblems must actually be solved, not just reduced further. Recognition is very often how this last step is done.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Subproblems closed by recognition are those whose answers the solver already holds in memory.

card.rule: Recognition ends a chain of reductions: the last subproblem is solved by recalling an answer already held.
card.limits: Recognition does not shorten the reduction itself; it only closes it.

concepts.title: Program structures that can recognise
concepts.question: Which program structures can implement recognition?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Recognition needs a mechanism inside the solver that maps a problem statement to its stored answer.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The authors name three structures. First, a series of conditional branch statements, forming an implicit tree of tests that can be converted into a discrimination net (Chapter 2). Second, a production system: problem-statement 1 gives solution 1, problem-statement 2 gives solution 2, and so on. Third, the pattern recognition programs found in the literature.

blocks.label: Limit
blocks.text: If a production system has no limit on size, any problem statement it recognises leads directly to its solution.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors support the claim by describing mechanisms: branching tests that can be converted to a discrimination net, a production system, and pattern recognition programs.

card.rule: Recognition can be built from branching tests, a discrimination net, a production system or pattern recognition programs.
card.limits: The authors list the structures to show the variety of programs that can recognise, not to rank them.

concepts.title: What the set-predicate formulation guarantees
concepts.question: What may a method assume when a problem is given in set-predicate form, and what can it not assume?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: We need a method for problems given as a set U and the goal of finding, producing or determining a member of a subset G, identified by a test on the elements of U.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: A method for this formulation can use only what the formulation implies. First, the set U exists for the solver, so there must be some way of obtaining its members. Second, there is some way of determining the elements of G, namely the test.

blocks.label: Limit
blocks.text: The test must not be a way of generating elements of G directly, since that would solve the problem instantly. So the method has no other information to go on.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors argue from the formulation itself: with only a set and a test, nothing else is available to a method, and a test that generated members directly would solve the problem at once.

card.rule: Given only a set and a test, a method can obtain members of the set and test them, and nothing more.
card.limits: Any extra information about where G lies is outside the formulation and lets a better method exist.

concepts.title: The generate-and-test method
concepts.question: What are the two steps of generate-and-test, and what does it do when the set is exhausted?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: With only a set and a test available, the authors say there is one method that makes sense, in fact the only sensible one.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: A process generates potential solutions from the set U. As each is generated, it is tested to see whether it is also a member of G. If it is, generation stops and the element is reported as the solution; if the generator is exhausted, the method reports no solution.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Figure 4.2 shows this as a short program: generate from U; test whether the element is in G; if true stop and report the element; otherwise continue; at the end report no solution.

card.rule: Generate elements of the set one at a time and test each until one passes or the set is used up.
card.limits: The method is general because the generator and test are independent, which is also why it is weak.

concepts.title: Variants that leave the method unchanged in character
concepts.question: What variants of generate-and-test are possible, and why do they not change its essential character?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A reader may ask whether changes such as wanting every solution, or receiving candidates in a batch, create new methods.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The authors say variants are conceivable but do not change its essential character. One variant is wanting several or all solutions rather than only the first.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Alternatively the main generator may provide a number of candidates at once, not one at a time. These are listed temporarily and a second generator goes through the list so the test can be applied to each element. The two generators taken together are equivalent to one overall generator of candidates.

card.rule: Wanting all solutions, or generating in batches, changes the bookkeeping but not the nature of generate-and-test.
card.limits: The claim concerns these variants; it does not say every search method reduces to generate-and-test.

concepts.title: The guarantee and the four sources of difficulty
concepts.question: What does generate-and-test guarantee, and what four things set the time to the first solution?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Generate-and-test is the most general method for the set-predicate formulation. What can be promised about it, and when is it slow?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: From Figure 4.2, the solution will always be found if the conditions of the formulation hold and the generator is allowed to run long enough. The interesting difficulty measure is therefore the time to the first solution.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: That time is set by four things: (1) the average effort to generate each element; (2) the average effort to test whether a candidate satisfies the solution conditions; (3) the size of the problem space to be searched; (4) the relative position of the solution in the order the generator produces new elements. In a given case any of these, or a combination, may be the source of difficulty.

card.rule: Generate-and-test finds a solution if one exists and it runs long enough; its difficulty is generation cost, test cost, space size and the solution's position.
card.limits: The guarantee says nothing about how long is long enough; for large spaces the time can be impractical.

concepts.title: Example: the extra chair
concepts.question: Why is generate-and-test an excellent method for finding an extra chair?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: An extra chair is needed from the living room to seat one more dinner guest.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The set U is small, perhaps four chairs, and accessible: step into the living room and look at each in turn. The test is rapid: reject large stuffed chairs and tacky chairs, and any other will do.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors conclude that generate-and-test is an excellent method here, since a small, accessible space and a fast test mean no more elaborate method is worth building.

card.rule: When the space is small and accessible and the test is rapid, plain generate-and-test is excellent.
card.limits: The conclusion holds for small cheap cases; the next examples show cases where the same method fails.

concepts.title: Example: the safe
concepts.question: Where does the difficulty lie when both generating and testing are cheap?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A safe has ten independent dials, each numbered 00 to 99, and a would-be safecracker does not know the combination.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Generating a setting and testing it are both cheap, but the space is huge: 100 to the tenth power, or 10^20, one hundred billion billion settings.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Only one combination opens the safe. On average it would take 50 billion billion trials. The authors conclude the problem is difficult, and that the difficulty lies entirely in the size of the space.

card.rule: With cheap generating and testing, difficulty can still be extreme because the space is enormous.
card.limits: The result assumes no information about the combination; a faint click per dial would change the problem, as a later example shows.

concepts.title: Example: choosing a chess move
concepts.question: Where does the difficulty lie when generate-and-test is used to choose a chess move?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A chess player on move has some twenty to thirty legal alternatives. Can generate-and-test pick a good one?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Generating moves is easy, even generating all of them with a little care. The great difficulty lies in determining whether a move is good: the problem lies in the verifier, not the generator.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: A principal way to evaluate a move is to look at the consequences of later moves by both players. The authors say looking ahead only five moves, with 30 alternatives at each step, means considering some 10^15 positions to evaluate a single move.

card.rule: In chess the generator is cheap but the verifier is very costly, so a more chess-sensitive formulation is needed.
card.limits: The authors conclude only that this formulation is poor; they do not say chess is unsolvable.

concepts.title: Example: the crossword word
concepts.question: What happens to difficulty when a generator is built from another generator and test?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: In a crossword one needs a word with three g's whose fourth letter is z.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Generate-and-test could use a generator of words with three g's and test the fourth letter. The space is probably small and the test cheap, but such a generator is likely expensive to build.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: One can build it from another generate-and-test: a generator that produces dictionary words in sequence and a test that counts three g's. Packaged together they make a generator of three-g words. Now generating and testing are both cheap, and the difficulty becomes the size of the space, the dictionary.

card.rule: Packaging a generator and a test makes a new generator; the difficulty moves from the generator to the size of the underlying space.
card.limits: The authors call the examples superficial; they show where difficulty can sit, not exact costs.

concepts.title: Recasting a search problem as set-predicate
concepts.question: Can generate-and-test solve a problem stated as a search for a path, and what does it cost?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The second formulation asks for a path from an initial element of the problem space to a desired element. The space has operators that generate neighbouring points, though not all operators apply at each point.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Any problem in this formulation can be recast as set-predicate. Take a goal test as the test, organize the operators to generate one element after another so that all elements eventually appear, and apply generate-and-test.

blocks.label: Limit
blocks.text: There is a subtle shift of task: finding a path has been replaced by finding the final element of the path. To solve the original problem a record of the successful path must be kept.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors argue by construction: take a goal test, organize the operators to generate every element eventually, and apply generate-and-test, while keeping a record of the successful path.

card.rule: A search problem can be recast as set-predicate and solved by generate-and-test, provided the successful path is recorded.
card.limits: The recasting throws away the guidance a search method could use, which is why it is general but weak.

concepts.title: Where the power of search comes from
concepts.question: Where must gains over random search come from?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Random search or generate-and-test uses no knowledge of the goal. How can a search method do better?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Gains over random search must come from exploiting additional information: controlling the search at each step in the light of what has been discovered and what remains to be done.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors illustrate the point with the combination safe and the algebra equation in the next ideas.

card.rule: A search method gains power by letting each step depend on the goal and on progress so far, at the cost of being specific.
card.limits: Information the method does not use gives no gain; power comes only from information it actually exploits.

concepts.title: Example: the safe that clicks
concepts.question: How does a faint click on each correct dial change the safe problem?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: With 10 dials of 100 settings each, the space has 10^20 elements and random search is impractical. Suppose the safe is defective.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: If a faint click can be heard each time a dial is turned to its correct setting, the average number of trials to find any one dial is 50, so about 500 trials open the safe. Ten clicks turn an impossible task into a trivial one for the safecracker.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors remark that it would not take a very elaborate heuristic generator to change the very large number into a quite small one.

card.rule: Feedback that confirms each part separately turns one huge search into many small ones.
card.limits: The gain relies on feedback per dial; a safe that gives no partial signal gets no benefit.

concepts.title: Example: solving ax + b = cx + d
concepts.question: How can the right values of k be found without searching?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Solve ax + b = cx + d for x. The admissible operators are Add[k], Sub[k], Mult[k] and Div[k]: adding, subtracting, multiplying or dividing both sides by the same number k. Each type has infinitely many operators, so there are infinitely many action sequences of any length.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Yet a solution sequence is easy to construct: Sub[cx], Sub[b], then Div[a - c]. The arguments k need not be guessed; they are provided by the problem expression and by the expressions obtained from it along the way.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The desired object has only a term in x on the left and a constant on the right. So subtract the x-term from the right side, subtract the constant from the left, and divide by the coefficient of x.

card.rule: Copy each operator's argument from the current expression and the first path generated is a solution.
card.limits: This is the limiting case, with search eliminated; it works only because the expression reveals the needed k.

concepts.title: Two ways to cut a search: test and copy
concepts.question: How do the safe and the algebra examples differ as search-reducing devices?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The safe and the algebra equation are both quick to solve, but not for the same reason.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: In the safe, many alternative settings are tried for each dial, but the click tells at once which is right, so exploration continues only along the correct path and the other branches are terminated. The click is a test that discriminates correct from incorrect paths. In algebra, the right values of k are generated directly by copying them from the expression, so only a single, unbranching path is explored.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Figure 4.3 shows the exploration tree for the safe-opening task: at each dial many branches are tried but all except the correct one are cut off.

card.rule: One device tests and prunes wrong branches; the other generates the right values directly and has no wrong branches.
card.limits: Many real methods mix the two; the examples show each device in its pure form.

concepts.title: Forward, backward and the tree to be grown
concepts.question: In which directions can a search run, and what is the task of a problem solving procedure?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: In the safe and algebra examples operators were tried in the same order as they appear in the solution. Must that always be so?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: It is common but not logically necessary. Most often search works forward from the initial object toward the desired object, or backward from the desired object toward the initial one, so each operator is applied to a known object to give a new known object.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Either way the search can be drawn as a tree of the paths actually explored, which says nothing of the order branches are added. The task of a problem solving procedure is to grow a tree of operator sequences that will not branch too luxuriantly and that includes at least one solution path.

card.rule: Search can run forward or backward, and its task is to grow a modest tree that contains a solution path.
card.limits: Disconnected segments joined later are possible; the authors say they discuss such methods later.

concepts.title: The heuristic-search program and its cycle
concepts.question: What are the steps of the basic cycle of heuristic search?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors want one program that shows every opportunity to apply information in the search formulation.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Figure 4.4 gives it. Insert the initial element on untried-problems. Select an element from untried-problems as current-element (stop and report failure if none). Select an operator for it. Apply the operator to give a new element. Test the new element for a solution; if it is, reconstruct the path and succeed. Otherwise evaluate it: reject it or insert it on untried-problems. Then decide the next step.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Figure 4.5 gives the same method as a flow diagram, with one extra box assigning the name current-element to new-element, which the program does in passing at line 8.

card.rule: The basic cycle selects an element, selects an operator, applies it, tests, evaluates and decides what to do next.
card.limits: The program is a scheme, not a prescription; real programs use only some of its mechanisms.

concepts.title: Evaluating and deciding: continue, advance or back up
concepts.question: What three-way choice ends each cycle, and what does evaluation do?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: After a new element is produced and tested, the search must decide what to do with it and where to go next.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Evaluation of the new element leads to accepting it, so it is remembered for later use on untried-problems, or rejecting it. The cycle ends with a three-way choice: continue applying operators to the current element; replace the current element by the new one (advance); or abandon the path and go back to untried-problems (back up).

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Backing up allows search to restart from any element remembered earlier. The cycle ends by finding a solution, which leads to reconstructing the path, or by exhausting untried-problems.

card.rule: Each cycle evaluates the new element and then continues, advances or backs up.
card.limits: The labels are the authors' names for the options, not a claim about which a given program chooses.

concepts.title: An encompassing scheme, not one method
concepts.question: Why do real programs use only parts of the heuristic-search scheme?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Many heuristic search programs have been built in artificial intelligence, yet almost none uses all of the mechanisms in the authors' program.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The program is better seen as an encompassing scheme from which more specific methods are derived. There are two reasons programs use only some of its mechanisms. The more important is that particular task environments permit some mechanisms and not others.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: If some mechanisms do not apply to a set of problems, one can generally write a more direct executive that incorporates only the heuristic mechanisms actually used.

card.rule: Heuristic search is a scheme; each program uses the part of it that its task environment allows.
card.limits: A program using fewer mechanisms is not thereby inferior; the task may not allow the rest.

concepts.title: The four undefined processes and Table 4.1
concepts.question: Which four processes does the scheme leave open, and how does Table 4.1 help?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The program of Figure 4.4 has four processes whose content is not fixed: select-element, select-operator, evaluate(new-element) and decide-next-step.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Table 4.1 lists some ways these have been specified in programs from the literature.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors use ease of applicability as an example for selecting operators. Operators too easy to apply could be rejected, difficult ones selected when they apply, or all ordered by ease. Programs exist that reject or select on ease of application, but the authors know of none that order on it. They say the table can serve as a check list when comparing programs.

card.rule: The four open processes are filled in differently by different programs; Table 4.1 is a check list of the ways.
card.limits: The table gives key notions, not complete specifications.

concepts.title: Fixed strategies: depth-first, breadth-first, scan-search
concepts.question: How do fixed choices in select-element and decide-next-step give depth-first, breadth-first and related searches?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Table 4.1 lists fixed strategies for choosing which element to work on and what to do after evaluation.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: For select-element, a fixed strategy can be last-in-first-out, which is depth-first search, or first-in-first-out, which is breadth-first search. Or selection can follow the evaluation of elements. For decide-next-step, the fixed strategies are always advance (depth-first), always continue (one-level breadth-first) and always go back (search and scan).

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The table groups the fixed strategies and the evaluation-based options under each of the four open processes of the heuristic-search program.

card.rule: Fixed rules for selecting and deciding yield the familiar searches: depth-first, breadth-first, one-level breadth-first and search-and-scan.
card.limits: These are fixed strategies; evaluation can replace them with choices that depend on how promising elements look.

concepts.title: The task: proving theorems in the propositional calculus
concepts.question: What is the Logic Theorist's task, and what is the calculus made of?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors take a single problem solver, the Logic Theorist (LT), and first describe its task environment. They plan to build a generate-and-test scheme for it, then describe LT's behavior and structure.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The task is to discover proofs of theorems in elementary symbolic logic, the propositional calculus, treated as a purely formal mathematics. Expressions are built from variables and constants with connectives: not (~), or (V) and implies. Five expressions are axioms, and rules of inference derive new theorems from axioms and other theorems.

blocks.label: Limit
blocks.text: A footnote warns that discovering proofs is not a deductive process, and that doing the task in logic does not make problem solving more logical than any other task, such as writing the book.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors support the description by stating LT's task environment (five axioms and rules of inference) and, in a footnote, noting that discovering proofs is not a deductive process.

card.rule: LT's task is to find proofs of propositional-calculus theorems from five axioms and rules of inference; finding them is problem solving, not deduction.
card.limits: The system is treated as purely formal; its interpretation as sentences and deduction is not needed.

concepts.title: The axioms, the rules and what a proof is
concepts.question: What four rules turn axioms into theorems, and what counts as a proof?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: To find a proof the solver needs the axioms and the legal moves for deriving new expressions.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The five axioms are those of Whitehead and Russell's Principia Mathematica. Three rules of inference plus a derived fourth turn known theorems into new ones. Substitution puts any expression for a variable throughout a theorem. Replacement swaps a connective for its definition, for example (P implies Q) for (not-P or Q). Detachment: if A and A implies B are theorems, B is a theorem. Chaining: if A implies B and B implies C, then A implies C.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Whitehead and Russell did not take chaining (their syllogism) as a separate rule but derived it by two successive applications of detachment to Axiom 1.6. A proof, the solution path, is a list of expressions each validly derived from earlier ones that leads from axioms and known theorems to the desired expression.

card.rule: Four rules act as operators on expressions, and a proof is a list of validly derived expressions ending at the target.
card.limits: Chaining is a derived rule, not an independent one, in Principia.

concepts.title: The set-predicate version of the proof task
concepts.question: How big is the set of possible proofs, and why is trial and error hopeless?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: To pose the task in set-predicate form, take as the set U all possible proofs, that is, arbitrary lists of logic expressions.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: With no limit on length that set is infinite, so restrict it: lists of at most 20 expressions, each at most 23 symbols long, using only variables P, Q, R, S, T and the connectives not, or and implies. The number of possible proofs meeting these restrictions is about 10^235.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Testing a member is also costly: each expression must be checked as an axiom or as following from earlier ones by the rules, and the target must appear. The authors conclude that choosing proofs by sheer trial and error is not feasible for humans or machines: the set is too large and the testing too costly.

card.rule: Posed as generate-and-test, proof finding has about 10^235 candidates and an expensive test, so it is hopeless.
card.limits: The size depends on the arbitrary restrictions chosen, as the next idea shows.

concepts.title: Why 10^235 is arbitrary
concepts.question: Why does the authors' 10^235 not reflect the task?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The first generator for logic proofs produced a space of about 10^235 lists.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: That size is exceedingly large but also arbitrary: it depends entirely on the simplicity restrictions imposed on the set. Nothing in this generator reflects the demands of the task except in the weakest sense of generating elements of the problem space, for instance not mixing in numerals or Greek letters.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors then ask for a more meaningful generator that takes account of conditions a solution must meet.

card.rule: A size set by arbitrary restrictions shows nothing about the task; a better generator must use the task's own demands.
card.limits: The point is about this generator; some size estimates in the book do track real task structure.

concepts.title: The British Museum Algorithm
concepts.question: How does the British Museum Algorithm generate, and what does that do to the verifier?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Can a generator be built that uses some of the conditions a proof must meet?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The authors call their scheme the British Museum Algorithm. It considers only lists of expressions that are valid proofs: initial expressions are axioms and each later one is derived from earlier ones by valid rules. It generates single-expression proofs first, then two-expression proofs, and so on. Given all proofs of length k, it makes those of length k + 1 by applying the rules in all permissible ways, so it grows a tree of proofs.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Because it generates only proofs (of something), most of the work of verification disappears. The verifier now only needs to check that the desired theorem occurs somewhere in the generated sequence of expressions, a quite simple process.

card.rule: Generating only valid proofs, shortest first, leaves the test with only one job: is the target in the list?
card.limits: The algorithm is far from efficient; it only shifts work from the test to the generator.

concepts.title: How few theorems the algorithm reaches
concepts.question: How quickly does the algorithm reach the theorems of Chapter 2 of Principia?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Principia's Chapter 2 holds sixty-odd theorems. How soon does the algorithm reach them?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Figure 4.7 shows how the number of proofs grows with steps at the start. Theorem 2.01 appears at step 4, within the first 42 theorems proved. Theorems 2.02, 2.03 and 2.04 arrive at step 6, within the first 115. Theorem 2.05 arrives at step 8, within the first 246. Only one more theorem, 2.07, is in the first 1000.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The proofs of the rest need complex substitutions or detachment. The authors cannot estimate how many proofs must be generated to cover Chapter 2, but it is almost certainly very large, and the first six theorems give no reason to expect the others early. It would take eons of eons of computation.

card.rule: After about a thousand theorems the algorithm has reached only six of Principia's sixty-odd.
card.limits: These counts cover only the simplest steps, so the later growth is much faster than they suggest.

concepts.title: Spectacularly inefficient, yet not random
concepts.question: In what sense is the algorithm not random?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Despite its inefficiency, the generating process of the British Museum Algorithm is not a random walk.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: In adding to sequences of expressions, it applies only admissible operators, so every sequence it generates is a valid proof of something. It does not explore the space of all possible sequences of expressions, only the space of proofs. Even within that space it proceeds in an orderly way from short to long proofs.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors use this to show that even an apparently blind generator has built-in selectivity, a theme taken up again in the discussion of LT's selectivity.

card.rule: The algorithm explores only the space of proofs, in order of length.
card.limits: Orderly is not the same as efficient; the algorithm remains hopelessly slow for most theorems.

concepts.title: Why study hopeless formulations
concepts.question: Why do the authors examine formulations they call impossible ways of solving the problem?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Both the arbitrary generator and the British Museum Algorithm are impossible ways to solve the logic problem. Why spend time on them?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: First, they reveal the structure of the task environment by showing how difficult the problems are for weak problem solvers, and so provide a standard against which more powerful formulations can be compared. Second, generate-and-test is a method of last resort: almost any problem can also be formulated so that it applies, so it can be tried when all else fails.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: If a problem is small, generate-and-test may even be best, since an elaborate efficient method costs more to build than it saves. The authors treat such methods as the standard against which stronger formulations are judged.

card.rule: Hopeless formulations measure how hard a task is for weak solvers and supply the method of last resort.
card.limits: A last-resort method is not a first choice unless the problem is small.

concepts.title: LT at work: three theorems
concepts.question: What do LT's runs on Theorems 2.01, 2.45 and 2.31 show?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Before opening up LT's structure, the authors describe how it behaves from outside. LT is given the five axioms as theorems it may assume, and it already holds the rules of inference and the definitions as processes.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Asked for Theorem 2.01, LT works about ten seconds and prints a four-line proof: copy Axiom 1.2, substitute, replace a connective, substitute again. Given the 38 theorems before 2.45, it takes about 12 minutes to produce a five-line proof. Given the 28 theorems before 2.31, it works about 23 minutes and then reports that it cannot prove it and has exhausted its resources.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: A footnote warns that absolute times are deceptive since they depend on the machine. LT ran on JOHNNIAC, a mid-fifties first-generation machine.

card.rule: LT quickly proves easy theorems, takes longer on harder ones, and sometimes gives up with a report that it has run out of resources.
card.limits: Times belong to the machine used; compare the relative times, not the absolute ones.

concepts.title: The first 52 theorems: 38 proved
concepts.question: How well did LT do on the first 52 theorems of Chapter 2, and how did time relate to proof length?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The first experiment gave LT the axioms and the first 52 theorems of Chapter 2 of Principia in book order.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: LT proved 38 of the 52 theorems, 73 percent. About half the proofs took under a minute each; most of the rest took one to five minutes; a few took 15 to 45 minutes (JOHNNIAC time).

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: There was a strong relation between time and proof length: time rose sharply, perhaps exponentially, with each added proof step.

card.rule: LT proved about three theorems in four, and the time needed grew sharply with the number of steps in the proof.
card.limits: The success depended on theorems being stored in order; the next ideas show what happens without them.

concepts.title: Taking away the earlier theorems
concepts.question: What happens to LT's success when the earlier theorems are removed from its memory?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: In the second and third experiments the authors restored the initial conditions by removing from LT's memory the theorems it had proved. They describe this as getting a new subject who knows how to solve logic problems but is unfamiliar with the particular problems.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Given Theorem 2.12 in that state, LT could not find a proof, although with the earlier theorems it had done so in about ten seconds. When Theorem 2.03 alone was stored with the axioms, LT succeeded.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The comparison shows that what is stored changes what can be proved.

card.rule: LT's success depends on what it has stored: removing earlier theorems can turn a ten-second proof into a failure.
card.limits: Adding even one relevant theorem can restore success, though at a longer proof and more time.

concepts.title: Casting proof finding as a search
concepts.question: What problems arise in turning proof finding into a search, and what choices must be made?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A tree of possible solution paths is a natural representation for a theorem-proving program. The solution condition: the theorem to be proved is obtained from the axioms and proved theorems by admissible operations. But the elementary operators do not fit the search formulation directly.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Replacement is simple: an expression in, an expression out. Substitution needs the new expressions and the variables. Detachment and chaining need a second theorem. The search can run forward from axioms or backward from the theorem. Backward, substitution replaces identical subexpressions with a variable, and detachment and chaining take one expression but give a pair, both of which must be shown true.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In the state language the objects are logic expressions and sets and sequences of them; in the process language the operators build sets or trees of expressions.

card.rule: To use search on logic, one must decide the element of the space, the direction, and how to handle operators that need extra inputs or give pairs.
card.limits: Different choices give different programs; LT's choices come next.

concepts.title: LT's four design choices
concepts.question: What choices define LT's problem space?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The previous idea left open the element of the space, the direction, and how operators should take inputs.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: LT chooses: first, the element of the space is a single logic expression. Second, it works backward, so the initial element is the theorem to be proved and the search goes toward the axioms and assumed theorems. Third, the operators come from detachment and chaining by always having a theorem or axiom enter as one input, so each operator takes one input and gives one output. Fourth, replacement and substitution are components of all the operators and of a test of whether a solution has been found.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors compare this to the parametrized operators of the algebra example: the set of axioms and proved theorems, called theorems, supplies the parameter, as in Q[T].

card.rule: LT works backward on single expressions, with operators parametrized by a stored theorem.
card.limits: Because operators take one theorem as parameter, certain proofs cannot be found, as a later idea shows.

concepts.title: Substitution test, detachment and chaining operators
concepts.question: What do the Substitution Test and the detachment and chaining operators compute?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: LT's operators are built from the rules, each with a theorem T from the list theorems as a parameter.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The Substitution Test SB(T) = X seeks, by substitutions and replacements, to transform theorem T into expression X. Detachment DT[A implies B](X) seeks to transform B into X by SB; if it succeeds it produces SB(A), the same substitutions made in A. Forward chaining CF[...](D implies B) needs X = (A implies C) and seeks SB(D) = A, producing SB(B) implies C. Backward chaining CB[B implies D](A implies C) seeks SB(D) = C, producing A implies SB(B).

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: An example: SB[P V Q for A, Q for B](A implies B) = ((P V Q) implies Q), which substitutes (P V Q) for A and Q for B.

card.rule: Each operator uses substitution to match part of a stored theorem to the current expression and then returns the rest of that theorem, modified the same way.
card.limits: These definitions are exact; matching either succeeds, producing an expression, or fails.

concepts.title: LT's executive and its submethods
concepts.question: How does LT's executive organize the operators into submethods?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: LT's operators and test must be organized by an executive program, a variant of the heuristic-search method of Figure 4.4.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Figure 4.8 shows the executive. Four specialized subroutines, called submethods, each organize one operator or the test: substitution, detachment, chaining forward and chaining backward. Each systematically tries its operator for all theorems on the list, in the order listed.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The substitution-submethod tests whether any theorem can be reached directly from the input and, if so, announces the proof. The others apply their operator to each theorem, test each new problem by substitution, and otherwise add it to the end of untried-problems. Each submethod can add at most one branch per theorem.

card.rule: LT's executive tries four submethods in turn on each problem and adds the surviving subproblems to a list.
card.limits: The executive is a particular variant of the general scheme, simplified for clarity.

concepts.title: A worked case: Theorem 2.45 in two steps
concepts.question: How did LT find the proof of 2.45, and what does the search tree contain?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: When LT had all 38 theorems that precede 2.45 together with the axioms, it found a two-step proof.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The detachment operator, applied to 2.45 and Theorem 2.16, added a new expression to untried-problems: P implies (P V Q). The substitution operator, applied to this new expression and Theorem 2.2, found that the latter could be made equal to it by substitution. That completed the proof.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Figure 4.9 shows the tree of sequences. The top node is the problem.

card.rule: A two-step proof: detachment makes one useful subproblem, then substitution closes it; a few other subproblems are made along the way.
card.limits: The proof is found only because the right theorems were on the list.

concepts.title: No guarantee, but a partial one
concepts.question: What does LT's method guarantee about a subproblem, and what does it not?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: LT is called a heuristic method. What does it promise?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: It gives no guarantee that it will work. There may be no suitable theorem on the list for any submethod. A subproblem generated may not belong to any proof; it can even be false. There is also no guarantee that the four methods together, with unlimited effort, can prove every theorem.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: What the operators do guarantee: any subproblem generated is part of a sequence of expressions that ends in the desired theorem.

card.rule: LT's operators guarantee that a subproblem leads toward the target; they do not guarantee that it can be proved.
card.limits: The guarantee concerns the form of the sequence, not whether the search succeeds.

concepts.title: Why LT cannot prove Theorem 2.13
concepts.question: Why can LT not find the Whitehead and Russell proof of 2.13?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: LT cannot prove Theorem 2.13, although all the new members of untried-problems after a certain point are false expressions that cannot lead to a proof.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Whitehead and Russell prove it with Axiom 1.06 and the earlier theorems 2.11 (call it A) and 2.12 (call it B), writing 2.13 as C. From B and the axiom B implies (A implies C), detachment gives A implies C. From that and A, detachment gives C. Working backward, LT must find a stored theorem of the form X implies C. But A implies C has not been proved yet, so the detachment-submethod fails.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The submethod treats the two premises A and A implies C asymmetrically. Had LT been asked first to prove A implies C, it would have found that, and then C. The authors conclude that LT will not find a large class of branched proofs unless given some intermediate expressions as subproblems in a suitable order.

card.rule: LT's backward detachment needs a stored implication ending in the target, so proofs that first need a new implication are out of reach.
card.limits: Giving LT the intermediate step first as a problem would let it succeed.

concepts.title: Built-in selectivity and the choice of generator
concepts.question: How does building a solution property into the generator cut the space, and which generator should be chosen?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Both LT and the British Museum Algorithm generate only sequences that are proofs of something. How general is that trick?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Many problems have the form: the solutions are all elements with properties p1, p2 and p3, and no generator gives all three, but generators exist for any two. Then three schemes arise. Generate elements with p1 and p2 until one has p3. Or generate p1 and p3 and wait for p2. Or generate p2 and p3 and wait for p1. Which is best depends on which constraint is hardest to satisfy and on relative cost.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: For proofs, p1: the list begins with known theorems. p2: every other expression follows from earlier ones. p3: the last expression is the target. p2 is hard, so waiting for it is foolish. The British Museum Algorithm satisfies p1 and p2 and waits for p3. LT builds backward from the target, satisfying p2 and p3, and waits for p1.

card.rule: Build the hardest conditions into the generator and let the cheapest one be what the test waits for.
card.limits: A property that is rare should be put into the generator; a common one can safely be left to chance.

concepts.title: Where the generator gets its information
concepts.question: Where does a selective generator get the information it uses?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A generator that is more than generate-and-test must have access to information in the situation that lets it construct required objects directly.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Take the detachment-submethod. It adds an expression only when certain special conditions hold, and those conditions determine what is added. It adds an expression only when a stored theorem of suitable form is found, and the form of that theorem fixes the expression added.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: These conditions keep theorems with property p1 and untried-problems with p2 and p3. Taken jointly the detachment and chaining submethods give a selective subset but usually no unique sequence, and they do not guarantee all proof properties, hence the need for the substitution test. LT beats the British Museum Algorithm because its generator is more selective.

card.rule: A selective generator acts only when special conditions hold, and those conditions fix what it adds.
card.limits: A selective generator still needs a test, because it does not guarantee every proof property.

concepts.title: Measuring selectivity in bits
concepts.question: How much does halving the alternatives at each branch point reduce a random search?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors want a way to measure the selective power of a generator.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Take a tree with m alternatives at each branch point and k branch points, with a single correct path. Random search needs on the order of m^k trials. A generator that produces only half the alternatives at each point leaves (m/2)^k trials, a reduction by a ratio of 2^k.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: For a search seven steps long the factor is 128; for ten steps it is just over a thousand.

card.rule: Cutting the alternatives in half at each of k steps cuts the search by a factor of 2^k.
card.limits: The calculation assumes a single correct path and random search within the reduced tree.

concepts.title: How fast the proof tree grows
concepts.question: How does the size of LT's tree grow with depth, compared with a working-forward algorithm?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors compare LT with a more selective working-forward algorithm, so that the comparison is on detachment and chaining alone and not on substitution.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: LT starts with U[0] = 1, and T theorems. The generator makes about aT new expressions, where a is the chance that the operators succeed with a given theorem. Each round multiplies the tree by aT, so the number of branches of length n or less is of the order (aT)^n: exponential growth. The working-forward algorithm takes pairs of members of T and adds about aT^2 new members; the number of branches grows of the order (aT)^(2^n).

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Table 4.2 gives estimates for a = 0.3 and T = 6. For LT the sizes for 1 to 6 steps are about 2, 3, 6, 10, 19, 34. The working-forward figures climb far faster, reaching astronomical values by n = 6.

card.rule: LT's search tree grows as (aT)^n; a working-forward algorithm grows doubly exponentially, as (aT)^(2^n).
card.limits: The estimates rest on a, the chance an operator succeeds, being constant, and are only orders of magnitude.

concepts.title: What makes a generator selective
concepts.question: What two characteristics give generators their selectivity?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The submethods of LT, and the generators of the working-forward algorithm and the British Museum Algorithm, belong to an important class of heuristics.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: They generate a selective tree of possible solution action sequences and paths. Their selectivity rests on two characteristics: (1) they generate only sequences that satisfy certain admissibility criteria, criteria that a solution path must also meet; (2) they use information extracted from partial sequences already generated to choose the directions in which to continue. Generators are more or less selective as they use more or less of this information.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Because problem spaces are so large, the authors say it is hard to exaggerate the amount of selectivity in even apparently blind generators.

card.rule: A selective generator generates only admissible sequences and uses information from what it has already built.
card.limits: Selectivity is a matter of degree; more information used means more selective.

concepts.title: Matching: a faster route than the British Museum Algorithm
concepts.question: Why is LT faster than the British Museum Algorithm even when both use only substitution?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: So far the analysis ignored how substitutions of variables and replacements of connectives are made. Matching, the process that does this, adds selectivity beyond what has been shown.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Even when only substitution is used, with no detachment or chaining, the British Museum Algorithm needs from five times to a hundred times and more as long as LT to prove even the simplest theorems.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Take Theorem 2.02, P implies (Q implies P), derived from Axiom 1.3, A implies (B or A). LT proved it in about 10 seconds. The British Museum Algorithm would make it the seventy-ninth theorem generated, and would need about 158 seconds, if machine speeds were comparable. Figure 4.10 shows the tree of the first twelve theorems from Axiom 1.3, with 2.02 at node (9).

card.rule: LT reaches a target by directly working out the substitutions, where the British Museum Algorithm must generate its way to it.
card.limits: The comparison covers substitution only; with detachment and chaining the gap is explained by other effects.

concepts.title: How matching works, step by step
concepts.question: How does LT compare an axiom with the target and decide each substitution?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: LT wants to turn Axiom 1.3, A implies (B or A), into the target P implies (Q implies P).

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Matching compares the two expressions piece by piece. First the main connectives are identical. Second, the left terms differ (the variable A, the constant P), so P is substituted for A throughout. Third, the connectives inside the parentheses differ: the or must become implies, but by the definition of implies a not-sign must stand before the variable before the or, so B is first replaced by not-B and the or then changed to implies. Fourth, the left terms inside differ (B and Q), so Q is substituted for B. Finally the far-right terms are identical.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The matching process went down the branch from node (1) through (5) to (9) without exploring the other branches. It looked at two expressions instead of eight, reducing the work of comparison by a factor of four.

card.rule: Matching compares expressions part by part and makes only the substitution or replacement that each difference calls for.
card.limits: Matching succeeds only if every difference can be removed by allowed substitutions and replacements.

concepts.title: Why matching is efficient: copying and componentwise feedback
concepts.question: From what two sources does the matching process draw its efficiency?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Matching avoided exploring other branches. What makes it so economical?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: First, it generates the correct substitutions instead of searching for them: by comparing the symbols of a given expression with those of a desired one, it determines exactly which substitution will partly transform one into the other, copying information from the desired expression. In this it resembles the algebra algorithm, not the clicking safe.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Second, it proceeds componentwise, getting feedback after each substitution or replacement that guides the next step. This resembles the clicking safe, and it is a form of factorization.

card.rule: Matching copies correct substitutions from the target and gets feedback component by component.
card.limits: Copying works only where the target shows the substitution; feedback guides the rest.

concepts.title: Matching also drops dead ends
concepts.question: What does matching do with axioms that cannot be made to fit?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: In the 2.02 example LT was assumed to pick Axiom 1.3 at once. In fact it does not know which axiom to use.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The substitution-submethod begins by matching with each axiom in turn, abandoning it for the next one if matching proves impossible.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors illustrate with Theorem 2.02 matched against Axiom 1.2. Thus the matching process lets LT abandon unprofitable lines of search as well as guiding it to correct substitutions.

card.rule: Matching quickly rules out theorems that cannot be made to fit, and it guides the substitutions for those that can.
card.limits: The quick rejection depends on the first difference that substitution cannot remove.

concepts.title: How often substitution alone works
concepts.question: How often did the substitution-submethod succeed on original problems and on subproblems?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: LT found proofs for 38 of the first 52 theorems of Principia. What part did substitution play?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The substitution-submethod was essential to all 38 proofs. Seventeen proofs, almost half, were done by it alone. These took three or fewer matching attempts each: 54 attempts for 17 theorems.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: On new subproblems, 338 attempts gave 21 successes, 6.2 percent. So there was about one chance in three of proving an original problem directly by substitution, but only about one in sixteen for a subproblem generated from it. The authors link this to the order of theorems in Principia.

card.rule: Substitution alone solves about a third of the original problems but a sixteenth of the subproblems.
card.limits: The difference is attributed to the order of theorems in Principia, so it may not carry over to other lists.

concepts.title: Matching in detachment and chaining, and the proof record
concepts.question: How many proofs did each combination produce, and how many subproblems did the other submethods generate?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Matching also drives detachment and chaining. A successful match here creates a subproblem and does not directly prove the theorem.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The average number of new subproblems per application was 3 for detachment, 2.7 for forward chaining and 2.2 for backward chaining: about one subproblem per 7.5 theorems tested. Applied to the original problem, the submethods generated 8 to 9 subproblems on average; applied to subproblems, only 2 or 3.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Of the 38 proofs, seventeen were one step (substitution alone), nineteen were two steps (twelve by detachment then substitution, seven by chaining forward then substitution), and two were three steps. Fourteen attempts failed, most ended by time or space limits; one theorem LT cannot prove and one more it is believed cannot.

card.rule: Detachment and chaining each generate a few subproblems per call, and most of LT's proofs were one or two steps long.
card.limits: These figures describe LT on one list of theorems, the first 52 of Principia's Chapter 2.

concepts.title: The executive searches in breadth
concepts.question: How does LT's executive order its search, and how does LT stop?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The submethods are organized by the executive of Figure 4.8. How does it build the search tree?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: It explores in breadth: first for one-step proofs, then two-step proofs, and so on. When all the submethods have been tried on a problem without a proof, the executive takes the next untried subproblem from untried-problems and repeats.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The proof of 2.01 used substitution only, so no subproblem list. The proof of 2.45 made one subproblem, closed at once by substitution, so no subproblem was ever selected from the list. On 2.31, LT considered all six subproblems on untried-problems, found nothing more to do, and reported so.

card.rule: The executive works breadth-first, so one-step proofs come before two-step proofs, and it ends with a proof or a failure report.
card.limits: Breadth-first is systematic but not selective, as a later idea shows.

concepts.title: Stop rules and the exponential cost of wrong branches
concepts.question: What do the two extra heuristics do, and why are such stop rules valuable?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Under a breadth-first executive every wrong branch costs effort that multiplies as the tree deepens.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Two heuristics were added in a second run on Theorem 2.45 with a smaller theorem list. One weeds out new expressions that appear unprovable by certain plausible criteria; the other weeds out expressions that look too complicated, with too many negation signs. They cut the search by a factor of 24/9, or 2.7, and the net saving after the cost of the extra tests was a factor of 2.3. Neither is foolproof; both can eliminate paths to solutions, even all of them.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Such heuristics are stop rules. Generating ten branches at a node with only one good one multiplies effort by ten; if each false branch itself branches tenfold, effort grows by 10^n for paths of length n.

card.rule: A stop rule cuts off a branch that looks wrong, saving effort that would otherwise grow exponentially, at the risk of cutting off a good branch.
card.limits: Stop rules are fallible; the net saving must be reckoned after paying for the extra tests.

concepts.title: A smaller theorem list can help
concepts.question: How does the size of the theorem list affect subproblems and effort?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Another way to reduce subproblems is to limit the theorems available for generating them, that is, to make the set T smaller.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: LT's statistics show that a submethod generates about one subproblem per seven theorems examined. The broad tree of Theorem 2.17 came from a list of twenty theorems; the deep tree of 2.27 from a list of only five, so fewer subproblems were made at each step.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: For Theorem 2.48, with all prior theorems LT needed two steps; starting only with the axioms and 2.16 it needed three steps but about one third of the time. The irrelevant theorems took much effort. A problem solver may be encumbered by too much information as well as handicapped by too little, if the extra reduces selectivity.

card.rule: More available theorems mean more subproblems; too much information can slow a solver.
card.limits: A short list can also fail, as removing theorems before 2.12 showed; the list must hold the right ones.

concepts.title: Choosing the next subproblem by value
concepts.question: How can LT use an evaluation function, and what is the scan-search heuristic?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Because LT keeps every expression it has produced on untried-problems, it need not take them in the order generated.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Each expression can be given a value when placed on the list, an estimate of how likely it is to lie on a short path to a proof. Expressions are then taken in order of value, highest first. In one version of LT a primitive evaluation function simply measured simplicity, so simpler expressions were taken before complex ones.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: This heuristic gave only a small average improvement to LT; it has since been used with more sophisticated evaluation functions to powerful effect. Selecting subproblems by an evaluation function is called the scan-search heuristic: scan the list for the most promising member, carry out a burst of search from it, evaluate and place the new nodes, and repeat.

card.rule: Giving each stored subproblem a value and working on the best first is the scan-search heuristic.
card.limits: LT's simple version helped little; the idea paid off with better evaluation functions in later programs.

concepts.title: The similarity test as an abstraction
concepts.question: What does the similarity test compare, and why does it count as abstraction?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Matching still involves a lot of search through the theorem list to find theorems to match, and most attempts fail.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: A screening step, the similarity test, rejects theorems with a low chance of matching. Two expressions are similar if their left sides and their right sides agree in (1) the maximum number of levels from the main connective to any variable, (2) the number of distinct variables, and (3) the number of variable places. Intuitively, they look alike.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Of (1) (P or Q) implies (Q or P), (2) P implies (Q or P) and (3) R implies (M implies R), expressions (2) and (3) are similar, but (1) is similar to neither. The test is an abstraction: it matches descriptions of expressions, which are cheaper to process than the expressions themselves. LT applies it before matching in every submethod.

card.rule: The similarity test compares simple descriptions of two expressions and lets matching run only if the descriptions agree.
card.limits: Agreement in the descriptions does not guarantee that matching will succeed.

concepts.title: What the similarity test gains on paper
concepts.question: How much does the similarity test raise the chance of a successful match?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Table 4.3 compares how many theorems were considered, how many passed the similarity test, and how many then matched.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The test reduces the matchings attempted a great deal and raises the probability of success correspondingly. In substitution it reduces attempts by a factor of ten and raises the chance of success by the same factor.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In Table 4.3, substitution considered 11,298 theorems, 993 passed (8.8 percent) and 37 matched (3.7 percent of those passing). Detachment considered 1,591: 406 passed (25.5 percent), 210 matched (51.7 percent). Forward chaining considered 869: 200 passed (23.0), 120 matched (60.0). Backward chaining considered 693: 146 passed (21.7), 63 matched (43.2).

card.rule: Of the theorems considered, about a fifth to a quarter pass the test for chaining and detachment, and many of those match.
card.limits: These are gross gains; the cost of the test itself is not counted in the table.

concepts.title: A heuristic that sometimes rejects good candidates
concepts.question: What kind of error can the similarity test make, and what happened with Theorem 2.07?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The similarity test is only a heuristic. It does not guarantee that all it passes will match, or that it passes every theorem that would match.

blocks.label: Model
