blocks.text: It rarely rejects a theorem that would match (a type II error in the statistical sense), but even rare errors can be costly. Theorem 2.07, P implies (P or P), follows by substituting P for Q in Axiom 1.3, P implies (Q or P). The test calls them dissimilar because 2.07 has one distinct variable and 1.3 has two.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: LT found the proof by forward chaining, where a direct match is checked before a subproblem is created, but at about five times the cost of running without the test. A weaker test comparing only the number of variable places does not make this error, and 2.07 is proved by substitution; otherwise it changed performance little.

card.rule: A heuristic screen can wrongly reject a good candidate, and a rare error can be expensive.
card.limits: The weaker test shows that a looser screen can be nearly as good, since the descriptive measures are highly correlated.

concepts.section: Processing Effort in the Logic Theorist
concepts.title: Measuring effort in elementary processes
concepts.question: Why must heuristics be judged by cost as well as selectivity, and how is cost measured?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: So far the analysis looked at selectivity. Each added test, search or description also costs processing effort.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The costs must always be balanced against the gains in performance, since other heuristics could be put in their place. Effort is stated as the total number of elementary information processes (eips) executed. The total is taken as an index of effort.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: LT is written in an information processing language whose elementary processes are subroutines in JOHNNIAC machine language. The average time per eip is quite constant at about 30 milliseconds on JOHNNIAC (about 300 microseconds on the IBM 360/65). Memory space is also a cost but is not discussed.

card.rule: Count effort in elementary information processes, and weigh the effort a heuristic costs against the search it saves.
card.limits: The count leaves out memory space, which is also a cost.

concepts.section: Processing Effort in the Logic Theorist
concepts.title: Effort is proportional to theorems considered
concepts.question: What predicts the effort LT spends on a proof, and with what weights?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Which simple quantity predicts the effort LT spends on a logic problem?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Effort is roughly proportional to the total number of theorems examined, whether tested for similarity or for matching. The fit is much improved by weighting theorems considered for chaining and detachment more than those for substitution: twice as many eips per theorem for chaining, three times for detachment.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: About 45 eips are executed per theorem considered with the substitution-submethod, so 135 for detachment and 90 for chaining. Table 4.4 shows estimates generally within a few percent of the actual, except for Theorem 2.06 where the estimate is too low.

card.rule: Effort is about 45 eips per theorem considered by substitution, 90 by chaining and 135 by detachment.
card.limits: These figures are for the full similarity test with precomputed descriptions; recomputing changes them.

concepts.section: Processing Effort in the Logic Theorist
concepts.title: Storing or recomputing the descriptions
concepts.question: What happens to effort when LT can no longer store the descriptions?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The similarity test needs a description of each theorem, and these must be computed from the expressions.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Since the descriptions of the theorems are used again and again, LT computes them at the start of a problem and stores them with the theorems. As the number of theorems grows, the space for the stored descriptions becomes prohibitive and LT switches to recomputing them whenever needed.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: With recomputation, effort is still roughly proportional to the number of theorems considered, but eips per theorem rise to about 70 for substitution, 210 for detachment and 140 for chaining.

card.rule: Storing descriptions saves effort but takes space; with too many theorems LT recomputes them and pays more per theorem.
card.limits: Proportionality to theorems considered holds in both modes, with different constants.

concepts.section: Processing Effort in the Logic Theorist
concepts.title: Is the similarity test worth its cost?
concepts.question: Under what conditions does the similarity test save effort, and when does it not?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The similarity test raised the chance of matching, but a heuristic must be judged net of its own cost.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: A number of theorems were run with the full test, with the modified test that checks only variable places, and with no test, using both stored and recomputed descriptions. With stored descriptions the full test saves between 10 and 60 percent (for 2.08, 3534 against 5206 eips). With recomputed descriptions the full test is about 15 percent more expensive than none (for 2.45, 26,739 against 22,914).

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors conclude that the similarity test is rather marginal and gives nothing like the improvement given by the matching process.

card.rule: The similarity test pays for itself only when its descriptions are precomputed; with recomputation it costs more than it saves.
card.limits: The modified test is somewhat better, but still a small gain.

concepts.section: Processing Effort in the Logic Theorist
concepts.title: Why the screen adds so little
concepts.question: Why do the performance figures overstate the similarity test's value?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Table 4.3 suggests large gains from the similarity test, yet the effort comparison shows only a marginal net gain. Why the discrepancy?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Matching has two parts: a testing part that locates the differences between elements and diagnoses the corrective action, and the part that carries out the substitutions and replacements. The latter is the major expense in a matching that works, but most of it is saved when the matching fails.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: So matching is inexpensive for just the expressions that the similarity test excludes. The test trims off the problem tree only stubs that matching would prune quickly anyway.

card.rule: Matching is cheap when it fails, so a screen that removes likely failures saves little.
card.limits: The argument applies to this pairing; a screen in front of a method that is expensive when it fails could pay off.

concepts.section: Processing Effort in the Logic Theorist
concepts.title: The plateau in LT's power
concepts.question: What does the distribution of effort show about LT's reach?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: LT proves many theorems but not all. What does the pattern of its successes and failures show?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Almost all proofs LT found took less than 30,000 eips (Figure 4.14). Among the many attempts that went past that limit, only a few succeeded, and those cost far more. Proofs by substitution, almost half the total, took about 1000 eips or less each. The longest proof, 89,000 eips, cost some 250 times the shortest. To prove the 12 further theorems that the authors believe LT can prove, the effort limit would need to rise to about a million eips.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors infer that LT's power is largely restricted to a class of problems. Good heuristics make differences of orders of magnitude, but a plateau is always reached that can be passed only with quite different heuristics, which again give orders of magnitude.

card.rule: A heuristic program reaches a plateau: big gains from good heuristics, then a limit passed only by new kinds of heuristic.
card.limits: The plateau claim is the authors' inference from LT; they say they believe it is typical.

concepts.section: Processing Effort in the Logic Theorist
concepts.title: Proof length and effort
concepts.question: How does the length of a proof relate to effort, and why?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Theorem 2.17 cost LT 89,000 eips. Its proof is longer than the two earlier examples.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The proof takes three steps: a forward chaining, a detachment, and a substitution. Length of proof is an important variable in total effort: short proofs are easy and long ones difficult, and difficulty rises more than proportionately with length.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: All one-step proofs need 500 to 1500 eips; two-step proofs need 3000 to 50,000. LT obtained only six proofs longer than two steps, needing 10,000 to 90,000 eips. Figure 4.12 shows the tree for 2.17 and Figure 4.9 the two-step tree for 2.45.

card.rule: Each added proof step multiplies effort, because more subproblems must be generated and examined.
card.limits: Per-theorem effort is about the same across proofs; length matters through the number of subproblems.

concepts.section: Processing Effort in the Logic Theorist
concepts.title: Why deeper proofs exhaust LT
concepts.question: Why does LT's unselective executive limit its reach to proofs of about three steps?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Theorem 2.27 is the only four-step proof LT achieved, from the axioms alone, at a cost of 38,367 eips.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Its tree branches little at each point, so LT reaches depth four with reasonable effort. If it had branched like the other two trees, LT would have processed about 250 subproblems and spent at least 250,000 eips. The authors hypothesize that the number of subproblems grows more or less exponentially with proof depth.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The difficulty is that LT's executive is systematic and unselective: it generates all subproblems that detachment and chaining can produce, with duplicates removed, and takes them in order of generation (breadth). With a theorem list averaging thirty expressions, one-step proofs are no problem, two-step searches are of reasonable size, three-step searches press LT against its computing limits, and four or five steps exceed any computing power that could practically be provided.

card.rule: Because LT generates all subproblems breadth-first, its search grows exponentially with depth and runs out of power at about three steps.
card.limits: A tree that happens to branch little, like that of 2.27, can be searched deeper.

concepts.section: Processing Effort in the Logic Theorist
concepts.title: Learning: using experience to change the program
concepts.question: What three things must hold for experience to improve LT, and what is the simplest scheme?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: All the heuristics so far were built into LT by design. But LT's own experience in solving problems carries information about its task.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Using that information needs three things: some aspect of LT's performance must be variable; some information from its experience must be gathered; and that information must be used to affect the variable behavior. The simplest method makes the list theorems variable, adding each new theorem LT proves, so LT becomes gradually more capable.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Given the right sequence, LT could then prove Theorem 2.13, which it cannot otherwise prove. In the authors' experiments the sequence of problems was set by the designers, though LT could be altered to pose problems for itself (Pitrat, 1966).

card.rule: Learning needs a variable part of the program, gathered experience, and a use of that experience; the simplest case adds proved theorems to the list.
card.limits: A backward worker like LT must pose its own problems before it can learn theorems in this way.

concepts.section: Processing Effort in the Logic Theorist
concepts.title: Valuable-theorem lists: help when the task is similar, hindrance when it is new
concepts.question: What happened when LT used lists of theorems that had worked before?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A more complex scheme gives each submethod its own list of valuable theorems, those that took part in earlier proofs with that operator, and a backup list of the rest.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The submethods work only from their valuable lists and fall back on the others if those prove insufficient. In the experiment LT tried the first 52 theorems, then its results were erased and it tried them again with the valuable lists. For the twenty non-trivial theorems proved in both runs, Figure 4.15 plots time in the test run against time in the pretest: the points form two straight lines, each with about half the points.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: On the upper line the test run took almost twice as long as the pretest; on the lower line less than half as long. The protocols explain it: when a problem yielded to a method that had worked before, the valuable lists found it fast; when the problem was of a new type, the program first wasted time on the valuable lists and then fell back on the full store.

card.rule: Experience speeds up problems like earlier ones and slows down problems unlike them, and it adds to LT's information.
card.limits: Ordering by past usefulness would not help a breadth-first search, which generates everything anyway; the lists must be used to select.

concepts.title: The chapter's framework in a sentence
concepts.question: How does the chapter describe problem solving, the solver's task and the source of difficulty?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: After the long study of LT the authors pull together the framework.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Problem solving is the selecting of an element with certain properties from a large set, or the traversing of a large space to find one of a rare set of paths with preferred properties. The solver is given a description of the solution and must find a process that generates it.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Problem difficulty arises usually from the size of the set of possibilities, which the chapter showed to be immense even in relatively simple situations.

card.rule: Solving is picking a rare element out of an immense set, and difficulty usually comes from the set's size.
card.limits: Size is the usual source of difficulty, not the only one; the cost of generating and testing also counts.

concepts.title: Three principles of selectivity
concepts.question: Which three selective principles did LT illustrate?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The chapter used LT to show how solutions are often found after looking at only a tiny part of an immense set.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: First, generate only elements that are already guaranteed to have some of the properties that define a solution, as LT's methods do. Second, use information obtained step by step while generating possible solutions to guide the continuing search, as the matching process does. Third, abstract from the detail of problem expressions and work with simpler abstractions, as the similarity test does.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors tie each principle to a part of LT: the methods, the matching process and the similarity test.

card.rule: Guarantee some properties in the generator, use feedback as you go, and abstract to cheaper descriptions.
card.limits: The third principle paid little here, since the similarity test's extra effort almost balanced its selectivity.

concepts.title: Effort, selectivity and machine speed
concepts.question: What does LT's effort tell us, and how much can faster machines help?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Does the explanation of LT's power lie in the program or in the task?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: LT needs a more or less constant amount of effort per subproblem generated, or equivalently per branch added to the tree. So its efficiency can be equated with its selectivity in exploring the problem space, and its behavior says more about the task environment than about its detailed make-up as an IPS.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: LT would run about 100 times as fast on an IBM 360/65 as on JOHNNIAC. But increases in speed, even much greater than 100 to 1, are minuscule next to the gains from selective heuristics. No conceivable speed-up lets the British Museum Algorithm or the working-forward algorithm compete with LT's weak heuristics, and LT in turn reaches a plateau lifted only by new heuristics.

card.rule: Selectivity, not speed, determines which problems a program can solve.
card.limits: LT's own plateau shows that selectivity too has limits.

concepts.title: Beyond LT: AND-OR trees
concepts.question: How can a later program overcome LT's restriction to single-output operators?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: LT's operators took a theorem as a parameter so that a working-backward operator would give a single output expression. This kept LT from proving a theorem such as P or not-P.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Soon after LT, a theorem-proving program was built (Gelernter, 1959) that accepts an operator's multiple outputs and sets the goal of proving them all. For instance the detachment operator would become DT(X), giving (A and A implies X).

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: This structure is known as an AND-OR tree. Some nodes give a set of subproblems all of which must be solved; others give a set of which only one need be solved.

card.rule: Allowing an operator several outputs, all of which must be proved, gives an AND-OR tree and removes LT's restriction.
card.limits: The chapter only mentions the extension; the book does not develop it.

concepts.title: Gelernter's diagram, and heuristics that belong to the environment
concepts.question: What did the geometry program show about one powerful heuristic, and whose theory do such results belong to?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Experience like LT's has been reported for other problem solvers. Gelernter, Hansen and Loveland studied a program that proves theorems in plane geometry.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Adding or removing one or two heuristic elements often changed time on simple problems by 2 to 1 or 3 to 1; in some cases the effect was much more dramatic. The program checked each subgoal against a diagram and rejected it if the property was false in the diagram. With that heuristic disconnected, storage was exhausted by the first several hundred first-level subgoals; about 1000 subgoals per stage were estimated against about 5 per stage with the diagram.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: That is a selectivity factor of 200 to 1 per step from a single powerful heuristic. Because the effectiveness of a heuristic depends on the structure of the problem space, the authors say such generalizations belong to the theory of problem environments, not to psychology.

card.rule: A single heuristic, consulting a diagram, can make a 200-to-1 difference per step, and such findings describe problem environments, not human minds.
card.limits: The results are about which heuristics suit which problem spaces, not about how humans think.

concepts.title: From the chapter to human problem solving
concepts.question: What does the chapter now allow us to do in the three task environments that follow?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The chapter began with two questions: how can a problem be solved, and what makes it difficult? Having answered them, how will the theory be used?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The chapter illustrated both the set-predicate and search formulations, showing how generate-and-test methods fit the first and heuristic search methods the second.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: This gives techniques for predicting problem difficulty and for making many predictions about the specific paths solutions will take. The authors say they are ready to use this general theory to understand human problem solving in cryptarithmetic, logic and chess.

card.rule: With a formulation and its method specified, the theory predicts difficulty and the paths solutions take; next it is applied to cryptarithmetic, logic and chess.
card.limits: The chapter's tools are general; whether they fit human behavior is the question of the later parts.

concepts.title: The DONALD + GERALD task
concepts.question: What are the rules of a cryptarithmetic task, and which puzzle does the chapter analyze?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors want to analyze how people solve cryptarithmetic puzzles. In DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT each letter stands for one digit, different letters stand for different digits, and the digit 5 is given for D.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: A cryptarithmetic task asks for an assignment of distinct digits to distinct letters that makes an arithmetic sum true. The best-known example in the United States is SEND + MORE = MONEY; the chapter works with DONALD + GERALD.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors took the puzzle from a study by Bartlett (1958). They know of no other psychological work that used cryptarithmetic, so this chapter builds the analysis of the task from the ground up.

card.rule: A cryptarithmetic task assigns distinct digits to distinct letters so that a stated sum comes out true.
card.limits: The given hint (D is 5) belongs to this one puzzle, not to cryptarithmetic in general.

concepts.title: The set-predicate formulation
concepts.question: How many candidate assignments does a generate-and-test approach face, and is that too many?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors first ask whether the puzzle fits the simplest formulation. The task has 10 letters and 10 digits that could be paired in many ways, and each complete pairing is a possible solution.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: In the set-predicate formulation every complete assignment is a candidate, and a plain addition check tests it. Solving then means generating candidates and testing each one: the generate-and-test method.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Counting the pairings gives 10! in all. With D already set to 5, the nine remaining digits can go to the other letters in 9! ways, about a third of a million cases.

card.rule: Set-predicate formulation plus generate-and-test is workable here: 9! assignments is sizable, though not overwhelming for a computer.
card.limits: A third of a million cases is workable for a computer, but the next formulation makes far better use of the task's structure.

concepts.title: The search formulation and problem spaces
concepts.question: What must a search formulation specify, and how many problem spaces can one task have?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Generate-and-test treats every complete assignment alike. The authors ask what is gained by seeing the puzzle as a search, where partial information builds up step by step.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: A search formulation needs nodes, which stand for the information gathered so far, and operators, which change that information. The start (no assignments, or only D set to 5) and the goal (all letters assigned, successfully) must both be expressible.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors say this formulation does considerably better wherever there is enough structure to apply it. A problem space is fixed by naming the expressions that can represent a state of information and the operators allowed on them.

card.rule: A problem space is defined by what a state of information can say and what operators may change it.
card.limits: A task has many possible problem spaces; none is the one true space, and some serve better than others.

concepts.title: The basic problem space and Add
concepts.question: What are the states and the single operator of the basic problem space?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors need a first problem space for the puzzle, one that can be built straight from the problem statement.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: An expression is a letter, an assignment arrow, then a digit, such as A set to 2. A knowledge-state is a list of one or more expressions, all taken to hold at once. The one operator, Add, takes an expression and adds that assignment to a state.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The definition is written in BNF, the notation of Chapter 2. Add on A set to 2, applied to D set to 5, gives the state with both. If the assignment is already in the state, Add leaves it as it was.

card.rule: In the basic space a state is a list of letter-digit assignments, and Add is the only operator.
card.limits: A state records what is known, not how it was found; duplicates are never kept.

concepts.title: Initial state and the test-for-solution
concepts.question: How do the instructions say where to start and how to recognize a solution?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A problem space is not yet a problem. The instructions must say where the search starts and how to tell when a state counts as a solution.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The start is the state holding D set to 5. The goal set is not written out but defined by a test process. The test has four parts: D still holds 5; no letter has several digits; no digit goes to several letters; and the addition is correct and complete.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Figure 5.2 lists these four parts. The last part also checks that every letter has been given a digit, so a finished state cannot pass with letters missing.

card.rule: Define the start state, and define success by a test with four checks instead of listing the goals.
card.limits: The test is an agreed check of the task's rules; it does not by itself say how to find a state that passes.

concepts.title: Depth-first search and early failure
concepts.question: How does a depth-first program use the test to prune the search?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Within the basic space many programs could search from the start state. The authors give a simple one and ask how much it saves compared with generate-and-test.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: A depth-first program makes a new state by applying one operator, then runs the test. A failed state is dropped; an incomplete but consistent state is searched further, and a success ends the search. Operators come from a generator that marks letters as used.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Branches end when a state gives one letter two digits, two letters the same digit, or a false column sum worked from the right. Letting failure show early removes an entire subtree at a time.

card.rule: Test each new state at once, drop failures, and go deeper only on consistent incomplete states.
card.limits: The method is simple and its test is wasteful; further heuristics can cut the search still more.

concepts.title: How big the depth-first search tree is
concepts.question: How large is the search tree, and why is it so much smaller than generate-and-test?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: How selective is the simple depth-first search on DONALD + GERALD? The authors count the tree of Figure 5.5 and compare it with the 9! terminals of generate-and-test.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The tree drawn has 87 terminals. Counting the final failing assignment on each branch, which the figure leaves out, gives 252 branches, three times as many. The threefold growth comes from using each column sum only to test, never to generate, assignments.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Failure shows up early and each failure removes a whole subtree. Had the program waited until every assignment was made, the tree would have 9! terminals, the same as generate-and-test.

card.rule: Testing early prunes whole subtrees, so a crude depth-first search needs only a small part of the 9! cases.
card.limits: Pruning helps only where failures show up early; branches that cannot be ruled out are still searched in full.

concepts.title: Heuristics that cut the tree to 23 nodes
concepts.question: How do the heuristics of Figure 5.6 shrink the basic search, and at what cost?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Even the depth-first tree has 87 terminals. The authors recall that the heuristics of Chapter 4 can cut a search further, at the price of more processing at each node.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The program of Figure 5.6 chooses a letter whose digit a column can fix. It computes that digit from the column sum and the carry, and if no digit can be computed the line of search ends. When the carry is unknown it tries 0 and then 1.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: With this generator the tree of Figure 5.7 comes down to 23 nodes, against 87 terminals before. The figure marks both the letter selected and its column.

card.rule: Computing a digit from a column, instead of trying all ten, trades work per node for far fewer nodes.
card.limits: The authors do not claim this is the best possible heuristic search; they stop and turn to other problem spaces.

concepts.title: Richer expressions in the augmented space
concepts.question: What kinds of partial information can the augmented space hold that the basic space cannot?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: In the basic space the only partial information is a set of exact assignments. Solvers often know less than that, such as that a letter must be odd.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The augmented problem space adds expressions describing classes of digits. A letter may be said to satisfy an inequality, to be odd or even, or to be one of an enumerated set of digits. A state can hold such facts.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Figure 5.8 extends the definition of an expression so that a state can hold these facts alongside exact assignments. A state may then record what a letter may be before it records what it is.

card.rule: The augmented space lets a state say what a letter may be, not only what it is.
card.limits: Richer expressions need new operators to produce and use them; the space alone does no solving.

concepts.title: Carries as variables
concepts.question: Why do the authors add carries to the variables of the augmented space?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The augmented space can already say more about letters. The authors ask whether it should also say something about the carries that every column sum produces.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The augmented space adds the carries to the variables. A carry such as c2 can then be given any kind of expression, just like a letter, so a state can say that a carry is 0, 1, or odd.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In the basic space a single temporary carry variable was enough to evaluate each column sum. In the augmented space letters and carries together are called variables, and every type of expression admits carries.

card.rule: Carries become variables in the augmented space, so what is known about them can be recorded.
card.limits: A solver can solve the puzzle without ever naming carries, as the basic space does.

concepts.title: Operators for the augmented space
concepts.question: Which four operators does the augmented space need?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Richer expressions help only if the system can produce them from the puzzle and put them to use. The operators of the basic space, which only add assignments, are not enough.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: At least four types of operator are needed: Assign-value (AV), Process-column (PC), Generate-numbers (GN) and Test-if-digits-admissible (TD). The column processor draws inferences from the columns of the sum.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: From the facts that G is even and G is below 5, the system must be able to generate 0, 2 and 4. From a zero carry into the leftmost column, D set to 5 and R odd, the column processor must infer that G is even.

card.rule: The augmented space needs operators that assign, infer from columns, generate digits from classes, and test digits.
card.limits: The details, above all the power of the column processor, can vary a good deal from one solver to another.

concepts.title: Replacing testing by generating
concepts.question: How does the augmented space change the balance of testing and generating?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The basic space made testing a heavy job. The authors ask how this changes once the space can express classes of digits and carries.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: In the augmented space much of the testing of the basic space is replaced by generating. What is left is a test of whether a digit is admissible.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In the basic space the digits were generated in a way that ensured they were disjoint. That is no longer possible, since digits now come from classes, so disjointness must be determined by a test.

card.rule: Inference does work before assignment, so less is left to testing, but disjointness still has to be tested.
card.limits: Less testing does not mean none: a candidate digit must still be checked before it is assigned.

concepts.title: The six column equations
concepts.question: How can the whole puzzle be stated as equations, and what are the states of the algebraic space?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A third representation drops assignments as the unit of knowledge. The authors instead write the constraints of the puzzle themselves and work on them directly.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT is equivalent to six equations, one for each column, in the letters and the carries. The units column, for example, reads 2D = T + 10c2. With the conditions that letters are distinct digits and carries are 0 or 1, they state the problem completely.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The six equations are the first element of the algebraic problem space. Derived equations are added to them, or replace specific expressions, to make a new element; a finished letter shows up as a derived equation such as R = 7 or a given D set to 5.

card.rule: In the algebraic space a state is a set of equations, and solving means deriving new ones.
card.limits: The six equations alone do not enforce distinct letters; that condition must be added.

concepts.title: A two-production system for the algebraic space
concepts.question: What do the two productions of Figure 5.9 do, and in what order?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Equations alone do not solve anything. Some process must act on them, so the authors give a small production system as the problem solver.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Production P1 fires when a variable has been given a digit: it substitutes the digit for the variable throughout the equations and marks the assignment used. Production P2 applies otherwise and infers consequences from the equations.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Marking an assignment used stops it from being matched again, so substitution is not repeated. The authors suggest a tag such as used on the equation and say the details do not matter.

card.rule: Substitute every known value first; when nothing is left to substitute, infer new consequences.
card.limits: The inference step is the hard part and is left loosely specified; the two productions are only a frame.

concepts.title: Solving DONALD + GERALD by inference
concepts.question: In what order does inference fix the letters, and where does trial still appear?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: How far can inference alone take a solver who starts from the six equations and the given D set to 5? The authors trace the production system on the puzzle.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: With D set to 5 the units equation gives T = 0 and c2 = 1. The second equation then makes R odd, and the sixth makes R above 5, so R is 7 or 9. The fifth equation gives E as 9 or 0; T is already 0, so E = 9, and R is then 7.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The solution path is D set to 5, then T = 0, E = 9, R = 7, A = 4, G = 1, L = 8, then N set to 6, B = 3 and O = 2. The final letters need only a short trial.

card.rule: Each inference fixes a letter or carry for certain, so the puzzle falls out in a short chain.
card.limits: The chain depends on the given D; it is not a general guarantee for every cryptarithmetic task.

concepts.title: Definite assignments instead of tentative ones
concepts.question: Why can the algebraic space make definite assignments where other spaces make tentative ones?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: In the basic and augmented searches a solver often makes an uncertain assignment and has to take it back if it fails. The walkthrough seems to avoid this.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The inference process deduces enough about one letter at a time, first T and then E, that a definite assignment can be made instead of an uncertain one. A fact such as R = 7 or 9 is kept as information, not turned into a tentative assignment, until one alternative is eliminated for certain.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In this way the walkthrough almost completely eliminates trial and error. The solution path from T through L is reached by deduction only.

card.rule: Hold alternatives as information, and assign a letter only when deduction leaves one value.
card.limits: Almost, not entirely: some trial remains, and not every cryptarithmetic task allows this.

concepts.title: When the hint is removed
concepts.question: What happens to the algebraic process on the puzzle if D set to 5 is not given?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The smooth walkthrough relied on the given D set to 5. The authors ask what the same inference process could do without that hint.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Without the hint, inference would stop almost immediately. It could infer that E is 0 or 9, that T is even, that R is above D, and then that A is 4 or 5. After that it has nothing more to add.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors say the almost complete elimination of trial and error is not possible in all cryptarithmetic problems. A tentative assignment becomes necessary.

card.rule: Without a decisive given, inference stalls early and tentative assignment must take over.
card.limits: How early inference stalls depends on the task and on the hint, so no general rule follows.

concepts.title: Spaces from special features or a global view
concepts.question: What other problem spaces might a solver use beyond the basic, augmented and algebraic ones?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The three spaces seem to cover most ways a solver might represent the task. But other spaces can be imagined, some tied to features of particular puzzles and some resting on a wider view of the task.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: For AA + BB = CBC one can work with multiples of 11: CBC must be a multiple of 11, and so equals 121, which makes BB = 22 and AA = 99. A global view instead searches the space of letter-digit correspondences, for example by matching letters to their alphabet positions.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors note that the first depends on special features not present in DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT, and that the second takes a more global view of what the solver is looking for.

card.rule: Besides the three main spaces there are special-feature spaces and global spaces of whole correspondences.
card.limits: The examples show that the list of spaces is open; they do not show that every solver uses one of them.

concepts.title: Describing spaces by entities and relations
concepts.question: How can the spaces be compared by what they admit?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: With several spaces in hand, the authors want a common way to compare them, and to see what further spaces might be built.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: A space can be described by the information it can express at an element, meaning its entities and the relations among them. The basic space admits letters, digits and assignment. The augmented space adds carries, disjunction, inequality and parity. The algebraic space adds arithmetic operations.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors offer this notation as a way to compare spaces side by side, and as a hint that further spaces can be built from it.

card.rule: Describe a space by the entities and relations it admits, and vary the list to invent new spaces.
card.limits: The list says what a space can express, not how good it is at guiding a search.

concepts.title: A space with no digits: counting equations
concepts.question: What can a space that records only which variables are assigned tell a solver?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors ask about a radical variant. What if a space could show that a letter or carry has been assigned, but not which digit it was given?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The space (letter carry, assignment) holds that kind of information. It is what one uses with systems of equations to count equations against variables, in order to see how many unknowns remain and which equations might conveniently be solved first.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: For DONALD, once D has been assigned, T and c2 are determined, and R and G are restricted a little, since one variable can be removed from the equation that links them. But this does not suggest a good order for the columns.

card.rule: A digit-free space supports counting equations and unknowns to choose an order of attack.
card.limits: In this task it does not carry the solution far: it gives no good order for taking up the columns.

concepts.title: The parity and high-low space
concepts.question: What can a solver infer when digits are known only as odd or even and high or low?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Another variant gives up exact digits for coarse description. Can a solver still draw useful inferences when a digit is known only roughly?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: In the space (letter carry, parity, high-low) a digit is described as odd or even and as low (below 5) or high. This gives four classes: low-even, low-odd, high-even and high-odd. Inference is still possible: two even digits sum to an even digit, and two high digits sum to a carry of 1.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: From the given D set to 5, which is high and odd, the solver infers that T is low and even and that c2 is odd. The actual carry is 1, but only its oddness is kept. Figure 5.10 traces a search in this space.

card.rule: Even coarse facts, parity and high or low, still allow real inferences about sums and carries.
card.limits: The space cannot name digits, so it can only plan, not complete, a solution.

concepts.title: Counting assignments that fit an abstract solution
concepts.question: How much does the abstract space narrow the search, and how is that counted?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The abstract space cannot name digits. The authors ask how many basic-space assignments remain consistent with its answers, to see how much it narrows the task.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The abstract solution is a box with T, A, O low-even; N, L high-even; G, B low-odd; D, R, E high-odd. With D set to 5, 6 x 2 x 2 x 2 = 48 basic assignments fit it. Search in the abstract space ends in five admissible boxes in all.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Jointly the five boxes fit 35 x 48 = 1680 assignments in the basic space. That is a factor of 216 below the 9! assignments of the basic space.

card.rule: Counting the basic assignments that fit each box shows how far abstract search cuts the task.
card.limits: The factor of 216 is not a real measure of gain, since a basic search never looks at all 9! cases.

concepts.title: Abstract spaces as spaces for plans
concepts.question: What are the abstract spaces for, and what do they save?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The digit-free and the parity and high-low spaces leave out detail. The authors ask what such spaces are good for, and what their use costs.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: A solver cannot express all the information about a solution in these spaces, so cannot solve the whole problem in them. They are spaces in which plans can be forged, to guide further action in a fully detailed space.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Searches in the basic space started from the abstract solutions explore only 17 final nodes, against 87 for the plain depth-first tree and 23 for the heuristic tree. The abstract search itself needs considerable processing to use the many constraints that partial results imply.

card.rule: An abstract space gives a plan that guides a short search in the detailed space, at the price of extra processing.
card.limits: The gain is measured in final nodes reached; the work of making the plan is not counted in that figure.

concepts.title: Many spaces as a baseline for human behavior
concepts.question: Why does the chapter describe so many spaces before looking at any person?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The chapter has presented many variations on one task, with no human data yet. The authors give the purpose of doing so.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The variations are a foundation for examining how humans attempt DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT. With so many spaces to hand, the authors stand a good chance of recognizing which one a person is using, especially if he has little experience of cryptarithmetic.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Whether humans will work in these spaces, or use these heuristic devices, is left open for the next two chapters. The authors do not expect subjects to work in the simpler spaces; these form a base line against which the intelligence a subject shows can be measured.

card.rule: The catalogue of spaces is a base line for recognizing and measuring the representations people use.
card.limits: It is a set of candidate descriptions, not a finding that humans use any of them.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: Thirteen questions for a single-subject study
concepts.question: Which four sets of questions does the chapter ask by studying one subject on one attempt?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Chapter 5 supplied tools for analyzing human data. This chapter uses them on one subject, S3, in one integrated problem solving attempt on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT, working from his protocol.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The authors list thirteen questions in four sets: the theoretical analyses (a problem space, its detail, known organizations, a matching IPS), the treatment of data, the testing of theory, and generality.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: They say one chapter cannot answer all thirteen directly, though evidence on many will emerge. Questions of generality are mostly postponed, because starting with one attempt obscures what subjects have in common.

card.rule: The chapter asks about theory, data, testing and generality, but answers mainly the first three for one subject.
card.limits: One subject cannot show whether the mechanisms found are unique to him; the authors defer that to later chapters.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: What a protocol is
concepts.question: What counts as the protocol, and what extra information accompanies the transcript?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The data for the analysis are what S3 said aloud while solving. The words alone leave out facts that bear on the whole performance.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: A transcript of a subject's verbalizations is called a protocol. The authors' protocol is augmented with indications that S3 wrote down various assignments, and with remarks of the experimenter, E.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: No separate record exists of what S3 wrote, nor of timing. Yet it is usually clear from the protocol when he wrote something, as at B9.

card.rule: A protocol is the transcript of thinking aloud, augmented with notes on writing and on the experimenter's remarks.
card.limits: The protocol gives no separate record of writing and no timing, so some facts must be read from the speech itself.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: Microtheories as data points
concepts.question: Why does each analyzed attempt count as a microtheory, and what role does it play for the general theory?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A general theory of problem solving must meet behavior as particular as one person's attempt at one puzzle. How can that meeting serve as a test?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Each attempt is represented by a specific IPS in a specific task environment. By the usual canons of science, a symbolic system that generates a segment of behavior is a theory of it, so the authors call these small theories microtheories.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Each microtheory is a single data point at which the more general theory is put to the test. The authors note the term is currently used more broadly, for a theory of a miniature domain such as rat behavior in a T-maze.

card.rule: One IPS fitted to one attempt is a microtheory, and each microtheory is a data point for the general theory.
card.limits: A single data point tests the general theory only a little. The authors rely on many microtheories, and Chapter 7 remains at the level of individual solvers too.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: Why look at one attempt in such detail
concepts.question: Why does the chapter pay such elaborate attention to a single problem solving attempt?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The level of detail in this chapter is beyond what one would want most of the time. The authors have to say why it is worth the cost.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Their argument is that the data are so sequentially interdependent that they cannot be unraveled without a highly specific IPS. The raw verbalizations make sense only seen through the lens of such an IPS.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors add that the detail is appropriate when asking if the theory fits, and that Chapter 7 carries out analysis at a more abstract level, whose validity depends partly on the correctness of this detailed kind.

card.rule: Detailed single-case analysis is justified because the data are sequentially dependent and the abstract analyses rest on it.
card.limits: The detail is not what one wants most of the time; it serves to check the theory's fit, not to describe every subject.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: How the protocol was taken
concepts.question: Under what conditions was S3's protocol collected, and how long did the attempt last?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A reader judging the analysis needs to know the conditions of the observation: who the subject was, what he had, and what he was asked to do.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The protocol was taken in spring 1960. S3 was a male college student at Carnegie Institute of Technology. He sat at a table with paper and pencil, heard the instructions, and was asked to speak aloud at all times; his talk was tape-recorded.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The protocol has 2186 words. At about two words a second, as in similar protocols, this means roughly 20 minutes. Timing is not critical, since the authors cannot use it in their analysis.

card.rule: S3 solved with paper and pencil, thinking aloud, for roughly twenty minutes, estimated from the word count.
card.limits: The twenty minutes is an estimate from a typical speaking rate, not a measured duration.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: The B-numbered phrases
concepts.question: How is the protocol cut into phrases, and what do the 321 phrases say about the density of the data?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: To refer to a point in the talk, the analysts need a unit smaller than the whole protocol. They also need to know how much data the protocol holds.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The protocol is cut into short phrases labeled B1 to B321, including both the subject's and the experimenter's remarks. The cutting rests on a naive judgment of a single task assertion or reference and serves to ease reference.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: With 321 phrases, there is one phrase every three to four seconds. The authors grant this may seem a low density of data, given how much can go on in a few seconds of human thinking.

card.rule: The protocol is cut into 321 short B-numbered phrases, each a rough unit of assertion, for reference.
card.limits: The phrasing does not affect the analysis explicitly; it is a tool for pointing at places, not a theory of units of thought.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: Why the talk is not coded into categories
concepts.question: Why do the authors keep the subject's words in their original form instead of coding them into formal categories?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: In much psychology, verbal data are coded into formal categories. A reader may ask why this analysis does not do the same.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The authors object in principle. Language already encodes information, so recoding into another language that keeps all meaning hardly encodes at all, and recoding that loses meaning throws away the data protocols are meant to give.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: They note that easy phrases, like making R a 9, need no coding, while hard ones, like a muddled self-correction, should stay in original form. Short phrases give a series of fairly unambiguous measurements of what S3 knew at particular times.

card.rule: Keep the subject's utterances in original form, because coding either adds nothing or discards meaning.
card.limits: The argument fits an analysis of full meaning. The authors say the usual practice codes the talk as an indicator of a few underlying attributes.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: An internal space apart from the written one
concepts.question: Why do the authors describe an internal problem space separately from what S3 writes down?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: S3 writes some things down, but long periods go by with no writing. The thinking that fills those periods cannot be read from the paper.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: There is an internal problem space clearly different from the space of written, externalized actions. Three kinds of internal action occur: assigning digits to letters, inferring relations from the columns of the sum, and generating digits that satisfy certain relations.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: S3 says he will assume L is 1 (assignment), reads that 1 plus 1 gives 3 or R (inference), and lists that R can be 1 or 3 but not 5, 7 or 9 (generation).

card.rule: S3 works mainly in an internal space of assigning, inferring and generating, not in the space of written marks.
card.limits: The internal space is inferred from talk, not seen. The authors add no operators for writing or for reading the paper, and leave open whether information is stored internally or on the paper.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: Equality, inequality and parity, apart from assignment
concepts.question: Which relations does S3 use, and why must equality be kept separate from assignment?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: S3 says many kinds of thing about a letter. To model what he knows, the analysts must sort these statements into types.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Three relations occur: equality, inequality, and parity (odd or even). Equality must be kept separate from assignment, since S3 appears to distinguish throughout whether a digit has been inferred to equal a letter or has been assigned to it.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: S3 says A would have to equal 5 (equality), R has to be greater than 5 (inequality), and R has to be an odd number (parity). At B95 he adds that this is all going on the assumption that R is 7, which he had assigned at B61.

card.rule: Keep inferred equalities, inequalities and parities separate from digits that S3 has merely assigned.
card.limits: The distinction rests on how S3 talks and acts; the authors are not saying that every solver keeps the two apart.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: Alternatives, free letters and last letters
concepts.question: How does S3 hold a letter that has several possible values, or one that nothing constrains?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A state of knowledge about a letter is often neither a single digit nor nothing. S3 holds partial information in more than one way.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: S3 can consider a disjunctive set: for example, that G is either 1 or 2. He also uses the concepts of a letter being free, constrained only by membership in the remaining unassigned digits, and last, the final digit that will remain among them.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: At B74 he says he now knows that G has to be either 1 or 2. At B242 he sees that the solution for O is independent of the rest of the column, so O is free. Last names the digit left when all others are placed.

card.rule: S3 can hold a set of alternatives for a letter, and can treat a letter as free of any constraint but the unused digits.
card.limits: Free means only that the letter is limited by the remaining digits; it does not say the letter is easy to find.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: Reading columns, and what S3 does with carries
concepts.question: What does S3 do with equations and carries as he works?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Other subjects rearrange the sum as equations. What S3 does with equations and carries decides which operators his space needs.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: S3 often states equations, but each corresponds to reading a column; there is no evidence that he manipulates equations algebraically. He uses carries in four ways: using them in inferences, inferring them, seeking them, and possibly assigning them.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Examples: 3 + 3 is 6, plus 1 is 7 (use); that he was then carrying 1 into the left-hand column (inference); no place where L plus L can exceed 10 (search); suppose I carry 2 from the column (assignment).

card.rule: S3 reads columns instead of manipulating equations, and treats carries as things to use, infer, seek and perhaps assign.
card.limits: The assignment of a carry of 2 is the one case that exceeds the legal carry values, so S3 is not strictly held to legal moves.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: A variant of the augmented problem space
concepts.question: How does the description of S3's problem space relate to the augmented space of Chapter 5?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors need a formal description of the problem space that covers most of the protocol, so that every state S3 reaches can be written down.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The space is a variant of the augmented problem space of Chapter 5, set out in BNF (Figure 6.1). It adds the digit variables x and y, for times when S3 processes a column without specific digits, and groups letters and carries as variables.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Letters and carries are combined because for several purposes they are equivalent for S3. A disjunction sign lets G = 1 V 2 be written instead of clumsier forms. The set free-letters changes over time, while all-letters is constant.

card.rule: S3's space is the augmented space with digit variables, letters and carries pooled as variables, and with sets of alternatives.
card.limits: The grammar describes the space of the protocol; it does not claim that S3 had this grammar in mind.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: A knowledge-state is a set of tagged expressions
concepts.question: How does the model say what S3 knows and how he holds each piece of knowledge?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The analysts must record what S3 knows at each moment. A fact may be firmly held, newly found, or in doubt, and these differences affect what he does next.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: A knowledge-state is a set of state-expressions. Each state-expression is an expression, a relation among variables and digits such as R > 5 or D <- 5, followed by a tag. The tag represents a mode of knowing.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Tags include new, meaning S3 has just come by the knowledge; an open box, meaning S3 knows the expression is impossible given the rest; and unclear, meaning he believes it but is uncertain of the grounds.

card.rule: A knowledge-state is a set of expressions, each marked by a tag for how S3 holds it.
card.limits: Tags are read from the protocol; they are the analysts' tools and not a claim that S3 has such labels.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: Tags are symbols, not mental concepts
concepts.question: Do the English glosses of the tags put concepts like belief and uncertainty into the IPS?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Reading tags as believes or is concerned may suggest that the model contains mental notions such as belief.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The authors say their renderings are not to introduce concepts such as belief, uncertainty or concern into the IPS. What exists in the IPS is a representation of the knowledge-state as a set of symbol structures, such as the list (R, >, 5, unclear).

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: How the IPS reacts to a state-expression is defined by the program, not by the English paraphrase. Of the tag combinations on a lone variable, only L with the open box and L unknown make sense; the rest do not occur and receive no meaning.

card.rule: The meaning of a tag lies in how the program reacts to it, not in its English paraphrase.
card.limits: The paraphrases still help the reader follow the analysis; they must not be mistaken for parts of the system.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: Constraint expressions and the two kinds of goal
concepts.question: What constraint expressions does S3 use, and what do get and check goals ask for?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: S3 often limits a letter's values without naming one digit, and he sets himself aims. The model needs forms for both.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Constraint expressions limit a variable without necessarily reducing it to one digit: a parity such as R odd, a set such as G = 1 V 2, an inequality such as R > 5, or a qualifier, free or last. Goals are of two types: get, to obtain an expression, and check, which works on information already in the knowledge-state.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Get R means obtain a value for R. Get c6 = 1 means infer that c6 is 1; it carries some wishful thinking, but S3 can form it instead of simply assuming it. Check column-set means check all the columns of the set.

card.rule: Constraints narrow a variable; get goals seek new information and check goals test what is already held.
card.limits: A get goal can be wishful: nothing guarantees that the sought fact is true or even possible.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: The four operators PC, GN, AV and TD
concepts.question: What does each of the four operators take as input and give as output?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: To find S3's moves in the protocol, the analysts define operators by the information they use and the information they produce.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Four operators generate new states of information. Process column (PC) infers information about the letters and carries of a column. Generate (GN) outputs the admissible values for a variable. Assign value (AV) assigns a digit to a variable. Test admissible value (TD) says whether a digit is admissible for a letter.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: PC on 5 + 5 gives T = 0 and c2 = 1. GN outputs values without regard to whether they have been assigned to other letters; R odd gives 1, 3, 5, 7, 9. TD checks that the digit is not already used and that it meets the known restrictions.

card.rule: PC infers from a column, GN lists admissible values, AV assigns one, and TD tests a digit for a letter.
card.limits: The four operators are defined by outside inputs and outputs; how each is carried out is left for later sections.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: Why a graph that keeps repetitions
concepts.question: Why does the analysis use a problem behavior graph and not an ordinary search tree?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Earlier trees were simple: no part was searched more than once, because systematic generators or specific tests for duplication prevented it. For LT a program was in hand and the aim was to understand its behavior.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Here the situation is reversed. Nothing is yet known about S3's program, and there is no assurance that he does not search the same part of the space again and again. So the authors modify the search tree into the problem behavior graph (PBG).

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The PBG retains the full information about the dynamics of search, including repetitions. If the structures of Figure 6.1 are S3's problem space, he should be seen wandering in it, each node described in that language and each move by an operator.

card.rule: A PBG records the search as it happened, repetitions included, because the subject's program is unknown.
card.limits: A graph of what the subject did is only as good as the space chosen for it; later the authors warn it could be superficial.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: The drawing rules of a PBG
concepts.question: How do nodes, arrows, vertical lines and the direction of time work in a PBG?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A graph that records revisits needs fixed conventions, or its shape would say nothing about order and returns.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: A state of knowledge is a node. Applying an operator to a state is a horizontal arrow to the right, whose head is the result. A return to the same state, say node X, is a new node below X, joined to it by a vertical line.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Time runs to the right, then down, so the graph is linearly ordered by time of generation: a node lower down was generated later than one above it.

card.rule: Right means an operator was applied, down means a return to an earlier state, and the whole graph reads in time order.
card.limits: Position shows order and returns only; the graph does not itself show which separate nodes hold identical states.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: Reading the model graph of Figure 6.2
concepts.question: What sequence of moves does the small example graph of Figure 6.2 record?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Before turning to S3's graph, the authors show the rules at work on an invented sequence of operators Q1, Q2 and Q3.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The subject starts at node 1. Q1 yields node 2, and Q2 leads to node 3. He then returns to the state of node 2, shown as node 4, and applies Q3 to reach node 5. He returns to the state of node 1 (node 6), written below nodes 4 and 5 because it came later.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: At node 6 Q1 is applied again, drawn as a double line, giving node 7. The move from node 3 to node 4 is not shown as an operation, since returning involved no operation such as recalling the prior state or abandoning what Q2 produced.

card.rule: Returns are drawn as new nodes without an operator, and an immediate reapplication shows as a double line.
card.limits: The graph does not mark that nodes 7, 2 and 4 hold the same state; the identity must be known from the analysis.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: Path information and past attempts
concepts.question: Why do nodes with the same facts count as separate nodes with different information?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A state of knowledge does not tell how the subject got there. Many paths lead to the same node, as 3 + 5, 2 x 4 and 24/3 all give 8.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: From the state, one can infer which operators were applied, but not their order or whether any was applied more than once. The subject also needs information about past attempts: at node 4 he must know he has been in this state and that Q2 was then applied.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Otherwise, being in the same state as at node 2 and assuming no randomness, he should apply Q2 again rather than Q3. Both path information and past attempts are functions of a node, so each node's state is expanded to include them; that is what makes nodes 7, 2 and 4 separate.

card.rule: A node holds the state of knowledge plus path information and information about past attempts.
card.limits: A subject can return to the same situation without knowing the full history of past attempts, as may happen at node 7.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: Marks and conventions in S3's graph
concepts.question: What do the corner labels, decimal B-numbers, circled numbers and jagged edges in Figure 6.3 mean?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: S3's graph covers 238 nodes and must be tied to the protocol and to the paper he wrote on, though writing operations are not drawn.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: An X number in a node's upper right corner names the new external display where something was written. The B-number in the upper left is the approximate starting point of the node's interval in the protocol; a decimal such as B64.1 means an occurrence somewhere after that phrase.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Circled footnote numbers mark rare items too unique for the formal space. A jagged right-hand boundary, as at B30.1, shows that a node is subordinated to a generator and executed repeatedly (the same marking at B99 and B103). Figure 6.4 outlines the whole tree and its main episodes.

card.rule: Corner labels and edge marks tie each node to the protocol, to the paper, and to repeated generate-and-test loops.
card.limits: An operator attempted without result still gets a node, because the lack of new information may only be seen late or remain in doubt.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: What counts as an operator in the coding
concepts.question: By what rule does the analyst decide which events in the talk become moves in the graph?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The talk contains many kinds of event. The analyst must decide which of them are moves in the graph and which are not.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The authors adopt the view that anything that changes the knowledge-state, as defined in Figure 6.1, should be treated as an operator. Other information, notably which column is being considered, is not shown explicitly in this problem space.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The four operators are the end result of coding and were not chosen a priori. B1, which clarifies the rules for the subject, is outside the problem space, so it is marked only by a special footnote; the initial display X1 is taken as set up by the experimenter.

card.rule: Treat as an operator whatever changes the knowledge-state; handle the rest inside a node or as footnotes.
card.limits: Which events change the state is judged from the talk, so the choice can be questioned, as later sections show.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: Coding B5: four questions, three working rules
concepts.question: What questions arose in coding B5, and what rules let the authors proceed without full answers?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: At B5 S3 considers the two D's, asserts their value, and concludes that T is zero. This is coded as PC on column 1, yet four questions remain open.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The questions are when the inference occurred, why column 1 was considered, whether S3 held the goal of finding T beforehand, and whether he also concluded c2 = 1. The authors do not need complete answers to all of them.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: They need only the approximate sequence of processing, which the protocol shows. They record no conjecture about a goal unless specific information is available. They treat c2 = 1 as plausible since 5 + 5 = 10, and B21 later shows the information was kept.

card.rule: Code what the protocol supports; do not record conjectures, and let later behavior confirm what was left unsaid.
card.limits: A coding choice without direct evidence rests on plausibility and later confirmation, and it can be wrong.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: Coding B8 to B22: one node with a goal
concepts.question: How do the authors turn about fifteen phrases of writing and searching into a node with the goal get R?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Between B8 and B22 S3 writes, searches for a next step without result, writes again, considers column 2, column 3 and the letters A, L and R, and then processes column 2.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Everything before B18, meaning the writing and the attempts to select columns, belongs within a node. S3's evident concern with R in B18 and B19 shows that the choice of column 2 was partly based on wanting information about R, so B8 is given the goal get R.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In B18 and B19 he noted how often A, L and R occur. No evidence shows any column being processed then, so the authors read it as simply selecting the next column.

card.rule: Writing and column choice stay inside a node, and a clear concern with one letter earns the node a get goal for it.
card.limits: The goal rests on the concern shown at B18 and B19. With weaker evidence only the operator PC on column 2 would be coded.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: A coding can be wrong; later evidence corrects it
concepts.question: How can the analysts find out that a coding of nothing new was wrong, and what do repetitions show?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Coding B14 to B19 as mere selection of a column could be wrong: S3 may have drawn conclusions he did not voice.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: If he derived information without saying so, it should surface later in a context with no apparent antecedents, and the reading can be revised. If he made an unsuccessful attempt, the reading is shown wrong only if some regularity of his behavior implied he would then have been processing columns.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: B23 and B25 repeat the reasoning of B20 and B22. The reason is unclear: it may be a check, or the experimental setting may push the subject to talk. A repetition can correct: B32 to B35 yield G even, and B36 to B38 show no such inference is possible.

card.rule: Treat a coding of nothing new as provisional; hidden information should reappear later with no visible source.
card.limits: A silent unsuccessful attempt leaves no trace, so only a known regularity of the subject's behavior can expose it.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: Generating odd digits for R, and the argument for parsimony
concepts.question: What did S3's listing of the odd digits for R show about generating and testing digits?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: At B26 to B30 S3 lists the odd digits for R just after concluding that R is odd. The authors ask what the listing shows about GN and TD.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The generation (GN of R) is not in doubt. In generating, S3 does not take account of digits already assigned: the used digit 5 is generated and then explicitly rejected rather than skipped. This supports the claim that TD was applied to GN's output.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: It is not clear that TD was applied to 1, 3, 7 and 9, since these were admissible and S3 gave no sign. Some assumptions of parsimony enter the coding, and the authors assume TD was applied uniformly. The loop is drawn at B30.1 with a jagged boundary.

card.rule: S3 generates first and tests afterwards; where evidence is silent, assume TD was applied uniformly.
card.limits: The uniform assumption is a convenience for coding, not proof that TD ran on every digit.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: A pause, a prod and a back-up
concepts.question: How do the authors code the pause at B31 and the place from which S3 resumes?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: At B31 the experimenter breaks in with a prod, urging the subject to talk. The graph must show what happened in the silence and where S3 picked up.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Nothing after B32 shows S3 using the refined fact that R is 1, 3, 7 or 9, instead of the plainer fact that R is odd. The authors infer that he backed up in his search to the state of knowledge at B26.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Some further processing may have gone on from B30.1 during the pause, but with no evidence for it, they make no explicit note of it.

card.rule: After a pause with no visible result, code a back-up to the last state the later talk uses.
card.limits: Silent thinking may have happened; the coding says only that no sign of it is found.
