concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: From an utterance to what S3 knows
concepts.question: How can an utterance such as R is odd count as evidence that the subject knows it?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The coding treats an utterance as showing what S3 knows. Yet a statement can be true by chance whether or not the speaker knows.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: If the question had been whether R is odd or even, the answer odd would have even odds of being true with no knowledge. Fortune-tellers appear informative by making statements broad enough that falsification is remote. Here the ensemble for S3's utterances is the language of the problem space, so R is odd is unlikely to be right by chance.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: More important than probabilities is the web of inference that relates an utterance to others, such as two L's equal an R. The web varies in coverage, and not all assertions can be made with considerable assurance.

card.rule: An utterance counts as evidence of knowledge when it fits a rich web of inference with other utterances.
card.limits: Coverage varies: some assertions rest on a thin web and cannot be claimed with confidence.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: Protocols are not introspections
concepts.question: In what sense are the thinking-aloud protocols not introspective reports?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Verbal data are often confused with introspection, and much confusion surrounds their use in psychology. The authors state how they use them.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: They do not treat protocols as introspections; there are very few introspective utterances. At B86 the experimenter asks what S3 is thinking and he replies that he was trying to think over what he had been saying, which gives essentially no evidence. An utterance at time t is taken to indicate knowledge or operation at time t.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The subject is not asked to theorize about his own behavior, only to report the information and intentions within his current awareness. All theorizing about the causes and consequences of his knowledge state is done and validated by the experimenters.

card.rule: Use the talk as a record of current knowledge and operation; the theorizing is the analysts' job.
card.limits: A running report covers only what is within current awareness, so it can leave gaps that the analysis must fill.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: The analyst as instrument
concepts.question: How do the authors answer the worry that a human analyst's coding may not be reliable?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The method needs a human analyst to extract the meaning of utterances, propose what knowledge and operation to attribute, and build the web of inference that supports each attribution.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: When psychology uses human analysts as instruments, for example to score tests or to measure interaction in small groups, measurements are generally duplicated by several judges and reliability is calculated. The authors have not adopted these methods for protocols.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: They believe it more appropriate to rely upon the persuasiveness of the web of inference.

card.rule: The authors rest the coding on the persuasiveness of its web of inference, not on duplicate judges.
card.limits: Without independent judges the coding's reliability is not measured; the authors say so and defer to later work.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: Two linguistic problems behind protocol analysis
concepts.question: Which two linguistic problems lie between a spoken protocol and the symbol structures of the theory, and which does the book take up?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The inputs to protocol analysis are natural language strings produced by the problem solver. The outputs are symbol structures read as parts of his deep-structure representation of his knowledge-state and actions.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Two problems link them. One is how the solver generates the strings from his internal representation. The other, the inverse, is how the analysts infer the deep structure from the strings. The authors do not address the first.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: They call the first genuine and important for linguistics, but its solution is not relevant to their theory, which postulates only deep structure (the internal representations) and not surface structure.

card.rule: The book takes up only the inverse problem: inferring deep structure from the strings the solver produced.
card.limits: How the solver generates his utterances is left open; the theory's claims concern the internal representation alone.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: Analysis cannot be evaded, but can be informal
concepts.question: Why must the authors face the problem of analysis, and how far do they go in solving it?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The problem of synthesis can be set aside, but the problem of analysis cannot be evaded if protocols are to be data for testing the theory.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The authors can, however, stop short of a full formal grammar that translates natural language strings into elements of deep structure. They rely on a systematic but informal set of procedures.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: These procedures are combined with their own knowledge of English and their consequent ability to extract meanings from the strings. The aim is to extract the most directly obvious components of the deep structures implicit in the protocols.

card.rule: Analysis is needed to use protocols as data, but an informal, systematic procedure suffices; no full grammar is built.
card.limits: An informal procedure rests on the analyst's judgment, which links back to the worry about reliability.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: What a successful encoding implies
concepts.question: What does the successful encoding of S3's behavior into the PBG claim about his problem solving?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The problem graph is a projection of the whole behavior into a space the analysts devised. They state in strong form what a successful encoding implies.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: First, S3 passed through the states of knowledge shown, from the initial state to the solution. Second, the operators PC, GN, AV and TD account for all his transitions to new states; returns to prior states are governed by other processes. Third, these operators plus processes for selecting operators, ending a line of search and choosing prior nodes suffice to explain the behavior at this level of detail.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In short, S3's basic method is search, hence trial and error, but in a space defined by intellectual operations of moderate sophistication. They define a basic competence like the abilities Gagne tried to identify in simpler arithmetic situations.

card.rule: The PBG claims that four operators plus selection, termination and return processes explain S3's behavior at this level.
card.limits: The claims are stated in strong form and are then qualified: the true situation may deviate from them in several ways.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: Three ways the graph could mislead
concepts.question: In what three ways might the true state of affairs deviate from what the PBG implies?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The graph is a projection into a space of the analysts' own making, so the true situation may differ from what it shows.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: It may be superficial: the essential problem solving may be done inside the operators or the selection and evaluation processes, if these need search in another space or some other intellectual process. It may be too disaggregated: it may show the means of a larger plan without any sign of that higher organization.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In the worst case it may be epiphenomenal: other processes using different or additional information might be responsible for the problem solving, and as a result the subject would come to know and reveal the information in the graph. An analogy for excessive disaggregation is a trace of the machine instructions of a program.

card.rule: A PBG may be superficial, too disaggregated, or epiphenomenal; each is a way the true process hides behind the graph.
card.limits: These are possibilities to be tested by the later work, not findings; the authors go on to argue that the method is less sensitive than they seem.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: The external problem space shows an epiphenomenal graph
concepts.question: What would the graph look like if the problem space were only the written display, and why does it fail?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: As true behaviorists, the authors might have taken as problem space the writing of assignments on paper, an objective indication of intermediate states.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Figure 6.5 gives a BNF for this external problem space, and Figure 6.6 the graph it yields for S3. That graph is epiphenomenal: it has very few clues to the processes that determine the sequence of actions.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The external space has no representation of the fact that R is 7 or 9, so nothing indicates why R was assigned 7 at B61 and 9 at B189. Evidence of S3's concern with E, O and column 5 does not appear before B249.

card.rule: A graph of the written display alone leaves out the knowledge that explains why each value was written.
card.limits: The external graph is not useless: it can still be used to test a theory, as the later sections show.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: The price of too fine and too coarse a graph
concepts.question: How much does the success of a PBG depend on choosing exactly the right level of aggregation?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: It might seem that a PBG explains behavior only if it sits at precisely the right level of detail: too coarse and it is superficial or epiphenomenal, too fine and it hides the larger units.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The authors argue the success of the method is not nearly so sensitive as this suggests, because the behavior is itself organized in a hierarchy of levels. The detailed processes are carried out as parts of more comprehensive acts.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Disaggregating too far costs two things: analysis of subprocesses that are not problematic for the subject, which is no burden, and a need to look beyond the local context to explain why a behavior occurred just where it did. Excessive aggregation loses information, and the price may be ruinous.

card.rule: Too fine a graph costs effort that a comprehensive IPS can repay; too coarse a graph loses information that cannot be regained.
card.limits: The insensitivity is a claim about this method and this behavior; the authors still treat excess aggregation as a heavy loss.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: A coarse graph can still test a theory
concepts.question: How can a graph in the wrong space still be used to test a theory about the subject?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Even where the aggregated external graph clearly does not match the space in which the subject works, it may still provide a great deal of data for testing theories.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Suppose there is reason to assume that the subject works in the augmented space. Then an IPS built in that space can simulate the behavior, and the information in the aggregated graph can be predicted by extracting the appropriate subset from the more complete simulated graph.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The prediction is likely to succeed, if the theory is roughly correct, to the extent that the missing subprocesses represent doing what the environment demands. In the case at hand, trying the values 7 and 9 for R and no others would become understandable, and might even be predicted.

card.rule: Simulate in the richer space, then read off the coarse graph's information as a subset of the simulation.
card.limits: The prediction works to the extent that the omitted subprocesses merely do what the task environment demands.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: The graph as problem space or as summary
concepts.question: What are the two ways of viewing a PBG, and why is the second extremely important?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A PBG can be read in two ways, and the way chosen decides how much detail must be right.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: It may be treated as the subject's problem space, in which case it must describe information and behavior at the right level of detail, or at least not too aggregated. Or it may be regarded simply as the experimenter's summary of the protocol, in a space that may or may not match the subject's. Even then it can test how well a hypothesized IPS predicts the behavior.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The second reading is extremely important. First, there is no reason a protocol should give a complete record of the state of knowledge at every moment. Second, some data lack complete protocols, such as Bartlett's data on DONALD + GERALD and Moore and Anderson's data on logic problems. Third, protocol analysis detailed enough for a PBG is costly.

card.rule: A PBG may be the subject's space or only the analysts' summary, and the summary reading keeps it useful when records are partial.
card.limits: The summary reading tests an IPS only through the part of behavior the graph records; it does not show the subject's own space.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: The first stage is done: the protocol is encoded
concepts.question: What has the PBG achieved, and what remains before a theory of S3's behavior exists?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The first stage of the analysis is the PBG. The authors ask what it has shown and what is missing.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The protocol has been encoded with a relatively high degree of objectivity and reproducibility, in concrete terms, so the content of the problem solving steps is kept. The subject can be viewed as working in a problem space, and that space can be specified in some detail.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The extraction of the PBG's information was not hard, partly because of the limited range of S3's linguistic behavior. The PBG is a basic description, so the next step is to build a bridge to a full theory by outlining a program that predicts the PBG and comparing its predictions with the graph.

card.rule: The PBG describes the behavior; a program that predicts the PBG is the bridge to a theory.
card.limits: The program will not be described in completely closed terms, so some looseness remains in how it fits the data.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: Three components of the program to come
concepts.question: What three kinds of component will the program for S3 need?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A program that predicts S3's PBG has to do more than the arithmetic. It also has to say how he decides what to do and what he remembers.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Three components are expected. First, processes for doing the arithmetic, i.e., drawing inferences from the relations of the problem, in which PC plays a central role. Second, processes for deciding what to do next: the subject's strategy. Third, assumptions about what he remembers and when he calls stored information to mind.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The strategy is synonymous with the set of processes and need not involve an overall plan, much less a conscious one. For example, after inferring D = 5 and then T = 0, the program must say what task S3 takes up next.

card.rule: The program needs arithmetic processes, a strategy for choosing what to do next, and assumptions about memory.
card.limits: Strategy here means only the set of choosing processes; it does not imply a conscious or overall plan.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: What belongs to the task and what to the subject
concepts.question: Which parts of the program come from the task environment, and which from the subject's psychology?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: In the program for S3, some features simply reflect what the task demands, and others reflect the person. The authors want to tell them apart.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The arithmetic operators are mostly set by the task environment, i.e., the rules of arithmetic, rather than by the subject's idiosyncrasies. S3's strategy is also conditioned by the task: he approaches it with the idea that he can deduce the assignments without trying all combinations, which is an objective property of the task, though another subject might not use it.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: A computer program without intent to simulate a human would remember any fact once validly inferred. So much of what is specifically psychological about S3 revolves around the limitations and vagaries of his memory. An example of a personal slip is his early invalid inference that R = 7 implies L = 3 and c3 = 0.

card.rule: Arithmetic and the chance to deduce come from the task; the limits of memory, and slips, come from the person.
card.limits: The line is not sharp: a subject may fail to use what the task offers, as another subject might not deduce.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.section: Analysis of the Protocol: A Production System
concepts.title: Why a production system fits the graph
concepts.question: Why is a production system a natural form for inducing S3's program from the problem behavior graph?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The PBG splits the protocol into 238 parts, each with an operator and a state of knowledge. If S3 uses definite processes for choosing and applying operators, enough repetition of similar situations may exist to induce them.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Repetition of decision situations is the key: if each situation called forth a unique process, no proposed process could be verified. But sameness is not given in advance. Each of the 238 states is unique, so how much repetition exists is defined afterwards by the proposed process and its proposed laws of evocation.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The data are correspondences between states of knowledge and the actions that followed. A production, which pairs specific information with an operator it evokes, is introduced to handle such situations. The whole program is the collection of productions plus an ordering that resolves conflict. Figure 6.7 was induced by examining the PBG.

card.rule: A production pairs a state condition with an action, so a program can be induced from state-action pairs, plus an order to settle conflicts.
card.limits: Sameness of situations is defined after the fact, so the same data could in principle support other proposed processes.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.section: Analysis of the Protocol: A Production System
concepts.title: Processes that steer attention
concepts.question: What are FC, FA, GNC, FL and FP, and why were they not counted among the operators?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The productions need processes beyond PC, GN, AV and TD, because S3 must pick columns, letters and earlier actions to consider.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: These new processes produce outputs that do not change the knowledge state as defined, so they were not among the operators. They control attention. They would be included in an expanded space that made control of attention explicit; here they are defined at the same level as the operators.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: FC finds a column containing a variable. FA finds the antecedent of an expression: the column or relation used to derive it. GNC generates the columns of a set from right to left. FL finds a letter of a set, for instance the undetermined letter that occurs most often. FP finds the production that produced an expression, and so is essentially a recall process.

card.rule: FC, FA, GNC, FL and FP select columns, letters, relations or past productions; they steer attention without changing the knowledge state.
card.limits: They are defined by what they take in and give out; how they find their answers is left for later sections.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.section: Analysis of the Protocol: A Production System
concepts.title: P1 and P2: new information versus a goal
concepts.question: How do P1 and P2 share an action sequence yet answer to different concerns?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: S3 often takes a fact about a variable and goes to a column to learn more, and at other times goes to a column because he wants a fact. One action sequence appears under two motives.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: P1: if a new expression determining an assignment has been produced, find a column containing the variable and process it, PC[column]. P2: if the goal is to evaluate a variable or establish a specific value, find a column containing the variable (FC) and process it for the variable (PC). If FC finds no column, PC is not evoked.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Both have fundamentally the same action sequence, yet P1 is evoked by new information about a variable and P2 by the goal of getting it. P1 loses its new tag after success, so it is not repeated; P2 can be applied again to the same variable to accumulate information. P2's goal can also be a relation, as in get c5 = 1.

card.rule: P1 is driven by new information and P2 by a goal; both go to a column and process it.
card.limits: When both conditions hold at once the system needs an ordering to say which acts; the data show P1 usually won.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.section: Analysis of the Protocol: A Production System
concepts.title: P3 and the minimal-generality principle
concepts.question: What does P3 do, and why is it stated only for letters?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: When a plain column look-up does not yield a letter's value, S3 has another means: pick a value for another letter in the column and use it. The authors must state this rule at the right generality.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: P3: if the goal is the value of letter.1, find a column containing it, assign a value to the other letter in the column, then determine letter.1 by PC. It is an alternative means to reach a goal, and gives the appearance, justified or not, of being less arbitrary than simply assigning a value to letter.1.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: P3 applies only to letters, though it could cover carries; S3 never used it with carries. P1 and P2 did occur with carries as well as letters. The principle: always use the smallest class in the problem space that covers the cases observed.

card.rule: Use the smallest class of the problem space that covers the observed cases; P3 is stated for letters because S3 never used it on carries.
card.limits: A narrower rule may fail to cover cases that simply did not happen to occur in this one protocol.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.section: Analysis of the Protocol: A Production System
concepts.title: P4 generates and assigns; P5 checks the columns
concepts.question: What do P4 and P5 do, and when is each used?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Two further productions govern longer stretches of behavior: one when S3 has narrowed a letter to a few values, and one at the end, when he checks the solution.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: P4: if the goal is to evaluate a variable that is constrained (it appears in a constraint-expression), generate its admissible values. If only a few values satisfy the constraint, assign one with AV; otherwise do nothing. P5: if the goal is to check a set of columns, generate them from right to left and execute PC on each.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: P4, like P1, strips the new tag from the constraint-expression. P5 is evoked only once in the whole problem solving, at the end, but it governs a rather long sequence of behavior.

card.rule: P4 generates the few values a constrained letter can take and assigns one; P5 checks every column, right to left.
card.limits: P4 does nothing if too many values qualify, and P5 occurs only when a candidate solution is being checked.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.section: Analysis of the Protocol: A Production System
concepts.title: P6 to P10: productions that set goals
concepts.question: Which productions create goals, and what does each respond to?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Besides acting, S3 sets himself goals in response to what he finds. Five productions turn conditions in the knowledge state into goals.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: P6: an unknown expression gives the goal get expression. P7: an expression marked impossible gives the goal get variable, accepting the fact and seeking another value. P8: a new expression to be checked gives the goal get expression. P9: a letter-set gives find one (FL) and get it. P10: a note-tagged expression, critical to a process, gives check expression.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Unknown arises only when another process tries to use an expression and finds it unknown, so not everything unknown is stored. P9 supplies something to work on when all else fails, since the initial problem is get all-letters. P10 is stated unconditionally, though S3 would not check D <- 5.

card.rule: P6 to P10 turn unknowns, impossibilities, new checks, letter sets and critical notes into goals.
card.limits: P10 is too broad as stated: the subject's degree of certainty also decides whether he checks, and the authors do not model it.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.section: Analysis of the Protocol: A Production System
concepts.title: P11 tests new digits; P12 backs up on a contradiction
concepts.question: How do P11 and P12 handle a newly derived digit and a contradiction?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A newly derived digit may clash with the rest of the knowledge state, and a clash must be traced back and undone.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: P11: whenever a digit is newly derived as the value of a letter, test whether it is admissible with TD. The result is a plus, or the tag changes from new to impossible together with the reason for the failure. P12: if one expression is impossible, find the expression used in deriving it, and declare that impossible also.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: P11 is also evoked when digits are generated while obtaining values for a variable. There is no similar check on the value of a carry. P12 provides backtracking on a succession of implications when a contradiction is discovered.

card.rule: P11 tests every new digit for a letter; P12 passes an impossibility back to the expression it was derived from.
card.limits: P11 is not applied to carries, and P12 depends on the system being able to recall what an expression was derived from.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.section: Analysis of the Protocol: A Production System
concepts.title: P13 repeats an unclear step; P14 repeats a past derivation
concepts.question: How do P13 and P14 use unclear results and memory of earlier productions?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: S3 sometimes repeats a step because he is unsure of it, or repeats an earlier derivation when asked to confirm a fact. The system needs rules for both.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: P13: if the result of an operator is unclear, repeat the operator with the goal of getting the variable involved. The operator is normally, but not always, PC. P14: if the goal is to check an expression derived earlier, find the production used for it and repeat it, after setting the goal of getting the expression.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Addition of two digits, as in 5 + 5 = T, is always clear. A complex determination, such as inferring R odd from 1 + L + L = R, is unclear at least the first time. Contradictions and inferences with no definite conclusion are also unclear. P14 implies some memory of production occurrences.

card.rule: P13 repeats an operator whose result is unclear; P14 re-runs the production that derived an expression S3 wants to check.
card.limits: What counts as unclear is not fixed in advance: the same inference may be unclear the first time and clear later.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.section: Analysis of the Protocol: A Production System
concepts.title: The system is incomplete in three ways
concepts.question: In what ways is the production system of Figure 6.7 incomplete?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors admit the system does not specify everything needed to predict S3's behavior.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: First, it gives no priority order: the order in the figure is essentially arbitrary, yet conflicts will occur, since some productions have identical conditions (P2 and P3) and others have different conditions that can both hold at one node (P1 and P2). Second, not all nodes of the graph are handled.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The productions were made from regularities in the PBG, so idiosyncratic or unclear nodes give no production. As a result the system cannot solve DONALD + GERALD, or many other cryptarithmetic tasks, without augmentation. The productions do form an integrated system, since the context for the conditions is supplied by the products of the productions themselves.

card.rule: The system lacks a priority order, leaves some nodes unexplained, and cannot solve the task alone.
card.limits: The integration is only within the restricted context; the conditions might fail in a larger context.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.section: Analysis of the Protocol: A Production System
concepts.title: Four functions the productions carry out
concepts.question: Which productions select operators, evaluate, select nodes and set goals?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Any system that generates a problem graph must select operators, evaluate states, choose nodes to continue from, and set goals. The authors sort the productions by these functions.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Operator selection: P1, P2, P3, P4, P5 and P11 pick one of the four operators; P3 and P4 specify a pair in sequence, and P13 and P14 select operators indirectly. Evaluation: a line ends when an impossibility or an unclear product arises. Node selection: P12, P13 and P14. Goal setting: P6, P7, P8, P9 and P10.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Termination on impossibility is implicit, since no production that selects operators does so on an impossibility. Productions that respond to it choose an old node, abandoning the current one. P13 and P14 fix the node to use, and P12 backs down the tree. With path memory, 'if at a node and not prohibited, select it' is equivalent to depth-first search. P6, P7, P10 and P13 form one component of means-ends analysis.

card.rule: The productions together select operators, end lines of search, pick nodes in depth-first order, and set subgoals in a means-ends way.
card.limits: These functions are read out of the system by the authors; they are not separate modules in S3.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: Two kinds of error to be counted
concepts.question: How do the authors plan to evaluate the production system, and what are errors of omission and commission?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A production system fitted to a graph might seem to fit by construction. The authors need a way to say how well it characterizes the problem graph.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: First, account for what the production system explains and what it does not. Then analyze two kinds of failure: errors of omission, where the system is silent on behavior that occurs, and errors of commission, where the system makes a specific assertion about behavior that is wrong.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The evaluation compares the system with the problem graph node by node. Later sections count the first kind of error (the question-mark nodes) and the second (wrong productions chosen according to the priority scheme).

card.rule: Omission means the system says nothing about a piece of behavior; commission means it says something wrong.
card.limits: The two kinds of error differ in meaning and should not be pooled without care, as the summary percentage later shows.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.section: How Much Does the Production System Explain?
concepts.title: Marking productions on the protocol itself
concepts.question: How do the authors record which production seems evoked at each node, and with what conventions?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: To count what the system explains, the authors must write for each node which production, if any, seems to have been evoked.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: They do this on the protocol itself (Appendix 6.1), not on the problem graph, so that productions can be compared with the verbal behavior that is the main evidence. Three conventions are used.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: First, a question mark where the information behind a condition cannot be discerned, or neither condition nor action can, sometimes with an English comment, as when behavior lies clearly outside the problem space. Second, a vertical arrow shows that a node is covered by the production named at the preceding node. Third, a variable d stands for the input to TD when it is applied to several members of a generator.

card.rule: Mark each node with its production, a question mark when none can be found, an arrow when the previous production still covers it.
card.limits: The marks are the authors' judgment from the protocol and carry the same interpretive uncertainty as the coding.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.section: How Much Does the Production System Explain?
concepts.title: From 238 nodes to 275 production occurrences
concepts.question: Why does the count rise from 238 nodes to 275 production occurrences, and what does node mean afterward?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Once a production occurs, a sequence of productions can follow automatically, since the outputs of one are the inputs of the next. Some of these occur within a single node of the graph.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: At B8 FC gives a failure, so two P1 occurrences happen within one node; at B7 and several other places P11 produces an occurrence of TD with no node in the graph, since TD gives a plus. The authors count these implied occurrences, expanding the data set from 238 nodes to 275 production occurrences.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The expansion is about 15 percent. From now on, node means a place where a production was, or should have been, evoked.

card.rule: Count implied production occurrences as well as graph nodes: 238 nodes become 275 occurrences.
card.limits: The expansion depends on judging which implied occurrences are not contradicted by the data.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.section: How Much Does the Production System Explain?
concepts.title: Positive and negative instances: the State-production Table
concepts.question: How does the State-production Table find the positive and negative instances of each production?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: For each production the protocol shows only its positive occurrences. To judge the system, the authors also need negative instances: nodes where the conditions held but something else happened.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: They ask, for each node and each production, whether its conditions were satisfied. The answers appear in the State-production Table (Appendix 6.2), built by recording the expressions produced by productions that occurred and by keeping a goal stack. Each production is matched at each context point and marked.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: A production cannot be evoked when its conditions are not satisfied, because a production is not recognized by its action part alone. At B185 the action looks like P5's, but a question mark is coded, since the condition for P5, the goal to check a set of columns, does not hold. Evidence for a condition is explicit protocol data or implicit data output by earlier productions.

card.rule: A production counts as present only if its condition held; a table of conditions at every node reveals the negative instances.
card.limits: Whether a condition was met is a matter of the authors' judgment about the subject's state, and some marks are questionable.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.section: How Much Does the Production System Explain?
concepts.title: The matrix of could-occur against did-occur
concepts.question: How does the matrix of Figure 6.8 compare the productions that could have occurred with those that did?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: To see how productions fared against each other, the authors need a table of competition: where each could have applied, which actually did.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: In Figure 6.8 the columns are the productions that did occur at a node, and the rows are those that could have occurred. Entry (i, j) is the number of times production i could have occurred but production j did. The diagonal entry (j, j) is the number of times j did occur.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Each cell has two entries: the top counts nodes where the conditions were definitely satisfied; the lower counts additional questionable nodes. Where P1 or P2 could have occurred in 10 cases, P1 did in 8 and P2 in 2; where P3 or P4 could have occurred, P4 did 14 times and P3 not at all.

card.rule: Entry (i, j) counts times production i could have occurred but j did; strong one-sided counts suggest an ordering.
card.limits: Counts are small for many pairs, and some cells rest on questionable nodes.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.section: How Much Does the Production System Explain?
concepts.title: Deriving a priority order, and what it leaves out
concepts.question: How is a priority order derived from the matrix, and does it describe the data perfectly?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The strong biases in the matrix are consistent with a priority ordering among productions. The authors try to impose a linear order on them.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: They place production j above production i whenever entry (i, j) is greater than entry (j, i). This could fail if the data were intransitive, but no intransitivities appear. Data are not everywhere numerous, and in several cases there are none. The isolates P14, P5 and P8 are put at the top, though they could be anywhere.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: One extra rule: once a production is evoked, no new production can be evoked until its action has run its course; the vertical arrow therefore has top priority. A transitive order does not mean a perfect fit: every nonzero entry above the diagonal in Figure 6.9 is a case where the lower production was selected, and the farther from the diagonal, the larger the inversion.

card.rule: Order the productions by head-to-head counts, and treat each entry above the diagonal as an inversion the order cannot explain.
card.limits: With sparse data some positions are arbitrary, and a transitive order can still misdescribe individual choices.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.section: How Much Does the Production System Explain?
concepts.title: Coverage rises and errors rise: Figure 6.10
concepts.question: How do coverage and errors change as productions are added in the order of how many nodes each covers?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Each production covers some nodes. The authors ask what the fit looks like as more of them are added, one by one.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Figure 6.10 orders productions by the nodes they cover: P13 first with 38 occurrences, P8 last with 2. Adding productions raises the total described, but with diminishing marginal utility, especially if an extra production is a cost in parsimony. The relevant total is 267 nodes, 8 fewer than 275, since eight contexts lie clearly outside the problem space.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Coverage starts at 16 percent with P13 alone and reaches 89 percent with all productions. Errors rise at the same time: definite errors climb from 0 for P13 alone to 23, and adding questionable errors raises it to 38. These counts are sums of entries above the diagonal of the matrix.

card.rule: More productions cover more nodes, from 16 to 89 percent, but with diminishing gains and growing errors.
card.limits: Coverage is bought with parsimony: the last productions add little and cost simplicity.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.section: How Much Does the Production System Explain?
concepts.title: The 80 percent figure and why it hides more than it shows
concepts.question: How is the 80 percent fit computed, and why do the authors call it not very informative?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors want one number for how much of the protocol the production system describes, after penalizing it for errors.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Of the 267 relevant nodes, 237 are covered by some production, leaving 30 errors of omission. Taking away the 23 definite errors of commission gives (237 minus 23) over 267, which is 80 percent. With the questionable errors added, (237 minus 38) over 267 gives 75 percent.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors say the number is not very informative, because it combines errors of omission and of commission. They would rather understand both kinds to see why the system could not do better.

card.rule: About 80 percent of the relevant nodes fit, or 75 percent counting questionable errors, but the two error types need separate study.
card.limits: A single percentage merges different kinds of failure and so cannot say how to improve the system.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: Where the omissions fall, and a false inference to avoid
concepts.question: How many omissions are there, where do they cluster, and what must not be inferred from the clustering?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The production system fails to find a production or sequence for 38 question-mark nodes. The causes range from lack of data to inability to construct a mechanism.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The authors discuss the failures under ad hoc headings. Two instances illustrate more than one type of problem, so 40 items are listed, not 38. Many failures are due implicitly to lack of information in the protocol. Most fall at terminations (26) or beginnings (8).

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: It would be false to infer that, because most question-mark nodes are terminals, the model makes most of its errors on evaluation. Failure to interpret the protocol leads to inferring termination, not vice versa, and lines of exploration are not long: once the thread is lost it is rarely picked up before a new line starts.

card.rule: Omissions cluster at the ends and beginnings of lines of search, but that is an artifact of losing the thread, not proof that evaluation fails.
card.limits: The headings are ad hoc, suggested by the omitted instances, so the counts per heading are descriptive, not a theory of the failures.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: Evaluation: persistence, switching and backing down
concepts.question: What does S3 do at points of explicit evaluation that the production system cannot represent?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: At several nodes S3 says outright what he thinks of a line of search, and the system cannot take that in.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: At B143.1 S3 states his options, R assigned 7 or R assigned 9, and decides to keep 7. He switches to 9 at B183, and back at B238.1. In these episodes he shows some persistence and then finally backs down.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: A related pair concerns whether the carry c5 exceeds 1: at B222.1 he chooses not to investigate it, while at B230 he does. The system fails on only one of these options, but there is a general problem of formulating the effect of multiple branchings at the same decision point.

card.rule: The system has no representation for evaluating a line of search, such as persisting with it and then backing down.
card.limits: Evaluation is built into the system only implicitly, so explicit weighing of options by S3 falls outside it.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: Two extra nodes kept in mind: the R point and the E point
concepts.question: Which earlier points does S3 keep available beyond the immediate path, and what jumps does the system fail to predict?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A system that backs up needs to know which earlier node to return to. S3's returns do not all fit the system's way of choosing.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Besides the immediate path and the initial situation, the subject appears to keep two additional nodes available: the decision situation for the assignment of R, and the one for E. The overall graph shows three substantial breaks in continuity, which are oscillations between E and R, as is one more that is hidden, when S3 decides to explore R assigned 9.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors have no formulation that predicts these jumps. They might be handled by better evaluation together with a better treatment of the goal stack: the return to E after a jump to R may occur because get E never leaves the goal stack, but is only pushed down.

card.rule: S3 shuttles between the R and E decision points, a pattern the system does not predict.
card.limits: The goal-stack explanation is offered as a possibility, not tested.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: Memories the system does not provide
concepts.question: What kinds of memory does the system assume, and where does S3 show more?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The problem space as used assumes several memory mechanisms. In a few places S3 shows evidence of more.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Assumed: knowledge of the current state, path memory, prior nodes, and a goal stack. Beyond these, at B158 S3 recalls that E equal to 0 leads to a contradiction found at B136. The system assumes memory of assigned values, but not this recognition that lets him follow a path he took before.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: At B188.1 he recovers at once from setting L to 9, an error he made at B105, where his recovery was much more involved; the system offers nothing for the quicker second recovery. At B275 there is a forgetting only partly explained, then a recall for which no mechanism is given.

card.rule: S3's memory of past paths and past mistakes goes beyond what the system supplies.
card.limits: The authors infer a more general memory from a few examples; its structure is not worked out.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: Mechanisms the system almost has: digit-oriented work, induction, Eureka
concepts.question: Which mechanisms similar to those in the system did the authors fail to formulate?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Some omissions involve mechanisms of the same kind as the system's, which the authors could not formulate properly.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: A digit-oriented step: after asserting that E equal to 0 is impossible, S3 at once asserts that A equal to 0 is impossible (B237), as if finding all the letters that cannot be paired with 0, now that 0 is assigned to T. At B238.1 the focus is the letter to be assigned to 9. Induction occurs at B155.1, where he sees a general case from several instances.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: At B244 S3 thinks first in terms of the full digit set, then uses only the remaining digits; at B281 and B282 he repeats this smoothly. At B303 there is no means to evoke the final check, which would need two productions: one to say Eureka, and one to say that, if Eureka, then check.

card.rule: The system lacks digit-oriented operations, induction, and a production that recognizes a solution and triggers the final check.
card.limits: Most of these gaps look fixable by extending the system, for example by making the inside of GN and AV explicit.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: Behavior outside the space, and blank periods
concepts.question: What parts of the protocol fall outside the problem space or consist of silence, and how are they treated?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Some nodes are so far outside the problem space that they were judged irrelevant to evaluating the production system, and some are long silences.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The extensions of the problem space concern the rules (B1, B50), new methods (B39), whether the top goal is to find a single solution or all solutions (B317 to B319), and the exit from the space to the larger world (B320). Interactions with the experimenter would need a new problem space, which should not be built on skimpy data.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: B169 is the one clear example of emotionally toned behavior, and B224.1 and B225 are task-oriented behavior by the experimenter. Blank periods (B30.1, B85.1, B103.1, B114.1) are silences broken by the experimenter.

card.rule: Talk about rules, goals and feelings lies outside the space, and blank periods form a separate kind of omission.
card.limits: If imported from a general model of such behavior elsewhere, the outside material might be handled well; the data here are too thin.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: When writing does shape the thinking
concepts.question: Why do the authors not model writing, and where does it show an effect?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: S3 writes on paper, but the production system has no writing operators. The authors say why, and note where that choice costs something.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The main reason for not making writing explicit is that, in this protocol, writing does not seem to affect very much what goes on in the internal problem space. B185 is an exception: S3 keeps two external displays and has a copy operation that takes information from one to build the other.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: A second example, not recorded as an omission, is at B12, where the response to finding D in column 6 is to write 5 for D instead of processing column 6. With a set of writing productions the authors might have found more interactions, especially in the control of attention.

card.rule: Writing is left out because it rarely alters the internal process, though B185 and B12 show it can.
card.limits: Adding writing productions would let one study when S3 chooses to write, which the present system cannot.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: Reading the table of commission errors
concepts.question: How is Table 6.1 organized, and how many errors of commission are definite and how many questionable?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: In 38 cases the production the system evoked differed from the one the priority scheme would choose. The authors discuss them pair by pair.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Of the 38 errors, 23 are definite and 15 questionable. Table 6.1 lists, for each error pair, the separation of the two in the priority ordering, the counts of definite and questionable errors, and the nodes concerned, with a question mark before nodes that are questionable.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In the top row, P3 over P2, the pair is adjacent in the ordering. P2 was chosen 16 times and P3 9 times in 25 co-occurrences, so there are 9 errors. More than one error can occur at a node; this happened four times, each a questionable error with a definite one, as in the single P7 over P10 error that also involved P7 over P12.

card.rule: Table 6.1 lists each pair of competing productions, how far apart they rank, the counts of errors, and the nodes concerned.
card.limits: A count of errors can mislead because some errors are repeats of one another, as the next sections show.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: P3 over P2: nine errors but three independent ones
concepts.question: Why is the count of nine P3-over-P2 errors deceptive?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The largest group of errors is P3 chosen where P2 should have been. Nine looks like a clear number, but the authors say it misleads.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The discriminators that tell when P3 is evoked are not known. The nine errors are all the occasions on which P3 was evoked. P3 is clearly a secondary method, never evoked until P2 has been tried at least twice. Only three evocations are essentially independent: getting R at B40, E at B120, and E at B218.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The rest are repetitions. B104 repeats B40, as does B186 when S3 starts over with R assigned 9, and B189 is an immediate repeat of B186 caused by an error in executing it. The acts of repetition are themselves part of what is to be explained.

card.rule: Nine errors reduce to three independent evocations plus repetitions, which are themselves behavior to explain.
card.limits: The number of independent errors is uncertain, since repetitions and originals are linked.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: P7: a production of marginal efficacy
concepts.question: What does the record of P7's errors suggest about whether P7 belongs in the system?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: P7 turns a failure into a goal of getting the value of the variable just affected. Its pairings with P12 and P4 produce several errors.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Of the eight occurrences of P7, all but one are implicated in some error, so P7 is clearly of marginal efficacy. A moderately careful look at goals shows that five of the eight occur when the goal is already at the top of the stack.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In the other two cases, B203.3/2 and B229.2, P7 makes a genuine switch of attention, and both involve the carry and are among the most obscure passages. In short, with only slight modifications one might dispense with P7 altogether.

card.rule: P7 is implicated in nearly all its occurrences as an error and may be removable with small changes.
card.limits: The two cases where P7 did switch attention are obscure, so removing it would need those cases explained another way.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: When does a critical feature trigger a check?
concepts.question: What do the P10-related errors show about when S3 checks a fact and when he does not?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: P10 says that a critical, note-tagged expression triggers a check. The data show that S3 does not check all such expressions.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The questionable errors on P12/P10 and the P7/P10 error all stem from the fact that S3 does not check D assigned 5 or T assigned 0, except that he checks the latter after the experimenter brings it to his attention. In the definite cases one can find plausible reasons why checking makes little sense.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: No clear pattern emerges when these are compared with the times when checking is evoked. There is a relatively thin line between getting a value and checking a value, and the authors' account of the difference is only marginally satisfactory.

card.rule: The system lacks the conditions that say which critical facts S3 will check; some he never checks without prompting.
card.limits: The authors did not add discriminating conditions to P10, though they say they are needed.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: Errors that come from repetition and from newness
concepts.question: What do the P2/P4, P2/P1 and P1/P11 errors show about memory and about what counts as new?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Three more pairings of errors have a common source: how the system handles repeating the past and judging an expression new.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: P2/P4: all four errors involve repetition, and show that the system is not explicit about what is remembered from the past and how processing is guided by it. The two definite errors (B116, B139) repeat the final path of a previous branched exploration, which implies not repeating the generation of values for the constrained variable.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: P2/P1: one error (B85) is simply an ambiguity, since both give the same result, the determination of c6; the other (B290.1) sits in a larger context than the system captures. P1/P11: the question is whether the relation is new. S3 does not evoke TD on old material, and failing to evoke TD on E equal to 0 at B129 and again at B207 is part of his major difficulty.

card.rule: Repeated paths, ambiguous triggers and the judgment of what is new produce errors; the last explains S3's main difficulty.
card.limits: The P1/P11 errors depend on deciding whether a relation is new, which the system does not model well.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: Why error counts are partial and biased
concepts.question: Why do the authors say any discussion of errors is partial and biased?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: After listing errors pair by pair, the authors qualify what the list can show.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Any discussion of errors is only partial and fundamentally biased, because it takes place against a background of choices about how to fashion the production system. A number of errors could become nonerrors if the system were modified.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: But an equivalent number of errors, actually somewhat more in the cases investigated during the analysis, would show up elsewhere. The discussion still gives some feeling for the places where the system is weak and for what remedial actions might be.

card.rule: Error counts depend on design choices; changing the system moves errors around, and it does not simply remove them.
card.limits: The list still marks weak places, but one should not read the total as a fixed measure of the theory.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: Each named process is to be a subroutine
concepts.question: What does it mean to treat PC, GN, FC and the others as single, well-defined processes?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: So far the processes have been described only by rough input and output. Using them in the graph and the productions implies more than that.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: A single process is associated with each name, not merely a type of process. The processes are to be subroutines: one should be able to write them in a process language so that the entire variation of output is determined by the variation of input. To predict the output, no information about the context beyond the inputs should be needed.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: To the extent this fails, the total errors in the description are underestimated, since some production occurrences would be judged correct when an algorithmic specification consistent with other occurrences of the process would lead to an error. So the errors in the basic processes need investigation.

card.rule: Treat each named process as a subroutine whose output depends only on its inputs, and check whether it really does.
card.limits: If a process depends on context beyond its inputs, errors hidden in the production fit would go uncounted.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: Errors in processes versus errors in productions
concepts.question: Why keep errors in the basic processes apart from errors in the production system?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A wrong result might come from the choice of the process, or from the process itself failing. Pooling the two would confuse the tests.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The errors in the basic processes should not necessarily be combined with those in the production system, since the productions can be correct even if the basic processes are faulty. For example, the subject may make an error in arithmetic while the processes postulate that he always adds correctly.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Such errors belong to the processes underlying PC and do not invalidate the productions that use PC. If such errors became too numerous they would compromise the whole system. The authors have independent knowledge that humans make errors of perception, memory and elementary processing, so a division is appropriate.

card.rule: Charge arithmetic and other elementary slips to the basic processes, not to the productions that call them.
card.limits: If slips are too numerous, they undermine the whole system; the present data do not allow predicting when they occur.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: Basic-basic processes, and the nine processes in six groups
concepts.question: What would a complete explanation of the basic processes need, and how does the chapter handle that?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: To explain the basic processes fully, one would have to say how each is built from still simpler processes.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The authors call these basic-basic or BB processes, at the level of elementary operations of perception, immediate memory and access to long-term memory. FC, for example, is a visual exploration of the board under the direction of assimilated information about the task display, and might take under a second. Even PC involves operations of the order of adding a pair of digits or recalling a letter's known properties.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: A model of the BB processes would be a detailed model of immediate memory and immediate processing, which this volume does not attempt. The authors give an informal, incomplete treatment, looking for inconsistency or complexity that does not fit calling the processes basic. They discuss the nine basic processes in six groups, each with a table of occurrences, their inputs and outputs.

card.rule: The basic processes rest on elementary perceptual and memory operations, which the chapter does not model but checks informally.
card.limits: The check is for inconsistency or too much complexity; it does not show how the processes are built.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: Process column: the most complex operator
concepts.question: Why is PC called the most complex basic process, and what does S3's power hinge on?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: PC occurs 88 times, enough to show much about its nature. If it were just a routine for adding pairs of numbers, as in 5 + 5 giving T equal to 0 and c2 equal to 1, understanding it would amount to understanding how a human does arithmetic.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: But PC produces a wide variety of final responses, so the power of S3's problem solving hinges strongly on the sophistication of PC. This shows when his behavior is compared with that of subjects whose PC admits only simple arithmetic.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Table 6.2 lists the 88 occurrences. The diversity implies that even if PC is a single subroutine, it is a highly conditional one. The key question is whether some uniform scheme of processing can yield this diversity, and the authors sketch a system for it in Figure 6.11.

card.rule: PC is a highly conditional subroutine that draws many kinds of conclusion from a column, and S3's power rests on it.
card.limits: The sketch of a uniform scheme is not a model of S3's arithmetic and omits a detailed theory of immediate memory.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: Five elements of the PC sketch
concepts.question: What five elements does the sketched PC system hold, and which productions define them?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: To show that one scheme could produce PC's variety, the authors sketch a system with a small working memory and productions that fill it.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Figure 6.11 arranges memory for PC with five elements: the unknown, the value, the operand, the target and the operator. At the start, in the context of a goal and a column, all five are undefined.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: A set of initial productions defines them from the context: the u-productions define the unknown, the v-productions the value, the single o-production the operand, the t-productions the target and the q-productions the operator. Then a production p1 can perform the operation, and the a-productions analyze the result, either causing new operations or packaging the output expression.

card.rule: PC is sketched as five working elements, filled in by u, v, o, t and q productions, then operated on by p1 and a-productions.
card.limits: This is a sketch to show feasibility; the authors say it does not model S3's detailed memory.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: Digits, parities, inequalities and quantities, and the conversions among them
concepts.question: Which kinds of value must PC combine, and how does it add things of different types?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The complexity of PC comes largely from the many kinds of symbol structure it must combine: it is not limited to digits.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The operations must handle digits, parity-values (even and odd), inequality-values (such as greater than 5) and quantities such as two L's, written 2:L. Various conversions allow an operation to be carried out when the types differ.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: To add 1 to 2:L, a digit to a quantity, both are converted to parity-values, so even plus odd gives odd. To add G to 5, a quantity to a digit, G is converted to an inequality (greater than 0) and added to 5 to give greater than 5. The operation is attempted if the inputs are of suitable types, and conversion routines are called if not.

card.rule: PC converts values of different types to a common type so that it can add digits, parities, inequalities and quantities.
card.limits: A conversion loses precision: parity and inequality are weaker than a digit, so the result may be only a class of digits.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: Two traces: 5 + 5 = T and 1 + L + L = R
concepts.question: How does the PC system carry out its two simplest example inferences?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: To show the system working, the authors trace it on two entries of Table 6.2: a plain sum and a parity inference.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: For 5 + 5 = T the first production defines T as the unknown, then 5 as the value, the other 5 as the operand, the target as the value and the operator as addition. Adding two digits gives 10, which is decomposed into a digit and a carry: T equal to 0 and c2 equal to 1.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: For 1 + L + L = R the two L's are quantities with the same letter and add to 2:L, which a production converts to even. Then the operand is set to 1 with addition. A digit meets a parity-value, so the digit is converted to a parity-value, and the sum is odd: R is odd.

card.rule: PC defines its five elements, adds, converts if needed, and packages the result as T equal to 0 and c2 equal to 1, or R odd.
card.limits: Both traces are chosen for being simple; the authors say the system has trouble with other entries.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: What the PC sketch shows, and what it does not
concepts.question: What three things does the PC system show, and why is it not a model of S3's arithmetic?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The sketch explains many of S3's uses of PC, but the authors do not claim it as a formal model of his PC operator.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: It has trouble with minor variations: for example, column 5, with O plus E equal to O, is handled awkwardly, and trying for the maximum value (line 64) is not represented. The authors do not wish to treat it as a model of his arithmetic, because that would require a detailed account of his immediate memory and immediate processing.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: It does show that (1) the kinds of inference and operation in S3's PC can be represented by a production system, (2) there are no gross inconsistencies in his PC, and (3) a great deal of knowledge stored in his memory is required for so diversified an operator. No intricate numerical algorithm is needed; each production is a bit of partial knowledge a human of S3's skills might have.

card.rule: The PC system shows feasibility, consistency and a heavy knowledge demand, not a full model of S3's arithmetic.
card.limits: Awkward cases such as column 5 and going for the maximum value show the sketch is incomplete.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: The carry is added last
concepts.question: In what order does S3 take the parts of a column, and when does he overlook the carry?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A model of PC must say in what order the operands of a column are taken, and whether the carry is always taken into account.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Table 6.2 shows one regularity: the carry from the previous column is attended to only after the other operands. There are eleven instances in which some evidence of the order exists, and in all of them the carry is dealt with last. There is no evidence of the carry being taken at any other position.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: On three occasions (B20, B32 to B36, B78 to B83), all at the beginning, the carry is not attended to at first, but it is always discovered eventually. After that, the assumption that the carry is always taken into account fits best, though when the carry is 0 or undefined, nothing in the protocol shows it was noted.

card.rule: S3 adds the carry after the other operands, and after a few early lapses he takes it into account throughout.
card.limits: Where the carry is 0 or undefined nothing in the protocol shows it was attended to, so the pattern rests on the eleven clear cases.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: Assign Value is generate plus associate
concepts.question: How is AV built from GN, and what is the associating step like?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Generate Variable (GN) and Assign Value (AV) occur 27 times each and are discussed together, because AV can be written in terms of GN.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: AV(variable) is GN(variable), which yields a digit, followed by associate(variable, digit). Associate is essentially the operation in a paired-associate learning task, where the variable is the stimulus and the digit the response, or the reverse, since recall can go either way.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Of the 27 AV occurrences, 13 are essentially just associate, because a single value was already delivered, either by GN in P4 or because P3 goes slowly enough for the generation to be seen. Whether the association is made by building a symbol structure such as D <- 5, or by a designation such as find digit of D giving 5, is not determined. The performance of the system is not affected by the choice.

card.rule: AV is a generate step followed by an associate step, like a paired-associate pairing of letter and digit.
card.limits: The text leaves open how the association is stored, and says the fit does not depend on that choice.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: Generation runs upward, starting from the low member
concepts.question: In what order does S3 usually generate values, and where does he start?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Adding the nine AV occurrences that contain a buried GN to the 27 explicit ones gives a total of 36 cases of generating.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The main form of the process, with 24 cases, starts at the low member of the set and generates values in ascending order. Three of these have a set of one or no element.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Included is B98.1, which generates E even starting from 2 rather than from 0. The authors say this is undoubtedly what occurred, since only programmers start counting from 0, even though for this problem 0 is the correct starting place. They add that a consequence of this will be apparent later.

card.rule: Most generation is ascending from the low end of the admissible set, and S3 starts counting at 2 for an even digit.
card.limits: Six cases follow other mechanisms, and a few generate from the top.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: Small sets: pick the other one
concepts.question: How does S3 handle a set of two values when one has just been ruled out?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Six cases of GN differ from the ascending pattern. Each involves a two-element set, one member of which has just been judged not possible.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Because the new information came just before GN was evoked, the basic set of values has not yet been modified, and GN can be viewed as performing the update. This could be done by generate-and-test using GN and TD. But with only two elements there is a strong possibility of a rule that amounts to: pick the other one.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The two mechanisms can coexist, since unique clues for evoking the second are clearly present. In general, an organism with a small immediate memory may be expected to handle small sets quite differently from large ones, which must be generated serially.

card.rule: With a two-element set, one member excluded, the subject can pick the other without serial generation.
card.limits: This reading needs the clues that mark the set as small, and it is the authors' proposal, not shown by the data.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: Generating from the top of the set
concepts.question: When does S3 generate from the top of a set, and why are these cases hard to explain?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Six cases of GN remain unexplained after the ascending and two-element patterns. Three are unimportant: incomplete GN's with no information (B155, B288) and an unsatisfactory digit-centered situation (B235).

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The final three give evidence both that a set of values exists and that generation begins with the top value rather than the bottom. Each involves generating only a single value: O <- 9 at B125, O <- 8 at B219, and N <- 6 instead of N <- 3 at B294.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In the first two there are complexities the authors can sense but have not captured: assigning 9 to O resolves the dilemma for E = 0 or 9, and O <- 8 is probably confused with E = 8, since it evokes c5 = 2. At B294 the choice followed an extensive comparison of the consequences of each value, which apparently ended indecisively. The failure is the authors' inability to discover the additional considerations in the decision.

card.rule: A few GN cases start at the top of the set, and their causes lie in considerations the model does not capture.
