card.limits: Each of the three cases generates one value only, so the evidence for top-first generation is thin.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: Test Digit checks availability and constraints
concepts.question: What two checks make up Test Digit, and which one is skipped for S3?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: TD(letter, digit) is the process by which a proposed pairing is checked before it is accepted. It occurs 31 times.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: It has two separate parts. One checks whether the digit is available, that is, not already used by another letter. The other checks whether the digit satisfies all the constraints known to hold for the letter.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Because S3 appears to work from letters to digits, he need not test whether a digit already carries the given letter: no instance in Table 6.5 has TD evoked with a variable that already had a value. In the other direction the digit may lie outside the admissible set for the letter, which happens in three cases: two for R greater than 5 and one for E even.

card.rule: TD asks whether the digit is free and whether it fits the letter's known constraints.
card.limits: The order of the two checks is unclear, and may vary with the circumstances.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: The order of the TD checks, and what TD cannot do
concepts.question: In what order might the two TD checks run, and what inference is beyond the program?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The program for TD in Figure 6.12 lists the checks in a fixed order, but the authors doubt that the order is fixed.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Whether the checks are done in the order shown, in the inverse order, or as a single access to a compound stimulus is unclear. The order may vary: the letter first and then the digit when a new assignment is proposed, but the digit first during a generation of digits. That requires either two different processes or enough conditional structure in TD to adapt.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The one other noteworthy occurrence is B295.1. S3 becomes aware that if he lets B equal 3, no other digits will be available, even though the letter O is still unassigned. This inference does not come from the program and requires other processing. If the model could handle noticing, it could handle this event, and B202-203, differently.

card.rule: The TD checks may run in either order, and some inferences, such as running out of digits, go beyond the program.
card.limits: The program is a sequential sketch, so the true order and the noticing mechanism are not established.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: Find Column: two selection rules
concepts.question: How do two simple rules about the current column decide most FC choices?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The input to FC is the variable whose column is sought, but several columns can contain the same variable, so extra mechanism is needed. Of the 64 cases, ten are repetitions and eight have uniquely determined columns.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: For the other 46, the key feature is whether the sought variable has been processed on the current column. Rule 1: if the current column is unprocessed for the variable, select it. Rule 2: if the current column is already processed for the variable, do not select it.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Rule 1 accounts for six cases. Rule 2 accounts for 30, because it reduces the set from which selection must occur to either one or no elements. That leaves ten cases in which one column was chosen from two or three eligible columns.

card.rule: Select the current column if the variable is not yet processed in it, and drop it if it has been.
card.limits: Ten cases still need a further rule, and FC is highly perceptual, so a sequential rule is a poor picture of it.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: Choosing the most constrained column
concepts.question: How are the ten leftover FC choices explained, and why is full comparison ruled out?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Ten FC cases select one column from two or three eligible ones: eight for R, one for D and one for E.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Any variation on a rule that selects the most constrained column accounts for all except B203 and B240. S3 would take column 2 or 6 for R rather than column 4, and column 1 for D rather than column 6.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors caution against this mechanism, since it could imply considerable computation and comparison of all columns before selecting, which clearly does not occur. B12 makes it highly probable that D's first column at B5 was not chosen by comparing columns 1 and 6. B203 is a genuine anomaly, and no clue explains B240. FC is highly perceptual, so the sequential program of Figure 6.18 is probably a poor representation.

card.rule: A most-constrained-column rule fits eight of ten leftover FC choices, but not by exhaustive comparison.
card.limits: Two cases remain unexplained, and the program is a sequential stand-in for a perceptual process.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: Find Antecedent and Find Production recall past behavior
concepts.question: Why are FA and FP grouped, and what does the text say about their mechanism?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Find Antecedent (19 occurrences) and Find Production (4) are grouped because the essential component in both is the recall of past behavior.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Even in P3, where FA seems only to call for a relation that determines the input variable, the result is never a new relation, but one already used. In B42, which concerns the assignment of L to get R, it is implausible that FA chooses between three columns for R as FC would; it returns to column 2, which was used to derive R odd.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: For FA, ten cases have no alternatives to the output and five others repeat prior sequences, leaving four worth discussing. The authors can say little about the mechanisms without a more detailed model of memory.

card.rule: FA and FP draw on memory of what was done before, rather than choosing among columns afresh.
card.limits: Without a detailed model of memory the mechanism cannot be specified, and only four FA cases raise issues.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: Generate Column and Find Letter: needed for sufficiency
concepts.question: Why does the system include GNC and FL, and how might FL choose a letter?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Generate Column and Find Letter appear only twice and four times, in Tables 6.9 and 6.10, so little can be said about their internal mechanisms.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Both are postulated in response to needs for sufficiency. For example, it is not possible to add up a sequence of columns serially, as at B304-B316, without sequencing through the columns.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The only FL instance that offers food for thought is the extended attempt at B14-B18 to select a letter for processing. S3 is considering letters and their multiple occurrences. A mechanism that chooses the unprocessed letter occurring the maximum number of times in the problem is as good an approximation as one can get, though it may differ from the actual process.

card.rule: GNC and FL are included because the system could not run without them; FL may pick the unprocessed letter that occurs most often.
card.limits: With so few instances their internal workings stay unspecified, and the most-frequent-letter rule is only an approximation.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: What the analysis shows about thinking aloud
concepts.question: What did the full analysis of S3 accomplish, and what do the 75 to 80 percent show?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The chapter has built a PBG from a protocol, defined operators, proposed productions, and scrutinized the fit between the production system and the PBG.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: All of this shows how a verbal thinking-aloud protocol can serve as raw material for generating and testing a theory of problem solving behavior. A sizable fraction, 75 to 80 percent, of the units of behavior was accounted for by the production system.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The detailed scrutiny of the discrepancies gives no reason to suppose the remainder is intrinsically incomprehensible or random. Most inadequacies of the model appear due either to the lack of a detailed account of attention and memory mechanisms or to missing data.

card.rule: A thinking-aloud protocol can be used to build and test a theory, and the unexplained remainder looks like model gaps, not randomness.
card.limits: The fit is for one subject on one problem, and the remainder is not shown to be explained, only not shown to be random.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: S3's arithmetic: close to ideal, with two shortfalls
concepts.question: How close is S3's arithmetic to what the task needs, and where does it fall short?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: S3's processes for drawing inferences from the columns are very close to those that are ideal for this task environment and to those postulated in Chapter 5.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: He infers properties of numbers, such as R odd, and limits assignments numerically, such as G equal to 1 or 2. He makes inferences about the carries into and out of a column as well as the letters in it.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In two respects he falls short. First, he is not always sure his inferences are correct, so he sometimes checks them by repeating them. Second, occasionally they are not correct, the inference to L = 3 from R = 7 being a notable example. Apart from these, S3 knows and uses all the arithmetic that could help him, so the environment does not test his arithmetic knowledge.

card.rule: S3's column inferences are near the ideal, apart from uncertainty that leads to repeats and a few actual errors.
card.limits: The assessment covers this one task; the environment is not a measure of his arithmetic skill.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: Confusing necessary and sufficient conditions
concepts.question: Where does S3 treat a consistent value as a necessary one?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The uncertainties and errors in S3's inferences seem sometimes associated with vagueness in his distinction between necessary and sufficient conditions.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: L = 3 is consistent with the hypothesis that R = 7, so S3 infers that L = 3 from R = 7. A consistent value is taken as if it were forced.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In column 5, S3 notices that E = 0 or 9 is consistent with O + E = O. It takes some experimentation to convince him that this conclusion is necessary, which the authors call another instance of confusion between necessary and sufficient conditions.

card.rule: Do not treat a value that fits the premise as one the premise requires, and test whether a conclusion is forced.
card.limits: The authors read the errors as vagueness in S3's distinction; this is their interpretation of the protocol.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: S3's strategy: depth first, with limited forward search
concepts.question: What is S3's main strategy, and how far does he leave it?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: S3's main strategy for deciding what to do next when a process is finished is depth-first search with means-ends analysis, similar to the strategies of Chapter 5.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: He substitutes known values for letters in the display and infers what he can, and if he obtains new information, he substitutes it back. He substitutes D <- 5 in both columns 1 and 6; when this gives no result, he follows the carry c2 = 1 into column 2, finds R odd, takes this to column 6 and concludes R = 7 or 9.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The problem can be solved to a single assignment by this precise strategy; S3 would have done so if he had not had difficulty determining E = 9. He did retreat from it. When columns 2 and 6 gave no precise value, he decided at B40 to try possible solutions in forward search, though to a very limited extent. He then divided his exploration into R = 7 and R = 9, pursuing them separately.

card.rule: S3 chains inferences from known values column to column, and drops to limited trial-and-error when inference stalls.
card.limits: The authors know the problem is solvable by the strategy; S3 did not, so this is hindsight.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: S3's memory: low strain, with known failures
concepts.question: How does S3 keep memory strain low, and what slips remain?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The ways S3 holds information in memory, and its fallibilities, have been discussed at length. Here the authors summarize.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: He keeps cognitive strain relatively low by trying not to make highly conditional hypotheses, a by-product of using a reasoning strategy rather than forward search. He does remember whether he is considering R = 7 or R = 9, and that other results may be conditional on these assumptions.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: He generally remembers deduced properties, such as R = 7 or 9 and E = 9 or 0, but not always how he derived them. So he sometimes repeats derivations to check for untested assumptions. His failure to recall T = 0 to refute E = 0 is not completely explained, though it fits evoking TD only on new results.

card.rule: S3 stores conclusions better than their derivations, so he repeats derivations to check them.
card.limits: The failure to recall T = 0 is only partly explained by the TD program.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: From detail back to general mechanisms
concepts.question: What did the minute detail of the chapter give back about problem solving in general?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The analysis became increasingly particularistic: it considered one individual on one problem, and more and more the minute detail of that behavior. The authors admit empathy with a reader who felt stifled.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The detail gave preliminary answers to some of the questions posed at the chapter's start. The subject uses several mechanisms of problem solving studied in earlier chapters, in his overall strategy and in particular heuristics such as the column selection process, FC.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: One can pass from general observations on heuristics to a precisely defined IPS, almost, as the authors stopped short of a full program. The production system makes the relation of the program to the search in the problem space, the PBG, transparent. No appreciable chunk of raw data is left unresponded to, down to individual linguistic utterances.

card.rule: Detailed analysis of one subject links general heuristics to a precisely stated production system tied to the PBG.
card.limits: The IPS is almost, not fully, specified, and its degree of detail cannot be given precise meaning.

concepts.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
concepts.title: Five techniques for inducing programs from data
concepts.question: Which five techniques does the chapter offer for getting from protocols to programs?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: For inducing programs from data, the chapter has provided a number of techniques.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: (1) Formalize the problem space, with both the knowledge states and operators, so changes of knowledge are easier to determine. (2) Build the Problem Behavior Graph, a plot of the subject's search through the problem space. (3) Write the production system, which extracts the regularities of behavior at a node of the PBG.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: (4) Determine the priority ordering of the production system by minimizing the number of errors in predicting behavior. (5) Display the performance of the production system in a graph showing its coverage and its errors, compared with the addition of new productions.

card.rule: Formalize the space, draw the PBG, write productions, order them by fewest errors, and plot coverage against errors.
card.limits: These are the chapter's own techniques for one task; the text does not claim they suit every protocol.

concepts.title: From one subject to many
concepts.question: What does the S3 theory predict for other subjects, and why do the authors expect that prediction to fail?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors ask whether the theory built for subject S3 explains the behavior of other subjects, and how far. Read literally, the theory is close to a specific computer program for S3 on DONALD+GERALD=ROBERT.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: As a general theory it would predict that every other subject given the same puzzle behaves exactly as S3 did and produces an identical protocol. The authors say at the outset that this prediction will fail; what matters is the manner and extent of the failure.

blocks.label: Assumed
blocks.text: Some failure is expected. Other subjects may differ in their basic processes, for example in the arithmetic behind column processing, and may organize them into somewhat different productions and problem spaces.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors offer no result yet; they state in advance that identical protocols will not occur and that the test is how and how far behavior departs from the theory.

card.rule: The test of a general theory is not whether it predicts identical protocols, which it will not, but how and how far real behavior departs from it.
card.limits: The chapter gives no verdict yet; it sets up the comparison, which is made at three levels in the pages that follow.

concepts.title: Three levels of comparison
concepts.question: At which three levels does the chapter compare S3 with the other subjects?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: To see how far the theory carries, the authors compare subjects at three levels instead of redoing the full protocol analysis for each one.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: First, problem spaces: do other subjects work in an augmented space like S3's? Second, episodes: the major features of the search paths. Third, a different cryptarithmetic task, CROSS+ROADS=DANGER, with eye-movement data as a second kind of independent evidence.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: For the second level the authors do not compare protocols line by line. They use diagrams of how episodes are organized in each protocol, enough to diagnose where differences come from.

card.rule: The chapter generalizes along subjects (problem spaces, then episodes) and along tasks (a second puzzle with eye movements).
card.limits: Episode diagrams are a coarse tool; they locate differences but do not explain every detail.

concepts.title: A problem space fixes what intelligence can choose
concepts.question: What does knowing a subject's problem space tell us, even before we know the production system?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: For S3 the authors specified a problem space in detail, the kinds of knowledge that are its elements and the operators for acquiring more, and then described behavior with a production system.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Even without the production system, the space already carries important information about the subject's capabilities. Once the space is fixed, intelligence is limited to choosing among the operations it admits, using the kinds of information it makes available.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors turn to the variety of spaces that are possible for a task and, among those, the ones humans actually use. Chapter 5 had already classified several by entities, relations and predicates.

card.rule: Fixing the problem space fixes the menu of operations; behavior is then a matter of choosing from that menu.
card.limits: The space alone does not say which operation is chosen when; that is what the production system adds.

concepts.title: Operators follow the space, but not in detail
concepts.question: How much of a space's operators does the type of knowledge fix, and what can still vary?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Chapter 5 did not describe the operators of each space separately. The authors now note that the kind of knowledge in a space follows from its states, but still leaves room for variants.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: A letter-digit space needs an operator for adding assignments, but could also have a delete-assignment operator that removes one assignment and keeps the rest, instead of returning to an earlier state. That would change problem solving a great deal. Whether it helps depends on how independent subsets of letters and columns are.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: For the augmented space the four operators PC, AV, GN and TD were argued plausible in Chapter 5, but their detail was left open. TD might be split in two: whether a digit is already used, and whether it fits the letter's known constraints.

card.rule: A space's states suggest its basic operators, yet equally valid variants exist, and the choice can make search better or worse.
card.limits: The authors do not claim any variant is what a subject uses; the point is that the space does not fix operator detail.

concepts.title: Do problem spaces apply to others, and do they vary?
concepts.question: Which two prior questions does the chapter ask about problem spaces of subjects other than S3?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Chapter 5 listed possible spaces for the task. Now the authors turn to how people behave, not to the range of possible spaces.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: They are not yet ready for a full ecological study of how often each space turns up in natural environments. They ask two prior questions: does the problem-space concept apply to problem solving by humans besides S3, and is there enough variation between subjects for the space to be a psychological datum?

blocks.label: Assumed
blocks.text: If a space only reflected the demands of the task, it would tell the psychologist nothing about the person. Variation between people is what makes it informative.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors give a reason, not data: a space that reflected only task demands would tell the psychologist nothing about the person, so variation between people is what makes it informative.

card.rule: Two things must be shown: other people also work in problem spaces, and those spaces differ enough to be informative.
card.limits: The chapter does not claim to establish how common each space is in everyday life.

concepts.title: Bartlett's subject I works in the augmented space
concepts.question: What in Bartlett's subject I shows that he used the augmented problem space?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The augmented space, the one S3 used, seems to be the space most technically educated people use on DONALD+GERALD. Of the eight short written protocols Bartlett (1958) printed, at least five clearly use it.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: A subject is taken to work in the augmented space when its relations (assignment, equality, inequality, parity, disjunction) appear in the protocol and its operators are used on them.

blocks.label: Term
blocks.text: The augmented space has knowledge about letters and carries, in the relations of assignment, equality, inequality, parity and disjunction. Its four operators are PC (process a column), AV (assign a value), GN (generate the digits still possible for a letter) and TD (test a digit against the exclusion rule).

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Subject I's written summary names equality, inequality and parity outright. Assignment is little used, since he infers well, but it appears. Restating his steps in PC, GN, AV and TD shows all four operators at work.

card.rule: Evidence for a subject's space is that the space's relations appear and that its operators are used on them.
card.limits: A written summary is thin data; it shows the space used at least part of the time, not that nothing more powerful was available.

concepts.title: What the protocol evidence cannot show
concepts.question: What can the figures of subjects in the augmented space not show, and why do the authors accept that?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Figure 7.1 shows a subject working at least part of the time in a space that included the augmented one. It does not show that he lacked further inference operations, or that his sophistication was not out of reach at some moments.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Such gaps are tolerated for two reasons. The task is understood well enough that the sufficiency of the reasoning is apparent. And the authors believe, from general experience, that human competence does not fluctuate violently over short periods in nonstressful situations.

blocks.label: Assumed
blocks.text: The second reason is an assumption from general experience, not a finding.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Figure 7.1 shows a subject working at least part of the time in a space that included the augmented one; the authors admit it does not show that he lacked further inference operations.

card.rule: Evidence of a space shows it was used, not that nothing more was available; the gap is covered by understanding the task and by a stated assumption.
card.limits: Where the data are thin, or the assumption of steady competence is doubtful, the conclusion about the space is less secure.

concepts.title: A protocol too obscure to classify
concepts.question: Why is Bartlett's subject VII a case where the evidence is insufficient to say which space was used?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Subject VII's protocol is the most obscure of Bartlett's. He substitutes 5 for D, juggles digits for a while, gives up after about ten minutes, and begins again.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Early on he appears to lack strong inference with PC, since he mostly makes assignments, and there is no evidence of parity, inequality or sets of possible digits. Then he infers that E must be 9 because O plus E has to give the O of ROBERT.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: After that inference he says the numbers seem to fit in easily, identified in the order L, A, R, G. We learn too little about the processes he used for the fitting. The authors move on to their own subjects rather than belabor insufficient data.

card.rule: When a protocol gives no view of how the later steps are made, the space cannot be identified with confidence.
card.limits: The early phase suggests weak PC, but one clear inference cannot be stretched to claim a particular space for the rest.

concepts.title: Which of the authors' subjects used the augmented space
concepts.question: Which of the authors' own subjects work in the augmented space, and which does not?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Besides S3 the authors have complete protocols for four more subjects on DONALD+GERALD, in the same style as S3's: S4, S5, S6 and S8.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: S4, S5 and S8 clearly work in the augmented space. S6 does not, and is discussed later. The protocols of the first three are printed in Appendices 7.1, 7.2 and 7.3.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: For each of the three the authors give a figure of examples: mentions of each kind of knowledge, and uses of the four operators. They pick examples where the knowledge is used as input to an operator, not only produced as output.

card.rule: Three of the four newly analyzed subjects use the augmented space; the fourth, S6, works in something simpler.
card.limits: A figure of illustrations does not prove other spaces were absent; the authors rely on reading the whole protocols.

concepts.title: Examples of each kind of knowledge in S4, S5 and S8
concepts.question: What do the figures show for use of carries, inequalities, parity, disjunctions and the four operators?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: To show a subject works in the augmented space, the authors extract from each protocol one or more lines for every kind of knowledge and every operator.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: S4 on carries: O plus 9 is O, so N plus R must exceed 10. On parity: R must be odd because the two D's add to 10. On disjunction: R is 1 or 2 greater than G. For PC: to have O plus E equal O, E must be 9. For TD: G must be 1, since it is 0 or 1 and T is zero.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: S5 and S8 give the same kinds of lines, for example S8's argument that R is 7 or 9, so L is 3 or 4. S5 tries L as 3, sees R would be 7, tries L as 2, sees R would be 5, which cannot be, and so on. Such trial values are AV.

card.rule: Each kind of knowledge and each operator can be matched to a line of protocol where it is used.
card.limits: Lines are chosen as examples; they do not show every use or that nothing else was used.

concepts.title: Same tools, varied activity
concepts.question: What does sharing the augmented space imply for comparing subjects' strategies?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: That Bartlett's subjects and the authors' S4, S5 and S8 all worked in the augmented space does not mean their activity was identical.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: There was substantial variation in what they did. Sharing a space means they used essentially the same intellectual tools. So it is meaningful to compare their strategies and heuristics.

blocks.label: Assumed
blocks.text: Comparing strategies makes sense only among subjects who share a space. For that reason the strategy analysis later in the chapter is limited to S3, S4, S5 and S8.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Bartlett's subjects and S4, S5 and S8 all worked in the augmented space while showing substantial variation in what they did; the authors therefore limit later strategy analysis to S3, S4, S5 and S8.

card.rule: A shared space gives a common set of tools; what differs between subjects is how they use them, and that can then be compared.
card.limits: Subjects in different spaces, such as S6, cannot be compared on strategy in the same way.

concepts.title: S6: a subject below the augmented space
concepts.question: What kind of subject is S6, and what marks his behavior as different from the other subjects?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors expect some spaces poorer than the augmented one. Their example is S6, an adult without college whose arithmetic and symbolic skills were below the other subjects'. He abandoned the problem unsolved after 25 minutes.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: His protocol is mostly assignments, sometimes interrupted by summing columns whose digits are already assigned. Sums always start from the two upper digits, as in 3 plus 3 giving E. There is no sign of inequalities, digit sets or parity.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: He lets inconsistent assignments stand for long stretches. The experimenter recorded his digits on the display, and column 6 stayed as 5 + 8 = 7 for four minutes. His protocol runs to 130 phrases, numbered B1 to B240.

card.rule: S6 shows a space poorer than the augmented one: assignments, plain sums from the upper digits, and tolerance of inconsistency.
card.limits: Poor arithmetic skill alone does not make a subject a basic-space case; S6 is described from his behavior, not from his schooling.

concepts.title: Firm and tentative columns
concepts.question: How does S6 divide the display, and what does that division tell us about his problem space?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: S6 allows inconsistent assignments to stay. The authors ask what this implies about the space he works in.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: He divides the display in two. The right-hand columns are considered firmly assigned. The columns to the left are tentative. He assigns digits to letters that occur only in the left columns without dealing with the consequences for those columns.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors draw the inference that S6 keeps in mind which columns are definitely assigned and which are tentative. This fact about status is part of his knowledge state, along with the assignments.

card.rule: S6's space includes the status of each column, firm or tentative, not only the letter-digit assignments.
card.limits: The division is inferred from behavior; it is the authors' model of what S6 retains, not something he states.

concepts.title: S6's seven operators
concepts.question: Which seven operators does S6's problem space have, and what does each kind do?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors induce a space for S6 from his protocol. His knowledge state holds the letter-digit assignments plus next-column, along with his current goals and temporary information.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Seven operators: four make assignments (AV assigns an unused digit, MD moves a digit from one letter to another, EX exchanges the digits of two letters, AEX assigns the digit just made free), one processes columns (PC), one tests whether a proposed digit is legitimate (TD), and one retracts a step (BU).

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Table 7.1 counts them over the whole protocol. Of 61 assignments, 49 are AV, 2 are MD, 3 are EX and 7 are AEX. PC occurs 42 times and BU only 4. TD occurs 32 times, 11 by S6 and 21 evoked by the experimenter.

card.rule: S6's space has four assignment operators, PC, TD and BU, and most of his actions are plain AV.
card.limits: The counts come from one protocol and one subject.

concepts.title: From AV to move, exchange and assign-exchanged
concepts.question: Why does S6 develop MD, EX and AEX out of the plain assignment operator?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: S6 reaches a tentative full assignment of digits quickly: nine letters assigned by B30, all ten by B69. From then on, every new assignment must use a digit already in use by another letter.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: He comes to see a new assignment as moving a digit from one letter to another (MD). MD occurs only twice and leads to EX, one operator making two assignments at once, which avoids breaking the rule that each digit goes to one letter. EX leads to AEX: he assigns, lets the experimenter evoke TD, then assigns the digit just freed.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The first MD is at B73 (taking 4 from E and giving it to O). The first EX is at B107, where he announces two assignments at once. The first AEX is at B133, also the time of the last EX.

card.rule: The operators MD, EX and AEX arise because once all ten digits are in use, any new assignment must take a digit from another letter.
card.limits: The chain is the authors' reconstruction from the order of occurrence, not a description the subject gives.

concepts.title: S6's rudimentary column processing
concepts.question: How limited is S6's column processing, and what evidence shows the limit?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: S6 processes columns 42 times. In essentially all cases the two upper digits are given, and in most the lower one as well, so the process is a consistency check.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: His column processing is extremely rudimentary, close to what the basic space offers. When he finds a column that does not check, he can set a letter without noticing the same letter also appears as an upper digit in that column.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: At B88 to B93 he adds right to left on a fully assigned display until column 5 fails. Computing O + E + c5, he sets O to 6 without noticing O is also an upper digit. In four cases he inferred a top letter from a known sum, each taking 10 to 30 seconds; generate-and-test is plausible.

card.rule: S6's PC is little more than adding two given digits and checking the result; it rarely runs backward to find an upper letter.
card.limits: Three of the four backward inferences came in the last minutes before he gave up, which makes them weak evidence of a general skill.

concepts.title: No GN, little testing, almost no backup
concepts.question: Which operators of the augmented space does S6 lack or hardly use, and what replaces them?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The augmented-space subjects generate the digits still possible for a letter (GN), test assignments (TD) and back up to earlier states after failure. The authors check whether S6 does these.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: S6 has no GN: he generates digits in only two other places, in the same circumstances. TD appears explicitly, but the checks are mostly built into his assignment operators or supplied by the experimenter. He almost never backs up; he keeps every digit assigned and reassigns to fix local trouble.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: At B41 S6 had given 7 to both R and N and caught it himself. Backups are rare, with one at B75 clear from his words. In the augmented space trial and error with backup is what makes a PBG interesting; S6 has no structure that lends itself to a graph.

card.rule: S6 replaces generation and backup with continuous reassignment of a fully assigned display, with the experimenter helping to enforce the one-digit rule.
card.limits: The absence of GN and of backup is read from rare occurrences, not from anything S6 says.

concepts.title: The evidence for next-column
concepts.question: What counts as evidence that S6 keeps a firm/tentative boundary in memory?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Next-column is a novel part of S6's space, and the authors claim he keeps it in memory. The evidence is indirect, so they first define it operationally.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Next-column is the first column from the right that contains an undefined letter or an inconsistency, not counting inconsistencies that depend on carries into or out of neighbors. Letters to its right are firm; all others are tentative.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Of 27 conflicts between a firm and a tentative letter, the tentative one was changed in 22. All four backups followed a breach of this rule. In 13 cases he made next-column consistent as far as his PC allowed, and 18 of 21 inconsistencies he found were in next-column.

card.rule: S6's choices fit the next-column rule: he changes tentative letters before firm ones, and finds inconsistencies in next-column.
card.limits: The rule is inferred from regularities, not from anything S6 says, and sometimes the result is not objectively correct.

concepts.title: Why S6 matters
concepts.question: Why do the authors spend so much space on S6's problem space?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The augmented space will seem natural to most readers. The authors want to show that humans work in other spaces too.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: They have been explicit about S6's space and the evidence for it for two reasons: to document spaces other than the augmented one, and to emphasize that much is known about a problem solver's power once his space is known.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: S6's problem can be solved in his space, but not easily: the solution needs extensive search. His rudimentary column processing and absent backup show why.

card.rule: S6 documents that spaces differ among people, and that knowing the space tells how hard the task is for that person.
card.limits: S6 is one subject; the authors do not claim his space is typical of any group.

concepts.title: S8's search for a way in
concepts.question: What did S8 do in the 25 minutes before he settled on the augmented space?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: S8 had just solved AA+BB=CBC by fairly exhaustive search among equal-digit numbers such as 11, 22, 33. Faced with LETS+WAVE=LATER he judged those techniques inapplicable and searched widely.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: He tries to characterize the task in some way, for example as adding two four-digit numbers to get a five-digit number, and sees whether that evokes a method. If so, he judges feasibility. If the verdict is negative, as it usually is, he looks for a new characterization or returns to an earlier method.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In about 25 minutes he generated fourteen methods using seven different problem spaces. He grew discouraged, but began trial assignments once he realized the problem might have many solutions, one of which he could find by starting anywhere. He then used the augmented space, and continued with it on DONALD+GERALD.

card.rule: S8's prelude is a search for a problem space: characterize, evoke a method, test feasibility, and try again.
card.limits: S8 does not describe it as a search for a space; the authors read it as one because each method implies a definite space.

concepts.title: A side result from the search
concepts.question: What useful problem information did S8 derive during his search, and why did he derive it?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: S8 sometimes derives significant problem information during his search, though not as a direct attempt to solve the puzzle.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: He settles whether a carry can be greater than 1 (it cannot). He does so as a subtask in judging an approach: adding up the vertical columns, which he considers hopeless if the carry is unknown.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: He sums up his thinking on column 2: either T and V, or T plus V plus 1, gives either E or a number whose second digit is E. He adds that one could start eliminating on this basis.

card.rule: Information found while evaluating a method counts as a by-product of the search for a space.
card.limits: S8 does not follow up this by-product; he sets it aside until he enters the augmented space.

concepts.title: The seven spaces S8 found
concepts.question: Which seven problem spaces did S8 consider, and in what order do the authors discuss them?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: S8's prelude is a rich source of data on problem spaces in cryptarithmetic. Figure 7.8 extracts the seven spaces he came across.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The authors list them from most familiar to least: basic, augmented, number, algebra, word-meaning, cryptogram and typographical. S8 met them in a different order.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The basic and augmented spaces need no further discussion. S8 refers to the basic space and wants no part of it: random substitution of numbers for letters would take enormous time or a machine. For each of the other five the authors give elements, operators, initial and final elements.

card.rule: The seven spaces run from the familiar letter-digit spaces to novel ones based on numbers, equations, meanings, rules and letter shapes.
card.limits: The order of the list is the authors' choice of presentation, not the order in which S8 thought of them.

concepts.title: The number space
concepts.question: What is the number problem space, and where did S8 use it?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A solver can view each word as a number, so WAVE is a four-digit number in the thousands, and look for a way to limit the admissible values so that instances can be generated.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Its element is a set of three numbers, one per word. Its operators obtain another number that fits a word's pattern, as ABAB yields 1212, 1313, 2323, taking account of excluded and forced values, and test whether the three numbers satisfy the addition test.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: S8 used it almost exclusively on AA+BB=CBC, ruling out equal-digit pairs one after another. On LETS+WAVE=LATER it gets him nowhere: the letters of the words show no pattern.

card.rule: The number space treats words as numbers and generates candidates by pattern; it works when words have a repeated-letter pattern.
card.limits: With distinct letters such as L, E, T, S, the pattern gives no handle, so S8 gets nowhere with it on LETS+WAVE.

concepts.title: The algebra space and why S8 gave it up
concepts.question: What is the algebra space, and what kept S8 from using it?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Chapter 5 defined the algebra space and used it for a parsimonious solution of DONALD+GERALD. In the protocols the authors have, it does not show up much.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: It represents the carries by variables, writes one equation per column, and manipulates the equations by substitution, addition and subtraction. Subjects usually approach its formulation and back off as too difficult.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: S8 tries twice. He cannot see how to represent the carries explicitly, and he holds that the number of unknowns should not exceed the number of equations. The authors say the space is beyond his sophistication (a college undergraduate), though if it were set up for him he could probably maneuver in it.

card.rule: The algebra space is compact, but it requires inventing explicit carry variables and tolerating more unknowns than equations.
card.limits: The authors' conclusion rests on one subject's remarks; it is not a general claim that no one can use algebra here.

concepts.title: The word-meaning space
concepts.question: Why might word meanings be a source of information in cryptarithmetic, and why did S8 reject them?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: It is an irrelevant feature that cryptarithmetic problems use patterns of letters that make English words. Any other set of distinct variables would do as well, so LETS+WAVE=LATER is essentially the same problem as one written with other symbols.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: When English words are used they could be a source of information, and the prevalence of anagram problems makes this plausible. If BILL leads to William, then to William the Conqueror, then to 1066, then in BILL+WAS=KING B is 1, I is 0 and L is 6.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: S8 tried several times to build such a space and always failed: he judged that the words LETS, WAVE and LATER would give no clue to any four- or five-digit numbers. The authors think it is a problem space (elements are words with meanings, operators search long-term memory) but do not press the point.

card.rule: Word meanings can in principle supply numbers by associations, so they define a possible space whose operators search long-term memory.
card.limits: The authors lack data and a model of long-term memory to settle whether this is a problem space; they only sketch it.

concepts.title: The cryptogram space: searching for a rule
concepts.question: What are the elements and operators of the cryptogram space, and who searched in it?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A solver might look for a single rule that gives every letter a unique digit, the simplest being A=1, B=2, C=3. Once the rule is found, one writes the correspondences and checks the sum.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Its elements are rules, functions from letters to digits, expressed in some language. Operators build new rules in that language. A few come directly from memory, such as assigning the integer i to the i-th letter. The rest must be constructed.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: S8 searched for such a rule twice: first the simple alphabet rule, then counting from the front or the end of the alphabet, which fails when L would be 12. Bartlett's subject VI wrote down two coding rules.

card.rule: The cryptogram space searches rules that map letters to digits; the plausibility rests on each letter getting a different digit.
card.limits: No such rule exists for LETS+WAVE, so the search cannot succeed; the space is still a genuine one by the authors' definition.

concepts.title: The typographical space
concepts.question: What does the typographical space search for, and why is it the hardest to put in space form?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A solver might hope that letters look like the digits they stand for, an onomatopoetic approach.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Its search is for a mapping from typographical features of letters to digits, such as E looks like 3 or S like 2, with operators that select ways of viewing letters (symmetry as in E and 3, deletion as in H and 4).

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: S8 states the idea, tests it through the digits up to 7, and sees it will not go far. Of all the approaches this one is the least easily put in the form of a problem space. The authors point to the EPAM program, which uses features to discriminate letters.

card.rule: The typographical space searches for visual resemblances between letters and digits, which the authors can sketch only loosely.
card.limits: It is the least formalizable of the seven spaces; the authors only suggest how a search over similarity criteria might be modeled.

concepts.title: What the survey of spaces is for
concepts.question: What two purposes do the authors give for surveying the problem spaces?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors have looked at a number of problem spaces, all arising in humans' attempts at cryptarithmetic. Some have extended evidence and some are sketched. Several, mainly the briefly noted ones, cannot support successful solving of this task, in the experimenters' belief.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Their first purpose is to stress the psychological reality and usefulness of the concept: other subjects than S3 work in problem spaces, and the spaces vary. Their second is to show that, for this class of problem, the problem space comes close to being a definition of the situation or world view.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: A problem space precisely identifies what the subject knows, what intellectual tools he has, and what he will extract from the situation.

card.rule: A problem space comes close to a subject's definition of the situation: it fixes what he knows, can do, and will extract.
card.limits: The point is made for this class of problem and for gross features of behavior, not for every task.

concepts.title: How stable is a problem space?
concepts.question: What do the authors admit they have not shown about the stability of a subject's problem space?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Nothing so far deals with whether a subject's problem space is stable.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The authors have not shown that a subject must stay in a given space. They have not shown that even a small hint, such as noting that R is odd and suggesting he use such information, would not change his space for the rest of the task.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: What is shown is that, in these tasks, the problem space is a useful construct for describing gross features of a subject's behavior.

card.rule: The chapter shows the problem space is useful for gross features of behavior, not that it is fixed or unchangeable.
card.limits: A hint might change the space; the authors have no evidence either way.

concepts.title: S3's problem-solving strategy in five points
concepts.question: Beyond the problem space, what five strategic habits did S3 show on DONALD+GERALD?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Knowing a subject's problem space tells only part of the story. Large variations in behavior and performance remain to be explained, so the authors extract from S3's production system the main strategic features, ignoring what the space itself determines.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: S3 (1) attended to whatever columns were relevant to the subgoal at hand (partly FC), (2) tried to exploit new information when he got it (P1), (3) tried to obtain information when he lacked it (P2), (4) backed off to the last prior state not disconfirmed when he reached a dead end (P12), and (5) checked every new piece of information for consistency with earlier assignments (P11).

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The list does not exhaust the productions' implications but shows what they contain. Chapter 6 showed limits to S3's obedience: a failure to evoke TD on E equal to 0 accounts for much of the inadequacy in his problem solving.

card.rule: S3's strategy: look at the relevant columns, use new information, seek missing information, back off from dead ends, and check consistency.
card.limits: S3 did not follow these habits perfectly; his departures, such as the missed TD on E equal to 0, explain much of his difficulty.

concepts.title: Two questions about strategies, one aggregate method
concepts.question: Which two questions about strategies do the authors ask, and why use a more aggregated analysis?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors ask to what extent other subjects use the same strategies as S3 and how they differ. They also ask to what extent the strategies are demanded by the task and to what extent they are psychological.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: To keep the comparison fair they limit it to subjects in the same problem space: S3, S4, S5 and S8. They analyze at a more aggregated level than S3's protocol analysis, for three reasons.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: (1) The production system does not always reveal as clearly as possible the role of the task environment. (2) Building a production system takes substantial effort; the alternative technique is easier and still captures much. (3) They wish to introduce as many tools as possible, since different tools serve different purposes at different costs.

card.rule: The analysis asks which strategies are demanded by the task and which are psychological, using a cheaper aggregated method on four subjects.
card.limits: An aggregated analysis loses detail; the authors do not claim it replaces the production system.

concepts.title: What counts as obvious
concepts.question: How do the task and the subject's intelligence together determine what is obvious?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: In Chapter 3 the authors defined invariances of the task environment: aspects that any problem solver must take into account to solve the problem. They also introduced intelligence as an upper and lower limit on what is available.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Given an upper limit on intelligence, some aspects of the task become invariant and show in all successful solvers below that limit; paths without them would need higher intelligence, such as inventing a new mathematics. Given a lower limit, some aspects become obvious: assumed to be discovered readily by all solvers above it.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Episodes are intervals when a solver is doing the obvious things in this sense. An episode's boundary is reached when he must do something not obvious to him. Chapter 3 illustrated this with everyday examples but did not make it operational; the chapter now does so for cryptarithmetic.

card.rule: Obvious is relative to the solver's intelligence, and an episode is a stretch of behavior made up of obvious moves.
card.limits: Chapter 3's treatment was not operational; the working definition of obvious comes only in the next ideas.

concepts.title: The operational rule for obviousness
concepts.question: What is the authors' operational assumption that makes a move obvious in the augmented space?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors need an operational meaning for obvious. It starts from the problem space: a subject in the augmented space who wants the digits available for a letter simply applies GN, while a subject in a poorer space might have to account for every assigned value.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: In every cryptarithmetic task the global goal is to accumulate knowledge about assignments, so there is a gradient from no information to complete, proven knowledge. It has little direction in problematic situations, such as whether R should be 7 or 9, but great direction when knowledge is available for the asking. The assumption: any immediate node from a given node that adds validated knowledge is obvious.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Nodes produced by PC, TD and GN can yield validated new information, true if the knowledge at the starting node is true. Nodes produced by AV give only the possibility of it later. So a solver acquires information one step away but does not see across a boundary of conjecture.

card.rule: A move is obvious when it adds validated knowledge in one step; assigning a value is not obvious, since it only conjectures.
card.limits: The solver may cross conjectural boundaries, but those crossings are his decisions and are what the analysis wants to observe.

concepts.title: Potential episodes and their heads
concepts.question: How do the authors divide a problem space into potential episodes, and what is an episode's head?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: With the obviousness rule the authors can cut the augmented space into potential episodes.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Connect each node to the nodes obvious from it. One and only one of these nodes, the one containing the most information, is the head of the episode. It holds the information that any subject entering the episode at all will obtain.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Movement from entry to head is then an obvious response to a demand of the task, because any rational man would acquire this information. So within-episode detail can be ignored and analysis can concentrate on moves from episode to episode.

card.rule: An episode runs from an entry node to its head, the node with the most information; analysis follows the moves between episodes.
card.limits: A degree-n notion of obviousness, seeing n conjectural steps ahead, would be an artificial measure like assuming chess players look ahead a fixed number of moves.

concepts.title: Testing the obviousness assumption
concepts.question: Why is the obviousness assumption an empirical claim, and which subject fails it?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors say they are making an empirical assertion: no subject who works in the augmented space is blind to opportunities for immediate gain of knowledge.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: If the claim is false, it will show in the protocols and the definition of obvious will have to change. S3 meets the condition in the main. S6 does not, since he left columns with obvious inferences untouched, such as column 2 with 3 + 3 = R, but he works in a version of the basic space, so a different criterion may be needed.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In production terms the assumption says that productions P1, P7, P11 and P12 are in every subject's program: the ways S3 responds at once to new information to derive further new information.

card.rule: The obviousness assumption is testable: a subject in the augmented space who leaves one-step inferences untouched would falsify it.
card.limits: S6 is not a counterexample to the claim for the augmented space, since he is not in it.

concepts.title: Columns as information sources
concepts.question: How does the structure of DONALD+GERALD make a chain of inferences an episode?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: To reanalyze S3 in episodes, the authors review the structure of the task in Figure 7.11. There are six columns, each imposing constraints on a subset of the variables.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Picture each column as an information source, a node, with lines linking it to the variables it constrains. A subject starts at any node and tries to get new information. If he succeeds he can move to any other node affected by it. The assumption is that he keeps going until no more information can be inferred; such a sequence is an episode.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Episodes are generated by assuming a state of knowledge, starting at the matching node and tracing the inferences until all obvious information has been produced. Doing this for all states would give an objective map of potential episodes against which a subject's behavior can be examined.

card.rule: The task is a network of columns linked by shared letters; an episode is a run of inferences through that network until nothing more follows.
card.limits: The figure shows column constraints only; the rule that no two letters share a digit is not drawn in it.

concepts.title: The exclusion rule and the limits of the episode map
concepts.question: Which source of information is missing from the column diagram, and how does the augmented space handle it?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The one source not shown in Figure 7.11 is the exclusiveness of assignments. Its obvious form says no two letters get the same digit. Less obvious forms exist.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: An example of a subtler form: digits greater than five cannot go to more than four letters. Chapter 5 explored a space using abstracted values (above or below five, even or odd) to make such inferences. In the augmented space they can come only through TD and GN.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: TD makes the elementary check whether a digit is available or outside the letter's range. GN considers only the variable's range and digits already assigned. So the authors ignore subtler inferences in defining episode boundaries, but would revise the definition of obviousness if such inferences were routinely made.

card.rule: Exclusion enters the augmented space only through TD and GN, so subtle exclusion inferences are left out of the episode boundaries.
card.limits: If users of the augmented space routinely made the subtler inferences, the definition of obviousness would need revising.

concepts.title: Episode schemas for DONALD+GERALD
concepts.question: What are episode schemas, and what does schema 1-2-6 contain?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Mapping every episode would be wasteful, since many sequences follow the same line of reasoning in Figure 7.11. The authors keep only the characteristic types, which they call episode schemas.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Figure 7.12 shows the main schemas, ignoring the given fact D set to 5, which they regard as adventitious. Each is labeled by the columns processed. Schema 1-2-6 starts from the assumption that D exceeds 5, infers in column 1 that T is even, in column 2 that R is odd, in column 6 that R exceeds 5, hence R is 7 or 9, and finally that G is below 5.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Starting from D set to 5 adds the knowledge that T is 0. That refines schema 5-3 by removing the possibility E equal to 0, leading on to schema 5-3-2-4-6 for L, G, B and N. Schema 2-6 yields all the remaining information except the final resolution of B, N and O, which needs a small trial and error search.

card.rule: Episode schemas are the characteristic inference chains of the task, named by the columns they pass through, such as 1-2-6.
card.limits: The schemas assume particular orderings of column inferences; other orderings are possible, so a schema is a pattern, not a fixed script.

concepts.title: Episodes as demands of the task
concepts.question: What can episodes in a protocol tell us about the subject, and what can they not?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The schemas represent the demands of the task environment for problem solvers working in the augmented space. Elements of all of them are needed to solve the problem. For example, E equal to 9 must be reached somehow, by inference or by assignment.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Once a subject enters any episode he runs through to its end, because the steps are obvious. So when episodes appear in behavior, we see the task's demands reflected. We learn only that the subject has reached a certain level of adaptivity to the environment, assuming adequate motivation.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The ordering of inferences in Figure 7.12 is the one reached when D set to 5 is processed first, followed by the critical fifth column. Many orderings are possible, especially once a correct value is assigned: with L set to 8 it follows that R is 7, G is 1, c3 is 1, E is odd and so E is not 0.

card.rule: Episodes mostly show what the task demands; the subject's own differences appear in which episodes he starts and in his errors.
card.limits: The claim assumes adequate motivation and that the subject is in the augmented space.

concepts.title: The episode abstract
concepts.question: What does an episode abstract record, and how does it relate to the problem behavior graph?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors call a description of behavior in terms of episodes an episode abstract. For S3 the abstract is Figure 7.13, with each line one episode.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The columns give: where the episode begins in the protocol (B-number), the episode's name (E-number), the new presuppositions or facts that bring the subject in, the matching schema from Figure 7.12, and a description of the episode. A few intervals that are not episodes, mainly rehearsals and repetitions, are noted in brackets.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Compared with the full problem behavior graph (Figure 6.4), the two correspond well. Episodes are long advances with short backups, and a new episode can usually be detected when the subject retreats to a prior base state of knowledge. Rehearsals inside an episode are not shown separately.

card.rule: An episode abstract compresses a protocol into labeled episodes, showing the logical structure without every step.
card.limits: Not all rehearsals are shown; the abstract aims only at the logical structure of the information generated.

concepts.title: S3 reanalyzed: task-determined and error-driven
concepts.question: Which parts of S3's protocol are fixed by the task and which by his error?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors check whether the episode abstract of S3 (Figure 7.13) tells the same story as the full analysis of Chapter 6.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Two portions correspond almost literally to the principal schemas: the beginning, E1 to E4, up to the point where S3 wrongly concludes that c3 is 0, and the end, E16 to E19, after the experimenter's intervention. These contain substantially all the analysis needed, so they are task-determined.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The middle, when S3 struggles with contradictions from his error, follows the same principal sequences with two changes: the erroneous premise c3 equal to 0 is added, and the forgotten fact T equal to 0 is omitted. That is why the middle can be described parsimoniously.

card.rule: S3's protocol is task-determined at its start and end; the middle is the same reasoning run under a false premise.
card.limits: The middle is described by the same schemas, but the error itself, the c3 equal to 0 premise, is not predicted by the theory.

concepts.title: Inside S3's error middle
concepts.question: How do the two schemas alternate in the middle of S3's protocol, and why can S3 not escape?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: In the middle of S3's protocol his erroneous premise c3 equal to 0 and the omitted T equal to 0 cause repeated contradictions.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: In E5, E7, E9 and E12 he follows schema 1-2-6: once to work out the consequences of R set to 7, twice to check earlier facts about R, and last for R set to 9. In the last case 5-3 follows 1-2-6 and ends in a contradiction. In E6, E8, E11, E13 and E14 he follows 5-3, in the first case until E even is derived and in the other three until a contradiction.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Each contradiction leads him to change his held value of E or his assumed value of R. All involve, directly or indirectly, that E even forces A equal to 5 in column 3, which conflicts with D equal to 5. He cannot give up E even, since c3 equal to 0 is held true.

card.rule: S3 cannot escape because the false belief c3 equal to 0 keeps forcing E even, which collides with D equal to 5.
card.limits: The contradiction is traced to the premise only after the experimenter's intervention; before that S3 changes E or R instead.

concepts.title: S4: the most direct route
concepts.question: How did S4 reach the solution so directly, and where did he nearly go wrong?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: S4 was the most efficient of the five subjects on DONALD+GERALD, taking about ten minutes. The brevity of his episode abstract (Figure 7.14) shows the directness of his route.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: After column 1 he considers L as 3 by schema 1-2-6, ignoring the carry c2, and concludes that G is 1. From column 6 he notices the solution for column 5 and follows path 5-3 back to columns 3 and 2. In E4, with column 4 drawing attention to R, he finds R is 7 by 1-2-6, using E equal to 9 to remove the alternative.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In E5 he checks his entries from right to left. L equal to 3 is still on the display, which gives E equal to 8 in column 3, and he finds the contradiction at column 5. Retracing by schema 5-3 (E5, E6) he corrects L to 8 and then reaches the remaining values, working right to left.

card.rule: S4 went by task-demanded episodes, with one slip that a right-to-left check exposed.
card.limits: S4's slip is the same one S3 made; the difference in outcome is in recovery, not in the error.

concepts.title: Why S4 recovered faster than S3
concepts.question: Why could S4 recover from the shared L equal to 3 slip much faster than S3?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Both subjects left the tentative value L equal to 3 on the display, but S4 recovered much more rapidly than S3.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The authors speculate that S4 remembered T equal to 0 when processing column 5, so he reached the definite conclusion E equal to 9 instead of the alternative E equal to 9 or 0. Knowing E equal to 9, he inferred R equal to 7 definitely. In his first exploration of schema 5-3 (E3) he followed the path to L above 5 in column 2 even with L equal to 3 on the display, apparently remembering the value was tentative.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: S3 faced several alternatives (E equal to 0 or 9, R equal to 7 or 9), which made it harder to fix on one source of the contradiction. The authors conclude that small but crucial differences in memory of previous results had a large effect on ease of recovery.

card.rule: Recovery from a shared error depends on what the subject remembers: definite facts shrink the set of alternatives.
card.limits: The explanation is the authors' speculation from the protocols, not something shown by direct memory tests.

concepts.title: S5's O equal to 1 error
concepts.question: How did S5 come to infer wrongly that O equals 1?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: S5 worked from right to left even more readily than S4, assigning R, inferring L, assigning A (E2 to E4). In E3 he made the same mistake as S3 and S4 (R equal to 7 gives L equal to 3), but it caused no later trouble.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: In E4 he correctly infers E equal to 9 and at the same time wrongly infers O equal to 1. This begins apparent contradictions from E6 through E21. It is another confusion between necessary and sufficient conditions.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: He processes column 5 from the top down, trying values for O and then for E. He rejects O equal to 0 because T is 0, then tries O equal to 1 and finds it satisfactory provided E is 9. He never explores other values of O, so never finds that O equal to 1 is not necessary.

card.rule: Finding one value that works (sufficient) is not finding the only value that works (necessary); S5 treated the first as the second.
card.limits: O equal to 1 is possible for column 5 but not required; the solution has O equal to 2.

concepts.title: How the error spreads through S5's protocol
concepts.question: How long did S5's false belief O equal to 1 mislead him, and how was it found?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Holding E equal to 9, S5 follows schema 3-2 back to column 2 and tries values 6, 7 and 8 for L, since L above 5 has been inferred.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: For each L he works from right to left trying to complete columns 4 and 6 with the remaining digits. Because O is taken as 1, each attempt ends in a contradiction. He repeats this twice (E6 to E7, E10 to E11). Then he tries R as 7 and as 9, using the wrong inference that L is 3 or 4, and again meets contradictions (E14 to E18).

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: At last he reexamines column 5 carefully (E19, E20), discovers the error and finds the solution. In E7, which should have led to the solution, the contradiction arises because 1 is already assigned to O, so only 2 remains for G in column 6.

card.rule: A wrong belief taken from one column poisoned many later attempts until a careful recheck of that column cleared it.
card.limits: The error's source, column 5, was not visited again until the end, which is why the middle was long.

concepts.title: S5's five tags for expressions
concepts.question: What five tags does S5 attach to an expression, and what do they mean?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: S5 handles conflicts in a way that looks unsystematic, but he has a consistent scheme. The authors say he distinguishes assignments from inferences, and truly known information from two kinds of inference.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: S5 keeps a consistent scheme: he tags each expression by how he obtained it, separating assignments from inferences and truly known facts from two kinds of inference.

blocks.label: Term
blocks.text: Each expression has one of five tags: a (assignment), da (derived from an assignment), df (derived from a fact), de (derived by exhaustion) and f (fact). An assignment has the form letter arrow digit. A fact is given directly on the display or by the experimenter, such as D equal to 5, c7 equal to 0 and O plus E equal to O.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Things derived from facts, however immediately, are df, such as T equal to 0 or E equal to 0 or 9. Derivation by exhaustion is, for instance, R equal to 9 when R is 7 or 9 and R set to 7 has led to contradictions. The classes da, df and de are hereditary: anything derived from a df expression is df, and S5 does not grade expressions by number of inference steps.

card.rule: S5 sorts what he holds into assignments, inferences from assignments, inferences from facts, inferences by exhaustion, and facts.
card.limits: The tags are the authors' reconstruction of S5's scheme; S5 does not state them.

concepts.title: S5's rule for settling conflicts
concepts.question: Which of two conflicting expressions does S5 reject?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: S5 faces 58 conflicts between pairs of expressions. Direct perusal makes his choices look haphazard, since sometimes he rejects the newly evoked one and sometimes the one established earlier.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: His decision rule is to reject the expression higher in the order a, da, df, de, f. So assignments yield to anything, expressions derived from assignments yield to those derived from facts, and knowledge derived from facts loses to knowledge derived by exhaustion. If the two belong to the same category he rejects the more recent.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Of 54 decisions between different categories, 47 (87 percent) agree with the rule. All four decisions within one category agree with rejecting the most recent. The authors credit R. Van Horn with first uncovering S5's consistent reaction.

card.rule: S5 gives up the less well-grounded expression: assignment, then derived-from-assignment, then derived-from-fact, with exhaustion above them.
card.limits: The rule describes S5; it is part of his program, not a law of problem solving, and can be overruled.

concepts.title: Exceptions and why rules are not absolute
concepts.question: What do S5's exceptions to his decision rule show about rules in a problem solver's program?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Seven of S5's 54 cross-category decisions go against the rule. Six of the seven were retracted almost at once.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Some are explorations of extremes. At B458 and B460 he tries L set to 0, first dropping T equal to 0 and then questioning the experimenter on D equal to 5. At B167 he rejects c6 equal to 1, that is E equal to 9, for a moment to see if E set to 8 could save a complete assignment, concludes it cannot, and abandons the line.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The one exception not retracted quickly (B421) rejects R equal to 9 (de) in favor of E equal to 9 (df). It came when column 5 was studied with unusual care and S5 had his back against the wall, right after rejecting E equal to 9 for R equal to 9. This was the time to abandon the principle.

card.rule: A decision rule belongs to the problem solver's program, not his structure, so it can be overruled and its exceptions may carry information.
card.limits: The authors read this exception as a higher rule coming into play; that reading is their interpretation.

concepts.title: S5 and S3 share the same underlying processes
concepts.question: Why do the authors say S5's and S3's different-looking protocols have the same underlying processes?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Superficially the search paths of S5 and S3 differ greatly.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Underneath they are basically the same. Both preoccupy themselves with schemas 2-6-5 and 5-3. Their long middle segments differ because each rests on a different error: S3's c3 equal to 0 and S5's O equal to 1.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Like S3, S5 sometimes rehearses derived facts when in difficulty (E15, E18). Each is faced with several alternatives and a long fallible line of reasoning, so each has trouble pinpointing the source of the contradiction. While not sure all possibilities were tried, he explores alternatives more or less systematically; once convinced all alternatives hit a genuine contradiction, he identifies it fairly rapidly.

card.rule: Same processes, different errors: paths diverge because of what each subject got wrong, not because of different programs.
