card.limits: The claim rests on the schemas and difficulties matching; it does not show the programs are identical in detail.

concepts.title: S8: working right to left
concepts.question: How did S8 search for most of his protocol, and what did he use to limit his search?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: S8 took even longer than the others, nearly an hour, to solve DONALD+GERALD. Like them, he first determined that R is 7 or 9, by schema 2-6.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: After that he showed an even stronger propensity than S5 to work from right to left, as in doing a real arithmetic sum. He assigns R and infers L, or the reverse, and then tries alternative values for A in column 3, beginning with 1 and working systematically upward.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The only fact he uses to make the search more selective is that R is 7 or 9. He systematically tries all admissible assignments of the letters, with considerable difficulty keeping in memory where he is and which alternatives he has tried.

card.rule: S8 searched systematically from the right, trying A upward from 1 under the single restriction that R is 7 or 9.
card.limits: He did use the column-selection reasoning at the start and end; the right-to-left search is the middle of his protocol.

concepts.title: S8's switch to column selection
concepts.question: What made S8 drop his right-to-left search?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: S8's right-to-left phase seldom came to column 5. Once he deduced the crucial fact that E is 9 (E22) he changed course.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: He abandons the right-to-left forward search for the select-column reasoning that the other subjects used and reaches the answer almost at once. The essential parts of his reasoning are E1 and E2 (schema 1-6-2) and E22 and E23 (schema 5-3-2).

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: These essential parts are almost the same as the essential parts of the three protocols analyzed before. His difficulties did not arise mainly from errors producing apparent contradictions.

card.rule: Once E equal to 9 is known, S8 abandons trial and reasons by column, as the other subjects did throughout.
card.limits: Why he handled column 5 differently on the occasion he finally reasoned from it is not explained by the protocol.

concepts.title: Why S8 took so long
concepts.question: Where did S8's difficulties come from, if not from errors?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: S8 made the usual error, R equal to 7 implies L equal to 3, in E2, but corrected it in E8, so it did no harm. His difficulties did not arise mainly from errors that led to apparent contradictions.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: He stuck so systematically to his right-to-left search that he seldom came to column 5. When he did, he came with a value for E assigned earlier from column 3. Given several iffy assumptions at any moment, he had no reason to localize an error in that assignment.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: His one important unsystematic act came the third time he reached column 5: he took seriously its special property, that O plus E gives O. The protocol gives no convincing reason why he treated it that way on that occasion.

card.rule: S8's delay came from the strategy itself, which kept him away from column 5, not from false beliefs.
card.limits: The protocol does not explain the third visit; the authors do not guess.

concepts.title: S8's three cases and his bad luck
concepts.question: Which three cases did S8's strategy require, and how did he choose their order?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: In one sense S8 had bad luck. His strategy required him to consider three major cases (E7).

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The cases were R equal to 7 with L equal to 3, R equal to 7 with L equal to 8, and R equal to 9 with L equal to 4. Because R equal to 7 allowed two values for L and R equal to 9 only one, he reasonably chose to explore R equal to 9 first (E10 to E17).

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Since 3 precedes 8 in digit order, he explored L equal to 3 before L equal to 8 (E18 to E23). The correct case, L equal to 8, came last. Even without the E equal to 9 inference at E22 he would eventually have found the answer, if no mistake had occurred.

card.rule: S8 ordered cases by number of alternatives and digit order, and the true case came last, so his search was long.
card.limits: A different order would have found the answer sooner; the length reflects luck in ordering, not weaker reasoning.

concepts.title: What the four subjects share
concepts.question: In what ways do S3, S4, S5 and S8 resemble each other, despite different paths?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The four subjects (S4, S3, S5, S8) took noticeably different courses, yet their programs show close resemblances.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: All four had the necessary arithmetic knowledge, though not beyond mistaken inferences. All had both the column-selection strategy and right-to-left search strategies, with different readiness to use each. All preferred column selection, which solves for the unknowns one by one as in simultaneous equations. All eventually recognized the central importance of E equal to 9.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: All four showed severe limits in the amount of information they could retain, and some of their difficulties trace to these limits. They retained derived properties of the letters better than they retained a memory of the path used to reach an inference.

card.rule: The four share arithmetic, both strategies, a preference for column selection, the key inference E equal to 9, and tight limits on memory.
card.limits: These are resemblances in programs, not identical paths; priorities and errors differ.

concepts.title: Two sources of path differences
concepts.question: What two things account for almost all the differences in the subjects' paths?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The four protocols differ in course, but the authors say the divergence does not imply fundamental differences in the governing programs.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: It is not difficult to build a common program that produces protocols resembling any of the four through minor variations in priority and in the breadth of the inferences drawn. The differences in paths are accounted for almost entirely by (1) differential priorities for the several strategies and (2) differences in the particular errors of reasoning or memory committed.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors have only rudimentary indications of what causes the errors. They say the component processes and the range of component strategies appear largely alike in all four cases.

card.rule: Different paths come from different priorities among shared strategies and from different particular errors, not from different programs.
card.limits: The causes of the errors are not known; the authors have only rudimentary indications.

concepts.title: Four simulated variants of one program
concepts.question: What do the four simulated abstracts (alpha, beta, gamma, delta) show?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: To show that one program can yield several subjects' paths, the authors give episode abstracts for four versions of a simple program (Figure 7.18).

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The common rules: follow FC whenever any information is produced, so an episode runs to its limit. An episode ends when no more can be inferred or a letter's value comes by exhaustion. With no specific instigator, the program scans right to left to find next-column, and assignments are made for letters in next-column.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Version alpha makes no trial assignments and resembles S4. Beta explores a letter's values when narrowed to two or fewer, and resembles S3. Gamma degrades beta by ignoring a possible carry into column 3, which gives the erroneous L equal to 3 and L equal to 4, and by discarding information from a failed branch, so it resembles S3 more. Delta cannot infer E equal to 9, allows assignment to any letter, and resembles S8.

card.rule: Small changes to one program, such as restricting assignments or degrading reasoning, give paths like S4, S3 and S8.
card.limits: Delta differs from S8 in starting with R equal to 7 and L equal to 3, and it is S8, not delta, who finally found E equal to 9.

concepts.title: Small causes, divergent paths
concepts.question: What general lesson do the authors draw from the simulations about comparing subjects' paths?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The simulations are simple and rather rigid, yet small parametric changes give a range of individual differences that correspond well with the differences among the subjects.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The lesson is that in large combinatorial spaces, small causes can bring about great divergences between search paths. So comparing temporal sequences in behavior directly may exaggerate the underlying differences among the programs that generate it.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The commonalities can be found by inducing a family of programs rich enough in capacity for minor variation to produce a number of different paths. The four subjects' protocols and the four simulated abstracts show this.

card.rule: Different search paths do not imply different programs, because in a large search space a tiny difference can send the search far away.
card.limits: This is the authors' conclusion from four simulations and four subjects; it does not show that no real program differences exist.

concepts.title: Testing the theory on a second task
concepts.question: Why do the authors turn to CROSS+ROADS=DANGER, and who attempted it?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: So far the chapter uses a single task. The authors say this is less severe a limit than it seems, because they did not treat the task as an unanalyzed variable against which to plot behavior, as in intelligence testing or work on functional fixity or the Einstellung effect.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: They tried to find the specific mechanisms producing each bit of task-oriented behavior. If the theory is any good, these mechanisms should work the same way on any cryptarithmetic task. It would still be comforting to verify this on a new task.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The new task is CROSS+ROADS=DANGER. S4 solved it immediately after a ten-minute break following DONALD+GERALD, and another subject, S2, attempted it. S2's main interest is his eye-movement data.

card.rule: A theory built from mechanisms, not from task scores, can be tested by showing the same mechanisms on another task.
card.limits: Two subjects on one new task is a small check, which the authors call comforting, not conclusive.

concepts.title: The structure of CROSS+ROADS
concepts.question: What makes CROSS+ROADS=DANGER harder than DONALD+GERALD, and where does inference stall?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors judge CROSS+ROADS somewhat harder, because no key step unlocks the puzzle the way E equal to 9 did for DONALD+GERALD.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Progress is easy at first. S4 was given R set to 6 as a start, just as he was given D set to 5 earlier, and columns 1 and 2 give full information. But there is no way to extract general information from the three left-hand columns, even though R, O and A each occur more than once.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Figure 7.19 shows how the variables enter the constraints, and Figure 7.20 gives the immediate processing sequences. Writing the equations for the left columns, assuming the right two correct (S equal to 3, E equal to 4, R set to 6), still leaves most of the trial-and-error search to be done.

card.rule: CROSS+ROADS gives easy information from the two right columns, then stalls: the left columns must be attacked by trial.
card.limits: The statement that no key step exists is the authors' judgment of the task, not a proof.

concepts.title: Reasoning the augmented space cannot do
concepts.question: What can algebra on the left columns show, and why is that reasoning outside the augmented space?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Suppose columns 1 and 2 are filled in (S equal to 3, E equal to 4, R set to 6) and the left columns are written as equations with carries. How far does algebra go?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The authors combine the equations to get G plus 10 equal to C plus N plus 11 times (c5 minus c4). The factor on the carries can be plus 1, 0 or minus 1, and minus 1 leads to a contradiction. So c5 equal to 0 with c4 equal to 1 is not possible.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: This is not a very strong conclusion and leaves almost all the trial-and-error search to be done. The authors add that this line of reasoning is a good example of reasoning that is not possible for someone working in the augmented space.

card.rule: A weak but valid inference exists from combining column equations, but it lies outside the augmented space.
card.limits: The inference rules out one carry combination only, so the search remains large.

concepts.title: S4 on CROSS+ROADS: still the augmented space
concepts.question: What evidence shows S4 stayed in the augmented space on CROSS+ROADS, apart from one small extension?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors ask whether S4's episode abstract (Figure 7.21) shows a more sophisticated space than the augmented one.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: They find little evidence for one. In E1 R set to 6 leads to S equal to 3 or 8 and he derives D equal to 1 at once. E equal to 4 or 0 from S equal to 3 or 8 was reached by rapid assignment and calculation (B17 to B19). The derivation of A and O as 2 or 3 in E5 combines GN and PC.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In that last case G was set to 5 and the unavailability of 0 and 1 rules out the pair (4, 1), leaving (2, 3) so either letter can have either value. This use of unordered sets of digits may be seen as an extra augmentation. S4 also neglected the carry into the column, which shows the nature of the inference.

card.rule: S4's reasoning on CROSS+ROADS uses the same operators as before, with one extension: unordered sets of digits.
card.limits: Neglecting the carry meant no pair of available digits summed to the needed 4, a sign the inference was approximate.

concepts.title: S4 on CROSS+ROADS: search and errors
concepts.question: How did S4 proceed once he had exhausted the immediate information, and what did errors cost him?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: S4 promptly exhausted the immediate information, recognized the situation (he says you really cannot tell anything about the rest of the letters), and went into a systematic attempt to assign values.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: He did not see the subtler inference that c4 equal to 1 implies c5 equal to 1. The task needs at least a double assignment before real consequences follow, such as assignments to G and O (column 3) when S is 8 and to C and O (columns 5 and 4) when S is 3. After each assignment the episode is completed at once and the contradiction found.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: S4 made a substantial number of errors, but recovery was rapid once a contradiction appeared. He never found that he had made an error; he found only a set of incompatible assignments. Some six and a half episodes of 21 arose from errors, yet they never caused him the difficulties S3 and S5 had.

card.rule: On a puzzle with no key step, S4 assigns systematically, finds contradictions quickly, and recovers without diagnosing his errors.
card.limits: S4 recovers by finding incompatible assignments, not by locating the faulty inference, so he would meet trouble if errors were harder to isolate.

concepts.title: Choices the systematic account does not explain
concepts.question: Which selections by S4 on CROSS+ROADS are not explained by systematic generation?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Three selection behaviors in S4's episode abstract are not explained by systematic generation.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: First, he assigned S as 8 before S as 3, with no cue in the protocol as to why. He generates assignments for G from large digits down but for O upward and later for C upward. Second, after columns 1 and 2 were exhausted he worked on column 3, possibly because he was working right to left and knew the carry into column 3 but not into columns 4 or 5.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Third is the order of assignments to G, O, A and C. In the first half (S as 8) it runs G, O, C, apparently set by the column considerations. In the second half (S as 3) it is C, O, A, with O after A in E12. The issue comes down to choosing C (column 5) after E equal to 4 in E9, and keeping A equal to 5 from E16 to E17.

card.rule: A few of S4's choices have no cue in the protocol; the authors list them, and offer a conjecture for one.
card.limits: The authors do not claim these can be explained from the episode abstract, which is too crude to compare in detail.

concepts.title: What the new task showed about S4 and S2
concepts.question: What do the authors conclude from S4 and S2 on CROSS+ROADS, and what could be studied next?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors summarize S4's CROSS+ROADS behavior against his DONALD+GERALD behavior.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: S4 operates essentially as he did before: same problem space, same level of episoding. They have not compared the two protocols in detail, because the episode abstract appears too crude, and some decisions and errors remain unexplained.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: For S2 and S4 alike, a different task in the same environment still leads to behavior analyzable in the same terms: the same augmented space, task demands showing as episodes of immediate inference, and systematic assignment between episodes. Further work would go down to the production-system level for the fine structure of linkage, and lower to the mechanisms of operators and memory.

card.rule: The same space, episodes and systematic assignment appear on the new task; finer analysis would have to go to productions and memory mechanisms.
card.limits: The check was whether the same terms apply; the authors do not claim fine-grained identity of behavior on the two tasks.

concepts.title: S2: the augmented space under different conditions
concepts.question: How do the experimental conditions for S2 differ, and what shows he used the augmented space?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: S2, also a college sophomore, was observed on CROSS+ROADS for the first 382 seconds. The arrangements differed: he wore an eye-movement helmet, and the display was a projected slide.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Assignments were not written on the display. S2 could ask the experimenter to remember an assignment and call for it later. The authors say this changes the operations used, as shown later, though not in the episode abstract (Figure 7.22).

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Evidence for the augmented space: D equal to 1 derived in the first episode and C above 6 in the second imply a reasonable PC. TD is routinely applied, and more than minimally: he concluded A equal to 0 is impossible because it makes O equal to G, even though neither has a value. AV is used systematically. Later he says S equals 3, R is six, and C can be five, seven or eight, which shows GN.

card.rule: S2 uses all the operators of the augmented space and none of greater power.
card.limits: S2's failure to recall E equal to 3 at E6 shows that his reasoning could not have excluded C equal to 9 even with a stronger mechanism.

concepts.title: Depth versus breadth, and why add eye movements
concepts.question: Which two research strategies do the authors alternate between, and what do eye movements add?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors' investigations alternate between two strategies. One examines a single problem-solving attempt in the greatest detail to see whether the theory fits the fine structure of behavior. The other asks whether the theory fits the facts across a substantial range of situations, trading depth for breadth.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Chapter 6 was the detailed kind, as will be Chapters 9 and 12. The episode abstracts here and Chapters 10 and 13 are the broad kind. The detailed strategy needs as much information as possible about a stretch of behavior. A verbal protocol gives a high density of data per minute of behavior.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Longer sessions do not give the same benefit, since they allow more new elements (facts, methods, stimuli) to enter and so add degrees of freedom. Gross eye movements recorded in parallel with the talk increase the number of points the theory must fit without adding degrees of freedom.

card.rule: Eye movements are valuable because they add data points to fit without adding freedom for the theory to bend.
card.limits: Longer sessions add data but also add new elements, so they are not an equivalent way to get more evidence.

concepts.title: How the eyes were recorded
concepts.question: How did the camera record eye position, and why was the less accurate arrangement chosen?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: To know where on the display the subject's eyes pointed at each instant, Winikoff used a commercially available adaptation of the Mackworth Eye Marker Camera.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: A spot of light is reflected from the cornea and carried by mirrors and lenses to a frame of film exposed to the scene the subject views. When the eye moves, the spot reflects at a slightly different angle and lands elsewhere on the film. After calibration the spot coincides with where the eyes point, to about plus or minus 1 degree horizontally and 2 degrees vertically.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The camera is mounted on a helmet because the head moves. A bite rod would improve accuracy, but subjects had to talk continuously, so the cruder system was used. Frames were taken at 0.2-second intervals, so almost no fixations were missed; time markers on the audio tape every tenth frame (2 seconds) tie speech to eye movements, imperfectly.

card.rule: The setup trades accuracy for the freedom to talk, and ties eyes to speech only to within about two seconds.
card.limits: Coordination is imperfect, because a human matched the heard time to the word.

concepts.title: Fixations, saccades and what the display allows
concepts.question: What are fixations and saccades, and what do they say about where a subject looks?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: On a stationary display like a cryptarithmetic puzzle, or a page, eye movements are a series of fixations, each followed by a saccade, a jump to another position.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: A saccade takes almost no time and nothing is seen during it, so all vision time divides into fixations, each localizable on the display. The fixation is the natural unit of analysis, as in reading studies. The region of clarity is about 2 degrees in radius, roughly one letter wide, so a fixation on D in column 2 means he is probably not looking at the neighboring letters.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Generally more fixations go to the upper half of a field than to the lower, and more to the right than the left. S2 on CROSS+ROADS shows a strong vertical effect, with very few fixations on the lower row. The display never changes, so after first orientation nothing new appears that he could miss.

card.rule: Fixations are the unit; on a still display, where the eyes rest says which letters the subject is attending to.
card.limits: Looking at a letter shows only that he is looking, not that he is seeing or thinking about it.

concepts.title: Attention, scan, transition and excursion units
concepts.question: What four kinds of eye-movement aggregates did Winikoff define, and which ones count as problem solving?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Winikoff found that cryptarithmetic eye-movement data can be aggregated into units of 1 to 20 seconds, called eye-movement aggregates (EMAs).

blocks.label: Term
blocks.text: An attention unit is a series of fixations devoted mostly to one task-relevant locale. A scan unit is a series of short fixations wandering widely over the display. A transition unit is a short series of brief fixations between attention units. An excursion unit is a short series of brief fixations within an attention unit that leave its locale and return.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: An attention unit is read as the subject attending to problem solving concerned with that part of the display. A scan unit is read as some kind of search. Transitions and excursions are not given problem-solving significance; they may work at a lower control level.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Winikoff found that cryptarithmetic eye-movement data aggregate into units of 1 to 20 seconds, the eye-movement aggregates (EMAs), which the authors then classify as attention, scan or transition units.

card.rule: Attention units mean working on a place, scan units mean searching, and transitions and excursions are treated as not meaningful for problem solving.
card.limits: The authors later concede that treating transitions and excursions as meaningless is undoubtedly false at a finer level of detail.

concepts.title: How the fixations were aggregated
concepts.question: How does the aggregation program build attention units, and what justifies a cutting point at 1.2 seconds?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A multiple-pass ALGOL program aggregates the time series of frames automatically. Task-relevant areas are the columns of the display.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Pass 1 aggregates fixations. Pass 2 joins consecutive fixations in the same column and absorbs short misfits as excursions. Pass 3 turns ABAB into one unit, and pass 4 absorbs B in ABA into A, when preset conditions hold. Pass 5 labels the remaining intervals scan units or transitions by duration.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Several preset parameters affect the decisions, but small variations leave the aggregation quite stable. Table 7.3 shows a sharp drop in the number of residual intervals at 1.2 seconds. So the long non-attention units are not the tail of one homogeneous distribution, which justifies a cutting point.

card.rule: The program builds attention units bottom-up, and a gap in the durations of the leftovers justifies splitting scans from transitions.
card.limits: Two scan units cannot be adjacent, and excursions inside a scan or transitions between a scan and an attention unit are impossible by construction.

concepts.title: Why matching eyes to thought is hard to judge
concepts.question: What four difficulties complicate evaluating the correspondence between eye movements and problem solving?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Winikoff evaluated how closely eye-movement units match the problem solving inferred from the verbal protocol. The authors list four distinct difficulties.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: First, there are two eye-movement measures, fixations and the aggregates built from them, and they are correlated. Second, the problem solving is inferred from speech, and some inferences rest on surface features of utterances, such as S2 saying S plus S has to equal R, which alone could predict eyes on S, S and R. Third, imperfect correspondence is expected and even useful.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Fourth, several measures could be used: numbers of units or total duration, and counts of eye movements without problem solving or the reverse. Any comparison has a rate of false positives, so a degree of correspondence must be judged against a null model of chance, which differs for each comparison.

card.rule: A claim that eyes track thought must beat chance for each pair of measures and must not depend on surface features of speech.
card.limits: Because correspondence should be imperfect, the absence of a match is not a failure of the method.

concepts.title: Winikoff's results
concepts.question: What did Winikoff's comparison of eye movements with problem solving find, and what conclusion do the authors draw?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Winikoff compared three correspondences: fixations with surface verbalizations, fixations with inferred problem solving, and eye-movement aggregates with inferred problem solving.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: All three far exceed chance, so their reality is not in doubt. Fit improves almost always as one goes from the first pair to the second to the third, which is the direction that justifies using aggregates. Correspondence is better when total duration is measured than when numbers of units are counted. The improvement from fixations to aggregates is stronger than that from surface verbalization to inferred problem solving.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In the one chess protocol, where the problem behavior graph added little beyond surface verbalizations, no improvement appeared. The net result gives confidence that aggregates can supplement verbal behavior. Often the two corroborate each other, sometimes eye movements add significant information.

card.rule: Eye-movement aggregates track inferred problem solving far above chance, well enough to supplement verbal protocols.
card.limits: The best fit came where the inference was richest; in the chess protocol, with thin inference, there was no gain.

concepts.title: The recall operators and eyes returning to a letter
concepts.question: What new operator did the eye-movement data force the authors to add for S2, and what is the evidence?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors build a production system for S2 from only the first 206 seconds (through E3). Of the four augmented-space operators only PC, AV and TD occur there; GN does not.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: One new operator, RV, recalls the value of a variable. It is needed because S2 records values by uttering them to the experimenter and later asking for them. Another operator, RA, recalls the antecedent situation, the path followed in the space, like FA for S3.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: RV is postulated directly from eye movements: whenever S2 tries to recall the digit of a letter, his eyes return to the place where it was assigned or derived. There is rarely any sign of this in his speech, so other subjects might have had such an operator unseen. In all eight places where recall could occur the protocol is consistent with it, good in six and needing reinterpretation in two.

card.rule: Eye movements reveal a recall step that speech does not, so RV is postulated because the eyes go back to where a value was set.
card.limits: The data cannot say whether the eye shift is the recall, an aid to it, or a consequence of it, since speech and sight may lag.

concepts.title: S2's production system compared with S3's
concepts.question: How does S2's production system differ from S3's, and in which respects does S2 resemble S5 and S8?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors built a production system for S2 as they had for S3, using the same names for analogous productions. Only one production has no counterpart in S3's set: the recall production P16.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: S3's P1 is split into three parts, because with assignment attention is already at the right column and FC is unnecessary. P3 is more direct, P4 simpler with no generation, and P5 is absent since S2's segment has no final checking. In responding to contradiction (P7), S2 sets the goal of assigning a new value, where S3 set the goal of getting a value.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: As its basic driver (P9) S2 uses FNC, finding the next column in the usual right-to-left sequence, where S3 used FL, which finds an appropriate letter. In this S2 resembles S5 and S8. P11 and P12 are in nearly the same form, and of the two repetition productions S2 has only P14. S2's system is, if anything, somewhat simpler than S3's.

card.rule: S2's productions parallel S3's, with a recall production added and right-to-left column finding as the driver.
card.limits: Differences in the small segment studied may not reflect real differences between S2 and S3.

concepts.title: The goal stack and its signals
concepts.question: How does S2's goal stack work, and why do the authors keep it outside the productions?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The top goal and the expressions are the information S2 uses to pick the next production. They form the relevant short-term memory of his problem space, not his full knowledge state; earlier assignments and deductions are presumably in long-term memory.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The goal stack is handled by rules, not productions. Each goal expression has a goal type, a signal giving its operational status, and sometimes a column or variable. Operations on the stack are automatic: they take no appreciable time and have no implications for eye movements.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: A new goal normally pushes the stack, unless the top goal's signal shows success or failure, in which case the top goal is replaced. A conditional-fail signal marks a goal that set up a subgoal such that nothing more can be done unless the subgoal produces new information, so there is no need to return if it fails. Operators produce goals directly, where in S3's system they produced expressions converted to goals by P6 and P10.

card.rule: The goal stack is automatic bookkeeping that holds the current goals and signals, separate from the productions that act.
card.limits: A different design, always returning to the prior goal first, would give different implications for eye movements.

concepts.title: Linking productions to eye movements
concepts.question: What two observation rules link S2's productions to his eye-movement units, and what are the minimum and maximum versions?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: To test the production system against eye movements, the authors need rules that say what eye-movement units each production should produce.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Rule 1: the subject always has an attention unit at the column named in the top goal, and covers or stresses the letter the top goal names, if any. Rule 2: the subject scans the display when he selects a new column undirected by the previous problem solving (FNC), or when a directed search (FC) fails.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: These two rules follow Winikoff in discarding transitions and in setting the boundary between attention units and transitions by the aggregation program's internal criteria. They are the minimum rules. The maximum rules shift the scan-attention boundary, give significance to transitions for FC and FNC, and add a few ad hoc interpretations. The truth lies somewhere between.

card.rule: Observation rules predict an attention unit at the goal's column and a scan when the next column is chosen without direction.
card.limits: The truth is expected to lie between the minimum and the maximum rule sets, so each coverage figure has a range.

concepts.title: How much behavior the production system covers
concepts.question: How well do S2's productions account for his verbal behavior and his eye movements?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors count, for each production added in turn, how much behavior it accounts for, using six quantities including nodes of the PBG covered, ad hoc operator outputs, and eye-movement units and time that correspond. Equal fractional credit is given when one unit covers several productions.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The system covers 94 production occurrences. The productions are ordered from P1 prime prime, covering the most PBG nodes (18), to P4, covering the fewest (1). Ad hoc operator outputs rise to about 10 percent of the total, mostly in two main productions.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: With the minimum rules the system covers 67.5 percent of eye-movement units and 87.5 percent of time; with the maximum rules 87 percent of units and 94.4 percent of time. Time is covered better than units, as in Winikoff's study. Most of the increase from minimum to maximum comes from the systematic reinterpretation, not from the additional ad hoc ones.

card.rule: S2's productions cover most of his eye movements, more by time than by number of units, and the gain from the maximum rules is mostly systematic.
card.limits: The distribution of time over productions is approximate, though the totals are exact.

concepts.title: What the S2 analysis shows overall
concepts.question: How well does the production system fit S2, and what does it say about the information processing models?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors took a 200-second segment of S2's protocol and fitted an information processing system to both his speech and his eye movements.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The fit is extremely close and better than S3's on DONALD+GERALD. Part of this is the shortness of the segment (200 seconds against about 1000), but part is the extra evidence from eye movements. The productions are about half again as dense: 0.47 per second against 0.32.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The production system for S2 is very much of a piece with the system for S3 and, by extension, with the structure of the other augmented-space subjects. So the eye-movement data substantially support the reality of the information processing models. The finer analysis also gave meaning to transitions, which Winikoff's study had set aside; occasionally the aggregation had simply over-aggregated.

card.rule: A second, independent kind of data fits the same kind of production system, supporting the reality of the models.
card.limits: The better fit is partly due to the shorter segment, so it cannot be compared with S3 directly.

concepts.title: The trilogy about cryptarithmetic
concepts.question: What did each of the three chapters on cryptarithmetic contribute, and what tools were added in this one?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The conclusion looks back on the three chapters about problem solving in the cryptarithmetic environment.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Chapter 5 analyzed the task environment and described a series of problem spaces. Chapter 6 analyzed one subject on one task, DONALD+GERALD, and found his behavior took place in the augmented space, explained by a production system with the largest part derived from a problem behavior graph. Chapter 7 extended the analysis to four other subjects, briefly to Bartlett's, and to two subjects on another puzzle.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: To do so it introduced two tools: a procedure for episoding behavior that allows summary treatment without the full problem behavior graph, and procedures for obtaining and analyzing eye-movement data along with the verbal protocol.

card.rule: Task analysis, then one subject in depth, then many subjects in breadth, with two new tools for the last step.
card.limits: The tools extend, but do not replace, the detailed single-subject analysis of Chapter 6.

concepts.title: What the extended analysis confirms
concepts.question: What are the authors' main findings from the extended analysis, and what do the errors show?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors say the extended analysis gives additional confirmation of the general conclusions of the previous chapter.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: It proved possible to characterize the problem spaces in which subjects worked. Three of the four subjects who did DONALD+GERALD in the laboratory worked in essentially the S3 augmented space, and the fourth worked in a simpler, more basic space. A very large part of the behavior was behavior demanded by the task in the spaces they used.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Some behavior was determined by particular errors, and these were not predicted by the theory. The errors were of simple kinds: elementary faults of reasoning, such as confusing sufficient with necessary conditions, and lapses of memory. Explaining them would call for detailed data on memory processes not obtainable from the protocols.

card.rule: Spaces can be identified, most behavior is task-demanded, and the leftover is simple errors the theory does not predict.
card.limits: The theory does not predict the errors, and the protocols cannot supply the memory data that would explain them.

concepts.title: From cryptarithmetic to logic
concepts.question: What is the next step in the authors' program, and what status do they give the tools?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: From the three chapters a detailed but particularistic theory of human problem solving begins to emerge, along with reasons for confidence in the technical devices used to obtain the data and extract the theory.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Moving from one subject to a comparison of several was the first cautious step toward generalizing the theory. The next step is a second trilogy of chapters on a second task environment: discovering proofs for theorems in a formal system.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors say their job of tool building is complete in all essentials. In the tasks of the remaining chapters they will use the same tools as before.

card.rule: The theory is detailed but particularistic so far; the next test is a different task environment, proof discovery in a formal system, with the same tools.
card.limits: Generalization is described as cautious: one task family has been covered in depth.

concepts.title: The logic task as a recoding game
concepts.question: What did the logic subjects believe they were doing, and what did they actually have to do?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: After cryptarithmetic, the authors turn to a second task: solving problems in a simple system of symbolic logic. The label is misleading for the subjects, who were never told it was logic.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Subjects were told to "recode" certain strings of symbols into other, specified strings, using a given set of rules. Facing a blackboard, each had a sheet of twelve rules for manipulating parenthesized expressions made of letters and connectors.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors describe the setting as the task was set up in earlier work. Their evidence for what subjects do comes later in the chapter, from two groups of subjects.

card.rule: The logic task is a recoding game: change given symbol strings into a target string, one permitted rule at a time.
card.limits: The word logic is the analysts' label for the task. It describes what the authors study, not what the subjects were told.

concepts.title: Handling the connectors by form, not meaning
concepts.question: Why do subjects treat dots, wedges, horseshoes and tildes as marks to rewrite rather than as and, or, implies, not?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: For analysts the four connectors stand for and, or, implies and not. The subjects are not told this, and in fact they do not discover this interpretation.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The subjects therefore treat the expressions entirely in terms of their syntactic properties, that is, their form and arrangement, with no reference to semantic meaning. The rules say what shapes can be rewritten into what other shapes.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors report that subjects had only the rule sheet and the instruction to recode, and that they did not discover the interpretation of the connectors.

blocks.label: Assumed
blocks.text: The authors take it that the rule sheet is enough to run the task; they build the analysis on form and do not ask subjects to know any logic.

card.rule: In this task the subject manipulates the form of expressions; meaning plays no part in the rules.
card.limits: Form-only handling describes what the rules demand. It does not say every mark is completely meaningless to every subject.

concepts.title: What a logic problem is
concepts.question: How is a logic problem posed to the subject, and which problems make up the set?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors need a definite meaning for a problem in this task environment before they can study how it is solved.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: A problem gives the subject a set of expressions and asks him to transform them into another specified expression. The desired expression is called L0, and the given expressions are L1 up to Ln.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The set of problems in Figure 8.2 holds three practice problems, a1 to a3, and sixteen regular ones. The regular problems systematically vary the number of given expressions between one and four.

card.rule: A logic problem is a set of given expressions L1 to Ln plus one desired expression L0 to be derived from them.
card.limits: This is the form used in the chapter. The task could be set up differently, as the extension question shows.

concepts.title: The blackboard display and the external record
concepts.question: How does the display keep a record of each move and show when the problem is solved?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The experimenter needs a checked, visible record of what the subject has done at each moment, so that later moves build on legitimate steps.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The desired expression L0 is written in the upper right quadrant. The subject asks the experimenter to apply a rule to an expression already on the board. If the move is legitimate, the experimenter writes the new expression in the left-hand column, continuing the numbering, with the rule name in the right-hand column.

blocks.label: Term
blocks.text: The expressions in the lower left quadrant are the derived expressions. As soon as one of them is the same as L0, the problem is solved.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Figure 8.3 shows the display for problem D1 with the solution of a subject called S4: a numbered column of expressions with the rule used beside each.

card.rule: Every accepted move goes on the board, numbered, with its rule, and the problem ends when a derived line equals L0.
card.limits: Our reading: the board records the officially made rule applications only. It does not show what the subject was thinking.

concepts.title: The two groups of subjects and what their data are
concepts.question: Which two groups supplied the logic data, and how do their data differ in kind?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors want human behavior to compare with their task analysis, so they draw on two bodies of data collected with the same display.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Sixty-four Yale undergraduates, run by Carpenter, Moore and others, each attempted all sixteen regular problems with fifteen minutes per problem. Ten Carnegie Tech undergraduate and graduate students attempted one to six problems each, with thirty minutes per problem.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In both studies the subjects told the experimenter aloud which transformations to make. The Yale data are the lists of transformed expressions with the rule used and the time elapsed. Carnegie times were not recorded, but the subjects thought aloud, giving protocols.

blocks.label: Assumed
blocks.text: The Yale experiment studied alcohol and problem solving. The authors pool all treatments, since the design was counterbalanced and the alcohol effects were small.

card.rule: Yale gives step records with times from many subjects; Carnegie gives think-aloud protocols from a few.
card.limits: Not every subject has protocols for every problem. The authors analyze all protocols available for a given problem.

concepts.title: The questions and plan of the task analysis
concepts.question: Which three questions guide the logic chapters, and in what order does Chapter 8 proceed?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: As with cryptarithmetic, the authors will first analyze the task environment, then examine human behavior in detail, then take a broader view. They respond to the nature of the task and the data, fairly independently of the earlier cryptarithmetic analysis.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Three questions recur: can humans be described as working in problem spaces; what problem solving organizations and heuristics do they show; and how far is behavior set by the task environment rather than by their own characteristics.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Chapter 8 takes up the basic problem space, then focuses on one program, GPS, as an example of a problem solving IPS for logic. It ends by examining sources of problem difficulty in the data of the sixty-four Yale subjects.

card.rule: The logic chapters ask the same three questions as the cryptarithmetic ones and begin with the task environment.
card.limits: This chapter only prepares the ground: GPS is not yet used as a model of human behavior.

concepts.title: The rule sheet and the direction of its arrows
concepts.question: How does the rule sheet say which forms may be rewritten into which, and in which direction?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Subjects need a fixed list of permitted moves. Anything outside the list is not a legitimate step.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Figure 8.1 gives twelve rules. Each shows an expression form at the tail of an arrow that may be changed into the different form at the head. A double-headed arrow means the change can be made in either direction.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The rule sheet appears as Figure 8.1, with notes under each rule about where it may be used, such as only with a wedge or dot, or only when the connective is the major one.

card.rule: A rule rewrites the form at the tail of its arrow into the form at the head; only double-headed arrows run both ways.
card.limits: Each rule has conditions on where it applies. Following an arrow is not enough on its own.

concepts.title: Sign changes inside the rules
concepts.question: How do the rules keep double negation from ever appearing in an expression?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: In the form of logic the authors considered for LT in Chapter 4, double negation was a separate matter. In the Moore-Anderson task, a pair of tildes might appear when a rule negates something already negated.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Double negation is handled implicitly: the rules themselves make changes in sign, so multiple negation signs never arise. When a rule would negate a negated part, the tilde is removed instead of a second one being added.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors give a worked case for rule 2, which turns A ⊃ B into ~B ⊃ ~A, applied to an expression with a negated part.

card.rule: Each rule states its own sign changes, so an expression never carries two tildes in a row.
card.limits: This is a convention of this task's rule sheet; it is not how every logical system treats negation.

concepts.title: What the twelve rules do
concepts.question: In broad terms, what does each of the twelve rules do, and which take two lines as input?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: To judge the size of the search and how GPS works, the authors need the rules as operators on expressions: what they accept as input and what they produce.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Rule 1 swaps the two sides of a wedge or dot. Rule 2 turns A ⊃ B into ~B ⊃ ~A. Rule 3 drops a repeated part (A V A or A.A to A). Rule 4 regroups a chain of wedges or of dots. Rule 5 links A V B with ~(~A.~B). Rule 6 links A ⊃ B with ~A V B. Rule 7 distributes a dot over a wedge or a wedge over a dot.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Rule 8 keeps either side of a dot. Rule 9 adds a wedge to a line, A to A V X. Rule 10 joins two lines with a dot. Rule 11 takes A ⊃ B and A and gives B. Rule 12 takes A ⊃ B and B ⊃ C and gives A ⊃ C. Rules 10, 11 and 12 use two lines as input (Figures 8.1 and 8.17).

card.rule: Rules 1 to 7 reshape one expression; rules 8 and 9 shorten or extend; rules 10 to 12 combine two lines.
card.limits: Two-line rules also carry conditions, such as the lines being positive and the horseshoe being the major connective.

concepts.title: The basic problem space for logic
concepts.question: What are the elements, operators, initial state and desired state of the basic problem space?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors want a natural formulation of the logic problems as search, so they can say how large the search is and what behavior in it looks like.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: In the basic problem space the elements are logic expressions and the operators are the given rules. The initial state is the expression, or expressions, L1 (L2, and so on); the desired final state is L0. Some operators take one expression as input and some (R10, R11, R12) take a pair.

blocks.label: Term
blocks.text: The knowledge state is the set of all expressions derived up to a given point. Each successful application of an operator adds a new expression to the collection.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors call this the natural basic problem space and say all behavior in these problems occurs in it. They note that these are clearly search problems.

card.rule: Basic space: expressions are the elements, rules are the operators, and each success adds an expression to the knowledge state.
card.limits: This is one way to formulate the task. GPS and the planning method later use other spaces alongside it.

concepts.title: The simplest estimate of the maze
concepts.question: How big is the maze if all twelve operators could be applied at every point of a seven-step proof?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: How much search would a brute-force solver face on a problem like D1? The authors want a first number.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Take the simplest scheme: assume the twelve operators are applicable at each point. Then finding the seven-step proof of D1 (embedded in Figure 8.3) means threading a 12^7 maze, about 4 x 10^7 paths.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The figure comes from simple arithmetic: twelve choices at each of seven steps, with each step multiplying the number of paths by twelve.

blocks.label: Assumed
blocks.text: The estimate assumes every operator is applicable to every expression. The authors say at once that this is not so.

card.rule: With b choices at each of n steps there are b^n paths: for 12 operators and 7 steps, about 4 x 10^7.
card.limits: The figure is a first, crude count. Real applicability and the growth factors that follow change it.

concepts.title: Three factors that make the space grow faster
concepts.question: Which three factors push the logic search space to grow faster than a simple count suggests?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A closer look at the operators shows effects that oppose each other on the size of the maze. One decreases growth; three increase it.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Decreasing: not every operator applies to every expression. Increasing: (1) many operators apply to subexpressions as well as the whole expression; (2) operators with two inputs add new expressions in proportion to the square of the number available, not linearly; (3) R9 can create arbitrarily many new expressions at any time by putting an arbitrary expression in place of X.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The clearest case of the second factor is R10, which combines derived expressions to form their conjunction. R9 is the case of the third factor, since X can be any coded expression.

card.rule: Subexpressions, two-input rules and R9 push the space to grow faster than 12 choices per step suggests.
card.limits: The three increasing factors are partly offset by rules that rarely apply. Together they call for a finer estimate.

concepts.title: Expression size and the picture of concentric rings
concepts.question: How does the picture of rings by expression size show the space and a solution path?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: All three growth factors relate to the size of the expressions involved: the number of subexpressions depends on size, and R9 and R10 produce larger expressions than their inputs.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Figure 8.4 draws the whole space as concentric rings, each holding expressions of one size. Size is the number of terms, that is, constants or variables. With three distinct letters, the number of expressions rises by a factor of about 100 with each increase of one in size.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Problem D1 starts with a four-term expression, L1, and seeks a two-term expression, L0. The figure shows a solid path, the direct search matching Figure 8.3, and a dashed hypothetical path that goes the long way around, adding complexity before it simplifies.

card.rule: Solving is a trip between rings of expression size, and each extra term makes the ring about a hundred times more crowded.
card.limits: Size counts terms only. Two expressions of equal size can be very different in how reachable they are.

concepts.title: How many expressions an operator produces
concepts.question: How is the average number of expressions an operator yields from one expression worked out?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: To estimate the growth of the space, the authors must find how often each operator applies to expressions of a given size and what size it produces.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Expressions of size four come from applications of R1, R2, R4, R5 and R6. R1 can apply at any of the three connective locations of a four-term expression, but only where the connective is a wedge or dot, which is two cases in three. R1 therefore yields on average 3 x (2/3) = 2 four-term expressions.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Not every contribution is below one. If expressions of size four are generated from one of size two, R9 applies to each possible two-term expression, contributing a total of 216 expressions.

card.rule: Expected output equals the number of places a rule can apply times the share of those places where its conditions hold.
card.limits: The averages describe typical contributions. They are not a guide to what a particular expression allows.

concepts.title: Growth per step and the effect of limiting expression size
concepts.question: How fast does the number of expressions grow per step, and how much does a size limit help?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Given the productivities, how many expressions will be available at each stage of search, starting from one expression of size four as in problem D1?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: From the number of expressions of each size at one stage the authors compute the numbers at the next. The top curve of Figure 8.5 totals expressions of ten or fewer terms. Plotted on a logarithmic scale, growth of 10^a is a line of slope a. The growth rate is about thirty-fold per step.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Two lower curves assume that no expression greater than 5 terms, or greater than 4 terms, is generated. The growth rate then falls to about 12 and 9 per step. Even so it is large enough to preclude brute-force forward search.

blocks.label: Assumed
blocks.text: The calculation leaves out the contributions of R9 and R10 and keeps expressions of all sizes unless a limit is stated.

card.rule: Left unchecked the space grows about thirty-fold per step; a size limit lowers that to about 9 to 12, still too fast for brute force.
card.limits: The curves rest on assumed limits and on leaving out R9 and R10. They give orders of magnitude, not exact counts.

concepts.title: Assumptions behind the estimate and its purpose
concepts.question: Which simplifications does the growth estimate make, and what is such a crude model good for?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The growth calculation rests on gross assumptions about problem solving strategy. The authors ask what each one leaves out and how much it matters.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: All expressions of whatever size are kept, although a solver might discriminate against large expressions, and many small ones arise by generating large ones and breaking them up. The count also lets every size category grow indefinitely, as for a solver that checks for no duplicates.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Only a limited number of distinct small expressions exist: 6 of size one and 216 of size two. If duplicates were removed, a category would reach a limit. Allowing for duplicates has so small an effect on the overall growth rate that it would not show on the graph, since the limit bites first on the smallest expressions.

card.rule: Removing duplicates would cap small expressions first, but those matter little for total growth, so the estimate stands.
card.limits: The estimate describes simple, undiscriminating procedures. A solver that discriminates among expressions faces a different space.

concepts.title: Where GPS came from and why it is called general
concepts.question: Where did the General Problem Solver come from, and what made it general?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The size calculations show that blind search is hopeless. The authors now turn to a program that works in the same space with more intelligence: GPS, a problem solving program developed initially by the authors and J. C. Shaw in 1957.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: GPS grew out of the work on LT described in Chapter 4, and its first task environment was the Moore-Anderson logic task. It earned the name general problem solver because it was the first problem solving program to separate cleanly a task-independent part, holding the general mechanisms, from a part holding knowledge of the task environment.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors point to the structure of the program itself: general mechanisms sit in one part and task knowledge in another, so the same mechanisms can be described without reference to logic.

blocks.label: Assumed
blocks.text: In this chapter the authors describe GPS in a task-independent way, which is the natural way to describe it, but they do not assess how well it suits other task environments.

card.rule: GPS is general because its problem solving mechanisms are kept apart from its knowledge of any one task.
card.limits: General here means separated mechanisms, not a claim that GPS solves every problem. This chapter does not test other tasks.

concepts.title: Objects, operators, features and differences
concepts.question: In what terms does GPS see a problem, and what are objects, operators, features and differences?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: To work on many tasks, GPS needs a task-independent vocabulary for describing a problem.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: GPS operates on problems that can be formulated in terms of objects and operators. An operator is something that can be applied to certain objects to produce different objects, as a saw applied to logs produces boards. Objects are characterized by the features they possess and by the differences observable between pairs of objects.

blocks.label: Term
blocks.text: Operators for a given task may be restricted to certain kinds of objects. Some operators apply to several objects as inputs and produce one or more objects as outputs, as adding two numbers produces their sum.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: One kind of problem in this vocabulary is to transform a given object into another. The logic task fits: expressions are objects and the twelve rules are operators.

card.rule: GPS describes a task by its objects, the operators that turn objects into objects, and the differences between pairs of objects.
card.limits: A task must be expressible as objects and operators for GPS to work on it. Not every task is.

concepts.title: Transform and apply goals
concepts.question: What are transform and apply goals, and what is attached to each goal type?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: To specify problems and subproblems, GPS needs a discrete set of goal types. The authors introduce two at first.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The transform goal type is: find a way to transform object 1 into object 2, which means by applying a sequence of operators from the task environment. The apply goal type is: apply operator to object 1, or to an object obtained from object 1 by admissible transformations.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In logic, a transform goal is to find L0 from L1. An apply goal is to apply a rule such as R7 to L1. With each goal type goes a set of methods for achieving goals of that type.

card.rule: A transform goal asks for any route from one object to another; an apply goal names the operator to be used.
card.limits: Two goal types are not the whole set. A third, reduce, is added when means-ends analysis is introduced.

concepts.title: The executive: evaluate, select, apply
concepts.question: What does the GPS executive do when it tries to achieve a goal?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: GPS needs one uniform procedure for going after any goal, whatever its type.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Figure 8.6 gives achieve(goal): (1) evaluate the goal and, if it is rejected, stop and report failure; (2) select a method for the goal and, if none exists, stop and report failure; (3) apply the method to the goal and, if it succeeds, stop and report success; otherwise go back to step 1.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: When an attempt is made to achieve a goal, the goal is first evaluated to see whether it is worth achieving and whether achievement seems likely. If so, a method is selected and executed. The method leads either to success or to a repetition of the loop.

card.rule: Achieve a goal by evaluating it, selecting a method, applying it, and looping back to evaluation if the method fails.
card.limits: The loop is only the executive. The behavior comes from the methods it calls.

concepts.title: Recursive methods and depth-first control
concepts.question: How do subgoals make GPS recursive and depth-first?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A simple executive could not by itself produce intelligent behavior. Something in the methods must build a rich structure from it.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Methods try to achieve a goal by creating subgoals whose achievement aids the main goal, then evoke the executive to attempt each subgoal. Attempting one goal thus leads to others, and these to still others, so the methods are recursive. Together they form an organized, cooperating system of heuristics, although each method on its own remains a rational approach to goals of its type.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Because each method attempts everything appropriate to a subgoal before returning control to the method of the goal that called it, GPS is basically a depth-first problem solver.

card.rule: GPS pursues each subgoal to the end before control returns to the goal that created it, so it is depth-first.
card.limits: Our reading: depth-first control can follow blind paths unless it is curbed. The summary of the chapter makes this point.

concepts.title: Means-ends analysis
concepts.question: What is means-ends analysis, and how does a common-sense argument about a car show it?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The main methods of GPS jointly embody a heuristic the authors touched on in cryptarithmetic: means-ends analysis. They introduce it through a common-sense argument.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Means-ends analysis classifies things by the functions they serve, and oscillates among ends, the functions required, and the means that perform them. This forms the basic system of heuristic of GPS.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: A parent wants to take a son to nursery school. The difference between what is had and wanted is one of distance. Distance is changed by an automobile; the automobile will not work, and what it needs is a new battery; an auto repair shop has new batteries.

card.rule: Ask what differs between what you have and what you want, what changes that kind of difference, and what that change requires.
card.limits: Following one means can raise a new difficulty, as the car story shows. The method does not by itself guarantee success.

concepts.title: What means-ends analysis assumes
concepts.question: What must be true of a task for the means-ends heuristic of GPS to be usable?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A heuristic works only if the task has the right structure. The authors list what the means-ends system assumes.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: First, if an object is given that is not the desired one, differences will be detectable between them. Second, operators affect some features of their operands and leave others unchanged, so operators can be characterized by the changes they produce and used to remove differences.

blocks.label: Assumed
blocks.text: A further assumption concerns an operator that is not applicable. Another is that some differences prove harder to affect than others, so it is worth working on the hard ones first.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The assumptions are stated for objects and operators in general, not for logic alone. GPS puts them to use through its three methods.

card.rule: Means-ends analysis needs detectable differences, operators with characteristic effects, and some ordering of differences by difficulty.
card.limits: If differences cannot be detected, or operators change everything at once, the heuristic has nothing to work with.

concepts.title: The reduce goal and the transform method
concepts.question: How does the transform method use a reduce subgoal to move one object toward another?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Transform and apply goals are not enough for means-ends analysis. The authors add a third goal type: reduce the difference between object 1 and object 2 by modifying object 1.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The transform method works in three steps. (1) Match object 1 to object 2 to find a difference. (2) Set up a reduce subgoal for that difference; if achieved, it yields a new object, object 3. (3) Set up a transform subgoal to turn object 3 into object 2. If that goal is achieved, so is the original transform goal.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Figure 8.7 shows the methods as a flow diagram and Figure 8.8 in the program notation of the book. The core of the system is three methods, one for each goal type.

card.rule: To transform A into B, find a difference, reduce it to get a new object, then transform the new object into B.
card.limits: The method relies on a reduce goal that can succeed. If reducing fails, the transform goal fails.

concepts.title: The apply-operator method
concepts.question: How does GPS apply an operator when the operator does not fit the object at once?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: An operator can be applied only to an object of the right form. When the object does not fit, GPS must change it first.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The apply-operator method: (1) decide whether the operator can be applied to the object now, and if so apply it; (2) if not, set up a reduce subgoal for the difference found between the object and condition(operator), the operator's input form; (3) if that difference is reduced, set up an apply subgoal on the new object. In step 1 or 3, the new object is made from product(operator), the output form.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The method suits operators defined by two forms, one describing the input conditions and one the output product. The logic task has operators of this kind.

card.rule: Apply an operator at once if it fits; otherwise reduce the difference from its input form, then apply it to the changed object.
card.limits: The method fits operators defined by input and output forms. Other operators need variants of it.

concepts.title: The reduce method and how the three methods fit together
concepts.question: How does the reduce method find an operator to remove a difference, and how do the three methods call each other?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A difference has been found. GPS needs an operator that can remove it.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The reduce method: (1) search for an operator relevant to reducing the difference; if none is found, stop and report failure; (2) set up the apply goal of applying that operator to the object, which on success produces the modified object.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The transform method sets up reduce goals; the reduce method sets up apply goals; the apply-operator method can set up reduce goals in turn. In problem a1 the first three goals run in this order: transform L1 into L0, reduce a difference, apply a rule.

card.rule: Reduce looks for an operator relevant to the difference and sets up an apply goal for it.
card.limits: Finding a relevant operator depends on the table of connections. A difference with no relevant operator ends in failure.

concepts.title: The six differences for the logic task
concepts.question: Which six differences does GPS use for logic expressions, and what does each one compare?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Means-ends analysis needs differences to bridge the perceptual world of objects and the action world of operators. For logic these are new information, unique to this problem space.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: GPS compares two expressions and names the ways in which they differ. These differences are what the means-ends methods try to reduce, choosing operators by the differences they affect.

blocks.label: Term
blocks.text: At: a variable is in one expression but not the other. An: a variable occurs a different number of times. As: the signs differ. Ac: the binary connectives differ. Ag: the grouping differs. Ap: the positions of components differ.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Examples: P V P differs by +t from P V Q, since it needs a Q. P . Q differs from (P . Q) ⊃ Q by +n, since it needs another Q. Q and ~Q differ in sign; P ⊃ Q and P V Q differ in connective. P V (Q V R) and (P V Q) V R differ in grouping; P ⊃ (Q V R) and (Q V R) ⊃ P differ in position.

card.rule: A difference is a way two expressions can differ: in terms, counts, sign, connective, grouping or position.
card.limits: These six are the differences GPS is given for logic. Another program or task would use different ones.

concepts.title: The table of connections and the criteria of progress
concepts.question: How does GPS know which operators affect which differences, and which differences to attack first?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The six differences alone do not tell GPS what to do. It must also know which operators bear on each difference and which differences are hardest.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The table of connections of Figure 8.9 associates with each difference the operators relevant to modifying it. A +, - or X in a cell means that the operator in that column affects the difference in that row. Criteria of progress are given as a list of differences in order of difficulty.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: For a pair of expressions the differences are ranked: +t, -t, +n, -n, As, Ac, Ag, Ap, from most important to least. As is the more important in comparing ~(P V Q) with R ⊃ Q, while Ac is the more important in comparing ~P V Q with P ⊃ Q.

card.rule: The table of connections says which operators affect which difference; the ranking says which difference to work on first.
card.limits: Both were given to GPS by hand. The chapter later asks how far they could be derived from the task itself.

concepts.title: GPS at work on the simple problem a1
concepts.question: How does GPS solve the simple problem a1, goal by goal?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Problem a1 gives L1 = R . (~P ⊃ Q) and asks for L0 = (Q V P) . R. The letter R is at the left end of L1 and at the right end of L0.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Goal 1: transform L1 into L0. The difference is Ap. Goal 2 reduces Ap; the table of connections points to rule 1, so goal 3 applies rule 1 to L1, giving L2 = (~P ⊃ Q) . R. Next an Ac difference in the left parts leads to rule 6 on left(L2), giving L3 = (P V Q) . R. A position difference leads to rule 1 on left(L3), giving L4 = (Q V P) . R, which is L0.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Figure 8.10 gives the trace of sixteen goals. The derivation is: apply rule 1 to L1; apply rule 6 to left(L2); apply rule 1 to left(L3); L4 = L0.

card.rule: GPS finds the biggest difference, picks a relevant rule, applies it, and repeats on the new expression until none remains.
card.limits: Problem a1 is simple. For harder problems the trace is much longer and includes rejected and failed goals.

concepts.title: Handling operators with two inputs
concepts.question: How does GPS cope with rules like R12 when it holds only one expression?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Solving D1 needs rules with two inputs (R10, R11, R12). With one expression in hand, picking R12 does not settle which of its two inputs the expression should be, nor where the other input will come from.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: GPS treats this as one more difficulty and sets up a reduce goal for it. Applying R12 to L3 creates the difference of a single expression against a set (the inputs of R12). Its subgoal selects one input to correspond to L3. Applying that input to L3 gives not a new expression but a partially specified one-input operator, Q12, of the form A ⊃ ~R, with ~R ⊃ Q, giving A ⊃ Q.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Goals G52 to G60 of Figure 8.11 show the scheme. Q12 is then applied to the expressions on the display, selecting L2; a position difference is removed with R2 and Q12 is reapplied, producing the desired P ⊃ Q.

card.rule: A two-input rule is handled as a difficulty: pick one input to match the expression in hand, and get a one-input operator that looks for the other.
card.limits: The authors note other ways to handle two-input operators; this is the one that fits GPS as described here.

concepts.title: GPS's search on problem D1
concepts.question: What does GPS's search on D1 look like overall: what does it try, reject and finally choose?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: D1 has L1 = (R ⊃ ~P) . (~R ⊃ Q) and L0 = ~(~Q . P). Figure 8.11 traces every goal GPS sets itself on the way to the solution.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: GPS first tries to eliminate terms, namely the R's, and considers in turn each rule that might eliminate something: R8, R7, R3, R11 and R12. Each is rejected, sometimes after long exploration. A path is rejected either because expressions become too complex or because GPS remembers that the result was already tried and failed or was rejected.

blocks.label: Evidence
