blocks.text: With direct ways to eliminate R exhausted, GPS looks over the whole set of expressions (G44) to see if it can go straight from one of them to L0. The one chosen is rejected at once, as it had been tried in G7. GPS then starts selecting earlier goals as new starting points; G2 comes to nothing, but G8, add P to L3, proves fruitful and leads, after a small detour on R11, to the R12 sequence and the solution.

card.rule: GPS tries each way to eliminate terms, rejects dead ends by complexity or memory, then restarts from an earlier goal that works.
card.limits: The trace is for one problem. It shows what GPS did, not that this is how people proceed; that comparison comes next chapter.

concepts.title: Problem behavior graphs of GPS and their modified forms
concepts.question: How are problem behavior graphs of GPS on D1 drawn, and why modify the first form?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Figure 8.12 plots GPS's search on D1 as a problem behavior graph (PBG) with rule applications as operators. This is equivalent to viewing GPS in the basic problem space. Something is missing: the graph does not explain, for example, why rules 5 and 6 are used in its third line, and the guiding role of R7 is nowhere apparent.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The graph can be modified in two ways. One includes all the goals as operators (a fragment is Figure 8.13). The other shows only the transform and apply goals as operators, putting the differences into the boxes as state information (Figure 8.14).

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors will use the second, more compact form for the PBGs of their subjects. It corresponds to an alternative organization of GPS, in which data structures are not created for reduce goals; differences are simply attached to the transform and apply goals.

card.rule: A PBG of rule applications hides the goals behind them; adding goals, or differences in the boxes, shows the guidance.
card.limits: Each graph form is a way of drawing the same search. None adds information GPS did not use.

concepts.title: How means-ends analysis cuts the search down
concepts.question: Why does means-ends analysis keep the actual search small however large the whole problem space is?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The space actually searched in solving a problem is very small beside the problem space estimated earlier. The authors ask why.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The problem space is generated by working outward from the initial objects in no particular direction. Means-ends analysis is given both the initial and the terminal objects. Generating and removing differences limits the search to objects between, or nearly between, them, and generally finds short, direct paths.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: So long as the search need never extend beyond a narrow band joining the initial and terminal objects, the size of the search stays small and independent of the size of the problem space. The expanse beyond the band becomes irrelevant, and almost all of the space is ruled out of bounds at once.

card.rule: Means-ends analysis confines the search to a narrow band between start and goal, so the size of the whole space stops mattering.
card.limits: It can be wrong: the only path between two small expressions might pass through a very large one.

concepts.title: Means-ends analysis compared with working backward
concepts.question: How does means-ends analysis differ from a simple working-backward method, and which way does GPS work?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Using the goal object to guide search might sound like working backward from the goal. The authors separate the two ideas.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Working-backward methods start from the goal object and use information about it to anchor the search. In fact GPS works forward. Means-ends analysis uses information about the relation between both terminals, the start and the goal, and so imposes a far more powerful directionality on the search than working backward alone.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors draw the contrast explicitly, taking as the simple working-backward case the method used by LT in Chapter 4.

card.rule: Means-ends analysis is forward search guided by the difference between start and goal, not backward search from the goal.
card.limits: Our reading: the difference between the two is one of what information is used, not only of direction.

concepts.title: The planning method
concepts.question: What is the planning method, and why does solving a simplified problem first reduce difficulty?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Means-ends analysis sees only one step ahead. A second system of heuristic, a form of planning, builds a proposed solution in general terms before the details are worked out. It uses a problem in a different problem space as an aid.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The planning method is added to the transform goal type. (1) Abstract by omitting certain details of the original objects and operators. (2) Form the corresponding problem in the abstract space. (3) When it is solved, use its solution as a plan for the original problem. (4) Translate the plan back into the original space and execute it.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The power of the method rests on two facts. The whole of GPS can solve the abstract problem, which is usually simpler, with fewer steps. And the subproblems that make up the plan are collectively simpler, each with fewer steps. Since exploration generally grows exponentially with the number of steps, several smaller problems whose lengths add up to the original length can cut difficulty by orders of magnitude.

card.rule: Solve a simplified version first, then use its solution as a plan whose steps are small problems in the original space.
card.limits: A plan is only as good as the abstraction: details left out may make a plan fail when it is carried out.

concepts.title: The standard abstraction applied to D1
concepts.question: How does the standard abstraction turn problem D1 into a short planning problem and a plan?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: To show planning, the authors apply it to D1: L1 = (R ⊃ ~P) . (~R ⊃ Q) and L0 = ~(~Q . P).

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The standard abstraction ignores differences among connectives, signs and the order of symbols. L1 becomes (PR)(QR) and L0 becomes (PQ). The operators are abstracted too, so that A V B to B V A becomes the identity operator and A . B to A becomes (AB) to A.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: One solution of the abstract problem is: apply R8 to the left of (PR)(QR), giving (PR); apply R8 to the right, giving (QR); apply R12 to the two, giving (PQ). For the original problem this becomes a plan: apply R8 to L1, apply R8 to the other side, apply R12 to the results, and transform the outcome into L0.

card.rule: Strip a problem of connectives, signs and order, solve what is left, and read the solution as a plan for the original.
card.limits: The abstract solution is a plan, not a proof. It must still be carried out in the original space.

concepts.title: Plans can fail, and planning is still powerful
concepts.question: Can an abstract plan fail in the original space, and is planning still worth using?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Like the other heuristics, planning offers no guarantees. The plan comes from a simplified problem, so what holds there need not hold in the original.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Planning may generate no plan, a single plan, or several. More seriously, a plan may be illusory: it may prove impossible to carry out in the original space.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In the D1 example the first plan generated, R8, R11, R12, does not give a valid derivation when translated back to the original task environment. The time wasted on invalid plans must be counted in judging the heuristic. Even so, the authors judge it a very powerful one.

card.rule: A plan from the abstract space may be illusory; count the wasted effort, and planning still pays.
card.limits: How often plans fail depends on the abstraction. A poor abstraction gives many illusory plans.

concepts.title: Many possible abstractions
concepts.question: How many abstractions are possible for the six differences, and what do some alternatives look like?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The standard abstraction was introduced without motivation. The authors ask whether anything in the task makes it particularly appropriate.

blocks.label: Term
blocks.text: Differences and operators that an abstraction eliminates are inessential; those that remain are essential. The standard abstraction is written (As, Ac, Ap), a list of the differences to be ignored.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: For a given set of differences, each subset is a possible basis for an abstraction. Six differences give 2^6 = 64 possible bases.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Other bases: (As) alone sends L1 to (R ⊃ P) . (R ⊃ Q). The basis (At, Ag) abstracts from the identity of terms and the structure of expressions. The basis (An, Ac, As) abstracts from counting occurrences as well as from connectives and signs.

card.rule: Each subset of the differences is a possible abstraction, so six differences give 64 bases.
card.limits: Most of the 64 are not sensible; later criteria narrow them down.

concepts.title: What makes an abstraction good
concepts.question: By what criteria is an abstraction judged, and what stays constant when the planning depth changes?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Not every basis works equally well. The criteria for a good abstraction are complex and involve three aspects.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: First, the size of the planning space and the difficulty of solving problems in it. Second, the number of spurious solutions obtained in the planning space. Third, the size of the implementation space, which is the original space, and the difficulty of solving problems in it.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors state these as the aspects to weigh. Some features of the problem situation remain unchanged by abstraction, as the extension question shows.

card.rule: Judge an abstraction by the planning space, the spurious plans it yields, and the implementation space.
card.limits: The three aspects pull against each other. No single basis wins on all three.

concepts.title: How the difference ordering limits abstractions
concepts.question: How does GPS's ordering of differences cut the 64 possible abstractions down?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: It might seem that all 64 bases must be considered. The authors point out that the ordering of differences used by GPS removes many of them.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: A difference is not considered for the abstraction basis if differences higher in the ordering are retained in the planning space. An abstraction that ignores two differences in the ordering, but not those between them, would violate the ordering. So the basis (Ap, At) does not fit the ordering GPS uses, though it fits some other orders.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Given the differences and their order, the possible planning spaces are the five divisions of the ordered list into two parts: the top set essential and the bottom set inessential. Figure 8.18 lists these possibilities and shows which operators become identity operators.

card.rule: With the differences ranked, an abstraction splits the list into a kept top and an ignored bottom, with no skipping.
card.limits: The constraint holds only for the ordering GPS uses. Another ordering would allow other bases.

concepts.title: Where to put the split between essential and inessential
concepts.question: Which considerations decide where the split between essential and inessential differences falls?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Exactly where should the split be made? The authors give three considerations.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Efficiency: search effort grows geometrically with depth, so the maximum depth is least when the differences are divided about equally, near the middle of the list. Applicability: if differences among connectives stayed in the abstract space, tracing plans through would be about as hard as solving in the original, so a workable abstraction must remove them, at least down to (Ap, As, Ac). Adding An loses much of the task's structure. Analogy: An and At fix what materials an expression contains; As, Ac, Ap and Ag fix how they are arranged.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The first two considerations leave two plausible abstractions, (Ap, As, Ac) and (Ap, As, Ac, Ag). The material-arrangement analogy makes (An, At) essential and the rest inessential, which is substantially the same distinction.

card.rule: Split the differences near the middle, remove connective differences, and match the materials-versus-arrangement analogy.
card.limits: The criteria do not settle whether Ag is essential. The authors leave that open.

concepts.title: Deriving the table of connections from the operators
concepts.question: How could GPS work out the table of connections for itself?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: In the logic version of GPS, the authors simply gave it the differences, the operators relevant to each, and the order of difficulty. This is fair, since a human subject arrives holding a great deal of structure about symbols in long-term memory. Still, how much of this information lives in the task environment itself?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The table of connections is the easiest to derive (Newell, 1962). An operator is relevant to exactly the differences it reduces, and these are found by matching the operator's output expression to its input.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Figure 8.19 lists each rule's input and output forms and the differences found by matching them; the result is exactly the table of connections. For rule 3, A V A to A, the match finds An. For rule 2, A ⊃ B to ~B ⊃ ~A, it finds Ap and As. The operators and objects determine the structure of the task environment, and the authors have found a way to extract a relevant part of it.

card.rule: An operator is relevant to the differences between its input form and its output form, so the table can be read off the operators.
card.limits: This derives which operators bear on which differences. It does not by itself give the differences or their order.

concepts.title: Deriving the differences and their ordering
concepts.question: Can the differences and their ordering be derived too, and what remains out of reach?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The table of connections is easy to derive. The differences themselves and the difference ordering are harder, and so is the planning space.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Differences have been derived by at least two programs (Ernst and Newell, 1969; Quinlan and Hunt, 1968), starting from generalized primitive perceptual differences, such as telling connectives apart from one another and from signs and terms. These programs use quite elementary differences, not ones like An, the number of variable places.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Eavarone (1969) wrote a program that produces a difference ordering from given differences and operators. If every operator relevant to a difference produces higher differences in its output, working on the higher ones first is doomed, since they are reintroduced. So the table of connections must be writable as a triangular array (Figure 8.21). For logic the program produced an ordering consistent with the authors' own.

card.rule: Differences can be built from primitive perceptual ones, and an ordering exists only if the table can be written triangularly.
card.limits: No program has produced its own planning space. That still depends on settling which differences are essential and on a representation for the abstract space.

concepts.title: Analysis versus induction as sources of task information
concepts.question: How do analytic extraction and induction from examples compare as ways to obtain task information?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Each extra kind of information GPS uses has its source in the structure of the task environment. The authors ask in what ways an IPS could obtain it.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Some can be extracted by simple analytic processes. All of it can also be extracted by induction from a series of examples. Induction has advantages: it can be simpler if the induction demanded is not too sophisticated, and it needs no fully formed model of the space.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Induction also has costs: the knowledge is gained at much greater cost in processing, bit by bit, and is more contingent. The authors' purpose was to expose the nature of the task environment, not to explore how its structure might be learned; they show only that the information needed for a planning scheme is relatively accessible to the IPS itself.

card.rule: Analysis uses a model of the task; induction uses examples and is slower and more contingent.
card.limits: The authors do not claim GPS learns its own structure here. They show the information is accessible.

concepts.title: Measuring problem difficulty from the Yale data
concepts.question: How was problem difficulty measured, and what does Table 8.1 show about hard and easy problems?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors want to explain why some of the sixteen problems were much harder than others. As often, human data are best viewed as revealing the structure of the task environment.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Table 8.1 lists the problems in order of difficulty, measured by the number of the 64 Yale subjects who solved each. B2 was solved by 5 subjects and C1 by 6, the most difficult; D1 and C3 were solved by 24 each, the least difficult.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Other columns give the median solution time, the number of steps without the givens, the number of binary connectives in the proof as a measure of size, the constructions involved, and the number of essential rule applications. All solutions of more than ten steps are among the seven hardest problems, and every problem has a solution of at most eight steps.

card.rule: Difficulty is the number of subjects who solved a problem; steps, size and constructions are compared against it.
card.limits: Number of solvers measures difficulty for these subjects. Another group or a different time limit could rank the problems differently.

concepts.title: Constructions in geometry and why they raise difficulty
concepts.question: What is a construction in geometry, and why does it make a problem harder?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Several features in Table 8.1 go with difficulty, but the one that correlates most closely is the presence or absence of constructions. The authors borrow the term from elementary geometry.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Proofs of certain theorems need auxiliary lines or other figures that are not in the problem statement. Constructions substantially increase difficulty, since the student must decide whether one is needed and which lines to draw out of infinitely many. Without constructions the number of segments, angles and triangles to compare is very limited; with them the student faces an immensely larger maze and needs new selective heuristics.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Wertheimer (1945) discussed finding the formula for the area of a parallelogram. The key is to drop perpendiculars from one side to the other. Then the problem becomes the area of a rectangle, obtained by adding and subtracting equal triangles.

card.rule: A construction adds something not in the problem statement, which enlarges the maze and calls for new selective heuristics.
card.limits: The geometric term is an analogy. The authors then define a construction for logic in their own terms.

concepts.title: Defining a construction in the logic task
concepts.question: How do the authors define a construction for logic, and which kinds of step are not constructions?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: In logic, the givens and the goal define a limited set of expressions that can be derived without excessive search: simplifications of the givens, rule applications that promise to reduce differences with L0, rules that conspicuously fit the forms of the givens, and expressions from inessential steps.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: A construction is a rule application (1) that produces a more complex object than its input, or than any of its inputs, and (2) does so without direct prior justification for the added complexity. Simplifications and inessential transformations fail the first condition. Difference-reducing and conspicuously fitting applications fail the second. All other applications are constructions.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors predict difficulty by postulating that subjects can generate expressions obtainable without constructions from those they already have, so problems will be difficult if they cannot be solved without constructions.

card.rule: A construction adds complexity with no direct justification; simplifications and well-motivated steps are not constructions.
card.limits: The definition is the authors' own operational one. It is stated in terms of rule applications, not of what subjects intended.

concepts.title: Which rule applications are constructions
concepts.question: Which uses of R5, R7, R9 and the two-line rules count as constructions in the book's examples?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Applying the definition to the rules, the authors find that the steps to treat as constructions are certain applications of R5, R7, R9 and the two-line rules R10, R11, R12.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: R9 and R10 produce more complex outputs and can produce a large number of different ones. R5 (adding a tilde to the whole expression) and R7 (in the direction that enlarges the expression) increase complexity without proliferating new expressions. The geometric analogy: drawing a line between two existing vertices (R5, R7) is a construction with little choice; drawing to new vertices (R9, R10) allows wide choice.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In problem A4 the goal is P V T and T occurs in no given expression. Getting P and adding T with R9 is not a construction, since the difference in variables motivates it. Two-line rules, especially R11 and R12, are constructions when one or both inputs must first be generated without motivation.

card.rule: A step is a construction when it adds complexity that the goal or the visible form does not call for.
card.limits: The same rule can be a construction in one problem and not in another, depending on motivation.

concepts.title: Path frequencies and linked steps
concepts.question: What do the counts of subjects along solution paths show about linked steps and planning?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: To test the construction hypothesis, the authors look at how many subjects wrote down particular expressions on the way to a solution in eight problems (Figure 8.23), to see which steps were difficult and which steps were linked.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Two steps are linked if the first was done in order to do the second, or the second was obvious once the first was done. The evidence is that almost all subjects who did the first also did the second. The authors find eleven such instances in the eight problems.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In D4 only half applied R9, but all of those went on to R11. In B3 only six used R10, and all but one of them used R7; three solved the problem, so R10 was used in order to apply R7. The data are consistent with the construction hypothesis, but show steady attrition, not full plans made in advance.

card.rule: A step that nearly everyone takes after another is linked to it; attrition shows where steps were hard, not that whole plans existed.
card.limits: Counts of paths can show linkage but not intention. The authors speak of conjecture where they cannot tell.

concepts.title: Functional fixity in problem C1
concepts.question: What other difficulty beyond the R10-R7 construction does problem C1 show?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: In C1, the R10-R7 construction was not the only difficulty. Only one quarter of the subjects applied R12.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: In C1 the solution calls for one term, P V Q, to do two different jobs. The authors count this, together with the R10-R7 construction, among the reasons the problem was hard.

blocks.label: Term
blocks.text: The authors name the phenomenon functional fixity. Our reading: a subject who has put an item to one use tends not to see it as available for another.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: C1 is the only problem in which the same term, P V Q, is put to two distinct uses in the solution. It is used as the left-hand input to R10 after having been used to construct one of the inputs to R12.

card.rule: C1 is hard partly because one term must serve two purposes, and subjects tend to keep it for one.
card.limits: The authors defer the evidence for the deterrence. The card relies on their account of what C1 requires.

concepts.title: A simple processor without constructions
concepts.question: What does a processor with a few simple heuristics and no constructions predict about easy and hard problems?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: To test the difficulty hypothesis further, the authors postulate a processing system and ask which expressions it would generate and whether it solves each problem, as they did for D1.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The postulates: R8 is applied to positive main expressions with dots as main connectives. Inessential rules are applied when useful to make essential rules fit, in particular R2 and R5 when they reduce the number of tildes. R11 and R12 are applied to eliminate unwanted letters. R7 is applied when a given expression has the form (AB)(AC). R9 is applied as the last step when L0 is A V B and B does not occur in the givens.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: By hand simulation, this processor solves all but one (B1) of the six easiest problems and none of the harder ones. It fails on all seven difficult problems because none of its heuristics makes a construction. The authors take it as a crude first approximation to the heuristics of the subjects who solved the easier problems but not the harder ones.

card.rule: A processor with simplification, difference-reduction and fit heuristics solves the easy problems and fails when a construction is needed.
card.limits: It is a crude first approximation. It is not offered as a model of any one subject.

concepts.title: The first four summary ideas: goals, means-ends, difficulty goals, self-built structure
concepts.question: Which four ideas about GPS does the chapter summary list, and what is risky in the third?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors say their task analysis of the logic problems was narrower than for cryptarithmetic. They described the basic space and estimated its size, then, rather than vary the spaces and heuristics, presented GPS as an existing program working in the basic space. GPS does more than simple forward search and introduces several important ideas.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: (1) Goal structures: the goal is a symbol structure holding the desired object, the methods of attaining it and the history of past attempts. (2) Means-ends analysis: select operators with a view to the goal; this needs differences as a bridge between objects and operators, and an ordering of differences to give direction. (3) Difficulties lead to goals to overcome them: being unable to apply an operator sets up a goal of applying it. (4) An IPS constructing its own structures: differences and connections can be obtained from the task definition.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Each idea was introduced in this chapter: goal structures through the executive and methods, means-ends through the three methods, difficulty goals through reduce goals, and self-built structures in the section on developing the task information.

card.rule: GPS brings goal structures, means-ends analysis, goals set by difficulties, and the possibility of building its own structures.
card.limits: Idea 3 is a dangerous heuristic: it can follow blind paths forever unless curbed.

concepts.title: The last two summary ideas and what comes next
concepts.question: What do the summary's ideas on constructions and planning spaces say, and what do the authors turn to next?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The chapter has already used some human data, in the section on sources of difficulty. The authors say this gives some evidence that their information processing analysis makes sense when applied to human behavior.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: (5) Constructions: an operation that increases complexity when there is no strong guideline. It was made operational for the logic task, and relative problem difficulty was understood as a combination of the need for a construction and the effect of large search spaces. As an independent measure of difficulty the authors used the 64 Yale subjects. (6) Planning spaces: the planning space is another problem space, but unlike the augmented space of cryptarithmetic it is not richer than the base space; it consists of less detail.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The role of a planning space is to guide action, rather than to serve as the site of the main problem solving. The authors now turn to examining the application to human behavior more deeply.

card.rule: Construction explains difficulty together with search size; a planning space has less detail and guides action in the base space.
card.limits: The difficulty explanation is tested against subjects only through counts so far. Closer tests of behavior come next.

concepts.title: What the chapter sets out to test
concepts.question: What does the chapter ask about human subjects and GPS, and in which problem space?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors have turned their task analysis of the Moore-Anderson logic task into one program, GPS, working in a definite problem space. They now ask whether a person working these logic problems behaves in a GPS-like way, and whether the likeness holds at a convincing level of detail.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The space is the basic one: logic expressions are the nodes and the twelve legal rules are the operators. Given the cryptarithmetic experience, the authors aim high: to leave only modest amounts of task behavior unexplained.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors say the order here reverses history. GPS was the first detailed simulation of human symbolic behavior and came after the Logic Theorist, which had been compared only generally with human problem solving. Cryptarithmetic comes first in the book because the basic issues are more transparent there.

card.rule: The chapter tests, in the basic space of logic expressions and twelve rules, whether subjects behave like GPS at a detailed level.
card.limits: The test concerns this one task; a good fit here would not by itself show that other tasks are GPS-like.

concepts.title: Why the fit is not circular
concepts.question: Why does the authors' fitting of GPS to some of the same protocols not make the match trivial?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: GPS was built by close study of some of the same protocols that the chapter discusses. A reader may suspect that any fit between program and data is then guaranteed.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The authors grant that GPS is partly adapted to the data, as any model with parameters is. They deny that the fit is tautological. GPS can be adequate only to the extent that the subject really behaves in a GPS-like way.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: All aspects of GPS (methods, heuristics, organization) are defined independently of the subjects' behavior, from the task environment and the theory of Chapter 4. So the authors say there is no a priori reason why humans, or any particular person, should behave this way.

card.rule: Partial adaptation to data does not make a fit trivial, because GPS is defined independently of the subjects' behavior and could fail to match.
card.limits: The argument shows the fit is testable, not that it is good; the later sections must show the match in detail.

concepts.title: GPS is a family of programs
concepts.question: In what sense is GPS not a single program, and what does that mean for the chapter's questions?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A reader may picture GPS as one fixed program. The authors say the name covers several variants that have run on computers, and the variants differ in many respects.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The differences go beyond settings of parameters, even nonnumerical ones such as tables of connections. At one time or another GPS has had five basic underlying IPS structures, which affect how methods and data structures are represented. There has also been one change of programming language, and methods have been added and removed.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Because of this, the chapter's questions are about the GPS-like behavior of the subjects. The authors promise to point out which aspects fit particular existing forms of GPS closely and which do not.

card.rule: GPS names a family of variants, so the chapter asks about GPS-like behavior and says where a particular version fits.
card.limits: A claim that people are GPS-like does not say which variant is right; it concerns the shared organization.

concepts.title: Comparing S9 with GPS on Problem a1
concepts.question: How is a subject's free-form protocol compared with a computer trace on Problem a1?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Problem a1 is a simple training problem, the first one subject S9 tried after studying the twelve rules. The protocol of S9 is set beside a trace of a working version of GPS solving the same problem.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The subject speaks freely, while the program's language is stylized. To compare them, each sentence is translated into the program's terms. For instance, a remark about looking at reversing two things is read as a goal to remove the difference in position of corresponding parts of two objects.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors say such translation has been shown to be not too difficult in practice. With a trace there is no need for a PBG, either of the protocol or of GPS. The analysis is essentially the same as an earlier one, except that the trace came from a working program rather than a hand simulation.

card.rule: To compare a protocol with a trace, translate the subject's everyday wording into the program's goals, then match similarities and differences.
card.limits: Translation involves interpretation; the comparison is only as good as the readings of the loose sentences.

concepts.title: Where GPS fell short on Problem a1
concepts.question: Which differences between S9 and the trace count against GPS as an accurate theory of S9?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Beside the match, the comparison shows differences that the authors call inadequacies of GPS in this form. They matter for judging GPS as an accurate account of S9's behavior.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: First, S9 solved the whole problem in his head and only then asked the experimenter to write the transformations on the blackboard. That version of GPS has no internal versus external distinction, so its trace corresponds only to the subject's covert, verbalized problem solving.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Second, the trace contains items with no correspondent in the protocol, most prominently references to R5 and R8. The authors cannot tell whether this is an error in the theory or whether the subject noticed the rules and did not mention them. In the second case, the program makes a genuine prediction of covert behavior.

card.rule: The trace and S9's protocol differ in the internal versus external split and in rules that appear only in the trace.
card.limits: A step with no correspondent in the protocol does not by itself refute the theory, since the subject may have thought it without saying it.

concepts.title: Correspondences on Problem a1
concepts.question: In what detailed ways do S9 and GPS agree on Problem a1?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Despite the differences, the authors point to striking agreement in detail between the trace and S9's protocol. They ask what that agreement shows about the problem space and the program.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: First, in noticing differences between expressions, both attend most to differences in positions of symbols, next to the presence or absence of signs (tildes), and least to differences in connectives. Second, both refuse to use R2 to reorder after mentioning or trying it, because it also changes a sign.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors conclude that, though the sample is miniscule, there is little doubt that S9 worked in the same problem space as GPS and that his program was GPS-like in many ways.

card.rule: Both S9 and GPS weight differences in order position first, sign second, connective last, and both avoid R2 after mentioning it because it also changes a sign.
card.limits: The sample is one subject on one simple problem; the authors call it miniscule and treat it as a first indication.

concepts.title: The structure of Problem a1
concepts.question: Why does Problem a1 have six solution paths of length three, and how do they differ?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Part of the likeness among subjects could come from the task itself. For Problem a1 there are six distinct solution paths of length three, and all are essentially permutations of the path that the subject and GPS used.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Stated in terms of function, the problem calls for three changes: put the R on the other side of the whole expression, change the signs and the horseshoe to a wedge, and swap P and Q. The three can be done in any order, so there are 3! = 6 orders. Each change can be recognized from the form of the resulting expression and done by one operation.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: S11 states the three changes in nearly these words: change the places of the R, change the signs and horseshoe to wedge, and reverse P and Q. The six paths are listed in Figure 9.3, using the label PQ for the subexpression holding P and Q.

card.rule: Problem a1 needs three independent changes, each done by one rule, so it has 3! = 6 shortest paths.
card.limits: The changes are not fully independent: the rule that swaps P and Q is R2 if their connective is still a horseshoe, but R1 once it has become a wedge.

concepts.title: Similarities among five subjects on a1
concepts.question: What do five subjects share on Problem a1 beyond what the task forces?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The protocols of S9 and four other subjects are alike. Some likeness comes from the shared task environment, but the authors point to similarities that go beyond what the task requires.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: All five map out the solution, partly or fully, before asking the experimenter to carry out the official transformations. They state the plan partly as functions to be performed (S9: reversing the two things) and partly as rules to apply (S15: use R1 and switch the two around).

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: All five mention first the reversal of left and right sides of the whole expression. Three then mention the change of connective followed by the swap of P and Q; two mention them in the reverse order. None interposes a transformation of the whole expression between the two operations on the parts.

card.rule: Beyond task demands, all five subjects plan the solution aloud before acting and mention the whole-expression reversal first.
card.limits: A few features vary: only some subjects mention rule R2, and only one mentions features that must not change.

concepts.title: Matching and functional language
concepts.question: What do subjects use matching for, and how do they word the differences they find?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors ask what small set of subprocesses lies behind the five protocols. The first is matching two expressions to discover one or more differences between them.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Differences are mostly worded as actions to remove them, such as connective change or change places, and rarely as plain descriptions.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: All five subjects match L1 with L0 at the outset. They notice the difference in order of terms across the whole expression before the differences in the P-Q terms, and they treat (Q V P) as similar to (~P horseshoe Q) even though these sit in different places of their expressions.

card.rule: Matching finds differences, and subjects word them as actions to remove them rather than as static descriptions.
card.limits: The wording is a pattern across five subjects on one problem, not a guarantee for other tasks.

concepts.title: Three kinds of rule search
concepts.question: What distinguishes a search for a rule that does a job from a search for one that applies?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A second subprocess searches for an operator relevant to reducing a difference or doing a function. A third searches for a rule that is applicable and gives an apparently desirable result. The authors ask how these appear in the protocols and in GPS.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Searching for a rule to meet a stated function is evoked by that function; S9 says he is looking for a way to get rid of the horseshoe and finds R6. Searching for a rule that applies and looks useful is a test of both points: S9 finds R3 inapplicable because two parts are not identical, and finds R4 applicable but with no switching of order, so undesirable.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In GPS a difference and a function are synonymous; in the protocols they differ. S15 shows the other way to find a relevant rule: apply the rule to a concrete expression, get the output, and match it with the wanted output to see whether the difference is gone.

card.rule: Searching by function asks what rule would do this job; searching by applicability asks which rule fits here and gives a good result.
card.limits: In GPS difference and function are synonymous, but in the protocols they can be separate, so the two searches should not be merged.

concepts.title: Table of connections or rule search
concepts.question: Why do these subjects search the rules so often, and what do they already know?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: There are two ways to find a rule for a difference or function: use an association already stored in memory, which is the GPS table of connections, or search the rules more or less systematically.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Because Problem a1 is the first these subjects have solved, they have stored little of a table of connections, so the protocols hold many rule searches motivated by a function to be performed.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In summary, the protocols are explicable by a small number of subprocesses that are contained in GPS or describable in GPS-like terms.

card.rule: On a first problem the table of connections is thin, so subjects search the rules; the same GPS subprocesses explain the protocols.
card.limits: This explains a first problem; it does not say how fast the table fills with practice.

concepts.title: How hard Problem D1 is
concepts.question: How many subjects solved Problem D1, and how did practice change the result?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Problem D1 was one of sixteen problems given to the Yale subjects. It was usually given to the Carnegie subjects immediately after the three training problems. It was one of the two easiest problems for the Yale subjects.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Even so, only 24 of 64 Yale subjects solved it in the fifteen minutes allowed. Among sixteen subjects who met it in the first one-hour session, one solved it; in the second session four, in the third five, and in the fourth fourteen of sixteen.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors conclude that it was not easy in an absolute sense for subjects without extensive practice. By the fourth session the subjects had practiced, successfully or not, on at least twelve earlier problems. Five of the seven Carnegie subjects with protocols solved D1 in their half hour.

card.rule: D1 is among the easier problems yet was solved by few unpractised subjects, so practice raised the rate sharply.
card.limits: The sessions confound practice with other changes; the authors read the rise as an effect of practice.

concepts.title: The shortest solution of D1
concepts.question: How long is the shortest solution of D1, and what are its main moves in plain terms?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: To read the subjects' behavior on D1 the authors first analyze the task. The shortest solution from L1 takes six steps (Figure 9.4): R8 applied to the left part of L1, R8 to the right part, R2 on one of these, R12 on the two parts, then R6 and R5.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: In functional terms, L1 is split into two parts by two uses of R8. One part, preferably the one beginning with a negated R, is commuted by R2 so that the two parts can be combined by R12, which removes the R's. The horseshoe in the result is changed to a dot by first making it a wedge (R6), then a dot (R5).

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Some orders can be swapped, for example L2 and L3 may be interchanged. Other changes make the solution longer. If R2 is applied to L2 instead of L3, a later R1 or R2 must reverse P and Q, so a subject may take seven steps without wasting any.

card.rule: D1's shortest solution has six steps: split with R8 twice, align with R2, combine with R12, then change the connective with R6 and R5.
card.limits: The six steps are the shortest path; longer routes can still be free of wasted steps.

concepts.title: Clues in the task environment of D1
concepts.question: What does the task environment offer to guide a solver beyond exhaustive search?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors ask what clues the task environment gives to the correct path, short of trying everything.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: A match between L1 and L0 detects the need to delete R. This is an essential difference, in the sense used for planning in Chapter 8. It suggests considering paths that solve the problem in an abstract space.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In that abstract space the expressions are the original ones with connectives, signs and the order of symbols ignored. The authors show five such plans (Figure 9.5), not all that could be generated, to analyze the subjects' behavior. They label each by its most characteristic essential rule.

card.rule: Matching L1 with L0 reveals that R must be deleted, and that essential difference suggests plans in an abstract space.
card.limits: The five plans are the most important ones, not an exhaustive list.

concepts.title: Five plans for D1
concepts.question: How do the five plans differ in how they get rid of the R's?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Each plan names the essential rule that seems most characteristic of it. They differ mainly in how the R's are eliminated.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: In two plans the R's go by successive uses of R8 (path.R10) or by R8 combined with R11 (path.R11), and the pieces are joined by R10. In two others the R's go by R7 followed by R8 (path.R7), or by R12 (path.R12). In the last (path.R9), R8 removes a part and later removes the remaining R.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In path.R12 in particular, R8 is used not to delete letters but to divide L1 into two separate parts to which the two-line rule, R12, can be applied. The authors say the plans are not the only ones that the protocols show but they are the most important.

card.rule: The five plans differ in how they eliminate the R's; path.R12 splits L1 with R8 and then applies the two-line rule R12.
card.limits: Other plans appear in the protocols; these five are the main ones the authors use.

concepts.title: Why repeated use of R8 fails
concepts.question: Why can R8 not be applied a second time to a part of L1?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Plans that try to pull a single letter out of L1 by successive uses of R8 cannot be carried out. The authors give the reason.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: R8 can be applied only to positive expressions whose main connective is a dot. The main connective of left(L1) or right(L1) cannot be changed to a dot without making the whole expression negative.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: So after R8 has produced one part, a second use of R8 on that part is blocked. The attempt fails because of a condition on sign and connective, not for want of the right idea.

card.rule: R8 needs a positive expression with a dot as main connective, and left(L1) cannot be given a dot without becoming negative.
card.limits: The explanation concerns R8 in D1; other rules have different conditions.

concepts.title: Equivalence classes of inessential rules
concepts.question: How many forms can one binary expression take under the four inessential rules, and how many classes do they fall in?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors want to know which forms an expression can be turned into by R1, R2, R5 and R6, the four rules that change tildes and connectives and permute the order of terms around the main connective.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Take two fixed subexpressions A and B. There are three connectives, two orders and three signs (one for A, one for B, one for the whole), each plus or minus. That gives 3 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 = 48 expressions. From any one of the six forms in Figure 9.7, each of the other five, and only those, can be reached.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: So six expressions form a class under the four rules, and there must be 48/6 = 8 such classes. Two expressions in the same class can be obtained from each other by R1, R2, R5 and R6; expressions in different classes cannot.

card.rule: The four inessential rules link six forms of an expression, which makes 48 forms fall into 8 classes.
card.limits: The counting holds for a binary expression of two fixed parts; with more structure the counts change.

concepts.title: What inessential means
concepts.question: Why does the name inessential mislead, and what would be a better description?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The four rules R1, R2, R5 and R6 are called inessential. A reader might take that to mean they can be ignored.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: As noted in Chapter 8, these rules do not add terms to expressions, delete terms, or change the grouping of terms in subexpressions. The authors say form-preserving would perhaps be more descriptive, since subjects almost uniformly regard expressions in one class as highly similar.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The word inessential alludes to planning: a plan can be made in terms of the essential rules, with the inessential ones serving for minor adjustments that fit the segments of the plan together. But labeling a rule inessential does not mean it can be ignored in deciding whether a plan is feasible.

card.rule: Inessential rules preserve the form of an expression; they are used for adjustments, but they matter for a plan's feasibility.
card.limits: The word marks a role in planning, not unimportance; ignoring them can make an infeasible plan look feasible.

concepts.title: Why the R7 plan fails
concepts.question: Why can L1 not be put into a form to which R7 applies, and why is this not obvious?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The R7 plan requires an expression like L1 to be put into a shape such as (R V P)*(R V Q), or (R*P) V (R*Q), or similar with tildes in front of both R's. The authors ask whether the inessential rules can do this.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: They cannot. The sign of R in any subexpression with a wedge or dot connective obtained from L1 is determined by the connective. So different changes cannot be made to the two signs of R without producing different connectives in the two subexpressions.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors stress that this result is by no means obvious. A person without Figure 9.7 might not be sure that L1 cannot be put into a form for R7, so the infeasibility of the R7 plan is also not obvious.

card.rule: In D1 the signs of the two R's are tied to the connectives, so the inessential rules cannot make R7 applicable to L1.
card.limits: The proof depends on Figure 9.7's structure; a solver without it may search a long time before seeing the block.

concepts.title: Counting the extended class of L1
concepts.question: How many forms does an expression made of three binary parts have under the inessential rules?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A subject attempting the R7 plan is expected to produce expressions from L1 by commuting it or applying R1, R2, R5 or R6 to its parts. The authors name the set he draws from.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The set of expressions obtainable by operating on the main expression of L1 as well as on its parts is the extended equivalence class of L1. Three binary expressions are involved, and each has six forms, so each extended class has 6 x 6 x 6 = 216 expressions.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The count rests on Figure 9.7: any binary expression has six forms under the four inessential rules. The whole of L1, its left part and its right part are three such expressions, and each may be in any of its six forms independently of the others.

card.rule: Operating on the main expression and on both parts of L1 gives an extended equivalence class of 216 forms.
card.limits: The count belongs to an expression with three binary parts; a different structure has a different count.

concepts.title: Weaker clues: simplification and applicability
concepts.question: Besides the start-goal match, what weaker clues could steer a solver on D1?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: So far the match between L0 and L1 has been the source of clues. The authors list weaker ones that a solver might also use to choose a path.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: One is simplification: if applying a rule yields an expression simpler than L1 by some measure, that suggests the step is appropriate. R6 might be justified partly because its product is simpler than L1. A still weaker clue is applicability: a rule is applied because it applies, which the authors compare to climbing a mountain because it is there.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: L1 has the shape (RP)(RQ), which looks like the right side of R7, (AB)(AC); that likeness may suggest R7. But rules differ widely in how likely they are to apply. It makes no sense to apply R9 because it is applicable, since R9 is always applicable.

card.rule: Simplification and mere applicability are weaker clues than the start-goal match, and applicability says nothing for a rule that always applies.
card.limits: A weak clue can start a search but does not settle that a step is part of the solution.

concepts.title: The GPS trace for S4 on D1
concepts.question: How does GPS begin Problem D1, which rules does it try, and why does it reject some?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors compare an initial segment of subject S4's protocol on D1 with a trace of a version of GPS over the same period (Figure 9.8). First they describe the trace.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: GPS matches L1 to L0 and finds R's in L1 but none in L0. That leads to a reduce goal, named Delete. Searching the rules finds R8, which has two admissible forms, and GPS chooses the first. R8 is applicable, so L2 is produced. The next goal, to transform L2 into L0, creates the goal of restoring a Q to L2, and that goal is rejected because adding a term is treated as harder than deleting one.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: GPS returns to its Delete goal, tries the other form of R8 with a similar excursion, and rejects R8 altogether. It then finds R7, selecting the variant that both decreases terms and has a dot as main connective. R7 is not at once applicable, so GPS removes the connective differences in each part with R6, and then a sign difference, again with R6.

card.rule: GPS sees R's in L1 but not L0, tries R8 in both forms and rejects it because the product lacks a letter L0 needs, then moves to R7.
card.limits: This is one version of GPS on one initial segment; the authors note its details differ from the version used on a1.

concepts.title: Avoiding cycles with a progress test
concepts.question: How does GPS avoid cycling forever over the inessential rules, and what is the alternative?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: In trying to make L1 an input for R7, GPS could cycle indefinitely over the inessential rules: change a connective, change a sign, change the connective back, and so on.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The version used applies a progress test to the successive differences between the obtained expression and the desired one (the input for R7). GPS arranges differences in a priority order. Removing a connective difference is progress, but reintroducing the connective difference in order to remove a sign difference is not.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: So the second move brings the series of transformations to a halt. The authors note that this is only one of several possible means of avoiding the cycle.

card.rule: GPS halts a cycle because reintroducing a connective difference to fix a sign difference is not progress under its priority order.
card.limits: A progress test can stop a search that a longer route would have solved; it depends on the chosen priority order.

concepts.title: Where S4's words match the trace
concepts.question: Which of S4's remarks match steps of the GPS trace, and what does each show?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors compare S4's protocol with the trace sentence by sentence, informally, to see whether the program is a detailed model of his symbol manipulation.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: S4's first sentence, about wanting to eliminate one of the sides by R8, corresponds to goals 1 to 3. His rejection (I can't do that because I will be eliminating the Q or the P) expresses a covert application of R8, a comparison of the result with L0, and rejection because a needed letter is lost. Applying R6 to both sides to get ready for R7 corresponds to goals 9 to 14.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors say it would be hard to find words that expressed these ideas more clearly, and that if the program's mechanism were not operating it would be hard to explain why S4 said what he did. His choice of R6 over R5 also suggests a preliminary feasibility test, as in the program's reduce goal.

card.rule: S4's sentences match the trace's goals closely: choose R8 to delete, reject it for deleting a needed letter, then use R6 to prepare R7.
card.limits: These are informal matches of single sentences; they do not show that the same motive lies behind each step.

concepts.title: A late agreement after a divergence
concepts.question: What happens in the last part of the S4 segment, and why is that agreement notable?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: In the last part of the S4 segment the authors look at his remarks after the abandoned try at R7: it can't be done because of the horseshoe; I scan the rules to change the R to a tilde R in the second equation but see no way; I am lost for a second.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The trace and the protocol come back into good agreement. Both record the futile search for further operators to remove the sign and connective differences, always with negative results.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors point out that paths that begin to diverge do not often merge in this way. They read the final comment of mild despair as the impact of several successive failures.

card.rule: After a divergence, S4's search and the trace agree again; the authors count such re-agreement as notable.
card.limits: Agreement on a failing search is weaker evidence than agreement on a distinctive success.

concepts.title: Where S4 and the trace part ways
concepts.question: Which differences between S4 and the GPS trace show where the program needs to change?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Besides the agreements, the comparison shows discrepancies. The authors treat them as clues to what the program lacks.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: S4 handles both forms of R8 together and both applications of R6 together, while GPS handles them one at a time. This grouping of similar items is likely real; the authors suggest GPS should treat them as compounds. S4 also corrected himself, saying he should have used R6 on only the left-hand side, which has no counterpart in GPS.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The version of GPS also draws no line between internal and external actions: S4 handled R8 covertly but commanded the experimenter to apply R6 on the board. Nor can it explain the phrase and I don't see it, since it has no copy of the rule sheet and does not distinguish searching the sheet from searching memory.

card.rule: The discrepancies are grouping of similar items, a hindsight correction, no internal versus external line, and no rule-sheet search.
card.limits: Not every discrepancy is serious: one comment may simply lack enough data to be explained.

concepts.title: The verdict on the S4 comparison
concepts.question: What do the authors conclude from the comparison of GPS with S4, and how confident are they?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors take stock of the agreements and disagreements between the trace and the protocol over the first episodes of S4 on D1.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: They say the program gives a complete explanation of S4's task behavior through this episode with five exceptions of varying seriousness. Two exceptions are generalized deficiencies that could be remedied: no internal versus external line, and the rule-sheet search spaces. One is the grouping of items, which GPS could be extended to include.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Two exceptions are clear task-oriented behavior with nothing corresponding in the program: the early complication comment, mostly a case of insufficient information, and the should-have passage, which is serious. The version used on D1 differs from the one used on a1, but the authors say they must be regarded as the same program, so an approximate fit to two subjects on two problems gives confidence in the main processes.

card.rule: GPS explains S4's episode with five exceptions; the authors read the fit across two subjects and problems as support for its main processes.
card.limits: The fit is approximate and based on informal comparison; the should-have passage points to a missing mechanism.

concepts.title: Why look at the Yale aggregate data
concepts.question: What do the aggregate data from 64 Yale subjects serve to check?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Before analyzing the protocols of the other subjects intensively, the authors take a comprehensive view of behavior on D1 from the performance of the 64 Yale subjects, who did not think aloud.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: These data serve three purposes. They check the authors' characterization of the task environment. They throw light on whether thinking-aloud instructions change the problem solving process in significant ways. And they give a background against which the protocol data can be read.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Table 9.1 shows the number of steps taken by the 24 Yale solvers and the 5 Carnegie solvers who thought aloud. Thirteen of the 24 Yale solvers took six or seven steps, as did two of the Carnegie group, so the distributions look quite similar.

card.rule: The Yale data check the task analysis, test whether thinking aloud alters search, and give a background for the protocols.
card.limits: Similar step counts show only that the distributions look alike; they do not by themselves show that the search paths are alike.

concepts.title: Four classes of expected expressions
concepts.question: Which four classes of expressions would the four main paths lead subjects to write down?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The 64 subjects wrote on the board 118 different expressions, with 519 occurrences in all, an average of 4.4 per expression. The authors ask whether these are the expressions one would expect from searching along the main paths, or whether behavior is highly idiosyncratic.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Pursuit of the paths should generate mostly expressions from four classes: the equivalence class of L1, the equivalence class of the left part of L1, that of the right part of L1, and that of L0.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: R8 applied to L1 yields a member of the left or right part's class, and its class is explored further when subjects try to make an expression positive with a dot so R8 can be used again. Members of left, right and L0 classes arise along the R12 path. The attempt to apply R7 yields members of the class of L1.

card.rule: If subjects follow the main paths, their expressions should fall in four classes: that of L1, of its left part, of its right part, and of L0.
card.limits: Expressions outside the four classes are not predicted by this simple reading, though some may be explained otherwise.

concepts.title: What the aggregate counts show
concepts.question: How much of the subjects' writing falls inside the four expected classes?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Table 9.2 gives the counts for the four classes and for all other expressions. The authors ask how far the four classes account for what subjects wrote.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The four classes hold 60 of the 118 different expressions, just over half. But those expressions occurred on average 7.3 times each, against 1.4 for the other 58. So the four classes account for 437 of the 519 occurrences, 84 percent, or five-sixths.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: All 6 members of each of the classes of left(L1), right(L1) and L0 occurred. Of the 72 members of the class of L1, 42 occurred. Of the other unusual expressions, 26 percent (29 percent of their occurrences) belong to the extended equivalence class of L1.

card.rule: The four classes cover about half the different expressions but 84 percent of all occurrences.
card.limits: Half of the different expressions lie outside the four classes, though they are rare ones.

concepts.title: Reaching the L0 class and solving
concepts.question: What do the data say about subjects who reach expressions of the L0 class?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors look at what happened once a subject produced an expression in the equivalence class of L0, and at what happened when a subject produced expressions in both the left and right classes.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Every subject who generated an expression in the class of L0 solved the problem. A solver must use at least three expressions of that class to change from a horseshoe to a dot. The 84 occurrences in the records of the 24 solvers exceed that minimum by only 12 occurrences, 0.5 per solver.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: So the subjects milled about very little once they had a member of L0's class. Of 32 subjects who generated expressions in both the left(L1) and right(L1) classes, 24 (75 percent) solved the problem.

card.rule: Reaching the L0 class meant solving, with almost no milling about; having both halves of L1 gave a 75 percent solving rate.
card.limits: These counts are association; the authors do not claim that producing both halves caused solving.

concepts.title: Does thinking aloud change the search?
concepts.question: What do the data on the seven thinking-aloud subjects say about thinking-aloud instructions?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Thinking aloud might change how people search. The authors compare the seven thinking-aloud subjects with the Yale group, who did not talk.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The seven generated 34 different expressions with 78 occurrences. Only 3 of those expressions (one occurrence each) were not used by the Yale subjects, and 30 of the remaining 31 belonged to the four classes. The two subjects who failed produced no member of left(L1), right(L1) or L0.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The five solvers produced 20 occurrences of left or right expressions and 19 of L0 expressions, against minimums of 15 each for five solutions. So few superfluous expressions were generated. The authors conclude that thinking-aloud instructions did not modify the directions of search.

card.rule: The talking subjects wrote almost the same expressions as the Yale subjects, so thinking aloud did not change the direction of search.
card.limits: The conclusion concerns this task and these counts; the authors add a footnote saying it is not a general statement.

concepts.title: A caution on thinking-aloud evidence
concepts.question: How far does the authors' finding on thinking aloud extend, and what does the literature they mention cover?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A footnote qualifies the finding that thinking-aloud instructions did not modify the search. The authors say it is not a general statement about the effect of such instructions on behavior.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: They cite one related study: Dansereau and Gregg (1966) found no difference in the times taken for mental multiplication problems in silent and thinking-aloud conditions.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Most research on effects of verbalization concerns either verbal instruction or requiring subjects to state reasons or to verbalize principles in problem solutions. The authors say such effects have no relevance to whether thinking aloud changes the course of problem solving behavior.

card.rule: The thinking-aloud result is limited to this task; most research on verbalization addresses a different question.
card.limits: A narrow finding should not be generalized, and the authors point to a gap in the research instead of closing it.

concepts.title: Expressions considered but not written
concepts.question: What do protocols show about expressions that subjects considered without writing them?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The protocols hold evidence of expressions that subjects generated in their search but did not ask the experimenter to write on the board. The authors ask whether these change the picture drawn from the written ones.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Subjects sometimes apply a rule mentally, work out the output and decide it is undesirable, so they do not request it. S4 sees at the outset that he could obtain two of his expressions by applying R8 to L1, but declines because each eliminates a letter he needs for L0.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Subjects also work backward from L0, for example deriving Q V ~P, and consider what expression they would need to make a rule applicable. S4 reasons that with (R V Q) he could apply R7 to derive R*(P V Q) and then R8 to derive (P V Q). The unwritten expressions fall in the same categories as the written ones, and so support using the written ones to characterize the activity.

card.rule: Expressions considered but not written fall into the same classes as the written ones, which supports using the board as a record.
card.limits: Unwritten expressions are known only through what subjects say, so the record is partial.

concepts.title: Expressions in the class of L1 and R7
concepts.question: How do the expressions in the class of L1 show that subjects were preparing to apply R7?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The expressions in the equivalence class of L1 should reflect attempts to make R7 applicable. The authors check this against S4's case and the other subjects.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Matching L1 with the input of R7, (A V B)*(A V C), shows three differences: a tilde on the right-hand R, and a horseshoe where a wedge is needed in each part. Applying R6 to the right part removes the first and third; R6 on the left part removes the second. S4's L2 and L3 are two of the three resulting expressions.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The other Carnegie subjects fit too: S5 produced all three, S8 two, and S11 two; S9 and S10, who made no preparation for R7, produced none. Among the Yale subjects' 122 rule applications to L1, 35 (24 of R6 to the left part and 11 to the right part, about 30 percent) were apparently preparatory to R7. The authors call the evidence convincing.

card.rule: Subjects who prepared for R7 produced the three expected class-of-L1 expressions; those who did not prepare, did not.
card.limits: These counts show the pattern in aggregate; they do not show each individual's reasons.

concepts.title: Left, right, L0 and miscellaneous expressions
concepts.question: What do the Yale records show about the left, right and L0 classes and the miscellaneous expressions?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Figures 9.9 to 9.11 show the main transformations in the classes of left(L1), right(L1) and L0. The authors read what these transformations were for.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Transformations to forms with dot connectives are probably attempts to delete the R's by a second use of R8, thwarted because the expressions cannot be made positive. In 24 cases, expressions of each class with horseshoe connectives served as inputs to R12, the crucial step in solving D1. In the L0 class, all but two of the 63 transformations moved toward the goal expression.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Even many miscellaneous expressions have plausible accounts. Subject 62 used R9 to produce (R horseshoe ~P) V Q and then, in eight steps using R4 among other rules, turned it into ~R V ~(~Q*P), but could not eliminate the left part. Plans calling for R9 followed by R4 probably account for 20 of the 43 miscellaneous expressions and 27 of their 58 occurrences.

card.rule: Even the odd expressions in these classes have accounts: dot forms try a second R8, horseshoe forms feed R12, and R9-then-R4 plans explain many miscellaneous ones.
card.limits: Some miscellaneous expressions remain unaccounted for; the explanations are plausible rather than complete.

concepts.title: The aggregate picture: orderly, task-driven search
concepts.question: What is the authors' summary of how subjects generated expressions on D1?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: After the counts, the authors summarize what the generation of expressions shows about how subjects searched.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The generation of expressions can be explained parsimoniously by postulating that subjects seek to follow paths suggested by noticeable differences between L1 and L0 and by noticeable features of these expressions. There is little that seems random about the generation once the problem structure is understood.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The summary draws on the counts. A little over half of the different expressions, and five-sixths of all occurrences, fell in the four classes predicted from the paths. The talking subjects wrote almost the same expressions as the Yale subjects.

card.rule: Subjects' written expressions follow paths suggested by noticeable differences in the task; little is random, and thinking aloud makes no detectable difference.
card.limits: The summary rests on this one problem and the counts; it does not cover other problems or cognitive tasks.

concepts.title: Episodes in the logic task
concepts.question: How is an episode defined in the logic task, and how does it differ from cryptarithmetic?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors now study the seven thinking-aloud protocols for D1. The earlier sections give enough understanding of the task to structure the analysis: attempts, right or wrong, revolve around making essential transformations, those that delete or diminish an R, while members of the equivalence classes get generated on the way.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: So protocols can be episoded at the level of goals that attempt essential changes. Once an essential step is decided on, obvious inessential steps are executed so the essential rule can be applied. Within an episode, behavior should be mostly GPS-like. These expectations are hypotheses still to be tested.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In Chapter 3 an episode was a segment of obvious behavior in pursuit of a goal. In Chapter 7, for cryptarithmetic, obviousness meant new information could be gained without positing a new assignment. The logic task has a different structure and needs a different notion: the subject arrives at an essential rule he wishes to apply but which is inapplicable to the current expression.

card.rule: In logic, an episode is the obvious work done to make a chosen but inapplicable essential rule applicable.
card.limits: The authors state that the expectation about episodes and their internal nature is still a hypothesis at this point.

concepts.title: Inside an episode and how it ends
concepts.question: What goes on inside an episode, and why does it usually end in failure?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The decision to apply an essential rule starts an episode. The obvious steps taken to make the rule applicable form its body.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The subject goes through a GPS-like means-ends cycle: a difference is detected, a relevant operator is selected and applied, and the result is judged by trying to reapply the original essential operator. The relevant operator may come from a direct association from the difference to an operator, or from a search of the rule sheet for a rule with the desired function. It may also be a search of the display for an expression that already meets the conditions.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: An episode usually ends with failure to apply the essential rule. Rarely is there a sharp sign that a rule is inapplicable to some variant, so the subject may continue for several minutes. A result that is available is obvious, so it is found quickly; but it is not obvious that no result is available, since that means exhausting the space of inessential transformations.

card.rule: An episode runs the means-ends cycle to make a wanted rule applicable, and usually ends only when the subject concedes failure.
