card.limits: If the essential rule does become applicable, the episode can continue to further essential rules under a plan or a principle.

concepts.title: Other sources of episodes
concepts.question: Besides a wanted essential rule, what else can start an episode, and how do episodes nest?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Episodes can arise in two other ways than by the decision to apply an essential rule.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: One is the direct attempt to reach the goal expression. This is the same as the episodes above with the goal expression in place of the operator condition. Each attempt to solve a1 was a single episode of this type, since no essential operators were involved. The other is the adoption of a specific method, for example working forward and trying each operator in turn.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Once such a method is adopted, a sequence of future actions becomes highly predictable, even obvious: a subject working forward will consider R4 after R3 and R5 after R4, whatever the content of the rule. This is like a plan, where the next essential rule does not start a new episode. Episodes are tied to goals, so they can be nested, one inside another, as subjects stay with particular paths for long periods and adopt methods.

card.rule: A direct attempt at the goal, or the adoption of a method, also starts an episode, and episodes can nest.
card.limits: What makes behavior obvious is commitment to a method or plan, not the content of any one rule.

concepts.title: S4's eleven episodes
concepts.question: How does the episoding scheme divide S4's behavior, and what marks the boundaries?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors use S4 to show how a logic protocol is episoded. Figure 9.12 gives S4's episode abstract and Figure 9.13 his problem behavior graph (PBG), so episodes can be checked from two viewpoints.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: S4's behavior breaks into eleven episodes, one of which (E3) consists of three subepisodes. Each is clearly set off in the PBG as a separate cluster of search. Most come from an attempt to follow path.R7 or path.R12. One is a clear case of working forward, marked WF at B99, and there are other notes, for example AC at B19 for the avoid-consequences method.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The start and end of episodes are often marked by distinctive language. The working-forward episode begins when S4 says he is looking through the rules one at a time to see how they might help rearrange the expression, and ends when he concludes that 7 seems to be the only one that can help. Episoding by points where the subject changes direction would often coincide, but the present scheme explains why episodes exist and how far they extend.

card.rule: S4's protocol divides into eleven episodes whose boundaries match his own changes of direction, and the scheme explains why they exist.
card.limits: The count of episodes depends on the scheme; the empirical rule of changes of direction would give a similar but not identical division.

concepts.title: Reading the problem behavior graph
concepts.question: What do the boxes, arrowheads and double lines of the logic PBG mean?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The PBG of S4 shows attempts to apply rules, which are a salient feature of the logic task. So the authors take goals as operators, not just the rules themselves.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The operators are the goals of applying a rule and of transforming one expression into another (abbreviated get). Inputs are sometimes written with the operator; when missing they are the current expressions. The boxes hold state information: the expression under consideration, or differences and features derived from it. Differences are treated as state information tied to a goal, though they may appear as operators when used explicitly.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: An arrowhead on the line between boxes means the operator was applied successfully, covertly or overtly, abstractly or in detail, accurately or with error. No arrowhead means the operator was not applied, and the next box then describes the difficulty. The goal of applying it stays in the goal stack, and a later reapplication is shown by a double-lined connection.

card.rule: In the PBG, an arrowhead means an operator was applied, no arrowhead means it was blocked, and a double line means a goal was reapplied from the goal stack.
card.limits: A PBG fills gaps in a plausible way, so it is a reconstruction, not a recording.

concepts.title: How the problem is put into words steers the path
concepts.question: How might the way a subject phrases the task influence the paths he tries?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Episode abstracts for the other six D1 protocols are in Figures 9.14 to 9.19, and the protocols themselves, with episode boundaries marked, are in the appendices. Uncertain points are footnoted.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Most protocols open with a statement of the problem expressions and the differences between L1 and L0. The needed change is most often put as I must eliminate the R's, sometimes followed by I must group the Q and P. There are strong hints that how the subject represents the problem, and so phrases the task, influences the paths he evokes and tries.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: R8 may be seen as a way to eliminate half of L1, as S4 sees it when he declines because he would lose Q or P. Or it may be seen as a way to get the two parts as separate lines, as S9 sees it when he says he can split them up. S15 shows a shift from one view to the other.

card.rule: How a subject phrases the task, such as eliminate half versus split into lines, influences which paths he tries.
card.limits: The authors call these strong hints, not proof; the effect of the representation is inferred from a few protocols.

concepts.title: Which plans the subjects followed
concepts.question: Which of the five plans did the seven subjects use, and how do the R12 episodes look?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors check the seven episode abstracts against the five plans. Most episodes fit one of them.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: All the solvers use path.R12. S4, S5 and S8 spend a great deal of time, and S10 and S11 briefly, on path.R7 and variants. Variants of path.R11 are prominent in S5's protocol and variants of path.R10 in S8's. S11 is a special case: only one of his seven episodes (E6) follows any of the paths.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The path.R12 episodes are all similar and fairly simple. After R12 yields (P horseshoe Q), subjects note the connective difference with L0, remove it, then commute, with few comments beyond their instructions to the experimenter. As in cryptarithmetic, protocols have more comments about differences and operators when difficulties arise than when sailing is smooth.

card.rule: Every solver used path.R12; others followed R7 variants, and the R12 episodes are simple and quiet.
card.limits: S11 is an exception, and a simulation would need extra abilities to start from any displayed expression.

concepts.title: S5 and the persistent R7 attempt
concepts.question: How did S5 try to make R7 applicable, and is his behavior understandable?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: S5 failed to solve D1, and three of his five episodes concern path.R7. He generated more members of the equivalence class of L1 (15) than any other subject. Afterwards he said, in effect, that he was stuck on one track, kept switching terms around, and ended up with the wrong sign in the wrong place.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Figure 9.20 shows his steps. After applying R6 to both sides of L1 to get L5, the protocol divides into three subepisodes. In E3.1 he tries to remove the tilde from the R in the left part by going around the right-hand cycle of Figure 9.7: change connective, change sign, change connective back, in both directions. In E3.2 he does the same around the left-hand cycle, using a dot instead of a horseshoe and back. In E3.3 he gives up on the left R and tries to add a tilde to the right R, again around the right-hand cycle, noticing the lack of progress a little sooner.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors read this as futile but understandable and systematic. Since S5 had not analyzed the effects of successive rule applications as Figure 9.7 does, and could not look more than a step or two ahead without writing the steps, he needed an extensive search to convince himself he would always return to the same expression without the sign he wanted.

card.rule: S5's long R7 attempt was systematic: he walked around the cycles of connective changes in Figure 9.7 to try to change an R's sign.
card.limits: Understanding his search does not make it effective; the authors do not claim persistence helped him.

concepts.title: Classifying each step by its mechanism
concepts.question: How can the authors test whether behavior inside episodes is GPS-like without a full simulation?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: So far the authors have described S5 and promised changes to GPS. They ask whether there is a way, short of simulation, to tell whether behavior within an episode is GPS-like rather than produced by other mechanisms, such as exhaustive search.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: GPS is a collection of steps: matching and trying to reduce a difference, selecting a rule relevant to a high-priority difference, and responding to an inapplicable rule by trying to make it applicable. These steps are integrated enough to be recognized in protocols. So one analysis lists the types of step in an episode and sees how much is GPS-like, using the PBG.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: S4's PBG has 79 rule applications (counting scans of the display and rule sheet that found nothing). Each is classified by what evoked it. At B10 the first R7 answers a difference from the goal (group terms): means-ends toward the goal object. The next R6 answers a connective difference because R7 was inapplicable: means-ends for applicability. The following R7 is a reapplication, and the last R6 answers a sign difference from R7: a second applicability case.

card.rule: Classify each operator occurrence by the mechanism that evoked it, and see what share is GPS-like.
card.limits: A classification counts types of step; it does not show how well the steps fit together.

concepts.title: Avoiding consequences
concepts.question: What is the avoid-consequences method, and why can a simple GPS not produce it?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: An important form of means-ends analysis not yet met is the avoidance of consequences. Take an operator that is applicable, so nothing needs to be done to make it applicable, but that has both desirable and undesirable consequences.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: A simple GPS-like system would take the resulting expression and try to remove the undesirable consequences. The avoid-consequences method instead searches beforehand for a rule to apply first, so that when the given rule is applied later it keeps the desired consequence without the undesired one.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In S8's protocol, R8 can plainly be applied and does something desirable (eliminates an R) and something undesirable (throws away a P or Q). His remark is that R8 would work if he could apply R7. R7 groups P and Q so that R8 would do only the desirable thing.

card.rule: Avoiding consequences means preparing the expression beforehand so that a rule's bad effect never happens.
card.limits: Examples of a good effect and a bad one that are seemingly independent are the clearest cases of this method.

concepts.title: Working forward in three forms
concepts.question: What are the ways of working forward that the protocols show?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Working forward means choosing a rule without reasoning back from the goal. The main type iterates through the rules systematically and evaluates each one.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: S4 gives a perfect example in his PBG when he looks through the rules one at a time. Two other types occur rarely: working forward by similarity of input form, and doing something just because it is different. Working backward rarely occurs in D1 and is discussed in Chapter 10.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: S11 applies R7 mentally and gets an expression of the form A(BC). The rules he then considers are chosen from the three-term form of the expression. There is no evidence of comparison with L0, so no means-ends analysis, and he did not consider the rules systematically since other rules also applied. S8, remembering advice not to stay in a rut, applies R5 to L1 to see what comes out; there is nothing functional about the result.

card.rule: Working forward can be a systematic scan, a choice by similarity of input form, or a deliberate try of something different.
card.limits: The two rare types are known from only a few examples.

concepts.title: Repetitions: goal stack, implementation, commands
concepts.question: What are the main kinds of repeated operator application, and what mechanism lies behind them?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A very large fraction of the operators in the PBG repeat earlier applications. The authors classify them.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The first kind comes from the goal stack: the prior goal of applying an operator is kept and reevoked after a remedial attempt at a subgoal. The remedial actions concern difficulty, specification, uncertainty about the output, errors such as stating the wrong input, and interruptions irrelevant to the problem. The common case is the reattempt after trying to overcome a difficulty.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The second kind is implementation of an operator already applied and examined. It appears in the PBG as an operator with an arrow where no expression was written on the display, followed by a later application all over again. Often the aim is to put an actual result on the display, sometimes to carry the calculation forward covertly. This is a variety of planning, taken up in Chapter 10.

card.rule: Many operators are repeats: goal-stack reapplications after a remedial subgoal, and implementations of an operator already tried.
card.limits: The kinds of repetition are classified from the PBG and some cases are uncertain.

concepts.title: Review, noticing and the leftover category
concepts.question: What do review, noticing and the leftover category add, and how much do the main types explain?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A third kind of repetition is review, a recapitulation of past actions. It arises when the subject tries to understand what went on, or when the experimenter asks for it. The category other holds the occurrences that cannot be shown to be GPS-like.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Most reviews are strictly reproductive. One review, made for diagnostic purposes, is the only one of its kind in all the protocols. Another subtype of other is noticing, where a subject working on one thing sees something useful, as when S4 suddenly sees path.R12 while he is concerned with R2.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The four main types (means-ends analysis, working forward, goal-stack repetition and implementation of plans) account for 82 percent of occurrences. Reviews and commands, which reproduce past behavior, add 9 percent. That leaves essentially the avoid-consequences method, the noticings and items with too few data.

card.rule: Review and commands reproduce past behavior; the four main types plus these account for 91 percent, leaving mainly avoid-consequences and noticings.
card.limits: Noticings vary in importance: S4's sight of path.R12 is critical, others are minor.

concepts.title: Reading Table 9.3 with care
concepts.question: What can and can't be inferred from the tally of mechanisms?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Table 9.3 is remarkable for the small number of mechanisms and because most belong to types already understood: GPS-like means-ends analysis, working forward, repetition from the goal stack and implementation of plans. The authors warn about what to infer from it.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: They compare the tally to the work of a centrifuge: the behavior is dissolved into little bits, each classified by a single property, and much of its integrated character is destroyed.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: What is shown is that no other collection of mechanisms seems required, and that fuller descriptions will probably fit within a GPS-like framework. The authors also say the use of the PBG overstates the GPS-like character, since it tends to fill gaps in a plausible, GPS-like way.

card.rule: The tally shows that no other mechanisms seem needed, not that the integrated behavior has been explained.
card.limits: The classification loses integration and consistency of selection, and the PBG itself leans toward GPS-like readings.

concepts.title: Mechanisms by subject
concepts.question: What does the breakdown by subject (Table 9.4) show about stability across subjects?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Table 9.4 gives the mechanisms by subject, ordered from left to right by the total number of operator occurrences (equivalently phrases or time). The authors ask what varies between subjects.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The major categories are very stable across subjects. This suggests they are set by the general structure of the task together with a basic GPS-like mechanism. The two nonsolvers (S11 and S5) do not differ much from the solvers. The only interesting differences are that the other category is almost absent for the efficient solvers (S10, S9 and S15), and that avoid consequences and review increase gradually as the protocols get longer.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors expect this, since good solvers have no occasion to depart from the basic mechanisms.

card.rule: The mechanism shares are stable across subjects, with other absent in efficient solvers and review and avoid-consequences growing with length.
card.limits: The stability supports the account but does not show the subjects reasoned in the same way inside each category.

concepts.title: How episodes get started
concepts.question: What can start an episode, and which starting points are more primitive?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Within episodes the subjects look GPS-like, but that does not yet explain the whole course of a protocol or why subjects follow different courses. The authors need processes for starting episodes, and for ending them.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: In GPS, the table of connections and the ordering of differences give a definite way to start an episode from a given pair of expressions. The pair may be L1 and L0, a derived expression and the input form of a rule, a derived expression and L0, or a derived expression and one held in memory by working backward from L0. In a GPS trace, a new episode is a match and its processing that was not evoked as a subgoal of a currently active goal.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: At the outset a subject has only L0, L1 and the rules. Three ways of starting appear: (1) match L0 and L1 to form differences (eliminate the R's, group Q and P); (2) look for rules that simplify L1; (3) search for rules that apply to L1. The authors judge 3 more primitive than 2, and 2 more primitive than 1, where primitive means less specifically adapted to the task. The GPS described uses only (1).

card.rule: An episode starts when a match not evoked by an active goal sets a difference to remove; the most task-specific start is the L0-L1 match.
card.limits: Most but not all subjects start with a match of L0 and L1; the protocols hold variants that the described GPS does not capture.

concepts.title: How episodes end, and what persistence means
concepts.question: How do subjects differ in ending an episode, and what do the authors say about persistence as a trait?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: As in GPS, an episode ends when the goal is reached or when the subject can think of nothing more to do toward it. But thinking of nothing more is highly ambiguous and hides real differences among subjects.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: S4 abandons path.R7 after only two expressions (it cannot be done; he sees no way) and after a second attempt that wrote nothing new (he cannot find a way). S8, like S4, gives up after two expressions. S5 goes through an elaborate search for indirect routes.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors say that a label like stereotypy could be put on S5's persistence, but unless such a trait is consistent from one problem to another it is neither testable nor useful for prediction. Nor can one say that persistence necessarily reduces effectiveness: if S4 had been more persistent when he first considered R12 as a means of eliminating R's, he would have found the solution much sooner.

card.rule: Subjects end episodes at very different points; calling the difference a trait like stereotypy is not useful unless it is consistent across problems.
card.limits: Persistence can help or hurt depending on the path being pursued.

concepts.title: What the chapter concludes
concepts.question: What does the chapter claim about GPS as a theory of human problem solving, and on what evidence?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The chapter tests how well GPS serves as a theory of human problem solving in the Moore-Anderson logic task environment.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The evidence was thinking-aloud protocols from the authors' own laboratory together with aggregate data from 64 Yale subjects. Subjects who talked aloud explored very much the same parts of the problem space as those who did not. For both groups, behavior was of the kind predicted by the GPS simulations.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The data cover two problems: a very simple one, compared with GPS in considerable detail, and a more difficult but not extremely difficult one from Moore and Anderson's set. For the latter, a task analysis based on the essential versus inessential distinction, and on the notions of construction and planning from the previous chapter, explained to a considerable extent why the subjects' explorations stayed mostly in limited, specified portions of the problem space.

card.rule: Subjects who talked aloud and those who did not explored the same parts of the problem space, and their behavior matched GPS's predictions on two problems.
card.limits: The claim rests on two problems in one task environment; the later chapters carry the analysis on to other aspects.

concepts.title: What the chapter adds to the logic analysis
concepts.question: Beyond behavior within single episodes, which further questions does the chapter take up?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Chapters 8 and 9 showed that people solving logic problems act like GPS inside single episodes: they analyse by function, build goal structures and set subgoals to reduce differences between expressions. Left open is how the episodes themselves are arranged and called up, and whether the account holds up on other problems.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The chapter looks at the macrostructure of the protocols, meaning how episodes are arranged and evoked, and so at planning. It then turns to a second problem, C1, and to a new heuristic, working backwards. Two further topics follow: differences among subjects and the learning of one subject over a series of problems.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The earlier chapters rested on protocols from several subjects, mostly on one problem. The new questions are tested on further problems and on protocols reproduced in the appendices.

card.rule: After within-episode behavior, the chapter asks how episodes are organized, how the account fares on a harder problem, and how subjects differ and learn.
card.limits: The chapter's account is built on a small number of subjects and a few problems, so it is a first picture, not a full survey.

concepts.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
concepts.title: Two ways GPS can organize episodes
concepts.question: How can GPS arrive at its sequence of episodes, with or without a planning routine?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Chapter 9 analysed D1 mostly within episodes, so it did not ask how subjects choose the goals that begin episodes. GPS as described in Chapter 8 offers two answers, and the authors say a range of possibilities lies between them.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Basic GPS does not separate essential from inessential differences. Add a heuristic that reduces the most serious differences first, and order the differences with every essential one ahead of the inessential ones, and it will behave as if it did. It sets the goal of reducing the most serious essential difference, uses inessential operators to prepare an essential one, then moves to the next essential goal.

blocks.label: Alternative
blocks.text: With the planning method, a planning routine solves an abstracted problem in a planning space. Each step of that solution is an essential operator and becomes a goal in the original space, and one episode is devoted to each.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Both routes are descriptions of the program given in Chapter 8. The chapter tests them by asking which one the structure of real protocols resembles.

card.rule: Episodes can be ordered by difference ranking with no plan, or by a plan made in an abstract space and then carried out episode by episode.
card.limits: These are two idealized extremes; the authors say real protocols may sit anywhere between them.

concepts.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
concepts.title: Telling which organization produced a protocol
concepts.question: What would a protocol look like if the planning routine, rather than difference ranking, had organized it?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The two ways of organizing episodes predict different protocols, so the authors can ask which one a given protocol shows.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: If the planning routine were responsible, the first part of the protocol would contain only abstracted actions in the planning space. The later part would consist of episodes in the original problem space, arranged in the order of the plan made earlier.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The test rests on the protocol itself: what comes first, and whether the later episodes follow the order of what came first.

blocks.label: Limit
blocks.text: Things get more complicated if a subject makes several plans before trying any, or makes a new plan after a failed attempt to carry out an earlier one.

card.rule: A planning protocol has an abstract first part and a later series of concrete episodes that follow the plan's order.
card.limits: Real protocols mix the pattern: plans may be several, revised, partial or interleaved with concrete work.

concepts.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
concepts.title: A looser test for planning
concepts.question: By what behaviors do the authors decide that a subject is planning?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors want to find planning in human protocols without requiring that the subject follow the GPS planning scheme in every detail.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: A subject plans when he contemplates a run of at least two abstracted transformations and then carries it out.

blocks.label: Term
blocks.text: Planning, by their looser criterion, means that the subject considers abstracted transformations of expressions, meaning transformations in which not every detail of the input or output expression is fixed. He also considers a sequence of at least two such transformations in a row.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The criterion is meant to be read off protocols. The next cards apply it to the remarks of one subject, S8, on several problems.

card.rule: A subject plans when he contemplates a run of at least two abstracted transformations and then carries it out.
card.limits: The test is looser than GPS's scheme; it does not demand that the plan be complete, fully worked out or even feasible.

concepts.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
concepts.title: Planning in people is partial and flexible
concepts.question: How does the planning of human subjects differ from the GPS planning routine?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: GPS's planning routine moves in a tidy way: abstract problem first, then episodes in the original space. Human protocols seldom look so tidy, yet planning shows up in many of them.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: By the looser criterion, planning may be partial and incomplete. A subject may plan one portion of a problem and not another. He need not show signs of switching consciously or systematically between the problem space and the planning space, and may move flexibly from one to the other.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors built the GPS routine inductively, after examining some of these human protocols. They say planning is very prominent in many of them, and call the GPS routine a formalized and stylized description of less formal and less comprehensive processes.

card.rule: In people, planning is partial and flexible; the GPS routine is a stylized description of it.
card.limits: The GPS routine is stylized: it captures the form of planning, not the looseness of the real processes.

concepts.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
concepts.title: S8 plans before acting: problem A4
concepts.question: What plan did subject S8 state for problem A4 before applying any rule?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: In A4 the board shows four given lines: P or Q; if not-R then not-Q; S; and if R then not-S. The goal is P or T. S8 talked for about a minute and a half before applying any rule.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: From his remarks the authors infer this plan. Get P alone, since one R9 then gives P or T. Combine lines two and four by R12 so the R's cancel, leaving S and Q. Combine that with line three by R11 to cancel the S's, leaving Q. Combine that with line one by R11 to cancel the Q's, leaving P.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The plan is an inference from remarks all made before any rule was applied. The authors check it against the rest of the protocol and show it in a nine-line outline in Figure 10.1.

blocks.label: Limit
blocks.text: S8 does not know whether R12 can be applied, since one of the two lines would first have to be reversed to give the same sign for R.

card.rule: S8 planned A4 by working back from the goal to P alone, then chaining three cancellations, with details left open.
card.limits: The plan is not a complete solution and may not be feasible: S8 does not know whether the cancellation steps will work or the exact form of the result.

concepts.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
concepts.title: How S8 carries out the A4 plan
concepts.question: What would show that S8 worked out the details only while carrying out his plan?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: S8 may have worked the whole solution out in detail and simply left it unspoken. If so, his plan tells us little. The authors need a way to test whether the details were really worked out only as he went.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: If the plan was only a skeleton, S8 should return to the goal of applying R12 and work it out in detail, then move to the two applications of R11. There should be little hesitation between one of these episodes and the next, but some search and problem solving within each.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: This is what the protocol shows. He reverses the fourth line with R2 so that it begins with S, applies R12 to the second line and the reversed fourth, then R11 with the third line to get not-Q. He changes the first line to a horseshoe with R6, reverses it, and applies R11 to get P. Last comes R9.

card.rule: A plan is a skeleton: the episodes carrying it out show real problem solving within each, with little hesitation between them.
card.limits: A smooth run does not prove the solution was found beforehand; the remarks that show open details are the evidence.

concepts.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
concepts.title: A plan that fails: S8 on D1
concepts.question: What does S8's failed plan on D1 reveal about how fully a plan is thought through?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Successful plans are easy to read as complete. An unsuccessful plan can show whether the whole of it was ever thought through. S8 had already worked a while on D1, converting the starting line step by step into forms with wedges and dots, when he stated a new plan.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: His plan: apply R8 to the first line to drop one of its two halves, change the connective of the remaining half to a dot, apply R8 again to eliminate R and leave P or Q, then apply R9 to add the other letter. It is stated in terms of functions, such as eliminate and add on.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors infer that he had not worked out the operations he did not mention, or the tildes and connectives of the expressions that would result. He had not yet decided whether to drop the left or the right half, and when he tried the plan it did not work.

card.rule: A plan that fails when carried out shows that its detail was left open and its essential steps were chosen by function.
card.limits: A failed plan shows incomplete foresight; it does not show that the planning was irrational.

concepts.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
concepts.title: More S8 plans: C3 and B2
concepts.question: What do S8's plans on C3 and B2 add to the picture of how people plan?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: S8's planning on C3 resembles that on A4. On B2 his plan is a different matter. In both problems the goal is not-Q.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: C3 plan: change the second line so the S's cancel against the first by R11, leaving R; then cancel R against the horseshoe third line by a second R11. S8 works out details as he goes, with hardly a pause. B2 plan: transform lines one and two each into not-Q, combine them with R10, then take them apart again with R3.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In C3 only a few remarks and small hesitations show that he did not already hold the full solution. After the plan he still needed to eliminate P from the expression not-(P implies Q), and nothing shows he had foreseen how. In B2 the plan is redundant: success on either of the first two goals would already solve the problem.

card.rule: S8's C3 plan fits the usual pattern of an incomplete skeleton, while his B2 plan was infeasible and redundant.
card.limits: Plans can be redundant or infeasible, which shows a plan is a guess about a route and not a guarantee.

concepts.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
concepts.title: Essential and inessential rules in the plans
concepts.question: Which rules did S8's plans mention, and which did they leave out?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: GPS's planning routine abstracts away the inessential differences and plans with the essential operators. Do the subjects' plans make a similar distinction?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: S8's abstractions correspond well with the distinction. His plans are about R11, R12, R8, R9, R10 and R3, rules that remove, add or combine whole parts. They are not about R1, R2, R5 or R6, the rules that rearrange order, invert a horseshoe or change a connective.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The pattern holds across A4, D1, C3 and B2. Whatever S8 omits in a plan, such as tildes and connectives, is what the later inessential operations adjust.

card.rule: In S8's plans the essential rules are named and the inessential ones are left to be fitted in during execution.
card.limits: The distinction is the authors' reading of which rules the plans name, not a division stated by the subjects.

concepts.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
concepts.title: Where might the distinction come from?
concepts.question: What three conjectures do the authors offer for the origin of the essential-inessential distinction?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The subjects separate the rules into essential and inessential ones, but nothing in the logic task tells them to. The authors ask where the distinction comes from, and can only conjecture.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: First conjecture: transfer from other mathematical tasks. In algebra, proficient people automatically simplify expressions by combining similar terms and arranging terms in patterns. Second: experience with material objects. Several subjects find that using R8 to disassemble an expression into parts is less drastic than using R8 to delete part of it. Third: a perceptual distinction between objects that keep an identity through time and the changeable properties of objects.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Offered as conjectures, not findings. Each points to a familiar source outside the logic task, from which the subjects might have brought the distinction with them.

card.rule: The authors suggest three possible sources of the distinction: other mathematics, handling objects, and perception; none is tested.
card.limits: These are conjectures; the authors show no data that choose among them.

concepts.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
concepts.title: The same contrast in algebra story problems
concepts.question: What two ways of representing a calculation appear in the algebra story-problem protocols?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors note that the contrast between operating upon an object and changing it into a new object also appears in protocols of subjects solving algebra story problems (Paige and Simon, 1966). The problem asked for an equation: a number is multiplied by 6, the product is increased by 44, and the result is 68.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: In one protocol, the subject says: call the number n; multiply it by 6 and add 44 to it; the result is 68. In the other, the subject says to multiply x by 6, writes 6x, adds 44, and writes the result is 68 as an equals sign and 68, taking each phrase in turn.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The first subject's repeated use of it, referring to a partly finished calculation, shows an entity he would call the result so far. The second subject's process looks more like building a symbolic object, the final equation, out of a set of parts.

card.rule: One subject treats a calculation as a thing that is changed step by step; the other builds the equation from parts.
card.limits: Two protocols illustrate the contrast; they do not show how common each way of thinking is.

concepts.title: Why problem C1 is examined
concepts.question: What earlier idea about problem difficulty does the difficult problem C1 help to test?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Looking at the relative difficulty of the sixteen problems the subjects attempted, the authors came to link problem difficulty closely with the need to make constructions in order to solve a problem.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: On the authors' reading, a problem that can be solved only by making a construction is the difficult kind. In C1, as the next cards show, the construction is to assemble an expression from two components by one rule and then apply a second rule to the result.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The idea rests on the relative difficulty of the sixteen problems attempted. A further, harder problem, C1, is needed to see whether the idea holds.

card.rule: Problems that require constructions are harder; C1 is a new, difficult problem on which to test that idea.
card.limits: The link between constructions and difficulty is the authors' explanation, tested on a few problems and subjects.

concepts.title: Where the Yale subjects' expressions fall
concepts.question: In which classes of expressions do the Yale subjects' attempts on C1 cluster?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: On problem C1 the Yale subjects wrote 121 different expressions in 487 appearances. Do those expressions spread over the whole problem space, as they did on D1, or cluster in a few places?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Almost all lie in a few equivalence classes tied simply to L1, L0 and the path between. About a quarter fall in the classes of L1 and its left and right sides, one tenth in the extended class of L1, and about a third in classes got from those by Rule 9. Only 5 percent lie in the classes leading to the solution.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Appearances are even more concentrated than distinct expressions. The class of L1 itself accounts for over a quarter of all appearances, and the left and right sides of L1 for over a third. The authors conclude that subjects did not stray far from what simple transformations of L1 produce.

card.rule: On C1 the subjects stayed close to L1: most distinct expressions and still more of the appearances lie in a few classes near it.
card.limits: The pattern describes the Yale group in aggregate; it does not say what any one subject did.

concepts.title: Yale and Carnegie subjects on C1
concepts.question: Did thinking-aloud instructions change which parts of the problem space the subjects explored on C1?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The Yale and Carnegie subjects worked under different conditions, and protocols depend on instructions to think aloud. If the instructions changed what subjects did, the protocols would not describe ordinary problem solving.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The authors say the thinking-aloud instructions did not substantially influence what part of the problem space the subjects explored. The two groups spread their appearances of expressions over the equivalence classes in strikingly similar ways.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Table 10.2 sets the two groups side by side, class by class, as percentages of all appearances. The columns for the two groups are close in nearly every class.

card.rule: The two groups explored the same parts of the space in nearly the same proportions, so thinking aloud did not substantially alter exploration.
card.limits: Similar exploration of the space does not show that the thinking process is unaffected in every other respect.

concepts.section: Sources of Problem Difficulty on C1
concepts.title: Who solved C1
concepts.question: What do the solutions and failures of the nine C1 subjects say about C1's difficulty?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors want further data on why problems are hard. For C1 they have protocols of nine subjects, reproduced in Appendices 10.5 to 10.13, with episode abstracts for each subject in Figures 10.3 to 10.11.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Three of the nine subjects solved C1 and six failed. For six subjects there are protocols for both D1 and C1. S8 and S9 solved both; S4 and S10 solved D1 but not C1; S5 and S11 failed both.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: These results agree with the earlier classification of C1 as more difficult than D1 (Table 8.1).

card.rule: Fewer subjects solve C1 than D1, and no subject solved C1 without solving D1, as C1's higher difficulty predicts.
card.limits: Six subjects are a very small sample, so the pattern is suggestive, not conclusive.

concepts.section: Sources of Problem Difficulty on C1
concepts.title: The construction in C1
concepts.question: Which step of C1 is a construction, and what makes the problem hard?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: C1 starts from L1, (P or Q) and (if Q then R), and asks for L0, P or (Q and R). The last step of the solution applies R7 to (P or Q) and (P or R). That pair first has to be put together by R10 from its two parts.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Assembling the pair by R10 and then applying R7 is a construction in the authors' earlier sense. The authors say the construction can be avoided by working backward from L0. What makes the whole problem hard is to discover that (P or Q) and (P or R) are wanted.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The right-hand part, P or R, comes indirectly. Split L1 by two uses of R8, change the connective of the left part to a horseshoe, and combine the two with R12, which eliminates the Q's and leaves not-P implies R.

card.rule: C1's difficulty lies in discovering that (P or Q) and (P or R) must be built and combined; working backward from L0 can reveal this.
card.limits: This is the authors' account of C1's difficulty; the next sections test it against the protocols.

concepts.section: Sources of Problem Difficulty on C1
concepts.title: Seven a priori paths for C1
concepts.question: How do the authors use seven plausible solution paths to interpret what the subjects wrote?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: To see whether the subjects' expressions relate to sensible routes, the authors list the routes first. They describe seven paths with some plausibility a priori, named by the key rule each uses: path.R4, path.R7, path.R9, path.R9', path.R10, path.R11 and path.R12.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Only the seventh, path.R12, is feasible; none of the other six yields a solution. Each path predicts which classes of expressions a subject following it would produce.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Path.R9 should give expressions in the class of left(L1) and expressions got from them by R9. Path.R9' should give expressions equivalent to right(L1). Path.R7 should give expressions in the class of L1, since R7 is not actually applicable. Path.R12 should give the classes of both sides of L1 and some further classes besides.

card.rule: Seven candidate paths each predict classes of expressions; only path.R12 would also produce the pair needed for the solution.
card.limits: The paths are the authors' list of plausible routes, not a proof that no other route could occur.

concepts.section: Sources of Problem Difficulty on C1
concepts.title: Two exceptions to the predicted classes
concepts.question: Which expressions fell outside the predicted classes, and why?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The nine subjects' expressions can be sorted into the classes the seven paths predict. A reader wants to know whether any fell outside, and why.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: All do, with two exceptions. S2 wrote six expressions derived from an incorrect expression, (P implies not-R), which the experimenter had put on the board by mistake. S5 wrote eleven expressions of the form (P or Q) or P and two of the form (P or Q) or (Q and R).

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: S2's six expressions come from the experimenter's mistake, not from his own plan. S5's come from a path of his own that pursues a different aim from the seven listed.

card.rule: Apart from an experimenter's error (S2) and one subject's own side path (S5), the expressions fell in the predicted classes.
card.limits: The fit is of the nine subjects' expressions, not of every possible subject.

concepts.section: Sources of Problem Difficulty on C1
concepts.title: An anomaly in the solvers and nonsolvers
concepts.question: What anomaly in who found the R10-R7 idea threatens the authors' account of difficulty?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: If the only construction needed is the R10-R7 sequence, then subjects who find it should be the ones who solve C1. The protocols seem not to fit this tidy picture.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Counting S2 as a solver, only the four subjects who solved C1 applied R12 to get not-P implies R, and everyone who applied it solved it. Three of the four solvers found, by working backward, that L0 follows from (P or Q) and (P or R) by R10 and R7.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Yet three of the five nonsolvers, S5, S10 and S11, also found the R10-R7 possibility by working backward and did not use it successfully. Unless this is explained, the hypotheses about the source of difficulty fail, since R10-R7 is the only construction required.

card.rule: Finding the R10-R7 idea by working backward did not ensure success, which the account of difficulty must explain.
card.limits: That S5 and S11 also failed D1 does not explain the anomaly; it does not say why they failed.

concepts.title: S2 and the puzzle of the missed finish
concepts.question: What happened in S2's first episode on C1, and what puzzle does it leave?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: S2 is counted among the subjects who worked backward and still failed to finish. His first episode on C1 shows how far he got.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: S2 first simplifies L1 by obtaining its two parts with R8. He searches for applicable rules, finds R12 and applies it. At this point he notices that R7 could be applied and appears to see that the expression he has just derived is a suitable input for it.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The experimenter then made an error in writing down an expression, so S2 worked from an incorrect line. He kept trying to apply R10 and R7, failed and gave up on the plan.

blocks.label: Limit
blocks.text: Even allowing for the error, the authors find the protocol mysterious.

card.rule: S2 derived what he needed, but an error in the board and an unexplained failure to complete the plan stopped him.
card.limits: Because of the experimenter's error, S2's case is hard to interpret, and the authors do not claim to explain it.

concepts.title: S5 sees the goal and misses the inputs
concepts.question: What did S5 notice at the start of C1, and what did he fail to plan?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Near the beginning of his protocol, S5 notices that if he had both (P or R) and (P or Q) he could get the answer directly by R7. He already has (P or Q).

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: S5 does not set the goal of getting (P or R). He turns the subproblem into one of applying R7 to L1 itself, which he cannot do. He then goes off to another plan.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors read S5's difficulty as a failure to evolve a plan for obtaining the appropriate inputs to R7. He never considers using (P or Q) and (if Q then R) in combination to obtain (P or R).

card.rule: S5 saw what the goal needed but replaced the subgoal of building the missing input with an attempt to make L1 itself fit R7.
card.limits: S5's case shows one way backward reasoning can go wrong, not that backward reasoning is difficult in general.

concepts.title: Two solvers' routes: S8 and S9
concepts.question: How did the solvers S8 and S9 reach the key step on C1?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Both S8 and S9 solved C1, but by different routes. Each began by noticing path.R7, the idea of applying R7 to L1, which does not work.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: S8 remembered from D1 that the signs in L1 cannot be changed to fit R7, and set R7 aside. He then derived a set of expressions and announced path.R12. The authors say he in effect solved it by working forward, using a simplification heuristic and examining the simplified expressions for new possibilities.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: S9 had not struggled with the signs in L1 on D1, so he had not learned from that problem about the equivalence class of L1, and he tried to put L1 in shape for R7 for some time. Then he worked backward from L0, taking R12 as the way to the answer.

card.rule: S8 reached the key step by working forward and simplifying; S9 by working backward after wasting time on R7.
card.limits: Two solvers are too few to show which route is better; they show that there was more than one way to the solution.

concepts.title: Functional fixity: S10 rejects R12
concepts.question: Why did S10 rule out R12 after working backward from L0?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: S10 worked backward from L0 and failed. He saw at once that P or (Q and R) would follow from (P or Q) and (P or R) by R7. In L1 he already had (P or Q), together with a horseshoe line, but only one P.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: S10 decided that he had to keep a P, a Q and an R, and so could not use R12, because R12 eliminates Q's. He then dropped path.R12 and never returned to it.

blocks.label: Term
blocks.text: The authors call this functional fixity (Duncker, 1945). S10 thinks of R12 by one function, eliminating Q's, and so will not use it on an expression he needs for another function, as an input to R10 and then R7.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors point to S10's protocol: he saw R12 could finish the proof, rejected it because it eliminates Q's, and never returned to it, which they call functional fixity (Duncker, 1945).

card.rule: S10 saw the right finishing step but rejected R12 because he thought of it only as eliminating Q's and he needed (P or Q).
card.limits: Functional fixity is the authors' reading of S10's remark; he does not describe it that way himself.

concepts.title: S11 and S13 on the double role
concepts.question: How did S11 and S13 each handle the double role of (P or Q)?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: S11 and S13 also worked backward from L0, and for both the same expression, (P or Q), had a second use that made trouble.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: S11 saw that R7 on (P or Q) and (P or R) would give L0. Comparing with L1, he needed to change the horseshoe line into (P or R), which would mean changing the first expression and changing it back. Turning the horseshoe into a wedge with R12 would take out the Q. He too assumed that R12 uses up (P or Q).

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: S13 was troubled by the same double role of (P or Q) but overcame it and found his way to the solution.

card.rule: S11 assumed R12 would consume (P or Q), as S10 did; S13 felt the same trouble but kept both needs in mind and overcame it.
card.limits: The authors have no solid ground for saying why S13 succeeded where S10, S11 and S5 did not.

concepts.title: Two ways to come to apply R12
concepts.question: How does the double-function argument explain who applied R12 and who then solved?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Among the Yale subjects, some applied R12 and some went on to solve. The authors ask how the double-function reluctance bears on this.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: R12 was sometimes applied for simplification, or some similar working-forward reason; S2 and S8 applied it without first working backward from L0 to see that (P or R) was needed. The more common way to arrive at the need for R12 was backward from L0.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: A subject who noted in this way that (P or R) had to be obtained would at the same time note that (P or Q) had to be kept, and would be reluctant to alter it.

card.rule: R12 was applied by those who simplified forward, while those who reasoned backward were deterred by the double function.
card.limits: The explanation fits the protocols described; the authors offer it as an account, not a proof.

concepts.title: The double-function test and where it fails
concepts.question: Why is a test against double functions wrong for logic expressions, though sound for wood or chess?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Double-function behavior does not need any new mechanism beyond those already in GPS. The question is why the behavior, which seems sensible, is an error on C1.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Suppose that, before an operator is applied officially, it is checked whether the differences it will produce are larger or more serious than those it removes; if so, it is not applied. This test is wrong here because any expression in the logic problems can exist in as many copies as desired and is not destroyed by transformation.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: If the expressions were made of wood and the transformations done by saws and drills, the test would be right: a piece of wood fashioned into the leg of a chair cannot also be used to make the chair back.

card.rule: A check that stops an operator from consuming something needed elsewhere is right for physical things but wrong for logic expressions, which can be copied.
card.limits: The test is valid where things are consumed; it is only a fallacy where, as in logic, nothing is used up.

concepts.title: What made C1 difficult
concepts.question: What are the sources of difficulty on C1 for subjects who work forward and for those who work backward?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The analysis of C1 had to explain why some subjects who had seen the R10-R7 route still failed, as well as those who had not.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: For subjects who work forward, the R10-R7 construction made C1 difficult. For subjects who work backward, the difficulty comes mainly from functional fixity arising from the double function of the subexpression (P or Q).

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The support is the set of episodes examined above: those of S2, S5, S8, S9, S10, S11 and S13.

card.rule: C1 is hard for forward workers because of the R10-R7 construction, and for backward workers because of the double function of (P or Q).
card.limits: The two sources of difficulty are the authors' account of the protocols, not a test run on new subjects.

concepts.title: Two displays and the knowledge state
concepts.question: Why do the rule sheet and the board raise a question about what counts as a subject's knowledge state?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The logic task has two displays: the rule sheet, which is static, and the board, which slowly accumulates the expressions written on it. They have important effects on performance. Doing C1, or even D1, in the head with perfectly memorized rules would be a very different matter.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: In the problem-space view, an element of the space is what the problem solver knows at the moment: the knowledge immediately available for the inputs to operators and for selecting an operator and judging the position. In the basic space, subjects tend to keep one expression in view and apply a rule to it to make a new current expression.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors ask whether all the information in the external memories is available. If it is not, it is not part of the knowledge state; if it is, they must say how the external memory fits into the problem space.

card.rule: Whether a display belongs to the knowledge state depends on whether its contents are available to the solver when needed.
card.limits: The question is posed for the logic task; the authors say that in other tasks the external memories may matter more.

concepts.title: Uneven access to the displays
concepts.question: What shows that the contents of the external displays are not equally available to the subjects?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: If every part of a display were as available as what the subject holds in mind, the display could be treated as part of the knowledge state. The authors look for signs that this is not so.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: There is little doubt that the contents are differentially accessible. Subjects have to search the displays repeatedly. They come to know some parts and not others.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Subjects know R5 and R6 well enough to apply them without looking at the rule sheet, but not R4 or R11. They know the expression they are working on, but may be unaware for some time that it is already on the board on a different line.

card.rule: Subjects know some contents of the displays well, others poorly, so the displays are not uniformly available.
card.limits: The experiments were not designed to study external memory, so the evidence is gathered from protocols and is only illustrative.

concepts.title: Four roles an external memory can play
concepts.question: What four roles may an external memory play in a problem space?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: An external memory such as the board or the rule sheet must be fitted into the idea of a problem space. The authors list four ways to do it.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: One: a repository of non-current elements reached by recall, not by operators that generate new knowledge. Two: wholly external to the knowledge state, so operators that access and search it count like any other. Three: built into processing at a node, so all relevant information in it is available. Four: an adjunct to the knowledge state with some but not all of its information available, the extended knowledge state.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The first three simply fold the external memory into the problem-space conception developed so far. The fourth is a real elaboration of it.

card.rule: An external memory can serve as a store of prior nodes, an outside source of new knowledge, a part of the knowledge state, or an extension of it.
card.limits: The list is a set of possibilities; which role applies is mostly an empirical question for each solver and each memory.

concepts.title: The board as a stock of prior nodes
concepts.question: How do subjects use the board as a store of earlier expressions to return to?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: In the first role, the board is a store of earlier expressions that are not current but can be recalled. The authors ask how subjects use it.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Subjects engage mainly in a depth-first search in which each newly generated expression succeeds the last as the current expression. This is why the knowledge state can be characterized roughly as a single logic expression. When the current expression is judged undesirable, they fall back to another expression on the display, most commonly the prior one or the initial one.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In the D1 protocols the evidence for these returns is widespread and clear, especially the return to L1.

card.rule: The subjects search depth-first and fall back to the previous expression or the starting one when the current one fails.
card.limits: The picture is a first approximation: subjects do sometimes return to other expressions on the board.

concepts.title: Backing up, and scanning the board
concepts.question: Besides simple backup, how did subjects occasionally use the whole display?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Almost all movement on the display fits depth-first search with backup. The authors look for the rarer cases where a subject goes to the display to find a new place to start.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: In C1, S3 tried R5 on an expression only to see what it would look like, judged it unhelpful and went back one node. That is backing up, with clear functional significance. Only occasionally is the display searched for a new starting place independent of how the earlier expressions arose.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: S8 on D1 gave up an extended try at path.R7 and went back all the way to L1. He then looked over the board: he reconsidered L3 and dropped it, thought of eliminating an R inside a subexpression, saw that this was impossible with wedges, and moved to dots and L5.

card.rule: Most moves on the display are depth-first with backup; a few are scans for a new starting place.
card.limits: Even S8's scan ended on the most recent expression, so the line between scan and backup is not sharp.

concepts.title: An external memory as a source of new knowledge
concepts.question: When does searching an external memory count as an ordinary operator of the problem space?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: In the second role the external memory is wholly outside the knowledge state. Its contents are not known to the solver until they are found.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Searching it and extracting data is then an operation like any other information-generating operation. References, books, maps and letters play this role. The operators in the space are then inhomogeneous: some are search operators for external memories and others are inference operators. Rules to select the search operators depend only on knowledge in the current state.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The rule sheet hardly works in this way, since subjects become familiar with it before the first problem. Among the board searches there are few cases where a subject responds to a difficulty by searching the display for an alternative expression instead of looking for a rule.

card.rule: An external memory unknown to the solver is searched by operators of its own kind, like any other information-generating step.
card.limits: The logic displays are only weakly of this type, since the subjects generated the board and quickly learned the rule sheet.

concepts.title: When a display is part of the knowledge state
concepts.question: What is the criterion for treating an external memory as part of the knowledge state, and why does a large board fail it?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The knowledge state is defined by function: it holds the knowledge available for use when the subject is in a given state. All of it must be in some memory, whether short-term, long-term or external. The authors ask when an external memory belongs in it.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The criterion is whether all its contents relevant to selecting operators and to the inputs of operators are in fact available, though not all need be equally accessible. A board with only a few expressions could be part of the knowledge state. When it grows large, with complex expressions such as the four-term ones in D1 and C1, it becomes truly external to the current state.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The best evidence is that subjects fail to notice duplications at once. S4 on D1 wrote L8 by R10 and did not notice that it repeated L2 until many segments later. When he saw it, he said he was clear back at the beginning again, so the discovery meant failure to progress and sent him back to start over.

card.rule: A display is part of the knowledge state only if its relevant contents are available; a large board is not, as missed duplicates show.
card.limits: The test is about availability for the next step, not about whether the contents are visible on the display.

concepts.title: The extended knowledge state
concepts.question: What does the idea of an extended knowledge state add, and how does the logic display fit it?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: An external memory used in a routine way but not totally available is hard to place. Treating it as part of the knowledge state overstates what is available, and treating it as outside understates it.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The authors define an extended knowledge state: the contents of memory X plus what can be obtained from memory Y by a retrieval program P. To be more than a relabeling, the accessing functions must be defined, so that what is actually available can be stated. The display can then be available for some functions and not for others.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Subjects are poor at spotting duplicates. They duplicate expressions because they do not search the display each time they write one and instead rely on noticing a repeat.

card.rule: The extended knowledge state is what is in mind plus what a retrieval process can fetch from the display.
card.limits: The authors cannot specify the accessing functions in detail for the logic task, because the experiments did not give enough information.

concepts.title: How subjects search the rule sheet
concepts.question: On what conditions do subjects search the rule sheet, and what slips through?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Even when rules are not fully known, subjects can find one by searching the sheet. The question is on what basis they search.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Working forward, they select almost entirely by the connective. S10 at the start of D1 looked at the first card, saw two horseshoe expressions and named R6 and R2. Otherwise subjects describe the situation by function, so the search has two conditions: function and feasibility, the latter based on the connective.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: When first attempts fail, subjects sometimes search by function alone, without feasibility. S8 on D1 asked how to get rid of a term with a horseshoe, decided it could not be done, and then took rules that delete terms, R8, R3 and R11, without checking applicability.

card.rule: Subjects search by connective when working forward, and by function plus feasibility, dropping feasibility when they fail.
card.limits: The search is described from protocols; the authors have not checked which rules are evoked in each search.

concepts.title: How the layout of the rule sheet shaped search
concepts.question: How can the layout of the rule sheet make a subject overlook a rule?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The rule sheet is a complexly structured memory. Its rules fall into three sets marked off by lines, with a description below each rule. The authors took over the form used in the earlier Yale studies.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The wording of the descriptions and the grouping of the rules have effects, though these are hard to pin down. The functional descriptions subjects use are no doubt affected by the sheet's wording.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: At the start of D1, S8 looked forward for a rule with a dot as major connective. He examined R1, R3, R4 and R7 aloud and then said he saw nothing to do on the scale of the whole. He did not mention R5 or R8.

card.rule: The layout of the rule sheet can hide rules that match a search condition, as it hid R5 and R8 from S8.
card.limits: The effects of the sheet's structure are hard to pin down systematically from these data.

concepts.title: What the external memory analysis shows
concepts.question: What do the authors conclude about external memory, and where does their conclusion stop?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The analysis of external memory in logic was only illustrative. The authors ask what it nevertheless shows.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: An external memory can be fitted into the process in several different ways, and all of these show up to some extent in logic. Because the logic task is dominated by the basic means-ends cycle, the structure of the two external memories can be ignored to a first approximation.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors say that in other tasks this would clearly not be so. They add that the concept of an extended knowledge state seems a necessary modification of the notion of the knowledge state.

card.rule: In logic, external memory structure can be ignored as a first approximation; the extended knowledge state is a needed modification.
card.limits: The conclusion is for the logic task; other tasks, such as chess, may depend more on external memory.

concepts.title: Similarity first, then subtle differences
concepts.question: When the authors look for individual differences among the subjects, what do they find first?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors have noted changes in the subjects' procedures over a series of problems and differences in style. They now ask what differences can be found.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: They list six places to look: the problem spaces in which subjects work, the operators they apply, the differences they notice, their ordering of differences, their abstracting procedures and distinctions between essential and inessential, and their methods. What strikes first is the similarity among subjects: with qualifications for S11, all work in essentially the same space and apply almost the same methods.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Differences are nevertheless detectable and are significant enough to make some subjects substantially better problem solvers than others.

card.rule: Subjects are alike in space, operators, differences and methods; the differences are subtle but large enough to matter.
card.limits: S11 is the main qualification to the similarity, as later cards show.

concepts.title: Style as a matter of methods
concepts.question: Which aspects of style do the authors find in the protocols, and what methods lie behind them?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Individual differences and learning are likely to be linked: a subject with a richer range of techniques may be moved toward it by practice. The authors look for aspects of style in the protocols.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: They find four: the number of rule applications carried out; forward search of the rules to find those applicable to given expressions; search of the rules for one that performs a desired function or reduces a difference; and working backwards from L0. They relate mostly to methods.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Number of rule applications depends on the availability of generators and the strength of stop rules. The second aspect is the method Find operator to transform X, the third Find operator to perform function F, and the fourth the working-backwards method.

card.rule: The four aspects of style correspond to methods: how many rules to apply, two ways of searching the rules, and working backward.
card.limits: The aspects were found in a few protocols; they are a description of style, not a full theory of individual differences.

concepts.title: Two styles of attacking the same problem
concepts.question: How do S9 and S11 differ in the way they first compare L1 with L0?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Figure 10.14 gives the opening of the protocols of S9 and S11 on D1 and C1. Comparing the same subject on the two problems shows persisting style; comparing the two subjects on one problem shows the effect of the task.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: At a surface level each subject has consistent habits of expression. At a deeper level the way they compare L1 with L0 differs. In both problems the form of L0 reminds S9 of a rule. S11, especially on D1, matches L1 with L0 symbol by symbol, with little abstraction from connectives.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: S9 speaks of what a form reminds him of and drops what he does not need. S11 speaks of removing, changing and what he can do on an expression.

card.rule: S9 characterizes the problem broadly and is reminded of a rule; S11 matches particulars symbol by symbol.
card.limits: Two subjects on two problems are an illustration of style, not a sample.

concepts.title: Consistent habits across two problems
concepts.question: How consistent is each subject's way of working across D1 and C1?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Table 10.3 compares six subjects who have protocols for both D1 and C1: how many expressions each wrote, whether each searched the rules or the expressions on the board, whether each persisted in one plan, whether each worked backward, and whether each characterized the problem in general terms.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: There is great individual consistency. S11 worked almost entirely in his head and wrote three expressions each time, while S5 wrote 17 on one problem and 19 on the other. Only S4 was inconsistent, with 13 expressions on D1, which he solved, and 6 on C1, which he failed. Four of the six searched the list of rules extensively on one or both problems, each consistently.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The two extreme writers, S11 and S5, were both subjects who solved neither problem. The two who did not search the rules were a nonsolver, S5, and a solver, S9.

card.rule: Each subject's habits, such as how much to write down and whether to search the rules, were stable from D1 to C1.
card.limits: The table covers six subjects on two successive problems, so it shows stability over a short span only.

concepts.title: Profiles from strongest to weakest
concepts.question: How do the authors describe the subjects, arranged by apparent problem solving power?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Given the consistent habits, the authors arrange the subjects in the apparent order of their problem solving power and describe each.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: S9 generates clear general plans, working both backward and forward, and executes them with moderate difficulty. S8 is at first much less planful. He works forward, searches the rules when necessary, scans the new expressions as he writes them and reformulates the problem in light of what he finds.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: At the other end, S11 concerns himself with the detail rather than the broad structure of the problems, and spends much time searching for rules he can apply. The ordering rests on the protocols, not on a separate test.

card.rule: The stronger solvers characterize the problem and plan broadly; the weakest attend to detail.
card.limits: The ordering is apparent, drawn from the protocols of a few subjects.

concepts.title: Depth-first, scan-and-search, and abstraction
concepts.question: Which earlier strategy labels do the authors apply to S5, S8 and S9?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Chapter 8 classified strategies for applying means-ends analysis. The authors now ask which of those strategies particular subjects show.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: S5 is a clear example of the depth-first strategy, and his inability to solve the problems can be attributed to the stereotypy it produces. S8 fits the scan-and-search strategy: he often reviews the expressions he has generated and continues his search from those that seem most promising. Most subjects alternate between abstractions and the detail of the concrete problem space, and S9's protocols perhaps show this alternation most clearly; he does most of his problem solving in abstracted expressions.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors say they can apply a label like stereotypy to S5's persistent behavior on path.R7, and they read S8's label from his frequent reviewing of the expressions he has generated. They add that stereotypy is neither testable nor useful for prediction unless it is consistent from one problem to another.

card.rule: S5 shows the depth-first strategy and its stereotypy; S8 shows scan-and-search; S9 shows the alternation between abstraction and detail most clearly.
card.limits: A strategy label summarizes tendencies seen in a few protocols and does not describe everything a subject does.

concepts.title: S11: working in the head
concepts.question: What follows from S11's choice to have almost nothing written on the board?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: All the subjects operate in the problem space of expressions and rules and use the same basic processes of finding differences, finding relevant operators and applying them. The range of individual differences looks narrower than in cryptarithmetic. S11 is the most idiosyncratic, yet the authors do not find him in a different space.

blocks.label: Model
