blocks.text: S11 told the experimenter to write down very few expressions, only two. His preference for working in his head had several consequences, or causes. His plans are vaguer, and there is a looser link between plans and rules. He will group the terms in L1 somehow, and the feasibility of the somehow is never tested carefully.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Since he does not generate new expressions, they are not available to him for scanning to produce new goals. He cannot follow a search-and-scan strategy, because of the limits on what he can hold in his head.

card.rule: S11's habit of working in his head left him with vague plans and no written expressions to scan.
card.limits: The authors say it is not easy to distinguish causes from symptoms in his idiosyncrasy.

concepts.title: S11's syntax and symptoms
concepts.question: What do S11's remarks on tildes and signs show about how he reads the expressions, and how do the authors treat these findings?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: At one point in his protocol on D1, S11 speaks of changing the sign on the Q from the horseshoe to the tilde and the sign on the P from a tilde to a dot before it.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The authors infer that he is matching symbols in a linear string without first detecting the hierarchical phrase structure. He seems unaware of the difference in function between binary connectives like the horseshoe or dot and the unary tilde.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: He is also preoccupied with avoiding introducing tildes. Other subjects treat tildes as details to be adjusted by inessential transformations, except when a tilde makes a whole expression negative and so blocks certain rules.

card.rule: S11 reads expressions as flat strings of symbols and fears tildes, which is a symptom of weaker abstraction.
card.limits: The authors call these symptoms and stress that they are not a fundamental characterization of S11.

concepts.title: S8 stops searching the rules
concepts.question: What changed in S8's behavior over his six problems, and what do his remarks suggest?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Style was studied over only two successive problems. The authors cannot tell whether a subject keeps the same style over a longer run, or whether rule searches fade as the functions and conditions of the rules are learned. They turn to S8, with six protocols in sequence: D1, C1, A2', B2, A4 and C3.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: After problem C1, S8 no longer searches through the rules. His remarks in the last four protocols show that he now knows the functions of the rules. His style moves gradually toward that of S9.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In A4, after solving, he says he does not have to refer to the paper much any more and is starting to remember the rules as he looks at them. In C3 he says that a term now reminds him of a certain rule, and that the rules seemed all mixed up at first but are getting far apart.

card.rule: After C1, S8 stops searching the rule sheet and speaks of knowing what each rule does.
card.limits: Part of his change may reflect the later problems being easy enough that no searches were needed.

concepts.title: What S8 learned
concepts.question: What three kinds of learning do the authors attribute to S8?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Over six problems S8's style moved toward S9's. The authors summarize what he learned.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: First, he gradually acquired a table of connections between features and differences on one hand, and rules on the other. Second, he shifted from a working-forward style to one based on abstract characterization of the main features of the problem and on planning. Third, he learned that certain goals can be achieved by fixed sequences of certain operators.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: S8 first worked backward from L0 in A4 and did so in all later problems. On the last three problems he characterized the problem at the outset, and on each of the last two he outlined a correct plan.

card.rule: S8 learned direct links from features to rules, a planful style based on abstract characterization, and fixed sequences of operators.
card.limits: This is one subject over six problems; it shows that these kinds of learning can occur.

concepts.title: Running the movie in reverse: S9's practice problems
concepts.question: Do S9's early practice problems look like S8's early behavior?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: S8's learning looked like a shift toward S9's style. To test whether the picture runs in reverse, the authors turn to S9's protocols on three practice problems, a1, a2 and a3, attempted just before D1.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: On a1, S9 made notes on his rule sheet about the function of each rule, because starting from the rules alone would be a hit-and-miss operation. He then noticed differences and searched the rules for one that suited the difference. On a2 he failed: he did not know that expressions can be split and the parts used as inputs to two-line rules.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: On a3 he characterized the problem fairly completely at the beginning and made one extensive search of the rules. The authors say his practice behavior resembles S8's early behavior more than his own later behavior.

card.rule: S9's early practice looks like S8's early work, and it begins to move toward his later style by the third practice problem.
card.limits: Three practice problems for one subject show only the start of a change.

concepts.title: The logic landscape and its explorers
concepts.question: How do the authors sum up the exploration of logic problems in Part III?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Part III has ranged widely over logic problems. The authors step back to ask what kind of terrain they have been exploring and who explored it.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The landscape strongly resembled the one met earlier in cryptarithmetic. The exploratory behavior of the human problem solvers reflected the structure and appearance of that landscape as seen by information processing systems with limited capacities to detect patterns, to infer consequences and to remember paths of exploration.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The evidence is the body of protocols and the analyses of Chapters 8 to 10, summed up here in a few lines.

card.rule: The logic terrain is like the cryptarithmetic terrain, and the subjects explored it as limited information processors would.
card.limits: This is a summary of a first approximation, which the following cards qualify.

concepts.title: The first approximation to the subjects' paths
concepts.question: On what three assumptions can the range of paths a group will explore be predicted?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors want a prediction of the range of paths a group of subjects will explore on a problem of this kind.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: As a first approximation, assume that they make exploration and solution plans based on three things: comparing the starting point with the desired goal and applying appropriate operators to reduce differences; simplifying the initial expressions; and applying operators whose inputs strikingly resemble given expressions.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The behavior of all of the subjects and all versions of GPS fit this first approximation. To varying degrees, subgoals are set up to find operators that will modify expressions to make them fit operators already selected for application.

card.rule: Subjects can be expected to reduce differences from the goal, simplify the givens, and apply operators whose inputs look like what they have.
card.limits: The approximation says what paths are likely, not which one a given subject will take.

concepts.title: Dimensions of variation, and what the theory achieves
concepts.question: In which dimensions do subjects vary, and what do the authors claim for the account as a whole?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Within the shared first approximation, subjects and the same subject at different stages of learning differ. The authors list the dimensions of variation.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: They differ in how they characterize the initial problem, and appear to learn gradually which differences to rank first in planning. They differ in persistence in a subgoal against readiness to return to the whole problem. They differ in priority given to working forward and restructuring versus working backward by a definite plan. They differ in cues used to detect cycling and lack of progress.

blocks.label: Model (continued)
blocks.text: They differ in how far they explore paths mentally rather than writing expressions on the board, and in how far operators are tied in memory directly to differences or features, so that no search is needed. They also acquire generalized knowledge that some differences are not remediable, and that some goals can be reached by fixed sequences of operators.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: To a large extent these differences can be detected in protocols and used to account for the variety in style of the explorations of different subjects.

card.rule: Subjects vary in characterization, persistence, direction of work, cues to lack of progress, mental versus written exploration, and learned knowledge.
card.limits: The list is of dimensions found in these protocols, not a complete theory of individual differences.

concepts.title: What the chess part sets out to ask
concepts.question: What questions does the chess part ask, and what will it do with the earlier task analyses?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Chess, the choice of a move, is the third and last task area. The authors put to it the same questions as before: can a human be viewed as an information processing system here, with problem spaces, search strategies, heuristics and goal structures that can be identified precisely?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: One function of the part is to confirm or qualify the earlier analyses, by separating what comes from the task environment from what comes from the subject. A second is to find new phenomena: new mechanisms, representations and heuristics.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The plan is stated in three steps: analyze the task, examine some behavior in detail, then take a broader view of human chess playing. The test for any new phenomenon is whether the basic apparatus of Part I can describe it.

card.rule: The chess part asks the old questions of a new task, to confirm or qualify earlier analyses and to understand new phenomena with the same basic apparatus.
card.limits: The aim is understanding by the Part I apparatus, not a fit to the specialized frameworks of earlier tasks, so a new phenomenon need not look like an old one.

concepts.title: Why a game, and why chess
concepts.question: What makes games, and chess in particular, good material for the study of problem solving?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors need a third task area. They could have chosen tic-tac-toe, the world of Hoyle, Go or a game of their own devising, so they must say why a game, and why chess.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: A game gives a relatively closed environment, defined by its rules, and a well-defined goal. Sometimes several top goals are incompatible, such as winning and drawing. The competitive side can be relied upon, in our culture, to motivate subjects.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Choosing a move in chess is acknowledged to be hard, and the game has not become barren or exhausted after 200 years of study. Nearly all serious games between grandmasters of the last century are preserved, so programs and people can be compared in detail.

card.rule: Games are closed, goal-defined and motivating, and chess adds real difficulty plus a vast recorded record against which programs and people can be compared.
card.limits: These are the authors' reasons for choosing chess, not claims that chess is typical of all problem solving.

concepts.title: The basic problem space of a game
concepts.question: What are the elements and operators of the basic problem space of chess, and what is the game tree?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A game such as chess, checkers or tic-tac-toe has a problem space that is defined at once, without further analysis. The question is what its elements and operators are.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The elements are the board configurations, called positions. The operators are the legal moves defined by the rules. The rules give a starting position and a way to recognize the terminal positions that win, lose or draw. Taking all legal moves at each position generates the game tree.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors compare choosing a move in a game to exploring a proof tree in logic and to exploring for a solution in puzzles: in each, exploring the tree teaches the consequences of the available steps. For interesting games the tree is of enormous size.

card.rule: In a game, positions are the elements, legal moves are the operators, and the tree of all legal moves from a position is the game tree.
card.limits: The analogy with theorem proving and puzzles is useful but not exact; the next ideas show where it breaks.

concepts.title: A proof is a path, a win is a strategy
concepts.question: How does showing a winning move differ from showing a proof, and why does it matter?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: In theorem proving, one problem solver makes every step. In a game, the two sides move alternately. The authors ask how this changes what counts as a solution.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: A proof is shown by a single path that leads to the desired theorem. A winning move is shown by a subtree of the game tree with the minimax property: for each reply the opponent might make there is a move for the player, and so on until a winning position is reached.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Hence a proof is a definite plan, while a win is a strategy setting out a tree of paths for all possible moves of the opponent. The authors say this difference has important consequences for the heuristics that game programs use.

card.rule: A proof is a single path; a win is a whole strategy covering every reply the opponent can make.
card.limits: Case analysis in a proof comes closer to the game situation, so the contrast is sharpest for proofs that are a single path.

concepts.title: Why logic space is a web and chess space a tree
concepts.question: In what way does the basic space of logic differ in shape from that of chess?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors compare chess with the Logic Theorist, a typical theorem-proving task, and note that the two spaces differ in shape even before the players are considered.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: In chess the legal moves are always a function of the current position alone. In logic, though not in cryptarithmetic, an operator that is a rule of inference can take more than one expression as input, as detachment does.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Because of this, the authors say, the basic problem space in logic is more like a web or lattice than a tree. The comparison of theorem proving with games therefore holds, but it is not exact.

card.rule: Chess moves depend on one position, but logic operators like detachment can depend on several expressions, so logic's space is a web rather than a tree.
card.limits: The difference concerns the shape of the basic space; it does not by itself say which task is harder.

concepts.title: Three different trees
concepts.question: Why must the problem solving search tree be kept apart from the proof tree and the game tree?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The words tree and search are used for several things in this chapter. The authors warn that confusion among them hides real differences between kinds of programs.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The problem solving search tree, when there is one, is not the proof tree of theorems and not the game tree of chess. In most game programs the search does run along some or all branches of the game tree, but the authors say this is not an essential feature.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: They will describe game-playing schemes that work in spaces larger than the tree of legal moves. They also cite a conceivable game player that does not search the game tree at all, while a theorem prover that finds no proofs cannot be conceived.

card.rule: The search a program carries out, the proof tree and the game tree are three distinct things, and a game player need not search the game tree.
card.limits: Most existing programs do search the game tree, so the distinction matters for what is possible, not for what is usual.

concepts.title: A move cannot be undone
concepts.question: Why does the first move from the current position play a different role from later moves in the search?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: In theorem proving the aim is to find a whole path, the proof, and there is no penalty for blind alleys or extra steps other than the time spent searching. In a game the aim at each point is to find only the first step of a path.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Once a move is made, it cannot be undone if it later proves wrong. So the first move from the current position plays a distinct role. The later moves of the search tree are explored not to choose a path but only for the information they give about how good the first move is.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Therefore proof paths are of the essence of theorem proving, but game paths are incidental to choosing moves, though they can be very informative. The contrast concerns the purpose of the search, not whether a game player searches.

card.rule: Only the first move is chosen and cannot be undone; later moves in the search serve just to evaluate it.
card.limits: The player still searches, and the search can be deep; only its purpose differs from that of a proof search.

concepts.title: Any proof will do; a move must be best
concepts.question: What is the player trying to find in a game, and when may the search stop early?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors list a fifth difference between proving theorems and playing games, having to do with what counts as success.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: In theorem proving the task is to find a proof, and any one will do. In a game it is to find the best move, or, if that cannot be guaranteed, at least a very good move. A move is suitable only in relation to an assessment of the other moves available.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The one exception is a move that can be shown to lead to a forced win, a win no matter what the opponent does. There, as in theorem proving, no further search is needed, unless esthetic criteria lead the solver to prefer one winning strategy, or proof, to another.

card.rule: A theorem needs any proof, but a game needs the best (or a very good) move, judged against the alternatives, unless a forced win is found.
card.limits: The standard of best is only attainable where it can be guaranteed; otherwise a very good move must do.

concepts.title: The common scheme of every chess program
concepts.question: What four-part scheme do all the chess programs share, and who described it first?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Many chess programs have been built. The authors want to know what they have in common before they compare them, and where they differ in search strategy and heuristics.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: All work in the basic problem space of legal moves, occasionally augmented by abstract moves. All follow the approach Shannon described in 1949: consider the alternative moves, obtain an evaluation of each by analysis, and choose the one preferred on that evaluation.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The analysis is the hard part. It has three steps: explore continuations to some depth, evaluate the positions reached at the ends by the pattern of men on the board (a static evaluation), and combine these by minimaxing into an effective value for the alternative.

card.rule: Every program considers alternative moves, explores continuations to a depth, evaluates the end positions statically, and minimaxes to choose.
card.limits: The scheme says what is common; the programs differ widely in how deep, how wide and how finely they carry out each step.

concepts.title: What chess adds to forward search
concepts.question: Which two features does chess add to the forward search of logic and cryptarithmetic, and what forces each?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The approach of the chess programs is one of forward search, as in the earlier tasks. The authors ask what is new in chess compared with logic and cryptarithmetic.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: There are two new features. The first is the evaluation, which stands in for the final desired position as a complete surrogate. The second is a complex procedure for inferring the effective values of alternative moves.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The evaluation is forced by the commitment to a sequence of irreversible moves long before the final position comes into view. A player must therefore judge positions by their features rather than by the result.

card.rule: Chess adds to forward search an evaluation that stands in for the unseen goal and a procedure for inferring the effective values of moves.
card.limits: These are the features of the programs the authors describe; they do not claim that no other design could exist.

concepts.title: Minimax: working back from the end
concepts.question: How is the minimax value of a position defined, and why is the name minimax apt?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors ask how the value of a move can be found from the end positions of the game, and whether that value can be defined in a way that applies to every position.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Start from the terminal positions, which have determinate payoffs of win, tie or loss, and work backwards. The value of a nonterminal position is the best of the values of the positions one move on. Best means the maximum when it is the player's move and the minimum when it is the opponent's move.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The name arises from this alternation of minimum and maximum. Values and the function best are relative to the player, and a next-position means one reached by a single move.

card.rule: A position's minimax value is the best of its successors' values, taking the maximum on one's own move and the minimum on the opponent's.
card.limits: The definition needs the whole tree; real programs apply it to a small part and so must use evaluations in place of true values.

concepts.title: The three-move minimax example
concepts.question: In the book's small tree, why does White prefer the sure draw to the move that might win?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: White is to move at position X and has three choices, W1, W2 and W3. To keep the example simple, every Black reply leads to a terminal position with a known payoff. How should White decide?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Whatever Black does, W1 leads to a draw, and W2 leads to a loss for White. W3 offers a win in one reply and a loss in another, with the outcome in Black's control. If White credits Black with enough skill, W3 ends as a loss.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: So White prefers W1 to W2, and W1 to W3, because the possible win from W3 is a chimera that can never be realized. White imputes the value tie to position X by reasoning backwards from the known values.

card.rule: Credit the opponent with skill: a move that gives the opponent the choice between your win and your loss is worth your loss.
card.limits: The reasoning assumes an opponent able to see the outcomes; against a weaker opponent a gamble might pay, but minimax does not rely on it.

concepts.title: The prototypic chess program
concepts.question: How do find-move and analyse together carry out the search, and what is left undefined?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Minimaxing must be fitted into a real program: values come from static evaluations, moves come from generators that need not produce all legal moves, and the search must stop before everything is exhausted. The authors give a prototypic program for this.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The main process, find-move, generates the base-moves, makes each, has the resulting position analysed, compares the value with the best so far and replaces the best move if the new one is better, then tests width-termination to decide whether to continue.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The analysis process first tests depth-termination. If the position is terminal for the search it computes a static-value and stops. If not, it generates analysis-moves, analyses each next position in the same manner, and finally computes an adjusted-value. Pure minimaxing would use the best-value itself.

card.rule: Find-move and analyse form a recursive loop: generate moves, evaluate by deeper analysis or a static value, keep the best, and stop by tests on width and depth.
card.limits: The prototype is a scheme: until its undefined processes are filled in, it does not specify a particular program.

concepts.title: Turing's dead position
concepts.question: What is a dead position, and how does it let Turing's program limit its search?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: In 1953 Turing described a program, simple enough to be hand-simulated, that considered all legal moves as alternatives. To limit computation it needed to be very careful about which continuations to explore.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Turing introduced the dead position: one in some sense stable, which can be evaluated without further search of the game tree. For example, there is no sense in counting material while an exchange of Queens is in progress; the exploration should run until the exchange is finished and the material will not change with the next move.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The program analyzed all the opponent's immediate replies. After that it considered further moves only from positions that were not dead.

card.rule: Evaluate only dead positions; keep exploring a position until nothing is about to change its static value.
card.limits: Deadness here is a judgment about stability; counting material in a live position gives a misleading value.

concepts.title: Turing's lexicographic evaluation
concepts.question: How did Turing's program compare two evaluations, and why did the static value act as a candidate?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Turing's program had to decide which of two moves was better when each had an evaluation made of several parts, and also how to handle that it analyzed only a subset of moves at most positions.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The static value was limited to material, mostly for computational reasons, though positional value was also considered at depth one. The evaluation was a list compared lexicographically: material dominates, and position counts only when the material is the same.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors spell out the position-value, with such features as King mobility, castling and defended pieces, to convey the range of features. Turing did not use simple minimax alone, since only some moves were analyzed.

card.rule: Compare evaluations as lists in order: the first component decides, and the next counts only when the first is equal.
card.limits: A strict order means a small gain in material outweighs any gain in position; the scheme does not trade the two against each other.

concepts.title: How Turing's program played
concepts.question: How well did Turing's hand-simulated program play, and what did that show?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Only one game with the program was published, as far as the authors know, so the evidence about its strength is slight. They set out what it shows.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The program proved weak. It lost against a weak human player who did not know the program, though it was not entirely a pushover. Its play was rather aimless, and it was capable of gross blunders, one of which cost it the game.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The subtleties of its evaluation were lost on it, since most of the numerous factors in the position-value rarely influenced the move chosen. In summary, it was not a very good player, but it reached the bottom rung of the ladder of human play.

card.rule: Turing's program, with minimal exploration, played at the bottom rung of human play: aimless, prone to gross blunders, and indifferent to most of its evaluation.
card.limits: One published game is thin evidence, and this was a hand simulation, so the verdict is a rough one.

concepts.title: The Los Alamos program: no selectivity at all
concepts.question: What is the simplest way to realize the chess scheme, as the Los Alamos program did?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A research group at Los Alamos wished to get a computer to play chess. The authors take its program as an almost perfect example of the simplest system that fits the framework.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: All base-moves are considered, and all continuations are explored to a depth of four plies, two moves for each side. The static evaluation is a sum of a material measure and a mobility measure, and the values are combined by minimaxing.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors call it an almost perfect example of the simplest type of system realizing the framework. As in the prototype, the alternative with the best effective value is chosen as the move.

card.rule: Explore every move to a fixed depth, evaluate by material plus mobility, minimax, and add no selectivity.
card.limits: This is the simplest type, not a good player; the next ideas show how weak that simplicity is.

concepts.title: The arithmetic of four plies
concepts.question: How many continuations does four plies mean, and what does that demand of the processor?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Exploring all moves to a fixed depth looks harmless until the count is made. The authors do the arithmetic for the Los Alamos program.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: There are on average about 30 legal alternatives at each move. Four plies ahead is therefore 30 to the fourth power continuations, almost a million. In the reduced 6 by 6 game there were about 160,000.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: To make a move in ten minutes, the processor would need to generate and evaluate a continuation in less than one millisecond. This forces the process to be very simple and straightforward.

card.rule: About 30 moves per position over four plies gives almost a million continuations, so each must be handled in under a millisecond.
card.limits: The figures are for the Los Alamos setting of ten minutes per move and about 30 legal moves; other limits give other budgets.

concepts.title: Anchor points on a continuum
concepts.question: What do Turing's and the Los Alamos programs show, taken together, about the two ways to simplify a chess program?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Chess programs can be simplified in two directions: by exploring very little, as Turing's did, or by examining each position very little, as the Los Alamos program did. The authors ask what the two extremes show.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The Los Alamos programs test the limits of simplification toward minimizing the information required for each position evaluated. Turing's program tests the limits toward minimizing the exploration of continuations. They are anchor points of a continuum along which chess-playing systems are distributed.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Both extremes play at the level of a human beginner, which shows that such a level can be reached with little complexity. The authors conclude this casts doubt on the prospects of a system at either extreme rising far above beginner level.

card.rule: The two extremes of simplicity, little exploring or little looking at each position, both stall near human beginner level.
card.limits: The conclusion concerns systems at either extreme; it does not forbid one that combines power with selectivity.

concepts.title: Plausible move generators
concepts.question: How does Bernstein's program decide which few moves to consider at each position?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: In 1957-58 Alex Bernstein, a chess player and programmer at IBM, built a program for the IBM 704 for the full 8 by 8 board. The authors say it takes an extremely important step toward greater sophistication: only a fraction of the legal alternatives and continuations are considered.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: A series of subroutines, called plausible move generators, propose the moves to be considered. Each is related to a feature of the game, such as King safety, development, defending one's own men or attacking the opponent's. The generators are run in priority order, the most important first, until seven moves have been collected.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The program explores four plies, as the Los Alamos program did, but uses the generators at every stage, so at most seven direct continuations are considered from any position. It minimaxes and chooses the alternative with the greatest effective value, with no adjustment to the dynamic value.

card.rule: Run feature-related move generators in priority order until seven moves are collected, and search only those.
card.limits: The generators carry the program's chess knowledge, so a good move that no generator proposes is never considered.

concepts.title: What radical selectivity buys, and what it risks
concepts.question: What does Bernstein's program show about selecting few moves, and what does selecting few moves risk?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Bernstein's program gives the authors their first information about radical selectivity in move generation and analysis. Its play is uneven, with striking blind spots, and sometimes very good for a series of moves.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: At seven moves per position it examines only about 2500 final positions four plies deep, out of about 800,000 legal continuations. That it still plays at all tolerably after a reduction in search by a factor of 300 implies that the selection mechanism is fairly effective.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The selections reflect the common and tested lore of the chess world, so the significance of the reduction is that this lore is captured successfully in the mechanism. It had never beaten anyone, as far as the authors know, and lost the reported game to a good player.

card.rule: Seven moves per position cuts the search by about 300 and still plays tolerably, which shows the generators capture real chess lore.
card.limits: Playing tolerably is not playing well: the program had never beaten anyone and was not tried against weak players.

concepts.title: Sophistication costs program and time
concepts.question: Why does the 300-fold saving in search not make Bernstein's program 300 times faster than Los Alamos?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Selectivity cuts the number of positions, but the authors point out that every increase in the sophistication of performance is paid for by an increase in the complexity of the program.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The move generators and the components of the static evaluation need varied and diverse information about each position. That means more program and more computing time per position than the Los Alamos program needs. Bernstein's program has 7000 instructions, the Los Alamos program 600, a factor of over 10.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors estimate that both would need about the same average time per move on a processor of the same power, say half a minute on an IBM 360/65. The greater processing per position approximately cancels the 300 to 1 gain in selectivity, even though Bernstein's program is coded for maximum speed.

card.rule: More selective means more work per position, and at four plies the extra work roughly cancels the saving in positions.
card.limits: The cancelation is an estimate for a particular depth; deeper search changes the balance, as the next idea shows.

concepts.title: Selectivity is powerful, speed is weak
concepts.question: Why does deeper search favor selectivity over speed as a way to improve a complex program?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The two programs perform alike by accident, say the authors. They ask which of the two, selectivity or speed, is better for improving complex programs.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The significant feature of chess is the exponential growth of positions with depth of analysis. As analysis deepens, greater computing effort per position soon pays for itself, since it slows the growth in the number of positions.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Suppose both programs went one move deeper. The Los Alamos program would take about 1000 times as long (30 squared), Bernstein's about 50 times (7 squared), gaining a factor of 20. For a tree of four branches searched n deep, doubling speed gives n plus a half, but halving the branches to two at each node gives 2n.

card.rule: Because positions grow exponentially with depth, cutting the branching factor helps far more than a faster machine.
card.limits: Selectivity pays only if the heuristics are good enough not to discard the useful moves.

concepts.title: Goals as the second level of organization
concepts.question: What is the NSS program's second level of organization, and what does each goal bring with it?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The NSS program was developed in 1958 with J. C. Shaw. It can be described in the same terms as the others, and shows Turing's dead position and Bernstein's move generators. The authors ask what it adds.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: It adds a second level of organization: a set of goals, each corresponding to a basic aspect of the chess situation, such as material balance or center control. Each goal has its own base-move generator, analysis-move generator and static-evaluation process. The program has no adjusted-value process.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: At the start of each move a preliminary analysis establishes which chess situation obtains, and that evokes the goals appropriate to it. A goal specification routine supplies the information for this choice, and the goals go on a current-goal-list, most crucial first. This list controls selection of alternatives, continuations and evaluation.

card.rule: Goals are modules that each bring their own move generators and evaluation, and the situation decides which goals are active and in what order.
card.limits: What kind of game the program plays depends on which goals are available and chosen for each move.

concepts.title: A generator proposes; the analysis disposes
concepts.question: What is the division of labor between move generators and analysis in the NSS program?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A program that proposes moves for reasons must also decide whether each proposal is acceptable. The authors ask how NSS divides these two jobs.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Each base-move generator finds positive reasons for doing things. For instance, only the center-control generator will propose P-Q4 in the opening, and only the material-balance generator will propose moving a piece that is en prise out of danger. The analysis procedure is concerned only with whether a move is acceptable once it has been generated.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors put it as: a generator proposes; the analysis procedure disposes. The value assigned to a move comes from a series of evaluations, one for each goal, so the value is a list whose components say how acceptable the position is from each goal's viewpoint.

card.rule: Generators supply reasons to make moves; analysis, using every goal's evaluation, judges whether each proposal is acceptable.
card.limits: A proposal made for one goal may be rejected by another goal's evaluation, so a proposed move is not yet a chosen move.

concepts.title: Values as lists, compared lexicographically
concepts.question: How can the NSS program compare two values that are lists of independent components?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Minimaxing requires that any two values can be compared, to decide which is preferable or whether they are equal. In NSS each value has several independent components, one for each goal selected.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Minimaxing needs a complete ordering of such values. NSS uses a lexicographic ordering: each component is completely ordered within itself, and values of higher-priority components dominate those of lower-priority components, as the goal list orders them.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: To compare two values, compare the first components. If one move is preferable on that, it is preferred. If they are equal, compare the second components, and so on down the list. Material balance would assess only gain or loss of material; development, the gain or loss of tempi; pawn structure, doubling and isolation of pawns.

card.rule: Compare value lists component by component in priority order; the first unequal component decides.
card.limits: The method makes high-priority goals absolute: no gain in lower components can offset a loss in a higher one.

concepts.title: Taking the first acceptable move
concepts.question: How does the NSS program choose a final move, and when is its choice not the maximum value?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: In the other programs the final choice was an extension of minimax: choose the move with the highest value. The authors point out that this rests on the assumption that the set of alternatives is fixed.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: If base moves are generated one at a time, other choice procedures become possible. The simplest, which NSS uses, is satisficing: set an acceptance or aspiration level as the final criterion and take the first move that reaches it.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The executive goes down the goal list, activating the move generators in priority order, so important moves are considered first. Width-termination at depth one is then simply whether a move reaches the specified level of acceptability.

card.rule: NSS takes the first move whose value reaches an aspiration level, because moves are generated one at a time in priority order.
card.limits: Satisficing can settle on a move before better ones are seen, so the result depends on the order of generation.

concepts.title: Dead with respect to every goal
concepts.question: How does NSS generalize Turing's dead position to decide how far to explore?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The analysis-move generators are the main agents of selectivity in NSS. They decide, at each position reached in analysis, which further branches are explored. So they set the average number of branches and the average depth of exploration.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: NSS generalizes Turing's dead position. Turing applied it to exchanges; NSS applies it to each feature of the board. The static evaluation of a goal means something only if the position is dead with respect to that feature, that is, if no move is likely to alter that component radically.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Each goal's analysis-move generator says whether the position is dead for its goal; if not, it generates the moves that are plausible and could seriously affect the static value. Exploration therefore continues until a position is dead with respect to all goals, and then a static evaluation can be made.

card.rule: Explore until a position is dead with respect to every goal's feature, generating only moves that could change that feature.
card.limits: There is no separate width or depth limit for analysis at depth greater than one; the dead tests control both.

concepts.title: Evaluating one move: the schematic example
concepts.question: Following the schematic example, how does NSS reach one effective value for a proposed move?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors give a schematic example. White, the machine, must move from position P0. Some generator proposes the move M1, which leads to P1, and the value of P1 will become the value of M1. The values are written as lists of three components, one per goal.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: For P1 the first and second goals can produce static values, 5 and 3, but the third goal does not find the position dead and generates two moves, M2 and M3. M2 leads to P2, which is dead for all goals, with the static value (4, 3, 1).

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: M3 leads to P3, where the first goal generates M4, to P4 with the value (2, 8, 1), and the second goal generates M5, to P5 with the value (4, 7, 3). The third goal finds P3 dead. White is to move at P3 and maximizes; the first component dominates, so M5 is chosen, and (4, 7, 3) is the value of P3.

card.rule: Explore until every branch ends in a dead position, then back values up by lexicographic maximum and minimum, level by level.
card.limits: The numbers are schematic; in the real program the ordered values are sets of symbols whose structure depends on the computation.

concepts.title: The alpha-beta procedure
concepts.question: How can a program stop exploring a node once it knows its value cannot matter?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Minimaxing in NSS is carried out at the same time as the branches are generated. That permits the so-called alpha-beta procedure, which lops off a large number of irrelevant branches.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: At each node keep the best value found so far: the highest at a maximizing node, the lowest at a minimizing node. Let a maximizing node have the highest value so far, alpha. Its child, a minimizing node, has the lowest value so far, beta. The move finally chosen at the child must have value beta or less, while the parent's choice will be alpha or more.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: So if a move is found at the child that makes beta smaller than alpha, the child can be abandoned at once. Its eventual value is guaranteed to be below alpha, and the parent can already get alpha elsewhere. In the schematic example, had P5 been generated before P4, no further moves from P3 would be needed, since Black will already prefer P2 to P3.

card.rule: Once a branch is guaranteed to be worth less than what is already in hand elsewhere, stop exploring it.
card.limits: The cutoff requires that the values already found elsewhere are available when the branch is explored.

concepts.title: What alpha-beta is, and what it is not
concepts.question: Why is the alpha-beta procedure not a heuristic, and where do heuristic questions remain?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A procedure that prunes branches might be taken for a heuristic, which is a risky shortcut. The authors explain why alpha-beta is different.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The alpha-beta procedure is not a heuristic. The branches it eliminates are guaranteed to have no effect on the final value that minimaxing produces, so they can be ignored with impunity. It costs a little, since alpha and beta must be computed and compared at each node, but the savings far exceed the costs.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: It has been used in all game-playing programs after the first few. It is easy to add the test to the width-termination process, provided the best value obtained so far by the opponent is available.

card.rule: Alpha-beta removes only branches that cannot change the minimax result, so it gives the same answer as full minimaxing for less work.
card.limits: It saves only what is provably irrelevant; further savings beyond it need heuristics, which can err.

concepts.title: What the NSS search depends on
concepts.question: On what does the NSS search depend to terminate quickly, given nothing guarantees it will?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors say the analysis procedure of NSS is not simple, conceptually or technically. There are many ways to terminate the search and reach an effective evaluation.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Success depends heavily on the ability to evaluate statically. The more numerous the situations that can be recognized as having a certain value without having to generate continuations, the more rapidly the search will terminate.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The number of plausible moves that affect the value is also of consequence.

card.rule: NSS search ends quickly when many situations can be valued statically and few plausible moves affect the value.
card.limits: Static evaluation covers only the features the goals know; positions outside them still need exploration.

concepts.title: The center-control goal
concepts.question: What does the center-control goal propose, and what does it leave to other goals to catch?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The center-control goal is the simplest of the three developed goals. It needs no special information, and it becomes irrelevant once all the center pawns have been moved to the fourth rank or beyond, or captured.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Its important part is the base-move generator. It proposes the two primary moves, P-Q4 and P-K4, if they are legal. If they cannot be made, it can prevent the opponent from making his primary moves, by occupying or attacking those squares, or prepare its own, by adding defenders or removing a block.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Its evaluation is essentially negative. It only assures that moves proposed by other goals will not be made if they jeopardize control of the center. A typical move it rejects is B-Q3 or B-K3 before the respective center pawns have moved.

card.rule: Center control proposes the central pawn moves and ways to prevent or prepare them, and its evaluation only vetoes moves that interfere.
card.limits: It never traces consequences itself, and it ignores moves from other goals that happen to help the center.

concepts.title: The material-balance goal and its exchanges
concepts.question: How does the material-balance goal handle gain and loss of material, and what is outside its sight?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Material-balance handles all questions about gain and loss of material in the immediate situation. It does not consider threats such as pins and forks, where the actual exchange is still a move away; other goals must take care of those.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Positive and negative aspects of material are kept in a single goal, since they compensate directly and material must often be spent to gain material. The goal works from a special data structure, the list of all exchanges. Each exchange gets a static-exchange-value.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: This value is a considerably better approximation to the true balance than the plain count of material, but considerably less accurate than a full dynamic analysis. It handles the order in which doubled pieces, such as a Queen preceding a Rook on a file, must capture, but takes no account of interactions between exchanges.

card.rule: Material-balance lists every exchange, values each separately, and so sees material well but not threats or interactions among exchanges.
card.limits: Because exchanges are valued one by one, an attacker used in one exchange may be counted again in another.

concepts.title: Playing off the exchanges
concepts.question: How does NSS improve on a raw material count when search stops early for lack of space?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Search in NSS was usually ended for reasons of space, so a forced static value, the plain balance of material, was too crude an evaluation.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: NSS adopted an adjusted static value that makes use of the information in the specification lists of exchanges. The exchanges are played off as if they were moves. When a player selects an exchange, his static-exchange-value is increased by it. The option to select the next exchange goes to the opponent of the player who made the last move in the previous exchange.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The player holding the option may choose to take none of the exchanges and end the playoff. This is always considered possible, so the playoff is not forced. Despite the simplifications, the adjusted values are very much better than the raw static values.

card.rule: Play the listed exchanges off alternately, letting either side stop, to get a material value much better than a raw count.
card.limits: The playoff still treats exchanges as independent, so interactions between them remain a basic simplification.

concepts.title: The development goal
concepts.question: How does the development goal generate moves and value a position?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The development goal is concerned, like center control, only with the initial deployment of the game, and uses highly specific information, such as the aim to develop a Knight to its B3 square. It must decide which pieces count as undeveloped.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: A specification list holds the undeveloped pieces, by criteria such as a Knight or Bishop still in its original position. The generator proposes legal developing moves first. It then proposes preparatory moves, built from developing moves described by how many men block them, zero, one or two. Moves with more than two blockers are ignored.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: If the blocker is the player's own man, the goal proposes any move that clears the way and leaves the other goals to weed out bad proposals. If the blocker is the opponent's, it is attacked. The static value has two numbers, the tempi count and the number of the mover's pieces wholly blocked, ordered with tempi first.

card.rule: Develop pieces by legal moves first, then by moves that clear blockers, and value positions by tempi and then by blocked pieces.
card.limits: The goal knows only opening deployment, so it has nothing to say once pieces are developed.

concepts.title: No-move: asking what if nothing is done
concepts.question: What is no-move, and why does it take the program beyond the basic space of legal moves?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: In situations with many alternatives, a quick way to put a floor under the value of a position is to ask what would happen if one side did nothing.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: NSS uses a no-move to curtail its search. It assumes that a no-move increases by exactly one tempo the value of a move for the player who makes it.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In using no-move, the program takes a first timid step to extend the problem space beyond the basic space of legal moves. The authors had said earlier that programs work in the basic space, occasionally augmented by abstract moves such as no-move.

card.rule: Ask what if I (or he) did nothing, and treat that as a move worth exactly one tempo, to put a minimum on a position's value.
card.limits: No-move is not a legal chess move; it is an abstract move added to the legal ones, so it leaves the basic space.

concepts.title: Strong where it has goals, blind where it has none
concepts.question: How do the NSS games link the program's strong and blind play to its set of goals?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Two kinds of experiment were run with NSS to see how it copes with the task: it played against several human players, and its play was compared with book games. Only three goals were available: material balance, center control and development.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Against one of the authors (HAS), then rated class A, the program played White and had rather the better of the first ten moves, until it ran out of things to do about development and center control. It had no goals for King safety, serious threats or pawn promotion.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In a game against a weak player, the absence of any goal about attacks on the King made it miss an obvious, devastating double check on move 14, after which its position deteriorated. The authors relate the erratic play directly to the presence and absence of specific goals: strong when the goals fit, blind when they do not.

card.rule: NSS plays strongly when the considerations on the board match its goals and is blind when the relevant goal is missing.
card.limits: Blindness from missing goals is a feature of this three-goal version; a program with more goals would be blind in different places.

concepts.title: Tracing NSS through recorded games
concepts.question: How did the authors trace NSS's reasoning, and why did the trace reject 2.P-Q4 after 1.P-K4 P-K4?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: To understand better how a system like NSS responds to its task environment, the authors studied its choice of moves in particular situations, taken from several games recorded in standard chess books.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: NSS was assigned the role of one of the players. Each of its moves was compared with the actual move in the recorded game. A trace printed all the continuations NSS examined, from which the working of the move generators and evaluations could be reconstructed.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In the example, after 1.P-K4 P-K4, the center-control generator proposes P-Q4 and material-balance proposes nothing. Black replies PxP, then White recaptures with the Queen, which is dead for material. Development finds the Queen exposed and generates N-QB3, a move that attacks it and adds a tempo. White's Queen must move, losing a tempo, so development rejects 2.P-Q4.

card.rule: Comparing each program move with the book move, and reading the trace, shows which generator proposed it and which goal rejected it.
card.limits: The trace shows reasons within the program's goals; it cannot show reasons the program has no goal to see.

concepts.title: How selective NSS was in the Morphy game
concepts.question: How few moves and positions did NSS examine in the Morphy game, compared with the other programs?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors had NSS play the role of Black, the Duke of Brunswick and Count Isouard, in Paul Morphy's seventeen-move game against them. They count how much NSS examined at each of Black's moves, and compare.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: On average NSS considered only three alternative moves in each position, out of close to thirty legal ones, about 10 percent. Only on the third and seventh moves did it consider more than three. In ten of the sixteen positions it accepted the first move it considered.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The average number of positions was 13, a little over four for each move considered. Bernstein's program investigates seven moves and about 2500 positions, and the Los Alamos program 30-odd moves and about 800,000. So NSS is more selective by a factor of about 200 over Bernstein's and about 60,000 over Los Alamos.

card.rule: In the Morphy game NSS looked at about three of thirty moves and thirteen positions, far less than Bernstein's or the Los Alamos program.
card.limits: The averages come from one game; the authors use them as an indication of selectivity, not a measure of playing strength.

concepts.title: What the situation requires, as the players saw it
concepts.question: What does agreement between NSS and the human players show about the requirements of a position?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: NSS agreed with the Duke and Count in more than half of the positions. The authors ask what this shows about how much a chess position dictates the move.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The agreement is strong evidence of the limits that the requirements of the situation place on choice. But the term requirements must be read with care: the players met the requirements only as they perceived them.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: If the players had perceived the real requirements, presumably they would not have lost the game in seventeen moves.

card.rule: Agreement between program and players shows how tightly the position limits choice, but only as the players perceived it.
card.limits: Perceived requirements may differ from real ones, as the players' loss in seventeen moves shows.

concepts.title: The problematic position after 3.P-Q4
concepts.question: What does the position after 3.P-Q4 show about how requirements are known, and how NSS erred?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: In the position after 3.P-Q4 in the Morphy game, the Duke and Count played B-N5. Sergeant's comment calls it following the bad example of Harrwitz, and in another place says the move is universally condemned by the analysts.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The authors read this comment as saying that historical experience among strong players has shown the move leads to bad consequences. It does not say that the weakness can be found by analysis in over-the-board play. Harrwitz lost after 59 moves, and Emanuel Lasker lost with the same move as late as 1889.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: So here the requirements of the situation do not reveal themselves easily or clearly. NSS examined ten moves and 43 positions, evidently finding it problematic too. It rejected B-KN5 because its analysis erroneously saw the loss of a pawn.

card.rule: A move can be condemned by historical experience though its weakness is not found by over-the-board analysis, and NSS also misjudged it.
card.limits: This is one position; it illustrates that requirements may be hidden, not that they usually are.

concepts.title: The Botvinnik-Kmoch opening, and what search is for
concepts.question: What do the Botvinnik-Kmoch results show about the first-acceptable-move criterion, and what is search for?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Table 11.6 gives the first ten moves of a game between Botvinnik, a former world champion, and Kmoch, a grandmaster. Only the beginning is considered because NSS has no middle-game goals. NSS played Black, with its three goals.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Using the criterion of the first satisfactory move, NSS considered an average of only two moves and 10.1 positions. At three moves (3, 5 and 10) it chose the same move as Kmoch, and at two others (1 and 6) a standard book move. At the other five it did not consider Kmoch's move or an opening-book move.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors attribute this partly to the trigger-happy choice criterion. At all those moves except 1, 6 and 9, it later gave the move imposed on it a value at least as high as its own choice. So its choice was sensitive to the order of move generation.

card.rule: With a first-acceptable criterion, NSS often settled on a move that merely satisfied it, so its choice depended on the order of generation.
card.limits: The sample is ten opening moves in one game, so it shows a tendency of the criterion, not a rate.

concepts.title: The Kotok program: one generator and tapered widths
concepts.question: How does the Kotok program generate moves, and how does it limit its search?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Around 1960 a group of students at MIT, under the aegis of John McCarthy, produced the Kotok or MIT chess program. A variant of it recently played a four-game correspondence match against USSR programs and did not fare well.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: It differs from the earlier programs in two respects. First, one generator serves both base moves and analysis moves: it makes each legal move, computes the static value of the result, and then yields the moves in order of that value. So no independent information goes into generating moves, though every move gets considered for inclusion.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Second, it adopts a fixed set of width limits, as Bernstein's program did, but tapered to give deeper penetration: typical widths for depths 1 to 8 are 4, 3, 2, 2, 1, 1, 1, 1. Its static value is a sum of many factors, with material balance calculated by an exchange analysis like the NSS program's.

card.rule: The Kotok program sorts all legal moves by static value, then searches few of them, fewer at each greater depth, with alpha-beta.
card.limits: Width settings are typical values that can be changed for any play; the schedule shown is only one example.

concepts.title: How strong the Greenblatt program was
concepts.question: What does the Greenblatt program's tournament record say about its playing strength?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A program built by Richard Greenblatt and associates at MIT gives the authors their first really accurate information about playing strength in relation to human players.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The program competed in at least two tournaments with rated players, so a rating could be given: provisionally 1239, class D. The authors' comments refer to its performance in the winter of 1966-67.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In the first tournament it drew with a player rated 1365 (class D) and lost four other games. In the second it defeated a player rated 1505 (class C) and lost four other games.

card.rule: In 1966-67 the Greenblatt program, provisionally rated class D, gave the authors their first accurate measure of a program against human players.
card.limits: The rating rests on a few tournament games and on one version of the program.

concepts.title: A won game, and the book moves
concepts.question: What does the Greenblatt program's won game show, and why do its book moves matter?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors give the program's tournament game with the class C player it defeated (Table 11.8) and ask what the game shows about how its play was organized.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: In the first nine moves the program concerns itself systematically and vigorously with center control and development. Its third move loses a tempo but is not amateurish, since the first three moves of both players are identical with a game between Mieses and Tarrasch in 1920. Black loses time with premature pawn moves, and by move 9 White has a distinct advantage in development.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Black blunders on move 11, and on move 14 falls into a trap that loses his Queen. The game is finished by an elegant checkmate beginning with a Queen sacrifice on move 20. White's early success is not unrelated to its ignoring its own King safety after Black's move 11.

card.rule: The won game shows the program playing the classical aims of the opening vigorously and winning after the opponent's blunders.
card.limits: One game against a class C player shows the program's style, not its general strength.

concepts.title: Plausibility, widths and extended depth
concepts.question: How does the Greenblatt program choose which moves to search and how deeply?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Like the Kotok program, the Greenblatt program generates moves by making all legal moves in a subsidiary pass, computing a plausibility score for each, and ordering the moves for actual consideration on that basis. Unlike the Kotok program, its plausibility value is entirely separate from its static value.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The plausibility value mainly reflects material and development, both combined in a system of weights on squares, and scores a move by how it changes the coverage of weighted squares. The program also shapes the search by making width-termination depend on depth, but the width is only a base value that several things can increase.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Depth-termination works the same way: a basic depth, extended for additional reasons such as plausible captures and forced defenses. In this the program moves some distance toward the structure of the NSS program, in which many separate kinds of reasons keep the search going.

card.rule: Order moves by a plausibility score separate from the static value, set a base width by depth, and extend width and depth for special reasons.
card.limits: The base widths are tournament settings; smaller values were used in casual play.

concepts.title: Secondary search along the principal variation
concepts.question: What is the Greenblatt program's secondary search, and what did its search statistics show?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: With every other chess program, search was a single sweep, shaped and limited by whatever heuristics were available. The one-level presearch for plausible moves was the first, small, change to this uniform pattern.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The Greenblatt program adds a secondary search. When a new alternative at depth one is found to be better than the reigning one, the program travels back out to the boundary of the previous search along the principal variation, the path that produced the minimax value of the new move. Then it pushes the search a couple of plies further and assigns the resulting value to the alternative.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors call this a substantially greater change than the presearch. They count it, with the goal organization of NSS, as one of two variations that are harbingers more than well-explored features, and note that it begins to relieve the program of considering any position only once.

card.rule: A newly best move is searched a couple of plies deeper along its principal variation before its value is accepted.
card.limits: It appears in a single program and is a harbinger rather than a well-explored feature.

concepts.title: What all six programs have in common
concepts.question: What do all six programs share, and what do they not do?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors have examined six chess programs and now step back to ask what they have in common.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: They are all very much of one type: forward search through a subtree of the tree of legal moves, selection heuristics, static evaluations and minimaxing. One more feature is common to them all: they choose moves in a chess position rather than play a game of chess.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The game is put together as a series of essentially independent choices of a move. So a program can easily be made to follow a book game by forcing it to play the book move, even when this differs from its own. This would not be possible in general if each move were based on a plan of play for the whole game.

card.rule: All six programs are forward searchers that choose a move at a time, with no plan carried from one move to the next.
card.limits: The summary concerns the six programs examined, not every possible way of playing chess.

concepts.title: How much each program searches, and why NSS searches so little
concepts.question: How do the programs rank by amount of search, and what limits the NSS search?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Despite the common features, the programs differ in important ways. One is the amount of search they carry out.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The Los Alamos program explores by far the largest game tree, Bernstein's the next largest, and the Greenblatt program a smaller one. The NSS and Turing programs explore very small trees indeed.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In NSS the severe limits stem from two things: the sharp distinction between generating moves and generating continuations, as in Turing's program, and the satisficing heuristic that accepts the first move meeting prior expectations.

card.rule: Search runs from the huge Los Alamos tree down to the very small NSS and Turing trees, and NSS is limited by its two-generator design and satisficing.
card.limits: The comparison is of the amount of search; it says nothing alone about the quality of the moves chosen.

concepts.title: Many generators or one
concepts.question: How do the programs differ in generating moves, and what concern does each approach express?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Another important variation among the programs is in how moves are generated. The authors set out two designs.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The Bernstein program and, more extensively, the NSS program have many separate move generators, each corresponding to a function to be served.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The Kotok program and the Greenblatt program have instead a single move generator that generates all the legal moves and orders them by an evaluation function.

card.rule: Bernstein and NSS use many function-specific generators; Kotok and Greenblatt use one generator that orders all legal moves by an evaluation.
card.limits: Both designs are choices within the common scheme; neither is shown to be better.

concepts.title: Where a program's chess information comes from
concepts.question: From what sources can a chess program obtain the information it needs, and how does NSS use means-ends knowledge?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Intelligent behavior in a task as complex as chess needs information, and the authors ask where it can come from. One source is actual exploration of the specific game position. This is, apart from the chess knowledge implicit in the static evaluation, the sole source for the Los Alamos program.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: A second source is chess theory applied to the actual position, where theory has its usual meaning of general rules or principles. The NSS move generators detect features of the position, such as a man under attack, and find legal moves relevant to those features. The features are tied to goals, such as gain of material or center control, which are important to the final goal of checkmate.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The relation of moves to features is one of means to ends. A feature shows a possibility of gain, such as an enemy piece under attack, or of loss, such as one's own piece under attack; moves are means to gain it (capturing) or avert the loss (interposing). This builds a bridge from the present situation to possible actions, instead of testing many actions systematically or at random in the hope that some prove relevant.

card.rule: A program can get information by exploring the position or from chess theory; NSS uses theory as means-ends knowledge linking features to relevant moves.
card.limits: The authors count this knowledge as the main organization of known generalizations about chess, not as everything a master knows.

concepts.title: Why first-acceptable can still give sensible moves
concepts.question: Why does NSS's first-acceptable-move rule produce sensible moves as often as it does?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The first-acceptable-move rule might be expected to give poor moves. The authors say it produces sensible moves as often as it does for a principal reason, tied to a general fact about chess and everyday life.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The amount of action that can be accomplished in a given time is limited, in chess as in real life. It is not important, or even relevant, to consider all the things it might be nice to do.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: There are three parts to the reason: the move is always proposed for a reason, since it is relevant to a goal in the light of specific features of the position; the most pressing problems and important considerations are taken up first; and a single move exhausts the program's capacity for action, so there is no point in dealing with the less important features.

card.rule: The first acceptable move is usually sensible because it is proposed for a reason, the pressing matters come first, and one move can answer only so much.
card.limits: The rule works when the program's goals include the pressing matters; when a goal is missing the move can be blind.

concepts.title: Concepts must emerge before search can succeed
concepts.question: Why do the authors say appropriate concepts matter more than a fast system for a task like chess?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: In a task environment as complex as chess, part of the success of play depends on fitting behavior to the objective requirements of the situation. The authors ask what such fitting needs.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: It depends on the emergence of appropriate concepts. Without them it will be impossible for a system, even a very fast one, to explore sufficiently to discover strong moves and to make reliable evaluations.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Chess history can be written largely in terms of the gradual emergence of a few central concepts, which were slowly arrived at by players and not by computation alone.

card.rule: In a complex task, success depends on a few central concepts having emerged, which speed alone cannot supply.
card.limits: This is the authors' view of what chess requires, argued from chess history and from NSS, not proved.

concepts.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
concepts.title: Chess is a deep task: what might fit a human
concepts.question: Which features of chess programs might fit a human player, and which cannot?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The previous chapter described chess programs: the basic problem space, a search for consequences, and logic to combine the results. Within those bounds a problem solver can be organized in many ways. Which of those organizations could a person actually use?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: According to the authors, a human lacks the speed, memory or precision of organization to examine 800,000 moves while taking a speck of information from each. Extreme organizations only give a background against which intelligence can be detected. Heuristic organizations may well fit: plausible move generators, evaluation functions, and rough-cut search followed by fine-cut search.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: No experiment is offered yet. The judgment rests on the earlier survey of chess programs set beside what a person can do; the test comes in the next step, a look at real human chess behavior.

card.rule: A human cannot comb through hundreds of thousands of moves, but plausible-move generation, evaluation and rough-then-fine search may fit him.
card.limits: The authors say these heuristic organizations 'may well fit'; at this point it is a hypothesis to be tested on a human protocol, not a finding.

concepts.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
concepts.title: The questions asked of one subject
concepts.question: What do the authors hope to learn by studying one subject choosing one move?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
