blocks.text: After a task analysis, the authors want to see what human chess behavior actually looks like. They ask the same fundamental questions as for the other tasks.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Can the human be viewed as an information processing system (IPS), and can that IPS be described in enough detail to make the view scientifically plausible? What part of the human's program is dictated by basic aspects of the task, and what part by features more properly psychological? What new mechanisms for reasoning or processing information are used in chess?

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: As before, they begin with one situation in detail: a single subject choosing a move in a given position. The evidence is therefore a single recorded analysis, studied closely.

card.rule: Study one subject on one position in detail, and ask whether he can be seen as an IPS, what the task dictates and what new mechanisms appear.
card.limits: A single position covers only part of chess, so conclusions from it are first steps, not a full theory.

concepts.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
concepts.title: Subject S2 and the talk-aloud setup
concepts.question: Who is S2, and under what conditions did he choose a move?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The data are a protocol from a study by de Groot (1965). A subject sees a middle-game position (position A) and is asked to choose White's next move.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: He may take as long as he wants, which in practice means a thorough analysis within the limits of normal over-the-board play. He is asked to talk aloud while analysing, and the talk is recorded on tape. The recorded talk is the data.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: S2 is a chess player of modest ability, active in a college chess club when the protocol was taken. He was by no means an expert or class A player. His play is undoubtedly better than the programs of the last chapter, with one exception noted later.

card.rule: The data are one modest club player's tape-recorded talk-aloud analysis of a position, with no time limit.
card.limits: S2 is not an expert, so the protocol shows how a modest player works, not how a master does.

concepts.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
concepts.title: Position A and de Groot's verdict
concepts.question: What problem does position A pose for White, and what did de Groot find?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Position A is a middle-game position from a game de Groot played in 1936, White to move. It mainly poses tactical problems. Black's last move left his Bishop on K2 in a hanging position, defended only by an exchangeable Knight on Q4, which ties down the Black Knight on B3.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The question is whether White can make profitable use of these tactical weaknesses. If not, White should strengthen his position with a calm move. Many exchanges are possible in the center.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: De Groot's thorough analysis finds that White can get the better of it, and that there is even a forced win. The winning move is 1. B x N/5.

card.rule: In position A, White asks whether Black's hanging Bishop can be exploited; de Groot's analysis says yes, by 1. B x N/5.
card.limits: The verdict comes from de Groot's analysis of this one position; it is the reference against which S2's analysis is read.

concepts.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
concepts.title: Reading the protocol: notation and gross features
concepts.question: How is the protocol coded, and what do its gross features show?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The protocol (Appendix 12.1) is segmented into short phrases and labeled like other protocols. Beside each phrase, where appropriate, the authors write the chess move or relation it gives, so that the information in the protocol can be scanned.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Notation is largely standard, with one departure: a prime marks Black. B x N'/5 means the White Bishop takes the Black Knight on the fifth rank, to distinguish it from B x N'/6. A prime is needed because men and moves are often named without context that fixes the side. Chess content is noted only where it is clear.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: S2 worked almost 17 minutes and was easy to get talking. He averaged 115 words per minute (low 90, high 145). His talk is task-oriented and free of stumbles and breaks.

card.rule: Code only the chess content that is clear in each phrase, and read the protocol's length and fluency as simple facts about the subject's behavior.
card.limits: Where a phrase has no single precise meaning, the authors leave it without notation rather than guess.

concepts.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
concepts.title: Episodes and scenes
concepts.question: How is S2's behavior divided into episodes and scenes?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: S2's seventeen minutes need structure. The authors find that his behavior falls naturally into a series of episodes, with relatively abrupt discontinuities of attention marking the boundaries.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Figure 12.2 lists 25 episodes, E1 to E25. Because 25 are too many for a reader to hold in mind, they are grouped into seven scenes. A scene is a set of explorations that seem to be under a common aim; occasionally an interruption within a scene is not devoted to the scene's main concern.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors present the whole as a drama in which the subject struggles to discover which things in the situation are good and which are dangerous. The subject did not have to remember the episodes; he only had to live them.

card.rule: Episodes are stretches of attention bounded by abrupt shifts; seven scenes group the 25 episodes by a common aim.
card.limits: Scenes are an aid for the reader, drawn by the authors; the episodes are the units of the subject's own behavior.

concepts.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
concepts.title: The seven scenes as a story
concepts.question: In what order did S2's seven scenes unfold, and what did each achieve?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Figure 12.2 lets us follow S2 from first look to final choice. How does he get from an orientation to a decision, and what does each scene add?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Scene 1 takes stock of material and threats. Scene 2 (80 s) explores 1. B x N'/5 down the exchange. Scene 3 (300 s) searches widely for other moves and finds nothing. Scene 4 (385 s) re-examines the exchange and concludes it is worth nothing for White. Scene 5 tries a mating idea and ends by favoring 1. B x N'/5.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Scene 6 (735 s) returns to the exchange and reviews Black's replies; every reply leads to complications. Scene 7 (980 s) decides on B x N' and gives the next move conditional on Black's reply. The summaries are the subject's own statements at episode ends.

card.rule: S2 explored his first candidate, searched widely, doubted it, tried something else, returned to it, and then decided on it.
card.limits: The scene titles and times are the authors' reading of the protocol, and the same candidate is chosen at the end that was first explored.

concepts.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
concepts.title: Considered moves and perceived relations
concepts.question: How do the authors tell a considered move from a perceived relation in a protocol?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: S2's protocol mentions both moves and relations on the board. To study his search, the authors must decide, for each remark, whether he considers a move or perceives a static relation.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: B22, 'The Bishop at Rook 2 can take the Knight', followed by what would answer it, shows a move being considered. B5, 'his Queen is threatening my Knight's pawn', states a relation: Q' x NP is possible, but this does not mean it has been considered. P x N and Q-QB3 are considered moves; attack and pin are relations.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The distinction rests on the information system that processes the board, not on the board's features. All future implications of an exploration are contained in the present position, like a system of axioms. Any could in principle be staticized as a perceived relation, such as potential-forking-square. In practice, the authors find the distinction easy to make in this protocol.

card.rule: Tag each remark as a considered move or a perceived relation according to what the solver is processing, not what is on the board.
card.limits: The labels depend on the authors' judgment of what S2 means; the same board fact could be a relation for one solver and a search result for another.

concepts.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
concepts.title: The exploration tree of Figure 12.3
concepts.question: What does the tree of all positions S2 considered show, and what does it leave out?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: What did S2's search actually cover? Putting together all the moves he considered gives the exploration tree of Figure 12.3, one branch per move considered.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The tree holds 64 positions, including the current one. Every node is mentioned explicitly by S2 except four, which are inferred. Dotted lines mark cases where it is inferred that he did not propose a move, and nonspecific moves such as Q-move mean he was no more specific. Averaged over the session, he examines about one new position every fifteen seconds.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors could have found a badly discontinuous tree, with branches missing because S2 was silent while traversing them. In fact, the nodes are all stated or inferred, so the tree is continuous. It does not, however, reveal how the tree was generated.

card.rule: The exploration tree is the set of positions S2 considered, built mostly from what he said; it shows coverage, not order.
card.limits: A tree loses the time order of the search: it cannot show which branch was explored first or how often he returned.

concepts.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
concepts.title: The PBG: deep, narrow, and back to the base
concepts.question: What pattern does S2's problem behavior graph show, and how does it define episodes?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The tree does not show how it was generated. The Problem Behavior Graph (PBG) of Figure 12.4 shows S2's search in the time order in which it was performed.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The pattern is distinctive: S2 searches deeply with little or no branching, and at the end of each search returns to the current position and starts over. He often reconsiders an initial move already analyzed: among 23 starts there are only eight distinct initial moves.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: All the moves are explicitly mentioned, apart from inferred ones, so the return to the start is direct evidence. The almost uniform return to the base position after each burst of exploration lets the authors segment the problem into 25 episodes. Boundaries are also marked by evaluative statements and proposals for what next, so there is little doubt the episodes are real.

card.rule: S2 searches deep and narrow, returns to the position on the board after each burst, and starts again; the returns mark the episodes.
card.limits: A few later episodes do not return all the way to the start; the pattern is almost uniform, not absolute.

concepts.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
concepts.title: Sufficient, not necessary: what a hypothesized strategy shows
concepts.question: What can the authors show about a hypothesized search organization, and what can they not?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: For computer chess programs, the authors could study the internal structure of existing programs. For S2 they must hypothesize mechanisms and ask what behavior would follow.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: At best, they can show that the hypothesized organization is sufficient to reproduce the subject's observed behavior. They cannot show it is necessary. A search strategy tells where to go next and what information must be kept for the search to be carried out; it does not say what else to gather at positions or what to do with it.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Our reading: this is the usual limit on arguing from a match to a mechanism. The authors proceed by proposing strategies and comparing the graphs they would predict with the PBG of Figure 12.4.

card.rule: Reproducing observed behavior shows a hypothesized organization is sufficient, not that it is the only one that could produce it.
card.limits: Sufficiency is still informative; it narrows the field when rival organizations fail to match the behavior.

concepts.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
concepts.title: Depth-first search
concepts.question: What is depth-first search, and why do chess programs use it?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Which search strategy do computer chess programs use, and does S2's behavior look like it?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The typical strategy is depth-first. Once a position has been generated, all deeper search beyond it is carried out before that part of the tree is abandoned. It is highly efficient for memory, since only a single line of positions from the position on the board up to the one being considered need be kept.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The strategy follows directly from the prototypic chess program of Figure 11.2. It suits minimaxing, which derives the value of a dynamic position from the values of all positions one level deeper: depth-first makes those values available one after another with minimum memory and retrieval effort.

card.rule: Depth-first search finishes everything below a position before leaving it; it needs little memory and fits minimaxing.
card.limits: Efficiency is for the program; the authors go on to test whether S2's search actually looks depth-first.

concepts.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
concepts.title: Breadth-first search
concepts.question: How does breadth-first search differ from depth-first, and what does it cost?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The alternative to depth-first search is the breadth-first strategy of Figure 12.5, used by the Logic Theorist (LT).

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Instead of going deeper and deeper, breadth-first search completes all positions at one level before going on to the next. New positions go at the end of a position-list and the first one is removed to be worked on. All positions must therefore be stored until they are considered.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Figure 12.6 shows how the search of Figure 12.3 would look as a PBG if breadth-first: highly discontinuous. The gap between the node being worked on and the node being generated gives the size of the position-list, which reaches a maximum of ten in the middle of the search.

card.rule: Breadth-first search finishes a whole level before the next, at the price of storing every unexamined position.
card.limits: Its storage cost and awkward minimaxing are why game-playing programs avoid it; it has other uses.

concepts.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
concepts.title: Simple progressive deepening
concepts.question: How does simple progressive deepening search, and why might it suit a person?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors ask what strategy could have produced S2's PBG. Neither depth-first nor breadth-first will do.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Simple-progressive-deepening search has two parts: one generates base-moves and one analyses each. The analysis is a simple loop, not a recursion, selecting only one move at each current position. A summary is kept with each base-move so that repeated analyses of it can differ. The expected behavior is a sequence of linear searches without any branching.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Figure 12.7 gives the program. The authors say it by no means describes Figure 12.4 exactly, but it is surely a closer approximation than either depth-first or breadth-first.

card.rule: Pick a base-move, follow one move at a time down a line, return to base, and use the kept summary to vary the next visit.
card.limits: It cannot produce the branching tufts that S2 sometimes shows, which is why the authors refine it.

concepts.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
concepts.title: Progressive deepening: a trunk with tufts
concepts.question: How does progressive deepening differ from the simple version, and what tree does it produce?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: S2's PBG sometimes branches at a position, so choosing a single move per position is too simple. A slight modification brings the strategy one step closer to what S2 did.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: In Figure 12.8 the base-move process stays the same. In the analysis, selecting one analysis-move is replaced by generating a set of analysis-moves, giving each a plausibility value, ordering them on the list, and considering each before one is selected for continuation.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Each exploration starts from the base position, but its tree resembles a skinny Christmas tree: a main trunk, with a tuft at each node of several branches, each one move deep. The term progressive deepening is taken from de Groot (1965), who introduced it for the tendency to extend analysis successively.

card.rule: Progressive deepening generates and ranks a set of moves at each node, tries each one move deep, and continues down one of them.
card.limits: The tuft is only one move deep; the strategy does not branch widely at every level.

concepts.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
concepts.title: How well progressive deepening fits S2
concepts.question: How well does progressive deepening match S2's PBG, and where does it fail?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Does the progressive-deepening strategy describe S2's PBG? The authors judge it by two features of the search: the return to the base position, and single-level tufts at each node.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Of the fifteen instances of multiple branching in Figure 12.4, eleven are exactly of the tuft form. The contrary examples are in E2, E18, E24 and E25. E2 is ambiguous: S2 refers to an exchange of Rooks (B28), which could be two moves or a single conceptual act.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors give each contrary case its own reading. In terms of the two features, return to base and single-level tufts, they conclude the strategy seems a plausible description of the PBG.

card.rule: Eleven of fifteen branchings are tufts, and the four exceptions are explicable, so progressive deepening is a plausible description.
card.limits: Plausible is the authors' word; it is a sufficiency claim from one protocol, with exceptions explained rather than eliminated.

concepts.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
concepts.title: What each episode is for: explore and rework
concepts.question: How do the authors establish each episode's function, and what do explore and rework mean?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Under progressive deepening, episode generation and move generation inside an episode are interwoven: the moves generated depend on the current position and on the state of the base-move being explored. The authors first treat episodes as wholes, the context for move generation.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: S2 makes explicit statements about each episode's function, so the function need not be inferred from the move pattern alone. The authors accept the naive hypothesis that episodes function as he indicates. Table 12.1 gives each episode's function and its result, positive or negative for White. Explore means to go down a new path; rework means to go down the specified path again, for whatever reason.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The comments make good chess sense and good problem solving sense, and are consistent with the subject's behavior throughout the episode.

card.rule: Take the subject's stated purpose for each episode as its function, and label episodes as explore (new path) or rework (path again).
card.limits: Accepting the subject's own account is a hypothesis the authors choose, checked against his behavior, not a proof.

concepts.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
concepts.title: R1: each base-move analysed on its own
concepts.question: What does rule R1 say, and how do the authors defend it?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Each episode is unique in the context of earlier ones, yet the authors write six rules that would generate a sequence of episodes not unlike Table 12.1. The rules cover which base-move is chosen next and what governs later episodes of the same base-move, but not behavior inside an episode.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: R1: the analysis of each base-move is independent of the analysis of other base-moves, except that it can be interrupted by other activity. Each episode in the analysis of a base-move is determined only by the results of prior episodes of that base-move.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: R1 says the total analysis factors into little analyses, one per base-move. Their only interaction is in the allocation of effort, including abandoning a base-move because others proved better. The authors find it difficult to refute: a refutation would need features within an episode that came from sources other than the base-move's earlier episodes.

card.rule: Analyse each base-move as its own small problem, linked to the others only by how effort is shared out.
card.limits: Independence is a rule about content, not effort: which move gets time still depends on how the others fared.

concepts.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
concepts.title: R2: from normal to unusual responses
concepts.question: What does R2 say about the order of episodes on one base-move?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: What decides which continuation S2 tries in each successive episode of the same base-move?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: R2: the first episode of a base-move uses normal moves, and later episodes use increasingly unusual moves. Take the responses to an attack in this order: defend; counterattack threatening equivalent material; counterattack threatening less material; move and ignore the attack. Defending the man attacked is the normal response. The others are more unusual, though they may be correct.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Table 12.1 shows very consistent conformity. Taking the sequence explore, extend, counterattack, counterattack with loss, recapture with loss as normal to unusual, each rework episode should lie further down than its predecessor, and the explore episodes should use only normal moves.

card.rule: On repeated visits to a base-move, move down the list from the usual reply to rarer and rarer ones.
card.limits: Normal and unusual belong to the subject's classification; they do not say which reply is best.

concepts.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
concepts.title: R3: stay with a winner, switch off a loser
concepts.question: When does S2 change base-moves, and what does the tally of cases show?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: When should the analysis of one base-move be dropped for another?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: R3: if the evaluation of an episode is favorable, analysis of its base-move continues; if unfavorable, a different base-move is analysed. In short: stay with a winner, switch off a loser. A single disconfirmation of the soundness of the move is enough to cause the switch.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Of the 21 cases in Table 12.1 relevant to R3, 16 are confirmatory. Three cases (E3, E6, E14) show other rules (R5 and R6) taking priority and so shed no light on R3. Two are negative instances: E18 and E20.

card.rule: Keep working a base-move while episodes go well; one bad result is enough to switch.
card.limits: R3 is silent on which base-move to pick next and how; this one protocol says little about that.

concepts.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
concepts.title: R4: biasing the search to test a possibility
concepts.question: What is R4, and how can an opponent's choices be biased without making the test useless?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: To find out whether any successful continuation exists for a base-move, S2 sometimes changes the search rules to obtain special information.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: R4: when exploring, moves for the opponent may be considered that are favorable to self, in order to place an upper bound on the possibilities. By biasing the choices in favor of White, S2 sees whether there is any possibility of a successful continuation.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: If a biased exploration succeeded, extra episodes to correct the bias would be expected, but the protocol offers no good chance to test this. The bias raises a problem: how to bias the opponent's choices without opening the floodgates of foolishness, which would give no useful information at all.

card.rule: When testing whether any success is possible, let the opponent reply favorably to you, as an upper bound, but not foolishly.
card.limits: Few cases bear on R4 and the rule gives no test for when to apply it, so negative instances cannot occur.

concepts.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
concepts.title: Means-ends analysis in E15, E16 and E18
concepts.question: How does S2 use a specific envisioned future situation to guide his search?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Most episodes work forward, exploring the consequences of base-moves, as computer chess programs do. In E15, E16 and E18, S2 uses a basically different approach.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: In E15 he envisions a future situation, the mating configuration with his Bishop at R6 and Queen at N7, and seeks moves leading to it. This reveals a difficulty, the Black Bishop on K2. E16 sets the goal of removing it, and E16 and E18 pursue that goal. The search still works forward, but with a definite end in view. This is means-ends analysis, familiar from GPS.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: It needs a future situation specified in enough detail that differences between present and desired state can be found. Wanting a checkmate position permits no specific inferences, whereas wanting the Bishop on R6 and Queen on N7 defines a specific desired state.

card.rule: Envision a detailed target, find the differences from now, and search for moves that remove them.
card.limits: Without a detailed target, such as a bare wish for checkmate, there are no differences to work on.

concepts.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
concepts.title: R5: moves discovered and tried next
concepts.question: What does R5 say about moves discovered during an exploration?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: An exploration can discover new moves worth trying as well as new facts about its base-move.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: R5: the analysis of a base-move is interrupted to pursue other moves, discovered during the episode, that seem to have merit either for self or for the opponent. It is a special form of the notion that moves can be considered independently of positions, and it adds interruption: exploring the new move next.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: All four relevant cases are positive. E3 is completely explicit: Q-KB3, discovered in E2, is explored next. In E14, S2 finds in E13 that N' can recapture and tries it elsewhere in the exchange. E17 returns to E16 afterwards. E19 returns to an old move, B x N'/5, last seen in E18.

card.rule: Try a promising move discovered in one place at the next opportunity, even if it interrupts the current analysis.
card.limits: The rule is plausible but little used in chess programs; its four positive cases come from one protocol.

concepts.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
concepts.title: R6: looking around when things go well
concepts.question: What does R6 say, and what do the six rules leave undecided?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: What does S2 do when an analysis goes well? Rules R1 to R5 concern staying, switching, bias and interruption.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: R6: before a base-move is finally chosen, a check is made for other alternative base-moves. It is the heuristic for looking around when things go well.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: There is only one positive instance, the wide search of E6 to E10 after the good result of E5, but it is clear and important. E25 is labeled a negative instance, since insistent use of R6 would require one final survey of the whole position before committing. The protocol does not show why R6 was evoked after E5 rather than earlier or later.

card.rule: When a line looks good, look around for other base-moves before committing.
card.limits: R6 rests on one clear instance, and the six rules together are incomplete.

concepts.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
concepts.title: Where move generation happens: new and repeated positions
concepts.question: In how many positions is a move generated, and how do new and repeated positions differ?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: To model move generation inside episodes, the authors consider only the positions in Figure 12.4 where it takes place.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: They exclude the base position, all terminal positions, all of E19 (the summary) and E25 (the recapitulation), and three apparent branchings where S2 does not return all the way to the base. That leaves 74 positions: 53 where new moves are generated and 21 where moves already made are repeated.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: At repeat positions the issue is whether to start a variation here. In 20 of the 21, only the repeated move is generated. The lone exception is in E4, where S2 recalls the Rook exchange of E2 (B50) without considering it seriously. No position poses a choice between new and old moves.

card.rule: Of 74 move-generation positions, 53 call for new moves and 21 repeat old ones, mostly with only the repeated move.
card.limits: The counts come from the authors' reading of one protocol and exclude summaries and terminal positions by choice.

concepts.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
concepts.title: Single moves and tufts
concepts.question: How many moves does S2 generate at a new position, and what patterns do the tufts show?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: At the 53 positions with new moves, how many alternatives does S2 generate?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Almost always only a single move is generated (43 positions), occasionally two (9), and once three (1). The 10 positions with multiple alternatives are called tufts.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Of the 10 tufts, 7 are Black positions and 3 White; among single-move positions, 18 are Black and 25 White. So S2 may treat himself (White) differently from his opponent (Black).

card.rule: One move per new position is the rule; the few tufts fall mostly on Black's side.
card.limits: Counts from one protocol suggest a pattern; the authors do not pursue these breakdowns.

concepts.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
concepts.title: Two ways to generate moves: all legal moves or by function
concepts.question: What two solutions exist for generating moves, and which does S2 appear to use?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Existing chess programs generate far larger sets of moves than S2 needs. Yet it is not easy to design a single integrated process that produces a modest collection of plausible moves, such as the eight S2 considers from the base position.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Chapter 11 described two solutions. The Kotok and Greenblatt programs generate all legal moves and pick the best by an evaluation function. The alternative is to develop specific generators, each devoted to a specific function, and use higher routines to select among them to build the set of moves considered at a position.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: A cursory look at S2's protocol shows much activity of the second sort. B46 says Black must recapture, which poses a function. B47 gives the only way to do it, pawn takes Knight, which generates the move that satisfies the function. With several ways to recapture, all would presumably be generated.

card.rule: S2's protocol suggests that he poses a function, such as recapture, and generates the moves that satisfy it.
card.limits: The evidence is a cursory reading of the protocol, not a full test.

concepts.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
concepts.title: From a situation to moves by a chain of functions
concepts.question: How do functions link a perceived situation to the moves that answer it?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: How does a recognized situation lead S2 to a set of candidate moves?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Suppose a piece Y is moved so that Y x Z becomes possible. We say Y attacks Z, which classifies the situation. From an attack we infer that a problem exists, and obtain defend Z as a class description of a solution.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Under defend sit more specific functions, such as capture-attacker and add-defender. At some point of elaboration there are ways of generating actual moves that accomplish them, for example all moves that capture the attacker.

card.rule: Classify the situation, infer the problem, name the class of solution, narrow to a specific function, then generate the moves.
card.limits: The chain is the authors' model of S2; each link is an assumption to be checked in the protocol.

concepts.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
concepts.title: One generator at a time, from public chess knowledge
concepts.question: What do the authors assume about which generator S2 evokes, and what guards against ad hoc generators?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Given functional generators, how does S2 use them, and how can the authors avoid inventing generators to fit the data?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: If S2 recognizes the situation, he generates the set of moves appropriate to that kind of situation, one move or more, and all serve the same function. Several generators may apply to one situation; they are ordered from normal to unusual, and only one is evoked on any occasion. This ordering is how R2 is carried out.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors treat the generators and their labels as public knowledge of the chess world, though tinged with the subject's own experience. The situations and generators must exist in common chess knowledge, which checks against creating ad hoc generators. For most cases in this protocol there is no difficulty of interpretation.

card.rule: Assume S2 recognizes a situation and evokes one generator from shared chess knowledge, in order from normal to unusual.
card.limits: Not every recognized situation need have an English name; the public-knowledge check is a requirement, not a proof.

concepts.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
concepts.title: Table 12.2: situation-response productions
concepts.question: How are the productions of Table 12.2 written, and what situations do they cover?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: What are S2's functional generators in concrete form? Table 12.2 lists situations and the responses they invoke.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The table has three groups: defensive situations, situations where the mover has the initiative, and information-gathering situations, whose responses suit analysis but not actual play. Each item has a mnemonic code with the situation left of the arrow and the response right. The first, x → r, means a capture occurred (x) and the response is to recapture (r). They are productions like those of Chapter 6.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The list is by no means complete: it holds only situations that actually occurred in the protocol. All the productions are extremely simple and well known in the chess literature. The information-gathering ones are seldom stated explicitly because they are part of everyday common sense.

card.rule: Each production pairs a recognized situation with a standard response, written as a code like x → r.
card.limits: The table shows only what this protocol evoked, so it is not the subject's whole repertoire.

concepts.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
concepts.title: Assessing the productions: the verdict and incomplete generation
concepts.question: How well do the productions account for S2's moves, and what is incomplete generation?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Figure 12.9 gives, for each new move, the code of the production that appears to govern it. Overall the account is reasonably good at 39 positions, and there is reason for dissatisfaction at 14. This tally obscures many ways the rules can fail.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: If a situation evokes a production, all the moves it generates should be considered. Positions where not all are marked i, for incomplete. Where S2 plainly believed he had generated them all, the authors blame a faulty application of the production, not the scheme. Seven cases remain, which seem genuine failures.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Four instances show S2 believing generation complete when it is not. In E2 he ignores N'xB, declaring N' pinned (it is not), and repeats this next move. Also in E2 he calls Q'-Q1 the only move defending both men, but two other Q' moves exist. In E17 he overlooks R'xN.

card.rule: Mark positions where the production's full set was not considered, and separate errors in applying a production from failures of the scheme.
card.limits: A tally of successes and failures hides cases where failures have explanations and successes are shaky.

concepts.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
concepts.title: More than one generator at a position?
concepts.question: How well does the one-generator-per-position idea hold up in the tufts?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: To explain the small number of alternatives at each position, the scheme posits that only one production is evoked. Single-move positions agree with this. The tufts could give counterexamples.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Two of the ten tufts show some evidence of multiple generators. The one-position-one-generator idea is somewhat ambiguous because functions form a hierarchy: defense can be realized by adding a defender or moving away, and the two may be functional equivalents for the subject.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In E2, 2...P'xN is a recapture (x → r) whereas 2...R'xR is a counterattack (x → c). At the end of E14 two perhaps equivalent defenses for the Bishop are considered, one of them the generalized B-retreat.

card.rule: Only two of ten tufts hint at more than one generator, and a hierarchy of functions softens even those.
card.limits: With so few tufts the evidence is thin either way.

concepts.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
concepts.title: Moves with two productions, and moves with none
concepts.question: What happens when two productions explain one move, or none does?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Sometimes more than one production can account for a single generated move; sometimes none can.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Multiple interpretation occurs in only two cases here. A move serving more than one function is important and well known in chess. Information processing suggests such a move is generated from one production and then recognized as meeting another's requirements; the production 2a → 2d builds in finding a double-function move. So ambiguity is no serious deficiency.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In E2, 3.Q-B3 can be generated by iP → a, reinforced in E22 (B202, B205), or by p → a, since S2 considers the double threat (B34, B35). In E5, 4.BxN' can add a defender to the N' in danger (a → d) or continue the original attack (c → g).

card.rule: A move can fit two productions when it serves two functions; this is expected and not a defect.
card.limits: Cases with no fitting production are different, and the authors treat them as gaps.

concepts.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
concepts.title: Plans and the assume-the-negation production
concepts.question: How does S2 generate moves while following a plan?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: In several situations S2 has a plan of action that implies a sequence of moves. The moves at eleven positions are accounted for by this plan production (g → g).

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: While implementing a plan, S2 operates in a very exploratory way. All the positions where the opponent's move is skipped, the no-move, occur at these times, and he almost never generates alternative moves. Some plans are so familiar they could be productions, such as doubling the Rooks in E9; others, such as the means-ends analysis of E15, are built for this situation.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Demonstrating a fact by assuming its negation and following out the consequences is used often enough to be a production (→ n). It generates a plan, since the next several moves are dictated by the attempt to elicit the consequences. The authors count six instances of planning, and given a plan, deriving the moves is easy.

card.rule: Once a plan exists, its moves follow with few alternatives; assuming the opposite of a claim sets up such a plan.
card.limits: Plans are often built for the case at hand, so they cannot all be reduced to stored productions.

concepts.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
concepts.title: The scheme in summary: recognition then response
concepts.question: What picture of move generation does the scheme give, and how firmly is it supported?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: After tabulating how well Table 12.2 accounts for S2's generated moves, what picture of move generation results, and how much weight can it bear?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Through prior experience with chess and its literature, S2 has a collection of fixed responses to specific classes of situations. Behavior directly follows recognition. Because only one generator is evoked and the position itself is specific, one or at most a few moves result. Most tufts being Black and defensive derives from the generators fitting this base position.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Figure 12.9 and the discussion show the scheme can account for an appreciable number of generations, but that detailed consideration of each instance is needed to make sense of the evidence.

card.rule: S2 recognizes a situation and applies a stored response, giving one or a few moves; support is real but must be argued case by case.
card.limits: Each instance must be argued on its own merits; a good fit does not show the response was stored rather than reasoned out.

concepts.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
concepts.title: Evaluation: one feature at a time
concepts.question: How does S2 evaluate positions when an episode ends, and how does that differ from program evaluation?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: What evaluation does S2 assign when an episode terminates? The fundamental logic of the game, maximizing for self and minimizing for the opponent, is used throughout.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: S2 acts as if permanent gain is unlikely from any position, so finding any permanent gain can end an episode. A gain a player holds while it is still his move is taken as permanent. So is a loss at his move with no immediate compensation, especially just after a capture with no recapture available.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The dominant characteristic is that evaluations involve a single feature, such as an isolated pawn. After each White-Black pair of moves, either the status quo holds and search continues, or an advantage exists and it ends. There is no balancing of a pro from one feature against a con from another, unlike the polynomial payoff functions of chess and checker programs. Balancing of material, such as a piece for a pawn, does occur.

card.rule: S2 ends a line on a single decisive feature, not on a weighted sum of pros and cons.
card.limits: Material balancing is the exception; and one subject's single-feature style does not show that all players evaluate this way.

concepts.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
concepts.title: Levels of aspiration
concepts.question: What is a level of aspiration, and where does S2 show one?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Closely allied to evaluation is the control of search by a threshold: only changes in the evaluation of a position that exceed it end the search.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: A level of aspiration starts at some reasonable level. If positions keep exceeding the threshold, the aspiration level is raised; if few positions exceed it, the level is lowered.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: With the evaluative procedure S2 uses, it is difficult to see such a mechanism operating. One striking example does occur in the scene where he looks for new possibilities, E6 to E10.

card.rule: Raise the bar when many positions clear it, lower it when few do.
card.limits: In S2's protocol only one clear case shows it, so the authors treat it as a hint.

concepts.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
concepts.title: What the study of S2 shows and leaves out
concepts.question: What does the analysis of S2 establish, and what is left incomplete?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: What does the detailed study of one subject on one position establish about human chess behavior?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: A human's behavior in one more task can be represented as search in a problem space specified with precision: the basic space defined by the rules of the game, augmented by a few abstract moves such as no-move and Q-move. Within it the search has a well-developed structure, progressive-deepening plus rules for its details.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The program for behavior is a symbolic system, and hardly anything but an IPS could realize it. It requires a basically serial processor able to symbolize situations, since otherwise the search could not repeatedly go down the same path, and to form and evoke associations, which are the productions.

card.rule: S2's behavior fits search in a precise problem space with progressive deepening, run by a serial symbolic processor with stored associations.
card.limits: The parts examined are incomplete: they show only what this one task evoked from the subject's repertoire.

concepts.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
concepts.title: Episodes in chess: what counts as obvious
concepts.question: How do chess episodes fit the general notion of an episode, and where does the unobvious step lie?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The analysis of this chapter was done before the general notion of an episode emerged, and the authors left it unchanged. Do its episodes fit that notion?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: An episode is a stretch of behavior carried out by the problem solver because it is obvious: any equally intelligent solver with the same start and goals will run through essentially the same episode. If the desired result cannot be had, the exact courses can differ, but the domain explored is the same. What is obvious must be determined separately in each task environment.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In chess, the situation-response productions give the notion of obvious behavior. Given the set from the base-move, behavior runs off in immediate action and reaction. Prior analysis conditions it, in that more unusual moves are considered in successive analyses, but decisions at each node are reached without major reflection.

card.rule: A chess episode is the run of immediate situation-response steps that follows a base-move.
card.limits: The authors say they will not give a more precise definition; they suggest only that S2's episodes are consistent with the general concept.

concepts.title: Why the chapter looks beyond one subject
concepts.question: Why does the chapter bring in other evidence than the single subject S2, and why does perception get special weight?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The last two chapters analyzed a set of chess programs and one subject, S2. A reader may worry that this is peculiar to that one player. Few psychological studies of chess exist, and most are too general to analyze at the level of information processing.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The authors take up several related topics: de Groot's study and his grandmasters on position A, how players define the situation, a program that finds mating combinations, and the role of perception and noticing. Together these check the earlier material and extend it.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Perception shows up more strongly in chess than in the authors' other two tasks. Cryptarithmetic and logic used naive subjects and plain displays. Chess has a long history, and the chess subjects were experienced, so they could recognize subtle board features that a novice would miss.

card.rule: The chapter tests the single-subject analysis against other studies and adds the topics that analysis left thin, above all perception.
card.limits: Agreement with other studies reassures but does not prove the theory; the authors present these topics as checks and extensions.

concepts.title: De Groot's procedure and subjects
concepts.question: How did de Groot's way of collecting protocols and his subjects compare with the authors' own study?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: To use de Groot's work as a check on S2, the authors must know whether his study is comparable. He asked chess players, from good club players to grandmasters, to analyze positions and choose a move while talking aloud.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The situation was essentially the same as with S2. The chief difference in observation was that the authors had tape recorders, so their protocols are more extensive, while de Groot had to take notes. De Groot did go over his notes with the subject immediately after each session, which the authors did not do.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: S2 sits at the lower edge of de Groot's range, and the grandmasters are incomparably better. Even so, a summary of de Groot's main findings shows that his subjects and S2 were alike in many ways.

card.rule: De Groot's studies used nearly the same task as the authors, with hand notes plus a review with the subject instead of tapes, and his wider range of players still resembled S2.
card.limits: S2 is a weaker player than de Groot's best subjects, so any likeness to grandmasters is a finding to examine, not an assumption.

concepts.title: Selective search
concepts.question: How much of the game tree do human chess players actually search?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Chess programs differ in how many positions they examine. The authors ask what human players do when they analyze a position to choose a move.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Humans spend much of their time searching the game tree for the consequences of moves they consider. The search is highly selective, attending to only a few of the multitude of possible continuations.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: No evidence shows that the total number of different positions considered in an analysis lasting up to fifteen minutes or so exceeds about one hundred. In position A, five grandmasters explicitly considered between 20 and 76 positions. The counts come from protocol analysis.

card.rule: Human chess players do search, but only a small, highly selective part of the tree: about a hundred positions at most in a fifteen-minute analysis.
card.limits: The counts come from what players say aloud, not from direct sight of their thought.

concepts.title: Chess concepts as a shared vocabulary
concepts.question: What are chess concepts, and why would human players and programs both have them?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Analysis of a chess position requires referring briefly to the features that matter. A long list of piece positions would be clumsy.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: A concept is a classificatory term for a feature or subpattern of the position. The phrase fianchettoed short-castled position names a pattern of Black pawns, a Bishop, a Rook and a King, six pieces in all, and lets a knowledgeable player evoke the whole pattern.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Superficially, the same elementary concepts appear in human play and in chess programs: attacks, defenses, pins, open files and isolated pawns, among others.

card.rule: Chess concepts are named features of a position that let a knowledgeable player evoke a whole pattern in a phrase.
card.limits: That humans and programs use the same names shows less than it seems; the next idea explains why.

concepts.title: Same concept, different use
concepts.question: Does a program using the same concept names as a player use them in the same way?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Programs and protocols share concept names. A reader might take this to mean programs and people reason alike.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: In programs a concept can appear in the condition of a production (if a piece is attacked, then ...), in the label of an action (checking move), or in the evaluation of a result (after the exchange, White has an isolated pawn). The same concept in both does not imply precisely the same extension, nor, more important, the same use. Concepts encapsulate information that may be used in many ways.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Human protocols also contain much more global concepts: a developed position, control of the center, a won position, a weak King's side, a closed position. The authors conclude there are still strong generic similarities from the common reliance on the standard vocabulary of chess.

card.rule: Sharing a concept name does not show the same extension or the same use, yet the common vocabulary gives strong generic similarity.
card.limits: The authors claim generic likeness only; the match is not close for the global concepts.

concepts.title: Episodes in chess analysis
concepts.question: How is a human chess analysis divided into episodes and phases?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A chess protocol runs for many minutes. The authors ask whether it breaks into recognizable parts.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Human analysis is broken into separate episodes. The subject first orients himself to the position, and at the end sums up when he picks the single move to play. The number of episodes between these is variable.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: De Groot distinguishes three major phases, exploration, elaboration and proof, and counts the initial orientation as a fourth. S2 clearly showed an orientation episode (E1) and a summing-up episode (E25). His episodes between were not easily put into functional categories.

card.rule: Chess analysis starts with orientation and ends with a summing up, with a variable number of episodes between; features of episode types matter more than a fixed phase order.
card.limits: S2's middle episodes did not sort neatly into de Groot's phases, so a fixed phase sequence is not assumed.

concepts.title: Progressive broadening and deepening
concepts.question: What is progressive deepening, and why did the authors adopt this label for S2's search?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Within a single analysis, the player's attention returns to moves already looked at. The authors ask what pattern this return follows.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: De Groot calls it progressive broadening and deepening: the analysis of a move is reworked repeatedly, going over old ground more carefully, exploring new side branches and extending the search deeper. The idea is summed up as rough cut, fine cut, a term proposed by J. C. Shaw.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: S2's episodes showed this so strongly that the authors borrowed the term progressive deepening as the label for the search strategy he was using.

card.rule: Progressive deepening means reworking the analysis of a move repeatedly, each time more carefully and deeper.
card.limits: The label comes from de Groot's description and S2's behavior; programs of the day mostly lack it.

concepts.title: Exploration and verification
concepts.question: How do exploring and verifying differ, and what does S2 show of each?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Not every episode of analysis does the same job. The authors ask what an episode is for.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Some episodes explore for new information; others try to prove or disprove a hypothesis, which is verification. Players frequently pick a favorite move quite early and then try to verify it is better than the alternatives. Search may be conducted differently in the two kinds of episode, since different information is sought.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In S2's protocol, his use of negation in E17 and E24 is a form of verification, and scene 3 (E6 to E10) is exploration. But although he investigates B x N'/5 time and again, there is little reason to view it as a favorite he is trying to prove: he returns to it because it is the only thing he has found of interest.

card.rule: Tell exploring (seeking information) from verifying (testing a hypothesis), and do not read repetition as verification.
card.limits: Repeated visits to a move may mean only that nothing else has been found.

concepts.title: Redefining the problem
concepts.question: What is redefining the problem in chess analysis, and how does it differ from forming a hypothesis?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: In de Groot's protocols, players now and then stop and restate what they are trying to do, in rather general terms, such as that White will have to extract some profit from a weakness after all.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Human players attempt periodically to redefine the problem. The redefinition is usually a conclusion drawn from the immediately preceding analysis, and it is accepted as the new working assumption.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: It may look like hypothesis formation, but it is not: after a redefinition there is normally no activity devoted to proving or disproving it.

card.rule: A redefinition is a summary conclusion adopted as the new working assumption, not a hypothesis put to the test.
card.limits: The authors know redefinition here from de Groot's protocols rather than from their own data.

concepts.title: How players evaluate positions
concepts.question: How do human chess evaluations differ from the evaluations most chess programs use?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A major difference between human play and most chess programs lies in how positions are evaluated.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: De Groot's subjects often evaluated in rather elementary terms, mentioning a single advantage, such as Black gains an open file. S2 did the same. This contrasts, though without contradicting, the elaborate polynomial evaluations used in most chess and checkers programs. Players seldom balance many factors, some pro and some con, to reach one estimate.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The comparison rests on de Groot's protocols (pp. 232-239) and on S2's protocol. The human style resembles more closely the NSS evaluation process.

card.rule: Human evaluation usually names one advantage rather than weighing many factors into one number.
card.limits: This is a contrast with polynomial evaluation, not a contradiction of it.

concepts.title: Perception separates strong from weak players
concepts.question: What test finally separated strong chess players from weak ones for de Groot?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: De Groot looked for measures that would separate strong from weak players, other than whether they found the correct move. Statistics of search and analysis, such as the number of positions examined, did not do it.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: He finally separated strong from weak players with perceptual tests: players were shown chess positions briefly, for three to seven seconds, and then reproduced them.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The grandmaster reproduced the positions perfectly, and performance fell off appreciably as chess ability decreased. S2's protocol gives little direct evidence on perception, so the authors postpone this topic to the end of the chapter.

card.rule: Memory for briefly seen positions, not the amount of search, separated strong players from weak ones in de Groot's work.
card.limits: S2's protocol cannot speak to this, so the authors look to other studies for it.

concepts.section: Comparison with de Groot's Protocols on Position A
concepts.title: De Groot's protocols on position A
concepts.question: What data from de Groot's subjects on position A does the authors' comparison use, and why?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A qualitative comparison with de Groot is not enough. The authors want to see how far the likeness comes from the objective demands of the task, and how far from shared features of human information processing.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: They use the data that de Groot summarized from 19 protocols of subjects placed before position A. The subjects include 5 grandmasters and 4 masters, and the rest range from expert to club level.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: One of the fullest protocols, that of the former World Champion M. Euwe, yielded the problem behavior graph (PBG) of Figure 13.1, where it can be set beside the PBG of S2.

card.rule: The comparison on position A uses de Groot's 19 protocols to separate task demands from features of the human processor.
card.limits: The two sources of likeness overlap, so the data alone may not always tell them apart.

concepts.title: How many first moves players consider
concepts.question: Out of 56 legal first moves in position A, how many did the 19 subjects consider, and how alike were they?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: There are 56 legal base-moves (candidate first moves) available to a player in position A. The authors ask how many the subjects actually mention and whether they pick the same ones.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Most of the 56 were not mentioned by any subject. Only 22 different initial moves were mentioned by one or more of the 19, and 15 of these by at least one of the nine masters or grandmasters. On average a subject considered fewer than 5 different base-moves.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: A total of 94 moves (not all different) were mentioned by the 19 subjects, and the seven moves mentioned by the most subjects accounted for about two-thirds of all mentions. One master considered 11 moves; no other master or grandmaster considered more than 6.

card.rule: Subjects looked at few of the 56 legal moves, and they looked largely at the same few.
card.limits: The counts are of moves mentioned in protocols, so they may undercount moves that were considered silently.

concepts.title: Where strong and weak players disagreed
concepts.question: Which move did strong and weaker players treat differently in position A, and what explains it?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Players of all levels agreed on most popular moves. The authors look at the one clear disagreement.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The authors speculate, rather than show, why. Bishops are somewhat stronger than Knights, but mainly in the endgame; the general statement is common lore, while the qualification is understood only in more sophisticated circles. Weaker players may have dismissed the move by the general rule, and stronger ones considered it because they meant to seek a decision before the endgame.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The move 1. BxN'/5, objectively the strongest in the position, was mentioned by all five grandmasters and chosen by four of them, but mentioned in only three of the other de Groot protocols. S2 mentioned and chose it.

card.rule: The strongest move was studied by the grandmasters and mostly passed over by weaker players, possibly because they used a general rule that the strong players knew to qualify.
card.limits: The explanation is the authors' speculation; the protocols show who mentioned the move, not why others did not.

concepts.title: Consensus within the search trees
concepts.question: Does the agreement among strong players go beyond first moves to whole search trees?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Agreement on first moves might not carry over to the lines that follow them. The authors look at the full search trees of the five grandmasters and four masters (Figure 13.2).

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The consensus extends further. For 1. BxN'/5, three Black replies were mentioned explicitly, two by eight of these players and the other by seven. One branch explored by eight of them was the objectively correct reply, the only one that did not lose material for Black.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Again there was considerable agreement on White's next move. A similar degree of agreement holds for the initial move N x B. The most explored branches also account for a large share of S2's exploratory activity.

card.rule: Strong players agree not only on which first moves to try but on which replies and follow-ups to examine.
card.limits: The agreement is among stronger players on one position; it does not show that every position produces such consensus.

concepts.title: A common chess culture
concepts.question: How do the authors explain the high consensus among players, and what is the alternative reading?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Why do players of such different strength agree so much on which moves to examine in position A?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: One explanation is sociological. All the players, even the weakest, belong to a common chess culture, passed on in across-the-board play, in conversation and in writing: published annotated games and books on strategy and tactics. They know that winning the exchange is usually decisive, that Bishops are usually slightly stronger than Knights, and that dynamic analysis is needed to evaluate exchanges.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: They know substantially all the heuristic principles in existing chess programs and a great many more, so they approach the position with a common body of beliefs. The beliefs are not identical, otherwise all the players would be grandmasters.

blocks.label: Alternative
blocks.text: Because chess is so vast, what the task requires is itself sociologically defined, by the best existing knowledge. The consensus can be viewed either as participation in a common culture or as a common response dictated by the requirements of the situation.

card.rule: High consensus reflects a shared chess culture, and since the culture also defines what the task requires, the two readings cannot be fully separated.
card.limits: The shared beliefs are not identical across players; if they were, all would be of grandmaster strength.

concepts.title: Dynamic and static analysis of moves
concepts.question: How did the grandmasters analyze exchanges and quiet moves in position A, and what did they see?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: What in the position led the stronger players to examine 1. BxN'/5, and how were its consequences worked out? Dynamic analysis plays out sequences of moves; static evaluation judges a position as it stands.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The exploration tree of Figure 13.2 shows that Black's reply B'xB loses a piece, N'xB loses the exchange, and P'xB, the only other possible move, leaves White with new attacking possibilities. The move generation analysis for S2 applies well to the grandmasters: piece exchanges are examined dynamically, as is the undefended capture, and quiet moves are generally evaluated statically.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors say the grandmasters' analysis was governed almost wholly by the objective requirements of the situation.

card.rule: Exchanges are played out dynamically, quiet moves are judged statically, and the few quiet moves considered all bear on central features.
card.limits: Some moves were seen but not mentioned, so the protocols show only part of the analysis.

concepts.title: Progressive deepening and short-term memory
concepts.question: Why do grandmasters return to the base position, and what does that suggest about memory?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The most striking feature of the grandmasters' graphs cannot be put down to the task's requirements but to the players' own limits: like S2, they keep returning to the base position and reexplore earlier variations. There is very little branching without a return.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The authors suggest the cause is the burden exploration places on short-term memory.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The grandmasters' graphs show very little branching without a return to the base position. There is one exception in Keres' protocol, one in Fine's and four in Euwe's, mostly after he has repeated a variation several times.

blocks.label: Alternative
blocks.text: In cryptarithmetic and logic a written display records tentative assignments. In chess pieces may not be touched, so there is nothing like it. The authors expect this difference in short-term memory demands to explain the different organization of the graphs.

card.rule: Progressive deepening is attributed to short-term memory limits, which chess's no-touch rule makes bite harder than a written display would.
card.limits: The memory account is called very likely and more plausible, not demonstrated.

concepts.title: Six sequencing rules tested on the grandmasters
concepts.question: How well do the six rules for sequencing S2's episodes fit the grandmasters' graphs?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors earlier proposed six rules (R1 to R6) governing the order of episodes in S2's graph. Do they fit the grandmasters?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: R1, that the analysis of each base-move is independent of the others, is satisfied by all the graphs. R2, that the first episode of a base-move uses normal moves, is hard to test but has no obvious violations. R3, stay with a good base-move and switch from a loser, fits four protocols (one violation in Fine's) but not Euwe's, who has about six violations.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: R4, considering less-than-optimum moves for the opponent, appears in one to four cases per protocol. R5, predicting interruption to pursue moves discovered during an episode, is not supported by any grandmaster protocol. R6, a check of alternatives before the final choice, is supported only by Alekhine's protocol.

card.rule: Of the six rules, R1 to R4 fit the grandmasters reasonably, R3 fails for Euwe, and R5 and R6 get little or no support.
card.limits: Several of the tests are weak because the protocols have few variations.

concepts.title: Working forward in position A
concepts.question: Did players in position A mostly work forward from the position, or toward goals by means-ends analysis?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors ask whether the protocols on position A show means-ends analysis, in which a player picks actions by noting what stands between the present position and a goal.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Mostly they show forward search. Players, strong as well as weak, tend to work forward from the current position, evaluating the consequences of considerable moves.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Explicit means-ends analysis is hardly evident, except for two cases: the general strategic consideration that an aggressive move must be sought since the endgame favors Black, and the interest of several players in finding moves that attack Black's weakened King's position.

card.rule: In position A players mostly searched forward from the current position, with only two general goals guiding them in a means-ends way.
card.limits: This describes position A only; the authors say other kinds of positions can look different.

concepts.title: Targets that were not used
concepts.question: Position A offered specific targets for means-ends analysis; why did the players not use them?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The working-forward style is not entirely inherent in position A. Several specific targets could be identified statically and used to build means-ends analysis, but the players seem not to have done so.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Besides the two general goals, position A offered more specific targets, such as the defensive goal of protecting a pawn. Two more were involved in the analysis of 1. BxN'/5 and 1. NxN', but in most protocols they were discovered in the course of dynamic analysis, or at least did not motivate it.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: De Groot also gives considerable evidence that, especially for stronger players, particular board features suggest specific moves in a highly automatic, overlearned way, without explicit verbalized problem solving.

card.rule: Specific targets were available but were found during analysis, and strong players often respond to features automatically, without stated goals.
card.limits: Automatic evocation leaves no spoken goal, so protocols cannot show it directly.

concepts.title: Why redefinition is rare in position A
concepts.question: Why did neither de Groot's subjects nor S2 redefine the situation in position A?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Defining the situation is an important kind of information processing to understand.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: In position A neither de Groot's subjects nor S2 redefined the chess situation in the course of the analysis. Elsewhere de Groot shows that such redefinitions often occur in chess play. The authors surmise that the few in position A are due to the tactical character of the particular task environment.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors examine instances from de Groot's protocols, setting aside the initial orientation phase.

card.rule: Redefinition was rare in position A, probably because the position was tactical, but it is an important process that contrasts with search.
card.limits: The tactical-position explanation is a surmise, not a demonstrated cause.

concepts.title: Three causes of redefinition
concepts.question: What three circumstances lead a player to redefine the situation, and what do they show about move analysis?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Instances of redefinition in de Groot's protocols differ on the surface. The authors ask what they have in common.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: One subject overlooks a key piece until late in the protocol, which invalidates a favorable analysis. Another decides on a calm move, reluctantly, once convinced that his hopes for the earlier move were excessive. A third keeps the intended move but plays it in the context of a different plan.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The examples show that redefinition may come about (1) because a feature that was overlooked is noticed, (2) because initial expectations about a move are disappointed, or (3) because exploring a move relates it to outcomes and goals other than those that suggested it. In such cases dynamic analysis looks more like information gathering than a simple forward search.

card.rule: Redefinition arises when a missed feature is noticed, when hopes for a move are disappointed, or when a move turns out to serve other goals.
card.limits: These are three examples from de Groot, not a complete list of the causes.

concepts.title: Mating combinations and the limits of search
concepts.question: Why are mating combinations a test case for the theory of search?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Chess players tell novices to check whenever they can, since it may be mate. The advice is ironic, because most checking moves are easily refuted and only cost the attacker time.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Even so, series of checking moves that end in mate give chess much of its spectacle, the brilliancies. Some recorded combinations are eight or more moves deep, that is, sixteen plies.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Mating combinations are of special interest in testing the limits of search, which is central to the theory in this part. They seem to require more search than a human, with limited processing ability, can do (Simon and Simon, 1962).

card.rule: Mating combinations seem to demand more search than humans can do, so they test how far a search-based theory can go.
card.limits: Most checks fail; only the rare combination ending in mate is spectacular.

concepts.title: MATER: checks only and mobility
concepts.question: What two ideas let MATER find mating combinations, and why does mobility matter?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A program must find forced mates without searching the whole tree. The authors describe MATER, a forward-search program for mating combinations.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: MATER rests on two ideas: generate only checking moves, and abandon a line as disadvantageous if it allows the opponent more than a very few legal replies (more than four, say). A few further rules set the order of exploring.

blocks.label: Term
blocks.text: Mobility, meaning how freely the opponent can move, lies at the heart. A King is checkmated when it is attacked and no legal move removes the attack, so its adjacent squares are blocked or attacked. A check must be answered at once, which limits the replies.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Of all unevaluated moves it takes next the one allowing the fewest replies, and rejects any move allowing more than four.

card.rule: MATER searches only checks and follows the line that leaves the opponent the fewest replies, because mating is a matter of restricting mobility.
card.limits: The program is built for forcing situations; it is not a program for playing a whole game.

concepts.title: MATER in the prototype program schema
concepts.question: How is MATER specified in the schema used for the regular chess programs, and what does it leave out?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: To compare MATER with the programs of Chapter 11, the authors specify it with the same prototype program: base-moves, analysis-moves, termination rules and values.

blocks.label: Model
