blocks.text: Base-moves are the checking moves, cut off at those with more than four replies, ordered by number of replies, with double checks first, then checks with no recapture. For analysis the attacker uses the same moves and the defender all legal moves, those likely to foil a mating threat first. The static values are only mate or no-mate, assigned in the attacker's position.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: There is no width or depth limit. Piece values and center control have no significance, since the game ends if the search succeeds, so MATER attempts sacrifices unhesitatingly.

card.rule: MATER's specification is simple: forcing base-moves, mate or no-mate values, and no depth or width limits.
card.limits: The specification shows only what MATER does; it is not an account of how people find mates.

concepts.title: The subproblem list and its price
concepts.question: How does MATER choose which node to expand next, what does it cost, and how do humans differ?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The program of Figure 13.3 searches depth-first, like the other prototype programs. The real MATER works differently.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: MATER keeps the tree of moves through a web of links to predecessors and successors, plus a subproblem list, as in the Logic Theorist, that orders all moves on the whole tree by number of replies. It takes next the move with fewest replies, wherever it lies on the tree.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Jumping around the tree costs extra processing, since the board position must be rebuilt for each new move, but growing the tree from the most promising node is worth the housekeeping.

blocks.label: Alternative
blocks.text: Progressive deepening, with its frequent returns to old positions rebuilt from the base position, can be seen as a human attempt to approach the subproblem list's freedom within human limits.

card.rule: MATER expands the most promising node anywhere in its tree at a processing cost, which humans cannot afford; progressive deepening is their approximation.
card.limits: The depth-first version and MATER propose equivalent mates but might choose different ones.

concepts.title: How common are forced mates by checks
concepts.question: How often do mates forced by checks arise, and are there cues that signal them?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: It is of slight interest that positions exist where checks force mate. The authors ask whether such positions are unusual, whether cues signal them, and whether the mate can be found with modest search.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: In Fine's chapter on mating attacks, 129 positions are considered. In 51 of them checkmate can be forced by a sequence of checks. In five more, the checks must be preceded by a one-move mating threat. In the other 73, the defender can avert mate by a sacrifice or the mate is not forced as MATER defines it.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Such positions arise quite frequently in tournament games. Reasonably reliable cues are almost always present: the opponent's King is exposed or could be exposed by a capture, one's own pieces are mobile and the opponent's constricted. Even a rough measure of relative mobility would usually do.

card.rule: Forced mates by checks arise fairly often, and an exposed King together with superior mobility signals them.
card.limits: The cues are reliable almost always, not in every case.

concepts.title: Exploration, discovery and verification trees
concepts.question: How do the exploration, discovery and verification trees measure the search for a mate?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: To say whether a mate can be found with reasonable search, the authors need measures of the amount of search.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The exploration tree is the positions on a search tree that are actually examined. The discovery tree is all the moves seen, examined or not; some moves on the try-list stay unexplored. The verification tree is the part of the exploration tree needed to prove the combination: the attacker's single best move at each node and every legal move of the defender.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In the example of Figure 13.4 the exploration tree has 16 positions and the discovery tree 36 moves (14 checks and 22 replies). The verification tree has five moves and six positions.

card.rule: The discovery tree holds all moves seen, the exploration tree those examined, and the verification tree only what proves the mate.
card.limits: The three trees are measured in different units, positions for exploration and moves for discovery.

concepts.title: What MATER achieved
concepts.question: How well did MATER find the mates in Fine's positions, and what does that show about the task environment?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Can a program using only checks and a four-reply limit find the mates in Fine's positions with modest search?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: With no limit on computing effort, MATER solves combinations of uninterrupted checks, provided the defender never has more than four replies in the verification tree. Of the 51 positions that qualify, it found 43. Table 13.1 shows that the verification tree grows about two moves for every move of depth, so the tree grows roughly linearly, not exponentially.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The discovery tree grows only slightly more than proportionally to depth and stays near five times the verification tree. A fifteen-ply combination needed a discovery tree of only 108 moves, where an exponential tree of depth fifteen with two branches per node would have some 32,000. The selective heuristics radically prune the tree in these forcing situations.

card.rule: In mating situations the search tree grows roughly linearly with depth, so a selective program finds deep combinations with little search.
card.limits: This holds in forcing situations; it does not show that all chess search is cheap.

concepts.title: The fewest-replies heuristic and the initiative
concepts.question: Why does exploring the move with the fewest replies work so well, and what is holding the initiative?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A key heuristic in MATER is always to examine first the moves that permit the opponent the fewest replies.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The heuristic has a dual significance. It allows the opponent the fewest alternatives to find a way out of the mating net, and it holds down the branchiness of the search tree, making the mate easier to discover.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In this task environment the contributions of the two factors cannot be disentangled. The heuristic, with the checking-move heuristic, illustrates holding the initiative: acting so forcefully that the opponent must devote all his effort to replying, so that the side holding the initiative picks where the struggle is waged.

card.rule: Fewest replies both narrows the opponent's escapes and shrinks the tree, and it is an instance of holding the initiative.
card.limits: In this task the two effects of the heuristic cannot be told apart.

concepts.title: MATER II and mating threats
concepts.question: How does MATER II go beyond checks, and how does it test a candidate move?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: MATER I considers only checking moves. MATER II, by G. Baylor, aims to broaden the moves allowed in a mating combination, so as to find moves threatening enough to lead into the constrained checking situation.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The executive has three parts. First it runs a slight modification of MATER I as an information-gathering search and keeps the whole tree. Second, it scans that tree for candidate moves that might threaten mate in one, testing each by making the move, making a no-move for the opponent, and seeing whether a mating move exists. Third, it searches again with the mate-in-one threats as base-moves.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: MATER II found the checkmates in all five of Fine's positions that need an initial mating threat before checks.

card.rule: MATER II finds quiet mating threats by sampling a search tree and testing candidates with a no-move for the opponent.
card.limits: Two schemes were tried for finding threats; only the first is described here.

concepts.title: How far search can go
concepts.question: What do MATER I and II say about the role of search and the need for noticing?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: After the chess programs of Chapter 11, MATER I and II let the authors state more clearly what search can and cannot do in finding mates.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Forward search remains the central mechanism. Owing to the task environment and to heuristics that use it, the search space near a successful combination is more linear than exponential, so, to make a pun, search goes a long way toward being a sufficient discovery mechanism.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: But search must be highly selective, so strong mechanisms must exist for noticing features of the board and for building specialized search strategies that depend on them.

card.rule: Search goes far toward finding mates, but its selectivity depends on noticing features of the board.
card.limits: The conclusion concerns mating combinations, where the task environment is unusually favorable.

concepts.title: A mate that needs a quiet move
concepts.question: Why would MATER I miss the winning move in Fine's position 97, and how does MATER II find it?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: In a position from a casual game among masters, mates are threatened on two squares near Black's King but both are protected. The winning move is N-N5. How does White discover it?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: White can choose N-N5 without seeing the combination to the end, since the move prevents Black's capture of the Queen and so adds an attacking piece with no loss of material. MATER I would not find it, since N-N5 is not a checking move.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: MATER II first explores the checks Q-N7 and QxRP'. The second leads to 1. ... K'xQ, 2. N-N5ch. Neither line ends in mate, but N-N5 has been discovered.

card.rule: MATER I cannot find a quiet winning move; MATER II discovers it during its check searches and then tests it.
card.limits: The example is one position, chosen because it needs a non-checking first move.

concepts.title: How humans found the quiet move
concepts.question: How did the two human experts find N-N5, and how does their search differ from MATER II's?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Two protocols gathered by G. Baylor for Fine's position 97 let the authors check MATER II against human experts.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Both experts found the combination by noticing N-N5, and the evidence suggests it was evoked by means-ends analysis. In the PBG shown, the player notes early the possibility of mate by QxRP'. But the pawn is defended by Black's King, so the Queen's attack needs support, and N-N5 provides it.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: MATER II discovered N-N5 not as a preparation for QxRP' but as a move to continue the attack after it, so the move's function at discovery differs.

card.rule: The humans found N-N5 as support for a planned Queen attack, MATER II as a continuation of it; both then explore it afresh.
card.limits: Neither protocol shows exactly how the move was noticed; the means-ends reading is suggested by the evidence.

concepts.title: Perceiving before searching
concepts.question: What do skilled players do in the first moments with a new position, and how do programs notice?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Most of the chapter has concerned the tree of continuations that players build, which gives chess thinking a working-forward flavor. But noticing keeps intruding: players notice a few considerable moves and do not mention the many other legal moves, and they sometimes notice new moves or features during their investigation, which then become the basis for more exploration.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: During the first moments, for example 15 seconds, a skilled player does not appear to search move sequences. He seems occupied with perceiving the essential properties of the position, embodying some of the chess concepts, which suggest moves and help him anticipate their consequences. He is gathering information about the problem, not seeking a solution.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: S2's first episode E1 illustrates this orienting behavior. De Groot, with later work by his students such as Jongman, supports the conclusion. The authors say that to understand chess thinking, perceptual processes must be taken into account along with the conceptual ones.

card.rule: In its first moments with a position a skilled player perceives its essential properties before searching.
card.limits: The evidence is for the opening moments; later analysis is largely search.

concepts.title: What eye movements can and cannot show
concepts.question: What do eye-movement records show about the first look at a position, and what do they leave open?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors want direct data on the first perceptual processes of chess players, before any search of move sequences.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: At each fixation the subject appears to take in the pieces at or near the fixation point, and also pieces in peripheral vision, within about 2 degrees of arc, that bear a significant chess relation to the fixated piece: attack, defend, block or shield.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The best data are eye-movement records gathered by de Groot and his associates, by Tichomirov and Poznyanskaya, and by Winikoff. They show fixations moving from one square to another at a maximum rate of about four per second.

blocks.label: Limit
blocks.text: Calibration and the human visual apparatus make it impossible to say with assurance which square is attended at a given moment. A single fixation discovers pieces on several neighboring squares.

card.rule: Eye-movement records show a succession of fixations at up to four per second, but not exactly what information is being taken in.
card.limits: The exact square attended cannot be established with assurance from such records.

concepts.title: The PERCEIVER program
concepts.question: How does PERCEIVER simulate the first eye movements, and what two assumptions does it make?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: To test the eye-movement hypothesis, Simon and Barenfeld wanted a program that could mimic the first fixations of a human player.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: They organized the noticing processes already in MATER into a chess-perception program, PERCEIVER, which simulates the initial sequences of human eye movements.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Two assumptions are basic. Concepts: when the eyes fixate a piece, neighboring pieces can be detected that defend it, attack it, are defended by it, or are attacked by it. Attention: when attention is on piece A and a relation to piece B is noticed, attention may return to A without change of fixation; if not, B is fixated next.

card.rule: PERCEIVER fixates a piece, notices who attacks or defends it, and moves on to a related piece, building a sequence of fixations.
card.limits: The program needs further assumptions, such as where to start, but its qualitative behavior is not very sensitive to them.

concepts.title: PERCEIVER against an expert's eye movements
concepts.question: How closely did PERCEIVER's simulated fixations match an expert's, and why?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Figure 13.10 shows a position used by Tichomirov and Poznyanskaya, Black to play. Figure 13.11 shows 20 fixations of an expert in his first five seconds, and Figure 13.12 shows 15 simulated fixations by PERCEIVER. Ten squares are shaded that a good player would take as critical to understanding the position.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Both the expert and PERCEIVER were mainly occupied with the relations among pieces on these squares, and there is considerable concordance between the objects of attention in the two cases.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: If attention follows a train of associations through a web of relations, it will be brought back repeatedly to the points where the relations are densest. The authors conclude that a very simple program using perceptual processes already used in chess programs moves its attention in a way resembling a human's eye movements.

card.rule: A simple relation-following program fixates much the same critical squares as an expert, because those squares are where relations are densest.
card.limits: The match is a resemblance in what is attended, not proof that the human process is the same.

concepts.title: Reproducing positions after a brief look
concepts.question: What do the reproduction experiments show about proficiency and the meaningfulness of a position?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Can the information extracted by such perceptual processes account for the ability of masters to reproduce positions after five or ten seconds of sight?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Experiments show that the ability to reproduce a position after a few seconds depends sensitively on the subject's chess proficiency and on the meaningfulness of the position.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: De Groot and Jongman report that (1) after five seconds a grandmaster or master reproduces a position almost without error, (2) the weaker the player below this level, the more errors, and very weak players place only half a dozen pieces correctly, and (3) on random boards the masters fall to the level of weak players, who do not get worse.

card.rule: Reproduction after a brief look depends on both skill and meaningfulness: masters excel on game positions and fall to the weak players' level on random ones.
card.limits: The experiments are described here only as summarized by the authors, who then ask how memory can explain them.

concepts.title: Chunking explains the expert's memory
concepts.question: How does recognizing familiar constellations let masters hold a whole position in short-term memory?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: It is well established that about seven plus or minus two chunks can be held in short-term memory, and probably no more than one chunk can pass to long-term memory per five seconds. A chunk is any configuration familiar to the subject that he can recognize. So the information for reproducing a position after five seconds must be mainly in short-term memory, in at best nine chunks.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The authors combine PERCEIVER with the discrimination and chunking of Feigenbaum's EPAM theory. A stimulus matching a symbol stored in memory is recognized and replaced in short-term memory by that symbol, so a configuration of many relations can be held as one symbol.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Masters recognize clusters of related pieces as familiar constellations and store each as one symbol. Less skilled players must describe the board in more, simpler chunks and cannot hold enough. On a random board few configurations are familiar even to grandmasters, so they need more symbols than memory can hold and do as badly as weak players.

card.rule: Experts remember more because familiar constellations of pieces count as single chunks, and random boards destroy that advantage.
card.limits: The explanation is a hypothesis built from earlier memory theories; the authors do not claim to have measured chunks.

concepts.title: Is the chunk vocabulary big enough
concepts.question: Are the numbers the chunking explanation needs of the right order of magnitude?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A chunking explanation is only believable if the quantities fit. A master must carry a vocabulary of familiar subpatterns large enough to describe the many possible positions.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: In the years needed to reach mastery a player might gain a vocabulary comparable to a reader's word-recognition vocabulary in English, or the Kanji vocabulary of a reader of Chinese or Japanese, of the order of ten thousand to a hundred thousand symbols. Sequences of seven such symbols could encode between \(10^{28}\) and \(10^{35}\) positions, since \((10^4)^7\) and \((10^5)^7\) bracket that range.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The number of positions arising from reasonable moves is estimated to be far inside that range, so such a vocabulary can give distinct seven-symbol descriptions to distinct positions. Simon and Barenfeld suggest one encoding of the position of Figure 13.10 into eight symbols, eight constellations familiar to many experts.

card.rule: A vocabulary of tens of thousands of familiar patterns is enough for seven-symbol descriptions to tell chess positions apart.
card.limits: Different players of similar skill may chunk the same board differently; the argument shows sufficiency, not a unique code.

concepts.title: Seeing continuations without stating them
concepts.question: How can grandmasters see continuations they do not mention, and what is symptom-remedy analysis?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The grandmasters show by their evaluations that they see continuations they do not mention, and their protocols are generally less full and explicit than the weaker players'. The authors list three possible causes: they search faster, they report less, or they see consequences with less search.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The master's richer vocabulary of concepts is held to evoke condensed analysis programs that look at few branches, evaluate exchanges to a dead position, and avoid updating the board after every move. With each familiar feature, move generators and dynamic analysis programs are stored in memory.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In position A, spotting Black's just-defended Knight evokes the moves that attack it, among those most mentioned after 1. BxN'/5 P'xB, and a pawn capture leads the master to see the open King's file and evokes KR-K1. This symptom-remedy pattern is means-ends analysis resting on past experience, not present reasoning, and a simple production system can produce it.

card.rule: Familiar features evoke stored remedies, so a master can analyze compactly without explicit goal structures.
card.limits: Silence in a protocol is not evidence of what the player saw.

concepts.title: What the chapter achieved
concepts.question: What did the chapter's four lines of inquiry add to the single-subject analysis?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The chapter looked at varied data on human chess play. The authors summarize what the data say about S2's analysis and what corners of the chess situation they pushed into.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: De Groot's general picture of chess thinking corroborates the more detailed but narrow analysis of S2. The comparison of the grandmasters on position A separated demands of the task environment from S2's particulars, though the sociology of chess means the task is defined only in comparison with other players' abilities.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The rest of the chapter pushed into corners that the detailed study left unexplored: the redefinition of the situation, which arises in positions more strategic than position A; the mating-combination task, a test of whether search was sufficient for a task that seemed to need enormous searches; and perceptual and noticing mechanisms, which the authors relate to means-ends analysis.

card.rule: The chapter corroborates S2's analysis with other data and extends it to redefinition, mating combinations and perception.
card.limits: The chapter's checks rest on a few studies and one position, so they support rather than prove the theory.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Five general propositions the theory must fit
concepts.question: What five general propositions about problem solving must the theory fit, and what hard question do they raise?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Across the book's three tasks, subjects differ from each other and tasks differ from each other, yet behavior is largely predictable from what the task demands. The authors ask whether one theory can cover this, or only a loose collection of separate theories.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Five propositions open the chapter: people in these tasks are representable as information processing systems (IPS); this can be done in great detail for a given person and task; subject differences are real differences of program structure, method and content; task differences are also structural; and the task environment plus the solver's intelligence largely fixes behavior, whatever the fine detail of the IPS.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors say the whole body of analysis in the book supports the five. They note that other psychologists have answered the puzzle by assuming a representative subject, treating psychology as only statistical, keeping only what all humans share, dropping contents, or falling back on learning.

card.rule: The theory must explain what is common across people and tasks while allowing real structural differences, even though the task environment shapes behavior so strongly.
card.limits: The propositions are claims about the kinds of tasks studied; the chapter itself notes the evidence cannot mark the edges of their scope.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Four propositions that shape the theory
concepts.question: What four propositions give the theory its shape, and in what order does each determine the next?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Given large differences among people and tasks, the authors need a theory that names what is invariant and also says what determines the parts that vary.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Four propositions: (1) only a few gross characteristics of the human IPS are invariant over task and solver; (2) these suffice to determine that a task is represented as a problem space and that problem solving happens in it; (3) the structure of the task environment determines the possible structures of the problem space; (4) the structure of the problem space determines the possible programs.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The chapter's main sections develop these four in turn. Because points three and four speak only of possibilities, a fifth section deals with which actual space and program a solver ends up with. The authors say the book's evidence supports different parts to different degrees.

card.rule: Few IPS invariants imply a problem space; the task fixes the possible spaces; the space fixes the possible programs; a final step picks the actual ones.
card.limits: Propositions three and four give only possibilities; they do not say which space or program a given person actually uses.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Why only gross IPS features show through
concepts.question: Why should only a few gross features of an adaptive information processor show up in its behavior?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: If a problem solver's behavior is shaped by its task, its inner structure should show little. The authors need to explain why that holds, and when it would fail.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Adaptive devices shape themselves to their environment, and a system too inflexible for its environment is not adaptive. So only rather general features of an adaptive IPS can show through to behavior.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors cite their own discussion in Chapter 2 and the book's examples. They add that in extreme environments, where adaptation breaks down, the IPS structure does show through, but the studied tasks are not extreme for intelligent, well-educated subjects. They say which features show through cannot yet be derived a priori.

card.rule: An adaptive system hides most of its inner detail behind its fit to the environment; only gross features remain visible in behavior.
card.limits: In extreme environments, where adaptation fails, the system's structure shows through; the argument also cannot yet say in advance which features will show.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Computers show the same pattern: memory and rates matter
concepts.question: Why do the authors point to general-purpose computers when explaining which features of the IPS show through?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors need support for the claim that only a few gross memory features determine performance in a flexible system.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: With general-purpose computers also, a few gross features largely determine performance, and again they are memory sizes and rates and ways of accessing. The reason is that the flexibility of the program mediates between the machine's detailed structure and the structure of the practical problems it is to serve.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The comparison is offered as an analogy supporting the argument. The authors present the human case as having a similar form and do not claim to have derived the human features from first principles.

card.rule: In flexible systems, program flexibility sits between hardware detail and problem structure, so mostly memory sizes, rates and access modes decide performance.
card.limits: An analogy shows the pattern is coherent, not that the human features are the same as a computer's.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Why the problem space is a major invariant
concepts.question: Why do the authors argue that all human problem solving occurs in some problem space?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors want to explain why every task they studied was handled by search in a problem space, rather than in some other way.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The particular memories and processing rates of human beings determine that the problem space is a major invariant: all problem solving occurs in some problem space.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors say the argument, developed later in the chapter, is not logically conclusive but has considerable force. They add that an IPS with different characteristics might not solve problems this way and might not use problem spaces at all.

card.rule: Human memory sizes and processing rates make the problem space an invariant of human problem solving.
card.limits: The argument is not logically conclusive, and a differently built IPS might not need a problem space.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: The task fixes the space; the space fixes the program
concepts.question: How do the authors say the task determines the problem space, and what the program can use?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A problem space must contain the information about the task that makes solving possible, and a program that searches it can use only what the space holds.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Solving is effective only if significant information about the objective environment is encoded in the space, so the task environment remains the overwhelming determinant of the space. A program must select operators and evaluate knowledge states, so the possible programs are sharply categorized by the information the space makes available.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors add that the solver's general intelligence plus knowledge in relevant domains is often enough to predict which space he will use.

card.rule: The task supplies the information in the space, and the space's information limits what decisions a program can make.
card.limits: The studies shed little light on how the actual space and program are selected or constructed.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: The narrow focus of the study
concepts.question: What slice of human activity does the theory's evidence actually cover?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A theory of human problem solving could be taken to cover all human behavior. The authors recall what they actually studied.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Quoting Chapter 1, the study concerns intelligent adults in their own culture solving short (half-hour), moderately difficult symbolic problems: chess, symbolic logic and cryptarithmetic. It is concerned with integrated activity, not centrally perception, motor skill or personality, and mainly with performance, only a little with learning and not at all with development or age differences.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Time scales are limited too: it deemphasizes elementary reactions of half a second or less, and gives no attention to long-term activity over days or years. The authors call this a focus, not a set of boundaries.

card.rule: The evidence comes from intelligent adults on short symbolic tasks, studied as integrated performance.
card.limits: A focus is not a boundary; the authors say it does not mark the limits of the theory's applicability.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: A general theory from narrow data
concepts.question: Why do the authors put the theory forward as general when their data are narrow?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The data are drawn from three tasks, yet the authors want to propose a general theory of problem solving.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The authors say the arguments from the data are more general than the data, especially those about the relation of task environment to adaptive organism. They therefore present a general theory without trying to assess its boundaries.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: They note they have used the same approach in broader domains elsewhere, for example concept formation, algebra word problems, music, verbal learning and scientific discovery, but chose not to assemble evidence from scattered realms here. They add that the evidence at hand is ill-suited to define the theory's limits.

card.rule: The theory is offered as general because its arguments are broader than the three tasks, but the book's evidence cannot fix its limits.
card.limits: The authors can name some conditions that must hold, such as the memory structures of the adult human IPS, but they do not map the full boundaries.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: The few invariants of the IPS
concepts.question: Which few characteristics of the IPS do the authors say stay the same across problem solvers and tasks?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Chapter 2 gave an IPS with symbols, memories, processors and programs, but that set of assumptions admits arbitrary programs and so arbitrarily varied behavior.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Beyond those assumptions the authors add only a few invariants: (1) the sizes, access characteristics and read and write times of the memories; (2) the serial character of processing and the rate of elementary processes; (3) two invariant aspects of global program organization, its production-like and goal-like character.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Many of these are independently supported by experimental psychology, but the authors do not review that literature, since only gross characterizations matter for problem solving and the literature's detail is too fine.

card.rule: Memories, seriality with rates, and a production-like, goal-like program organization are the invariants the theory adds.
card.limits: Other characteristics are also invariant in humans but are left aside when they do not affect problem solving.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Long-term memory: unlimited and associative
concepts.question: How large is long-term memory and how does it hold information associatively, according to the authors?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The theory must say what long-term memory (LTM) can hold and how items link to each other.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: There is no evidence that LTM can be filled in a lifetime, so the IPS is assumed to have a potentially infinite vocabulary of symbols and an essentially infinite capacity for symbol structures. Associativity comes from storing information as symbol structures, sets of symbols joined by relations. A newly stored structure gets a name drawn from the vocabulary, and that name can be embedded in other structures.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors admit they lack operational specifications of human associative memory, so other forms of association, such as content addressing, may be needed. They judge this form adequate for the tasks studied, even the chess perception data, which involve little processing in LTM.

card.rule: LTM is treated as unlimited and associative: named symbol structures built from symbols joined by relations.
card.limits: The scheme may need extras, such as content addressing, for tasks that make heavy use of LTM.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Chunks: recognizable patterns with one symbol
concepts.question: What is a chunk, and how can many chessmen be a single one for an expert?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Players, readers and solvers treat some complex stimuli as single units. The theory needs a way to say what a unit is in the IPS.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Through learning, certain stimuli or patterns of stimuli from the input channels come to be designated by particular symbols, and so become recognizable. These recognizable stimulus patterns are called chunks. On recognition, a chunk evokes its stored designator, which serves as its internal representation.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Chunks are not innate but develop through learning. For the subjects the letter D, the number 4 and a chess Bishop were chunks. For an experienced chess player, a fianchettoed short-castled position is also one chunk, represented by a single symbol although it is an arrangement of six chessmen.

card.rule: A chunk is a stimulus pattern that learning has made recognizable, with a single symbol standing for it.
card.limits: Chunk size depends on experience, so the same pattern may be one chunk for an expert and many for a novice.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Reading LTM takes a few hundred milliseconds
concepts.question: How long does it take to read a symbol structure from LTM, and does it depend on memory size?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The theory needs the time cost of retrieving information, because the pace of problem solving depends on it.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Reading a symbol structure from LTM takes of the order of a few hundred milliseconds. Reading does not seem to call for scanning, which would make read times proportional to the size of memory.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Reaction-time and recognition experiments support it. Associative reaction times, such as naming a color or giving a superordinate, usually run from half a second to a second or a little more. Times grow somewhat with difficulty and with the size of the retrieval ensemble, but never become much longer; the reactions never take many seconds.

card.rule: Retrieval from LTM takes about a few hundred milliseconds, and it does not grow in proportion to memory size.
card.limits: Repeated attempts to remember something not retrieved at once do not count as a longer access time in this sense.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Writing LTM is slow: 5K to 10K seconds
concepts.question: How long does it take to fixate a new structure in LTM?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Retrieval is quick, but problem solving also needs to store new information. The theory needs its cost.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Storing (fixating) a symbolized internal representation of a stimulus containing K familiar subpatterns, including the ability to recognize the new chunk, takes about 5K to 10K seconds of processing time. That is roughly five to ten seconds per chunk.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Rote-learning data support the figure. Fixation of a low-meaningful nonsense-syllable pair is estimated at about seven new chunks and a serial-list syllable at about four. With these assumptions, experiments by Underwood and Schultz give 8 to 13 seconds per chunk and Hovland about 8 to 10 seconds.

card.rule: Writing in LTM costs about five to ten seconds per chunk, many times the cost of reading.
card.limits: Less is known about this parameter than about reaction times; other studies give lower values.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: How firm is the fixation figure?
concepts.question: What evidence supports five to ten seconds per chunk, and where does it vary?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors rely on a figure from rote-learning studies, but they admit it is not firmly established.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: From several experiments they take five to ten seconds per chunk as the typical fixation time, with some confidence it is correct within half an order of magnitude. Counts of chunks come from the EPAM model: about seven new chunks per low-meaningful nonsense-syllable pair, and about four per serial-list syllable.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Underwood and Schultz found about 8 to 13 seconds per chunk; Hovland about 8 to 10, and a revised count gives 13.3 and 9.3; Bugelski's experiments gave about nine. Ebbinghaus and Lyon, using themselves as subjects, found about two or three seconds per chunk, and mnemonic schemes can give two or three seconds for meaningful words.

card.rule: Five to ten seconds per chunk is the authors' working figure, supported by several studies and contradicted in part by faster self-experiments.
card.limits: The faster results may reflect subject experience or intelligence, or learning methods; the authors do not know which.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Writing is much slower than reading
concepts.question: What does the large difference between writing and reading times in LTM imply for problem solving?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Retrieval is fast and storing is slow. The authors ask what this gap does to the strategies a problem solver can use.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Writing in LTM takes at least a half order or a full order of magnitude, five or ten times, longer than reading it. So although an IPS can fixate some new symbols during a ten-minute problem solving episode, the total will be modest, almost certainly less than fifty.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Most of the IPS's activity is devoted to processes other than fixation. The authors say this difference in reading and writing times has much to do with the problem solving strategies available to a human IPS. They also say little is known of the accessing potentialities fixation creates, except that the learner has little direct control.

card.rule: Because writing to LTM is five to ten times slower than reading, a solver can store only a few new things during a short task.
card.limits: The count of fewer than fifty is a bound for ten-minute episodes, not a general limit on lifelong learning.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Short-term memory holds five to seven symbols
concepts.question: How large is short-term memory and what does each of its slots hold?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Problem solving requires a working store for the immediate inputs and outputs of processes.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The IPS has a short-term memory (STM) of very small capacity. Its contents are a small set of symbols, each of which can designate an entire structure of arbitrary size and complexity in LTM. Capacity is measured in symbols, equivalently chunks.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Digit-span experiments show a capacity of about five to seven symbols, George Miller's seven plus or minus two, and the capacity does not vary much over a wide range of tasks.

card.rule: STM holds about five to seven symbols, each able to stand for a whole structure in LTM.
card.limits: Capacity falls when the person is also doing another task; a symbol is worth as much as the structure it designates.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: STM contents are immediately available
concepts.question: How do the authors define STM functionally, and what do other tasks do to its capacity?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The details of how STM is accessed are unknown, yet the theory needs to say what STM does for processes.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: STM is defined functionally as the set of symbols available to an IPS process at a given instant, immediately and completely. At the problem solving level it makes no difference whether access works by rapid scanning, fixed cells or content addressing. The inputs and outputs of processes are plausibly held in STM at execution time.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The evidence is circumstantial. Only perhaps two symbols can be retained when even a simple task, such as counting backward by threes, comes between presentation and recall, and tasks that need attention reduce the measured capacity. The authors suppose the missing capacity holds process inputs and outputs, possibly a stack of subprocesses.

card.rule: STM is the set of symbols available to processes at an instant, and active processing uses up part of its capacity.
card.limits: The evidence for process inputs and outputs residing in STM is circumstantial; the question has not been posed experimentally.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Decay and rehearsal matter little for problem solving
concepts.question: Why do the authors treat STM decay as unimportant for explaining problem solving, and what error does it leave?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Information in STM decays, which could in principle limit problem solving. The authors ask whether the theory needs a parameter for it.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Decay and rehearsal are details unimportant for explaining problem solving. Problem solving is self-paced, so the solver can adjust rate and style so that he appears neither to have a rapidly decaying STM nor to rehearse. A more reliable STM might permit faster work, but that effect can be absorbed by the parameters for processing speed.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Controversy over whether decay comes from interference or time is called irrelevant here. The authors grant that STM errors, caused perhaps by decay with rehearsal strategies, will be infrequent but can have large effects: S3 spent long on a cryptarithmetic problem because he did not recall that T = 0, so E could not be 0.

card.rule: Self-pacing lets solvers hide STM decay, so no separate decay parameter is needed.
card.limits: Rare STM errors can have large effects and would need an explicit decay model to be predicted rather than taken as outside events.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: The human IPS is a serial system
concepts.question: What does it mean to say the IPS is serial, and what does the claim not mean?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The brain is physiologically highly parallel, so the claim of seriality is often misunderstood and rejected. The authors want to state it carefully.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The human IPS is basically a serial system: it can execute one elementary information process at a time. This does not mean memories are accessed by serial scan, which would make read time proportional to memory size, and it does not mean the IPS cannot be aware of many things at once in the sense of detecting when one of them occurs.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The claim asserts more than the bare logical necessity that behavior is serial when the output of one process is the input of the next. The authors say LTM clearly does not operate by scanning and STM acts as if it does not.

card.rule: A serial IPS runs a single elementary information process at a time, whatever the memories' access methods.
card.limits: Seriality is about processes, not about memory scanning or about awareness of many stimuli.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: A test for seriality: time proportional to K
concepts.question: How can an experiment tell whether an operation is carried out serially?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Seriality is a claim that can be tested by timing.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Take an operation Q that the solver knows well and that yields yes or no for a symbol of a given class. Present K symbols at once and ask for all K answers as fast as possible. If the time is proportional to K, the IPS is serial for Q; if the time does not depend on K, it is parallel for Q.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors' example: decide whether numbers are exactly divisible by 7, for example 35642, then the pair 35642 and 69416. A parallel processor would do the pair as fast as the single number, allowing for the time to state two answers. The authors add that a processor could be parallel for two activities but not three or four.

card.rule: If the answer time rises in proportion to the number of items, the process is serial for that operation.
card.limits: Time to state several answers must be allowed for, and parallelism for two items does not imply it for four.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Where seriality is qualified: automated and motor activity
concepts.question: In which activities does the authors' claim of seriality need qualification?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Everyday activity often looks parallel, so the authors state the limits of the seriality claim.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The human is a completely serial IPS for almost all information processing operations. Uncertainty remains for highly automated activities, where some parallelism appears but with concomitant changes in the actual task being performed. Motor activities can run in parallel when the motor systems are physically independent, but whenever central control is involved, seriality reestablishes itself.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors cite patting one's head with one hand while rubbing the stomach in a clockwise direction with the other, which shows both the extent and the limits of parallelism in motor activity.

card.rule: Seriality holds for almost all processing; automated and physically independent motor activities show limited parallelism.
card.limits: Where parallelism does appear, central control brings seriality back.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Elementary processes take about 40 milliseconds
concepts.question: How fast are the elementary processes, and why does that rate fit with memory access times?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The amount of processing an IPS can do depends on the time each elementary process takes. The authors ask what limits it.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Memory access time sets an ultimate lower bound on processing time, because a process either takes inputs already in STM or gets them from another memory. Access to LTM or the external environment takes about 100 milliseconds, and careful experiments show elementary processes in STM take of the order of 40 milliseconds.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: That duration might be identified with the unit access time from LTM. Processing times slightly shorter than access time yield a balanced system. A footnote argues against a microsecond processing time on evolutionary grounds: the system would sit idle waiting for the next structure from LTM or the display.

card.rule: Elementary processes take about 40 ms, slightly less than memory access, which gives a balanced system.
card.limits: A process that stays within STM avoids access time, but the small STM would soon leave it with only itself to use.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Elementary processes are compare and replace
concepts.question: What are elementary processes like, and how are more complex processes built?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The time that processes take also depends on how much work each does.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The elementary processes, the 40-millisecond ones, seem to be the simplest imaginable compare and replace operations. The small STM implies most involve only one or two input and output symbols. More complex processes involve access to LTM or are divided into sequences of subprocesses, that is, programs.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Someone who knows all two-digit by two-digit products can multiply 37 by 43 almost as fast as 7 by 3 by reading the product from LTM. Someone who knows only the 12 by 12 table must carry out a sequence of digit operations. The authors find no evidence for a third kind of process that computes 37 times 43 entirely within STM.

card.rule: Elementary processes are simple compare and replace steps with one or two symbols; anything larger is either an LTM lookup or a program of subprocesses.
card.limits: The authors cannot select a unique set of basic processes; many alternative bases suffice to build arbitrary programs.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Time for a composite algorithm is a sum
concepts.question: What does the theory say about the time of a composite process, and how well is it confirmed?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: If complex processes are sequences of elementary ones, their time should be predictable.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The time for a composite algorithm can be viewed as the sum of the times of its elementary component processes, given the actual sequence executed.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Empirically the matter is cloudy. Simple linear times appeared for linear searches such as running down the alphabet (Landauer), but composite models of more complex processes ran into difficulties (Olshavsky). One recent study of mental multiplication had some success predicting total times by adding component times, mostly memory transfers (Dansereau). The authors say the evidence is incomplete and do not attempt detailed time accounting.

card.rule: The time of a composite process is the sum of the times of the steps actually executed, though the evidence is incomplete.
card.limits: Success with simple linear searches does not carry over to complex composite processes.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Perceptual detail does not matter for these tasks
concepts.question: Why can the theory ignore most details of sensory processing for the studied tasks?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Humans have separate sensory systems and very short-term sensory stores, and much is known about them. Does the theory of problem solving need all of that?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: None of the problem solving data depend critically on these details. For the purpose of understanding problem solving, the effects of the sensory processes can be summarized simply: externally written letters are recognized directly and produce corresponding internal symbols in STM.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The visual buffer store, found by Sperling's partial-recall tasks, does not matter here because the displays remain visible; the theory need not distinguish retrieval from the display and from the buffer. Recognition of the elements takes perhaps forty or fifty milliseconds and is taken as an unanalyzed primitive process.

card.rule: Because displays stay visible and elements are simple, perception can be summarized as direct recognition producing symbols in STM.
card.limits: The detail might matter for other tasks or for explaining how information is read or written externally.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Simple displays and cultural expectations
concepts.question: What about the three tasks' displays makes pattern-recognition details unlikely to matter?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Visual pattern recognition is complex. The authors argue the studied displays avoid that complexity.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: In all three tasks the displays are simple arrangements of discrete elements that subjects recognize immediately. Their geometry is also simple, and subjects' cultural expectations encode it in standard ways, which gives assurance that unknown properties of visual pattern recognition did not greatly influence behavior.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Cryptarithmetic uses roman letters and arabic numerals in rows and columns; logic uses letters, punctuation and four symbols (horseshoe, wedge, dot, tilde), as horizontal strings readable as trees and arranged in a column; chess is an 8 by 8 board with six types of man, encoded by the sixteen directions of legal moves.

card.rule: Simple discrete elements in familiar layouts make the vision system's finer properties unlikely to influence the behavior studied.
card.limits: The assurance comes from the displays and the subjects' conventions; different displays might not give it.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Central memories are independent of sensory modality
concepts.question: How does the theory treat the sensory modality of stored information?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Information may arrive through sight or hearing. Does the memory structure differ by modality?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The basic structural characteristics of LTM and STM are independent of the original sensory modality of the stored information. The IPS can still distinguish visual from aural stored information, but information acquires its modality not by hardware differentiation in the central structures but by the specific ways these capabilities are used to organize it.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors point to the analysis of chess perception in Chapter 13. They add that there is only modest evidence in the protocols for any role played by sensory modalities in internal encodings, though the external visual stimulus itself played a major role, so programs would need processes for scanning and recognizing the display.

card.rule: Memory structure is the same for all modalities; modality lies in how information is organized, not in separate hardware.
card.limits: Only modest protocol evidence bears on modality; the external display's role was major.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: When is an encoding visual or aural?
concepts.question: By what two criteria can an internal encoding be said to preserve a sensory modality?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: If modality is a matter of organization, how can one tell which modality an encoding has?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: An encoding preserves modality to the extent that (1) externally similar stimuli have similar encodings, and (2) directly related parts of stimuli correspond to internal symbols with directly coded relations, so that external and internal structures are isomorphic.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: For similarity: an encoding of words is aural if taut and taught have identical encodings, and visual if tout and taut are more alike than taut and taught. For relational isomorphism, in Number Scrabble without a display, building a winning triplet from 3 and 9 would show the representation was not visual, since these numbers do not lie in a line in the magic square.

card.rule: An encoding is visual or aural to the extent that its similarities and relations mirror those of the external stimuli.
card.limits: Both criteria are matters of degree, and the protocols give only modest evidence.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: External memory changes the whole problem
concepts.question: How much does an external memory such as paper change problem solving?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: An IPS with only STM and LTM behaves very differently from one that also has external memories (EM) such as paper or a chessboard.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The EM must be specified in the same terms as the internal memories: symbol capacities, accessing characteristics and read and write times (and decay times if relevant). The problem solving program adopted depends on the available EM as intimately as on the built-in STM and LTM.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Multiplying two four-digit numbers with paper and pencil takes about one-hundredth the time of doing it mentally. Chess analysis with the board in view is much easier than blindfold, and DONALD+GERALD is much easier with the display than entirely in the head, even when only scanning, not writing, is allowed.

card.rule: External memory is part of the system: the program a solver uses depends on the external stores available as much as on the internal ones.
card.limits: Specifying the EM is essential for the theory, and the effect is not only due to slow LTM writing.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: STM plus the foveal view acts as one memory
concepts.question: How do the authors redefine STM functionally when a display is in view?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A subject looking at a display can use what is in foveal view without storing it. The authors ask what this does to the idea of STM.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Functionally, STM should be defined not as an internal memory alone but as the combination of the internal STM and the part of the visual display in the subject's foveal view. The foveal part is read-only, but it increases short-term capacity and makes the memory more stable.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors say how the two merge is unclear. It is not known whether information in the display must be read into internal STM and symbolized there, or whether recognized foveal symbols that stay in view are part of STM without further reading. Reaction-time experiments do not decide it, since they involve a change of stimulus that requires a fresh recognition.

card.rule: For a detailed model, STM is the internal short-term store together with the read-only part of the display in foveal view.
card.limits: The extent of the merge is open: it is not known whether a region larger than the fovea, reached by indexed saccades, also counts.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Reading and writing external memory
concepts.question: How do the access and writing times of external memory compare with LTM and STM?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Like LTM, EM must be deliberately accessed, and the theory needs its read and write costs.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: EM is essentially infinite in capacity but not associative: it is accessed by means ranging from linear scanning to random accessing from addresses held in STM. Reading from a fixated domain, or making a saccade to another point, takes a few hundred milliseconds, similar to reading LTM. More remote EMs take longer as motor behavior and distance grow.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Writing in EM is much quicker than the five to ten seconds per symbol for LTM, though slower than writing in STM, and depends on easily recorded external symbols. About a second per symbol for overlearned symbols is typical; the alphabet can be written in under half a second per letter, and typists manage about one word per second. A beginner writing Chinese ideograms for words already known orally would be very slow.

card.rule: EM is read about as fast as LTM and written far faster than LTM, but only when the internal symbols have easy external forms.
card.limits: Writing is slow or problematic if internal symbols lack simple recordable external names.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: How the three tasks' external memories shaped programs
concepts.question: How did the external memory arrangements in chess, cryptarithmetic and logic shape subjects' programs?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The three tasks differed in what the subject could write on the display. The authors ask what difference this made.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: All three tasks had displays larger than could be held in immediate attention, so scanning was an integral part of the programs. Each arrangement of EM profoundly affected the programs used, and the inferred programs incorporate searches of the EM. A program cannot be specified independently of its EM.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In chess no writing was allowed (the touch-move rule), and progressive deepening, returning to the initial position and retracing, stands out. In cryptarithmetic the blackboard held digits written beside letters; other information such as parity could not be recorded. In logic new expressions were annexed without erasing earlier ones.

card.rule: The EM differs by task, and each difference shows in the strategies subjects adopt.
card.limits: The link between progressive deepening and no writing is the authors' interpretation within these tasks, not a general law.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Why program organization is discussed at all
concepts.question: Why do the authors discuss program organization even though any language can express the same behavior?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The book used many programming techniques: flow control, subroutines, recursion, iteration, local naming, production systems and interpreters. Does the evidence narrow the choice?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Few experimental data beyond the book bear on this. From one viewpoint the question is as irrelevant as perceptual organization, since all programming languages have about the same expressive power. The authors still discuss it for two reasons.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: First, to discuss problem solving methods in detail one must adopt some language. Second, the representation may have second-order effects, such as making it easier to identify the program in use or to understand learning and assembling of programs. A footnote says language differences lie in naming, data structures and memory allocation, which are irrelevant given associative LTM and fully accessible STM.

card.rule: Program organization cannot be ignored: a language is needed to discuss methods, and it can have second-order effects.
card.limits: The choice of language does not change what behaviors can be produced.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Productions: calculation, homogeneity, easy growth
concepts.question: What three first advantages do the authors list for production systems?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors have a strong premonition that human programs resemble production systems, but cannot prove it. They list features that make productions an appropriate construct.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: (1) A production system can express arbitrary calculations, so it gives the IPS the capabilities we know it has. (2) It encodes the instructing information homogeneously, whereas a flow diagram splits program information into box contents and flow structure. (3) Each production is independent, a fragment of potential behavior, so composition is simple: make a new production and add it.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors list these without explicit support, saying ultimate verification may depend on the organization proving satisfactory in many small ways. Production systems are the most homogeneous form of programming organization known, and they offer simple ways to grow naturally from incremental experience.

card.rule: Production systems can compute anything, store behavior in one uniform format, and grow by adding independent productions.
card.limits: These are plausibility arguments, not proof; ordering of productions can add some further information.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Productions: the S-R kernel and meaningful parts
concepts.question: How do the authors relate productions to stimulus-response theory and to meaningful components?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors want to place productions relative to older stimulus-response (S-R) psychology and to show that productions are not arbitrary fragments.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: A production has a strong stimulus-response flavor, but identifying the two is overly simple, because productions also have matching, operand identification and subroutine calling that ordinary S-R formulations lack. Productions might express the kernel of truth in the S-R position. Productions also seem to be meaningful components of the problem solving process, not just odd program fragments.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors concede that the meaningful-component finding is partly because the scientists sought to define productions that way, but say it remains true that an organization of meaningful pieces describes the data, and promise further support later in the chapter.

card.rule: A production is like a stimulus-response pair with extra machinery, and the productions found correspond to meaningful steps.
card.limits: The meaningfulness is partly a product of how the authors defined productions, so it is weaker support than it first appears.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Productions: STM as working memory, control in STM
concepts.question: How does a production system tie the program to STM, and how is control handled?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Other program organizations contain unexplained machinery. The authors ask which one connects best to psychological constructs such as STM.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: In a production system the dynamic working memory, the memory on which productions are contingent and which they modify, is the STM. This fits the functional definition of STM as what the subject is aware of at a moment. Matching, operand definition, subroutining and control flow remain to be specified, but all seem amenable to explanation.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: If each production has a single action operator, a sequence such as FC followed by PC in cryptarithmetic is shorthand for an iteration through STM in which the first production outputs a unique linking symbol identifying the next stage. The subroutine pointer stack then consists of linking symbols in STM, so almost all control is assimilated to STM. The gap between organization and the psychology of immediate memory seems smaller than for other organizations.

card.rule: In a production system the working memory is STM and control can be carried by linking symbols in STM.
card.limits: Awareness here means only that behavior can depend on the information, not that the subject can report it.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Might LTM itself be a production system?
concepts.question: What intriguing possibility do the authors raise about LTM and productions?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Normally programs and data are separate. The authors ask whether human LTM might hold facts apart from the productions.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: There is an intriguing possibility that a production system offers a viable model of LTM: perhaps there is no LTM for facts distinct from the production system, no basic distinction between data and program, and LTM is only a very large production system. Then taking a new item into LTM would be equivalent to creating a new production or productions.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: This is offered as a suggestion, explored further in the section on the determination of programs. Retrieval from LTM would then be just selecting a production from memory, the most obvious way to arrange it.

card.rule: LTM may be one very large production system, so learning an item means creating a production.
card.limits: The authors present this as a possibility, not a conclusion.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Productions balance stimulus-bound and independent activity
concepts.question: How can a production system seem both stimulus-bound and stimulus-independent?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Critics have said that programming models are overly focused and nondistractable, as if always bound to a stimulus.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: A production system is totally stimulus-bound if stimulus means the contents of the dynamic working memory, since all connection between adjacent actions is mediated by it. But that stimulus is neither internal nor external, because STM combines the internal short-term store with the foveal parts of the visual field plus symbols just stored upon recognition of external stimuli.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: If most productions react to internally produced symbols, the system appears not to be stimulus-bound; if almost all take an external symbol in their condition, it appears very stimulus-bound. The nondistractable character that critics such as Reitman and Neisser attributed to programming models is therefore not structural but depends on the productions the system contains.

card.rule: Whether a production system looks stimulus-bound depends on whether its productions respond to internal or external symbols.
card.limits: Sequential action parts break the pure stimulus-boundness, but can be eliminated by linking symbols.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: What productions make of the elementary processes
concepts.question: What do discriminating, creating and reading amount to in a production system?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Adopting production systems makes the elementary processes more definite.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Discriminating becomes selecting the next production, that is, matching the conditions of productions to the contents of STM, with selectivity as broad as the number of productions. Symbol structures are created when a production places a new expression in STM, perhaps assembled from parts of existing expressions found by matching. The elementary read operation is extracting those parts.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: It would be hard to tell whether new expressions were freshly created or generated by modifying old contents: with (A = 4 new) then (A = 4), the tag may have been deleted or another expression created. No shuffling processes within STM are needed, since matching treats STM as content-addressed. Writing in LTM and reading and writing EM lie outside what the data can specify.

card.rule: In a production system, discriminating is matching conditions to STM, creating is placing an expression in STM, and reading is extracting parts by matching.
card.limits: Writing in LTM and EM operations are not specified by the book's data.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: The authors' judgment on production systems
concepts.question: How firmly do the authors recommend production systems as the form of program organization?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Several of the advantages are untested, and some of the arguments raise difficulties.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The authors do not think a conclusive case can be made yet for production systems as the appropriate form of program organization. Nevertheless, they judge that production systems should be the preferred language for expressing programs and program organization, and they use it for the rest of the chapter.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The case is cumulative: verification may depend on the organization proving relatively satisfactory in many small ways, none decisive. Few experimental data beyond the book bear on program organization, since such questions have not yet been posed experimentally.

card.rule: Production systems are chosen as the preferred language for programs, though the case is not conclusive.
card.limits: Using the language does not commit the authors to the claim that human programs are productions.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: A goal is a symbol structure with a test and control
concepts.question: What makes goal-directed behavior structural rather than just apparent?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Human behavior is clearly goal-directed, and the book has assumed so throughout. The open question is whether goal-directedness has structural significance in the IPS, since teleological behavior can arise in many ways, as when water seeks its own level or a stone falls.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The authors postulate that the IPS has goals, where a goal is a symbol structure with two characteristics: it carries a test to determine when some state of affairs has been attained, in which case the goal is satisfied; and it can control behavior under appropriate conditions, evoking patterns of behavior (methods) that stand in a rational relation to the goal.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The test may itself be a symbol structure fed to a testing process defined elsewhere. The authors say they have no good empirical information about the variety of goals, which may differ mostly in how desired situations are specified. The key issue is whether goals are incorporated in symbolic structures or the equivalent behavior is encoded into the program in other ways.

card.rule: A system has goals in the structural sense only if a symbol structure carrying a test and control power exists in it.
card.limits: Directed behavior that arises without any such goal structure does not count as having goals in this sense.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Goals in cryptarithmetic: P1 versus P2
concepts.question: How do two cryptarithmetic productions differ in whether they use an explicit goal?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The book offers examples of both goal-using and non-goal behavior. The authors contrast two productions from cryptarithmetic.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: P1 says: given a new piece of information about a letter, find an occurrence of that letter and try to use the information. The subject appears to have a goal of using new information, but internally no data structure is the goal; a single production produces the behavior.
