P2 says: to get the value of a letter, go to an occurrence of the letter and process its column.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The to-get condition in P2 is satisfied only if an explicit symbol structure exists that can be interpreted as the goal of obtaining a letter's value. A system containing P2 uses goals.

card.rule: P1 produces goal-like behavior without a goal structure; P2 needs an explicit goal structure in STM.
card.limits: From behavior alone the two cannot always be told apart; one must look at the program.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: What having goals demands of the IPS
concepts.question: What must a program contain if the IPS uses goals, and what behavior do goals produce?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Using goals has real consequences for the structure of the IPS, and the authors ask how to distinguish goal behavior from other directed behavior.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: If there are goals, the program must contain processes for creating, testing, updating, selecting methods for, evoking and discarding them. All criteria for goal behavior rest on the fact that the symbolized goal gives the system a way to remember both that it has a goal and where it is along the way.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Other systems of directed behavior are more stimulus-bound, since they keep no explicit data on progress toward goals. A key behavioral feature of goals is therefore that they produce correlations of behavior over long time intervals. A footnote adds the general principle that the data types of an IPS imply that the operations proper to them must be in its repertoire.

card.rule: Goals require processes to manage them and make behavior at different times correlated through remembered progress.
card.limits: Not all directed activity needs goal structures; other systems are more stimulus-bound.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Six criteria for a goal-directed IPS
concepts.question: What six behaviors show that an IPS is goal-directed?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Directed behavior must be told apart from behavior that merely looks directed.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Six criteria: interruptibility (after a distraction the IPS returns to directed activity at the same point); subgoaling (the IPS interrupts its activity to do a means to the goal, then returns and uses the result); depth-first subgoaling (subgoaling several levels deep, particularly conclusive); equifinality (if one method fails, another toward the same goal is tried); avoidance of repetition (memory of attempts prevents repeating); consummation (effort ends when the goal is attained).

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors say the evidence for goal activity is abundant in the protocols studied. Each criterion depends on the symbolized goal giving the system a memory of where it stands.

card.rule: Interruptibility, subgoaling, depth-first subgoaling, equifinality, avoidance of repetition and consummation mark goal-directed behavior.
card.limits: Fulfilling the criteria in protocols does not mean all directed activity is done through goal structures.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: The IPS has goal structures, but not all direction does
concepts.question: What do the authors conclude about goals in the human IPS and in directed activity?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Abundant evidence of goal activity could tempt a reader to say all directed behavior uses goals.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The authors conclude that the human IPS invariably has goal structures. They warn that it must not be assumed that all or most directed activity is achieved by means of goal structures.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The evidence for goal activity is abundant in the protocols. The P1 case shows behavior that looks goal-directed but is produced by a single production without a goal data structure.

card.rule: The IPS has goal structures, but much directed behavior can arise from productions that carry no goal.
card.limits: Observed direction is not proof of a goal structure.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: The IPS characteristics in summary
concepts.question: What eight characteristics of the human IPS influence its problem solving programs?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The section collected many details. The authors summarize those that influence programs for problem solving.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: (1) A serial system with a processor, input and output systems, LTM, STM and EM. (2) LTM unlimited and associative, writing K familiar symbols in about 5K to 10K seconds, reading in a few hundred milliseconds. (3) STM about five to seven symbols, two retained during an unrelated task, all available to processes. (4) STM and LTM homogeneous across modalities. (5) Elementary processes about fifty milliseconds, overall rate limited by read rates from LTM and EM. (6) EM access about a hundred milliseconds, reads about fifty, writes about a second for overlearned symbols. (7) Production system with conditions on STM plus foveal EM. (8) Goal structures.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Each item is developed and supported earlier in the section; the numbers are order-of-magnitude estimates.

card.rule: A serial processor with unlimited slow-to-write LTM, tiny STM, helpful EM, productions and goals.
card.limits: The numbers are estimates of order, not exact constants.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Problem solving takes place by search in a problem space
concepts.question: What does it mean to say problem solving is search in a problem space, and what does the claim not say?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors want to state the central invariant of problem solving behavior across tasks and subjects.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Problem solving takes place by search in a problem space. Over the range of tasks and individuals studied, a problem space is always used. This does not mean all behavior relevant to problem solving is such search: a problem must first be recognized and understood, a space constructed or, if one exists in LTM, evoked, and spaces can be changed during solving. These activities need not themselves be searches in a problem space.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Chapter 3 stayed neutral between a set-predicate formulation and a search formulation and left other formulations open. The evidence from the three tasks indicates that a human preferentially uses the search formulation.

card.rule: Humans preferentially formulate problems as search in a problem space, though recognizing, building and changing the space are not themselves such search.
card.limits: The authors do not know what part of all human problem solving uses a problem space; the claim holds over the tasks and individuals studied.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: The five parts of a problem space
concepts.question: What are the five components in the definition of a problem space?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The problem space was introduced loosely in Chapter 3; the authors now give a precise definition.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: A problem space consists of: (1) a set U of elements, symbol structures each representing a state of knowledge about the task; (2) a set Q of operators, information processes that produce new states of knowledge from existing ones; (3) an initial state of knowledge u0; (4) a problem, posed by specifying a set G of final desired states to be reached by applying operators from Q; (5) the total knowledge available to the solver in a given knowledge state.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors illustrate with chess: the elements are positions, the operators are moves, the initial state is the given position, and the final state depends on evaluations but is related to checkmate.

card.rule: A problem space is states, operators, an initial state, a goal set, and the knowledge available at each state.
card.limits: The final states may be given by evaluations rather than listed, as in chess.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: What the solver knows in a state: six layers
concepts.question: What kinds of knowledge are available to the solver in a knowledge state, from most transient to most stable?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Part five of the definition lumps all available knowledge together. The authors split it by how long it lasts.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: From most transient to most stable: (a) temporary dynamic information used only within one knowledge state; (b) the knowledge state itself, the dynamic information about the task; (c) access information to further structures in LTM or EM, the extended knowledge state; (d) path information about how the state was reached and what was tried in it before; (e) access information to other knowledge states reached earlier; (f) reference information that is constant during solving.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In chess: temporary information is where a move generator stands in listing defenders; path information includes that Bishop moves in this position were already looked at; constant information includes the conventional piece values in LTM; the extended state is the static relations not yet extracted from the displayed board.

card.rule: Available knowledge ranges from transient scratch information to stable reference facts, with path and access information in between.
card.limits: The extended knowledge state holds only access information, not the structures themselves.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Available means forthcoming when called for
concepts.question: What does 'available' mean, and why must the solver hold access information for other states?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The definition says the total knowledge is available to the solver. The authors qualify the word.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Available means the information may be used in decision processes or in applying operators and will be forthcoming if called for. The knowledge state itself is directly available, but the extended knowledge state offers only access information.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Similarly the solver does not have the information in other states he might go to if he abandoned the current one, but he has access information enabling him to recall them; otherwise he could never get to them.

card.rule: Available information is usable on call; extended and other states are reached through access information only.
card.limits: Access information being present does not guarantee the retrieval succeeds.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Invariants: small, finite spaces
concepts.question: Which invariant features say problem spaces are small and finite?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors list eight generalizations that hold for the tasks and subjects studied.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Four concern size. (1) The knowledge states are generated from a finite set of objects, relations and properties, so they form a closed space of knowledge. (2) The set of operators is small and finite, or at least finitely generated. (3) The set of alternative nodes the solver might return to is very small, usually one or two. (8) The knowledge state is of moderate size, at most a few hundred symbols and more typically a few dozen.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: These are postulated as invariant features of problem spaces used by humans for the tasks and subjects studied, and later related to the memory and processing characteristics of the IPS.

card.rule: Human problem spaces are closed, with few operators, few return points and knowledge states of a few dozen symbols.
card.limits: These are generalizations over the studied tasks, not logical necessities.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Invariants: seconds per state, tens of minutes per space
concepts.question: Which invariants concern time and the manner of search?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Besides size, the invariant features describe duration and the way search proceeds.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: (4) Residence time in each knowledge state before generating the next is of the order of seconds. (5) The solver remains within a given problem space for at least tens of minutes. (6) Problem solving is search: considering one knowledge state after another until a desired one is reached, with moves mostly incremental. (7) Search involves backup, returning from time to time to old knowledge states and abandoning knowledge-state information, though not necessarily path information.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: These generalizations hold for the tasks and subjects studied. The authors then relate the space and its regularities to the characteristics of the IPS.

card.rule: Spaces are occupied for tens of minutes, each state for seconds, with incremental moves and occasional backup.
card.limits: Abandoned states give up their dynamic information but may keep path information.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Measured residence times: two to eight seconds
concepts.question: What do the measured residence times in Table 14.1 show?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The claim that residence times are seconds needs data from the three tasks.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: From protocol data, the time between moves that change current knowledge is typically of the order of seconds. Table 14.1 gives averages from 1.9 seconds to 7.7 seconds.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: S2 on CROSS+ROADS: 1.9 s; S5 on DONALD+GERALD: 5.6 s; S2 on chess position A: 6.2 s; S8 on logic problem D1: 7.7 s. The lowest came from protocol plus eye-movement data and allowed finer analysis, including recall operators. Each average is total time divided by total number of nodes in the PBG, for a few subjects only, as an order-of-magnitude estimate.

card.rule: Average residence times in a knowledge state run from about two to eight seconds across the three tasks.
card.limits: The averages cover only a few subjects and serve as order-of-magnitude estimates.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.section: Residence Times and the Size of the Knowledge State
concepts.title: Where the current knowledge state lives
concepts.question: Given seconds per state, where can the knowledge state be stored?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A move between states generally means storing new information. Write times then say where the state can be held.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: In very short intervals, under about 100 milliseconds, symbols can be stored only in STM, where most within-state temporary symbols also reside. Over several seconds, symbols can also be stored in LTM or EM. The knowledge state is thus the content of STM together with a small quantity in LTM and a variable amount in EM.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: At about five seconds per node, little can go into LTM, which needs about 5K seconds to fixate K symbols, but something can, especially if knowledge is incremental. Subjects add to EM only sporadically in these tasks, but with marked effect. Someone solving equations or writing a program writes almost continuously, putting much of the state in EM.

card.rule: The knowledge state is STM plus a small part in LTM plus a variable part in EM.
card.limits: Tasks that encourage constant writing, like equations or programming, put much more of the state in EM.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.section: Residence Times and the Size of the Knowledge State
concepts.title: Availability and the extended knowledge state
concepts.question: Why do the authors need an extended knowledge state larger than the immediate one?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The state must be available when the solver chooses the next move. Is everything in memory actually available?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Information in STM is immediately available. Part of the state in LTM is retrievable within a few hundred milliseconds on simple recognition, and the situation favors recall because the information is recent and in context, though without absolute assurance (S3's failure to recall T = 0). Information in EM is part of STM while in foveal view; outside it, scanning programs are needed to guarantee availability.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Human behavior in logic and chess suggests EM access is by specific searches triggered by specific conditions, except for initial orientation. So an extended knowledge state is defined, larger than the immediate state, accessible selectively during residence at one node. The immediate state is kept small by availability while the extended state may grow.

card.rule: The immediate state stays small to remain available; the extended state can grow because it is reached by selective access.
card.limits: Retrieval of LTM parts is likely but not guaranteed.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.section: Residence Times and the Size of the Knowledge State
concepts.title: EM works with an index in LTM
concepts.question: Why does a large external memory need an internal index?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: External memory is quick to write but slow to search; LTM is the reverse. The authors consider how the two cooperate.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The most severe limit on LTM is the five-second-per-symbol write time; the most severe limit on EM is the search time to find a relevant item. So it is sometimes efficient to store information in EM because it can be recorded rapidly and to store index entries, that is access information, in LTM so the EM can be read quickly. An EM of more than very modest size is almost useless without a complementary internal index.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: A physical limit also applies: when the blackboard is full, nothing more can be written unless something is erased. A footnote notes that recognition is a powerful selective accessing mechanism for internal memory, which explains why the internal knowledge state is limited far less than the EM part.

card.rule: Put bulk information in EM and the quick index in LTM; large EM without an index is nearly useless.
card.limits: Physical space in the EM is also a limit.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Why residence times are seconds, not minutes
concepts.question: Why do the authors expect the time per knowledge state to be seconds rather than minutes?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Why not spend several minutes choosing each operator?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: During residence the IPS explores the extended knowledge state and then selects and executes an operator. The operators actually used are characteristically algorithmic subroutines, such as applying a rule in logic or processing a column in cryptarithmetic, which take a few seconds. A long search through a large knowledge state commits a lot of time to deciding, rather than to many small decisions each on a new base of information.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The problematic character of the task situations argues against the long preparation, since the solver's information is not shaped precisely enough to profit from it. A better balance between decision times and operator execution times uses the serial processing capacity better and implies residence times of seconds.

card.rule: Many small incremental decisions, each on fresh information, use serial capacity better than long deliberation.
card.limits: This is a heuristic argument, not a proof.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Why knowledge does not simply accumulate in one state
concepts.question: Why does search return to earlier states instead of growing a single cumulative state?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Problem solving surely accumulates knowledge, so one might expect a single growing state with no returns. LTM does work that way over a lifetime.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The observed organization is instead discrete current knowledge states with limited backup. The reason lies in the IPS: STM is too small to hold a continually growing state; assigning the accumulation to EM would make access cost grow unacceptably; accumulating in LTM avoids that but at large time costs of storing.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Search often returns to earlier states, which would not be needed with a single cumulative state. The authors contrast problem solving with the way LTM grows week by week without returning to earlier ignorance.

card.rule: Memory limits force problem solving into discrete states with backup rather than one ever-growing state.
card.limits: LTM itself is cumulative; the argument concerns the working knowledge state.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Memory requirements for backup
concepts.question: Why can a solver return to only one or two earlier states?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Solvers do return to earlier states, yet not to every node visited.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: At any point in search only one or two nodes are commonly available as backup. Alternative states must be held in LTM or EM, since STM is preempted by the current state and transient information, and the limiting factor is how many such states can be recorded in the available time.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The IPS could spend most of its time storing states, but only by slowing its exploration and discovery of new information. The programs studied avoid this expense and so have only rudimentary backup capabilities.

card.rule: Recording states costs time, so programs keep only one or two return points.
card.limits: Cryptarithmetic in the basic space may involve almost no backup at all.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Why keep any ability to go back
concepts.question: Why is a system with some capacity to return to earlier states more efficient?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Memory limits explain why the knowledge state stays small, but not why any states are kept for returning.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: A system that can return to earlier states is usually more efficient. A knowledge state may contain false information from processing or recall errors, or conditional information, assumptions made deliberately to work out consequences (conditional assignments in cryptarithmetic, alternative chess moves). If an error is found, everything implicated may need to be dropped; if a hypothesis proves infeasible or undesirable, all inferences that depend on it should be removed.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Some organizations need no backup: in the basic cryptarithmetic space a contradiction could be resolved by changing assignments in any order, so order information need not be kept (S6 to some extent). Purging irrelevant information also pays, since search costs rise with state size, like odd pages of a draft best put in the wastebasket.

card.rule: Backup lets the solver drop errors and rejected assumptions along with everything that depended on them.
card.limits: Where order of assignments does not matter, backup is not needed.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: How backup is done: dropping out and external records
concepts.question: By what mechanisms can a solver return to an earlier state?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Returning to a previous state can be easy or hard depending on how the knowledge is held.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: If the state is a collection of symbol structures, each expressing part of the whole, abandoning some simply drops them out and the IPS automatically returns to a prior state, which need not be stored separately. In EM this means erasing or discarding the workspace; in STM symbols can apparently be written over; in LTM elimination seems subject to little if any systematic program control, perhaps only through loss of the recognition that indexes it.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: A different kind of backup is provided by external displays such as the chessboard, which record the initial problem state for confident recovery. Whether a permanent external display of the initial state exists may largely determine the backup procedure adopted.

card.rule: Backup works by dropping symbol structures or by recovering the initial state from an external display.
card.limits: Humans have little systematic control over eliminating information from LTM.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Noncumulative memories: the 15-puzzle
concepts.question: Why is a noncumulative representation like the 15-puzzle display hard to back up in?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Some tasks store the knowledge state so that earlier states cannot be recovered from it.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: In the basic cryptarithmetic space, a move replaces one piece of information with another, so the earlier state is not recoverable from the display, nor at all unless path information is kept elsewhere. The 15-puzzle is a pure example: a state changes by sliding a block next to the empty space into it, and the aim is to reach the numbered order.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Doing it mentally is extremely hard because the number of blocks is too large for STM, so most people manipulate the display. Their knowledge state then consists almost entirely of the current display, and return depends on remembering a few recent moves in STM and undoing them with inverse operations.

card.rule: When each move overwrites the display, the past is lost unless the solver remembers recent moves and undoes them.
card.limits: Ability to return is limited to the few most recent moves held in STM.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Models and descriptions as poles of representation
concepts.question: How do a model and a description differ as ways of representing a knowledge state?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A knowledge state can be held so that earlier states are easy or hard to recover. The authors distinguish two poles of representation.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: A model, typified by the 15-puzzle, the chessboard and a cryptarithmetic display holding the current assignments, is a vector of fixed dimensionality. A move changes the value of one or more components, so earlier states are recoverable only if prior values and path information, or the change operators and their inverses, are kept. A description, typified by the display of initial and derived expressions in the logic task, is a set of statements whose conjunction describes the current extended state and whose validity is unconditional.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In a description, statements known at one node may be unknown at another but are not false there, so descriptions cumulate and need no erasing. Model elements can be read as statements only if made conditional, for instance by subscripting with the node's name. The chess mating program of Chapter 13 used retained inverse operators to back up in a model.

card.rule: A model is overwritten by each move and needs extra information to go back; a description cumulates statements that stay true.
card.limits: Real knowledge states mix both, and a model's representation of the present is independent of the route that led to it.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Where models and descriptions occur in memory
concepts.question: Which parts of a knowledge state tend to be descriptive and which model-like?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: An actual knowledge state can combine model and descriptive aspects.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The part held in LTM is apt to be descriptive, partly because some order information is almost always recorded with it and partly because there are no systematic erasing mechanisms such as a model requires. The part in EM, especially a formatted display, is likely to be a model. If the memory has ordering properties, such as a list on paper, a description's elements are usually entered in the order added, so earlier states can be recovered by ignoring later items.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: There are exceptions: a problem small enough to solve in the head with STM alone is most apt to be represented by a model, and the external display in the logic problems is description-like.

card.rule: LTM tends to be descriptive, formatted displays tend to be models, with exceptions on both sides.
card.limits: These are tendencies; small problems held in STM are model-like, and logic displays are description-like.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Short-run moves ride on long-run cumulation
concepts.question: How are moves within a problem related to long-term learning?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Within a problem, knowledge states are abandoned and revisited. Over days or years, knowledge simply accumulates.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Because EM can accumulate information indefinitely, the immediate and extended knowledge states had to be distinguished. Over periods much longer than a problem, an indefinite amount can accumulate in LTM, and the IPS does not return to earlier states. This longer-run cumulation goes by many names: learning, education, training, experience. No sharp line separates short-run changes (moves) from long-run changes (learning).

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Search should be thought of as a short-run component of exploring and returning riding atop a slower, gradual cumulation. The time scales of the experiments gave little evidence of this two-level movement, though some effects of learning appeared in logic, and the authors assert with reasonable assurance that it occurs generally.

card.rule: Exploring and returning within a session ride on top of a slower accumulation we call learning.
card.limits: The book's short experiments show little of the two-level movement.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: The problem space is empirically closed
concepts.question: What does closure of the problem space mean, and why is it not trivial?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A person has an essentially infinite LTM and access to a vast external environment, yet a solver usually uses only a small part of either. The authors call this closure.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The space is closed, empirically and approximately and not formally, under the operations that transform one current knowledge state into another. On exposure to a task a collection of symbol structures and processes is evoked; these define what can be noticed and done. If the IPS is a production system, they are the conditions and actions of its productions, and because that set is finite, so is the space, at least initially.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The hypothesis for why it stays finite: the information produced by problem solving is all of a piece with the information initially evoked and has no associations, via the productions, to other materials that would enlarge the space. If only algebraic operations are applied to algebraic expressions, only algebraic expressions result, which evoke only algebraic operations. Closure is akin to functional fixity.

card.rule: The solver's knowledge states stay within what the task evoked, because their contents evoke only more of the same kind.
card.limits: Closure is empirical and approximate; no absolute bar keeps the solver from going outside.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: When closure fails and why it matters
concepts.question: When might a task escape closure, and why does the concept of a problem space depend on it?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: If closure is only empirical, there should be tasks where it fails.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: In the tasks examined, closure was the rule. But one can conceive of tasks where a program is evoked that causes extensive search through LTM (free association), physical search of the environment (a manned landing on the Moon) or of a library (browsing). Only with at least approximate closure is it useful, or even operationally meaningful, to say that problem solving takes place in a problem space.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: S8 in cryptarithmetic spent forty minutes exploring alternative methods before settling into the standard augmented problem space. The concept lets one mark off a small portion of internal and external memory and information sources and postulate that outside the boundary is irrelevant: the processes will never, or seldom, carry thought past it.

card.rule: A problem space is meaningful only when thinking seldom crosses its boundaries; open-ended search breaks closure.
card.limits: Closure was the rule only in the tasks examined; the authors warn against extrapolation.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Closure keeps the production system small
concepts.question: Why can a relatively small production system describe a solver, and where does analysis stop?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A solver has far more productions in LTM than any analysis can list. How can a relatively small system describe behavior?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Closure of the space permits a relatively small production system to guide, or from the psychologist's viewpoint to describe, the behavior. The exact size is not an important descriptive parameter, though it must be small enough to be discovered and analyzed. Additional productions come into use with every significant new variety in the task environment, and analysis stops where the frequency of evoking a production is too low.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Figures 6.10 and 7.29 show diminishing marginal explanatory utility of successive cryptarithmetic productions. The subject surely has others, especially for error conditions, that went undetected; in chess the catalog of move-generation productions (Table 12.2) was insufficient for an entire game. A context may select a subset of LTM productions as the operative system, but the study does not identify the mechanism.

card.rule: A small production system suffices because later productions are evoked too rarely to matter; analysis stops by frequency.
card.limits: The catalog is incomplete, and the mechanisms that select context are unknown.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.section: When Does the Problem Space Exist?
concepts.title: A skilled multiplier: is that problem solving?
concepts.question: Does a skilled person doing long multiplication on paper count as having a problem space and goals?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Whenever behavior stays within a closed space, is it useful to call the space a problem space? The authors illustrate with multiplying 1492 by 1762 on paper.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: A problem space can be described: all complete and incomplete arrays of the familiar layout, with carries held briefly in STM. One could name subgoals such as one-digit multiplications, shifting left and a final addition. But for a reasonably skilled subject that goal description would not be a veridical analysis: a protocol would show no goal statements or explicit goal structures, and in common sense he follows a well-learned algorithm mechanically.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: If interrupted after the second multiplication he would probably resume; if interrupted in the middle of a multiplication he would redo it all, not trusting STM to hold the carry. So acceptable interruption points are where no essential information is held in STM.

card.rule: The skilled multiplier has a describable space, but goals and problem solving are not a veridical description of what he does.
card.limits: A schoolchild might show traces of a verbal recipe, so mechanization is a matter of degree.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.section: When Does the Problem Space Exist?
concepts.title: From recipe to mechanized algorithm, and understanding
concepts.question: Through what stages does a learner pass in mastering an algorithm, and how does understanding relate to them?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The same problem space describes performance at different levels of mastery. The authors outline the typical development for algorithms like square roots or casting out nines.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Four stages: (1) the algorithm is followed step by step from a recipe stored in EM; (2) the recipe is memorized, but still executed by step-by-step interpretation; (3) the memorized recipe is mechanized, compiled in the internal language of programs and executed directly without interpretation; (4) independently, an understanding of why it works may be acquired.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: High mechanization can occur without understanding, and high understanding can occur while still following an external recipe (likely only for elaborate algorithms such as the simplex method). Understanding likely affects recovery from error or interruption, the ease of retaining the algorithm, and flexibility in using shortcuts; high mechanization may inhibit special procedures for special cases.

card.rule: Mastery runs from external recipe to interpreted memory to compiled program, with understanding developing separately.
card.limits: The same problem space describes behavior at every stage.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.section: When Does the Problem Space Exist?
concepts.title: Programmed versus unprogrammed activity
concepts.question: What do the authors call behavior governed by a specific algorithm, and how does it differ from problem solving?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: When a subject executes a specific algorithm mechanically and with few errors, it adds little to say he is problem solving.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Such behavior can be called programmed activity. It takes place in problem spaces, but is distinguished, at least as a matter of degree, from unprogrammed activity: less stereotyped and mechanized behavior, involving search and backup, which this book treats as problem solving.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The algorithm has been tailored to guarantee solution of problems of its class, to operate smoothly within the limits of the IPS and its EM aids, and to avoid search as much as possible. So the phenomena that make problem solving interesting are unlikely to appear. The authors cite March and Simon (1958) for the distinction.

card.rule: Programmed activity follows a specific algorithm with little search; unprogrammed activity searches and backs up.
card.limits: The two differ in degree, not by a sharp line.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.section: When Does the Problem Space Exist?
concepts.title: Plans are programs
concepts.question: How are plans like algorithms, and how do programmed and unprogrammed behavior mix in using them?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Problem solving in the context of a plan resembles executing a specialized algorithm.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Plans are structurally identical to programs: symbolic structures available in LTM or EM, used to guide action in exploring the problem space. They involve the same kind of commitment as following an algorithm like the simplex method: some prior activity, the development of the plan, yields a conviction that it is worth pursuing, and then implementation activity carries it out.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Plans like those in the logic task range from two-step affairs to lengthy sequences. There is no rigid boundary between searching in the problem space (unprogrammed activity) and following a predetermined plan (programmed activity). The two are so interwoven that the authors treat both as interrelated components of problem solving.

card.rule: A plan is a program devised by prior activity and then executed; planning and searching are interwoven.
card.limits: No rigid boundary separates searching from following a plan.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Consistency, not derivation, of space and IPS
concepts.question: What did the discussion of the problem space show about the IPS, and what did it not prove?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors tried to link the problem space regularities to the basic IPS characteristics.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: They discussed most of the regularities listed at the start of the section, silent only on the nature of path information, and tried to show their consistency with the IPS characteristics, making plausible that problem solving takes the form of search through a problem space.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: They did not derive the problem space from the IPS in the sense of showing that, for this kind of IPS, searching a problem space is necessary. A proof, even if it exists, is beyond current understanding: it would need a representation of the set of all possible programs accomplishing given functions under specified structural limits, and none is known.

card.rule: The problem space is shown to be consistent with and plausible given the IPS, not logically derived from it.
card.limits: A derivation would need a way to represent all programs meeting given functions under given limits, which is unavailable.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: The task environment delimits possible problem spaces
concepts.question: What do the two symmetric propositions say about the relation between task structure and problem space?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors want to show the structure of the space is largely determined by the structure of the task environment. Chapter 3 stressed that no objective, vantage-free description of a task environment is possible, so the thesis is restated symmetrically.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The thesis: the task environment delimits the set of possible structures of the problem space, though nothing forces a space to incorporate all aspects of the task, and all spaces are abstractions from it. Two propositions: (1) the only aspects of the task environment relevant to solving in a particular space are those reflected in that space's structure; (2) the effectiveness of a problem solving scheme depends wholly on its reflecting aspects of the task structure.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The second proposition is obvious, since problems lie in the objective task environment and only information about it can bear on their solution. The first is shown whenever behavior is described as taking place in a problem space, as in the earlier chapters. The task now is to show how structural information is embedded in the space and used.

card.rule: Only what a space reflects of the task matters to solving in it, and a scheme works only as far as it reflects task structure.
card.limits: Spaces are abstractions; the task structure fixes possibilities, not which are realized.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: A tic-tac-toe isomorph: a nine-by-nine game tree
concepts.question: How can a uniform tree with nine branches at every node be made equivalent to tic-tac-toe?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors want to show that task structure is objective and can be expressed in different representations. They add a third isomorph of tic-tac-toe, after Number Scrabble.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Draw a symmetric game tree, uniformly nine nodes deep with exactly nine branches from every non-terminal node: 9 to the 9th power, 387,420,489 branches. Mark terminal branches as win, lose or draw. Make it equivalent to tic-tac-toe by identifying each branch with placing an x or o in one of nine squares, marking branches that are illegal because the square is occupied, and giving the legal terminal branches (362,880) the tic-tac-toe values.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Every statement about the new tree translates into a synonymous statement about tic-tac-toe or Number Scrabble and conversely; one could play either game in the other's space. Symmetries such as corner squares correspond to invariance of the marked tree under permutation of subtrees, so the information about symmetry is present in the tree as surely as in the display.

card.rule: A huge uniform game tree, with illegal branches marked and values set, expresses exactly the same task as tic-tac-toe.
card.limits: The translation can be complex, though it can be carried out by finite means.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Structure as what isomorphs preserve
concepts.question: How do the authors define the structure of a task environment, and when can a space have too much or too little?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: One cannot discuss a task environment without representing it. How can one still speak of its structure objectively?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: By the structure of the environment the authors mean precisely the set of invariants preserved under translation from any one of its isomorphic representations to any other. A problem space may contain more structure than the environment, such as the square shape of the usual tic-tac-toe array, which is spurious and at best useless, at worst harmful; or less, in which case it may not permit full use of the available structural information.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Structure alone does not settle problem difficulty: tic-tac-toe, Number Scrabble and the tree space would otherwise be equivalent for solving, which they clearly are not. The further issue is availability: how far information can be made explicit in the current state or readily derived from it.

card.rule: Structure is what stays invariant across isomorphs; spaces can add spurious structure or omit usable structure, and availability still matters.
card.limits: Equal structure does not mean equal ease, since availability differs.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Four decision points in search
concepts.question: What four decisions does a problem solver make in searching a problem space, and which two carry most of the burden?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Structural information helps only by influencing choices at the decision points of search.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: A problem solving IPS makes four kinds of decisions: (1) at a knowledge state, which operator to apply; (2) at a new state, whether to continue from it; (3) at a state, whether to remember it so it can be returned to; (4) on abandoning a state, which other state to select as backup. The main burden falls on the first pair, which guide search by selecting operators and evaluating new states.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The second pair usually offers fewer opportunities for applying structural information. For reasons of memory, only one or two prior states are retained as backup, and one of them is usually the initial state.

card.rule: Select an operator, decide whether to continue, decide whether to remember a state, and select a backup: the first two matter most.
card.limits: In tasks other than the three studied, remembering and backup decisions could matter more.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Backup is mostly automatic
concepts.question: Why do the authors find little explicit decision making about what to remember or where to return?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The second pair of decisions seemed to offer few chances to use structural information in the three tasks.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: When the knowledge state is descriptive, an accumulation of small symbol structures, which states are kept for backup depends on which predicates are retained long enough, by use, to enter LTM, so no explicit decisions are made. The choice of which prior state to return to is handled in relatively automatic ways, and only one or two states are usually available. Much of the backup observed simply resulted from abandoning a knowledge state.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In cryptarithmetic there were periodic decisions to record predicates in EM instead of LTM, but those recorded the current state even if later used for backup. Other tasks might make the choice of backup information a major part of problem solving, but not the three studied, and the authors warn against extrapolation.

card.rule: In the studied tasks, backup states were kept and chosen automatically, not by explicit decisions.
card.limits: In other tasks the decision about what backup to keep might be a major aspect.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Search-scan strategies are absent in humans
concepts.question: What is the search-scan strategy, and why did human subjects not use it?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Some of the most effective computer heuristic programs use a strategy that depends heavily on backup.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Search-scan: (1) keep enough information about prior nodes that any previously visited state can be recovered; (2) evaluate the promise of each state from which search has not yet been undertaken; (3) make each burst of search from the currently most promising state, evaluating the new nodes created.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Strong arguments support its effectiveness in many problem spaces, but the subjects did not use it. Since it places heavy demands on memory for backup information, its absence from the repertory of human programs is, the authors say, a consequence of the structure of the human IPS.

card.rule: Search-scan needs to recover any visited state; the human IPS lacks the memory for that, so people do not use it.
card.limits: The argument concerns the human IPS; computers with ample memory can use the strategy.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Extra aids as operators, not new spaces
concepts.question: How do aids such as working backward, planning and using EM enter the problem space?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Some aids to problem solving may or may not be represented in a given problem space: working backward, working abstractly as in planning, and using various external memories.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: They provide means of extracting information about the structure of the space. As in Chapter 5, they can be thought of as multiple problem spaces used at once, such as a working-backward space, a planning space or an external space, just as an augmented space can exist beside the basic one. Which exist depends on the structure of the task environment.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In logic, human solvers did not keep the spaces entirely separate: planning and working backward were embedded in the main space, the decision to use either was local to the knowledge state, and scanning EMs was the same. The authors treat these as additional operators in the space, so the decision to use them falls under the decision about which operator to apply.

card.rule: Planning, working backward and scanning EM behave like extra operators chosen locally, not like switches to another space.
card.limits: The task environment determines whether such possibilities exist at all.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Structure is redundancy that makes information predictive
concepts.question: In what ways can structure in a problem space be exploited for problem solving?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: How does knowing something about one part of a space help in another part?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Structure in a problem space is equivalent to redundancy: information in one part becomes predictive, at least heuristically, of properties in another. Nodes are described in a state language and operations in a process language. Structure helps in two basic ways: (1) correlating state-language information about nodes with process-language information about operators, giving selectivity in choosing operators; (2) correlating state-language information about one node with information about another, whether connected and how near, giving selectivity in deciding whether to proceed and in choosing a backup.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: A third way is information about symmetries or other regularities in the tree, so repetitive searches can be avoided. Recognizing symmetry in tic-tac-toe reduces the distinct first moves from nine to three: center, side and corner.

card.rule: Structure lets correlations between states and operators, between nodes, and between symmetric branches cut search.
card.limits: Symmetry helps only if recognized; the representation must make the correlation usable.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Structure as functions on states, goals and operators
concepts.question: How can the structural information used in the first two decisions be described formally?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors want a formal description of structural information.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Take the product space of current states U, desired states G and operators Q: U x G x Q. Information for the first decision is a function from U x G to Q. Information for the second is a predicate on U x G that is true (continue from the node) or false (discontinue). The predicate may also depend on other previously visited states.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: At the extreme, the function may be definable only by listing every value in extenso, one per pair of current and goal state. That would be known only if the whole space had been explored, so such a space would be no more tractable than one with random connections, which is arguably what random means. Actual spaces are more manageable: they are approximately factorable, and their functions can be written compactly with variables.

card.rule: Operator selection is a function from state-goal pairs to operators; the continue-or-not decision is a predicate on state-goal pairs.
card.limits: A function that must be listed pair by pair gives no help, and is no better than random.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: How operator choice can depend on state and goal
concepts.question: On what can the operator-selection function depend, and what strategies and tests correspond?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The function from U x G to Q suggests the operator depends on both the current and desired state, but special cases depend on only one or neither.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Means-ends analysis is the main case where the function depends on both u and g, specifically on their difference. A pure working-forward strategy may depend only on u, a pure working-backward strategy only on g. If operators are tried in a fixed priority order, as in some versions of the Logic Theorist, the function is constant, independent of both.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The predicate for evaluating a state also may depend on both or only on u. A progress test, depending on both, measures the distance of u from g. A simplicity criterion, depending only on u, rejects states that are too complex.

card.rule: Means-ends uses state and goal; forward uses the state; backward uses the goal; a priority list uses neither.
card.limits: The same dependency analysis applies to the continue-or-stop predicate.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Factorability: features that point to operators
concepts.question: How does describing states by features shrink the function from states to operators?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Listing the operator for every state is hopeless unless the space has more structure.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Suppose each state is described by presence or absence of n features. Suppose a function maps features to operators, so that if feature j is present, an operator q_j is relevant. There are 2 to the n distinguishable states, but only n feature-operator pairs need be known instead of 2 to the n state-operator pairs.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors simplify by taking the goal as invariant and the mapping as single-valued. If the space has this structure, the mapping can be found by searching only a small part of the space. A weak interdependence can be reintroduced by ordering the features, calling an operator relevant if its feature is present and no higher-ordered feature is present.

card.rule: If each feature calls for its own operator, n pairs replace 2 to the n pairs, and the mapping is easy to discover.
card.limits: Real spaces are only approximately factorable.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Differences and the kernel of means-ends analysis
concepts.question: How do difference vectors relate to means-ends analysis?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Often what matters is not the absolute features of the current state but how it differs from the goal.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Suppose an operator's relevance depends only on the components of a difference vector d(g, u), each component being difference-present or difference-absent. A relevance function from the set of difference vectors D to operators Q is the formal kernel of means-ends analysis.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The claim that means-ends analysis is frequently a powerful method is the claim that relevance functions from D to Q can be defined in many task environments. Such functions factor the state space, since an operator's relevance depends on a single feature independently of the others.

card.rule: Means-ends analysis is a function from differences to operators.
card.limits: Its power depends on such relevance functions being definable in the task at hand.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Complete factorability, abstraction and goal classes
concepts.question: What follows when a space is completely factorable, and how do abstraction and goal sets use feature vectors?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: In the limit, operators affect only their own feature. The authors ask what this implies and how vectors of features allow abstraction.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: A space is completely factorable if applying an operator relevant to a feature removes that feature and affects no other. Then paths from start to goal are permutable: the differences can be removed in any order. Such spaces are rather uninteresting, solvable trivially once the function is known. The real spaces are nearly, never completely, factorable.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Feature vectors allow abstracted spaces that keep most structural information but drop detail: the planning spaces. The dropped features and operators are called inessential and the retained ones essential. The vector form also allows a goal to be a set of features defining a class of states, as checkmate is a class of arrangements, not one.

card.rule: Complete factorability makes paths permutable and the space trivial; abstraction drops inessential features to form planning spaces.
card.limits: Real spaces are only nearly factorable, so permuting steps is not always safe.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Variables describe classes of operators and states
concepts.question: How do variables let one operator and one path stand for a whole class?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Many spaces have more structure than fixed vectors: whole classes of states and operators can be described by variables.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: An operator with a variable, q(x), applied to a state u(v) fixes x to match the value v the variable takes in the state, giving q(v). The commute operator of arithmetic takes A + B for any A and B and gives B + A with the same values. Such operators abstract: they define paths from a class of states to a class of states, so whole classes of paths can be searched at once.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: There is complete freedom in choosing when to select the particular members of interest, and if the selection can be postponed until a single member has been identified, search is avoided entirely. Variables can also state that an operator leaves some things invariant: if A(B + C) becomes AB + AC, the A positions in input and output correspond and the symbol is left invariant.

card.rule: A variable lets one operator apply to a whole class of states and states what the operator leaves unchanged.
card.limits: Binding must be consistent between the operator and the state it is applied to.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Foresight and hindsight: operator selection versus state evaluation
concepts.question: Why is operator selection foresight and state evaluation hindsight, and what is hindsight good for?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Information to evaluate states does not mention operators, which seems paradoxical if evaluation is to help the selective use of operators.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Operator selection is an application of foresight; state evaluation is an application of hindsight. The first answers which operator to apply next to build the path toward the goal; the second answers whether the current path is promising or should be abandoned. Foresight uses information available statically in the current state, while hindsight uses partial dynamic searches of alternatives.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The evaluation judges the efficacy of past actions: it computes the value of the action sequence that reached the state, standing in for prior knowledge of the space's structure. Hindsight is useful only if there is some capability for backup, since it serves to leave the current path for another.

card.rule: Foresight picks operators from static information; hindsight evaluates results and needs backup to be useful.
card.limits: Hindsight information is useless without some ability to go back.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Staticizing dynamic information in chess
concepts.question: How can chess concepts replace dynamic search with static analysis, and what risk comes with it?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: In some tasks, information normally got by searching ahead can be read off the current state.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Chess offers the best examples of staticizing dynamic information. Terms for describing positions, such as a forking square (a square from which a piece could attack two or more pieces at once) and a pinned piece (one so located that if it moved another piece would come under attack), let a player find geometrically in the original position what a trial move would reveal after the fact.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: A pinned Knight can be recognized without making its move, so all Knight moves may be eliminated unseen. Static features may be relevant to many dynamic paths and may persist over sequences of moves, reducing recomputation. A risk is that static descriptions must be revised as the position changes; a blunder can occur when moving a piece to use a forking square destroys another feature, such as a defended pawn, that depended on it.

card.rule: Static position features can replace dynamic lookahead, but must be revised as the position changes.
card.limits: Typical blunders arise when a static feature goes stale after a move.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Where the three tasks show each kind of structural information
concepts.question: Which task best illustrates each form of structural information the chapter has described?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The forms of information about problem space structure have been described abstractly. The authors point to the three tasks for illustrations.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Chess shows features correlated with relevant moves: a Rook move goes with an open file, a defender's move with an attack on a piece, a King's-side capture with a weakened King's position. Logic gives the best case of features as differences between initial and goal states, of explicit variables in the notation, and of planning spaces with essential and inessential features.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Information acquired by dynamic analysis and hindsight is illustrated by chess evaluation functions and by contradictions derived after conditional assignments in cryptarithmetic. Information about the branchiness of the environment is shown most clearly by the problem space of the chess mating program MATER.

card.rule: Chess shows feature-to-move correlations, logic shows differences, variables and planning spaces, and cryptarithmetic and chess show hindsight.
card.limits: These are illustrations from earlier chapters, not new evidence.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: From task structure to problem-space structure: summary
concepts.question: What do the authors conclude about how far a problem solver's characteristics can be inferred from task structure?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Chapters 5, 8 and 11 analyzed the three tasks in detail. What follows from them about the relation of environment to problem solver?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: A great many characteristics of the problem solving systems studied can be inferred, at least in broad outline, from the structure of the environments in which they operate. To be effective in enormous problem spaces, problem solvers must be able to extract from the environment the information about its structure that is stored there.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The forms in which this information is available, such as feature-operator correlations, differences, variables and static properties, condition the possible modes of exploiting it.

card.rule: Task structure explains much about problem solvers, and the form of the stored information limits how it can be exploited.
card.limits: Inference is in broad outline only; the details of any solver also depend on what it actually extracts.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Methods are determined by the structure of the problem space
concepts.question: What role do methods play in the theory, and how are named methods related to whole systems?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The book has named many methods: working forward, working backward, means-ends analysis, planning. For some mechanisms, such as the cryptarithmetic production systems, a whole system was built with no labeled methods.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The essential point of the section is that methods are determined by the structure of the problem space. A whole system such as the cryptarithmetic production system may be viewed in toto as a single idiosyncratic method.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors add that this is not quite the whole story, so some preliminaries are needed first: what a method is, and what other things beyond the problem space structure it depends on.

card.rule: Methods are largely fixed by problem-space structure, and any complete system can be regarded as one idiosyncratic method.
card.limits: Method also depends on aspects of the situation beyond problem-space structure, which the section later specifies.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: A method is a rational program, partly specified
concepts.question: What is a method, and how is it related to a program and to a plan?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Could methods and the programs that realize them be separate levels of organization?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: A method is an organization of behavior that bears a rational relation to solving a problem: if its premises are granted, it could produce a solution. This is a functional characterization; structurally methods are programs. Methods can leave aspects only partly specified, so the authors identify method and program, allowing programs to contain functionally specified subprocesses, which amounts to including goals in programs.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The quadratic formula calls for a square root without saying how to compute it, so time and error chances vary. A chess method that says to add a defender does not fix which man. As a consequence, no sharp line separates plans from methods; to paraphrase Polya, a method is simply a plan that you use twice.

card.rule: A method is a rational, possibly partly specified program; a method is a plan that you use twice.
card.limits: Rationality is minimal: it says only that the premises could produce a solution, not how likely.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: The space of methods is modest in problematic situations
concepts.question: How large is the space of methods, and what limits it?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: If each solver had unique methods, theory of methods would be hopeless. The authors ask how big the repertory is.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Methods are represented as production systems, so the set of all methods is the set of production systems realizing rational courses of action for given goals and environment. A solver has a repertory under whose control behavior comes. The variety of methods appears quite modest, depending primarily on the structure of the problem space, with qualifications.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: First, the claim concerns only unprogrammed activity in genuinely problematic situations; the set of all methods, including the quadratic formula and the simplex algorithm, is very large. Such methods must be discovered by someone highly skilled and passed on; only exceedingly rarely are they found by a solver who lacked them, and when available the situation is nonproblematic. Second, method depends on aspects beyond the space structure. Third, mixtures are discussed later.

card.rule: In genuinely problematic situations the variety of methods is modest, set mainly by problem-space structure.
card.limits: Specialized algorithms like the quadratic formula are outside the claim and are rarely discovered by a solver who lacked them.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: A method is a pattern of decisions
concepts.question: What does a method ultimately do, and which decisions let intelligence play most?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The function of a method is to produce behavior rationally related to an end. The authors translate this into demands on production systems.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Given the problem space, intelligence enters problem solving through a small set of decisions that determine goals, states and operators. Determining goals and operators and evaluating new states seem the important controlling decisions; saving states, selecting old states to retry and rejecting goals usually offer less scope. A method is ultimately a device for generating a coordinated pattern of such decisions that produces rational behavior.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In different task environments the decision points differ both in frequency and in the room they allow for the play of intelligence.

card.rule: A method coordinates decisions about goals, states and operators; goal, operator and evaluation decisions leave most room for intelligence.
card.limits: How much room there is for intelligence differs from task to task.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: The method translates embedded information into decisions
concepts.question: What information can a method use, and when are two production systems the same method?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A method makes decisions using information, but the only information it has is what the problem space embeds.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The information available to make decisions is that embedded in the task environment's structure as captured in the problem space. The method's main task is to translate it into the pattern of decisions. Any two production systems giving identical translations, identical patterns as a function of problem-space information, are in some important sense the same method, and often end up with a common name.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The information actually available to a production system comprises the symbol structures of goals, states and operators and its own structure. The correlations and redundancies that constitute space structure are not symbolized directly but are assumed by the method in the way it uses the symbol structures.

card.rule: A method maps the information in goal, state and operator symbols to decisions; identical mappings count as the same method.
card.limits: The structure of the space is assumed by the method, not represented in it.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: A working-forward production system and the recognition method
concepts.question: What four types of productions make up a working-forward system?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: To make methods concrete, the authors give paradigmatic production systems. They take the state to be descriptive: an ordered conjunction of small expressions, as in cryptarithmetic or chess.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Working-forward has four types of productions: (1) recognize the solution state, producing the symbol solution; (2) evaluate the present state, affixing a reject tag to a new expression, which stops that expression entering further solving and in effect returns the solver to the prior state; (3) determine how far to back up, spreading reject tags to other information; (4) select the operator for the next forward move from the current state, which may or may not depend on the new expression.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Operator selection alone does not make a method; evaluative information must be added unless the solver pursues one fixed goal that is built in. The same figure also characterizes the recognition method of Chapter 4, which consists of the productions recognizing a solution and those selecting the operator; it applies in principle to any problem, provided the solving operator is already in LTM.

card.rule: Working-forward recognizes solutions, evaluates and rejects new states, backs up, and selects operators from the current state.
card.limits: The recognition method works only if the solution, or the operator producing it, is already in LTM.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Means-ends analysis as productions: two forms
concepts.question: How is means-ends analysis realized in productions, and how do forms A and B differ?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Working-forward uses only the current state to choose operators. Means-ends analysis uses state and goal.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The paradigmatic means-ends system has a production recognizing final success and, in form A, productions that select an operator as a function of the current state and the goal state. No state evaluation is needed if operator selection is good, and no backup, since action can always continue from the new position. In form B, productions create difference goals as functions of the current state, and operators are then selected solely as a function of those goals.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Form B seems unadaptive since it ignores the state, but goals are created from the state and so encode information about it. Difference goals describe difficulties to be surmounted or gaps to be filled. The forms are functionally equivalent in making selection depend on goal and state, but not otherwise: a goal implies continuing effort until reached, whereas choosing an operator as a joint function of state and goal is a one-time action leaving no trace beyond its effects.

card.rule: Means-ends selects operators from state and goal directly (A) or through difference goals (B), which persist until satisfied.
card.limits: Not all means-ends schemes are so powerful; many include some evaluation and backup.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Where information sits changes the production system
concepts.question: How do production systems for selecting operators vary with where the operators are stored?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A system with several memories must adapt its programs to deal with information wherever it occurs.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Information about states, goals and operators can reside in STM, LTM or EM. For operator selection, the authors show four variants: in A the operators are part of the selection system itself, so selecting leads at once to the result appearing in STM; in B the operators are separate production systems to which selection transfers control; in C a single operator held in STM is selected or rejected and then executed; in D operators held in EM must be searched, each evaluated for rejection or execution, under control of a tag symbol, select.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: STM is too small to hold operators, so C involves only one at a time. In the normal arrangement the current state is mostly in STM with a little in LTM; the current goal is in STM with perhaps one or two others in a stack; higher pervasive goals are in LTM, and the top goal may be recorded in the environment. Keeping parts of the state in EM gives the extended knowledge state and requires scanning programs.

card.rule: Operators in LTM are embedded or separate systems; in STM one at a time; in EM they must be scanned and evaluated.
card.limits: Knowing the operators so that selection is embedded in a production system implies having them in LTM.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Assimilated versus interpreted operators
concepts.question: What is the difference between an assimilated operator and one that must be interpreted?
