blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Methods differ in whether their information is directly available or must be interpreted. Logic subjects showed the contrast.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Assimilation means the operation is available as a production system; interpretation means the controlling production system is an interpreter and the operator is a symbolic structure, in LTM or EM or perhaps STM if very small. Subjects who applied the logic rules from the rule sheet like a recipe interpreted them, while those who had assimilated the inessential rules just performed them.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Assimilated rules are encoded as productions whose evoking conditions are the rule's applicability conditions; many productions are needed but action is immediate and no stacks are required. An interpreter works symbol by symbol through two expressions, needs stacks because it does not know how big an expression or rule will be, but works for any operators, while adding a new operator to the assimilated system needs new productions.

card.rule: Assimilated operators are productions that act at once; interpreted operators are data run by a general interpreter that is slower but general.
card.limits: Parts of one skill can be mixed: most logic subjects matched and substituted for variables as assimilated operations.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Feature extraction must stay simple
concepts.question: Why do feature computations in productions remain simple, and when do they not?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: In the examples the features to be responded to are given directly as production conditions. That need not be so.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: An alternative is the logic match in GPS, where a complex comparison produces a difference, a symbol structure summarizing the match, which is then used to select an operator or reduce goal. The paradigms may need to be augmented with clusters of productions computing features and differences, but the short residence times within a knowledge state imply these remain simple, since they occur before any action the solver sees as producing new knowledge.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Even the match takes only a second or two, though it needs its own production system because it scans large expressions. The argument for simplicity rests on the solver's postulated inability to withhold problem solving merely for information gathering. When that fails, as in orientation periods at the start of a new problem, as in chess perception of Chapter 13, the extended knowledge state is built up before search.

card.rule: Feature computation before acting stays short because the solver cannot pause problem solving for pure information gathering.
card.limits: Orientation periods at the start of a problem are the exception.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Parametrized operators: attention and production
concepts.question: How does parametrization split operators into productive and attentional ones?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Operators are often given not as full sets of productions but as forms with variables.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Parametrization lets one choose among many possibilities in stages: first the form, then the free variables are fixed one by one, sometimes after a delay until a determining condition arises. It divides the choice of operator into parts that can be attended to separately. In productions it separates productive operators, which produce new information, from attentional operators, which select an aspect of the state for input to the productive ones.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The two can be coupled so the attentional operator simply precedes the productive one, as FC before PC in the cryptarithmetic productions. Or, when the productive operator is evoked, gaps in its specification are symbolized as difficulties to be removed by other productions with that goal, which is more flexible and an instance of means-ends analysis. States can contain variables too, and goals are often parametrized, as check(letter), though real acts of selecting a goal's variable were rare in the data.

card.rule: Parametrization separates choosing a form from filling in its variables, via attentional and productive operators.
card.limits: The rarity of selecting a goal's variable may be an artifact of the tasks studied.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Sources of structural variation in methods
concepts.question: Which functions account for structural variation among methods, and what stays the same?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The variety of production systems is not well enough understood for a definitive analysis. The authors summarize.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The functions described, with their structural counterparts, seem to cover the main sources of variation. The last three, location of information, need to interpret, and parametrization, account for some of the structural variability of methods. They do not alter the main function of a method, which is to effect a pattern of decisions about goals, states and operators as a function of information embedded in the problem structure.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: They solve only the subsidiary problems of effecting that pattern, given the many ways information can be encoded.

card.rule: Location, interpretation and parametrization vary the form of methods without changing their function.
card.limits: The authors say their analysis of the structure of methods is not definitive.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Are named methods ideal types mixed in real solvers?
concepts.question: Why might real solvers be mixtures of named methods rather than users of discrete complete methods?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Naming methods suggests each is a complete organization, that the solver has a discrete set, and that a selection mechanism evokes one.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: That picture is supported by the way a method's parts fit only in the context of the whole, and almost all multimethod artificial intelligence programs are organized so. But it implies a large number of distinct methods for human solvers; S3's cryptarithmetic system might be an idiosyncratic method. Alternatively, named methods may be ideal types and real solvers mixtures of them.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Making that operational needs units from which methods are built; a single production is too small, since it gives the class of all programs. But clusters of productions from various methods may be mixed so behavior is a composite. A footnote notes sociology's ideal types, which need explicit laws of composition to be viable.

card.rule: Real solvers might mix clusters of productions from several ideal-type methods rather than own many discrete methods.
card.limits: A mixture theory needs explicit units and laws of composition, which the authors do not fully supply.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: S3's production system as a mixture of two methods
concepts.question: How was S3's cryptarithmetic production system divided between working-forward and means-ends analysis?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Can an actual subject's program be shown to be a mixture of basic methods?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Figure 14.8 divides S3's production system into clusters. Working-forward is realized by P1 and part of P4. Means-ends analysis is realized by P6, P7 and P10, which go from the current state to goals reflecting differences, and by P2, P3 and half of P4, which select operators for those difference goals. P13 contains a whole sequence of difference determination and operator selection; P9 and P14 begin with difference goals and generate other goals; P8 changes goal types from check to get.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Both methods share a common set of evaluation productions, P11, P12 and P5, the last being the final evaluation. Working-forward controls behavior every time new information comes in, and means-ends analysis controls it whenever difficulties arise, so behavior oscillates between the two. The authors cannot say that all programs divide so or whether the mixing is psychologically real.

card.rule: S3's system fits as working-forward on new information and means-ends on difficulties, sharing evaluation productions.
card.limits: The psychological reality of the mixing is the crucial open issue.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: A manageable space of methods
concepts.question: How do the authors reduce the large set of methods to a manageable one, and how independent is method?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The whole set of methods is clearly very large. The authors seek a small kernel.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Mixtures reduce the total to the ideal types; the functional analysis abstracts away inessential variation of information location, parametrization and interpretation; allowing functionally specified subparts reduces it more. What remains is a manageable space reflecting the basic ways that information about the structure of the problem space maps into patterns of operator selection, state evaluation and goal creation.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Method is not a completely independent variable to be added to the task environment, the goals and the choice of problem space. It is partly independent, since a range of methods is available and a solver need not use the best ones; which he uses is partly a measure of intelligence and education. His choices are highly circumscribed. The analysis covers methods in problematic situations, not the highly specific methods of science, mathematics and the practical arts.

card.rule: Method is largely but not wholly fixed by the space; the set shrinks to patterns of operator selection, evaluation and goal creation.
card.limits: The analysis excludes the specific methods of science, mathematics and the practical arts.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.section: Determination of Individual Problem Spaces and Programs
concepts.title: Narrowing to one problem space and program
concepts.question: How does a solver move from the class of admissible spaces to one particular space and program?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The task environment fixes the class of admissible spaces and the space limits the possible programs. A real subject still ends up with one space and one program.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The theory of how this narrowing happens is tentative and incomplete. It is linked to individual differences, since the invariants so far hold over tasks and persons, while the space and program adopted differ across people and occasions. If determination depends on history, the program changes gradually with experience, but on a time scale of hours, not the minutes of a single search.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Most relevant behavior occurs before the subject reaches the laboratory, and the rest occurs in the first minutes or seconds while instructions are read. The subjects were not naive: they knew the symbols and arithmetic of logic and cryptarithmetic, and the chess players had spent many hours at the game. An initial program is therefore assembled rapidly and then stays fairly stable.

card.rule: Space and program are chosen from the admissible class by history and instructions, quickly, and then stay fairly fixed.
card.limits: The record of pre-session behavior and of initial responses is very thin, so the account is speculative.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Six sources for determining space and program
concepts.question: Which six sources of information help fix a problem space and program when a task is given?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: At the moment instructions are given, what can contribute to the choice of space and program?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Six sources: (1) the task instructions, giving fuller or poorer descriptions of objects, operators, initial and goal states, and perhaps imposing a form of EM such as the chessboard; (2) previous experience with the same or a nearly identical task, where the instructions may only evoke a stored program; (3) experience with tasks recognized as analogous; (4) stored LTM programs of wide generality; (5) stored programs that construct spaces and programs from external information and memory; (6) the course of problem solving itself, which may augment, modify or even change the space or program.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The sources are not exclusive. They can combine, as when a construction program (5) uses the instructions (1) as data, and different aspects of one situation can come from different sources. The instructions give more explicit information about the space than about the program.

card.rule: Instructions, same-task experience, analogy, general programs, construction programs and the course of solving all feed the choice.
card.limits: The treatment is illustrative, not systematic, so spaces and programs are discussed together.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Instructions give a representation, not only a definition
concepts.question: What does the critical experiment on tic-tac-toe and number scrabble predict about the problem space?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The task out there can be known only through a representation, and no neutral description of it exists. So the instructions do more than define the task.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Task instructions supply a specific representation that can define an initial problem space and parts of an initial program. In the thought experiment, one task T is described in its ith representation, tic-tac-toe or number scrabble, in condition Ci. The prediction is that subjects in condition Ci use the space defined by the ith representation, with the objects and operators of that game.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors admit the outcome is obvious and the experiment has been run only informally with friends. They state it tediously because the source of a space is sometimes treated as mysterious, and some say the real problem solving is the earlier process of fixing the space. A footnote refutes that: if it held, only the first of several tasks from one environment would be a problem. A further isomorph is JAM, the dual of tic-tac-toe, where lines are jammed through a point.

card.rule: Subjects work in the space defined by the representation in the instructions, even when the underlying task is the same.
card.limits: The experiment is a prediction, not a reported study.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Cryptarithmetic and logic subjects followed the instructions
concepts.question: What shows that the subjects' spaces in cryptarithmetic and logic matched their instructions?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: In both tasks the subjects had to build a space from a description. Did the spaces mirror it?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: In cryptarithmetic, a new task for the subjects, the spaces used were close to the instructions. All but S6 used the augmented space, which keeps the structure of the basic space and adds relations to the knowledge state with matching operators. None used the algebraic space or any abstract one. In logic, all subjects built spaces matching the instructions.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Had logic been introduced as a formal system, with dot for and and wedge for or, problem solving would differ. For problem A1, where L1 is (~P.Q) V (P.~P), subjects would then worry over the contradiction P.~P in the right side and what it implies.

card.rule: Spaces mirrored the instructions: basic or augmented in cryptarithmetic, rule-and-syntax spaces in logic.
card.limits: The formal-logic prediction is a conjecture and was not tested.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.section: Previous Experience with the Same Task
concepts.title: Prior experience with the same task evokes a stored program
concepts.question: How does prior experience with the same task shape what the subject does and what the protocol shows?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Chess is almost a perfect example of a highly familiar task.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Telling a subject to behave as a player in a shown position is enough to evoke from LTM the program for playing chess. So chess protocols tell little about how the game was learned, though the first segment may show how a new position is transferred to internal memory. The same applies to component tasks such as addition and subtraction in cryptarithmetic and substitution in logic.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: A principal criterion for treating a process as an operator in a problem space is that it represents a task in which the subject already has much experience and for which he has a performance program.

card.rule: Familiar tasks evoke stored programs; a process counts as an operator when the subject already has a program for it.
card.limits: Protocols from familiar tasks reveal performance, not learning.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.section: Previous Experience with the Same Task
concepts.title: Analogy transfers a space, with costs and benefits
concepts.question: What are the costs and benefits of treating a new task as analogous to a familiar one?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: When a new task resembles a familiar one, the solver may borrow the familiar space and program.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Borrowing requires adapting knowledge to the new task, and pays off only if the recognized similarity reflects real isomorphism and the adaptation succeeds. In logic, subjects treated the tilde as the negative sign of algebra. S8 asked whether a tilde times a tilde makes a positive and said he could think only in terms of mathematics. This cost something, but it was more than repaid since the algebra space and its associative, distributive and commutative laws largely applied.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In cryptarithmetic the instructions mention the similarity to arithmetic, and a subject can work from right to left as in addition. That ignores that constrained columns yield information independently of position, but it supplies a systematic procedure for breaking the task into parts, which S8 lacked in his numerical space. In logic the essential-inessential distinction may come from the physical world of rearranging versus removing or adding material.

card.rule: Analogy gives a ready space and a systematic procedure at the price of errors where the analogy fails.
card.limits: Analogy is useful only if it reflects real isomorphism between the tasks.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Low-level operations run on one general program
concepts.question: Why must simple operations such as addition use one general program across tasks?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Subjects working at a specific task may use programs far more general than the task.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Adding two numbers must use one program that takes digits and returns a sum in STM. There is no separate process for removing two pawns from eight, and another for taking N = 2 from B = 8 in DONALD+GERALD. The operation is used in a context each time, such as an exchange evaluation in chess or column processing in cryptarithmetic, but the general program works on the pair of digits, not on their interpretation.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The case for generalized subroutines is easy at the level of arithmetic. For problem solving programs it is less clear how much commonality can be extracted and packaged, and whether human subjects actually have such general programs.

card.rule: Arithmetic is one general program applied in many contexts; whether whole problem solving programs are general is open.
card.limits: The argument holds for low-level operations, not yet for whole problem solving programs.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: The cryptarithmetic and chess programs are task specific
concepts.question: What evidence suggests that the cryptarithmetic and chess programs are tied to their tasks?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Are there empirical clues that the problem solving programs themselves are general?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: In cryptarithmetic the production systems were specific to the task. P1, which takes a new digit assignment to a variable, finds the column and processes it, would be evoked only in cryptarithmetic and not in solving algebraic equations, where it would be as meaningful. A general version, P1*, could be written: new information about X leads to finding X's place and deriving consequences. A similar general production was used in Chapter 8 for algebra, yet there was no empirical ground for saying subjects used it.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In chess a single prototypic program was described, with all programs obtained by filling open subprocesses such as base-moves. This chess executive is specific to chess and could not be used for cryptarithmetic or logic.

card.rule: Both the cryptarithmetic productions and the chess executive are specific to their tasks, with no evidence of the general versions.
card.limits: A general version of P1 is conceivable, but there is no empirical evidence that subjects had it.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: GPS is organized in task-free terms
concepts.question: What makes GPS general, and what must be supplied to apply it to a task?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: GPS, used for the logic task, has substantial elements of generality.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Its basic program works with symbol structures for objects, operators, features and differences. Goals take such general forms, as in transform object 1 into object 2, and its methods refer to matching objects, obtaining a difference and setting goals from differences. Extra structures like the table of connections and the ordering of differences are described by the same four concepts.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: To work in a task, GPS needs coordinating definitions linking object, operator, feature and difference to classes of entities in that task, together with task-specific programs for detecting features and differences and applying operators. The original version showed this with logic and trigonometric identities. GPS-2-6 handled eleven tasks, from formal integration to puzzles, parsing a sentence and series extrapolation.

card.rule: GPS has a task-free core, plus per-task definitions and programs for detecting features and applying operators.
card.limits: These are synthetic programs; the generality is not tested against behavioral data.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Instructions to GPS resemble instructions to a human
concepts.question: How do the instructions to GPS-2-6 for Fathers and Sons compare with those given to a person?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Figure 14.9 gives the English statement of Fathers and Sons and the matching GPS-2-6 instructions.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The GPS instructions start with definitions linking task words to GPS's vocabulary, so sail is an operator and a son's location is an attribute of an object. Then come descriptions of operators, the initial and final situations, the goal and the ordering of differences. GPS already has two general kinds of operators and a scheme for detecting features and differences, so those need not be written out.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: A human also brings general knowledge of what operators do and capacities to detect features and differences. The word boat carries for the person prior knowledge about crossing, which is spelled out for GPS in the sail definition. Facts not universal, such as the 200 pound load limit, must be told to the human too. GPS could not order differences, though a later scheme in Chapter 8 would let that part be dropped.

card.rule: Both GPS and a human need the task-specific facts told, and neither needs general knowledge of operators and features spelled out.
card.limits: The difference between instructions comes from the human's familiar story setting, which is shown to be removable.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Constructing a space out of familiar components
concepts.question: How can a problem space be constructed so quickly from stored components?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A space and program may be assembled in response to instructions from general components. S8 offers the best example, as he considers how to approach LETS+WAVE=LATER.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Building a space means building (1) a representation for the knowledge state, (2) operators that produce new knowledge, and (3) processes that test whether operators apply and positions are desirable. The raw components are overlearned: addition, subtraction, symbol comparison and simple predicates such as R odd. They are not column processors or digit tests, but assembly into a space takes place in the first minute or two, or during the instructions.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: At B83 S8 turns from the cryptogram space to a typographical space, reading letters as digits with similar shapes, as E looks like 3. The knowledge state resembles that of the cryptogram space and the basic tests of disjointness and completeness are already formed. Only the operators, which are manipulations of how symbols are perceived, are new. Construction may mean a large selection of one organization from many, without much processing.

card.rule: A space is quickly built from overlearned parts, so construction involves selection among organizations more than heavy processing.
card.limits: The authors state this is no definite theory, only a framing of the issue.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: EDPS builds a performance program from worked examples
concepts.question: How does Williams' Example-Driven Problem Solver assemble a program from the test instructions?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Few programs shed light on how human programs are built. Compilers do not count since they work from process descriptions.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Donald Williams' EDPS handles concept-formation tasks from intelligence tests. Each test gives written instructions, a few worked examples, then a series of problems. EDPS works from the examples alone, with enough general context to ignore the written text. It determines the form of the answer, such as filling a blank, choosing an item that fits or fails to fit a rule, or stating the rule, and the relations that must be detected.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: It builds a trial program, tests it on the worked examples, and tackles the test items when satisfied. Its range is limited, mostly by intelligence-test tasks. Its construction processes are not problem solving but recognition of salient features of the task with direct selection of components, which is direct means-ends analysis.

card.rule: EDPS reads worked examples to fix the answer form and relations, builds a trial program, and checks it against the examples.
card.limits: The range of tests it handles is limited, and it is only an initial model.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: A space can grow during problem solving: S3 adds a production
concepts.question: What shows that a production system may be modified while the solver works?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The space and methods need not stay constant through a whole attempt, since the space may be built gradually as pieces are needed.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: S3 on DONALD+GERALD finishes a first episode establishing T = 0 and R odd, fails to establish anything about G, and says he will forget it for a minute and try possible solutions. This evokes production P3, which gets a letter, finds a column, assigns a value and processes the column, and for the first time the assignment operator is executed with L = 1.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The earlier analysis assumed that S3's space had the assignment operator and the program had P3 from the beginning, with this the first evocation. The production may instead have been added here, when the existing system, apparently a pure reasoning system, offered no way to continue. The authors do not know what adding a production to a system involves in structure of the IPS.

card.rule: P3 may have been added once the reasoning productions ran out of ways to continue.
card.limits: Data cannot separate use of an existing production from adding a new one.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: S8's discovery about the carry: space, program or knowledge?
concepts.question: What changed for S8 when he realized the carry takes only values 0 or 1?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: S8 near the end of DONALD+GERALD discovers the carry can only be 0 or 1. He then finishes at once.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: He gets E = 9 from E = 0 or 9 and T = 0, then follows familiar ground to the rest of the inferences. He calls the discovery important at the time and just after the solution. A priori the change could be in the problem space, in the specific program, or only in the knowledge state.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: It is likely a small part of the space changed, namely his general knowledge of the range of carries. The program would have changed if the form of inference, a letter must take a value since other values are exhausted, had been evoked for the first time, but he had used it several times. As he made no further use of the fact, it is unclear whether the space changed or he only made one inference, c5 = 0 or 1. Generality of wording is not a reliable guide, since earlier, in E24, he had concluded that the carry cannot be 2 or more.

card.rule: The change is probably in the space's knowledge of carries, but the data cannot confirm it.
card.limits: Without later use of the fact, the change cannot be located.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Waterman's poker program adds productions with experience
concepts.question: How does Waterman's draw poker program modify itself, and what does it support?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Programs that modify themselves are usually called learning programs, but few help here. An exception learns draw poker.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Waterman's program is a production system acting on a knowledge state made of a fixed vector of poker features, such as pot size and opening bet. It starts from a null production making a random bet, and with play it creates and adds productions until it plays quite passable poker. Diagnostic processes detect unsatisfactory behavior and fashion a production or cluster to remedy it.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Productions suit it for the reasons they suit the authors: each heuristic is a production or cluster, and the system is the collection. Location matters since productions near the head screen later ones, so specializations must precede general rules. This resembles S3 adding P3 when the existing system failed to continue, though the programs are likely not alike structurally. The adding processes are no more complex than the problem solvers themselves, and the program reinforces production systems as a representation of the IPS.

card.rule: A production system can grow by diagnosing failures and adding specialized productions ahead of the general ones.
card.limits: There is no reason to think S3's program resembles the poker program structurally.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Tasks differ through the capabilities they draw from other tasks
concepts.question: How does the six-source view explain differences and transfer among tasks?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: There are six ways a space and program can be determined, and several may act together.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Only the first (instructions) and the last (the course of solving) look mainly at the present task. The other four draw capability from other tasks: having the space already, adapting an analogy, using general methods, and constructing from available parts. In these cases performance on a task depends on performance on other tasks because they share processes and symbol structures. This is intertask transfer, and the aim is the structural means, not a correlation of performances.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The problem space gives a glimpse of communality, since a space covers a range of tasks defined by different start and end points. S4 used one space for DONALD+GERALD and CROSS+ROADS, S8 used one space in all logic problems, and six subjects who did D1 and C1 used the same space for both. The other three mechanisms are poorly understood, and they could all give functionally identical programs, which makes them hard to separate.

card.rule: Tasks are related through shared spaces and programs; the space shows communality, while the other mechanisms are poorly known.
card.limits: No mechanism has been tested directly against behavioral data, and the mechanisms may produce identical behavior.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Why GPS is a misleading model of generality
concepts.question: Why do the authors call GPS a misleading model of how tasks relate?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Relations among tasks depend on the actual structure of knowledge about the world, which brings back the aim of describing all knowledge.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Formal tasks hold a privileged place among tasks, and resource control, and the Piagetian concepts of causality, time, space, seriation and conservation have general import. Their content affects strongly how tasks relate and the possibility of learning programs that adapt programs and spaces from one task to another.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: GPS suggests a level of task-free generality neatly separated from the content of each space. Then generality would lie in the general mechanisms and the processes that identify a task so they apply. That organization is possible, but so are others, and each implies a different relation between tasks. For this reason GPS was discussed as just one of several ways to determine a space and program.

card.rule: GPS implies a clean split between general mechanisms and content, but other organizations of generality are possible.
card.limits: Which organization human problem solvers actually have is not established.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Two levels of commonality still leave wide freedom
concepts.question: What commonalities do all human problem solvers share, and how much freedom remains?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The world has many problem solvers, each a distinct information processing system. In what ways are they the same and different?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The theory gives two levels of commonality: all humans are IPS's with common organizational features, and all share a few structural constants such as nearly identical memory parameters. These produce common behavior among problem solvers. Yet a human IPS can still produce almost arbitrary behavior toward a task, from attempting it to going to sleep, arguing, redefining it, failing deliberately, ignoring it or striking.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The structural limits require only that these things be done in a certain style: not too fast, not remembering too much. The invariants are not absolute. STM size varies in the population and the variation matters for function, probably in the difference between the young and the mature and between the subnormal and the normal. Even so, the range is small compared with the variation across man-made IPS's.

card.rule: Basic IPS organization and near-constant memory parameters bound behavior in style but not in content.
card.limits: The analysis that follows concerns differences independent of variation in these parameters.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: The task environment shapes behavior, mediated by LTM contents
concepts.question: Where must any commonality beyond basic structure be located in the IPS?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A second source of commonality is the task environment. Humans in the same situation, with the same goals and enough ability, show many features given the same shape.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The shape holds even when they cannot quite solve the problem, since the same task features appear obvious to all. If there are strikingly different ways of attacking a task, there need be no behavioral similarity, and similarity depends on shared goals and situations. This commonality is mediated through the IPS and is not structural, so it must be represented in the IPS.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Since the IPS factors into basic structure and the contents of LTM, any commonality not due to basic structure must be an identity or similarity in the contents of LTM, in the productions or other stored structures. The variables usually invoked in behavioral science, such as culture, education or class, are differences of experience: jobs, people, books. The theory says little about what behavioral differences these contents produce.

card.rule: Commonalities not due to basic structure must lie in similar LTM contents.
card.limits: The theory in present form says little about the behavioral effects of culture, education and class.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Man mirrors the universe: elusive psychological laws
concepts.question: Why are psychological laws elusive, and where does the theory place the constraints on behavior?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The theory says little about behavior differences from different LTM contents, but proposes a system that can absorb any specification, even an encyclopedia.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The theory places the determination of similarities and differences of behavior on the causes that define LTM content, which depend on the details of life history. This is not arbitrary or unlawful. It means contents are as varied as the physical, biological and social phenomena the individual extracts them from. This fundamental characteristic accounts for the elusiveness of psychological laws: man is the mirror of the universe he lives in, and all he knows shapes his psychology, subject to a few basic constraints.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The view is not extreme cultural relativism nor the slogan that man can be anything. The universe mirrored includes a lawful physical and biological universe, including the body. Constraints on human behavior are placed in the environment, as limits on knowledge and how to obtain it, instead of limits on the ability to perform according to assimilated knowledge.

card.rule: Behavior reflects the content of what is known, so constraints sit in the environment and in how knowledge is acquired.
card.limits: The view does not equate with cultural relativism or with the claim that man can be anything.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Biological limits act as extra constraints outside the normal situation
concepts.question: Which internal constraints beyond the IPS structure does the card admit, and how does it handle them?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Are there no other internal constraints on human cognition?

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: When the biological system, especially the sensory system, is pushed to a limit, structural constraints appear. There are general limits in sensory capacity and odd phenomena such as after-images, illusions and ringing in the ears. Emotionality and altered states such as drowsiness are also internal and affect the IPS.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: These constraints are sources of both commonality and individual difference: all human visual systems have after-images, while hearing acuity can substantially affect behavior. A normal situation is one where these limits are not exceeded, and the theory applies to normal situations. So the theory is a first approximation, to be refined by sensory and other biological limits as extra constraints.

card.rule: Sensory and biological limits are extra constraints on a first-approximation theory that covers normal situations.
card.limits: The theory is stated for situations in which biological limits are not exceeded.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Development and learning as sources of invariant structure
concepts.question: Why might the need to develop and to learn imply further invariants of human cognition?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: A second source of constraints on cognition is the set of processes by which an adult's LTM contents are acquired, namely development and learning. The studies give little information about them.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The human IPS must grow to its adult state from a poorly understood neonatal one. At each moment, the changes must be assimilated by the existing system, which must keep working. This capacity to develop while performing may imply structural similarities among all human cognitive systems beyond those discussed in the chapter.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: A similar possibility comes from the need to learn continually. The systems studied create new knowledge all the time in STM and LTM, and the strong proposal is that all increments are cast as productions. The acquisition process has not been examined, and proposals like Waterman's poker learner are too unspecific to answer the important psychological questions. Learning at normal human time scales and amounts probably implies more invariant features.

card.rule: The requirements to develop while working and to learn continually probably imply additional common structure.
card.limits: The data of the book give only glimpses of development and learning.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Behavior depends on specific content
concepts.question: What do the authors conclude about the role of content in the behavior of an IPS?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The part on determination did not try to specify the process by which spaces and programs are determined, even speculatively.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: It listed in detail the sources of information that could be used, illustrating some with subjects' behavior and others with synthetic programs. It then summarized the relations among tasks and the sources of common and different behavior among solvers. Repeatedly the discussion returned to the content of the solver's knowledge: behavior is not a function of aggregate features of the content, such as how much there is or how it is expressed, but of the specific detail of content.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Content governs almost all aspects of the behavior of the IPS. It cannot be understood from syntax alone, abstracted from the vocabulary and semantics of what is said and done. Methods and programs are themselves content. Development and learning are two more sources of invariant structure, and the book gives only glimpses of them.

card.rule: Behavior depends on the specific detail of content, including methods and programs, not on aggregate features of it.
card.limits: The process by which spaces and programs are determined is not specified.

concepts.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
concepts.title: Summary: environment, space and program
concepts.question: What are the three things the chapter says must be described to understand human problem solving?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The chapter drew on the data of the preceding nine chapters to construct a theory of human problem solving.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Human problem solving is to be understood by describing (1) the task environment, (2) the space the solver uses to represent the environment, the task and the knowledge gradually accumulated about it, and (3) the program the solver assembles to approach the task. The authors characterized environments, spaces and programs, and showed how the solver's program extracts some of the structural information embedded in the environment to find solutions by highly selective search through the space.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The emphasis fell on the performance program. In the last section the chapter gave what evidence it could on how a solver generates a space and program for a new task and on commonalities and differences among solvers. The answers were sketchy, since these are the largest and most important terra incognita on the map of the theory. With that, the task set in Chapter 1 is complete as far as data and understanding allow, and an epilogue follows.

card.rule: Task environment, problem space and program together explain problem solving as highly selective search guided by extracted structure.
card.limits: How spaces and programs arise for new tasks, and how solvers differ, is the main unexplored territory.

concepts.title: What the computer gave the authors
concepts.question: What did the computer give the authors beyond a metaphor for the mind?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Problem solving was regarded as so complex that, for a whole generation, psychologists avoided it in the laboratory in favor of behaviors that seemed simple. The computer's arrival after World War II gave the authors and others the courage to return to complex cognitive performance as a source of data.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: A computer is a mechanism bound by the laws of physics, yet it manipulates symbols with great generality. The authors treat a programmed computer and a human problem solver as two species of one genus, the information processing system (IPS). The species differ in memory organization, elementary processes and program organization.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Simulation let the authors compare theory with data in detail and derive many empirical predictions. Still more important, they say, were the new concepts of information processing systems and the formalisms and languages for describing them precisely. In this book the computer recedes, and the IPS is specified directly for human behavior.

card.rule: According to the authors, the computer's chief gift was precise concepts and languages for information processing systems, and a human and a program are two species of one genus.
card.limits: The two species differ in memory organization, elementary processes and program organization, so the analogy is to a shared genus, not to identity.

concepts.title: Adaptivity and the three layers
concepts.question: How can behavior that looks complex come from a simple information processing system, and what lies between environment and system?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: Problem solving behavior looks highly complex. The authors say the key to understanding human problem solvers is their flexibility, or programmability: they survive by behaving adaptively across a wide range of environments, so organism and environment must be understood together.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: Factor the task environment apart from the hardware, and a very simple IPS suffices for chess, logic and cryptarithmetic. Its complex behavior comes from the environment's demands interacting with a few basic parameters of the system, above all its memories. Between them lie three layers, moving inward: the problem space, where solving is search; the methods, the means of that search; and the production system, the program organization that realizes the methods.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors say all this intermediate structure, though invariant, is for many purposes of explanation and prediction totally transparent: only knowledge of the demands of the environment, the general level of intelligence of the human, and the basic cognitive limits of the IPS are required to explain behavior.

card.rule: According to the authors, complex problem solving arises from a simple IPS meeting the demands of a task, through three layers: problem space, methods, production system.
card.limits: The claim rests on three tasks and on the assumption of adaptivity. The layers are still real mechanisms, not empty: the authors say they fill the gap between environment and IPS.

concepts.title: An outer and an inner theory
concepts.question: In what sense do the authors have an outer and an inner theory, and how does their link differ from thermodynamics and kinetic theory?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The authors argue that, for many purposes, only the demands of the environment, the general level of intelligence of the human and the basic cognitive limits of the IPS are needed to explain behavior. They therefore speak of an 'inner' and an 'outer' theory and reach for an analogy from physics.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The authors speak of an outer theory, which explains behavior from the environment's demands, and an inner theory of the mechanisms within. The outer theory provides the main, gross results. The inner theory provides the fine structure: dynamic details over time, and lapses from adaptation such as errors, confusions and wrong explorations.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors hesitate to evoke thermodynamics and kinetic theory, because the link there between macroscopic and microscopic theory is statistical. Here the link is adaptational: matters are simple because things line up in a means-ends chain in which only the end points count (equifinality), not because the law of large numbers cancels details. In other respects the analogy is apt.

card.rule: According to the authors, the outer theory gives the main, gross results and the inner theory the fine structure, joined by adaptation rather than by statistics.
card.limits: The analogy is partial. The authors themselves hesitate to use it, because the physics link is statistical and theirs is adaptational.

concepts.title: Reach, gaps and a progress report
concepts.question: How far does the authors' theory reach beyond its three tasks, and what do they say remains open?

blocks.label: Problem or observation
blocks.text: The theory of Chapter 14 is framed in general terms, but its empirical base is three tasks: chess, logic and cryptarithmetic. A reader must ask how far a theory built on so narrow a base can be trusted.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.text: The authors say the base gives strong clues to a general theory without defining the limits of the induction. The gaps are not only gaps of extent: many aspects of the basic IPS are unexplored, such as how large the effective short-term memory is when a person uses scratch paper, or what the specifications for associative access in long-term memory are.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors did not go outside their three tasks for extra verification. They look ahead to tasks of greater complexity and openness, such as everyday reasoning and scientific discovery, and to the whole developmental continuum. They call the volume a progress report and invite extensions, emendations or even refutations.

card.rule: According to the authors, the theory goes beyond its three tasks and yields strong clues, but the limits of the induction are undefined and many aspects of the IPS remain unexplored.
card.limits: The authors claim an essentially correct view, not a finished one. Reach beyond chess, logic and cryptarithmetic is argued, not tested.

concepts.title: A personal view of the antecedents
concepts.question: Why do the authors call the addendum a personal view rather than a history, and where do they draw the line?

blocks.label: Context
blocks.text: The addendum closes the book. In the main text the authors cite sources only where scholarly obligation requires it. Here they allow themselves more detail about where the work came from, especially its less obvious links to other streams of research.

blocks.label: What happened
blocks.text: The authors say this is not the place for a full-scale history of the developments behind the book, and that they are not the ones to write it. They offer notes they call a somewhat personal view of history.

blocks.label: Why
blocks.text: They take World War II as a convenient boundary between pre-history and history. The pre-history has two main strands. The post-war history needs particular attention to the ideas gathered under the label of cybernetics.

blocks.label: Result
blocks.text: The reader gets the participants' own account of their roots, organised around that boundary, not a neutral survey by outside historians.

card.rule: According to the authors, the addendum is a personal view of antecedents, divided at World War II into pre-history and history.
card.limits: Our reading: a personal account shows how the authors saw their roots, but it covers only what they chose to include and cannot settle how others would tell the story.

concepts.title: Cognitive psychology before 1945
concepts.question: Who counts as a forerunner of the authors' work before 1945, and why do they mostly look to Europe?

blocks.label: Context
blocks.text: In America, from the time of William James to about World War II, research on complex human thought had a great gap. Behaviorism, the nonsense syllable and the rat dominated. Hull's 1920 thesis on concept formation was an exception.

blocks.label: What happened
blocks.text: Hull left the problem for others that fitted the Zeitgeist, and this was read as showing the futility of a direct approach to higher mental processes. Of American psychologists, the authors name Tolman and Brunswik as the real forerunners. Tolman treated the organism as goal-seeking and shaped by its environment. Brunswik described that environment in probabilistic terms.

blocks.label: Why
blocks.text: European psychology cared less about methodological rigor and used verbal protocols more. Bartlett studied how information is represented inside the head, and the Wurzburg school, with Selz, stressed central processes.

blocks.label: Result
blocks.text: Wertheimer's and Duncker's work on problem solving was hardly known in America until after the war. Tracing concepts and citations, the authors find clear lineages: their own work and de Groot's owe large debts to Selz.

card.rule: According to the authors, the American forerunners were Tolman and Brunswik, and the stronger lineage ran from the European work on thought.
card.limits: Our reading: the authors trace lineage through concepts and citations, so a forerunner here means a shared line of ideas, not a claim that the earlier author held their views.

concepts.title: Filling the empty organism
concepts.question: What do the authors accept and what do they deny in the physiological psychologists' call to fill the empty organism?

blocks.label: Context
blocks.text: Quoting Boring, the authors describe the physiological psychologists' standard viewpoint. Skinner's empty organism links stimulus and response with nothing in between. Boring argued these correlations are early steps and the organism must be filled with explanatory mechanisms.

blocks.label: What happened
blocks.text: The authors split Boring's assumption in two. Part one is that the empty organism is to be filled with explanatory mechanisms, which all but radical behaviorists accept. Part two is that the mechanisms are to be neurological.

blocks.label: Why
blocks.text: They accept the first part and deny the second. This is not a denial of reduction in principle. They hold that, because of the complexity of the phenomena, the reduction of stimulus-response regularities to neural processes takes several successive steps, with layers of theory between, as in physics, chemistry and molecular biology.

blocks.label: Result
blocks.text: Information processing theories are one such layer, between behavior and neurology. The authors say Hebb's insistence that his theory was physiological shows the confusion they mean.

card.rule: According to the authors, mechanisms must fill the empty organism, but they need not be neurological, because the reduction needs layers of theory.
card.limits: Our reading: a middle layer is not a rejection of neuroscience; the authors keep reduction in principle and deny only a one-step reduction.

concepts.title: What formal logic gave psychology
concepts.question: What did formal logic contribute to information processing psychology, given that logic is not human thinking?

blocks.label: Context
blocks.text: Formal logic grew from the work of Peano, Frege and Whitehead and Russell around the turn of the century. The authors say the greatest weakness of the antecedents was the lack of a language that made psychological concepts clear and operational.

blocks.label: What happened
blocks.text: Logic supplied such a language. Even so, logicians and psychologists agree that logic is not human thinking. Logicians say inference has objective formal standards, which exist in Plato's heaven and not in heads. Psychologists say thinking is often not rigorous or step-by-step.

blocks.label: Why
blocks.text: The authors say the fundamental contribution was to show by example that symbol manipulation can be described as concrete processes. Symbols can be copied, compared, rearranged and concatenated as definitely as boards can be sawed, planed, measured and glued.

blocks.label: Result
blocks.text: This eased the apparent gap between ideas and the physical nervous system. Even a metaphorical use of logic's symbol manipulation liberated ways of conceptualizing thought, problem solving and decision making.

card.rule: According to the authors, logic showed that manipulating symbols can be described as concrete processes, while thinking itself is not logic.
card.limits: Our reading: the authors keep logic and thinking apart, so the lesson is about describing processes on symbols, not about thought being logical.

concepts.title: Decision theory, Turing and mathematics
concepts.question: Which pre-war developments beyond formal logic fed into the Zeitgeist the authors describe?

blocks.label: Context
blocks.text: Alongside formal logic, economics developed formal theories of rational decision making, the economic man. The authors say he was patently too rational by human standards, so psychology disputed or ignored his relevance.

blocks.label: What happened
blocks.text: Economics still reasoned about courses of action, and statistical decision theory was a close relative. Statistics linked to philosophy through the foundations of probability and the problem of induction. In 1936 Alan Turing described the Turing machine, the culmination of the drive to formalize processing. Carnap, Church, Curry and Post formalized logical syntax, later a model for formal grammar.

blocks.label: Why
blocks.text: The authors point to a growing belief that mathematics could do for biological, psychological and social phenomena what it had done for physics. Lotka's 1924 book foreshadowed cybernetic concepts, and Rashevsky carried the work forward.

blocks.label: Result
blocks.text: The authors see a growing Zeitgeist with faith in mathematics and a focus on symbols and their manipulation. Symbols became as tangible as wood or metal, and the Turing machine was an all-purpose planer and lathe for symbols.

card.rule: According to the authors, decision theory, the Turing machine and mathematical biology joined logic in a Zeitgeist centred on symbols and their manipulation.
card.limits: Our reading: the authors call this a Zeitgeist, a shared climate of ideas, not a single program of research or a claim that these workers cooperated.

concepts.title: The label cybernetics and its logic ties
concepts.question: What did cybernetics cover, how did early work tie to logic, and what role did the computer play at first?

blocks.label: Context
blocks.text: The authors take 1956 as a critical year, about a decade after the war, and sketch the mid-fifties. The developments they trace came to public notice at the war's end under the label cybernetics, a term Norbert Wiener devised. It embraced information theory, feedback systems theory and the electronic computer. Behind the Iron Curtain it also covered game theory, mathematical economics, statistical decision theory, management science and operations research.

blocks.label: What happened
blocks.text: The earliest publications, before and during the early war years, tied closely to logic: Shannon's 1938 master's thesis used Boolean algebra for switching circuits, and the 1943 Pitts-McCulloch paper gave a Boolean analysis of nerve networks. Most prominent figures had been immersed in symbolic logic.

blocks.label: Why
blocks.text: The authors read the broad use of the term as further evidence for the unity of the Zeitgeist. They say the war did not produce the cybernetic developments; it more likely delayed them slightly.

blocks.label: Result
blocks.text: Despite its logic ties, the computer as a symbolic machine played a muted role at first. The main underpinnings were feedback and information theory.

card.rule: According to the authors, cybernetics joined information theory, feedback and the computer, was tied to logic from the start, and gave the symbolic computer only a muted role at first.
card.limits: Our reading: the muted role is the authors' account of early expositions, not a claim that nobody saw the computer's importance later.

concepts.title: Work ahead of its Zeitgeist
concepts.question: According to the authors, what happens to work that is too early for, or fits, its Zeitgeist, and how did the brain-computer analogy fare?

blocks.label: Context
blocks.text: The authors build their account on a Zeitgeist, a shared climate of ideas. They note it is well known, or at least widely believed, that work which too far anticipates its Zeitgeist is ignored, while work fitting it is recognized promptly.

blocks.label: What happened
blocks.text: Von Neumann's game theory of the twenties was known to few before 1940, Lotka was read by few biologists, and few logicians knew the discoveries of Godel, Turing, Church and Post. All this changed in the early post-war years.

blocks.label: Why
blocks.text: Biology and the sciences of man soon used feedback ideas, most enthusiastically in Britain. The brain-computer metaphor appeared almost at once, and warnings against taking it seriously followed almost as fast.

blocks.label: Result
blocks.text: Feedback had considerable but unspecific impact on psychology. Information theory's influence was clear and precise, but its high-water mark came about 1955 and by 1962 it was a useful, specialized tool.

card.rule: According to the authors, work too far ahead of its Zeitgeist is ignored, and the brain-computer analogy came with warnings from the start.
card.limits: Our reading: the authors give the ignored-if-early rule as widely believed, and illustrate it with cases, not as a law.

concepts.title: Streams within psychology
concepts.question: Which strands of mid-fifties psychology did the authors see as converging on the new approach?

blocks.label: Context
blocks.text: By the mid-fifties the authors identify several strands in psychology, each gaining outlets and supporters after the war.

blocks.label: What happened
blocks.text: European work on thought was becoming available: translations of Duncker and of Wertheimer appeared in 1945, and Humphrey's 1951 book gave the first extensive English discussion of Selz. Concept formation was revived by information theory, decision theory and game theory, with Hovland in 1952 and Miller and Bruner, Austin and Goodnow in 1956.

blocks.label: Why
blocks.text: The war produced a vast increase in research on human skills, called human factors, much of it on human members of man-machine systems such as pilots, gunners and radar personnel. Researchers thus saw analogies between human information processing and servomechanisms and computers.

blocks.label: Result
blocks.text: Human factors and concept formation overlapped in ideas and people, and together they bridged mainstream psychology and computer science. Broadbent's 1954 model of attention and memory illustrates the concepts that emerged.

card.rule: According to the authors, European thought research, concept formation and human factors all fed psychology's new approach, with human factors and concept formation as the bridge to computer science.
card.limits: Our reading: the strands are the authors' selection from a mid-fifties picture, not a full account of psychology then.

concepts.title: Linguistics in the early fifties
concepts.question: How did the authors see linguistics, formalization and the computer relating in the early fifties?

blocks.label: Context
blocks.text: The authors say linguistics had a long-standing concern with formalization and methodological clarity. They write as outsiders and say they cannot judge how far developments there reflected the larger picture.

blocks.label: What happened
blocks.text: Harris's Methods in Structural Linguistics (1951) gave new impetus. Chomsky's work began in 1955, though it had little impact until a few years later (1957). It would redirect much of linguistics from structure toward processing, meaning generative systems.

blocks.label: Why
blocks.text: Some connections with logic are clear, for example in Chomsky's 1954 work.

blocks.label: Result
blocks.text: Efforts at mechanical translation, which might seem to tie linguistics to the computer, were made outside the main stream of linguistics.

card.rule: According to the authors, linguistics was moving from structure toward generative processing, while mechanical translation stayed outside its mainstream.
card.limits: Our reading: the authors speak as outsiders, so their link between linguistics and the larger Zeitgeist is cautious.

concepts.title: Computers as numeric machines
concepts.question: How were digital computers seen in the early fifties, and what simulation work already existed?

blocks.label: Context
blocks.text: The authors call digital computers a prominent event of the early post-war era. Their general theoretical character as universal machines was clearly understood.

blocks.label: What happened
blocks.text: They were viewed as mathematical machines working with numbers, not symbols. Programming was rudimentary: the first book on programming appeared in 1951 (Wilkes, Wheeler, Gill), and languages other than assembly languages only began toward the end of the period, with FORTRAN begun in 1954.

blocks.label: Why
blocks.text: So the powerful experience of working with a system that seemed to interpret symbols as the user did was not available in the early fifties.

blocks.label: Result
blocks.text: Some simulation of cognition existed. Building robots to illustrate psychological theories predated the computer (Boring 1946; Walter 1953; Ashby 1952), but it was separate from computer simulation, which moved toward game playing and other symbolic activities. The first checker program was coded in 1952, and Turing in 1950 stated the problem of simulation in a sophisticated form.

card.rule: According to the authors, early-fifties computers were seen as numeric machines, programming was primitive, and robot-building stayed separate from symbolic computer simulation.
card.limits: Our reading: the authors describe how computers were viewed then; their later pages show that view changing.

concepts.title: Starting with chess in 1954
concepts.question: Why did Newell begin with chess in 1954, and why did the team shift to theorem proving?

blocks.label: Context
blocks.text: In late 1954 A. Newell began in earnest to program a digital computer to learn to play good chess. The context was the Systems Research Laboratory at RAND, which simulated an air defense radar center. The proximate cause was the work of Selfridge and Dineen (1955), which made clear how computers could become non-numerical processors.

blocks.label: What happened
blocks.text: Newell's first description (1955) proposed aspiration values and a notion of satisfactory solution for judging moves. It also called for rules of thumb, later called heuristics, to cut the huge problem space. By early 1955 Shaw and Simon had joined him.

blocks.label: Why
blocks.text: The group weighed which programming language to use and whether to continue with chess or first design a theorem-prover in geometry or logic. For several reasons, the latter appeared somewhat simpler for an initial effort.

blocks.label: Result
blocks.text: Attention gradually shifted to theorem proving.

card.rule: According to the authors, the project began with chess in late 1954 and shifted to theorem proving because that looked simpler for a first effort.
card.limits: Our reading: the shift is described as gradual and for several reasons, so no single cause is given.

concepts.title: From Logic Theorist to machine proofs
concepts.question: What steps led from choosing propositional calculus to the first machine proof, and why did the languages suit psychology?

blocks.label: Context
blocks.text: By late October 1955 proving theorems in the propositional calculus, within the system of Whitehead and Russell, was chosen as the first target.

blocks.label: What happened
blocks.text: On December 15, 1955 the first successful hand simulation of a Principia Mathematica proof (Theorem 2.15) used the methods and flow diagram that went into the Logic Theorist. IPL-I was published in September 1956, after an unpublished RAND report of May 1, 1956 read on May 2 in Washington. The first versions of LT run on a machine were in IPL-II on the JOHNNIAC at RAND, and the first complete machine proof, of Theorem 2.01, came on August 9, 1956.

blocks.label: Why
blocks.text: Features of human memory, especially its associative organization, were exploited in the design of the information processing languages. That cue from psychology was probably one important hint toward list processing.

blocks.label: Result
blocks.text: The languages were then used to write programs expressing psychological theories.

card.rule: According to the authors, hand simulation in December 1955 came before the August 1956 machine proof, and the languages were designed for complexity and suited psychology.
card.limits: Our reading: the dates are the authors' record of their own project; the card does not weigh other claims to priority.

concepts.title: The Dartmouth summer seminar
concepts.question: Who gathered at Dartmouth in 1956, and which two concrete schemes did they bring?

blocks.label: Context
blocks.text: A research project in artificial intelligence was organized at Dartmouth for June 1956 by McCarthy, Minsky, Rochester and Shannon. Attendees included a large share of all those then active in the field, among them Selfridge, Solomonoff, More, Gelernter, Newell and Simon.

blocks.label: What happened
blocks.text: Many ideas for programs doing problem solving, pattern recognition or game playing were in the air. Only two concrete new schemes were brought: the Logic Theorist, and More's program for the propositional calculus using natural deduction. More had a flow diagram and had hand simulated it. The LT description, later presented in Cambridge in September, was distributed, and early debugging output was shown.

blocks.label: Why
blocks.text: The Logic Theorist was the only fully described program; its early debugging outputs were exhibited, and More's scheme existed on paper.

blocks.label: Result
blocks.text: Minsky's essay Steps Toward Artificial Intelligence, drafted and circulated as a report late in 1956 and published years later, reflected and helped codify the knowledge pooled there.

card.rule: According to the authors, Dartmouth gathered most active AI workers, but only the Logic Theorist and More's scheme were concrete new programs.
card.limits: Our reading: the count of two concrete schemes is the authors' report as participants, not an exhaustive survey.

concepts.title: From thinking-aloud tapes to GPS
concepts.question: How did comparing LT with human thinking-aloud tapes lead to the General Problem Solver?

blocks.label: Context
blocks.text: Serious attempts to interpret LT as a psychological theory began in autumn 1956. The authors had learned that Moore and Anderson at Yale used logic theorem-proving problems, disguised as decoding exercises, in problem-solving research. Their formal system was close to that of Whitehead and Russell, so it could serve to compare people with LT.

blocks.label: What happened
blocks.text: Peter Houts, a graduate student at Carnegie, made tape recordings of thinking-aloud sessions on the Moore-Anderson task. The first tapes were transcribed in spring 1957.

blocks.label: Why
blocks.text: Analysis showed that LT's organization did not fit the detail of human behavior, which showed signs of what the authors now call the means-ends method.

blocks.label: Result
blocks.text: Discussion of the tapes in a seminar on organizational behavior at Carnegie in summer 1957 moved the analysis toward the first versions of the General Problem Solver. Its flow diagram was produced before the end of October 1957, and the planning method a few days later.

card.rule: According to the authors, comparing LT with thinking-aloud protocols showed that LT did not fit, and the means-ends method seen in people led to GPS.
card.limits: Our reading: GPS grew from a program that failed to match the data, so fitting data was the aim, not defending LT.

concepts.title: The Elements paper and first public GPS
concepts.question: What thesis did the 1958 Elements paper state, and when was GPS first publicly described?

blocks.label: Context
blocks.text: The first published attempt to draw implications of the theorem-proving programs for the psychology of problem solving was Elements of a Theory of Human Problem Solving, in the Psychological Review for July 1958. It was written more than a year earlier and drew on LT experience.

blocks.label: What happened
blocks.text: The paper stressed broad resemblances between a heuristic problem-solving program and human problem solving, without detailed behavioral comparisons. Its thesis was that an explanation of an observed behavior of the organism is provided by a program of primitive information processes that generates the behavior.

blocks.label: Why
blocks.text: It explored the methodological assumptions of the approach and its relation to neurological, associationist and Gestalt explanations.

blocks.label: Result
blocks.text: The authors call it the first explicit and deliberate statement of the position now known as information processing psychology, though that phrase was not used. GPS was first publicly described, without its name, in a paper read on May 14, 1958 at a Colorado symposium and again at the RAND seminar, but published only in 1962.

card.rule: According to the authors, the Elements paper held that a program of primitive information processes explains behavior, and GPS was first described publicly in May 1958.
card.limits: Our reading: the authors say the paper fixed the position but did not use its name, so the label came later.

concepts.title: Chess resumed and de Groot
concepts.question: How did work on chess resume, and what led to collaboration with de Groot?

blocks.label: Context
blocks.text: Work on a chess program had been nearly dormant since 1955 and was resumed toward the end of 1957.

blocks.label: What happened
blocks.text: Meanwhile the discovery of de Groot's 1946 work on the thinking of the chess player led to contact and collaboration with him and his colleagues in Amsterdam. The authors say the collaboration has continued down to the present.

blocks.label: Why
blocks.text: The authors give no further reason for the pause.

blocks.label: Result
blocks.text: The NSS chess program became operational in 1958. Its history and that of earlier chess programs appear in the 1958 paper Chess-playing Programs and the Problem of Complexity.

card.rule: According to the authors, chess work was nearly dormant from 1955, resumed late in 1957, and led through de Groot's work to a lasting Amsterdam collaboration.
card.limits: Our reading: the addendum gives the sequence but no reason for the pause, so a reader should not supply one.

concepts.title: The 1958 RAND Summer Seminar
concepts.question: What was the 1958 RAND Summer Seminar for, and what followed from it?

blocks.label: Context
blocks.text: By spring 1958 LT had been tested extensively, GPS had been conceived and hand simulated, NSS was operative, EPAM was being built and protocol data were being analyzed. Apart from the RAND-Carnegie group and the MIT group there were no large-scale programs using computer simulation for problem solving, and communication with other streams was weak.

blocks.label: What happened
blocks.text: A committee of the Social Science Research Council (Hovland, Miller, Simon) organized a 1958 seminar at RAND in Santa Monica, directed by Newell and Simon. Its aim was to acquaint social scientists, especially psychologists, with simulation techniques. Lectures came from Newell, Simon, Hovland, Miller, Minsky and Shaw, with programming instruction in IPL-IV.

blocks.label: Why
blocks.text: The curriculum was built around the main programs: LT, GPS, NSS and EPAM.

blocks.label: Result
blocks.text: Participants spread the methods: Berlyne in 1965, Abelson's hot cognition in 1963, Green's BASEBALL program, and Hovland and Hunt's models of concept formation. Further seminars followed in 1962 and 1963.

card.rule: According to the authors, the 1958 RAND seminar taught simulation to psychologists and linked the RAND-Carnegie group to other streams of work.
card.limits: Our reading: the influence claims are the authors' own, drawn from participants' later writing, so they reflect how the authors saw the seminar.

concepts.title: Where the history stops and what came later
concepts.question: Why does the history stop at 1958, and which parts of the theory came later?

blocks.label: Context
blocks.text: The authors say the basic ideas of the theory emerged from late 1954 to 1958, and they give an almost blow-by-blow account of those critical years. They say even parochial history must stop with 1958; later work broadened into developmental psychology, psycholinguistics and cognitive psychology.

blocks.label: What happened
