blocks.text: Not every ingredient was in place by 1958. They single out two features that postdate the critical years: production systems as a preferred form for specifying the information processing system, and the postulated relation between environment and organism. The problem space descends by a continuous path from heuristic search, itself an attempt to formulate what the early AI programs shared.

blocks.label: Why
blocks.text: Production systems were, in the authors' words, a well-prepared formalism waiting for a scientific mission. They come from Post's work in symbolic logic and appear as Markov algorithms and as rewrite rules in linguistics. They gained currency when programming languages put them to use.

blocks.label: Result
blocks.text: The authors first used production systems in the chess analysis (1965) and made the link explicit in the cryptarithmetic work (1966). They trace the environment theme to economics and Simon's 1947 book.

card.rule: According to the authors, the history stops at 1958 because later work broadened too far, and production systems and the environment-organism relation postdate it.
card.limits: Our reading: the authors say the critical years are almost blow-by-blow, but later ingredients such as production systems came afterward, so the story does not end in 1958.

concepts.unit: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.section: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: What kind of theory this is
concepts.question: What kind of theory do the authors build, and what do they ask of it first?

paragraphs: The authors do not offer laws that say what behavior must be. They posit internal mechanisms, processes that handle symbols, which produce the behavior, so the theory explains and does not only describe. They decline to say where in the brain these processes sit.

The theory models one person on one task at a time, as a precise symbolic system from which behavior can be calculated. Because it can be calculated, it is more than a metaphor. What all people share is a question asked afterward.

Before fitting fine detail, the authors ask whether a system working within human limits, such as processing rate and immediate memory, is able to do the task at all. Only then do they refine it against specific data.
card.rule: According to the authors, the theory posits mechanisms, models one individual precisely, and asks first that those mechanisms be sufficient to do the task.
card.limits: Sufficiency is a first approximation: a system that can do the task need not be the way people do it, and the model's neat discrete symbols are an approximation.

concepts.unit: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.section: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: The chain from task to program
concepts.question: In what order do task, problem space, methods and production system limit one another?

paragraphs: The book's argument runs inward in steps. A few general traits of the human processor lead any task to be represented as a problem space. The task environment limits which spaces are possible. The space limits which methods and programs are possible.

The epilogue names the layers between environment and processor: the problem space, where solving is search; the methods, the means of that search; and the production system, the program organization that realizes the methods.
Each step fixes possibilities, not the actual choice. Which space and program a particular solver ends with depends on history and instructions, and the authors call their account of that tentative.
card.rule: According to the authors, the task limits the possible problem spaces, the space limits the possible methods and programs, and history and instructions pick the actual ones.
card.limits: Each link states what is possible, not what a given person does, and the account of how an actual space is chosen is tentative.

concepts.unit: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.section: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: Memory limits and the shape of search
concepts.question: How do the processor's memory limits help explain solving as many small steps of a few seconds each?

paragraphs: Chapter 14 gives the human processor a few gross traits. It runs one elementary process at a time. Its short-term memory holds about five to seven symbols. Writing new structures to long-term memory costs several seconds per chunk, far more than reading.

The authors argue these limits shape problem solving. Short-term memory is too small to hold one ever-growing state of knowledge, so the solver works through discrete states, keeps only one or two return points, and spends of the order of seconds in each.
Many small steps, each on fresh information, use a serial processor better than long deliberation. The authors offer this as a heuristic argument and not as a proof.
card.rule: According to the authors, a serial processor with a tiny short-term store and slow writing is why solving is a series of seconds-long steps with little backup.
card.limits: The link from limits to shape is argued from the three tasks, and the measured times are order-of-magnitude averages from a few subjects.

concepts.unit: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.section: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: Where the power of search comes from
concepts.question: Why can search succeed in huge spaces, and where must its power come from?

paragraphs: Chapter 4 frames solving as picking a rare element out of an immense set, so size is the usual source of difficulty. Blind generation finds a solution only if run long enough, which is impractical for large sets. Such hopeless methods serve as the standard against which stronger ones are judged.

Power over blind search comes only from information a method actually uses. The logic program LT shows three kinds: generate only elements already guaranteed to have some solution properties, use feedback gathered while generating, and work with simpler abstractions of the problem.

Chapter 14 says why such information exists: structure in a space is redundancy, so what is known in one place predicts something about another. Selective search then needs the solver to notice the right features.
card.rule: According to the authors, search beats blind generation only by using structure in the task, through guaranteed generators, step-by-step feedback and abstraction.
card.limits: Even strong selectivity depends on noticing features, and it paid little in one case: LT's abstraction cost nearly as much effort as it saved.

concepts.unit: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.section: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: How the book builds its evidence
concepts.question: How is each of the three tasks used as evidence, and what counts as a test of the theory?

paragraphs: Each task gets three chapters. First a task analysis shows which problem spaces and methods the task allows. Then a program is compared with the recorded thinking aloud of one subject, which the authors call a microtheory, a single data point for the general theory. Last comes a broader view across subjects.

A theory fitted to one subject, read literally, predicts that every other subject produces an identical protocol. The authors expect that to fail. What matters is how and how far real behavior departs from it.
The same ideas recur across puzzles, logic and chess: problem spaces, search and production systems. That sharing is what lets three different tasks support one theory.
card.rule: According to the authors, each task supplies a task analysis, a microtheory for one attempt and a comparison across subjects, and the test is the manner and extent of departure.
card.limits: Three tasks with a few subjects each is all the evidence there is, and the authors call the book a progress report.

concepts.unit: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.section: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: What a program-and-protocol match shows
concepts.question: What does a close match between program and protocol show, and what does it leave open?

paragraphs: A match between a program and a protocol is the book's main evidence, so the authors weigh it. They can show that a hypothesized organization is sufficient to reproduce the behavior. They cannot show that it is the only organization that could.

They also answer the charge of circularity. GPS was shaped partly by studying protocols, yet its methods and heuristics were defined independently from the task and theory, so it could have failed to match.
A single percentage can mislead, because it mixes errors of omission and errors of commission. And evidence that a space was used does not show that nothing more was available to the subject.
card.rule: A fit shows sufficiency and testability, not uniqueness; read the kinds of miss behind any single number.
card.limits: Sufficiency still narrows the field when rival organizations fail to match, and the authors accept some gaps by assuming competence does not swing wildly over short periods.

concepts.unit: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.section: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: One core, many paths
concepts.question: How can subjects' paths differ so much while the authors still claim a shared theory?

paragraphs: The subjects' paths differ, yet the authors find a common core. In cryptarithmetic, one program with small changes in the priority of strategies and in the particular errors made can produce protocols that resemble any of the four subjects.

In a large search space a small cause can send the search far away, so comparing paths directly may exaggerate the differences between the programs behind them. In logic the differences appear as style, such as how many rules to apply or whether to work backward.
Beyond that, the theory fixes the processor's organization and a few memory constants. These bound the style of behavior but leave its content open.
card.rule: According to the authors, different paths can come from shared strategies with different priorities and errors, and the invariants bound style, not content.
card.limits: The causes of the errors are not known, and the list of dimensions of style comes from a few protocols and is not a full theory of individual differences.

concepts.unit: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.section: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: Displays and boards as part of the system
concepts.question: How does the book bring paper, boards and displays into its theory of the solver?

paragraphs: Paper, a chessboard or a display of letters is not left outside the theory. The book describes an external memory in the same terms as the internal ones, by capacity, access and read and write times, because the program a solver uses depends on it as much as on short-term and long-term memory.

The effect is large. Tasks are much easier with the board or display in view, even when the solver only looks and never writes. Functionally, short-term memory plus the part of a display in foveal view acts as one memory.
When a display is only partly available, the authors define an extended knowledge state: what is in mind plus what a retrieval process can fetch from the display.
card.rule: According to the authors, external memory is part of the system, specified like the internal memories, and the knowledge state may include what can be retrieved from it.
card.limits: The accessing functions could not be specified in detail for the logic task, and how far the foveal-view merge extends is open.

concepts.unit: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.section: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: An outer theory and an inner theory
concepts.question: Why can the task environment explain so much, and what is left for the inner mechanisms?

paragraphs: The authors argue that an adaptive system hides most of its inner detail behind its fit to the environment. Only a few gross features of the processor show through, which is why the demands of the task explain so much.

They call this the outer theory: it explains the main behavior from the environment's demands. The inner theory of the mechanisms supplies the fine structure, which means dynamic detail over time and lapses from adaptation such as errors and wrong explorations.

A property shared by every path to a goal is a demand whoever the solver is, so the outer theory needs no assumption about the solver. Still, what a task requires can itself be set by a culture, as the chess players show.
card.rule: According to the authors, adaptation lets the task environment explain the gross results, and the inner mechanisms explain fine structure and lapses.
card.limits: In extreme environments, where adaptation fails, the processor's structure shows through, and the authors cannot yet say in advance which features will.

concepts.unit: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.section: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: How far the theory reaches
concepts.question: How far do the authors say the theory reaches, and what does the evidence leave unsettled?

paragraphs: The theory is stated in general terms but rests on three tasks, mostly adults solving short symbolic problems. The authors say their arguments are more general than their data, yet they also say the evidence cannot define the theory's limits.

Some limits are stated. Problem solving is search in a problem space over the tasks and subjects studied, not necessarily all problem solving. A space is meaningful only if thinking seldom crosses its boundary. The theory is a first approximation for normal situations, not for cases where biological limits are exceeded.

Open territory includes how a solver gets a space and program for a new task, how solvers differ, and many details of the processor. The authors call the book a progress report and invite extensions, emendations or even refutations.
card.rule: According to the authors, the theory is offered as general and gives strong clues from three tasks, but its limits are undefined and the book is a progress report.
card.limits: Reach beyond chess, logic and cryptarithmetic is argued here, not tested.

questions.q: A lab sets out to explain every part of human thinking in one report. What outcome would the authors of this book expect?
options: Coverage that stays shallow, since one work aiming at all of thinking cannot probe deeply
A deeper theory, because a wider scope forces more careful reasoning on every topic at once, in turn
A complete theory, because science advances all at once when the aim is set high enough in advance
A theory trusted more widely, because a larger scope gives readers more reasons to accept it all
optionExplain: Right: Spreading over everything is the trade-off the authors name. The card next sets this out.
It sounds plausible that breadth forces care, but the authors say wide aims make a work superficial.
The authors say the opposite: not all things can be done at once.
Trust is not what the authors discuss; they warn about shallowness.
questions.explain: The authors say aiming at all of human thinking in a single work makes the work superficial. The card next sets out the trade-off.
questions.rule: According to the authors, one work must trade breadth for depth, and this book chooses depth.

questions.q: The authors describe science as a series of successive ____.
questions.explain: Science proceeds by approximations that improve over time, so a work may start with a limited piece.

questions.q: A garden club plans a study of soil. Which plan follows the trade-off the authors describe?
options: Study every crop, pest and climate at once
Study one crop but promise to explain all garden science from it
Study one crop's root growth in depth, accepting that other soil questions stay untouched
Study nothing yet, since no single study can advance understanding at all
optionExplain: Covering everything is the aim that, per the authors, makes a work superficial.
Depth in one place does not give coverage of others; the trade-off remains.
Right: Depth costs coverage; the authors accept that aspects "however important" are left out.
The authors say no single work advances understanding very far, not that none advances it.
questions.explain: Probing deeply on one piece gives up coverage of the rest. The authors choose this, and accept the cost.
questions.rule: Depth in one place means gaps elsewhere.

questions.q: The authors list limits on any scientific work. Which of these belong to their list? Select all that apply.
options: The types of subjects it studies
How many readers agree with its conclusions
The formal character of the theory
The size of the publisher's print run
The data it gathers
optionExplain: Right: The authors name the kinds of subjects as a limit.
Agreement is not among the limits listed; the limits concern what the work itself covers.
Right: The kind of theory used limits what a work can say.
Nothing like this appears; the list concerns the work's content and method.
Right: The data a work collects limit what it can show.
questions.explain: The authors name five limits: the formal character of the theory, the phenomena it covers, the experimental situations it uses, the types of subjects it studies, and the data it gathers.
questions.rule: Theory form, phenomena, situations, subjects and data all limit a work.
questions.teaches: The authors list five limits on a single work: the formal character of the theory, the phenomena covered, the experimental situations used, the types of subjects studied and the data gathered.

questions.q: A reviewer concludes that, because the authors leave much out, they must think those aspects unimportant. What is wrong with this?
options: The authors say the aspects left untouched may be important; leaving them out is a cost of depth
Nothing; leaving something out shows the authors rank it low, and the text says so directly
The authors left nothing out
The authors cannot say what is left out
optionExplain: Right: The text says aspects are left untouched "however important", so omission is not a verdict.
The text does not rank the omitted aspects as unimportant; it says they may be important.
The authors say the opposite: a work covering all thinking would be superficial.
They do plan to indicate what is included and excluded in the next section.
questions.explain: Probing in depth means many aspects "however important" stay untouched. Omission follows from the trade-off, not from a low ranking.

questions.q: A weather model built on one valley's data also predicts a neighbouring valley well. How would the authors view this?
options: As proof that the first valley's limits were never real
As a flaw, because a theory should stay within the base on which it was first built and tested
As irrelevant, because success in a second case says nothing about a theory built on the first
As the outcome all scientists hope for: a theory that speaks beyond its initial base
optionExplain: The limits are real; reaching beyond them is a hope, not a guarantee.
The authors say the opposite: speaking beyond the base is what scientists hope for.
It does speak to the theory's reach, which the authors welcome.
Right: The authors say a theory may speak beyond its initial base, and all scientists hope for just that.
questions.explain: The authors accept that a work starts from a limited base, and add that a theory may speak beyond it.
questions.rule: A limited base can still carry a theory further.
questions.teaches: The authors say a theory may speak beyond its initial base, and that all scientists hope for just that.

questions.q: True or false: The authors usually distinguish a person performing a task from one learning or developing with respect to it.
questions.explain: The authors usually distinguish a person performing a task from one learning or developing with respect to it. The card next shows the three dimensions.
questions.rule: Locate a study by its task, by whether people perform, learn or develop, and by which people are compared.

questions.q: The three dimensions of Figure 1.1 are task, performance-learning-development and ____ difference.
questions.explain: The third dimension compares individuals, from members of different cultures to different species.

questions.q: A study compares how seven-year-olds in two countries learn to ride a bicycle. Which dimensions does it involve?
options: Only the task dimension
All three: cycling is the task, learning is the second dimension, and country or age is the third
Only the individual-difference dimension
Task and performance only
optionExplain: Learning and the comparison of groups are further dimensions the study uses.
Right: The study fixes a task, studies learning, and compares populations.
The study also names a task and a learning process.
The authors keep learning apart from performing, so the second dimension is learning here.
questions.explain: Cycling is a task, learning to ride puts the study at the learning end of the second dimension, and comparing countries uses the third.
questions.rule: Place a study on all three dimensions.

questions.q: Match each dimension of Figure 1.1 to the kind of variation it describes.
pairs: Doing mathematics versus driving a car
Performing a task versus learning to perform it
questions.explain: Each dimension varies one thing: the situation, the stage of the person with respect to it, or who the person is.
questions.rule: One dimension, one kind of variation.

questions.q: Where does Figure 1.1 place age-related differences between people, according to the authors?
options: Along the temporal axis, because differences dependent on age are strongly related to development
On the task dimension, because older and younger people face different situations in daily life
On the individual-difference axis only, since age is one more way people differ from each other
Nowhere, since the figure leaves out every difference among people of one species
optionExplain: Right: Age differences are tied to development, which the figure shows on the time axis.
Age is not a task; it is tied to development.
The authors say age differences go with development, shown on the temporal axis.
The figure includes cultural, demographic and species differences.
questions.explain: The authors place age differences on the temporal axis with development. Cultures and demographic groups sit on the individual-difference dimension, and the vertical axis reaches other species.
questions.rule: Age goes with development, not with task.
questions.teaches: Differences dependent on age are strongly related to development and sit on the temporal axis, while the vertical axis extends beyond humans to other species.

questions.q: A sports scientist maps a goalkeeper's tasks and training stages; a colleague calls it the full picture. What fits the authors' use of maps?
options: It is a complete theory of the subject
It is useful only if the best list of subsystems is first known with certainty
Its purpose is to mark which portions a study includes, not to give a new or total view
It should be redrawn until the dimensions no longer overlap or blur into each other
optionExplain: The authors say the opposite about their own figure.
The authors say the uncertainty about subsystems makes little difference.
Right: The authors say the figure marks the portions included, not a total view.
The authors accept that the distinctions are imperfect.
questions.explain: A map of dimensions locates a study; it does not claim to be a total view of the subject.
questions.rule: A scope map locates; it does not explain.
questions.teaches: The purpose of the figure is to demark the particular portions included in the book, not to provide a new or total view.

questions.q: Which task fits best into a study of the kind of problem solving this book describes?
options: Learning to ride a bicycle over the whole of a summer
Working through a half-hour logic puzzle on paper
Catching a ball thrown from a few meters away
Drawing up a five-year plan for a whole company
optionExplain: This is learning over a long period, which the book hardly treats.
Right: A short symbolic problem solved by an adult is the book's central case. The card next lays out the focus.
This is a motor skill, outside the central focus.
This activity lasts years, which the book does not examine.
questions.explain: The book looks at symbolic problems lasting about half an hour. The card next lays out the whole focus.
questions.rule: The central focus is adult performance on short symbolic problems, studied as integrated activity.

questions.q: The book's three main tasks are chess, symbolic logic and ____ puzzles.
questions.explain: Cryptarithmetic puzzles are the algebra-like puzzles the authors name as the third main task.

questions.q: Which study would the authors count as inside their central focus?
options: Toddlers acquiring their first words over two years
Adults working a twenty-minute symbolic puzzle, observed from start to finish
Reaction times to a flash of light, measured in milliseconds
A manager's staffing decisions tracked across several years
optionExplain: This concerns development, which the book does not treat at all.
Right: Short symbolic problems solved by adults are exactly the central case.
Elementary reactions of half a second or less are deemphasized.
Activities lasting years receive no attention.
questions.explain: The focus is short, integrated, symbolic performance by adults. The other studies are about development, elementary reactions or long activity.

questions.q: Which of these are outside the book's central focus? Select all that apply.
options: Details of perception and motor skill
Differences in problem solving related to age
The integrated activities that make up problem solving
Personality variables
The performance of intelligent adults
optionExplain: Right: The study is not centrally concerned with these.
Right: Development and age-related differences are left out entirely.
This is the book's center, so it is inside the focus.
Right: The authors say these are not a central concern.
Adult performance is the central subject.
questions.explain: The book concerns integrated problem solving by adults. Perception, motor skill, personality and development lie outside its center.
questions.rule: Performance in, development and personality out.

questions.q: A reader summarizes that the book excludes learning altogether. What does the text say that corrects this?
options: It treats learning as the main topic of the whole book, with performance receiving only a little
It is concerned equally with learning and with performance, and both get a full part of their own
It says nothing about learning at all, which the reader is left to infer from the tasks it studies
It is concerned primarily with performance and only a little with learning, so learning is not excluded
optionExplain: The proportions are reversed: performance is the primary concern.
The text says performance is primary and learning is treated only a little.
The text speaks of learning directly.
Right: Only development, not learning, is entirely excluded in the text.
questions.explain: The wording is "primarily with performance, only a little with learning, and not at all with development". Learning is thin, not absent.
questions.rule: Performance first; learning a little; development not at all.

questions.q: A solver speeds up late in a forty-minute puzzle. A critic wants the data dropped as learning. How would the authors answer?
options: That the data should indeed be dropped, because any sign of learning breaks the central focus of the book
That learning never occurs in puzzles of this kind, so the critic has misread the solver's late speed-up
That learning may be at work in tasks lasting tens of minutes, since the focus is not a boundary
That the speed-up proves the theory right, because learning is the main subject of the whole book
optionExplain: The authors call the focus central, not a boundary, so the data stay.
The text allows that learning may occur.
Right: The text says learning cannot be excluded in complex tasks lasting tens of minutes.
Learning is only a small part of the book's concern.
questions.explain: The focus is central, not a set of boundaries. Learning during a long task cannot be ruled out, and how important perception is, is an empirical question.
questions.rule: A focus is not a boundary.
questions.teaches: Because the focus is not a set of boundaries, learning cannot be excluded in tasks lasting tens of minutes, and how far perception matters is an empirical question, not a matter of definition.

questions.q: Before the mid-1950s, what had psychology mostly studied, according to the authors?
options: Chess, logic and puzzles solved by intelligent adults
The physiology of the central nervous system in human adults
Complex internal symbolic mechanisms, stated explicitly in computer programs
Learning, lower organisms and tasks that are simple for an adult human
optionExplain: These are the new focus of the book, not the earlier one.
The authors do not describe the earlier focus as physiological.
This is the new emphasis dated from 1956.
Right: The authors describe the earlier focus this way. The card next describes the change.
questions.explain: For several decades psychology concentrated on learning, lower organisms and simple tasks. The card next describes what changed.
questions.rule: Around 1956 several fields began to treat complex processes and explicit internal symbolic mechanisms as the thing to study.

questions.q: The authors date the change in scientific outlook roughly from the year ____.
questions.explain: The year is marked by works in psychology, linguistics and computer science.
questions.rule: The change in outlook dates from about 1956.

questions.q: Which research plan matches the new emphasis the authors describe?
options: Write out, step by step, the internal symbolic mechanisms of a complex task
Count how often rats press a lever for food under several different schedules of reward
Measure how many seconds adults need to react to a flash of light on a screen
Rank people on a single trait score and then compare the groups of people with each other
optionExplain: Right: The new emphasis is complex processes and explicit internal symbolic mechanisms.
This is learning in lower organisms, the older emphasis.
This concerns elementary reactions and says nothing of internal symbolic mechanisms.
This treats the person as a static collection of traits, not as a process.
questions.explain: The shift is toward complex processes and explicit symbolic mechanisms inside the organism.

questions.q: True or false: The four works the authors cite for 1956 were all investigations of problem solving.
questions.explain: The text says the common emphasis was not the investigation of problem solving but the exploration of complex processes and explicit internal symbolic mechanisms.
questions.rule: The shared emphasis was complex processes, not problem solving.

questions.q: A historian asks where the tools for the new study of man came from. What do the authors point to?
options: A single school of psychology that was founded by the authors of the four works of 1956 itself
The study of lower organisms learning simple tasks, extended step by step to adult human beings
Physiological research on the central nervous system, which supplied the basic mechanisms needed
Control theory, information theory, game and decision theory, and computers, from World War II
optionExplain: The text says the four works did not stem from a specific common lineage.
This is the older emphasis, which the new approach moved away from.
The authors say physiological mechanisms were inadequate for these tasks.
Right: The authors name this applied mathematics and technology as the broad background.
questions.explain: The authors trace the shared background to technologies that emerged in World War II and spread through the late forties and early fifties.
questions.rule: A shared technological background, not one school.
questions.teaches: The background of the new approach is applied mathematics and technology, such as control theory, information theory, game and decision theory, and computers, which emerged in World War II.

questions.q: A friend says the brain is a computer. When would a scientist stop calling this a metaphor?
options: When specific aspects of behavior can be calculated from a detailed model
When the comparison is repeated often enough that people accept it
When the computer used in the comparison is large enough to be called powerful
When every part of the brain has been matched to a part of the machine
optionExplain: Right: Calculation from detail is the authors' test. The card next spells it out.
Repetition does not turn a comparison into a model.
Size is not the test; the model's precision is.
The authors say such physiological matching is not possible yet.
questions.explain: The test is whether detailed calculations can be made from the comparison. The card next spells it out.
questions.rule: According to the authors, a precise symbolic model from which specific behavior can be calculated is no metaphor.

questions.q: Something ceases to be metaphor when detailed ____ can be made from it.
questions.explain: A metaphor stays rich in features whose relevance is problematic; a model supports calculation.
questions.rule: Calculation separates a model from a metaphor.

questions.q: Which statement about the weather goes beyond metaphor by the authors' test?
options: A remark that the atmosphere behaves like a giant kitchen stove on a summer day
A model of air-pressure rules from which tomorrow's valley temperature is computed
A poem in which clouds are described as slow ships crossing a pale sea
A claim that storms and tempers are alike in how they build and break
optionExplain: This stays a comparison; no detailed calculation follows.
Right: A detailed model from which a specific quantity is calculated passes the test.
This is imagery; nothing is calculated from it.
Rich in features, with no calculation behind it, this remains metaphor.
questions.explain: Only the model supports a calculation. The others are comparisons whose relevance is problematic.
questions.rule: If you can calculate from it, it is a model.

questions.q: Which features of the digital computer do the authors say faded in the search for the essence of an information processor? Select all that apply.
options: Its fast arithmetic
Its manipulation of discrete symbols
Its memory arranged in a plain order
Its construction from binary elements
Its use of precisely defined elementary processes
optionExplain: Right: The authors name fast arithmetic among the features that made it seem machinelike.
The model still assumes discrete symbols; this did not fade.
Right: This is another feature that faded in the search.
Right: This too is named as having faded.
The model keeps a small set of precisely defined processes.
questions.explain: Fast arithmetic, a plainly ordered memory and binary construction made the computer seem machinelike; these faded as scientists looked for the essential concept.
questions.rule: Drop the machine-like features; keep the abstract concept.
questions.teaches: The features that make a computer seem machinelike (fast arithmetic, a plainly ordered memory, binary elements) all faded in the search for the essential concept of an information processor.

questions.q: A student summarizes that the authors think man is a digital computer, so the theory is only a metaphor. What is wrong?
options: They use an abstract information processing system, tailored to their needs, to calculate behavior
Nothing is wrong; the authors state that man is to be modeled as a digital computer in every respect
The authors say metaphors have no place in science and so they reject the computer comparison outright
The theory is a model of the brain's continuous electrical and chemical mechanisms, step by step
optionExplain: Right: The authors separate the abstract concept from the computer metaphor.
This is the metaphor reading the authors set aside.
The authors say metaphors have their own good place in science.
The authors steer away from physiological models of that kind.
questions.explain: The abstract information processing system replaces the computer analogy; it is precise enough to calculate from.
questions.rule: An abstract system, not a computer analogy.

questions.q: A hospital wants to model how a nurse triages patients but cannot place each step in brain tissue. Should it wait, on the authors' reasoning?
options: Yes: a model with no physiological basis cannot be calculated from, so it can only be a metaphor
Yes: the authors insist that every step must first be mapped to some part of the brain tissue
No: the authors say the mechanisms known in neuropsychology were inadequate for such tasks
No: because the nurse's task is simple in the first place, it needs no model of any kind at all
optionExplain: The authors say calculation, not physiology, is what separates a model from a metaphor.
The authors do the opposite and avoid physiological speculation.
Right: The authors say they could not have built their theories restricted to physiologically based mechanisms.
Simplicity is not the reason; the reason is that physiology cannot yet supply the mechanisms.
questions.explain: The nonphysiological nature of the theory is not as disadvantageous as it first seems, because neuropsychology could not provide for these tasks.
questions.rule: Model the symbols; do not wait for the physiology.
questions.teaches: The authors say the mechanisms currently understood in neuropsychology are not adequate to the tasks of the book, so they could not have built their theories had they been restricted to physiologically based mechanisms.

questions.q: Why might a psychologist of thinking in 1970 pick chess over poetry writing as a task?
options: Chess is considered more important to human life than writing or any other creative work
Chess players are easier to find as volunteers than poets in a typical laboratory
Chess had working computer programs that suggested possible mechanisms of thought
Chess involves no sequential thinking, so it is simpler to describe in full
optionExplain: The choice is not about importance.
Availability of subjects is not the reason given.
Right: Available programs gave a stock of mechanisms to test. The card next gives the authors' reasoning.
The authors stress that sequential integrated behavior is at the heart of thinking.
questions.explain: The reason is the supply of plausible mechanisms from artificial intelligence. The card next gives the authors' reasoning.
questions.rule: Choose task environments in which artificial intelligence has already supplied an array of plausible mechanisms.

questions.q: The field devoted to getting computers to perform tasks requiring intelligence is called ____ intelligence.
questions.explain: This part of computer science supplied the mechanisms that the authors use as candidates for human problem solving.
questions.rule: Pick tasks where artificial intelligence has plausible mechanisms.

questions.q: Two candidate tasks exist. Task A has many working programs; Task B has none. Which does the authors' reasoning favor?
options: Task B, since a task with no programs cannot be biased by earlier machine ideas
Task A, since existing programs give an inventory of plausible mechanisms to compare with human behavior
Task B, since an untouched task is always more important to study
Either; the number of programs is irrelevant when subjects are intelligent adults
optionExplain: The authors want the inventory, not freedom from it.
Right: The authors need such an inventory to surmise what humans actually do.
Importance is not their criterion here.
The programs matter because they supply candidate mechanisms.
questions.explain: A theory needs both a task analysis and a stock of candidate mechanisms. Only Task A supplies the second.
questions.rule: No inventory of mechanisms, no basis to surmise the human ones.

questions.q: Match each area to the authors' reason for treating it as they do.
pairs: Artificial intelligence has supplied plausible mechanisms
Work has centered on grammar rather than use; later programs are less developed
Machines are built around a single act, not sequential behavior
questions.explain: The chosen tasks have mechanisms ready; language and pattern recognition each have a gap the authors name.
questions.rule: Each area has its own reason.

questions.q: True or false: The authors assume that artificial intelligence develops independently of psychology.
questions.explain: They call this assumption demonstrably wrong: much of artificial intelligence started from psychological concerns.
questions.rule: Artificial intelligence and psychology are linked.

questions.q: A linguist notes that the book skips language processing and concludes it has nothing to say about language. What do the authors say?
options: That language is outside their theory in every respect, so that no implication for it is possible
That language is the central task of the whole book, studied through the games of chess and logic
That they will treat language fully in a later chapter devoted to grammar and to competence
That their theory of problem solving has strong implications for the deep structure of language
optionExplain: The authors claim implications for deep structure.
Language is set aside as a task.
They say they will have little to say about language processing as such.
Right: They say so explicitly, even while having little to say about language processing as such.
questions.explain: Setting language aside as a task does not mean the theory is silent about it.
questions.rule: A task left out can still be touched by the theory.
questions.teaches: Although the book has little to say about language processing as such, the authors say their theory of problem solving has strong implications for what the linguist calls the deep structure of language.

questions.q: Why might one understand how a chess player plays before studying how they improve?
options: Improvement is rare in adults, so it can be left out without any loss
Improvement is a change made to the player, so one needs a model of the player to describe it
Playing and improving cannot be told apart, so only one can be studied at a time
Improvement depends on the opponent, which makes it outside science altogether
optionExplain: The authors say humans learn continuously.
Right: Learning changes a performing system. The card next says so.
Their distinction, though imperfect, is used.
No such claim is made.
questions.explain: To describe change, one needs a system that changes. The card next states the point.
questions.rule: Understand the performing system first; learning, as a second-order change to it, comes later.

questions.q: The authors call learning a ____-order effect.
questions.explain: It transforms a system capable of some performances into one capable of more.

questions.q: A firm wants to model how users learn a thermostat's menus. What does the authors' reasoning put first?
options: A learning curve alone, without any model of how a user performs a task
A study of the user's childhood, to see how the final system developed
A model of the performing user, against which learning can be shown as changes
A model of the brain's chemistry
optionExplain: A precise study of learning must start from a performance model.
The authors say prediction from development to final structure is not yet possible.
Right: Learning is represented as changes in the model of a performing organism.
The authors do not ground their model physiologically.
questions.explain: Describe the performing user first; then learning can be written as changes in that description.
questions.rule: Model performance, then represent learning as change.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, leaving learning out of the study has a price.
questions.explain: They say they pay a price: they might otherwise draw inferences about the performance system from the fact that it must be capable of modification through learning.

questions.q: How does the prototype of the mathematical theories of learning, mentioned by the authors, represent the organism?
options: As a set of probabilities of a fixed set of responses, with learning changing them
As a store of symbolic structures that grow through reading and through discussion with others
As a chain of chemical reactions that grow stronger with each repeated experience of a task
As a fixed set of skills that never change, with only the surrounding environment varying
optionExplain: Right: The prototype represents the organism through response probabilities.
This is closer to the information processing view, not the prototype of those theories.
The prototype is not physiological.
Learning in these theories does change the organism's representation.
questions.explain: In the prototype version, the organism is a set of response probabilities and learning is a change in them.
questions.rule: A learning theory needs a representation of the organism.
questions.teaches: In the prototype version of the mathematical theories of learning, the organism is represented by a set of probabilities of occurrence of a fixed set of responses, and learning is a change in these probabilities under the impact of experience.

questions.q: A shopper asks where men's suits are, is told, and follows the directions. Why is this a poor case of hard problem solving?
options: The shopper does not process any information, so no system is involved
Language is involved, and language is outside any theory of problem solving
The shopper is a child, and development is not treated at all in the book
The task is contrived so that simple learning substitutes for most of the work of problem solving
optionExplain: The authors say this is certainly the behavior of an information processing system.
Language production and reception are named as close to the book's interests.
The case concerns an adult who is following directions.
Right: The authors say this about the department-store case.
questions.explain: Being told the answer replaces most of the problem solving with plain learning; the case is allied to the book's interests but not a hard problem.
questions.rule: When told the answer, little problem solving remains.
questions.teaches: In the department-store example, language use, asking for information and following directions are allied to the book's interests, but the task is contrived so that simple learning substitutes for most of the work of problem solving.

questions.q: A theory of how people play chess leaves out emotion. What is the most likely reason the authors would give?
options: Emotion has no effect on thinking, so a theory of thinking can ignore it
Emotion cannot be studied by science, so the question is closed
Emotion matters too much to be treated inside a book on problem solving
Emotion should be studied after the cognitive models are in order, since it works through cognition
optionExplain: The authors say they are not claiming this.
No such claim is made.
Importance is the reason they say they are not using.
Right: Order of development is the authors' stated reason. The card next explains.
questions.explain: The authors cite the order in which theory should develop. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Leaving a topic out can be a claim about the order of theory building, not about the topic's importance.

questions.q: True or false: The authors leave out motivation by reason of convictions about the order in which theory should develop, not about its importance.
questions.explain: They say they exclude it by reason of convictions not about importance but about the order in which theory should develop.
questions.rule: Excluded for order, not for importance.

questions.q: A cooking-class researcher builds a model of how learners follow a recipe plan but skips their nerves. Which reasoning matches the authors?
options: Nerves play no part in cooking, so they can be skipped for good
Get the cognitive model in order first, since feelings often operate through the cognitive system
Nerves must be measured first, since they decide how every plan is carried out
Nerves are best studied by chemistry, since cognitive models cannot touch them
optionExplain: The authors do not deny the importance of such phenomena.
Right: This is the authors' strategy for emotion and motivation.
The authors say cognitive models come first.
The authors suggest cognition is a lens through which emotion operates.
questions.explain: The strategy is cognitive models first, then motivation, because emotional phenomena operate through the cognitive system.

questions.q: Match each thinker or work to the point the authors cite it for.
pairs: Made motor skills the key metaphor for thinking
Used perception as the touchstone of central activity
Indicated emotion works through the lens of cognition
questions.explain: The first two offer rival starting points (motor skills or perception); the third supports the authors' own order of work.

questions.q: Why did Bartlett compare thinking with motor skills, according to the authors?
options: He felt sequential behavior was central to both thinking and motor skills, which had been studied intensively
He thought motor skills were fully symbolic, like language, and therefore very easy to model by machine
He held that thinking depends on motivation, a trait which motor skills are thought to share with it
He wanted to avoid the study of sequences in behavior, which he judged to be unscientific by nature
optionExplain: Right: The authors give this as his reason.
The authors say motor skills seem in considerable part nonsymbolic.
Motivation is not given as his reason.
He took sequential behavior to be central.
questions.explain: Bartlett saw sequence as the shared core of thinking and motor skills. The authors agree sequence is central but find motor skills poorly represented as mechanisms.
questions.rule: Sequential behavior is central; motor skills lack a mechanistic account.
questions.teaches: Bartlett chose to compare thinking with motor skills because he felt sequential behavior was central both in thinking and in motor skills, where it had been studied intensively.

questions.q: A lab models better how people take in a chess board. What do the authors expect for the line between perceptual and symbolic behavior?
options: That the boundary will become sharper as time goes on
That perception will prove irrelevant to problem solving in all tasks, whatever symbols are involved
That the boundary may not hold for long if work pushes toward better models of the immediate processor
That the boundary is fixed by definition, so that no model of the processor can ever move it again
optionExplain: The authors expect it to blur, not sharpen.
The importance of perception is an open question for them.
Right: The authors say this in discussing the perceptual side.
The authors say the matter is empirical, not a matter of definition.
questions.explain: The omission of perception is plausible for now, but the authors say the boundary may not hold up as models of the immediate processor improve.
questions.teaches: The authors say the boundary between perceptual and symbolic behavior may not be maintainable for long, especially if work pushes toward better models of the immediate processor.

questions.q: How would the authors describe classical astronomy in a short phrase?
options: Empirical, but not experimental
Axiomatic and deductive
A large catalog of mechanisms
The human as a static collection of traits
optionExplain: Right: Astronomers observe the sky but cannot experiment on it. The card next gives the full list.
This is the authors' description of Newtonian mechanics.
This is the label for part of biochemistry.
This is the label for intelligence testing.
questions.explain: The authors call astronomy empirical but not experimental. The card next gives the full list of examples.
questions.rule: A theory's shape is its overall framework, not its detailed content.

questions.q: Match each field to the shape the authors give it.
pairs: In part, a large catalog of mechanisms
The human as a static collection of traits or factors
questions.explain: Each label gives a framework for the field, not a full account of it.
questions.rule: Shape is a field's overall framework.

questions.q: A field guide consists mostly of hundreds of separate pollination mechanisms, one per plant family, with no overarching law. Which of the authors' labels describes what such a work consists of?
options: Axiomatic and deductive, as in Newtonian mechanics
A large catalog of mechanisms, as in part of biochemistry
Empirical but not experimental, as in classical astronomy
A static collection of traits, as in intelligence testing
optionExplain: There is no set of axioms from which the rest follows.
Right: A list of many separate mechanisms matches this label.
Whether the guide's authors experiment is not what the label is about; the guide's content is a long list, not a method of testing.
The guide lists mechanisms, not traits of a person.
questions.explain: The authors say of biochemistry that it consists in part of a large catalog of mechanisms; a work made mostly of many separate mechanisms matches that label.
questions.rule: Match the framework, not the subject.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say that a statement of shape tells you how successful a theory is.
questions.explain: They say such statements convey neither the content of a theory nor how successful it is.

questions.q: Besides giving a framework, what else can a statement of a theory's shape suggest, according to the authors?
options: Which experiments the theory has already passed and which ones the theory has failed to pass
Which researchers will come to accept the theory and which of them will in time reject it
How many chapters the theory will need before it can be fully explained to a reader in detail
What issues will matter, that is, which problems the theory must face again and again
optionExplain: The authors say shape does not convey success.
Acceptance is not discussed.
Length is not part of the claim.
Right: The authors say shape sometimes points to the issues that matter.
questions.explain: A label such as this does more than classify: it can point toward the issues a theory will have to face again and again.
questions.teaches: A statement of shape also suggests which issues will be important, meaning which problems the theory will have to contend with repeatedly.

questions.q: A sociologist sorts shoppers into a few characteristic types and models each type. Which shape do the authors mention for this?
options: Axiomatic and deductive, as in classical mechanics
A static collection of traits, as in intelligence testing
Humans treated as ideal types, as in a part of sociology
A catalog of mechanisms, as in biochemistry
optionExplain: Types are not deduced from axioms.
That is the shape of intelligence testing, which scores traits, not types.
Right: The authors list this as the shape of part of sociology.
The shoppers are types, not mechanisms.
questions.explain: The authors give "ideal types" as the shape of a part of sociology.
questions.rule: A part of sociology: humans as ideal types.
questions.teaches: The authors give the treatment of humans as ideal types as the shape of a part of sociology.

questions.q: What does a process theory of thinking add to a set of laws relating situations to behavior?
options: Averages over many people, which show how behavior varies across a population
Measurements of the brain areas active during each step of thought
Mechanisms that produce the behavior, which explain it rather than only describe it
A longer list of laws, so that more behavior can be predicted with confidence
optionExplain: Averages describe populations; they do not posit mechanisms.
The authors decline physiological localization.
Right: Mechanisms are the addition. The card next explains.
More laws would still be description.
questions.explain: A process theory posits the mechanisms behind behavior. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Posit the internal mechanisms that produce behavior, and do not assign them to places in the brain.

questions.q: A theory that posits mechanisms to produce behavior is called ____ by the authors.
questions.explain: It reduces behavior to underlying processes, though the elementary processes themselves are not explained.

questions.q: Account A says sleepwalking rises after late nights; Account B posits internal steps that produce it. Which is a process theory?
options: Account B, since it posits internal mechanisms that produce the behavior
Account A, since a reliable relation is the strongest kind of explanation
Both, since any account of behavior counts as a process theory
Neither, since no process theory can be applied to sleep
optionExplain: Right: A process theory posits the producing mechanisms.
A relation describes; it does not posit what produces the behavior.
Only mechanism-positing accounts count.
Nothing in the card limits process theories to waking behavior.
questions.explain: Account A relates behavior to a condition; Account B posits mechanisms that produce the behavior.

questions.q: True or false: The theory assigns each of its processes to a named structure in the brain.
questions.explain: The processes are presumed internal and in the central nervous system, but the authors decline to localize them; no plausible localization exists yet.

questions.q: How do the authors treat the great debates over the empty organism, behaviorism, intervening variables and hypothetical constructs?
options: As open questions the book will settle with a series of new experiments reported in the later chapters
As proof that internal mechanisms cannot be posited in any theory that aims to be scientific in method
As the starting point of the theory, which each later chapter takes up in turn and tries to resolve in full
As a phase in the history of psychology; the theory posits internal mechanisms and links them to visible evidence
optionExplain: The authors do not plan to settle them.
They do posit internal mechanisms of great extent.
They call these debates a phase of history.
Right: The authors dismiss the debates as a past phase.
questions.explain: The theory posits internal mechanisms of great extent and complexity and makes contact between them and visible evidence of problem solving. For the authors that is all there is to it.
questions.rule: Posit mechanisms; connect them to visible evidence.
questions.teaches: The authors treat the debates about the empty organism, behaviorism, intervening variables and hypothetical constructs as a phase in the historical development of psychology.

questions.q: A critic says the theory's explanation is only a description. What do the authors admit about this view?
options: That the critic is right, and the theory only describes behavior in the most economical way it can
That some would dispute the distinction, though they hold that their theory explains
That nobody holds this view, so that it needs no reply and no discussion anywhere in the book at all
That the dispute proves the theory cannot explain anything at all about human behavior or its causes
optionExplain: They maintain that the theory explains behavior.
Right: The authors acknowledge the dispute in a parenthesis.
They say they are aware that some would dispute the distinction.
They maintain their theory explains, despite the dispute.
questions.explain: The authors say they are aware that some would dispute the distinction between explanation and description.
questions.rule: The explain-describe line is itself disputed.
questions.teaches: The authors acknowledge that some would dispute the distinction between explaining and describing, viewing all causal explanations as descriptions.

questions.q: Which data would the authors trust most for testing a theory of how people solve problems?
options: A detailed record of one person working through a problem
Average scores from several hundred people on the same problem
Ratings of difficulty given by a panel of experts after the fact
The percentage of people in a sample who solve it correctly
optionExplain: Right: The models describe individuals. The card next explains why.
The authors avoid grouped data when they can.
These do not record what a person actually does.
This is a statistic about a population, not a record of one solver.
questions.explain: The authors test their models on individuals and avoid grouped data. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: Model the individual first, then ask what is common to all human information processors.

questions.q: Efforts that deal with the individual in all his uniqueness are called ____.
questions.explain: Idiographic efforts are clinical; nomothetic efforts treat the individual as an intersection of populations.
questions.rule: Idiographic: the individual in all his uniqueness.

questions.q: A researcher has step-by-step notes from forty bakers. Which choice follows the authors' approach?
options: Build a model of one baker's sequence and test it, then ask which parts all bakers share
Average the forty notes into one typical baker, then test the average against each baker
Group the bakers by age and treat each group as one subject
Ignore the notes until a physiological account of baking is available
optionExplain: Right: Individual first, then what is common.
The authors avoid grouped data for testing.
This is the statistical-population treatment the authors reverse.
The authors proceed without physiology.
questions.explain: The model fits one person in full detail; commonality is the later and harder step.
questions.rule: One person, in full; commonality later.

questions.q: True or false: In the authors' theory, individual differences are not a topic tacked on to the main body of the theory.
questions.explain: Individual differences are built in, because the models describe individuals.
questions.rule: Individual differences are not tacked on.

questions.q: A footnote backs the view of the human as a decipherable mechanism by pointing to geology: its general theory of geological processes and its specific hypothesis of continental drift. What does the comparison suggest about the authors' own theory?
options: A general theory is credible only once grouped data from many particular cases have been averaged into it
A general theory can coexist with specific hypotheses about particular cases, without being replaced by them
Specific hypotheses about particular cases should be dropped once a general theory has been stated
A general theory holds only if each particular case it covers turns out to behave in exactly the same way
optionExplain: This is the statistical, nomothetic route the authors avoid; the geology comparison is not about averaging.
Right: the footnote relates a general theory to specific hypotheses about particular cases, as with their general theory and models of individuals.
The footnote presents the specific hypotheses as standing beside the general theory, not as discarded.
The footnote does not require identical cases; continental drift and the Moon's surface are different particular cases.
questions.explain: The footnote cites the relation of the general theory of geological processes to specific hypotheses such as continental drift or the Moon's surface, so a general theory and particular-case models coexist.
questions.rule: General theory and particular case coexist in other sciences.
questions.teaches: A footnote cites the relation of the general theory of geological processes to specific hypotheses, such as continental drift or the character of the Moon's surface, as a comparison for the view of the human as a decipherable mechanism.

questions.q: A modeler cannot explain one step in a person's chess protocol. What is the authors' stance on using a random generator for it?
options: They do so freely, since human behavior is fundamentally stochastic
They do so only reluctantly, since the natural assumption is that all behavior is caused
They never do so under any circumstance, since chance has no place in a theory
They do so for every step, since averages alone reveal the regularities
optionExplain: They reject this as the natural assumption.
Right: The authors say they only reluctantly assign some aspects to probabilistic generators.
The text says "only reluctantly", not never.
This is the statistical view they set aside.
questions.explain: The default is that behavior is caused; randomness is a last resort.
questions.teaches: The authors only reluctantly assign some aspects of behavior to probabilistic generators, because they take it as natural that all behavior is caused.

questions.q: A good theory of how a good player chooses chess moves would, in the authors' view, be able to do what?
options: Predict only the average rating of players in a tournament
Play good chess itself
Describe the player's moves, yet produce no moves of its own
Explain chess but only in terms of the player's brain chemistry
optionExplain: That is a statistical claim, not a performance.
Right: The authors say the theory performs the tasks it explains. The card next explains.
The authors say it performs the task.
The theory is not physiological.
questions.explain: The authors claim the theory performs the task. The card next explains.
questions.rule: A content-oriented theory is one that can carry out the task it explains.

questions.q: The authors' theory is unusual in that it performs the ____ it explains.
questions.explain: A good theory of a chess player can play chess.

questions.q: A team claims a theory of how an experienced baker judges dough readiness. Which result would show it is content-oriented in the authors' sense?
options: A chart shows the average proofing time reported by thousands of bakers
It explains why dough rises, using the chemistry of yeast
It ranks bakers by how often they agree with a panel
Run as a program, it judges dough readiness itself
optionExplain: This is a statistical summary, not a performance of the task.
This is a physical explanation, not a performance of the judgment.
This measures agreement, not the task.
Right: The theory performs the task it explains.
questions.explain: A content-oriented theory does the task, and the dough case needs a theory that judges dough.
questions.rule: Test a content-oriented theory by running it on the task.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say that content and process are not truly opposed, because it is of the nature of information processes to deal with content.
questions.explain: The contrast fails: it is of the nature of information processes to deal with content.

questions.q: A colleague argues that, since the theory plays chess, it will also write poems. What is the flaw?
options: Nothing; any theory that performs one task well will also perform every other task of the human mind
Poems are physical objects on a page, which no information processing theory can ever describe
No system now understands a poem; faith that one might goes beyond the evidence
The authors prove that poetry needs motor skills which their own theory has deliberately left out
optionExplain: The authors say there is no compelling evidence for this.
The limit is about content, not physical form.
Right: The authors state this limit directly.
No such proof is offered.
questions.explain: The kinds of content the theories demonstrably handle may not typify all human content.
questions.rule: Do not extrapolate beyond the evidence.

questions.q: The authors say a content orientation matters. If content strongly shapes behavior, what advantage do they claim for theories that handle it?
options: They can describe human behavior truly, in ways closed to theories unable to cope with content
They are shown to be correct on every kind of content that a human being can handle in any setting
They need no data at all
They replace the need for process models altogether
optionExplain: Right: The authors claim this opportunity for content-handling theories.
The authors admit the evidence does not go that far.
The authors still rely on data.
The authors say content and process are not opposed.
questions.explain: The orientation toward content removes a barrier to extending the theory and, if content is a major determinant of behavior, gives a chance to describe it truly.
questions.rule: A content orientation removes a barrier and widens the theory's reach.
questions.teaches: The importance of the content orientation is twofold: it removes a barrier toward extension of the theory, and if content is a substantial determinant of human behavior, such theories can describe behavior veridically where theories unable to cope with content cannot.

questions.q: In classical physics, what describes how a system's state changes through time?
options: A table of averages, which gives the typical state at each time
A list of axioms, which gives the final state without any steps
A diagram of the parts, which gives their positions but not their change
Differential equations, which give the laws of motion
optionExplain: Physics uses laws, not averages, for the time course.
Axioms are a different formal tool.
A diagram would not specify change through time.
Right: They set out the change of position and momentum. The card next gives the information processing counterpart.
questions.explain: Differential equations state how position and momentum change. The card next gives the counterpart.
questions.rule: In this theory a program does what differential equations do in classical physics: it says how the state changes.

questions.q: The natural formalism of the theory is the ____.
questions.explain: The program plays the role that systems of differential equations play in classical physics.

questions.q: Which best describes the state of a thinking person at one moment in this theory?
options: The set of positions and momenta of the body's parts
A single trait score that places the person among others
The probabilities with which the person gives each response
The collection of symbolic structures held in memory
optionExplain: This is the state of a physical system, not of this theory.
This is the intelligence-testing view.
This describes the prototype learning theories.
Right: This is how the authors define the state.
questions.explain: In a physical system the state is positions and momenta; here it is symbol structures in memory.

questions.q: Match each item to what it specifies or contains.
pairs: State as symbolic structures in a memory
Infinitesimal changes in all coordinates at once
A discrete change in one symbol structure at a moment
questions.explain: The two pairs mirror each other: continuous states with simultaneous infinitesimal change, and symbolic states with one discrete change.
questions.rule: Continuous and simultaneous versus discrete and single.

questions.q: A student says dynamic here means the theory is about drives and unconscious motives, as in depth psychology. What is wrong?
options: Nothing is wrong; the authors adopt the depth-psychology sense of the word dynamic throughout the book
Dynamic here means describing the change of a system through time, not the depth-psychology sense
Dynamic here means that the theory itself is expected to change a good deal over the coming years
Dynamic here means that the theory has been fully solved in closed form for every system it covers
optionExplain: They explicitly set that sense aside.
Right: The authors say so directly.
It concerns the system's change in time, not the theory's.
The authors say closed-form solution is rarely possible.
questions.explain: The word is used in the sense of change through time.

questions.q: A coach wants to predict a player's next move in the authors' terms. What does the theory make the next act a function of?
options: The immediately preceding state of the organism and of its environment
The player's long-run average over the whole season
The player's age and place of birth
The player's hidden motives, as in depth psychology
optionExplain: Right: The authors characterize each new act this way.
The theory is about the next act, not averages.
These are population variables the theory does not use.
The authors set that sense aside.
questions.explain: A dynamic theory characterizes each new act as a function of the preceding state of the organism and its environment.
questions.rule: Next act = function of the preceding state.
questions.teaches: The theory characterizes each new act as a function of the immediately preceding state of the organism and of its environment.

questions.q: You know today's exact weather and the rules for the next hour. Applying the rules hour after hour to see what follows is called what?
options: Simulation, tracing a system from a specific initial state
Integration, expressing the final state as a function of the initial one
Invariance, finding a property that never changes during the process
Averaging, replacing the course of events with a typical day
optionExplain: Right: This is the name for it. The card next sets out all three strategies.
That solves the laws instead of tracing them.
That looks for a conserved property, not for the course of events.
Averaging is a statistical tool, not a dynamic strategy.
questions.explain: Tracing from a specific starting state by repeated application of the laws is simulation. The card next sets out all three strategies.
questions.rule: When a dynamic system cannot be solved, simulate it step by step, or look for steady states, long-run behavior and invariants.

questions.q: Tracing a system from a specific initial state by repeatedly applying its laws is often called ____.
questions.explain: It is one of the chief uses of computers in engineering and science, and a mainstay of this work.
questions.rule: Simulation: apply the laws step by step.

questions.q: A kettle model is to find the temperature at which heating stops changing the water. Which strategy looks for it?
options: Simulation from the initial temperature, for a fixed number of steps
Integrating the laws to give temperature at every minute
Exploring the steady-state solutions, where the laws say nothing changes
Looking for an invariant such as total energy in the closed kettle
optionExplain: Simulation traces a course; it does not look for the resting point as such.
That gives the whole course, not just the resting point.
Right: A steady state is a point where nothing changes.
An invariant holds throughout, not only at rest.
questions.explain: A steady state is where the laws of motion say nothing changes.

questions.q: Match each strategy to what it does.
pairs: Traces the course from a specific initial state by applying the laws repeatedly
Expresses the state at each time as a function of the initial state
Looks for places where the laws say nothing changes
Looks for a property that holds despite variation elsewhere
questions.explain: Simulation runs the system, integration solves it, and the last two skip the full solution.

questions.q: Which of these do the authors give as an invariant from classical physics?
options: The position of a body at a given instant
Conservation of energy
The initial state of the system
A steady state in which nothing changes
optionExplain: This changes through time, so it cannot be an invariant.
Right: The authors list energy, momentum and angular momentum.
This is the starting point, not a property that holds throughout.
This is a different strategy, not an invariant property.
questions.explain: Conservation of energy, momentum and angular momentum are the authors' examples of properties that hold despite changes elsewhere.
questions.rule: An invariant holds while other things vary.
questions.teaches: In the systems of classical physics, conservation of energy, momentum and angular momentum are the authors' examples of invariants.

questions.q: A team cannot fully solve its model of a complex system. What is the authors' attitude toward complete detailed solutions?
options: They are required, since no theory can be considered legitimate without a full and explicit solution
They are easy to get for the systems of this book, so the team must have made an error somewhere
They are irrelevant, because simulation was invented only for the purpose of replacing all of them
They are not always necessary or even illuminating, so theorists try to circumvent them
optionExplain: The authors say the opposite.
The authors say they cannot be used for such theories yet.
The authors do not claim this; they say solutions may be unnecessary.
Right: The authors say this.
questions.explain: Theorists often spend their time trying to circumvent solving the system explicitly.
questions.rule: Do not insist on a full solution.
questions.teaches: Complete detailed solutions are not always necessary, or even illuminating, and the theorist of dynamic systems often spends his time trying to circumvent solving the system explicitly.

questions.q: Which data would help most to find out how one person is solving a puzzle?
options: The final answer alone, together with the time taken to give it
Average results of a control group that did not attempt the puzzle
A record of what the person says while working on it
Scores from a standard intelligence test taken some weeks earlier
optionExplain: This hides how the person got there.
A control group does not reveal one person's steps.
Right: A rich record identifies the information and its processing. The card next explains.
A test score does not trace a solution.
questions.explain: A running record of speech reveals steps. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Use rich data on each individual, especially verbal protocols, since classical control-group experiments rarely fit.

questions.q: Verbal protocols are used because verbal behavior has a high ____ rate.
questions.explain: Speech yields many data points per minute from one person.
questions.rule: Verbal behavior gives a high output rate.

questions.q: A team wants to learn how one user navigates a new banking app. Which design follows the authors' approach?
options: Show the app to two large groups and compare their average completion rates
Count the number of taps for the whole user base and report the mean
Collect detailed spoken accounts from each user as they work, and analyze each one
Wait until a physiological measure of attention is available
optionExplain: This is the control-group design they find rarely useful.
This groups data and loses the individual.
Right: Rich data on each individual, with speech as data.
The authors do not wait for physiology.
questions.explain: The authors want enough detail on each individual to tell what he knows and how he processes it.
questions.rule: Detail on each individual, not group averages.

questions.q: True or false: Because the theory is not experimental, the authors pay little attention to data.
questions.explain: They say there is no lack of orientation toward data; they use little classical experimental design.
