questions.q: Which reasons do the authors give for why classical control-group experiments are rarely useful? Select all that apply.
options: The phenomena depend strongly on their history
There are too few human subjects willing to take part
The focus is on the individual
Verbal reports are known to be unreliable
Much goes on within a single problem solving encounter
optionExplain: Right: One of the three reasons.
No shortage of subjects is cited.
Right: One of the three reasons.
The authors rely on verbal protocols.
Right: One of the three reasons.
questions.explain: History dependence, the individual focus, and the richness of a single encounter are the three reasons given.

questions.q: Two explanations fit a solver's transcript equally well. What do the authors say is a continuing search?
options: For new sources of data that can be joined to the existing data to ease identification
For a larger control group whose averages are expected to settle the matter between the two views
For a statistical test that picks between the two explanations automatically from the transcript
For a physiological measure that is expected to show directly which explanation is the true one
optionExplain: Right: The authors mention gross eye movement data as an example.
This is the approach they set aside.
They make little use of standard statistics.
They do not rely on physiology.
questions.explain: The nature of the theory leads to a continuing search for new data; gross eye movements, reported in Chapter 7, are one case.
questions.rule: Join new data to old to identify the process.
questions.teaches: The nature of the theory leads to a continuing search for new sources of data that can be joined to existing data to ease the problem of identification; data on gross eye movements, briefly reported in Chapter 7, is a case in point.

questions.q: Whose style of data analysis do the authors say theirs resembles?
options: The agricultural experimenter's, comparing treated and untreated plots
The biochemist's or the archaeologist's
The opinion pollster's, sampling large numbers of people
The insurance actuary's, pricing risk from long-run averages
optionExplain: The authors say theirs resembles this less.
Right: These fields piece together mechanisms or histories from detailed evidence. The card next explains.
Sampling many people is not their approach.
Averages over populations are not their approach.
questions.explain: The authors compare themselves with the biochemist and archaeologist. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Compare theory and data directly, in the manner of the biochemist or archaeologist, and use standard statistics sparingly.

questions.q: The book's data analysis techniques resemble those of the biochemist or the ____.
questions.explain: Both fit detailed evidence to a structure rather than average over many cases.
questions.rule: Biochemist or archaeologist, not the agricultural experimenter.

questions.q: Which method would mirror the authors' approach to checking a model of a solver?
options: Assign two hundred people to two groups and test the difference between their mean solving times
Report only the percentage of solvers who reach the right answer, however each one got there in the end
Skip comparison altogether
Compare the model's predicted steps with one solver's record in detail, and tabulate the matches
optionExplain: This is the agricultural-experimenter style.
This ignores the detail of how they got there.
The authors still compare and tabulate.
Right: This is direct comparison of theory and data, with tabulation.
questions.explain: Detailed, case-by-case comparison, with some measured tabulation, is the authors' approach.
questions.rule: Match model to record, in detail.

questions.q: True or false: The authors make no comparison of theory with data in numerical form.
questions.explain: They say some attempts are made to measure and tabulate such comparisons; what they make little use of is the standard statistical apparatus.

questions.q: A student asks why behavior cannot be plotted against theory on one simple graph. What reason do the authors give?
options: Graphs are banned in psychology journals by a long-standing custom among the editors of such journals
There is not even a well-behaved Euclidean space of measurements for comparing behavior with theory
Human behavior is random in nature, so that no graph of it could ever show any pattern at all in it
The theory predicts only the average of a group, which a graph of one person's behavior cannot show
optionExplain: No such custom is mentioned.
Right: The authors give this as part of the difficulty.
The authors do not treat behavior as fundamentally random.
The theory models individuals, not averages.
questions.explain: Diverse symbolic content gives no tidy numerical space in which to lay behavior beside theory.
questions.rule: No tidy numerical space for symbolic content.
questions.teaches: Because behavior is saturated with diverse meaningful symbolic structures, there is not even a well-behaved Euclidean space of numerical measurements in which to plot and compare human behavior with theory.

questions.q: A theory of how children learn to talk has mechanisms that could not produce speech at all. What is wrong with it?
options: Its mechanisms are too fast for children, so it fails to match human data
Its mechanisms are physiological, which a psychological theory must avoid
Its mechanisms are not sufficient: they cannot explain how the behavior can be performed
Its mechanisms are about individuals, which cannot be tested by any method
optionExplain: This concerns fidelity, a later step.
Sufficiency is not about physiology.
Right: Sufficiency asks whether the mechanisms could do the job. The card next explains.
The authors accept individual models.
questions.explain: A theory whose mechanisms cannot perform the behavior fails the sufficiency test. The card next explains.
questions.rule: First show a system, within human limits, that can do the task; then refine it toward fit with specific data.

questions.q: A theory meets the sufficiency test if its mechanisms can ____ the task.
questions.explain: The first question is whether the proposed mechanisms can do the task at all.
questions.rule: Sufficient = able to perform the task.

questions.q: Which check tests the sufficiency of a proposed model of how people solve a sliding-tile puzzle?
options: Run it, with human-like limits on speed and memory, to see whether it solves the puzzles
Count how many people agree that the model sounds reasonable once the model has been explained to them
Show which brain regions light up while people solve the puzzle, and match them to the model's parts
Compare its average solving time with a published population average gathered from many other studies
optionExplain: Right: Sufficiency asks whether a system within gross human limits can do the task.
Agreement does not test whether the mechanisms perform the task.
Sufficiency does not rest on physiology.
This is a fidelity check, and a later one.
questions.explain: A sufficiency test asks whether the mechanisms, under human limits, perform the task.

questions.q: True or false: A system that performs the task within human processing limits is, for the authors, a first approximation, to be followed by a revised system of higher fidelity to specific data.
questions.explain: It is a first approximation; the next step is a revised system with higher fidelity to specific data.

questions.q: A reviewer says sufficiency tells us nothing new, since psychologists routinely ask whether a theory could perform the behavior. What do the authors say?
options: That the reviewer is right, and that sufficiency is already the standard test applied throughout psychology
That sufficiency is irrelevant
Almost never has this been asked of a psychological theory, and the emphasis is foreign to psychology
That sufficiency belongs to physiology alone, and that psychology as a whole has no use for the question
optionExplain: The authors say the opposite.
Sufficiency is the first requirement.
Right: The authors say this directly.
The authors do not treat it as physiological.
questions.explain: The sufficiency question is rarely put to psychological theories, which is why the authors stress it.
questions.rule: Ask whether it could do the job.

questions.q: Which question do the authors cite as a lively case of the sufficiency concern in psycholinguistics?
options: Whether children prefer long or short sentences at the time when they first begin to speak their words
Whether classical stimulus-response learning mechanisms can account for a child's learning of language
Whether the grammar of a language can be written down in a finite set of rules by a trained linguist
Whether adults forget the languages they learned in childhood after many years of living abroad from it
optionExplain: This is not the example given.
Right: This is the example the authors give, and they report the answer is no.
This is not the example given.
This is not the example given.
questions.explain: The authors note that the stimulus-response mechanisms are generally concluded not to be sufficient, a conclusion they call unsurprising.
questions.rule: Ask whether the proposed mechanisms suffice.
questions.teaches: In psycholinguistics it is a lively question whether the mechanisms of classical stimulus-response learning theory are sufficient to account for the child's learning of language, and the conclusion is that they are not.

questions.q: Which three task environments does the book use for its empirical parts?
options: Cryptarithmetic, elementary symbolic logic and chess
Chess, poetry writing and map reading
Cryptarithmetic, language translation and bridge
Elementary logic, motor skill and perception
optionExplain: Right: These are the three tasks. The card next gives the plan.
Poetry and maps are not tasks of the book.
Translation and bridge are not tasks of the book.
The authors set motor skill and perception aside.
questions.explain: The three empirical parts are cryptarithmetic, symbolic logic and chess. The card next gives the plan.
questions.rule: First the groundwork, then three task environments, and last the theory stated as a whole.

questions.q: Put the five parts of the book in order.
items: Technical groundwork
Cryptarithmetic
Elementary symbolic logic
Chess
Statement of the theory
questions.explain: The groundwork comes first, then the three task environments in the order of cryptarithmetic, logic and chess, then the theory.

questions.q: A reader wants the book's comprehensive statement of the theory. Where should they go?
options: Part I, which defines the information processing system in its first chapters
Part IV, which gives a broader view of human problem solving in chess
The historical appendix, which records the relation of the work to wider trends
Part V, which is Chapter 14 alone
optionExplain: Part I is groundwork, not the full theory.
That is the broad view of one task, not of the whole theory.
The appendix gives history, not the theory.
Right: The final part states the theory as a whole.
questions.explain: Part V is a single chapter that states the theory covering all three task areas.
questions.rule: The full statement is Part V.

questions.q: True or false: Part V extends the theory by adding new task environments with fresh data.
questions.explain: Part V states a theory encompassing the phenomena that emerged in the three task areas already studied.
questions.rule: Part V states; it does not add tasks.

questions.q: A reader wants the historical context of the work in twentieth-century psychology. Where is it?
options: In Chapter 2, which defines the information processing system
In Part V, as the first section of the theory chapter
In a historical appendix, since the body refers only to research drawn on directly
Nowhere, since the authors decided to leave out all history
optionExplain: Chapter 2 defines the system.
Part V states the theory.
Right: The authors recorded their picture of the work's relation to broader trends there.
They included it in an appendix.
questions.explain: The body makes no attempt to give the historical context beyond direct references; the appendix does that.
questions.teaches: The authors made no attempt in the body of the book to give the historical context beyond references to research drawn on directly; instead they recorded in an historical appendix their picture of the work's relation to the broader trend of events during the century in psychology and other disciplines.

questions.q: A theory explains how an adaptive solver tackles a puzzle. Is it a theory about the solver, about the puzzle, or about both?
options: Both: the total system always includes the environment as well as the organism
The solver alone, since the puzzle is only a stimulus and holds no explanatory weight
The puzzle alone, since a highly adaptive solver mirrors whatever it faces
Neither, since a theory of problem solving describes only the answers produced
optionExplain: Right: The authors say so. The card next explains.
The authors take up this very question and do not reduce the task to a stimulus.
The authors say the total system includes the environment and the organism both, so neither alone is the theory's subject.
A theory describes the process, not only the answers.
questions.explain: The authors say the total system includes both environment and organism. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Part I defines the system, the environment it works in, and the kind of system that solves problems.

questions.q: Heuristics, as the authors use the word, are devices that aid ____.
questions.explain: Chapter 4 introduces generate-and-test, selective search and heuristics.

questions.q: A reader wonders whether a result tells about the person or about the structure of the puzzle. Which chapter takes this up?
options: Chapter 3, on the task environment and its role in a theory
Chapter 2, which defines the information processing system in a somewhat axiomatic way
Chapter 4, which discusses generate-and-test, search and the Logic Theorist in detail
Chapter 14, which states the theory as a whole in comprehensive form for the reader
optionExplain: Right: This chapter takes up whether the theory is about humans or about the task environment.
Chapter 2 gives the definition of the system.
Chapter 4 is about the problem solving system.
Chapter 14 is Part V.
questions.explain: The person-versus-task question is the major issue of Chapter 3.

questions.q: Match each Part I chapter to its subject.
pairs: The task environment and its role in a theory
Problem solving systems, search and the Logic Theorist
questions.explain: Each chapter adds one piece of the groundwork: system, environment, problem solver.

questions.q: What is the Logic Theorist, which Chapter 4 examines in detail?
options: A recent program that models a single subject's eye movements
A statistical test used to compare theory with data
A scheme for storing symbols in the central nervous system
A venerable program that was the first theorem-proving program
optionExplain: Eye movements appear in Chapter 7.
The book makes little use of standard statistics.
The theory is not physiological.
Right: The authors describe it this way.
questions.explain: The Logic Theorist is introduced as a specific example of an information processing system operating in a task environment.
questions.rule: LT: the first theorem prover, a worked example.
questions.teaches: The Logic Theorist is a venerable program that was the first theorem-proving program, and it consolidates the lessons of Part I by showing an information processing system at work in a task environment.

questions.q: A skilled cook adapts to any kitchen, so results may tell of cook or kitchen. What do the authors say of such organisms?
options: The boundary becomes sharper
The boundary becomes obscured, so Chapter 3 spends most of its length clarifying the question
The question has no sense
The question is settled in the first paragraph of the chapter, and the rest of the chapter applies it
optionExplain: The authors say the boundary becomes obscured.
Right: The authors say this about highly adaptive and intelligent organisms.
The authors say the total system always includes both.
Most of the chapter is devoted to clarifying it.
questions.explain: In an adaptive organism the line between person and setting blurs, so the issue needs careful treatment.
questions.rule: An adaptive organism blurs the organism-environment boundary.
questions.teaches: In a highly adaptive and intelligent organism the boundary between organism and environment becomes obscured, and most of Chapter 3 is devoted to clarifying this question.

questions.q: In a study of how people solve puzzles, which order of chapters seems most natural?
options: Start with broad averages over many people, then drop into one person's protocol
Analyze the task, then one person's protocol, then broader evidence from other subjects
Analyze one person's protocol before the task is analyzed, to avoid bias
State the full theory first, then test it against a single subject
optionExplain: The authors work from the individual outward.
Right: This is the order the authors follow. The card next sets out the chapters.
The authors analyze the task first.
The theory is stated last, in Part V.
questions.explain: The authors go from the task to a single protocol and then to broader evidence. The card next sets out the chapters.
questions.rule: Each empirical part moves from task analysis to an individual's protocol to a broader view.

questions.q: In Chapter 6 the subject whose protocol is analyzed is called ____.
questions.explain: S3 works a single cryptarithmetic puzzle aloud, giving the first protocol analysis.

questions.q: A reader wants to see attempts to simulate two protocol fragments with the General Problem Solver. Which chapter?
options: Chapter 9, in Part III
Chapter 6, in Part II
Chapter 8, in Part III
Chapter 12, in Part IV
optionExplain: Right: This chapter discusses simulating two fragments of protocols with GPS.
Chapter 6 is the first analysis of a human cryptarithmetic protocol.
Chapter 8 discusses the task environment and describes GPS.
Chapter 12 analyzes an individual chess protocol.
questions.explain: Chapter 8 introduces GPS and Chapter 9 uses it to simulate protocol fragments.
questions.rule: Chapter 8 introduces GPS; Chapter 9 simulates with it.

questions.q: Match each item to its role in Chapters 6 and 7.
pairs: A way of plotting a subject's search behavior
A representation of a subject's program
A tool of analysis introduced in Chapter 7
Further evidence from one more subject in Chapter 7
questions.explain: The graph and the production system come with Chapter 6; the episode and the eye movement data come with Chapter 7.
questions.rule: Graph and production system in 6; episode and eye movements in 7.

questions.q: Why does Chapter 6 contain a good deal of methodological discussion?
options: It repeats the groundwork of Chapter 2 for readers who skipped it
It is the only chapter that uses verbal evidence from more than one subject
It is the first chapter that deals with protocol data
It argues against the use of statistics in all of the later chapters
optionExplain: Chapter 2 is separate groundwork.
It treats a single subject, S3.
Right: The authors give this as the reason.
The nonstatistical approach is stated in the introduction.
questions.explain: Being the first protocol chapter, it explains the methods that later chapters then reuse.
questions.rule: First protocol chapter, so methods are explained.
questions.teaches: Chapter 6 contains a good deal of methodological discussion because it is the first chapter that deals with protocol data.

questions.q: Part III has three chapters. What does its last chapter, Chapter 10, do?
options: It defines the General Problem Solver for the first time and shows how the program is built from parts
It moves back to a broader base: various subjects on various logic tasks, many aspects of behavior
It states the theory in comprehensive form for the whole book, covering all three task environments
It analyzes one chess protocol in the way that Part II did for cryptarithmetic puzzles and their subjects
optionExplain: GPS comes with Chapter 8.
Right: The authors describe Chapter 10 this way.
The theory is stated in Chapter 14.
Chess belongs to Part IV.
questions.explain: Part III repeats Part II's pattern, ending with a broader base of subjects.
questions.rule: The last chapter of a part broadens the base.
questions.teaches: Chapter 10 moves back to a broader base, giving analyses of various subjects working on various logic tasks and examining a number of aspects of their behavior.

questions.q: A book claims people think as information processing systems and gives a chapter to it. What would you expect that chapter to do first?
options: Present the experiments that prove the claim is true
Make clear what the claim means before anyone tests it
Argue that the claim is plausible to most readers
Compare the claim with rival theories one by one
optionExplain: Experiments come, but a claim must be stated clearly first; this chapter is described as an explanation.
Right: a claim has to be understood before it can be tested.
Plausibility is a weak test; the next idea shows the authors distrust it.
Comparison with rivals is possible later; the opening task is to say what the claim is.
questions.explain: A claim has to be understood before it can be tested. The card shows how the authors divide the work.
questions.rule: This chapter explains what the IPS claim means and fixes the notation; it does not try to prove the claim.

questions.q: The chapter clarifies what the postulate means, while empirical ____ is the task of later chapters.
questions.explain: The authors say the explication does not justify the postulate; empirical verification comes later.

questions.q: A cookbook's first chapter defines its cooking terms and explains its recipe layout; recipes come later. Which pair of jobs matches Chapter 2?
options: Showing through tasting trials that the techniques work well
Arguing that readers should prefer this cookbook over all others
Listing every dish that the later chapters will go on to cover
Saying what the key terms mean and fixing the notation used later
optionExplain: Tasting trials would be the kind of evidence the authors leave to later chapters.
Persuasion about the book is not the chapter's stated aim.
Chapter 2 previews the next chapters only briefly, in its conclusion; its tasks are meaning and notation.
Right: Chapter 2 explains the central notion and sets up the notation used later.
questions.explain: Chapter 2 explains the IPS idea and fixes the notation, much as the cookbook chapter does for its terms.
questions.rule: This chapter explains what the IPS claim means and fixes the notation; it does not try to prove the claim.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, working out what the IPS postulate means also shows that the postulate is true.
questions.explain: They say the explication does not justify the postulate but only clarifies its meaning.
questions.rule: Clarifying a claim is not confirming it.

questions.q: A reviewer says Chapter 2 defines the IPS in detail, so it already gives strong evidence that humans are IPS's. What is wrong?
options: A definition clarifies a claim; the evidence is to come later
Nothing: a detailed definition is itself good evidence
The chapter never defines the IPS at all
The evidence is in the notation section of this chapter
optionExplain: Right: the authors separate saying what the claim means from testing it.
A detailed definition can be accurate and still say nothing about whether people fit it.
The chapter does define it, through eight postulates.
The notation section sets up tools for describing behavior, not evidence.
questions.explain: The authors keep meaning and verification apart: this chapter does the first, later chapters the second.
questions.rule: This chapter explains what the IPS claim means and fixes the notation; it does not try to prove the claim.

questions.q: A card-game guide first explains what the rules mean and ends with scoring shorthand. Which order does Chapter 2 follow?
options: Notation first, then the meaning of the postulates a little later on
Verification of the postulates first, then their meaning
Meaning of the postulates first, notation in the last section
Notation and meaning mixed together on every page of the chapter
optionExplain: The notation is held back until the final section.
Verification is not in this chapter at all.
Right: the conclusion says the first four sections spell out the postulates and the final section sets out the notation.
The chapter keeps the two jobs in separate stretches.
questions.explain: The authors spend the first four sections on the meaning of the eight postulates, then close with the notation section.
questions.teaches: The chapter spends its first four sections on the meaning of the eight postulates and puts the notation in its final section.
questions.rule: This chapter explains what the IPS claim means and fixes the notation; it does not try to prove the claim.

questions.q: A new scientific hypothesis strikes most people as odd. As evidence for it accumulates, what usually happens to how plausible it seems?
options: It becomes more plausible
It stays fixed, because plausibility belongs to the idea itself
It becomes less plausible, as familiar ideas lose their charm
It changes only if the hypothesis is first made simpler
optionExplain: Right: support and explanatory success raise plausibility.
That would make plausibility a fixed property; the authors call it time-dependent.
Evidence for a hypothesis does not usually make it seem less likely.
Simplicity is not the factor the authors name.
questions.explain: Plausibility moves with evidence. The card gives the authors' reasoning.
questions.rule: Do not judge a fundamental hypothesis by how plausible it sounds now; judge it after the empirical evidence is in.

questions.q: The authors say the plausibility of a fundamental hypothesis typically depends on ____.
questions.explain: A hypothesis is seldom thought plausible when it is new and becomes more so as the evidence builds.

questions.q: A friend dismisses a new theory of why bread rises because it sounds wrong to them. What would the authors advise?
options: Poll people on how plausible it sounds and go with the majority
Weigh the empirical evidence and the range of facts it explains
Wait a night and see whether it feels more right
Accept it, since ideas that sound wrong are usually correct
optionExplain: A poll measures first impressions, the very thing the authors distrust.
Right: the authors want the judgment made on empirical evidence.
A night's reflection changes feelings, not evidence.
The authors do not say odd-sounding ideas are usually right; they say sound is a poor test.
questions.explain: Judge by evidence and explanatory range, not by how the idea sounds at first.
questions.rule: Do not judge a fundamental hypothesis by how plausible it sounds now; judge it after the empirical evidence is in.

questions.q: Sort each item by whether the authors say it raises a hypothesis's plausibility.

items.t: Empirical tests that support it
Success in explaining a significant range of phenomena
Many readers finding it appealing at first sight
Its being new and not yet widely accepted
Surviving empirical tests across several generations

questions.explain: The authors tie plausibility to empirical support and explanatory success. Newness and first impressions do not raise it.
questions.rule: Evidence and explanatory range raise plausibility.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a hypothesis that keeps surviving empirical tests over generations is likely to be thought more plausible.
questions.explain: Support over time raises plausibility; the authors add that it may even come to seem self-evident.
questions.rule: Long survival of tests raises plausibility.

questions.q: An old gardening maxim is called self-evident by everyone. How do the authors' remarks suggest we read that self-evidence?
options: It shows the maxim needs no further testing of any kind at all
It proves the maxim already seemed plausible when first stated
It shows the maxim has stopped being a hypothesis at all
It may reflect surviving tests over generations, not inborn truth
optionExplain: Self-evidence today says little about whether tests were passed.
The authors say new hypotheses are seldom thought plausible at first.
Being obvious does not change a hypothesis into something else; it only changes how it is regarded.
Right: for the authors, self-evidence can be the end of a long record of empirical survival.
questions.explain: The authors say a hypothesis that survives empirical tests for several generations is likely to be regarded not merely as plausible but as self-evident.
questions.teaches: If a hypothesis survives empirical tests for several generations, it is likely to be regarded not merely as plausible but as self-evident.
questions.rule: Do not judge a fundamental hypothesis by how plausible it sounds now; judge it after the empirical evidence is in.

questions.q: Which list best names the parts of a system that thinks by handling symbols?
options: A keyboard, a screen, a memory and a power source
A sensory store, a motor store and a long-term store
A memory, a processor, receptors and effectors
A processor and a program, with nothing else
optionExplain: These are parts of a desktop computer, not the abstract parts the authors list.
The authors do not divide the system into stores of this kind.
Right: this is how the authors define an IPS.
A program is not a separate part; memory and receptors and effectors are also in the definition.
questions.explain: The authors name four parts. The card gives them.
questions.rule: An IPS is a memory holding symbol structures, a processor, receptors and effectors.

questions.q: An IPS consists of a memory containing symbol structures, a processor, effectors, and ____.
questions.explain: The definition lists memory, processor, effectors and receptors.

questions.q: Match each part of a robot vacuum to the part of an IPS it plays.
pairs: Chip that chooses the next move
questions.explain: The sensor brings in information from outside, the motors act on the world, the map is a stored structure, and the chip decides what to do next.
questions.rule: Receptors take in, effectors act, memory stores, the processor decides.

questions.q: True or false: In this chapter the authors treat the details of sensory and motor processing at length.
questions.explain: They say they abstract from the complications of sensory and motor processing and do not treat these in detail.
questions.rule: The chapter's focus is the central parts.

questions.q: A student summarizes: An IPS is a processor that runs programs; memory is optional. What does the authors' definition say instead?
options: A memory containing symbol structures is a defining part, along with the other three
Memory is the only defining part; the processor is optional
Memory and processor are defining, but receptors and effectors are optional by definition
A processor is defined as the memory
optionExplain: Right: all four components appear in the definition.
The processor is also in the definition.
Receptors and effectors are named in the definition as parts.
The processor is a separate component with its own definition.
questions.explain: The definition lists four parts; none is optional in the statement itself.
questions.rule: An IPS is a memory holding symbol structures, a processor, receptors and effectors.

questions.q: A friend expects this theory to explain how the eye turns light into nerve signals. What is the best reply?
options: Yes, since receptors are the main subject of the whole book
The authors set aside sensory and motor detail, so not their aim
Yes, but only for the motor side of the system and nothing else
No, because the IPS is defined without any receptors at all
optionExplain: Receptors are named in the definition, but the authors do not treat them in detail.
Right: the text says they abstract from the complications of sensory and motor processing.
Neither side is treated in detail.
The definition does include receptors.
questions.explain: The authors name receptors and effectors but set aside the complications of sensory and motor processing, so they do not treat them in detail.
questions.teaches: The authors abstract from the complications of sensory and motor processing, so they name receptors and effectors but do not treat them in detail.
questions.rule: An IPS is a memory holding symbol structures, a processor, receptors and effectors.

questions.q: A shopping list is a few items written in order. In the language of symbols, what would the whole list be?
options: A single symbol with no parts of its own at all
A process that takes some inputs and gives outputs
A memory, since it is where the list is kept for later
A structure of tokens linked by an ordering relation
optionExplain: A list has parts; a single symbol would not.
A list is stored; a process acts.
The memory is the place where the list could be kept.
Right: items in an order are tokens connected by a relation, which is what the authors call a symbol structure.
questions.explain: A symbol structure is tokens plus relations. The card gives the definition.
questions.rule: Symbols are elements; a symbol structure is tokens linked by relations; an information process takes or gives symbol structures.

questions.q: A symbol structure consists of a set of ____ of symbols connected by a set of relations.
questions.explain: Tokens are the instances or occurrences of symbols that are connected by relations.

questions.q: A phone stores a contact as three entries linked in order: first name, surname, number. Which statement fits the authors' definitions?
options: The contact is an information process
The contact is a structure, and searching for it is a process
Only the number counts as a symbol structure, not the names
The search is a symbol
optionExplain: A stored structure is data, not a process.
Right: the stored entries linked by relations are a structure, and a process that outputs it is an information process.
The three linked entries together form the structure.
A search is a process; a symbol is an element.
questions.explain: Structures are what is stored; information processes take or give them.
questions.rule: Symbols are elements; a symbol structure is tokens linked by relations; an information process takes or gives symbol structures.

questions.q: Sort each item: symbol structure or information process, in the authors' sense.

items.t: The list of three dashes in the order they came
Finding the item that comes after a given item in a list
A description pairing an attribute with a value
Copying a list into a new list
A tree built from tokens and left and right relations

questions.explain: Structures are things built from tokens and relations. Processes are things done with such structures as inputs or outputs.
questions.rule: Structures are stored things; processes act on them.

questions.q: True or false: A process that neither takes nor produces a symbol structure is not an information process, by the definition.
questions.explain: The definition requires symbol structures among some of the process's inputs or outputs.
questions.rule: No symbol structures, no information process.

questions.q: A system owns a sealed box of index cards that nothing can open or read. Does it really hold those symbol structures?
options: Not really, since no process can manipulate or access them
Yes, because the cards are tokens connected by relations
Yes, because storing alone is what having a structure means
No, because cards of paper cannot serve as symbols at all
optionExplain: Right: the authors say processes must be able to manipulate and access a structure, or the system would not have it.
The cards fit the structure definition, but the authors add a condition about access.
Storage is not enough on the authors' account.
Cards can serve as tokens; the problem is access, not the medium.
questions.explain: The authors require information processes that can manipulate and access the symbols in a structure; otherwise the IPS could not use the structure and would not have it.
questions.teaches: Without information processes that can manipulate and access the symbols in a structure, the IPS could not make real use of it and would not have it.
questions.rule: Symbols are elements; a symbol structure is tokens linked by relations; an information process takes or gives symbol structures.

questions.q: A processor in a thinking system must do three jobs. Which set of jobs is the best guess?
options: Sense the world, move the body, and store past events
Read the program, compile it, and print out the result
Hold basic operations, hold their data, and decide what runs next
Remember some facts, forget others, and rank all the facts
optionExplain: Sensing and moving belong to receptors and effectors, not the processor.
Compiling is a feature of computer software, not the authors' definition.
Right: these are the three parts of the processor in the authors' definition.
The processor does not itself rank memories; memory is a separate component.
questions.explain: The processor is operations, a short-term store and a controller. The card names them.
questions.rule: A processor is a fixed set of eip's, a short-term memory for their inputs and outputs, and an interpreter that picks the sequence.

questions.q: Match each part of the processor to its role.
pairs: A fixed set of basic operations
Holds the inputs and outputs of the eip's
Determines the sequence of eip's to execute
questions.explain: The eip's do the work, STM holds what they take and give, and the interpreter chooses what runs next.

questions.q: A decorating robot has fixed moves, a work tray and a controller. Which part plays the interpreter?
options: The controller that picks the next move from the tray
The set of fixed moves such as piping and swirling
The tray holding the cake and the toppings in hand
The cake that is being decorated on the tray
optionExplain: Right: the interpreter determines the sequence of eip's from what is in STM.
The moves are the eip's.
The tray plays the role of STM.
The cake is an object being worked on, not a part of the processor.
questions.explain: The controller corresponds to the interpreter because it chooses the next move from what is in the short-term store.
questions.rule: A processor is a fixed set of eip's, a short-term memory for their inputs and outputs, and an interpreter that picks the sequence.

questions.q: True or false: If the symbol structures in STM change, the interpreter may select a different eip to execute next.
questions.explain: The interpreter determines the sequence of eip's as a function of the symbol structures in STM, so a change there can change what runs next.
questions.rule: The sequence depends on the contents of STM.

questions.q: A student writes: The interpreter is one of the elementary information processes in the fixed set. What is wrong with this?
options: Nothing is wrong: the fixed set includes the interpreter
The interpreter is a separate component that sequences the eip's
The interpreter is the same thing as the short-term memory
The interpreter belongs to memory, not to the processor at all
optionExplain: The eip's are what the interpreter sequences; it is listed apart from them.
Right: the definition lists the eip's, STM and interpreter as three distinct parts.
STM holds symbol structures; the interpreter acts on them.
The definition puts the interpreter inside the processor.
questions.explain: The three parts are listed separately: operations, short-term memory and interpreter.
questions.rule: A processor is a fixed set of eip's, a short-term memory for their inputs and outputs, and an interpreter that picks the sequence.

questions.q: A relay coach tracks which runner is running and who runs next after the baton passes. Which processor part does the coach resemble?
options: STM, which holds the runners' times as inputs and outputs
An eip, which carries out the whole race by itself
The memory, since it stores every race ever run before
The interpreter, tracking the current process and the next
optionExplain: STM holds inputs and outputs, not the order of execution.
The eip's are the single steps, not the sequencer.
Memory stores structures; the sequencing role is the interpreter's.
Right: the Morse example describes the interpreter as tracking the current process and finding the next one.
questions.explain: In the Morse example the interpreter keeps track of the current elementary process being executed and, after execution, finds the next process to execute.
questions.teaches: The interpreter keeps track of the elementary process currently being executed and, after execution, finds the next process to run.
questions.rule: A processor is a fixed set of eip's, a short-term memory for their inputs and outputs, and an interpreter that picks the sequence.

questions.q: When does a symbol structure count as designating an object, if the definition is framed in terms of processes?
options: When a process given it can affect the object or give dependent output
When the structure looks a great deal like the object itself
When some person declares that it refers to the object
When it is kept in memory in the same place as the object
optionExplain: Right: the authors define designation by what processes can do with the structure.
Resemblance is not part of the definition.
The definition does not turn on anyone's say-so.
Being stored beside something does not make a process able to reach it.
questions.explain: Designation is tied to processes. The card gives the exact definition.
questions.rule: A structure designates an object when some information process, given the structure, affects the object or produces outputs that depend on it.

questions.q: A symbol structure designates an object if processes that take it as input either ____ the object or produce outputs that depend on the object.
questions.explain: Condition (a) says the processes affect the object; condition (b) says they produce outputs depending on it.
questions.rule: Affect the object, or produce outputs that depend on it.

questions.q: A process takes a barcode as input and prints the matching book's title and price. Does the barcode designate the book in the authors' sense?
options: No, because the process never changes the book itself
No, because a barcode is a mark and not a symbol structure
Yes, but only if a person is the one who runs the process
Yes, since a process given it outputs what depends on the book
optionExplain: Condition (a) is only one of two ways; (b) needs no change to the object.
A barcode is a pattern that can be a symbol structure.
The definition does not require a person to run the process.
Right: condition (b) is met when the output depends on the object.
questions.explain: Printing the title and price depends on which book the barcode names, so (b) holds.
questions.rule: A structure designates an object when some information process, given the structure, affects the object or produces outputs that depend on it.

questions.q: True or false: A doodle that closely resembles a cat designates the cat, according to the authors' definition, even if no process ever uses it.
questions.explain: Our reading: the definition rests on the existence of processes that use the structure, not on resemblance.
questions.rule: Designation rests on processes, not on resemblance.

questions.q: A student says: A symbol structure designates an object only if some process changes the object. What does the definition add?
options: A process must both change the object and produce outputs
A process whose outputs depend on the object also suffices
The process involved must be one of the elementary processes
Only a program is able to designate an object at all
optionExplain: The two conditions are alternatives joined by either, not both.
Right: there are two alternatives, (a) affecting the object or (b) producing dependent outputs.
The definition mentions information processes, not only elementary ones.
Any symbol structure can designate, not only programs.
questions.explain: The definition says either affect the object or produce outputs that depend on it.
questions.rule: A structure designates an object when some information process, given the structure, affects the object or produces outputs that depend on it.

questions.q: A designer says a wristband code identifies a patient only together with its scanner and database. How does this fit the authors' view?
options: It conflicts: a code ought to designate the patient by itself
It fits only because a wristband is a physical thing in the world
It fits: designation is defined together with the processes that use it
It conflicts: designation needs no processes at all to exist
optionExplain: The authors define designation by processes, so a code alone is not enough.
The physical form of the wristband is not the point.
Right: the authors say each part of such a system remains essentially undefined except together with the others.
Processes are written into the definition.
questions.explain: The authors say that in definitions of abstract systems each part remains essentially undefined except when taken in conjunction with the other parts, and they assume the needed information processes exist.
questions.teaches: In definitions of abstract systems each part remains essentially undefined except together with the other parts, so designation always assumes underlying information processes.
questions.rule: A structure designates an object when some information process, given the structure, affects the object or produces outputs that depend on it.

questions.q: A recipe card is a list of steps. When could such a list count as a program for a cooking machine?
options: It is written in clear and complete sentences throughout
It designates a process that the machine's interpreter can run
It is kept in the machine's memory for later use
It lists all of the inputs the machine receives each time
optionExplain: Clear writing is not part of the definition.
Right: both conditions are needed, a designated process and an interpreter able to execute it.
Storage alone does not make a structure a program.
Listing inputs does not designate a process.
questions.explain: A program ties a structure to an executable process. The card states both conditions.
questions.rule: A program is a symbol structure that designates a process the interpreter can execute; a primitive symbol has its designation fixed from outside the symbol structures.

questions.q: A symbol structure is a program if the object it designates is an information process and the ____ can execute the designated process.
questions.explain: The definition has two conditions: the designated object is an information process, and the interpreter can execute it.
questions.rule: Designated process plus an interpreter that can run it.

questions.q: A card designates a mail-sorting process, but nothing in the building can execute that process. Is the card a program?
options: Yes, because designating a process is all that is needed
Yes, because it is stored in the building somewhere
No, because (b) fails: no interpreter can execute that process
No, because mail sorting is not an information process
optionExplain: Condition (a) holds but (b) does not.
Storage is not the test.
Right: a program needs an interpreter able to execute the process it designates.
Whether sorting is an information process is not the issue here; the missing executor is.
questions.explain: Both conditions must hold. Here the designated process cannot be executed, so the card is not a program.
questions.rule: A program is a symbol structure that designates a process the interpreter can execute; a primitive symbol has its designation fixed from outside the symbol structures.

questions.q: Sort each item: is it a program in the authors' sense, assuming the interpreter can run whatever is designated?

items.t: A list designating a sequence of elementary processes
A list of three dash tokens
A description pairing a chessman with its color
A sublist that designates a subprogram
A list of method names the interpreter can execute in order
A single primitive symbol for a letter

questions.explain: A program designates a process the interpreter can execute. Lists of tokens and descriptions designate things that are not processes.

questions.q: True or false: If a structure designates an information process but the interpreter could not execute it, it would still count as a program.
questions.explain: Condition (b) requires that the interpreter can execute the designated process.

questions.q: A kitchen carries out any menu plan whose ticket number it is handed. How does the authors' parenthetical remark apply here?
options: It is given an input designating the program, such as the ticket
The kitchen has to be handed the whole plan on paper
The ticket number should be counted as the plan itself
The kitchen need not execute anything it is handed at all
optionExplain: Right: the authors say the definition should literally read given an input that designates the program.
Handing over the whole plan is not required.
The ticket designates the plan; it is not the plan.
Execution is still needed.
questions.explain: The authors note that literally condition (b) should read: if given an input that designates the program.
questions.teaches: Literally, the interpreter is given an input that designates the program, not the program itself.
questions.rule: A program is a symbol structure that designates a process the interpreter can execute; a primitive symbol has its designation fixed from outside the symbol structures.

questions.q: In the phrase a symbol structure designates an object, what can the object be?
options: Only a physical object that lies in the outside world
Only another symbol structure that is kept in memory
A stored structure, a process, or something in the environment
Only a program that the interpreter is able to run
optionExplain: That leaves out the internal objects.
That leaves out processes and external stimuli.
Right: the authors include all three sorts.
Programs are one kind of stored structure, not the only object.
questions.explain: Object is broader than it first looks. The card lists three sorts.
questions.rule: An object may be a stored symbol structure, a process the IPS can execute, or something in the external environment.

questions.q: Match each sort of object to its description.
pairs: Processes the IPS can carry out
questions.explain: The three sorts are stored structures, processes the IPS can execute, and the external environment.

questions.q: In a school office run by an IPS, sort each item by where it sits.

items.t: A student's record stored on the office computer
The sound of the school bell
The routine that prints report cards
A paper note on the counter that someone could read
A stored list of room numbers
The routine that checks attendance

questions.explain: Stored records and lists are structures in memory; routines are processes. The bell and the paper note are stimuli in the environment.
questions.rule: Memory and processes inside; stimuli outside.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, programs count as a kind of stored symbol structure, so they too can be designated as objects.
questions.explain: Sort (1) includes data structures and programs, so programs are objects of the first sort.

questions.q: A student says: Objects are only things outside the IPS. Which sorts did the student leave out?
options: Stored symbol structures and processes the IPS can execute
Only the stimuli that the receptors are able to detect
Only the programs that are stored in the IPS's memory
Only the responses that the effectors produce outside
optionExplain: Right: the authors list stored structures and executable processes as well as the environment.
Stimuli are the external sort the student already counted.
Programs are inside the stored-structure sort, but processes also count.
Responses belong to the external environment too.
questions.explain: Objects include things inside the system: stored structures and executable processes.
questions.rule: An object may be a stored symbol structure, a process the IPS can execute, or something in the external environment.

questions.q: A courier app reads the address from a parcel label and later prints a delivery receipt. In the authors' terms, what is the first act?
options: Producing a response in the environment designated by an internal structure
Creating an internal symbol structure that designates the external label
Executing a stored program
Deleting a data structure
optionExplain: That describes writing, the inverse operation.
Right: for the authors reading is creating internal symbol structures that designate external stimuli.
Execution of a program is a separate matter.
Deleting is not what the app does when it reads.
questions.explain: The authors define reading as creating in memory internal symbol structures that designate external stimuli; writing is the inverse, creating responses in the environment that are designated by internal structures.
questions.teaches: Reading is creating internal symbol structures that designate external stimuli; writing is the inverse, creating responses in the environment designated by internal structures.
questions.rule: An object may be a stored symbol structure, a process the IPS can execute, or something in the external environment.

questions.q: Can a symbol structure point to something that itself only points onward to something else?
options: Yes, to any depth
No, designation is always one step
Only once
Only if the final object is outside the IPS
optionExplain: Right: the authors allow any degree of indirectness.
The authors say the relation can have any degree of directness or indirectness.
They set no limit of one level.
The chain can end in a program, as their example shows.
questions.explain: Designation can be chained. The card shows the authors' example.
questions.rule: Designation can be as indirect as needed: a structure may point to a structure that points to a program.

questions.q: A symbol structure can point to a symbol structure that points to a symbol structure that points to a ____.
questions.explain: The authors' example chain ends at a program.
questions.rule: Chains of pointing can end at a program.

questions.q: A board entry names a list, which names an engineer, whose number is stored. How is the entry's designation of the number described?
options: Direct, since the entry is next to the number
Absent, since the entry is not a symbol
External, since the number is outside the IPS
Indirect, through several linked structures
optionExplain: Closeness on the page does not make the designation direct.
The entry is a symbol structure that designates.
The number is stored in memory in this scenario.
Right: the entry reaches the number only through further designating structures.
questions.explain: The entry designates the list, the list designates the engineer, and so on, so the designation is indirect.
questions.rule: Designation can be as indirect as needed: a structure may point to a structure that points to a program.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the book's focus on central processes means it often deals with structures designating other structures in memory.
questions.explain: They say the focus on central processes makes such designations frequent.
questions.rule: Central processes mean many memory-to-memory designations.

questions.q: Order these designations of a program from the most direct to the most indirect.
items: A structure that points straight to the program
A structure that points to a structure that points to the program
A structure that points to a structure that points to a structure that points to the program
questions.explain: Each extra link in the chain adds a degree of indirectness.

questions.q: A museum audio guide keeps a track code for each painting, and visitors only handle the codes. Which of the authors' remarks does this resemble?
options: Every symbol must designate some external object directly, in one step
Stimuli and responses are encoded internally, so designations are dealt with
Programs are not allowed to designate any other structures
Designation is limited to a single step of pointing at most
optionExplain: The authors allow chains and internal designations.
Right: the authors say that when they deal with stimuli and responses, these are already encoded internally.
Programs can be designated by structures, which the authors discuss.
They allow any degree of indirectness.
questions.explain: The authors say that, by the time they deal with stimuli and responses, these will already be encoded internally, so they almost always deal with the designations rather than the external objects designated.
questions.teaches: By the time the book deals with stimuli and responses they are already encoded internally, so it almost always deals with their designations rather than the external objects.
questions.rule: Designation can be as indirect as needed: a structure may point to a structure that points to a program.

questions.q: How many primitive symbol types would the Morse IPS need for the four basic external signals?
options: Two
Four
Three
Twenty-six
optionExplain: Two would cover only the signals, not the intervals.
Right: dot, dash, letter space and word space each evoke their own primitive symbol type.
Three would drop one of the four basic stimuli.
Twenty-six is the number of letters, which are a separate set of symbol types.
questions.explain: One symbol type per basic stimulus gives four. The card lists them.
questions.rule: A Morse IPS maps four kinds of external signal onto four primitive symbol types and strings them into lists using next.

questions.q: In the Morse example, sequences of stimuli are represented as lists composed with the relation ____.
questions.explain: Each token of a sequence is next to the following one.

questions.q: A system represents a morning routine as wake, wash, dress, eat, each following the previous. Which relation builds this list?
options: Above
Left
Next
Designates
optionExplain: Above would stack items, not sequence them.
Left would suit tree structures with a left and a right part.
Right: a sequence is a list built with next.
Designates links a symbol to an object, not each item to its follower.
questions.explain: A sequence is built with the relation next, as in the Morse lists.
questions.rule: A Morse IPS maps four kinds of external signal onto four primitive symbol types and strings them into lists using next.

questions.q: Match each external feature to the symbol token it evokes inside the Morse IPS.
questions.explain: Each of the four external features evokes a token of its own primitive symbol type.
questions.rule: One primitive symbol type per feature.

questions.q: True or false: In the Morse IPS, two dots then a dash would be stored as a list of three tokens linked by next.
questions.explain: Sequences of stimuli become lists of primitive tokens composed with next.
questions.rule: Three signals give a three-token list.

questions.q: An IPS reading semaphore flags has tags for flag positions and further tags for the letters they spell. What do the letter tags designate?
options: Only other tags held inside the IPS
External objects, namely the letters
Elementary processes that read flags
The flag positions themselves, not letters
optionExplain: Right: the Morse IPS also has symbol types for letters, which the authors call external objects.
Letter symbol types designate letters, not just other tags.
Letters are not processes.
The flag positions have their own tags.
questions.explain: In the authors' Morse example the symbol types for letters of the Roman alphabet designate external objects.
questions.teaches: The symbol types for the Roman letters designate letters, which the authors describe as external objects.
questions.rule: A Morse IPS maps four kinds of external signal onto four primitive symbol types and strings them into lists using next.

questions.q: In an IPS, what does a read process do?
options: Creates an internal structure designating what is at an outside location
Copies a stored structure out into the environment as a response
Chooses the next process to execute from the structures in STM
Deletes the old structures that are no longer needed in memory
optionExplain: Right: reading brings a designation of the stimulus into STM.
That is closer to writing.
Choosing the next process is the interpreter's job.
Deleting is not what reading does.
questions.explain: Reading takes the outside in. The card explains the other three processes.
questions.rule: Reading puts a designation of the outside into STM, writing does the reverse, and encoding and decoding convert letters and signal lists.

questions.q: A writing program designates the ____ of the reading process: it produces in the environment the object designated by an internal structure.
questions.explain: Reading creates an internal designation of a stimulus; writing creates the external object an internal structure designates.
questions.rule: Writing is the inverse of reading.

questions.q: A voice assistant hears the word timer and stores a tag for it; later it plays a beep. Which is reading and which is writing?
options: Storing the tag is writing; playing the beep is reading
Both are reading
Storing the tag is reading; playing the beep is writing
Both are encoding
optionExplain: That reverses the two.
The beep is an output into the environment, which is writing.
Right: reading creates an internal designation of a stimulus; writing produces an external response.
Encoding converts between letters and signal lists, not between world and memory.
questions.explain: The tag is an internal symbol structure for an outside stimulus, so storing it is reading; the beep is an external response, so producing it is writing.
questions.rule: Reading puts a designation of the outside into STM, writing does the reverse, and encoding and decoding convert letters and signal lists.

questions.q: Order the steps for the Morse IPS to echo a received letter.
items: Read the incoming signals into STM as a list of tokens
Decode the list into a letter token
Encode the letter token back into a list of signal tokens
Write the signals out into the environment
questions.explain: The signals come in, are turned into a letter, turned back into signals and sent out.

questions.q: True or false: If the designator in STM is the list for three dashes, the writing program would produce three dashes in the environment.
questions.explain: The writing program produces in the environment the object designated by the internal structure.
questions.rule: Writing realizes what a structure designates.

questions.q: An app keeps the word milk as a list of four letters, each letter itself kept as a pattern. Which description fits the authors' scheme?
options: A single primitive symbol with no parts of its own inside it
A higher-order list whose members designate lower structures
A program that designates a process the IPS can execute
An association pairing an attribute with a value for a symbol
optionExplain: A word list has members, so it is not a single primitive symbol.
Right: the authors build words as lists of letters, each member designating the appropriate letter token or its code list.
The list designates a word, not a process.
Attribute-value pairs are a different structure.
questions.explain: In the Morse example the word was is the list of W, A and S, where each member designates the appropriate symbol token or, alternatively, the appropriate list of Morse code.
questions.teaches: Each member of a higher-order list may designate either a letter token or the list of signal tokens for that letter.
questions.rule: Reading puts a designation of the outside into STM, writing does the reverse, and encoding and decoding convert letters and signal lists.

questions.q: To decide whether two shopping lists are identical, which two simple operations are the best guess for what you need?
options: Count the items in each list and then add up the totals
Move to the next item on each list, and compare the two items
Sort both of the lists into alphabetical order, then look
Copy the items of one list over the items of the other
optionExplain: Counting totals would not tell you whether the items match.
Right: stepping along and comparing are the building blocks.
Sorting would change the lists and ignore order.
Copying would overwrite rather than test.
questions.explain: A comparison is built from stepping and comparing. The card gives the authors' version.
questions.rule: Larger processes are composed from elementary ones; two lists are identical only if every token matches and both end together.

questions.q: The identity test for two lists combines finding the next symbol token with testing whether two tokens are ____.
questions.explain: The two elementary processes are finding the next member of a list and testing token identity.
questions.rule: Find the next token, test identity.

questions.q: Following the process, what is the result for the lists (R, E, D) and (R, E, D, S)?
options: Identical, because every token of list-1 matches in turn
Not identical, because the first tokens of the lists differ
The process never stops, as it goes on cycling through the lists
Not identical, since list-2 still has a token left over
optionExplain: Matching all of list-1 is not enough; step 4 checks list-2.
The first tokens R and R match.
Step 4 ends the process either way.
Right: after matching all of list-1 the process finds another token in list-2 and reports not identical.
questions.explain: All tokens of list-1 match, but step 4 finds S left in list-2, so the report is not identical.
questions.rule: Larger processes are composed from elementary ones; two lists are identical only if every token matches and both end together.

questions.q: True or false: If list-1 runs out of tokens first, the process reports identical whenever every token so far has matched.
questions.explain: It still checks list-2; if another token is found there, it reports not identical.

questions.q: Order the actions of the identity test on lists (A, B) and (A, B).
items: Find the next token in list-1
Find the next token in list-2
Compare the two tokens, and repeat while they match
Find that list-1 has no more tokens
Find that list-2 has no more tokens, and report identical
questions.explain: The process steps through both lists together and finishes only when both end.

questions.q: A coach wants a card-sorting process built only from take-next and compare-equal. How would the authors expect the larger process to be executed?
options: By an interpreter following a program that designates the steps
By a new elementary process added for each larger task needed
By the receptors alone, taking in each signal as it comes
By storing every possible answer in advance in memory
optionExplain: Right: the authors say the composite could be executed by an interpreter with a program that designates the sequence.
The point is to compose bigger processes from existing ones.
Receptors bring in stimuli and do not sequence processes.
Storing all answers would not be composing processes.
questions.explain: The authors say the composite process could be executed by an interpretive process in which a program, a symbol structure, designates the sequence of elementary processes.
questions.teaches: A composite process can be executed by an interpretive process: a program, which is a symbol structure, designates the sequence of elementary processes.
questions.rule: Larger processes are composed from elementary ones; two lists are identical only if every token matches and both end together.

questions.q: Digital computers can be programmed to fit the IPS postulates. According to the authors, what does that show about human thinking?
options: Nothing yet; only that such systems can be realized by a mechanism
That humans are information processing systems, as the postulates say
That humans are digital computers built from electronic circuits
That the postulates are specific to electronic circuits and wires
optionExplain: Right: realizability is shown; whether humans are well modeled is left for later.
The authors say computer realizations do not prove that humans are well modeled.
They do not say humans are computers.
The postulates are abstract, making no claim about how they are realized.
questions.explain: A computer shows realizability, not a model of humans. The card gives the authors' wording.
questions.rule: The postulates are abstract; a computer shows an IPS can be built, not that humans are one.

questions.q: The postulates characterize the memory, processes and structures ____, with no assertion about how they are realized physically or biologically.
questions.explain: The characterization is abstract.

questions.q: A laptop flight simulator behaves like a plane, and a pilot says this proves planes are laptops. What is the better statement?
options: The simulator proves the plane works the way the laptop does
The plane must contain a laptop somewhere inside its cockpit
A mechanism reproducing behavior does not show the real thing works so
Behavior can never be reproduced by any mechanism whatever
optionExplain: That draws the very inference the authors warn against.
Nothing in the text suggests this.
Right: the authors say a computer realization does not prove humans are well modeled by the system.
Reproducing behavior by a mechanism is exactly what the computers do.
questions.explain: A realization by a mechanism shows a model can be built, not that the real thing is organized that way.
questions.rule: The postulates are abstract; a computer shows an IPS can be built, not that humans are one.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the postulates require an IPS to be built from electronic circuits.
questions.explain: They make no assertions about how the structures and processes are realized physically or biologically.
questions.rule: The postulates are silent on realization.

questions.q: Argument: computers can be programmed to fit the IPS postulates, so humans, who think, must fit them too. What is the flaw?
options: Computers cannot in fact be programmed to fit the postulates
Humans do not actually think in any way that can be modeled
The postulates are physically specific to electronic circuits
Being realizable by a mechanism does not show humans are modeled by it
optionExplain: The authors say computers can be so programmed.
The argument does not need that claim to fail.
The authors call the postulates abstract.
Right: the authors separate showing the system can be realized from showing humans are modeled by it.
questions.explain: The step from a computer can realize an IPS to humans are IPS's is not licensed; the authors leave it to later chapters.
questions.rule: The postulates are abstract; a computer shows an IPS can be built, not that humans are one.

questions.q: A student argues that a human simulating a computer that simulates a human proves the computer's model adequate. How does the authors' footnote answer?
options: The argument is sound, because humans simulate quite slowly
The human's behavior differs observably from the human solving the problem
The footnote says humans cannot simulate computers at all
The footnote says the computer's behavior is the same as the human's
optionExplain: Speed is mentioned only as a small point; the argument fails for another reason.
Right: the footnote says that behavior differs observably, so the ability to simulate proves nothing.
The footnote grants that a human can simulate a computer, albeit slowly.
The footnote says the computer's behavior may match but the human's does not.
questions.explain: The footnote grants that a human can simulate anything a computer can, but a human simulating a computer simulating a human differs observably from a human solving the problem, so that ability proves nothing about the adequacy of the computer's simulation.
questions.teaches: A human can simulate any computer, but a human simulating a computer that simulates a human behaves observably differently from the human solving the problem, so the ability to simulate proves nothing about the computer simulation's adequacy.
questions.rule: The postulates are abstract; a computer shows an IPS can be built, not that humans are one.

questions.q: How many symbols appear in the list (B, A, N, A, N, A)?
options: Six, counting every occurrence of every letter
Three, counting only the different kinds of letter
Two, counting only the letters that appear again
It depends on whether tokens or types are counted
optionExplain: Six counts tokens only.
Three counts types only.
Two does not match either count.
Right: there are six tokens but only three types.
questions.explain: The question is ambiguous until you say tokens or types. The card gives the terms.
questions.rule: A token is one occurrence; a type is the class of tokens the system judges identical; say which you are counting.

questions.q: A class of all tokens that are judged to be identical is called a symbol ____.
questions.explain: Tokens of the same type differ only in being distinct occurrences.
questions.rule: Type: the class; token: the occurrence.

questions.q: How many tokens and how many types are in the list (R, E, D, R, E, D, R)?
options: 7 tokens and 3 types
3 tokens and 7 types
7 tokens and 4 types
4 tokens and 3 types
optionExplain: Right: there are seven occurrences of three kinds.
That reverses the two counts.
The three kinds are R, E and D.
Seven items are present, not four.
questions.explain: Count occurrences for tokens (7) and distinct kinds for types (3: R, E, D).
questions.rule: A token is one occurrence; a type is the class of tokens the system judges identical; say which you are counting.

questions.q: Sort each item: a token or a type?

items.t: The second D in the list (R, E, D, R, E, D)
The class of all D's the system judges identical
One occurrence of a dash in a Morse list
The dash symbol as a kind
The first R in the list (R, E, D, R)
The letter E as a kind

questions.explain: Tokens are single occurrences; types are the classes of tokens the system treats as identical.

questions.q: True or false: If the IPS judges two tokens identical, they belong to the same symbol type.
questions.explain: A symbol type is the class of all tokens judged identical.

questions.q: One writer says the word the appears five times in this paragraph; another says the is the commonest English word. Which speaks of tokens?
options: The first speaks of a type and the second counts tokens
The first counts tokens and the second speaks of a type
Both are about tokens
Both are about types
optionExplain: That reverses them.
Right: five occurrences are tokens; the word as a kind is a type.
The second statement is about the word as a kind.
The first statement counts occurrences.
questions.explain: The authors use the word symbol for either token or type and let context decide; the same holds for the word the in ordinary writing.
questions.teaches: The term symbol is used for either the token or the type, context making clear which is meant.
questions.rule: A token is one occurrence; a type is the class of tokens the system judges identical; say which you are counting.

questions.q: Is a single left-to-right ordering relation enough to record a printed formula that has exponents and subscripts?
options: No, other relations such as above and below are needed
Yes, since all writing runs from left to right on a page
Yes, if the symbols are small enough to fit in a line
No, because formulas cannot be stored as symbol structures
optionExplain: Right: exponents and subscripts need relations other than next.
Position above or below the line carries meaning that order alone cannot.
Size does not change what relations are needed.
Formulas can be stored as symbol structures.
questions.explain: Some structures need more than one relation. The card gives the authors' take.
questions.rule: A structure is tokens plus relations; a single relation such as next gives sequences, and several relations give richer structures.

questions.q: With the single relation ____ one can build sequences of symbols.
questions.explain: A sequence is built from tokens each next to the following one.

questions.q: A seating plan records who sits next to whom around a table and also who sits across. What does it need beyond a single relation?
options: Nothing: next is enough
A second relation, such as across
A new symbol type for each guest's mood
A program
optionExplain: Next alone cannot say who is across.
Right: two kinds of connection call for two relations.
Moods are not part of the plan.
A program is not needed to record the layout.
questions.explain: Different kinds of connection between tokens call for different relations.
questions.rule: A structure is tokens plus relations; a single relation such as next gives sequences, and several relations give richer structures.

questions.q: True or false: A symbol structure can use several relations at once.
questions.explain: The authors say there may be several relations; written mathematical notation is their example.

questions.q: A student says: A symbol structure is a string of symbols in order and nothing more. What does the text say?
options: Strings are not symbol structures of any kind at all
Order is irrelevant to symbol structures in general
Structures may use several relations, not only next
Structures use only the relation prior in every case
optionExplain: A string with next is a structure.
Order is encoded by next.
Right: the string is the single-relation case.
Prior is the inverse of next, not the only relation.
questions.explain: The one-relation sequence is a special case of the general idea of relations connecting tokens.
questions.rule: A structure is tokens plus relations; a single relation such as next gives sequences, and several relations give richer structures.

questions.q: The chemical formula H2O puts the 2 below the line, next to H. What does recording it need, beyond the relation next?
options: No further relation
A relation called above
A new primitive symbol type for the number 2
A second relation, below
optionExplain: The 2 is lowered, so next alone would lose that.
The 2 sits below, not above.
The digit 2 is a symbol; the lowering is a relation.
Right: the authors say normal mathematical notation uses next plus above and below for exponents and subscripts.
questions.explain: In writing normal mathematical notation one uses not only next but also above and below, to represent exponentiation and subscripting.
questions.teaches: Normal mathematical notation uses next together with above and below, to represent exponentiation and subscripting.
questions.rule: A structure is tokens plus relations; a single relation such as next gives sequences, and several relations give richer structures.

questions.q: What gives a symbol its symbolic character, in the authors' view?
options: Its visual form, which must look distinct from others
Its ability to designate something that processes can reach
