Its being stored in memory for later use by processes
Its place in a natural language like English or Greek
optionExplain: Right: a symbol is symbolic by having a referent that processes can gain access to.
Form alone does not make a symbol; processes must be able to use it.
Storage is not the test.
Language is not required; the book treats natural language as one case.
questions.explain: Symbols are symbolic by designating. The card gives the details.
questions.rule: A symbol is symbolic because processes can use a token of it to reach its referent and read it, change it or build with it.

questions.q: What makes symbols symbolic is their ability to ____, that is, to have a referent.
questions.explain: Designation is the property that gives a symbol a referent.

questions.q: A process uses the token ORD-17 to reach a customer order. Which of these uses of access do the authors list?
options: Read it
Modify it
Build a new structure with it
Judge how pleasing it looks
Replace the token with a picture of the order
optionExplain: Right: reading is one use.
Right: modification is another.
Right: building a new structure with the object is a third.
Aesthetic judgment is not on the authors' list.
Swapping the token for a picture is not a use of the referent.
questions.explain: The authors give reading, modifying and building a new structure with the referent as examples of using access.
questions.rule: A symbol is symbolic because processes can use a token of it to reach its referent and read it, change it or build with it.

questions.q: True or false: A token that no information process could use to gain access to anything would still be symbolic in the authors' sense.
questions.explain: Symbolic character comes from the ability of processes to use a token to reach a referent.

questions.q: A student says: Only single symbols can designate; structures do not. What do the authors say?
options: Structures designate, but single symbols do not designate
Designation applies to symbol structures, not only to symbols
Neither designates; only processes can do the designating
Only programs are able to designate anything at all
optionExplain: Symbols designate too.
Right: the authors say designation applies to structures although it is easier to think of single symbols.
Designation is a relation of symbols and structures to objects.
Designation is not limited to programs.
questions.explain: The authors state that designation applies to symbol structures, not just symbols.
questions.rule: A symbol is symbolic because processes can use a token of it to reach its referent and read it, change it or build with it.

questions.q: A process is given the pair (owner, bike) and outputs the name Dana. What does the pair designate?
options: Only the bike, since the owner is not part of the pair
Nothing at all, since the pair has two separate parts
Dana, and indirectly the owner of the bike in question
Only the word owner, which is the first part of the pair
optionExplain: The pair gives access to a value about the bike, not just the bike.
The authors say structures designate.
Right: like the authors' (color, house) giving white, the pair designates the value and indirectly the thing described.
The attribute word is part of the pair, not what it designates.
questions.explain: In the authors' example the pair (color, house) yields the symbol white, so the pair designates white and, indirectly, the color of the house.
questions.teaches: A structure such as (color, house) designates the symbol white that a process produces from it and, indirectly, the color of the house in question.
questions.rule: A symbol is symbolic because processes can use a token of it to reach its referent and read it, change it or build with it.

questions.q: In discussions of language, which relation is usually taken as the model case of designation?
options: A verb and the subject that it is attached to
A proper name and the particular object it names
A sentence and the truth value that it can take
A word and the spelling that it is written with
optionExplain: Grammatical roles are not designation.
Right: names such as a particular president's name are the usual starting point.
Truth is one of the harder cases linguists extend to.
Spelling relates a word to its letters.
questions.explain: Proper names come first in linguistic discussion. The card gives the authors' contrast.
questions.rule: Linguists model designation on name to person; the authors model it on a symbol naming a symbol structure.

questions.q: In the authors' theory the prototypic designatory relationship is between a symbol and a symbol ____.
questions.explain: X2 naming the list (A, B, C) is the authors' model case.

questions.q: MUM stands for a stored list (name, number, address); fetching its first element gives the name. Which relation does this illustrate?
options: A proper name designating a particular man long ago
A word designating an abstract idea such as truth or justice
A program designating a process that the IPS can run
A symbol designating a structure and giving access to its parts
optionExplain: That is the linguists' model case, not the authors'.
The entry designates a stored list, not an abstract idea.
The entry designates data, not a process.
Right: this is the authors' X2 and (A, B, C) pattern.
questions.explain: MUM names a list in memory, so the entry designates a symbol structure and gives access to its first element.
questions.rule: Linguists model designation on name to person; the authors model it on a symbol naming a symbol structure.

questions.q: Match each case to the setting it belongs to.
pairs: Proper name to a named man
Symbol X2 to the list (A, B, C)
Harder cases linguists try to reach
questions.explain: Linguists begin with names and work toward abstract words; the authors begin with symbols naming structures.

questions.q: True or false: Given a token of X2, which designates (A, B, C), a process can obtain the first element of the list, A.
questions.explain: Designation gives access to the structure, including its parts.

questions.q: A logbook describes a storm so fully that later crews plan from the log alone. Which idea about symbol structures does this illustrate?
options: A symbol structure can act as a surrogate for what it describes
A name is the same thing as the object that it names
A structure can designate only other structures in memory
A log is a primitive symbol fixed by the environment
optionExplain: Right: the authors say structures can encode information about any conceivable thing and so act as its surrogate.
Names and objects are distinct in the authors' theory.
Structures can stand in for external things as well.
Primitive symbols have designation fixed by eip's or environment.
questions.explain: Because symbol structures can encode information about any conceivable thing, including an external object, they can serve as a surrogate for it.
questions.teaches: Symbol structures can encode information about any conceivable thing, including an external object, and so can act as surrogates for it.
questions.rule: Linguists model designation on name to person; the authors model it on a symbol naming a symbol structure.

questions.q: Do concepts like designation apply only to elementary information processes?
options: No, they apply to arbitrary information processes
Yes, they apply only to the elementary information processes
Only to the interpreter that controls the processor
Only to processes that take no inputs from memory
optionExplain: Right: they apply at all levels.
The authors say they apply to arbitrary information processes.
The interpreter is not singled out.
Inputs are not the issue.
questions.explain: The authors apply their concepts at all levels. The card gives the wording.
questions.rule: Notions such as designation hold at every level of processing, and processes that follow indirect designations can be composed.

questions.q: Many of the concepts apply to arbitrary information processes and not only to ____ information processes.
questions.explain: Designation, for example, applies to structures and to composed processes.

questions.q: A lookup made of simple steps (find the letter, find the page, scan the names) is composed. Can it follow a designation?
options: No, only elementary processes are able to follow designations
Yes, since processes that follow designations can be composed
No, because a lookup that has several steps cannot qualify
Yes, but only if the whole lookup is reduced to a single step
optionExplain: The authors say they need not be elementary.
Right: composition is allowed.
Several steps are fine in a composed process.
A single step is not required.
questions.explain: The authors say the processes that interpret indirect designations can be built up out of other processes.
questions.rule: Notions such as designation hold at every level of processing, and processes that follow indirect designations can be composed.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the processes that interpret indirect designations must be elementary processes.
questions.explain: They say these processes need not be elementary but can be composed.

questions.q: A reader infers that notions hold only for elementary processes since the authors do not say otherwise each time. What is wrong?
options: Nothing: silence in the text means the notion is limited
The authors in fact state the opposite in every section
The authors say they will not often repeat the qualification
The notion applies only to the interpreter of the processor
optionExplain: Silence is explained by the authors as a matter of style.
They do not state the opposite in every section; they say they will not always be explicit.
Right: the omission is announced, not a restriction.
No limitation to the interpreter is stated.
questions.explain: The authors say they will not often use the circumlocution needed to emphasize that a notion applies at all levels.
questions.rule: Notions such as designation hold at every level of processing, and processes that follow indirect designations can be composed.

questions.q: In a post office no single machine reads addresses; staff routines combined do the reading. Which authors' remark does this resemble?
options: Every designation needs one dedicated machine to carry it out
Designation does not involve information processes at all
Addresses are primitive symbols fixed by the environment
Elementary designatory processes may be very simple or even absent
optionExplain: The authors allow composed processes to do the work.
Designation always involves processes.
Primitive symbols are a separate topic.
Right: the authors say there will usually be elementary designatory processes, but they may be very simple and in the limit absent.
questions.explain: The authors say there will usually be some elementary designatory processes, but they may be very simple and in the limit can be absent altogether.
questions.teaches: There will usually be some elementary designatory processes, but they may be very simple and in the limit can be absent altogether.
questions.rule: Notions such as designation hold at every level of processing, and processes that follow indirect designations can be composed.

questions.q: Which symbols can an IPS treat as having a built-in, fixed meaning?
options: Symbols for external events and symbols for elementary processes
Symbols for every list that has been built up in memory
Symbols created afresh for each new record the IPS makes
Symbols for the spellings of other symbols in memory
optionExplain: Right: these are the two kinds the authors name.
Lists in memory are built from other symbols.
Newly created symbols get their meaning from what they are set to designate.
Spelling is not part of the authors' account.
questions.explain: Primitive symbols have fixed meaning from outside the structures. The card names two kinds.
questions.rule: Primitive symbols are those whose designation is fixed by elementary processes: symbols for external events or structures, and symbols for elementary processes.

questions.q: Primitive symbols designate either specific events or structures in the external environment, or ____ information processes.
questions.explain: The second kind designates elementary processes so they can be executed by means of the symbols.
questions.rule: Symbols for external things, symbols for eip's.

questions.q: A coffee machine is described as an IPS. Sort each item.

items.t: The signal evoked when a cup is placed under the spout
The symbol that runs the heating routine
The symbol that makes the pump start
A stored recipe list built from earlier symbols
A list of last week's orders

questions.explain: Symbols tied to external events or to elementary processes are primitive. Structures built from them, such as the recipe and the order list, are not.
questions.rule: Primitive: fixed by eip's or the environment.

questions.q: True or false: The collection of symbols that is primitive stays the same for every IPS, whatever the application.
questions.explain: The authors say it varies with the particular application.
questions.rule: The primitive set depends on the application.

questions.q: A student says: primitive means simple-looking. What is the authors' meaning?
options: A symbol that is written with only a single letter or digit
A symbol that cannot be stored in any memory of the IPS
A symbol with no designation of any kind or meaning
A symbol whose designation is fixed by the eip's or the environment
optionExplain: Length is not the test.
Primitive symbols can be stored.
They do designate, but their designation is fixed.
Right: primitiveness is about where the designation is fixed.
questions.explain: The definition ties primitiveness to where designation is fixed, not to appearance.
questions.rule: Primitive symbols are those whose designation is fixed by elementary processes: symbols for external events or structures, and symbols for elementary processes.

questions.q: A theory of music recognition takes pitches and durations as its smallest symbols. Which point from the text does this fit best?
options: All theories must use letters as the primitive symbols
The set of primitive symbols depends on the application
Primitive symbols must be physical objects in the world
Primitive symbols are the same in vision and in speech
optionExplain: Letters are chosen for this book, not for every theory.
Right: the authors say vision theories often use a two-dimensional array of zeros and ones and a speech theory might use phoneme features.
Primitives are symbols, not physical things.
The text says choices vary.
questions.explain: For visual pattern recognition the sensory input is usually described as a two-dimensional array of zeros and ones; for speech a theory might take as primitives the features into which phonemes are assumed to be analyzed.
questions.teaches: Visual theories usually take a two-dimensional array of zeros and ones (more generally intensities) as primitive input, and a speech theory might take phoneme features.
questions.rule: Primitive symbols are those whose designation is fixed by elementary processes: symbols for external events or structures, and symbols for elementary processes.

questions.q: Why might a theory of problem solving treat every printed c as the same symbol?
options: Because all printed c's are physically identical in shape
It assumes the subject does not discriminate between such tokens
Because the eye is known to recognize letters perfectly
Because problem solving never involves letters at all
optionExplain: Printed c's differ physically; the point is about the subject's discriminations.
Right: the authors state this as an assumption about the subject.
The authors do not claim recognition is perfect; they set it aside.
Letters are used in the book's tasks.
questions.explain: The treatment of all c's as one type rests on an assumption about the subject. The card states it.
questions.rule: The book takes letters and similar marks as primitive, assuming the subject treats all tokens of a letter alike under the experiment's conditions.

questions.q: The authors take letters, digits and punctuation marks as ____ symbols designating external stimuli.
questions.explain: This divorces the theory from detailed concern with sensory mechanisms.
questions.rule: Letters are primitive in this book.

questions.q: A study of word puzzles treats every printed A as one symbol. What does this assume about the solver?
options: That the solver is not able to read the letters at all
That all printings of A are physically identical in shape
That the solver does not discriminate between printings of A
That the solver has no memory for the shapes of letters
optionExplain: Reading ability is not at issue.
Physical sameness is not claimed.
Right: all tokens of A are treated as one type, which assumes no discrimination among them.
Memory is unrelated.
questions.explain: Treating all tokens of a letter as one type is the same as assuming the subject does not discriminate among them.
questions.rule: The book takes letters and similar marks as primitive, assuming the subject treats all tokens of a letter alike under the experiment's conditions.

questions.q: True or false: If the primitive-letter assumption is wrong in an application, the authors expect the theory to fail to account for the observed behavior.
questions.explain: They say the error will be revealed by the inability of the theory to account for the observed behavior.
questions.rule: Wrong assumptions show up as unexplained behavior.

questions.q: A critic says: The authors prove from first principles that all c's belong to one type. What is wrong with this?
options: It is an assumption to be settled empirically
They prove it by the structure of the alphabet
They prove it by computer simulation
They do not make this assumption at all
optionExplain: Right: the authors say suitability depends on the experimental setting and can be settled only empirically.
The alphabet's structure does not decide it.
Simulation is not their argument here.
They do make the assumption.
questions.explain: The authors treat it as an assumption whose suitability is settled in the last instance only empirically.
questions.rule: The book takes letters and similar marks as primitive, assuming the subject treats all tokens of a letter alike under the experiment's conditions.

questions.q: Participants hunt for faint smudges on printed text. How does this bear on treating every printed letter as one type?
options: It shows that all printed letters are physically identical
It proves that the primitive-symbol assumption is correct
It has no bearing, since type is fixed by the alphabet itself
Under a proofreader's set, subjects may tell clear c's from broken ones
optionExplain: The smudges show the opposite of physical identity.
It shows when the assumption may fail, not that it is proved.
The authors tie type to the subject's discriminations.
Right: the authors say inducing a proofreader's set can make a subject discriminate a clear c from a broken one.
questions.explain: By inducing the psychological set of a proofreader a subject can be made to discriminate between a clearly printed c and a broken one, so not all tokens of c belong to one type.
questions.teaches: Inducing the psychological set of a proofreader can make a subject discriminate a clearly printed c from a broken one, so then not all tokens of c are of one type.
questions.rule: The book takes letters and similar marks as primitive, assuming the subject treats all tokens of a letter alike under the experiment's conditions.

questions.q: If letters are primitive symbols, can a theory say that s resembles z more closely than it resembles t?
options: No, primitive symbols are only the same type or different types
Yes, by comparing the shapes of the letters directly
Yes, since the alphabet is ordered in a fixed sequence
Only if the letters are written as capital letters
optionExplain: Right: there is no degree of difference among primitives.
Shapes are not available if letters are primitive.
Order is primitively defined and says nothing about similarity.
Case is irrelevant.
questions.explain: Primitives have no internal parts to compare. The card explains how to get similarity.
questions.rule: Primitive letters are the same or different, never more or less alike; similarity needs descriptions built from simpler features.

questions.q: Primitive symbols can only be tokens of the same type or tokens of ____ types.
questions.explain: There is no degree of difference among primitive symbols.
questions.rule: Same or different, nothing in between.

questions.q: A system stores each color name as a primitive tag: RED, ORANGE, BLUE. Can it say orange is closer to red than to blue?
options: Yes, because RED comes earlier than BLUE in the list of tags
Yes, because tags have degrees of similarity built in
Not as primitives; it would need descriptions by simpler features
No, and giving the tags descriptions could not help either
optionExplain: List order is not similarity.
Primitive tags have no degrees of similarity.
Right: similarity needs organization of simpler characteristics.
Descriptions are the authors' remedy.
questions.explain: As primitive tags the colors are only same or different; to compare them, describe each by simpler features.
questions.rule: Primitive letters are the same or different, never more or less alike; similarity needs descriptions built from simpler features.

questions.q: The authors want to make predictions that depend on how alike two letters are. What should they change?
options: Add many more primitive letters to the available stock
Describe each letter by simpler characteristics, not as a primitive
Order the alphabet in a different sequence than usual
Treat every letter as a program that the system runs
optionExplain: More primitives would still have no degree of difference.
Right: descriptions give a basis for degrees of similarity.
Ordering is primitively defined and does not capture likeness.
Letters are not programs.
questions.explain: Similarity needs structure: describing letters by features such as loops and intersections.
questions.rule: Primitive letters are the same or different, never more or less alike; similarity needs descriptions built from simpler features.

questions.q: True or false: Because the alphabet has a fixed order, the authors say we can speak of degrees of difference among primitive letters.
questions.explain: They say the ordering is primitively defined and does not give degrees of difference.

questions.q: An analysis describes letters by loops and crossings and predicts which get confused. Which theory in the text works this way?
options: The Logic Theorist problem solver
The thermostat program for the furnace
The Morse IPS for sending and receiving
The EPAM theory of verbal learning
optionExplain: The Logic Theorist is introduced later as a problem solver.
The thermostat has nothing to do with letters.
The Morse IPS takes letters as designated external objects.
Right: EPAM describes letters this way and so predicts effects of similarity.
questions.explain: The authors say EPAM represents letters by descriptions, such as whether they contain a closed loop or intersection of lines, and so permits predictions about similarity among letters; in their example t has an intersection while s and z have a single zigzag curve.
questions.teaches: The EPAM theory of verbal learning represents each letter by a description of simple features, so it can predict behavioral effects of similarity among letters.
questions.rule: Primitive letters are the same or different, never more or less alike; similarity needs descriptions built from simpler features.

questions.q: How could a program store that a certain chessman is a white knight on a given square?
options: By drawing a picture of the board in the program's memory
By storing the whole record of the game so far played
By giving each square on the board its own piece type
By attaching type, color and position pairs to the man's symbol
optionExplain: A picture is not an attribute-value scheme.
The record is about moves, not the single piece.
Squares are not piece types.
Right: attribute-value pairs describe the man.
questions.explain: A symbol can carry a description. The card shows the authors' scheme.
questions.rule: A described symbol carries attribute-value pairs; a chessman has type, color and position.

questions.q: A description is a set of ____-value pairs associated with a symbol.
questions.explain: Each pair gives an attribute and its value for that symbol.

questions.q: A library book symbol has the pairs title, author and shelf. In shelf: B12, which is the attribute and which the value?
options: Shelf is the attribute and B12 is the value
B12 is the attribute and shelf is the value
Both are values
Both are attributes
optionExplain: Right: the attribute is followed by its value.
That reverses the roles.
The pair names an attribute and its value.
B12 is the value, not an attribute.
questions.explain: In an attribute-value pair the attribute comes first and the value follows it.
questions.rule: A described symbol carries attribute-value pairs; a chessman has type, color and position.

questions.q: Sort each item from a chessman's description: attribute or value?

items.t: Type
Black
Position
Knight
Color
White

questions.explain: Type, color and position are the attributes; Black, Knight and White are values of them.
questions.rule: Attribute names the slot; value fills it.

questions.q: True or false: The attribute position of a chessman has as its value the name of a square.
questions.explain: The text says the attributes of a chessman include his position, the name of the square he stands on.
questions.rule: Position's value is a square name.

questions.q: A seating chart links each seat to its occupant, if any, and its neighboring seats in each direction. Which chess structure is this like?
options: A single chessman's description with its attribute pairs
A position, linking each square to its occupant and neighbors
The list of piece types that the program knows about
A program that the interpreter executes on the board
optionExplain: A single man's description does not cover the board.
Right: the authors define a position this way, and squares are themselves described symbols.
Piece types are just one attribute's values.
A position is data, not a program.
questions.explain: The authors say squares are also described symbols, and a position associates with each square the man on it, if any, and the names of adjacent squares in various directions.
questions.teaches: A chess position is a symbol structure associating each square with the man on it, if any, and with the names of the adjacent squares in various directions.
questions.rule: A described symbol carries attribute-value pairs; a chessman has type, color and position.

questions.q: How can the grouping of a logic expression with brackets be stored without storing the brackets?
options: By keeping only the letters, in alphabetical order, in a list
By storing a small picture of where the brackets were
By building lists inside lists so the grouping is in the structure
By storing the number of brackets used in the expression
optionExplain: Alphabetical order loses the structure.
A picture is not a symbol structure.
Right: nesting carries the grouping.
A count does not say what groups with what.
questions.explain: The grouping can live in the organization of lists. The card shows how.
questions.rule: A bracketed expression can be a flat list of tokens or a nested list whose positions encode connective, left part and right part.

questions.q: In the nested list, the first position holds the connective, the second the left part and the third the ____ part.
questions.explain: The authors' list uses first, second and third positions for connective, left and right.

questions.q: Using the nested-list scheme, how is (S or T) and U written, with A naming the list for S or T?
options: (A, and, U), where A designates (S, or, T)
(and, A, U), where A designates (or, S, T)
(and, U, A), where A designates (or, S, T)
(or, S, T, and, U)
optionExplain: That puts the connective in the middle.
Right: connective first, then left, then right.
That swaps left and right.
That flattens the structure and loses the grouping.
questions.explain: The scheme puts the connective first, then the left part A, then the right part U.
questions.rule: A bracketed expression can be a flat list of tokens or a nested list whose positions encode connective, left part and right part.

questions.q: True or false: In the flat list representation the brackets are themselves tokens in the list.
questions.explain: The authors say the parentheses are symbol tokens in the list.
questions.rule: The flat list keeps the brackets.

questions.q: True or false: In the nested list, an item's position tells whether it is the connective, the left part or the right part.
questions.explain: The nested list uses first, second and third positions for connective, left part and right part, while the flat list carries the grouping in its bracket tokens.
questions.rule: Position carries the roles in the nested list.

questions.q: To store flour and (eggs or milk) without tying left and right to list positions, what would let it be a tree?
options: Using the single relation above for both of the parts
Writing it out as one long English sentence of words
Using only the relation next between all the items
Separate relations called left and right for the two parts
optionExplain: Above alone does not distinguish left from right.
A sentence is a string, not a tree.
Next alone puts everything in a line.
Right: with relations left and right the expression can be a tree structure.
questions.explain: The authors say that with relations left and right, read as left and right sub-expression, the same logic expression could be represented as a tree structure.
questions.teaches: With relations left and right the same logic expression can be represented as a tree structure.
questions.rule: A bracketed expression can be a flat list of tokens or a nested list whose positions encode connective, left part and right part.

questions.q: Can a logic expression be stored as nothing but labelled pairs of names, with no list or tree?
options: Yes, attribute-value namings can carry structure and content
No, a list is needed to hold the structure somewhere
No, only a tree can show the grouping of the parts
Yes, but only for single symbols and not whole expressions
optionExplain: Right: this is the authors' association representation.
The authors show it can be done.
Trees are one option, not the only one.
The scheme covers whole expressions.
questions.explain: Namings alone can encode a structure. The card shows how.
questions.rule: Attribute-value associations can carry an expression's structure and content with no list or tree.

questions.q: In the association scheme, left(x1) = x2 means that the left part of node x1 is node ____.
questions.explain: The attribute left of x1 has the value x2.

questions.q: Node x3 is Q implies R, with right(x3) = x7 and term(x7) = R. What is the right-hand side of the implication?
options: Q
P
x6
R
optionExplain: Q is the left side, reached through left(x3) = x6 and term(x6) = Q.
P belongs to the other node.
x6 is the left node, not the right side.
Right: following right and then term gives R.
questions.explain: Follow the right link from x3 to x7 and then read its term, which is R.
questions.rule: Attribute-value associations can carry an expression's structure and content with no list or tree.

questions.q: Given connective(x2) = or, left(x2) = x4 with term(x4) = P, and right(x2) = x5 with term(x5) = Q, what expression is node x2?
options: Q or P
P and Q
P or Q
Q implies P
optionExplain: The left side is P, not Q.
The connective is or, not and.
Right: the connective is or, with left P and right Q.
Implication is node x3's connective.
questions.explain: Read the node's connective, its left term and its right term.
questions.rule: Attribute-value associations can carry an expression's structure and content with no list or tree.

questions.q: True or false: The attribute-value version is a list in disguise, using list positions to encode the structure.
questions.explain: The authors say it involves no symbol structure at all, only a pattern of namings.

questions.q: A display reads plus 3 times 4 5, each operator fixing how many operands follow it. Which notation is this?
options: Polish prefix notation
Attribute-value association
A tree with left and right relations
The flat bracketed list
optionExplain: Right: the authors' Polish prefix notation uses each connective to specify the exact number of operands that follow.
There are no attributes here.
No relations left or right are used.
There are no brackets.
questions.explain: The authors give Polish prefix notation as a further scheme: each connective specifies the exact number of operands that should follow it to its right.
questions.teaches: In Polish prefix notation each connective specifies the exact number of operands that follow it to its right.
questions.rule: Attribute-value associations can carry an expression's structure and content with no list or tree.

questions.q: Two systems store one logic expression, as a nested list and as a tree. Can their answers alone tell which is which?
options: Not always, since similar representations can give equal outputs
Yes, the tree gives faster answers than the list does
Yes, the list gives longer answers than the tree does
No, because they store two different logic expressions
optionExplain: Right: the authors say output may not reveal the representation.
Speed is not what the authors claim.
Length is not a guaranteed difference.
They store the same expression.
questions.explain: Outputs may not reveal the representation. The card gives the authors' comment.
questions.rule: Many representations can carry the same information; what matters is a scheme of associations and processes that can read the connections.

questions.q: All that is needed for a representation is some scheme of ____, together with processes that can extract the connections.
questions.explain: The authors say a scheme of associations plus processes to extract the connections is enough.

questions.q: Two apps store the same phone list, one alphabetically and one as a tree, and users see identical search results. What would the authors say?
options: The two apps must be using the same internal representation
One of the two apps must be giving out wrong answers
Output alone may not reveal the internal representation in use
Representation matters nothing at all to behavior in any case
optionExplain: Identical output does not force identical representation.
Neither app need be wrong.
Right: closely isomorphic representations can behave identically.
The authors add that sometimes the choice has striking consequences.
questions.explain: The authors say it is not always possible to tell from output which representation an IPS uses, especially when representations are isomorphic.
questions.rule: Many representations can carry the same information; what matters is a scheme of associations and processes that can read the connections.

questions.q: Match each representation to how it encodes structure.
pairs: Positions in the list encode connective, left, right
Separate primitive relations for left and right
A pattern of namings with no symbol structure
questions.explain: Each scheme encodes the same distinctions in a different way.

questions.q: True or false: If two representations are closely isomorphic, observing the system's output will reveal which one it uses.
questions.explain: The authors say it is not always possible to tell from output.
questions.rule: Isomorphic representations can look alike from outside.

questions.q: Two people solve one sliding-tile puzzle with different representations (a grid, a list of moves) and behave differently. What do the authors say?
options: Representation cannot change behavior in any observable way
In problems, the choice of representation can show up in behavior
Representation matters only for logic expressions, not problems
Only isomorphic representations can affect behavior at all
optionExplain: The authors say the choice sometimes matters.
Right: the authors say that especially in representing problems the choice may have striking consequences for external behavior.
They apply the remark to problems in general.
Isomorphic ones may not differ in behavior.
questions.explain: The authors say that in other cases, especially in representing problems, the choice of representation may have striking observable consequences for external behavior.
questions.teaches: In representing problems, the choice of representation may have striking observable consequences for external behavior.
questions.rule: Many representations can carry the same information; what matters is a scheme of associations and processes that can read the connections.

questions.q: Which two kinds of structure do the authors call the core of their representational capability?
options: Lists and attribute-value associations
Trees and graphs, with nothing besides
Tables and charts of numbers and names
Sentences and paragraphs of plain text
optionExplain: Right: these are the two core structures.
Trees and graphs are special-purpose uses built from these.
Tables and charts are not the authors' terms.
Natural-language units are not their basis.
questions.explain: The authors name two core structures. The card gives them.
questions.rule: The book's core symbol structures are lists, built with next, and attribute-value associations.

questions.q: In an attribute-value association, each attribute designates a ____ value.
questions.explain: The attribute designates a unique value in each association.

questions.q: Sort each item: list structure or attribute-value association?

items.t: A queue of customers in order
A person's record: eyes brown, height tall
A book's details: title, year
The steps of a recipe in order
Chapters, each a list of sections

questions.explain: Ordered sequences, including lists of lists, are list structures; records of named properties are associations.
questions.rule: Ordered things: lists; named properties: associations.

questions.q: True or false: A list may contain a symbol that names another list, so lists can be built up into hierarchies.
questions.explain: Because symbols can designate lists, hierarchical structures of lists may be built.

questions.q: A student says: an attribute may designate several different values in a single association. Is that right?
options: Yes, it may designate any number of different values
No, in each association an attribute has a unique value
Yes, but only when all of the values are numbers
No, because attributes themselves are not symbols at all
optionExplain: The authors state uniqueness.
Right: the authors say the attribute designates a unique value.
Numbers are not singled out.
Both attribute and value are symbols.
questions.explain: Each attribute designates a unique value in an association.
questions.rule: The book's core symbol structures are lists, built with next, and attribute-value associations.

questions.q: A designer limits a notes app to plain text lines and packs contact details in with special codes. Which risk do the authors name?
options: The memory of the IPS will fill up with the special codes it uses
Lists will no longer be able to name other lists in memory at all
Too limited a repertoire turns encoding into an exercise in virtuosity
The same attributes will be duplicated across many separate records
optionExplain: Memory is not the issue they raise.
Lists can name lists.
Right: the authors warn against a repertoire of structures that is too limited.
Duplication is not their point.
questions.explain: The authors say that if too limited a repertoire of structures and designations is provided, encoding complex information becomes an exercise in virtuosity that yields little benefit of any other kind.
questions.teaches: If the repertoire of structures and designations is too limited, encoding complex information becomes an exercise in virtuosity that yields little benefit of any other kind.
questions.rule: The book's core symbol structures are lists, built with next, and attribute-value associations.

questions.q: Why would solve-problem make a poor elementary process in a theory of problem solving?
options: It takes far too long to run on any known machine
It would assume the very thing the theory is meant to explain
It has too many inputs for a single elementary step
It is not a standard word in the English language
optionExplain: Speed is not the authors' reason.
Right: a system with such a primitive would not show how problem solving is accomplished.
Inputs are not the issue.
Wording is not the issue.
questions.explain: Elementary processes must explain, not hide. The card states two requirements.
questions.rule: Elementary processes must be well defined and realizable, and together powerful enough to compose all the system's behavior.

questions.q: Elementary means that these processes are not further analyzed in the theory into still simpler ____.
questions.explain: The theory does not break eip's down.

questions.q: A model of how people bake bread includes one basic step called make-good-bread. What do the authors' criteria say?
options: It is fine, since baking is such a common human skill
It is fine, since it is general enough to cover baking
It is poor only because it would take too long to run
It is poor: it is not well defined and hides how baking is done
optionExplain: Familiarity does not make a step well defined.
Generality is not enough; it also must be realizable.
Duration is not a criterion.
Right: like solve-problem, it hides the process to be explained.
questions.explain: An elementary step must be well defined and realizable; make-good-bread would hide what the theory should explain.
questions.rule: Elementary processes must be well defined and realizable, and together powerful enough to compose all the system's behavior.

questions.q: Which pair of requirements do the authors place on elementary processes?
options: Powerful enough to compose behavior, and well defined and realizable
Fast enough to run in real time, and cheap enough to build
Unique in form, and unchanging from one theory to another
Small in number, and named in ordinary English words
optionExplain: Right: the authors name these two requirements.
Speed and cost are not mentioned.
They say the choice depends on the application.
Count and naming are not criteria.
questions.explain: The requirements are sufficiency for composing behavior and well-definedness.
questions.rule: Elementary processes must be well defined and realizable, and together powerful enough to compose all the system's behavior.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, an elementary process can be anything the theorist finds convenient, provided it is named.
questions.explain: It must be well defined and realizable by known mechanisms; otherwise there is no point in taking it as primitive.

questions.q: One theorist debates which symbols stand for outside objects, another which basic operations the system has. Whose choice changes the mechanics of processing?
options: The first, since the symbols decide the mechanics of processing
Both equally, since both choices fix the processing mechanics
The second, since mechanics follow from the operations, not primitives
Neither, since the mechanics are fixed by the environment alone
optionExplain: The authors say the nature of the symbols as internal entities stays the same whatever they designate.
They treat the two choices differently.
Right: the authors contrast the two choices.
Elementary processes do shape the mechanics.
questions.explain: The authors say that for primitive symbols the mechanics of processing are determined by the processor and not by what the symbols designate, whereas the elementary processes must be general and well defined.
questions.teaches: Choices about primitive symbols concern how the external world is symbolized and leave the mechanics of processing unchanged, whereas the choice of elementary processes does matter for what the system can do.
questions.rule: Elementary processes must be well defined and realizable, and together powerful enough to compose all the system's behavior.

questions.q: How large a set of basic operations is needed for general information processing?
options: One operation for every task
An unlimited set
A single set that every machine must share
A relatively small set
optionExplain: Task-by-task operations would be unlimited.
They say the set is small.
They say there is no unique basis.
Right: the authors say a relatively small set suffices.
questions.explain: Generality comes from a small set. The card explains.
questions.rule: A small set of elementary processes is enough for general information processing, but many different sets will do.

questions.q: The authors say a relatively ____ set of elementary processes suffices for the full generality of information processing.
questions.explain: They add that there is no unique basis, so many sets will do.

questions.q: Two calculators use different primitive operations yet can compute the same range of results. Which of the authors' points does this match?
options: Only one single set of operations can be adequate
There are many adequate sets of elementary processes
Sufficient sets of operations must be very large ones
Elementary processes are not ever combined together
optionExplain: The authors deny uniqueness.
Right: many bases exist.
They say a small set suffices.
Composition is how larger processes arise.
questions.explain: Different sets can be adequate when combined with corresponding schemes of composition.
questions.rule: A small set of elementary processes is enough for general information processing, but many different sets will do.

questions.q: True or false: Different adequate sets of elementary processes all incorporate certain fundamental types of operations.
questions.explain: The authors say all of the ways incorporate certain fundamental types, though not in a single form.

questions.q: A student says: since machines differ in primitives, the number of primitives needed must grow with the variety of tasks. What do the authors say?
options: A relatively small set suffices for all information processing
The number of primitives must grow with the variety of tasks
Only a single primitive is needed for every information process
The set of primitives must be chosen afresh task by task
optionExplain: Right: generality comes from a small set.
They say the opposite.
They do not say one primitive suffices.
They say the choice is not entirely task dependent.
questions.explain: The authors reject the thought that the set varies without limit with the task.
questions.rule: A small set of elementary processes is enough for general information processing, but many different sets will do.

questions.q: A kitchen produces hundreds of dishes from a few techniques. Which of the authors' remarks is closest?
options: Every dish must be given a primitive operation of its own
Techniques are unique to each kitchen and cannot be shared
A small set of elementary processes underlies the computer's flexibility
Cooks need an unlimited stock of techniques to cover dishes
optionExplain: That would defeat the point of a small set.
There is no unique basis, but many sets do.
Right: the authors say general flexibility rests on this foundation stone.
The sufficient set is small.
questions.explain: The authors say the general-purpose flexibility of the digital computer rests firmly on the fact that a small set suffices.
questions.teaches: The general-purpose flexibility of the digital computer rests firmly on the fact that a relatively small set of elementary processes suffices.
questions.rule: A small set of elementary processes is enough for general information processing, but many different sets will do.

questions.q: Which basic ability lets an IPS act differently depending on what is in STM?
options: Discrimination
Symbol creation
Storing
Writing externally
optionExplain: Right: discrimination is behaving in alternative ways depending on STM.
Creation makes new symbols.
Storing keeps structures.
Writing externally produces responses.
questions.explain: Branching on contents is discrimination. The card gives the full description.
questions.rule: Discrimination lets behavior depend on STM contents; tests and comparisons decide whether two tokens are of one type.

questions.q: A test or comparison determines whether two symbol tokens do or do not belong to the same symbol ____.
questions.explain: Comparison tests sameness of type.

questions.q: A vending machine checks whether an inserted coin matches the symbol for a valid coin, then dispenses or rejects. Which processes are involved?
options: Symbol creation of new symbols for each coin
Storing a structure of the coin for later use
Writing out a new symbol structure for the coin
A comparison coupled with conditional behavior
optionExplain: Creation is not the main step.
Storing is not.
Writing is not.
Right: comparing and then branching.
questions.explain: The machine compares and then acts differently depending on the result.
questions.rule: Discrimination lets behavior depend on STM contents; tests and comparisons decide whether two tokens are of one type.

questions.q: Match each ability to its description.
pairs: Behave differently depending on what is in STM
Decide whether two tokens are of the same type
Pass control to an independent program
questions.explain: These are the first two types, with transfer of control as part of discrimination.

questions.q: True or false: A comparison must lead directly to a branch in behavior.
questions.explain: It may instead produce a conventional symbol such as true or false that is discriminated later.
questions.rule: Comparison can leave its result as a symbol.

questions.q: A spreadsheet cell shows TRUE after comparing two entries, and a later formula branches on that cell. Which of the authors' points does this illustrate?
options: Comparisons always branch the behavior at once on the result
A comparison may yield a symbol like true or false for later use
Comparison is not possible between two symbol tokens
Symbols cannot be tested for their type by any process
optionExplain: The authors say often, not always.
Right: comparison results can be kept as symbols for later discrimination.
Comparisons are a basic type of process.
Symbols are tested by comparison.
questions.explain: The authors say comparisons are often coupled with conditional behavior but may equally lead to a conventional symbol, such as true or false, that can later be discriminated.
questions.teaches: A comparison may lead to the production of a conventional symbol, such as true or false, that can be discriminated later.
questions.rule: Discrimination lets behavior depend on STM contents; tests and comparisons decide whether two tokens are of one type.

questions.q: What does a newly created symbol mean in an IPS?
options: Whatever meaning its shape might happen to suggest
It has no meaning at all, not even a designation
Only that it designates the structure it was set to designate
It means the time at which the symbol was created
optionExplain: Shape is not meaning here.
It does have a designation.
Right: a created symbol carries no meaning beyond its designation.
Time is not stated.
questions.explain: A new symbol gets its meaning from what it is set to designate. The card says so.
questions.rule: Symbols can be created arbitrarily and set to designate structures; structures can be created, copied and modified.

questions.q: A newly created symbol carries no meaning other than that it ____ the desired symbol structure.
questions.explain: Creation sets the symbol to designate a specified structure.

questions.q: A to-do app issues ticket T-481 for a new job description and links it to that description. In the authors' terms, what is this?
options: Discrimination: branching on what is found in STM
Symbol creation: a new symbol set to designate a structure
A primitive symbol for an event in the external environment
Reading a stimulus from the environment through a receptor
optionExplain: Discrimination is branching.
Right: a new symbol was created and set to designate.
The ticket is not tied to an external event.
Reading brings in a stimulus.
questions.explain: The ticket is a new symbol set to designate a structure.
questions.rule: Symbols can be created arbitrarily and set to designate structures; structures can be created, copied and modified.

questions.q: True or false: Writing eip's must permit building up arbitrary structures.
questions.explain: The authors say many variations are possible as long as they permit building arbitrary structures.

questions.q: A student says: a writing capability must include exactly create, copy and delete, no more and no fewer. What do the authors say?
options: Variations are fine if they permit building arbitrary structures
The student is right, since exactly these three are required
Writing must be limited to appending new tokens to a structure
Writing should not include copying an existing structure
optionExplain: Right: the authors allow variations.
The authors permit variation.
Appending is one allowed operation, not the only one.
Copying is listed.
questions.explain: The test is the ability to build arbitrary structures, not a particular list.
questions.rule: Symbols can be created arbitrarily and set to designate structures; structures can be created, copied and modified.

questions.q: An archive has unlimited storage. Does it need a process to destroy symbols?
options: Yes, every archive has to destroy symbols to stay usable
No, because symbols cannot be destroyed in an IPS at all
Yes, in order to keep the stored symbols meaningful
It depends on whether memory capacity is limited
optionExplain: The authors do not make it universal.
They do not say symbols cannot be destroyed.
Meaning is not the reason.
Right: the authors say whether destroy is needed depends primarily on whether memory is limited.
questions.explain: The authors say whether the system must also be able to destroy symbols depends primarily on whether memory capacity is limited.
questions.teaches: Whether the system must be able to destroy symbols depends primarily on whether memory capacity is limited.
questions.rule: Symbols can be created arbitrarily and set to designate structures; structures can be created, copied and modified.

questions.q: Which requirement of an IPS says that no part of a structure may be in principle inaccessible?
options: Designating parts of symbol structures
Symbol creation of new designations
Discrimination between alternatives
Reading and writing externally
optionExplain: Right: it must always be possible to designate parts and reach others.
Creation makes new symbols.
Discrimination branches.
Reading brings in stimuli.
questions.explain: Access to every part is a requirement of the designating operation. The card lists all three.
questions.rule: An IPS must be able to read and write externally, reach every part of a structure, and store and retrieve structures by designation.

questions.q: Storing means remembering a structure for later use and retrieving it at any time via a symbol structure that ____ it.
questions.explain: Retrieval goes through a designating structure.

questions.q: Match each everyday act to the kind of operation.
pairs: Turning a seen traffic sign into an internal structure
Finding the third item of a stored list
Filing a note to fetch it next week by its title
questions.explain: Bringing in a stimulus is reading, reaching a part is designating, and filing for later is storing.

questions.q: True or false: In a system with very limited memory, the complexity of the totality of stored structures is unaffected.
questions.explain: The authors say how much memory is available conditions strongly how complex the stored structures may be.

questions.q: A student says: some parts of a structure can be sealed off from designation as long as the rest works. What do the authors require?
options: Only the first part of a structure must be reachable
Only parts that have been stored must be reachable
Accessible parts may be chosen at random each time
No part of a structure may be in principle inaccessible
optionExplain: The requirement covers all parts.
Storage is not the criterion.
Random access is not the point.
Right: every part must be reachable in principle.
questions.explain: The requirement is that there must not be any parts of symbol structures that are in principle inaccessible.
questions.rule: An IPS must be able to read and write externally, reach every part of a structure, and store and retrieve structures by designation.

questions.q: A notebook randomly loses pages overnight. Which of the authors' requirements does it fail?
options: Symbol creation: new symbols must be creatable at will
Storing: the memory must be highly reliable over time
Discrimination: behavior must alter on STM contents
Reading externally: stimuli must be designated inside
optionExplain: Creation is not the problem.
Right: the authors say the memory must be highly reliable over time.
Discrimination is not the problem.
Reading a page is not the problem.
questions.explain: The authors say the memory must be highly reliable over time.
questions.teaches: The memory must be highly reliable over time.
questions.rule: An IPS must be able to read and write externally, reach every part of a structure, and store and retrieve structures by designation.

questions.q: What may the interpreter of an IPS consult to decide what to do next?
options: Only the information stored in STM
Any structure in long-term memory at once
Only the external environment
Only the last eip executed
optionExplain: Right: the authors' final assumption restricts it to STM.
The interpreter does not see all of memory at once.
The environment influences behavior only through what reaches STM.
Last step alone is not the whole STM.
questions.explain: The interpreter bases sequential behavior solely on STM. The card gives the full assumption.
questions.rule: The interpreter chooses what to do next from STM contents alone, and since STM keeps changing this limits nothing in the long run.

questions.q: The interpreter bases its determination of sequential behavior solely on information stored in the ____.
questions.explain: STM holds the input and output structures of the eip's.

questions.q: A cook picks each move only from the pan; an order slip on the wall is out of view. What does this resemble?
options: The slip controls the cook directly even from the wall
The slip cannot affect the next step until it gets into STM
The cook's behavior cannot change from one step to the next
The slip has already been stored in the cook's long-term memory
optionExplain: Out of view means no immediate effect.
Right: only STM contents control the next step.
Behavior changes when STM contents change.
The scenario does not say it is stored.
questions.explain: Our reading: on the authors' assumption, what is not in STM has no immediate effect on the next step.
questions.rule: The interpreter chooses what to do next from STM contents alone, and since STM keeps changing this limits nothing in the long run.

questions.q: True or false: Because STM contents change with almost every eip executed, the STM-only assumption imposes no essential limitation on behavior in the long run.
questions.explain: The authors say it localizes the immediate stimulus in the short run but does not limit behavior in the long run.

questions.q: A student says: if the interpreter looks only at STM, an IPS cannot carry out a long task. What do the authors say?
options: The student is right, since STM holds so little at once
STM is permanent, so long tasks are easy to carry out
The assumption applies only to short tasks, not long ones
STM changes with almost every eip, so there is no long-run limit
optionExplain: The authors explicitly deny a long-run limit.
STM changes rapidly, not permanently.
The assumption applies to all tasks.
Right: the authors rule this inference out.
questions.explain: The STM-only rule limits only the immediate stimulus for behavior.
questions.rule: The interpreter chooses what to do next from STM contents alone, and since STM keeps changing this limits nothing in the long run.

questions.q: An engineer flowcharts a copier's behavior, and a colleague asks whether the copier holds that flowchart internally. Which of the authors' two problems is this?
options: The first: hypothesizing rules that describe observed behavior
Neither: the question is really about receptors and effectors
The second: whether the IPS runs a program stored in its memory
The first: whether the STM is large enough for the task
optionExplain: The flowchart is the answer to the first problem.
The question concerns the program, not receptors.
Right: the first problem is the observer's description; the second asks whether the program is stored in the system.
STM size is not the issue.
questions.explain: The authors say the second problem is to what extent the IPS runs according to a program stored in its memory; the interpreter need contain only enough mechanism to interpret a stored program, not the whole specification.
questions.teaches: The interpreter need not contain the whole of the process specification, only enough mechanism to interpret a program stored in memory.
questions.rule: The interpreter chooses what to do next from STM contents alone, and since STM keeps changing this limits nothing in the long run.

questions.q: A thermostat program keeps checking temperature and switching a furnace forever. Which structural feature does it need?
options: A loop
A random choice
A deleted memory
A new symbol per check
optionExplain: Right: repetition is a loop.
Randomness is not needed.
Deleting memory is not repetition.
New symbols are not what repeats the checks.
questions.explain: Endless checking is a loop. The card explains how loops end.
questions.rule: A program is a structure of processes with numbered steps, branching on tests, and loops that need a conditional exit.

questions.q: Every loop must contain at least one conditional ____ so that the loop can finally be left.
questions.explain: A conditional branch lets the condition finally be satisfied and control leave the loop.

questions.q: Read the watering program in the code. Which statement is right?
options: The program has no loops
Steps 1 and 3 are loops, each with a conditional exit
The loop at step 3 has no way out of it once entered
Step 2 is a conditional branch that tests the soil
optionExplain: Going back to a step is a loop.
Right: each waiting loop exits when its test comes out the other way.
Step 3 exits when the soil is wet.
Step 2 simply acts.
questions.explain: Steps 1 and 3 wait in loops until their conditions hold. The whole program then returns to step 1.
questions.rule: A program is a structure of processes with numbered steps, branching on tests, and loops that need a conditional exit.
questions.code:
1. test if soil dry, if false go to 1
2. turn sprinkler on
3. test if soil wet, if false go to 3
4. turn sprinkler off, go to 1

questions.q: True or false: If none of a step's control statements is satisfied, execution continues with the next step in the order written.
questions.explain: The authors say the program then proceeds in the order the steps are written.

questions.q: A student says: a loop with no conditional branch is fine because it will stop eventually. What is wrong?
options: Nothing is wrong: the loop will stop by itself in time
Loops must have exactly two branches to be able to end
Loops of every kind are unable to end under any condition
A loop needs a conditional branch so that it can be left
optionExplain: Loops do not stop by themselves.
Two branches are not required.
Loops with a conditional exit do end.
Right: without a condition to satisfy, nothing ends the loop.
questions.explain: The authors require at least one conditional branch in every loop so that the action can terminate.
questions.rule: A program is a structure of processes with numbered steps, branching on tests, and loops that need a conditional exit.

questions.q: A dishwasher program tests water level, opens the inlet and starts the pump. Which of these basic steps work only inside the system?
options: All of them, since each step uses the inside of the system
Only the tests, since actions reach the outside world
None; each one detects or affects something external
Only the actions, since tests read the outside world
optionExplain: Tests and actions both touch the outside here.
Tests detect external things.
Right: because of the simplicity of the situation every eip in the thermostat example touches the outside.
Actions affect external things.
questions.explain: The authors note that, because of the simplicity of the thermostat, all its eip's either affect or detect something external to the IPS itself.
questions.teaches: In the thermostat program every elementary process either detects or affects something external to the IPS.
questions.rule: A program is a structure of processes with numbered steps, branching on tests, and loops that need a conditional exit.

questions.q: In a list of if-then rules where several conditions are true at once, what decides which rule acts?
options: Position in the list: a rule higher up takes priority
The rule that was written last in the whole list
The rule with the longest condition on its left side
A random draw among all of the rules that are true
optionExplain: Right: this is the authors' convention.
Later rules do not override earlier ones here.
Length does not matter.
The choice is not random.
questions.explain: List order resolves conflicts. The card gives the authors' example.
questions.rule: In a production system each condition-action pair is a production, and the topmost true condition wins.

questions.q: In a production system each conditional statement is called a ____.
questions.explain: A system of productions is a production system.

questions.q: Rules run top to bottom. With the door open, the light on and the room empty, which action comes first?
options: Switch the light off
Lock the door
None, since several conditions hold
Close the door
optionExplain: That rule is lower in the list.
That rule is lowest.
Priority settles conflicts.
Right: the first rule's condition is true and it is topmost.
questions.explain: The highest true production takes priority, so close-door runs first.
questions.rule: In a production system each condition-action pair is a production, and the topmost true condition wins.
questions.code:
1. door-open then close-door
2. light-on and room-empty then switch-light-off
3. room-empty then lock-door

questions.q: True or false: With the traffic light red, the walker does not move even if the lower move conditions are also satisfied.
questions.explain: The red-light production is highest and takes priority.

questions.q: Match each example to the notation the authors use for it.
questions.explain: The authors deliberately use a different scheme for each to stress the conventional character of the description.

questions.q: A kettle's rule list has only conditions and actions, with no step that says check the water. Which production-system feature is this?
options: Tests must be written as separate steps
The act of executing the tests is implicit
Productions cannot have conditions
Every production needs a go to
optionExplain: That describes sequential programs.
Right: the authors say the tests are implicit in a production system.
Productions have conditions by definition.
Productions have no go to.
questions.explain: The authors say that in the walker's production system the act of executing the various tests is implicit.
questions.teaches: In a production system the act of executing the various tests is implicit; the system is assumed to perform the action when its condition becomes true.
questions.rule: In a production system each condition-action pair is a production, and the topmost true condition wins.

questions.q: A bimetallic-strip thermostat bends and breaks a circuit when warm. Does it follow a program?
options: Yes, a program is stored somewhere in the bending strip
No: it behaves by physical law; the program only describes it
Yes, because it controls a furnace on the basis of heat
No, because thermostats cannot be described by programs
optionExplain: Nothing in the strip stores a program.
Right: the strip simply behaves, and the program describes its behavior.
Controlling a furnace does not require following a program.
It can be described by a program; it does not follow one.
questions.explain: A description is not the same as an internal program. The card explains.
questions.rule: A program may merely describe a system from outside; only some systems hold and follow a program internally.

questions.q: A program as first described is purely ____ to the IPS: it is our way, as outside observers, of describing the system.
questions.explain: The program belongs to the description, not necessarily to the system.

questions.q: A wind-up toy walks in a square because of its cams, and a student flowcharts its path. Where does the flowchart live?
options: In the observer's description; the toy need hold nothing like it
Inside the toy, as its stored memory of the route it walks
In the cams, as a stored program that the toy follows
In the toy's wind-up spring that supplies the energy
optionExplain: Right: nothing inside has to correspond to the program.
The toy has no memory of the flowchart.
Cams shape motion but need not be a stored program.
The spring supplies energy.
questions.explain: The toy behaves in the manner described without following a program.
questions.rule: A program may merely describe a system from outside; only some systems hold and follow a program internally.

questions.q: True or false: A system with no internal representation of a program cannot behave in the manner a program describes.
questions.explain: The thermostat strip behaves as the program describes with nothing inside corresponding to it.
questions.rule: Behavior and internal program are different things.

questions.q: A student says: because the thermostat acts as the flowchart says, it must contain the flowchart. What is the flaw?
options: The thermostat does contain the flowchart in its parts
Flowcharts cannot be used to describe thermostats at all
A mechanism can behave as a program says with no program inside
The flowchart is itself a physical law of the device
optionExplain: The strip holds no flowchart.
They can be described by flowcharts.
Right: the authors say there may be nothing in the system that corresponds to the program.
A flowchart is a description.
questions.explain: The program is the observer's description; there may be only a mechanism that behaves as the program describes.
questions.rule: A program may merely describe a system from outside; only some systems hold and follow a program internally.

questions.q: An oven switch bends when hot; a washing machine reads a punched card to run its cycle. Which holds a program and an interpreter?
options: The oven switch, with the bending strip as its program
Both of them equally, since each controls a machine
Neither of them, since neither has any memory of its own
The washing machine, with card as memory and reader as interpreter
optionExplain: The strip only reacts physically.
Only one has the specialized parts.
The card and reader are the specialized parts.
Right: like the player piano, it has a record of the scheme and a part that interprets the record.
questions.explain: The authors say what separates the player piano from the thermostat is a specialized subpart that records the scheme of behavior, a memory containing the program, and another that interprets the record, the program interpreter.
questions.teaches: A player piano differs from a thermostat in having a specialized subpart that records the scheme of its behavior, a memory containing the program, and another that interprets it, the interpreter.
questions.rule: A program may merely describe a system from outside; only some systems hold and follow a program internally.

questions.q: Two systems find the first S in a list, one by a built-in mechanism, the other by a stored program. Can outputs alone tell which?
options: Not without examining their microstructure
Yes, the program version is slower
Yes, the mechanism version is always wrong sometimes
No, because both are programs
optionExplain: Right: the authors say it would be impossible to distinguish them.
Speed is not claimed to differ.
The mechanism is not wrong.
One is a mechanism.
questions.explain: From outside the two can look alike. The card gives the authors' remark.
questions.rule: Outer behavior alone often cannot show whether a process is a mechanism or an interpreted program.

questions.q: Unless we could examine the system's ____, it would be impossible to tell whether the find was a mechanism or an interpreted program.
questions.explain: Only internal structure could separate them.

questions.q: One calculator multiplies by a dedicated circuit, another by repeated addition under a stored program, with equal answers. What would the authors say?
options: The first one must be the program running on the circuit
Answers alone cannot show which is mechanism and which is program
Their answers prove which of the two is the faster one
Both of them must be mechanisms rather than programs
optionExplain: Nothing in the answers marks the first as program.
Right: the same reasoning applies.
Speed is not what answers prove.
One uses a stored program.
questions.explain: The authors' point about find applies to any process realized in two ways.
questions.rule: Outer behavior alone often cannot show whether a process is a mechanism or an interpreted program.

questions.q: True or false: Seen only through inputs and outputs, a direct mechanism and an interpreted program would give different results.
questions.explain: The authors say that without microstructure information they could not be distinguished.
questions.rule: Same inputs and outputs, no way to tell.

questions.q: The Figure 2.8 program for finding S in a list has three steps: (1) find the first symbol, if none stop and report false; (2) test if it equals S, if so stop and report true; (3) find the next symbol, if there is one go to step 2, else stop and report false. Order what it does on the list (A, S) when looking for S.
items: Find the first symbol in the list (A)
Test whether it equals S (no)
Find the next symbol in the list (S)
Test whether it equals S (yes)
Stop and report true
questions.explain: The program tests symbols one by one and stops with true when it meets S.

questions.q: Searching a guest list for Dana, the program of Figure 2.8 is given an empty list. What happens?
options: It loops forever, since there is nothing left to find
It reports true, since an empty list has no mismatch
Step 1 finds no symbol, so it stops and reports false
It tests Dana against nothing and then goes on to step 3
optionExplain: Step 1 ends it.
True is reported only when a match is found.
Right: step 1 fails and the program stops with false.
The fail branch of step 1 stops the program.
questions.explain: The first step finds the first symbol in the list; if that fails, the program stops and reports false.
questions.teaches: In the program of Figure 2.8, if the first find fails because the list is empty, the program stops and reports false.
questions.rule: Outer behavior alone often cannot show whether a process is a mechanism or an interpreted program.

questions.q: What does it mean for a process to recognize a word, in this chapter?
options: It prints the word out on paper for the reader to see
It outputs the designation of a structure of the word's meaning
It checks the spelling of the word and nothing more
It deletes the word from memory once it has been read
optionExplain: Printing is writing, not recognizing.
Right: recognition gives access to a structure of meaning.
Spelling is one aspect among several.
Deleting is not recognition.
questions.explain: Recognition connects a word to its meaning-structure. The card gives the authors' definition.
questions.rule: Recognition gives access to a symbol structure for a word, and that access is what makes the word a symbol.

questions.q: A recognition process makes the word into a ____, since it provides a way to gain access to an appropriate symbol structure.
questions.explain: Access to a structure is what designation is.

questions.q: A contact app takes the typed name Dana and returns the stored entry with number and photo. Is this recognition in the authors' sense?
options: No, because the app prints nothing out for the user
No, because only words of English can be recognized at all
Yes, it gives access to a structure of what the name stands for
Yes, but only if the app is built as a discrimination net
optionExplain: Printing is irrelevant.
The type of word does not matter.
Right: input form leads to a structure.
The method is left open.
questions.explain: The authors define recognition as outputting the designation of a structure that contains aspects of the meaning.
questions.rule: Recognition gives access to a symbol structure for a word, and that access is what makes the word a symbol.

questions.q: True or false: The output of recognition is the symbol structure itself copied into STM.
questions.explain: The process outputs to STM the designation of a symbol structure, which gives access to it.

questions.q: True or false: Recognition and discrimination in the sense of selecting different behaviors are the same operation.
questions.explain: Recognition identifies a symbol structure on which to base later differential behavior, rather than itself selecting different behaviors.
questions.rule: Recognition prepares behavior; it does not select it.

questions.q: A photo-sorting app calls its face-matching step classification although it only finds the stored profile. Which remark of the authors is similar?
options: They rename discrimination as recognition everywhere in the book
They reject the discrimination net as an unhelpful device
They say that recognition is not really a process at all
They keep the name discrimination even though it clashes with theirs
optionExplain: They keep the usual name.
They use the net as the example.
They treat it as a process.
Right: they keep the common name despite the clash.
questions.explain: The authors say the mechanism is often called discrimination, and a discrimination net, even though its result is to identify a structure rather than select behaviors, and they keep the name though it clashes somewhat with their terminology.
questions.teaches: The mechanism is often called discrimination and a discrimination net, and the authors keep the name even though it clashes somewhat with their own terminology.
questions.rule: Recognition gives access to a symbol structure for a word, and that access is what makes the word a symbol.

questions.q: In a discrimination net, how do you get from an input word to its meaning?
options: Apply tests at nodes, following outcomes to a terminal node
Look the word up in an alphabetically sorted list
