Compare the word with every stored word, one after another
Ask the processor to guess at the most likely meaning
optionExplain: Right: tests lead from node to node.
A sorted list is another scheme.
The net avoids comparing with everything.
Guessing is not part of it.
questions.explain: Tests route a word through the net. The card gives the authors' example.
questions.rule: A discrimination net sorts a word through tests until a terminal node, which holds the meaning structure.

questions.q: The net-interpreter keeps following test outcomes until it reaches a ____ node.
questions.explain: Terminal nodes hold the meaning structures.

questions.q: In the invented net shown in the code, which terminal does CAT reach?
options: The terminal car
The terminal dog
No terminal
The terminal cat
optionExplain: R would lead to car.
D would lead to dog.
Both tests have outcomes.
Right: first letter C, then last letter T.
questions.explain: The first test gives C and the second gives T, so the terminal is cat.
questions.rule: A discrimination net sorts a word through tests until a terminal node, which holds the meaning structure.
questions.code:
test first letter:
  C: test last letter: T gives cat, R gives car
  D: dog

questions.q: In the invented net shown in the code, what happens with the word COT?
options: It reaches no terminal, since COT is not a word in the net
It reaches the terminal cat, since the tests treat it like CAT
It reaches the terminal dog, since O resembles the O in DOG
The net reports an error at the middle letter of the word
optionExplain: COT passes both tests.
Right: the net sees only what its tests ask.
It does not begin with D.
The middle letter is never tested.
questions.explain: A net recognizes by its tests; COT and CAT agree on every test.
questions.rule: A discrimination net sorts a word through tests until a terminal node, which holds the meaning structure.
questions.code:
test first letter:
  C: test last letter: T gives cat, R gives car
  D: dog

questions.q: Order the net-interpreter's steps for the word DOG in the authors' fragment.
items: Apply the first node's test, test-first-letter, to DOG
Follow the link for the result D to the next node
Apply that node's test, test-last-letter, giving G
Follow the link for G onward to a terminal node
Output the designator of the structure for the word
questions.explain: The interpreter alternates tests and links until a terminal node supplies the structure.

questions.q: A parcel-sorting net tests postcode area, and no link exists for a certain area. What does the authors' net-interpreter do when a link is missing?
options: It guesses the nearest link
It loops back to the start forever
It stops and reports not recognized
It outputs the last terminal it saw
optionExplain: Guessing is not in the program.
It stops.
Right: failed finds end with a not recognized report.
No old terminal is output.
questions.explain: In the net-interpreter program, failing to find the first node, a test, or the node for a result stops the process and reports that the word is not recognized.
questions.teaches: In the net-interpreter, if it fails to find the first node, a node's test or the node for a test result, it stops and reports not recognized.
questions.rule: A discrimination net sorts a word through tests until a terminal node, which holds the meaning structure.

questions.q: What does an interpreter trade away, and what does it trade for?
options: Much mechanism, for a small interpreter plus much symbolic structure
Speed, for memory capacity in the symbol structures held
Memory, for sensors that take in the outside world
Programs, for effectors that act on the outside world
optionExplain: Right: the interpreter exchanges mechanism for structure.
Speed is a separate matter.
Sensors are not involved.
Effectors are not involved.
questions.explain: Interpreters shift complexity into structure. The card gives the authors' wording.
questions.rule: A small interpreter plus large stored structure gives unlimited complexity: the limits lie in the programs, not the IPS.

questions.q: The limitations of behavior reside in the content of the ____ stored in the IPS, not in inherent features of the IPS.
questions.explain: Programs hold the complexity.

questions.q: A game console runs thousands of different games from cartridges with one fixed chip design. Which of the authors' points does this illustrate?
options: Each separate game needs a chip that is designed for it
A more complex interpreter is needed for more complex games
A simple fixed interpreter can show varied behavior from stored structure
Games are limited by the design of the chip alone, not the code
optionExplain: One chip serves all games.
The interpreter stays simple.
Right: the chip is the interpreter and the cartridge is the stored structure.
The structures set the limits.
questions.explain: Variety of behavior comes from stored programs, not from a complicated interpreter.
questions.rule: A small interpreter plus large stored structure gives unlimited complexity: the limits lie in the programs, not the IPS.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, more complex behavior needs a more complex interpreter rather than more complex programs.
questions.explain: The behavior is limited only by the complexity of symbol structures, not by the simplicity of the interpreter.

questions.q: A student argues: the interpreter is simple, so the IPS's behavior must be limited. What is the flaw?
options: Simple interpreters cannot run complex programs at all
The student is right: a simple interpreter caps the behavior
Behavior is limited by the number of receptors in the system
Behavior is limited only by the complexity of structures built
optionExplain: Simple interpreters can run complex programs.
The authors argue the opposite.
Receptors are not mentioned as the limit.
Right: complexity comes from the structures.
questions.explain: A simple interpreter does not cap behavior, since the eip's let the system build arbitrarily complex structures.
questions.rule: A small interpreter plus large stored structure gives unlimited complexity: the limits lie in the programs, not the IPS.

questions.q: A translation app can in principle handle any text, yet a novel takes a week on a slow phone. Which limit is this?
options: A limit in the design of the app's interpreter itself
Speed: long sequences of eip's cannot be speeded up
A limit on the complexity of the programs that are stored
A limit on what the stored symbols are able to designate
optionExplain: The design is not the limit here.
Right: the authors name speed as a limit.
Program complexity is not the issue.
Designation is not the issue.
questions.explain: The authors say there are limits on the speed at which the IPS can accomplish complex endeavors, since these may require very long sequences of eip's and there may be no way of speeding up the elementary processes.
questions.teaches: There are limits on the speed of an IPS, because complex endeavors may require very long sequences of eip's and there may be no way of speeding up the elementary processes.
questions.rule: A small interpreter plus large stored structure gives unlimited complexity: the limits lie in the programs, not the IPS.

questions.q: When does it matter whether an IPS has a true interpreter rather than a mechanism that behaves as a program describes?
options: When it wants to analyze, construct or modify a program
Whenever it executes a program, however simple
Only when the IPS happens to have no memory
In no case, since the two behave alike under all inputs
optionExplain: Right: only then must it treat the program as a symbol structure.
Executing alone does not require it.
Memory is not the issue.
The authors say it sometimes matters.
questions.explain: True interpretation is needed to work on programs as data. The card gives the authors' point.
questions.rule: A true interpreter is needed only when the IPS must treat a program as data: to analyze, construct or modify it.

questions.q: If the IPS wants to analyze, construct or modify a program, it must operate in a truly ____ mode.
questions.explain: It must deal with the program as a symbol structure.

questions.q: One robot rewrites its own routine to run faster; another repeats a routine wired into its circuits. Which needs a true interpreter?
options: The second
The first
Both
Neither
optionExplain: Repeating a wired routine needs no interpreter.
Right: modifying a routine means treating it as a structure.
Only one of them modifies.
The first does.
questions.explain: Modification calls for a true interpreter; fixed repetition does not.
questions.rule: A true interpreter is needed only when the IPS must treat a program as data: to analyze, construct or modify it.

questions.q: True or false: A mechanism that only produces a sequence of behaviors can have its internal structure described in information processing terms.
questions.explain: If the interpreter is only a mechanism, we have no way of describing its internal structure in information processing terms.

questions.q: Sort each task by what it requires.

items.t: Executing a fixed routine
Modifying a routine while it runs
Constructing a new routine from parts
Analyzing a routine to find a mistake
Repeating a wired-in sequence

questions.explain: Only tasks that treat the program as data need a true interpreter.

questions.q: A cook expands a shorthand recipe to find the sequence of steps. How does this resemble the authors' view of the interpreter?
options: The interpreter is the recipe itself, written in shorthand
The interpreter stores the ingredients for later use
It unravels statements to find the sequence of processes
The interpreter decides what the cook is going to make
optionExplain: The recipe is the program.
Storage is memory.
Right: the authors say the interpreter must unravel program statements.
Choice of dish is outside the interpreter.
questions.explain: The authors say the interpreter is just a process-oriented view of the conventions of the language, since it must unravel the program statements to determine the sequence of elementary processes.
questions.teaches: The interpreter is a process-oriented view of the conventions of the programming language, since it must unravel program statements to find the sequence of elementary processes.
questions.rule: A true interpreter is needed only when the IPS must treat a program as data: to analyze, construct or modify it.

questions.q: A program is a list whose items are either basic steps or names of other lists. What must an interpreter remember while running a sub-list?
options: Where it was in the calling list, so it can resume
The total number of steps in the whole program
Which of the steps in the program are the longest
Which of the lists in the program is the biggest
optionExplain: Right: it needs to return to the place it left.
Totals do not help resume.
Length is irrelevant.
Size is irrelevant.
questions.explain: Resuming needs a record of the place. The card shows the stack that does this.
questions.rule: A stack keeps the interpreter's place so that sub-programs run in full and then control returns to the calling list.

questions.q: A stack is a list that can have a symbol added to its front (pushing) and removed from its front (____).
questions.explain: Pushing adds a place-marker and popping returns the prior one.
questions.rule: Push to descend, pop to return.

questions.q: With R1 = (e1, R2, R2) and R2 = (e2, e3), where each e is an eip, in what order are the eip's executed?
optionExplain: That interleaves the two runs of R2.
That puts R2 before e1.
Right: each use of R2 runs both of its steps in full.
That runs R2 once.
questions.explain: Run e1, then R2 in full (e2, e3), then R2 in full again.
questions.rule: A stack keeps the interpreter's place so that sub-programs run in full and then control returns to the calling list.

questions.q: True or false: When a subprogram's execution is complete, popping the stack returns the earlier symbol so the system can proceed to the next step.
questions.explain: The authors say popping the stack returns the prior symbol to the top and lets the system proceed.

questions.q: A student runs P = (e1, S, e4) with S = (e2, e3) and gets e1, e4, e2, e3. Where is the mistake?
options: S should be skipped, since it is only a name
S should run in full where named: e1, e2, e3, e4
e4 should run first, before anything else does
S should run twice, once for each of its steps
optionExplain: S is part of the program.
Right: a named sub-list runs where it is named, then the calling list resumes.
e4 follows S in the list.
S appears once.
questions.explain: The stack lets S run to completion and then returns to e4.
questions.rule: A stack keeps the interpreter's place so that sub-programs run in full and then control returns to the calling list.

questions.q: A manager's instructions are carried out by an assistant, and a friend asks who interprets the assistant. Which remark of the authors answers this?
options: Another interpreter must interpret it, and so on without end
The interpreter is a program that a stack interprets in turn
Interpreters do not really exist in any information system
At some level the interpreter is a mechanism acting directly
optionExplain: They deny the endless chain.
The stack is for place-keeping, not for interpreting the interpreter.
They accept interpreters.
Right: the authors block the regress.
questions.explain: The authors say that describing the interpreter as a program does not mean another interpreter interprets it; at some level it is a mechanism that directly carries out the actions.
questions.teaches: Describing the interpreter as a program does not mean another interpreter interprets it: at some level it is just a mechanism that accomplishes the actions directly.
questions.rule: A stack keeps the interpreter's place so that sub-programs run in full and then control returns to the calling list.

questions.section: The Relation of an IPS to Language
questions.q: In modern linguistics, what does a grammar do?
options: It determines which strings of elements are admissible
It stores the meanings of the words of the language
It parses the speech sounds into separate phonemes
It sets the speed at which the speech is delivered
optionExplain: Right: a grammar determines well-formed strings.
Meanings are in the deep structure.
Parsing yields structures.
Speed is not a grammar matter.
questions.explain: Grammar separates admissible strings from others. The card sets this beside the IPS.
questions.rule: IPS symbols and lists correspond to linguistic elements and strings, and stored structures play the role of deep structures.

questions.section: The Relation of an IPS to Language
questions.q: Match each linguistic notion to its IPS counterpart.
questions.explain: The authors pair elements with symbols, strings with lists, and deep structures with stored symbol structures.

questions.section: The Relation of an IPS to Language
questions.q: A spell checker accepts only letter sequences allowed by a set of rules. Which linguistic notion does the rule set resemble?
options: A lexicon that stores the meanings of the words
A grammar, which determines the well-formed strings
A deep structure underlying the string's meaning
A surface structure obtained by parsing the string
optionExplain: A lexicon stores information about symbols.
Right: a grammar decides which strings are admissible.
Deep structures are meaning representations.
Surface structures come from parsing.
questions.explain: The rule set decides which strings are allowed, as a grammar does.
questions.rule: IPS symbols and lists correspond to linguistic elements and strings, and stored structures play the role of deep structures.

questions.section: The Relation of an IPS to Language
questions.q: True or false: The authors say the IPS's stored symbol structures are strings that can be read directly as sentences in a natural language.
questions.explain: They say the structures are not strings and cannot be interpreted directly as sentences.

questions.section: The Relation of an IPS to Language
questions.q: A student says: the authors claim their theory is a complete theory of linguistics. What do they say?
options: A complete theory of language and of its use in speech
No theory of language at all
A partial theory, of the deep structures used in problem solving
A theory of speech sounds as the ear receives them
optionExplain: They do not claim completeness.
They say it can be viewed as partial.
Right: they claim only a partial theory.
Sounds are not their subject.
questions.explain: The authors say they have little to say explicitly about linguistics but their theory is partly one of deep structures.
questions.rule: IPS symbols and lists correspond to linguistic elements and strings, and stored structures play the role of deep structures.

questions.section: The Relation of an IPS to Language
questions.q: A tool parses a sentence into a phrase tree, then derives a meaning structure with a dictionary. Which linguistic order is this?
options: The meaning comes first and the tree is derived from it later
The dictionary is the deep structure of the sentence itself
The phrase tree is the lexicon that the tool consults
Parsing gives surface structure, which is transformed to deep structure
optionExplain: The order is reversed.
The lexicon is a component, not the structure.
The tree is the surface structure.
Right: the authors describe this order.
questions.explain: The authors describe the surface structure as obtained by parsing, then transformed into a deep structure, with a lexicon in the system for extracting it.
questions.teaches: The surface structure of a string is obtained by parsing and is then transformed into a deep structure, with the help of a lexicon that stores information about the symbols.
questions.rule: IPS symbols and lists correspond to linguistic elements and strings, and stored structures play the role of deep structures.

questions.q: A book presents many programs created at different times and wants readers to follow them. Which choice of notation fits this aim?
options: A readable informal notation that could in principle be formalized
A fully formal language, whatever the cost in readability
A different formal language for each separate program
No notation at all, only plain prose descriptions
optionExplain: Right: this is the authors' compromise.
Formal languages tend to be unreadable.
Many languages would hide the relations among programs.
Prose alone would not be systematic.
questions.explain: The authors trade formality for readability. The card names the four uses of the notation.
questions.rule: The notation defines programs, task environments, traces and protocols, and is informal so that it can be read.

questions.q: Match each use of the notation to its description.
pairs: Substantive theories of an individual's behavior
External situations that set the tasks
Step-by-step accounts of a program run in a task environment
Records of human subjects' behavior and verbalizations
questions.explain: Programs are the theories, task environments the settings, traces what the program does, protocols what subjects did.

questions.q: A researcher writes down, line by line, what a program did while it solved a puzzle. Which use of the notation is this?
options: Defining a task environment
Encoding a protocol
Describing a trace
Defining a program
optionExplain: The environment is the puzzle itself.
A protocol records a human subject.
Right: a trace is the step-by-step account of a program run in a task environment.
The program is the theory, not its run.
questions.explain: A trace records what a program did; a protocol records what a human did.
questions.rule: The notation defines programs, task environments, traces and protocols, and is informal so that it can be read.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say the notation's syntactic details are of secondary importance because the programs are to be read, not written.
questions.explain: They say so when explaining their informal approach.

questions.q: Sort each item: trace or protocol?

items.t: A step-by-step account of what the model did
A transcript of a subject thinking aloud
The sequence of structures a program produced on a puzzle
A subject's written notes during the task
The record of which processes the program executed
A subject's spoken remarks while moving chessmen

questions.explain: Traces come from running a program; protocols come from human subjects.
questions.rule: Program run: trace. Human record: protocol.

questions.q: A lab wants its model simulated on a computer. What does the authors' remark say is needed, and what did they use?
options: No language is needed, only a diagram or a flowchart
A formal language with an interpreter; the book mostly used IPL-V
A natural-language summary written in plain English
Only a production system, with no interpreter at all
optionExplain: Diagrams cannot be run.
Right: the authors say simulating requires a formal language with an interpreter or compiler, and name IPL-V.
Summaries cannot be run.
An interpreter is still needed.
questions.explain: The authors say to simulate on a computer one must define a formal language with an interpreter or compiler, and that most of the simulations in the volume were carried out in Information Processing Language V.
questions.teaches: Information Processing Language V (IPL-V) was used to carry out most of the computer simulations discussed in the volume.
questions.rule: The notation defines programs, task environments, traces and protocols, and is informal so that it can be read.

questions.q: Why would a book hyphenate several words into one name, such as untried-problems?
options: So that it is clear what counts as a single simple identifier
So that the name reads like an ordinary English sentence
So that the computer can read the name more easily
So that the name carries a hidden internal structure
optionExplain: Right: hyphens make the unit unambiguous.
Sentences would be ambiguous.
The book is for human readers.
A simple identifier has no implied composition.
questions.explain: Hyphens mark a single name. The card gives the authors' conventions.
questions.rule: Hyphenated words name things, lists are parenthesized without commas, a colon assigns a name, and operands may follow prepositions.

questions.q: The authors use a ____ to indicate the assignment of an identifier to a process or a symbol structure.
questions.explain: The top line of Figure 2.12 gives an identifier and follows it with a colon.

questions.q: In the authors' notation, how is the list of three theorems theorem1, theorem2, theorem3 written?
options: (theorem1, theorem2, theorem3)
theorem1-theorem2-theorem3
[theorem1 theorem2 theorem3]
(theorem1 theorem2 theorem3)
optionExplain: Commas were used only earlier in the chapter, for emphasis.
Hyphens would make a single identifier.
Square brackets mark parameters.
Right: parenthesized, with no commas.
questions.explain: Lists are parenthesized sequences without commas.
questions.rule: Hyphenated words name things, lists are parenthesized without commas, a colon assigns a name, and operands may follow prepositions.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say a process name such as xyz would not be allowed because it does not describe what the process does.
questions.explain: Identifiers are arbitrary, and xyz could be used, except that it gives no mnemonic help to the reader.

questions.q: In insert problem on untried-problems at end, how are the operands marked?
options: By square brackets around each operand
By prepositions that act as separators
By a colon placed before each operand
By commas placed between the operands
optionExplain: Square brackets mark parameters.
Right: the choice between functional and prepositional form is made when a process is defined.
A colon assigns an identifier.
Prepositions separate the operands here.
questions.explain: Operands may be given by phrases in which prepositions are separators.
questions.rule: Hyphenated words name things, lists are parenthesized without commas, a colon assigns a name, and operands may follow prepositions.

questions.q: Substitute[expression for variable](expression) is written with some items in square brackets and one in parentheses. What do the two kinds of bracket mark?
options: Operands are in square brackets and parameters in parentheses
Both mark operands
Parameters are in square brackets and the operand is in parentheses
Both mark parameters
optionExplain: That reverses them.
They are different.
Right: the authors distinguish parameters from operands.
They are different.
questions.explain: The authors say it is sometimes convenient to parametrize processes and think of parameters as distinct from operands.
questions.teaches: It is sometimes convenient to parametrize a process, with the parameters given in square brackets and the operand in parentheses.
questions.rule: Hyphenated words name things, lists are parenthesized without commas, a colon assigns a name, and operands may follow prepositions.

questions.q: In the authors' convention, what comes first in a line of a sequential process?
options: The name that is to be given to the result
The process itself, a calculation or observation
The jump to the next line to be executed
A comment explaining what the line is for
optionExplain: Names are subordinate.
Right: process definition has first place.
Control is subordinate.
The authors do not mention comments.
questions.explain: The process leads. The card shows the reasoning.
questions.rule: Write the process first; the name given to its result and the control that follows are subordinate clauses.

questions.q: The double arrow => can be read as and ____.
questions.explain: It introduces the output symbol structure, often a new identifier.

questions.q: Which line follows the authors' convention of process first, then control?
options: find status of problem, if proved go to 10
go to 10 if status of problem is proved
x <- status(problem); if x = proved go to 10
if proved go to 10 after finding status of problem
optionExplain: Right: the find comes first and the control clause follows it.
That puts control first.
That uses assignment first, as in FORTRAN and ALGOL.
That puts control before the process.
questions.explain: The process definition leads, followed by subordinate control clauses.
questions.rule: Write the process first; the name given to its result and the control that follows are subordinate clauses.

questions.q: The step select first from untried-problems produces the problem itself. Can the control clause if too-complex stop follow it directly?
options: Yes, because select returns all of the problem's information
Yes, because every control clause can accept any kind of test
No: select yields the problem, so its status must be found first
No, because select cannot ever be used together with stop
optionExplain: The result is the problem, not its attributes.
Control is limited to simple discriminations on the result.
Right: control senses only the result just produced.
The problem lies in the test, not in stop.
questions.explain: Control actions depend on the nature of the result just produced; the status is an attribute that must be found first.
questions.rule: Write the process first; the name given to its result and the control that follows are subordinate clauses.

questions.q: True or false: A control clause can test any property of the thing selected, including attributes not yet found.
questions.explain: Control actions are limited to simple discriminations on the result just produced, so the attribute must be found first.

questions.q: In a vending process, pay returns succeed or fail, while dispense returns released or jammed. Which of the authors' ideas does this fit?
options: Control never depends on the results of the processes
Every process yields a signal, general or defined for it
Only the processor ever sees the signals, not control
Signals are written in by the reader of the program
optionExplain: Control depends on results.
Right: control senses these signals.
Control senses them.
The reader does not write them.
questions.explain: The authors say all processes produce signals to indicate their result, which may be general, as succeed or fail, or uniquely defined for the process, as generation-stopped and generation-completed for generate.
questions.teaches: All processes produce signals indicating their result; they may be general, such as succeed or fail and true or false, or uniquely defined for the process, such as generation-stopped.
questions.rule: Write the process first; the name given to its result and the control that follows are subordinate clauses.

questions.q: Why do the authors avoid writing F(a + b) in place of two separate steps?
options: Because the function F cannot take a sum as its input
Because brackets are unreadable in printed programs
Because assignment runs faster than embedding does
Because embedding obscures the sequential control flow
optionExplain: F can take sums; the issue is clarity.
Brackets are used elsewhere.
Speed is not their concern.
Right: nested expressions hide the order of steps.
questions.explain: The authors want control flow to stay visible. The card gives their alternatives.
questions.rule: Avoid nested calls; refer to results by the process's name or by the word result.

questions.q: The special term ____ indicates the most recently obtained result.
questions.explain: It can be used in later lines too.

questions.q: In the program shown in the code, what are the values of the three occurrences of result?
optionExplain: Right: each use refers to the most recent result: 12, then 14, then 2.
Each occurrence refers to a different result.
That reverses the order.
The order follows the lines.
questions.explain: The product is 12; adding 2 gives 14; dividing by 7 gives 2.
questions.rule: Avoid nested calls; refer to results by the process's name or by the word result.

questions.q: True or false: In the authors' example, all occurrences of result in successive lines refer to the same value.
questions.explain: They say the three occurrences are all different.
questions.rule: Each result is the latest at its line.

questions.q: Sort each way of referring to a result.

items.t: x <- a + b; then F(x)
Using the word result for the latest result
Naming the result of effort-used as effort-used
tmp1 <- f(y); tmp2 <- g(tmp1)
z <- apply(method, problem)

questions.explain: Assignment creates a temporary identifier; the authors' conventions avoid doing so.
questions.rule: Assignment needs names; conventions do not.

questions.q: A program uses forty temporary names x1 to x40 and is hard to follow. Which remark of the authors does this match?
options: Temporary names make long programs clearer to the reader
Embedding is not possible in any programming language
Temporary identifiers greatly add to the obscurity of programs
Names should be made longer so they read as words
optionExplain: The authors say the opposite.
Embedding is possible but avoided.
Right: that is why the authors look for ways to keep them down.
Length is not the point.
questions.explain: The authors say that embedding reduces the need for temporary identifiers, which are a major contributor to the obscurity of programs, but they avoid embedding for its effect on control flow.
questions.teaches: Temporary identifiers are a major contributor to the obscurity of programs, which is what embedding reduces.
questions.rule: Avoid nested calls; refer to results by the process's name or by the word result.

questions.q: Which basic process do the authors use for all repetitive operations?
options: Generate
Find
Report
Apply
optionExplain: Right: generate steps through the elements of a set.
Find locates a value.
Report outputs text.
Apply runs a process once on operands.
questions.explain: Repetition is done by generate. The card describes all five basic processes.
questions.rule: Generate repeats a subprocess over each element of a set; test, find, apply and report do the single steps.

questions.q: A generate takes as operand a ____ and produces its elements in sequence, giving each to a subprocess.
questions.explain: The subprocess sees each element in turn.

questions.q: In generate orders (=> current-order): pack current-order, what does current-order refer to in the body?
options: The whole set of orders, handled all at the same time
The element of orders being processed at that moment
The last order only, once the generate has finished
The generate process itself, as a named subprocess
optionExplain: The set is generated one element at a time.
Right: the name is given to each element in turn.
It changes with each element.
The name is for the element.
questions.explain: The => clause names the element currently produced.
questions.rule: Generate repeats a subprocess over each element of a set; test, find, apply and report do the single steps.

questions.q: In generate methods: apply method to current-problem, how is each element of the set of methods referred to?
options: By a fresh name that has to be defined beforehand
By the term result, which stands for any element
It cannot be referred to inside the subprocess body
By the set's name, method, without further definition
optionExplain: A fresh name is optional.
Result means the latest result, which is something else.
It can be referred to.
Right: the authors usually allow an element to be named by its set name.
questions.explain: The authors say they usually also allow an element to be named by its set name.
questions.rule: Generate repeats a subprocess over each element of a set; test, find, apply and report do the single steps.

questions.q: Match each basic process to its function.
pairs: Produce the elements of a set in sequence
Try to get a relation's value or a designated structure
Evaluate a condition of Boolean connectives and relations
questions.explain: Each has a special form for its operands.

questions.q: A rule says file the report in the cabinet without saying which drawer. When do the authors say leaving the place unspecified is acceptable?
options: Never: an insert must always say exactly where it goes
Only when the list that is receiving the item is empty
When the place makes no difference or is an open parameter
Only when the item inserted is a report or a record
optionExplain: The authors allow it.
No such condition is mentioned.
Right: the authors say insert may be used without specifying where.
The rule is general.
questions.explain: The authors say an insert may be used without specifying exactly where on the list when the place makes no substantial difference, or when it is still an open parameter to be determined by some other process.
questions.teaches: An insert may leave the place unspecified when the place makes no substantial difference to the discussion or is still an open parameter to be determined by another process.
questions.rule: Generate repeats a subprocess over each element of a set; test, find, apply and report do the single steps.

questions.q: In a production system, after an action sequence has run, where does control go?
options: Back to the top of the list of productions
On to the next production further down the list
To the production named by a go to statement
To the last production at the bottom of the list
optionExplain: Right: control starts over from the top.
The system does not just continue down.
There is no go to.
The last is not special.
questions.explain: Control restarts at the top. The card gives the details.
questions.rule: A production system runs from the top: the first true condition fires, then control starts again at the top.

questions.q: Each production has a condition and an ____-sequence.
questions.explain: The condition decides whether the action sequence runs.

questions.q: Rules run top to bottom. With temperature 25 and the heater on, which action runs first?
options: Heater-on
Open-window
Heater-off
No action
optionExplain: Rule 1 needs a temperature below 5.
Rule 3 needs a temperature above 30.
Right: rule 1 fails, rule 2 holds and is the first true condition.
Rule 2 is true.
questions.explain: Control goes down from the top to the first true condition, which is rule 2.
questions.rule: A production system runs from the top: the first true condition fires, then control starts again at the top.
questions.code:
1. temp below 5 and heater-off then heater-on
2. temp above 20 and heater-on then heater-off
3. temp above 30 then open-window

questions.q: True or false: After the action of the first true production has run, control starts over at the top of the list.
questions.explain: The authors say control starts over at the top.

questions.q: A student says: a production can jump to any other production with go to. What do the authors say?
options: Yes, go to is the main control action in productions
Only stop is forbidden; every other jump is allowed
Only conditional jumps are forbidden; plain ones are fine
No: control by go to is impossible; the only other action is stop
optionExplain: They say the opposite.
Stop is allowed.
No jumps are possible.
Right: control is by position in the list.
questions.explain: In a production system control is by order and restart, not by jumps.
questions.rule: A production system runs from the top: the first true condition fires, then control starts again at the top.

questions.q: Is a production condition such as: the total of x and y exceeds the difference of u and v, allowed?
options: Yes, any test at all can be written as a condition
No: conditions are limited to simple matching and detection
Yes, but only when the rule also contains a go to
No, because conditions are required to be numbers only
optionExplain: Conditions are restricted.
Right: the authors rule out test if (a + b) > (c - d).
There is no go to.
Conditions need not be numbers.
questions.explain: The authors say a condition is an operation involving only matching and detection, just as control actions in sequential processes allow only simple discriminations, so a test such as (a + b) > (c - d) is not permitted.
questions.teaches: A production condition may involve only matching and detection, so an arithmetic test such as (a + b) > (c - d) is not permitted.
questions.rule: A production system runs from the top: the first true condition fires, then control starts again at the top.

questions.q: How could you say compactly that a word is either one letter or two letters?
options: Write out all fifty-two one-letter words in full
Name the class letter and write letter | letter letter
Write the allowed word length as a single number
Give each possible letter its own separate program
optionExplain: That lists letters, not the class.
Right: alternatives and a class name do it.
A length number does not define the class.
Programs are not needed.
questions.explain: Alternatives let one rule cover several shapes. The card shows the notation.
questions.rule: BNF names classes in angular brackets, builds patterns by concatenation, offers alternatives with a bar and names classes with ::=.

questions.q: In BNF the bar | means that the class is A ____ B.
questions.explain: A | B means either A or B.

questions.q: Given small-word ::= letter | letter letter, which of these strings belong to the class small-word?
options: T
TO
TOO
TOOT
T2
optionExplain: Right: one letter.
Right: two letters.
Three letters are too many.
Four letters are too many.
A digit is not a letter.
questions.explain: A small word is one or two letters.
questions.rule: BNF names classes in angular brackets, builds patterns by concatenation, offers alternatives with a bar and names classes with ::=.

questions.q: With small-word as above and bigger-word ::= small-word | letter small-word, how many letters can a bigger word have?
options: Two only
Two to three
One to three
One to four
optionExplain: That ignores the first alternative.
That ignores one-letter words.
Right: small words have one or two; with an added letter, two or three.
The longest is a letter plus two letters.
questions.explain: The alternatives give lengths 1 and 2 from small-word and 2 and 3 from the second.
questions.rule: BNF names classes in angular brackets, builds patterns by concatenation, offers alternatives with a bar and names classes with ::=.

questions.q: A student says the pattern letter A letter D includes WORD. Is that right?
options: No, because the second character must be the letter A itself
Yes, since any four letters at all would match it
Yes, since D is a letter and the pattern allows it
No, because the final letter D is not allowed there
optionExplain: Right: the pattern fixes the second and fourth characters.
Only the first and third are free.
D is literal in the pattern.
D appears literally and is allowed.
questions.explain: WARD, BARD, BAAD and ZAPD fit; WORD has O in second place.
questions.rule: BNF names classes in angular brackets, builds patterns by concatenation, offers alternatives with a bar and names classes with ::=.

questions.q: A form checker describes valid license plates as three letters then three digits. Which standard tool does the text name for describing such grammars?
options: Flow diagrams, which show sequences of steps in a picture
Production systems, which are lists of condition-action rules
Discrimination nets, which sort words into their meanings
BNF, a metanotation for grammars of programming languages
optionExplain: Flow diagrams show sequences.
Production systems are rule lists.
Nets are for recognition.
Right: BNF is a metanotation for grammars.
questions.explain: The authors call BNF a standard metanotation used to describe the grammars of programming languages.
questions.teaches: Backus Normal Form is a standard metanotation used to describe the grammars of programming languages.
questions.rule: BNF names classes in angular brackets, builds patterns by concatenation, offers alternatives with a bar and names classes with ::=.

questions.q: How can a short rule describe an unlimited set of strings, such as all whole numbers?
options: By letting the definition use its own class name
By listing every one of them out in a table
By limiting the length of the numbers allowed
By using a clock to count them as they come
optionExplain: Right: recursion.
There are infinitely many.
A limit would make it finite.
A clock has no role.
questions.explain: A definition that mentions itself can keep building. The card shows how.
questions.rule: A recursive definition uses its own class name, so a finite rule describes an unlimited class.

questions.q: A definition that uses the class it is defining is called ____.
questions.explain: Recursive definition gives infinite classes.

questions.q: Using the definitions in the code, which string is NOT a well-formed expression?
options: (P or Q)
~(P and S)
(P or Q and R)
optionExplain: ~~P is a tilde before the expression ~P.
One connective with two expressions is allowed.
A tilde before a bracketed expression is allowed.
Right: each use of a connective needs its own brackets.
questions.explain: (P or Q and R) would need Q and R bracketed as an expression of its own.
questions.rule: A recursive definition uses its own class name, so a finite rule describes an unlimited class.
questions.code:
<constant> ::= P | Q | R | S
<connective> ::= or | and | implies
<expression> ::= <constant> | ~<expression> | ( <expression> <connective> <expression> )

questions.q: True or false: By the definition, ~~P is a well-formed expression.
questions.explain: ~P is an expression, so ~ followed by it is one too.

questions.q: Order the steps that show 334 is an integer under integer ::= digit | digit integer.
items: 4 is a digit, hence an integer
34 is a digit followed by an integer, hence an integer
334 is a digit followed by an integer, hence an integer
questions.explain: Each step uses the previous result as the integer that follows a digit.

questions.q: A pattern for street addresses is written house-number street-name. In the authors' view of patterns as symbol structures, what does each concatenation represent?
options: A new class name defined for each part
A distinct relation in a symbol structure
A bar that marks an alternative form
A recursive call to the same class
optionExplain: Class names are separate.
Right: each concatenation stands for a relation.
A bar marks alternatives.
Recursion is a different matter.
questions.explain: The authors say each concatenation in a BNF expression represents a distinct relation in a symbol structure, and the relation of the tilde to its expression is one.
questions.teaches: Each concatenation in a BNF expression represents a distinct relation in a symbol structure, such as the relation of left-hand subexpression.
questions.rule: A recursive definition uses its own class name, so a finite rule describes an unlimited class.

questions.q: A rule matches the pattern expression or (expression and expression). How can its action name the particular sub-expressions matched?
options: By indexing the class names so each occurrence is labelled
By reading them off a screen at the time of matching
By guessing which part is which each time it is applied
By matching only the first part and ignoring the others
optionExplain: Right: indexing distinguishes the occurrences.
The system is not seeing a screen.
Guessing is not a method.
All three parts must be named.
questions.explain: Indices tell occurrences apart. The card shows the authors' example.
questions.rule: Index the class names so each occurrence in the condition can be named in the action.

questions.q: BNF identifies class membership but does not automatically provide designations for ____.
questions.explain: Variables are needed to refer to the matched parts.

questions.q: Apply the production expression.1 or (expression.2 and expression.3) gives (expression.1 or expression.2) and (expression.1 or expression.3) to P or (Q and R). What is produced?
options: (P or Q) and (Q or R)
(P or Q) and (P or R)
(P and Q) or (P and R)
(P or Q) and (P or Q)
optionExplain: The second part uses expression.1, which is P.
Right: P is expression.1, Q is expression.2 and R is expression.3.
That swaps the connectives.
The last part uses expression.3, which is R.
questions.explain: Substitute P, Q and R for the indexed names in the right-hand side.
questions.rule: Index the class names so each occurrence in the condition can be named in the action.

questions.q: True or false: In the production, the expression bound to expression.1 is copied into both parts of the output.
questions.explain: Expression.1 appears twice on the right-hand side.

questions.q: A student says the condition pattern alone tells the action which sub-expression to copy. What is missing?
options: Nothing is missing, because the pattern already names parts
A bar placed between the matched parts of the pattern
Indexed names, since BNF alone gives only class membership
A recursive definition of the class of expressions
optionExplain: The action cannot say which part.
A bar means or.
Right: the parts must be named.
Recursion is for unlimited classes.
questions.explain: Without indexed names the action cannot say which matched part it means.
questions.rule: Index the class names so each occurrence in the condition can be named in the action.

questions.q: A tool states that its output is a symbol structure of the class invoice. Which use of patterns from the text does this match?
options: Patterns describe the inputs of a process and nothing else
Patterns are used only for giving names to symbols
Patterns replace productions as the basic rule form
Patterns can also describe the output of a process
optionExplain: They also describe outputs.
They describe structures.
Productions still use them.
Right: the authors write an example in which a process's output is a column.
questions.explain: The authors say patterns can be used wherever classes of symbol structures need to be described, for example for the output of a process.
questions.teaches: Patterns are useful wherever classes of symbol structures need to be described, including the output of a process, as when FC produces a symbol structure of the class column.
questions.rule: Index the class names so each occurrence in the condition can be named in the action.

questions.q: What is the basic hypothesis whose specification the chapter begins?
options: That humans operate as information processing systems
That computers can think in the same way as humans do
That every problem has exactly one single solution
That language is itself a formal system of rules
optionExplain: Right: this is the book's basic hypothesis.
The authors say computer realization does not show this.
This is not their claim.
Language is a related topic, not the hypothesis.
questions.explain: The hypothesis is that humans are IPS's. The card says what Chapter 2 did with it.
questions.rule: Chapter 2 specifies the hypothesis and the notation; testing it is for later chapters.

questions.q: The chapter describes, by means of ____ postulates, the basic characteristics of the hypothesized information processing system.
questions.explain: The postulates are listed at the start of the chapter.

questions.q: Sort each task by where it is done.

items.t: Saying what the IPS postulates mean
Setting out the notation for programs and traces
Testing the postulate against human data
A careful analysis of the task environment
A general framework for problem solving

questions.explain: Chapter 2 specifies the hypothesis and the notation; testing and framework come later.
questions.rule: Meaning and notation now, testing later.

questions.q: According to the conclusion, what will the next chapter do?
options: Test the postulate on a group of chess players
Define Backus Normal Form and its notation in full
Describe the Logic Theorist program in complete detail
Make a careful analysis of the concept of task environment
optionExplain: Testing comes later.
BNF is in this chapter.
The Logic Theorist is for Chapter 4.
Right: Chapter 3 is announced as this analysis.
questions.explain: The next chapter, also introductory, analyzes the task environment.
questions.rule: Chapter 2 specifies the hypothesis and the notation; testing it is for later chapters.

questions.q: True or false: Chapter 2 tests and confirms the hypothesis that humans operate as IPS's.
questions.explain: The authors say it specifies the hypothesis and that empirical verification is for later chapters.

questions.q: A textbook's early chapters define terms and tools, then analyze the setting, then propose a framework. Which chapters of this book fit that order?
options: Chapter 3 first, then Chapter 2, then Chapter 4 for the framework
Chapter 4 for the notation and Chapter 2 for the framework
Chapter 2 for notation, 3 for task environment, 4 for framework
Chapter 2 for the framework, Chapter 3 for the notation
optionExplain: Chapter 2 comes first.
The notation is in Chapter 2.
Right: the conclusion lays out this order.
The framework is in Chapter 4.
questions.explain: The authors say that after the task environment in the next chapter they will be ready in Chapter 4 to propose a general framework for the study of problem solving behavior.
questions.teaches: Chapter 3 will analyze the concept of task environment, and Chapter 4 will propose a general framework for the study of problem solving behavior.
questions.rule: Chapter 2 specifies the hypothesis and the notation; testing it is for later chapters.

questions.q: In a BNF definition, how can the vertical bar itself appear as a character in an expression?
options: By putting it in quotation marks
By doubling it
By putting it in angular brackets
It cannot appear
optionExplain: Right: quotes show that it is not the metasymbol.
Doubling is not described.
Angular brackets name classes.
The appendix shows it can.
questions.explain: Quotes turn a metasymbol into a plain character. The card shows the sample.
questions.rule: In a BNF definition, alternatives are separated by bars, recursion makes infinite classes, and quotes turn a bar into a plain character.

questions.q: In X ::= A | B C, the class X has ____ alternatives.
questions.explain: A is the first and B followed by C is the second.

questions.q: Given the two definitions shown in the code, which string is NOT a member of X?
options: FFAGG
DKK
DKKK
BC
optionExplain: F, then FAG, then G.
D followed by KK.
Right: E is K or KK, so DKKK is too long.
B followed by C.
questions.explain: D must be followed by a member of E, which is K or KK.
questions.code:
<X> ::= A | B C | D <E> | F <X> G | H "|" G
<E> ::= K | K K
questions.rule: In a BNF definition, alternatives are separated by bars, recursion makes infinite classes, and quotes turn a bar into a plain character.

questions.q: Suppose a class X may be an A or an F, then an X, then a G (among other forms). True or false: FFFAGGG is a member of the class X.
questions.explain: It fits F X G with X = FFAGG, and so on down to A.

questions.q: Order the steps showing FFAGG is a member of X.
items: A is a member of X
FAG is a member of X, since F, a member of X, and G are joined
FFAGG is a member of X, since F, the member FAG, and G are joined
questions.explain: Each step wraps the previous member in F and G.

questions.q: When the language being defined is BNF itself, how do the authors keep its symbols distinct from the metasymbols?
options: They invent a different bar symbol for the purpose
They use quotation marks, as the pattern language is BNF
They avoid using patterns in the definition at all
They define the whole language in plain prose only
optionExplain: No new bar is introduced.
Right: the authors say quotes are needed.
Patterns are defined in the appendix.
The appendix is formal syntax.
questions.explain: The authors say the pattern language is just BNF itself, so quotes are needed to define it.
questions.teaches: The pattern language is just BNF itself, so the appendix needs quotation marks to define it.
questions.rule: In a BNF definition, alternatives are separated by bars, recursion makes infinite classes, and quotes turn a bar into a plain character.

questions.q: How is the formal language of the appendix divided?
options: A common part, then sequential processes, then production systems
Into letters, digits and punctuation marks, in turn
Into programs on the one side and data on the other
Into sensing on the one side and acting on the other
optionExplain: Right: three parts.
That is the list of marks.
That is a different split.
That is not the appendix's split.
questions.explain: The language has a shared part and two process languages. The card gives the structure.
questions.rule: A common first part serves two languages: sequential processes with control statements, and production systems with restricted conditions.

questions.q: The appendix defines the syntax of the language but leaves out its ____.
questions.explain: The authors say they will not define the semantics here.

questions.q: Where in the appendix would a definition of the class identifier belong?
options: In the production system part of the appendix
In the sequential process part of the appendix
In the report part, with the other special syntax
In the first part, which underlies all the definitions
optionExplain: Production systems use identifiers but do not define them.
The same holds for sequential processes.
Report is a special syntax process.
Right: identifiers underlie everything.
questions.explain: The first part introduces identifiers, symbols, symbol structures and process names.
questions.rule: A common first part serves two languages: sequential processes with control statements, and production systems with restricted conditions.

questions.q: Match each item to its part of the appendix.
pairs: Symbols, structures and naming of processes
Control statements such as if, otherwise and go to
A condition with a single level of conjunction
questions.explain: The appendix separates a common base from the two kinds of process language.

questions.q: True or false: In the appendix, classes of expressions are defined before they are used.
questions.explain: The definitions are given from the bottom up.

questions.q: A designer lets production conditions nest and, or and not to any depth. How does this differ from the authors' syntax?
options: The authors allow conditions to nest to any depth at all
Only a single level of conjunction and of negation is allowed
The authors allow no conjunction in a condition at all
The authors allow negation only, with no conjunction
optionExplain: That is the designer's version.
Right: only simple discriminations are allowed.
Conjunction is allowed.
Negation is also single-level.
questions.explain: The appendix notes that the condition part of a production cannot be an arbitrarily complex test: only a single level of conjunction and a single level of negation are permitted.
questions.teaches: A production condition permits only a single level of conjunction and a single level of negation.
questions.rule: A common first part serves two languages: sequential processes with control statements, and production systems with restricted conditions.

questions.q: A beginner and an expert both find the only move that saves a game. What does that shared move mainly reveal?
options: The structure of the position they both faced
The shared habits that both players' minds have built up
The emotions both players happened to feel at the board
The long training each of the players went through earlier
optionExplain: Right: when the situation allows one good move, finding it points to the position.
Habits can matter, but a shared answer points to what the position forced.
Emotion is a guess; the shared move does not show it.
Training may differ widely between the two, yet the move is the same.
questions.explain: A move that the position forces says more about the position than about either player. The card next gives the authors' reasoning.
questions.rule: Behavior demanded by the situation reveals the task environment, not the person.

questions.q: Behavior that suits the goal in light of the problem environment is called adaptive, or ____.
questions.explain: The authors use adaptive and rational as two names for behavior appropriate to the goal given the environment.
questions.rule: Behavior demanded by the situation reveals the task environment, not the person.

questions.q: Everyone who wants the cheapest fare on a booking site ends up sorting by price. By the authors' view, what does this mainly show?
options: All customers share the same underlying personality type
The site's options make price sorting the demanded step
The customers all feel the same emotions while shopping online
Customers copy one another without any reasons of their own
optionExplain: A shared trait is a far-fetched reading when the step is simply what the goal needs.
Right: a shared, goal-suited step points to the structure of the situation.
Emotion is not what the shared action reveals.
Copying is a guess; each shopper can reach the step alone.
questions.explain: Because the step is what the goal demands, it tells us about the site's structure; the customers need only want the fare and be able to find the step.
questions.rule: Behavior demanded by the situation reveals the task environment, not the person.

questions.q: True or false: If the same motivated person is placed in a different task environment, the authors expect the demanded behavior to change.
questions.explain: The behavior is demanded by the situation, so a different situation demands different behavior.
questions.rule: Change the situation and the demanded behavior changes.
questions.hint: Where does the behavior come from?

questions.q: According to the authors, problem situations with motivation secure and emotion not aroused suit the study of what best?
options: The nature of emotions in decision making
How motivation differs between people
The structure of task environments
The physiology of the behaving organism
optionExplain: Emotion is deliberately left out of these settings.
Motivation is assumed to be present, not varied.
Right: such settings are better for studying task environments than organisms.
Physiology is not what these settings isolate.
questions.explain: With motivation not in question and emotion absent, behavior mostly follows the situation, so the authors see the structure of the task environment as the natural object of study.
questions.teaches: Problem solving situations without emotion or doubtful motivation seem better suited to investigating the structure of task environments than the nature of behaving organisms.
questions.rule: Behavior demanded by the situation reveals the task environment, not the person.

questions.q: Every volunteer must slide a red tile aside first, or no solution works. A reviewer says this shows how minds are wired. What fits?
options: The step proves that every human mind shares one inborn rule for sliding tiles in puzzles
The step shows that the volunteers lack the imagination to try any other approach at all
The step shows the volunteers were all taught the same method by the same teacher earlier
The shared step reflects the puzzle's demands, so it says little about the volunteers
optionExplain: That jumps from a demanded step to a claim about minds that the evidence does not support.
Imagination is not tested by a step that is required.
No shared teaching is needed to explain a required step.
Right: a step needed by every solution is a demand of the puzzle.
questions.explain: A step every solution needs is demanded by the task. The volunteers' own limits show up only where they depart from what is demanded.
questions.teaches: Behavior that departs from what the situation demands is where the subject's own limits, and so his psychology, show.
questions.rule: Behavior demanded by the situation reveals the task environment, not the person.

questions.q: An economist predicts a firm's output from its costs, without studying the owner's mind. What must be assumed about the owner?
options: The owner wants to maximize profit and can find and carry out the best action
The owner has the same personality and outlook as the other owners in the industry
The owner has no emotions of any kind that could disturb the business choices
The owner picks among the available options at random, with no regard to costs
optionExplain: Right: motivation plus ability are the only psychological assumptions needed.
Shared personality is not required.
Emotion is not ruled out; it is simply left aside.
Random choice would make prediction from costs useless.
questions.explain: Prediction from costs works only if the owner can be trusted to pursue the best action. The card next gives the authors' account.
questions.rule: Assume motivation and ability, then infer behavior from the structure of the choices.

questions.q: Economic man is assumed to be motivated to maximize his ____ (or, in some uses, his profit).
questions.explain: Utility is the quantity economic man maximizes in the authors' description.
questions.rule: Assume motivation and ability, then infer behavior from the structure of the choices.

questions.q: A planner predicts commuters take the faster route, taking their wish for speed as given. In the authors' scheme, where does that wish sit?
options: Among the behavior variables the theory must predict
Among the given data of the problem
Among the limits of short-term memory
Among the rival explanations of the environment
optionExplain: Treating it as an output would reopen questions of preference that economics sets aside.
Right: like the utility function, the wish is a given.
Memory limits belong to the subject's psychology, not to the givens.
Rival explanations are not what a given is.
questions.explain: The authors say economics places the utility function among the data given, so preference is not itself explained.
questions.rule: Assume motivation and ability, then infer behavior from the structure of the choices.

questions.q: True or false: On the economist's route, a theory takes preferences as given instead of explaining them.
questions.explain: Preferences are placed among the givens, so the theory does not explain them.
questions.rule: Assume motivation and ability, then infer behavior from the structure of the choices.

questions.q: According to the authors, what does the economist's stratagem let economics study instead of decision-making psychology?
options: The memory limits of the buyers and sellers who take part in the market
The way that preferences are first formed in childhood and later adulthood
The environment of choice, such as markets and cost functions
The emotions of the traders during the heat of trading in the market
optionExplain: Memory limits are a psychological matter the stratagem avoids.
Preference formation is exactly what gets treated as given.
Right: economics turns to the environment of choice.
Emotion is not part of the environment of choice.
questions.explain: By assuming motivation and ability, economics can turn its attention to the structure of the choice environment.
questions.teaches: By assuming motivated, able economic man, economics turns to analyzing the environment of choice, such as markets and cost functions.
questions.rule: Assume motivation and ability, then infer behavior from the structure of the choices.

questions.q: A theory predicts a hungry rat takes the shortest path to food, needing only that it wants food and finds the path. What is it?
options: A full psychological theory of rat memory and the way rats retain maze routes
A theory of how rats learn to prefer one kind of food over another kind
A theory of rat emotion under stress, including fear of open maze spaces
A theory of the task environment's structure, not a psychological theory
optionExplain: Nothing in the theory depends on memory.
Preferences are taken as given, not learned in the theory.
Emotion plays no part in the prediction.
Right: if the subject enters only as motivated and able, the theory describes the task environment.
questions.explain: The authors say a theory of how perfectly rational man behaves in a task needs nothing about the subject beyond adequate motivation, so it is a theory of the environment.
questions.teaches: A theory of how perfectly rational man would behave in a task environment is not a psychological theory but a theory of the structure of that environment.
questions.rule: Assume motivation and ability, then infer behavior from the structure of the choices.

questions.q: A volunteer with good eyesight and real motivation guesses a hidden rule far more slowly than the best strategy allows. Where should we look first?
options: At limits on what the volunteer can work out or carry out
At a flaw in the best strategy itself, which probably does not really work
At the dim lighting of the room, which probably blurred the stimuli
At whether the volunteer really wants the reward offered for success
optionExplain: Right: with motivation and sight secured, the gap points inside the subject.
The best strategy is taken as sound for a given set of possible concepts.
Lighting was stipulated as adequate.
Motivation was stipulated as adequate.
questions.explain: Once motivation and perception are secured, the remaining explanation must be inside the person. The card next shows the authors' account.
questions.rule: When a motivated subject falls short of the rational model, look for limits inside the subject.

questions.q: In simple concept attainment experiments, the key limit on strategy is how many symbols the subject can hold in ____ memory.
questions.explain: The authors name the limit on retaining and manipulating symbols in short-term memory.
questions.rule: When a motivated subject falls short of the rational model, look for limits inside the subject.

questions.q: A student told right or wrong after each guess keeps testing one feature of a hidden rule. What is a likely reason, per the authors?
options: The hidden rule has no optimal strategy that could be followed
Holding several features at once exceeds short-term memory
The student is not paying attention to the sorting task at all
The room is too dim for the student to see the features properly
optionExplain: Such tasks presuppose a set of possible concepts, so an optimal strategy exists.
Right: memory limits explain why efficient strategies are not adopted.
Inattention would reclassify the experiment instead.
Poor sight would turn it into a perception experiment.
questions.explain: Keeping many features in mind at once taxes short-term memory, so the student falls back on a simple strategy.
questions.rule: When a motivated subject falls short of the rational model, look for limits inside the subject.

questions.q: True or false: A subject who tries to spoof the experimenter is still a good case for studying concept formation.
questions.explain: The authors say that if a subject refuses the task or tries to spoof, it would not count as a concept attainment experiment.
questions.rule: When a motivated subject falls short of the rational model, look for limits inside the subject.

questions.q: According to the authors, when does the gap between rational prediction and behavior tend to vanish?
options: Whenever the subject is paid more money for each correct classification made
Whenever the set of possible concepts is small enough to list in full on one page
Whenever the experimenter is present in the room during the whole experiment
Only when the rational behavior is transparently obvious, and not always then
optionExplain: Payment is not the authors' reason.
Set size is not mentioned as the condition.
Presence of the experimenter is not mentioned.
Right: gaps shrink for obvious rational behavior, though not reliably.
questions.explain: The authors add that if a subject does not behave rationally, we may take that as showing the rational behavior was not obvious to him.
questions.teaches: The discrepancies tend to vanish only when the rational behavior is transparently obvious, and even then not always; if the subject fails to act rationally, the behavior was not obvious to him.
questions.rule: When a motivated subject falls short of the rational model, look for limits inside the subject.

questions.q: A taster told right or wrong must name one spice from ten, but needs far more tries than the best strategy. What follows?
options: Study the taster's limits in judging or applying the best strategy
Conclude that the list of ten spices must have been wrong from the start
Conclude that the taster did not really want the prize at all
Conclude that the stew is not a task environment in any proper sense
optionExplain: Right: with motivation assumed, the shortfall points to internal limits.
The set of possible answers is given by the setup.
Motivation is assumed adequate in this case.
A stew with a goal is a task environment.
questions.explain: As in concept attainment, a motivated subject whose behavior falls short of the optimal strategy points to the subject's own limits.
questions.teaches: Experiments of this kind can serve to reveal the structure of human short-term memory, which is why cognitive strain is central in the Bruner-Goodnow-Austin account.
questions.rule: When a motivated subject falls short of the rational model, look for limits inside the subject.

questions.q: A grandmaster plays a perfect defence and a club player errs. What can each performance teach a researcher?
options: Both performances reveal only the different personalities of the grandmaster and the club player
The perfect defence shows the position's structure; the error shows the player's limits
Both performances reveal only the structure of the position
Neither performance says anything beyond who won the game and who lost the game that day
optionExplain: Personality is not what either performance isolates.
Right: matches to the demand reveal the environment; departures reveal the subject.
The error cannot be explained by the position alone.
Both performances carry information.
questions.explain: Fitting behavior points to the environment and departures point to the subject. The card next states this as a two-bladed theory.
questions.rule: A theory of problem solving needs two blades: demands of the task environment and the psychology of the subject.

questions.q: The authors compare their theory to scissors, which cannot cut paper without two ____.
questions.explain: One blade is the analysis of task environments, the other the limits of rational adaptation.
questions.rule: A theory of problem solving needs two blades: demands of the task environment and the psychology of the subject.

questions.q: A study of a delivery driver's routes finds most follow the quickest roads, but one driver often takes odd detours. Which pairing fits the authors?
options: Quick routes inform about the driver's skill; the detours inform about the road network itself
Both kinds of route inform only about the driver
Quick routes inform about the road network; the detours inform about the driver
Both kinds of route inform only about the road network
optionExplain: This reverses the pairing.
The shared quick routes are the demanded behavior.
Right: behavior that fits the demands informs about the environment; departures about the subject.
The detours are what the environment does not explain.
questions.explain: The demanded behavior reflects the road network, while departures from it point to the driver's own mechanisms.
questions.rule: A theory of problem solving needs two blades: demands of the task environment and the psychology of the subject.

questions.q: True or false: A psychologist following the authors' view should attend to the demands of the task environment as well as to the subject.
questions.explain: The authors say the two aspects are like figure and ground, so both belong in the theory.
questions.rule: A theory of problem solving needs two blades: demands of the task environment and the psychology of the subject.

questions.q: Match each piece of behavior with what the authors say it tells us about.
pairs: Moves exactly as the situation demands
The structure of the chess problem space
questions.explain: Fitting behavior points to the environment, departures to the subject, and a grandmaster's play gives information about the chess problem space.
questions.rule: A theory of problem solving needs two blades: demands of the task environment and the psychology of the subject.

questions.q: An exam tutor wants to explain results on a hard question. Using the two-blade idea, which pair of analyses does a full account need?
options: The mood of the examiner and the temperature of the examination room
The students' handwriting and the colour of the pens that they used
The age of the school building and the location of the school itself
The structure of the question and the limits of the students
optionExplain: Mood and temperature are not the two blades.
Handwriting is irrelevant to demands and to limits.
School age and location do not give either blade.
Right: the task's demands plus the solver's limits.
questions.explain: Both parts are needed: what the task requires, and what limits the solver's adaptation to it.
questions.teaches: The authors treat the two aspects as figure and ground: which one is figure depends on the momentary viewpoint, so both stay in the theory.
questions.rule: A theory of problem solving needs two blades: demands of the task environment and the psychology of the subject.

questions.q: A subject looks at a drawing of a cube and reports a box in three dimensions. Which three things should a researcher keep apart?
options: The drawing itself, the subject's reading of it, and the researcher's description
The subject's eyes, the sheet of paper, and the lighting conditions in the experimental room
The subject's age, current mood, and previous training in perception experiments of any kind
The first reading, the second reading, and the final answer the subject gives aloud
optionExplain: Right: the thing, the subject's version, and the theorist's version.
These are physical conditions, not the three distinctions.
These are subject variables, not representations.
These are two readings and an answer, not environment, representation and description.
questions.explain: The drawing, the subject's reading of it and the researcher's account of it are three different things. The card next names them.
questions.rule: Keep apart the environment, the subject's representation of it, and the theorist's description.

questions.q: The figure used to illustrate the perception demonstration is called the ____ cube.
questions.explain: The authors use the Necker cube, a two-dimensional drawing, to illustrate the distinction.
questions.rule: Keep apart the environment, the subject's representation of it, and the theorist's description.

questions.q: Visitors study a printed floor plan of a maze. Which item is the visitor's internal representation, in the authors' sense?
options: The printed plan hanging on the wall of the museum
The mental picture of the layout the visitor uses to plan routes
The curator's written description of the maze, which visitors never read
The actual maze walls in the building that the visitors walk between
optionExplain: The plan is part of the stimulus the visitors are shown.
Right: the representation is internal to the subject.
That is the theorist's description.
That is the environment itself.
questions.explain: The environment is the maze, the description is the curator's, and the problem space is what the visitor builds in the mind.
questions.rule: Keep apart the environment, the subject's representation of it, and the theorist's description.

questions.q: True or false: Since the Necker cube is really two-dimensional, either three-dimensional reading counts as a veridical interpretation of it.
questions.explain: Neither reading is veridical, because the geometric object is two-dimensional.
questions.rule: Keep apart the environment, the subject's representation of it, and the theorist's description.

questions.q: According to the authors, how can the Necker cube stimulus be described adequately?
options: By the subject's internal three-dimensional reading alone
By a complete list of everything the subject says, does and reports while looking at the figure during the whole experiment
By the three-dimensional box that the figure resembles, together with the name that experimenters usually give to the box
By the two-dimensional figure, the conditions of showing it (size, distance, illumination) and the verbal instructions
optionExplain: That would describe the representation, not the stimulus.
Reports of the subject are behavior, not the stimulus.
The box is the subject's reading, not the stimulus.
Right: figure, conditions and instructions.
questions.explain: The stimulus is described by showing the figure, stating the conditions under which it is shown and quoting the instructions.
questions.teaches: The Necker stimulus is described by the two-dimensional figure, the conditions of presentation (size, distance, illumination) and the verbal instructions given.
questions.rule: Keep apart the environment, the subject's representation of it, and the theorist's description.

questions.q: A taste test says: the same juice served cold. Later, results differ with the colour of the cup. What does this show about the description?
options: How much detail a description needs can only be settled empirically
