Descriptions of a juice are veridical once the juice has been named
Cups never matter in taste tests, so the result must be an error
Colour can safely be ignored once the juice itself has been named exactly
optionExplain: Right: whether a detail matters is found by experiment.
The result shows the description left out something that mattered.
The result shows a cup did matter.
The result shows colour mattered here.
questions.explain: Any description short of exhibiting the setup abstracts, so detail that affects behavior can be omitted by accident.
questions.teaches: The amount and fineness of detail needed for a veridical description can in the last analysis be determined only empirically; small imperfections or the experimenter's intonation might matter.
questions.rule: Keep apart the environment, the subject's representation of it, and the theorist's description.

questions.q: When is a written description of an experimental stimulus good enough?
options: When it is long enough to list every physical property that the original stimulus is known to have
When something built from it makes subjects behave as they did with the original
When the experimenter is confident that the description reads well and sounds natural to others
When the subjects themselves agree that the written description of the stimulus is accurate
optionExplain: Length does not guarantee that the behavior-relevant details are included.
Right: the test is the subjects' behavior.
Confidence does not test it.
Subjects need not be able to judge a description.
questions.explain: The test is behavioral: rebuild from the description and see whether subjects respond alike. The card next states this.
questions.rule: A description is veridical only if it matches the vocabulary in which subjects first encode the stimulus.

questions.q: A stimulus description is veridical if a stimulus built from it produces the same ____ in subjects as the original.
questions.explain: The authors give this as the basic test of veridicality.
questions.rule: A description is veridical only if it matches the vocabulary in which subjects first encode the stimulus.

questions.q: Which stimulus could the authors say is easily described in words?
options: A famous oil painting seen under gallery lighting at a museum
A colour photograph of that same famous painting, shown on paper
A plain line drawing of a cube, for human subjects
A bird's song as heard by another bird in the wild
optionExplain: No verbal description would be veridical for the painting.
Even a photograph could not be described except by reproducing it.
Right: line drawings are encoded as lines and plane figures.
The text gives no ground to describe an animal's encoding in our words.
questions.explain: A line drawing can be described because subjects can be assumed to encode it as line segments.
questions.rule: A description is veridical only if it matches the vocabulary in which subjects first encode the stimulus.

questions.q: Researchers use the same line description for a drawing shown to humans and to frogs. What does the authors' view predict?
options: It will hold for any species
It holds only for the most intelligent species among those tested
It fails for humans too
It may fail for frogs, who may encode the drawing in other ways
optionExplain: Species can differ in encoding.
Intelligence is not the issue in the authors' remark.
Human experience supports line descriptions.
Right: the authors call line descriptions rash for a frog.
questions.explain: Veridicality depends on the subject's encoding, which experience can vouch for only with subjects like us.
questions.rule: A description is veridical only if it matches the vocabulary in which subjects first encode the stimulus.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say that describing a stimulus also postulates something about the subject's initial processing of it.
questions.explain: A description predicts the vocabulary of elements and relations the subject will use in his initial encoding.
questions.rule: A description is veridical only if it matches the vocabulary in which subjects first encode the stimulus.

questions.q: A team finds a vision program cannot pick out straight lines in photos though people do it with ease. What do the authors' remarks suggest?
options: Seeing lines needs a nontrivial encoding scheme, inborn or learned
The photos contain no lines, so no program could ever find any in them
People cannot really see lines and only think they do when they look
Programs rarely fail at pattern recognition, so this failure must be a bug
optionExplain: Right: the program's difficulty shows the encoding is not trivial.
The authors take lines in drawings to be present; the issue is encoding.
People do perceive lines; they have an encoding scheme.
The difficulty of pattern-recognizing devices is the authors' evidence.
questions.explain: The authors cite the trouble of building pattern-recognizing devices as evidence that representing stimuli as lines needs an encoding scheme.
questions.teaches: Only a subject whose inborn mechanisms provide a line-encoding scheme, or who has acquired one by learning, perceives the Necker cube as a few line segments.
questions.rule: A description is veridical only if it matches the vocabulary in which subjects first encode the stimulus.

questions.q: A chess player is deciding on a move. Which set best describes the space in which her thinking happens?
options: Only the legal moves that are actually available to her on the board at that moment
Positions and moves she considers, including ones she imagines and may reject
The chess board and all of the pieces standing on it, which she looks at while thinking
The moves that she finally makes in the game, written down by the scorekeeper in the game record
optionExplain: Legal moves are only part of what she may consider.
Right: thinking covers considered and imagined alternatives.
The board is the environment, not the space of thought.
Final moves are only the overt part.
questions.explain: The space is wider than what is played. The card next names it.
questions.rule: A problem space is the subject's internal representation of initial, goal and intermediate states and of the changes possible among them.

questions.q: The space in which a subject's problem solving activities take place is called the problem ____.
questions.explain: The authors call it the problem space.
questions.rule: A problem space is the subject's internal representation of initial, goal and intermediate states and of the changes possible among them.

questions.q: Dana plans a route home and imagines a shortcut that turns out to be closed. Was the shortcut part of her problem space?
options: No: only routes that are actually open belong to the problem space at all, not imagined ones
No: only the single route that she finally walks belongs to her problem space
Yes: behaviors considered in thought count even if they prove infeasible
Yes, but only if she says the shortcut aloud so that an observer can record it
optionExplain: Feasibility is not the test; consideration is.
The space includes unchosen alternatives.
Right: the space includes considered behaviors.
Speaking aloud gives evidence but is not required.
questions.explain: The problem space contains what the subject considers, not just what is possible or done.
questions.rule: A problem space is the subject's internal representation of initial, goal and intermediate states and of the changes possible among them.

questions.q: True or false: A subject's problem space is the list of legal moves in the rulebook, and nothing more.
questions.explain: The space is the subject's own representation, including states and moves he considers that may be illegal.
questions.rule: A problem space is the subject's internal representation of initial, goal and intermediate states and of the changes possible among them.

questions.q: How do the authors say they will describe the subject's behavior?
options: In molar terms, not by coordinates of body parts or sound waves
In molecular terms, by the space-time coordinates of body parts and sound waves
Only by what he says aloud while solving
Only by his final answer
optionExplain: Right: molar rather than molecular.
The authors rule out molecular detail.
Speech is only one source of evidence.
Final answers omit the thinking responses they want to describe.
questions.explain: The description is molar, but it still includes internal thinking responses and the set of behaviors from which they are drawn.
questions.teaches: The description of behavior will be molar rather than molecular: the authors will not refer to space-time coordinates of body parts or sound waves from the mouth.
questions.rule: A problem space is the subject's internal representation of initial, goal and intermediate states and of the changes possible among them.

questions.q: Two classmates solve the same puzzle. How should a teacher describe each pupil's problem space, in the authors' terms?
options: Read it off the puzzle's rule sheet, which is the same for both pupils and therefore fixes both spaces
Build a representation of each pupil's space from the instructions and what the pupil does
Measure the pupil's body movements and sound waves in great detail until the space shows itself
Assume that both pupils' problem spaces are identical
optionExplain: The rule sheet gives the stimulus, not each pupil's space.
Right: the space is the subject's representation and must be constructed.
Body movements are molecular, not the space.
Spaces may differ between subjects.
questions.explain: The subject encodes the instructions and stimuli into goals, rules and states, so the teacher must infer each space.
questions.teaches: The subject must himself encode the presented instructions and stimuli, defining goals, rules and other aspects of the situation, in some kind of space.
questions.rule: A problem space is the subject's internal representation of initial, goal and intermediate states and of the changes possible among them.

questions.q: A two-player game of perfect information has a finite tree of plays. What does this guarantee?
options: The first player must be able to win the game whenever he plays well enough
The game cannot ever end in a draw
An optimal strategy can be found with a finite number of calculations
The players will find the best play unaided, without needing any calculation at all
optionExplain: Nothing says the first player wins.
Draws are possible in number scrabble.
Right: examine the whole tree and the strategy follows.
Finding the strategy is possible in principle, not guaranteed for players.
questions.explain: Finiteness makes exhaustive calculation possible. The card next shows how the authors use it.
questions.rule: A finite game of perfect information has a game tree, and minimax works backward through it.

questions.q: Every possible play of number scrabble can be represented by a ____ of the nine digits.
questions.explain: The order in which the digits are drawn is a permutation of the nine digits.
questions.rule: A finite game of perfect information has a game tree, and minimax works backward through it.

questions.q: A game has three tokens, drawn one at a time until all are gone. How many complete plays does its tree hold?
optionExplain: 3 is the number of first moves, not the number of complete plays.
9 adds the numbers instead of multiplying.
27 would allow tokens to repeat.
Right: 3 x 2 x 1 orders, as with permutations of nine digits.
questions.explain: Each complete play is an ordering of the three tokens, and there are six orderings.
questions.rule: A finite game of perfect information has a game tree, and minimax works backward through it.

questions.q: At your opponent's turn, minimax offers you the outcomes win, draw and lose from three sub-branches. What value does that node get?
options: Lose
Win
Draw
The average of the three
optionExplain: Right: assume the opponent picks the worst for you.
Win assumes the opponent helps you.
Draw is not the worst outcome.
Minimax takes the opponent's choice, not an average.
questions.explain: At the opponent's nodes assign the worst outcome for you; at your own, the best.
questions.rule: A finite game of perfect information has a game tree, and minimax works backward through it.

questions.q: Put the steps of the minimax procedure in order.
items: Examine all branches of the game tree
Give each terminal a value of win, draw or lose
Work backward from the terminals through the tree
Give own-turn nodes the best outcome and opponent-turn nodes the worst
Read off the best first move
questions.explain: The procedure runs from the terminals backward, applying best at own turns and worst at the opponent's.
questions.rule: A finite game of perfect information has a game tree, and minimax works backward through it.

questions.q: A new game ends as soon as someone completes a line, even with tokens left. Why can parts of its full tree be left out?
options: The tree can never be finite for games that are allowed to end early
Branches that continue after the game has ended are never played
Players avoid the early branches
Minimax does not apply to games that can end before all pieces are drawn
optionExplain: Early ending shortens plays and keeps the tree finite.
Right: moves after the end are not part of real plays.
Avoiding branches is a matter of choice, not structure.
Minimax applies to any finite tree.
questions.explain: Such branches are inessential because the game would already be over.
questions.teaches: Some branches of the number scrabble tree are inessential, because the game can end before the ninth move.
questions.rule: A finite game of perfect information has a game tree, and minimax works backward through it.

questions.q: A player holding 5 and 8 considers a 2 that was already drawn. What should a theory of his thinking do with that idea?
options: Drop it, since the move is illegal and so cannot count
Drop it, since the move was never actually played in the game
Include it, since the player considered it
Include it only if the idea would have led to success in the end
optionExplain: Illegal moves can still be thought of.
Unplayed moves can still be considered.
Right: considered moves belong in the representation.
Success is not the test.
questions.explain: The player's thought of the 2 happened, even though the move is unavailable. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Represent the moves a subject considers, even those that are illegal or impossible.

questions.q: The authors say we must represent the subject's wishes and ____ as well as his more realistic thoughts.
questions.explain: They use wishes and dreams for considered behaviors that prove infeasible or illegal.
questions.rule: Represent the moves a subject considers, even those that are illegal or impossible.

questions.q: A player in a word game thinks of a word, then finds it was already used. Where do the authors place the word?
options: outside the problem space altogether
relevant to the problem space only after the word has been played
evidence that the player misread the rules of the word game completely
part of the problem space, though outside the legal moves
optionExplain: Legality does not remove it from the space.
Playing is not needed.
Considering it need not signal a misreading.
Right: considered moves are in the space.
questions.explain: The authors count considered-but-illegal moves inside the subject's problem space.
questions.rule: Represent the moves a subject considers, even those that are illegal or impossible.

questions.q: True or false: If a theory represents only legal moves, it cannot account for a player who says aloud that there is no 3.
questions.explain: Such a remark shows the player went outside the game tree, which a legal-moves-only representation lacks.
questions.rule: Represent the moves a subject considers, even those that are illegal or impossible.

questions.q: A chess student plans a bishop move, then realizes the bishop would be pinned and cannot move. Which representation describes the student's thinking best?
options: One that includes the pinned move as something considered
One that includes only the moves that are actually available to her
One that includes only the moves that the teacher would approve of
One that includes only the final move that the student plays
optionExplain: Right: the considered move is part of the thinking.
Available moves omit what the student actually considered.
Teacher approval is not the test.
The final move leaves out the deliberation.
questions.explain: The representation must hold what the subject considered, as the authors say of wishes and dreams.
questions.teaches: An overt remark such as saying there is no 3 gives concrete evidence that the subject has gone outside the game tree.
questions.rule: Represent the moves a subject considers, even those that are illegal or impossible.

questions.q: Two games are formally equivalent. Does a champion of the first immediately play the second at champion level?
options: Yes: the games are the same game, so skill at one transfers to the other at once
Not necessarily: the strategy must be translated or the representation recoded
No: formal equivalence means that the two games are unrelated in structure and rules
Yes, but only against beginners
optionExplain: The authors say transfer is not at all easy.
Right: equivalence in structure does not give automatic transfer.
Equivalence means the structure is shared.
Level of the opponent is not the point.
questions.explain: Formal sameness differs from psychological ease of transfer. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Formally equivalent games can be played with different internal representations, and strategy does not transfer automatically.

questions.q: In the magic square used to link the two games, every row, column and diagonal sums to ____.
questions.explain: Each line of the magic square is a triple of digits that sums to 15.
questions.rule: Formally equivalent games can be played with different internal representations, and strategy does not transfer automatically.

questions.q: Using the magic square, a number scrabble player wants the digit that plays the role of the center square. Which digit is it?
optionExplain: 1 is a side square.
9 is a side square.
Right: the center square is 5.
3 is a side square.
questions.explain: In the magic square, 5 is in the center, even digits are corners and the other odd digits are sides.
questions.rule: Formally equivalent games can be played with different internal representations, and strategy does not transfer automatically.

questions.q: A tic-tac-toe expert plays number scrabble with no pencil and no knowledge of the magic square. What do the authors expect?
options: Perfect play at once, since the games are equivalent
The expert will refuse to play the unfamiliar game
The expert will lose every single game against any opponent
Transferring the strategy is not easy
optionExplain: Formal equivalence does not give instant transfer.
The authors do not predict refusal.
They do not predict certain defeat.
Right: experts will find transfer hard.
questions.explain: Tic-tac-toe experts can readily persuade themselves the transfer is not easy.
questions.rule: Formally equivalent games can be played with different internal representations, and strategy does not transfer automatically.

questions.q: Match each tic-tac-toe term to its number scrabble translation.
pairs: The ten's complement of the digit
questions.explain: The authors translate squares into digits: center is 5, corners even, sides odd but not 5, and opposite means ten's complement.
questions.rule: Formally equivalent games can be played with different internal representations, and strategy does not transfer automatically.

questions.q: Two players must play number scrabble using tic-tac-toe skill, with no pencil. One has strong visual imagery. Which route suits her?
options: Memorize the magic square and picture each drawn piece as a mark on it
Count the digits remaining in the center and play whichever digit is left
Translate each move into a chess opening and play the opening's reply
Ignore the digits and play only by the position names of the squares
optionExplain: Right: this is the visual-imagery route the authors describe.
Counting remaining digits does not use the tic-tac-toe strategy.
Chess openings are unrelated to the equivalence.
Digits have no positions unless the square is used.
questions.explain: A player with imagery can see two-in-a-row, center, side and corner on the memorized square.
questions.teaches: A player gifted with visual imagery can memorize the magic square and visualize each drawn piece as an O or X on it; the authors verified this is feasible for at least some subjects.
questions.rule: Formally equivalent games can be played with different internal representations, and strategy does not transfer automatically.

questions.q: Subjects playing the same game use different internal pictures of it. Which description should the experimenter treat as the true one?
options: The one the experimenter personally finds simplest to use
None can claim to be the only correct one
The one that the largest number of subjects happen to use
The one set out in the printed rulebook of the game
optionExplain: Simplicity does not make it true.
Right: no description has exclusive veridicality.
Popularity does not make it exclusive.
The rulebook gives one representation, not the privileged one.
questions.explain: No representation is privileged. The card next states the authors' position.
questions.rule: No single representation of a task environment is the true one, so a theory cannot assume it.

questions.q: The authors call the problem of choosing a single description a ____ knot.
questions.explain: They ask whether the Gordian knot can be cut instead of untied.
questions.rule: No single representation of a task environment is the true one, so a theory cannot assume it.

questions.q: Two cooks describe a recipe, one by steps and one by the dish wanted. Which describes the task truly, as the authors see it?
options: The step version must be the true description of the recipe
The dish version must be the true description of the recipe
Neither has an exclusive claim to be the objective one
The longer of the two descriptions must be the true one
optionExplain: Steps are one representation among others.
The target is also just one representation.
Right: both are descriptions that subjects could use.
Length does not make a description true.
questions.explain: As with the two games, no particular description gets an exclusive claim.
questions.rule: No single representation of a task environment is the true one, so a theory cannot assume it.

questions.q: True or false: Because the experimenter chooses the description, the experimenter's description is automatically more objective than the player's.
questions.explain: The authors say the experimenter's description would be no less subjective than the player's.
questions.rule: No single representation of a task environment is the true one, so a theory cannot assume it.

questions.q: A researcher writes down the representation she thinks a subject uses and tests it on behavior, not describing one true task. What is she doing?
options: Replacing the stimulus with the real problem that only the experimenter fully knows about
Assuming that every subject shares one and the same internal representation of the task
Dropping the study of behavior and relying on the subjects' own reports instead
Putting hypotheses about the subject's internal representation into the theory
optionExplain: The real problem is exactly what she is not describing.
Nothing assumes all subjects share one representation.
Behavior is what tests the hypothesis.
Right: this is the first way out the authors name.
questions.explain: Instead of an objective problem space, the theory carries hypotheses about the subject's own representation.
questions.teaches: One way out is to omit a description of the objective problem space and instead incorporate in the theory hypotheses about the internal representation the subject will himself use.
questions.rule: No single representation of a task environment is the true one, so a theory cannot assume it.

questions.q: A researcher wants to predict how a rewording of a puzzle changes solving. What must the theory describe?
options: The wording and the feedback the solver receives
The puzzle's true nature, independent of any subject's view of it
The solver's full life history, including schooling and past puzzles
The best possible solution to the puzzle and nothing else besides
optionExplain: Right: stimulus and feedback rules are the independent variables.
No one knows the real problem independently of a subject.
Life history is not required.
The best solution omits the stimulus differences.
questions.explain: The subject responds to what is presented, not to the real problem. The card next states this.
questions.rule: Use the stimulus and feedback rules as the independent variables, not an unknowable real problem.

questions.q: The independent variable in this approach is the ____, including feedback from the environment.
questions.explain: The stimulus including feedback enters as the independent variable.
questions.rule: Use the stimulus and feedback rules as the independent variables, not an unknowable real problem.

questions.q: Two groups see the same maze with different instructions. To predict their routes, what must be specified?
options: The designer's private intention in building the maze
The instructions and the feedback each group gets
The maze's hidden best answer that nobody has yet found
The weather on the day each group took the test
optionExplain: The designer's intention is not what subjects respond to.
Right: instructions and feedback are the stimulus.
The best answer is not the stimulus.
Weather is irrelevant to the stimulus.
questions.explain: Subjects respond to the stimulus including feedback, so these are what the theory should describe.
questions.rule: Use the stimulus and feedback rules as the independent variables, not an unknowable real problem.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, subjects' behavior depends on the stimulus they are shown, not on what the problem really is.
questions.explain: Behavior can depend only on the stimulus, since neither subject nor experimenter knows what the problem really is.
questions.rule: Use the stimulus and feedback rules as the independent variables, not an unknowable real problem.

questions.q: A teacher describes only the prompt the pupils get and her replies, not the true problem. Which part of the authors' view does this match?
options: The problem space must be described objectively and in full
The problem is identical for every pupil who takes part
Stimulus and feedback rules enter as independent variables
The teacher's replies are irrelevant to what the pupil does
optionExplain: The teacher is avoiding an objective problem space.
Pupils may see different problems.
Right: this is the stimulus-plus-feedback approach.
Feedback is part of the stimulus.
questions.explain: Prompt plus feedback are what the pupil actually meets.
questions.teaches: Differences in problem statements can be studied by describing only the stimulus and feedback rules, without describing the external task environment.
questions.rule: Use the stimulus and feedback rules as the independent variables, not an unknowable real problem.

questions.q: People study a task at length until new ways of viewing it appear rarely. What can a researcher then take as the real task?
options: Only the single most popular way that people have found
Whatever the researcher happened to guess at the start
The way that was found first, before all the others
The whole set of ways found, with their mappings
optionExplain: Popularity does not define the environment.
The first guess has no special status.
Order of discovery does not define it.
Right: the set generated up to the asymptote, with mappings.
questions.explain: The idea is to wait until the supply of representations dries up. The card next states it.
questions.rule: Equate the real environment with the set of representations people generate until new ones stop appearing, plus the mappings among them.

questions.q: The rate at which subjects generate new representations gradually decreases toward an ____.
questions.explain: The authors equate the real environment with the representations generated up to the time this asymptote is reached.
questions.rule: Equate the real environment with the set of representations people generate until new ones stop appearing, plus the mappings among them.

questions.q: A forum has produced twelve distinct ways to analyze a puzzle, none new this year. Under the authors' strategy, what stands for the puzzle itself?
options: The twelve ways together with the mappings between them
The longest thread on the forum about the puzzle's analysis
The method used by the person who founded the forum
The newest way, as the latest way supersedes all the older ones
optionExplain: Right: all representations plus mappings.
Length does not define the puzzle.
Authority is not the test.
Recency is not the test.
questions.explain: Once new representations stop appearing, the set and the mappings among them serve as the real environment.
questions.rule: Equate the real environment with the set of representations people generate until new ones stop appearing, plus the mappings among them.

questions.q: True or false: The requirement is easier to meet when the situation is complex relative to the time subjects have to analyze it.
questions.explain: With a lot of complexity and little time, subjects cannot exhaust it, so an experimenter with more time can approximate the full set.
questions.rule: Equate the real environment with the set of representations people generate until new ones stop appearing, plus the mappings among them.

questions.q: According to the authors, for which of their three tasks do they fall short of this strategy?
options: Cryptarithmetic
Chess
Elementary logic
All three
optionExplain: They say they conform reasonably for cryptarithmetic.
Right: with masters they cannot out-analyze the subjects.
They say they conform reasonably for elementary logic.
Only one task is named as falling short.
questions.explain: The authors can study cryptarithmetic and logic more thoroughly than their subjects, but not chess masters' domain.
questions.teaches: The authors conform reasonably with this strategy for cryptarithmetic and elementary logic but fall short with chess, since they cannot understand the task better than masters and grandmasters.
questions.rule: Equate the real environment with the set of representations people generate until new ones stop appearing, plus the mappings among them.

questions.q: A researcher with no special talent wants a full list of ways to see a card game. What lets her approximate it, per the authors?
options: Being more intelligent than every one of the subjects she studies
Asking one single expert player for the way he sees the game
Spending far more time analyzing the game than any subject has
Playing the game once herself, from beginning to end, with care
optionExplain: The authors say she need not be more intelligent.
One expert gives only one representation.
Right: time, even without superior intelligence, can meet the requirement.
One game gives little coverage.
questions.explain: Time spent on analysis can compensate for equal intelligence.
questions.teaches: The experimenter, even if no more intelligent than his subjects, can meet the requirement by devoting much more time to the analysis than any subject has, or by withholding some information from them.
questions.rule: Equate the real environment with the set of representations people generate until new ones stop appearing, plus the mappings among them.

questions.q: A researcher guesses that a subject pictures the magic square. Which later behavior would count most against the guess?
options: Scanning rows, columns and diagonals for two marks that stand in a row together
Taking the digit 5 first, as the center of the magic square
Naming the corner squares when talking about where to play
Adding two digits that share no line and working out a third one needed
optionExplain: Scanning lines fits the magic square.
Taking the center fits too.
Corner talk fits the square.
Right: arithmetic on non-collinear digits points to another space.
questions.explain: Behavior that the magic square representation would not produce counts against it. The card next explains.
questions.rule: A hypothesis about a subject's problem space is testable when rival spaces predict different behavior.

questions.q: On the magic square, any three digits that sum to 15 lie in a row, column or ____.
questions.explain: The eight triples that sum to 15 are exactly the eight lines of the square.
questions.rule: A hypothesis about a subject's problem space is testable when rival spaces predict different behavior.

questions.q: A subject holding 1 and 2 says that makes 3, so he needs 12, and looks for one. What does this suggest about his representation?
options: He is using arithmetic reasoning, not the magic square
He is using the magic square to find the digit that he needs
He has misread the rules of tic-tac-toe in an odd way
He has no representation of the game at all in mind
optionExplain: Right: 1 and 2 share no line, so a square user would not build on them.
The square gives no basis for this pair.
The subject is playing number scrabble.
Any search for a needed piece shows a representation.
questions.explain: Digits 1 and 2 lie on no common line of the magic square, so the behavior fits an arithmetic problem space.
questions.rule: A hypothesis about a subject's problem space is testable when rival spaces predict different behavior.

questions.q: True or false: If two representations would produce different moves on some task, that task can tell which one a subject uses.
questions.explain: Testing works when rival spaces lead to different behavior.
questions.rule: A hypothesis about a subject's problem space is testable when rival spaces predict different behavior.

questions.q: Why do the authors say hypotheses about representations are a major source of predictive power?
options: They always turn out to be true, so no later experiment is needed to confirm them at all, ever
They need no testing against behavior
An assumed problem space has many consequences for behavior, permitting many predictions
They remove the need for any description of the task environment in the theory at all
optionExplain: The authors test them rather than assume truth.
They are empirically testable.
Right: one assumption yields many predictions.
They are used alongside the task environment.
questions.explain: A single assumption about the space fixes many details of expected behavior.
questions.teaches: Assuming that a particular problem space is used generally has many consequences for behavior, hence permits many predictions.
questions.rule: A hypothesis about a subject's problem space is testable when rival spaces predict different behavior.

questions.q: A lab finds children use one of three ways of picturing fractions across many tasks. What does that do for the authors' kind of theory?
options: It makes the theory untestable
It makes each task need its own separate problem space, one task at a time
It removes the need for any hypotheses about what subjects represent
It makes it more parsimonious: few representations reused across tasks
optionExplain: Fewer spaces leave it more testable.
Reuse across tasks is the opposite of one space per task.
Hypotheses remain needed.
Right: few, widely reused representations greatly enhance parsimony.
questions.explain: A modest number of representations used across many tasks gives the theory economy.
questions.teaches: Parsimony is greatly enhanced if the number of representations available to human subjects is quite modest and the same representations are used across a considerable range of tasks.
questions.rule: A hypothesis about a subject's problem space is testable when rival spaces predict different behavior.

questions.q: A person solves a puzzle in silence, with no sentences in mind. How does the authors' account treat this?
options: Thinking happened in internal symbol structures, not necessarily sentences
Thinking cannot happen without sentences, so the person must have used words
Nothing was processed at all
Only gestures were used
optionExplain: Right: surface sentences are inessential.
This is the view that thought equals language.
Silence does not mean nothing processed.
Gestures are not required.
questions.explain: The authors separate surface sentences from deep structure. The card next states their position.
questions.rule: Surface language is clothing for conveying thought; deep structure, the internal symbol structures, is necessary for thinking.

questions.q: The authors say surface structure is the garb, or clothing, of thought, needed only for ____ it.
questions.explain: Surface structure conveys thought but is not needed for thinking.
questions.rule: Surface language is clothing for conveying thought; deep structure, the internal symbol structures, is necessary for thinking.

questions.q: A mathematician thinks through a proof wordlessly and then writes it up. In the authors' terms, what is the write-up?
options: Deep structure itself, written out in full on paper
Surface structure used to convey the thought
The only place where the proof really exists at all
Unrelated to the thought that the mathematician had earlier
optionExplain: The deep structure is the internal symbol structure.
Right: surface strings convey thought.
The authors do not make writing the only home of the proof.
Writing conveys what was thought.
questions.explain: The written sentences are surface strings that convey the internal structure.
questions.rule: Surface language is clothing for conveying thought; deep structure, the internal symbol structures, is necessary for thinking.

questions.q: True or false: The authors argue that thinking cannot occur without any language in any sense.
questions.explain: If language means deep structure, it is essential; surface language is not.
questions.rule: Surface language is clothing for conveying thought; deep structure, the internal symbol structures, is necessary for thinking.

questions.q: How do the authors say their internal structures differ from linguists' deep structures as sketched so far?
options: They are shorter than single sentences and tied to single words instead
They are identical to the spoken words of ordinary natural language speech
They are large, interrelated contexts extending beyond single sentences
They are limited to one language, the one the subject speaks natively
optionExplain: They are larger, not shorter.
They are not the words themselves.
Right: contexts beyond sentence boundaries.
They are not tied to one language.
questions.explain: Such contexts may help explain how context determines the meaning of otherwise ambiguous strings.
questions.teaches: Linguists tie each deep structure to a single sentence, but the authors' problem structures form large complex contexts beyond sentence boundaries, a route to explaining how context settles ambiguous strings.
questions.rule: Surface language is clothing for conveying thought; deep structure, the internal symbol structures, is necessary for thinking.

questions.q: A critic proposes that the mind carries sentence-level deep structures in parallel with the problem representations. How do the authors respond?
options: It is the simplest option
It is required by the data, which cannot be explained without it
It is already proven, so the authors accept it with no hesitation
It multiplies hypothetical entities without evidence
optionExplain: They prefer the simpler course.
They deny the data require it.
They deny it has evidential support.
Right: they call it unnecessary and unparsimonious.
questions.explain: They prefer identifying deep structures with semantics and the internal symbol structures.
questions.teaches: The authors prefer the simpler course that identifies deep structures closely with semantics, hence with the internal symbol structures that are the media of thought.
questions.rule: Surface language is clothing for conveying thought; deep structure, the internal symbol structures, is necessary for thinking.

questions.q: In an information processing system, how would the pieces a player holds in a card game be stored?
options: As a list attached to the player
As a single number held by the player
As a process that runs once the game begins
As a rule written into the game
optionExplain: Right: sets of objects are lists.
A number would lose the set.
Processes represent moves, not sets.
Rules would be programs, not stored sets.
questions.explain: The card next states the correspondence.
questions.rule: Objects are symbols, sets are lists, relations are associations, and moves are processes that edit those structures.

questions.q: Match each part of the problem to how the IPS represents it.
questions.explain: These four correspondences are the core of the encoding.
questions.rule: Objects are symbols, sets are lists, relations are associations, and moves are processes that edit those structures.

questions.q: At the start of number scrabble, what do the lists hold in this representation?
options: Each player holding four pieces, with one piece left in the unmoved list
Both players' lists empty and unmoved-pieces holding all nine pieces
Unmoved-pieces empty and the pieces already shared out between the players
Player 1 holding all nine pieces, with player 2 holding no pieces at all
optionExplain: Pieces are held only after drawing.
Right: nothing has been drawn.
Unmoved-pieces starts full.
Player 1 starts with none.
questions.explain: A move later deletes a piece from unmoved-pieces and inserts it on the mover's own-pieces list.
questions.rule: Objects are symbols, sets are lists, relations are associations, and moves are processes that edit those structures.

questions.q: True or false: When player 2 draws piece 6, the move process removes it from unmoved-pieces and adds it to player 2's own-pieces.
questions.explain: A move process changes the internal structures to correspond with the external change.
questions.rule: Objects are symbols, sets are lists, relations are associations, and moves are processes that edit those structures.

questions.q: A librarian's system records which books each reader has out and which are on the shelf. Which mapping matches the authors' encoding?
options: Each reader as a process, each book as a relation, and the act of checking out as a symbol
The shelf as an association; checking out as an object; and each reader as the list of books
Books as lists of readers; readers as processes; and the shelf as the relation between them all
Shelf and each reader's books as lists; checking out as a process moving a book between them
optionExplain: Readers are objects, not processes.
The shelf is a set, not an association; checking out is a move.
Books are objects, not lists.
Right: sets are lists and moves are processes.
questions.explain: The same scheme carries over: sets as lists, moves as processes that shift items between lists.
questions.teaches: The primitive processes can themselves be expressed as programs in terms of still more primitive processes for manipulating and testing lists and associations, at the level of counting fingers for arithmetic.
questions.rule: Objects are symbols, sets are lists, relations are associations, and moves are processes that edit those structures.

questions.q: A player holds digits 6 and 8 in number scrabble. Which digit completes a winning triple?
optionExplain: 7 would make 21.
9 would make 23.
3 would make 17.
questions.explain: The needed digit is the 15's complement of the sum. The card next shows the procedure.
questions.rule: Generate own pairs, compute the 15's complement of each sum, and search the unmoved pieces for it.

questions.q: The complement process takes an integer and produces its difference from ____.
questions.explain: The complement here is the 15's complement.
questions.rule: Generate own pairs, compute the 15's complement of each sum, and search the unmoved pieces for it.

questions.q: Order the steps the program takes to find a winning move.
items: Generate a pair from the player's own pieces
Sum the integers on the pair
Compute the complement of the sum
Search the unmoved pieces for that integer
Move the matching piece, or report no move
questions.explain: The program runs from a pair, to its sum, to the needed digit, and then to a search of unmoved pieces.
questions.rule: Generate own pairs, compute the 15's complement of each sum, and search the unmoved pieces for it.

questions.q: A player holds 2, 9 and 5. The unmoved pieces are 3, 4 and 7. Which draw wins at once?
options: 7, the sum of 2 and 5
4, completing 2 + 9 + 4
3, the smallest unmoved digit
No draw wins
optionExplain: 7 is the sum of 2 and 5, not the digit they need; the digit needed is 8, which is gone.
Right: 2 + 9 = 11 and 4 brings it to 15.
Smallest does not mean winning; 3 completes no pair.
A winning digit is available.
questions.explain: Check each pair: 2 and 9 need 4; 2 and 5 need 8; 9 and 5 need 1. Only 4 is unmoved.
questions.rule: Generate own pairs, compute the 15's complement of each sum, and search the unmoved pieces for it.

questions.q: Efficiency idea: after each move, which pairs does a smarter version need to examine?
options: All of the pairs again, starting from the very beginning of the game
Only pairs made up of unmoved pieces on the table
Only the pairs containing the most recently moved piece
No pairs at all, since the search is now complete
optionExplain: That repeats work.
Unmoved pieces are not the player's.
Right: older pairs were examined already.
Pairs are needed.
questions.explain: Older pairs were checked on earlier moves.
questions.teaches: A more efficient process examines only pairs containing the most recently moved piece, since the others were already considered on a previous move.
questions.rule: Generate own pairs, compute the 15's complement of each sum, and search the unmoved pieces for it.

questions.q: The two games are equivalent, yet spotting a fork is easier on a tic-tac-toe grid. Why?
options: The grid has fewer winning lines than the number scrabble layout
The games are not really equivalent after all, despite appearances
Forks do not exist in number scrabble, so there is nothing to find
The grid makes the needed lines directly available to scanning
optionExplain: Both have the same eight lines.
They are formally equivalent.
Forks exist in both.
Right: what is easy to read off differs by representation.
questions.explain: Ease depends on what the representation makes accessible. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Equivalent representations differ in which information is readily accessible, and that decides how costly a process is.

questions.q: A forking move sets up two possible winning moves for the next ____, so the opponent cannot counter both.
questions.explain: The opponent can block only one of the two threats.
questions.rule: Equivalent representations differ in which information is readily accessible, and that decides how costly a process is.

questions.q: One group gets a road network as a map, another as junction pairs. Both must find where two roads meet. Whose task is cheaper?
options: The map group's, since the lines are directly scannable
The list group's, since a list of pairs is exact and complete
Equal, since both groups are given exactly the same network
Neither group can find the town, since no map shows meetings
optionExplain: Right: accessible information is cheap to use.
Exactness does not give accessibility.
Same network does not mean same cost.
Both can, at different cost.
questions.explain: The same facts are costly to extract from one format and easy from another.
questions.rule: Equivalent representations differ in which information is readily accessible, and that decides how costly a process is.

questions.q: A number scrabble player memorizes, for each digit, the triads that contain it. What do the authors expect for her fork search?
options: It stays as costly as before
Essentially the simple tic-tac-toe process becomes available
It becomes impossible, since memorizing disturbs the other lists
It no longer needs the unmoved pieces, which are dropped
optionExplain: Memorized lists remove the cost.
Right: the missing accessible information is exactly what she has added.
Memorizing makes it easier.
The search still needs unmoved pieces.
questions.explain: The authors say the lists could be stored in memory and the same process used.
questions.rule: Equivalent representations differ in which information is readily accessible, and that decides how costly a process is.

questions.q: True or false: Finding a fork is hard in number scrabble because the game itself is harder than tic-tac-toe.
questions.explain: The games are formally equivalent; the difference lies in which information the representation makes readily accessible.
questions.rule: Equivalent representations differ in which information is readily accessible, and that decides how costly a process is.

questions.q: A tic-tac-toe program already finds forks cheaply. What further saving do the authors mention?
options: Searching through all of the pairs afresh on every turn
Dropping the triad lists to save on storage space
Using only the corner squares for every forking move
Marking triads that are already blocked
optionExplain: That would add cost.
Removing the lists removes the shortcut.
Squares are not restricted to corners.
Right: marking blocked triads further cheapens the search.
questions.explain: A blocked triad cannot yield a win, so it can be skipped.
questions.teaches: In the tic-tac-toe representation, triads already blocked could be marked, further cheapening the search for forking moves.
questions.rule: Equivalent representations differ in which information is readily accessible, and that decides how costly a process is.

questions.q: A theory says a player finds the pairs of his digits that sum to 15. Must it spell out how the system adds?
options: Not when the process is definite and elementary
Yes, every step of the arithmetic must be spelled out
Yes, in binary, since that is how the machine adds
Never, in any theory, because detail is not needed
optionExplain: Right: some encoding and programs can be assumed.
Spelling out every step is not required.
Binary is not required.
There are cases where detail is given.
questions.explain: Definite, elementary processes can be assumed. The card next states the authors' practice.
questions.rule: For definite, elementary processes, assume an encoding and programs exist and describe at a higher level.

questions.q: The authors say they will generally ____ above the level of detailed encodings and programs.
questions.explain: They float above that level except where the encoding becomes important.
questions.rule: For definite, elementary processes, assume an encoding and programs exist and describe at a higher level.

questions.q: True or false: A recipe saying fold the egg whites, without describing hand motions, parallels assuming definite, elementary processes need no spelled-out detail.
questions.explain: The cook is assumed to have the lower-level skill, as the theory assumes an encoding and programs exist.
questions.rule: For definite, elementary processes, assume an encoding and programs exist and describe at a higher level.

questions.q: According to the authors, what makes lists and associations convenient as representations?
options: They run fastest on every kind of computer on which a theorist might try them out
They need fixed addresses in memory, so that each item has exactly one place
New information can be added to memory without destroying what is encoded
They keep all information in one fixed order that new items cannot disturb at all
optionExplain: The authors do not claim speed.
Linear addresses are the contrast, not the advantage.
Right: additions do not destroy earlier information.
Order is not what they preserve.
questions.explain: This makes the representation task much simpler.
questions.teaches: Lists and associations make it possible to add additional information to memory without destroying the information already encoded, which greatly simplifies the representation task.
questions.rule: For definite, elementary processes, assume an encoding and programs exist and describe at a higher level.

questions.q: Suppose the authors had begun with a linearly addressed memory like a standard computer's. What would they have faced?
options: No questions at all, since every memory encodes tasks equally well
A need to drop number scrabble as an example of a task environment
Faster programs, because such memory is quicker to use than lists
Questions about how particular task environments could be encoded
optionExplain: Such a memory does raise encoding questions.
Number scrabble would remain usable.
Speed is not what they say.
Right: encoding questions would have arisen.
questions.explain: Lists and associations spare the theorist those encoding questions.
questions.teaches: Starting with a linearly addressed memory, as in a standard computer, would have raised questions about how particular task environments could be encoded.
questions.rule: For definite, elementary processes, assume an encoding and programs exist and describe at a higher level.

questions.q: In number scrabble, why can the card color be left out of the problem space?
options: It has no bearing on the goal of three digits summing to 15
Colors cannot be represented in any symbol structure the system could hold
The cards have no color, so there is nothing to leave out
The authors forgot to mention it when they described the game
optionExplain: Right: the goal is what makes a property relevant.
Colors can be encoded; they are simply irrelevant.
Nothing says the cards lack color.
It was assumed irrelevant on purpose.
questions.explain: The goal decides what matters. The card next states this.
questions.rule: Include in the problem space only what the goal makes relevant.

questions.q: The problem space is restricted to task-____ aspects of the environment.
questions.explain: Only the aspects relevant to the goal are included.
questions.rule: Include in the problem space only what the goal makes relevant.

questions.q: A puzzle asks you to fit boxes into a trunk. Which property of the boxes belongs in the problem space?
options: Their color
Their dimensions
The brand on them
The name of who packed them
optionExplain: Color does not affect fitting.
Right: dimensions affect fitting.
Brand does not affect fitting.
Packer's name does not affect fitting.
questions.explain: Relevance is tied to the goal of fitting.
questions.rule: Include in the problem space only what the goal makes relevant.

questions.q: True or false: If the goal changes from fitting the boxes to sorting them by color, color becomes task-relevant.
questions.explain: Relevance depends on the goal, so a new goal can make a property relevant.
questions.rule: Include in the problem space only what the goal makes relevant.

questions.q: The processes an IPS has must be supplied before it meets any specific problem. How does the goal-environment link help, according to the authors?
options: It makes processes unnecessary
It decides who will win each game before the first move is made
It lets those processes be applied to specific task environments
It removes the need for goals when a system meets a new problem
optionExplain: Processes are still required.
The link does not decide winners.
Right: the link brings the available processes to bear.
Goals remain central.
questions.explain: Knowing what is relevant to the goal connects general processes to particular tasks.
questions.teaches: The processes the IPS has must be provided before it meets a specific problem, and the goal-environment interdependence enables them to be brought to bear on the tasks posed by specific task environments.
questions.rule: Include in the problem space only what the goal makes relevant.

questions.q: Who has a problem in the authors' sense?
options: Someone who wants coffee and already knows the route to the coffee machine
Someone who already holds a finished proof of the theorem in hand
Someone who has no wants at all and so nothing to work toward
Someone who wants a proof and does not yet know the steps
optionExplain: The way is known, so there is nothing to work out.
The goal is already reached.
Without a want, there is no problem.
Right: a want plus no known way.
questions.explain: A want plus not knowing the way defines a problem. The card next states it.
questions.rule: A problem exists when something is wanted and the way to get it is not immediately known.

questions.q: A person has a problem when he wants something and does not know ____ what series of actions will get it.
questions.explain: If the way is known at once, there is no problem.
questions.rule: A problem exists when something is wanted and the way to get it is not immediately known.

questions.q: Which can be the desired object of a problem, according to the authors? Select all that apply.
options: An apple to eat
An elegant proof for a theorem
Something to appease hunger
A series of steps already rehearsed and known
optionExplain: Right: a tangible, specific object.
Right: an abstract object.
Right: a general object.
This is a means already known, not an object desired with the way unknown.
questions.explain: The authors list tangible, abstract, specific and general objects.
questions.rule: A problem exists when something is wanted and the way to get it is not immediately known.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say limiting the discussion to symbolic entities and processes limits their analysis little, except at the physiological boundaries.
questions.explain: The limitation matters mainly at the physiological boundaries, such as sensory and motor skills.
questions.rule: A problem exists when something is wanted and the way to get it is not immediately known.

questions.q: A student says picking an apple shows problem solving is mostly physical. What would the authors reply?
options: The crucial activities are still central symbol manipulation
Physical problems are not problems at all in the authors' sense
Orchards are not task environments, so the example does not count
Symbols are never used when a person acts on physical objects
optionExplain: Right: central processing is crucial even for physical goals.
They count physical objects as desirable.
Nothing excludes orchards.
Symbols are used.
questions.explain: Even going to the orchard to pick an apple depends on symbol-manipulating activity.
questions.rule: A problem exists when something is wanted and the way to get it is not immediately known.

questions.q: A coordinator must produce a seating plan meeting several rules. How do the authors' ideas treat this?
options: As a purely physical task of moving people into the right chairs
As finding a symbol structure that has the required properties
As not a problem, since the coordinator knows what she wants
As a perception experiment about how people look at the seating plan
optionExplain: The plan is an arrangement of symbols.
Right: like a proof, the plan is a symbol structure to be found.
The want and unknown path make it a problem.
The task is not about perception.
questions.explain: A proof is a list of list structures, and finding a proof is finding a list structure with the right characteristics.
questions.teaches: A proof is a sequence of axioms and theorems ending in the theorem to be proved, so it can be represented as a list of list structures, itself a list structure; proving is finding a list structure with appropriate characteristics.
questions.rule: A problem exists when something is wanted and the way to get it is not immediately known.

questions.q: A homework sheet says: Given a triangle; Prove a fact about it. What must the student bring for this to be a problem for her?
options: Nothing more, since the sheet of paper is itself the whole problem to be solved
A copy of the answer, so that she can compare her own work with it
An interpretation of the terms and of Given and Prove, plus motivation
A calculator, since every textbook problem needs some way to compute it
optionExplain: A sheet alone is only a stimulus.
The answer would end the problem.
Right: interpretation and motivation.
A calculator is not required.
questions.explain: The sheet becomes a problem only through the solver's interpretation. The card next states this.
questions.rule: A problem is information about goal, conditions, tools, start and resources, plus the solver's interpretation of it.

questions.q: The two general representations of problems the authors introduce are the set representation and the ____ representation.
questions.explain: The set and search representations cover large classes of problems.
questions.rule: A problem is information about goal, conditions, tools, start and resources, plus the solver's interpretation of it.

questions.q: Match each element of a trip-planning problem to the kind of information it supplies.
questions.explain: Each element fills one role in the given information.
questions.rule: A problem is information about goal, conditions, tools, start and resources, plus the solver's interpretation of it.

questions.q: True or false: The authors define general problem representations in terms of symbol structures, not English statements.
questions.explain: They define representations directly in terms of essential symbol structures, so natural-language understanding is not at issue.
questions.rule: A problem is information about goal, conditions, tools, start and resources, plus the solver's interpretation of it.

questions.q: True or false: The authors guarantee that every problem fits either the set or the search representation.
questions.explain: They leave open that some important classes of problems have not yet been represented.
questions.rule: A problem is information about goal, conditions, tools, start and resources, plus the solver's interpretation of it.

questions.q: A lab wants to study problem solving apart from skill at understanding language. What do the authors suggest?
options: Present every problem as an English sentence, so the subject can read it plainly
Test only native speakers of English, so that language skill is equal for all
Ignore the problem statement and judge only the answer that the subject gives
Define representations directly in terms of the essential symbol structures
optionExplain: English statements would require language understanding.
Language skill would still interfere.
The problem still has to be given.
Right: symbol structures need not be English.
questions.explain: Assuming English statements would imply capabilities of natural language understanding that are beside the main issue.
questions.teaches: The authors avoid assuming problems arrive as English statements, since that would imply natural-language understanding beside the main issue; they define representations in terms of deep structures.
questions.rule: A problem is information about goal, conditions, tools, start and resources, plus the solver's interpretation of it.

questions.q: Which problem is well defined in the authors' sense?
options: Find a number whose square is 169
Make a person happy
Write a poem readers will love in fifty years
Choose the best way to spend a life
optionExplain: Right: squaring a candidate is a quick test.
No performable test exists for happiness.
No quick test exists for love in fifty years.
No quick test settles best life.
questions.explain: The key is a quick test of any proposed answer. The card next states it.
questions.rule: A problem is well defined if candidate solutions can be tested with small effort.

questions.q: A problem is well defined if a test exists that determines whether a proposed object is a ____.
questions.explain: The test checks candidate solutions.
questions.rule: A problem is well defined if candidate solutions can be tested with small effort.

questions.q: Find a key that opens this lock. Is the problem well defined, and why?
options: No: there are far too many keys that could be tried
Yes: trying a key is a quick test
No: locks have no solutions that anyone could recognize
Only if the right key has first been found by someone
optionExplain: Many candidates do not remove the test.
Right: a candidate can be tested with little effort.
The lock supplies the test.
The test exists before the key is found.
questions.explain: Well defined concerns testing a candidate, not how many candidates there are.
questions.rule: A problem is well defined if candidate solutions can be tested with small effort.

questions.q: A colleague says a problem is well defined only if its solution can be found quickly. What is wrong?
options: The requirement is that the solution be unique, whatever the effort of testing
The requirement is that the problem be stated in symbols rather than words
The requirement is a quick test of a candidate, not quick finding
Nothing is wrong, because a well defined problem is one that is solved quickly
optionExplain: Uniqueness is not required.
Symbols are not required.
Right: the test is cheap, the search may not be.
Finding and testing are different.
questions.explain: The authors say the test is performable with relatively small effort.
questions.rule: A problem is well defined if candidate solutions can be tested with small effort.

questions.q: True or false: A problem is well defined even if testing every candidate needs enormous processing effort.
questions.explain: Performable means with relatively small processing effort.
questions.rule: A problem is well defined if candidate solutions can be tested with small effort.

questions.q: To search for a five-letter word meeting some clues, how could the authors' style define the candidate set?
options: As the words that the solver already knows and has used before in other puzzles
As the clues themselves, taken one at a time in order
As the single correct word, which the solver has yet to find
As all strings an enumerative procedure generates from an alphabet
optionExplain: Known words are a subset the solver may use, not the defined set.
Clues are tests, not candidates.
The correct word is the answer, not the set.
Right: an enumerative procedure over an alphabet.
questions.explain: For symbolic expressions the candidate set is all possible expressions the generator can produce.
questions.teaches: Where the solution is a symbolic expression, the set of possible solutions can be taken as all possible symbolic expressions, defined more precisely as the set generated by an enumerative procedure from an alphabet of elementary expressions.
questions.rule: A problem is well defined if candidate solutions can be tested with small effort.

questions.q: You hunt for a lost key among all the drawers of a house. How is this best described as a set problem?
options: U is all places it might be; G is where it actually is
U is the key that was lost; G is the house in which it was lost
U is the number of drawers; G is the person who lost the key
U is the time spent searching; G is the effort that was used
optionExplain: Right: candidates and the goal subset.
The key is the goal object, not the candidate set.
The person is not a goal-set.
Time and effort are costs.
questions.explain: A set of candidates contains a goal subset. The card next states this form.
questions.rule: State the problem as: given U, find a member of the goal subset G.

questions.q: In the set representation, the problem is to find a member of the goal-set G, a subset of U having specified ____.
questions.explain: G is the subset with the specified properties.
questions.rule: State the problem as: given U, find a member of the goal subset G.

questions.q: For a sudoku puzzle, what are U and G?
options: U: the digits that are given at the start; G: the empty squares that must be filled in by the solver
U: all ways to fill the grid with digits; G: fillings meeting the rules and the given digits
U: the rules of the puzzle; G: the printed grid in which the solver writes down the digits
U: one row of the grid; G: one column of the grid that crosses that row
optionExplain: Givens and blanks do not define candidates and goals.
Right: candidate fillings and valid ones.
Rules and grid are not a set and subset of candidates.
Rows and columns are parts, not the whole.
questions.explain: G is picked out from U by the stated properties.
questions.rule: State the problem as: given U, find a member of the goal subset G.

questions.q: Match each term with its role in the set representation.
questions.explain: U contains the candidates and G the solutions; solving means finding a member of G.
questions.rule: State the problem as: given U, find a member of the goal subset G.

questions.q: A student says G is the set of all candidates. What is the error?
options: G is empty by definition until a solution has been found
G is a single number that picks out the answer
G is only the subset with the specified properties
G is the set of tests used to check each candidate
optionExplain: G is not empty.
G may hold one or several elements.
Right: all candidates are U.
Tests pick G out; they are not G.

questions.q: A detective knows exactly one suspect fits all the clues. Which sentence matches the set representation, and what does it show about G?
options: U is all suspects and G must hold several suspects who fit the clues together
U must be empty before the detective starts, and G is filled in later by clues
G is the list of clues, and U is the one suspect who matches that list
U is all suspects and G holds the one who fits, so G may have a single member

U cannot be empty.
The clues define G; they are not G.

questions.explain: The set of possible solutions contains the solution or solutions, so G can have one member or several.

questions.rule: State the problem as: given U, find a member of the goal subset G.

questions.q: A hunter must dig at one of ten thousand sites; only one holds treasure, and each dig takes a week. What makes this a problem?
options: Many candidates, one winner, and costly tests
The treasure itself is very heavy, and it is hard to carry back to the shore
The map of the island is old, and parts of it are hard to read
The hunter is tired after so many weeks of digging in the hot sun
optionExplain: Right: large U, sparse G, costly testing.
Weight is not in the authors' reasons.
Age of the map is not the structure.
Fatigue is a subject matter, not the problem structure.

questions.rule: A problem is hard when U is huge, G is sparse, or generating and testing candidates is costly.

questions.q: The problem solver is not really given the set of possible solutions; he is given a process for ____ its elements.
questions.explain: A generator produces elements in some order, at some cost.
questions.rule: A problem is hard when U is huge, G is sparse, or generating and testing candidates is costly.

questions.q: Match each feature of a password search to the authors' reason it illustrates.
questions.explain: Each feature matches one of the three reasons.
questions.rule: A problem is hard when U is huge, G is sparse, or generating and testing candidates is costly.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say it may or may not be possible to change the order in which a generator produces elements.
questions.explain: The order is one of the generator's own properties, which problem statements usually do not specify.
questions.rule: A problem is hard when U is huge, G is sparse, or generating and testing candidates is costly.

questions.q: A student says a problem is hard only when the set U is large. What is the error?
options: Size of U never matters
Sparseness of G and the cost per element also matter, and the list is not complete
U is in practice always small, so the size of the set is not a reason that counts for much
Cost is close to zero in the end, so only the size of U and the sparseness of G count

U is often immense.
Cost can be very high.
questions.explain: The authors give size of U, sparseness of G and cost as three of the reasons.
questions.rule: A problem is hard when U is huge, G is sparse, or generating and testing candidates is costly.

questions.q: Two searches share U and G. One generator yields an element each second, the other each hour. With one day, which can be solved?
options: Neither one, since both searches have exactly the same set U to cover
Both of them, since the goal set G is the same in the two searches
The one whose costs fit the time and computing power available
Only the slow one, since a slow generator gives more careful candidates
optionExplain: Same U does not make costs equal.
Same G does not make costs equal.
Right: solvable if costs are not too large relative to resources.
The slow one is the less affordable.

questions.teaches: A problem can be solved if the costs of generating and testing are not too large relative to the time and computing power available for solution.
questions.rule: A problem is hard when U is huge, G is sparse, or generating and testing candidates is costly.

questions.q: In a crossword, each answer must fit its clue and cross other answers. What does the crossing letter do to the separate word problems?
options: It makes each word problem independent of the others
It makes the separate word problems unsolvable
It removes the need for the clues
It links their solution sets
optionExplain: Independence would mean no shared squares.
They remain solvable.
Clues remain.
Right: shared letters tie the problems together.
questions.explain: Shared squares link the subproblems. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Split a set problem into subproblems of the same kind, but expect their solution sets to be interdependent.

questions.q: In the crossword decomposition, U_i is taken to be the set of all English ____.
questions.explain: Each subproblem searches among English words.
questions.rule: Split a set problem into subproblems of the same kind, but expect their solution sets to be interdependent.

questions.q: A school timetable makes each class a subproblem, but two classes share one teacher. What does the shared teacher do?
options: Introduces interdependency between the subproblems, like crossing letters
Makes the classes independent of one another
Removes the need for a timetable
Makes the timetable unique
optionExplain: Right: a shared element links the solution sets.
Sharing creates dependence.
Timetables are still needed.
Uniqueness is not implied.
questions.explain: The shared teacher plays the part of the shared letter.
questions.rule: Split a set problem into subproblems of the same kind, but expect their solution sets to be interdependent.

questions.q: True or false: Once one word is fixed, the words crossing it must match its letter at the intersection, so their goal sets narrow.
questions.explain: Our reading of the intersection condition: a fixed letter excludes words that do not carry it.
questions.rule: Split a set problem into subproblems of the same kind, but expect their solution sets to be interdependent.

questions.q: According to the authors, which generator and test split do expert solvers usually find best?
options: A generator for definition and length, then a test of the crossing letters afterward
A generator with no conditions at all, then a test of all three conditions together
A generator meeting the definition and crossing letters, then a test for length
Random words drawn from the dictionary, with no test applied to any of them

Random generation is not discussed.

questions.rule: Split a set problem into subproblems of the same kind, but expect their solution sets to be interdependent.

questions.q: A hiring team can let a generator propose only candidates with the right degree and test the rest, or generate more narrowly. What fits?
options: Generators must do all the work, with tests left to confirm the final answer
Tests must do all the work, with generators supplying anything at all at random
The way work is divided never matters for how well the search performs overall
Responsibilities of generator and test can be divided in different ways
optionExplain: Nothing requires generators to do all the work; the text allows responsibility to be divided differently.
Nothing requires tests to do all the work; the text allows responsibility to be divided differently.
