Right: the responsibilities of generator and test can be divided in different ways.
questions.explain: How the work is split between generating and testing is a design choice.
questions.teaches: The respective responsibilities of generators and tests in obtaining and verifying solutions can be divided in different ways.
questions.rule: Split a set problem into subproblems of the same kind, but expect their solution sets to be interdependent.

questions.q: A student's lines end with the target theorem, but line 4 is neither an axiom nor derived from earlier lines. Is the list a proof?
options: No: a step lacks support
Yes: it ends in the theorem
Yes: lines can appear freely
Only if line 4 is short
optionExplain: Right: every step needs support.
Ending right is only one condition.
Unsupported steps are not allowed.
Length is irrelevant.
questions.explain: Two properties are needed: supported steps and the right last step. The card next states them.
questions.rule: A proof is a sequence whose every step is an axiom or follows from earlier steps, and whose last step is the theorem.

questions.q: The second property says the final subexpression of the sequence is the theorem to be ____.
questions.explain: The last line must be t.
questions.rule: A proof is a sequence whose every step is an axiom or follows from earlier steps, and whose last step is the theorem.

questions.q: A chain of reasoning ends exactly on the claim wanted, and each line follows from earlier lines or from accepted premises. Which properties hold?
options: Only p2, since the chain ends exactly on the claim wanted
Both p1 and p2, so the sequence is a proof
Only p1, since every line is supported by earlier lines
Neither, since a chain of reasoning is not a formal proof
optionExplain: p1 also holds.
Right: supported steps and correct ending.
p2 also holds.
Both hold.
questions.explain: Support of each step is p1; ending on the claim is p2.
questions.rule: A proof is a sequence whose every step is an axiom or follows from earlier steps, and whose last step is the theorem.

questions.q: Which part of the sequence does the test for the second property need to look at?
options: Every subexpression in the sequence in turn
Only the first subexpression of the sequence
Only the final subexpression
The overall length of the sequence of steps
optionExplain: That is the test for p1.
The first line is not tied to p2.
Right: only the last line.
Length does not matter.
questions.explain: The test for p2 concerns only the characteristics of the final subexpression.
questions.rule: A proof is a sequence whose every step is an axiom or follows from earlier steps, and whose last step is the theorem.

questions.q: True or false: Under p1, a step must be an axiom or follow from earlier steps in the sequence.
questions.explain: Allowable derivations are from previous subexpressions, never later ones.
questions.rule: A proof is a sequence whose every step is an axiom or follows from earlier steps, and whose last step is the theorem.

questions.q: A checker validates contract clauses by comparing each only with the one or two it relies on. Which observation of the authors does this echo?
options: Each test needs the whole sequence of clauses before any judgment can be made at all
Only the last clause matters
Tests cannot be factored into parts, so the checker must treat the contract as one block
Tests for p1 are relational, comparing a step with the earlier steps it derives from
optionExplain: The authors say the tests can be factored into parts.
That is p2 only.
They say tests factor.
Right: each test is relational and local.
questions.explain: Local checks suffice because each step links to a few earlier ones.
questions.teaches: The tests for p1 are relational: each is satisfied if the last subexpression of the partial sequence stands in a certain relation to one or two prior subexpressions from which it is directly derived.
questions.rule: A proof is a sequence whose every step is an axiom or follows from earlier steps, and whose last step is the theorem.

questions.q: In planning a trip, which describes the target by what it is rather than by how to get there?
options: Arriving at the hotel by evening
Take the 9:10 train, then take a taxi
Turn left, then turn right at the lights
Follow the signs for the town centre
optionExplain: Right: this names the end state.
This is a sequence of actions.
This is a sequence of actions.
This is an action rule.
questions.explain: Naming the goal and naming the route use different kinds of language. The card next gives the authors' terms.
questions.rule: State language names expressions and their features; process language names operators and their sequences; a proof needs both.

questions.q: Symbols that designate operators belong to the ____ language.
questions.explain: Operators are named in the process language.
questions.rule: State language names expressions and their features; process language names operators and their sequences; a proof needs both.

questions.q: Sort each item into the language it belongs to.

items.t: The expression last(u_t)
The difference between two expressions
A characteristic of an expression
The operator Q_3
A sequence of rules of inference
A characteristic of an operator

questions.explain: Expressions, their parts, characteristics and differences are state language; operators, their sequences and their characteristics are process language.
questions.rule: State language names expressions and their features; process language names operators and their sequences; a proof needs both.

questions.q: For u_t to count as a proof of t, what must be true of all the operators Q_i?
options: They are chosen at random from all possible operators
They correspond to admissible rules of inference
They are as few as possible, whatever the proof needs
They are all identical, so the same rule is repeated
optionExplain: Random operators may be inadmissible.
Right: the chain must use admissible operators.
Fewness is not required.
Identity is not required.
questions.explain: Admissible means corresponding to the rules of inference.
questions.rule: State language names expressions and their features; process language names operators and their sequences; a proof needs both.

questions.q: True or false: State language and process language are two names for the same set of symbols.
questions.explain: State language names expressions and their characteristics; process language names operators.
questions.rule: State language names expressions and their features; process language names operators and their sequences; a proof needs both.

questions.q: A baker describes a cake either directly or as the result of applying recipe steps to ingredients. Which point of the authors does this match?
options: Cakes cannot be described at all
Only the steps may be described
The same object can be designated as a state or as the output of a sequence of operators
Only the end may be described
optionExplain: Both descriptions are possible.
The end description is also available.
Right: two ways of referring to the same thing.
The step description is also available.
questions.explain: The theorem t is both the final expression and the result of applying the operators to u_0.
questions.teaches: The theorem can be designated in several ways: as the final subexpression of the sequence, or as last(u_t), generated by applying the sequence of operators to u_0.
questions.rule: State language names expressions and their features; process language names operators and their sequences; a proof needs both.

questions.q: A person reaches for a cup. Which is closer to state language, and which to process language?
options: The commands to her arm are state, while the image of the cup in her mind is process
Both the image and the commands are state
Both the image and the commands are process
The image of the cup in her hand is state; the commands to her arm are process
optionExplain: This reverses them.
The commands are operations.
The image is a state.
Right: goal as state, commands as process.
questions.explain: The goal is a state; getting there is a series of operations. The card next gives the authors' terms.
questions.rule: Solutions are defined by start, end, admissible transformations and sometimes intermediate states; the state-process split is basic.

questions.q: State language is related to the operation of the ____ system.
questions.explain: Process language is related to the efferent system.
questions.rule: Solutions are defined by start, end, admissible transformations and sometimes intermediate states; the state-process split is basic.

questions.q: A thermostat compares the sensed temperature with a target and switches the heater. Which part is process language?
options: The signals that switch the heater on or off
The target temperature that has been set by the user
The sensed temperature that the thermostat measures now
The temperature of the room as it rises or falls
optionExplain: Right: instructions to the effector.
The target is a goal state.
The sensed value is a state.
The room temperature is a state.
questions.explain: Signals that act on the world are process; descriptions of conditions are state.
questions.rule: Solutions are defined by start, end, admissible transformations and sometimes intermediate states; the state-process split is basic.

questions.q: True or false: The conditions that define a solution can include characteristics of intermediate states.
questions.explain: The authors say sometimes the definition also includes intermediate states.
questions.rule: Solutions are defined by start, end, admissible transformations and sometimes intermediate states; the state-process split is basic.

questions.q: A student says the goal object is represented in the process language. What is the error?
options: The goal has no representation inside the problem solver
The goal is symbolized in the state language
The goal is a motor signal sent to the effectors
The goal is the afferent system of the organism
optionExplain: The goal is internally represented.
Right: the goal is a state.
Motor signals are process.
The afferent system is not a goal.
questions.explain: The internal representation of the goal object is in the state language.
questions.rule: Solutions are defined by start, end, admissible transformations and sometimes intermediate states; the state-process split is basic.

questions.q: A baker decides a loaf is done by its look and smell. In the authors' picture, what supplies the test of the solution?
options: The baker's arm movements as she takes the loaf out
The oven's design and the way it was installed
New stimuli received through the afferent channels
The recipe's page number in the baker's cookbook
optionExplain: Arm movements are efferent.
The oven is part of the environment.
Right: tests apply to new afferent stimuli.
The page number is irrelevant.
questions.explain: The problem is solved by translating stimuli into responses, and results are tested on new stimuli.
questions.teaches: The problem is solved by an appropriate translation of afferent stimuli into efferent responses, and tests of the solution are applied to new stimuli received through the afferent channels.
questions.rule: Solutions are defined by start, end, admissible transformations and sometimes intermediate states; the state-process split is basic.

questions.q: In a crossword, a friend says: I have the solution. What do they most likely hold?
options: The order in which they filled words
The list of pencil strokes
The clue sheet
The filled-in grid
optionExplain: That is a path.
That is an action sequence.
That is the problem.
Right: the terminal state.

questions.q: Match each term with its example.
pairs: The sequence of expressions in a proof

questions.rule: Solution can mean the path, the action sequence, or the object reached; say which when it matters.

questions.q: A hiker's route notes read: left, left, right, right. Which kind of solution is that list?
options: A solution-action-sequence
A solution-object, the place finally reached
A solution-path listing the places passed
Not a solution of any of the three kinds
optionExplain: Right: the sequence of actions.
The object is the place reached.
The path would list the places passed.
It is one meaning of solution.
questions.explain: A list of operators is the action sequence.
questions.rule: Solution can mean the path, the action sequence, or the object reached; say which when it matters.

questions.q: True or false: The authors distinguish solution-path, solution-action-sequence and solution-object as three senses of solution.
questions.explain: They say solution is used in several different ways and name these three where it matters.
questions.rule: Solution can mean the path, the action sequence, or the object reached; say which when it matters.

questions.q: In theorem proving, which does the authors' usage call the solution?
options: The theorem alone, which is already given at the start of the task
The sequence of expressions ending in the theorem
The list of operators alone, without the expressions
The axioms alone, which are given at the outset of the proof

In theorem proving the sequence of expressions is meant.

questions.q: A judge in a puzzle contest looks only at the final board, not the moves. What is she treating as the solution?
options: The solution-path, the sequence of states
The solution-action-sequence, the moves made
The goal-object, the terminal state
The problem statement that began the contest

The moves are not judged.

questions.q: A hiker meets a junction with three options; each leads to a second junction with two options. How many distinct routes are there?

3 counts only the first choice.
2 counts only the second choice.

questions.rule: Applying every admissible operator at each state yields a search tree; a branch whose end meets the goal conditions is a solution path.

questions.q: The branching tree of paths is called a search tree or ____ tree.
questions.explain: The authors give both names.
questions.rule: Applying every admissible operator at each state yields a search tree; a branch whose end meets the goal conditions is a solution path.

questions.q: A chess-like game offers 4 legal moves at each turn. How many move sequences are there after 3 turns?
optionExplain: Right: 4 x 4 x 4.
12 adds 4 three times.

questions.rule: Applying every admissible operator at each state yields a search tree; a branch whose end meets the goal conditions is a solution path.

questions.q: More admissible operators apply at each state. What happens to the search tree?
options: It becomes narrower overall
It becomes much wider
It stays exactly the same size
It disappears from the analysis
optionExplain: Fewer operators would narrow it.
Right: more branches at every node.
Branching affects size.
The tree remains.
questions.explain: More operators means more branches at each node.
questions.rule: Applying every admissible operator at each state yields a search tree; a branch whose end meets the goal conditions is a solution path.

questions.q: True or false: Any branch that ends anywhere in the search tree counts as a solution path.

questions.rule: Applying every admissible operator at each state yields a search tree; a branch whose end meets the goal conditions is a solution path.

questions.q: Rail travel is treated as a search space. What are the nodes and links, in the authors' description?

Passengers as the nodes and seats as the links, with each seat joining two different passengers

Stations as states of affairs and rides as the actions that change one state into another
optionExplain: Trains and tickets are not the states and actions.

questions.q: A chess player pictures a checkmate position she is unsure she can reach, then looks for moves leading to it. What is she doing?
options: Searching among imagined, conjectured states in an internal space
Replaying a past game that she remembers, move by move, from the start
Following the rulebook step by step without any thinking of her own
Waiting for the opponent to move before she thinks about anything
optionExplain: Right: conjectured intermediate states are searched internally.
No past game is involved.
Rules limit moves, not this search.
She is actively thinking.

questions.q: A solver may work ____ from the desired state, applying operators that are roughly the inverses of the admissible actions.

questions.q: Lee first fixes the hotel she wants, then finds flights that reach it. Which idea does this match?
options: Searching only the external world, trying each hotel in person one after another
Working backward from a desired state, using a conjectured goal
Running every possible flight at once and then keeping the cheapest one
Skipping the planning and letting the airline decide for her

Nothing is run at once.

questions.q: A chess player explores many future lines before choosing a move. What is the explored tree?
options: The solution action sequence that she will actually play out over the next several moves of the game in order
The set of her opponent's possible replies only
A structure for predicting consequences and evaluating the move before her, not part of the solution
A record of all the past games that she has stored in memory and consults when a new game starts
optionExplain: The tree contains many lines that will not be played.
It includes her own moves too.
Right: the solution is the next move, not the tree.
It is about the future.
questions.explain: The solution to choosing a move is a good next move, not the whole explored tree.
questions.rule: Search can occur among imagined states, conjectured goals or plans, so the search space belongs to the solver as well as to the task.

questions.q: True or false: The structure of the search space depends only on the states and admissible actions of the task environment.

questions.rule: Search can occur among imagined states, conjectured goals or plans, so the search space belongs to the solver as well as to the task.

questions.q: Before packing a suitcase, Sam decides which item to pack next, preferring items that fix the most constraints. What kind of search is this?
options: Search in the external world, by actually trying out each item in the case
A random walk through the items with no guide to choice at all

questions.rule: Search can occur among imagined states, conjectured goals or plans, so the search space belongs to the solver as well as to the task.

questions.q: A bike lock has four dials, each 0 to 9. What is the set U?
options: All 10,000 possible dial settings
The one opening setting only, once found
The four dials taken together as a whole
The digits 0 to 9 that appear on each dial

That is G.

Digits are not whole settings.

questions.q: Match each problem with its set U.
questions.explain: Each problem has a candidate set from which the goal subset is picked.
questions.rule: Name the set of candidates and the subset that qualifies, and many problems fit the set form.

questions.q: A bike lock has four dials, each 0 to 9. How many elements does U have?
optionExplain: 40 adds the dial values.

10 counts one dial.
9,999 would drop the all-zero setting.

questions.rule: Name the set of candidates and the subset that qualifies, and many problems fit the set form.

questions.q: True or false: For practical machine design, the set U is small enough to examine every element.

questions.rule: Name the set of candidates and the subset that qualifies, and many problems fit the set form.

questions.q: A student writes G for translation as: all English word sequences with correct syntax. What is missing?
options: The requirement that the translated sequences must be short
The requirement that the translated sequences must rhyme in each line
The requirement of the same meaning as the German original
Nothing is missing, since correct syntax already fixes the meaning
optionExplain: Shortness is not required.
Rhyme is not required.
Right: syntax, style and meaning.

questions.rule: Name the set of candidates and the subset that qualifies, and many problems fit the set form.

questions.q: A planner fixes budget and floor area, then layout, then finishes. What shape of search tree do the authors expect for definite priorities?
options: Flat, with all of the choices on budget, layout and finishes made at the very same stage
Random, since no priorities can determine the order in which choices are made at all

questions.rule: Name the set of candidates and the subset that qualifies, and many problems fit the set form.

questions.q: A program reproduces a person's moves in a puzzle. Another researcher says the puzzle demanded those moves. Must one be wrong?
options: No: if the program solved the puzzle, both can hold
Yes: demands and programs exclude each other, so one is wrong
Yes: only programs explain behavior, and demands explain nothing
No: but only if the puzzle was easy enough to solve at all
optionExplain: Right: effective symbol manipulation is a way of meeting the demands.
The authors see no necessary conflict.
Demands also explain behavior.
Easiness is not the condition.
questions.explain: Both explanations can describe the same behavior. The card next explains.
questions.rule: A program that matches behavior and a demand that explains the behavior can both hold; the first may show only adaptation.

questions.q: The second kind of explanation says the behavior was ____ by the task environment.
questions.explain: The behavior is what the situation called for.
questions.rule: A program that matches behavior and a demand that explains the behavior can both hold; the first may show only adaptation.

questions.q: All pilots lower the flaps to land. One researcher cites their training programs; another says landing demands flaps. What fits the authors?
options: Only the training explanation counts as a scientific explanation
Both can be right; there is no necessary conflict
Only the demand explanation counts as a scientific explanation
They must be merged into a single explanation to be useful
optionExplain: The authors use both.
Right: two routes to the same behavior.
The authors use both.
They remain two kinds of explanation.
questions.explain: If the pilots succeeded, their programs were effective means for the task's demands.
questions.rule: A program that matches behavior and a demand that explains the behavior can both hold; the first may show only adaptation.

questions.q: True or false: The demands explanation can still predict the obvious moves of a solver who fails to solve the problem.
questions.explain: It can predict the obvious things to do to attain the goal, even if they are insufficient.
questions.rule: A program that matches behavior and a demand that explains the behavior can both hold; the first may show only adaptation.

questions.q: A researcher infers a program from behavior and says it must reveal the person's lasting makeup. What caution do the authors add?
options: It is a permanent part of the person that will appear in every task the person ever meets
It is certainly wrong, because behavior cannot be used to infer a program at all
It is identical across tasks
It may be idiosyncratic to the task and show only that the person could adapt
optionExplain: The authors warn the opposite.
The authors do not call it wrong.
Different tasks generate different structures.
Right: tasks can produce different, ephemeral structures.
questions.explain: The program may be simply what the task demanded.
questions.rule: A program that matches behavior and a demand that explains the behavior can both hold; the first may show only adaptation.

questions.q: Why do the authors want to understand what the task environment demands before interpreting behavior?
options: To understand by elimination which aspects of behavior the person's psychology determines
To avoid studying people altogether and to study only the task environments in their place instead
To prove that the person is irrational whenever the task demands something else of him
To replace the programs that explain behavior by tables of the task's demands
optionExplain: Right: what remains after demands is psychology.
They still study people.
They study rational and limited behavior.
Programs remain central.
questions.explain: Knowing the demands lets them subtract what the task forced.
questions.teaches: One main task of the book is to understand what the task environment demands, so that by elimination one can see which aspects of behavior are determined by the psychology of the problem solver.
questions.rule: A program that matches behavior and a demand that explains the behavior can both hold; the first may show only adaptation.

questions.q: A mountain pass exists in a range. Does the range make demands on a traveler?
options: Yes, whatever the traveler happens to want to do
Only through the traveler's goal of crossing
No, since mountains are lifeless and have no wants
Only if the traveler happens to be a trained climber
optionExplain: Without a goal no behavior is required.
Right: the goal turns features into demands.
The point is the goal, not the object's life.
Climbing skill is not the issue.
questions.explain: Demands come from goals. The card next states the definition.
questions.rule: A demand is a constraint that behavior must satisfy to reach the goal, and it arises from the goal, not from the environment alone.

questions.q: A demand of the task environment is a ____ on the solver's behavior that must be satisfied for the goal to be attained.
questions.explain: That is the authors' working definition.
questions.rule: A demand is a constraint that behavior must satisfy to reach the goal, and it arises from the goal, not from the environment alone.

questions.q: To bake bread, the oven must be hot. In the authors' account, where does this demand on the baker's behavior come from?
options: The oven alone, which has the hot temperature
The flour alone, which sets what the bread must be
The goal of baking, through the baker's commitment to attain it
The kitchen walls, which keep the heat in
optionExplain: The environment per se does not make demands, so the oven alone cannot be their source.
Flour is part of the environment and does not make demands by itself.
Right: the goal makes the demand via the solver's commitment to attain it.
Walls are environment and do not make demands by themselves.
questions.explain: The authors say the environment per se does not make demands; the problem or goal makes them via the problem solver's commitment to attain it, and a demand is a constraint on behavior that must be satisfied for the goal to be attained.
questions.rule: A demand is a constraint that behavior must satisfy to reach the goal, and it arises from the goal, not from the environment alone.

questions.q: True or false: If the solver does not hold the goal, there is a demand on his behavior in the authors' sense.
questions.explain: The concept is conditioned on the goal being held and adequate motivation.
questions.rule: A demand is a constraint that behavior must satisfy to reach the goal, and it arises from the goal, not from the environment alone.

questions.q: True or false: The authors worry that demands might depend on the solver's own program, which would undermine the split into task environment and solver.
questions.explain: They call this the risk that the factorization is a mirage.
questions.rule: A demand is a constraint that behavior must satisfy to reach the goal, and it arises from the goal, not from the environment alone.

questions.q: Why do the authors begin each main empirical part with a chapter on task analysis?
options: Behavior is much easier to describe than tasks are, so tasks are taken up afterward
Tasks never change from one experiment to the next, so the analysis is done once
Readers prefer short chapters, so the analysis is kept apart from behavior
Demands seem to be a framework outside the solver to which behavior can be related
optionExplain: They find tasks hard to describe, not easy.
The reason is the framework, not constancy.
Reader preference is not their reason.
Right: analysis before behavior.
questions.explain: Each main task starts with task analysis, followed by chapters on behavior.
questions.teaches: Because demands appear to give a framework outside the problem solver, the authors organize each main empirical part with a task analysis chapter first, then chapters on behavior.
questions.rule: A demand is a constraint that behavior must satisfy to reach the goal, and it arises from the goal, not from the environment alone.

questions.q: Every way of winning tic-tac-toe involves three marks in a row. What kind of fact is that?
options: A demand of the task shared by every successful player
A habit of good players that weaker players tend to lack
A rule that only experts follow and beginners can ignore
A matter of luck that depends on which squares are free
optionExplain: Right: it holds along all paths to the goal.
Habits vary; this does not.
Nonexperts must also meet it.
It is not luck.
questions.explain: A property shared by all winning paths is demanded by the task. The card next names it an invariant.
questions.rule: A property shared by every path to the goal is a demand, whoever the solver is.

questions.q: Aspects of behavior that are constant along all paths leading to a goal are called task ____.
questions.explain: Invariants are demands of the situation.
questions.rule: A property shared by every path to the goal is a demand, whoever the solver is.

questions.q: Which statement is a task invariant of number scrabble?
options: Every winner is the player who moved first in the game
Every winning hand contains three digits that sum to 15
Every winner holds the digit 5 somewhere in the winning hand
Every game ends before the ninth digit has been drawn
optionExplain: Second players can win.
Right: this is part of every winning path.
Winning hands such as 2, 4, 9 lack a 5.
Draws can run to nine pieces.
questions.explain: Only the first property is shared by every path that wins.
questions.rule: A property shared by every path to the goal is a demand, whoever the solver is.

questions.q: True or false: A clever solver and a weak solver who both reach the goal must both satisfy the invariants of the task.
questions.explain: An invariant is shared by all paths to the goal, so any successful solver exhibits it.
questions.rule: A property shared by every path to the goal is a demand, whoever the solver is.

questions.q: A student says a property is a task invariant only if it is easy to see. What is the flaw?
options: Invariants never involve proofs, so a hard proof cannot reveal one
Easy properties cannot be invariants
Invariants depend on the solver, so each solver has his own set
Invariance holds however much analysis it takes to reveal it
optionExplain: Some need difficult proofs.
Easy ones can be invariants too.
They do not depend on the solver.
Right: invariance is independent of how hard it is to show.
questions.explain: The authors say invariance is quite independent of the analysis required.
questions.rule: A property shared by every path to the goal is a demand, whoever the solver is.

questions.q: A mathematician proves that every proof of a theorem from given axioms must use axiom A7. What is that fact, in the authors' terms?
options: A demand of the task environment, though proving it may be difficult
A habit of mathematicians who have worked on that kind of theorem for years
A feature of one particular proof, not of every proof of the theorem
A property of the mathematician's mind, not of the task of proving
optionExplain: Right: shared by all proofs, so a demand.
Habits vary; this is required.
It holds for all proofs.
It does not depend on the mind.
questions.explain: The authors give this as an example: all proofs of a theorem may involve a specific axiom. Likewise, squaring the circle, doubling a cube and trisecting an angle with straight-edge and compass were proved impossible only after many centuries.
questions.teaches: All proofs of a given theorem from a set of axioms may involve the use of a specific axiom, and squaring the circle, duplicating the cube and trisecting an angle by straight-edge and compass took many centuries to prove impossible.
questions.rule: A property shared by every path to the goal is a demand, whoever the solver is.

questions.q: A canyon has one bridge, and a traveler arrives with a helicopter. Is crossing the bridge still a demand on her?
options: Yes: bridges have to be used by any traveler who crosses the canyon
No: the original statement assumed travelers without such means
Yes: helicopters are not allowed in such problems about bridges
No: the bridge does not exist for travelers who can fly at all
optionExplain: Her means change the demand.
Right: the demand depended on the assumed solver.
Nothing excludes helicopters.
The bridge exists but is not required.
questions.explain: The demand held only for solvers lacking other means. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Treat possibilities of physical action as environment, but keep the solver's own processing to describe him.

questions.q: The authors place possibilities of actual ____ actions in the description of the environment.
questions.explain: The information-processing activities describe the solver.
questions.rule: Treat possibilities of physical action as environment, but keep the solver's own processing to describe him.

questions.q: A cook's task includes stirring a pot. Does having a spoon belong to the environment or the cook, by the authors' boundary?
options: The cook, since she is the one who holds the spoon in her hand
Neither side, since a spoon is only a tool and not part of anything
The environment, since it concerns physical action possibilities
Both sides equally, since the cook and the kitchen share the spoon
optionExplain: The solver is described by information processing.
One of them must hold it in the description.
Right: physical actions possible belong to the environment.
The boundary puts it in one side.
questions.explain: What can physically be done is part of the environment; the cook's internal search describes her.
questions.rule: Treat possibilities of physical action as environment, but keep the solver's own processing to describe him.

questions.q: True or false: Mathematical proof raises the same difficulty as the bridge, because its operators are an empirical matter.
questions.explain: In proof the admissible operators are defined formally and accepted by both experimenter and subject.
questions.rule: Treat possibilities of physical action as environment, but keep the solver's own processing to describe him.

questions.q: If all means, even the ability to do arithmetic, are assigned to the environment, what happens to the theory of the solver?
options: Nothing is left to describe him
It becomes simpler and complete as a result
It covers the physical actions that the solver takes
It no longer needs a goal to be specified
optionExplain: Right: all he is would be specified by the environment.
It would vanish, not become complete.
Physical actions belong to the environment.
Goals remain.
questions.explain: The authors warn the problem solver would disappear.
questions.rule: Treat possibilities of physical action as environment, but keep the solver's own processing to describe him.

questions.q: A team models a bookkeeper. Which of her features belongs to the solver, by the authors' suggested boundary?
options: The calculator on her desk that she uses to add up the accounts
Her processes for searching through her internal problem space
The office doors that she walks through on her way to the files
The paper forms that she fills in when she records each entry
optionExplain: The calculator is a physical resource.
Right: information processing describes the solver.
Doors are environment.
Forms are environment.
questions.explain: The suggested boundary: physical action possibilities in the environment, information-processing activities in the solver.
questions.teaches: The suggested boundary treats possibilities of actual physical actions as part of the environment and the information processing activities, the processes for searching through the internal problem space, as describing the problem solver.
questions.rule: Treat possibilities of physical action as environment, but keep the solver's own processing to describe him.

questions.q: A test measures how well people solve one kind of puzzle. Where will it predict performance best?
options: On all tasks equally
On tasks unrelated to puzzles
On very similar puzzles
Nowhere
optionExplain: Prediction weakens as environments differ.
It is weakest for unrelated tasks.
Right: closeness of environments matters.
It predicts within the class.
questions.explain: Closer environments predict better. The card next gives the authors' view.
questions.rule: An adaptivity measure predicts well in similar environments and less well in different ones.

questions.q: Such a measure is highly predictive in a very ____ environment.
questions.explain: It is less predictive in environments with different characteristics.
questions.rule: An adaptivity measure predicts well in similar environments and less well in different ones.

questions.q: A scale is built from crossword scores. Which prediction does the authors' view support best?
options: Performance at playing chess games
Performance at singing in a choir
Performance at sprinting in a race
Performance on other crosswords
optionExplain: A different environment is less predictable.
Unrelated.
Unrelated.
Right: a similar environment.
questions.explain: The measure suits tasks in the class it was built from.
questions.rule: An adaptivity measure predicts well in similar environments and less well in different ones.

questions.q: What do the authors want class-specific measures to allow? Select all that apply.
options: Predicting performance in tasks of that class
Scaling tasks by difficulty
Scaling solvers by adaptivity or ability
Proving there is one general intelligence
optionExplain: Right: prediction.
Right: task difficulty scale.
Right: solver scale.
The authors do not need or claim this.
questions.explain: These three uses follow common psychometric practice.
questions.rule: An adaptivity measure predicts well in similar environments and less well in different ones.

questions.q: True or false: The authors assert that intelligence is a single general trait that applies equally across all task domains.
questions.explain: Generality across domains is called an empirical question, not assumed.
questions.rule: An adaptivity measure predicts well in similar environments and less well in different ones.

questions.q: A hospital builds a score from nurses' triage accuracy. Using the authors' approach, what is it fit to do?
options: Predict triage-like performance and scale the nurses and cases
Prove that nurses have a general intelligence that applies to all tasks
Predict how well the same nurses would write poetry in their free time
Replace the cases by the score, so that no case needs to be seen
optionExplain: Right: class-specific prediction and scaling.
General intelligence is not needed or implied.
Poetry is a different environment.
Scores do not replace cases.
questions.explain: The measure is specific to a class of tasks.
questions.teaches: Class-specific measures permit predicting performance in tasks in the appropriate environment, scaling such tasks according to difficulty, and scaling problem solvers according to adaptivity, ability or intelligence.
questions.rule: An adaptivity measure predicts well in similar environments and less well in different ones.

questions.q: Two solvers differ widely in inventiveness. Should a single description of the environment fit both?
options: Yes: the task is the same, so the description must be the same
Not necessarily: the actions each can think of differ
Yes: tasks are independent of the solvers who attempt them, so one description fits
No: solvers of such different inventiveness cannot be studied together at all
optionExplain: Same task does not mean same thinkable actions.
Right: thinkable actions differ.
That ignores what each can think of.
They can be studied with separate descriptions.
questions.explain: What is demanded depends on what solvers can think of. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Describe the environment for a given level of intelligence; demands are the invariants of the paths that level can reach.

questions.q: The authors assume the solvers studied come from a reasonably ____ range on the intelligence scale.
questions.explain: This keeps the environment description common to the group.
questions.rule: Describe the environment for a given level of intelligence; demands are the invariants of the paths that level can reach.

questions.q: To cross a river, adults think of building a raft; toddlers do not. How should the environment be described when studying toddlers?
options: Include rafts, since adults think of them and so they are part of the task
Leave out the river, since toddlers would not see it as a problem
Include only the external actions thinkable by toddlers
Describe it exactly as for adults
optionExplain: That uses the wrong group.
The river remains.
Right: only actions thinkable by the group studied.
Their space is smaller.
questions.explain: Descriptions fit the group's range of intelligence.
questions.rule: Describe the environment for a given level of intelligence; demands are the invariants of the paths that level can reach.

questions.q: If intelligence is scalable along one dimension, how does the search space of a less intelligent solver relate to a more intelligent solver's?
options: It is larger and denser than the space of the more intelligent solver
It is unrelated to the space of the more intelligent solver, though similar in name
It is identical to the space of the more intelligent solver in every respect
It is a smaller, sparser subpart of the more intelligent solver's
optionExplain: The reverse of nested.
Scalability implies a relation.
They differ.
Right: nested spaces.
questions.explain: The inventor's space contains branches missing from the others.
questions.rule: Describe the environment for a given level of intelligence; demands are the invariants of the paths that level can reach.

questions.q: True or false: Crossing the bridge is a demand on every solver, whatever their inventiveness.
questions.explain: A solver who invents or charters an airplane has no such demand.
questions.rule: Describe the environment for a given level of intelligence; demands are the invariants of the paths that level can reach.

questions.q: Once a search space for a given intelligence level is specified, what are the demands of the environment?
options: Properties of the space invariant over all paths that lead to a solution
The shortest path only
Each solver's preferred path
The initial state only
optionExplain: Right: invariants over all solution paths.
The shortest path is one path.
Preferences vary.
The start is not a property of all paths.
questions.explain: The authors note an analogous notion can be introduced for the set representation, but restrict themselves to search.
questions.teaches: Demands of the environment become properties of the specified search space invariant over all paths leading to a solution, and an analogous notion can be introduced into the set-theoretic representation.
questions.rule: Describe the environment for a given level of intelligence; demands are the invariants of the paths that level can reach.

questions.q: According to the authors, what correlates more strongly with chess skill?
options: A standard intelligence score
Chess knowledge
Height
Age
optionExplain: Some correlation, but lower.
Right: much higher correlation with chess knowledge.
Not mentioned.
Not mentioned.
questions.explain: The authors judge knowledge the better predictor. The card next states this.
questions.rule: Domain ability reflects domain knowledge as well as aptitude, and players of similar strength see similar things.

questions.q: In the American rating system, a class A player has a rating between 1800 and ____.
questions.explain: Class A runs from 1800 to 2000.
questions.rule: Domain ability reflects domain knowledge as well as aptitude, and players of similar strength see similar things.

questions.q: Order the American rating classes from lowest to highest.
items: Class A
Expert
Master
Senior master
questions.explain: Class A, expert, master and senior master rise in that order.
questions.rule: Domain ability reflects domain knowledge as well as aptitude, and players of similar strength see similar things.

questions.q: Two players are about the same strength and examine the same position. What do the authors expect about how they see it?
options: Entirely different things, so no common description of the task can be made
Nothing at all, since a position means nothing until it has been played out
Roughly the same things, so the demands can be inferred for both
Only what their rating numbers say
optionExplain: That would contradict the claim.
They see the position.
Right: similar strength, similar view.
Ratings are a measure, not their perception.
questions.explain: The task environment can be described in about the same way for them.
questions.rule: Domain ability reflects domain knowledge as well as aptitude, and players of similar strength see similar things.

questions.q: A writer says rating-based ability reflects intelligence alone. What do the authors say instead?
options: Ratings ignore knowledge and reflect general intelligence and nothing else
Ratings measure only how many years a player has spent playing the game
Ratings have no value as a measure of skill at the game of chess
Such measures reflect domain knowledge in addition to aptitude
optionExplain: The reverse.
Not at all.
They use them.
Right: knowledge is part of it.
questions.explain: Chess ratings track chess knowledge strongly.
questions.rule: Domain ability reflects domain knowledge as well as aptitude, and players of similar strength see similar things.

questions.q: How does a task analysis proceed at a given level of intelligence?
options: Remove paths too difficult for that level, then look for features invariant over the paths left
Include all possible paths whatever their difficulty, then look for the features that all of them have in common
Use only the shortest path to the goal, then describe that one path in full detail and no other
Ignore the difficulty of the paths and describe every path equally, then pick the one the solver took
optionExplain: Right: drop the paths too hard, then find invariants.
Too-hard paths are not available.
Shortest is not the rule.
Difficulty is central.
questions.explain: At a given level, some paths are not available as paths to the goal because they are too difficult.
questions.teaches: An analysis of the task environment describes the constraints that must be satisfied to attain the goal at a specified level of intelligence; paths too difficult for that level are removed and the invariant features of the remaining paths are sought.
questions.rule: Domain ability reflects domain knowledge as well as aptitude, and players of similar strength see similar things.

questions.q: A guide describes a cross-country trip for someone who must explain why it was difficult. Which details matter most?
options: The flat roads that make up most of the journey
The hard stretches such as mountain passes
The color and make of the car used for the trip
The number of road signs counted along the way
optionExplain: Flat roads are easy.
Right: difficulty lies in the passes.
Color is irrelevant.
Signs are not the difficulty.
questions.explain: Difficulty is concentrated in a few segments. The card next states the method.
questions.rule: Merge nodes that are obviously reachable from one another and describe in detail only the hard passages.

questions.q: The difficulty of search for a solver is measured by the expected size of his search ____.
questions.explain: The measure can be applied to path segments too.
questions.rule: Merge nodes that are obviously reachable from one another and describe in detail only the hard passages.

questions.q: A tutor analyzes a pupil's long division. Writing digits is obvious; finding each quotient digit is hard. How should the analysis proceed?
options: Detail every pen stroke the pupil makes, whether the stroke is hard or easy
Skip the whole division
Merge the obvious steps and give detail on the quotient-digit steps
Detail only the final answer
optionExplain: That keeps the plains.
That drops the passes.
Right: simplify the plains, keep the passes.
That drops the process.
questions.explain: Obvious steps are treated as a single unit.
questions.rule: Merge nodes that are obviously reachable from one another and describe in detail only the hard passages.

questions.q: True or false: A good task description must keep the detail of every link inside a cluster of nodes easily reachable from one another.
questions.explain: Such clusters can be treated as single nodes.
questions.rule: Merge nodes that are obviously reachable from one another and describe in detail only the hard passages.

questions.q: The authors assume their adult subjects follow rules at the level of executing chess moves. Why would this assumption fail for young children?
options: Children never play chess at all, so legal moves cannot matter for them
Legal moves do not exist for children, who cannot yet see the board
Children are too fast at the game to be described in terms of episodes
Making a legal move can itself be a problem for a child or beginner
optionExplain: Some children do play.
They exist.
Speed is not the point.
Right: obviousness depends on the solver.
questions.explain: Legal moves are declared immediately available processes for adults.
questions.teaches: Making a legal move in chess can be a problem for a child or a beginner, so the assumption that legal moves are immediately available processes would not be viable for young children.
questions.rule: Merge nodes that are obviously reachable from one another and describe in detail only the hard passages.

questions.q: In a solved maze, getting from C to D took a second, but D to E took an hour. What does this show about difficulty?
options: Difficulty can be measured for segments, and segments can differ greatly
Difficulty exists only for whole paths and cannot be assigned to segments
All segments are equally hard, so the difference is only a measuring error
The step from D to E must have been the easy one of the two segments
optionExplain: Right: segments differ.
The measure applies to segments.
They differ.
It was the hard one.
questions.explain: The authors give such an A-to-G path as an example of uneven difficulty.
questions.teaches: The difficulty of getting from A to G can be spoken of for the whole path and also for any segment, and a segment such as C to D may be easy while D to E is very hard.
questions.rule: Merge nodes that are obviously reachable from one another and describe in detail only the hard passages.

questions.q: A chef's evening is described as: make stock, sear meat, plate. What are these in the authors' sense?
options: Invariants, each a property shared by every path to the goal
Episodes, each a segment devoted to a goal
Problem spaces, each a whole representation of the task
Rules of inference, each a step allowed in a formal proof
optionExplain: Invariants hold across all paths.
Right: goal-directed segments.
A problem space is the whole representation.
Rules of inference belong to proofs.
questions.explain: Each step is a goal-directed unit of behavior. The card next defines an episode.
questions.rule: Treat behavior as a sequence of goal-directed episodes and study what starts and ends each.

questions.q: An episode is a segment of behavior associated with attaining a ____.
questions.explain: Each episode is devoted to a goal.
questions.rule: Treat behavior as a sequence of goal-directed episodes and study what starts and ends each.

questions.q: Mia's packing is described as gather clothes, fold, zip. What should a theory of her behavior attend to mainly?
options: Every finger movement she makes while packing the case
The brand and make of the suitcase she packs
What starts each episode and what ends it
The weather forecast for the day of her trip
optionExplain: That is molecular detail.
Irrelevant.
Right: initiation and termination of episodes.
Irrelevant.
questions.explain: Episodes are treated as units.
questions.rule: Treat behavior as a sequence of goal-directed episodes and study what starts and ends each.

questions.q: True or false: If an episode's goal is easy for the solver, the authors say its detailed behavior need not be studied closely.
questions.explain: If the goal is sufficiently easy, we need not be concerned with the details.
questions.rule: Treat behavior as a sequence of goal-directed episodes and study what starts and ends each.

questions.q: A researcher says episodes of hard goals can also be skipped as units. What is wrong?
options: Hard goals have no episodes
Episodes cannot be hard
Nothing is wrong, since every episode can be treated as a unit however hard its goal may be
The unit treatment is justified when the goal is easy relative to the solver's power
optionExplain: Hard goals have episodes too.
Episodes can be hard.
The condition matters.
Right: the condition is an easy goal.
questions.explain: For hard goals the detail is the interesting part.
questions.rule: Treat behavior as a sequence of goal-directed episodes and study what starts and ends each.

questions.q: A new clerk finds filing trivial, so a researcher predicts the filing episodes from the task alone. What do the authors say makes this possible?
options: The goal is easy enough relative to the clerk's power, so episodes follow from task analysis
Clerks are all alike in what they can do, so one clerk's episodes serve for every clerk and every office
Filing has no goals of its own, so a researcher can only predict from outside the task itself
The researcher watches every motion of the clerk and records each one in full and careful detail
optionExplain: Right: easy goals let episodes come from task analysis.
Likeness is not the claim.
Filing has a goal.
Watching each motion is what the unit view avoids.
questions.explain: When the goal is easy enough, episodes can be derived from the task environment.
questions.teaches: If the goal is easy enough relative to the power of the problem solver, the episodes can be derived from analysis of the task environment and treated as units.
questions.rule: Treat behavior as a sequence of goal-directed episodes and study what starts and ends each.

questions.q: A study measures skill in chess, cryptarithmetic and logic. Must it assume that the best chess player is also the best at logic?
options: Yes: ability is general, so the best at chess is best at logic
No: it assumes only an ability within each domain
Yes: all three are the same game in different clothes
No: it assumes no ability of any kind within a domain
optionExplain: The authors leave this to evidence.
Right: no cross-domain ordering is assumed.
The domains differ.
It assumes a unidimensional ability within each.
questions.explain: The authors do not postulate agreement across domains. The card next states their restrictions.
questions.rule: Restrict to a homogeneous class of tasks and to subjects for whom the tasks are neither impossible nor trivial.

questions.q: Whether intelligence generalizes over different task domains is, the authors say, an ____ question.
questions.explain: It is settled by evidence, not definition.
questions.rule: Restrict to a homogeneous class of tasks and to subjects for whom the tasks are neither impossible nor trivial.

questions.q: A researcher studies spelling-bee skill. Which subject group follows the authors' restriction?
options: Professional lexicographers only
Toddlers who cannot yet read
Pupils who understand the task and find it neither trivial nor impossible
Anyone at all, since the choice of subjects makes no difference to the analysis
optionExplain: Experts would find it trivial.
Toddlers cannot accept the task.
Right: not too naive, not too expert.
The authors restrict subjects.
questions.explain: Subjects should be able to understand and accept the task and find it non-trivial.
questions.rule: Restrict to a homogeneous class of tasks and to subjects for whom the tasks are neither impossible nor trivial.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say their three task domains are as diverse as the tasks of an intelligence test battery.
questions.explain: They call these domains extremely homogeneous by comparison.
questions.rule: Restrict to a homogeneous class of tasks and to subjects for whom the tasks are neither impossible nor trivial.

questions.q: If one solver ranks higher at chess and lower at logic, does that contradict the authors' plan?
options: Yes: it refutes the assumption of scalable intelligence altogether
Yes: it refutes the claim that chess is a unidimensional skill at all
No: since such a case of different orderings never happens
No: they do not require the orderings to agree
optionExplain: Scalability is within a domain.
Chess is unaffected.
It can happen; they do not rule it out.
Right: no cross-domain ordering is postulated.
questions.explain: The unidimensional ability is assumed domain by domain.
questions.rule: Restrict to a homogeneous class of tasks and to subjects for whom the tasks are neither impossible nor trivial.

questions.q: What does choosing subjects who are neither too smart nor too knowledgeable do for the authors' tasks?
options: The tasks are then real problems for them, not trivial
It makes the subjects identical in what they know and can do
It raises their motivation
It removes the need for tasks
optionExplain: Right: tasks must pose a problem.
It does not make them identical.
Motivation is a separate matter.
Tasks remain.
questions.explain: A task that is trivial for the subject does not display problem solving.
questions.teaches: The authors use a restricted class of subjects who are intelligent enough to understand and accept the tasks, yet not so smart or knowledgeable that the tasks are trivial for them.
questions.rule: Restrict to a homogeneous class of tasks and to subjects for whom the tasks are neither impossible nor trivial.

questions.q: Two subjects attack the same puzzle with radically different mental pictures. What do the authors expect to do?
options: Average the two pictures into a single picture
Make two separate analyses of the task
Discard one of the two subjects from the study
Assume that the two pictures are really identical
optionExplain: Averaging merges incompatible spaces.
Right: separate analyses and perhaps different measures.
Both are valid subjects.
The pictures differ.
questions.explain: Different problem spaces call for separate analyses. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Fix the problem space assumed, put shared knowledge in the environment, and pick naive subjects to cut variance.

questions.q: The authors' main technique for reducing variance in representation is to select subjects who are ____ in certain dimensions.
questions.explain: Naive subjects have not seen the particular problems or the specific kind of task.
questions.rule: Fix the problem space assumed, put shared knowledge in the environment, and pick naive subjects to cut variance.

questions.q: A study of mental arithmetic assumes every participant knows that doubling a number gives an even number. Which restriction is this?
options: Restricting the domain to a single definite class of task environments
Choosing naive subjects who have not seen the particular problems before
Treating an informational resource as part of the task environment
Fixing the intelligence scale so that it measures one ability only
optionExplain: The domain is arithmetic.
Naivete concerns unseen problems.
Right: shared knowledge goes into the environment.
Intelligence scaling is separate.
questions.explain: The even-number fact is regarded as a feature of the task environment, not of each solver.
questions.rule: Fix the problem space assumed, put shared knowledge in the environment, and pick naive subjects to cut variance.

questions.q: True or false: If two subjects use radically different problem spaces, the authors expect two separate analyses of the task.
questions.explain: They expect separate analyses, perhaps with different difficulty measures and invariants.
questions.rule: Fix the problem space assumed, put shared knowledge in the environment, and pick naive subjects to cut variance.

questions.q: A reviewer says the authors require naive subjects in every task. What is the exception?
options: In chess the subjects are untrained, but the positions are familiar ones to them
In logic the subjects are experts, and the problems are well known to them in advance
There is no exception: naive subjects are required in every one of the tasks
In chess the subjects must be chess players, but the positions must be new to them
optionExplain: Untrained subjects would not play chess.
Logic uses naive subjects.
The authors note the exception.
Right: kind-of-task naivete is relaxed for chess.
questions.explain: The requirement not to have seen the particular problems is kept.
questions.rule: Fix the problem space assumed, put shared knowledge in the environment, and pick naive subjects to cut variance.

questions.q: How do the authors regard the final demonstration that scalable intelligence is tenable?
options: It comes from the analyses undertaken in later chapters
It is proved in full within this chapter, using the examples given
It needs no demonstration at all
It is shown by the definitions of the terms alone, with no data
optionExplain: Right: the later analyses.
They only establish the method here.
They call for a demonstration.
They say not by definition.
questions.explain: This chapter only sets the methodological basis.
questions.teaches: The final demonstration that the assumption of scalable intelligence is tenable comes from the analyses undertaken in later chapters; this chapter establishes only the methodological basis.
questions.rule: Fix the problem space assumed, put shared knowledge in the environment, and pick naive subjects to cut variance.

questions.q: Which question did the chapter open with and return to at its end?
options: How to build a computer whose memory can store lists and associations together
How far behavior is demanded by the task environment rather than the solver
How to measure short-term memory span in a way that is the same for every subject
How to teach chess to beginners in a way that makes the game easy to learn
optionExplain: Not a chapter question.
Right: the relation of task environment to problem solver.
Not a chapter question.
Not a chapter question.
questions.explain: The opening claim about demanded behavior returns in the last question. The card next lists all four.
questions.rule: Four issues structure the chapter: the environment, the problem space, the representation of problems, and the demands of the task.

questions.q: Put the chapter's four questions in order.
items: How to represent the external environment
How the subject represents it internally
How to represent problems and their goals
How task environment and solver relate
questions.explain: The chapter moves from environment to problem space to problems to the relation between environment and solver.
questions.rule: Four issues structure the chapter: the environment, the problem space, the representation of problems, and the demands of the task.

questions.q: Match each concept to the question it answers.
questions.explain: Each concept is the main answer to one of the four questions.
questions.rule: Four issues structure the chapter: the environment, the problem space, the representation of problems, and the demands of the task.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say experimenters have no privileged access to the real world that forms a subject's environment.
questions.explain: We have no privileged access to the real world that constitutes the environment of another human.
questions.rule: Four issues structure the chapter: the environment, the problem space, the representation of problems, and the demands of the task.

questions.q: True or false: The authors claim the set and search representations cover every kind of problem.
questions.explain: They leave open that other problem representations exist.
questions.rule: Four issues structure the chapter: the environment, the problem space, the representation of problems, and the demands of the task.

questions.q: A pupil proposes a move the game rules forbid. What caution from the chapter's summary applies to the teacher's model of the pupil?
options: Treat the move as an error
Ignore the move, since moves outside the rules tell nothing about the pupil
Do not assume the pupil's problem space lies inside the legal space
Assume the pupil has no problem space
optionExplain: That assumes the legal space.
The move is evidence.
Right: the subject's space may extend beyond legal moves.
The pupil has a space.
questions.explain: The summary says one must not assume automatically that the subject's space lies within a legal problem space.
questions.teaches: One must not assume automatically that the subject's problem space will lie inside a legal problem space as understood by the experimenter.
questions.rule: Four issues structure the chapter: the environment, the problem space, the representation of problems, and the demands of the task.

questions.q: What provides the interface between the problem solver and the task environment, according to the authors?
options: The experimenter's instructions to the subject
The physical room in which the experiment is held
The solver's long-term memory and what it holds
The goal accepted by the problem solver
optionExplain: Instructions are stimuli, not the interface.
The room is part of the environment.
Memory is a part of the solver.
Right: the accepted goal.
questions.explain: The goal links the two components of the theory. The card next states this.
questions.rule: The accepted goal is the interface between the IPS and the task environment; later parts apply the concepts to real tasks.

questions.q: The three later parts of the book deal with cryptarithmetic, elementary logic and ____.
questions.explain: These are the three task domains analyzed in detail.
questions.rule: The accepted goal is the interface between the IPS and the task environment; later parts apply the concepts to real tasks.

questions.q: Why did the authors use simple examples and metaphors in this chapter?
options: A real task environment would obscure the broad issues in technical particulars
Real task environments do not exist, so only simple examples and metaphors are possible
Metaphors are exact, and a simple metaphor can replace a detailed analysis
Readers asked for simple examples, and the authors wished to please their readers
optionExplain: Right: simple cases keep the issues visible.
Real tasks are used later.
Metaphors are illustrative.
No such reason is given.
questions.explain: Detail would have buried the general issues.
questions.rule: The accepted goal is the interface between the IPS and the task environment; later parts apply the concepts to real tasks.

questions.q: True or false: The authors claim this chapter fully makes its general concepts operational.
questions.explain: They say full understanding requires analysis of an environment in detail.
questions.rule: The accepted goal is the interface between the IPS and the task environment; later parts apply the concepts to real tasks.

questions.q: Put the sequence of the book's preliminary chapters in order.
items: Chapter 2: the information processing system
Chapter 3: the task environment
Chapter 4: how an IPS goes about solving a problem
questions.explain: Chapters 2 and 3 describe the two components; Chapter 4 describes the problem solving activity.
questions.rule: The accepted goal is the interface between the IPS and the task environment; later parts apply the concepts to real tasks.

questions.q: What will the next chapter use to illustrate its general discussion of how an IPS solves a problem?
options: An extensive analysis of a chess grandmaster's play
An extensive analysis of the Logic Theorist
A detailed study of crossword solvers at work
A survey of the limits of human short-term memory
optionExplain: Chess comes in a later part.
Right: the Logic Theorist.
Crosswords were a short example here.
No survey is promised.
questions.explain: The Logic Theorist was one of the first problem solving systems programmed for a digital computer.
questions.teaches: Chapter 4 illustrates its general account of problem solving with an extensive analysis of the Logic Theorist, one of the first problem solving systems programmed for a digital computer.
questions.rule: The accepted goal is the interface between the IPS and the task environment; later parts apply the concepts to real tasks.

questions.q: A theory of problem solving should answer which pair of questions?
options: How is intelligence measured, and how does it grow with age?
How can a problem be solved, and what makes a problem difficult?
Why do solvers differ in motivation, and how can it be raised?
How are problems posed, and who ought to pose them?
optionExplain: Intelligence testing is a different field; the chapter does not set out to measure intelligence.
Right: solution and difficulty are the two questions the chapter sets itself.
Motivation matters to people, but it is not one of the chapter's two questions.
Posing problems is a topic the authors mention later only for LT's learning; it is not the chapter's pair.
questions.explain: The chapter asks how a problem can be solved and what makes it hard. The card next gives the full statement.
questions.rule: Solution and difficulty are the two questions.

questions.q: The theory is meant to apply to man, beast and ____ alike.
questions.explain: The authors say the theory should apply to man, beast and machine, insofar as each can be represented as an information processing system.
questions.rule: The theory covers anything representable as an IPS.

questions.q: A lab builds a robot vacuum and models it as an IPS of the Chapter 2 type. Does the chapter's theory reach it?
options: No: the theory is limited to humans because only humans solve problems
Yes: the theory is meant for any system representable as such an IPS, machines included
Only if the robot copies the errors that people make on the same task
Only if the robot's program is the Logic Theorist or a close relative
optionExplain: Tempting if problem solving is thought uniquely human, but the authors extend the theory to beast and machine.
Right: the claim is about systems representable as an IPS, not about humans alone.
Matching human errors is a later test of a human theory, not a condition for the general theory to apply.
LT is only the worked example; the theory is not restricted to it.
questions.explain: The condition is representability as an IPS, not who or what the system is.
questions.rule: Representable as an IPS is the test.

questions.q: True or false: In this chapter the authors set out to demonstrate the full breadth of their theory.
questions.explain: They say they need not demonstrate the breadth here. They give an overview with simple examples and then study one program in depth.
questions.rule: This chapter supplies tools, not the whole demonstration.

questions.q: Why do the authors study the Logic Theorist in depth instead of surveying many programs?
options: It is the only problem solving program that had been written when the book appeared
It reproduces the way a human subject proves logic theorems, step by step
It can prove every theorem of elementary logic given enough time
It was among the first heuristic problem solving programs and illustrates many of the theory's basic ideas
optionExplain: Other programs existed; the authors say many have been written since 1956.
Matching a human subject is a later question; LT is introduced as an example of a problem solver.
The chapter later shows LT cannot prove every theorem, for example Theorem 2.13.
Right: the authors cite its historical interest and its many illustrations of the theory.
questions.explain: The authors choose LT for its historical place as one of the first heuristic programs and for what it illustrates.
questions.rule: An example is chosen for what it illustrates.
questions.teaches: The authors pick LT partly for its historical interest as one of the first heuristic problem solving programs, and because it illustrates many basic ideas of the theory.

questions.q: Before a solver applies any method, which process comes first in the authors' scheme?
options: Translating the external situation into an internal representation and problem space
Testing a candidate solution against the goal
Choosing which of several rival methods to trust
Abandoning the problem if it looks too hard
optionExplain: Right: the input translation comes first and sets the stage.
Testing needs candidates, which need a space to come from; that is later.
Method selection follows once a representation exists.
Abandoning is one of the options after a method has ended.
questions.explain: The authors place the input translation first. The card next describes it.
questions.rule: Represent first, then choose a method.

questions.q: The first process, which builds the internal representation, is called the input ____.
questions.explain: The authors name the initial process the input translation; it builds the representation and selects a problem space.
questions.rule: The first process is the input translation.

questions.q: A hiker reads a trail map and decides the trail is a path of junctions, ignoring elevation. What is this reading in the authors' terms?
options: A method that has been halted by a monitoring process
A subgoal that has been set aside for a later branch
An internal representation chosen by input translation, which fixes what can be solved
A test that distinguishes correct paths from incorrect ones
optionExplain: No method has run yet; the picture is what a method would work in.
Subgoals come from methods in operation, not from the first translation.
Right: the hiker's junction picture is the representation, and it limits what questions are easy.
A test is part of a method; the picture is the space in which tests are applied.
questions.explain: Choosing to see the trail as junctions is the translation step; elevation questions become hard or impossible in that picture.
questions.rule: The representation fixes what is easy and what is out of reach.

questions.q: True or false: An internal representation is guaranteed to make the solution easier to find than the raw problem was.
questions.explain: The authors say the representation may render solutions obvious, obscure or perhaps unattainable.
questions.rule: A representation can help or hinder.

questions.q: A student reads a word problem as a picture of two trains and cannot make progress. By the authors' scheme, what is one option open to the student?
options: Keep the same picture and run the same method with more speed
Wait for the environment to supply the answer
Treat the lack of progress as a sign that the problem is unsolvable
Select a different internal representation and reformulate the problem
optionExplain: Speed does not fix a representation that hides the answer.
The environment may supply new information, but waiting is not one of the listed options.
The authors list abandoning as an option, but not as a verdict that the problem is unsolvable.
Right: one of three options after a method ends is to choose a different representation and reformulate.
questions.explain: After a method is terminated, the solver may try another method, select a different representation and reformulate, or abandon the attempt.
questions.rule: A poor representation can be replaced.
questions.teaches: When a method ends, one option is to select a different internal representation and reformulate the problem.

questions.q: Who or what may end a running problem solving method, in the authors' scheme?
options: Only the external environment, when it changes the task
The method itself, or more general processes that monitor how it is going
Only the solver's memory, once the answer is stored
Nothing; a method must run until it reaches the goal
optionExplain: The environment can interrupt (a footnote says so), but it is not the only halting source.
Right: the authors name both the method's own processes and general monitors.
Memory is not named as a halting mechanism.
Methods can be halted, which is why other options exist after termination.
questions.explain: Halting can come from the method or from monitoring. The card next sets out the steps.
questions.rule: Methods can be halted from inside or outside.

questions.q: The selected method comes to ____ the behavior, both internal and external, of the problem solver.
questions.explain: The authors say the applied method controls the solver's behavior, internal and external, until it is halted.

questions.q: A cook stirring custard by a recipe smells scorching and stops stirring. Which statement fits the authors' account?
options: The recipe method reached its goal and so ended
The cook changed the problem space by input translation
The method was halted by a monitoring process that is not part of the recipe itself
The cook set a subgoal aside in favor of another branch
optionExplain: The goal of cooked custard was not reached; the method was interrupted.
The scorch smell does not change the problem space; it halts the method.
Right: monitoring processes can halt a method whose own steps have not finished.
No subgoal was generated or set aside in this story.
questions.explain: The recipe says nothing about scorching; a more general monitor noticed and stopped it.
questions.rule: A monitor can stop a method that does not know it is failing.

questions.q: True or false: Because a method is rational, it must be rational about the external problem even when the internal representation is poor.
questions.explain: The method bears a rational relation to attaining the solution as formulated and seen in the internal representation, so a poor representation carries over.
questions.rule: Rationality is relative to the representation.

questions.q: A person tries three different ways, one after another, to open a jammed jar. How does the authors' scheme describe this?
options: One goal attacked by a sequence of methods, so behavior under one goal can look sharply divergent
Three separate goals, one for each technique tried
A single method that is repeated three times unchanged
A failure of the input translation, which must be redone each time
optionExplain: Right: the authors say a goal may be attacked by a whole sequence of methods.
The goal is the same each time; only the methods change.
The techniques differ, so these are different methods.
Changing methods does not require redoing the input translation.
questions.explain: The authors note that a goal may be attacked by a sequence of methods, so one stretch of behavior aimed at one goal may contain several quite different sequences.
questions.rule: One goal, several methods in turn.
