questions.teaches: Because a goal may be attacked by a whole sequence of methods, one segment of behavior aimed at a single goal can contain sharply divergent sequences.

questions.q: A method has stopped without a solution. Which set lists the options the authors give?
options: Try another method, choose a new representation, or abandon the attempt
Restart the same method, ask for help, or guess
Change the goal, change the solver, or change the environment
Rest, review the failed steps, or lower the standard for success
optionExplain: Right: these are the three options (a), (b) and (c).
Restarting and guessing are not on the authors' list.
The solver does not replace itself or its environment in this scheme.
Resting and lowering standards are not options the authors list.
questions.explain: There are three options. The card next states them.
questions.rule: Another method, another representation, or stop.

questions.q: Put these three options in the order the authors list them.
items: Attempt another method
Select a different representation and reformulate
Abandon the attempt
questions.explain: The authors list (a) another method, (b) a different representation, then (c) abandoning the attempt.

questions.q: A carpenter's first technique for joining two boards fails, so she redraws the joint as a flat plan instead of a 3-D object. Which option is this?
options: Attempting another method on the same representation
Abandoning the attempt to solve the problem
Selecting a different representation and reformulating the problem
Halting a method with a monitoring process
optionExplain: Option (a) would keep the same drawing and change the technique.
She keeps working, so she has not abandoned the attempt.
Right: redrawing the problem in another form is option (b).
Halting is what ended the first technique, before the options came into play.
questions.explain: Changing how the problem is pictured is a change of representation, not just of method.

questions.q: True or false: By the authors' list, a solver whose method has failed must try another method.
questions.explain: Trying another method is one option of three; the solver may instead change representation or abandon the attempt.

questions.q: While a solver is mid-method, a friend shouts a useful hint. Per the authors, what may happen?
options: Nothing, because the method controls behavior until it ends
New information from outside may interrupt current activity and prompt different attempts
The solver must abandon the attempt, since the method was disturbed
The solver must restart the input translation from scratch
optionExplain: That treats the method as uninterruptible, but the footnote says influx can interrupt.
Right: the footnote says continuous influx of new information may interrupt the solver.
A hint offers new possibilities; it does not force abandonment.
Interruption does not require redoing the translation; it may prompt different attempts.
questions.explain: A footnote adds that incoming information may offer new solution possibilities or demands and make the solver break off to try something different.
questions.teaches: A footnote adds that the continuous influx of new information from the external environment can offer new solution possibilities and cause the solver to interrupt its current activity.

questions.q: A running method creates a new problem for itself. What do the authors call it?
options: A representation
A recognition
A termination
A subgoal
optionExplain: A representation is how the problem is held internally, not a new problem.
Recognition is a method of solving by recalling an answer.
Termination is how a method ends.
Right: the authors call new problems produced by a method subgoals.
questions.explain: New problems from a method are subgoals. The card next states what the solver may do.

questions.q: A new problem produced during a method is called a ____.
questions.explain: The authors define a subgoal as a new problem produced by a method in operation.
questions.rule: A method may produce a subgoal.

questions.q: Planning a dinner, you need an ingredient you lack. You decide to finish chopping first and shop later. In the authors' terms, you have...
options: abandoned the attempt to solve the problem
set a new subgoal aside and continued with another branch of the original method
selected a different representation and reformulated
halted the method by a monitoring process
optionExplain: You are still making dinner, so the attempt continues.
Right: the missing ingredient is a subgoal; you postponed it and carried on.
The problem is pictured as before; only the order of work changes.
No monitor stopped the method; you chose to proceed.
questions.explain: The solver has the option of setting a subgoal aside and continuing with another branch.

questions.q: True or false: A solver that meets a subgoal must attempt it at once.
questions.explain: The authors say the solver may elect to attempt a subgoal but may also set it aside and continue with another branch.
questions.rule: Subgoals are optional to pursue now.

questions.q: An assistant tidies the desk but sets a jammed drawer aside to fetch a screwdriver first. What does this show about how subgoals relate to the main goal?
options: Subgoals are new problems raised in service of the original method, and the order of pursuing them is a choice
Subgoals replace the original goal, which is then forgotten
Subgoals can only be solved after the original goal is reached
Subgoals are produced only by the external environment
optionExplain: Right: subgoals arise inside a method, and the solver chooses what to attempt next.
The original goal stays; the next sections discuss how pending goals are stored.
Subgoals support the original goal and so usually come before it.
The authors place subgoals inside methods, not outside.
questions.explain: Subgoals are produced by a method in operation, and the solver chooses among them and the other branches.
questions.teaches: A method itself produces subgoals while it runs, so the solver's choice among them and the other branches is made inside the method's operation.

questions.q: How many problem solving methods does the authors' solver activate at one time?
options: As many as there are subgoals
Two, a main one and a monitoring one
All applicable methods, with the best result kept
One
optionExplain: Subgoals are handled by goal control, but still one method is active at a time.
Monitoring processes exist, but they do not make the system run two methods at once.
Running every method together would be parallel; the authors say the opposite.
Right: the IPS is fundamentally serial in evoking methods.
questions.explain: The solver is serial in its methods. The card next adds what may happen in parallel.

questions.q: True or false: The solver may take in many things at once while it perceives, yet does one thing at a time about them.
questions.explain: The authors allow some parallel capability in scanning the environment or representation, while holding that only one method is active at a time.

questions.q: A chess player glances over the whole board in one look, then works through one plan of attack. How does the authors' account describe this?
options: Both perception and the use of methods must be strictly serial
The player must be running several methods in parallel
Perception may be parallel while the choice of method is serial
The player is not an information processing system
optionExplain: The authors allow some parallel processing at the perceptual level.
A single plan at a time is what the serial claim says.
Right: seeing many squares at once is allowed; working through one plan at a time is the rule.
A human player is exactly the kind of system the authors want to describe.
questions.explain: The authors let perception be parallel but keep method use serial.
questions.rule: Look in parallel, act one method at a time.

questions.q: Methods run serially, but scanning of the display may take place in ____.
questions.explain: The serial claim is about activating methods; the allowance for parallel processing is about perceptual scanning.

questions.q: A theory says people cannot read a map and plan a route at the same time. What would the authors' picture predict about reading while planning?
options: Both must wait their turn, one symbol at a time, because the system is serial throughout
Both can proceed together, since a human is not a serial system
Reading the map is perception that may be parallel; planning the route is a method, and only one runs at a time
Neither is possible without a monitoring process present
optionExplain: The authors allow parallel capacity at the detailed perceptual level.
The serial claim is about methods, and the authors apply it to people as IPSs.
Right: the authors separate the perceptual level from the method level.
Monitoring is irrelevant to the serial point.
questions.explain: The serial constraint is on evoking methods, while the scanning of the display may take in many items at once.
questions.rule: Serial applies to methods, not to every perceptual act.
questions.teaches: The authors tie the serial structure to a symbol-manipulating IPS: only such a system can switch methods and representations and make decisions as the scheme requires.

questions.q: Which cycle do the authors say the solver's behavior repeats?
options: Select a goal, select a method, evaluate the results, select a goal again
Perceive, remember, forget, perceive again
Generate, test, reject, generate again
Plan, act, rest, plan again
optionExplain: Right: this is the circuit the authors describe.
These are memory events, not the goal-method circuit.
Generate-and-test is one particular method, not the whole cycle.
Resting is not part of the authors' circuit.
questions.explain: The cycle runs from goal to method to evaluation and back to goal. The card next explains why goals pile up.

questions.q: Goals that wait while new goals are handled are said to be held in ____.
questions.explain: Pending goals are held in abeyance while new goals are attended to and are re-evoked when the new goals are reached.

questions.q: You are baking, you need to melt butter first, and while melting it you must find a pan. Which order do pending goals return in?
options: Continue baking, then melt the butter, then find a pan
Melt the butter, then continue baking, then find a pan
Find a pan, then continue baking, then melt the butter
Find a pan, then melt the butter, then continue baking
optionExplain: This returns to the oldest goal first, the opposite of a stack.
Melting cannot finish before the pan is found.
Baking is the oldest pending goal and would be resumed last.
Right: the most recent goal is satisfied first and the earlier goals are re-evoked in reverse order, like a stack.
questions.explain: Goals pushed down last are popped up first, so the latest sub-need is settled before the earlier goals return.

questions.q: True or false: Because goals are stored and re-evoked, behavior directed at one goal can be tied to behavior that happened long before.
questions.explain: The authors say recursiveness creates dependencies between behaviors that are remote from each other in time.
questions.rule: Recursion links behaviors far apart in time.

questions.q: A manager keeps a to-do list where each new urgent task goes on top and is finished before older ones. Which structure does this resemble?
options: A parallel scanner that reads every item together
A pushdown list, or stack, where the newest item is handled first
A discrimination net that sorts items by their features
A generator that produces items in random order
optionExplain: A scanner reads items together, but the to-do list handles one item at a time, newest first.
Right: newest on top, handled first, is the pushdown pattern the authors name.
A discrimination net sorts by features, a recognition device from Chapter 2, not a store of waiting goals.
Nothing is random in a to-do stack; the order is fixed by when items arrive.
questions.explain: Goals pushed down last are popped up first. The authors add that the interpreter of Chapter 2 uses stacks with programming languages for essentially the same purposes.
questions.rule: Waiting goals sit on a stack.
questions.teaches: In the Chapter 2 interpreter (their Figure 2.11), stacks are used with programming languages for essentially the same purposes as the goal stack of a problem solver.

questions.q: Into which two principal parts does the authors' theory of problem solving divide?
options: Perception of problems and memory of solutions
Representations and their selection, and problem solving within a given representation
Easy problems and difficult problems
Human solvers and machine solvers
optionExplain: Perception and memory are components of an IPS, not the theory's two parts.
Right: representation, and methods within a representation.
Difficulty is a topic of the chapter but not the split of the theory.
The authors want one theory for both kinds of solver.
questions.explain: The split is between representations and solving within them. The card next gives the details.

questions.q: The second part of the theory defines a set of methods together with executive ____ for selecting and evaluating them.
questions.explain: The second part defines methods and executive organizations for selecting and evaluating them.

questions.q: A study looks at how people choose between ways of picturing a puzzle, such as a list versus a diagram. Which part of the theory does it address?
options: The within-representation part: methods and their executives
Neither, since both parts are about methods only
The part about difficulty, which is separate from both
The representation part: possible representations and their selection
optionExplain: The second part starts after a representation is in place.
The first part is about representations, not methods.
Difficulty is a separate question, but this study concerns selection of pictures.
Right: choosing among pictures is the first part.
questions.explain: How representations are chosen belongs to the first part of the theory.
questions.rule: Choosing a picture belongs to part one.

questions.q: True or false: The authors claim the theory of how representations are selected is well developed.
questions.explain: They say the first part has not received much attention as yet, and that most progress concerns methods.
questions.rule: Representation theory is the thin part.

questions.q: What reason do the authors give for treating the book's emphasis on methods as not too damaging?
options: Some studied representations have wide applicability, and human subjects barely change their representations during the tasks studied
Methods and representations are the same thing under another name
Representation problems turn out to be easy to solve by recognition
No problem in the book depends on a representation at all
optionExplain: Right: the authors give both reasons.
They treat the two as separate parts of the theory.
Recognition is a different method for a different purpose.
Representations do matter; the book simply assumes the representation is fixed.
questions.explain: The authors argue that the studied representations are widely applicable and that subjects in the tasks studied do not change representation appreciably.
questions.rule: The focus fits the tasks studied.
questions.teaches: The authors note that the human subjects in the tasks they studied do not in fact change or modify their representations appreciably during problem solving.

questions.q: How do the authors describe our knowledge of how representations are selected and modified?
options: It is better understood than the study of methods
It is fully worked out for human solvers
Much less has been learned than about methods
It is irrelevant to problem solving
optionExplain: The authors say the opposite.
They say the first part has received little attention.
Right: representation is the less developed part.
They accept it matters; it is simply less studied.
questions.explain: The authors say much less is known. The card next gives their reason for going on anyway.

questions.q: The authors say the limit may not be too damaging because some representations have very wide ____.
questions.explain: Some of the representations that have been studied have very wide applicability.

questions.q: A researcher studies adults solving puzzles in which everyone keeps the same picture of the problem throughout. Which authors' point supports a focus on methods here?
options: Representations are irrelevant to puzzles of any kind
Methods and representations can never be separated
Only machines ever change their representations
Subjects who do not change representation make the within-representation theory enough for that task
optionExplain: Representations matter; they are held fixed in this case.
The authors separate the two parts of the theory.
The claim concerns their human subjects, not machines.
Right: the authors rely on subjects not changing representation appreciably.
questions.explain: If subjects keep one representation, a theory of methods inside it captures most of the behavior.
questions.rule: A fixed representation lets a theory of methods carry the load.

questions.q: True or false: If a task required subjects to keep switching representations, the book's emphasis on methods would explain less of their behavior.
questions.explain: The authors' defense rests on their tasks involving little change of representation. This is our reading of their argument.
questions.rule: The defense depends on the tasks.

questions.q: In which kind of problem would the authors accept that the representation part of the theory matters most?
options: One that can be solved by recognition alone
One where the whole difficulty lies in finding the right representation
One with a very large search space but a good representation
One where a ready-made method exists for the formulation
optionExplain: Recognition bypasses both difficulty and representation.
Right: the authors point to problems where, once the representation is found, solving is trivial.
A large space with a good representation is a difficulty of methods and space size.
A ready method makes the representation less central.
questions.explain: The authors note that some problems have all their difficulty in finding the right representation, as in the Nine Dot Problem of the next card.
questions.rule: Some problems turn on representation alone.
questions.teaches: Some problems have their whole difficulty in finding the right representation; once found, solving is a trivial matter.

questions.q: In the Nine Dot Problem, what usually keeps solvers from finding a four-line solution?
options: The huge number of possible line combinations
A rule that forbids lifting the pencil
An assumed restriction that the lines may not extend beyond the square of dots
The need to count the dots correctly
optionExplain: The space is not huge; the difficulty is the hidden restriction.
No-lift is part of the statement but does not block the solution.
Right: the stay-inside restriction comes from the representation.
Counting plays no role.
questions.explain: Most subjects add a restriction the problem never states. The card next explains.
questions.rule: The solver, not the problem, adds the restriction.

questions.q: In the Nine Dot Problem the subject must draw ____ straight lines through all nine dots.
questions.explain: The task is four straight lines without raising the pencil, passing through all nine dots.

questions.q: A solver stuck on a seating plan assumes every guest must sit inside the table's rectangle, though the host did not say so. This resembles the Nine Dot Problem because the block is...
options: a restriction from the solver's representation, not from the problem statement
a rule stated by the host in the problem
the huge number of possible seatings
a lack of any method for the task
optionExplain: Right: the rectangle limit is self-imposed, like the stay-inside limit.
The host never stated it, so it is not part of the problem.
The count of seatings is not what blocks the solver here.
The block is in the picture, not in missing methods.
questions.explain: The Nine Dot difficulty is an assumed limit that the representation imposes.
questions.rule: Check whether a limit is in the problem or in your picture.

questions.q: True or false: A subject who considers lines extending outside the square finds a solution very quickly.
questions.explain: The authors say that once the subject considers such lines, a solution comes quickly; the restriction came from the representation.
questions.rule: Lift the assumed limit and the problem opens up.

questions.q: A friend says the Nine Dot Problem is typical of the problems imported into the psychological laboratory. How do the authors see it?
options: As the best sample of all laboratory problems
As a task that proves methods do not matter
As perhaps untypical of the problems imported into the laboratory
As a task no human has ever solved
optionExplain: They say the opposite: it is perhaps untypical, not the best sample.
Methods still matter for most tasks the book studies; this one just turns on representation.
Right: they call it perhaps rather untypical.
People do solve it, and quickly once the representation changes.
questions.explain: The authors flag the problem as perhaps untypical and add that how representations are selected has not received much attention yet.
questions.rule: Do not generalize from an untypical case.
questions.teaches: The authors call the Nine Dot Problem perhaps untypical of the problems imported into the psychological laboratory.

questions.q: What is the best short description of a method in this theory?
options: A guaranteed procedure that always produces a solution
A single operation applied once to the problem
A collection of information processes combining a series of means to attain, or attempt to attain, an end
A way of measuring how difficult a problem is
optionExplain: Methods attempt; many fail.
A method combines a series of means, not one operation.
Right: means combined toward an end, attempted but not guaranteed.
Difficulty is analyzed separately.
questions.explain: A method combines means toward an end. The card next states what fixes the means.
questions.rule: A method is means plus an end.

questions.q: A method can be understood only in reference to its ____.
questions.explain: The authors say a method can be understood only in reference to its goal, whether explicit or implicit in the method.

questions.q: In a board game you may move only along marked lanes. Which part of the theory decides which means your method may use?
options: The solver's memory of previous games
The problem space, specified by the internal representation
The speed of the solver's processing
The number of players at the table
optionExplain: Memory may supply information but does not set the means.
Right: the problem space fixes how the situation can change.
Speed does not determine which means are allowed.
Players are not mentioned as a determinant of means.
questions.explain: The means are dictated by the nature of the internal representation, since the problem space determines the ways the situation can change.

questions.q: True or false: A goal in a method must be written out in every method as an explicit symbol structure.
questions.explain: A goal may be represented explicitly as a symbol structure or may be implicit in the structure of the method itself.

questions.q: A thermostat aims at one temperature but has no stored goal symbol. How does the authors' account treat such a goal?
options: It does not count as a goal until a symbol is stored
It must be a subgoal produced by the thermostat's method
It is the representation, not the goal
It can be implicit in the structure of the method, not represented as a symbol structure
optionExplain: The authors say explicit symbols are optional.
A subgoal is a new problem raised by a method; the target temperature is not one.
A goal and a representation are different things in the theory.
Right: the authors allow goals implicit in the method.
questions.explain: The authors say a goal may be represented explicitly as a symbol structure or implicit in the structure of the method itself.
questions.teaches: A goal need not be stored as an explicit symbol structure; it may be implicit in the structure of the method itself.

questions.q: Which method does the authors' theory pair with the set-predicate formulation of a problem?
options: Heuristic search
Generate-and-test
Recognition only
Working backward
optionExplain: Heuristic search is paired with the search formulation.
Right: generate-and-test is paired with set-predicate.
Recognition is a universal method that applies to every formulation, not the paired one.
Working backward is a direction of search, not the paired method.
questions.explain: Generate-and-test is paired with set-predicate. The card next adds the other pairing.

questions.q: Match each problem formulation to its associated method.
questions.explain: Chapter 3's two formulations each get a single basic method; recognition is the one method that applies to all formulations.
questions.rule: Pair the formulation with its method.

questions.q: A problem is stated as: find some member of a given set that passes a given test. Which method is associated with it?
options: Generate-and-test
Heuristic search for a path
Parameter passing
Working backward
optionExplain: Right: a set and a test is the set-predicate formulation.
Heuristic search goes with the search formulation, a path from initial element to goal.
Parameter passing is a footnote technique for interpretation.
Working backward concerns direction in search.
questions.explain: A set U with a test for a subset G is the set-predicate formulation, whose method is generate-and-test.

questions.q: True or false: Because each basic formulation has a method, no formulation can have more than one method.
questions.explain: The authors say several methods may exist for a single formulation, though in general only one is associated with each basic type.
questions.rule: One basic method, not the only possible method.

questions.q: Why do the authors say the name heuristic search covers both the formulation and its method?
options: The method and the formulation were invented by the same author
Heuristic search is the only method that exists for any formulation
The formulation was found by running the method
The two are essentially in one-one correspondence, as set-predicate is with generate-and-test
optionExplain: The reason given is correspondence, not authorship.
Other formulations have other methods.
Nothing in the text says the formulation came from running the method.
Right: the footnote draws the parallel with set-predicate and generate-and-test.
questions.explain: A footnote says the name has been used for both because the two are essentially in one-one correspondence, as with set-predicate and generate-and-test (Newell and Ernst, 1965).
questions.teaches: A footnote says the name heuristic search has been used for both the problem formulation and the method because the two are essentially in one-one correspondence.

questions.q: A general-purpose method meets a specific problem. What must happen before it can act on the problem?
options: The method must be rewritten from scratch for each problem
The problem must be solved by recognition first
The problem must be matched to symbol structures built into the method
The method must be halted by a monitor
optionExplain: Methods exist in the solver beforehand and are not rewritten.
Recognition is a different method, not a prerequisite.
Right: interpretation matches the method's abstract structures to the problem.
Halting is unrelated.
questions.explain: The method needs an interface to the problem. The card next names it.
questions.rule: A method needs an interface to the problem.

questions.q: Fitting a particular situation to a general method is a process of ____, in the sense in which logicians use that term.
questions.explain: The authors call the process of fitting a particular situation to the method interpretation, in the logicians' sense.

questions.q: A recipe card reads: bake X cakes for Y guests. Using the card for 12 guests means filling in Y. Which idea from the chapter does this resemble?
options: Halting: a monitoring process stopping the method
Recognition: recalling an answer already in memory
Interpretation: matching the method's variables with particular elements of the problem
Stop rules: pruning branches that lead nowhere
optionExplain: Nothing is stopped in this case.
Filling a slot is not retrieving a stored answer.
Right: the variable slot is filled by a specific value, as in parameter passing.
No branch is cut off here.
questions.explain: The recipe's variables are matched to particular values for this use, which is interpretation.
questions.rule: Fill the method's variables with the problem's particulars.

questions.q: True or false: A method whose symbol structures cannot be matched to a problem as presented still receives the information it requires.
questions.explain: The problem must be capable of interpretation in the method's terms, both to guarantee the information the method requires and to set limits on what is available.

questions.q: Why does the authors' footnote use the example of computing sin(30) with a routine written for sin(x)?
options: It shows interpretation in simple form: a value is stored in the variable cell by a special process called parameter passing
It shows that routines for sine cannot be reused for other angles
It shows that recognition is the only computing method
It shows that goals are stored on a stack
optionExplain: Right: the routine is general, and parameter passing supplies the particular.
The point is the opposite: one routine works for any angle.
The footnote is about interpretation, not recognition.
Stacks are discussed elsewhere in the chapter.
questions.explain: The footnote says the technique of writing the routine with a variable name and then storing a particular value in that cell is parameter passing, a simple instance of interpretation.
questions.rule: Parameter passing is a simple interpretation.
questions.teaches: A footnote calls the process that stores the particular value 30 into the variable cell x parameter passing, a simple form of the same interpretation technique.

questions.q: In a problem space that holds very little information, what kind of methods are likely to be usable?
options: Many powerful methods
No methods at all
Only recognition
Only one or two weak methods that proceed inefficiently
optionExplain: Powerful methods need information to exploit.
Weak methods still work.
Recognition is a separate universal method, not the only one left.
Right: weak methods can still proceed, though inefficiently.
questions.explain: A poor space leaves a few weak methods. The card next states the contrast with a rich space.

questions.q: In an information-____ problem space many methods may become applicable as one uses less and less of the total information.
questions.explain: In an information-rich problem space, many methods become applicable as less of the total information is used.

questions.q: A cook has a pantry stocked with every ingredient and also a detailed recipe book. A second cook has only salt and rice. Which statement fits the authors' point?
options: Both cooks are limited to the same single method
The first cook's space can support many methods; the second's leaves only a few weak methods
The second cook has more methods because there is less to consider
Neither cook can use any method
optionExplain: The point is a difference between rich and poor spaces.
Right: more information means more methods can be applied.
Poor spaces limit the choice, not enlarge it.
Weak methods still apply in the poor space.
questions.explain: An information-rich space supports many methods; an information-poor one only weak ones.
questions.rule: Information widens the choice of methods.

questions.q: True or false: If a problem space contains information, a solver must use all of it.
questions.explain: The authors say a space can contain more information than a method and its formulation require, since information need not be utilized simply because it is there.

questions.q: A recipe method is promised the oven temperature as a given. What must the kitchen's problem space be able to do for the method to work?
options: Hold exactly the information the method uses and nothing more
Generate, from the information and transformations it holds, the kind of information the formulation promises the method
Contain at least as many elements as the goal set
Solve the whole problem before the method starts
optionExplain: A space can hold more information than the minimum, so exactness is not required.
Right: the space must be able to yield what the formulation guarantees to the method.
Element counts are not the coupling condition.
If the space solved the problem, no method would be needed.
questions.explain: The formulation guarantees the method certain information, so the space must be able to generate it from what it contains; extra information is allowed.
questions.rule: The space must supply what the formulation promises.
questions.teaches: The problem formulation must be coupled with the problem space: out of the information and transformations in the space it must be possible to generate the kinds of information the formulation guarantees to the method.

questions.q: According to the authors, what determines how difficult a problem is?
options: The task environment alone, whoever the solver is
The solver's intelligence alone, whatever the task
The number of words in the problem statement
The interaction between the task environment and the solver's program of methods and executive
optionExplain: A task is easy or hard only relative to the methods that meet it.
The solver's program matters, but only in interaction with the task.
Statement length is not the authors' determinant.
Right: difficulty comes from the interaction of environment and program.
questions.explain: Difficulty depends on task and program together. The card next lists how to measure it.

questions.q: Which of these does the chapter list as ways to measure difficulty? Select all that apply.
options: Whether a solution is attained
The time required to find a solution
The quality of the solution
How confident the solver feels
The age of the solver
optionExplain: Right: attainment is a measure.
Right: time is a measure.
Right: quality is a measure.
Confidence is not on the authors' list.
Age is not a difficulty measure in the list.
questions.explain: The authors list attainment, time and quality, and say they are related but imperfect.

questions.q: Two cooks finish the same dish, one in 20 minutes and one in an hour, but the dish from the slower cook tastes better. Which measures give conflicting verdicts?
options: Time and quality, which are related only imperfectly
Attainment and time, which must always agree
Quality and attainment, since both cooks finished
None: every measure of difficulty agrees
optionExplain: Right: the measures can disagree.
Both cooks attained the goal; the conflict is elsewhere.
Both reached the goal so attainment does not separate them.
The authors say the measures are related only imperfectly.
questions.explain: Time and quality point in different directions here, an example of the measures being imperfectly related.

questions.q: True or false: A single global measure of solution time can be split into the time spent in each method and each component process.
questions.explain: The authors want exactly this: each part of the program contributes an increment of time to the solution.
questions.rule: Dissect total time into component times.

questions.q: A programmer says she has found the cause of a program's slowness in one routine, so she knows everything that makes the task difficult. How would the authors respond?
options: She is right because difficulty always has a single cause
She is wrong because difficulty cannot be traced to components at all
One cause can be isolated, but they do not expect all determinants to be isolated without examining the whole program and problem structure in detail
She is right because difficulty depends only on the task environment
optionExplain: The authors do not say difficulty has one cause.
They do want to trace difficulty to components.
Right: they want to attribute difficulty to components but doubt that all can be isolated cheaply.
They say it depends on the interaction of task and program.
questions.explain: The authors would isolate major determinants but warn that finding all of them would need a look at the entire program and problem structure down to the last detail.
questions.rule: Expect to isolate the major determinants, not all.
questions.teaches: The authors do not expect to isolate all determinants of difficulty unless they examine the entire program and problem structure down to the last detail.

questions.q: A solver tries one method after another until one works. What happens to the chance of eventually solving as more methods are tried?
options: It stays the same, since each method is independent of the rest
It falls, because each failure makes the next less likely
It reaches certainty after the second method
It rises with each added method, but the time spent also rises
optionExplain: Independent methods each add their own chance.
A failure does not lower the next method's chance in the formula.
The formula only approaches certainty with more methods.
Right: more tries add chance and cost.
questions.explain: More methods mean more chance and more time. The card next gives the formulae.
questions.rule: More tries, more chance, more time.

questions.q: The basic structure of a problem solver is described as ____: it selects one method and, if that fails, selects another.
questions.explain: The authors describe the solver's basic structure as disjunctive.

questions.q: Each method has a 0.3 chance of success, and the chances of different methods are assumed mutually independent. By the formula probability-of-solution = 1 - [1 - probability(method)]^N, what is the chance that at least one of N = 2 methods succeeds?
optionExplain: This adds the chances (0.3 + 0.3) and ignores overlap.
This multiplies the chances (0.3 x 0.3), which is the chance both succeed.
This is the chance for one method only.
questions.explain: The probability of at least one success is 1 - (0.7)^2 = 0.51.
questions.rule: Chance of at least one success is 1 - (1 - p)^N.

questions.q: Setup takes 5 seconds, and each method costs 2 seconds to select and 10 to execute. By the second formula, how long do three methods take?
options: 36 seconds
17 seconds
41 seconds
31 seconds
optionExplain: This leaves out the setup time.
This counts the setup and one round only.
This counts selection once for all three.
questions.explain: The time is the setup plus N rounds of selection and execution: 5 + 3 x 12 = 41 seconds.

questions.q: True or false: Because subjects in the experiments use only a few methods, an estimated average time per method is enough to assess difficulty.
questions.explain: The authors say that with only one or two methods used, it is essential to consider the structure of each individual method; an average would suit a large number of methods.
questions.rule: With few methods, study each one.
questions.teaches: Because the subjects in the authors' experiments use only a few methods, often one or two, it becomes essential to consider the structure of individual methods in assessing difficulty.

questions.q: Which assumption do the authors flag as doubtful in their success formula?
options: That the chance of success of different methods is independent
That a solver tries methods at all
That time is measured in seconds
That the problem has a goal
optionExplain: Right: failures can inform the next choice.
The disjunctive structure is the point of the formulae.
Units are not the issue.
A goal is a basic element of the theory.
questions.explain: Independence is one of the doubts. The card next lists the rest.

questions.q: Which are limitations the authors state for the formulae? Select all that apply.
options: A method may either solve the problem or not, so probability is unclear
A failed method may give diagnostic information about what to try next
Execution time and chance of success are assumed constant
Methods always take exactly one second
The formulae are known to be exact
optionExplain: Right: the meaning of probability is questioned.
Right: failures can be informative.
Right: constancy is an assumption.
The authors never fix a method time.
The authors call them exceedingly approximate.
questions.explain: The authors list the unclear meaning of probability, dependence among methods, and the assumed constants.
questions.rule: Probability, independence and constants are the weak points.

questions.q: A chess engine tries a first plan, which fails but reveals a weakness on one wing. It then picks a second plan aimed at that wing. Which assumption of the formulae does this break?
options: That the engine tries methods one at a time
That a problem has a solution
That the success chances of different methods are independent
That time is spent on execution
optionExplain: The engine does try one at a time.
Nothing here denies a solution exists.
Right: the failure informed the next method.
Execution time still applies.
questions.explain: Failure of one method gave diagnostic information about which method to select next.
questions.rule: Failures can guide the next choice.

questions.q: True or false: The authors treat the formulae as exact and as reflecting the quality of solutions.
questions.explain: They call the formulae exceedingly approximate and say they do not reflect qualitative differences among solutions.

questions.q: A chef's failed sauce leaves a useful reduction that she reuses in a later dish. Which limit of the formulae does this show?
options: A method always has the same chance of success
A method may fail to solve the problem yet produce a symbol structure that turns out to be useful later
All methods take the same time
Methods are tried in parallel
optionExplain: That is an assumption of the formulae, not the limit shown.
Right: a failed method can still leave something useful.
That is another assumption, not what the story shows.
The formulae and the story are about serial tries.
questions.explain: The authors say a method may fail to solve the problem but still produce a symbol structure that proves useful later.
questions.rule: A failure can still yield something.
questions.teaches: A method may fail to solve the problem but still produce a symbol structure that turns out to be useful later.

questions.q: A method that must look through an entire problem space is run on a space ten times larger. Roughly how does the time to solution change?
options: It stays about the same
It grows by about ten seconds
It shrinks, since larger spaces hold more solutions
It grows roughly in proportion, about ten times as long
optionExplain: Search time depends on the number of elements to examine.
The authors speak of proportion, not a fixed addition.
A bigger space has not more solutions as a rule.
Right: time is roughly proportional to the size for elementary methods.
questions.explain: Time is roughly proportional to space size for elementary methods. The card next says why.
questions.rule: Elementary method: time scales with space.

questions.q: For the most elementary methods, time to solution is roughly ____ to the total size of the space.
questions.explain: The authors say time is roughly proportional to the total size of the space for methods that search through the entire space.

questions.q: A lock has 1,000 possible codes and a guesser tries them one by one in a fixed order. A second lock has 10,000 codes. By this rule, how do the average search times compare?
options: About the same
About ten times longer for the second lock
About one hundred times longer
About twice as long
optionExplain: Size matters for elementary search.
Right: ten times the space, roughly ten times the time.
Proportional means ten times, not a hundred.
A tenfold size gives a tenfold time here, not a double.
questions.explain: Time is roughly proportional to the size of the space: 10,000 / 1,000 = 10.
questions.rule: Ten times the space, ten times the time.

questions.q: True or false: A sophisticated method that explores only part of a space can solve a problem faster than its space size alone would suggest.
questions.explain: The authors say more sophisticated methods can often be described as cutting down the part of the space that must be explored.
questions.rule: Sophisticated methods shrink the effective space.

questions.q: Which statement best expresses how the authors treat sophisticated methods?
options: Their effect can often be described as cutting down the part of the space that has to be explored to find a solution
They explore a larger space than elementary methods, so they are slower
They need no problem space at all
They make time independent of the solver
optionExplain: Right: the gain is a smaller region to explore.
Sophisticated methods reduce the part examined.
All methods work on a problem space.
The solver's program still matters.
questions.explain: Sophisticated methods change the cost by cutting down the part of the space that needs exploring.
questions.teaches: The effect of more sophisticated methods can often be described as effectively cutting down the part of the problem space that must be explored in order to find a solution.

questions.q: A solver has used all the relevant information it has and still has not found the answer. What does the authors' picture say it must do?
options: Return to the original space and begin again
Declare that no subspace exists
Wait for the problem statement to change
Adopt a method that examines all the elements of the remaining subspace
optionExplain: Starting over discards the reductions.
A subspace remains; it simply cannot be reduced further.
Waiting adds no information.
Right: with no information left, the remaining subspace is searched in full.
questions.explain: Without more information, the solver examines everything left. The card next explains the picture.
questions.rule: When information runs out, exhaust the subspace.

questions.q: Applying a piece of relevant information limits the solver to a more relevant ____ of the original space.
questions.explain: Each relevant piece of information cuts the space down to a more relevant subspace.

questions.q: Looking for a lost key, you rule out the car because you did not take it, and the garden because it rained all day. What have you done in the authors' terms?
options: Switched to a recognition method
Abandoned the attempt
Used relevant information to reduce the space to a more relevant subspace
Increased the size of the space
optionExplain: No answer was recalled.
You are still searching.
Right: each fact removes part of the space.
Ruling places out shrinks the space.
questions.explain: Excluding places on relevant information narrows the region to search.

questions.q: True or false: The olympian view assumes that having information is enough to use it to reduce the space.
questions.explain: The authors call their description olympian because of that implicit assumption; in fact a solver may not know how to use the information.
questions.rule: Having is not the same as using.

questions.q: A student owns a table of identities but does not recognise that one applies to her problem. By the authors' remark, what happens to the reduction?
options: She reduces the space fully, since she holds the information
The space becomes smaller by itself
She may fail to reduce the space even though she holds the information
The problem becomes solvable by recognition
optionExplain: Holding it is not enough.
Spaces do not shrink without the solver's use of information.
Right: the problem solver may not know how to use information to reduce the space.
Recognition requires the answer to be in memory.
questions.explain: The authors admit the olympian view overstates: a solver may not know how to use information to reduce the space.
questions.teaches: In fact, the problem solver may not know how to use information to reduce the space, even when he has it.

questions.q: Two problem solvers of about equal ability attack the same problem. What do the authors predict about their behavior?
options: Highly similar behavior, since they reach about the same subspace
Completely different behavior, since each solver is unique
Identical keystrokes, step for step
No prediction is possible without testing each one
optionExplain: Right: similar subspaces mean similar demands.
The authors predict similarity for similar solvers.
The claim is about similar behavior, not identical steps.
They say the observed space can be used to predict behavior.
questions.explain: Equal ability means similar subspaces and similar behavior. The card next explains.

questions.q: Solvers at widely different levels may achieve different reductions and so face different problem ____.
questions.explain: Different reductions give different demands, so separate analyses may be needed.

questions.q: A researcher finds that a novice and an expert are working in different problem spaces on one chess position. What should she do?
options: Use one analysis for both, since the position is the same
Discard the expert's data
Assume the novice will soon behave like the expert
Analyse the two separately, since different reductions mean different demands
optionExplain: Same position, different demands.
Nothing in the account suggests discarding data.
No claim is made that the novice will converge.
Right: widely different levels may call for separate analyses.
questions.explain: Different reductions mean different demands and call for separate analyses.

questions.q: True or false: If we can observe which problem space a subject is operating in, we can use this to predict the subject's later behavior.
questions.explain: The authors say this directly: determining the subject's problem space by observation helps predict subsequent behavior.
questions.rule: Observe the space, predict the behavior.

questions.q: Two taxi drivers of equal skill are asked to find the fastest route between two stations using the same map. What should the account lead us to expect?
options: Very similar route choices, because both pick out about the same relevant information
Unrelated routes, because routes cannot be predicted
That the driver with the longer career will use a bigger space
That both will search every street in the town
optionExplain: Right: equal ability, equal reduction, similar behavior.
The account predicts similarity, not unrelated routes, when ability is equal.
Equal skill means about equal reduction in the account, so a longer career is not the factor.
Both reduce the space with information instead of searching everything.
questions.explain: Equal ability gives about the same reduction. The demands of the situation, defined by the subspace, are then essentially the same for both, and highly similar behavior is predicted.
questions.teaches: Since the demands of the situation, defined by the subspace, are essentially the same for two solvers of similar ability, highly similar behavior is predicted for them.

questions.q: A person asked the value of pi answers 3.1416 instantly. What kind of solving is this in the authors' scheme?
options: It was found by generate-and-test over all real numbers
The answer was recognised: it was in memory and evoked by understanding the question
It was found by heuristic search through a tree
It is not problem solving, so the theory has nothing to say
optionExplain: That would be a slow way to answer.
Right: the answer was already stored.
No search was needed.
The authors say the situation fits the set-predicate definition of a problem.
questions.explain: The answer was simply evoked. The card next gives the authors' view.

questions.q: Recognition is called the one ____ method of solving problems.
questions.explain: The authors call it the one universal method: it applies to all problem formulations.

questions.q: A child asked what 7 times 8 is says 56 at once. A second child must add eight sevens. What distinguishes them in the authors' terms?
options: The first uses generate-and-test and the second uses recognition
Both use recognition, but at different speeds
Neither is solving a problem
The first recognises the answer; the second uses another method because the answer is not in memory
optionExplain: Recognition is the fast case.
Recognition fails if the answer is not in memory.
The authors count even trivial cases as problems under the set-predicate definition.
Right: the first has the answer stored.
questions.explain: Whether the problem is easy depends on the solver's repertoire: the first child has recognition available, the second does not.
questions.rule: Easy for one solver, hard for another.

questions.q: True or false: Because recognition is immediate, ordinary measures of problem difficulty such as search time do not apply to it.
questions.explain: The authors say that when a problem is solved by recognition the usual measures of difficulty do not apply, for the result is immediate.
questions.rule: Immediate results have no difficulty to measure.

questions.q: Why does the authors' pi example say the problem is not easy for every solver?
options: A solver who knows pi only as the ratio of circumference to diameter might have to circumscribe a polygon about the circle
Pi is a hard number to remember for all people
Recognition cannot be used by people, only by machines
Only mathematicians count as solvers
optionExplain: Right: with a different repertoire the same problem needs another method, not recognition.
The point is the solver's repertoire, not the number's difficulty.
People use recognition all the time; the pi answer is a case of it.
No such restriction on who counts as a solver is stated.
questions.explain: The authors observe that a solver who knows pi only through its definition might have to circumscribe a polygon about a circle: the triviality is a function of repertoire.
questions.rule: Triviality depends on the solver's methods.
questions.teaches: A solver who knows pi only as the ratio of circumference to diameter might have to circumscribe a polygon about the circle, which is not a recognition process at all.

questions.q: Why is recognition important for solving hard problems, per the authors?
options: It solves most hard problems directly
It replaces the need to reduce problems
It is often the way the last subproblem in a chain of reductions is solved
It proves the problem has no solution
optionExplain: They say it seldom solves hard problems directly.
Reduction is still needed.
Right: reduction must end somewhere, often in recognition.
Recognition does not prove unsolvability.
questions.explain: Recognition ends reductions. The card next states the point.

questions.q: A hard problem is solved by replacing it with ostensibly ____ problems.
questions.explain: That is reduction: replace a hard problem with easier ones until some can be solved directly.

questions.q: To tile a bathroom, you split it into three rectangles, then recall the tile count for each rectangle from a chart. Which step is recognition?
options: Splitting the room into rectangles
Deciding to split into three
Adding up the three counts
Recalling each rectangle's tile count from the chart
optionExplain: Splitting is the reduction.
Choosing the split is part of reduction.
Summing is a further processing step.
Right: the stored answer is evoked.
questions.explain: Splitting reduces the problem; recalling the stored counts closes it.
questions.rule: The last step of the reduction is recalled.

questions.q: True or false: If a reduction succeeds, every subproblem must eventually be solved rather than only reduced further.
questions.explain: The authors say that some subproblems must actually be solved, not just reduced further, if reduction is to succeed.

questions.q: A mathematician says a proof was easy because it reduced the claim to a lemma she already knew. Which words of the authors does this echo?
options: The problem was solved by generate-and-test
He reduced the problem to something he already knew
The problem was abandoned
The representation was selected by input translation
optionExplain: No generating and testing is described.
Right: this is the phrase the authors quote.
The proof was completed.
Representation is not the point.
questions.explain: The authors note that people say 'he reduced the problem to something he already knew', which describes recognition closing a reduction.
questions.rule: Reducing to the known is recognition.
questions.teaches: The ordinary phrase 'he reduced the problem to something he already knew' describes recognition as the last step of a reduction.

questions.q: Which of these is a production-system recognition scheme?
options: A generator that produces candidate solutions in turn
A tree search that grows until a path reaches the goal
Each problem statement paired with its solution, so a recognised statement leads straight to the solution
A table of probabilities for each method
optionExplain: That describes generate-and-test.
That describes heuristic search.
Right: statement to solution pairs.
That is not a recognition scheme in the text.
questions.explain: A production system pairs statements with solutions. The card next lists the three structures.

questions.q: Put the authors' three recognition structures in the order they list them.
items: Series of conditional branches (implicit test tree)
Production system of statement-solution pairs
Pattern recognition programs from the literature
questions.explain: The authors mention conditional branches first, then the production system, then the pattern recognition programs.

questions.q: A phone menu says: if the caller presses 1 go to billing; if 2 go to repairs; if 3 go to sales. Which recognition structure does this resemble?
options: A series of conditional branches forming a tree of tests
A production system with unlimited size
A pattern recognition program for geometric figures
A heuristic search with backing up
optionExplain: Right: each test branches to its handling.
A production system would pair statements with solutions directly.
No figures are involved.
No search or backing up occurs.
questions.explain: A chain of tests forming a decision tree matches the conditional-branch scheme.
questions.rule: Conditional branches form a test tree.

questions.q: True or false: In a production system with no size limit, any recognised problem statement leads immediately to its solution.
questions.explain: The authors say so: if no limits are placed on the size of the production system, a recognised problem statement leads immediately to its solution.

questions.q: Why do the authors say that most pattern recognition programs do not all lead to recognisers of problem statements?
options: They need more memory than any production system
They cannot recognise anything at all
They mostly work with continuous signal spaces or two-dimensional spaces of geometric figures such as characters
They were designed only for chess
optionExplain: Memory is not the stated reason; the stated reason is the kind of space they work in.
They recognise well within their domains, which are signals and figures.
Right: their spaces differ from problem statements.
The text does not tie them to chess.
questions.explain: The pattern recognition literature mostly deals with continuous signals or two-dimensional figures, so these programs do not immediately give recognisers of problem statements.
questions.rule: Check that a technique fits the material.
questions.teaches: Most pattern recognition programs operate with continuous signal spaces or two-dimensional spaces holding geometric figures such as characters.

questions.q: In the set-predicate formulation, what is the solver guaranteed?
options: A way to generate members of G directly
A guarantee that G is small
A way to obtain members of the set U and a way to test whether an element is in G
A list of the elements of G
optionExplain: Generating G directly would solve the problem instantly.
Nothing is guaranteed about the size of G.
Right: obtain members and test them.
A list of G would be the solution.
questions.explain: The formulation guarantees a set and a test. The card next states the limits.
questions.rule: A set to draw from and a test to check.

questions.q: In the set-predicate formulation the goal is to find a member of a subset G of the set ____.
questions.explain: The goal is to find, produce or determine a member of a subset G of the set U.
questions.rule: Find a member of G within U.

questions.q: You must find a customer named Lee in a card file you can flip through, and you can recognise Lee when you see the card. Which parts of the formulation does this match?
options: The test is the file and U is the name Lee
The card file is U, the test is recognising Lee, and Lee's card is in G
G is the whole file and U is the single card
There is no set involved, only a test
optionExplain: U is the set, not the test.
Right: set, test, subset.
G is the subset of U that passes the test.
A set is always present in the formulation.
questions.explain: The file is the set, the check is the test, and Lee's card is the subset member.
questions.rule: Identify the set, the test and the subset.

questions.q: True or false: A method for the set-predicate formulation may use a procedure that produces members of G directly.
questions.explain: If members of G could be produced directly the problem would be solved instantly; the formulation guarantees only a test for them.
questions.rule: A direct generator of G would end the problem.

questions.q: A friend gives you a lock puzzle with the hint that the answer is a number divisible by 7. How does this hint relate to the set-predicate formulation?
options: It is part of the guaranteed formulation
It makes the test unnecessary
It shows the set does not exist
It is information beyond the bare set and test, so it can support a more selective method
optionExplain: The bare formulation does not include such hints.
A test is still needed.
The set remains.
Right: extra information about G lies outside the formulation.
questions.explain: The authors say the method is limited to the formulation's information; extra facts such as a divisibility hint would let a more selective method be built.
questions.teaches: Because the formulation guarantees only a set and a test, any further information about where members of G lie is outside it and could support a more selective method.

questions.q: A generate-and-test method generates an element and finds that it fails the test. What does the method do next?
options: Stops and reports no solution
Generates another element and tests it
Changes the test
Reports the failed element as the solution
optionExplain: No solution is reported until the generator is exhausted.
Right: it continues generating until success or exhaustion.
The test is part of the formulation.
A failed element is not a solution.
questions.explain: It keeps going. The card next states the full method.

questions.q: Put the generate-and-test steps in order.
items: Generate an element from U
Test whether it is in G
If it passes, stop and report it
If the generator is exhausted, report no solution
questions.explain: Generate, then test, then stop and report on success, or report no solution when the generator runs out.

questions.q: You look for a matching sock by pulling socks from a drawer one at a time and checking against the one in your hand. Which part is the test?
options: Checking each pulled sock against the one in hand
Pulling socks out of the drawer
The drawer as a whole
Putting socks back
optionExplain: Right: the test checks membership in G.
Pulling is the generator.
The drawer is the set U.
Putting back is not part of the method.
questions.explain: The comparison decides whether an element is in G, which is the test.
questions.rule: Pulling is the generator and comparing is the test.

questions.q: True or false: If the generator in generate-and-test runs out of elements without a success, the method reports that there is no solution.
questions.explain: Figure 4.2 ends by stopping and reporting no solution after the generator is exhausted.

questions.q: In generate-and-test, why are the generator and the test described as completely independent?
options: They run on different computers
The test chooses what the generator produces
The generator can only produce correct answers
Each need only meet minimal conditions of its own, which is the method's generality and weakness
optionExplain: The text is about logical independence, not hardware.
In this method the generator ignores the test results.
If the generator produced only correct answers no test would be needed.
Right: independence gives generality but no use of progress made.
questions.explain: The authors name this independence as the generality and weakness of the scheme.
questions.rule: Independence is both strength and weakness.
questions.teaches: The generality and the weakness of generate-and-test lie in the fact that the generation process and the test process are completely independent, each fulfilling only minimal conditions of its own.

questions.q: A user wants every solution rather than the first one. How does the method change?
options: The test is removed
The method stops after the first success anyway
The generator keeps operating and stores solutions as they are found
The set U is replaced by G
optionExplain: Testing is still needed to tell solutions.
That would give only the first.
Right: continue and store.
G is not directly available.
questions.explain: The generator continues and stores solutions. The card next adds the other variant.
questions.rule: All solutions: keep generating and store.

questions.q: Two generators working together, one listing candidates and one passing them to the test, are equivalent to one overall ____ of candidates.
questions.explain: The authors say the two generators taken together are equivalent to a single overall generator.

questions.q: A hotel clerk prints a list of free rooms and then checks each against a guest's needs. Which variant does this match?
options: A method for finding all solutions
A heuristic search with backing up
A main generator providing candidates at once, with a second generator going through the list for the test
A recognition method
optionExplain: Only one fit is needed.
No search tree is involved.
Right: batch then list.
No stored answer is evoked.
questions.explain: A list of candidates produced at once and then examined is the batch variant.
questions.rule: Batch candidates need a second generator.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say that generate-and-test with a batch generator is a different method from generate-and-test with a one-at-a-time generator.
questions.explain: They say variants do not change its essential character and that the two generators together are equivalent to one overall generator.

questions.q: A librarian wants all books on a topic from a shelf, scanning shelf by shelf and noting those that fit. What additional resource does the method need?
options: A memory to store solutions as they are found
A second kind of test
A smaller set U
A method for choosing representations
optionExplain: Right: all solutions require storage.
The same test applies.
The set stays the same size.
No change of representation is needed.
questions.explain: Collecting all solutions needs a store for the ones already found, since the generator must continue.
questions.teaches: If all solutions are wanted, the generator must continue to operate and the solutions must be stored in some memory as they are found.

questions.q: A generate-and-test method is slow on a problem. Which of these could be the reason?
options: Only the space size, since nothing else matters
Only the test, since generation is free
The method has no guarantee of ever finding the solution
Generating is costly, testing is costly, the space is big, or the solution comes late in the order
optionExplain: Size is one of four.
Generation can cost too.
The solution will be found if the generator runs long enough.
Right: all four can contribute.
questions.explain: Four factors set the time. The card next lists them.

questions.q: Which of these set the time to the first solution in generate-and-test? Select all that apply.
options: Average effort to generate each element
Average effort to test a candidate
Size of the space searched
Position of the solution in the generator's order
The colour of the problem statement
optionExplain: Right.
Right.
Right.
Right.
Not a determinant.
questions.explain: The authors list generation effort, test effort, space size and the solution's relative position.

questions.q: You search a messy bookcase for a red book, picking up books at random, and the red book happens to be the last book you reach. Which of the four factors made it slow?
options: The cost of testing each book
The relative position of the solution in the generator's order
The cost of generating each book
The size of the bookcase alone
optionExplain: Checking colour is cheap.
Right: the solution came last.
Picking a book is cheap.
Size matters, but the unlucky position was decisive here.
questions.explain: The solution's position in the order of generation is factor (4).
questions.rule: Late position slows the first success.

questions.q: True or false: If the conditions of the formulation hold and the generator is allowed to run long enough, generate-and-test finds a solution.
questions.explain: The authors say the solution will always be found under those conditions, as the program in Figure 4.2 shows.

questions.q: A friend wants to know which single quantity best measures how hard generate-and-test finds a problem. What does the account suggest?
options: The number of solutions that exist
Time to find the first solution, which depends on several factors
The elegance of the generator
The age of the solver
optionExplain: Number of solutions is not the measure named.
Right: time to first solution.
Elegance is not a measure.
Age is irrelevant.
questions.explain: Because the solution is guaranteed, the interesting measure is the time to find the first one.
questions.rule: Because success is guaranteed, time is the measure.
questions.teaches: Because a solution is guaranteed under the stated conditions, the interesting measure of problem difficulty for generate-and-test is the amount of time it takes to find the first solution.

questions.q: Which conditions make generate-and-test an excellent method for a simple household task?
options: A huge set and a slow test
A set that cannot be seen
A test that needs expert help
A small, accessible set and a rapid test
optionExplain: That makes the method poor.
Access is needed to generate.
A slow test makes the method costly.
Right: small set, easy access, quick test.
questions.explain: Small, accessible and fast. The card next shows the chairs.

questions.q: In the chair example the set U is about ____ chairs.
questions.explain: The authors say the set is small, say four chairs.

questions.q: You need one spare mug and your cupboard holds five. You pick up mugs one at a time and reject chipped ones. How good is generate-and-test here?
options: Excellent: the set is small and accessible and the test is rapid
Poor: the space is huge
Poor: the test is very slow
Impossible: no generator exists
optionExplain: Right.
Five mugs is not huge.
Checking for chips is quick.
The cupboard supplies the generator.
questions.explain: It matches the chair case: a small accessible set and a quick test.
questions.rule: Use the plain method when it is cheap.

questions.q: True or false: Generate-and-test would remain an excellent method for the chair problem even if the living room held a million chairs.
questions.explain: With a million chairs the set would no longer be small, and the time would grow with the space size (our reading from the four factors).
questions.rule: Method quality depends on set size.

questions.q: Why would the authors not bother to design a clever method for the chair problem?
options: Because clever methods do not exist for chairs
Because the test cannot be written down
Choosing or building a more efficient but elaborate method would cost more than generating and testing
Because chairs are not a set
optionExplain: Clever methods are possible but not worth it.
The test is given in the text.
Right: the elaborate method would cost more than it saves.
The chairs form the set.
questions.explain: The authors say that if a problem is small, generate-and-test may be the best way since building an efficient elaborate method is more costly than simply generating and testing.
questions.rule: Do not build what costs more than it saves.
questions.teaches: If a problem is small, generate-and-test may be the best way to solve it, because selecting or constructing a more efficient but elaborate method is more costly than simply generating and testing.

questions.q: A safe has ten dials, each with 100 settings. How many settings are there in all?
options: 10^10, ten billion
10^20, one hundred billion billion
optionExplain: This adds up wrongly.
That would be ten dials of ten settings.
Multiplying gives only 1,000, ignoring independence of dials.
Right: 100 to the tenth power.
questions.explain: The dials are independent, so the counts multiply: 100^10 = 10^20. The card next gives the consequence.

questions.q: In the safe problem the difficulty lies entirely in the ____ of the space.
questions.explain: Both generating and testing are cheap; only the size of the space makes the problem hard.

questions.q: A combination padlock has four dials of 10 digits each, with no clue. About how many settings must be tried on average?
options: About 10,000
About 5,000
About 40
About 400
optionExplain: This is the whole space, not the average.
Right: 10^4 = 10,000 settings, and half on average.
This adds the dial sizes: 4 x 10.
Wrong power.
questions.explain: The space is 10^4 = 10,000 settings; on average you try half before success.
questions.rule: Average trials are about half the space.

questions.q: True or false: The safe is hard because testing a setting is expensive.
questions.explain: The authors say both generating and testing are cheap; the difficulty lies entirely in the size of the space.
questions.rule: Do not blame the test when the space is the problem.

questions.q: Why does the authors' safecracker have no recognition process available?
options: Because recognition is forbidden by the rules of safes
Because the test is expensive
Because he does not know the combination, so the correct setting cannot be recognised and sits at random in the generator's order
Because there is more than one combination
optionExplain: No such rule is mentioned.
The test is cheap.
Right: with no knowledge, the combination appears at a random position.
Only one combination opens the safe.
questions.explain: A safecracker who does not know the combination cannot recognise it, so it lies at a random place in any generator's sequence.
questions.teaches: Only one combination opens the safe, and it is situated at random in the sequence of any generator available to a would-be safecracker who has no recognition process.

questions.q: In choosing a chess move by generate-and-test, which part is the source of difficulty?
options: The test of whether a legal move is good
Generating the legal moves
Counting the pieces
Writing down the move
optionExplain: Right: the verifier is the problem.
Only twenty to thirty moves need generating.
Not part of the method.
Not part of the method.
questions.explain: Evaluating a move is the hard part. The card next explains.

questions.q: A chess player on move has some twenty to ____ legal alternatives.
questions.explain: The authors say on average there are some twenty to thirty legal alternatives.

questions.q: A mapping app lists three routes in a second but needs several minutes to check traffic along each. Which part is like the chess problem?
options: The verifier is costly while the generator is cheap
The generator is costly while the verifier is cheap
Both are cheap and the space is huge
Neither is costly
optionExplain: Right.
That would match the crossword example.
That would match the safe.
Not so here.
questions.explain: Cheap listing with costly checking has the same shape as chess.
questions.rule: Compare generator cost with verifier cost.

questions.q: True or false: In the authors' chess example, difficulty would fall greatly if a cheaper way of judging a move were found.
questions.explain: The difficulty lies in the verifier, so a cheaper test would reduce it (our reading); the authors draw the conclusion that a formulation more sensitive to chess is needed.
questions.rule: Fix the part that is costly.

questions.q: What do the authors conclude from the 10^15 count?
options: Chess programs cannot exist
Generate-and-test is the best method for chess
A problem formulation more sensitive to the structure of chess must be adopted to find good moves
Chess has too few legal moves
optionExplain: They do not say that.
The count shows the opposite.
Right: they conclude a better formulation is needed.
There are twenty to thirty moves.
questions.explain: The authors say this only shows that a formulation more sensitive to chess must be used if the solver is to find good moves.
questions.rule: Change the formulation when the method is hopeless.
questions.teaches: The authors conclude that a problem formulation more sensitive than generate-and-test to the structure of chess must be adopted if the problem solver is to find good moves.

questions.q: To make a generator of words with three g's, one could generate dictionary words and keep those with three g's. What becomes the main difficulty?
options: The cost of testing the fourth letter
The size of the space, the dictionary
The lack of any generator
The lack of a test
optionExplain: The test is cheap.
Right: both steps are cheap, so size remains.
A generator now exists.
A test exists.
questions.explain: Difficulty moves to space size. The card next shows the chain.
questions.rule: Packaged generators leave size as the difficulty.

questions.q: Packaging a generator of words and a test for three g's together makes a new ____ of three-g words.
questions.explain: The pair of processes together forms a generator of three-g words.
questions.rule: Generator plus test makes a generator.

questions.q: You need a song with the word love in its title. You skim a list of all song titles and keep those containing love, then check each for another clue. What does skimming plus keeping play the role of?
options: A recognition method
A heuristic search
A stop rule
A generator of love-titles built from a generator of all titles and a test
optionExplain: No answer is recalled.
No search tree.
No pruning of paths.
Right.
questions.explain: A generator and a test, packaged, make a generator of the narrower set.
questions.rule: Package generator and test to narrow a set.
