questions.q: True or false: In the crossword example the authors say the generator of three-g words is cheap to build directly.
questions.explain: They say the generator is likely to be very expensive, unless built from a dictionary generator and a count of g's.
questions.rule: A direct narrow generator can be costly.

questions.q: Why do the authors call these examples superficial?
options: Because the examples are wrong
They illustrate the method and show how difficulty can be localised in different parts, without detailed analysis
Because the method cannot be applied to them
Because they were taken from a laboratory
optionExplain: Nothing says they are wrong.
Right: illustrative, not detailed.
They are applications of the method.
They are everyday examples.
questions.explain: The authors say all these examples are superficial but serve to illustrate generate-and-test and to show how difficulty can be localised in different parts of the method.
questions.teaches: The four examples are superficial, but they show how problem difficulty can be localised in the various parts of the generate-and-test method.

questions.q: A problem asks for a path from a start to a goal. Can generate-and-test be applied to it?
options: Yes, by treating the goal check as the test and generating elements with the operators
No, because paths cannot be tested
Only if the space is small
Only if there is a single operator
optionExplain: Right: any search problem can be recast.
The goal check serves as the test.
Size affects the time, not the possibility.
Many operators are allowed.
questions.explain: It can be recast. The card next explains the shift of task.
questions.rule: Search can be recast as set-predicate.

questions.q: Recasting replaces finding a path with finding the final ____ of the path.
questions.explain: The task shifts from finding the path to finding its final element; a record of the path must still be kept.
questions.rule: Record the path as well as the element.

questions.q: A maze program finds the exit by generating every square in some order and testing each for the exit. What must it also store to report the route?
options: A copy of the exit test
A second maze
Nothing; the exit square is the route
A record of the path that led to the successful square
optionExplain: The test is already in the program.
No second maze is needed.
The square alone does not give the route.
Right: the route was the original goal.
questions.explain: The recast finds only the final element, so the path must be retained separately.
questions.rule: Keep the path when you recast a path problem.

questions.q: True or false: After recasting a search problem as set-predicate, finding the desired element is the same task as finding the path to it.
questions.explain: The authors point to a subtle shift of task: the final element is found, and the path must be retained to solve the original problem.
questions.rule: Element and path are different outputs.

questions.q: Why must there be a test of whether an element is a desired one in any search formulation?
options: Because operators need testing
Because the space must be tested for size
Otherwise the solver could not know that the solution had been reached
Because the path must be tested for length
optionExplain: Operators are not tested here.
Size is not tested.
Right: some test marks success, which is what recasting uses.
Length is not the point.
questions.explain: The authors argue that in the search formulation there must exist a test of whether an element is a desired one, hence whether the solution has been reached; that test becomes the test of generate-and-test.
questions.rule: Every search needs a goal test.
questions.teaches: In the search formulation there must exist a test of whether an element of the space is a desired element, and this can be taken as the test of the generate-and-test method.

questions.q: What must a search method exploit to do better than random search?
options: A faster computer
A larger problem space
Information about what has been discovered and what remains to be done
A longer time limit
optionExplain: Speed does not change the search.
A larger space makes search worse.
Right: information guides the next step.
Time does not add selectivity.
questions.explain: Information guides the search. The card next says how.
questions.rule: Use information to control each step.

questions.q: The generality and weakness of generate-and-test lie in the ____ of the generation process and the test process.
questions.explain: Generator and test are completely independent in generate-and-test.

questions.q: Hunting for a lost phone, you call it and follow the sound as it gets louder. Which feature of search does this use?
options: Controlling each step by feedback on progress toward the object
Independence of generator and test
Exhausting the whole space
A fixed order of checking rooms
optionExplain: Right.
That would ignore the sound.
Following the sound does not need that.
A fixed order ignores the sound.
questions.explain: Each step depends on how close you are, which is dependence on progress.

questions.q: True or false: A method whose steps depend on the object sought is more specific than one whose generator ignores it.
questions.explain: The authors pair power with specificity: dependence on the object sought gives power but ties the method to the task.

questions.q: A burglar-proofing firm is told that a lock-picking tool which works on every lock must be very powerful. How would the authors' pairing of power and specificity answer?
options: Generality guarantees power
Power lies in depending on the particular object sought, so a tool that fits every lock uses little about any one lock
Power comes only from speed
A tool cannot be both general and weak
optionExplain: The authors tie power to specificity; generate-and-test is general and weak.
Right: dependence on the object sought gives power and specificity.
Speed is not the source of power in their account.
They say generate-and-test is exactly both general and weak.
questions.explain: Generate-and-test is general because generator and test are independent. Conversely, the power and specificity of a search method lie in its dependence on the nature of the object sought and the progress made toward it.
questions.teaches: Conversely, the power (and specificity) of a method for the search formulation must lie in the dependence of the search process upon the nature of the object being sought and the progress being made toward it.

questions.q: A defective safe clicks whenever one dial reaches its correct setting. About how many trials will open a 10-dial safe with 100 settings per dial?
options: About 10^20
About 500
About 50 billion billion
About 100
optionExplain: That is the whole space with no clicks.
Right: about 50 per dial, ten dials.
That is the no-click average.
That is the number of settings of one dial.
questions.explain: 50 trials per dial on average, ten dials. The card next states the lesson.

questions.q: With the click, the average number of trials to find the correct setting of any one dial is ____.
questions.explain: Each dial has 100 settings; on average half must be tried.

questions.q: A padlock with 4 dials of 10 digits gives a click when a dial is right. About how many trials on average open it?
options: About 5,000
About 20
About 40
About 100
optionExplain: That is the average for no clicks (10^4 / 2).
Right: 4 x 5 = 20 on average.
That is 4 x 10, the worst case per dial.
Wrong count.
questions.explain: With clicks each dial averages 5 trials of 10, so 4 dials need about 20.
questions.rule: Add per-dial averages, do not multiply.

questions.q: True or false: If the clicks were removed, the average number of trials would rise from about 500 to about 5 x 10^19.
questions.explain: Without clicks half of the 10^20 settings must be tried on average, about 5 x 10^19 (50 billion billion).
questions.rule: Without the signal the space is the whole problem.

questions.q: Why does the click allow the problem to be factored into ten small problems?
options: Because the safe has fewer dials than stated
Because the dials are tried in parallel
Because the clicks reveal the combination
Each dial's correct setting is confirmed independently, so success on one dial is known before the next is attempted
optionExplain: The dials remain ten.
Parallelism is not mentioned.
The click only confirms a dial.
Right: success per dial is known.
questions.explain: The authors stress knowing when each small problem has been solved; the click tells the safecracker so.
questions.rule: Know when each part is solved.
questions.teaches: Information that factors a large problem into several small ones and tells when each small one has been solved reduces the search task tremendously.

questions.q: The algebra operators have an infinite number of possible arguments k. How does the authors' solver choose them?
options: It copies the needed values from the current expression
It tries values at random until one works
It tries all values in order
It asks the user for each value
optionExplain: Right: the expression supplies k.
Random trial would be hopeless with infinitely many values.
There are infinitely many.
The text mentions no such step.
questions.explain: The expression itself tells the solver what to use. The card next shows how.
questions.rule: Read the argument off the expression.

questions.q: Put the solution steps for ax + b = cx + d in order.
items: Sub[cx]: remove the x-term from the right
Sub[b]: remove the constant from the left
Div[a - c]: divide by the coefficient of x
questions.explain: Subtract cx, subtract b, then divide both sides by (a - c).

questions.q: For 3x + 4 = 5x + 10, which sequence follows the pattern of the authors' solution?
options: Add[5x], Add[4], Mult[3 - 5]
Sub[3x], Sub[10], Div[3 - 5]
Sub[5x], Sub[4], Div[3 - 5]
Div[5], Sub[4], Sub[5x]
optionExplain: Adding is the wrong direction.
This removes the wrong terms.
Right: k = cx = 5x, then b = 4, then divide by a - c = 3 - 5.
The order puts division first, which fails.
questions.explain: Each k is copied from the expression: 5x, 4, and the coefficient (3 - 5).

questions.q: True or false: In the algebra example the first solution sequence generated is already a solution, so trial-and-error search is eliminated.
questions.explain: The authors say the algebra example illustrates the limiting case: trial-and-error search is eliminated entirely and the first path generated is a solution path.

questions.q: In the authors' account, which information tells the solver to divide by (a - c)?
options: A table of common divisors
A random choice among Div operators
The original equation alone, before any step
The equation (a - c)x = (d - b) obtained after the two subtractions
optionExplain: No table is used.
Nothing is chosen at random.
The coefficient appears only after regrouping.
Right: the intermediate equation shows the coefficient.
questions.explain: After the first two subtractions, the equation shows (a - c)x, which names the divisor.
questions.teaches: After the two subtractions and regrouping the new expression (a - c)x = (d - b) informs the solver that k must be set to (a - c) in the division.

questions.q: In the clicking safe, what happens to wrong settings on a dial?
options: They are never tried
They are tried, then dropped because the click tells which is correct
They are all kept for later
They are copied from the problem statement
optionExplain: Wrong settings are tried.
Right: wrong tries are pruned.
The click removes them.
Copying is the algebra device.
questions.explain: The click prunes. The card next contrasts it with algebra.

questions.q: Match each example to its search-reducing device.
pairs: A test that discriminates correct from incorrect paths
Generating the correct values directly by copying
Independent generator and test with no guidance
questions.explain: The safe uses a test that prunes; the algebra example copies the right argument and explores one path.

questions.q: A cook follows a recipe that says to add exactly the quantity written on the pack. Which device is this closer to?
options: A click that discriminates after trying
Random generation
Copying values from the problem expression, with no branching
A stop rule
optionExplain: No trying and pruning.
Nothing is random.
Right.
No branches arise to stop.
questions.explain: The amount is read off the expression, as in algebra.

questions.q: True or false: The safe example produces an exploration tree in which wrong settings are tried and then cut off, while the algebra example follows a single unbranching path.
questions.explain: The click lets the safecracker drop wrong settings after trying them, giving a tree of Figure 4.3; the algebra copying yields one path with no wrong branches.
questions.rule: Safe branches and prunes; algebra does not branch.

questions.q: A spellchecker flags each misspelled word as you type and you fix each at once before going on. Which device is it like?
options: The algebra copy: it writes the right word without trying
The click: immediate information on each part lets you continue along the correct path only
Generate-and-test with no feedback
A recognition method
optionExplain: The checker points out errors; you still try fixes, so nothing is copied.
Right: feedback per part prunes the wrong branches.
Feedback is the feature here, so it is not feedback-free generate-and-test.
No stored answer is evoked by the checker.
questions.explain: A test that discriminates correct from incorrect steps at once is the click device. In both book examples the order in which operators are tried follows their order in the solution sequence, which is common but not logically necessary.
questions.teaches: In both the safe and the algebra problems the order in which operators are tried is related to their order in the solution action sequence, a common characteristic but not a logically necessary one.

questions.q: Which two directions does search most often take?
options: Upward and downward in memory
Left to right, or right to left on the page
Forward from the initial object, or backward from the desired object
Fast, or slow
optionExplain: Not search directions.
Page layout is irrelevant.
Right.
Speed is not direction.
questions.explain: Forward or backward. The card next gives the reason.

questions.q: The task of a problem solving procedure is to grow a ____ of operator sequences that will include at least one solution path.
questions.explain: The procedure grows a tree of operator sequences without too much branching.
questions.rule: Grow a tree with a solution in it.

questions.q: To plan a trip you start from your destination and work out how to arrive, leg by leg, back to home. Which direction is this?
options: Working forward from the initial object
Working backward from the desired object toward the initial object
A disconnected segment
Generate-and-test
optionExplain: That would start at home.
Right.
A disconnected segment is built apart.
Not the point.
questions.explain: Starting at the goal and moving toward the start is working backward.

questions.q: True or false: The order in which operators are tried must match the order in the final solution sequence.
questions.explain: The authors say this is common but not logically necessary: disconnected segments could be built and connected later.

questions.q: A builder constructs the roof frame and the wall frame separately and joins them later. What does this resemble in the authors' account?
options: Working strictly forward
A recognition method
A stop rule
Constructing disconnected segments of the final action sequence and connecting them afterwards
optionExplain: Forward would build in order.
No answer is recalled.
Nothing is pruned.
Right.
questions.explain: The authors note that segments can be built apart and joined later, a feature of some methods discussed later.
questions.teaches: The authors say it would be admissible to construct various disconnected segments of the final action sequence and subsequently connect them, and that they will discuss methods that operate this way later.

questions.q: In the heuristic-search program, what is done to a newly produced element immediately after it is created?
options: It is discarded
It is tested for being a solution
It is converted into an operator
It is added to the goal set
optionExplain: Evaluation and decision follow the test.
Right: the solution test comes first.
Elements and operators are different things.
Goals are not enlarged.
questions.explain: The test comes right after applying the operator. The card next lists all steps.

questions.q: Put the basic cycle in order.
items: Select an element from untried-problems
Select an operator
Apply the operator to get a new element
Test the new element for a solution
Evaluate the new element
Decide the next step
questions.explain: The program selects an element and operator, applies the operator, tests, evaluates, then decides.
questions.rule: Select, select, apply, test, evaluate, decide.

questions.q: In the program of Figure 4.4, a newly applied operator produces an element that is not a solution and is accepted by evaluation. Where does it go?
options: It is inserted on untried-problems for later use
It is reported as the solution
It is thrown away
It replaces the goal
optionExplain: Right: accepted elements are remembered.
It failed the test.
Rejection is the other outcome.
The goal is unchanged.
questions.explain: Accepted elements are inserted on untried-problems.

questions.q: True or false: If untried-problems becomes empty and no solution has been found, the program stops and reports failure.
questions.explain: The cycle terminates either on finding a solution or by exhausting untried-problems.

questions.q: The program offers an additional exit that Figure 4.4 does not show. What is it?
options: Termination when the operator list is empty
Termination when a monitor is bored
Termination when the goal changes
Termination on external criteria such as time or space limits
optionExplain: Not mentioned.
Not mentioned.
Not mentioned.
Right.
questions.explain: The authors say that although not shown there could also be an exit from decide-next-step on time or space limits.
questions.rule: Real searches also stop on resource limits.
questions.teaches: Although not shown in the program, there could be an additional exit from decide-next-step to terminate on external criteria such as time or space limits.

questions.q: At the end of a cycle, the search may continue applying operators to the current element, advance, or ____.
options: stop the program
restart the whole problem
back up to untried-problems
change the goal
optionExplain: Stopping is a termination, not part of the three-way choice.
Restarting discards memory.
Right: backing up returns to the remembered elements.
The goal is not changed.
questions.explain: The third choice is to back up. The card next defines all three.

questions.q: Match each choice to its meaning.
pairs: Keep applying operators to the current element
Replace the current element by the new element
Abandon this path and go back to untried-problems
questions.explain: Continue stays, advance moves to the new element, and back up returns to earlier remembered elements.
questions.rule: Stay, move on, or go back.

questions.q: Exploring a cave system, a diver reaches a dead-end passage and returns to the last junction noted on her list. Which choice is this?
options: Advance: move to the new element
Continue: apply more operators to the same element
Back up: abandon the path and return to untried alternatives
Reject: delete the junction from memory
optionExplain: Advance goes deeper.
Continue stays at the same place.
Right.
Rejection concerns a new element, not returning.
questions.explain: Going back to remembered alternatives is the back-up option.
questions.rule: Back up to resume from a remembered element.

questions.q: True or false: Backing up allows further search to start from any element previously remembered on untried-problems.
questions.explain: The authors say the latter choice allows further search to be initiated from any previously remembered element.
questions.rule: Back up resumes from stored elements.

questions.q: Why does it matter that evaluation can attach information to an element as well as accept or reject it?
options: The information can be used later when selecting which element to work on
It stops the cycle at once
It makes the element a solution
It removes the need for a test
optionExplain: Right.
It does not stop the cycle.
Solution status is tested separately.
A test is still needed.
questions.explain: The authors say evaluation can associate with the element information to be used for later selection.
questions.rule: Evaluation can label elements for later use.
questions.teaches: Evaluation can also associate with the element information to be used for later selection, not only accept or reject it.

questions.q: Why does almost every heuristic search program use only some of the mechanisms in the full scheme?
options: The scheme has never been written down
Programmers dislike complex programs
The other mechanisms are always harmful
Particular task environments permit some mechanisms but not others
optionExplain: It has been written down in the figure.
No such claim is made.
Not harmful as such; unused where inapplicable.
Right.
questions.explain: Tasks differ in what they permit. The card next adds the second reason.
questions.rule: The task decides which mechanisms apply.

questions.q: The authors treat the heuristic-search program as an encompassing ____ from which more specific methods can be derived.
questions.explain: They call it an encompassing scheme.
questions.rule: A scheme, not a single method.

questions.q: A maze program has no need to evaluate positions because every square is equally good. Which statement follows?
options: It is not a search program
It can use a more direct executive with only the mechanisms it needs
It must still run the evaluation step
It cannot find solutions
optionExplain: It still searches.
Right.
Unused mechanisms can be omitted.
It can find solutions.
questions.explain: Where mechanisms are inapplicable, a more direct executive can be written with only those used.
questions.rule: Use only the mechanisms the task allows.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say a program that uses only some of the scheme's mechanisms must be an earlier, underdeveloped design.
questions.explain: Underdevelopment is one reason, but the more important reason is that tasks permit only some mechanisms.
questions.rule: Fewer mechanisms can mean a better fit.

questions.q: Besides the task environment, what other reason do the authors give for programs using only part of the scheme?
options: Early programs were slow
Computers had little memory
The scheme was never written down
Earlier programs are underdeveloped because the full generality of heuristic search was discovered gradually
optionExplain: Speed is not given as a reason.
Memory is not given as a reason.
The scheme is written down in the figure.
Right: some early programs are simply underdeveloped.
questions.explain: The authors name a gradual process of discovery of the full generality of heuristic search, so some earlier programs are underdeveloped.
questions.rule: Some programs predate the full scheme.
questions.teaches: There has been a gradual process of discovery of the full generality of heuristic search, so some of the earlier programs are simply underdeveloped.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the four undefined processes in the heuristic-search program?
options: Select-element
Select-operator
Decide-next-step
Reconstruct-path
optionExplain: Select-element is one of the four.
Select-operator is one of the four.
Decide-next-step is one of the four.
Right: reconstruct-path is defined in the program.
questions.explain: The four are select-element, select-operator, evaluate and decide-next-step. The card next gives details.

questions.q: Which are among the four undefined processes? Select all that apply.
options: Select-element
Select-operator
Evaluate(new-element)
Decide-next-step
Reconstruct-path
optionExplain: Right.
Right.
Right.
Right.
It is defined in the program.
questions.explain: The four open processes are select-element, select-operator, evaluate and decide-next-step.

questions.q: A program orders all its operators by how easy each is to apply and tries the easiest first. Which of the authors' possibilities is this?
options: Ordering all operators on ease of applicability
Rejecting operators that are too easy
Selecting only difficult operators
Choosing operators at random
optionExplain: Right: ordering.
That removes some.
That keeps only some.
Not random.
questions.explain: The authors list reject, select and order as three uses of the same criterion; this is ordering.
questions.rule: Reject, select or order on a criterion.

questions.q: True or false: The authors know of programs that order operators on ease of applicability.
questions.explain: They say programs exist that reject or select on ease of application but know of none that order on this measure.
questions.rule: Not every possibility has been tried.

questions.q: How do the authors say Table 4.1 can be used as the book proceeds?
options: As a proof that heuristic search is correct
As a list of mistakes to avoid
As a check list against which various programs and partial programs can be compared
As a substitute for reading the programs
optionExplain: It proves nothing.
It lists mechanisms, not mistakes.
Right.
It supplements, not replaces.
questions.explain: The authors say the table can be used as a check list and give it as a backdrop for the detailed example in the next section.
questions.rule: Use the table as a check list.
questions.teaches: The authors say the table lists only key notions and does not indicate whether a mechanism is to select on a value, reject on a value, or order all candidates by that characteristic.

questions.q: Selecting the most recently stored element first is called what in the table?
options: Breadth-first search (first-in-first-out)
Scan-search
Random search
Depth-first search (last-in-first-out)
optionExplain: Breadth-first takes the oldest first.
Scan-search uses evaluation.
Not random.
Right.
questions.explain: Last in, first out gives depth-first. The card next gives the others.

questions.q: Match each rule to its search name.
questions.explain: LIFO and always-advance give depth-first; FIFO gives breadth-first; always-go-back gives search and scan.

questions.q: A librarian keeps a stack of boxes to check and each time opens the box most recently added. Which search is this?
options: Breadth-first
Depth-first
Search and scan
One-level breadth-first
optionExplain: That would open the oldest first.
Right.
Search and scan returns to the list after each step.
One-level always continues on the same element.
questions.explain: Taking the newest item first is last-in-first-out.

questions.q: True or false: First-in-first-out selection corresponds to breadth-first search.
questions.explain: Table 4.1 lists first-in-first-out as breadth-first search.

questions.q: Which of these does Table 4.1 list as a limit on a heuristic search?
options: The age of the solver
The colour of the nodes
Depth of search
The number of solvers
optionExplain: Not a limit.
Not a limit.
Right.
Not a limit.
questions.explain: The table lists number of operators (width), depth of search, effort or space, and limits from evaluation.
questions.rule: Limits can be width, depth or effort.
questions.teaches: Table 4.1 lists as limits on a heuristic search the number of operators (width), the depth of search, effort and space, and limits set on evaluation of the new element.

questions.q: What is LT asked to do?
options: Discover proofs of theorems in elementary symbolic logic
Play chess against a human
Translate sentences into logic
Check whether a given proof is valid
optionExplain: Right.
Chess comes in Part 4.
Not LT's task.
Checking is the test; finding is the task.
questions.explain: LT finds proofs. The card next gives the setting.
questions.rule: LT finds proofs of logic theorems.

questions.q: In the system used, ____ expressions are taken as axioms.
questions.explain: Five expressions are taken as axioms, with rules of inference to derive new theorems.

questions.q: A student says LT's work in symbolic logic must itself be an especially logical process of thought. How does the authors' footnote respond?
options: Discovering proofs is not a deductive process, and the logic task makes problem solving no more logical than other tasks
She is right because logic always yields deduction
She is right because LT applies only axioms
She is wrong because LT does not use logic
optionExplain: Right.
The footnote says otherwise.
Applying axioms is the proof, but finding proofs is not deduction.
LT does work in logic.
questions.explain: The footnote separates the logical form of the task from the nature of the search process.
questions.rule: Task content is not process type.

questions.q: True or false: The authors treat the propositional calculus here as a purely formal mathematics with no need of its interpretation.
questions.explain: They say the system is to be dealt with as purely formal mathematics and will have no further need of the interpretation.

questions.q: Which of these connectives does the chapter say it uses?
options: Only and
Not, and, and exclusive-or
Not, or, and implies
None; only variables
optionExplain: Not the stated set.
Not stated.
Right: and is mentioned but not needed.
Connectives are used.
questions.explain: The authors introduce negation, or and implies, mentioning that other connectives such as and exist but are not needed.
questions.teaches: The authors mention other connectives such as and, but say they will not need them in the chapter.

questions.q: In the authors' system, what is a proof of a theorem?
options: A single expression equal to the theorem
A list of expressions, each validly derived from the previous ones, leading from axioms and known theorems to the desired expression
A random list of expressions
Any list that contains the theorem
optionExplain: A single expression is not a derivation.
Right.
Validity matters.
Mere presence is not enough.
questions.explain: A proof is a validly derived list. The card next gives the rules.
questions.rule: A proof is a valid derivation list.

questions.q: Match each rule of inference to what it does.
pairs: Put an expression for a variable throughout a theorem
Swap a connective for its definition or back
From A and A implies B, get B
From A implies B and B implies C, get A implies C
questions.explain: These are the four rules in the chapter.

questions.q: You know P implies Q and Q implies R are theorems. Which rule gives P implies R?
options: Detachment
Substitution
Replacement
Chaining
optionExplain: Detachment needs A and A implies B.
Substitution changes variables.
Replacement swaps connectives.
Right.
questions.explain: Chaining joins two implications that share a middle term.
questions.rule: Chain implications that share a term.

questions.q: True or false: In Principia, chaining was assumed as a separate rule of inference.
questions.explain: Whitehead and Russell derived it by two applications of detachment to Axiom 1.6.

questions.q: In the authors' framing, how do the rules relate to the problem's state and process languages?
options: Rules are objects and expressions are operators
Rules act as operators, and expressions are the objects, in the process and state languages respectively
Both are operators
Both are objects
optionExplain: Reversed.
Right.
Expressions are objects.
Rules act.
questions.explain: Applying a rule to an expression produces a new one, so rules are operators and expressions are objects.
questions.teaches: Applying a rule to one expression produces a new one, so rules can be interpreted as operators and expressions as objects in the process language and state language of the problem domain.

questions.q: How large is the authors' restricted set of possible proofs?
options: About 10^235
About 10,000
About a million
About 20 x 23
optionExplain: Right.
Far too small.
Far too small.
That multiplies the limits and says nothing about the set.
questions.explain: The number is astronomically large. The card next states the restrictions.
questions.rule: The proof space is astronomically big.

questions.q: Posing the task as a set of arbitrary lists of expressions makes the number of possible proofs ____ if no limits are set.
questions.explain: With no limits on length the number is infinite.

questions.q: Why does checking one candidate list in this formulation take real effort?
options: The list must be rewritten in a new alphabet
The list must be run on a different machine
The test needs the solver to know the answer
Each expression must be checked as an axiom or as derivable from earlier ones, and the target must appear
optionExplain: No new alphabet.
Machine is irrelevant.
Knowing the answer would not be a test.
Right.
questions.explain: Verification of validity is costly.
questions.rule: The verifier has work to do.

questions.q: True or false: In this formulation, difficulty comes from both the size of the space and the cost of testing a candidate.
questions.explain: The authors say the set is too large and the testing too costly.

questions.q: A cryptographer proposes to attack a cipher by checking all keys of 128 bits one by one. Using the authors' account, what is the main obstacle?
options: The test of each key is expensive
There is no set of keys
The space of keys is far too large, even if each test is cheap
Keys cannot be generated
optionExplain: Here the test is cheap.
A set exists.
Right.
Keys can be generated.
questions.explain: As with the safe, a huge space defeats generate-and-test even when each trial is cheap; with the proof task both space and test are costly.
questions.teaches: Each expression in a candidate proof must be checked as an axiom or as derivable from earlier expressions, so the test as well as the space makes sheer trial and error infeasible.

questions.q: Why do the authors call the 10^235 figure arbitrary?
options: It is an exact count of all theorems
It was found by experiment
It depends on the simplicity restrictions imposed, not on the task
It was chosen to match the computer's memory
optionExplain: It counts candidate lists.
It is a computed size.
Right.
Memory is not mentioned.
questions.explain: The restrictions set the size. The card next shows what a better generator uses.
questions.rule: Restrictions, not the task, fix the number.

questions.q: The authors say nothing in this generator reflects the ____ of the task, except in the weakest sense.
questions.explain: Nothing reflects the demands of the task except in the weakest sense.
questions.rule: A good generator reflects task demands.

questions.q: A password cracker limits guesses to lowercase letters of length 8 because that is easiest to enumerate. By the authors' reasoning, what does the resulting size tell us about the task?
options: Little: it reflects the restrictions chosen rather than the demands of the task
Everything about how hard passwords are
That passwords contain only lowercase letters
That the test is cheap
optionExplain: Right.
The size is set by the chosen restriction.
That is an assumption of the enumeration.
Test cost is separate.
questions.explain: As with 10^235, the number follows from a chosen restriction.
questions.rule: Be wary of sizes set by convenience.

questions.q: True or false: Tightening the simplicity restrictions would change the 10^235 figure, though not the task.
questions.explain: The figure depends entirely on the restrictions imposed.
questions.rule: Change the restriction, change the number.

questions.q: How do the authors make the generator more meaningful than the arbitrary one?
options: By lengthening the lists
By adding more symbols
By generating only lists that are valid proofs, which meet some conditions of a solution
By removing the test
optionExplain: Longer lists enlarge the space, not the selectivity.
More symbols enlarge the space.
Right: valid proofs satisfy some solution conditions by construction.
A test is still needed for the target.
questions.explain: They propose to generate only lists of expressions that are valid proofs, which removes the major part of the verification task.
questions.rule: Build the task's constraints into the generator.
questions.teaches: The generator can be made meaningful by generating only lists of expressions that are valid proofs, which eliminates the major part of the verification task.

questions.q: What does the British Museum Algorithm generate?
options: Every possible list of symbols
Only lists of expressions that are valid proofs of something, shortest first
Only the target theorem
Random lists of axioms
optionExplain: That is the first generator.
Right.
It does not know the target.
Not random.
questions.explain: It generates valid proofs from short to long. The card next explains.

questions.q: Put the algorithm's growth steps in order.
items: Generate one-expression proofs (the axioms)
Generate two-expression proofs
Build proofs of length k + 1 from all proofs of length k
Check whether the desired theorem appears
questions.explain: It starts with the axioms and grows proofs by one step at a time, while the target is checked for.

questions.q: Because the algorithm creates only valid proofs, what does the test have to do?
options: Check every inference for validity
Check that the desired theorem occurs somewhere in the generated sequence
Re-derive each expression
Choose which axiom to use
optionExplain: Validity is built into the generator.
Right.
Not needed.
The generator uses all axioms.
questions.explain: Validity is guaranteed by construction, leaving only the occurrence test.
questions.rule: Move the checking into the generator.

questions.q: True or false: The British Museum Algorithm still has to verify the validity of each inference after generating a list.
questions.explain: By generating only valid proofs it eliminates the major part of the task of verification.

questions.q: In the algorithm's tree of proofs, what does each branch leading from a choice point stand for?
options: A different axiom to start from
A guess at the target theorem
A legitimate way of deriving a new expression as an immediate consequence of the expressions in that proof
A proof that has been rejected
optionExplain: Axioms are the starting one-expression proofs, not the branches.
The algorithm does not know the target.
Right: each branch adds one admissible derived expression.
Rejected proofs are not shown as branches.
questions.explain: The authors describe a tree each choice point of which represents a proof, with branches representing the legitimate ways of deriving new expressions as immediate consequences.
questions.teaches: The generated tree has a proof at each choice point, and the branches from it are the legitimate ways of deriving new expressions as immediate consequences of the expressions in that proof.

questions.q: How many of Principia's Chapter 2 theorems are among the first 1000 the algorithm proves?
options: Six
About fifty
All of them
None
optionExplain: Right: 2.01 to 2.05 and 2.07.
Far more than reached.
Far more than reached.
Some are reached.
questions.explain: Only six. The card next lists them.

questions.q: Theorem 2.01 is obtained at step ____ of the generation.
questions.explain: Theorem 2.01 is obtained in step 4, among the first 42 theorems proved.

questions.q: Theorem 2.05 appears at step 8. Which statement fits the authors' count?
options: It is among the first 42
It is among the first 115
It is among the first 246 theorems generated
It is not generated in the first 1000
optionExplain: That is for step 4.
That is for step 6.
Right.
It is within the first 1000.
questions.explain: Step 8 gives 2.05 within the first 246.

questions.q: Which theorems are reached within the first 1000 proofs? Select all that apply.
optionExplain: Right.
Right.
Right.
Right.
Not reached; it needs detachment.
questions.explain: The authors list 2.01 to 2.05 and 2.07 only.

questions.q: What do the authors conclude about the algorithm from these counts?
options: It will soon prove all theorems
It is more efficient than a human
It does not use detachment
Proofs of the remaining theorems need complex substitutions or detachment and would take eons of computation
optionExplain: They say the opposite.
They say it is spectacularly inefficient.
Detachment is a rule it could use.
Right.
questions.explain: The proofs of all the remainder require either complex substitutions or detachment, which the early steps leave out.
questions.rule: Early successes do not predict later ones.
questions.teaches: The enumeration in Figure 4.7 extends only to replacements and substitution of negated variables; no detachments and no complex substitutions are included.

questions.q: What does the British Museum Algorithm explore?
options: The space of all sequences of expressions
The space of proofs, not the space of all sequences of expressions
Only the space of theorems
The space of axioms only
optionExplain: That was the first generator.
Right.
It builds proofs, not just theorems.
It uses axioms and their consequences.
questions.explain: It explores proofs only. The card next says how it proceeds.

questions.q: The algorithm proceeds in an orderly way from ____ to long proofs.
questions.explain: It proceeds in order of increasing proof length.

questions.q: A cook tries only recipes that are valid (every step uses available tools), in order of number of steps. Which feature of the algorithm is this?
options: Random generation
Recognition of a stored answer
Orderly generation within the space of valid items
A stop rule on negations
optionExplain: Not random.
No answer stored.
Right.
Not a stop rule.
questions.explain: Only valid items, shortest first, matches the algorithm.

questions.q: True or false: The authors describe the British Museum Algorithm as a random search.
questions.explain: They say that in spite of its spectacular inefficiency its generating process is far from random.

questions.q: Why is it significant that the algorithm applies only admissible operators?
options: Every sequence it produces is a valid proof of something
It runs faster than LT
It needs no test at all
It generates only the target
optionExplain: Right.
It is slower.
A test is still needed.
It does not know the target.
questions.explain: Admissible operators mean every sequence is a proof, which is the built-in selectivity.
questions.teaches: Even apparently blind trial-and-error generators contain a great deal of built-in selectivity, because they exclude many irrelevant parts of the space of possible solutions.

questions.q: Why do the authors study generate-and-test even though it cannot solve the logic problem?
options: It shows how hard the task is for weak solvers and is a method of last resort
It is the method LT actually uses
It solves most problems quickly
It is the only method that works
optionExplain: Right.
LT uses a more selective method.
It is slow.
Other methods exist.
questions.explain: Two reasons: a standard of difficulty and a last resort. The card next explains.

questions.q: Generate-and-test is described as a method of last ____.
questions.explain: Almost any problem can be formulated so that generate-and-test applies, so it can be tried when all else fails.

questions.q: A technician cannot find a faulty cable by reasoning, so she tries each cable in turn. In the authors' terms, she...
options: uses recognition
uses heuristic search with evaluation
falls back on generate-and-test as a method of last resort
reduces the representation
optionExplain: No stored answer.
No evaluation.
Right.
No change of picture.
questions.explain: When nothing better is available, trying elements in turn is available.

questions.q: True or false: Almost any problem can also be formulated so that generate-and-test becomes a possible method.
questions.explain: The authors say that, however else a problem is formulated, it can almost always be formulated so that generate-and-test applies, which is why it is a method of last resort.

questions.q: Why are weak but general-purpose methods like generate-and-test valuable to the strategy of reducing a hard problem to many small subproblems?
options: They let the small subproblems at the bottom of the reduction actually be solved
They make the hard problem easy at once
They replace the need for subproblems
They show that reduction is impossible
optionExplain: Right: without them the reduction could not end in solved problems.
They are weak and do not make the hard problem easy.
Subproblems are still needed for the strategy.
The reverse: they make reduction feasible.
questions.explain: The authors say that without weak but general-purpose methods the basic strategy of reducing a single hard problem to a myriad of small subproblems might not be feasible.
questions.rule: Reduction needs weak methods at the bottom.
questions.teaches: If it were not for weak but general-purpose methods such as generate-and-test, the basic strategy of reducing a single hard problem to a myriad of small subproblems might not be feasible.

questions.q: LT is asked to prove a theorem it cannot prove with the theorems it has. What does it do?
options: It prints a false proof
It crashes without a message
It runs forever without any report
It works for a time, then reports it cannot prove it and has exhausted its resources
optionExplain: LT's operators guarantee valid steps, so a false proof is not produced.
The report is an explicit output of the program.
LT stops when resources are exhausted, as the text describes.
Right: for 2.31 LT gave up with a report after about 23 minutes.
questions.explain: LT reports failure explicitly. The card next gives three runs.
questions.rule: LT reports failure as well as success.

questions.q: LT ran on a first-generation machine called ____.
questions.explain: LT was run on JOHNNIAC, a mid-fifties machine no longer in service.

questions.q: A reader says LT took 12 minutes on Theorem 2.45, so a modern laptop would need 12 minutes too. Why is that reasoning unsafe?
options: Because 2.45 was proved instantly
Because LT does not run on laptops
Because the 12 minutes were spent printing
Absolute times depend on the particular machine the program was run on
optionExplain: The text says about 12 minutes on JOHNNIAC, not instantly.
The point is machine dependence, not whether LT can be run elsewhere.
No time is attributed to printing.
Right: the footnote says absolute times are deceptive.
questions.explain: The authors stress that times depend on the particular computer, so they should be read as JOHNNIAC times.

questions.q: True or false: When LT is given more of the earlier theorems, the number of lines in its proof of 2.45 can only increase.
questions.explain: Theorem 2.45 was proved with 38 earlier theorems in five lines; later results show longer theorem lists can shorten proofs but cost effort (our reading of the sequence).

questions.q: On an IBM 360/65, roughly how long would LT's ten-second JOHNNIAC run on Theorem 2.01 take?
options: About ten seconds
About a thousand seconds
About a tenth of a second
About a minute
optionExplain: That would mean no speed difference between the machines.
That would be slower than JOHNNIAC.
Right: the 360/65 was about 100 times faster.
That also would be slower than JOHNNIAC.
questions.explain: A footnote says the 10-second JOHNNIAC time corresponds to about 0.1 second on the IBM 360/65, which is about 100 times faster.
questions.rule: Convert times by the machine ratio.
questions.teaches: JOHNNIAC's addition time was 50 microseconds, and the IBM 360/65 is about 100 times faster, so the 10-second run corresponds to about 0.1 second.

questions.q: In the first experiment, about what share of the 52 theorems did LT prove?
options: About a tenth
All of them
About half
About three quarters
optionExplain: This would be around 5 theorems.
LT failed on 14 theorems.
Half would be 26, but LT proved 38.
Right: 38 of 52 is 73 percent.
questions.explain: 38 of 52, or 73 percent. The card next gives the timing.

questions.q: LT proved ____ of the first 52 theorems.
questions.explain: The authors report 38 proved, 73 percent.

questions.q: In the experiment, 38 of 52 theorems were proved. How many were not proved?
optionExplain: 12 is the number the authors say LT could prove with enough resources.
That is the number proved.
That is the percent proved.
questions.explain: The remainder, 14, were not proved within the limits.

questions.q: True or false: In the first experiment, time to prove a theorem rose sharply, perhaps exponentially, with each extra proof step.
questions.explain: The authors found a strong relation between time and length of proof.
questions.rule: Time grows sharply with proof length.

questions.q: In the first experiment, what did LT do with a theorem it failed to prove?
options: It was deleted from memory
It was reported as false
It was stored in memory with the axioms and available for later proofs
It was proved at the end
optionExplain: Deleting would make it unavailable.
Failing to prove is not a finding of falsity.
Right: the program stored theorems whether or not proved.
No second pass is described.
questions.explain: The authors say regardless of whether a theorem was proved it was stored and available as material for later proofs.
questions.teaches: LT's program stored every presented theorem on the list with the axioms regardless of whether it had been proved, making it available for building proofs of subsequent theorems.

questions.q: LT could prove Theorem 2.12 in about ten seconds with all earlier theorems. What happens if all the earlier theorems are removed?
options: LT cannot find a proof
LT finds the same proof as before
LT finds a shorter proof
LT proves it faster
optionExplain: Right: the second experiment failed.
The one-step proof used an earlier theorem.
Removing resources does not shorten proofs.
Without helpful theorems LT cannot proceed.
questions.explain: Without earlier theorems LT fails. The card next gives the details.

questions.q: LT succeeded on Theorem 2.12 once the axioms and Theorem ____ were stored.
questions.explain: In the third experiment the axioms and Theorem 2.03 were stored, and LT then proved 2.12.

questions.q: A chess club's coach erases all of a player's studied games and asks him to play the same openings again. How does the authors' second experiment compare?
options: It is like giving LT extra theorems
It is like changing the rules of logic
It is like asking LT to prove a falsehood
It is like removing LT's earlier theorems: the player has the skill but not the specific stored material
optionExplain: Erasing removes material.
The rules of the system do not change.
No falsehood is involved.
Right: the authors liken it to a new subject who knows the method but not the problems.
questions.explain: The authors translate the removal as a new subject who knows how to solve problems but is unfamiliar with the particular ones.

questions.q: True or false: With only the axioms and Theorem 2.03 stored, LT was able to prove Theorem 2.12.
questions.explain: It succeeded, in fifteen minutes with a three-step proof, whereas the full list had given a one-step proof in about ten seconds.
questions.rule: A sparse list can still succeed, slowly.

questions.q: What does the contrast between the first and third experiments show about a problem solver's stored knowledge?
options: Knowledge never changes what a solver can do
A solver can be handicapped by missing knowledge, and a single relevant item can restore success at higher cost
All stored items contribute equally
A solver needs all knowledge to succeed
optionExplain: The results show it does matter.
Right.
One item made the difference here.
One theorem sufficed.
questions.explain: Adding just 2.03 turned failure into success, though the proof was longer and took about fifteen minutes.
questions.rule: Key knowledge can matter more than amount.
questions.teaches: With the axioms and Theorem 2.03 stored but not the other theorems before 2.12, LT proved 2.12 in fifteen minutes with a three-step proof where all prior theorems had given a one-step proof.

questions.q: Why can detachment not be used directly as an operator on a single logic expression?
options: It cannot be applied to expressions at all
It needs a second theorem as input
It always produces false results
It requires a new alphabet
optionExplain: It does apply to expressions, with the extra input.
Right: detachment needs both A and A implies B.
Its results are valid when it applies.
No alphabet change is involved.
questions.explain: It needs a second theorem. The card next lists the other issues.

questions.q: Match each operator to what it needs in the forward direction.
pairs: Only the expression and the connective
The expressions to substitute and the variables
A second theorem as the premise
A second theorem linking two implications
questions.explain: Replacement is simple; the other operators need extra inputs.
questions.rule: Substitution, detachment and chaining need more.

questions.q: Working backward, LT's detachment takes a single expression X. What does it produce?
options: A single expression that is already proved
No output
A new axiom
A pair of expressions, both of which must be shown true
optionExplain: The pair is not already proved.
It produces a pair.
Axioms are given, not made.
Right: to prove B you must prove both A and A implies B.
questions.explain: In reverse, detachment turns one goal into two.

questions.q: True or false: Working backward changes only the direction of search; the operators keep exactly the same inputs and outputs.
questions.explain: Backward, substitution replaces identical subexpressions with a variable, and detachment and chaining give pairs, so the operators are reversed.

questions.q: In the authors' state and process language for this problem, what are the elements and what are the operators?
options: Logic expressions (and sets or sequences of them) are objects; operators construct sets or trees of expressions
Operators are objects and expressions are processes
Both are processes
Both are states
optionExplain: Right.
Reversed.
Expressions are objects.
Operators act.
questions.explain: The state language holds expressions; the process language holds operators that build sets or trees.
questions.teaches: In the process language the elementary operators each add one more logic expression to a set, and the list in generation order is the sequence generated by the operator sequence.

questions.q: In which direction does LT search?
options: Forward, from the axioms toward the theorem
Both directions at once
Backward, from the theorem to be proved toward the axioms
Sideways among theorems
optionExplain: That is the British Museum direction.
LT does one direction.
Right.
Not described.
questions.explain: LT works backward. The card next lists all four choices.

questions.q: In LT the element of the problem space is a single logic ____.
questions.explain: The first choice: the element is a single logic expression.

questions.q: A tutor asks a student to prove a target by looking for any known fact that would let the target follow. Which LT choice matches?
options: Working forward from the axioms
Substituting without a target
Replacing connectives only
Working backward from the target
optionExplain: Forward would start from known facts and generate.
A target is always present.
Replacement is only a component.
Right.
questions.explain: Starting from the goal and asking what would give it is working backward.

questions.q: True or false: In LT the stored theorems enter the problem in two roles, as parameters of operators and as the goal set.
questions.explain: The goal set is the set theorems, and theorems also enter as parameters of the operators.
questions.rule: Theorems are both goals and parameters.

questions.q: Why does LT require a theorem to enter each operator as an input?
options: To make operators more expensive
So that each operator has a single input and a single output when working backward
To remove the need for substitution
To search forward
optionExplain: Cost is not the aim.
Right.
Substitution is still used.
LT works backward.
questions.explain: Having a theorem as a parameter makes the operators one-input one-output.
questions.teaches: The goal set G is the set theorems, so a proof has been found when the sequence finally contains some T in theorems; thus members of theorems enter the proof in two roles.

questions.q: In LT's detachment operator, given the expression X to prove, what does it seek in a stored theorem A implies B?
options: To transform A into X
To find X inside A
To transform B into X by substitution and replacement
To delete B
optionExplain: B is the conclusion that must match X.
X is not searched inside A.
Right: if B can become X, the new problem is A.
Nothing is deleted.
questions.explain: B must match X; then A becomes the new problem. The card next gives all operators.
questions.rule: Match the conclusion, produce the premise.

questions.q: Match each operator to its output.
pairs: SB(A), the premise of the matched theorem
Success or failure in transforming T into X
questions.explain: Each operator returns the part of the theorem that was not matched, modified by the same substitutions.

questions.q: LT holds the theorem A implies B and wants to prove X. SB turns B into X. What new problem does detachment create?
options: Prove SB(A)
Prove SB(B)
Prove X again
Prove nothing; the problem is solved
optionExplain: Right: if SB(A) is proved, detachment gives X.
SB(B) equals X, which is the target.
That would loop.
Detachment creates a subproblem.
questions.explain: If A can be proved, B follows by detachment, and B matches X.

questions.q: True or false: Substituting (P V Q) for A and Q for B in A implies B gives (P V Q) implies Q.
questions.explain: The authors give exactly this example of the SB operation.

questions.q: Why does the authors' SB notation write substitutions explicitly, as in SB[a for A, b for B](T), but not the replacements?
options: Replacements never occur in LT
Replacements are done by hand
Replacements are always clear without being stated
Substitutions are unimportant
optionExplain: Replacements do occur; they are components of every operator.
Nothing is done by hand in LT.
Right: the authors say replacements are always clear.
Substitution is the core of the test.
questions.explain: To make the parameters explicit they write SB[a for A, b for B](T) for substituting a for A and b for B in T; replacements are always clear without being stated.
questions.teaches: When the parameters of SB are made explicit, only the substitutions are written, because replacements are always clear without being stated.

questions.q: How many submethods does LT's executive use?
options: One
Two
Four
Ten
optionExplain: There are several.
Two covers only part.
Right: substitution, detachment, chaining forward and chaining backward.
Too many.
questions.explain: There are four. The card next describes them.

questions.q: Put LT's executive steps on one problem in order.
items: Substitution-submethod: try for an immediate proof
Insert the problem on untried-problems
Take the current problem from untried-problems
Detachment, chaining forward and chaining backward submethods
questions.explain: LT first tries substitution, then adds the problem to untried-problems and works through the list with the other submethods.

questions.q: The detachment-submethod produces a new subproblem and checks it by substitution without success. What happens to the new subproblem?
options: It is discarded
It is added to the end of untried-problems
It is reported as the proof
It replaces the original theorem
optionExplain: Failure to prove is not rejection.
Right: it will become a current problem later.
It has not been proved.
Theorems are not replaced.
questions.explain: Each unsolved new problem is inserted at the end of untried-problems.

questions.q: True or false: Each submethod can add at most one branch for each theorem in the theorem list.
questions.explain: The authors say each submethod is an independent unit adding at most one branch for each member of theorems.
questions.rule: At most one branch per theorem.

questions.q: In the original LT, the submethods were called methods. Why do the authors now call them submethods?
options: Because they are smaller programs
Because LT has only one method now
Because the term method is banned
Only later did it become clear that the fundamental units were the operators and the test; submethods package their application
optionExplain: Size is not the reason.
LT has complete-organization methods in the authors' use.
No such ban.
Right.
questions.explain: A footnote explains that method is now reserved for a complete organization that has a chance to solve the problem.
questions.rule: Use method for the whole organization.
questions.teaches: A footnote says the fundamental units were later seen to be the three operators and the test, with submethods simply a way of packaging their application, and that method is now used for a complete organization that has a chance to solve the problem.

questions.q: In LT's proof of 2.45, what completed the proof once the subproblem had been created?
options: A second detachment
A substitution that made a stored theorem equal to the subproblem
A chaining step
A new axiom
optionExplain: Not used here.
Right.
Not used here.
Axioms are given.
questions.explain: Substitution closed it. The card next gives the steps.

questions.q: LT's proof of 2.45 took ____ steps.
questions.explain: A two-step proof, detachment followed by substitution.

questions.q: In the proof of 2.45, detachment with 2.16 added P implies (P or Q) to untried-problems. What closed the proof?
options: The substitution operator showed that Theorem 2.2 could be made equal to that expression
A second detachment with Theorem 2.16
A chaining step with Axiom 1.6
Nothing; the expression was the proof
optionExplain: Right: substitution into 2.2 matched the new subproblem.
A second detachment is not part of the two-step proof.
No chaining step is used in this proof.
The expression was only a subproblem until it matched a stored theorem.
questions.explain: The expression was a subproblem, closed when substitution made a stored theorem (2.2) equal to it.
questions.rule: A subproblem closes when it matches a stored theorem.

questions.q: True or false: If Theorem 2.16 had been missing from the theorem list, LT would still have produced the same two-step proof.
questions.explain: Detachment used 2.16 to make the useful subproblem, and a smaller theorem list leads to a deeper search in later figures (our reading).
questions.rule: The proof used particular stored theorems.

questions.q: Which pair of theorems did the proof of 2.45 use with its two operators?
options: Axiom 1.6 with chaining
Theorem 2.11 with substitution
No theorems were used
Theorem 2.16 with detachment, then Theorem 2.2 with substitution
optionExplain: Not in this proof.
Not in this proof.
Theorems are the parameters.
Right.
questions.explain: The tree shows detachment with 2.16 and substitution with 2.2.
questions.rule: Match each operator to its theorem.
questions.teaches: Before producing the expression that figured in the final proof, the detachment operator had added seven other expressions to untried-problems that played no part in the proof.

questions.q: What does LT's operators guarantee about every subproblem they generate?
options: It is true
It will lead to a proof
It belongs to a sequence of expressions ending in the desired theorem, each derived by the rules
It is simpler than the problem
optionExplain: Subproblems can be false.
No such guarantee.
Right.
Not guaranteed.
questions.explain: The guarantee concerns form, not success. The card next explains.

questions.q: True or false: A subproblem LT generates may be a false expression.
questions.explain: The authors say a subproblem may not be part of any proof sequence, for example because it is false.

questions.q: A detective builds a chain of reasoning from the conclusion backward, each step following legitimately from the next, but cannot connect it to any known fact. Which is the analogue?
options: Connection to known theorems guaranteed
A false chain
Valid form guaranteed, but not connection to the known theorems
A proof
optionExplain: That is what is not guaranteed.
The steps are valid.
Right.
It is not yet connected.
questions.explain: Backward steps are valid by construction but may fail to reach the stored theorems.
questions.rule: Valid links do not ensure connection.

questions.q: A reader says LT's valid steps guarantee success. In fact there is no guarantee that the four methods form a sufficient set to prove all ____.
questions.explain: The authors say there is no guarantee that the combination of the four methods, used in any fashion and with unlimited effort, can prove all theorems.
questions.rule: Valid steps do not make the method complete.

questions.q: Which distinction does this idea draw?
options: Completeness is guaranteed, while soundness is not
Both are guaranteed
Neither is guaranteed
Soundness of each step is guaranteed, while completeness of the method is not
optionExplain: Reversed.
The authors say no guarantee of success.
Steps are valid.
Right (our wording of the authors' point).
questions.explain: Operators guarantee that subproblems form sequences ending in the target, but the whole method may fail to connect to the theorem list.
questions.teaches: What the operators do not guarantee is that a generated sequence can be connected with the axioms and previously proved theorems, that is, with the list theorems.

questions.q: Why does LT fail to prove 2.13 by two detachments working backward?
options: It has no detachment operator
It looks for a stored theorem of the form X implies the target, and the needed implication is not yet proved
The theorem is false
It runs out of memory at once
optionExplain: It has one.
Right.
2.13 is a theorem.
The cause is the missing intermediate.
questions.explain: The needed implication is not stored. The card next explains.

questions.q: LT's detachment-submethod does not treat the two premises ____ symmetrically.
questions.explain: It treats the two premises asymmetrically: it needs one already stored as an implication to the target.

questions.q: How could the designers get LT to prove 2.13?
options: Remove the axioms
Give it the problem of proving A implies C first, so that this becomes a stored theorem
Speed up the machine
Change the proof to a forward one
optionExplain: Axioms are needed.
Right.
Speed does not help with an impossible search.
LT is designed backward.
questions.explain: Once A implies C is stored, detachment finds it.

questions.q: True or false: If LT had already proved A implies C, it would then succeed on C by detachment.
questions.explain: The authors say that with that implication in memory the detachment-submethod would discover it.

questions.q: The authors say there is a very large class of proofs LT will not discover. Which class?
options: All proofs longer than one step
Proofs using axioms
Proofs of false theorems
Branched proofs, unless some intermediate expressions are given as subproblems in a suitable sequence
optionExplain: It does find two-step proofs.
It uses axioms.
False theorems have no proofs.
Right.
questions.explain: Branched proofs need intermediate expressions to be proved first.
questions.teaches: The authors say Whitehead and Russell's proof of 2.13 uses Axiom 1.06 and the earlier theorems 2.11 and 2.12 in two detachments, the first of which produces the implication LT needs but cannot find.

questions.q: A solution must have three properties. A generator exists for any two. Which should it make sure of?
options: The two that are hardest to satisfy by chance
The two that are easiest to satisfy
Any two; it makes no difference
Only the first listed
optionExplain: Right.
Waiting for the hardest is slow.
It matters a lot.
Order of listing does not matter.
questions.explain: Fix the hard ones in the generator. The card next gives the proof case.

questions.q: Match each proof generator to the properties it builds in.
pairs: p1 and p2: starts with known theorems, every step valid
p2 and p3: valid steps, ends at the target
p1 and p3: starts and ends right, steps unchecked
questions.explain: BMA waits for p3; LT waits for p1; the foolish generator waits for p2.

questions.q: A job seeker needs a role that pays well, is nearby, and uses her skills. Listings of nearby roles using her skills are easy to get, pay is rare. Which generator is sensible?
options: List roles that use her skills and wait for pay
List all roles
List roles that pay well and are nearby, and wait for one that uses her skills
List nothing
optionExplain: That waits for the rare property.
No constraint is used.
Right: fix the rare property (pay).
No candidates.
questions.explain: If a property is rare, build it into the generator; the common ones can wait.

questions.q: True or false: If property p1 is common among generated elements, it is reasonable to generate elements with p2 and p3 and wait for p1 to show up.
questions.explain: The authors say that if there are lots of elements satisfying p1, generating with p2 and p3 is reasonable.
questions.rule: Common properties can be left to chance.

questions.q: Which generator does the proof task make foolish, and why?
options: One that satisfies p2 and p3
One that satisfies p1 and p2
None is foolish
One that satisfies p1 and p3 and waits for p2, since valid inference is the difficult condition
optionExplain: That is LT.
That is the British Museum Algorithm.
One is foolish.
Right.
questions.explain: Writing lists that start with theorems and end with the target is easy; valid steps are hard, so waiting for them would be foolish.
questions.rule: Never wait for the hard property.
questions.teaches: The generator satisfying p1 and p2 reduces the size of the space of possibilities from the order of 10^235 to the order of 10^7.

questions.q: When does LT's detachment-submethod add a new expression?
options: Whenever it likes
Only when it finds a stored theorem of the form A implies X for the expression X being proved
For every stored theorem
Only at random
optionExplain: It is conditional.
Right.
Only matching theorems count.
Not random.
questions.explain: It acts only under special conditions. The card next explains.

questions.q: The superiority of LT over the British Museum Algorithm arises because its generator is more ____.
questions.explain: Both have selective generators, but LT's is more selective.

questions.q: A librarian only pulls books whose catalogue entry names the topic requested. Which feature of LT is this like?
options: Generating every book
Recognition from memory
Taking action only when special conditions are met, so the conditions determine the action
Random sampling
optionExplain: No: conditional.
No answer is recalled.
Right.
Not random.
questions.explain: Conditional action driven by the target is the detachment pattern.

questions.q: True or false: LT's detachment and chaining submethods guarantee that each generated sequence has all the properties of a proof.
questions.explain: The authors say they do not guarantee this, hence the need for a test process, the substitution-submethod.

questions.q: What do LT and the British Museum Algorithm have in common?
options: Both use selective generators that build trees of possible solutions, and a simple test checks each possibility
Both search forward
Both use no test
Both are random
optionExplain: Right.
LT goes backward.
Both use a test.
Neither is random.
questions.explain: The authors say there is no fundamental difference in these respects.
questions.teaches: The detachment-submethod uses the information that the proof being constructed contains X and that only a theorem of the form A implies X in the theorem list is of interest.

questions.q: A heuristic halves the alternatives at each of seven branch points. By about what factor is random search reduced?
optionExplain: That adds 2 seven times.
That is the number of steps.
That is 7 squared.
questions.explain: The reduction is 2^7. The card next gives the general rule.

questions.q: Halving the alternatives at each of k branch points reduces random search by a ratio of 2 to the power ____.
questions.explain: A reduction from m^k to (m/2)^k trials is a ratio of 2^k.

questions.q: A tree has 10 steps. Halving the alternatives at each step reduces the search by about what factor?
options: A little over a thousand
A million
optionExplain: That is 2 x 10.
That is 10 squared.
That is 2^20.

questions.q: True or false: A heuristic that keeps only one third of the alternatives at each step reduces random search by more than one that keeps half.
questions.explain: Keeping fewer alternatives gives a larger reduction (3^k against 2^k); this extends the authors' calculation.

questions.q: A tree has 6 alternatives at each of 3 branch points and one correct path. A heuristic halves the alternatives at each point. About how many trials does random search now need?
optionExplain: That is 6^3, the unreduced count.
That is 6 x 3, adding instead of multiplying.
That is 3^2, using the wrong exponent.
questions.explain: (m/2)^k = 3^3 = 27, a reduction by 2^3 = 8 from 216. Halving the alternatives gives the search one bit of information per step.
questions.teaches: The information provided by a heuristic that halves the alternatives at each branch point is one bit per step.

questions.q: Which grows faster with proof depth n: LT's backward tree or a working-forward algorithm's?
options: LT's tree
They grow at the same rate
Neither grows
The working-forward tree
optionExplain: LT's grows more slowly.
The exponent differs.
Both grow.
Right.
questions.explain: The forward algorithm pairs theorems, so it grows faster. The card next gives the formulas.

questions.q: LT's tree grows as (aT) raised to the power ____.
questions.explain: The number of branches of length n or less is of the order (aT)^n.

questions.q: With a = 0.3 and T = 6, about how many branches does LT's tree have at depth 4?
options: About 4
About 10
About 2
About 1,300
optionExplain: That is just n.
Right: aT = 1.8 and 1.8^4 is about 10.5.
That is the depth 1 value.
That is far too large.

questions.q: True or false: If a doubled, the base aT of LT's tree would double, so each extra step would multiply the tree by twice as much.
questions.explain: Each round multiplies by aT, so doubling a doubles the factor per step.

questions.q: Why does the working-forward algorithm grow faster than LT?
options: Its operators take pairs of known theorems, so the number of new expressions per round grows with the square of the list
It uses fewer theorems
It is slower on each step only
It has no operators
optionExplain: Right.
It uses the same list.
The difference is in growth, not cost per step.
It has operators.
questions.explain: A pair of members of T is needed for each operator, giving aT^2 new members.
questions.teaches: In the working-forward algorithm the operators take a pair of members of T and attempt to construct a new expression to add to T, so the number of new members after one round is of the order aT^2.

questions.q: What are the two sources of selectivity in these generators?
options: Speed and memory
Randomness and luck
Number of theorems and number of axioms
Generating only admissible sequences, and using information from partial sequences already generated
optionExplain: These are costs, not selectivity.
Selectivity is not luck.
These are inputs, not sources.
Right.
questions.explain: Admissibility and information use. The card next explains.

questions.q: Generators are more or less selective as they use more or less of the ____ extracted from partial sequences.
questions.explain: Selectivity depends on how much information from partial sequences is used.

questions.q: A GPS device offers only roads, and picks each next turn using how far the destination still is. Which sources of selectivity does it use?
options: Neither
Random turns
Admissible paths (roads only) and information from the partial route so far
Only the destination name
optionExplain: It uses both.
Turns are chosen, not random.
Right.
More than the name is used.
questions.explain: Roads-only is admissibility; distance remaining is information from the partial route.

questions.q: True or false: Even apparently blind trial-and-error generators have a great deal of built-in selectivity.
questions.explain: The authors say it is hard to exaggerate the amount of selectivity exercised even by such generators.

questions.q: What do the authors say small differences between heuristics can do in such immense problem spaces?
options: Make no real difference
Change only the speed of the machine
Change the goal of the search
Make very large differences in selectivity and so in problem solving efficacy
optionExplain: The authors say the opposite.
The effect is on selectivity, not on machine speed.
The goal is not affected by heuristics.
Right: immense spaces magnify small differences.
questions.explain: Because the spaces are so large, apparently small differences between heuristics may make very large differences in their selectivity.
questions.teaches: Apparently small differences between heuristics may make very large differences in their selectivity, and hence in their problem solving efficacy.

questions.q: Using only substitution and replacement, how does the British Museum Algorithm compare with LT on simple theorems?
options: It takes from about five to over a hundred times as long
It takes about the same time
It is faster, since it is exhaustive
It cannot prove them at all
optionExplain: Right: the authors give factors from five to a hundred and upwards.
The authors report large factors, so equal time is wrong.
Being exhaustive makes it slower, not faster, as the factors show.
It can prove them, only much more slowly.
questions.explain: The factors run from five to a hundred or more. The card next gives the example.
questions.rule: LT is faster by large factors.

questions.q: Theorem 2.02 would be the ____th theorem generated by the British Museum Algorithm.
questions.explain: The authors say it would be the seventy-ninth theorem generated.

questions.q: LT needs about 10 seconds for Theorem 2.02 and the British Museum Algorithm about 158 seconds. About what is the ratio?
options: About 5 to 1
About 100 to 1
About 2 to 1
About 16 to 1
optionExplain: Five is the smallest factor in the range, not this ratio.
A hundred is the largest factor quoted, not this one.
That underestimates the gap by far.
Right: 158 / 10 is close to 16.
questions.explain: Dividing 158 seconds by 10 seconds gives about 16.

questions.q: True or false: In the 2.02 comparison, the difference arises mainly because LT uses detachment and chaining.
questions.explain: The comparison is for substitution alone; the difference comes from how the matching process finds the substitutions.
questions.rule: The gap here is due to matching.

questions.q: In the tree from Axiom 1.3, how is Theorem 2.02 reached?
options: By detaching a second theorem
