By substituting not-Q for Q to reach node (5), then replacing the connective to reach node (9)
By chaining two implications
By copying the axiom unchanged
optionExplain: No detachment is involved.
Right.
No chaining is involved.
The axiom itself is not 2.02.
questions.explain: The authors trace 2.02 as the ninth theorem derived from Axiom 1.3, by one substitution and one replacement.
questions.rule: Trace the steps in the tree.
questions.teaches: The ninth theorem generated from Axiom 1.3 is the seventy-ninth generated from the five axioms considered together.

questions.q: When matching meets a variable on one side and a constant on the other, what does it do?
options: Gives up at once
Substitutes the constant for the variable throughout the expression
Replaces the constant by a new variable
Tries every possible constant
optionExplain: Giving up is only for differences that cannot be removed.
Right: substitution removes the difference, as with P for A.
That would move away from the target.
That is the search the matching process avoids.
questions.explain: A variable can be replaced by the constant throughout. The card next walks through the full example.
questions.rule: Fix a difference by the matching substitution.

questions.q: Put the matching steps for 1.3 against 2.02 in order.
items: Main connectives found identical
Substitute P for A throughout
Replace B by not-B, then or by implies
Substitute Q for B
Far-right terms found identical
questions.explain: The matching works from the main connective inward, one difference at a time.
questions.rule: Left to right, difference by difference.

questions.q: Matching expression X = A implies (B or A) with target Y = P implies (B or P). What is the one change needed?
options: Replace or by implies
Substitute B for P
No change; they already match
Substitute P for A throughout X
optionExplain: The connectives already agree.
That goes the wrong way and would not fix A.
The A and P differ, so a change is needed.
Right: after replacing A with P, the two expressions are identical.
questions.explain: Only the first term differs, so one substitution is enough.
questions.rule: Fix each difference where it occurs.

questions.q: True or false: In the 1.3 to 2.02 example, matching examines the whole set of eight expressions in the tree before choosing.
questions.explain: It followed the single branch (1), (5), (9) and looked at two expressions instead of eight.
questions.rule: Matching goes directly along one branch.

questions.q: Why does the authors' count of two expressions instead of eight understate the saving?
options: Matching handles a single pair of elements at a time instead of whole expressions
Matching skips the first expression
Matching is run on a faster machine
The count of eight was wrong
optionExplain: Right: the comparison is of individual symbols.
It does not skip.
Speed is not the reason.
The text does not say so.
questions.explain: The authors note the saving is even greater since the matching procedure does not deal with whole expressions but with single pairs of elements.
questions.rule: Count work in the unit actually compared.
questions.teaches: The matching process required replacing B by not-B first because, by the definition of implies, a not-sign must stand before the variable ahead of the or before the connective can be changed.

questions.q: Which two features give the matching process its efficiency?
options: Searching all substitutions, then choosing the best
Using a faster machine and a bigger memory
Copying correct substitutions from the desired expression, and working component by component with feedback
Choosing substitutions at random but quickly
optionExplain: That is the exhaustive search matching avoids.
Hardware is not the source named.
Right: copying and componentwise feedback.
Random choice would not be efficient.
questions.explain: Copying and feedback. The card next relates each to earlier examples.

questions.q: Match each feature of matching to the earlier example it resembles.
pairs: Copying substitutions from the desired expression
Solving one dial at a time
questions.explain: Copying resembles the algebra algorithm; componentwise feedback and factorization resemble the safe.

questions.q: A tailor altering a jacket to match a pattern checks one seam at a time and fixes each before moving on. Which feature of matching is this?
options: Copying the answer from the pattern
Generate-and-test
A stop rule
Componentwise processing with feedback that guides the next step
optionExplain: Copying would mean reading each fix off the pattern.
There is no blind generation.
Nothing is pruned by a rule.
Right: one component at a time with feedback.
questions.explain: Fixing one seam at a time is componentwise factorization.

questions.q: True or false: Matching resembles the algebra algorithm in copying substitutions from the desired expression, and the clicking safe in giving feedback at each component.
questions.explain: The authors tie the two sources of efficiency to the two earlier devices: copying to algebra, componentwise feedback to the safe.

questions.q: When the correct substitution cannot be read off immediately, what does matching still avoid?
options: Any use of feedback
Substitution altogether
A search through the whole space of possible substitutions for various combinations of variables
The need for a target
optionExplain: Feedback is what it uses.
Substitution is its work.
Right.
A target is essential.
questions.explain: Componentwise feedback keeps the search on the correct path even when copying fails.
questions.teaches: The componentwise character of matching is a form of factorization: feedback after each step avoids a search through the whole space of substitutions for combinations of variables.

questions.q: How does LT treat an axiom that cannot be matched to the target?
options: It abandons it for the next axiom after a short test
It tries every possible substitution first
It reports that the theorem is false
It rewrites the axiom
optionExplain: Right: failure is found early and the next axiom is tried.
That would waste effort; matching fails fast.
A failed match says nothing about truth.
Axioms are not altered.
questions.explain: Matching abandons impossible fits. The card next gives the 1.2 example.

questions.q: The substitution-submethod begins by matching the target with each ____ in turn.
questions.explain: In fact the submethod tries each axiom in turn and abandons it for the next if matching proves impossible.
questions.rule: It tries each axiom in turn.

questions.q: A shopper compares a dress to a photo and sees at once that the colour cannot be altered to match. What does this resemble?
options: Abandoning an axiom as soon as matching shows a difference substitution cannot remove
Copying a substitution from the target
Recognition from memory
Backing up in a search
optionExplain: Right.
Nothing is copied.
No stored answer is evoked.
Backing up concerns remembered elements.
questions.explain: A difference that cannot be removed ends the attempt early.
questions.rule: Reject early on an impossible difference.

questions.q: True or false: LT chooses the right axiom directly, without matching the target against the others.
questions.explain: The authors say that in actual fact the submethod begins by matching with each axiom in turn, abandoning it for the next one if matching proves impossible.
questions.rule: It tries each axiom in turn.

questions.q: Against Axiom 1.2, what does the matching process find almost immediately in the 2.02 example?
options: That 1.2 is false
That (R or P) cannot be made into P by substitution
That 1.2 equals 2.02
That P can be replaced by R
optionExplain: Axioms are true; the match simply fails.
Right: the mismatch is found, so 1.2 is eliminated.
They differ, which is why 1.2 is dropped.
Replacing P by R would not remove the mismatch.
questions.explain: Matching finds on the second test that (R or P) cannot become P by substitution, so Axiom 1.2 is eliminated.
questions.rule: Fail fast on an impossible difference.
questions.teaches: Matching against Axiom 1.2 finds almost immediately, on the second test, that (R or P) cannot be made into P by substitution, and so eliminates the axiom.

questions.q: How many of LT's 38 proofs were achieved by the substitution-submethod alone?
options: All 38
Seventeen
Two
Nineteen
optionExplain: Other submethods were needed for the rest.
Right: almost half.
That is the number of three-step proofs, not substitution-only proofs.
Nineteen is the number of two-step proofs.
questions.explain: Seventeen, almost half. The card next gives the rates.

questions.q: On subproblems, substitution succeeded in about ____ percent of attempts.
questions.explain: 21 successes in 338 attempts is 6.2 percent.

questions.q: Substitution is tried on 160 new subproblems at the observed rate of one in sixteen. About how many successes?
options: About 53
About 2
About 100
About 10
optionExplain: That uses a one in three rate.
That is far too low.
That would be more than half.
questions.explain: 160 divided by 16 is 10.

questions.q: True or false: The authors found that the substitution-submethod does about as well on subproblems as on original problems.
questions.explain: About one in three originals but only one in sixteen subproblems.
questions.rule: Subproblems are much harder to close by substitution.

questions.q: To what do the authors attribute the lower success on subproblems?
options: Faulty programming
The kind of selectivity implicit in the order of theorems in Principia
Slow machine speed
A random effect
optionExplain: No fault is claimed.
Right.
Speed does not change success rates.
They give an explanation.
questions.explain: They think the order in which Principia lists theorems makes original problems close to the earlier ones, favouring direct substitution.
questions.rule: A source list's order can favour original problems.
questions.teaches: The theorems proved by substitution alone looked like corollaries of the theorems they were derived from and occurred close to them in the chapter.

questions.q: Of LT's 38 proofs of the first 52 theorems, how many were two-step proofs?
options: Nineteen
Seventeen
Two
Thirty-eight
optionExplain: Right: twelve by detachment, seven by forward chaining.
Seventeen were one-step proofs.
Two were three-step proofs.
That is all the proofs.
questions.explain: Nineteen. The card next gives the split.

questions.q: Match each submethod to its average number of new subproblems per application.
questions.explain: Detachment 3, forward chaining 2.7, backward chaining 2.2.

questions.q: Of the nineteen two-step proofs, seven used chaining forward. How many used detachment?
options: Seven
Nineteen
Seventeen
Twelve
optionExplain: Seven is the forward chaining count.
That is the whole set.
That is the number of one-step proofs.
questions.explain: Detachment plus substitution made twelve; chaining forward plus substitution made seven.

questions.q: True or false: When these submethods work on subproblems rather than the original problem, they generate fewer subproblems per application.
questions.explain: On the original problem 8 to 9 subproblems were generated; on subproblems only 2 or 3.

questions.q: Why are there no two-step proofs by backward chaining?
options: Because backward chaining is not an operator
Because it is too slow
For two-step proofs, a proof by backward chaining implies a proof by forward chaining
Because it needs three steps
optionExplain: It is one of the three operators.
The reason is logical, not speed.
Right.
The text does not say that.
questions.explain: For two-step proofs only, whenever backward chaining works, forward chaining also works, so the forward proof is the one found.
questions.rule: For two steps, forward covers backward.
questions.teaches: There are no two-step proofs by backward chaining since, for two-step proofs only, if a proof by backward chaining exists, one by forward chaining also exists.

questions.q: How does LT's executive explore the tree of subproblems?
options: In depth: following one chain as far as it goes
At random
In breadth: one-step proofs first, then two-step, and so on
From the longest proof to the shortest
optionExplain: Depth-first is a different fixed strategy.
The order is systematic.
Right.
Short proofs come first.
questions.explain: Breadth-first. The card next gives examples.

questions.q: On Theorem 2.31, LT considered all ____ subproblems on untried-problems and then reported that it could think of nothing more to do.
questions.explain: There were six subproblems on untried-problems in that case.

questions.q: A detective checks all leads one step from the crime scene before checking leads two steps away. Which search order is this?
options: Breadth-first
Depth-first
Back-up
Random
optionExplain: Right.
Depth-first follows one chain at a time.
Back-up returns to remembered elements.
The order is systematic.
questions.explain: Exploring all one-step possibilities before two-step is breadth-first.

questions.q: True or false: For failures, the most common reason LT stops is that it has run out of things to try.
questions.explain: The authors say termination by time or space limits is the most common result; running out of things to do is rare.

questions.q: Why did the proof of 2.45 not require selecting a subproblem from the list?
options: No subproblem was created
The list was empty
Substitution failed
The one subproblem created was proved at once by the substitution-submethod
optionExplain: One was created.
The list was not consulted.
Substitution succeeded.
Right.
questions.explain: A subproblem that is solved at creation never needs to be taken from the list.
questions.teaches: In none of the examples cited did LT terminate because of time or space limits, but this is the most common result in cases where LT does not find a proof.

questions.q: What is a stop rule in the authors' sense?
options: A command that halts the whole program
A heuristic that cuts off branches that appear unprovable or too complicated
A rule that forbids substitution
A rule that adds new axioms
optionExplain: A stop rule prunes branches, not the program.
Right.
Substitution is still used.
Axioms are not changed.
questions.explain: A stop rule weeds out branches. The card next gives the numbers.

questions.q: The two stop rules cut the search by a factor of 24/9, or about ____.
questions.explain: 24/9 is 2.7; net of the extra testing the saving was 2.3.

questions.q: A search tree has ten branches per node and paths of length 3. How much more effort do false branches add if each false branch also branches tenfold?
options: A factor of 30
A factor of about 1,000
A factor of 10
A factor of 3
optionExplain: That is 10 x 3.
Right: 10^3.
That is only one level.
That is the depth.
questions.explain: Effort multiplies by 10 at each level, so 10^3 at depth 3.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say neither stop rule is foolproof, and both can eliminate some paths to solutions.
questions.explain: Both can eliminate paths that lead to solutions, even all of them.

questions.q: Why is the net saving of 2.3 smaller than the gross saving of 2.7?
options: The stop rules fail on half the problems
The theorem list was larger
The machine was slower
The additional testing required by the stop rules has its own cost
optionExplain: That is not stated.
The list was smaller in this run.
The same machine was used.
Right.
questions.explain: The authors say that when the cost of the additional testing is taken into account the saving was 2.3.
questions.rule: Count the cost of the screening.
questions.teaches: Even if the false branches at a node cannot be avoided in generation, almost all the consequent inefficiency can be avoided if a test discriminates false branches from the correct one after generation, as the click does in the safe.

questions.q: A submethod generates about how many subproblems per theorem it examines?
options: About one per seven theorems
About seven per theorem
About one per theorem
About one per hundred
optionExplain: Right.
That is the reverse ratio.
That would be far too many.
That is too few.
questions.explain: About one per seven. The card next gives the consequences.

questions.q: The broad proof tree of 2.17 came from a list of twenty theorems, the deep tree of 2.27 from a list of ____.
questions.explain: Fewer theorems gave fewer subproblems at each step.

questions.q: A submethod examines 56 theorems. About how many subproblems would it generate at one-per-seven?
options: About 56
About 392
About 8
About 2
optionExplain: That is the number of theorems.
That multiplies instead of dividing.
That is too few.
questions.explain: Divide the theorems examined by seven.

questions.q: True or false: In the Theorem 2.48 comparison, the proof from the shorter theorem list took about a third of the time of the proof from the longer list.
questions.explain: Three steps from the short list took about one-third the time of the two-step proof from the long list.

questions.q: For Theorem 2.48 the authors expected the shorter theorem list to make the proof harder. What happened?
options: The shorter list gave no proof
The shorter list gave a three-step proof in about one third of the time of the longer list's two-step proof
The shorter list gave a longer time
Both lists gave the same proof
optionExplain: A proof was found.
Right: they were wrong; the irrelevant theorems cost effort.
The time was shorter, not longer.
The proofs differed in length.
questions.explain: The authors had conjectured the shorter list would need a longer chain and so be harder. They were wrong: it took three steps but only about one third of the time.
questions.rule: Test conjectures; extra information can cost.
questions.teaches: The authors had conjectured the proof would be more difficult under the shorter theorem list because a longer proof chain would have to be built; they were wrong.

questions.q: What does an evaluation function do in this context?
options: Proves the theorem
Estimates how likely each expression is to lie on a short path to a proof
Counts the axioms
Orders the axioms by length
optionExplain: It does not prove anything.
Right.
It values expressions, not axioms.
It values subproblems.
questions.explain: It estimates promise. The card next gives the details.

questions.q: Taking subproblems from the list in order of an evaluation function is called the ____-search heuristic.
questions.explain: The authors call it the scan-search heuristic.

questions.q: A chess engine ranks candidate lines by how good they look and expands the best-looking one next. Which heuristic is this?
options: Breadth-first search
Depth-first search only
Scan-search, selecting by evaluation function
Random search
optionExplain: Breadth-first ignores values.
Depth-first uses recency.
Right.
Not random.
questions.explain: Selecting the most promising member of a list by value is scan-search.

questions.q: True or false: The simplicity measure used in one version of LT gave a large average improvement in performance.
questions.explain: It gave only a small average improvement, although it changed the ranking of proofs by difficulty.
questions.rule: A weak evaluation function helped little.

questions.q: What happened to the evaluation-function idea after LT?
options: It was used with more sophisticated evaluation functions in later programs, to powerful effect
It was abandoned as useless
It was replaced by random selection
It was shown to be wrong
optionExplain: Right.
The authors say it has been used to powerful effect.
No such shift is stated.
No such finding is stated.
questions.explain: The authors say the idea has been used in subsequent programs with more sophisticated evaluation functions.
questions.rule: A weak first try may still be a good idea.
questions.teaches: The primitive simplicity-based evaluation function changed considerably the ranking of proofs by difficulty even though the average improvement was small.

questions.q: What is the main idea of LT's similarity test?
options: Screen out theorems that are unlikely to match by comparing simple descriptions
Prove theorems by comparing their length
Choose the shortest theorem
Remove variables from theorems
optionExplain: Right.
It does not prove theorems.
It screens, not selects the shortest.
Variables are counted, not removed.
questions.explain: It screens by description. The card next defines similarity.

questions.q: Which of these does the similarity test compare for the left and right sides? Select all that apply.
options: Maximum number of levels from the main connective to any variable
Number of distinct variables
Number of variable places
The names of the variables
The truth value
optionExplain: Right: the first criterion.
Right: the second criterion.
Right: the third criterion.
Names are not compared; R and M versus P and Q need not match.
Truth values are not used.
questions.explain: The three criteria are depth, number of distinct variables and number of variable places.

questions.q: Compare P implies (Q or P) with R implies (M implies R). Are they similar?
options: No: the variable names differ
No: the connectives differ
Yes: left sides have one variable at one level, right sides two distinct variables at two levels and two places
Only if P equals R
optionExplain: Names are not part of the description.
The inner connectives are not compared.
Right: the descriptions agree on both sides.
Identity of names is not required.
questions.explain: The authors say (2) and (3) are similar by the definition.

questions.q: True or false: (P or Q) implies (Q or P) is similar to P implies (Q or P).
questions.explain: The authors say (1) is not similar to (2) or (3): the left sides differ in the number of variables and levels.

questions.q: Why does the authors call the similarity test an abstraction?
options: It removes the expressions from memory
It matches certain descriptive characteristics instead of the detail of the expressions, so less processing is needed
It generates new expressions
It proves the expressions equal
optionExplain: It does not remove anything.
Right.
It does not generate.
Matching decides equality.
questions.explain: Descriptions need less processing than whole expressions, which makes the abstraction potentially useful.
questions.teaches: LT's overall chances of a successful match are 0.3 percent for substitution, 13.4 percent for detachment, 13.8 percent for forward chaining and 9.4 percent for backward chaining.

questions.q: In substitution, the similarity test changes the number of matchings attempted by about what factor?
options: A twofold reduction
No change
A tenfold increase
A tenfold reduction
optionExplain: It is much larger.
There is a big change.
It reduces attempts.
Right.
questions.explain: A factor of ten. The card next gives the numbers.

questions.q: Of the 11,298 theorems considered in substitution, ____ passed the similarity test.
questions.explain: Table 4.3 gives 993 passing.

questions.q: In detachment, 406 of 1,591 theorems passed. About what percent is that?
options: About 5 percent
About 25 percent
About 52 percent
About 8 percent
optionExplain: That is closer to the substitution pass rate.
Right: 406 / 1,591 is 25.5 percent.
That is the matched-of-similar rate.
That is substitution's pass rate (8.8).
questions.explain: The table gives 25.5 percent.

questions.q: True or false: Given that a theorem passes the similarity test for forward chaining, the chance it then matches is higher than the unscreened chance.
questions.explain: 60.0 percent of those passing matched, against about 13.8 percent overall.

questions.q: Why does Table 4.3 show only a gross gain from the similarity test?
options: It uses a different machine
It counts only successes
It leaves out substitution
The test is only a heuristic that may let through or reject wrongly, and it is not costless
optionExplain: The table uses the same runs.
It counts all theorems considered.
Substitution is included in the table.
Right: errors and cost both erode the gross gain.
questions.explain: The authors give two reasons the entire gross gain may not be realized: the test is only a heuristic with no guarantee of passing only matching expressions or of rejecting only failing ones, and it has a cost of its own.
questions.teaches: The gross gain of the similarity test may not be fully realized for two reasons: the test is only a heuristic with no guarantee, and it is not costless.

questions.q: What does a screening heuristic risk, besides passing candidates that fail?
options: Proving a false theorem
Using too little memory
Making the goal unreachable by definition
Rejecting a candidate that would have succeeded
optionExplain: Proofs remain valid.
Memory is not the issue.
The goal is unchanged.
Right: a type II error.
questions.explain: It may reject good candidates. The card next gives the case.

questions.q: The similarity test can commit an error corresponding to a type ____ statistical error.
questions.explain: Rejecting what would have matched corresponds to a type II error.

questions.q: Theorem 2.07 and Axiom 1.3 are called dissimilar because...
options: 2.07 is longer
1.3 is false
2.07 has one distinct variable and 1.3 has two
They use different connectives
optionExplain: Length is not compared.
Axioms are true.
Right.
Both use implies and or.
questions.explain: The test demands equal numbers of distinct variables.

questions.q: True or false: Using the weaker test that compares only the number of variable places would make LT reject 2.07 as dissimilar to Axiom 1.3.
questions.explain: The weaker test does not commit that error, and 2.07 is then proved by substitution.
questions.rule: A weaker test avoids this error.

questions.q: What explains the small change in performance under the weaker test?
options: It rejected most theorems
It was run on a faster machine
The descriptive measures are highly correlated
It was never used
optionExplain: It admitted only 10 percent more.
Speed was not the reason.
Right.
It was tested on ten problems.
questions.explain: The authors say there is a high correlation among the descriptive measures.
questions.teaches: On a sample of ten problems the weaker test admitted only about 10 percent more similar theorems and about 10 percent more subproblems.

questions.section: Processing Effort in the Logic Theorist
questions.q: How do the authors measure processing effort in LT?
options: By the total number of elementary information processes executed
By wall-clock time on any machine
By the number of theorems proved
By the length of the program
optionExplain: Right: the eip count is machine-independent.
Clock time depends on the machine.
That is a performance measure, not an effort one.
Program length is not effort.
questions.explain: They count eips. The card next says why.

questions.section: Processing Effort in the Logic Theorist
questions.q: The average time per eip on JOHNNIAC is about ____ milliseconds.
questions.explain: About 30 milliseconds, quite constant.

questions.section: Processing Effort in the Logic Theorist
questions.q: A heuristic saves 2,000 eips of search but costs 2,500 eips to run. Per the authors' reasoning, what should be concluded?
options: It is a gain, since it saves search
The cost does not matter
It is neutral
It is a net loss, since costs must be balanced against performance gains
optionExplain: That ignores the cost.
The authors say costs must always be balanced.
It loses 500 eips.
Right: 2,500 is more than 2,000.
questions.explain: A heuristic is worthwhile only if its saving exceeds its cost.

questions.section: Processing Effort in the Logic Theorist
questions.q: True or false: An eip count would give about the same ranking of programs on a faster computer.
questions.explain: Because the count is of elementary processes and not of time, it does not depend on the machine (our reading).

questions.section: Processing Effort in the Logic Theorist
questions.q: Why is the total count of elementary processes an adequate index of effort even though the processes differ in kind?
options: Their relative frequencies are reasonably constant
All elementary processes take identical time in every program
Memory use is included in the count
Effort does not matter for LT
optionExplain: Right: with steady proportions of each kind, the total tracks the effort.
Their times are only reasonably constant on average, not identical.
Memory space is a cost the authors do not count.
Effort is the quantity being measured.
questions.explain: Because the relative frequencies of the different eips are reasonably constant, the total number of eips is an adequate index.
questions.rule: A mix that stays steady lets a total stand for effort.
questions.teaches: Because the relative frequencies of the different elementary processes are reasonably constant, the total number of eips is an adequate index of effort.

questions.section: Processing Effort in the Logic Theorist
questions.q: What best predicts the effort needed for LT to prove a theorem?
options: The length of the theorem statement
The number of theorems examined by the submethods
The age of the program
The number of axioms alone
optionExplain: Statement length is not the predictor.
Right.
Irrelevant.
Axioms are part of the list but not the predictor.
questions.explain: Effort follows theorems examined. The card next gives the weights.

questions.section: Processing Effort in the Logic Theorist
questions.q: Match each submethod to its eips per theorem considered.
questions.explain: Chaining is twice and detachment three times the substitution figure.

questions.section: Processing Effort in the Logic Theorist
questions.q: LT considers 20 theorems with detachment and 10 with substitution. Using 135 and 45 eips per theorem, what total effort is predicted?
options: 1,050 eips
2,250 eips
450 eips
3,150 eips
optionExplain: That uses 45 for everything.
That misses the substitution term.
That counts only the substitution work.
questions.explain: Detachment contributes 2,700 eips and substitution 450.

questions.section: Processing Effort in the Logic Theorist
questions.q: True or false: The authors say the estimates in Table 4.4 are generally accurate within a few percent, except for one theorem.
questions.explain: The estimates are accurate within a few percent except for Theorem 2.06, for which it is too low.
questions.rule: A good fit with one exception.

questions.section: Processing Effort in the Logic Theorist
questions.q: Under what conditions does Table 4.4 compare actual and predicted effort?
options: With no similarity test and including all theorems
With only the axioms stored
With the full similarity test included, and excluding theorems proved by substitution
With the weaker similarity test only
optionExplain: The table includes the full similarity test.
The theorem list is not restricted that way.
Right: that is how the authors describe the comparison.
The weaker test is discussed separately.
questions.explain: The authors compare actual and predicted efforts with the full similarity test included and excluding theorems proved by substitution.
questions.teaches: Actual and predicted efforts in Table 4.4 are compared with the full similarity test included and excluding theorems proved by substitution.

questions.section: Processing Effort in the Logic Theorist
questions.q: Why does LT switch from stored to recomputed descriptions as its theorem list grows?
options: Recomputing is always cheaper
The descriptions become wrong
Storing the descriptions takes too much space
The similarity test is dropped
optionExplain: Recomputing costs more eips.
They remain right.
Right.
The test continues.
questions.explain: Space becomes prohibitive. The card next gives the costs.

questions.section: Processing Effort in the Logic Theorist
questions.q: With recomputed descriptions, substitution costs about ____ eips per theorem.
questions.explain: About 70 for substitution, 210 for detachment and 140 for chaining.

questions.section: Processing Effort in the Logic Theorist
questions.q: Detachment costs 135 eips per theorem with stored descriptions and 210 with recomputed ones. By how many eips per theorem does recomputation add?
optionExplain: That is the total recomputed cost.
That is the stored cost.
That adds instead of subtracting.
questions.explain: Subtract the stored cost from the recomputed cost.

questions.section: Processing Effort in the Logic Theorist
questions.q: True or false: With recomputed descriptions, effort for a proof is no longer roughly proportional to theorems considered.
questions.explain: Effort is still roughly proportional, with a larger constant per theorem.

questions.section: Processing Effort in the Logic Theorist
questions.q: How do the authors say a good heuristic reduces effort, given that effort follows the theorems considered?
options: By making each elementary process cheaper
By proving theorems twice
By skipping the executive
By securing consideration of the right theorems early, reducing the expected number considered before a proof is found
optionExplain: The cost of an eip is fixed by the machine.
Doubling work is not a saving.
The executive remains in place.
Right: a smaller count of theorems considered means less effort.
questions.explain: In first approximation the number of theorems considered is an effort measure for evaluating a heuristic, so a good heuristic reduces the expected number considered.
questions.teaches: A good heuristic, by securing the consideration of the right theorems early in the proof, reduces the expected number of theorems considered before a proof is found.

questions.section: Processing Effort in the Logic Theorist
questions.q: With descriptions recomputed every time, is the full similarity test cheaper or dearer than no test?
options: Cheaper, by about 60 percent
The same
Dearer, by about 15 percent
Cheaper, by about 10 percent
optionExplain: The 10 to 60 percent saving was for stored descriptions.
There was a difference.
Right.
That too is a stored-description saving.
questions.explain: It costs more. The card next gives examples.

questions.section: Processing Effort in the Logic Theorist
questions.q: With stored descriptions, the full similarity test saved between 10 and ____ percent of the effort.
questions.explain: The saving ranged from 10 percent to 60 percent, for example 3534/5206 for Theorem 2.08.

questions.section: Processing Effort in the Logic Theorist
questions.q: For Theorem 2.08 the full test needed 3534 eips and no test needed 5206. About what share of effort did the test save?
options: About 32 percent
About 68 percent
About 15 percent
About 5 percent
optionExplain: That is the ratio 3534/5206, the remaining effort.
That is the recomputed penalty, not this saving.
Too small.
questions.explain: The saving is 1,672 out of 5,206, about 32 percent.

questions.section: Processing Effort in the Logic Theorist
questions.q: True or false: With precomputed descriptions, the saving from the full similarity test ranged from 10 to 60 percent.
questions.explain: The authors give that range, with 3534/5206 for 2.08 as an example.

questions.section: Processing Effort in the Logic Theorist
questions.q: With recomputed descriptions, how does the weaker test (variable places only) compare with the full test on Theorem 2.45?
options: It needs more eips than the full test
It needs fewer eips than the full test, and also fewer than no test at all
It needs the same as the full test
It cannot prove the theorem
optionExplain: The weaker test costs less, not more.
Right: 18,035 against 26,739 and 22,914.
The figures differ.
It does prove 2.45.
questions.explain: For Theorem 2.45 the modified test needs 18,035 eips, against 26,739 for the full test and 22,914 for no test.
questions.rule: A cheaper screen can pay when a dearer one does not.
questions.teaches: With recomputed descriptions, the modified similarity test proves Theorem 2.45 in 18,035 eips, against 26,739 for the full test and 22,914 for no test.

questions.section: Processing Effort in the Logic Theorist
questions.q: Why is the similarity test worth little in net effort?
options: Matching is very expensive on failures
The test is slow
Matching already fails cheaply on the expressions the test rejects
The test is inaccurate
optionExplain: Failures are cheap.
Speed is not the issue.
Right.
Accuracy is a separate matter.
questions.explain: Failures are cheap anyway. The card next gives the reasoning.
questions.rule: Cheap failure limits the screen's value.

questions.section: Processing Effort in the Logic Theorist
questions.q: Matching has a testing part and a part that carries out ____ and replacements.
questions.explain: The second part carries out the substitutions and replacements.

questions.section: Processing Effort in the Logic Theorist
questions.q: A security guard checks bags at the door to bar items a cashier would reject in two seconds anyway. How much does the guard save?
options: A lot
Little, as the later check already rejects them cheaply
Everything
Nothing, as the guard works for free
optionExplain: The cashier would have rejected them at once.
Right.
Rejects are cheap anyway.
The guard has a cost.
questions.explain: A screen is worthwhile only if the later step is costly on what it rejects.
questions.rule: Screen only what is costly to reject later.

questions.section: Processing Effort in the Logic Theorist
questions.q: True or false: The most expensive part of matching is spent on expressions that do not match.
questions.explain: The substituting and replacing effort is the major expense when matching works; most of it is saved when matching fails.
questions.rule: Success is where the cost lies.

questions.section: Processing Effort in the Logic Theorist
questions.q: Which measure shows the similarity test's gross gain but hides its small net gain?
options: The count of eips
The number of theorems
The size of the theorem list
The performance figures of Table 4.3 on matchings attempted and their success rate
optionExplain: The eip count shows the small net gain.
That is not a gain measure.
That is not a gain measure.
Right.
questions.explain: The table counts matchings avoided and raised success rate, but not the cost of what was avoided.
questions.rule: Count avoided cost, not avoided attempts.
questions.teaches: The authors split matching into a testing part that locates differences and diagnoses corrective action, and a part that does the substituting and replacing, which is the major expense only when matching works.

questions.section: Processing Effort in the Logic Theorist
questions.q: What does the authors' plateau claim say about heuristic programs like LT?
options: More computing time alone always lifts the plateau
Good heuristics give big gains, but a plateau is reached that only quite different heuristics can pass
Heuristics cannot improve performance
A plateau never occurs
optionExplain: They say large expenditures are impractical.
Right.
They say heuristics give orders of magnitude.
They say it invariably occurs.
questions.explain: Gains then a plateau. The card next gives the evidence.

questions.section: Processing Effort in the Logic Theorist
questions.q: Almost all proofs LT found took less than ____ eips.
questions.explain: Figure 4.14 shows almost all under 30,000.

questions.section: Processing Effort in the Logic Theorist
questions.q: The longest proof cost 89,000 eips, about 250 times the shortest. About how many eips did the shortest cost?
options: About 360
About 22 million
About 89
About 1,000
optionExplain: Right: 89,000 / 250 is about 356.
That multiplies instead of dividing.
That is the longest proof's figure scaled by a thousand.
Substitution proofs took about 1,000, a different group.
questions.explain: Divide 89,000 by 250.

questions.section: Processing Effort in the Logic Theorist
questions.q: True or false: By the authors' estimate, getting LT to prove the 12 extra theorems it can in principle prove would need an effort limit of about a million eips.
questions.explain: They estimate the limit would have to extend to about a million.

questions.section: Processing Effort in the Logic Theorist
questions.q: A chess program improves 100-fold through a new evaluation heuristic and then stops improving. What do the authors say about reaching beyond such a plateau?
options: More computer time alone will do it
The program should be discarded
Major adjustments in the program are needed to extend its powers to essentially new classes of problems
Nothing can be done
optionExplain: Large expenditures of effort are logically possible but impractical.
The authors do not recommend discarding.
Right: new kinds of heuristics are needed.
They say new heuristics can lift the plateau.
questions.explain: The authors say that although LT could in principle solve others by large expenditures of effort, major adjustments are needed to extend its powers to new classes of problems.
questions.teaches: While it is logically possible for LT to solve more problems by large expenditures of effort, major adjustments are needed in the program to extend its powers to essentially new classes of problems.

questions.section: Processing Effort in the Logic Theorist
questions.q: How does effort grow as a proof gets longer?
options: Exactly in proportion to its length
Not at all
More than in proportion to its length
Less than in proportion
optionExplain: The authors say more than proportionately.
Length matters a lot.
Right.
It grows faster, not slower.
questions.explain: Effort grows faster than length. The card next gives the figures.

questions.section: Processing Effort in the Logic Theorist
questions.q: All one-step proofs need between 500 and ____ eips.
questions.explain: One-step proofs need 500 to 1500 eips.

questions.section: Processing Effort in the Logic Theorist
questions.q: A two-step proof costs 3,000 eips at the low end and 50,000 at the high end. About how many times larger is the top of that range than the bottom?
options: About 50 times
About 3 times
About 17 times
About 2 times
optionExplain: That divides by 1,000.
That is the ratio of 9,000 to 3,000.
Right: 50,000 / 3,000 is about 16.7.
Too small.
questions.explain: Divide the high end by the low end.

questions.section: Processing Effort in the Logic Theorist
questions.q: True or false: LT obtained many proofs longer than two steps.
questions.explain: LT obtained only six proofs longer than two steps; the difference in effort for longer proofs is the main theme.
questions.rule: Long proofs are rare for LT.

questions.section: Processing Effort in the Logic Theorist
questions.q: Why did Theorem 2.17 cost far more than the two-step proof of 2.45?
options: Many more subproblems were generated, since the problems were similar in effort per theorem considered
Each theorem considered cost much more effort
The machine was slower
The theorem was false
optionExplain: Right: the extra depth multiplied the subproblems.
Effort per theorem was roughly similar for the two problems.
The same machine was used.
2.17 is a theorem.
questions.explain: The authors compare the trees and find the problems similar in effort per theorem, so the difference in total effort is largely due to the number of subproblems generated.
questions.teaches: The problems 2.17 and 2.45 are roughly similar in effort per theorem considered, so the difference in total effort can be attributed largely to the difference in the number of subproblems generated.

questions.section: Processing Effort in the Logic Theorist
questions.q: About how deep a proof can LT's systematic executive search with practical computing power?
options: Ten steps
Any depth
One step only
Two to three steps in the usual case
optionExplain: Far deeper than practical.
Depth is limited.
It does two-step proofs.
Right.
questions.explain: Two to three steps. The card next gives the reason.

questions.section: Processing Effort in the Logic Theorist
questions.q: The number of subproblems to examine increases more or less ____ with the depth of the proof.
questions.explain: The authors support the hypothesis that it grows exponentially with depth.

questions.section: Processing Effort in the Logic Theorist
questions.q: A tree with about 250 subproblems per proof and 1,000 eips each would cost how many eips?
options: About 1,000
About 250,000
About 25,000
optionExplain: That is one subproblem's cost.
Right.
That divides by 10.
That multiplies by 10.

questions.section: Processing Effort in the Logic Theorist
questions.q: True or false: If the tree for 2.27 had branched as widely as those for 2.17 and 2.45, its four-step proof would have cost at least 250,000 eips.
questions.explain: The authors say about 250 subproblems and at least 250,000 eips.

questions.section: Processing Effort in the Logic Theorist
questions.q: What is the root of LT's difficulty with deep proofs, according to the authors?
options: A shortage of axioms
A systematic unselective procedure for generating subproblems and taking them in order of generation
A slow machine
A lack of detachment
optionExplain: Axioms are not the issue.
Right.
Speed does not change exponential growth.
Detachment is present.
questions.explain: The authors say the difficulty is the systematic, unselective principles in the executive.
questions.teaches: LT considers subproblems in order of generation so that a proof will not be missed through failure to consider a subproblem that has been generated.

questions.section: Processing Effort in the Logic Theorist
questions.q: Which of these is needed for experience to improve a problem solver, in the authors' account?
options: A larger memory only
A new representation every time
A teacher
A variable aspect of performance, gathered experience, and a way to use it
optionExplain: Size alone does not change behavior.
Representations are not required.
None is mentioned.
Right.
questions.explain: Three conditions. The card next lists them.

questions.section: Processing Effort in the Logic Theorist
questions.q: The simplest learning scheme makes the list ____ variable, adding each new theorem LT proves.
questions.explain: The list theorems becomes variable.

questions.section: Processing Effort in the Logic Theorist
questions.q: A student keeps a notebook of every identity she proves and consults it on later problems. Which scheme is this?
options: Making the stored list variable by adding new results
Valuable-theorem lists
A stop rule
A similarity test
optionExplain: Right.
That is a different scheme discussed next.
No pruning here.
No screening.
questions.explain: Adding each new result to the list is the simplest scheme.

questions.section: Processing Effort in the Logic Theorist
questions.q: True or false: With a suitable sequence of problems, LT with a growing theorem list could become capable of proving Theorem 2.13.
questions.explain: The authors say that with the right sequence it could become capable of proving 2.13.

questions.section: Processing Effort in the Logic Theorist
questions.q: Why does a backward-working program like LT need to pose problems for itself in order to gain new theorems automatically?
options: Working backward, none of the expressions it generates is known to be a theorem
Working backward, all expressions are theorems
Because forward programs cannot pose problems
Because it has no memory
optionExplain: Right: only a proved result can enter the stored list.
That describes working forward.
That is not the stated reason.
LT has a memory of theorems.
questions.explain: Working forward, every generated element is a theorem and a candidate for the stored list; working backward, none is known to be one.
questions.rule: Backward search yields goals, not facts.
questions.teaches: Working forward, all generated elements are theorems and so candidates for the stored list; working backward, none is known to be a theorem, so LT needs an active process of problem posing.

questions.section: Processing Effort in the Logic Theorist
questions.q: A solver tries first the methods that have worked before. What is the likely effect on a new type of problem?
options: It solves the new problem faster
No effect
It cannot solve it at all
It wastes time on the old methods before falling back on the full set
optionExplain: Old methods help only on similar problems.
There is a cost.
The backup list still works.
Right.
questions.explain: Old methods can hinder. The card next gives the experiment.

questions.section: Processing Effort in the Logic Theorist
questions.q: In Figure 4.15 the points of the scatter diagram fell on two straight ____.
questions.explain: The authors note the remarkable fact that the points form two straight lines.

questions.section: Processing Effort in the Logic Theorist
questions.q: A chef starts each time with the dishes that sold best last season. This season's menu is entirely new in style. What does the LT result predict?
options: She will finish faster than before
Starting with last season's best sellers will cost time before she falls back on the wider repertoire
No change in time
She will need no repertoire
optionExplain: That is for similar tasks.
Right.
There is a cost.
The fallback is needed.
questions.explain: Past experience helps on similar tasks and hinders on novel ones.

questions.section: Processing Effort in the Logic Theorist
questions.q: Which are true of the experiment? Select all that apply.
options: Points on the upper line took almost twice as long in the test run
Points on the lower line took less than half as long in the test run
Each line held about half the points
All points fell on one line
The test run was always faster
optionExplain: Right: valuable lists misled on new-type problems.
Right: valuable lists helped on similar problems.
Right: the points split about evenly.
There were two lines.
The upper line shows it was slower for half of the problems.
questions.explain: Two straight lines, one slower and one faster.

questions.section: Processing Effort in the Logic Theorist
questions.q: What two general lessons about learning do the authors draw from LT's examples?
options: Learning is unnecessary and rarely useful
Learning requires a teacher and a large memory
Experience is one more source of information to exploit, and to affect performance it must find a variable aspect of the program
Learning always improves performance
optionExplain: They say experience is information.
Neither is stated.
Right.
The experiment shows it can hinder.
questions.explain: The authors say they will deal hardly at all with learning in the book but draw these two lessons.
questions.teaches: The authors say the approach to learning shown here, with the performing program laid out, shows that experience is one more source of information and that it must find a variable aspect of the program's structure to specify.

questions.q: According to the authors' conclusion, what usually makes a problem difficult?
options: The size of the set of possibilities
The age of the problem
The number of solvers
The wording of the question
optionExplain: Right.
Not mentioned.
Not mentioned.
Wording is not their account.
questions.explain: Size of the set. The card next gives the framework.
questions.rule: Size of the set of possibilities.

questions.q: The solver is given a description of the solution in the ____ language and must find a process description.
questions.explain: The description is in the state language; the solver finds the process language description.

questions.q: A detective must find the one culprit among 10,000 suspects. In the authors' terms, where does the difficulty lie?
options: In the size of the set of possibilities
In the colour of the evidence
In the length of the question
In the choice of language
optionExplain: Right.
Not relevant.
Not relevant.
Not relevant.
questions.explain: A rare element in a large set.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say problem difficulty does not depend on the size of the set of possibilities.
questions.explain: They say difficulty arises usually from the size of the set of possibilities.

questions.q: In the authors' framing, in what do the solver's given description and the sought description differ?
options: Both are in the state language
The given description of the solution is in the state language; the sought description says how to generate it, in the process language
Both are in the process language
The given description is of the process, the sought one of the state
optionExplain: That ignores the sought generating process.
Right: state language in, process language out.
That ignores the given description of the solution.
That reverses the two.
questions.explain: The solver is given a description of the solution in a language called the state language and is required to find an alternative process description that will specify how to generate it.
questions.rule: Given: what it is; sought: how to make it.
questions.teaches: The solver is given a description of the solution in a language called the state language and must find an alternative process description specifying how to generate it.

questions.q: Which principle does LT's matching process illustrate?
options: Generating only valid proofs
Using information obtained in the course of generating to guide the continuing search
Abstracting to simpler descriptions
Learning from experience
optionExplain: That is the first principle, shown by the methods.
Right.
That is the similarity test.
That is a later section.
questions.explain: Feedback in generation. The card next lists all three.

questions.q: Match each LT component to the principle it illustrates.
pairs: Generate only elements guaranteed to have some solution properties
Use information gained while generating to guide search
questions.explain: The three principles map to methods, matching and similarity.

questions.q: A job board shows only listings in your city and sorts them by how well each fits your last application. Which principles are at work?
options: Abstraction only
Learning only
Recognition only
Guaranteed properties (city) and guidance from information gained so far (fit)
optionExplain: More than one principle is used.
Not learning.
Not recognition.
Right.
questions.explain: City filter guarantees a property; fit ranking uses information so far.

questions.q: True or false: The authors credit the similarity test with the third principle, abstraction from detail.
questions.explain: Abstraction is illustrated by the similarity test.

questions.q: Which of the three principles did the authors find almost cancelled out by its processing cost?
options: Guaranteed properties in the generator
Abstraction through descriptions, as in the similarity test
Feedback-guided matching
None
optionExplain: That one gave large gains.
Right: the description processes almost balanced the selectivity gain.
Matching gave the largest gains.
One did.
questions.explain: The authors say in the description processes the increased selectivity was almost balanced by the added effort.
questions.rule: Gains from abstraction can be eaten by cost.
questions.teaches: In some cases, for example in the description processes, the increased selectivity was almost balanced by the increased processing effort required to produce it.

questions.q: Which raises a problem solver's reach more: a 1000-fold faster processor or effective selective heuristics?
options: Effective selective heuristics
The faster processor
Both equally
Neither
optionExplain: Right.
Speed gains are minuscule by comparison.
The authors say heuristics dominate.
Both help but unequally.
questions.explain: Selectivity wins. The card next gives the reasoning.

questions.q: LT would run about ____ times as fast on an IBM 360/65 as on the JOHNNIAC.
questions.explain: The authors give a factor of about 100.

questions.q: A team doubles the clock speed of a brute-force search. By the authors' view, what is the likely effect on the problems it can solve?
options: It now rivals LT
It solves every problem
It becomes selective
Little: speed-ups are minuscule next to gains from selective heuristics
optionExplain: No conceivable speed-up would let it compete.
Not so.
Speed does not add selectivity.
Right.
questions.explain: The gains from speed are small compared with selectivity.

questions.q: True or false: Because LT's effort per subproblem is roughly constant, a program's problem solving power depends on how many branches it must add to reach a proof.
questions.explain: Effort is proportional to the branches added, so selectivity in the tree decides power.

questions.q: About how large is the search tree LT generated for a hard case like Theorem 2.17?
options: Millions of branches
About 2 branches
About 250 branches
Modest, about 33 branches
optionExplain: That would be unreachable for LT.
That is too few for a three-step proof.
250 subproblems is the figure for a wider tree that would have been needed for 2.27.
Right: the trees remain small.
questions.explain: Even for problems like 2.17 the search trees LT generates are of modest size, about 33 branches in that instance.
questions.teaches: Even for a problem like 2.17 the search trees LT generates are of modest size, about 33 branches in that instance.

questions.q: In an AND-OR tree, what distinguishes an AND node from an OR node?
options: An AND node is a solution
An OR node is always false
An AND node gives subproblems all of which must be solved; an OR node gives subproblems of which only one need be solved
There is no difference
optionExplain: A node is not a solution.
OR nodes need one.
Right.
They differ.
questions.explain: All versus one. The card next explains.
questions.rule: AND needs all; OR needs one.

questions.q: A tree whose nodes give sets of subproblems that must all be solved or of which one must be solved is called an ____ tree.
questions.explain: The authors name it an AND-OR tree.

questions.q: To approve a loan a bank needs proof of income and proof of address, but to prove identity it accepts a passport or a licence. Which nodes are these?
options: Income and address: AND; passport or licence: OR
Income and address: OR; passport or licence: AND
All AND
All OR
optionExplain: Right.
Reversed.
Identity needs one only.
Income and address both needed.
questions.explain: Both needed means AND; either suffices means OR.

questions.q: True or false: LT's single-output operators prevented it from proving the theorem P or not-not-not-P (Theorem 2.13).
questions.explain: The authors say the restriction to operators that yield a single output expression made it impossible for LT to prove this theorem.
questions.rule: The restriction cost LT some theorems.

questions.q: In the extension that accepts multiple outputs, what must the executive remember after proving one of an operator's two output expressions?
options: That the other expression still has to be proved
That the theorem is now proved
That the operator should be removed
That the first expression was false
optionExplain: Right: both must be proved.
One of two is not enough.
Operators remain available.
The first was proved, not false.
questions.explain: The necessary additional executive structures are added so that the solver knows, after proving one of the expressions, that it still has to prove the other.
questions.teaches: The additional executive structures let the solver know, after it has proved one of an operator's output expressions, that it still has to prove the other.

questions.q: What did the geometry program do with a diagram to cut its search?
options: Drew a new diagram for every subgoal
Rejected a subgoal if its property was false in the diagram
Used the diagram to count steps
Ignored the diagram
optionExplain: It consulted the existing diagram.
Right.
Not used that way.
It was crucial.
questions.explain: Subgoals false in the diagram were rejected. The card next gives the effect.

questions.q: With the diagram, the program accepted about ____ subgoals per stage, against about 1000 without it.
questions.explain: About 5 against about 1000: a factor of 200 to 1.

questions.q: A heuristic cuts 1000 candidates per stage to 5. About what factor is that?
options: 50 to 1
5 to 1
optionExplain: That uses 250 candidates.
Right.
That is the output count.
That is the input count.
questions.explain: 1000 divided by 5 is 200.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say LT's and the geometry program's results depend on specific properties of the information processing system that carries out the search.
questions.explain: They say such generalizations belong to the theory of problem environments and are independent of specific characteristics of human cognitive processes.
questions.rule: These are facts about the environment.

questions.q: Why might a heuristic that is effective in LT also be useful in the geometry program?
options: Both were written by the same people
Both run on the same computer
Both work backward, use a powerful matching heuristic, and keep generated subproblems on a list, so the same heuristics apply
Both prove only logic theorems
optionExplain: Authorship is not the reason given.
Hardware is not the reason given.
Right: shared structure explains shared heuristics.
One proves geometry theorems, not logic ones.
questions.explain: The authors list the shared features: working backward, matching for substitutions, and a list of subproblems.
questions.teaches: Gelernter's geometry theorem prover and LT share many heuristics: both work backward, use a powerful matching heuristic for substitutions, and keep generated subproblems on a list, though the diagram heuristic has no close analog in LT.

questions.q: Which three tasks will the next parts of the book analyse, with the chapter's theory?
options: Cryptarithmetic, logic and chess
Algebra, geometry and music
Memory, perception and learning
Safe-opening, crosswords and chairs
optionExplain: Right.
Not the tasks of the book.
Those are topics, not tasks.
Those are examples within this chapter.
questions.explain: Cryptarithmetic, logic and chess. The card next explains how the chapter prepares for them.

questions.q: The chapter shows generate-and-test fitting the set-predicate formulation and heuristic search fitting the ____ formulation.
questions.explain: Heuristic search is paired with the search formulation.

questions.q: Given the formulation and method for a new puzzle, what can the theory estimate in advance?
options: The exact solution
The solver's mood
The size of the problem space and so the likely difficulty
The author's name
optionExplain: It does not give the solution.
Not part of the theory.
Right.
Irrelevant.
questions.explain: The demands of the task become a description of the space with an estimate of size.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say the general theory lets them make predictions about the specific paths that problem solution will take.
questions.explain: They say they arrive at techniques for predicting difficulty and for making many predictions about the specific paths.

questions.q: As formulation and method are specified, what becomes of the notion of the demands of the task?
options: It is dropped from the theory
It becomes a description of the problem space explored by generators or search operators, with estimates of its size
It becomes a list of axioms
It becomes a measure of the solver's intelligence
optionExplain: The authors use it to predict difficulty.
Right: the demands are expressed as the space to be explored and its size.
Axioms belong to logic tasks.
Intelligence is not the measure.
questions.explain: In this way the authors arrive at techniques for predicting problem difficulty and the specific paths solution will take.
questions.rule: Demands become a space and its size.
questions.teaches: As problem formulation and method are specified, the notion of the demands of the task is transformed into a description of the problem space that will be explored by generators or search operators, and into estimates of its size.

questions.q: In a cryptarithmetic puzzle such as a letter sum, what does each letter stand for?
options: Any whole number, so two letters may stand for the same value
One digit, and different letters stand for different digits
A word whose length is the digit being coded
An operation such as plus or minus that the solver must find
optionExplain: Tempting because algebra reuses values, but here each letter has its own digit.
Right: letters are placeholders for digits, with no digit used for two letters.
Letters are not words; each one stands for a single digit.
The operations are given in the sum; only the digits are unknown.
questions.explain: Each letter is a distinct digit from 0 to 9. The card next states the rules in full.

questions.q: True or false: Each letter in the task stands for a digit different from the digit of every other letter.
questions.explain: Each letter is a distinct digit, so no letter other than D may equal 5 once D has been given that value.
questions.rule: No digit is shared between letters.

questions.q: In a puzzle TO + GO = OUT, which proposal breaks the rules of the task itself?
options: O stands for 1 and T stands for 2
The result OUT has three digits though TO and GO have two
No digit is given for any letter at the start
G and U both stand for the digit 0
optionExplain: This is allowed: different letters, different digits.
A longer result is allowed; the sum may carry into a new column.
A puzzle need not give any hint; the rules do not require one.
Right: two different letters would share one digit, which the task forbids.
questions.explain: The only rule broken is sharing a digit between letters. The other three are legal features of such a puzzle.

questions.q: According to the authors, what happens to the DONALD + GERALD puzzle if the hint D is 5 is removed?
options: It still has exactly one solution
It has no solution, because D must be known
It has several solutions, one for each possible D
It has solutions only if leading letters may be zero
optionExplain: Right: the authors say the puzzle has a unique solution even without that hint.
The hint helps the solver; the sum itself already fixes D.
The authors say the solution is unique even without the hint.
The authors raise no such condition; the solution is unique without the hint.
questions.explain: The hint makes the puzzle easier to solve but is not needed for a unique answer.
questions.rule: A hint can shorten the work without changing the answer.
questions.teaches: The DONALD + GERALD puzzle has a unique solution even when D is 5 is not provided as given information.

questions.q: Which of these are general features of cryptarithmetic tasks, not features of this puzzle alone? Select all that apply.
options: Each letter stands for one digit
The digit 5 is given for D
Distinct letters must have distinct digits
Replacing letters by digits must make the sum correct
optionExplain: Right: this holds for every such task.
A given digit is a hint that only some puzzles carry.
Right: a general rule of the task.
Right: the defining goal of every such puzzle.
questions.explain: The letter-digit link, distinctness and a true sum are general. The D hint belongs to this puzzle.
questions.rule: Separate the general rules from this puzzle's hint.

questions.q: A psychologist wants to study how people solve a new kind of puzzle. Following this part of the book, what comes first?
options: Record many solvers first and infer the task from them
Study one solver only, since a single case shows everything
Analyze the task itself, then examine one solver, then several
Write a program, then compare it with a published solver
optionExplain: The authors begin with the task, not with the solvers.
They do study one solver in detail, but after the task analysis and before the broader view.
Right: the authors analyze the task in Chapter 5, one subject in Chapter 6, and a number of subjects in Chapter 7.
A program is not the first step; the task analysis comes first.
questions.explain: Task analysis is the base on which the later chapters read human behavior.
questions.rule: Analyze the task, then one subject, then many.
questions.teaches: The part has a fixed plan: Chapter 5 analyzes the task, Chapter 6 examines one subject's attempt, and Chapter 7 examines a number of subjects.

questions.q: A puzzle has 10 letters and 10 digits and every pairing is allowed. How could a computer find the answer by brute force?
options: Reason column by column and never try a full pairing
Check only the last column and assume the others work
Try each complete pairing and check whether the sum holds
Ask which letters begin a number and fix them first
optionExplain: This is a cleverer method, not brute force.
A partial check cannot confirm a full solution.
Right: this is the generate-and-test idea, which the card names.
This is a heuristic; brute force makes no such choices.
questions.explain: Brute force generates complete assignments and tests each. The card next gives the size of that job.
questions.rule: Generate every assignment, test every one.

questions.q: Producing every complete assignment and then checking each with an addition is called generate-and-____.
questions.explain: The generate-and-test method fits the set-predicate formulation directly.

questions.q: Five guests are seated in five chairs and every seating is tried and checked against some rules. How many seatings are tested?
options: 120, since each guest gets one chair
25, one for each guest and chair pair
3125, because each guest may pick any chair
5, one for each of the chairs in the room
optionExplain: Right: 5 x 4 x 3 x 2 x 1 = 120, the same kind of count as 9! for the puzzle.
This counts pairs, not whole seatings.
This allows two guests in one chair, which the setup forbids.
This counts chairs, not arrangements.
questions.explain: A one-to-one pairing of n items gives n! complete assignments: 5! = 120.
questions.rule: n items paired one-to-one give n! cases.

questions.q: True or false: If the hint that D is 5 were removed, a generator would face 10! complete assignments instead of 9!.
questions.explain: With D free as well, all ten digits go to the ten letters in 10! ways. Each fixed assignment removes one factor.
questions.rule: Each fixed assignment removes one factor.

questions.q: How do the authors say the condition in this formulation could be tested?
options: By checking each letter against a table of known results
By asking a person to judge whether the digits look right
By testing only whether the digits are all distinct
By a straightforward addition test on each assignment
optionExplain: No such table is mentioned.
The check is mechanical, not a judgment.
Distinctness alone does not make the sum correct.
Right: the check is plain addition of the substituted numbers.
questions.explain: Because the test is a simple addition, generate-and-test can proceed mechanically.
questions.rule: A formulation is usable when its test is cheap and exact.
questions.teaches: In this formulation the condition a solution must satisfy can be checked by a straightforward addition test.

questions.q: Eight volunteers are matched to eight jobs, one job each. A colleague lets one volunteer do several jobs. What changes for a try-everything checker?
options: Nothing changes, because the number of jobs is the same
Far more cases, since the one-to-one rule no longer limits them
Fewer cases, because freer choices let the checker finish sooner
The checker no longer needs to test the pairings it builds
optionExplain: The count depends on the pairing rule, not only on the number of jobs.
Right: the authors note their generator already uses the rule that a digit goes to one letter.
Freer choices create more cases, not fewer.
Every case still needs testing.
questions.explain: Even the crude generator in the chapter uses the rule that a digit goes to one letter. Without it, hundreds of millions of cases would arise instead of a third of a million.
questions.rule: The task's own constraints already shrink the crude search.
questions.teaches: Even this primitive generator uses the task constraint that a digit goes to only one letter; without it hundreds of millions of cases, not a third of a million, would be considered.

questions.q: To treat a puzzle as a search, what must you first be able to describe?
options: States of information, and the moves that change them
Only the final answer, since a search is aimed at nothing else
The number of people who have tried the puzzle before you
A catalogue of all the complete solutions to the puzzle
optionExplain: Right: states of information and the operators that alter them.
The answer is the goal, but a search also needs states and moves.
That is a fact about people, not a part of the search.
Listing solutions would make searching unnecessary.
questions.explain: Search needs nodes for states of information and operators for changing them. The card next defines both.

questions.q: In a search formulation, positions or nodes hold the information so far and ____ modify that information.
questions.explain: Operators are the processes that change one node into another.
questions.rule: Nodes hold information; operators change it.

questions.q: A courier plans a delivery round by search, where a node is the partial route so far. Which is an operator?
options: The finished route that visits every stop
The list of parcels waiting at the depot
The driver's name and vehicle number
Adding one more stop to the end of the route
optionExplain: That is a goal state, not an operator.
That is information about the task, not a move.
These do not change the information in a node.
Right: it turns one partial route into a longer one.
questions.explain: An operator is a process that produces a new node from an old one.
questions.rule: An operator makes a new node from an old one.

questions.q: Two solvers model the same puzzle, one with nodes that list only assignments, the other with nodes that also note parity. What do the authors allow?
options: Only one is a true space; the other is a mistake
Both may be problem spaces for the same task
Both are valid only if they give the same number of nodes
Neither is valid until the solver has a solution
optionExplain: The authors stress that many problem spaces can exist for one task.
Right: a task can have many problem spaces, each fixed by its expressions and operators.
The size of the tree is not what makes a space valid.
A space is a way of representing the task, set up before solving.
questions.explain: Each problem space is defined by its expressions and operators, so one task can have several.

questions.q: What principle do the authors use to arrange the basic, augmented and algebraic problem spaces?
options: The year in which each space was first proposed
How hard each space is for human subjects
How much information each one uses to limit the search
How many letters each space can represent
optionExplain: No dates are given as the ordering.
Human difficulty is the topic of later chapters.
Right: they are arranged by the amount of information used to limit search.
All three represent the same letters.
questions.explain: The three spaces run from the least to the most information used to cut down search.
questions.rule: Order spaces by how much information they use.
questions.teaches: The basic, augmented and algebraic problem spaces are arranged according to how much information they use to limit search.

questions.q: True or false: A single task can have more than one problem space, each defined by its own expressions and operators.
questions.explain: The authors emphasize that there can be many problem spaces for one task, each defined by its expressions and operators.
questions.rule: The task does not fix the space.

questions.q: A team plans a wedding seating chart as a search. Which pair is an expressible start and an expressible goal?
options: Start: the finished chart. Goal: an empty room with no guests seated
Start: every guest seated. Goal: no rules checked or applied at all
Start: one table named. Goal: a printed list of all the tables
Start: no guests seated. Goal: all guests seated, rules met
optionExplain: This runs the search backwards and loses the point of searching.
A start with all assigned would leave nothing to search.
A list of tables is not a successful assignment.
Right: the start may be nothing known, and the goal is a complete, successful assignment.
questions.explain: In the chapter the start is no assignments or only D set to 5, and the goal is a complete, successful assignment.
questions.rule: Both ends of the search must be expressible.
questions.teaches: The initial state of information may be no assignments or only a given one, and the final state must be expressible as a complete, successful assignment.

questions.q: While working a letter-digit puzzle, what is the most basic thing a solver could know?
options: That the answer is an even number
That one letter stands for one digit
That the sum has six digits in its result
That some letter is bigger than another letter
optionExplain: A property of the answer is a richer kind of knowledge than one assignment.
Right: a specific assignment is the simplest piece of knowledge here.
This is part of the problem statement, not a step toward its solution.
A comparison needs more machinery than a single assignment.
questions.explain: The basic space admits only specific assignments. The card next defines it.

questions.q: In the basic space a knowledge-state is a list of one or more ____.
questions.explain: A state is a list of expressions, each a letter, an arrow and a digit.
questions.rule: A state is a list of assignments.

questions.q: Add of B set to 3 is applied to the state with D set to 5 and T set to 0. What is the result?
options: The state holding only B set to 3
The unchanged state with D set to 5 and T set to 0
The state holding B set to 3, D set to 5 and T set to 0
A state with B set to 3 listed twice
optionExplain: Add keeps what the state already knew.
B set to 3 is new, so the state changes.
Right: Add puts the new assignment into the list.
Add never creates duplicate expressions.
questions.explain: Add extends a state by one assignment and removes nothing.

questions.q: True or false: Applying Add of T set to 0 to a state that already holds T set to 0 leaves the state unchanged.
questions.explain: Duplicate expressions are redundant, so Add does nothing when the assignment is already in the state.

questions.q: The authors say an expression could be stored as a list of three symbols or as attributes. What follows for their analysis?
options: Such details of encoding need not concern the analysis
They must choose the list encoding for the space to be valid
The two encodings give different problem spaces
The analysis fails until the encoding is chosen
optionExplain: Right: the system is assumed to have processes that find the letter and the digit in an expression.
The pattern does not settle the encoding, and either serves.
The space is fixed by expressions and operators, not by storage.
The authors move on without fixing it.
questions.explain: Processes for finding the letter and the digit shield the analysis from how an expression is stored.
questions.rule: Analyze at the level of expressions, not storage.
questions.teaches: The pattern for an expression does not fix its representation, and the analysis can ignore the encoding because the system has processes for finding the letter and the digit.

questions.q: A student says the basic space is called basic because it has the fewest possible letters. What is the actual reason?
