options: It uses the fewest operators of any space, namely none
It admits only the explicit, specific assignments
It is the only space that a computer can run
It is the space that humans always use
optionExplain: It has one operator, Add.
Right: it holds only the basic elements stated in the problem.
All three spaces are defined for an information processing system.
The authors do not claim that humans use it.
questions.explain: The name refers to the kind of knowledge allowed, not to the number of letters.
questions.rule: Basic means only the explicit assignments.

questions.q: A planner wants the simplest problem space for a seating puzzle. In the authors' sense of simple, which is it?
options: The space in which the search tree has the fewest nodes
The space with the shortest program for solving the puzzle
The space in which the answer is reached the soonest
States of explicit guest-table pairs, built from the text
optionExplain: Tree size is a matter of search, not of the simplicity of the space.
Program length is not the authors' measure of simplicity.
Speed of solving does not define a simple space.
Right: simplicity is the directness and ease with which the space can be built from the explicit instructions.
questions.explain: The basic space is the simplest in which the whole problem can be defined, because it can be built so directly from the statement.
questions.rule: Simple means directly built from the instructions.
questions.teaches: Simplicity of a space refers to the directness and ease with which it could be built from the explicit problem instructions.

questions.q: How could a solver decide that a finished set of letter-digit assignments is a solution?
options: Check the given hint, the distinctness rules and the addition
Check that the digits come out in increasing order
Check that no two letters of the sum are the same
Check that the first assignment tried was the last kept
optionExplain: Right: the rules of the task are exactly what a solution must satisfy.
Order of digits is not a rule of the task.
Letters repeat in the sum; digits must not repeat across letters.
The order of trying is not a test of a solution.
questions.explain: A solution must respect the hint, the distinct-digit rules and the sum. The card next lists the four checks.
questions.rule: Test against the task's own rules.

questions.q: Put the four parts of the test-for-solution in the order the authors list them.
items: D is still assigned 5
No letter has more than one digit
No digit is given to more than one letter
The addition is correct and every letter has a digit
questions.explain: The four checks run from the hint, to letter consistency, to digit consistency, to the sum.

questions.q: A state holds D set to 5, T set to 0 and R set to 5. Which check does it fail?
options: The one that D is still assigned 5
The one that no letter has more than one digit
The one that no digit goes to more than one letter
The addition check, since no sum can be worked yet
optionExplain: D is still 5, so this check passes.
Each letter has one digit; the clash is between letters.
Right: D and R both hold 5.
The digit clash fails first and for certain.
questions.explain: Two letters hold the digit 5, so the third check fails.
questions.rule: A shared digit fails the digit check.

questions.q: A state passes the first three checks but only some letters have digits. What does the test report?
options: Fail, because every letter needs a digit before the test can pass
Succeed, because nothing in it is wrong
Incomplete, which is a weak evaluation that it has not yet failed
Nothing, because the test runs only on full assignments
optionExplain: Only a contradiction is a fail; an unfinished state is incomplete.
Success needs the addition correct and complete.
Right: the tests distinguish succeed, fail and incomplete.
The test is written to handle partial states too.
questions.explain: The three-way answer lets a partial state with no contradiction go on being searched.
questions.teaches: The test processes distinguish succeed, fail and incomplete, so a partial state can get a weak evaluation: incomplete but not yet fail.

questions.q: True or false: If the letter and digit tests quit at once whenever a letter is unassigned, errors in the addition on partial states would be masked.
questions.explain: The authors say quitting immediately on incompleteness would hide addition errors, so the tests report incomplete and go on.
questions.rule: An early quit can hide a later error.

questions.q: A team must define what a finished jigsaw is. Following the authors, which approach to the goal is simpler?
options: Write a test that checks a picture against the rules
List every possible finished picture in advance, one by one
Declare the first picture that gets reached to be the goal
Define the goal by how long the puzzle took to finish
optionExplain: Right: defining goals by a test process is simpler than writing the goal set as an expression.
That is the explicit goal set, which would be considerably more elaborate.
The first picture reached need not satisfy the rules.
Time is a cost, not a definition of success.
questions.explain: Goal sets are often defined by a test; writing the goal set itself would need a considerably more elaborate space.
questions.rule: A test defines the goal more cheaply than a list.
questions.teaches: A goal set could be written as an expression, but a problem space able to do so would be considerably more elaborate than one that defines the goal by a test process.

questions.q: Why check partial assignments during a search instead of waiting for complete ones?
options: Complete assignments cannot be checked by a computer
Partial assignments cannot be wrong, so checking them adds nothing
It makes every assignment equally likely to succeed in the end
A failure found early rules out all completions of it
optionExplain: They can be checked; they are simply many.
Partial assignments can already contain a clash.
Checking early does not change what the solution is.
Right: one early failure removes a whole group of later candidates.
questions.explain: Early failure prunes a whole branch. The card next shows how the program does it.

questions.q: The search goes deeper only when the test reports a state as incomplete but ____.
questions.explain: A consistent state has no clash yet, so it may still lead to a solution.

questions.q: A search fills seats one guest at a time and puts two guests in the same seat. What does a depth-first program with this test do?
options: It keeps filling seats and checks only when all are full
It drops that branch and tries the next alternative at the previous step
It restarts the whole search from the first guest
It accepts the clash if the rest of the seating looks good
optionExplain: That would be the generate-and-test pattern, not early failure.
Right: a clash ends the branch, as a repeated digit does in the chapter.
Only the failed branch is dropped.
A clash makes every completion of that branch invalid.
questions.explain: The test marks the branch failed, so the program backs up and tries another move.
questions.rule: A clash ends that branch only.

questions.q: True or false: A generator that marks letters as used avoids generating the same letter a second time.
questions.explain: The authors say the generator must record when a letter is used so that it does not generate it again.

questions.q: Which inefficiency do the authors point out in this program's test-for-solution?
options: It restarts its addition check from the far right
It skips the check of the hint that D is 5 in every state
It tests only complete assignments, never partial ones
It never checks the final column of the sum at any point
optionExplain: Right: the check is repeated more than the order of assignment requires.
The first part of the test checks the hint.
It tests partial states too.
Every column is eventually reached.
questions.explain: Because assignments go from the right, only the newest column can have changed.
questions.teaches: The test-for-solution restarts its addition check from the far right each time, though by the way assignments are generated only the currently active column need be checked.

questions.q: A cashier checks a long receipt total, starting at the units. In which order does the authors' generator take up the sum's columns and rows?
options: Columns from left to right, and within a column from bottom to top
Rows first, finishing the whole top row before the next
Letters in alphabetical order
Columns from right to left, and from top down within each
optionExplain: That order starts from the carry-free side only in the leftmost column.
The program works column by column.
Alphabetical order is not the order in the program.
Right: it follows the order of occurrence in the display, right to left, top to bottom within each column.
questions.explain: The generator walks the columns right to left, top to bottom, which fits how a carry moves.
questions.teaches: The generator produces operators in the order the letters occur in the display, right to left in the columns and top to bottom within each column.

questions.q: A search tests each partial state and drops failures. How does its tree compare with one tested only when complete?
options: It is the same size, since every state is visited anyway
It is much smaller, as each failure removes whole subtrees
It is larger, since each test adds more branches to the tree
It is smaller only if the first branch tried is correct
optionExplain: States below a failed state are never visited.
Right: pruning early means whole subtrees are never built.
Tests remove branches; they do not add them.
The saving does not depend on luck with the first branch.
questions.explain: Early failure keeps the tree small. The card next gives the chapter's figures.

questions.q: The depth-first tree drawn in Figure 5.5 has 87 terminals; counting the undrawn final failing branches gives ____ branches.
questions.explain: Each branch ends with one more failing assignment that is not drawn, which makes the whole three times larger.

questions.q: A tester builds 3-digit codes from digits 0 to 9, dropping a prefix once a digit repeats. How many full codes does it reach?
optionExplain: This is the count with no pruning; repeated digits are dropped as soon as they appear.
This starts from 9 digits; the first digit may be any of the 10.
Right: 10 x 9 x 8 codes with no repeated digit.
This adds 10 + 9 + 8 instead of multiplying the choices.
questions.explain: Pruning at each step leaves 10 x 9 x 8 = 720 complete codes instead of 1000.
questions.rule: Count the survivors of each step.

questions.q: Suppose the program used each column sum to generate a letter's digit instead of only to test. What would happen to the tree?
options: It would grow further, since sums add branches
It would stay the same
It would become the 9! tree of generate-and-test
The threefold growth over the drawn tree would disappear
optionExplain: Computing a digit from the sum creates fewer branches, not more.
The role of the sum changes what is generated.
Using sums prunes more than the plain depth-first version does.
Right: that growth comes from generating every digit and keeping only the one the sum allows.
questions.explain: With the sum as a test, all ten values of T are generated and only T = 0 survives the last column. As a generator, only T = 0 is produced.
questions.rule: Generate from the constraint, do not just test it.

questions.q: In Figure 5.5, how much of the possible search is done before the first and only solution is found?
options: About half, as an average over orders would give
About 99 percent, since the last unexplored branch ends at once
About 10 percent, since a tree finds solutions early
None, since the tree never reaches a solution
optionExplain: The half is an average over random orders; this order is not random relative to the answer.
Right: the solution lies at the end of the search, so almost the whole tree is explored.
The solution is found late, not early.
The tree does contain the solution.
questions.explain: The branch with L set to 9 is left until last, and it ends immediately by implying R = 9.
questions.rule: An average is not a guarantee for one order.
questions.teaches: In Figure 5.5 the search to the first and only solution covers 99 percent of the possible search, because the last unexplored branch (L set to 9) ends at once by implying R = 9.

questions.q: True or false: The depth-first search of Figure 5.5 has 9! terminals.
questions.explain: That is the count for generate-and-test, or for a search that tests only complete assignments. The drawn tree has 87 terminals.
questions.rule: Early tests are what shrink the tree.

questions.q: Files are checked in an order unrelated to where the one match lies. What does the authors' estimate of search to the first match assume?
options: The match is always in the middle of the list
Every file takes the same time to open
The order of generation is random relative to where the solution is
The manager stops at the first file that looks promising
optionExplain: The estimate rests on a random order, not on a fixed middle.
Time per item is not part of the estimate.
Right: the estimate of about half assumes this.
Stopping rules are not what the estimate assumes.
questions.explain: On that assumption the first match is reached after about half the possibilities on average.
questions.rule: Averages depend on how the order relates to the answer.
questions.teaches: The actual number of alternatives searched to the first solution is usually estimated at one half of the total, on the assumption that the order of generation is random relative to the location of a solution.

questions.q: In a column sum where the other digits are known, how can a solver find the missing digit?
options: Compute it from the sum, instead of trying all ten digits
Try every digit and keep the largest that works
Leave it until every other letter has been guessed
Ask which digit has been used least so far
optionExplain: Right: the sum fixes the digit, up to the carry.
Trying all ten wastes the information in the sum.
Waiting adds nothing; the sum already determines it.
Past use of digits does not determine the missing one.
questions.explain: A column sum can give a digit directly. The card next describes the program that does this.

questions.q: Heuristics usually need more processing at each node but reduce the number of ____ that must be examined.
questions.explain: The extra work at a node is repaid when the tree has fewer nodes.
questions.rule: More work per node, fewer nodes.

questions.q: A column has top digit 6 and middle digit 7, with carry-in 0. Which digit does the program compute for the bottom letter?
options: 13, the full sum of the two digits
3, with a carry of 1 into the next column
1, the carry alone
7, copied from the middle row
optionExplain: A column holds only one digit; the 1 is carried.
Right: 6 + 7 = 13, so the bottom digit is 3 and the carry is 1.
The carry goes on to the next column; the digit written is 3.
The bottom digit is the sum's units digit, not a copy.
questions.explain: The units digit of 6 + 7 is 3, and the tens digit 1 becomes the carry.
questions.rule: Units digit stays, tens digit is carried.

questions.q: A column's carry-in is unknown when the program must compute a digit. What does it do?
options: It stops and reports that the whole task is unsolvable
It assigns the carry the value 9 and works backwards
It skips the column and does not return to it later
It tries the carry 0 first, then the carry 1
optionExplain: It tries both carries before giving up.
A carry can only be 0 or 1.
The column is handled by trying each carry value.
Right: it tries the two possible carries in that order.
questions.explain: Since a carry is 0 or 1, the program tries 0 first and then 1.
questions.rule: Try the two carries in turn.

questions.q: The authors suggest freeing the order of assignment, instead of working strictly right to left. What ability does that require?
options: Detecting a column contradiction with parts unknown
Knowing the answer to the puzzle in advance of the search
Using fewer letters than the puzzle itself has in it
Giving up the test-for-solution at the end of the search
optionExplain: Right: out-of-order assignments mean columns are examined with missing parts.
The program must find the answer, not know it.
The number of letters is fixed by the puzzle.
The test is still needed.
questions.explain: Without a rigid order, columns are examined with unknown carries or letters, so inference must work on partial columns.
questions.teaches: Freeing the order of assignment, rather than working rigidly right to left, requires the ability to detect contradictions in a column even though not all its components are known.

questions.q: True or false: The heuristic program does more work at each node, yet its search tree has far fewer nodes.
questions.explain: The extra processing per node pays off: the tree falls to 23 nodes from 87 terminals.
questions.rule: Work per node and number of nodes trade against each other.

questions.q: A clerk first handles invoice lines with one unknown, then works bottom-up. Which feature of the authors' selection process is this?
options: It picks the letters at random and then sorts them afterwards
It always starts at the left-most column and works rightward
It prefers a letter alone in a column, else goes right to left
It assigns every letter first and does all checking at the end
optionExplain: The selection is not random.
The fallback is right to left.
Right: that is the order of preference in the program of Figure 5.6.
Checking goes on during the search.
questions.explain: A letter alone in a column is easiest to fix. Only when none exists does the program work from the right.
questions.teaches: The selection process first tries to find a letter that occurs alone in a column, and only if that fails does it proceed from right to left like the original generator.

questions.q: A solver reasons that a letter must be odd and above 5. Which kind of knowledge is this?
options: A complete assignment of the letter to a digit
Knowledge that the letter is already used elsewhere
A restriction to a class of digits, not one digit
A fact about the carries of the sum, not the letter
optionExplain: No single digit has been named.
Nothing about other letters is stated.
Right: the letter is narrowed to some digits but not fixed.
The fact concerns the letter itself.
questions.explain: Partial information can narrow a letter to a class. The card next names the forms it takes.
questions.rule: Know a class, not yet a digit.

questions.q: Match each statement about a letter to the kind of expression the augmented space uses.
questions.explain: The augmented space uses an inequality, a parity and a listed set of digits, among other forms.
questions.rule: Know the forms of partial information.

questions.q: A door code digit is known to be even and less than 7. Which digits are still possible?
options: 2, 4 and 6 only
1, 3 and 5
optionExplain: Right: these are the even digits below 7.
Zero is even and below 7, so it stays.
8 is not below 7.
These are odd, not even.
questions.explain: Intersecting the two conditions leaves 0, 2, 4 and 6.
questions.rule: Combine class conditions by intersecting them.

questions.q: A state holds that R is 7 or 9. Later the solver shows that R is not 7. What does the state now allow?
options: R is 8, the digit between them
R is any odd digit again
Nothing, since R has no value
R is 9
optionExplain: 8 was never listed.
The earlier narrowing still holds.
One listed value remains.
Right: with one listed alternative removed, only the other remains.
questions.explain: Removing 7 from the pair 7 or 9 leaves 9.
questions.rule: Eliminate an alternative, keep the rest.

questions.q: Two expressions say the same thing, though one excludes a single digit and the other lists the nine that remain. How do the authors view them?
options: They are identical in every way, so only one is needed
They are redundant, but may differ for a process
They contradict each other and cannot share a state
They differ only in being easier for people to read
optionExplain: The authors say they may be quite different for processing.
Right: the form of the information matters to the processes that use it.
They say the same thing, so no contradiction.
The difference noted is in processing, not readability.
questions.explain: A process may use the exclusion directly but must scan the listing, so equivalent facts can be unequal in cost.
questions.rule: Equal in content, unequal to a process.
questions.teaches: Relations in the augmented space are redundant, but from a processing viewpoint knowing that a letter is not one digit may be quite different from knowing it is one of the nine others.

questions.q: True or false: The augmented space can express facts, such as parity, that the basic space cannot.
questions.explain: The basic space admits only specific assignments. The augmented space adds inequalities, parity, enumerated sets and exclusions.
questions.rule: Compare what each space can express.

questions.q: A guest list note says only that a guest at table 3 is not Dana. Which form of augmented-space expression is this?
options: An exclusion, ruling a certain assignment out
An inequality, comparing one quantity with another
A parity, a statement that a quantity is odd or even
A complete assignment of Dana to one particular table
optionExplain: Right: the authors list exclusion, such as a letter being not zero.
No comparison is made.
Parity concerns odd and even digits.
Dana's table is not named.
questions.explain: An exclusion rules out one value without naming the right one.
questions.teaches: Besides inequalities, parity and enumerated sets, the augmented space can state that certain assignments must be excluded, for example that E is not 0.

questions.q: When adding two numbers by hand, which numbers help the work yet are not printed in the sum?
options: The digits that form the answer to the sum
The headings written above the columns
The total number of columns in the sum
The carries passed to the next column
optionExplain: Those are printed.
Headings are not numbers used in the sum.
That is visible in the layout.
Right: carries are hidden quantities of the sum.
questions.explain: Carries are part of the arithmetic but not of the display. The card next treats them as variables.

questions.q: In the augmented space, letters and carries together are called ____.
questions.explain: Figure 5.8 defines a variable as either a letter or a carry.

questions.q: In the sum 47 + 38, what is the carry into the tens column?
optionExplain: The units add to more than 9, so a carry occurs.
Right: 7 + 8 = 15, so 1 is carried.
5 is the units digit written, not the carry.
A carry is a single digit, here 1.
questions.explain: The units column gives 15: write 5, carry 1.
questions.rule: Carry is the tens digit of a column total.

questions.q: A solver records that c6 equals 0 for DONALD + GERALD. What does this say about the leftmost column?
options: The digits of the leftmost column must add to zero
The letter at the left of the answer stands for 0
No carry arrives from the column on its right
The puzzle has no carries in any of its columns
optionExplain: A zero carry does not make the sum zero.
The carry is separate from any letter's digit.
Right: c6 is the carry into the leftmost column, and 0 means none arrives.
Other carries can still be 1.
questions.explain: A carry of 0 into the leftmost column leaves its two digits to produce the answer's digit alone.
questions.rule: A carry variable can be known before the letters.

questions.q: What do the authors call the peculiarity of cryptarithmetic problems about their variables?
options: All variables are carries, and the letters are only names for them
Every variable is given its value in the puzzle statement itself
Variables may take any real value, not only whole numbers
Letters are named explicitly, while carries are left implicit
optionExplain: Letters and carries are different variables.
Only some puzzles give a hint.
Digits and carries are whole numbers.
Right: the carries are hidden unless the problem space names them.
questions.explain: The puzzle names the letters but not the carries, though both matter to the solution.
questions.rule: Name the hidden variables to use them.
questions.teaches: It is a peculiarity of cryptarithmetic problems that they introduce some variables (the letters) explicitly but leave others (the carries) implicit.

questions.q: True or false: The basic problem space could not evaluate a column sum without recording a carry as a separate variable.
questions.explain: The basic space solved the task with one temporary carry variable used only to evaluate column sums.
questions.rule: Temporary carry is not a recorded fact.

questions.q: When two three-digit numbers are added, which values can a carry into any column take?
options: Any digit from 0 to 9
0 or 1
Only 1, since a carry is always there
optionExplain: A carry from two digits and a carry is at most 1.
Right: two digits plus a carry of at most 1 total at most 19, so a carry is 0 or 1.
Some columns produce no carry.
The largest column total is 9 + 9 + 1 = 19, so the carry is never 2.
questions.explain: In the chapter's equations the carries are set to be 0 or 1, independently of each other.
questions.teaches: In the problem statement as equations, each carry is to be assigned 0 or 1, independently of the others.

questions.q: A solver knows a digit is even and below 5. Besides recording this, what must the solver be able to do with it?
options: Forget it until the digit is named
Replace it with a guess of 9
List the digits that satisfy both conditions
Count how many letters remain
optionExplain: Unused knowledge does nothing.
9 is neither even nor below 5.
Right: the facts only help if they can be turned into candidates.
Counting letters does not use the digit's class.
questions.explain: Class facts must be used, not only recorded. The card next names the operators that do this.
questions.rule: Use class facts by generating from them.

questions.q: Match each operator of the augmented space to its job.
pairs: Records a specific digit for a variable
Draws inferences from a column of the sum
Produces the digits belonging to a class
Checks a digit against what is known
questions.explain: AV assigns, PC infers from columns, GN generates from classes and TD tests admissibility.

questions.q: A column reads 4 plus G equals R, with no carry in. The solver knows R is odd. What can the column processor infer?
options: G is odd
G is even
G is 3
Nothing, since G has no digit yet
optionExplain: Right: 4 is even, so an odd R needs an odd G.
An even plus an even gives an even, not an odd.
Odd is all that follows; several odd digits fit.
Parity can be inferred without a digit.
questions.explain: Even + odd = odd, so G must be odd. This is an inference from the column.

questions.q: The generate-numbers operator receives the facts that H is odd and H is less than 6. What does it produce?
options: 1 and 3 only
1, 3 and 5
0, 2 and 4
optionExplain: 5 is odd and below 6, so it belongs.
Right: the odd digits below 6.
7 is not below 6.
These are the even digits below 6.
questions.explain: Intersecting odd with below 6 leaves 1, 3 and 5.
questions.rule: Generate the intersection of the classes.

questions.q: Where do the authors expect to find the largest variation among problem solvers' operators?
options: In the way digits are written on paper
In the number of letters in the puzzle
In how fast the assignment operator runs
In the power of the column processor
optionExplain: The operators are not about writing.
The puzzle fixes the letters.
Speed is not the variation noted.
Right: the authors say variation is greatest there, and they will see it in the human behavior that follows.
questions.explain: Some solvers draw few inferences from a column; others draw many.
questions.rule: Look at the column processor to tell solvers apart.
questions.teaches: There can be substantial variation in the details of the operators, most especially in the power of the column processor (PC), and some of this variation will appear in the human behavior in the next two chapters.

questions.q: True or false: Process-column and generate-numbers do the same job: both list the digits that belong to a class.
questions.explain: Process-column infers facts from the columns of the sum; generate-numbers lists the digits of a class. One produces class information, the other uses it.
questions.rule: Produce class facts, then use them.

questions.q: A scheduler learns that a meeting room must be one of the rooms free at 2 pm. Why must it also be able to list those rooms?
options: Class facts must be used, such as by generating members
Listing rooms replaces the need to know they are free
A class cannot be recorded without naming every member
Listing members is needed only for letters, not for rooms
optionExplain: Right: producing the class is not enough.
The class fact is what the listing is built from.
A class can be stated without listing members.
The same need arises in any problem with classes.
questions.explain: The most obvious use of class information is to generate the individual digits that belong to a class.
questions.rule: Facts about classes need operators that use them.
questions.teaches: Introducing a column processor is not enough, since class information must be not only produced but used, most obviously by generating the individual digits that belong to the classes.

questions.q: A solver does more reasoning before naming any digit. What is likely to happen to the checking done afterwards?
options: More of it is needed, since reasoning adds errors
It stays the same, since every digit is checked in full
Less of it is needed, since fewer unsuitable digits are tried
It moves to the end and is done only once
optionExplain: Reasoning removes candidates; it does not add errors.
The point of reasoning first is to save checking.
Right: reasoning in advance replaces some testing.
Checking still occurs at each assignment.
questions.explain: Generating from inference reduces testing. The card next shows what remains.

questions.q: In the augmented space much of the testing of the basic space is replaced by ____.
questions.explain: The augmented space makes information, so the basic tests are largely replaced by generation.

questions.q: A code digit must be odd and must not have been used earlier in the code. Which check matches the test that remains in the augmented space?
options: Adding up the whole code to see whether it is correct
Counting how many digits the code has
Asking whether a candidate digit is unused and within the allowed class
Asking whether the first digit is the largest
optionExplain: That is a test of the full solution, not of one digit.
Length is fixed by the puzzle, not tested per digit.
Right: admissibility means not yet assigned and compatible with what is known.
No such rule applies.
questions.explain: The remaining test looks at one digit at a time: not used elsewhere, and within its class.

questions.q: True or false: In the augmented space, generating each letter's digit from its class still guarantees that no two letters get the same digit.
questions.explain: Two letters may be allowed the same digit by their classes, so disjointness must be determined by a test.
questions.rule: Generation from classes needs a disjointness test.

questions.q: How do the authors describe the test for a solution in the basic space?
options: A substantial process, with distinctness and the sum
A single glance at the last column of the sum
A light test of the hint and nothing else
No test at all, because generation was exact
optionExplain: Right: the basic test did a great deal of work.
The basic test checked much more than that.
The hint was just the first of four parts.
The basic space relied on a full test.
questions.explain: Much of that work moves into generation in the augmented space.
questions.rule: Compare the work of the two tests.
questions.teaches: In the basic problem space the test for a solution was a substantial process, involving the tests that all digit assignments were distinct and requiring evaluation of the problem sum.

questions.q: A student says that in the augmented space no testing of digits remains. What is wrong?
options: Testing returns only at the very end of the search
Testing is done by the carries, not by the solver
Testing is replaced by guessing
A test of whether a digit is admissible is left
optionExplain: The remaining test is applied to individual digits.
Carries are variables, not testers.
Guessing does not replace a test.
Right: a digit must still be tested before it is accepted.
questions.explain: The test that remains is smaller but real.

questions.q: A caterer picks dishes that fit a diet, then checks each pick before adding it to the menu. What two conditions does the authors' admissibility test have?
options: The digit is the smallest digit still available and is even
The digit is unused and lies in the set compatible so far
The digit has appeared in the hint and is also below 5 in value
The digit makes the whole sum correct and no letter is left over
optionExplain: Neither condition is part of the test.
Right: not taken, and within its class.
Only D has a hint, and no such rule applies.
That tests a solution, not a digit.
questions.explain: A digit is admissible if it is not already used and is still compatible with what is known about its letter.
questions.teaches: A digit is admissible if it has not already been assigned to some other letter and is within the set of digits still compatible with the known conditions on the particular letter.

questions.q: How could the constraint of one column of a sum be written, with no assignments at all?
options: As an equation of the column's digits, result and carries
As a list of the digits that may not be used in the column
As a single word naming the letter on top of the column
As a count of how many letters the column holds in all
optionExplain: Right: the column rule becomes an equation in letters and carries.
That would be a restriction on digits, not a column equation.
A name carries no arithmetic.
A count says nothing about the sum.
questions.explain: A column of an addition is an equation: digits plus carry-in equal digit plus ten times carry-out. The card next writes all six.

questions.q: The algebraic space starts from ____ equations, one for each column of the sum.
questions.explain: DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT has six columns and so six equations.

questions.q: For the sum TO + GO = OUT, which equation holds for the units column, with c2 the carry into the tens column?
options: 2O = T
T + G = O + 10c2
O + T = O + 10c2
optionExplain: This ignores the carry into the next column.
This mixes the tens-column letters into the units column.
The units digits of the top rows are both O, not T.
Right: the two units digits are both O, and the result's units digit is T.
questions.explain: In the units column O plus O gives T with possible carry c2: 2O = T + 10c2.
questions.rule: Write each column with its carry.

questions.q: True or false: The six column equations alone already require that different letters stand for different digits.
questions.explain: The authors add that each letter is to be a distinct digit and that carries are 0 or 1; these conditions are not in the equations.
questions.rule: Equations plus conditions state the problem.

questions.q: What do the authors say about writing out a formal definition of the algebraic space?
options: It cannot be done, because equations are not expressions
It follows the other spaces and is left as an exercise
It is given in full in Figure 5.9, beside the productions
It must wait until the human data have been examined
optionExplain: They say it can be done.
Right: they do not formalize it.
Figure 5.9 gives productions, not the definition of the space.
The definition does not depend on human data.
questions.explain: The definition would follow the form used for the basic and augmented spaces.
questions.rule: The spaces share one pattern of definition.
questions.teaches: The authors do not formalize the algebraic problem space, noting that it can be done along exactly the same lines as the other spaces and calling it a good exercise for the reader.

questions.q: A budget sheet has the constraints a + b = 10 and b = 6. Which step is a move in the algebraic style?
options: Trying every value for a and checking each
Crossing out b because it is a letter
Substituting 6 for b to derive a = 4 as a new equation
Asking which value a was used last month
optionExplain: That works with assignments, not with derived equations.
Nothing is crossed out for that reason.
Right: derived equations join or replace earlier ones to make a new element.
Outside facts do not enter the space.
questions.explain: Algebraic and logical manipulations derive new equations that augment the set or replace specific expressions.
questions.rule: Derive new equations, do not guess values.
questions.teaches: Various algebraic and logical manipulations derive new expressions that augment the existing set of equations, or replace specific expressions, to form a new element of the space.

questions.q: A rule-based solver has two rules: one applies when a value is newly known, the other applies when the first does not. Which is tried first?
options: The one for the other case
Whichever was written last
Neither, since only one rule fires in a lifetime
The one for a newly known value
optionExplain: It applies only when the first does not.
Order of writing is not the order of use.
Rules fire repeatedly in a production system.
Right: the second applies only otherwise.
questions.explain: A production system tries the specific rule and falls back to the other. The card next gives the two rules.
questions.rule: Specific rule first, general rule otherwise.

questions.q: Match each part of the production system to its job.
pairs: P1: a variable has been given a digit
Substitute the digit for the variable and mark it used
Stops the same substitution from being matched again
questions.explain: P1 substitutes, P2 infers, and the mark prevents repetition.

questions.q: R1 substitutes any known value; R2 applies otherwise. The state holds y = 6 and x + y = 10. Which rule fires?
options: R2, since the equation has two unknowns
R1, giving x + 6 = 10
Both at once, in either order
Neither, since 10 is not a variable
optionExplain: R2 fires only when R1 cannot.
Right: a value is known, so substitution comes first.
The rules are tried in order, not together.
y has a known value, which is enough for R1.
questions.explain: Because y is known, R1 applies and replaces y by 6.
questions.rule: Known values get substituted before anything is inferred.

questions.q: True or false: If the system did not mark a used assignment, the substitution production could match the same assignment again and again.
questions.explain: A used tag is what keeps P1 from matching an assignment it has already used.

questions.q: How do the authors treat the two processes of substitution and inference?
options: Both are fully defined in the productions of Figure 5.9
Inference is trivial, while substitution is the hard part
Substitution is simple; inference is less well defined
Neither needs any explaining
optionExplain: The figure lists the productions, not the inference process.
It is the other way round.
Right: they say infer-consequences needs more explanation.
They explain the inference step by example.
questions.explain: Substitution is simple; deducing as many new consequences as possible is the open-ended part.
questions.rule: The hard work lies in inference.
questions.teaches: Substitution involves only straightforward processing, whereas the process of inferring consequences, meaning deducing as many new algebraic and arithmetic consequences as possible, is less well defined.

questions.q: A clerk copies each confirmed figure into linked cells, and otherwise deduces what else follows. What pattern does the clerk's work show?
options: It alternates between substituting and inferring
It repeats a single step until the whole form is full
It makes guesses and keeps only those that fit the form
It checks the form once, at the end of all the work
optionExplain: Right: the two productions oscillate between these two activities.
Two different steps alternate.
Neither instruction involves guessing.
The checks run throughout.
questions.explain: Substitution makes new facts usable, inference produces further facts, and the cycle repeats.
questions.teaches: The two productions simply oscillate between inferring consequences from previous assignments or inferences and substituting any newly made or derived assignments for letters or carries.

questions.q: Given 2D = T + 10c2 and D = 5, what follows for T and for the carry c2?
options: T = 5 and c2 = 0
T = 0 and c2 = 1
T = 10 and c2 = 0
T = 1 and c2 = 0
optionExplain: Doubling 5 gives 10, not 5.
Right: 2D is 10, so T is 0 and the carry is 1.
T is a single digit; the 1 of 10 is the carry.
The units digit of 10 is 0, and the 1 is carried.
questions.explain: Substituting 5 gives 10 = T + 10c2, so T is 0 and c2 is 1. The card next follows the whole chain.
questions.rule: Substitute, then read off the digit and carry.

questions.q: Put these letters in the order the inference process fixes them.
questions.explain: The solution path runs T, E, R, A, G, L before the trial values for N, B and O.

questions.q: Given c5 + E = 10c6 with carries 0 or 1 and E a digit, which values may E take?
options: Only 9
Any digit from 0 to 9
1 or 10
0 or 9
optionExplain: E = 0 also fits when both carries are 0.
The equation is very restrictive.
10 is not a digit, and 1 does not satisfy the equation.
Right: c6 = 0 forces c5 = 0 and E = 0; c6 = 1 forces c5 + E = 10, so E = 9 and c5 = 1.
questions.explain: Only two combinations satisfy the equation, giving E = 0 or E = 9.
questions.rule: A carry equation leaves few possibilities.

questions.q: T has been fixed at 0 and E must be 0 or 9. What follows, given that letters have distinct digits?
options: E = 0, since 0 is the smaller choice
E remains open until R is known
T must change to 9
optionExplain: Right: E cannot share the digit 0 with T.
T already holds 0 and digits are distinct.
Distinctness settles E immediately.
T = 0 was derived and stays.
questions.explain: Distinct letters cannot share a digit, so the choice of E narrows to 9.

questions.q: After L = 8 the program stops. How does the solver finish?
options: It guesses N among all ten digits and tests each guess
It restarts the whole puzzle with a new hint from outside
A short trial: 2, 3 and 6 remain and N is greater than B
It reports that no solution exists for these equations
optionExplain: Only 2, 3 and 6 remain, and N is above B.
No new hint is given.
Right: with N above B only two trial values are left.
A solution exists and is found.
questions.explain: Since N is greater than B, only two trial values for N remain, 6 and 3, and 6 works.
questions.teaches: After L = 8 the program takes the solver no further; the digits 2, 3 and 6 remain for N, B and O, and since N is greater than B there are only two trial values for N, 6 and 3.

questions.q: True or false: In this walkthrough the solver guesses R as 7 and takes the guess back if it later fails.
questions.explain: R = 7 or 9 is held as information until E = 9 rules out 9, so R gets the definite value 7 with no guess.
questions.rule: Hold alternatives until one is eliminated.

questions.q: A bookkeeper's balancing sheet shows a fully satisfied relation after two of its quantities are fixed. What happens to such a relation in the chapter's solution?
options: It stays in the set and is checked at every later step
It forces the solver to restart from the beginning
It drops out, as it no longer constrains the others
It turns into a new unknown in the problem space
optionExplain: The authors show it dropping out.
A satisfied relation does not restart anything.
Right: equations 1 and 5 drop out of the set in the same way.
It is simply no longer needed.
questions.explain: After substitution, a fully used equation imposes no condition on the remaining variables.
questions.teaches: Equations (1) and (5) drop out of the set once substituted values leave them imposing no conditions on the remaining variables.

questions.q: A solver knows a letter is 7 or 9. What is the careful way to proceed?
options: Keep both possibilities on record until one is ruled out
Assign 7 and go on, correcting it if later steps fail
Assign 9 since it is larger
Drop the letter from the puzzle
optionExplain: Right: a definite assignment waits for deduction.
That is a tentative assignment, which this approach avoids.
Size gives no reason to choose.
A letter cannot be dropped; it has a digit.
questions.explain: Alternatives held as information cost nothing. The card next shows when they are used.
questions.rule: Keep alternatives; assign only when certain.

questions.q: The inference process makes ____ assignments, not tentative ones, once deduction leaves a single value.
questions.explain: A definite assignment is one that deduction guarantees.

questions.q: A password's last digit is 3 or 8; 8 is already used elsewhere in it and digits are distinct. What does the algebraic style do?
options: Assigns 8 and checks later
Keeps both open until the end
Asks for a hint
Assigns 3 as a definite value
optionExplain: 8 is already used, so it is ruled out.
One alternative has been eliminated, so a definite value follows.
No hint is needed.
Right: the alternative 8 is eliminated for certain.
questions.explain: Distinctness removes 8, which leaves 3 as the only possibility.

questions.q: True or false: When deduction leaves a letter with two possible digits and nothing can separate them, the process can go on without any tentative assignment.
questions.explain: The algebraic process removes most trial but not all: when inference stalls, a tentative assignment has to take over.
questions.rule: Trial takes over where deduction stops.

questions.q: Why do the authors say classical theory of Diophantine equations does not help much here?
options: Diophantine equations cannot have integer solutions at all
Special conditions make the theory largely inapplicable
The puzzle has no equations in it at all, only letters
The theory deals only with one equation at a time
optionExplain: They are exactly equations in integer values.
Right: the peculiar conditions of the puzzle fall outside the classical theory.
The puzzle can be written as six equations.
No such limit is stated.
questions.explain: Classical Diophantine theory is built for integer solutions of equations without these special conditions.
questions.rule: Special conditions can defeat general theory.
questions.teaches: Equations in integer-valued variables are called Diophantine equations, but the additional conditions here (some variables only 0 or 1, others in a fixed range and all disjoint) make the classical theory largely inapplicable.

questions.q: A ticket order must be a whole number from 0 to 4, and it must be even and above 2. Why can a solver deduce its value?
options: Because fixed whole-number values can be cut down by conditions
Because the variable can take any real number between 0 and 4
Because guessing works better on small whole numbers than large
Because the conditions contradict each other and leave nothing
optionExplain: Right: the fixed set of values permits logical inferences that reduce it.
Real numbers would not allow elimination in this way.
The reasoning is deduction, not guessing.
They do not; they leave the value 4.
questions.explain: With values limited to 0 to 4, even and above 2 leaves only 4.
questions.rule: Fixed sets of values permit elimination.
questions.teaches: The inference process works with fixed sets of nonnegative integer values for the variables, and this limitation permits logical inferences that reduce the set of possible values for a variable.

questions.q: A deduction process cannot narrow any variable to a single value. What must the solver do to go on?
options: Repeat the same deductions until a value appears
Assume the first value in the list
Stop, since no solution can exist
Make a tentative assignment and follow its consequences
optionExplain: Repeating the same steps changes nothing.
That is a tentative assignment under another name, with no check.
A solution may still be there.
Right: when deduction stalls, trial must begin.
questions.explain: Deduction without a decisive fact runs out. The card next shows this on the puzzle.

questions.q: Without D set to 5, the inference process would stop almost ____.
questions.explain: The process would infer only a few facts before stopping.

questions.q: In a number puzzle a solver has deduced that X is 0 or 9, Y is even, and nothing else follows. Which description fits?
options: The puzzle is solved, since two facts about it are known
Inference has stalled, so a tentative assignment comes next
Inference should be repeated several times until it succeeds
The puzzle must contain an error in its statement
optionExplain: Neither variable has a single value.
Right: nothing more can be deduced.
It has no more to add.
Stalling is not a sign of error.
questions.explain: With no further deductions, the solver must commit to a trial value.
questions.rule: A stalled deduction calls for a trial.

questions.q: True or false: In the no-hint case, once the deductions that follow a tentative E set to 0 are used up, a new tentative assignment is again needed.
questions.explain: The authors say further inferences would not be forthcoming, so another tentative assignment would be necessary.
questions.rule: Each stall asks for a new trial.

questions.q: What does the E set to 0 trial yield in quick succession before inference stalls again?
options: Every letter's digit, so the puzzle is then fully solved
Only that E is not 9, and nothing more follows from it
A contradiction at once, which ends that line of search
optionExplain: Inference stalls again before that.
Many more facts follow.
Right: the authors list these as deduced in quick succession.
No immediate contradiction is reported.
questions.explain: A single tentative assignment can be followed by many deductions, though not by all of them.
questions.rule: A trial can pay off quickly.
questions.teaches: Once E was tentatively set to 0, the authors say c5 = 0, c6 = 0, A = 5, c3 = 0, c4 = 1 and L below 5 would be deduced in quick succession.

questions.q: A planner has narrowed a delivery time to a few values but not to one. By the authors' remarks on this puzzle, what comes next?
options: Careful argument will always fix a single value in the end
The planner should discard the argument and start again
The remaining values can be added together
A tentative value must still be chosen
optionExplain: The authors say it does not.
The narrowing is useful, not wasted.
Adding values is not a step in the method.
Right: even careful argument that cuts the letters down to a few values leaves a tentative assignment for L.
questions.explain: Narrowing the choices helps trial, but trial may still be needed.
questions.teaches: Even a careful argument that narrows R and L to a few values still leaves one having to assign a tentative value for L.

questions.q: In a sum such as AA + BB = CBC, each addend has a repeated digit. What property might a clever solver notice?
options: The sum must be an even number, as both addends are
AA and BB are multiples of 11, so the sum is too
The letters A and B must be consecutive digits
The result CBC must begin with the digit 9, as it comes from large addends
optionExplain: Nothing in the pattern forces an even sum.
Right: a repeated two-digit number is 11 times its digit.
No such relation follows from the pattern.
C is not forced to be 9.
questions.explain: Repeated digits give multiples of 11, a feature of this puzzle's layout. The card next uses it.
questions.rule: Look for features of the puzzle itself.

questions.q: In AA + BB = CBC the sum CBC must be a multiple of ____.
questions.explain: AA is 11 times A and BB is 11 times B, so the sum is a multiple of 11.

questions.q: In KK + MM = NMN, which fact lets a solver start from multiples of 11?
options: K and M are both even digits
N is the first letter in the alphabet
KK and MM are each a multiple of 11, so NMN must be one as well
The sum has three digits while the addends have two
optionExplain: Nothing says the digits are even.
Alphabet order plays no part here.
Right: the sum of two multiples of 11 is a multiple of 11.
A longer sum does not by itself give a multiple of 11.
questions.explain: Repeated-digit addends are multiples of 11, so the sum must be too. Only a few numbers of the form NMN qualify.
questions.rule: Use the structure of the puzzle.

questions.q: Match each representation to what it uses.
pairs: Multiples of 11 for AA + BB = CBC
A special feature of one puzzle
A global view of letter-digit correspondences
The main spaces developed in detail
questions.explain: The multiples-of-11 space depends on one puzzle's features, the alphabet mapping is a global correspondence, and the three main spaces are the ones the chapter develops.
questions.rule: Sort spaces by the knowledge they use.

questions.q: What do the authors say about proving that their list of problem spaces is complete?
options: A formal demonstration of completeness would not be easy to provide
Completeness is proved in Figure 5.8
It is unnecessary, since only three spaces can exist
It has been proved by Bartlett
optionExplain: Right: they do not claim the list is complete.
Figure 5.8 defines the augmented space.
They say other spaces exist.
Bartlett did not prove any such thing.
questions.explain: The three spaces seem to cover most representations, but the authors stop short of a proof.
questions.rule: A list of spaces is not a proof of coverage.
questions.teaches: It would not be easy to provide formal demonstrations of the completeness of the list of problem spaces, and there are other spaces that might be considered.

questions.q: A researcher calls it far-fetched that a solver would match letters to digits by alphabet position, A as 1, B as 2. What do the authors say?
options: It is far-fetched, and no subject has ever used it
It is not far-fetched: one of Bartlett's subjects used it
It is the representation the authors expect most people to use
It is the same as the basic space, only written differently
optionExplain: The authors cite a subject who did.
Right: a real subject used it.
They make no such claim.
It is a global space of correspondences, which differs from the basic space.
questions.explain: Even unlikely-looking representations can occur in human solvers.
questions.teaches: One of Bartlett's (1958) subjects used precisely the representation that maps letters to digits by their numerical positions in the alphabet.

questions.q: Two note-taking systems allow different statements. How might you compare what each can express?
options: Count how many pages each of the systems uses up
Ask which of the two systems is the older one
Test which is the faster for one person to use
List the things and relations each lets you write
optionExplain: Size does not show what can be said.
Age says nothing about expressive power.
Speed measures use, not what can be expressed.
Right: the entities and relations show what a system can express.
questions.explain: Comparing means listing entities and relations. The card next does this for the three spaces.

questions.q: Match each space to what it admits.
pairs: Adds carries, disjunction, inequality and parity
questions.explain: Each space adds to the one before: carries and class relations, then arithmetic.

questions.q: A calendar app stores dates and names. A second also stores durations and before-or-after relations. How would the authors describe the second?
options: It admits more entities and relations: a richer space
It is the same space with only a different layout
It is a simpler space, because it has more labels in it
It is a different task, not a different space
optionExplain: Right: richness is measured by what is admitted.
More entities and relations make a different space.
More admitted information does not make a space simpler.
The task is the same; the representation differs.
questions.explain: Adding durations (entities) and before-or-after (a relation) enlarges what can be expressed.
questions.rule: More entities and relations, richer space.

questions.q: True or false: A space that admits letters, digits, carries, assignment and inequality, but not parity, disjunction or arithmetic, lies between the basic and augmented spaces.
questions.explain: It admits more than the basic space but fewer relations than the augmented space, so it is a minor variant between the two.
questions.rule: Subsets of entities and relations make new spaces.

questions.q: Is a space better described by its entities and relations or by its operators, according to the authors?
options: Operators are more basic, since they do the work
Entities and relations are more basic, since operators come later
Neither is more basic, since each depends on the other
Neither can describe a space
optionExplain: The authors say neither is more basic.
They rule this out as well.
Right: they characterize spaces equally well.
Either can; they choose entities and relations here.
questions.explain: A space can be characterized by the information it holds or by the operators that make and react to it; the two descriptions go together.
questions.rule: Information and operators define each other.
questions.teaches: Problem spaces can be characterized either by the types of information expressible at an element or by the operators that produce and react to such information, and neither characterization is more basic than the other.

questions.q: A team lists what a notes app can say, then removes one feature to see what is left. Which idea from the chapter is this?
options: Proving that the list of problem spaces is complete
Choosing the one space that human solvers actually use
Varying the subsets of entities and relations
Forming a plan in an abstract space of the puzzle
optionExplain: Removing a feature does not prove completeness.
Nothing about human use is tested.
Right: varying the list gives new spaces to examine.
The change here is to the list of what can be expressed, not planning.
questions.explain: Each subset of entities and relations defines another space, some of them interesting.
questions.rule: Vary the subsets to find new spaces.
questions.teaches: The notation suggests generating other interesting problem spaces by ringing changes on subsets of the entities and relations, with minor variants made by excluding relations from the algebraic space.

questions.q: Before solving a set of equations, what can you learn by counting unknowns and equations, without solving anything?
options: How many unknowns remain, and which equation comes first
The exact value of each of the unknowns in the system
Whether a proposed solution to the system is wrong
The number of digits that each answer will have
optionExplain: Right: counting shows where the system is most determined.
Counting does not produce values.
No solution has been proposed yet.
Digit counts do not come from counting equations.
questions.explain: Counting gives structure, not values. The card next uses this for the puzzle.
questions.rule: Count to find the order of attack.

questions.q: The space (letter carry, assignment) records that an assignment has been made but not which ____.
questions.explain: It keeps the fact of assignment and drops the value.

questions.q: The equations are a + b = 9, a = 4 and b + c = 8. Counting unknowns, which should be solved first?
options: b + c = 8, because it has the most letters
a + b = 9, because it is the first sum
Any order, because the counts are identical
a = 4, then a + b = 9, then b + c = 8
optionExplain: It has two unknowns when reached first.
It has two unknowns until a is known.
The order matters: one equation has a single unknown.
Right: each equation then has a single unknown.
questions.explain: Starting from the equation with one unknown lets each step leave one unknown in the next.

questions.q: True or false: In the DONALD puzzle, knowing only that D has been assigned is enough to suggest a good order for taking up the columns.
questions.explain: It fixes T and c2 and restricts R and G, but the authors find it insufficient to suggest a good order for the columns.

questions.q: When can the authors say whether this digit-free space guides solution well?
options: At once, from the definition of the space
Only after it has been tried
Never, since no digits are involved
Only when humans have used it
optionExplain: They state it cannot be known in advance.
Right: its inadequacy cannot be known until it has been tried.
It can be tried on a task.
Trying it does not need human data.
questions.explain: A space may disappoint on one task and help on another, so it has to be tested on the case.
questions.rule: Judge a space by trying it.
questions.teaches: The inadequacy of the digit-free space to guide solution efforts cannot be known until it has been tried, since in other cases it might be more useful.

questions.q: A student has 2p + q + 3r = 25, p = 3 and p + 2q = 11. In what order does counting unknowns suggest solving?
options: p first, then q from the third equation, then r
r first, since it has the largest coefficient
q first, since it appears in two of the equations
All three at the same time, as a single block
optionExplain: Right: p = 3 gives q = 4 and then r = 5.
r has the most unknowns around it and is reached last.
q needs p first.
The equations are solved one after another.
questions.explain: p = 3 makes the third equation give q = 4, and then 6 + 4 + 3r = 25 gives r = 5.
questions.rule: Use counts to order simultaneous equations.
questions.teaches: In other cases this digit-free space might be more useful, for example by suggesting the order of solving simultaneous equations.

questions.q: Adding two even digits gives which kind of result?
options: An odd result
Either, depending on the digits
A result that is always 0
An even result
optionExplain: Odd results come from adding an even digit and an odd one.
The parity of the result is fixed by the parities of the addends.
Even digits need not be 0.
Right: even plus even is even.
questions.explain: Parity passes through addition, and so coarse facts can drive inference. The card next defines the space.

questions.q: Match each description of a digit to its class in the parity and high-low space.
questions.explain: The two dimensions, parity and high or low, give four classes.

questions.q: True or false: In this space, adding two high digits is known to produce a carry of 1 into the next column.
questions.explain: Two high digits sum to at least 10, so a carry of 1 follows even though the digits themselves are unknown.

questions.q: Figure 5.10 relates N and B by a relation meaning opposite on the high-low dimension. If B is found to be low, what follows for N?
options: N is low as well
N is high
N is even
N is the same digit as B
optionExplain: That would follow from a relation meaning the same on the high-low dimension, not from one meaning opposite.
Right: opposite on the high-low dimension means one is high and the other low. The other relation means both high or both low.
Parity is a different dimension; the relation concerns high and low only.
Two letters never share a digit, and the relation does not name digits.
questions.explain: The authors use one relation for letters that must be the same on the high-low dimension and another for letters that must be opposite. With B low, opposite means N is high.
questions.rule: Relations link letters in a coarse space.
questions.teaches: The relation N ~ B means that N and B must be the same on the high-low dimension, both high or both low, while N -|- B means that they must have opposite values on that dimension.

questions.q: One sensor reports a liquid only as warm; another reports exactly 41 degrees. Which supports finer conclusions about the liquid?
options: The coarse report, as it leaves fewer cases to track
Both equally, since each is only a single report
The exact reading, as it allows finer inference
Neither, since sensors cannot support inference
optionExplain: Coarser knowledge allows weaker inferences.
The strength of an inference depends on how exact the premise is.
Right: finer information supports finer inference.
Either can; the finer one supports more.
questions.explain: From D high and odd the solver could infer only that T is even; from D set to 5 it infers that T is low and even.
questions.teaches: From D set to 5 the solver can infer T low and even, whereas from D known only to be high and odd, all that can be inferred is that T is even.

questions.q: If the digits 0 to 9 are sorted into low and high (5 or more) and into odd and even, how many fall in the low-even class?
options: 2, namely 0 and 2
5, namely every even digit
4, namely 0, 2, 4 and 6
3, namely 0, 2 and 4
optionExplain: 4 is even and below 5.
Only the even digits below 5 are low.
6 is not below 5.
Right: the even digits below 5.
questions.explain: Class sizes decide how many arrangements a box allows. The card next counts them.

questions.q: With D set to 5, the abstract solution box is consistent with ____ assignments in the basic space.
questions.explain: The count is 6 x 2 x 2 x 2 = 48.
questions.rule: Multiply the arrangements in each cell.

questions.q: A cell holds 3 digits and 3 letters must fill it, while another cell holds 2 digits for 2 letters. How many ways fill both cells?
optionExplain: This adds the letters instead of arranging them.
Right: 3! x 2! = 6 x 2.
This is 5!, treating all five letters as freely interchangeable across cells.
This counts only the first cell.
questions.explain: Letters can be arranged within each cell independently, and the counts multiply.

questions.q: True or false: Because 1680 assignments are 216 times fewer than 9!, a basic-space search guided by the abstract space examines 216 times fewer cases than before.
questions.explain: The authors say this reduction does not really measure the usefulness of the search, since a search in the basic space would not examine all 9! possibilities anyway.
questions.rule: A raw ratio can overstate the gain.

questions.q: One box fixes B only as low, O only as even, and N as high exactly when B is low. How many basic assignments does it fit?
options: 48, the same as for every one of the boxes
16, because fewer of the letters are fixed
144, which is 3 x 48, since less is fully fixed
Zero, since the box is inconsistent with the sum
optionExplain: The authors say three of the boxes fit more than 48.
Less fixed means more assignments, not fewer.
Right: less information per letter means more consistent assignments.
The box is admissible.
questions.explain: The more precisely a box fixes its letters, the fewer assignments it fits.
questions.teaches: Box 5 fits 3 x 48 = 144 basic assignments, because of B it is known only that it is low, of O only that it is even, and of N that it is high if and only if B is low.

questions.q: A scout narrows a search to five zones and searches each in fine detail. Which step of the chapter's method is this?
options: Using each admissible box to start a basic search
Ranking the five zones by size and searching only the largest
Averaging the zones together to give one single answer
Throwing away the zones that look odd or hard to search
optionExplain: Right: each box is checked for an actual solution consistent with it.
The method tests each box.
No averaging is done.
Boxes are tested, not discarded on looks.
questions.explain: Each of the five boxes starts a search in the basic space to see whether an actual solution fits it.
questions.rule: Coarse answers seed the detailed search.
questions.teaches: Each of the five admissible assignments in the abstract space can be taken as the starting point for a search in the basic problem space to determine whether an actual solution consistent with it exists.

questions.q: A traveller picks a route on a rough map, then follows detailed signs. What is the rough map doing?
options: Replacing the need to move at all
Giving a plan that guides the detailed steps
Showing every sign along the way
Proving that the route is the shortest
optionExplain: The journey still has to be made.
Right: coarse planning can shape fine action.
A rough map omits detail.
Planning does not guarantee shortest routes.
questions.explain: Coarse spaces can steer detailed search. The card next gives the numbers for the puzzle.

questions.q: Match each search of the chapter to the number of final nodes or nodes it reaches.
pairs: Basic-space searches guided by the abstract boxes
questions.explain: The chapter gives 87 for the first tree, 23 for the second, and 17 for the searches the abstract plan guides.

questions.q: An architect sketches room sizes first, then draws full plans for one sketch. Which is the plan space?
options: The full plan, since it has the most detail
The building itself, once it has been finished
The list of materials ordered for the building
The sketch of room sizes, which guides the full plan
optionExplain: That is the detailed space the plan guides.
A finished building is no space for planning.
A materials list is not an abstraction of the design.
Right: a plan space is an abstraction used to guide detailed work.
questions.explain: A plan space leaves out detail on purpose and is used to guide action in the detailed space.

questions.q: True or false: A solver who works only in the parity and high-low space can write down the complete solution of the puzzle.
questions.explain: These spaces cannot express exact digits, so they cannot hold all the information about the solution; they can only guide the detailed search.
questions.rule: Abstract spaces plan, they do not finish.

questions.q: What weakness do the authors say all three searches share?
options: They fail to infer promptly that E equals 9
They all ignore the given hint
They all need more than 9! steps
They all make the same tentative assignments
optionExplain: Right: the authors say all three suffer from this.
The hint is used in each.
None comes close to that count.
The authors do not say that.
questions.explain: Seeing E = 9 early would have shortened every one of the searches.
questions.rule: All three miss an early inference.
questions.teaches: All three searches (the 87-terminal and 23-node trees and the 17-node search from abstract solutions) suffer in efficiency from failing to infer promptly that E equals 9.

questions.q: A hiker finds that a rough map saves walking and concludes that planning is free. What do the authors note about planning in the abstract space?
options: It requires no effort, since the space is simple
It requires a human subject to run the whole thing
It takes much processing to use many constraints
It requires the full basic search to be done first
optionExplain: The authors say the search needs considerable processing.
Nothing is said about needing a human.
Right: the plan costs effort, though the final search is short.
The abstract search comes before the basic one.
questions.explain: The short final search hides the work of making the plan.
questions.rule: Count the cost of planning too.
questions.teaches: The search in the abstract space requires considerable processing to take advantage of the multiplicity of constraints that are implicit in the partial results attained along the way.

questions.q: Why list several ways to represent a task before watching anyone solve it?
options: So that every person will be forced to use one of them
So that the computer can replace the person
So the representation a person uses can be recognized when it appears
So that the task is made easier to solve
optionExplain: The aim is to observe, not to force.
Replacing the person is not the aim.
Right: a prepared catalogue makes recognition possible.
Easing the task is not the purpose.
questions.explain: Candidates prepared in advance let observers see which one a person is using. The card next states the authors' purpose.

questions.q: The simpler spaces form a base ____ from which the intelligence a subject shows can be measured.
questions.explain: The authors call them a base line for measuring a subject's intelligence.
questions.rule: A base line to measure from.

questions.q: A teacher lists three ways pupils might add fractions before watching the class work. Which purpose from the chapter does this serve?
options: Recognizing which method each pupil is using
Making all pupils use the first method
Proving that the three methods are the only ones
Replacing the pupils' work with a computer program
optionExplain: Right: a prepared set of methods allows recognition.
The aim is recognition, not instruction.
Completeness is not claimed.
No program is mentioned.
questions.explain: Having the candidates ready lets the observer identify the one in use.

questions.q: What do the authors say would happen to a subject who knew only enough to operate in a space as simple as the basic space?
options: He would solve it quickly
He would solve it only if he was given an extra hint
He would use the algebraic space instead of the basic
He would find it difficult or impossible to track so much
optionExplain: Simplicity of definition does not mean ease of use.
No such rule is given.
He is assumed to know only the basic space.
Right: the size of the basic space defeats human limits.
questions.explain: Humans cannot track large amounts of information or operate in highly systematic ways, so a subject confined to the basic space would struggle.
questions.rule: Human limits make the simple spaces hard.
questions.teaches: Since humans generally cannot keep track of large amounts of information and operate in highly systematic ways, a subject who knew only enough to operate in a space like the basic problem space would find the problem difficult or impossible.

questions.q: True or false: The authors expect human subjects to operate in the simple spaces they have described.
questions.explain: They say they would not expect a subject to operate in the simpler spaces, which instead form a base line for measuring the intelligence he shows.
questions.rule: Spaces are a base line, not a prediction.

questions.q: A researcher watches a veteran puzzle fan solve an unfamiliar puzzle. What do the authors say may happen when the subject is a cryptarithmetic buff?
options: The expert will use the basic space exactly as defined
The tables may be turned, and the researchers may learn
The study becomes invalid and must be set aside
The expert's moves cannot be analyzed at all by the authors
optionExplain: An expert is more likely to go beyond it.
Right: an expert may use representations the analysts had not thought of.
The authors see a chance to learn, not an invalid study.
They can be analyzed; they may also teach the analysts.
questions.explain: A skilled subject may reveal spaces beyond those in the catalogue.
questions.teaches: If a subject is a cryptarithmetic buff, the tables may be turned and the authors may learn a thing or two themselves.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A psychologist holds one recorded problem solving session. Which question can that single record not settle on its own?
options: Whether this person worked in some problem space
What the person said at each step of the work
Whether other people use the same mechanisms as this person
How the person's statements compare with a model
optionExplain: A single record can show this, because it is about that person's own behavior.
The record itself holds this directly.
Right: one case cannot show how widely its mechanisms are shared.
A model can be compared with one record, though the comparison is hard.
questions.explain: A single record speaks about one person. The card next lists the authors' questions.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: The authors group their thirteen questions into ____ sets.
questions.explain: The sets concern the theoretical analyses, the treatment of data, the testing of theory, and generality.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Which set holds the question: how does one compare the induced IPS with the behavior it is meant to explain?
options: Testing of theory
Treatment of the data
Generality
Theoretical analyses
optionExplain: Right: comparing a model with the behavior it explains is a test of the theory.
This set asks how to get information from verbal behavior.
This set asks whether the mechanisms are unique to the subject.
This set asks whether a problem space and an IPS can be found at all.
questions.explain: Comparing model with behavior and judging the goodness of approximation are the testing questions.
questions.rule: Match the question to its set.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Match each question to the set it belongs to.
pairs: Can the subject be viewed as working in some problem space?
How does one extract information from verbal behavior?
How can we evaluate the goodness of approximation?
Are the mechanisms for this subject unique to him?
questions.explain: Each question belongs to one of the four sets the authors list.
questions.rule: Sort questions by what they ask about.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A lab studies how one nurse triages patients, using a recording of her talking aloud. Which of its questions would the authors leave for later chapters?
options: Whether her talk can be turned into a record of what she knew
Whether a system can be written that behaves as she does
Whether the written system fits her recorded behavior
Whether other nurses triage with the same mechanisms
optionExplain: This is a data question the single case helps to answer.
This is a theoretical question tackled with the single case.
This is a testing question that the single case supports.
Right: questions of communality wait until more than one subject is studied.
questions.explain: A single subject cannot show what is common to many, so the authors postpone that.
questions.rule: Communality needs more than one subject.
questions.teaches: Because the chapter starts from a single attempt, questions of communality are mostly postponed; the authors still expect other subjects may fit the framework of the task analysis, an expectation to be tested.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: In this study, what is the raw material from which S3's problem solving is analyzed?
options: A questionnaire that he filled in after solving
A transcript of what he said aloud while working
Timings of every keystroke he made at the table
A rating by the experimenter of how hard he tried
optionExplain: A later account was not the data; the talk was recorded while he worked.
Right: the verbalizations are the main data.
