The authors say no timing information is available.
No such rating is part of the data.
questions.explain: The talk during the work is the data. The card next gives its name and its additions.
questions.rule: Data come from the talk during the work.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A transcript of a subject's verbalizations while solving is called a ____.
questions.explain: The word protocol names the transcript, together with the additions described on the card.
questions.rule: Protocol is the name for the transcript.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Which item would the authors count as an augmentation of a protocol?
options: A mark awarded for the elegance of his reasoning
An indication that the subject wrote an assignment on the paper
An essay the subject wrote about the puzzle a week later
The average time taken by other subjects on the puzzle
optionExplain: The text names no such grade.
Right: indications of writing are named as augmentations.
A later essay is not among the augmentations.
Timings of others are not named as augmentations.
questions.explain: The augmentations are about the subject's writing and the experimenter's remarks.
questions.rule: Augmentations bear on the performance itself.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: The authors had no separate record of S3's writing and no timing information.
questions.explain: True: the protocol shows when something was written, but there is no separate record of writing and no timing information.
questions.rule: Check what the record does and does not contain.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A researcher has only an audio recording of a cook talking aloud while planning a menu. How could she tell the cook jotted something on a list?
options: She cannot tell, so writing must be ignored completely
She must time the recording to the second
She must ask the cook to rate her own thinking
The speech itself usually makes it clear, as the authors found at B9
optionExplain: The authors found the speech usually shows when writing happened.
Timing is not what reveals writing; the authors had no timing.
Asking for self-ratings is not the authors' method.
Right: the protocol shows that something was written even without a separate record.
questions.explain: Talk and the experimenter's remarks often reveal actions that no separate record captured.
questions.teaches: Although no separate record of what S3 wrote was available, it is usually clear from the protocol when he wrote something, as in B9.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A theory claims that people solve puzzles in a certain general way. How could one test it against one person's recorded attempt?
options: Build a specific system that reproduces that attempt and see how well it fits
Compare that person's speed with a national average for puzzles
Ask the person whether the theory sounds right
Count the words spoken and compare them with another puzzle
optionExplain: Right: a specific system for the attempt makes the general claim testable.
Speed says little about the way the person solved the puzzle.
Opinion about a theory is not a test of how behavior fits it.
Word counts do not show what processes produced the behavior.
questions.explain: A general claim meets one attempt through a specific system for that attempt. The card next names it.
questions.rule: Fit a specific system to a specific attempt.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: The authors call a specific IPS fitted to one attempt a ____ and treat it as one data point.
questions.explain: Many such small theories are the places where the general theory is put to the test.
questions.rule: A specific IPS for an attempt is a microtheory.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Which item is a microtheory in the authors' sense?
options: The broad claim that people use heuristics on all tasks
A table of how long ten students took on the puzzle
A symbolic system that generates the behavior of S3's one attempt on the puzzle
The remark that cryptarithmetic puzzles are hard
optionExplain: That is the general theory, not a theory of one attempt.
A table of times is data, not a symbolic system that generates behavior.
Right: it is a specific IPS for one segment of behavior.
An opinion about difficulty does not generate behavior.
questions.explain: A microtheory is a symbolic system that generates a segment of behavior; by scientific canons that makes it a theory.
questions.rule: A generating system is a theory.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: Although a microtheory covers only one attempt, it serves as a single data point at which the more general theory is put to the test.
questions.explain: True: the authors treat each microtheory as a single data point at which the more general theory is put to the test.
questions.rule: Small theories are data points for the large one.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: The authors use the word microtheory in a narrower sense than its current one, which covers a theory of a whole miniature domain such as rat behavior in a T-maze.
questions.explain: The footnote says the term is currently used in a somewhat broader sense, for a theory applying to a miniature domain of behavior, while the authors use it for one IPS fitted to one attempt.
questions.rule: Say what the term means in this book.
questions.teaches: In current usage a microtheory means a theory applying to a miniature domain of behavior, for example a theory of rat behavior in the T-maze; the authors use it more narrowly.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A coach writes an exact rule set that reproduces how one club player picked her moves in one game. What is that rule set in the authors' terms?
options: The general theory of chess playing
A microtheory of that game, and one data point for a general theory
A protocol of the player's words
An error of omission in the player's reasoning
optionExplain: A rule set for one game is specific, not the general theory.
Right: a specific system for a specific attempt is a microtheory.
A protocol is a transcript; the rule set generates behavior.
Errors of omission are shortfalls of a fitted system, not the system itself.
questions.explain: Specific system, specific attempt, so a microtheory.
questions.rule: Specific IPS plus specific attempt equals microtheory.
questions.teaches: Because the raw data of an attempt are sequentially interdependent, each microtheory has to be highly specific to its attempt; a general scheme alone cannot unravel them.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Why might a researcher need a detailed model of one person before the person's talk can be understood?
options: People speak too quickly for a transcript to be accurate
A model is needed only to satisfy journal editors
Each statement depends on what came before, so it cannot be read in isolation
Every person solves a puzzle in an entirely unique way
optionExplain: Transcript accuracy is not the authors' reason.
The reason given is about the data, not publication.
Right: sequential dependence is the reason the authors give.
The authors expect common mechanisms, so uniqueness is not the reason.
questions.explain: Sequential interdependence means a statement's meaning depends on the state reached. The card next states the argument.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: The raw verbalizations make sense only when seen through the lens of an appropriate ____, because the data are sequentially interdependent.
questions.explain: The data cannot be unraveled without a highly specific IPS.
questions.rule: Read the data through a specific IPS.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A reader asks why Chapter 6 bothers with so much detail on one man. Which reply follows the authors?
options: The detail is appropriate for asking if the theory fits, though not what one wants most of the time
The detail is needed because one man represents everyone
The detail is unneeded, and Chapter 7 drops it entirely
The detail is required by law for all protocols
optionExplain: Right: they admit the level is beyond what one would usually want.
They do not claim that one man represents everyone.
Chapter 7 is more abstract, but its validity rests partly on this detail.
No such requirement is mentioned.
questions.explain: Detail is costly but suited to testing fit.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: If the detailed analysis of S3 had shown that no specific IPS could fit his behavior, the validity of Chapter 7's abstract analyses would be in doubt.
questions.explain: The authors say the validity of the abstraction depends in part on the essential correctness of detailed analysis of this kind.
questions.rule: Abstractions inherit the risk of the detail beneath them.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A school adviser wants to understand one pupil's quarrel with a long homework task by recording the pupil thinking aloud. Why might a detailed model of that pupil's steps help?
options: Each remark depends on the earlier steps, so a specific model can show what the remark meant
Every remark stands alone, so the model only counts words
A model removes the need to listen to the recording
A detailed model proves the same steps work for all pupils
optionExplain: Right: sequential interdependence is what a specific model unravels.
The point is that remarks do not stand alone.
The recording remains the data.
A model of one pupil does not by itself show what holds for all.
questions.explain: A step's meaning depends on the state the solver was in, which a specific model reconstructs.
questions.rule: Interpret each step by the state it came from.
questions.teaches: The authors also note that Chapter 7 carries out a great deal of analysis at a more abstract level, but the validity of that abstraction depends partly on the essential correctness of detailed analysis like this chapter's.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A subject speaks about two words a second and the transcript has 2000 words. About how long did the session last?
options: About 200 seconds
About 4000 seconds
About 1000 seconds, or a quarter of an hour or more
About 20 seconds
optionExplain: That would imply ten words a second.
That would imply half a word a second.
Right: 2000 words at two a second is 1000 seconds.
That would imply a hundred words a second.
questions.explain: Duration is the word count divided by the speaking rate. The card next gives the authors' figures.
questions.rule: Words divided by rate gives time.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: S3 was asked to ____ aloud at all times while he worked, and his words were tape-recorded.
questions.explain: Thinking aloud produces the verbalizations that form the protocol.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A protocol has 1800 words and the authors' rate of about two words a second applies. About how long did the session last?
options: About 30 minutes
About 15 minutes
About 7 minutes
About 90 minutes
optionExplain: That would need 3600 seconds, or twice the words.
Right: 1800 divided by 2 is 900 seconds, which is 15 minutes.
That would be 450 seconds, or half the words.
That would be 5400 seconds, far above the rate implied.
questions.explain: Divide words by two to get seconds, then convert to minutes: 900 seconds is 15 minutes.
questions.rule: Estimate time from words and rate.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: No timing information is available for S3's attempt; the authors estimated about 20 minutes from the word count and a typical speaking rate.
questions.explain: True: no timing information is available; they estimated about 20 minutes from the word count and a typical rate.
questions.rule: Distinguish an estimate from a measurement.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A study of a mechanic thinking aloud has a transcript but no stopwatch record. Following the authors, how should the analyst treat time?
options: Refuse to use the protocol at all
Invent a stopwatch record from memory
Assume each word took exactly one second
Estimate it from the word count if needed, and avoid analysis that depends on it
optionExplain: The authors used theirs without timings.
Inventing a record would add no evidence.
The authors use about two words a second, not one.
Right: the authors did the same, since they cannot use timing.
questions.explain: An estimate suffices when the analysis does not rely on timing.
questions.rule: Use an estimate only where timing is not needed.
questions.teaches: The authors say timing information is not critical, since they have no way of making use of it in their analysis.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Why might an analyst number every short phrase of a transcript?
options: So that each phrase can be counted as one unit of thought
So that the subject can read it back aloud
So that any point in the talk can be referred to exactly
So that the experimenter's remarks can be left out
optionExplain: The numbering does not claim to mark units of thought.
The numbering is for the analysts, not for the subject.
Right: numbering eases reference.
Experimenter remarks are numbered too.
questions.explain: Numbered phrases give names to places in the protocol. The card next says how the authors did it.
questions.rule: Number the phrases to refer to them.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: The protocol is labeled B1, B2, ..., B____.
questions.explain: There are 321 numbered phrases, including both subject and experimenter.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A reader sees the label B189 in the book. What does it point to?
options: A numbered phrase of the protocol, such as one of S3's utterances
The 189th second of the recording
A production in the production system
A column of the sum
optionExplain: Right: B numbers label the short phrases of the protocol.
No timing exists; the numbers label phrases.
Productions are labeled P1, P2, and so on.
Columns are labeled col. 1 to col. 6, or numbered as in the problem space.
questions.explain: B-numbers label phrases of the protocol; P-numbers label productions.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: The phrase boundaries were chosen on a precise theory of what makes one unit of thought.
questions.explain: The authors say the phrasing rests on a naive assessment of a single assertion or reference and does not affect the analysis explicitly.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A team splits a 40 minute interview into numbered lines to refer to them. Following the authors, what should they claim for the numbering?
options: That each line is exactly one unit of thought
That the numbering fixes the length of the interview
That the numbering must be redone by several judges
That it aids reference, without claiming each line is one unit of thought
optionExplain: The authors make no such claim.
Numbering says nothing about duration.
Reliability by multiple judges is a different matter.
Right: the authors use the phrasing to facilitate reference.
questions.explain: Numbering is a convenience for pointing at places in the talk.
questions.rule: Do not read theory into labels.
questions.teaches: The 321 phrases come at a rate of about one every three to four seconds, which the authors admit may seem a rather low density of data.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A researcher wants the full meaning of what each speaker said. What is a danger of coding every remark into a few categories first?
options: The remarks become too easy to analyze
Meaning that the categories cannot hold is lost
The categories are always too numerous to use
The speakers become aware of being recorded
optionExplain: Coding does not cause an excess of ease.
Right: a coarse code throws away the very content one hoped to get.
The worry is loss of meaning, not too many categories.
Coding happens after recording and does not affect the speakers.
questions.explain: Coding that loses meaning discards data. The card next gives the authors' argument.
questions.rule: Coding can discard what you came for.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Language is already a device for ____ information, so recoding it with all meaning kept hardly encodes it at all.
questions.explain: A lossless recode adds nothing, and a lossy recode discards data.
questions.rule: A lossless recode is no recode.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: S3 says that he will make R a 9. How do the authors treat such a phrase?
options: It must be recoded into a number and a letter before use
It is easy to read as it stands and needs no special coding
It is thrown out, since it is only an intention
It is replaced by the experimenter's summary
optionExplain: The authors say easy parts need no recoding.
Right: parts that are easy to code do not need it.
Such a phrase gives clear evidence of an assignment.
The original words are kept.
questions.explain: Clear utterances are usable directly; recoding would add nothing.
questions.rule: Do not recode what is already clear.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: The authors most want to keep in original form the half-finished, self-correcting remarks that are hard to code, and see little need to clean up a plain statement such as making R a 9.
questions.explain: Parts that are easy to code do not need recoding; parts that are not easy to code should stay raw so that whatever information they hold is kept.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A team studying how families decide on holidays has recordings of meetings. One analyst proposes five tick-box categories for every sentence. What would the authors' objection be, if the aim is to capture full meaning?
options: Five categories are too few to be statistically valid
The sentences are too short to be coded
Families never speak in sentences
The ticks would discard much of the meaning the recordings were made to capture
optionExplain: The authors' objection is about meaning, not number of categories.
Short phrases are what make unambiguous measurement possible.
The authors make no such claim.
Right: lossy coding throws away the very data sought.
questions.explain: When the goal is meaning, the content must be kept.
questions.rule: Decide on coding by what you want to learn.
questions.teaches: The authors note that the common practice in psychology is to code verbal data to indicate a few underlying attributes, but here they want the full content of the utterances, meaning included.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A person solving a puzzle writes only now and then, but talks throughout. What does this suggest about where the work happens?
options: Much of it happens internally, between the written marks
All of it happens on the paper, so silence means rest
None of it can be known, so the talk is useless
It happens only when the experimenter speaks
optionExplain: Right: long periods of talk with no writing point to internal work.
Talk during unwritten periods shows work with no writing.
The talk is the main evidence about internal steps.
The experimenter's remarks are not the source of the thinking.
questions.explain: Periods of talk without writing reveal internal work. The card next names the internal actions.
questions.rule: Look for work behind the marks.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Match each of S3's internal actions to its kind.
pairs: Reading a column to conclude that R is odd
Listing the odd digits R could be
questions.explain: The authors list three kinds of internal action: assigning, inferring relations, and generating digits.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: S3 reads column 2 and concludes that the digit for R must be odd. Which kind of internal action is this?
options: Assigning a digit to a letter
Generating digits that satisfy a relation
Inferring a relation from a column
Writing the answer on the paper
optionExplain: No digit is given to R by this step.
Generation would list the odd digits afterwards.
Right: he draws a conclusion from the structure of a column.
No writing is involved in this step.
questions.explain: Reading a column and concluding something about a letter is inference.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: Long stretches of S3's work pass with no writing, so a space of written actions alone would miss most of it.
questions.explain: True: long stretches pass with no writing, so a space of written actions would miss most of his work.
questions.rule: Written marks leave out most thinking.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Compared with a subject who has no pencil and paper, what does the authors' analysis expect for S3?
options: He solves much faster, since writing does the inferring
He can no longer think aloud
He needs separate operators for reading the paper
He has little trouble remembering his assignments
optionExplain: Writing does not do the inferring; it holds assignments.
Thinking aloud was requested of all subjects.
The authors define no operators for writing or reading.
Right: the main effect of writing is that S3 does not have much difficulty remembering assignments.
questions.explain: Paper acts as an external memory for assignments, not as the place where inferences happen.
questions.teaches: The distinction between internally and externally stored information does not seem an essential part of the knowledge-state; the important effect of writing is that S3 has little difficulty remembering assignments.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Which statement narrows a letter's value without naming its digit?
options: The letter is 7
The letter has to be greater than 5
The letter was given the digit 9
The letter equals the digit 4
optionExplain: This names a digit.
Right: an inequality limits the possibilities without fixing one digit.
This also names a digit.
This names a digit too.
questions.explain: A letter can be limited without being fixed. The card next lists the kinds of limit.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Match each of S3's statements to its relation.
pairs: R has to be a number greater than 5
R has to be an odd number
questions.explain: S3 uses equality, inequality and parity relations.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Which of S3's statements is an assignment, as against an inferred relation?
options: A would have to equal 5
R has to be greater than 5
Let us start back here and make R a 7
R has to be an odd number
optionExplain: This is an equality inferred from the column.
This is an inequality.
Right: he chooses a digit for R as a trial.
This is a parity.
questions.explain: An assignment chooses a digit; the others state what the sum forces.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: The authors keep equality and assignment apart because S3 distinguishes between a digit inferred to equal a letter and one assigned to it.
questions.explain: True: they keep them apart because S3 distinguishes between a digit inferred to equal a letter and one assigned to it.
questions.rule: Inferred is not the same as assumed.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A bookkeeper tries filing an unclear receipt under travel to see if the totals work, then later finds the totals force it to be 40. Which pair matches S3's two moves?
options: The trial filing is like an assignment; the forced total is like an inferred equality
Both are assignments, since both name an amount
Both are inferred equalities, since both name an amount
Neither compares with S3, since he never trialed anything
optionExplain: Right: one is chosen as a trial, the other follows from the structure.
The forced amount follows from the structure, as an inferred equality does.
The trial filing is chosen, not forced.
S3 trialed values such as R equal to 7.
questions.explain: The trial is chosen; the forced value is deduced. S3 keeps the two apart.
questions.rule: Mark which values are trials and which are forced.
questions.teaches: At B95 S3 remarks that all of this is going on the assumption that R is 7, which he had assigned at B61, showing he keeps assigned digits distinct from inferred ones.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A solver knows a letter is either 1 or 2 and nothing else. How should this be recorded?
options: As a set of two alternatives, not as one digit
As the digit 1, the smaller one
As no knowledge at all about the letter
As the digit 3, the sum of the two
optionExplain: Right: a disjunction keeps both possibilities open.
Choosing one would lose the other possibility.
The solver knows something definite.
Nothing makes the letter the sum of the alternatives.
questions.explain: Partial knowledge can be a short list of alternatives. The card next names this form.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A letter that is limited only by the digits not yet assigned is called ____.
questions.explain: Free letters are constrained only by membership in the remaining unassigned digits.
questions.rule: Free means unconstrained except by the pool.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: S3 says the solution for O is independent of the rest of the column. Which concept is this?
options: O is last
O equals 1 or 2
O is free
O is greater than 5
optionExplain: Last means O will be the final digit remaining; that is a different claim, made later.
That would be a disjunctive set.
Right: nothing in the column constrains O beyond the unassigned digits.
That would be an inequality.
questions.explain: Independence from the column is what free means.
questions.rule: Free is independent of the column.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Match each statement to the concept it expresses.
pairs: O may be any digit still unassigned
O will get the only digit that remains
questions.explain: The notation has a disjunction, a free qualifier and a last qualifier.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A planner knows guest A sits at table 1 or 2, guest B can sit at any table left, and guest C will take whichever seat remains. Which guest corresponds to a last letter?
options: Guest A, who has two options
Guest C, who gets the one seat left over
Guest B, who can go anywhere left
None of them, since last concerns only guests
optionExplain: A has a disjunctive set.
Right: the last element takes whatever remains in the free set.
B is like a free letter.
The concept applies to anything drawn from a shrinking pool.
questions.explain: Last means the final item left in the pool.
questions.teaches: Both qualifiers occur for the same letter: S3 sees O as free at B242 and, at B248, as probably the last one he will ever find.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A solver reads the rightmost column and says that two L's plus a carry of 1 gives R. What is the best description of this step?
options: Solving a system of simultaneous equations
Looking up the answer in a table of results
Guessing digits at random until the column fits
Reading what a single column implies, rather than rearranging an equation
optionExplain: No equations are combined.
No table is involved.
The step is reasoned, not random.
Right: it uses the column as it stands.
questions.explain: Reading a column is different from rearranging equations. The card next says which S3 does.
questions.rule: Read the column as it stands.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: S3 shows clear evidence of manipulating equations algebraically.
questions.explain: His equations all correspond to reading a column; algebraic manipulation shows clearly in the protocols of other subjects, not S3.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Match each remark about carries to the way S3 handles carries.
pairs: Adding 3 and 3 and then the carry to get 7
Concluding that 1 is carried into the left-hand column
Asking where L plus L could exceed 10
Supposing that 2 is carried from the column
questions.explain: S3 uses, infers, seeks and possibly assigns carries.
questions.rule: Four ways to handle a carry.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A reader sees S3 say suppose I carry 2 and decides the transcript must be wrong, since carries can only be 0 or 1. What do the authors conclude?
options: The transcript was mistyped and the line should be dropped
S3 has misunderstood the rules of addition entirely
For S3 the values of the carry are not restricted to 0 and 1
Carries in this puzzle can in fact reach 2
optionExplain: The authors take the remark as evidence about S3.
The authors do not draw that conclusion from one remark.
Right: the remark shows he is not held to legal carry values.
The remark concerns S3's thinking, not the arithmetic of the puzzle.
questions.explain: A record of an apparent mistake is data about how the subject thinks.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Another subject rewrites L + L + 1 = R as R minus 1 equals twice L. How does this compare with S3?
options: The other subject manipulates the equation algebraically; S3 reads the column
The same; S3 also rearranges every equation first
S3 does worse, since only algebra can solve the puzzle
S3 also rewrites the equation but silently
optionExplain: Right: such manipulations show up in other subjects' protocols, not S3's.
The authors find no evidence of that.
The authors say nothing of the kind.
There is no evidence of silent rewriting.
questions.explain: S3's equations come from reading columns.
questions.rule: Compare methods by what the protocol shows.
questions.teaches: Algebraic manipulations of equations show up clearly in the protocols of other subjects, so S3's method is a feature of this subject, not of the task.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Why might a formal grammar for a solver's states include a placeholder for some digit, besides the ten digits themselves?
options: The solver is unsure how many digits there are
Placeholders replace the letters of the puzzle
Placeholders are needed only for the carries
The solver sometimes works through a column without naming specific digits
optionExplain: The ten digits are known.
The letters remain.
The need arises with digits in a column.
Right: a placeholder stands for a general value.
questions.explain: A general digit stands for a value not yet pinned down. The card next gives the authors' choice.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: The chapter writes the description of S3's problem space in ____ notation, a formal grammar.
questions.explain: Figure 6.1 gives the space in BNF.
questions.rule: Describe the space by a grammar.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: In Figure 6.1 letters and carries are put in one class called variables. What reason do the authors give?
options: Because both are single digits
For several purposes they are equivalent for S3
Because the grammar cannot name them separately
Because the experimenter ruled it
optionExplain: Letters stand for digits, but a carry is a different kind of thing.
Right: S3 treats them alike in several ways.
It could have named them apart.
No such rule is mentioned.
questions.explain: Pooling letters and carries as variables follows S3's treatment of them.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: The set free-letters loses members as S3 assigns digits, while all-letters is a constant set.
questions.explain: True: free-letters loses members as letters are assigned, while all-letters is a constant set.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A teacher writes a rule for a game state using the sign V so that one square can be marked X V O. Why do the authors adopt a similar sign?
options: It marks a digit that has been assigned
It writes alternatives like G = 1 V 2 more cleanly than the other forms
It stands for the carry between columns
It replaces the need for a tag on expressions
optionExplain: Assignment uses a different arrow.
Right: the other ways of writing it are clumsier or somewhat ambiguous.
Carries are written with c and a number.
Tags are unaffected.
questions.explain: A sign for or avoids awkward notations such as lists.
questions.teaches: The authors use the disjunction sign to write G = 1 V 2 rather than G = (1 2), G = 1 2 or G = 1, 2, all of which are either clumsier or somewhat ambiguous.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Why might a model of someone's knowledge store how the fact is held, as well as the fact?
options: Facts are stored only in order to be forgotten later
The way a fact is held never changes behavior
It makes the model shorter than a list of facts
Whether it is new, in doubt or ruled out affects what the person does next
optionExplain: Facts are stored for use.
How sure someone is can change what they try.
Added tags make the record longer, not shorter.
Right: the mode of knowing guides later action.
questions.explain: How a fact is held matters for action. The card next gives the authors' tags.
questions.rule: Record the fact and its mode.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Match each tag to its meaning for an expression such as R > 5.
pairs: S3 has just come by the knowledge
S3 knows it is impossible given the rest
S3 believes it but is uncertain of the grounds
questions.explain: Each tag is a mode of knowing attached to an expression.
questions.rule: Tags say how an expression is held.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: Once S3 has verified that R is greater than 5, the analysts would attach the same tag as when he first believed it without grounds.
questions.explain: A different mode of knowing calls for a different tag; the tag records how he holds the expression at that moment.
questions.rule: Tags track the mode of knowing.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: S3 holds that R is greater than 5 but cannot say why. Which tag would the analysts attach?
options: unclear
new
open box
no tag at all
optionExplain: Right: he believes it but is uncertain of the grounds.
New means he has just come by it, not that grounds are missing.
The open box marks an impossibility.
The mode of knowing is recorded by a tag.
questions.explain: Belief without known grounds is unclear.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: S3 is concerned with whether R > 5 holds, but he does not know whether it is true. Which tag expresses that?
options: unclear
note
unknown
new
optionExplain: Unclear means he believes it already.
Note marks a known fact important to other considerations.
Right: unknown marks concern with an expression whose truth he does not know.
New marks fresh knowledge, not concern.
questions.explain: Concern without knowledge is unknown.
questions.rule: Unknown means asked but not answered.
questions.teaches: The tag unknown means S3 is concerned for some reason with whether the expression is true but does not know; the tag note means he knows it and the fact has become important to other considerations.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A student circles one date in her notes, saying she knows it, and it keeps mattering to other questions. Which of S3's tags matches this?
options: unknown
unclear
new
note
optionExplain: She knows the date, so it is not unknown.
She is not unsure of the grounds.
She is not just now learning it.
Right: the fact is known and has become important to other considerations.
questions.explain: Known and important to other thinking is note.
questions.teaches: A tag is only a mode of knowing attached to an expression: the same expression R > 5 can carry any of several tags, depending on how S3 holds it at that moment.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A program stores an item marked uncertain. Where does the meaning of that mark lie in an information processing view?
options: In the feeling of doubt the program has
In how the program reacts when it meets the marked item
In the English word chosen by the person who wrote it
In a number that records the strength of doubt
optionExplain: The authors do not put such feelings in the IPS.
Right: the program's reactions define the meaning.
The word is only a paraphrase.
No such number is part of the representation described.
questions.explain: A mark means what the program does with it. The card next explains the authors' position.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: In the IPS a state-expression is a ____ structure, such as the list (R, >, 5, unclear), and not a mental concept.
questions.explain: The paraphrases are not part of the IPS; the program's reactions define what a tag means.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Which of these is how the IPS represents R > 5 marked unclear?
options: A feeling of doubt attached to R
The sentence S3 spoke aloud
A list of symbols such as (R, >, 5, unclear)
A number between 0 and 1 for confidence
optionExplain: The IPS has no feelings.
The utterance is data, not the representation.
Right: a symbol structure isomorphic to a sequence of symbols.
No such number appears in the representation.
questions.explain: The representation is a symbol structure.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: In the authors' scheme the state-expression L unclear, with a tag on a lone variable, has a meaning.
questions.explain: Only L with the open box and L unknown make sense on a lone variable; the other combinations have no meaning and do not occur.
questions.rule: Check which tags fit a lone variable.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A thermostat stores the list (temperature, >, 20, warm). Does that show that the thermostat believes the room is warm, on the authors' view?
options: No; what the item means is fixed by how the device reacts to it
Yes, since any stored item is a belief
Yes, since the word warm is in the list
No, because thermostats store no symbols
optionExplain: Right: reaction defines the meaning, not the English gloss.
The authors deny that a gloss adds the concept.
The word is a label for readers.
The point is the gloss, not whether symbols exist.
questions.explain: A gloss is not a mechanism.
questions.rule: Do not read English glosses as mechanisms.
questions.teaches: The combinations with no meaning do not occur in the protocol, so the authors give them no meaning rather than excluding them formally from the grammar, which would only complicate Figure 6.1.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A solver hopes that a carry will turn out to be 1, though it might not be possible. Is it sensible to model that hope as a goal?
options: Yes: a goal to infer it differs from assuming it is so
No, since a goal must always be reached
No, since only digits can be goals
Yes, but only if the solver already knows the carry
optionExplain: Right: setting out to obtain a fact is not the same as taking it for granted.
A goal can fail.
Goals can concern relations too.
If he already knew it, there would be nothing to obtain.
questions.explain: A hope to obtain a fact differs from assuming it. The card next names the goal types.
questions.rule: A goal is not an assumption.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A goal of type ____ seeks to obtain an expression, whereas a goal of type check works on information already in the knowledge-state.
questions.explain: Get goals obtain new expressions; check goals test existing ones.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: S3 wants to see whether his final assignment satisfies every column of the sum. Which goal is this?
options: A get goal on R
A get goal on c6 = 1
A check goal on the set of columns
A constraint such as R odd
optionExplain: This seeks one letter's value.
This seeks one carry.
Right: the aim is to test information already held.
A constraint limits a variable and is not a goal.
questions.explain: Checking all columns tests an existing result.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Which of these are constraint expressions rather than assignments? Select all that apply.
options: R odd
G = 1 V 2
optionExplain: Right: a parity limits R.
An arrow marks an assignment.
Right: a set of alternatives.
Right: an inequality.
This is an equality fixing T, not a constraint.
questions.explain: Parity, sets of alternatives and inequalities limit a variable without fixing it.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A planner sets the goal of finding a train that arrives before nine, though none may exist. How does the authors' account see forming such a goal?
options: As a mistake, since goals must be known to be possible
As trying to obtain the fact, which differs from assuming the train exists
As a check goal, since a train is already known
As an assignment of a train to the plan
optionExplain: The authors accept a degree of wishful thinking.
Right: S3 can set a goal such as get c6 = 1 without assuming it.
Nothing is known yet, so it is a get goal.
Nothing has been assigned.
questions.explain: Goals can be wishful.
questions.rule: A goal is an attempt to obtain.
questions.teaches: The goal get c6 = 1 has a degree of wishful thinking, since there may be no possibility that c6 could be 1 given the rest of the knowledge-state, yet S3 is capable of forming it.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A solver who knows R is odd writes 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 as candidates for R without checking which digits are used. Which kind of step is this?
options: Testing whether a chosen digit is allowed
Reading a column to infer a new fact
Writing the digit on the paper
Generating the values consistent with what is known about R
optionExplain: Nothing has been chosen or tested yet.
No column is read.
The digits are listed, not written.
Right: listing the candidates that fit what is known.
questions.explain: Listing what fits is a separate step from choosing or testing. The card next names the four operators.
questions.rule: Generate, assign and test are separate.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Match each operator to its job.
pairs: Infers information from a column's letters and carries
Lists the admissible values for a variable
Assigns a digit to a variable
Reports whether a digit is admissible for a letter
questions.explain: These are the four operators of the problem space.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: R is known to be odd and above 5, and 7 is already used by another letter. What does GN output for R?
options: 9 only, since 7 is taken
7 and 9, since GN ignores which digits are already used
No digits, since 7 is taken
optionExplain: Removing used digits is the work of TD.
The restriction R > 5 removes 1, 3 and 5.
Right: GN gives admissible values without taking assignments into account.
GN does not check use.
questions.explain: GN works from the known restrictions; TD later rejects digits already used.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: GN removes the digits that are already assigned to other letters.
questions.explain: GN outputs admissible values without regard to previous assignments; TD checks for a digit being already used.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A hotel clerk lists free rooms, picks one, and then checks that no other guest holds it. Which step is like TD?
options: The final check that no other guest holds the room and that it suits the guest
Listing the free rooms
Picking one room
Reading the booking sheet for conclusions
optionExplain: Right: TD tests that the digit is unused and satisfies the known restrictions.
Listing is like GN.
Picking is like AV.
Reading and concluding is like PC.
questions.explain: TD tests both use and restrictions.
questions.teaches: When a digit is not admissible, TD reports the expression that caused the failure; it determines whether the digit is already used for another letter and whether it satisfies the known restrictions on the letter.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A tree for a computer program's search has no repeated node. Why can one not assume the same of a human solver?
options: Humans have far more nodes to search than computers
Humans do not use search at all
Computers cannot repeat a search
Nothing guarantees the human avoids searching the same part again
optionExplain: The issue is repetition, not number of nodes.
The authors assume S3 searches in a problem space.
A program can repeat unless it is built to prevent it.
Right: a person's search may repeat.
questions.explain: A program can be built to avoid repetition, but a person's program is unknown. The card next gives the graph the authors use.
questions.rule: Do not assume a person never repeats.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: The PBG keeps the full dynamics of search, including ____.
questions.explain: That is why it is preferred to a simple tree here.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: In Chapters 4 and 5 trees could be drawn without repeated parts. What made this safe?
options: The subjects were instructed never to repeat
Systematic generators, or specific tests for duplication
The trees were drawn after the solutions were known
The tasks were too small for repetition
optionExplain: No such instruction is mentioned.
Right: these built-in devices prevented any part from being searched twice.
Knowing the solution does not prevent repetition.
Size was not the reason given.
questions.explain: The earlier trees were of programs that could not repeat; S3's program is not known to be like that.
questions.rule: Trees suit programs built not to repeat.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: The PBG was devised because the authors knew nothing yet of S3's program and had to induce it.
questions.explain: True: the situation is that they know nothing yet of his program and must induce it.
questions.rule: Here the data come first and the program is induced.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: An analyst maps how a student redrafts an essay, sometimes returning to earlier wording. Which of the authors' reasons for a PBG carries over?
options: The student has a program in hand which one wants to understand
The student's own procedure is unknown, so repeated visits must be kept in the record
A tree is always shorter than a graph with repeats
The student can be assumed to avoid revisiting
optionExplain: That was the situation for LT, not for S3.
Right: with the program unknown, repetition has to be recorded.
Brevity is not the authors' reason.
That is exactly what cannot be assumed.
questions.explain: When the program is unknown, keep the repeats.
questions.teaches: In analyzing LT a program was already in hand and the aim was to understand its behavior; the PBG reverses this, since the subject's program is what the analysis must induce.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: In a diagram of a search over time, a new node appears directly below an earlier one, joined by a vertical line. What might that line stand for?
options: A new operator applied to the earlier state
A move to an entirely new state of knowledge
The end of the protocol
A return to the state of knowledge the earlier node shows
optionExplain: Operators are drawn as horizontal arrows.
A new state would follow along an arrow.
Nothing marks the end this way.
Right: coming back to a state is drawn below it.
questions.explain: A vertical line records a return. The card next gives the full set of conventions.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Match each element of a PBG to what it shows.
pairs: A horizontal arrow to the right
An operator applied to a state
A vertical line to a new node below
A return to the same state of knowledge
questions.explain: These three elements carry most of the meaning of the graph.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Node P is on a lower row than node Q. What do the PBG rules say about their order?
options: P was generated later than Q
P was generated earlier than Q
P and Q hold the same state
P comes from Q by one operator
optionExplain: Right: time runs right, then down.
Lower rows come later in time.
Position alone does not show this.
An operator would show as a horizontal arrow.
questions.explain: Rows later in the graph are later in time.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: A doubled horizontal line shows a repeated application of the same operator to the same state of knowledge.
questions.explain: True: a doubled line shows a repeated application of the same operator to the same state of knowledge.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A hiker tries the north path from a fork, comes back, and tries the north path again. Using the PBG conventions, how is the second attempt drawn?
options: A single arrow to a new node, as for any first attempt
A vertical line only, with no further arrow
A node below the fork for the return, then a doubled line for the repeated move
A dotted line back to the start
optionExplain: The repeat would be hidden.
The second attempt is a move and needs an arrow.
Right: return goes down, and a repeated application of the same operator doubles the line.
No dotted lines belong to the conventions.
questions.explain: Return is down; repetition is a doubled arrow.
questions.rule: Mark the return, then mark the repeat.
questions.teaches: A repeated application of the same operator to the same state of knowledge is shown by doubling the horizontal line.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A subject applies Q1 then Q2, then goes back to the state he had after Q1. Is that move back an operator in the graph?
options: Yes, as an operator for undoing Q2
Yes, as the operator Q3
No, because the subject did not really go back
No; going back involves no operation, so it is not drawn as one
optionExplain: Returning is not treated as an operator.
Q3 is a different operator, applied later.
He did go back; the issue is only what the graph draws.
Right: no operation, no operator.
questions.explain: A return is a change of place, not an operation. The card next walks through Figure 6.2.
questions.rule: A return is not an operation.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Put the events of Figure 6.2 in order.
items: Q1 is applied to the first state
Q2 is applied
The subject returns to the state of node 2
Q3 is applied
The subject returns to the state of node 1
Q1 is applied again
questions.explain: The sequence runs from the start through two moves, a return, a third move, a second return and a repeat.
questions.rule: Follow the nodes in time order.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: At node 6 the subject, back at the state of node 1, applies Q1 again. What state of knowledge does the resulting node 7 hold?
options: The same state as node 3
The same state as nodes 2 and 4
The same state as node 5
A new state not seen before
optionExplain: Node 3 came from Q2, not from Q1.
Right: Q1 applied to the state of node 1 gives the same result as before.
Node 5 came from Q3.
Applying the same operator to the same state gives the same state.
questions.explain: The same operator on the same state gives the same result, though the graph does not mark the identity.
questions.rule: Same operator, same state, same result.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: Node 6 is drawn below nodes 4 and 5 because it occurred later in time.
questions.explain: True: it is drawn below them, because it occurred later in time.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A reader sees nodes 2, 4 and 7 in a graph and asks whether the graph tells her they hold identical states. What does the authors' graph do?
options: It marks them with a common color
It joins them with a vertical line
It does not indicate it; the identity must come from the analysis
It leaves them out entirely
optionExplain: No such marking is part of the conventions.
Vertical lines join a node to the one a return came from, and not all three.
Right: the identity of those states is not shown in the graph.
All three are drawn as nodes.
questions.explain: The graph records order and returns, not equality of states.
questions.rule: Do not read equality from position.
questions.teaches: The identity of the knowledge states at nodes 7, 2 and 4 is not indicated in the graph itself.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Two solvers hold exactly the same facts about a puzzle but reached them by different routes. Is their position the same for deciding what to do next?
options: Not necessarily; what they remember of the route and earlier attempts can differ
Yes, since only the facts count
Yes, since both will be bored of the puzzle
No, because one solver must have cheated
optionExplain: Right: the facts do not fix the history.
History can matter even when the facts are identical.
Boredom is not at issue.
Different routes need not mean cheating.
questions.explain: The same facts can come from different routes. The card next says what a node must add.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Information about how the subject reached a node is called ____ information.
questions.explain: The authors distinguish path information from information about past attempts.
questions.rule: Path information records how he got there.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: At node 4 the subject chooses Q3, though in the same state at node 2 he chose Q2. What must he know, on the authors' account?
options: That he has been in this state before and applied Q2 then
That Q3 is always better than Q2
That the experimenter wants Q3
Nothing; the choice is random
optionExplain: Right: otherwise he would apply Q2 again.
Nothing about better operators is said.
The experimenter is not part of the account.
The account assumes no randomness.
questions.explain: Without memory of past attempts, the same state would produce the same choice.
questions.rule: Same state plus memory gives a different move.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: Given a state of knowledge, one can infer which operators were applied, but not their order or whether they were applied more than once.
questions.explain: True: one can infer which operators were applied, but not their order or whether they were applied more than once.
questions.rule: A state does not record its history.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A chess player returns to a position she analyzed earlier and now plays a different move. What would the authors say about the two visits?
options: They are the same node, since the position is identical
They cannot be compared, since chess is different from cryptarithmetic
They are separate nodes, because her memory of the earlier visit makes the situation different
Only the second is a node; the first is background
optionExplain: The nodes are distinguished by path and past-attempt information.
The principle is general to the PBG.
Right: past attempts are part of what distinguishes the nodes.
Both are nodes.
questions.explain: Memory of earlier attempts makes the second visit a different situation.
questions.rule: Count the memory as part of the state.
questions.teaches: Returning to the same situation does not require knowing the full history of past attempts; this may be the case at node 7 of Figure 6.2.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A graph of a talk-aloud record gives each node a phrase number. What does that number let the reader do?
options: Read the digit the subject assigned at that point
Find roughly where in the protocol the node's interval begins
Learn how many seconds the node lasted
See which operator was applied
optionExplain: The number points at the protocol, not at a digit.
Right: it ties the node to the record.
No timing exists.
Operators are written in the node.
questions.explain: Numbers tie the graph back to the protocol. The card next lists the marks.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Match each mark in Figure 6.3 to its meaning.
pairs: X number in the upper right corner
A new external display after writing
An occurrence somewhere after phrase B64
A rare item outside the formal space
A node run repeatedly under a generator
questions.explain: Each mark carries one piece of information about the node.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: S3 generates the odd digits for R and rejects the digit 5, which is already used. How does the graph show the loop between generating and testing?
options: With one node for each digit generated
With a doubled horizontal line
With a circled number
With a jagged right-hand boundary on one node, rather than drawing every cycle
optionExplain: The authors avoid depicting the whole loop.
A doubled line marks a repeated operator on the same state.
Circled numbers mark rare items outside the space.
Right: the generated digits are tested in a loop shown by the edge mark.
questions.explain: The convention saves the figure from drawing each pass through the loop.
questions.rule: A jagged edge compresses a loop.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: An operator that produced no new information is left out of the graph.
questions.explain: A new node is still placed at the head of the arrow, because the inference that nothing new was produced may be made late or remain in doubt.
questions.rule: Draw the attempt even without a result.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A team maps a salesperson's calls and records every attempt as a step, even a call with no result. Which authors' reason supports this?
options: Resultless calls are the most informative
The graph must have the same number of steps as the protocol
Whether a call yielded anything may only be judged late, or remain doubtful
Leaving them out would shorten the graph too much
optionExplain: The authors give no such claim.
Nodes number 238 against 321 phrases.
Right: the same reason lets the PBG keep resultless attempts.
Brevity is not at issue.
questions.explain: Judging that nothing was learned can come late, so the attempt is kept.
questions.rule: Keep the attempt; judge the result later.
questions.teaches: Figure 6.4 shows the outline of the entire tree, which has 238 nodes, and also provides a summary of the main problem solving episodes.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: In coding a talk-aloud record into moves, what is a sensible test of whether an event counts as a move?
options: Whether it changes what the subject knows
Whether the subject says it loudly
Whether the experimenter wrote it down
Whether it takes more than a few seconds
optionExplain: Right: moves are events that change the state of knowledge.
Volume has no bearing.
The experimenter's notes are not the test.
Duration is not the test, and none is known.
questions.explain: A move is an event that alters the state. The card next gives the authors' rule.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: The authors treat as an operator anything that changes the ____, as defined in Figure 6.1.
questions.explain: The four operators are the end result of coding and were not chosen a priori.
questions.rule: Operators are whatever changes the state.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: S3 moves attention from column 2 to column 3 without drawing any new conclusion. How is this handled in the graph?
options: It is coded as a new operator, PC
It is coded as an assignment
It is coded as a test of a digit
It is not an operator; choosing columns is internal to the node
optionExplain: PC requires information to be inferred.
No digit has been assigned.
No digit is being tested.
Right: the authors declare column selection internal to the node.
questions.explain: Attention shifts do not change the state as defined, so they are not operators.
questions.rule: Attention is internal to a node.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: B1, in which the rules are clarified with the experimenter, lies outside the problem space and is marked only by a special footnote.
questions.explain: Talk about the rules is not a move in the space of digits and letters.
questions.rule: Rule talk is outside the space.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: An analyst codes a mechanic's talk and finds the mechanic asks the owner about the car's history. Following the authors' practice, how is the question coded?
options: As the most important node in the graph
As lying outside the problem space, noted by a footnote and not as a node
As a repeated application of the first operator
As an error of the subject
optionExplain: The authors set such exchanges aside.
Right: like B1, it is not a move in the space.
It is not a repeat of an operator.
It is not an error.
questions.explain: Exchanges that clarify the task are outside the space.
questions.rule: Footnote what lies outside the space.
questions.teaches: The authors explain only the first 4 percent of the protocol this way; to examine it all would need another 70 pages, much of it as transparent as the first part and equally dull.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: An analyst cannot tell whether a speaker already had a goal before acting. What is the cautious policy?
options: Always record the most likely goal
Record no conjecture about the goal unless specific information supports it
Discard the whole remark as useless
Ask the subject years later
optionExplain: That would add unsupported claims.
Right: the authors take this view.
The remark still shows what the subject did.
Retrospective accounts are not used.
questions.explain: Unsupported conjectures are not recorded. The card next shows the authors' choices.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: S3's inference at B5 that T is zero is coded as the operator PC on column ____.
questions.explain: The coding is clear even though four questions about it stay open.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: S3 did not say that c2 was 1 at B5. How do the authors justify listing it as known?
options: He wrote c2 = 1 on the paper at B5
The experimenter stated it
It is a rule that all carries are recorded
Five plus five is ten, and B21 later shows the information was retained
optionExplain: The text does not say so.
The experimenter is not the source.
No such rule is given.
Right: plausibility plus later evidence.
questions.explain: A plausible inference later shown to be used is accepted.
questions.rule: Let later use confirm an inference.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: The authors say they need only the approximate sequence of processing for B5 and decline to settle all four questions.
questions.explain: True: they need only the approximate sequence of processing, and they decline to settle the rest.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: An analyst of a commentator's talk cannot tell when she noticed a threat on the chess board. Which working rule of the authors helps?
options: It is enough to know the approximate order of processing, which the talk usually shows
Wait until the commentator is asked to explain
Assume the threat was noticed at the start
Drop the remark from the analysis
optionExplain: Right: exact timing of the inference is not needed.
The authors do not wait for retrospective accounts.
That would be a conjecture.
The remark still supports the sequence.
questions.explain: Approximate sequence is enough to place a node.
questions.teaches: As to when the inference occurred, we need only know the approximate sequence of processing, which is evident from the protocol.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A subject counts how often each of three letters appears in a sum, then works on one column. What is the most reasonable reading of the counting?
options: He has already solved those three letters
He is checking a finished answer
He is choosing which column to work on next
He is assigning digits to the three letters
optionExplain: Counting does not give values.
Nothing has been finished.
Right: counting occurrences is a way of selecting.
No digits are named.
questions.explain: Counting is a step toward a choice. The card next gives the authors' reading.
questions.rule: Counting selects; it does not solve.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: In B18 and B19 S3 notes how often A, L and R occur; the authors read this as selecting the next ____.
questions.explain: There is no evidence of column processing during the counting, so no new information is credited.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Why does the coding give the node starting at B8 the goal get R?
options: He said at B8 that he wanted R
R is the first letter in the puzzle
The experimenter named R as the target
His concern with R at B18 and B19 shows column 2 was chosen partly to learn about R
optionExplain: The goal is inferred from B18 and B19, not stated at B8.
Position in the puzzle does not decide it.
The experimenter did not name it.
Right: the concern points to the goal.
questions.explain: The goal is attributed from later evidence of concern.
questions.rule: Attribute a goal from clear concern.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: Had S3 shown no concern with R at B18 and B19, B8 to B22 would be coded as a single node whose operator is PC on column 2.
questions.explain: That is the authors' fallback when the goal is unclear.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A cook scribbles a figure on a pad after noticing it on a label and says nothing more. What should an analyst following the authors claim?
options: A discovery, because the cook wrote something
A writing step, without claiming new information was found
Nothing, because writing is outside the analysis
A deliberate decision to stop cooking
optionExplain: Writing alone does not show a discovery.
Right: new information is conceivable, but there is no evidence for it.
Writing is noted, as in the graph's X displays.
Nothing in the scribble shows that.
questions.explain: Treat an unexplained act as an act, not as a result.
questions.rule: Claim only what the evidence shows.
questions.teaches: At B12 and B13 S3 writes 5 for D on noticing D in column 6; the authors count this as a writing step, noting that new information is conceivable but that no evidence for it appears.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: An analyst coded a stretch of talk as producing nothing new. Later the subject uses a fact that has no visible source. What does this suggest?
options: The subject has invented the fact on the spot
The experimenter must have supplied it
The fact may have been derived earlier without being said, so the earlier coding needs revising
The recording is faulty and should be discarded
optionExplain: That is possible but not the natural reading.
Nothing suggests this.
Right: unexplained facts point back to hidden steps.
A gap in coding does not make the recording faulty.
questions.explain: A fact with no source hints at an unseen step. The card next gives the authors' view.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: If S3 derived information without mentioning it, the authors expect it to surface later in some context without apparent antecedents.
questions.explain: That reappearance is how the analysts would correct the interpretation of the earlier segment.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: At B32 to B35 S3 concludes that G is even, and at B36 to B38 he repeats the step and sees no such inference is possible. What does this show?
options: A repetition can correct an earlier inference
Repetitions never add anything
G is in fact even
The experimenter gave a hint
optionExplain: Right: the second pass overturned the first.
Here the repeat changed the conclusion.
The repeat concluded the opposite.
No hint is mentioned.
questions.explain: A repeat can correct as well as confirm.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Which explanations do the authors offer for the repetition at B23 to B25? Select all that apply.
options: S3 checked the processing to be sure of the inference
The experimental situation pushes the subject to talk
S3 had forgotten the first result
The experimenter asked him to start the puzzle again
optionExplain: Right: a check is one explanation.
Right: the structuring of the setting is another.
The authors do not offer forgetting here.
No such request is described.
questions.explain: The authors give two possibilities, a check and the pressure to talk, and admit the reason is not apparent.
questions.rule: Say what you do not know.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A worker repeats a calculation and gets the same answer. The analyst records the first result as a node and then the repeat. Why record the first result separately?
options: The repeat is a return to an earlier state, so the first result must be a node to return to
The two results must differ, and one is wrong
Each calculation takes the same time
The worker must have two goals
optionExplain: Right: the authors create B22.1 for the first PC on column 2 and back up for B23.
They need not differ.
Time plays no part.
A repeat does not imply two goals.
questions.explain: A repetition needs a node to return to.
questions.rule: Mark the first result so the return has a target.
questions.teaches: Because B23 repeats the reasoning of B20, the authors create a node B22.1 for the result of the first processing of column 2 and then back up to it for the repetition at B23.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A solver lists 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 and then says that 5 is taken. What does rejecting after listing, rather than skipping, show?
options: That the solver cannot count the digits
That the solver is guessing at random
That generating ignores used digits and a separate test then catches them
That 5 was never used
optionExplain: Rejecting after listing is not a failure to count.
The list is systematic.
Right: generation and test are separate steps.
The solver said it was taken.
questions.explain: The order of listing then rejecting shows two steps. The card next gives the authors' reading.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: S3 generated the digit 5 and explicitly rejected it, which supports applying ____ to the output of GN.
questions.explain: TD is the operator that checks whether a digit is already used.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: S3 says nothing special on passing 1, 3, 7 and 9. How do the authors code TD for these digits?
options: As not applied, since S3 did not comment
As applied uniformly, on grounds of parsimony
As applied only to those digits he later used
As applied once for the whole set
optionExplain: Silence is not read as absence.
Right: the simplest assumption is that TD ran on every digit.
The text gives no basis for that.
The authors treat each generated digit as tested.
questions.explain: Uniform application is the simpler assumption.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: An analyst may conclude that TD was applied only to the digit 5, because S3 commented on that one alone.
questions.explain: The authors reject this: a process deciding when to apply TD would itself have to do what TD does.
questions.rule: A silent step is not an absent step.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A clerk checks each cheque number against a blocklist but speaks aloud only when one is blocked. How should an analyst treat the silent ones?
options: As unchecked, since no check was spoken
As checked at random
