As unknowable, so drop them
As checked too, since a rule for choosing when to check would itself need the same check
optionExplain: The authors do not read silence that way.
Nothing supports random checking.
The parsimony argument gives a coding.
Right: this is the authors' parsimony argument.
questions.explain: If checking were sometimes skipped, some process would have to decide when, and that process would do the checking job anyway.
questions.teaches: If S3 applied TD sometimes and not always, he would need a process to decide when, and that process would have to perform the same function as TD, namely to determine whether a digit is already assigned.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A subject falls silent and the experimenter prompts him to go on talking. How should the analyst treat the silent period?
options: Credit the subject with the best possible reasoning
Record that the subject gave up
Make no note of processing in it unless the talk gives evidence for it
Remove the period from the study
optionExplain: That would add unsupported claims.
Nothing shows he gave up.
Right: unsupported steps are not recorded.
The pause is data of a kind.
questions.explain: Without evidence, nothing is recorded. The card next gives the authors' handling of B31.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: The authors infer that after the pause S3 resumed from the state of knowledge at B____.
questions.explain: He seems not to use the refined list of odd digits, so he is taken to have backed up.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: After a pause S3 says nothing that uses the list 1, 3, 7, 9 for R, only that R is odd. What do the authors conclude?
options: He had backed up to the plainer state, R odd
He had solved R during the pause
He had forgotten that R is odd
He had been told the answer
optionExplain: Right: the later talk uses only the earlier fact.
No value of R is voiced.
He continues to use that fact.
Nothing says so.
questions.explain: The state is read from what the later talk uses.
questions.rule: Read the state from later use.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: Because S3 was silent at B31, the authors add no operator to the graph for the pause.
questions.explain: True: no operator is added; with no evidence, the authors make no explicit note of any processing in the pause.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A student goes quiet and then restarts from an earlier step. How can the analyst test whether the silence hid a discovery?
options: Ask the student a year later what happened
Assume a discovery, since silence means thought
Count the seconds of silence
Look for the new fact right after the prod or later, where its origin would be unexplained
optionExplain: Retrospective accounts are not the authors' method.
That would be unsupported.
No timing is available.
Right: hidden results should show up in one of those places.
questions.explain: A real discovery would show itself at the next remark, or later with no visible source.
questions.rule: Test silence by what follows it.
questions.teaches: If S3 obtained new information in the pause, it should show up at B31 itself, which it does not, or at some later time in facts whose origin would not be accounted for.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Asked is the number odd or even, a person answers odd. How much does the answer show about what the person knows?
options: Everything, since the answer was correct
Little, since a guess is right half the time
Nothing at all about anything
That the person is lying
optionExplain: A correct guess shows nothing.
Right: a two-way question gives even odds with no knowledge.
It shows something, but weakly.
No reason to suspect lying.
questions.explain: Answers to narrow questions can be right by chance. The card next gives the authors' remedy.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: The authors rely on the ____ of inference that links an utterance to other utterances.
questions.explain: The web gives support beyond the chance that one short statement is correct.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: S3 says two L's equal an R, and in other places that R is odd. How does this strengthen the claim that he knows R is odd?
options: The words two L's are longer than R is odd
The utterances fit together in a web of inference, not by chance alone
The experimenter agreed with him
He said both in a hurry
optionExplain: Length is irrelevant.
Right: related utterances support one another.
Agreement by the experimenter is not mentioned.
Speed is not evidence here.
questions.explain: A fact that connects with others is less likely to be accidental.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: An answer of odd to the question is R odd or even is weaker evidence of knowledge than the same remark made unprompted alongside related statements about R.
questions.explain: A forced two-way answer has even odds of being right by chance, while an unprompted remark linked to others rests on a web of inference.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A fortune-teller says someone close to you is worried about money. Why is this weak evidence of insight, on the authors' reasoning?
options: Money worries are rare
Fortune-tellers speak too quickly
The statement has no words in common with the problem
The statement is general enough that falsification is remote
optionExplain: The point is the generality, not the rarity.
Speed is not the issue.
The issue is how easily it could be falsified.
Right: broad statements are rarely wrong.
questions.explain: The more general the statement, the less it shows.
questions.teaches: The authors note that some interesting computer programs make effective use of this principle, appearing to give information by making statements broad enough to be hard to falsify (they cite Weizenbaum, 1966).

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Which report is more trustworthy for what a person knew at a given moment: a running commentary or an account given afterwards?
options: The running commentary
The account given afterwards, since it is calmer
Both equally
Neither, since people never know what they know
optionExplain: Right: it is closer to the moment it describes.
Calm does not remove the mixing of past and present.
Time gaps invite error.
A running commentary does carry information.
questions.explain: Closeness in time limits distortion. The card next shows how the authors use talk.
questions.rule: Prefer reports made at the time.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Under thinking aloud, S3 reports information and intentions within his current awareness, while the ____ do the theorizing.
questions.explain: All theorizing about causes and consequences of his knowledge state is carried out and validated by the experimenters.
questions.rule: The subject reports; the analysts explain.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: At B87 the experimenter asks what S3 is thinking, and he replies that he was trying to think over what he had said. How do the authors use the reply?
options: As a full account of his reasoning
As proof that he cannot introspect
For the evidence it gives of knowledge or operation, which here is essentially none
As a new operator in the graph
optionExplain: It is not a full account.
The authors draw no such conclusion.
Right: the reply tells almost nothing.
No operator is added.
questions.explain: An introspective remark is used only for the evidence it holds.
questions.rule: Use remarks only for their evidence.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: On the authors' method the subject reports information and intentions at hand while the experimenters theorize about causes.
questions.explain: The subject is not asked to theorize; the experimenters carry out and validate all theorizing.
questions.rule: Keep theory on the analyst's side.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A coach asks a golfer to narrate each shot as she plays, rather than explain her round afterwards. Which feature of thinking aloud does this match?
options: It gives the golfer more time to theorize
It makes the report a measure of strength
It removes the need for any analysis
Reports made at the time leave less room for mixing current and past knowledge
optionExplain: Thinking aloud does not ask for theory.
No measure of strength is involved.
The analysts still interpret the talk.
Right: retrospective accounts give more opportunity for such mixing.
questions.explain: Contemporary reports resist the blending of old and new knowledge.
questions.rule: Ask for reports at the time.
questions.teaches: Retrospective accounts leave much more opportunity for the subject to mix current knowledge with past knowledge, making reliable inference from the protocol difficult.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A study asks a person to score essays. What safeguard does psychology usually add?
options: The scorer is told the right answers in advance
Several judges score the same essays and agreement is calculated
The scorer works faster each time
The essays are shortened
optionExplain: That would defeat the purpose.
Right: duplication by judges and a reliability measure.
Speed is not a safeguard.
Length is not the safeguard.
questions.explain: Duplication by several judges is the common practice. The card next shows what the authors do instead.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: In place of several judges, the authors rely on the persuasiveness of the web of ____.
questions.explain: The web of inference supports each attribution to the subject.
questions.rule: Rely on the web of inference.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A reviewer complains that only one analyst coded S3's protocol. Which reply fits the authors' position?
options: The coding is defended by the analyst's long experience alone
The coding is defended by S3's later approval of it
The coding is defended by laying out the web of inference that supports each attribution
The coding is defended by the number of words in the protocol
optionExplain: Experience is not the defence the authors give.
S3's later view is not used.
Right: they rely on the persuasiveness of that web.
Length does not support the attributions.
questions.explain: The authors answer with the strength of the reasoning, not with agreement counts.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: The authors did not adopt duplication by judges or reliability measures for their coding of S3.
questions.explain: True: they did not adopt duplication by judges or reliability measures.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A researcher shows colleagues her full reasoning behind each attribution to a speaker, instead of showing that other raters agree. Whose stance is this?
options: The authors', who rely on the persuasiveness of the web of inference
The standard practice of psychology with human judges
A fully mechanized method with no analyst
A retrospective method based on the subject's memory
optionExplain: Right: the support lies in the reasoning laid out.
That would rely on agreement.
A human still makes the attributions.
The subject's later memory is not used.
questions.explain: Laying the web open lets readers judge for themselves.
questions.rule: Show the web, and let readers judge.
questions.teaches: The authors add that the long-run solution to these questions is mechanization, and that it is too early to report progress on current efforts toward it.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: One linguist studies how a speaker turns an inner meaning into a sentence. Another studies how a listener recovers the meaning from the sentence. Which is the analysts' problem with a protocol?
options: The listener's problem of recovering the meaning from the strings
The speaker's problem of generating the sentence
The problem of translating one language into another
The problem of how children learn grammar
optionExplain: Right: analysts infer the internal representation from what was said.
The authors set this problem aside.
No translation between languages is involved.
Learning grammar is not the subject.
questions.explain: Analysts run from strings to meaning. The card next names the two problems.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: The theory postulates only deep structure, the internal representation, and not ____ structure.
questions.explain: That is why the generation of utterances is not relevant to the theory.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A phone engineer wants to recover the intended request from messy calls and does not care how callers choose their words. Which of the authors' two problems is hers?
options: The problem of how the callers produce their sentences
The problem of choosing a theory of problem solving
The inverse problem of inferring the deep structure from the strings
The problem of timing the calls
optionExplain: She is not concerned with generation.
This is not a linguistic problem of the kind described.
Right: recovering the intended meaning from what was said.
Timing is not the problem.
questions.explain: Recovering meaning from strings is the inverse problem.
questions.rule: Recovery runs from strings to meaning.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: The authors solve the problem of how the problem solver generates his utterances, as part of their theory.
questions.explain: They leave it unaddressed: it is genuine and important to linguistics, but not relevant to the theory.
questions.rule: Set aside what the theory does not need.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: The authors say the two problems are identical with central problems of linguistics. By what names are they known?
options: Analysis for generating the strings, and synthesis for inferring the deep structure
Synthesis for generating the strings, and analysis for inferring the deep structure
Encoding and recording
Surface and deep, respectively
optionExplain: The names are the other way round.
Right: these are the central problems of modern structural linguistics.
These are not the names the authors use.
Those are kinds of structure, not names of problems.
questions.explain: Synthesis builds the strings; analysis recovers the structure.
questions.rule: Synthesis is generating; analysis is inferring.
questions.teaches: The two problems are identical with the central problems of modern structural linguistics: synthesis, the generation of strings from internal representation, and analysis, the inference of the representation from the strings.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A researcher must pull meaning from speech but has no formal grammar of the language. What can she do?
options: Give up, since meaning cannot be extracted without a full grammar
Replace speech by a questionnaire
Ask the speaker to write a grammar
Use systematic but informal procedures and her knowledge of the language
optionExplain: The authors proceed without one.
The speech is the data.
That is not the authors' method.
Right: that is what the authors do.
questions.explain: Informal but systematic procedures can extract meaning. The card next gives the authors' stance.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: The authors stop short of constructing a full formal ____ for translating strings into elements of deep structure.
questions.explain: They use systematic but informal procedures instead.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Which resources do the authors rely on to extract components of deep structure from the protocols?
options: A computer program that parses each sentence
The subject's own parsing of his sentences
Informal systematic procedures and their own knowledge of English
A table of word frequencies
optionExplain: They say the mechanizing of the procedure lies in the future.
The subject is not asked to analyze his speech.
Right: these are what they name.
No such table is mentioned.
questions.explain: The analysts use systematic informal procedure plus their command of the language.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: The authors say they can evade the problem of analysis because their theory postulates only deep structure.
questions.explain: That reasoning lets them set aside synthesis; analysis cannot be evaded if protocols are used to test the theory.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A team studying customer calls wants only the plainly stated complaints coded, using a trained reader's judgment and a written checklist. Which feature of the authors' approach does this share?
options: It extracts the most directly obvious components from the strings and does not seek a complete grammar
It builds a full formal grammar of the callers' speech
It relies on the callers to report their own intentions in theory terms
It ignores the callers' words and uses recorded timings
optionExplain: Right: the aim is the directly obvious components.
The authors do not.
The subject is not asked to theorize.
The words are the data.
questions.explain: Take the obvious components by informal procedure.
questions.teaches: The aim of the informal procedure is to extract from the protocols the most directly obvious components of the underlying deep structures that are implicit in them.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A diagram shows a solver moving by four kinds of step. What else must be true for the diagram to explain the behavior?
options: Nothing else; the steps explain everything on their own
The solver must have used all four steps equally often
The solver must be unable to repeat a step
Something must govern which step is taken, when to stop, and which earlier point to return to
optionExplain: The steps do not say why one is chosen.
No such condition is needed.
Repetition is allowed.
Right: selection, termination and return processes are needed too.
questions.explain: Steps alone do not choose themselves. The card next states the three implications.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: On the PBG view, returns to prior states are governed by ____ processes, not by the four operators.
questions.explain: The four operators account for all transitions to new states of knowledge.
questions.rule: Operators make new states; others handle returns.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Which of these is part of what a successful encoding implies?
options: S3 has the same operators as every other subject
The four operators account for all of S3's transitions to new states of knowledge
S3 never returned to a prior state
S3 solved the puzzle without any search
optionExplain: Generality is not implied by this encoding.
Right: that is the second implication.
Returns occur but are governed by other processes.
The basic method is search.
questions.explain: The encoding speaks about S3's transitions, using four operators.
questions.rule: The operators account for new states.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: On the authors' account, S3's basic problem solving method is search, so it rests on trial and error in a space of very simple operations.
questions.explain: It is search in a space defined by intellectual operations of a moderate degree of sophistication.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A teacher says her pupils' competence at sums can be described by a short list of basic operations. Which comparison do the authors make for the four operators?
options: They define the limit of what any human can learn
They define a basic competence, similar to abilities Gagne tried to identify in simpler arithmetic situations
They reproduce Gagne's results exactly
They replace Gagne's abilities with simpler ones
optionExplain: No limit is claimed.
Right: the authors draw this comparison.
The comparison is one of kind, not identity.
No replacement is claimed.
questions.explain: The operators sit at a level comparable to Gagne's abilities.
questions.teaches: The four operators provide a definition of basic competence, similar to the abilities Gagne tried to identify in somewhat simpler arithmetic situations (the authors cite Gagne and Paradise, 1961, and Resnick, 1969).

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A computer trace lists every machine instruction a program ran but does not show the plan the program followed. Which concern about an analysis does this illustrate?
options: The description is too coarse to show any detail
The description is correct but unreadable
The description is false
The description is too fine to show the larger organization
optionExplain: A list of every instruction is the opposite of coarse.
The concern is missing organization, not readability.
A trace can be true and still hide the plan.
Right: detail can hide the plan.
questions.explain: Excess detail hides organization. The card next names three concerns.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Match each concern about the PBG to its description.
pairs: The essential problem solving is done inside the components
It shows means but not the larger plan they serve
Other processes with other information produce what the graph shows
questions.explain: Each concern names a way the graph may fail to explain.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Other processes, using information the graph does not show, might lead S3 to know and report exactly what the graph records. Which concern is this?
options: Epiphenomenal
Superficial
Too disaggregated
Correct and complete
optionExplain: Right: the graph would be a by-product of other processes.
Superficial means the key work is inside the components.
Disaggregated means the larger plan is hidden.
That would be no concern at all.
questions.explain: A by-product graph is epiphenomenal.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: For the superficial concern, the basic issue is how much selection is done inside the components.
questions.explain: The issue is whether the selection requires problem solving, either search in another space or some other intellectual process, not how much selection occurs.
questions.rule: Ask whether the hidden work needs problem solving.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: An audit trail lists every keystroke of an accountant but shows no plan. How would excessive detail reveal itself, on the authors' reasoning?
options: In a trail that is shorter than the real work
In keystrokes that are all identical
In capricious-looking selections, whenever the next action was fixed by an unrecorded higher-level plan
In a trail that matches the accountant's own account exactly
optionExplain: Excess detail makes the trail longer, not shorter.
Identical keystrokes are not the sign.
Right: local choices look arbitrary when a plan decided them.
A match would not reveal a problem.
questions.explain: Choices that look unmotivated locally may have been fixed by a plan.
questions.rule: Capriciousness hints at a hidden plan.
questions.teaches: Excessive disaggregation would reveal itself in the capriciousness of various selections viewed in terms of the local context, whenever the next action was in fact determined by the structure of a higher-level plan.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A researcher records only what a subject writes on paper. What can that record not explain?
options: How many marks were made
Which letters appear in the puzzle
Whether the subject used a pencil
Why one value was written rather than another the subject had narrowed it to
optionExplain: The record shows the marks.
The puzzle is on the paper.
That is visible.
Right: the narrowing happens in the head, not on paper.
questions.explain: What is written does not show what was known. The card next gives the authors' example.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: The graph in the external problem space is ____: it holds very few clues to the processes that determine the sequence of actions.
questions.explain: The authors use this word for a graph that may not reflect the real processes.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Why can the external graph not explain assigning 7 to R at B61 and 9 at B189?
options: S3 changed his mind about the rules
It has no representation of the fact that R is 7 or 9
The experimenter chose the digits
The two values were chosen at random
optionExplain: The text gives no such reason.
Right: the narrowing is not in the external space.
The experimenter did not choose them.
The authors do not suggest randomness.
questions.explain: Without the alternatives in the space, the choice of 7 then 9 cannot be explained.
questions.rule: Represent the alternatives to explain choices.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: In the external problem space, S3's concern with E, O and column 5 does not show until B249.
questions.explain: True: it does not show until B249.
questions.rule: The external space misses long stretches of work.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A manager reads only a log of final entries in a spreadsheet and sees no sign of an analyst's main preoccupation. Which of the authors' findings does this parallel?
options: S3 spent most of his time writing assignments
S3 ignored column 5 entirely
E, O and column 5 held S3's attention for almost half the total time, yet show in the external graph only at B249
The experimenter hid the data
optionExplain: The writing was sparse.
He attended to it long.
Right: the external space hid most of the real work.
Nothing like that occurs.
questions.explain: What dominated attention was invisible in the written record.
questions.rule: Attention can be invisible on paper.
questions.teaches: Concern with E, O and column 5 dominated S3's attention from B80 to B162 and from B219 to B243, almost half the total time, yet the external graph gives no evidence of it until B249.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A map shows every paving stone of a town. Compared with a map that shows only main roads, what is the main cost of the over-detailed map?
options: Extra effort in reading, though nothing is lost
Important information is lost
The map cannot be used for any purpose
The map becomes false
optionExplain: Right: excess detail costs effort but keeps information.
Detail adds information; coarse maps lose it.
It remains usable.
More detail does not make it false.
questions.explain: Fine detail costs effort; coarse maps lose information. The card next says how the authors weigh these.
questions.rule: Detail costs effort; coarseness costs information.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Excessive aggregation exacts a price because aggregation means loss of ____.
questions.explain: The price may be heavy, or even ruinous.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Which is the heavier of the two prices of disaggregating too far, according to the authors?
options: Having to look beyond the local context to explain why a behavior occurred exactly where it did
Analyzing subprocesses that are not problematic for the subject
Having too little data in the protocol
Being unable to draw the graph at all
optionExplain: Right: this is the heavier price, paid by building a comprehensive IPS.
The authors call this price not burdensome.
This is not one of the two prices.
The graph can still be drawn.
questions.explain: The second price is heavier but can be paid by constructing a comprehensive IPS and testing its predictions.
questions.rule: Pay the heavy price with a comprehensive IPS.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: The authors say the method is not nearly so sensitive to the level of aggregation as the warnings imply, because behavior is organized in a hierarchy of levels.
questions.explain: True: they say it is not nearly so sensitive as the warnings imply, because the behavior is organized in a hierarchy of levels.
questions.rule: Hierarchy makes the level less critical.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: In a kitchen, a cook sieves flour as part of making a sauce. How does this fit the authors' reason for the method's insensitivity?
options: Every step in cooking is independent of the others
Detailed steps never matter to the larger act
A detailed step is a subroutine within a more comprehensive act, as processing column 2 is within getting R
Larger acts are the sum of equal steps
optionExplain: The point is that steps nest in larger acts.
They are components of it.
Right: the authors give this example.
The structure is hierarchical, not flat.
questions.explain: Detailed processes are components of larger acts.
questions.teaches: The authors illustrate the hierarchy by noting that a subject might process column 2 as one component of an act intended to infer an assignment for R.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A coarse record shows only which values a subject tried. How could a richer model of the subject's reasoning be tested against it?
options: Ignore the record and trust the model
Run the model and see whether the values it tries match those in the record
Ask the subject to explain each value
Throw away the model and keep the record
optionExplain: That is no test.
Right: extract the matching subset from the simulation.
The authors do not ask for such explanations.
The record alone does not explain.
questions.explain: A model can be tested on the part of its output that the record shows. The card next states the method.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: The aggregated graph's information is predicted by extracting the appropriate ____ of the more complete simulated graph.
questions.explain: The simulated graph holds more than the aggregated one, so the aggregated information is a part of it.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A model in the augmented space gives R the values 7 and 9 only. Which fact about the coarse graph would this account for?
options: That S3 wrote the digit 5 for D
That S3 spoke 2186 words
That S3 made an arithmetic error
That S3 tried 7 and 9 for R and no other values
optionExplain: D is given by the puzzle.
The model does not predict word counts.
The model does not predict errors.
Right: the model makes this understandable.
questions.explain: The model predicts which values would be tried for R.
questions.rule: A fuller model explains a coarse record.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: Prediction from the simulated graph succeeds whether or not the omitted subprocesses do what the task environment demands.
questions.explain: It succeeds to the extent that the missing subprocesses represent doing what the environment demands.
questions.rule: Omitted steps must be demanded by the task.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A school wants to test a model of how pupils solve sums, but has only their final answers. Which feature of the authors' method would apply?
options: Reject the model since answers alone cannot test anything
Change the answers to fit the model
Simulate the pupils with the model and compare the simulated answers with the recorded ones
Ask pupils to guess what the model does
optionExplain: The authors show that coarse data can test a theory.
That would defeat the test.
Right: use the part of the simulation the data can be compared with.
Pupils are not the test.
questions.explain: Coarse data can still bear on a detailed model.
questions.teaches: The authors assume the subject works in the augmented space on grounds drawn from data on other subjects, from other problems attempted by the same subject, or from theory.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A detailed analysis of one session is very expensive. Once a model has been built from it, how could the model be tested more cheaply on other data?
options: Test it against coarser data that are easier to obtain
Repeat the detailed analysis for every session
Stop testing, since the model came from real data
Test it only against the session it came from
optionExplain: Right: coarser data can test a hypothesized model.
That is the expensive route.
The model still needs tests.
That would not be an independent test.
questions.explain: Cheaper data can test a model built from costly analysis. The card next gives the authors' reasons.
questions.rule: Test cheaply once the model exists.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Match each reason the second reading matters to its description.
pairs: A protocol need not show the state of knowledge at every moment
Some data recorded only external behavior, as with Bartlett and Moore and Anderson
Detailed analysis is expensive, so cheaper aggregated tests are valuable
questions.explain: These are three reasons the authors give for valuing the summary reading.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Bartlett recorded only the external behavior of subjects on DONALD + GERALD. How can such data be used?
options: They cannot be used at all
They reveal each subject's full state of knowledge
They replace the need for any IPS
As aggregated data to test a hypothesized IPS, though they cannot reveal successive states of knowledge
optionExplain: The authors find such data highly informative.
They are too aggregated for that.
The IPS is what they test.
Right: the second reading allows this.
questions.explain: Aggregated data test theories without showing each state.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: The authors say there is no a priori reason for a protocol to give a complete record of the subject's state of knowledge, and expect gaps and omissions even in a fairly full protocol.
questions.explain: True: there is no a priori reason it should be complete, and they expect gaps and omissions even in a fairly full protocol.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A hospital has full recordings of a few doctors thinking aloud and only summary logs for hundreds more. How does the authors' reasoning suggest they proceed?
options: Discard the logs, since only full recordings count
Build a model from the few full recordings and test it on the logs
Discard the recordings, since only logs are cheap
Mix the two sets into one list
optionExplain: The authors use aggregated data.
Right: this follows the logic of building on costly detail and testing on cheaper data.
The recordings supply the model.
That would lose the distinction between model and test.
questions.explain: Model from detail, test on the coarse.
questions.rule: Induce from detail; test on the aggregate.
questions.teaches: A large part of the evidence for the theory of problem solving in cryptarithmetic, examined in Chapter 7, is of an aggregated kind, tested with the help of data that are easier to obtain from the protocol.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: After describing a person's solving steps in detail, what must be added to turn the description into a theory?
options: A longer list of the same steps
A program that predicts those steps, to be compared with what happened
The subject's opinion of the steps
A ranking of the steps by difficulty
optionExplain: More description is not a theory.
Right: a description becomes a theory when it generates the behavior.
Opinions are not predictions.
A ranking does not generate behavior.
questions.explain: Description and theory are different. The card next names the authors' plan.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: The PBG is a basic ____ of the subject's behavior, and a program that predicts it is the next step.
questions.explain: The authors build a bridge from description to a full theory.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Which feature of S3's talk does the authors give as partly explaining why extracting the PBG was not hard?
options: His fast speaking rate
His use of written notes to explain his steps
The help of a second coder
The limited range of his linguistic behavior, so complicated interpretations are infrequent
optionExplain: Speed is not given as a reason.
Notes are not the reason.
No second coder is mentioned.
Right: simple talk eased the coding.
questions.explain: The task's narrow language made interpretation easy.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: The authors say a certain degree of looseness will remain in fitting the program they outline to the data.
questions.explain: True: a certain degree of looseness will remain in fitting the program to the data.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A team has coded one pupil's talk into a graph of steps and now wants to explain it. Following the authors, what comes next?
options: Outline a program that would produce the pupil's graph and compare its output with the actual graph
Publish the graph as the finished theory
Ask more pupils to repeat the same talk
Remove the steps that the program cannot explain
optionExplain: Right: predict, then compare in detail.
The graph is a description.
Repeating talk does not build the theory.
Failures are examined, not removed.
questions.explain: Predict the graph, compare, and look at the failures.
questions.teaches: The authors will compare the program's predictions with the PBG in some detail, to see how closely it matches and in what particular respects it fails.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A cook has worked out one fact about a recipe. What else does a model of the cook need, beyond the cook's arithmetic skill, to predict what she does next?
options: Only the list of ingredients
Only the cook's age and training
A way of choosing the next task, and assumptions about what she remembers
Nothing further, since skill decides everything
optionExplain: The next action depends on more than the task data.
The model concerns processes.
Right: strategy and memory both shape what comes next.
Skill does not choose the next step.
questions.explain: Choosing and remembering are parts of the model. The card next names the three components.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Match each component of the program to what it does.
pairs: Draw inferences from the relations of the problem
Say what is remembered and when it is called up
questions.explain: These are the three components the authors expect.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: After S3 infers D = 5 and then T = 0, which component of the program decides what task he takes up next?
options: The memory assumptions alone
The arithmetic processes alone
The experimenter's remarks
The strategy, the set of processes that choose the next task
optionExplain: Memory affects the choice but is not the strategy.
Arithmetic produces inferences, it does not choose.
The experimenter is not a component of the program.
Right: strategy is the deciding component.
questions.explain: Deciding the next task is strategy.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: On the authors' account, strategy is synonymous with the set of processes and need not involve an overall plan, much less a conscious one.
questions.explain: True: strategy is synonymous with the set of processes and need not involve an overall plan, much less a conscious one.
questions.rule: Strategy need not be a plan.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A traveler follows the rule of taking the exit nearest the platform edge, with no plan of the whole route. Is that a strategy in the authors' sense?
options: No, because a strategy requires a plan of the whole route
Yes; a set of processes that decides what to do next counts, without an overall plan
No, because it is conscious
Yes, but only if written down
optionExplain: The authors say it need not.
Right: no overall or conscious plan is needed.
Consciousness is not a condition either way.
Writing is not a condition.
questions.explain: A choosing rule is a strategy.
questions.rule: Strategy can be a simple rule.
questions.teaches: The authors say the subject's strategy may be implicit or explicit, and that the program's components must bear an appropriate relation to the task environment if the program is to be effective.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A program solves a puzzle and keeps every fact it has validly inferred. What does a human solver add that the program lacks?
options: The ability to add digits
Knowledge of the rules of the puzzle
Limits and vagaries of memory
A wish to finish the puzzle
optionExplain: Arithmetic is set by the task, which the program shares.
Both know the rules.
Right: forgetting is what is specifically human here.
The authors do not locate the difference there.
questions.explain: Perfect memory belongs to programs, not people. The card next sorts task from subject.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A great deal of what is specifically psychological about S3 revolves around the limitations and vagaries of his ____.
questions.explain: Arithmetic is set by the task, but memory is the person's.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: S3 infers that if y = 2x + 1 with integers x and y, then y is odd. Where do the authors place this kind of rule?
options: With the task environment, as arithmetic operators determined by the rules of arithmetic
With S3's idiosyncrasies
With the experimenter's instructions
With S3's memory limits
optionExplain: Right: the inference is dictated by arithmetic, not by the subject's quirks.
Any solver who knows arithmetic could use it.
The instructions do not contain it.
The rule is not about memory.
questions.explain: Rules of arithmetic belong to the task.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: S3's early inference that R = 7 gives L = 3 and c3 = 0 was an invalid inference, a difficulty particular to S3 rather than dictated by the rules of arithmetic.
questions.explain: True: it was an invalid inference, a difficulty particular to S3, so it was not dictated by the rules of arithmetic.
questions.rule: A slip belongs to the person.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Two students face the same sum. One tries every combination of digits; the other deduces assignments column by column. What does this show about the task, on the authors' view?
options: Deducing is possible in the task, but whether a subject uses it is a matter of the subject
The task forces deduction on all subjects
The task forbids deduction
The two students must have different arithmetic
optionExplain: Right: the task offers the option; the subject may or may not take it.
The authors say another subject might not use it.
S3 uses it.
Both have the same arithmetic available.
questions.explain: The option is the task's; the use is the subject's.
questions.teaches: That S3 can deduce the assignments without trying all combinations is an objective property of the task environment, although another subject might very well not make use of it.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: Analysis of the Protocol: A Production System
questions.q: You have a long record of what a person knew at each step and what they then did. What kind of program is easiest to induce from such a record?
options: A fixed script of steps in order
A single formula for the total time taken
A set of rules pairing specific information with an action
A list of the person's favorite digits
optionExplain: A script ignores the state at each step.
A formula for time does not explain choices.
Right: the record is a list of state and action pairs.
Preferences are not what the record shows.
questions.explain: Pairs of state and action suggest condition-action rules. The card next names them productions.
questions.rule: State and action pairs suggest rules.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: Analysis of the Protocol: A Production System
questions.q: The total program is the collection of productions plus an ____ of the productions that resolves conflict.
questions.explain: Several productions may have conditions met at the same time, so an ordering decides which acts.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: Analysis of the Protocol: A Production System
questions.q: Why must repetition of decision situations exist for a proposed process to be verified?
options: Because repeated situations make the protocol longer
If every situation evoked a unique process, there would be no way to check that a proposed process was in fact used
Because the subject was told to repeat himself
Because the computer needs repeated input
optionExplain: Length is not the reason.
Right: verification needs repeats.
The subject was not told so.
No computer is used in this analysis.
questions.explain: A process shown by one case cannot be checked against another.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: Analysis of the Protocol: A Production System
questions.q: True or false: The sameness of two decision situations is fixed in advance, before any process is proposed.
questions.explain: Each of the 238 states is unique; how much repetition exists is defined afterward by the proposed process and its laws of evocation.
questions.rule: Sameness is defined after the fact.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: Analysis of the Protocol: A Production System
questions.q: A bank studies one clerk's choices over a day and finds she handles two kinds of cheque the same way. How does this match the authors' reasoning on repetition?
options: Every cheque is identical, so repetition is given
A rule cannot be checked with more than one cheque
The clerk's choices are random, so no rule exists
Grouping cheques by a proposed rule makes a repetition, and the rule can then be checked on other cheques
optionExplain: Each situation differs in detail.
Several cheques are what check it.
Nothing implies randomness.
Right: repetition is defined by the proposed process, then verified.
questions.explain: A rule defines which situations count as the same.
questions.rule: A proposed rule defines the repetition.
questions.teaches: The production system of Figure 6.7 was induced by examining the problem graph in the light of various notions of how problem solving might proceed in the cryptarithmetic task, and the notation follows that of earlier chapters with a few additions.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: Analysis of the Protocol: A Production System
questions.q: A solver decides which column of the sum to look at next. Does this choice change what the solver knows about the letters?
options: Yes, since it fixes a digit for a letter
Yes, since it infers a new relation
No; it changes where attention goes, not what is known
Yes, since it tests a digit
optionExplain: Fixing a digit is assignment.
Inference comes from processing the column.
Right: choosing where to look does not add knowledge by itself.
Testing is a different step.
questions.explain: Selecting is not the same as learning. The card next names the selecting processes.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: Analysis of the Protocol: A Production System
questions.q: Match each attention process to its job.
pairs: Finds a column containing a given variable
Finds the column or relation used to derive an expression
Generates the columns of a set from right to left
Finds the production that yielded an expression
questions.explain: These are four of the five attention processes.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: Analysis of the Protocol: A Production System
questions.q: The goal is to check all six columns. Which process puts the columns in order for processing, from right to left?
options: GNC
FC
FL
FP
optionExplain: Right: it generates the columns of a set from right to left.
FC finds a column for one variable.
FL finds a letter, not a column.
FP recalls a production.
questions.explain: Generating columns in order is GNC's job.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: Analysis of the Protocol: A Production System
questions.q: True or false: FC, FA, GNC, FL and FP change the knowledge state, so they are counted among the four operators.
questions.explain: They produce outputs that do not change the knowledge state as defined, so they were left out of the original operators; they control attention.
questions.rule: Not changing the state means not an operator.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: Analysis of the Protocol: A Production System
questions.q: A librarian picks the shelf that holds a book on her list, and separately remembers which search she ran last time. Which pair of S3's processes does this resemble?
options: PC for finding the place, and AV for recalling
GN and TD for the two tasks
FL for both tasks
FC for finding the place, and FP for recalling the earlier procedure
optionExplain: PC and AV are operators that change the state.
GN and TD are operators.
FL finds a letter from a set.
Right: one finds a location, the other recalls a past production.
questions.explain: Finding a place and recalling a past action are two attention processes.
questions.teaches: FL can use the display and current knowledge about letters to select, among those still undetermined, the particular letter that occurs the maximum number of times in the display; FP differs from FA in outputting a production rather than a column or relation.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: Analysis of the Protocol: A Production System
questions.q: A solver has learned a digit for a letter and goes to a column containing that letter to see what follows. Another wants to know a letter's value and goes to a column containing it. What differs?
options: The first uses algebra, the second does not
The first is driven by new information, the second by a goal
The first is correct, the second is wrong
The first needs the experimenter, the second does not
optionExplain: Neither uses algebra here.
Right: same move, different trigger.
Both can be sound.
The experimenter plays no part.
questions.explain: Information-driven and goal-driven moves can look alike. The card next names the productions.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: Analysis of the Protocol: A Production System
questions.q: P1 is evoked by new information, whereas P2 is evoked by a ____.
questions.explain: Both then find a column containing the variable and process it.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: Analysis of the Protocol: A Production System
questions.q: S3 has inferred that R is 7 and turns to another column containing R without having set any aim. Which production is this?
options: P2, evoked by a goal to get R
P1, evoked by the new assignment
P5, checking the columns
P11, testing a digit
optionExplain: No goal is in play.
Right: new information about a variable triggers P1.
P5 concerns checking.
P11 tests; it does not go to a column.
questions.explain: Fresh information sends him to another column.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: Analysis of the Protocol: A Production System
questions.q: True or false: After P1 succeeds, the new tag is removed, so the production will not be repeated on the same expression.
questions.explain: True: successful execution removes the new tag, so the production will not be repeated on the same expression.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: Analysis of the Protocol: A Production System
questions.q: A shopper sees a price drop on one item and checks other shelves; another shopper, with a list to fill, checks shelves for a missing item. Which shopper acts like P2?
options: The one reacting to the price drop, since fresh information moves her
Both, since both visit shelves
Neither, since shelves are not columns
The one filling a list, since a goal sends her to the shelves
optionExplain: That is P1.
They differ in what drives them.
The comparison is by trigger, not by object.
Right: P2 is goal-driven.
questions.explain: A goal, not new information, drives P2.
questions.teaches: P2 can be applied repeatedly to the same variable, gradually accumulating information about it, and its goal can be either information about a variable or a relation such as get c5 = 1.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: Analysis of the Protocol: A Production System
questions.q: To find a letter's value, a solver picks a value for another letter in the same column and uses it. How does this compare with picking the first letter's value directly?
options: It looks less arbitrary, though it is still a guess
It is a proof, so no guessing remains
It is slower and always worse
It is the same step by another name
optionExplain: Right: the guess is moved to a letter that then fixes the first.
A value was still assigned.
Nothing says it is always worse.
It differs by what is assigned.
questions.explain: Assigning a neighbor can look less arbitrary. The card next states the production.
questions.rule: Guess a neighbor, derive the target.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: Analysis of the Protocol: A Production System
questions.q: P3 applies only to ____, although it could equally well be generalized to include carries.
questions.explain: S3 never performed P3 with carries, so the authors keep P3's condition narrow.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: Analysis of the Protocol: A Production System
questions.q: S3 wants the value of letter.1, finds a column containing it, assigns a digit to the other letter there, and then uses PC. Which production is this?
options: P1
P4
P3
optionExplain: P1 starts from new information.
P4 generates admissible values of a constrained variable.
Right: assign the other letter, then determine letter.1.
P12 backtracks on a contradiction.
questions.explain: Assigning the other letter and processing the column is P3.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: Analysis of the Protocol: A Production System
questions.q: True or false: The authors state P3 for letters and carries together, since the rule would work equally well on both.
questions.explain: They keep P3 to letters because S3 never used it with carries; the principle is to use the smallest class that covers the observed cases.
questions.rule: Do not generalize beyond the data.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: Analysis of the Protocol: A Production System
questions.q: A teacher notes that a pupil uses a trick only on fractions and not on decimals, although it would work on both. Following the authors' principle, how should the teacher describe the pupil's rule?
options: As applying to all numbers, since it would work
As applying to nothing in particular
As an accident, so no rule is stated
As applying to fractions, the smallest class that covers the observed cases
optionExplain: The principle says to stay with the observed cases.
It was used on fractions.
A repeated use is a regularity.
Right: do not widen it beyond what was seen.
questions.explain: State a rule as narrowly as the observations allow.
questions.rule: State rules as narrowly as the data allow.
questions.teaches: The organization of the problem space dictates the generalizations that take place: P1 is genuinely general in having an assignment-expression as its condition, because not all combinations of letters and digits occurred.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: Analysis of the Protocol: A Production System
questions.q: A letter is known to be 7 or 9. What would a sensible solver do next with the letter?
options: Wait until the letter is forced to a single value
List the two values and pick one to try
Try all ten digits
Give up on that letter
optionExplain: He can act on two candidates.
Right: with few candidates, choosing one is practical.
Ten digits ignore what is known.
Two candidates are few enough to try.
questions.explain: A short list of candidates invites trying one. The card next states P4.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: Analysis of the Protocol: A Production System
questions.q: P5 generates the columns from ____ to left and executes PC on each.
questions.explain: P5 governs the final check of all columns.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: Analysis of the Protocol: A Production System
questions.q: S3 knows R is 7 or 9 and decides to try one. Which production does this?
options: P5, checking the columns
P3, assigning a neighbor letter
P4, generating the admissible values and assigning one because few remain
P9, picking a letter from a set
optionExplain: P5 comes at the end.
P3 assigns another letter in a column.
Right: a small set leads to an assignment.
P9 selects a letter, not a value.
questions.explain: A constrained variable with few values is P4's case.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: Analysis of the Protocol: A Production System
questions.q: True or false: P4 assigns a value if only a few values satisfy the constraint on a letter; otherwise it does nothing.
questions.explain: True: if only a few values satisfy the constraint it assigns one; otherwise it does nothing.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: Analysis of the Protocol: A Production System
questions.q: A packer has a fixed order for checking a finished crate: each side, right to left, once at the end. Which production is it like?
options: P5, a check run once at the end that governs a long sequence
P1, evoked by new information each time
P4, generating a few admissible values
P12, backing up after a contradiction
optionExplain: Right: P5 is evoked once, at the end.
P1 repeats with new information.
P4 concerns constrained variables.
P12 is evoked by impossibility.
questions.explain: One final sweep is P5.
questions.teaches: P5 is evoked only once during the course of problem solving, namely at the end, yet it governs a rather long sequence of behavior.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: Analysis of the Protocol: A Production System
questions.q: A solver learns that a value he tried for a letter is impossible. Does he deny the news or accept it and look elsewhere?
options: He accepts it and looks for another value of the letter
He denies it and checks the fact
He ends the whole attempt
He picks a different puzzle
optionExplain: Right: the production for impossibility sets a goal to get the variable again.
That would be a check goal, not P7.
Nothing ends the attempt.
The task is fixed.
questions.explain: Accepting an impossibility leads to seeking a new value. The card next names the productions.
questions.rule: Accept the news; seek another value.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: Analysis of the Protocol: A Production System
questions.q: Match each production to what it responds to.
pairs: An expression that is relevant but unknown
A set of letters to be evaluated
An expression critical to a process, tagged note
questions.explain: These four productions each set a goal in response to a condition.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: Analysis of the Protocol: A Production System
questions.q: S3 finds that R = 5 is impossible and goes back to finding a value for R. Which production produced the new goal?
options: P10, which sets a check goal
P8, which bridges check and get for a new expression
P7, which sets the goal get variable for the variable of an impossible expression
P6, which responds to an unknown expression
optionExplain: P10 responds to a note-tagged expression.
P8 concerns new expressions to be checked.
Right: acceptance of the impossibility leads to a new search.
The expression is impossible, not unknown.
questions.explain: Impossibility leads to P7.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: Analysis of the Protocol: A Production System
questions.q: True or false: P7 represents the subject's attempt to deny the new information that an expression is impossible.
questions.explain: P7 represents his acceptance of it, which leads him to look for another value; denial would lead to a check goal.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: Analysis of the Protocol: A Production System
questions.q: A planner finds one route closed and immediately sets herself the task of finding another route. Which production's logic is this?
options: P10, checking a critical fact
P7, accepting an impossibility and seeking a new value
P6, learning something relevant is unknown
P9, picking a letter from a set
optionExplain: She is not checking the closure.
Right: the closure is accepted and a new goal set.
The closure is known.
No set is being picked from.
questions.explain: Accept, then seek another.
questions.teaches: P9 provides something to work on when all else fails, since the initial problem is stated as get all-letters; it selects a member from a set of letters.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: Analysis of the Protocol: A Production System
questions.q: A solver finds that a conclusion cannot hold. What should she do about the step that led to it?
options: Keep the earlier step, since it came first
Discard the whole problem
Ignore the clash
Trace back and mark that earlier step as impossible too
optionExplain: It led to the clash.
Only the chain needs undoing.
A clash cannot be ignored.
Right: backtracking undoes the implication chain.
questions.explain: A contradiction is passed back along the chain that produced it. The card next gives the production.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: Analysis of the Protocol: A Production System
questions.q: P11 tests a newly derived digit for a letter by means of the operator ____.
questions.explain: The result is either a plus or an impossibility with its reason.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: Analysis of the Protocol: A Production System
questions.q: S3 derives a new digit for a letter and finds it already belongs to another letter. Which production carries out the test?
options: P12, which backs up on a contradiction
P5, which checks the columns
P11, which applies TD to the newly derived value
P3, which assigns a neighbor letter
optionExplain: P12 acts after an impossibility is known.
P5 acts at the end.
Right: new digit values are tested.
P3 assigns, it does not test.
questions.explain: New digit for a letter means test.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: Analysis of the Protocol: A Production System
questions.q: True or false: There is no check on the value of a newly derived carry like the one P11 makes on the value of a letter.
questions.explain: True: there is no similar check on the value of a carry.
questions.rule: Carries are not tested by P11.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: Analysis of the Protocol: A Production System
questions.q: A scheduler finds that an appointment clashes with another and then withdraws the booking that caused the chain of changes. Which production is it like?
options: P12, which declares the expression used in the derivation impossible too
P11, which tests a new digit
P4, which generates admissible values
P13, which repeats an unclear operator
optionExplain: Right: it follows the derivation back.
P11 detects the clash but does not follow it back.
P4 concerns values for a constrained variable.
P13 concerns unclear results.
questions.explain: Withdrawing the cause is backtracking.
questions.teaches: P11 is also evoked when digits are generated in the context of obtaining values for a variable, so every generated digit is tested as well as every newly inferred one.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: Analysis of the Protocol: A Production System
questions.q: A solver gets an answer he is not sure of. What is a natural next move?
options: Accept it and say nothing
Delete the step from memory
Switch to a new puzzle
Repeat the step to confirm it
optionExplain: Doubt invites a repeat.
Deleting does not settle it.
The task is fixed.
Right: repetition is a way to settle doubt.
questions.explain: Doubt leads to repetition. The card next shows how the authors state this.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: Analysis of the Protocol: A Production System
questions.q: P13 repeats an operator, normally PC, when its result is tagged ____.
questions.explain: An unclear result leads to the goal of getting the variable again.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: Analysis of the Protocol: A Production System
questions.q: Which result would the authors call clear from the first time?
options: The inference that R is odd from 1 + L + L = R
The sum of two known digits, as in 5 + 5 giving T equal to 0
A line of reasoning ending in a contradiction
An inference that gives no definite conclusion
optionExplain: This is unclear the first time.
Right: adding two digits is always clear.
Contradictions are unclear.
These are unclear too.
questions.explain: Simple addition is clear; complex inference is unclear at first.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: Analysis of the Protocol: A Production System
questions.q: True or false: P14 needs no memory of what happened earlier in the protocol.
questions.explain: P14 finds the production used in an earlier derivation, so it implies some memory of production occurrences.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: Analysis of the Protocol: A Production System
questions.q: A teacher asks a pupil to check an earlier answer, and the pupil redoes the same working. Which production does the pupil's move resemble?
options: P13, repeating because the result was unclear
P14, repeating the production that derived the expression
P11, testing a new digit
P6, setting a goal for an unknown
optionExplain: The pupil is asked to check, not unsure.
Right: checking by repeating the earlier derivation.
No new digit is tested.
The answer is known.
questions.explain: Checking by redoing is P14.
questions.teaches: The tag unclear also covers processes that lead to contradictions and those from which no definite conclusion can be drawn, not only the first use of a complex inference.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: Analysis of the Protocol: A Production System
questions.q: A set of rules has two whose conditions can both be met at the same moment. What does the set still need to predict behavior?
options: A third rule that repeats both
Nothing; both act at once
A longer list of conditions
A rule for which of the two acts
optionExplain: Repeating does not settle which acts.
The behavior shows one action.
More conditions do not choose between two.
Right: a priority order settles conflict.
questions.explain: Conflicting rules need an order. The card next lists what is missing.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: Analysis of the Protocol: A Production System
questions.q: Match each gap in the production system to its consequence.
pairs: Conflicts between productions are not resolved
They give rise to no production
The system cannot solve the task by itself
questions.explain: Each gap limits what the system can predict.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: Analysis of the Protocol: A Production System
questions.q: P2 and P3 have identical conditions. What does the system say about which acts?
options: It does not say; the order in the figure is essentially arbitrary
P2 always acts first, by its number
P3 always acts first, being newer
They both act at once
optionExplain: Right: the priority order is not specified.
The figure's order carries no such meaning.
No such rule is given.
Only one acts at a node.
questions.explain: The system is silent on priority until the data are examined.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: Analysis of the Protocol: A Production System
questions.q: True or false: The system of Figure 6.7, as it stands, is capable of solving DONALD + GERALD.
questions.explain: Nodes that were idiosyncratic or unclear gave no productions, so the system cannot solve the task without augmentation.
questions.rule: A fitted system need not be a solver.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: Analysis of the Protocol: A Production System
questions.q: A team builds rules from a chess player's repeated habits and leaves out one-off moves. Which limitation of the authors' system would this share?
options: The rules would play better than the player
The rules would predict every move
The rules may not be able to play a full game without additions
The rules would need no ordering
optionExplain: Nothing makes them better.
One-off moves are left out.
Right: rules built from regularities leave out the unique cases.
Conflicts would still need an ordering.
questions.explain: Rules from regularities lack the odd moves.
questions.teaches: The productions form an integrated system in one nonobvious way: the context in which conditions are tested is provided by the products of the productions themselves, so the conditions can be adequate within the restricted context even if inadequate in a larger one.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: Analysis of the Protocol: A Production System
questions.q: A search program must decide what to do at each point. Which four jobs must it do?
options: Add numbers, subtract numbers, multiply and divide
Read, write, speak and listen
Start, pause, stop and restart
Choose a step, judge the state, pick where to continue, and set goals
optionExplain: Those are arithmetic skills.
These are modes of communication.
These are controls, not search functions.
Right: selection, evaluation, node choice and goal setting.
questions.explain: Search needs four jobs. The card next sorts the productions among them.
questions.rule: Select, evaluate, choose node, set goals.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: Analysis of the Protocol: A Production System
questions.q: Match each function to the productions that carry it out.
pairs: P1, P2, P3, P4, P5 and P11
P6, P7, P8, P9 and P10
questions.explain: Each function is carried out by a group of productions.
questions.rule: Know which productions do which job.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: Analysis of the Protocol: A Production System
questions.q: Which production backs down the tree, eliminating nodes as candidates for restarting?
options: P6
P1
optionExplain: P13 helps fix the node to use, with P14.
Right: P12 does the backing down.
P6 sets a goal.
P1 selects an operator.
questions.explain: P12 carries out the backing down.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: Analysis of the Protocol: A Production System
questions.q: True or false: The authors treat an impossibility as ending a line of search by an explicit termination production.
questions.explain: Termination on impossibility is implicit, because no production that selects new operators does so with an impossibility tag.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: Analysis of the Protocol: A Production System
questions.q: A hiker returns to the last fork whenever a path ends in a cliff and tries the nearest untried path there. Which search strategy does this equal?
options: Breadth-first search
Random search
Depth-first search, in the authors' account of selecting prior nodes
Means-ends analysis
optionExplain: That would try all paths at one level first.
The hiker follows a rule.
Right: continuing at the current node unless prohibited, with path memory, is depth-first.
That is about subgoals, a different function.
questions.explain: Stay at the current node unless it is ruled out; back up when it is.
