questions.teaches: Productions P6, P7 and P10, along with P13, form one component of means-ends analysis, namely the immediate reaction to a difficulty by setting up a goal to deal with it, which builds hierarchic subgoals within subgoals.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A model of a driver says nothing about a turn the driver made, and also predicts a turn the driver did not make. Are these the same kind of failure?
options: No; one is silence and the other is a false assertion
Yes; both are failures to predict the driver's behavior
Yes; every model error is a false assertion
No; only the silence counts against the model
optionExplain: Right: they are different kinds of failure.
Both fail, but in different ways.
Silence asserts nothing.
A false assertion counts against it too.
questions.explain: Silence and false assertion differ. The card next names them.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Match each kind of error to its description.
pairs: The system is silent on behavior that occurs
The system makes a specific but wrong assertion
Writing down which production, if any, seems evoked at each node
questions.explain: The evaluation first accounts for the fit, then looks at the two kinds of error.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: At one node the system evokes P3, but the subject, by the priority scheme, should have had P2. What kind of error is this?
options: Commission, since the system made a specific but wrong assertion
Omission, since the system was silent
No error, since both are productions
An error in the protocol itself
optionExplain: Right: a wrong production was evoked.
The system was not silent.
A wrong production is an error.
The error is the system's.
questions.explain: A wrong choice is commission.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: A node at which no production can be found to fit is an error of omission: the system is silent on behavior that occurs.
questions.explain: True: it is an error of omission, since the system is silent on behavior that occurs.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A weather model leaves out a storm that happened and also forecasts a storm that did not happen. How would the authors classify the two failures?
options: Both are omissions
Both are commissions
The missed storm is an omission; the false forecast is a commission
The missed storm is a commission; the false forecast is an omission
optionExplain: The false forecast is an assertion.
The missed storm is silence.
Right: silence versus a wrong assertion.
The classification is reversed.
questions.explain: Missing events are omissions; false assertions are commissions.
questions.teaches: Later the authors count both kinds on the same set of nodes, finding 30 errors of omission and 23 definite errors of commission, and note that combining them in a single percentage hides what each tells us.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: How Much Does the Production System Explain?
questions.q: Why might an analyst write the rule used at each step beside the original words of a speaker rather than on a separate diagram?
options: Because a diagram cannot be drawn for rules
To compare each rule directly with the words that are its evidence
To hide the words from readers
To shorten the record
optionExplain: A diagram can be drawn; the authors have one.
Right: the talk is the main evidence.
The aim is the opposite.
Shortness is not the reason.
questions.explain: Placing the mark beside the evidence lets readers check it. The card next gives the conventions.
questions.rule: Put the mark beside the evidence.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: How Much Does the Production System Explain?
questions.q: The authors mark a node with a ____ mark when the information behind a production's condition cannot be discerned.
questions.explain: A question mark records that the evidence does not permit a call.
questions.rule: Mark the unknown with a question.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: How Much Does the Production System Explain?
questions.q: Two nodes in a row are covered by the same production, whose action runs over both. How is the second node marked?
options: With the production number repeated and a new question mark
With the letter d
It is left blank
With a vertical arrow pointing to the production named at the previous node
optionExplain: A repeat would hide that the production is the same occurrence.
d stands for the input to TD.
Blank is not a convention here.
Right: the arrow shows it is covered by the preceding production.
questions.explain: The arrow carries a production across nodes.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: How Much Does the Production System Explain?
questions.q: True or false: The authors mark the productions on the protocol itself, to permit comparison of the productions with the verbal behavior.
questions.explain: True: they mark them on the protocol itself, to permit comparison of the productions with the verbal behavior.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: How Much Does the Production System Explain?
questions.q: A coder annotates a transcript and sometimes finds a passage that is plainly a conversation about the task rules. What does the authors' convention suggest she writes?
options: A new production number invented for the passage
Nothing, since such passages do not matter
A question mark with a comment such as outside the problem space
An arrow to the previous production
optionExplain: No production is invented.
They are noted.
Right: the authors comment in English when behavior lies outside the space.
An arrow means the same production continues.
questions.explain: Out-of-space behavior gets a question mark and a comment.
questions.rule: Comment on what is outside the space.
questions.teaches: When TD is applied to several members of a generator, the authors write the input with a variable d, though this can look as if TD interrupts another production, since it is applied to each output.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: How Much Does the Production System Explain?
questions.q: A rule's output feeds straight into another rule, which fires, and then another. Should the second and third firings be counted as separate events when scoring a model?
options: Yes, since each is a place where a rule applies
No, because only the first firing is observed
No, because they cannot be wrong
Only if the speaker says them aloud
optionExplain: Right: they are occurrences of rules.
Implied firings are part of the model's account.
They can be wrong.
The model's own sequence implies them.
questions.explain: Chained firings are occurrences too. The card next gives the authors' count.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: How Much Does the Production System Explain?
questions.q: The data set grows from 238 nodes to ____ production occurrences.
questions.explain: The expansion is about 15 percent.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: How Much Does the Production System Explain?
questions.q: At B7, TD is applied to a digit and gives a plus, so no node is drawn in the graph. How does the accounting treat it?
options: As nothing, since it has no node
As an error of omission
As an outside conversation with the experimenter
As a production occurrence of P11, although no graph node exists
optionExplain: The authors count it.
It is part of the system's account.
It is internal.
Right: implied occurrences are counted.
questions.explain: A passing test with no graph node is still an occurrence.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: How Much Does the Production System Explain?
questions.q: True or false: The expansion from 238 to 275 is an increase of about 50 percent.
questions.explain: It is about 15 percent: 275 divided by 238 is a little more than 1.15.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: How Much Does the Production System Explain?
questions.q: A school counts only the lessons on the timetable, but each lesson holds several short tasks. Which counting choice parallels the authors' decision?
options: Count only the lessons, as the timetable lists
Count the tasks inside the lessons too, and call each such place an occurrence
Count only the first task in each lesson
Count only the tasks pupils mention
optionExplain: That would be like keeping 238 nodes.
Right: expand the units to include implied occurrences.
That would hide later occurrences.
Mention is not the criterion.
questions.explain: Count the units the model says occur.
questions.teaches: Subsequent evocations of productions to implied products are carried along only as long as they are not contradicted by the data, which is how the number of nodes handled rises from 238 to 275.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: How Much Does the Production System Explain?
questions.q: A rule says: if A holds, do B. The analyst sees a person do B. Can the analyst say the rule was used?
options: Yes, since B is what the rule does
Not unless A held, since B may have come from another rule
No, since rules are never used by people
Yes, if the person says B aloud
optionExplain: B alone does not identify the rule.
Right: the condition must have held.
The model does posit rules.
Saying B is not evidence of A.
questions.explain: An action does not identify the rule; its condition does. The card next shows how the authors handle this.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: How Much Does the Production System Explain?
questions.q: The State-production Table is built by recording the expressions produced and by maintaining a goal ____.
questions.explain: With the state recorded, each production is matched at each context point.
questions.rule: The table tracks a goal stack.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: How Much Does the Production System Explain?
questions.q: At B185 the action resembles P5's, yet the authors code a question mark. Why?
options: P5 never occurs in the protocol
The action is of a different kind from P5's
B185 is outside the problem space
The condition for P5, the goal to check a set of columns, is not satisfied
optionExplain: P5 occurs once, at the end.
The action is similar.
The reason is the unsatisfied condition.
Right: a production is not recognized by its action part alone.
questions.explain: Without the condition, the production is not credited.
questions.rule: Credit the condition, not just the action.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: How Much Does the Production System Explain?
questions.q: True or false: The authors count a production as evoked whenever its action part is observed, even if its condition does not hold.
questions.explain: It is not possible for a production to be evoked when its conditions are not satisfied; productions are not recognized by their action part alone.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: How Much Does the Production System Explain?
questions.q: A teacher sees a pupil write 12 under a sum and credits the rule of adding units first, but the pupil had copied it. Which of the authors' principles does she break?
options: She credits a rule from its outcome without evidence that its condition was met
She counts a negative instance as a positive
She uses the pupil's own words as evidence
She expands the data set
optionExplain: Right: the condition must be shown.
She did not consider a negative instance.
No words were used.
That is not the issue.
questions.explain: Outcomes do not credit a rule.
questions.rule: Do not credit a rule by outcome alone.
questions.teaches: The authors accept as evidence for the condition part either explicit data from the protocol or implicit data output by prior productions that have been evoked.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: How Much Does the Production System Explain?
questions.q: Two rules both applied at 10 moments. One was used 8 times and the other 2. What might this suggest?
options: That the rules are the same
That the data are random
That one rule takes priority over the other
That the second rule is wrong
optionExplain: They behaved differently.
Eight to two is not an even split.
Right: a strong bias suggests an ordering.
It was used twice, which shows nothing about being wrong.
questions.explain: One-sided counts suggest priority. The card next gives the matrix.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: How Much Does the Production System Explain?
questions.q: In Figure 6.8 the diagonal entry (j, j) gives the number of times production j did ____.
questions.explain: Off-diagonal entries show how often another production was chosen when j could have occurred.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: How Much Does the Production System Explain?
questions.q: In the cases where P3 or P4 could have occurred, which production did the subject use?
options: P3 in 14 cases and P4 in none
P3 and P4 equally often
Neither, since both are goal setters
P4 in 14 cases and P3 in none
optionExplain: The counts are reversed.
The counts were far from equal.
They are operator-selecting productions.
Right: P4 dominated entirely.
questions.explain: The matrix shows P4 beating P3 in every competition.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: How Much Does the Production System Explain?
questions.q: True or false: In 10 cases where P1 or P2 could have occurred, the authors found P2 chosen in 8 and P1 in 2.
questions.explain: P1 was chosen in 8 and P2 in 2.
questions.rule: Read the entries the right way round.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: How Much Does the Production System Explain?
questions.q: A scorer tallies, for a tennis player, how often she chose a lob when a volley was also possible, and the reverse. What does this tally resemble?
options: An error of omission
A matrix of could-occur against did-occur, whose lopsidedness suggests a preference order
A state-production table
A graph of the priority ordering
optionExplain: It counts choices, not silences.
Right: pair counts reveal the order.
That table records conditions per node.
The tally comes before an ordering.
questions.explain: Pair counts show how two options fare against each other.
questions.rule: Count pairs to find an order.
questions.teaches: For any pair of productions, the symmetric off-diagonal entries (i, j) and (j, i) tell how those productions fared against each other; if no nodes had both conditions satisfied, both entries would be zero.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: How Much Does the Production System Explain?
questions.q: Rule A beat rule B in most of their head-to-head cases, and rule B beat rule C. Is it safe to put A above C?
options: Yes, always, since order is transitive
No, since A and C never met
Not without checking, because the data might contradict that order
Yes, since A is alphabetically first
optionExplain: The data need not be transitive.
They may have met.
Right: transitivity must be checked, not assumed.
Alphabet is irrelevant.
questions.explain: Pairwise results need not line up. The card next states what the authors found.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: How Much Does the Production System Explain?
questions.q: Production j is placed above production i when entry (i, j) is ____ than entry (j, i).
questions.explain: That is, j beat i more often than i beat j.
questions.rule: Winner of the pair goes higher.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: How Much Does the Production System Explain?
questions.q: Rule X was chosen over rule Y in 9 of 12 cases where both could occur. Where does the authors' method place them?
options: X above Y
Y above X
X and Y tied
Neither can be placed
optionExplain: Right: X won more often.
Y won fewer cases.
Nine against three is not a tie.
The data suffice to place them.
questions.explain: Majority wins the higher place.
questions.rule: Place the more frequent winner higher.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: How Much Does the Production System Explain?
questions.q: True or false: Because the priority ordering is transitive, it describes the subject's choices perfectly.
questions.explain: Every nonzero entry above the diagonal in Figure 6.9 is a case where the lower production was selected, so inversions remain.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: How Much Does the Production System Explain?
questions.q: A team ranks four restaurants by head-to-head visits. Three have no visit records against any other. Where should they go in the ranking, on the authors' treatment of P14, P5 and P8?
options: Anywhere, since the data give no reason to prefer one position over another
At the bottom, because they have never won
Left out of the study
Ranked by the number of letters in their names
optionExplain: Right: with no data the position is arbitrary.
No data means no losses either.
The authors keep the isolates.
Names are irrelevant.
questions.explain: With no data to specify their order, the isolates could equally well be anywhere in the ordering; their placement is bookkeeping.
questions.teaches: The three productions that are essentially isolates, P14, P5 and P8, are placed at the top, but they could equally well be anywhere in the ordering.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: How Much Does the Production System Explain?
questions.q: A model adds rules one at a time, most useful first. How should its coverage of the data grow?
options: In steps of the same size each time
In larger and larger steps
In smaller and smaller steps
Not at all after the first
optionExplain: The best come first.
Later rules cover fewer cases.
Right: the best rules come first, so later rules add less.
Later rules still add something.
questions.explain: Ordered by usefulness, gains shrink. The card next gives the authors' figures.
questions.rule: Gains shrink as rules are added.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: How Much Does the Production System Explain?
questions.q: With P13 alone the production system covers about ____ percent of the nodes.
questions.explain: Coverage climbs to 89 percent with all the productions.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: How Much Does the Production System Explain?
questions.q: Why does the relevant total stand at 267 and not 275?
options: Eight nodes were lost from the protocol
Eight contexts lie plainly outside the problem space, such as talk with the experimenter
Eight productions were removed from the system
Eight nodes were coded twice
optionExplain: Nothing was lost.
Right: they are excluded.
The productions are unchanged.
Double coding is not the reason.
questions.explain: Out-of-space contexts are excluded from the total.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: How Much Does the Production System Explain?
questions.q: True or false: In Figure 6.10, the number of definite errors is highest when only P13 is included.
questions.explain: With P13 alone there are no errors, as there is no conflict with other productions; errors climb to 23 with all of them.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: How Much Does the Production System Explain?
questions.q: A repair manual covers 16 percent of faults with its first rule, and each later rule adds less. The mechanic must decide when to stop adding rules. Which consideration do the authors raise?
options: Every rule must be added, since coverage is the only aim
Only the first rule is worth having
Errors fall as rules are added
Each extra rule has a cost in parsimony against the shrinking gain
optionExplain: The authors weigh parsimony.
Later rules still add coverage.
Errors grow with more rules.
Right: marginal utility falls while the description grows.
questions.explain: Weigh the gain against the added complexity.
questions.teaches: The error counts of Figure 6.10 come from adding up the appropriate subsets of entries above the diagonal in the matrix, with a solid curve for definite errors and a dotted curve that adds the questionable ones.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: How Much Does the Production System Explain?
questions.q: A model covers most of the data but also asserts some false things. Which single number best tells how to improve it?
options: The percentage of data covered
The percentage of false assertions
None; the two kinds of failure need separate study
The sum of both failure counts
optionExplain: It ignores false assertions.
It ignores silences.
Right: omission and false assertion call for different repairs.
A sum hides what kind of repair is needed.
questions.explain: One number merges two failures. The card next gives the authors' computation.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: How Much Does the Production System Explain?
questions.q: The authors compute the penalized fit as (237 minus 23) divided by ____, which they put at 80 percent.
questions.explain: 237 nodes are covered, 23 definite errors are subtracted, and 267 is the relevant total.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: How Much Does the Production System Explain?
questions.q: Using the authors' method with the questionable errors included, what is the penalized fit?
options: About 75 percent, from (237 minus 38) divided by 267
About 80 percent, the same as before
About 89 percent, the coverage figure
About 86 percent, from (237 minus 8) divided by 267
optionExplain: Right: the authors give 75 percent.
More errors lower the figure.
That is coverage before penalizing errors.
The 8 is the number of out-of-space contexts, not errors.
questions.explain: Subtract all 38 errors from the 237 covered nodes and divide by 267.
questions.rule: Include the questionable errors for the lower bound.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: How Much Does the Production System Explain?
questions.q: True or false: The authors call the 80 percent figure highly informative because it separates omission from commission.
questions.explain: They say it is not very informative because it combines the two kinds of error.
questions.rule: A merged figure hides the kinds.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.section: How Much Does the Production System Explain?
questions.q: A school says its model of pupils' sums fits 80 percent of answers. The model leaves out many answers and also gets some wrong. What would the authors ask next?
options: Whether 80 percent is a good round number
Whether the pupils liked the model
Whether 20 percent can be ignored
How many of the missing 20 percent are omissions and how many are wrong assertions
optionExplain: Roundness is not the matter.
Liking is not a test.
The authors study the failures.
Right: break the figure into its two kinds.
questions.explain: Split the shortfall by kind.
questions.teaches: The 38 errors of commission when questionable ones are included consist of 23 definite errors and 15 questionable ones.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A model fails most often at the points where the subject stops a line of thought. Does that show the model's account of how people decide to stop is the weak part?
options: Yes; failures at stopping points always reveal the stopping rule
Not necessarily; losing track of the thread also looks like a stop
Yes; models are weakest wherever people stop
No; failures at stopping points are random
optionExplain: A lost thread produces the same pattern.
Right: failure to interpret can itself be read as termination.
Nothing supports that.
They are systematic, but their cause is the lost thread.
questions.explain: A lost thread resembles an ending. The card next shows the authors' reading.
questions.rule: A lost thread looks like an ending.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: The authors list ____ items under their headings of omission, though there are only 38 question-mark nodes.
questions.explain: Two instances illustrate more than one type of problem.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Most question-mark nodes are terminals (26) or beginnings (8). What do the authors say this does not show?
options: That the protocol lacks information
That the model makes most of its errors on evaluation
That omissions exist
That there are 38 question-mark nodes
optionExplain: Lack of information is acknowledged as a cause.
Right: the clustering at terminals is an artifact.
They exist.
The count stands.
questions.explain: Failure to interpret leads to inferring termination, not the other way round.
questions.rule: Do not read the clustering as evaluation failure.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: Lines of exploration in the protocol are long, so a lost thread is quickly picked up again.
questions.explain: Lines of exploration are not very long, so once the thread is lost it is unlikely to be picked up until the subject has started a new line.
questions.rule: Short lines mean lost threads stay lost.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A support team finds most of its unanswered tickets end a conversation. Before blaming how the team closes tickets, what should it check, following the authors?
options: Whether tickets are numbered correctly
Whether more tickets begin than end
Whether the team works long hours
Whether tickets were marked closed because the thread was lost
optionExplain: Numbering is not the issue.
Counting beginnings does not test the artifact.
Hours are not the issue.
Right: a lost thread is read as an ending.
questions.explain: The location of failures can come from the way failures are detected.
questions.teaches: The omissions are sorted under seven ad hoc headings: evaluation, selection of prior nodes, memory mechanisms, extensions of the production system, interaction with the external problem space, extensions of the problem space, and blank periods.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A solver says aloud that he will keep his current guess though he sees an alternative. What does the model need in order to predict this?
options: A way of weighing options and sticking with one
A larger table of arithmetic facts
A louder microphone
A list of all possible digits
optionExplain: Right: evaluation of competing lines.
Arithmetic is not the issue.
The talk is already recorded.
Digits are already known.
questions.explain: Choosing between options needs evaluation. The card next gives S3's examples.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: At B143.1 S3 states his options, R equal to 7 or R equal to 9, and decides to keep ____.
questions.explain: He later switches to 9 at B183 and back at B238.1.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: S3 states his options at B143.1, decides to keep one, switches at B183 and returns at B238.1. How do the authors classify these episodes?
options: As memory failures, which need a larger goal stack
As blank periods, since he is silent
As evaluation, which the production system has no representation for
As commissions, since a wrong production was evoked
optionExplain: These are not classified as memory failures.
He speaks in each case.
Right: the system cannot capture explicit evaluation.
Nothing is evoked wrongly; the system is silent.
questions.explain: Persisting, switching and backing down are evaluative acts.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: At B222.1 and B230 the system fails on both the choice not to investigate and the later choice to investigate whether c5 exceeds 1.
questions.explain: The system fails on only one of the two options.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A shopper repeatedly considers two phones, sticks with one, switches, and then returns to the first. What problem does this raise for a model, in the authors' terms?
options: Locating where the shopper keeps the phones
Counting how many words the shopper says
Deciding which phone has more features
Formulating the effect of multiple branchings at the same decision point
optionExplain: Storage is not the issue.
Words are not the issue.
The issue is the model of choosing, not the facts.
Right: the same decision point is revisited with changing evaluations.
questions.explain: A revisited choice needs a model of evaluation across visits.
questions.rule: Model repeated choices at one point.
questions.teaches: The authors face a general problem of formulating the effect of multiple branchings at the same decision point, as when S3 chooses not to investigate (c5 > 1) at B222.1 and does at B230.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A solver leaves one unresolved question to work on another and later comes back. What might a model need in order to predict the return?
options: A rule that forbids leaving questions
A memory that keeps the unresolved question available
A random generator for choosing
A way of erasing the first question
optionExplain: He did leave one.
Right: a stored goal or decision point.
Returns are not random.
He comes back to it.
questions.explain: Returns need a stored point to return to. The card next names S3's two extra nodes.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Besides the immediate path and the initial situation, S3 keeps available the decision situations for R and for ____.
questions.explain: The jumps in the graph are oscillations between these two.
questions.rule: The two extra points are R and E.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: The authors see three substantial breaks in the continuity of the search. What do the breaks represent?
options: Pauses prompted by the experimenter
Errors in the arithmetic of columns
Oscillations between the decision situations for E and for R
Changes of the problem space
optionExplain: Pauses are a separate matter.
The breaks are about search, not arithmetic.
Right: S3 jumps between the two.
The space stays the same.
questions.explain: The breaks are jumps between two unresolved decision points.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: The production system predicts the jumps between R and E through its depth-first node selection.
questions.explain: The authors have no formulation that predicts these jumps.
questions.rule: The system does not cover them.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A mechanic sets a stuck bolt aside to work on the brakes and then returns to the bolt. Which explanation do the authors suggest for such returns?
options: The unresolved goal never left the goal stack; it was only pushed down
The mechanic forgot the bolt and rediscovered it
The bolt is chosen at random each time
A new goal replaced the old goal entirely
optionExplain: Right: the earlier goal remains stored beneath the later one.
The suggestion is that it was never lost.
Choices are not random.
The old goal stays on the stack.
questions.explain: A pushed-down goal can be resumed.
questions.teaches: Besides the three substantial breaks, the authors list other apparent breaks that are all intermediate nodes where S3 backs up to a previous state, so not every jump needs a special explanation.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A solver makes the same slip twice, and the second time repairs it at once. What does this suggest about his memory?
options: That he remembers the earlier slip and its repair
That he is careless
That the second slip was easier
That he forgot the first slip
optionExplain: Right: memory of the earlier episode speeds recovery.
The quick repair does not show carelessness.
The slip is the same.
Forgetting would not speed the repair.
questions.explain: Quicker repair suggests memory of the first episode. The card next gives S3's examples.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Match each memory item to the example the authors give.
pairs: At B158 S3 recalls that E equal to 0 leads to a contradiction
At B188.1 S3 recovers at once from setting L to 9
At B275 there is a forgetting only partly explained, then a recall
questions.explain: Each example shows memory beyond what the system provides.
questions.rule: Link the memory to its example.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: The system assumes memory for assigned values, which TD needs. Which of S3's acts goes beyond that?
options: Remembering that D is 5
Writing 5 for D on the paper
Recognizing at B158 that E equal to 0 had led to a contradiction before
Following the carry c2 into column 2
optionExplain: The system supplies memory of assigned values.
Writing is not memory beyond the system.
Right: the system has no recognition that lets him follow the path by memory.
Following a carry is within the system.
questions.explain: Recalling that a path failed goes beyond assigned values.
questions.rule: Remembering paths goes beyond remembering values.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: The authors conclude that memory should be kept completely tied to the service of the problem space.
questions.explain: They conclude that a more generalized memory is needed, not completely tied to the problem space.
questions.rule: Memory is wider than the task.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A cook who once burned a sauce by adding wine too early now avoids it at once. Which view of memory do the authors take, by analogy?
options: A memory serving only the present recipe
A general memory may deliver useful information, though it cannot be relied on to do so
A memory that always delivers the right fact
No memory at all, only rules
optionExplain: That is the view they find too narrow.
Right: it is not tied to the task and not always dependable.
They say it could not be relied on.
They argue for a wider memory.
questions.explain: Wider memory helps sometimes.
questions.rule: General memory is useful but unreliable.
questions.teaches: The authors say such a generalized memory would on occasion deliver some information of value, although it could not be relied upon to do so, and that this impression is reinforced by much else known about human memory.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Having found a solution, a solver now wants to confirm it. What must a model contain to explain why he starts checking?
options: A rule that forbids checking
A table of all possible solutions
A louder signal from the experimenter
Something that recognizes the solution and then calls for a check
optionExplain: He checks.
That is not needed to start a check.
The need is internal to the model.
Right: recognition followed by a check.
questions.explain: Finding the answer and then checking it are two steps. The card next gives the authors' proposal.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: At B237 S3 works from the digit 0 to find all the ____ that cannot be paired with it.
questions.explain: That is a digit-oriented step: the focus is a digit rather than a letter.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: The authors say the final check at B303 would need two productions. What would they be?
options: One to generate digits and one to test them
One to assign a digit and one to erase it
One to say Eureka on finding a solution, and one to say that, if Eureka, then check
One to repeat PC and one to stop
optionExplain: Those are GN and TD.
Erasing is not proposed.
Right: recognition and its consequence.
Stopping is implicit in the system.
questions.explain: Eureka and then check.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: The two examples of digit-oriented operations in the protocol are far apart.
questions.explain: The authors say the two examples are close together, at B237 and B238.1.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A pupil sees that three answers each follow one pattern and says that it is almost so whatever the situation. Which mechanism does this match?
options: Induction, seeing the general case from several instances
A digit-oriented operation
An error of commission
A blank period
optionExplain: Right: the authors name induction for this.
That works from a digit to letters.
That is a wrong production.
That is silence.
questions.explain: Induction goes from several cases to a general one.
questions.teaches: The system has no place for partial glimpses such as the connection at B100 between E being even and E not being 9, which causes S3 to go back and check.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A subject falls silent several times and the experimenter urges him to go on. What is the most likely reading, if no discovery shows up later?
options: He solved the problem silently
He had forgotten the task
He was ignoring the experimenter
He did not know how to proceed
optionExplain: A solution would show up later.
Nothing suggests he forgot it.
Nothing suggests defiance.
Right: no later trace of a discovery suggests no progress.
questions.explain: Silence with no later trace most likely means no progress. The card next gives the authors' reading.
questions.rule: Silence without trace means no progress.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Match each protocol passage to the concern it shows.
questions.explain: These are the extensions of the problem space the authors list.
questions.rule: Link each passage to its concern.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Why do the authors leave the interactions with the experimenter outside the space instead of building a space for them?
options: The experimenter's remarks are inaudible
Such a space would have to be built on skimpy data, unless a model were imported from elsewhere
The interactions did not occur
The interactions are all emotional
optionExplain: They are in the protocol.
Right: the data are too thin.
They are listed.
Only B169 is emotionally toned.
questions.explain: A new space should not rest on skimpy data.
questions.rule: Do not build on thin data.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: B169, in which S3 remarks that he feels as though he is baring his soul, is a clear example of task-oriented behavior by the experimenter.
questions.explain: B169 is the one clear example of emotionally toned behavior; B224.1 and B225 are task-oriented behavior by the experimenter.
questions.rule: Do not mix up the passages.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A recording of a chess player has long silences that end when the umpire reminds her to speak. If nothing in her later play uses new ideas, how should the analyst read them?
options: As periods of brilliant hidden analysis
As periods when she probably did not know how to proceed
As periods outside the game
As errors of commission
optionExplain: A later trace would be expected.
Right: no later trace implies no hidden discovery.
Silence in the game is part of the game.
Silence makes no assertion by the model.
questions.explain: Hidden gains should leave a mark.
questions.rule: Expect hidden gains to leave a trace.
questions.teaches: If S3 obtained critical information during a silence, the authors would expect it to show up at some later time; as there is no clear evidence of this, the silences likely show that he did not know how to proceed.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A system models a person's thinking but not their jotting on paper. Under what condition is that a reasonable simplification?
options: When the person writes constantly
When the paper is blank
When the person cannot write
When the jotting seldom changes what goes on in the head
optionExplain: Constant writing would matter.
A blank paper gives no information.
The case concerns a writer.
Right: then little is lost.
questions.explain: Writing can be ignored when it has little effect. The card next gives the authors' reasoning.
questions.rule: Ignore writing where it matters little.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: At B185 S3 has two external displays and a ____ operation that takes information from one to build the other.
questions.explain: This is the exception to the claim that writing does not much affect internal processing.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: At B12 S3 finds D in column 6. What does he do, and why does the authors' account note it?
options: He writes 5 for D rather than processing column 6, a case of writing shaping his next move
He processes column 6 at once
He asks the experimenter about D
He erases D
optionExplain: Right: writing as a response.
He writes instead.
He did not ask.
D is written, not erased.
questions.explain: Writing here replaces processing the column.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: The authors say writing has no effect on what goes on in the internal problem space.
questions.explain: They say it does not seem to affect it very much in this protocol, and name B185 as an exception.
questions.rule: Not very much is not never.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A study of cooks leaves out their note-taking, but one cook copies notes from one sheet to another to build a shopping list. Which authors' case is this like?
options: B1, where the rules are clarified
B169, an emotionally toned remark
B185, where information is copied from one external display to build another
B303, the missing final check
optionExplain: That concerns rules.
That concerns feeling.
Right: a copy operation between displays.
That concerns checking.
questions.explain: Copying between displays is the exception.
questions.rule: Spot the exception to ignoring writing.
questions.teaches: The authors say they might have found more interactions with the external problem space, especially in attention control, had they incorporated a set of writing productions and tried to determine the conditions under which writing is evoked.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Two rules compete at 25 moments. The higher-ranked rule is chosen 16 times and the lower 9 times. How many errors against the ranking are there?
options: 16, the number of times the higher rule was chosen
25, the number of co-occurrences
7, the difference between the counts
9, the number of times the lower-ranked rule was chosen
optionExplain: Those agree with the ranking.
Not all are errors.
Errors are counted, not differenced.
Right: each such choice goes against the order.
questions.explain: An error is a choice against the order. The card next shows the table.
questions.rule: Errors are choices against the order.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Of the 38 errors of commission, ____ are definite and 15 are questionable.
questions.explain: A question mark before a node in the table marks a questionable error.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: In Table 6.1 the top row is P3 over P2, with P2 chosen 16 times and P3 9 times. How are these numbers read?
options: P3 is chosen in 16 of 25, so there are 16 errors
In 25 co-occurrences, P3 was chosen against the ordering 9 times, giving 9 errors
P2 and P3 co-occur 9 times
P3 and P2 are 9 places apart in the order
optionExplain: 16 counts P2, the favored production.
Right: the lower-ranked production was chosen 9 times.
They co-occur 25 times.
They are adjacent.
questions.explain: Counting the lower-ranked choices gives the errors.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: In Table 6.1 each node has at most one error.
questions.explain: More than one error can occur at a node; this happened four times.
questions.rule: A node can hold two errors.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A referee's log lists each pair of teams with a count of clear upsets and a separate count of disputed ones. One pair shows 9 clear upsets and none disputed. How many of its upsets are certain?
options: None, since a pair with disputes is unreliable
Four or five, about half
All nine, since the disputed column is empty
Nine, but only if the referee agrees
optionExplain: The pair has no disputes.
Nothing supports a split.
Right: with no disputed cases, every counted case is clear.
The log's own columns settle it.
questions.explain: A separate column for doubtful cases leaves the other column certain.
questions.rule: Read the definite and questionable columns apart.
questions.teaches: In the top row of Table 6.1, P3 over P2, there are no questionable errors at all, so all nine of its errors are definite.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A machine counts nine faults, but six of them are the same fault coming back after a restart. How many independent faults are there?
options: Three, with the rest being repetitions
Nine, since each fault is counted
One, since all faults are the same
Six, the number of repeats
optionExplain: Right: count the independent ones.
Repeats are not independent.
Three differ.
The repeats are not the independent ones.
questions.explain: Repeats are not independent. The card next gives the authors' count for P3.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: P3 is a secondary method, evoked only after P2 has been tried at least ____ times.
questions.explain: All nine P3 errors are the occasions on which P3 was evoked.
questions.rule: P3 comes after two tries of P2.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: B104 repeats B40, and B186 repeats it again with R assigned 9. How should the authors count the errors at B40, B104 and B186?
options: As one independent evocation with two repetitions
As three independent errors
As two independent errors
As none, since repeats are harmless
optionExplain: Right: only B40 is independent.
Two are repetitions.
B104 and B186 both repeat B40.
Repeats still count as errors of the system.
questions.explain: Repeats are not independent evocations.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: The authors say the repetitions of P3 are noise to be removed before explaining the behavior.
questions.explain: They say the acts of repetition are themselves part of what is to be explained.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A pupil uses a long method for a sum after trying the short method twice, and then uses the long method again on three similar sums. How many independent evocations of the long method does this match, in the authors' sense?
options: Four, one for each sum
Three, one for each later sum
One, with the other three as repetitions of the pattern
None, since the pupil tried the short method first
optionExplain: The later uses repeat a pattern.
They repeat the first.
Right: related repetitions are not independent.
The long method was used.
questions.explain: A repeated pattern counts once as a source of error.
questions.rule: A repeated pattern is one source.
questions.teaches: B125 shifts B120 to column 5 with O in place of column 3 with A, and this whole pattern is repeated at B144 and B149, so a single choice recurs in three places.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A rule appears eight times in a record and is involved in an error seven of those times. What might be a fair conclusion?
options: The rule is the best in the system
The rule is of marginal use and may be removable
The record is wrong
The rule must be duplicated
optionExplain: Seven of eight errors suggest otherwise.
Right: it seldom works cleanly.
Nothing suggests that.
More copies would not help.
questions.explain: Frequent involvement in errors signals a weak rule. The card next states the authors' view.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Of the eight occurrences of P7, all but ____ are implicated in some error.
questions.explain: That is why the authors call P7 of marginal efficacy.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: In five of the eight P7 occurrences, the goal was already at the top of the stack. What does this suggest about P7 there?
options: It switched attention to a new variable
It caused the five errors
It cancelled the goal
It added nothing, since it set a goal that was already in place
optionExplain: That happens in only two cases.
The point is redundancy.
P7 sets a goal.
Right: it was redundant.
questions.explain: Setting a goal that is already on top changes nothing.
questions.rule: A redundant goal setting adds nothing.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: The two cases in which P7 makes a genuine switch of attention are among the clearest passages in the protocol.
questions.explain: Both involve the carry and are among the most obscure passages.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A team reviews a rule in its software that fires eight times, seven of them in error reports, five when the system was already in the right state. What would the authors' reasoning suggest?
options: Keep the rule and add more rules like it
Ignore the reports
Consider removing the rule, after checking the two cases where it did real work
Replace all rules with one
optionExplain: That adds to the problem.
The reports are the evidence.
Right: marginal rules may be dropped, with care for the real cases.
That does not follow.
questions.explain: Remove a marginal rule, minding its real uses.
questions.teaches: Of the eight occurrences of P7, all but one are implicated in some error, and five of the eight occur when the goal is already at the top of the stack; in the other two P7 makes a genuine switch of attention.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A rule says: check any fact that matters. A solver does not check the digit he was told at the start. What does this reveal?
options: The rule needs conditions that exclude facts a person already trusts
The solver is careless in general
The rule is correct as stated
The fact is false
optionExplain: Right: certainty conditions the checking.
Not all checking is absent.
It over-predicts checking.
A trusted fact need not be false.
questions.explain: Trust limits checking. The card next gives the authors' cases.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: S3 does not check D assigned 5, and checks T assigned 0 only after the ____ brings it to his attention.
questions.explain: These cases account for the questionable errors on P12/P10 and P7/P10.
questions.rule: The experimenter prompted the T check.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Why do the authors say there is a thin line between getting a value and checking a value?
options: Because getting and checking use the same operator
Because S3 never gets values
Because the experimenter does both
Their explanation of the difference is only marginally satisfactory
optionExplain: No such claim.
He gets many.
The experimenter does not.
Right: they admit the distinction is weakly explicated.
questions.explain: The distinction is not sharp in the account.
questions.rule: The get and check line is thin.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: The authors added discriminating conditions to P10 so that it only fires when S3 would plausibly check.
questions.explain: They did not add them, even though they say discrimination is clearly necessary.
questions.rule: A needed condition was left out.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A pilot checks the fuel gauge each flight but does not re-check the runway length given in the briefing, except when a controller mentions it. What problem does this pose for a rule to check every critical fact?
options: The rule is too weak, as pilots check nothing
The rule needs conditions that tell which critical facts are checked
The rule works as stated
The controller should do the checking
optionExplain: The pilot checks the gauge.
Right: not all critical facts trigger a check.
It over-predicts checks.
That is beside the point.
questions.explain: Checking depends on more than being critical.
questions.teaches: In one case, P10 is preferred over P13, which is one of the few places where a critical feature is generated by a process other than TD; the attention to c3 equal to 0 at B94 is quite clear.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A solver re-runs an earlier line of reasoning and skips the step of listing candidate values. What does a model need to explain this?
options: A rule that forbids repetition
A record of what was done before and a way to use it
A bigger list of candidates
A louder prompt
optionExplain: The solver repeats.
Right: guided repetition needs memory.
He skips the list.
The prompt is not the issue.
questions.explain: Repeating the final path of an earlier exploration relies on memory. The card next gives the authors' cases.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: S3 does not evoke TD on ____ material, and failing to do so on E equal to 0 is part of his major difficulty.
questions.explain: TD is applied only to relations judged new.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: At B85 both P1 and P2 lead to the same result, the determination of c6. How do the authors treat the error there?
options: As a serious failure of memory
As a mistake by S3
As an error of omission
As an ambiguity
optionExplain: Memory is not the issue.
The question is how to code, not his mistake.
A production was chosen.
Right: either production gives the same result.
questions.explain: Same result means ambiguous coding.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: The authors say S3's failure to evoke TD on E equal to 0 at B129 and B207 is minor and unrelated to his difficulty in solving the problem.
questions.explain: They say it is part of his major difficulty in solving the problem.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A teacher notices a pupil repeats the last working of a previous attempt without re-listing the options. What does this share with the P2/P4 errors?
options: It repeats the final path of an earlier branched exploration and does not generate the values again
It repeats the first step only
It checks a value already trusted
It begins a new method
optionExplain: Right: that is the P2/P4 pattern.
The final path is repeated.
That is a P10 matter.
That is a different matter.
questions.explain: Repeating the final path skips generation.
questions.rule: Repeat the final path, skip generation.
questions.teaches: In one questionable P2/P4 error (B299), S3 errs in determining the set of available digits, then returns to get B and could repeat PC or generate values from the restricted set, a choice that arises only at this one point in the protocol.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A model is revised to fix an error at one point. What often happens to the total errors?
options: They fall to zero
They double automatically
They tend to reappear elsewhere, in a similar number
They stay exactly where they were
optionExplain: Zero is unlikely.
Not necessarily.
Right: fixes move errors around.
The fix changes the place.
questions.explain: Error totals depend on design. The card next gives the authors' remark.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Any discussion of errors takes place against a background of ____ about how to fashion the production system.
questions.explain: That is why the discussion is partial and biased.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A reviewer says that a change to the production system would remove the P3/P2 errors. How do the authors' remarks bear on this?
options: The change would improve the theory with no cost
The change would be impossible
The change would introduce no errors
An equivalent number of errors, or somewhat more, would likely show up elsewhere
optionExplain: They say otherwise.
They accept changes could be made.
They expect new ones.
Right: errors tend to move.
questions.explain: Error totals move with design.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: The authors say the listing of errors is useless, since it is biased.
questions.explain: They say it still gives some feeling for where the system is weak and what remedial actions might be.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A school adjusts its marking scheme so that a common mistake no longer loses marks. Which of the authors' points does this illustrate?
options: A scheme with no errors is possible
Error counts depend on how the scheme is designed, and fixing one place can shift errors elsewhere
Marks are unrelated to errors
Errors vanish when the scheme is simplified
optionExplain: The authors doubt it.
Right: errors are relative to design choices.
They are related.
They tend to reappear.
questions.explain: Counts are relative to design.
questions.teaches: The authors say the errors investigated during the analysis suggest that modifications would, if anything, produce somewhat more errors elsewhere than they removed.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A function in a program is supposed to return a value that depends only on its inputs. A test shows it gives different answers to the same input on different days. What does this say about the function?
options: It is working correctly, since answers may vary
It has too few inputs, so add more tests
It depends on context beyond its inputs, so it is not a well-defined subroutine
It must be a faster routine
optionExplain: A subroutine's output is fixed by input.
More tests do not remove the dependence.
Right: output must follow from input alone.
Speed is not the matter.
questions.explain: A subroutine's output follows from its input. The card next states the authors' requirement.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: To predict the output of a basic process we should not need information about the ____ in which it occurs, beyond its inputs.
questions.explain: The processes are to be subroutines.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Suppose PC gave different outputs for the same column and the same knowledge on two occasions. How would this affect the count of errors in the fit?
options: Errors would be underestimated, since some occurrences judged correct would not match a single specification
Errors would be overestimated, since PC would look worse
Errors would be unchanged
Errors would vanish
optionExplain: Right: the hidden dependence masks errors.
Hidden dependence hides errors.
The authors say they are underestimated.
They would remain but be uncounted.
questions.explain: A single specification would label some occurrences wrong.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: The authors say the names of the processes stand only for types of process, not for a single process each.
questions.explain: They say a single process is to be associated with each name, so the processes are subroutines.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A bank's rule for approving a loan is supposed to depend only on the application form. An auditor finds approvals also depend on which clerk handled the case. What follows, on the authors' reasoning?
options: The rule is not a subroutine, and the bank's error count under the written rule is understated
The rule is fine, since clerks are part of the form
The rule is sounder, since it uses more information
The rule needs no change, since clerks differ
optionExplain: Right: hidden context breaks the specification.
The form is the declared input.
The aim is output fixed by input.
The rule fails its own specification.
questions.explain: Dependence on unlisted context breaks the subroutine idea.
questions.teaches: The authors treat errors in the basic processes separately from errors in the production system and judge that these errors in processes need investigation.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A pupil chooses the right method for a sum but adds 7 and 6 as 12. Where does the fault lie?
options: In the choice of method
In both equally
In the elementary arithmetic, not in the choice of method
In neither, as nothing went wrong
optionExplain: The method was right.
Only the arithmetic failed.
Right: the choice was correct.
A wrong sum is a fault.
questions.explain: Choice and execution are separate. The card next gives the authors' division.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A subject may make an error in ____ while the processes postulate that he adds correctly.
questions.explain: Such an error is charged to the processes underlying PC.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: S3 evokes PC on the right column, as the productions say, but adds two digits wrongly. How is this scored?
options: As an error of commission by the production system
As an error of the process underlying PC, which does not invalidate the production
As an error of omission by the production system
As no error, since the answer was reached
optionExplain: The right production was evoked.
Right: the production was right.
A production was found.
A wrong addition is a process error.
questions.explain: Wrong execution under a right production belongs to the process.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: The authors say errors in the basic processes must be added to the production system's errors to give the total.
questions.explain: They say the two need not be combined, since the productions may be correct even if the processes are faulty.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A navigator picks the right chart but misreads a number on it. Which of the authors' points does this illustrate?
options: A wrong reading shows the chart was wrong to pick
All faults must be charged to the navigator's plan
A misreading makes the whole voyage void
The decision can be correct while an elementary process fails, so the two errors are kept apart
optionExplain: The chart was right.
That would pool the errors.
Nothing says that.
Right: choice and execution are different.
questions.explain: Errors of perception are process errors.
questions.teaches: The authors' independent knowledge is that human subjects do make errors of perception, memory and elementary processing; if such errors are too numerous, they compromise the entire system.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A description of how a person sums two digits breaks the step into recalling the digits, holding them in mind and recalling their sum. At what level is this description?
options: At the level of overall strategy
At the level of the whole puzzle
At the level of elementary perception and memory operations
At the level of group behavior
optionExplain: Strategy concerns choosing tasks.
That is far larger.
Right: these are the building blocks of the step.
A single person is described.
questions.explain: Elementary operations lie beneath the named processes. The card next names them.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: The authors call the processes beneath the basic processes ____ processes, for basic-basic.
questions.explain: They are at the level of perception and immediate memory.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Why do the authors say a model of the BB processes is not for this volume?
options: It would be a detailed model of immediate memory and immediate processing
They have no data on arithmetic
The BB processes do not exist
The BB processes are irrelevant to problem solving
optionExplain: Right: too large a task for this book.
They have data on PC.
They postulate them.
They underlie the basic processes.
questions.explain: The model needed would be a different book's worth.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: There are nine basic processes, discussed in nine separate groups.
questions.explain: They are discussed in six groups.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A manual for forklift drivers lists tasks such as lift, tilt and turn, but does not explain the operator's hand-eye coordination. Which of the authors' moves does this resemble?
options: Modeling every muscle movement
Denying that tasks have parts
Treating coordination as a separate task
Naming the basic processes while leaving the elementary perception beneath them unmodeled
optionExplain: That would be the BB level and more.
The tasks are parts of the job.
It underlies the tasks.
Right: the BB level is left aside.
questions.explain: Name the level you use and leave the lower one.
questions.rule: Choose a level and say so.
questions.teaches: The authors count the occurrences of each basic process: PC 88, GN and AV 27 each, TD 31, FC 64, FA 19, FP 4, and the two remaining processes, GNC and FL, 2 and 4.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Two solvers can both add digits in a column. One can also conclude that a letter must be odd from the structure of the column. Which has the more powerful way of dealing with columns?
options: The first, since sums are exact
The second, who draws richer conclusions than a sum
Both equally
Neither, since columns are simple
optionExplain: Exact sums are less powerful than inferences like parity.
Right: richer inferences give more power.
The second has more.
Columns support many inferences.
questions.explain: Richer conclusions from a column give more power. The card next states the authors' claim.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: PC occurs ____ times in the protocol, and its occurrences are listed in Table 6.2.
questions.explain: It is the most complex of the basic processes.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Why do the authors say that understanding PC would amount to understanding human arithmetic if it were only a routine for adding?
options: Because PC is a program for a computer
Because adding pairs of digits is how a human does arithmetic, involving immediate memory and attention
Because adding is never done by humans
Because PC only occurs once
optionExplain: PC is a process in a theory of S3.
Right: PC would be arithmetic itself.
Humans do add.
It occurs 88 times.
questions.explain: A pure adding routine is just human arithmetic.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: The authors say S3's problem solving power hinges little on the sophistication of PC.
questions.explain: They say it hinges strongly on it, as seen by comparison with subjects whose PC admits only simple arithmetic.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A clerk who can only add figures is compared with one who can also say from the layout of an invoice that a total must be even. What do the authors' remarks suggest about their problem solving power?
options: Both have equal power, since both add
The first has more, being simpler
Neither can solve problems
It hinges on the sophistication of the column processing, so the second has more power
optionExplain: Added inferences count.
Simplicity does not add power.
Both can solve some.
Right: richer processing yields greater power.
questions.explain: Power follows from the richness of what each can infer.
questions.rule: Compare by the range of inferences.
questions.teaches: Even if PC is in some sense a single subroutine, its diversity means it is highly conditional, so that the key question is whether a uniform underlying scheme can yield all its varied outputs.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A routine to infer something from a column must hold the thing sought, a running value, and what to do with them. Why might that need several separate stored items?
options: Because each plays a different role in the operation
Because a computer cannot store one item
Because each digit needs its own name
Because several items are faster
optionExplain: Right: roles differ, so they are stored separately.
One item can be stored.
Roles, not names, are the point.
Speed is not the reason.
questions.explain: Different roles need different stores. The card next lists the five.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Match each kind of initial production to the element it defines.
questions.explain: The single o-production defines the operand.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Which production family defines the operand in the sketched system?
options: The v-productions
The a-productions
The single o-production
The t-productions
optionExplain: They define the value.
They analyze results after the operation.
Right: one production sets the operand.
They define the target.
questions.explain: There is only one o-production, for the operand.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: At the start of PC, all five elements of the sketched system are already defined by the previous column.
questions.explain: They start undefined, and the initial productions define them from the goal and the column.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A cashier's routine begins with no totals set, fills in which sum is wanted, which figure to start with, what to add, where to put the result and whether to add or subtract, then adds. Which stage matches the sketch's p1?
options: Setting which sum is wanted
Choosing add or subtract
Wrapping the result in a receipt
The act of performing the addition after all elements are set
optionExplain: That matches the unknown.
That matches the operator.
That matches packaging by a-productions.
Right: p1 performs the operation once the elements are defined.
questions.explain: Define the elements, then operate, then package.
questions.teaches: After p1, a number of a-productions analyze the results of the operation, either causing new operations to be performed or simply packaging the output expression.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: You know a number is even and you add 1 to it. What can you say about the result?
options: It is even
It is odd, though you do not know which odd number
It is exactly 1 more than a known number
Nothing can be said
optionExplain: Adding 1 changes parity.
Right: even plus 1 is odd.
No number is known.
Parity is preserved in a known way.
questions.explain: Parity can be added to digits. The card next shows how PC does it.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Match each kind of value PC handles to an example.
questions.explain: PC must be prepared to meet any of these as operand or as value.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: PC must add G, a letter known only as nonzero, to the digit 5. Following the authors' scheme, what is the result?
options: Exactly 5, since G adds nothing
Exactly 6, the next digit
Greater than 5, after converting G to the inequality greater than 0
Undefined, since types differ
optionExplain: G is not zero.
G need not be 1.
Right: that is the authors' example.
Conversion makes the addition possible.
questions.explain: A nonzero quantity added to 5 gives more than 5.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: To add 1 to 2:L, PC converts both to parity-values and obtains even.
questions.explain: Converting 1 to odd and 2:L to even gives odd.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A packer knows that a box holds an even number of items, and she adds one loose item. What does this mimic in PC's way of working?
options: Converting to parity and adding, so the total is odd without a known count
Assigning a digit to a letter
Testing a digit for admissibility
Generating all totals in order
