optionExplain: Right: parity arithmetic gives a class, not a number.
No digit is assigned.
That is TD.
That is GN.
questions.explain: Conversion to a weaker type yields a class result.
questions.teaches: The operation attempts to perform the arithmetic if the two inputs are appropriate, that is both digits, both parity-values and so on, and evokes the conversion routines only if they are not.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Adding two fives in a column gives ten. What do you write in the answer position, and what do you carry?
options: Write 0 and carry 1
Write 10 and carry nothing
Write 1 and carry 0
Write 5 and carry 5
optionExplain: Right: ten splits into a digit and a carry.
A column holds a single digit.
The units digit is 0.
That does not follow from 5 + 5.
questions.explain: Ten splits into a digit and a carry. The card next shows the authors' trace.
questions.rule: Split ten into digit and carry.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Put the steps of the PC trace on 5 + 5 = T in order.
items: T is defined as the unknown
The value, operand and operator are defined
The two digits are added to give 10
The 10 is decomposed into a digit and a carry
questions.explain: The trace first defines the elements, then adds, then splits the result.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: In the trace of 1 + L + L = R, what does the system do with the two L's first?
options: It assigns each L the digit 1
It tests each L for admissibility
It adds them to get the quantity 2:L
It converts R to a digit
optionExplain: No digit is assigned.
That is TD.
Right: two quantities with the same letter combine.
R is the unknown.
questions.explain: Two L's make 2:L.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: In the 1 + L + L = R trace, the final result is that R is even.
questions.explain: 2:L is even and adding 1 gives odd, so R is odd.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A kitchen scale shows twice an unknown weight W plus a 1 gram weight for a total T. A cook who knows W is a whole number says T is odd. Which step of the PC trace does her reasoning use?
options: Assigning a digit to W by trial
Converting 2W to even and the weight 1 to odd, then adding to get odd
Decomposing a ten into a digit and a carry
Generating W values in ascending order
optionExplain: No trial is made.
Right: parity conversion, as in the second trace.
That is the first trace.
That is GN.
questions.explain: Twice anything is even, and even plus odd is odd.
questions.rule: Twice a whole number is even.
questions.teaches: In the trace of 1 + L + L = 7, where the unknown is the target, the system adds the two L's to 2:L, subtracts the carry from the digit to get 6 as the new value, and then divides to obtain L equal to 3.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A rough program reproduces most but not all of a person's calculations. What may the programmer fairly claim for it?
options: That it is the person's exact method
That it proves the person is a computer
Nothing, since it fails sometimes
That the kinds of step can be represented, without claiming it is the person's exact method
optionExplain: It fails on some cases.
No such claim.
It shows feasibility.
Right: feasibility without a claim of identity.
questions.explain: A partial fit shows feasibility. The card next gives the authors' three claims.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Match each claim for the PC system to its content.
pairs: The kinds of inference of S3's PC can be expressed by a production system
There are no gross inconsistencies in S3's PC
A great deal of stored knowledge is needed for so diversified an operator
questions.explain: These are the three things the sketch shows.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Which feature of the PC system is an example of what the authors say it handles awkwardly?
options: Column 1, where D plus D gives T
The decomposition of ten into digit and carry
Column 5, where O plus E equals O
The conversion of 2:L to even
optionExplain: That is the simple case.
That works well in the trace.
Right: the authors name this case as awkward.
That works well in the trace.
questions.explain: Column 5 resists the scheme.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: The authors say a complex numerical algorithm is needed to do the task of PC.
questions.explain: They say no intricate numerical algorithm is required; each production is a bit of partial knowledge.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A team builds a rule set that reproduces most of a chess tutor's explanations but not the unusual ones, and declines to call it a model of the tutor's mind. Which authors' reason applies?
options: A true model would need a detailed account of the tutor's immediate memory and processing
The rule set is too long to be a model
Tutors are not people
Unusual explanations do not matter
optionExplain: Right: the same reason the authors give.
Length is not the reason.
Irrelevant.
They show the limits.
questions.explain: A model of the mind needs a model of memory.
questions.rule: Do not claim more than you model.
questions.teaches: The authors add that the system shows nothing like a requirement for intricate numerical algorithms; the same holds for the entries in the conversion matrix, each of which is a bit of partial knowledge.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: When adding a column with a carry coming in, which order of taking the parts would you expect many people to use?
options: Add the carry first and then the digits
Take the carry in the middle of the digits
Ignore the carry throughout
Add the digits first and bring in the carry last
optionExplain: S3 does not do this.
There is no evidence of this.
He eventually takes it into account.
Right: this is the order S3 uses.
questions.explain: One regular order is visible in the protocol. The card next gives the evidence.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: In all eleven instances where the order of addition is evident, the ____ is dealt with last.
questions.explain: No evidence shows the carry being considered at any other position.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: At B20, B32 to B36 and B78 to B83 the carry is not attended to at first. What do the authors say about this?
options: It happens throughout the protocol
It happens early on, and the carry is always discovered eventually
It shows S3 does not know about carries
It shows the carry is added first
optionExplain: They say the lapses are all at the beginning.
Right: the lapses are early and corrected.
He discovers it.
The evidence is for last.
questions.explain: Early lapses, then consistent use.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: The authors say there is evidence for the carry being added in the middle, after the first operand.
questions.explain: They say there is no evidence of any kind for the carry being considered at any other position than last.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A shopkeeper adds item prices first and adds tax last. A second shopkeeper adds tax to the first price and then adds the rest. Which matches S3's order?
options: The second, who adds the extra after the first operand
The first, who brings in the tax-like extra last, as S3 does with the carry
Both, since both reach a total
Neither, since carries are not taxes
optionExplain: S3 shows no such order.
Right: the extra comes last.
The order is the point.
The analogy is of order.
questions.explain: S3's order puts the carry last.
questions.teaches: Very often, when the carry is 0 or undefined, nothing in the protocol indicates explicitly that the carry has been noted, so the evidence for the order comes from the eleven instances listed.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: To give a letter a value, you may first pick a candidate digit and then pair it with the letter. Which two steps does that involve?
options: Testing a digit and then finding its column
Finding a column and then processing it
Backing up and then repeating the goal
Generating a digit and then associating it with the letter
optionExplain: Those are other processes.
Nothing is paired there.
That is not assignment.
Right: pick a value, then pair it.
questions.explain: Assignment pairs a chosen digit with a letter. The card next gives the authors' form.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: The associate operation resembles a ____ learning task, in which a stimulus is paired with a response.
questions.explain: The variable is the stimulus and the digit the response.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: In 13 of the 27 AV occurrences, what leaves AV as essentially only the associate step?
options: A single value was already delivered, by GN in P4 or by a visibly slow P3
The letter had no digit available
The digit was tested and found impossible
The column had been processed twice
optionExplain: Right: the generating was already done.
That would block the pairing.
That would be TD.
Columns are not the cause.
questions.explain: When the value is already given, only the pairing is left.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: The authors show that the association is made by building a symbol structure such as D <- 5, rather than by a designation.
questions.explain: They say this is not determined, and the performance of the system is unaffected.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A teacher hands each pupil a card with a letter on it, and the pupil attaches a number tag from a pile. Which part is the associate step?
options: Picking a number from the pile
Reading the letter on the card
Attaching the tag so that letter and number go together
Counting the pile
optionExplain: That resembles generating.
That is perception, not pairing.
Right: the pairing is the associate step.
Not part of the process.
questions.explain: Generating picks the value; associating binds it.
questions.teaches: There are five cases where AV assigns a digit-variable as the value, as in O <- x at B248; such symbols stand for a general value and are not more complex than digits.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Asked to name an even digit, a person who has not counted from zero before would likely begin with which number?
optionExplain: Only programmers count from 0.
1 is odd.
9 is odd and at the top.
Right: people begin counting at 2 for even numbers.
questions.explain: Everyday counting does not begin with zero. The card next gives the authors' view.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: In 24 of the 36 cases of generating, values are produced in ____ order, starting at the low member of the set.
questions.explain: The main form starts at the low member.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: At B98.1, S3 generates E even starting from 2. Why do the authors consider this the likely start?
options: Because 0 is not a digit in the puzzle
Because only programmers start counting from 0, though 0 is correct here
Because E cannot be 0
Because 2 is the only even digit
optionExplain: 0 is a legal digit here.
Right: they give this reason.
Later in the protocol 0 is considered for E.
There are several even digits.
questions.explain: An ordinary person starts evens at 2.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: The authors say S3 starts the even generation at 0, the correct starting place for this problem.
questions.explain: They say he starts from 2, even though 0 is the correct starting place.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A child asked to list all even numbers under ten begins with 2 and the correct list also contains 0. What does this show, by the authors' reasoning?
options: The child cannot count
Zero is not even
A natural starting habit can leave out a correct value, which shows up later
Ascending order is not used
optionExplain: The habit is ordinary.
Zero is even.
Right: the start matters for later consequences.
The order is ascending.
questions.explain: Starting at 2 skips 0.
questions.teaches: The 36 cases of GN divide as follows: 24 ascending from the low member, six with a two-element set, three unimportant incomplete or digit-centered ones, and three that begin from the top value.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A drawer has two keys, and you have learned a moment ago that one does not fit the lock. What is the quickest way to choose?
options: Pick the other key without trying them in turn
Test the first key again
Try every key in the building
Wait for a hint
optionExplain: Right: only one candidate remains.
It is already ruled out.
Only two keys are in the drawer.
The elimination answers it.
questions.explain: Elimination from two leaves one. The card next shows the authors' reading.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: With a two-element set, the rule may amount to: pick the ____ one.
questions.explain: One member has just been ruled out.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Why do the authors say a small immediate memory leads to different handling of small and large sets?
options: Large sets must be generated serially while small ones can be dealt with at once
Small sets cannot be stored at all
Large sets are always ignored
Memory size has no effect
optionExplain: Right: size changes the mechanism.
They are the easiest to hold.
They are generated serially.
The authors say it does.
questions.explain: Serial generation is for sets too big to take in at once.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: The authors say the pick-the-other rule replaces generate-and-test in all cases of GN.
questions.explain: They say the two mechanisms can coexist, since clear clues evoke the second one.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A waiter must seat a guest at one of two free tables, and one is reserved. A second waiter has twenty free tables. Whose method resembles serial generation?
options: The first waiter's, who takes the other table
Both, since both seat guests
The second waiter's, who must go through many candidates in turn
Neither, since seating is not a search
optionExplain: That is the pick-the-other rule.
The set sizes differ.
Right: a big set needs serial work.
Both pick among options.
questions.explain: Big sets are scanned in turn.
questions.teaches: Three further cases of GN, each generating only a single value, show both that a set of values exists and that generation can begin at the top value rather than the bottom.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A person picks the largest digit from a short list after weighing the outcomes of each choice. What does that suggest about the choice?
options: It came from counting upward from the smallest
It came from weighing consequences, not from counting upward
It was a random pick
It shows the list was empty
optionExplain: The largest was taken.
Right: a considered choice differs from serial generation.
Weighing took place.
A list existed.
questions.explain: A weighed choice differs from serial counting. The card next gives S3's cases.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: The three top-first cases generate only a single ____, so the evidence is thin.
questions.explain: Each involves one value only.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: At B294, what led to N <- 6 instead of N <- 3?
options: A rule that even digits are taken first
Counting upward from the lowest value
An instruction from the experimenter
An extensive comparison of the consequences of each value, apparently ending indecisively
optionExplain: No such rule is given.
The top value was chosen.
No instruction is described.
Right: the authors describe this.
questions.explain: The comparison was long and unresolved.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: The authors say they fully captured the considerations behind the top-first cases in their formal scheme.
questions.explain: They say they can sense complexities but have not captured them, and could not discover the extra considerations at B294.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A coach has two candidate lineups and, after a long comparison with no clear winner, picks the stronger one. Which authors' case is this like?
options: B98.1, counting up from 2
The pick-the-other rule
B294, a choice after comparing consequences that ended without a clear result
A Test Digit availability check
optionExplain: That is ascending generation.
No option was excluded.
Right: comparison without resolution.
No digit supply is at issue.
questions.explain: Comparison that fails to settle.
questions.teaches: Assigning 9 to O resolves the dilemma for E equal to 0 or 9, which is one of the complexities in the O <- 9 case at B125 that the formal scheme does not capture.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Before putting a number in a slot, you check that it is unused and also that it suits the slot's rules. How many checks is that?
options: Two, one for availability and one for fit
One, for availability alone
One, for fit alone
Three, adding a count
optionExplain: Right: two separate checks.
Fit is also checked.
Availability is also checked.
No third check is described.
questions.explain: Two questions are asked of a candidate. The card next names them.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: TD checks whether the digit is ____ and whether it satisfies the constraints known for the letter.
questions.explain: The first part concerns whether another letter has the digit.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: S3 proposes R equal to 3 where R is known to be greater than 5. Which part of TD catches this?
options: The part checking that the digit is available
Neither, since the proposal is a guess
The part finding the column
The part checking the constraints known for the letter
optionExplain: 3 may be free.
TD catches such cases.
That is FC.
Right: 3 lies outside the admissible set.
questions.explain: A digit outside the admissible set fails the constraint check.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: The authors say TD was evoked in Table 6.5 with letters that already had a value.
questions.explain: They find no instances in which TD was evoked with a variable that already had a value.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A locker clerk offers a student locker 14 for a rule that only upper-floor lockers may be assigned. Which TD part applies if the locker is free but on the ground floor?
options: The availability check, which rejects it
The constraint check, which rejects it though it is available
Neither check, since the locker is free
Both checks would pass it
optionExplain: It is free.
Right: free is not enough.
The rule still applies.
The rule fails.
questions.explain: A free item can still break the rule.
questions.teaches: At B229 two values of E are discarded, one because T = 0 and the other because R <- 9, which indicates additional structure beyond the two parts.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A clerk checks a proposed entry against a list of used items and against a rule. Does the order of the two checks change the outcome?
options: Yes, always, since results flip
Not for the final verdict, though it may change which failure is found first
No, and the first failure is the same too
It is impossible to say
optionExplain: The verdict is the same.
Right: the verdict is the same, the first failure may differ.
A different first failure is possible.
Reasoning settles it.
questions.explain: Order affects which problem is spotted first. The card next gives the authors' view.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: At B295.1, S3 notices that if B is 3, no other ____ will be available, even though a letter is still unassigned.
questions.explain: This inference does not come from the TD program.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: When might S3 check the letter first and the digit second, by the authors' account?
options: During a generation of digits
Only when the column is done
Whenever the subject is tired
When a new assignment is being proposed
optionExplain: There the digit leads.
Columns are not the cue.
Fatigue is not mentioned.
Right: the letter leads in a proposal.
questions.explain: The proposal starts from a letter.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: The authors claim the order of the TD checks is fixed and shown by the data.
questions.explain: They say it is unclear and may vary with circumstances.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A pupil seats guests and suddenly sees that the last guest will have no chair even though a table is still empty. Which feature of S3's B295.1 does this resemble?
options: Noticing that available digits would run out, a thing the TD program does not do
Checking one digit against a letter's constraints
Generating digits in order
Finding a column for a letter
optionExplain: Right: a global look-ahead beyond the checks.
That is the TD program.
That is GN.
That is FC.
questions.explain: A look at the whole supply goes beyond a single check.
questions.teaches: The authors say that if the model had some way of handling noticing, B295.1 could be handled differently, as could B202-203, which raises some of the same issues.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: You are looking for another place where item R appears, and you have finished working through the place you are in. Should that place be a candidate?
options: Yes, repeat it
Yes, but only after the last
No, you look elsewhere
Only if there are no others
optionExplain: It has already been used.
No ordering is stated.
Right: a processed place is passed over.
The authors drop it.
questions.explain: A used place is passed over. The card next gives the rules.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Of the 46 FC cases needing a rule, rule ____ accounts for 30, by excluding the current column when already processed.
questions.explain: Rule 1 accounts for six.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: S3 has not yet processed the variable in the column he is attending. What do the authors' rules say?
options: Drop the current column
Choose the most constrained column
Search all columns before choosing
Select the current column
optionExplain: That would be rule 2, for a processed column.
That is for the ten left over.
The authors say deliberate comparison does not occur.
Right: rule 1 applies.
questions.explain: Unprocessed means select it.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: The authors say rule 1 and rule 2 together settle the 64 FC cases.
questions.explain: Ten are repetitions, eight are uniquely determined, six and 30 are covered by the rules, and ten remain.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A mail sorter looks for a second sack of items for one town. She has finished emptying the sack in her hands. By rule 2, what does she do?
options: Picks the same sack again
Leaves that sack out of the choice and picks from the remaining sacks
Stops, as the job must be done
Picks the largest sack at random
optionExplain: It is already processed.
Right: the finished sack is out.
Other sacks remain.
The rule drops the current one first.
questions.explain: A finished place is excluded.
questions.teaches: Rule 2 does not always choose a column; it reduces the set to one or no elements, so the choice among remaining columns can still need a further mechanism.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Choosing which of three boxes to open first, you take the one with the most clues pointing to it. What kind of rule is that?
options: Choosing at random
Choosing the first in line
Choosing the most constrained option
Choosing the last used
optionExplain: A clue-based pick is not random.
Order is not the reason.
Right: the option with most constraints is taken.
Past use is not the reason.
questions.explain: More clues, more constraint. The card next gives the authors' use.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Of the ten leftover FC cases, most-constrained-column explains all but B203 and ____.
questions.explain: B203 is a genuine anomaly.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Why do the authors doubt that S3 compares all columns before choosing?
options: It would imply considerable computation, and B12 shows D's first column was not chosen so
Because S3 cannot read columns
Because only one column exists
Because comparison gives wrong answers
optionExplain: Right: the evidence cuts against it.
He reads them.
There are several.
Cost, not correctness, is the issue.
questions.explain: Exhaustive comparison is costly and not evident.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: The authors say the most-constrained rule explains all ten leftover FC cases.
questions.explain: It accounts for all except B203 and B240.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A mechanic picks which of three loose bolts to tighten first by feel, choosing the one with the least play, with no measuring of all three. Which of the authors' cautions does this match?
options: A constraint-driven choice without a full comparison of all options
A deliberate comparison of every bolt
A random choice among bolts
A choice fixed by order of arrival
optionExplain: Right: the choice is quick, not exhaustive.
No measuring is done.
Feel guides it.
Not by order.
questions.explain: Perceptual cues guide a quick pick.
questions.teaches: B203 is a genuine anomaly in which concern for R leads the subject to evoke P1 on R <- 9 rather than to consider E <- 9, and for B240 the authors have no clue why column 5 was chosen over column 4 after E <- 9.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: To find why you believe a fact, you retrace the path by which you reached it. What does this mostly use?
options: A fresh search of all sources
A guess from nearby facts
Memory of your past reasoning
A new derivation from scratch
optionExplain: The path was already taken.
Recall, not guessing.
Right: the path is recalled.
A past derivation is reused.
questions.explain: Past reasoning is recalled. The card next gives the authors' view.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: FA and FP are grouped because the essential component in both is the recall of past ____.
questions.explain: They return to something already done.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: In B42, what does FA return to, by the authors' account?
options: A new column chosen among three for R
Column 2, which was used to derive R odd
Column 6, a fresh derivation
No column, since none exists
optionExplain: That would be FC.
Right: an old relation, not a new one.
The relation is an old one.
A column is returned.
questions.explain: FA returns an earlier relation.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: The authors say FA in P3 yields a new relation each time.
questions.explain: They say the result is never a new relation, but one that has been used already.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Asked why she thinks the store is closed, a woman goes back to the sign she read earlier. Which process does this resemble?
options: Find Column, choosing among many places
Test Digit, checking constraints
Generate Variable, producing candidates
Find Antecedent, returning to an earlier relation
optionExplain: No choice among places is made.
Nothing is tested.
No candidates are generated.
Right: she recalls the earlier source.
questions.explain: Going back to the source used before is recall.
questions.teaches: The authors say two different forms of memory are involved, path memory in FA and production-occurrence memory in FP, but they are probably not distinct and are interwoven in the memory of past behavior.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: To total six numbers one by one, which supporting step must exist in any method?
options: A way to forget the total
A way to skip every other number
A way to move on to the next number in turn
A way to guess the answer
optionExplain: The total must be kept.
All are used.
Right: sequencing is needed.
The sum needs the numbers.
questions.explain: Serial work needs sequencing. The card next gives the authors' point.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: GNC and FL are postulated in response to needs for ____, as the system could not otherwise complete certain steps.
questions.explain: The sufficiency needs are given by the system's tasks.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Which rule do the authors offer as a fair approximation of FL at B14-B18?
options: Choose the unprocessed letter occurring the maximum number of times
Choose the letter at the left end
Choose the letter with the smallest value
Choose a letter at random
optionExplain: Right: the most frequent unprocessed letter.
Position is not the rule.
No value is known yet.
S3 weighs occurrences.
questions.explain: S3 considers letters and their multiple occurrences.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: The authors say they have detailed evidence about the internal mechanisms of GNC and FL.
questions.explain: They say the instances are so few that nothing can be said about the internal mechanisms.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A gardener must choose which weed to pull first and picks the kind that appears most often in the bed. Which process does this resemble?
options: Test Digit, checking constraints
Assign Value, pairing items
Process Column, adding digits
Find Letter, taking the item that occurs most often
optionExplain: No test is made.
No pairing is made.
No arithmetic is done.
Right: frequency guides the pick.
questions.explain: Pick by frequency.
questions.teaches: The authors add that the mechanism they suggest may differ from the actual process the subject uses.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A theory explains most but not all of a person's moves. What is the fairest reading of the leftovers?
options: They prove the person acted randomly
They may reflect gaps in the theory or the data, to be checked case by case
They prove the theory is wrong
They can be ignored
optionExplain: That needs evidence.
Right: examine them before judging.
Most moves are explained.
Scrutiny is the point.
questions.explain: The remainder needs scrutiny. The card next gives the authors' finding.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: The production system accounted for ____ to 80 percent of the units of behavior.
questions.explain: The fit is 75 to 80 percent.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: What do the authors conclude about the behavior the production system did not account for?
options: It is random and cannot be studied
No reason to think it is intrinsically incomprehensible or random; gaps in memory and attention accounts explain most
It is proof that S3 guessed
It is a copy of the explained behavior
optionExplain: They deny this.
Right: the gaps are in the model.
No such claim.
No such claim.
questions.explain: The remainder looks like model gaps.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: The authors say the chapter shows that a thinking-aloud protocol is useless as raw material for theory.
questions.explain: They say it shows how a protocol can be used to generate and test a theory.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A model of a chess club member's moves predicts 78 percent of them. A critic says the other 22 percent show the player is random. Which authors' response fits?
options: Accept the critic, as random moves are likely
Discard the model, as 22 percent is large
Ignore the misses, as they are few
Scrutinize the misses: they may come from missing data or an incomplete memory account
optionExplain: Not shown by scrutiny.
Most moves are explained.
Scrutiny is needed.
Right: that is the authors' approach.
questions.explain: Do not call the rest random without checking.
questions.teaches: The text says the detail gives no reason for supposing the remainder to be intrinsically incomprehensible, while stating the inadequacies as lack of an account of attention and memory or missing data.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A pupil does nearly every needed sum correctly but sometimes redoes one to be sure. How would you describe the arithmetic?
options: Close to ideal, with some uncertainty
Poor, since redoing shows weakness
Perfect, since no sum is wrong
Irrelevant to the task
optionExplain: Right: sound but not fully sure.
Redoing is a check.
Some uncertainty remains.
It is needed.
questions.explain: Checking shows uncertainty, not failure. The card next gives the authors' view.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: S3 infers properties of numbers, such as R ____, and limits assignments, such as G equal to 1 or 2.
questions.explain: Properties and limits both occur.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Which is one of the two shortfalls in S3's arithmetic?
options: He cannot add single digits
He cannot use carries
He is not always sure his inferences are right, so he repeats them
He never infers parity
optionExplain: He can.
He uses them.
Right: uncertainty leads to repeats.
He infers R odd.
questions.explain: One shortfall is lack of certainty.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: The authors say the cryptarithmetic task is a good measure of S3's arithmetic knowledge and skills.
questions.explain: They say the environment is not, in this sense, a test of or a measure of his arithmetic knowledge and skills.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A mechanic uses every tool a repair needs, but twice gives a wrong diagnosis. A report says the job does not test his skill. Which part of S3's summary does this resemble?
options: S3 has no arithmetic knowledge
S3 solves the puzzle at once
S3 avoids all inference
S3 uses all the help available, yet a few inferences are wrong
optionExplain: He has it.
He does not.
He infers often.
Right: tools used, errors present.
questions.explain: Full use of means, with a few errors.
questions.teaches: The authors name the inference to L = 3 from R = 7 as a notable incorrect inference.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: The ground is wet. Rain would explain that. Does it follow that it rained?
options: Yes, since rain explains wet ground
No, because other causes would also fit
Yes, if it often rains
Only if the ground is dry later
optionExplain: Other causes fit too.
Right: fitting is not forcing.
Frequency does not force it.
Not related.
questions.explain: A fit is not a proof. The card next gives S3's case.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: S3 infers L = 3 from R = 7 because L = 3 is only ____ with R = 7.
questions.explain: He takes a consistent value as forced.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: In column 5, what did it take to convince S3 that E = 0 or 9 was necessary?
options: A rule given by the experimenter
A fresh look at column 1
Some experimentation
Nothing, he saw it at once
optionExplain: No rule was given.
Column 5 was the one.
Right: he tested it.
It took experimentation.
questions.explain: He needed to test the claim.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: The authors say S3 does not confuse necessary and sufficient conditions.
questions.explain: They say the uncertainties and errors seem sometimes associated with such a confusion.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: S3 infers L = 3 from R = 7 because L = 3 is consistent with R = 7. A buyer who finds that a coat fits concludes that it must be the only size the shop has. What error do both share?
options: Treating a condition that is consistent as one that is required
Checking a conclusion twice before relying on it
Choosing a value at random from a short list of candidates
Dropping a premise once it has been used in an earlier inference
optionExplain: Right: consistency with the premise is not the same as being forced by it, which is S3's vagueness about necessary and sufficient conditions.
Repeating inferences to check them is something S3 does, but it is not the error the authors point to.
The inference from R = 7 to L = 3 was not a random choice; it rested on consistency.
The error is in the strength of the inference, not in dropping premises.
questions.explain: The authors say S3's errors seem associated with vagueness about necessary and sufficient conditions: L = 3 is consistent with R = 7, so he infers L = 3 from R = 7.
questions.teaches: L = 3 is consistent with the hypothesis that R = 7; hence S3 infers that L = 3 from R = 7, an inference that is actually not correct.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: When a new fact is learned, a good solver puts it back into every place where it applies. Which strategy is this?
options: Substituting the new information back into the display
Guessing a fresh value
Stopping the search
Starting a new problem
optionExplain: Right: it feeds the new fact back in.
The new fact is applied, not guessed.
Search continues.
The same problem continues.
questions.explain: New information is fed back. The card next names S3's strategy.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: S3 substitutes D <- 5 in columns 1 and 6, and when that gives no result he follows the ____ into column 2.
questions.explain: The carry c2 equals 1.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: What did S3 do at B61 to handle uncertainty about R?
options: Chose R = 7 and dropped R = 9
Left R unassigned for the whole protocol
Split the work into R = 7 and R = 9 cases and pursued them separately
Asked the experimenter for R
optionExplain: Both were pursued.
R was explored.
Right: two cases, two solutions.
No help was given.
questions.explain: The cases were split.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: The authors say S3 used forward search extensively from the start.
questions.explain: They say he did so only to a very limited extent, after inference stalled at B40.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A detective follows each clue to the next, but when clues run out, she tests two suspects in turn. Which part of S3's strategy matches the second step?
options: Substituting known values in the display
The limited forward search, trying cases when inference stalls
Following the carry into the next column
Testing a digit for availability
optionExplain: That is the first step.
Right: trial after inference stalls.
That is inference.
That is TD.
questions.explain: Cases are tried when chaining stops.
questions.teaches: The bulk of the protocol consists of passages concerned with the value of R, involving columns 2 and 6, and passages concerned with E, involving columns 5 and 3.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: You remember a conclusion but not how you got it. What is a sensible thing to do before relying on it?
options: Trust it, as a memory is proof
Drop it, as unproven things are useless
Ask someone else to forget it
Rederive it to check for untested assumptions
optionExplain: The basis is lost.
It may be right.
Not relevant.
Right: a recheck is wise.
questions.explain: A conclusion without its basis needs a check. The card next shows S3 doing this.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: S3 keeps cognitive strain low by trying not to make highly ____ hypotheses.
questions.explain: This follows from a reasoning strategy rather than forward search.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Why does S3 sometimes repeat a derivation, by the authors' account?
options: He forgets the problem itself
He enjoys repetition
He remembers the result but not always how he derived it
He cannot do the arithmetic
optionExplain: He remembers the problem.
Not stated.
Right: the basis is not kept.
He can.
questions.explain: Results are kept better than derivations.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: The authors say S3's failure to recall T = 0 to refute E = 0 is completely explained by their model.
questions.explain: They say it is not completely explained, though consistent with evoking TD only on new results.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A student keeps the answers from earlier problems but not the working, and recomputes some to be safe. Which of S3's habits is this?
options: Repeating derivations to see whether they rest on untested assumptions
Making highly conditional hypotheses
Using forward search throughout
Forgetting the problem statement
optionExplain: Right: the same habit.
He avoids them.
He uses it little.
Not described.
questions.explain: Rechecking derivations.
questions.teaches: S3 does remember whether he is working in the case R = 7 or the case R = 9, and that other results may be conditional on those assumptions.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A study examines one person in great detail. What may it fairly offer about people in general?
options: Final laws for all people
Nothing at all
Proof that the person is typical
Preliminary answers, to be tested elsewhere
optionExplain: One person cannot show that.
It gives preliminary answers.
That needs more subjects.
Right: tentative, not final.
questions.explain: One case gives preliminary answers. The card next gives the authors' view.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: The production system makes the relation of the program to the search in the problem space, the ____, transparent.
questions.explain: The PBG plots the search.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Which general mechanism from earlier chapters does the text point to as appearing in S3's behavior?
options: A fixed table of memorized answers
Heuristics such as the column selection process FC
A random choice process
A ban on all search
optionExplain: No such table is described.
Right: FC is a named example.
The authors find structure.
S3 searches.
questions.explain: FC is a heuristic of the kind studied earlier.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: The authors say the IPS was specified as a full program with every detail.
questions.explain: They say it is precisely defined, or almost so, since they stopped short of a full program.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A researcher studies one pianist's practice sessions in fine detail and finds links to general learning methods. Which of the authors' admissions applies?
options: Detail is worthless for general questions
The detail may feel stifling, but it gives preliminary answers to general questions
One case settles all questions
General questions should be dropped
optionExplain: The authors say otherwise.
Right: the same two-sided view.
Only preliminary answers.
Not suggested.
questions.explain: Detail helps with caution.
questions.teaches: The authors say that no appreciable chunk of raw data, the verbalizations of the protocol, is left unresponded to, down to the level of individual linguistic utterances.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: To turn a recorded think-aloud into a model, which first step makes later work easier?
options: Writing the final program at once
Counting the words spoken
Ignoring pauses and repeats
Stating the states of knowledge and the moves that change them
optionExplain: A space comes first.
Words are not the unit.
Not the first step.
Right: formalize the space first.
questions.explain: Formalizing comes first. The card next lists the five techniques.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Put the chapter's five techniques in order.
items: Formalize the problem space
Build the problem behavior graph
Write the production system
Set the priority order by minimizing errors
Display coverage and errors against added productions
questions.explain: The list runs from space to graph to productions to ordering to display.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: Which technique is used to decide which production wins when two apply at a node?
options: Determining the priority ordering by minimizing prediction errors
Drawing the PBG
Formalizing the problem space
Plotting coverage against productions
optionExplain: Right: the order is set by fewest errors.
That records the search.
That defines states and operators.
That shows performance.
questions.explain: Priority ordering settles conflicts.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: True or false: The graph of coverage and errors is used to build the problem space.
questions.explain: It displays the performance of the production system, with coverage and errors, as new productions are added.

questions.unitTitle: Cryptarithmetic: Behavior of a Single Subject, S3, on DONALD + GERALD = ROBERT
questions.q: A researcher records a cook's think-aloud, lists the cook's kitchen states and actions, and plots the sequence of states. Which two techniques is this?
options: Priority ordering and coverage display
Writing productions and priority ordering
Formalizing the problem space and building a behavior graph
Coverage display alone
optionExplain: Those come later.
Productions come after the graph.
Right: space then graph.
Not what was done.
questions.explain: States and actions, then the plot of the path.
questions.teaches: The authors count the production system's role as extracting the regularities of behavior at a node of the PBG.

questions.q: A theory fits one person's problem-solving protocol in fine detail. What would you expect when other people try the same puzzle?
options: Identical protocols, since one theory fits every person
Similar broad features, with differences of detail that need explaining
Unrelated behavior, since one successful case says nothing at all about any other person
Identical answers reached by completely different methods
optionExplain: Tempting, but individuals differ in details.
Right: the card shows this is the authors' expectation.
Too pessimistic; shared structure is the open question.
The answer is shared by definition, but the methods are the question.
questions.explain: A detailed fit to one person leaves open how much carries over. The card next states the authors' view.

questions.q: True or false: The authors expect their S3 theory, read literally, to fail as a prediction of identical protocols for all subjects.
questions.explain: True: they expect the prediction to fail. What interests them is how and how far it fails.
questions.rule: The prediction fails; the pattern of failure is the data.

questions.q: A coach writes a model of one runner's pacing that reads like a program. Following the authors, what is the key question about other runners?
options: Whether their pacing matches the model exactly, lap by lap
Whether one runner who differs is enough to discard the model
Whether the runners agree with the coach about the model
How far and in what way their pacing departs from the model
optionExplain: Exact matching is not expected; that standard would reject any general theory.
A single difference is expected, so it cannot settle the matter alone.
Agreement of opinion is no test; the behavior is.
Right: the manner and extent of departure is the question.
questions.explain: The measure is the size and kind of the differences, not a yes or no on identity.

questions.q: Which differences between S3 and another subject would the authors not be surprised to find? Select all that apply.
options: Different details in the arithmetic processes
Basic processes organized into somewhat different productions
A somewhat different problem space
The other subject accepts two letters standing for one digit
optionExplain: Right: they name this as expected.
Right: also named as expected.
Right: also named as expected.
This breaks the rules of the task, not a difference of process.
questions.explain: The authors list differences in processes, productions and problem space as unsurprising.

questions.q: A bakery models one baker's routine and finds a second baker differs in oven timing. According to the authors, what decides if the model is more than a description of one baker?
options: How large the differences are and in what circumstances they appear
Whether the second baker accepts the model as correct
Whether a third baker can be found who matches the model exactly in every detail
Whether the model can be written as a program at all
optionExplain: Right: this is the authors' criterion.
The model's status depends on behavior, not acceptance.
One exact match shows little about breadth.
The theory is only close to a program; being program-like is not the test.
questions.explain: The authors say significance depends on the extent of differences and the circumstances where they appear.
questions.teaches: Whether the theory is only a description of idiosyncratic behavior or has broader significance depends on the extent of the differences and the circumstances in which they appear.

questions.q: You want to know whether a model of one expert transfers to other experts. Which comparison levels might you use?
options: Only their final answers
Only a line-by-line copy of each full transcript
The space they work in, the paths they take, and a new task
Only their opinions of the model afterwards
optionExplain: Final answers hide the process.
The authors explicitly avoid this.
Right: the chapter uses these three.
Opinions are not behavior data.
questions.explain: A fair guess uses several grains of comparison. The card names the three.

questions.q: Put the chapter's three comparison levels in the order the authors take them.
items: Problem spaces of the subjects
Episodes and search paths
A different task with eye-movement data
questions.explain: The chapter moves from spaces, to episodes, to a second puzzle.

questions.q: A researcher has diagrams of how episodes are organized for five students on one puzzle and wants no full transcript comparison. Which statement fits the authors' plan?
options: The diagrams replace any further need to ask what caused the differences at finer levels
The diagrams prove the students share one program
The diagrams give a framework to find what causes differences at finer levels
The diagrams are useful only when the puzzle changes
optionExplain: They are a start for diagnosis, not a substitute.
They give clues, not proof.
Right: the diagrams serve as a tight framework for diagnosis.
They are used with the same puzzle in the second section.
questions.explain: The authors use episode diagrams as a framework for diagnosing the causes of path differences.

questions.q: True or false: If subjects use different problem spaces, the authors expect them to follow somewhat different paths through the problem space.
questions.explain: The chapter says differences in basic processes, productions and spaces should cause different paths, and the paths point back to the cause.

questions.q: A teacher sees two pupils reach the same sum by different routes. Following the authors' tracing idea, what is a sensible move?
options: Work backwards from the differing routes to the differences in the pupils' underlying methods
Conclude that the pupils must have the same method, despite the differences in their routes to the sum
Ignore the routes and score only the sums
Ask both pupils to use the first pupil's route
optionExplain: Right: trace backwards from path differences to underlying program differences.
Different routes are evidence of different methods.
That discards the process data the approach relies on.
This changes the behavior rather than explaining it.
questions.explain: Differences in the paths are the evidence from which causes are traced back.
questions.teaches: The authors treat differences in search paths as clues that can be traced backwards to the divergence in the subjects' underlying programs.

questions.q: A player is limited to a kitchen's tools. What does knowing the tools tell you before watching them cook?
options: Exactly the dish they will make in every case
Nothing, because only the recipe matters
How quickly they will cook, independent of the recipe they have chosen to follow
What they are able to do, though not yet what they will choose
optionExplain: The tools allow many dishes.
The tools already bound what is possible.
Speed is not set by the tool list.
Right: the space limits the options without choosing among them.
questions.explain: Tools fix what is possible, not what is chosen. The card applies this to problem spaces.

questions.q: Once the problem space is fixed, intelligence is constrained to selecting among the ____ it admits.
questions.explain: The card says the choice is among the operations the space admits.

questions.q: Subject X can only record letter-digit assignments and check sums, while Subject Y can also record inequalities and parity. What follows from the authors' view?
options: X and Y differ only in how fast they work
Y's space admits inferences that X's cannot, so their capabilities differ before any strategy is considered
Nothing can be said about their capabilities until both production systems have been written out in full detail
X must be less intelligent in every respect
optionExplain: Speed is not what the space defines.
Right: the space already settles what each can do.
The authors say the space already carries information.
The claim concerns the space, not general ability.
questions.explain: A richer space admits richer operations; this is information about capability.

questions.q: True or false: A problem space and a production system say the same thing about a subject, so one makes the other unnecessary.
questions.explain: The space tells what is available; the production system tells how the subject selects and orders operations.

questions.q: A club moves from a plain chess set to a board that shows legal moves automatically. In the authors' terms, what has changed?
options: The operations and information available to players, so the space itself differs
Only the players' strategies, which stay within the same space whatever the board shows
Nothing, since the rules of chess are the same
Only the players' intelligence, which grows with the board
optionExplain: Right: the space changes what is available.
Showing legal moves changes the information available, not only strategy.
The rules stay but the space of usable knowledge changes.
The tool changes the space; it need not change the player's ability.
questions.explain: A space is defined by the knowledge and operators available, so aids that change them change the space.
questions.teaches: A human can use any problem space the experimenter can specify, but possibly not in reasonable time nor without error unless supplied with external memory and computational aids.

questions.q: A word-processing program has only an undo for the last action. A rival adds a way to delete one earlier edit and keep the later ones. Which holds?
options: The rival must be better
The two are the same because both remove an edit
Neither matters to how work is done
The rival changes how problems are handled and may be better or worse depending on how independent the edits are
optionExplain: More options do not always help.
They differ when later edits depend on the removed one.
Operator choice changes the process.
Right: this is the card's logic.
questions.explain: Variant operators can alter the whole search. The card applies this to cryptarithmetic.

questions.q: A delete-assignment operator removes one assignment and leaves all the ____ intact.
questions.explain: The card describes this variant as different from returning to an earlier state.

questions.q: In the augmented space, TD could be split in two. Which pair fits the authors' example?
options: Test whether the sum is correct; test whether the subject is too tired to continue with the puzzle
Test whether the digit is already assigned; test whether it fits the letter's known constraints
Generate possible digits; assign the first one
Process a column; back up to the last state
optionExplain: Fatigue is not an operator in the example.
Right: the two checks the card names.
Generation and assignment are other operators (GN, AV).
These are PC and a backup step, not a split of TD.
questions.explain: TD checks two things at once, and the text imagines separate operators for each.
questions.rule: TD can be split in two.

questions.q: True or false: If TD were split in two and each part were evoked on independent cues, the authors suggest problem-solving power would probably improve.
questions.explain: They say independent evocation would probably be to the detriment of the power of the problem solving.

questions.q: A navigation app can recompute a whole route after a wrong turn, or drop only the one bad leg and keep the rest. When would dropping a single leg be better?
options: Always, since it keeps more of the work that has already been done
Never, since a clean restart is safer
When the other legs do not depend on the dropped one
Only when the route has no turns
optionExplain: Not when later legs depend on the removed one.
If parts are independent, a restart wastes work.
Right: this mirrors the independence condition on letters and columns.
Turns do not decide independence; dependence does.
questions.explain: A delete-style operator pays off only if the remaining pieces do not depend on the deleted one.
questions.rule: Independence decides whether partial deletion helps.
questions.teaches: The authors say a modified space with such an operator could be better or worse than the basic one, depending on how far subsets of letters and columns are independent of each other.

questions.q: If every person solving a puzzle used exactly the same representation, what would that say about the representation?
options: It would prove that the representation is built into the minds of all people everywhere
It would prove people are not intelligent
It would make the representation useless to study
It might only reflect the task's demands rather than anything about the people
optionExplain: Task demands are a simpler explanation.
Uniformity says nothing about intelligence.
It would only tell us about the task.
Right: no variation, no psychological information.
questions.explain: Variation is what makes a representation psychologically informative. The card links this to problem spaces.

questions.q: The authors say they are not ready for a serious ____ study of how often various problem spaces occur in natural environments.
questions.explain: They cite Brunswik's idea of ecological study as something not yet attempted.

questions.q: A survey finds that all 30 testers used the same method on a task where one method is forced. Following the authors, what can be concluded?
options: That the method is a deep trait of human thought that is shared by every person who tries
Little about the testers, since the sameness may reflect only the task's demands
That the method is wrong
That the testers must have copied each other
optionExplain: A forced method is explained by the task.
Right: demands of the task explain the uniformity.
Nothing here suggests that.
The authors give no reason to suppose copying.
questions.explain: Uniformity under forced demands is not psychological evidence.
questions.rule: Look for variation not forced by the task.

questions.q: Which are the two prior questions the authors ask? Select both.
options: Does the problem-space concept apply to humans other than S3?
Is there enough variation among subjects to make the space a psychological datum?
How often does each space occur in natural environments?
Can the subjects be ranked by intelligence?
optionExplain: Right: first question.
Right: second question.
This is the ecological study they say they are not ready for.
No ranking is proposed.
questions.explain: Applicability and variation are the two prior questions; frequency in nature is explicitly postponed.

questions.q: A linguist asks if speakers of different dialects use different internal rules for forming questions. Which situation would make the rules a real datum about speakers?
options: All speakers use the same rule
The rule can be listed in a textbook
The rules differ from speaker to speaker in ways not forced by the language's grammar
Nobody can say the rule aloud
optionExplain: That would only reflect the demands.
Being listed says nothing about variation.
Right: this is the analogue of variation not forced by the task.
Inability to verbalize is not variation.
questions.explain: A feature becomes psychological data when it varies and is not imposed by the task.
questions.teaches: The authors' interest centers on the spaces that are in fact used by humans, not on the whole range of spaces that could be specified.

questions.q: A solver's notes state that R must be odd and that G cannot be zero because T is zero. What kind of knowledge do such notes show?
options: Relations such as parity and exclusion, not only plain letter-digit assignments
Only plain assignments of digits to letters
Random guessing about letters
Only knowledge of how to read the words that the puzzle happens to be written in
optionExplain: Right: the notes use richer relations.
A plain assignment would name one digit for R, not a property.
The notes give reasons, not guesses.
Odd and zero refer to digit properties.
questions.explain: Parity and exclusion are relations beyond bare assignment. The card names the full set.

questions.q: The four operators of the augmented space are PC, AV, GN and ____.
questions.explain: TD tests a digit; the other three process columns, assign values, and generate possible digits.

questions.q: A solver writes: 'Column 5 gives E as 9. That makes N plus R more than 10.' Which operator best describes the first step?
options: GN, generating the digits still possible for a letter
PC, processing a column to get a value
AV, assigning a trial value to a letter
TD, testing a digit already used
optionExplain: No set of candidate digits is listed.
Right: a column is processed to derive E.
E is inferred, not tried.
No check of availability is shown.
questions.explain: Deriving a value by adding in a column is PC.
questions.rule: Column in, value out is PC.

questions.q: True or false: A relation that appears only as the output of an operator shows as well as an input use that the subject can employ it.
questions.explain: The authors want relations to occur both as input and as output; output alone does not show the subject can use the information.

questions.q: A cook's notes link two steps: a hot oven means browning is skipped, and skipping browning means the rack is lowered. What do the notes show?
options: Only that the cook knows the recipe by heart
Only that the notes were written afterwards
Nothing, since only the final dish can be used as evidence of the cook's thinking
Facts are used as inputs to reach new facts, a chain of use
optionExplain: Memorization would not show chaining.
Nothing about timing is shown.
The chain of use is the evidence.
Right: this parallels relations as input and output.
questions.explain: Chaining facts through steps is the sign of using a knowledge space, not just holding it.
questions.teaches: Subject I's protocol is only a written summary prepared by the subject, not a think-aloud record, yet the authors say it gives ample evidence of his problem space.

questions.q: A diary shows you ate well on three days. What can it not show about the days it does not cover?
options: It cannot show that the other days looked the same, though a steady habit would make that plausible
It shows that the other days were identical to the days it covers, in food and in every other habit
It shows the other days were skipped
It shows nothing at all about habits
optionExplain: Right: same logic as the card.
A sample does not prove the rest.
Absence from the record is not skipping.
It shows something, just not everything.
questions.explain: A sample supports a steady-pattern assumption without proving it. The card applies this to protocols.

questions.q: Figure 7.1 shows the subject working at least part of the time in a space that ____ the augmented space.
questions.explain: The figure shows use of a space including the augmented one; only by indirection does it speak to operations he did not use.

questions.q: A teacher sees a pupil solve three fraction problems correctly with one method. The authors' reasoning would let her say:
options: The pupil knows only that one method
The pupil has mastered every method
The pupil used that method, and probably can use it steadily, though better methods are not ruled out
Nothing can be said until she has given the pupil a further and fuller test on fractions of every kind
optionExplain: That would claim an absence the data do not show.
Three problems do not show that.
Right: use shown, absence of more not shown, steadiness assumed.
She can say something; just not everything.
questions.explain: Evidence of use is not evidence of a limit, and steadiness is assumed.

questions.q: True or false: The authors present the claim that competence does not fluctuate violently over short periods in nonstressful situations as a belief from general experience, not as a result of their data.
questions.explain: They say they believe it from general experience; it is an assumption that supports reading the protocols.

questions.q: A sports scientist watches a runner for 10 relaxed minutes and infers a typical stride. Which extra condition does the authors' stance need?
options: That the runner is chased by someone
That 10 minutes are replaced by 10 seconds
That ability does not swing wildly in short spans under calm conditions
That the runner changes stride every minute without any cause that could be observed
optionExplain: Stress is the condition the authors avoid assuming away.
Shorter data would weaken the claim.
Right: the same assumption lets sparse data stand.
Wild fluctuation would undermine the inference.
questions.explain: The assumption of stable competence in calm settings underwrites the inference.
questions.teaches: The authors say the full protocols for S4, S5 and S8 settle the question of their space with reasonable certainty, though the figures alone do not prove other spaces were unused.

questions.q: A solver reports that the rest fell into place easily, without saying how. What does that tell you about their method?
options: Very little about the method, since the steps are not described
That the method was a simple lookup
That the method was the most advanced one available to anyone solving it
That the solver made no errors
optionExplain: Right: the report hides the process.
Nothing supports a lookup.
Ease does not show advanced methods.
Errors are not ruled out by a casual report.
questions.explain: A bare claim of ease does not reveal process. The card shows the case of subject VII.

questions.q: Subject VII's key inference was that E had to be ____, because O plus E gives the O of ROBERT.
questions.explain: O + E = O forces E to 9 (with a carry) given that 0 is excluded for E.

questions.q: A tutor's note says: 'Pupil Z juggled numbers for ten minutes, restarted, found one key fact, then everything fitted easily.' What would the authors say?
options: The note proves the pupil used algebra
The note proves the pupil guessed
The note shows the pupil used a perfect method throughout
The note shows an insight but not the processes used afterwards, so the method is only partly known
optionExplain: No algebra is mentioned.
Guessing is not shown.
The early juggling argues against that.
Right: parallels subject VII.
questions.explain: The key fact is visible; the fitting that followed is not.
questions.rule: Say what is shown, not what is hidden.

questions.q: True or false: The authors find no evidence that Subject VII's early protocol uses parity, inequality or disjunctive sets.
questions.explain: True: they find no evidence he uses parity, inequality or disjunctive sets.

questions.q: A reviewer must classify a solver whose written record is thin. What is the better practice per the authors' handling of VII?
options: Force the solver into the most common category
Leave the solver unclassified or use better data, and turn to cases with complete protocols
Assume the solver's method was random
Ask the solver to guess their own method
optionExplain: That would claim more than the data give.
Right: they turn to their own full protocols.
Thin data give no support for randomness.
Introspection after the fact is no replacement for process data.
questions.explain: The authors do not belabor insufficient data; they go to protocols in the style of S3's.
questions.teaches: Subject VII himself called stage 3 the difficult one, since it was hard to break away from an approach leading to nothing definite; once stage 6 was reached the rest was much easier.

questions.q: Out of four newly analyzed subjects, how many would you expect to share the space of a fifth, S3, if the space is common among technically educated people?
options: Most of them, with perhaps one exception
None, since individuals differ completely
All four without exception
Exactly one
optionExplain: Right: three of the four do.
The authors found considerable sharing.
One subject, S6, does not.
Three share it.
questions.explain: The authors report that three of four share S3's space.

questions.q: Sort each subject by whether he worked in the augmented problem space.

items.t: S3
S4
S5
S8
S6

questions.explain: S4, S5 and S8 work in the augmented space as S3 did; S6 does not.

questions.q: S5 states that R has to be greater than 5 and less than 10, so it is 6, 7, 8 or 9. Which kind of knowledge is this?
options: A parity fact about R
A plain assignment of one definite digit to the letter R, such as R equals seven
A carry out of a column
An inequality about a letter, used to narrow its possible digits
optionExplain: No odd or even statement is made.
R is not given one value.
No carry is mentioned.
Right: it states bounds on R.
questions.explain: Bounds on a letter are inequality relations.

questions.q: True or false: To show that a subject uses a piece of knowledge, the authors choose examples where it is used as input to an operator, not only produced as output.
questions.explain: They explain that use as input shows the subject can employ the information.

questions.q: A researcher asks 40 people to solve a puzzle and finds 30 use one representation. What does the authors' chapter suggest as the next step?
options: Drop the 10 who differ as noise
Check the others for different representations, and study what each representation allows
Declare that representation the only possible one for people
Stop, since majority use settles everything
optionExplain: S6's different space is treated as informative.
Right: the interest lies in both the shared and the exceptional space.
The chapter documents other spaces.
The minority tell about variation.
questions.explain: Exceptions such as S6 reveal variation in spaces.
questions.teaches: The authors reproduce the S4, S5 and S8 protocols in appendices at the end of the chapter, with S6's protocol also given in full in an appendix.

questions.q: A solver notes that the two D's add to 10, so a carry of 1 reaches column 2 and R must be odd. Which relation is the claim about R?
options: Equality between two letters
Inequality, because the leading column forces a bound on the letter
Parity: the carry-in and doubling mean an odd result
Assignment of R to a digit
optionExplain: No two letters are set equal.
No bound is given.
Right: this is the form of S4's parity line.
R is only shown to be odd.
questions.explain: A statement about odd or even is parity. The card gives the S4 example.

questions.q: Match each S4 line to the kind of knowledge it shows.
pairs: N plus R must exceed 10 to make column 5 come out
R must be an odd number
R is 1 or 2 greater than G
E must be 9 for O plus E equal O
questions.explain: Each line illustrates one element of the augmented space.

questions.q: S8 says R is 7 or 9, so L is either 3 or 4. What kind of knowledge is the statement about L?
options: A parity fact, since three and four differ in whether they are odd or even
An assignment of L
A carry into column 2
A disjunction, a small set of digits a letter can take
optionExplain: Three and four have different parity, so parity does not state it.
L is not given one value.
No carry is stated.
Right: it is a set of possible digits.
questions.explain: A small set of digits for a letter is a disjunction.

questions.q: True or false: S5 trying L as 3, then as 2, then as 1 and noting what R would be each time, is an example of PC alone.
questions.explain: Trying values is AV; computing R from each is PC. The sequence combines the two.

questions.q: A planner tries a meeting time, works out the seating needed, and checks it against a room of 10 seats. Which operator pair is parallel?
options: Only generating a list of the possible values for a letter, like GN, with no test of any value
Trying a value and testing it against a constraint, like AV and TD
Only processing a column, like PC
Backing up to an earlier state with no test
optionExplain: No list is generated.
Right: a trial then a check.
No column is summed.
A test happens in the example.
questions.explain: Trial and test correspond to AV and TD.
