questions.teaches: S5 rejects L as 1 because 1 is already assigned to O, so a trial value from AV is followed by a TD check against the digits in use.

questions.q: Two chess players know the same rules and pieces but play differently. What is a sensible way to compare them?
options: Compare their rules, which must differ
Declare that they cannot be compared
Compare their strategies, since they share the same basic tools
Compare only their final results and not how they played, since the results are what count
optionExplain: They share the rules.
Shared tools make comparison meaningful.
Right: common tools make strategy a fair comparison.
Strategies are the point of interest.
questions.explain: Strategy comparison needs shared tools. The card applies this to problem spaces.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, although several subjects worked in the augmented space, substantial variation existed; only the intellectual tools were essentially shared.
questions.explain: True: substantial variation existed; only the intellectual tools were essentially shared.

questions.q: Subject Q solved the puzzle by working only in plain letter-digit assignments, while S3 used parity and inequalities. Per the authors, a strategy comparison of Q and S3 is:
options: Not straightforward, since they work in different problem spaces
Perfectly meaningful, since both of them solve cryptarithmetic puzzles in the end
Unnecessary because S3's way is the standard
Meaningful only if Q finishes faster
optionExplain: Right: comparison of strategy needs a shared space.
Different tools change what strategies are possible.
The authors do not treat S3's way as the standard.
Speed is not the criterion.
questions.explain: Strategies are compared within a space.

questions.q: The strategy analysis covers S3, S4, S5 and S8 but leaves out ____, who does not work in the augmented space.
questions.explain: Restricting the comparison to subjects who share a space keeps it fair.

questions.q: Three cooks use the same pantry and stove but follow different orders of steps. Following the authors' logic, what is the best question to ask?
options: Why do their pantries differ?
How do their strategies differ, given they share the same tools?
Whether any cook has a hidden stove
Which cook is the most intelligent overall, judged by the finished dishes
optionExplain: The pantry is shared.
Right: this is the point of shared tools.
No such assumption is relevant.
The question is about strategy, not a ranking of ability.
questions.explain: With shared tools, differences lie in strategy and heuristics.
questions.teaches: The strategy analysis that follows is carried out at a more aggregated level than the production-system analysis done for S3.

questions.q: A student keeps a wrong sum on the page for four minutes while trying other digits. What does this suggest about the student's way of working?
options: The student has solved the puzzle and is double-checking
The student is using parity to prune options
The student is waiting for the experimenter to correct the sum when he gets round to it
The student is not checking the whole display for consistency as he goes
optionExplain: A wrong sum is not a check.
Parity use would expose the wrong sum.
The authors do not give this reading.
Right: that is S6's pattern.
questions.explain: Leaving a sum such as 5 + 8 = 7 on the display means the whole display is not being watched. The card describes S6.

questions.q: S6 abandoned the problem unsolved after ____ minutes.
questions.explain: The card gives 25 minutes.

questions.q: A solver sums columns only from the top two digits to get the bottom one, and does not work from a known result back to an unknown top digit. Which S6 trait does this resemble?
options: Column processing that always starts from the two upper digits
Use of parity to infer odd digits
Use of inequality to bound letters
Backing up to the last known state of the display after a failure
optionExplain: Right: this is how S6 sums.
No parity inference is shown.
No bounds are used.
Backup is a different trait.
questions.explain: S6 starts column sums from the two upper digits.
questions.rule: Upper digits in, lower digit out.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say S6 is a subject with lower arithmetic skill, and that any such subject can be described as working in the basic space.
questions.explain: They note that at much lower skill, such as young children, behavior may not be characterizable as working in the basic space at all.
questions.rule: Low skill is not the same as a basic space.

questions.q: A teacher finds a six-year-old's attempt to the same puzzle cannot be read as assigning digits to letters at all. Following the authors, what is the right reading?
options: The child works in the augmented space but makes many arithmetic errors along the way and fails
The child is using the typographical space
Behavior can fall below even the basic space when arithmetic competence is very low
The task has no problem space for anyone
optionExplain: The child lacks the competence the augmented space needs.
No evidence is given for that.
Right: this is the authors' remark about young children.
Other subjects do work in problem spaces.
questions.explain: The authors caution that descending in skill may leave the basic space behind entirely.
questions.rule: Skill can fall below the basic space.
questions.teaches: Descending in arithmetic skill toward young children may give behavior that is not characterizable at all as working in the basic problem space.

questions.q: A builder fixes the foundation firmly but leaves the upper floors loosely planned. What does the builder have to remember in order to work this way?
options: The exact dimensions of every brick
The names of every previous builder who worked on the site
Which parts are fixed and which are still open
Which floor was most expensive
optionExplain: Dimensions are not what makes the work staged.
Names are irrelevant.
Right: the status of each part.
Cost does not guide the staging.
questions.explain: Staged work depends on knowing status. The card shows S6 doing this with columns.

questions.q: S6 treats the right-hand columns as firmly assigned and the ones to the left as ____.
questions.explain: Left columns are tentative; right columns are firm.

questions.q: S6 assigns a digit to a letter that occurs only in the left columns. What does he do about the consequences?
options: He does not deal with them at that moment
He checks all columns at once for consistency
He asks the experimenter to remove the digit
He backs up to the first state
optionExplain: Right: left columns are tentative, so consequences are left alone.
That would remove the tentative/firm distinction.
Not described.
S6 almost never backs up.
questions.explain: Assignments to purely left letters go in without working out their consequences.

questions.q: Match each part of S6's display to its status.
pairs: A letter in a firm column
Kept in preference to tentative ones
questions.explain: These are the elements of the firm and tentative division.

questions.q: A copy editor fixes the first chapters of a book for good and drafts the later ones loosely. Which part of the editor's knowledge matches S6's next-column?
options: The total number of pages in the book, counted from the first page
The list of authors
The name of the printer
The point in the book up to which the text is final
optionExplain: Page count does not mark status.
Not a status marker.
Not related.
Right: next-column marks where firm ends.
questions.explain: Next-column plays the role of a boundary between firm and tentative.
questions.teaches: S6 keeps knowledge of the assignments externally on the display, so internally he remembers only next-column, his goal stack, the immediate products of operators, and the column he is working on.

questions.q: A puzzle solver mostly types guesses, sometimes adds a column, sometimes checks a guess against the rules, and rarely undoes a step. What is the main operator type?
options: Backing up
Making assignments
Generating all possible digits for a letter
Using parity
optionExplain: Backup is rare.
Right: assignments dominate S6's protocol.
S6 has no such operator.
S6 shows no parity inference.
questions.explain: Assignment dominates S6's behavior; the card gives the counts.

questions.q: Match each S6 operator to what it does.
pairs: Assigns an unused digit to a letter
Moves a digit from one letter to another
Tests whether a proposed digit is legitimate
questions.explain: These are four of S6's seven operators.
questions.rule: Four assign, one processes, one tests, one retracts.

questions.q: Of S6's 61 assignments, how many were AV?
optionExplain: Right: Table 7.1 gives AV as 49 of 61.
That is the total of all assignment operators.
That is the number of column processing instances.
That is the number of TD occurrences.
questions.explain: AV is 49 of 61; MD 2, EX 3, AEX 7.
questions.rule: AV is the main assignment operator.

questions.q: True or false: Of the 32 TD occurrences in S6's protocol, only 11 were produced by S6 himself and 21 were evoked by the experimenter.
questions.explain: True: only 11 were by S6; 21 were evoked by the experimenter.

questions.q: S6's seven operators include four assignment operators (AV assign-value, MD move-digit, EX exchange, AEX assign-exchanged-digit), PC (process column), TD (test digit) and BU (back up). A novice's log shows 61 edits: 49 new entries, 2 moves, 3 swaps and 7 swap-and-fill actions. Which operator class does this log match?
options: The assignment operators AV, MD, EX and AEX
Column processing, PC, which adds the digits of a column
Testing, TD, which checks proposed values for legitimacy
Backup, BU, which retracts steps
optionExplain: Right: Table 7.1 gives 61 assignments, split 49 AV, 2 MD, 3 EX and 7 AEX.
PC is a separate class, counted as 42 occurrences.
TD is a separate class, counted as 32 occurrences.
BU is a separate class, counted as 4 occurrences.
questions.explain: The four assignment operators together make 61 in S6's protocol.
questions.teaches: Table 7.1 gives 61 assignment operators in S6's protocol: AV 49, MD 2, EX 3 and AEX 7.

questions.q: A child has all ten counters placed on ten squares. To change one square the child has to take a counter from another. What new moves appear?
options: Moves that add a new counter
Moves that shift a counter from one square to another, or swap two
Moves that remove all the counters from the squares and start the game again
Moves that only count the counters
optionExplain: None is left to add.
Right: this is what S6 develops.
Not needed.
Counting does not change a square.
questions.explain: When all digits are used, new assignments must reuse digits. The card shows what S6 does.

questions.q: Put S6's assignment operators in the order they first appear in the protocol.
items: AV: assign an unused digit
MD: move a digit from one letter to another
EX: exchange the digits of two letters
AEX: assign the digit just freed
questions.explain: AV starts, then MD at B73, EX at B107, AEX at B133.

questions.q: S6 says to take the 4 from E and give it to O. Which operator is this?
options: AV, assign-value
EX, exchange
MD, move-digit
BU, back-up
optionExplain: AV assigns an unused digit.
EX swaps two letters' digits.
Right: a digit moves from one letter to another.
BU restores a previous digit.
questions.explain: Taking a digit from one letter for another is MD.

questions.q: True or false: Once S6 has all ten digits assigned, a plain AV on an unused digit is still the usual way he makes each new assignment.
questions.explain: All digits are in use, so each new assignment takes a digit from another letter; this is why MD, EX and AEX arise.

questions.q: A seating planner has every seat taken and must seat one more guest. Which approach resembles EX?
options: Seat the new guest on top of someone who is already seated, as a spare
Remove all guests and begin again
Ask the new guest to stand
Swap two guests' seats in one step so no seat holds two guests
optionExplain: That breaks the one-seat rule, like a doubled digit.
That is a restart, not an exchange.
This leaves the problem unsolved.
Right: exchange gives two assignments at once.
questions.explain: EX avoids breaking the rule of one digit per letter by exchanging.
questions.teaches: After the first AEX at B133, the experimenter's evoked TDs became frequent: 70 percent of the 21 evoked TDs came after that point, with only 40 percent of the time remaining.

questions.q: A solver finds a column that does not add up. What does the solver need in order to repair it by reasoning, not by trial?
options: A faster pencil
The ability to work backward from the sum to the missing digit
A bigger display on which all ten letters can be seen at one time
Willingness to change the experimenter
optionExplain: Speed is not the issue.
Right: this is what S6 lacks.
Display size is not the issue.
Not relevant.
questions.explain: Reasoning backward is the skill missing from S6's PC. The card shows the evidence.

questions.q: S6 performed column processing ____ times in his protocol.
questions.explain: Table 7.1 gives PC as 42 occurrences.

questions.q: A solver adds a column and sets a letter to the result, though that letter also appears as an upper digit in the same column. Which S6 trait is this?
options: Using parity to infer R
Backing up to the first state of the puzzle after each failed column
Setting O to 6 at B93 without noticing O was an upper digit
Generating the digits for a letter
optionExplain: S6 does not use parity.
He almost never backs up.
Right: this is the episode the authors cite.
S6 has no such operator.
questions.explain: The longest explicit arithmetic sequence ends with this error.
questions.rule: Check where the letter also appears.

questions.q: True or false: In S6's protocol there were only four backward inferences of an upper letter from a known sum, and three of them came in the last minutes before he gave up.
questions.explain: True: there were only four, and three of them came in the last minutes before he gave up.

questions.q: A trainee checks a ledger by adding each column from right to left until one fails, then changes a single entry to make it balance. Which comparison to S6 holds?
options: The trainee uses a check-and-patch routine like S6's right-to-left check until a column fails
The trainee uses algebra on all of the columns at once to find all the digits directly without any trial
The trainee searches for the digits by parity
The trainee avoids all trial and error
optionExplain: Right: S6 does this at B88 to B93.
S6 does not.
No parity is used.
S6 relies on trial and error.
questions.explain: S6 states a strategy of working right to left until a column fails, then making it consistent.
questions.rule: Right to left until a column fails.
questions.teaches: S6 makes explicit the strategy of working from right to left until he reaches an inconsistent column, which he then tries to make consistent (B88 to B94).

questions.q: A solver who keeps every cell filled and fixes problems by overwriting, rather than by returning to an earlier clean state, will rarely need what?
options: Any digit at all
A step to retract an action
A way to read the puzzle aloud to the experimenter
A pencil
optionExplain: Digits are still used.
Right: backup becomes rare.
Reading is needed.
Writing is still needed.
questions.explain: Overwriting replaces going back. The card describes S6's habit.

questions.q: True or false: S6 rarely backs up to earlier states, in contrast to the augmented-space subjects; he reassigns instead.
questions.explain: True: he rarely backs up; he reassigns instead.

questions.q: At B41 S6 notices he has given 7 to both R and N. Which operator's job does his remark perform?
options: GN, which generates the digits that are still possible for a given letter
PC, which processes a column
AV, which assigns a value
TD, which checks that a digit is assigned to only one letter
optionExplain: No digit set is produced.
No column is processed.
The remark is a check, not an assignment.
Right: the remark catches a violation of the one-digit rule.
questions.explain: Catching a doubled digit is TD.

questions.q: Which of these are true of S6, compared with the augmented-space subjects? Select all that apply.
options: He lacks a GN operator
He almost never backs up
The experimenter took over part of the work of preventing duplicate digits
He uses disjunctive sets to prune options
optionExplain: Right: he has none.
Right: he reassigns.
Right: this explains the shift of TD.
No digit-set reasoning appears in his protocol.
questions.explain: The first three are in the text; disjunctive sets are used by the other subjects.

questions.q: A proofreader sets no marker to return to and keeps changing the text in place to patch each error. Compared with S6, which is closest?
options: Patching in place instead of backing up to an earlier version
Keeping an exhaustive list of all the variants of the text, edit by edit
Pruning options with parity
Backing up after each error
optionExplain: Right: this is S6's habit.
S6 generates nothing like that.
S6 does not use parity.
S6 almost never backs up.
questions.explain: S6 patches instead of returning to a prior state.
questions.teaches: The experimenter gradually stepped out of his passive role and took on responsibility for not allowing multiple assignments, which is why explicit TD by S6 is rarer than TD evoked by E.

questions.q: A solver, when a conflict arises between an old firm fact and a new tentative one, usually changes the tentative one. What does this suggest?
options: The solver picks at random
The solver prefers the newest fact whatever its firm or tentative status
The solver keeps a record of which facts are firm
The solver cannot tell the facts apart
optionExplain: A strong regularity is not random.
The tentative one is changed, regardless of age.
Right: the status must be remembered.
He treats them differently, so he can.
questions.explain: A consistent preference implies a retained status. The card gives S6's numbers.

questions.q: In 27 firm-versus-tentative conflicts, S6 changed the tentative letter in ____ of them.
questions.explain: He changed the tentative one in 22 cases, all but 5.

questions.q: In 21 inconsistencies S6 discovered, how many were in next-column?
optionExplain: Three were elsewhere.
That is the number of attempts at consistency.
Right: 18 of 21.
That is the number of failures of the firm/tentative rule.
questions.explain: The text gives 18 out of 21.

questions.q: True or false: S6's four backups all occurred after he followed the rule of changing tentative letters before firm ones.
questions.explain: All four backups followed a failure of the rule, a firm letter changed in preference to a tentative one; they were lapses caught at once.

questions.q: An accountant considers the first line counting from the right that is blank or contradictory as the next one to repair. Which element matches this?
options: S6's operational definition of next-column
S6's GN operator, which generates the digits possible for a letter
S6's MD operator
S6's goal stack
optionExplain: Right: first problem column, counted from the right in the puzzle.
GN generates digits.
MD moves digits.
The stack holds goals.
questions.explain: Next-column is defined as the first column from the right with an undefined letter or inconsistency.
questions.teaches: On the few occasions when S6 changed a firm letter, he attended to the new next-column immediately, and four of the five failures to keep firm letters were lapses caught at once.

questions.q: A teacher spends time documenting one student's unusual method. What is a good reason?
options: It proves the student's method is best
It replaces the need to look at any other students
It shows the student cheated
It shows methods differ among students and what each method can and cannot do
optionExplain: S6's space makes the task hard.
One case cannot do that.
Nothing suggests it.
Right: the authors' reason.
questions.explain: An unusual method shows variation and its consequences. The card gives the authors' two reasons.

questions.q: The authors describe S6's space so explicitly partly because the augmented space will seem ____ to most readers.
questions.explain: They want to show that other spaces occur in human behavior.

questions.q: Given S6's space, what does the problem require of him?
options: No search, because the space makes inference trivial
Extensive search, because he lacks inferences that prune it
An impossible amount of search, so that the puzzle cannot be solved at all
A machine for processing data
optionExplain: Just the opposite.
Right: the problem can be solved but only with extensive search.
The authors say it can be solved in this space.
The machine remark was S8's about the basic space.
questions.explain: The problem is solvable in S6's space but demands extensive search.

questions.q: True or false: By describing S6, the authors want to show that the problem space is a psychological datum, since it varies from person to person.
questions.explain: This is the second prior question the chapter sets out to settle.
questions.rule: Variation makes the space a datum.

questions.q: A language teacher learns that one pupil translates every sentence word by word. What does knowing this method tell her?
options: How much the pupil can do and how hard some sentences will be for that pupil
Nothing about difficulty
That the pupil has no real language ability, so the sentences will be hard for any method
That other pupils use the same method
optionExplain: Right: knowing the space tells the power.
Knowing the method tells a good deal.
The method is a limited tool, not zero ability.
Variation is the point.
questions.explain: Once the space or method is known, much about the person's power is known.
questions.rule: Know the space, know the power.
questions.teaches: One of Bartlett's subjects (V) appears to use inequality information systematically but not parity, and to ignore prospective carries, but the record is too brief for the authors to use him as an example.

questions.q: A person faced with a new kind of puzzle says aloud what the puzzle looks like and tests whether any known method fits. What are they doing?
options: Solving the puzzle by trial and error with a digit for each letter
Checking the answer
Memorizing the puzzle
Looking for a way to represent the problem before working on it
optionExplain: No trials yet.
No answer exists yet.
Memory is not the aim.
Right: this is S8's prelude.
questions.explain: Characterizing the task and testing methods is the search for a representation. The card describes S8.

questions.q: In his prelude S8 generated fourteen methods using ____ different problem spaces.
questions.explain: Fourteen methods, seven spaces.

questions.q: S8 realizes the puzzle may have many solutions, one of which he could find by starting at the beginning. What follows?
options: He gives up the puzzle
He starts making trial assignments in the augmented space
He returns to the number space
He asks for the algebra space to be set up for him by the experimenter
optionExplain: He had said he was near it, but this thought ends the search.
Right: his estimate of success changes and the search ends.
The number space had got him nowhere.
Not described.
questions.explain: Believing many solutions might exist changed his estimate and ended the search for a space.

questions.q: True or false: S8 himself describes his prelude as a search for the right problem space.
questions.explain: He sees himself as searching for a method or approach; each method implies a space the authors infer.

questions.q: A new employee tries one way of organizing a messy spreadsheet, judges it too slow, then tries another, and finally settles on one after noticing many arrangements would work. Which parallel to S8 is right?
options: The employee has no way to find a method
The employee should always choose the first method tried
Search over methods ends when a change in the estimate of success makes trial worth it
The employee has proved all methods impossible
optionExplain: Methods are tried.
S8 rejects several.
Right: S8's commitment came with a changed estimate.
No proof is involved.
questions.explain: A change in the estimated chance of success ended S8's search.
questions.teaches: S8 resisted trial assignments because he was convinced they were futile, a one-in-a-skillion chance of stumbling on the answer.

questions.q: While deciding whether a method is worth trying, a solver proves a small fact useful for the puzzle. This is best called:
options: The solution itself
A mistake
Proof that the method works and should be used for the puzzle
A by-product of evaluating the method
optionExplain: It is not the answer.
The fact is correct.
It does not show the method works.
Right: the fact comes out of the feasibility check.
questions.explain: Evaluation can yield facts. The card gives S8's carry result.

questions.q: S8 settled for himself that a carry in column addition cannot be greater than ____.
questions.explain: At most 1 can be carried.

questions.q: Why did S8 settle the carry question?
options: To prove a theorem about carries
To judge whether adding up the vertical columns was hopeless because the carry is not known
Because the experimenter had asked him to settle that question before he went any further with the puzzle
To start assigning digits at once
optionExplain: No theorem was aimed at.
Right: it was a subtask in evaluating that approach.
Not described.
He did not begin assignments yet.
questions.explain: The carry question served the evaluation of a method.

questions.q: True or false: S8's remark on column 2 means that the second column's sum yields either E or a number whose second digit is E.
questions.explain: He says T and V, or T plus V plus 1, gives E or a number ending in E.
questions.rule: Sum is E or ends in E.

questions.q: A planner rejects a delivery route because a bridge might be closed, and in doing so works out the bridge has only two states, open or closed. Which parallel holds?
options: The route is chosen because the bridge is open, and the rest follows from that
The bridge fact is a proof the route is best
A fact about the task is learned as a subtask of judging a method
The planner has solved the whole delivery
optionExplain: The parallel is about the fact found, not the route.
It is only a fact.
Right: like the carry result.
No.
questions.explain: S8's carry result was a fact learned while testing an approach.
questions.teaches: S8 says explicitly that he is at a loss how to attack the problem and cannot think of a method, which the authors take as evidence that he is searching for a method.

questions.q: A student asked how to crack a letter-substitution puzzle says: try numbers for letters at random. Another says: look for a rule. Which basic way to define the puzzle differs?
options: The rule-seeking way defines a different kind of thing to search, rules, not assignments
They are the same way of working
The rule-seeking way has no operators of its own
The random way requires inequalities
optionExplain: Right: this is a different space.
Random assignment and rule search differ in what is searched.
It has operators for making rules.
Random assignment uses no inequalities.
questions.explain: Spaces differ in what their elements are. The card lists seven.

questions.q: Put the seven spaces in the order the authors discuss them, from most familiar to least.
items: Basic space
Augmented space
Number space
Algebra space
Word-meaning space
Cryptogram space
Typographical space
questions.explain: The authors discuss them in the order basic, augmented, number, algebra, word-meaning, cryptogram, typographical.

questions.q: Match each space to what its elements are.
pairs: A set of three numbers, one per word
A collection of equations in letters and carries
A rule mapping letters to digits
A recognition of digits in the shapes of letters
questions.explain: These are the element types in Figure 7.8.

questions.q: True or false: S8 does not consider the basic space promising for LETS+WAVE=LATER and settles on the augmented space.
questions.explain: True: he says random substitution is virtually hopeless without enormous time or a machine; he wants no part of it and settles on the augmented space.

questions.q: A codebreaker lists these approaches: try each key, look for letter frequencies, guess a meaning, find a pattern rule. Which question mirrors the authors' use of the S8 list?
options: Which approach is guaranteed to work if the solver has enough time?
What does each approach take as its elements and operators?
Which approach came first?
Which approach is cheapest?
optionExplain: S8's list does not guarantee success.
Right: each space is defined by its elements and operators.
The authors do not order by time.
Cost is not the criterion.
questions.explain: Each space is described by elements, operators and initial and final elements.
questions.teaches: For each space S8 uncovered, Figure 7.8 gives the elements, the operators, an initial element and a final element.

questions.q: A puzzle is AA + BB = CBC. What property of the words might help a solver narrow the numbers?
options: All letters stand for 0
The sum must be 100
Letters are unrelated to digits, so no property of the words could help
Each of AA and BB is a repeated-digit number like 11, 22, 33
optionExplain: Letters stand for different digits.
No such rule is given.
They are linked by the puzzle.
Right: the pattern limits the candidates.
questions.explain: A repeated-letter pattern restricts candidate numbers. The card describes the number space.

questions.q: In the number space the element is a set of three numbers, one for each ____ of the puzzle.
questions.explain: Each word is viewed as a number.

questions.q: Which pattern could the number space generate numbers from, per the authors?
options: ABAB giving 1212, 1313, 2323
LETS giving 1234
ROADS giving any digits at all
WAVE giving 5555
optionExplain: Right: the authors give this example.
Distinct letters have no repeated pattern.
No pattern limits it.
Distinct letters cannot all be one digit.
questions.explain: A repeated-letter pattern lets the operator generate instances.

questions.q: True or false: On LETS+WAVE=LATER the number space works as well as on AA+BB=CBC.
questions.explain: S8 finds no repeated letter pattern in LETS, WAVE, LATER and gets nowhere.

questions.q: A treasure hunt gives three keys whose digits repeat in a regular way. Which spaces mirror the number space?
options: Search over digit-by-digit assignments with no pattern
Search over word meanings
Search over whole keys that fit the repeated pattern
Search over letter shapes
optionExplain: That is the basic space.
That is word-meaning.
Right: view each item as a whole number with a pattern.
That is typographical.
questions.explain: The number space generates whole numbers fitting a pattern.
questions.teaches: In the AA+BB=CBC protocol S8 rules out 11 with 22, 11 with 33, 22 with 44 and 33 with 44, then judges that 33 with 55, or 22 with 66, just about reaches 99.

questions.q: A student faces a puzzle where each column gives one equation, but there are more unknowns than equations. What is the likely reaction of someone trained on ordinary algebra?
options: Confidence that more unknowns make it easier, as more can be tried
Immediate success with substitution
Doubt that the puzzle can be solved by equations
Switching to a different alphabet
optionExplain: More unknowns do not.
Not with too many unknowns.
Right: this is S8's belief.
Not relevant.
questions.explain: Ordinary algebra expects unknowns not to exceed equations. The card shows S8 holding this belief.

questions.q: In the algebra space the carries are represented by ____.
questions.explain: Carries are variables in the equations.

questions.q: A solver says: I do not see how to write the carries down, so I cannot form the equations. Which difficulty of S8 is this?
options: His inability to invent a way to represent the carries explicitly
His belief that carries can exceed 1, which blocked him from forming the equations
His inability to add
His distrust of the experimenter
optionExplain: Right: the authors name this.
He settled that they cannot.
He can add.
Not described.
questions.explain: S8 could not represent the carries explicitly.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say that if the algebra space were set up for S8 he could probably maneuver in it.
questions.explain: True: they say that if the space were set up for him he could probably maneuver in it.

questions.q: Which are reasons a solver may fail to use a space that exists? Select all that apply.
options: He cannot invent the representation the space needs
He holds a belief carried over from other domains that blocks the space
The space is not logically valid
The experimenter forbids it
optionExplain: Right: like S8 with carries.
Right: S8's unknowns-versus-equations belief.
The algebra space is valid; the barrier is the solver's.
Not in the text.
questions.explain: Both of S8's barriers are about the solver, not the space's validity.
questions.teaches: S8's belief that the number of unknowns should not exceed the number of equations comes from his experience with algebraic equations in continuous variables, and it blocked him from this space.

questions.q: In a letter-for-digit puzzle, the letters happen to spell English words. Should the meanings of the words matter to the solution?
options: Yes, the rules of the puzzle require that the words make sense as ordinary English words
No, and no solver would ever look at them
Yes, because the digits are the words' lengths
By the rules, no; but a solver might still search the meanings for clues
optionExplain: The rules do not.
S8 did look.
Not the rule.
Right: irrelevant in principle, tempting in practice.
questions.explain: The words are an irrelevant feature that could still be exploited. The card gives the BILL example.

questions.q: In the authors' example, BILL leads to William the Conqueror and the year ____.
questions.explain: BILL, William the Conqueror, 1066.

questions.q: Using the authors' example BILL WAS KING with BILL as 1066, what digit does L stand for?
optionExplain: That is B.
Right: B is 1, I is 0, and both L's are 6.
That is I.
L is a single digit.
questions.explain: 1066 maps B, I, L, L to 1, 0, 6, 6.

questions.q: True or false: The authors state firmly that word-meaning clues form a problem space as they define the term.
questions.explain: They say it seems to them that they can, but do not wish to press the issue nor have the data to establish it.

questions.q: A puzzle writer picks the letters so they spell a famous phrase. Which statement about solving by the phrase's meaning matches the authors' view?
options: The meaning could give clues but is not part of what the puzzle's rules require
The meaning is required by the rules of the puzzle, so that every solver has to use it in the end
The meaning can never help
The meaning replaces the arithmetic
optionExplain: Right: irrelevant by the rules, possibly useful.
Not so.
The BILL example shows it can.
The addition test still applies.
questions.explain: The word pattern is an irrelevant feature but can be a source of information.
questions.teaches: The authors cannot define the operators of the word-meaning space precisely, because no good models of long-term memory are available.

questions.q: A cryptic message may be decoded by guessing a rule like A is 1, B is 2. What is searched in this approach?
options: Individual letter-digit pairs, one at a time, with no overall rule
Column sums only
Meanings of words
A rule that maps the whole alphabet to digits
optionExplain: That is the basic space.
That is column processing.
That is word-meaning.
Right: rules, not individual assignments.
questions.explain: In the cryptogram space the search is for a rule. The card describes it.

questions.q: In the cryptogram space the elements are ____ mapping letters to digits.
questions.explain: Elements are rules, functions from letters to digits.

questions.q: S8 tries counting from the end of the alphabet for letters near the end, and finds L would be 12. What follows?
options: The rule is accepted, since 12 is allowed as a code for a letter
The rule cannot make L a one-digit number, so S8 drops it
He concludes the puzzle has no solution
He moves to the algebra space
optionExplain: A digit is a single digit.
Right: he tests and abandons.
Only the rule fails.
Not described.
questions.explain: He tests the rule at once and abandons it when L cannot be a digit.

questions.q: True or false: Bartlett's subject VI and S8 both appear to search in the cryptogram space.
questions.explain: Both look for letter-to-digit coding rules; VI wrote two such rules.

questions.q: A puzzle fan assumes the clues follow a rule such as every other letter, wrote down one rule, found it fails, and wrote another. Which space is this?
options: A space of equations in letters and carries, like the algebra space
A space of meanings like word-meaning
A space whose elements are rules, like the cryptogram space
A space of letter shapes like typographical
optionExplain: No equations are formed.
Meaning is not the aim.
Right: constructing and testing rules.
Shapes are not examined.
questions.explain: Constructing and testing rules is the cryptogram space.
questions.teaches: The authors say that problem spaces whose elements are rules can be constructed, since several programs developed to find concepts defined by rules (Simon and Kotovsky, 1963; Evans, 1964; Johnson, 1964; D. Williams, 1969) supply the essential ingredients.

questions.q: A solver notes that an E looks like a 3 and an S like a 2. Which kind of resemblance is being used?
options: The sounds of the letters when they are said aloud
The alphabetical order
The meanings of the words
The visual shapes of letters and digits
optionExplain: No sound is used.
That is the cryptogram idea.
That is word-meaning.
Right: this is the typographical idea.
questions.explain: Shape resemblance is the typographical space. The card gives S8's examples.

questions.q: S8 said an E looks a lot like a ____.
questions.explain: S8 mentions E and 3.

questions.q: Which of these views of a letter did the authors list as typographical operators?
options: Position in the alphabet
Symmetry, as E with 3, and deletion, as H with 4
The carry out of a column
How frequently the letter occurs in ordinary English text
optionExplain: That is the cryptogram idea.
Right: the two examples in Figure 7.8.
That belongs to the augmented space.
Not in the text.
questions.explain: Symmetry and deletion are the typographical operators' examples.

questions.q: True or false: The authors consider the typographical approach the least easily put in the form of a problem space of the seven.
questions.explain: True: they say it is the least easily put in that form.

questions.q: A designer wants to test if shoppers associate product icons with initials by shape. What research aid do the authors suggest for a similar idea?
options: A table of word frequencies
A record of eye movements only, taken from subjects who are talking
Programs that discriminate letters by features, such as EPAM
A list of carry values
optionExplain: Not mentioned.
Eye movements come later in the chapter.
Right: they mention EPAM and feature work on letters.
Not relevant.
questions.explain: EPAM uses features to discriminate letters and could simulate similarity judgments.
questions.teaches: Eleanor Gibson's work (1966) tells something about the cues children use to discriminate letters, and a great deal more is known about features used in auditory discrimination of phonemes; this could help sketch search in a space of similarity criteria.

questions.q: Two people read the same news article but pick out different facts. What would you say about their view of the situation?
options: Their definitions of the situation differ, in what they know and extract
They disagree about the facts only, and otherwise see the situation in the same way
They are both wrong
There is no difference to study
optionExplain: Right: this is the authors' world-view idea.
A view of the situation is more than facts.
Nothing says so.
There is.
questions.explain: A definition of the situation fixes what a person extracts. The card states the authors' second purpose.

questions.q: The authors say the problem space comes close to being a ____ of the situation.
questions.explain: A definition of the situation, or world view.

questions.q: Two cooks have different kitchens and knowledge. According to the authors' idea, what does knowing a cook's space tell you?
options: Only how fast the cook works
What the cook knows, has available as tools and will extract from the situation
The cook's age
Which dish the cook will choose, from among all the dishes that the kitchen could make
optionExplain: Speed is not named.
Right: the authors' three things.
Not named.
Selection is not fixed by the space.
questions.explain: The space gives a precise identification of knowledge, tools and what will be extracted.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say every one of the spaces they surveyed is capable of supporting successful problem solving on the task.
questions.explain: They say several, especially the briefly noted ones, are not capable of supporting success, in the experimenters' belief.

questions.q: A manager sees two employees treat the same customer complaint as a billing issue and a trust issue. Following the authors, what has been learned?
options: The employees are guessing
The complaint has no real content
The employees have identical views of the situation, so they will extract exactly the same things
The employees work in different problem spaces, and so will extract different things
optionExplain: Nothing says so.
Content exists.
They differ.
Right: different definitions of the situation.
questions.explain: Different spaces mean different views of the situation.
questions.teaches: For the more briefly noted spaces it is not easy to demonstrate that a human's search will reside within the space while he is problem solving.

questions.q: A student working on a puzzle in one way is given a small hint. What might change?
options: The whole way the student represents the puzzle
Nothing at all, since a hint cannot affect the representation
Only the answer
The rules of the puzzle
optionExplain: Right: a hint could shift the space.
That has not been shown.
Representation may change too.
Rules stay.
questions.explain: A hint may re-represent a problem. The card states the authors' caution.

questions.q: The authors say the problem space is a useful construct for describing the ____ features of a subject's behavior in these tasks.
questions.explain: The claim is limited to the gross features of behavior.

questions.q: The authors say they have shown that the problem space is useful for what?
options: Predicting every move exactly
Proving that a subject cannot change his space once he has entered it
Describing the gross features of a subject's behavior in these tasks
Replacing the production system
optionExplain: Not claimed.
They say this is unshown.
Right: this is the claim.
The space does not do that.
questions.explain: The claim is limited to gross features.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say they have not presented evidence that a subject must keep working in the space he begins with.
questions.explain: True: they explicitly say they have not presented such evidence.

questions.q: A researcher wonders if telling subjects that R is odd would change the way they approach the puzzle. How do the authors classify this question?
options: As settled: hints never change the space
As settled: hints always change it
As open: their data do not decide it
As irrelevant to the theory
optionExplain: Not claimed.
Not claimed.
Right: they raise exactly this possibility.
It bears on stability.
questions.explain: The effect of hints on the space is an open question in the chapter.
questions.teaches: S8 spends his time deciding which space to enter, and once he moves into the augmented space all the alternative spaces disappear from view.

questions.q: A detective follows the habits: look where the clues are, use each new fact, seek missing facts, drop a disproved theory, check new facts against old. What is this a list of?
options: A problem-solving strategy beyond the choice of representation
A list of the tools that the detective owns and is able to use in the case
A set of the detective's mistakes
A record of how long the case took
optionExplain: Right: strategy sits on top of the space.
Tools would be the space.
These are good habits.
Time is not in the list.
questions.explain: Strategy is how the tools are used. The card lists S3's five habits.

questions.q: Put these S3 habits in the order the authors list them.
items: Attend to the columns relevant to the subgoal
Exploit new information
Obtain information that is lacking
Back off to the last undisconfirmed state
Check new information for consistency
questions.explain: The list runs from attention, to exploiting, to obtaining, to backing off, to checking.
questions.rule: Attend, exploit, obtain, back off, check.

questions.q: A solver reaches a contradiction and returns to the last state not shown wrong. Which of S3's habits is this?
options: Exploiting new information (P1)
Obtaining missing information when none is available to exploit at the moment (P2)
Checking consistency (P11)
Backing off to the last prior state of knowledge not disconfirmed (P12)
optionExplain: Exploiting moves forward.
No missing information is sought.
The check found the contradiction; the return is another habit.
Right: this is habit four.
questions.explain: Returning to the last undisconfirmed state is P12.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say there are limits to how far S3 followed the five habits, and that departures such as the failure to evoke TD on E equal to 0 account for much of the inadequacy.
questions.explain: True: they say there are limits to how far he followed them, and departures such as the failure to evoke TD on E equal to 0 account for much of the inadequacy.

questions.q: A student fixes a wrong proof by returning to the last line known to be sound, then checks every new line against the earlier ones. Which two S3 habits does the student show?
options: Attending to relevant columns and exploiting new information
Backing off and checking consistency
Obtaining missing information and attending to columns
Only exploiting new information
optionExplain: Different habits.
Right: habits four and five.
Different habits.
Both back off and check appear.
questions.explain: Return to the last sound state is P12; checking new lines against old is P11.
questions.teaches: Each of the five habits is described as only partly embodied in a production (for example, attending to relevant columns partly in FC), so the productions hold more than the list.

questions.q: Two engineers solve a bridge problem in the same way. One could say the method is forced by physics, or that it is a personal habit. What would help decide?
options: Seeing which parts of the method appear in every successful attempt
Asking which engineer is older
Counting the pages of calculation that each engineer produced in solving the problem
Waiting for a third method
optionExplain: Right: demands of the task show up in all successful attempts.
Age does not decide.
Length does not decide.
Waiting does not settle it.
questions.explain: What is demanded by the task shows in all successful solvers. The card poses this question.

questions.q: The strategy comparison is limited to subjects who use the same problem ____.
questions.explain: Only subjects in the augmented space are compared.

questions.q: Which are among the authors' three reasons for the aggregated technique? Select all that apply.
options: The production system does not always bring out the role of the task environment
Building a production system takes substantial effort
They wish to introduce as many tools as possible for dealing with data
Production systems cannot be applied to human protocols
optionExplain: Right: reason one.
Right: reason two.
Right: reason three.
They used one for S3.
questions.explain: The first three are given; the last contradicts Chapter 6.

questions.q: True or false: The authors want to tie their analysis to a single technique, since different tools only add confusion.
questions.explain: They say different tools serve different purposes and have different costs, so one should not be tied to any single way of analyzing data.

questions.q: A school leader reviewing 30 teachers decides on a short checklist rather than full lesson transcripts, which are too costly. Which authors' reason does this echo?
options: The aggregated technique removes the task environment's role from the analysis altogether
The aggregated technique needs no data
The aggregated technique is perfectly precise
The aggregated technique is easier to apply yet still captures much of what goes on
optionExplain: It aims to show the role better.
Data are still needed.
It is coarser.
Right: reason two.
questions.explain: The cost saving is the second reason.
questions.teaches: The authors will first describe the alternative data-analysis technique, then analyze S4, S5 and S8 with it, and also reanalyze S3 briefly so as to have a comparable base.

questions.q: A beginner and an expert both solve a chess endgame. Which of the expert's moves are likely to be obvious to the expert but not the beginner?
options: No moves at all, since all of the moves are obvious to everyone who plays
Moves that the expert sees readily because of the expert's level
Only moves that lose
Moves chosen at random
optionExplain: Obviousness varies.
Right: obviousness depends on the solver.
Not relevant.
Random choices are not obvious ones.
questions.explain: What is obvious depends on the solver. The card links this to episodes.

questions.q: An episode ends when the solver faces the problem of doing something that is not ____ to him.
questions.explain: Episode boundaries arise when the next step is not obvious.

questions.q: A route-planner takes the only open road without comment, then must choose between two similar routes and pauses. Where does an episode end?
options: At the start
At the end of the journey only, when the planner finally arrives
At the pause, where the next step is no longer obvious
At each road
optionExplain: Nothing ends the walk at the start.
The pause already marks a boundary.
Right: the boundary is the non-obvious choice.
Obvious moves lie within an episode.
questions.explain: Obvious moves are inside an episode; the boundary is the first non-obvious problem.

questions.q: True or false: Solution paths that omit a task invariant would require higher intelligence than the solvers in question have, such as inventing a new mathematics for cryptarithmetic.
questions.explain: This is how the authors describe aspects that are invariant below an upper limit of intelligence.

questions.q: A recipe step says whisk eggs until frothy. For a trained cook this is one smooth stretch of behavior; for a novice it needs checks. How does this fit the authors' notion?
options: The step is obvious to nobody, whatever their skill or training may have been in the kitchen
Skill is irrelevant to episodes
Only novices have episodes
The same step is obvious to one solver and a boundary of an episode for another
optionExplain: It is obvious to the trained cook.
Skill sets the limit.
Everyone has them.
Right: obviousness depends on intelligence or skill.
questions.explain: Episodes depend on a solver's level.
questions.teaches: The authors want the construct of intelligence to give operational meaning to two phrases: the subject will obviously do X in situation Y, and the subject must show behavior X if he is to solve problem Y in situation Z.

questions.q: A solver can either add two known digits to learn a result, or guess a value for a letter. Which is a move any rational solver would make at once?
options: Guessing a value, since it saves time compared with working anything out first
Adding the two known digits, since it gives knowledge that must be true
Neither, since both need a hint
Both equally
optionExplain: A guess is conjecture.
Right: validated knowledge.
Adding needs none.
They differ in what they validate.
questions.explain: A move that adds sure knowledge is obvious; a guess is not. The card states the rule.

questions.q: The authors assume that any immediate node that adds ____ knowledge is obvious.
questions.explain: Validated knowledge is knowledge true provided the starting knowledge is true.

questions.q: Which operator produces nodes that add new validated knowledge, per the authors?
options: Only AV, because it adds assignments to the knowledge the solver holds
Only GN, because it lists digits
PC, TD and GN, though they might not give new facts in fact
None of them
optionExplain: AV adds conjecture.
PC and TD also do.
Right: they create the possibility of validated information.
That would leave no obvious moves.
questions.explain: PC, TD and GN can yield validated information; AV only possibilities.

questions.q: True or false: A solver in the augmented space is expected to see and acquire information that lies only one step away in the problem space.
questions.explain: He will see one-step gains but not across a boundary of conjecture.

questions.q: A mechanic can test a fuse and read the result at once, or guess that the radio is faulty and replace it. Which does the rule call obvious?
options: Testing the fuse, since it gives validated knowledge in one step
Replacing the radio, since it saves time
Both, since both are quick
Neither, since a mechanic needs a manual before testing or replacing anything
optionExplain: Right: testing parallels PC, TD, GN.
That is a conjecture.
Only the first validates.
The first is obvious.
questions.explain: Tests that give sure knowledge are obvious; conjectural repairs are not.
questions.rule: Tests are obvious; guesses are not.
questions.teaches: The authors say the global goal gives a gradient with very little directive value in problematic situations (for example, whether R should be 7 or 9) but great value when obvious knowledge is available for the asking.

questions.q: In a maze, every time you reach a junction with one open path you follow it. What is the natural unit of analysis?
options: Each single step
The stretch between real choices, not each step along a forced path
The whole maze only, taken as one single unit for the purposes of analysis
The walls
optionExplain: Forced steps carry no information.
Right: forced steps are inside an episode.
Too coarse.
Walls are not behavior.
questions.explain: Forced steps group into stretches. The card calls such stretches episodes.

questions.q: The node of an episode that contains the most information is called its ____.
questions.explain: One node, the head, contains the most information.
questions.rule: The head holds the most information.

questions.q: A subject enters an episode at a node and keeps drawing obvious inferences until nothing more follows. Where does he end?
options: At the starting node
At a random node
At the solution of the whole puzzle, once nothing remains to be done
At the head of the episode, the node with the most information
optionExplain: He moves on.
The head is unique.
Only if the episode completes it.
Right: movement runs from entry to head.
questions.explain: Obvious inferences end at the head.

questions.q: True or false: Because movement within an episode is an obvious response to the task, the authors treat the fine detail inside an episode as the main object of analysis.
questions.explain: They say within-episode detail can be ignored and attention concentrated on moves from episode to episode.

questions.q: A teacher of two classes counts how many different ways pupils start new topics, not every step within a topic. Which authors' step does this echo?
options: Ignoring within-episode detail and studying moves from episode to episode
Counting every step within the episode
Averaging over all the episodes together without distinguishing between any of them
Ignoring the starting points
optionExplain: Right: the same coarse grain.
That is the detail the authors skip.
Episodes remain distinct.
Starting points are what the analysis tracks.
questions.explain: Coarse grain focuses on transitions between episodes.
questions.teaches: The authors note that one could define obvious of degree n, with the solver seeing across n conjectural steps, but as n increases this becomes an artificial measure, analogous to assuming chess players look ahead a fixed number of moves.

questions.q: A theory says every skilled typist will fix an obvious typo at once. What would count against it?
options: A beginner who leaves typos
A skilled typist who fixes typos
A skilled typist who regularly leaves obvious typos untouched
A typist who prefers another keyboard to the one in front of her
optionExplain: The theory covers skilled typists.
That fits.
Right: a counterexample in the stated group.
Irrelevant.
questions.explain: An empirical claim names its group and what would refute it. The card states the authors' claim.

questions.q: True or false: The authors treat the obviousness assumption as an empirical assertion that could fail.
questions.explain: If false, its failure would be evident from the protocols.

questions.q: S6 leaves column 2 untouched even though it holds 3 + 3 = R. How do the authors treat this?
options: It refutes the assumption for the augmented space
It shows S6 used parity
It fails the assumption, but S6 works in the basic space, so another criterion is needed
It is ignored as a typing error
optionExplain: S6 is not in that space.
No.
Right: S6 is outside the claim's scope.
The authors discuss it.
questions.explain: The assumption concerns the augmented space; S6 needs a different criterion.

questions.q: Which productions do the authors say all subjects' programs include under the assumption? Select all that apply.
options: P1, responding to new information
P11, checking consistency of new information
P12, backing down a chain of implications
P15, assigning when GN leaves one digit
optionExplain: Right: one of the four.
Right: another of the four.
Right: the third of those listed here.
The authors only propose this as a possible addition.
questions.explain: P1, P7, P11 and P12 are included in all programs; P15 is an extra the authors could add.

questions.q: A coach says all trained goalkeepers will dive for a shot on target. A trainee does not dive, but is on a smaller training pitch with other rules. What is the sound reading?
options: The trainee is outside the claim's scope, so a different criterion may apply
The claim is refuted, since a trained goalkeeper did not dive when the shot came
The claim is proved
The trainee is not a person
optionExplain: Right: like S6.
Scope excludes the trainee.
No.
Silly.
questions.explain: A claim for one condition is not refuted by a case outside it.
questions.teaches: The one inference not yet in the mini production system is deriving information from GN when the set is small, for example if R is odd and only one odd digit is unassigned, then R has to be that.

questions.q: Several clues in a crossword share letters. After finding one answer, which next step is likely?
options: Starting an unrelated clue elsewhere in the grid
Stopping after one answer
Guessing the longest clue
Moving to the other clues that share the new letters and continuing while they give more
optionExplain: A shared letter makes related clues available.
More follows.
Guesses are not the pattern.
Right: this is the episode pattern.
questions.explain: New information passes along shared variables. The card describes this as an episode.

questions.q: In Figure 7.11 the task has ____ columns, each an information source.
questions.explain: DONALD+GERALD=ROBERT has six columns.

questions.q: A subject learns the value of R and then applies it in every column where R appears, deriving more, until nothing new follows. This sequence is:
options: Several separate episodes
One episode
A conjecture
A repetition of an earlier step
optionExplain: Nothing breaks the run.
Right: a run of obvious inferences until none remain.
It rests on validated knowledge.
It generates new facts.
questions.explain: Keep inferring until no more follows is an episode.

questions.q: True or false: Starting an episode from a different state of knowledge can yield a different episode from the same network of columns.
questions.explain: Episodes are generated by assuming a state of knowledge and tracing inferences; different starts give different episodes.

questions.q: A mechanic's wiring diagram shows components as nodes and wires as links; a fault found in one node leads to checking the connected nodes. Which feature of the authors' account does this mirror?
options: Information found at one node moves attention to the linked nodes it affects
Every node is checked in a fixed order regardless of what is found at the others
Only the first node matters
The links carry no information
optionExplain: Right: same network logic.
Order depends on new information.
Links matter.
They carry the variables.
questions.explain: Nodes are information sources; variables link them.
questions.teaches: Many of the potential episode sequences are essentially the same, differing only by irrelevant extra information or by one having a further piece of relevant information, so only characteristic episode schemas need be considered.

questions.q: Four digits are above five (6, 7, 8, 9). How many letters can be given digits above five?
options: Any number of letters, since digits can repeat among letters
Exactly ten
At most five
At most four, one for each such digit
optionExplain: No two letters share a digit.
Only four digits exceed five.
Five is not above five.
Right: this is the subtler exclusion fact.
questions.explain: A subtler form of the exclusion rule. The card gives the authors' example.

questions.q: In the augmented space, inferences from the exclusion rule can be made only through TD and ____.
questions.explain: TD and GN carry them.

questions.q: Which description fits what GN takes into account?
options: Only the carries between columns
The range of the variable and the digits already assigned to other letters
Any inference about how many letters can exceed five, taken over all letters
The final check of the whole sum
optionExplain: That is PC's concern.
Right: the card's description.
That subtler inference is not part of GN.
Not GN.
questions.explain: GN uses range and exclusions by assignment.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say subtler exclusion inferences are ignored in defining episodes, but they would revise the definition if users of the augmented space routinely made them.
questions.explain: They state both the simplification and its condition.

questions.q: A seating chart rule says no two guests share a seat. A subtler consequence is that at most six guests can sit in the six front seats. Which authors' point does this parallel?
options: A fact stated directly in the puzzle that the solver is given to start with, as D is 5
A guess about names
A subtler consequence of a simple exclusion rule that a subject may not routinely draw
An error in the rules
optionExplain: It is derived.
Not a guess.
Right: parallels the five-digit example.
The rule is fine.
questions.explain: Counting consequences of exclusion are subtler than the exclusion itself.
questions.teaches: Chapter 5 explored a space that made such inferences by abstracting values to greater or less than five and even or odd.

questions.q: A manual lists a few standard repair routines, not every possible sequence of checks. What advantage does this have?
options: It guarantees that every repair carried out will be identical in every detail
It removes the need for any test
It makes the machine simpler
It captures the essential structure without listing every variation
optionExplain: Variations still exist.
Tests remain.
The machine is unchanged.
Right: schemas are characteristic types.
questions.explain: Schemas keep the essential structure. The card applies this to episodes.

questions.q: Put the inferences of schema 1-2-6 in the order the authors give them, starting from the assumption D exceeds 5.
items: T is even (column 1)
R is odd (column 2)
R exceeds 5 (column 6)
R is 7 or 9
G is below 5
questions.explain: The schema runs through columns 1, 2 and 6 and ends with G below 5.

questions.q: What extra knowledge does starting from D set to 5, instead of D above 5, add in column 1?
options: T is 5
T is 0, and not only even
R is 7
E is 9
optionExplain: T is the digit written in the bottom row, not the given one.
Right: 5 + 5 gives 10.
R is determined later.
E comes from column 5 with T known.
questions.explain: Doubling 5 gives 10, so T is 0 and the carry is 1.

questions.q: True or false: The authors ignore the information D set to 5 in drawing the schemas because they regard it as adventitious.
questions.explain: They want to exhibit the structure of the task without special given information.

questions.q: A detective notes that some case reasoning runs from clue A to clue B to clue C whatever the suspect. Which authors' notion fits?
options: An episode head
An exclusion rule, which forbids any two different letters from sharing the same digit
A schema, a characteristic chain labeled by the nodes it passes through
A conjecture
optionExplain: A head is the end node.
Not a chain.
Right: the same idea as 1-2-6.
The chain is validated.
questions.explain: Schemas are named by their nodes.
questions.teaches: In schema 2-6, the sequence obtains all remaining information about the letters except the final resolution of B, N and O, which still requires a small trial-and-error search.

questions.q: Every successful driver stops at a red light. What does seeing a driver do so reveal about that driver?
options: Little beyond having adapted to the demands of the road
A distinctive personal style of driving that identifies the driver
A wish to break rules
Poor eyesight
optionExplain: Right: the behavior is demanded, not personal.
Style is not shown.
The opposite.
No.
questions.explain: Task-demanded behavior reveals adaptivity, not individuality. The card states this for episodes.

questions.q: Once a subject enters an episode, he runs through to the end because the steps are ____.
questions.explain: Obvious steps are carried through.

questions.q: In every successful protocol the inference E equal to 9 appears, by inference or by assignment. What does this show?
options: A special insight of one subject that the others did not have in the study
A demand of the task, not a feature of the individual subject
An error common to all
A feature of the experimenter
optionExplain: All have it.
Right: all successful solvers must reach it.
It is correct.
It is a feature of the task.
questions.explain: Needed by all successful solvers means demanded by the task.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, what we learn about a subject from seeing a standard episode is how he differs from other subjects.
questions.explain: We learn only that he has attained a certain level of adaptivity to the environment.

questions.q: A coach sees two players both pass to the open teammate each time. What is the authors' inference?
options: Each has a unique passing style of his own, which the coach can now describe in some detail
Both lack skill
The teammate is fast
The behavior is demanded by the situation and shows both are adapted, not how they differ
optionExplain: Not shown.
Not implied.
Irrelevant.
Right: analogous to standard episodes.
questions.explain: Differences must be sought elsewhere than in standard episodes.
questions.teaches: If L is set to 8, the subject will conclude R is 7 and G is 1, also c3 is 1 so E is odd and therefore not 0, even if some of those relations had not been established previously.

questions.q: A film summary lists scenes with start times, titles and what triggers each. What does it lose compared with the full film?
options: Detail within each scene, but it keeps the structure of the story
The order in which the scenes of the film are shown to the audience
The whole plot
The start times
optionExplain: Right: same trade-off.
Order is kept.
The plot is kept.
Start times are in the summary.
questions.explain: A summary keeps structure and loses detail. The card describes the abstract.

questions.q: In the episode abstract each line represents a single ____.
questions.explain: One line per episode.

questions.q: In S3's abstract a new episode starts after the subject returns to an earlier base state of knowledge. What does this retreat usually signal?
options: The end of the protocol
A rehearsal inside an episode
The start of a new episode
An error by the experimenter
optionExplain: The protocol continues.
Rehearsals inside are subsumed.
Right: retreat to a base state marks a new one.
Not related.
questions.explain: Short backups end an advance; the retreat marks the next episode.

questions.q: Match each column of the episode abstract to its content.
pairs: Where the episode begins in the protocol
The new facts that instigate it
questions.explain: These four columns come before the description of the episode.

questions.q: A coach summarizes a match by listing each attacking phase, what triggered it and which standard move it matched. Which is the closest analogue?
options: A full ball-by-ball log of every play in the match
A table of final scores
An episode abstract with instigators and schemas
A list of players
optionExplain: That is the full graph.
Too coarse.
Right: same structure.
Not structure.
questions.explain: Listing phases with triggers and schema names mirrors the abstract.
questions.teaches: Rehearsals occurring within an episode are subsumed under the episode description, which aims only to show the logical structure of the information generated.

questions.q: A student solves a puzzle correctly at the start and end but struggles in the middle after assuming something false. What best explains the struggle?
options: The same reasoning run under a false premise
A different kind of thinking in the middle of the problem
A lack of motivation
Luck
optionExplain: Right: the middle follows the same schemas with an error.
The authors find the same sequences.
Not suggested.
Not a satisfying account.
questions.explain: Same reasoning, wrong premise. The card gives S3's case.

questions.q: S3's middle section differs from the task-determined sections by an added false premise, c3 equal to 0, and an omitted fact, T equal to ____.
questions.explain: He forgot T equals 0.

questions.q: Which episodes of S3 correspond almost literally to the principal schemas?
options: E5 to E15, in the middle of the protocol where he struggles
E1 to E19 equally
Only E10
E1 to E4 at the start, and E16 to E19 at the end
optionExplain: The middle is the error-laden portion.
The middle differs.
Not so limited.
Right: the task-determined portions.
questions.explain: The beginning and the end are task-determined.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say the experimenter's intervention is part of the portion where S3 follows the principal schemas almost literally.
questions.explain: The end, E16 to E19, after the experimenter's intervention, corresponds almost literally to them.

questions.q: A sailor's route is straightforward at the harbor and arrival, but wanders in the middle after trusting a wrong chart. How would the authors classify the wandering?
options: A different method entirely
The same navigation rules under a false premise, not a new method
Proof that the sailor is unskilled at reading any chart that he is given
A feature of the harbor
optionExplain: Not the authors' reading.
Right: like S3's middle.
Not implied.
No.
questions.explain: False premises produce long detours without new processes.
questions.teaches: The authors say the two task-determined portions contain substantially all the analysis necessary to solve the problem.

questions.q: A solver keeps meeting contradictions and changes several beliefs, but not the one that causes them. What is the likely reason?
options: The solver holds the root belief to be true and does not question it
The solver likes contradictions
The solver lacks arithmetic skill
The solver is distracted by noise from other people moving outside the room
optionExplain: Right: that is S3's situation.
No.
Arithmetic is fine.
Not suggested.
questions.explain: A belief held true is not abandoned. The card describes S3's c3 equal to 0.

questions.q: True or false: In S3's middle episodes, the contradictions all trace back to E even forcing A equal to 5, which conflicts with D equal to 5.
questions.explain: All involve, directly or indirectly, that conflict.

questions.q: In E12 S3 follows schema 1-2-6, then 5-3, and ends in a contradiction. What was he exploring?
options: The consequences of assuming R equal to 7
A check of earlier facts about R
A final check of the solution at the end of the protocol
The consequences of assuming R equal to 9
optionExplain: That was E5.
Those were E7 and E9.
That came at the end of the protocol.
Right: E12 is the last use of 1-2-6.
questions.explain: The four uses of schema 1-2-6 are E5 (R equal to 7), E7 and E9 (checks) and E12 (R equal to 9).

questions.q: Put the cause chain in order from false premise to contradiction.
items: S3 holds that c3 equals 0
Column 3 then makes E even
E even makes A equal to 5
A equal to 5 conflicts with D equal to 5
questions.explain: From the premise c3 equals 0 follows E even, then A equals 5, which collides with D equals 5.

questions.q: A company keeps adjusting its forecasts but not its assumption about next year's demand, which is the real cause of the misses. Which part of S3's story does this resemble?
options: Backing up to the first state at once and starting the problem anew
Changing E or R repeatedly while holding c3 equal to 0
Recalling T equal to 0
Using TD correctly
optionExplain: S3 does not.
Right: adjusting the symptoms.
S3 forgot it.
The TD miss is another matter.
questions.explain: The cause stays untouched while its symptoms are patched.
questions.teaches: In E6, E8, E11, E13 and E14 S3 follows schema 5-3, in the first of these until E even is derived and in the others until a contradiction is reached.

questions.q: A solver who leaves a tentative value on the page and later checks all entries from right to left will probably:
options: Never see any conflict
Delete every entry
Discover that the leftover value conflicts with another entry
Solve everything at once, with no further trouble from any earlier error
optionExplain: A full check should expose one.
Not necessary.
Right: a full check exposes it.
Not guaranteed.
questions.explain: A full check exposes leftover tentative values. The card describes S4's E5.

questions.q: S4 solved the problem in about ____ minutes.
questions.explain: He was the most efficient of the five, taking about ten minutes.

questions.q: S4 leaves L equal to 3 on the display and later works out E equal to 8 in column 3. Where does the contradiction surface?
options: At column 1
At column 6 only
He never finds it, however carefully he checks
At column 5, during his right-to-left check
optionExplain: Column 1 was settled first.
The check fails earlier.
He does.
Right: E equal to 8 fails there.
questions.explain: Column 5 requires E equal to 9.

questions.q: True or false: S4's error in assuming L equal to 3 came from ignoring a carry, the same slip S3 made.
questions.explain: Both left L equal to 3 on the display after ignoring the possible carry.

questions.q: An accountant realizes a total contradicts a later line, retraces her steps and fixes one earlier figure. Which part of S4's story is this?
options: Assigning R to 7 using the fact that E is 9, in episode four
Retracing the path by schema 5-3 to correct L to 8
Considering L equal to 3
Starting from column 6
optionExplain: That came earlier.
Right: retrace, then fix the earlier value.
That was the slip.
That was a different step.
questions.explain: Retracing the contradiction to its source corrected L.
questions.teaches: S4's attention was called to R by column 4 in E4, where he found R equal to 7 by schema 1-2-6 using E equal to 9 to eliminate R equal to 9.

questions.q: Two detectives make the same wrong assumption. One quickly corrects it. What most likely differs?
options: Their intelligence ranking on a general test given beforehand
Their ability to guess
What each remembers of the established facts
The weather
optionExplain: Not shown.
Not the factor.
Right: facts that cut alternatives make the error easy to isolate.
Irrelevant.
questions.explain: The card says memory of earlier results differs. This is the authors' account of S4.

questions.q: S4 recalled that T equals ____ when processing column 5, which led to E equal to 9 definitely.
questions.explain: T equal to 0 removes E equal to 0.

questions.q: Why did S3's alternatives make recovery harder?
options: Several open possibilities blurred where the contradiction came from
He had no memory at all of any of the facts that he had worked out earlier
The experimenter blocked him
He ran out of time
optionExplain: Right: many alternatives, no single suspect.
He remembered much.
Not the reason given.
Time is not the point.
questions.explain: Alternatives such as E equal to 0 or 9 and R equal to 7 or 9 made it hard to pinpoint the source.

questions.q: True or false: If S3 had remembered T equal to 0 when he processed column 5, the authors' account suggests his recovery would have been quicker.
questions.explain: S4's recovery was fast partly because he recalled it and reached E equal to 9 definitely.

questions.q: Two cooks both leave out salt. One quickly notices because she remembers which steps were done; the other has to re-check everything. How does this fit?
options: Cooks differ in basic processes
Small memory differences produce large differences in ease of recovery
The first cook must be more intelligent than the second cook in every respect of the task
The second cook did nothing wrong
optionExplain: The processes are shared.
Right: the authors' conclusion.
Not the claim.
Both erred.
questions.explain: Memory differences, not process differences, explain the gap.
questions.teaches: S3 always generated columns by FC and so never searched systematically from right to left until his final check, whereas S4 showed a systematic right-to-left search to check partial results.

questions.q: A solver finds one value that makes a column work and assumes it is the only one. Which logical slip is this?
options: Treating a necessary condition as if it were sufficient
Circular reasoning
Contradiction
Treating a sufficient condition as necessary
optionExplain: The reverse.
No circle.
No contradiction is involved.
Right: it works, but it need not be required.
questions.explain: One working value does not exclude others. The card names the slip.

questions.q: S5 confused necessary and ____ conditions when he decided that O equals 1.
questions.explain: The authors call it confusion between necessary and sufficient conditions.

questions.q: S5 tries O equal to 0, rejects it because T is 0, tries O equal to 1 and accepts it if E is 9. What does he fail to do?
