options: Explore other values for O that also satisfy column 5
Check that T equals 0
Process column 5 at all
Consider E at all
optionExplain: Right: he stops at the first workable value.
He used it.
He did.
He did.
questions.explain: He stops at the first value that works.
questions.rule: He stops at the first fit.

questions.q: True or false: S5's error in E3, deducing L equal to 3 from R equal to 7, caused him the same long trouble that O equal to 1 later did.
questions.explain: The L equal to 3 error turned out not to cause him later troubles; the O equal to 1 error did.

questions.q: A student finds that 4 times 3 equals 12 and decides 12 can only be made that way, then misses 2 times 6. Which authors' point does this mirror?
options: Failing to know the multiplication table well enough to see the other pair
Using too many alternatives
Accepting a sufficient case as necessary and never exploring the others
Forgetting a given fact
optionExplain: Skill is not the issue.
The opposite.
Right: the same slip as O equal to 1.
Not the issue.
questions.explain: The first fit is taken for the only fit.
questions.teaches: S5 processes column 5 from the top of the column to the bottom, trying values for O first and then for E, rejecting O equal to 0 on the strength of T equal to 0.

questions.q: A navigator keeps ending in the wrong place because an early waypoint is misrecorded. How is the fault likely found?
options: By switching to a different compass
By trying more routes
By carefully rechecking the early waypoint
By waiting
optionExplain: The compass is fine.
More routes keep failing.
Right: the source must be revisited.
Nothing changes.
questions.explain: Rechecking the source clears the error. The card shows S5 doing this at column 5.

questions.q: S5 finally found his error by reexamining column ____.
questions.explain: Column 5 was reexamined at E19 and E20.

questions.q: In E7 S5 chose L correctly but reached a contradiction. Why?
options: Because 1 had already been given to O, leaving only 2 for G in column 6
Because L was wrong
Because column 5 failed
Because the experimenter intervened and told him that the earlier step was wrong
optionExplain: Right: the false belief blocked G equal to 1.
L was right in E7.
E equal to 9 was correct.
Not described.
questions.explain: The wrong O blocked the right G.
questions.rule: A right step blocked by a wrong belief.

questions.q: True or false: S5 tried L as 6, 7 and 8 because he had inferred that L must exceed 5.
questions.explain: L above 5 followed from E equal to 9 and column 3.

questions.q: A technician replaces three parts in turn, each time the fault persists because the real cause lies upstream. Which authors' idea does this match?
options: A failure of arithmetic
A random fault
A problem with the display on which the digits were written down for him
A wrong earlier belief makes correct later steps appear to fail
optionExplain: Arithmetic was correct.
The fault is systematic.
Not the cause.
Right: like S5's G equal to 1 blocked by O equal to 1.
questions.explain: A wrong premise causes right steps to fail.
questions.rule: Right steps fail under a wrong premise.
questions.teaches: After the false inference O equal to 1, S5 reaches a sequence of apparent contradictions from E6 to E21, and he repeats the L-trial sequence twice, in E6 to E7 and again in E10 to E11.

questions.q: A detective marks notes as: given by the police, deduced from police facts, deduced by ruling out alternatives, deduced from a hunch, or a hunch. What is this?
options: A list of suspects, ordered by how likely the detective thinks each one is
A scheme that grades information by how it was obtained
A timetable
A random order
optionExplain: Not suspects.
Right: S5's idea.
No times.
It is graded.
questions.explain: Information graded by origin. The card gives S5's five tags.

questions.q: Match each S5 tag to its meaning.
pairs: An assignment of a digit to a letter
A fact given on the display or by the experimenter
questions.explain: These four tags, with df, make up S5's scheme.

questions.q: T equal to 0 is derived at once from D equal to 5. Which tag does it get?
options: df, derived from a fact
f, a fact
a, an assignment
de, by exhaustion
optionExplain: Right: derived from the fact D equal to 5.
A fact must be given directly.
It is not an assignment.
No exhaustion is used.
questions.explain: However immediately, things derived from facts are df.

questions.q: True or false: S5 treats an expression reached through many steps of inference as less well established than one reached in a single step.
questions.explain: The authors say S5 does not distinguish gradations within a category.

questions.q: A reporter classifies claims as: stated on the record, deduced from record claims, deduced from deduced claims by ruling out alternatives. Which feature from S5's scheme is closest to the hereditary rule?
options: Each claim must be re-graded as more steps are added to the chain of reasoning
Only record claims count
All claims are equal
A claim deduced from a record-derived claim keeps the record-derived class
optionExplain: S5 does not grade by steps.
Others are used.
They are graded.
Right: derived from df is df.
questions.explain: The classes are hereditary.
questions.teaches: An expression belongs to class a only if it has the form letter arrow digit, and it is a fact only if given directly on the display or by the experimenter, for example D equal to 5.

questions.q: Your notes say two things that conflict: one is a guess, the other was derived from solid facts. Which do you drop?
options: The solid derivation
The guess
Both
Neither, until a third arrives
optionExplain: Better grounded.
Right: a rule grading by grounding says so.
Only one must go.
A conflict forces a choice.
questions.explain: Grounding decides the conflict. The card shows S5's rule.

questions.q: When two conflicting expressions are in the same category, S5 rejects the ____ one.
questions.explain: The rule for equals: reject the more recent.

questions.q: S5 holds R equal to 9 derived by exhaustion (de) and E equal to 9 derived from column 5 (df), and they conflict. By his rule, which is rejected?
options: R equal to 9, the de expression, since it came later than E equal to 9
Neither
E equal to 9, the df expression, since df loses to de
The older one
optionExplain: de ranks above df and is kept.
A conflict needs resolving.
Right: df is higher in the order than de.
Order is by category first.
questions.explain: Knowledge derived from facts loses to knowledge derived by exhaustion.

questions.q: True or false: Under S5's rule, an assignment (a) conflicting with an expression derived from a fact (df) will usually be rejected.
questions.explain: Assignments yield to anything.

questions.q: A manager's policy: drop a rumor before a firsthand report, drop a firsthand report before a verified document, and drop the newer of two equal items. Which S5 feature matches the last clause?
options: Rejecting assignments first
Keeping assignments longest
Averaging the items
Rejecting the more recent within one category
optionExplain: That is the first clause.
The reverse.
No averaging.
Right: same-category tie-break.
questions.explain: A tie-break for equals.
questions.teaches: The authors report 58 conflicts in S5's protocol, of which 54 were between different categories and 4 within a single category.

questions.q: A chess player usually follows a rule but breaks it in one critical game and wins. How should an analyst read the broken rule?
options: As evidence that the rule never existed in his program in the first place
As possibly a higher-level rule at work, not only noise
As measurement error only
As cheating
optionExplain: It fits most moves.
Right: the authors' reading.
Not necessarily.
No.
questions.explain: Exceptions may reflect higher rules. The card gives the authors' view of S5.

questions.q: Six of the seven exceptions in S5's protocol were almost immediately ____.
questions.explain: He quickly took them back.

questions.q: At B458 and B460, S5 tries L set to 0, dropping T equal to 0 and questioning D equal to 5. How do the authors classify this?
options: A confirmation of the rule
A random slip
An exploration of extreme possibilities
A guess of the experimenter
optionExplain: It breaks the rule.
It is purposeful.
Right: he tests the limits.
Not so.
questions.explain: S5 was testing extremes.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say decision rules like S5's are part of the problem solver's structure and cannot be revised.
questions.explain: They say such rules are part of his program and always open to revision.

questions.q: A teacher notices a pupil who rechecks unfamiliar items first but once skips a familiar item under time pressure, which proves right. How should this skip be read?
options: Possibly a higher rule overriding the usual one, not mere noise
As proof that the pupil does not follow any rules when checking items
As a measurement mistake
As unrelated to rules
optionExplain: Right: like B421.
Most choices follow.
Not necessarily.
It relates to them.
questions.explain: Overruling a decision rule may be needed to succeed.
questions.teaches: In one exception S5 reached a complete assignment ending with G equal to 2, inferred from column 6 that c6 was 0, then found c6 equal to 1 already followed from column 5 and E equal to 9.

questions.q: Two drivers take different routes to the same town because each followed a different wrong signpost. What does the difference show?
options: Different skills in driving
Different errors on the same way of driving, not necessarily different drivers
Different towns
Different maps
optionExplain: The skills may be the same.
Right: this is the authors' reading of S3 and S5.
Same town.
Not suggested.
questions.explain: Different errors can create different paths from one program. The card says so.

questions.q: Both S3 and S5 are preoccupied with schemas 2-6-5 and ____.
questions.explain: Both share these two.

questions.q: S5, like S3, finds it hard to pinpoint the source of his contradictions. What do the authors give as the reason?
options: He has no memory
He does not use columns
He avoids checking
At each moment he faces several alternatives, and the contradiction comes at the end of a long, fallible chain
optionExplain: He remembers facts.
He does.
He checks.
Right: that is the stated reason.
questions.explain: Several alternatives and a long chain hide the source.

questions.q: True or false: Once S5 is convinced that every alternative reaches a genuine contradiction, the authors say he identifies it fairly rapidly.
questions.explain: Until then he keeps exploring; afterwards he finds the cause quickly.

questions.q: Two students both retrace their work after errors; one retraces in an hour, the other in minutes, because the first had several unfinished lines of thought. Which authors' point is this?
options: Difficulty localizing an error comes from the number of live alternatives
Fast students use different processes from the slow students, whatever the errors
Errors are unrelated to alternatives
Only the fast student is correct
optionExplain: Right: matches S3 and S5.
The processes are the same.
They relate.
Not the point.
questions.explain: Live alternatives slow localization.
questions.teaches: S5, like S3, several times (E15, E18), when in difficulties, rehearses the facts he has previously derived.

questions.q: A student faced with a long addition puzzle decides to work as in a real sum, starting from the rightmost column and trying values in order. What kind of search is this?
options: A random guess
A left-to-right inference starting from the leftmost column of the display
A systematic right-to-left trial of admissible values
An algebraic solution
optionExplain: It is systematic.
The direction is right to left.
Right: S8's style.
No equations are formed.
questions.explain: Right-to-left systematic trial. The card describes S8.

questions.q: S8 tried values for A in column 3 beginning with ____ and working upward.
questions.explain: He started at 1.

questions.q: Apart from the order of trial, which single fact did S8 use to make his search more selective?
options: E is 9
T is 0
R is 7 or 9
G is below 5
optionExplain: He did not have it yet.
He did know this, but R is the one the card names.
Right: the only fact he used.
Not the one named.
questions.explain: R equal to 7 or 9 was the one fact.

questions.q: True or false: S8's right-to-left search is described by the authors as a strategy the other subjects lacked entirely.
questions.explain: All four had both the column-selection and right-to-left strategies; they differed in readiness to use them.

questions.q: A technician checks each of ten switches in order from the left until the lights work, knowing only that the fault is in an odd-numbered switch. Which part of S8's strategy is this like?
options: Systematic trial in a fixed order, with one restricting fact
Reasoning from column interactions to find some values directly
Random trial
Backing up to start
optionExplain: Right: same structure.
That is the other strategy.
Not random.
Not relevant.
questions.explain: Fixed order trial limited by a single fact.
questions.teaches: S8 had considerable difficulty during the systematic search phase in keeping in memory just where he was and what alternatives he had tried.

questions.q: A solver tries many values in order, then discovers one crucial fact and finishes quickly by reasoning. What caused the switch?
options: Fatigue
Boredom
The experimenter's hint about which column to look at next
The new fact made reasoning from the constraints possible
optionExplain: No.
No.
Not described.
Right: S8's switch.
questions.explain: A crucial fact opens reasoning. The card shows S8's E22.

questions.q: S8 changed strategy when he deduced that E is ____.
questions.explain: E equal to 9 at E22.

questions.q: Which episodes contain the essential parts of S8's reasoning?
options: E5 and E6
E1 and E2, and E22 and E23
E10 to E17
E25 only
optionExplain: These are early in the right-to-left systematic search; the book names other episodes as essential.
Right: the essential parts are E1-E2 (schema 1-6-2) and E22-E23 (schema 5-3-2).
These are the exploration of the R = 9 hypothesis within the systematic search, not the essential reasoning.
E25 is not among the episodes the book names as essential.
questions.explain: The authors say that once S8 deduces E = 9 at E22 he abandons right-to-left search; the essential parts are E1-E2 and E22-E23.

questions.q: True or false: After E equal to 9, S8's reasoning resembles the essential reasoning in the three protocols analyzed earlier in the chapter.
questions.explain: His essential parts are almost the same as theirs.

questions.q: A cook tries all combinations of spices in order, then reads on a label that one spice is key and finishes the dish by reasoning. Which authors' point matches?
options: A crucial inference lets the solver abandon brute force for reasoning
Brute force always ends in failure for puzzles of this kind and this size
Reasoning never helps
The cook must restart
optionExplain: Right: like E22.
Not claimed.
It does here.
Not needed.
questions.explain: Insight replaces enumeration.
questions.teaches: S8's essential reasoning is almost the same as that in the three protocols analyzed before it: schema 1-6-2 at E1 and E2, and schema 5-3-2 at E22 and E23.

questions.q: A student methodically works in one direction and does not look at the one clue that would unlock the puzzle. What is the likely problem?
options: A mistake in arithmetic
Too many clues
Poor memory only
The method, not an error
optionExplain: No error is described.
The reverse.
The method itself.
Right: the method avoids the key clue.
questions.explain: A method can hide a key clue. The card shows S8.

questions.q: S8 made the usual error that R equal to 7 implies L equal to 3 in E2, and corrected it in E____.
questions.explain: Corrected in E8, so it did no harm.

questions.q: When S8 did reach column 5 in his right-to-left phase, how did he arrive?
options: With no value for E
With a value for E assigned earlier from column 3
With the carry unknown
With the answer already found by some other means earlier
optionExplain: He had one.
Right: that value stayed unquestioned.
Not the point.
No.
questions.explain: The earlier E value masked the property of column 5.

questions.q: True or false: The authors explain why S8 processed column 5 differently on the third occasion.
questions.explain: They say there is no convincing evidence in the protocol as to why.

questions.q: A proofreader finds the same unusual sentence on a third pass and finally studies it, though the first two passes skipped it. What do the authors say about such a change?
options: The change was caused by a hint
It proves the proofreader is intelligent
The records often do not tell us why the change came when it did
It shows the sentence is wrong
optionExplain: Not shown.
No.
Right: S8's third visit is unexplained.
No.
questions.explain: The cause of the change is not in the protocol.
questions.teaches: S8's one important piece of unsystematic behavior occurred when, on his third arrival at column 5, he took seriously its special property that O plus E equals O.

questions.q: A detective has three suspects and checks the one with the fewest possible alibis first. What else decides the order among the rest?
options: The detective's favorite suspect among the three, whatever the evidence
A coin toss
The longest alibi
A convention such as the natural order of the cases
optionExplain: Not S8's rule.
Not S8's rule.
Not S8's rule.
Right: S8 used digit order.
questions.explain: Ordering cases by simple conventions. The card gives S8's.

questions.q: Put S8's exploration in the order he took the cases.
items: R equal to 9 with L equal to 4
R equal to 7 with L equal to 3
R equal to 7 with L equal to 8
questions.explain: He explored R equal to 9 first, then L equal to 3, and L equal to 8 last.

questions.q: Why did S8 explore R equal to 9 before R equal to 7?
options: R equal to 9 is larger
R equal to 9 allowed only one value for L, so it was a smaller case
R equal to 7 had been rejected
The experimenter suggested it to him during the first trials of the protocol
optionExplain: Size of R was not the reason.
Right: fewer alternatives.
It had not.
Not described.
questions.explain: Fewer alternatives first.

questions.q: True or false: Had S8 explored L equal to 8 before L equal to 3, he would have reached the solution sooner.
questions.explain: The true case was L equal to 8, which he reached last.

questions.q: A locksmith tries the three possible lock types, starting with the one with the fewest key variants, then the lowest-numbered. The right type is last. What do the authors' remarks imply?
options: The locksmith lacked reasoning about the three lock types
The locksmith made an error
The search was reasonable but unlucky in order
The order cannot affect time
optionExplain: He reasoned.
No error.
Right: S8's situation.
It does.
questions.explain: A reasonable ordering can still be unlucky.
questions.teaches: Even if S8 had not arrived at E equal to 9 in E22, he would sooner or later have arrived at the correct answer, barring a mistake along the way.

questions.q: Four students solve the same puzzle by different routes. What would let you say they share one method?
options: The same component skills and strategies, used with different priorities
The same steps taken in the same order and at the same moments in each protocol
The same speed
The same mistakes
optionExplain: Right: this is the authors' claim.
Paths differ.
Speeds differ.
Mistakes differ.
questions.explain: Shared parts, different priorities. The card states the authors' claim.

questions.q: Which are shared by all four subjects, according to the authors? Select all that apply.
options: The necessary arithmetic knowledge
Both column-selection and right-to-left strategies
Recognition of the central role of E equal to 9
Identical protocols
optionExplain: Right.
Right.
Right.
The courses were noticeably different.
questions.explain: The first three are stated; the protocols differed.

questions.q: The authors say the subjects remembered which of two things better?
options: The path better than the properties of the letters that were derived along it
Derived properties of letters, better than the path used to derive them
Neither
Both equally well
optionExplain: The reverse.
Right: the stated pattern.
They remembered properties.
They differ.
questions.explain: Properties were retained better than paths.

questions.q: True or false: All four subjects preferred making arbitrary conditional assignments to solving for the unknowns one by one.
questions.explain: They preferred column selection, which solves for unknowns one by one, as with simultaneous equations.

questions.q: A team can recall the facts it established but not how it got them. What difficulty does the authors' finding predict?
options: Trouble adding numbers
No trouble at all
An inability to form hypotheses about what each letter is
Trouble localizing the source of a contradiction
optionExplain: Not the issue.
Memory limits matter.
Not implied.
Right: without the path, errors are hard to trace.
questions.explain: Without the path the cause of a contradiction is hard to find.
questions.teaches: All four subjects eventually recognized the central importance of the inference E equal to 9, whichever route they took to reach it.

questions.q: Four chefs bake the same cake with different timings because each switched steps or slipped on one. What would you say?
options: They share one recipe but differ in priorities and slips
They have four quite different recipes that happen to look alike in the result
None can bake
The oven differs
optionExplain: Right: the authors' account.
Not necessarily.
No.
Not relevant.
questions.explain: Same program, different priorities and slips. The card gives this for the subjects.

questions.q: Differences in paths come from differential priorities for the strategies and from differences in particular ____ of reasoning or memory.
questions.explain: Priorities and errors.

questions.q: A subject prefers right-to-left search while another prefers column selection. Which source of difference is this?
options: Particular errors of memory made by the subject
Different problem spaces
Differential priorities for the strategies
A different task
optionExplain: Not an error.
Same space.
Right: source one.
Same task.
questions.explain: Priority among strategies.

questions.q: True or false: The authors claim to understand well the causes of the errors that shaped the subjects' paths.
questions.explain: They have only rudimentary indications of the causes of the errors.

questions.q: A school finds that students' essays differ in structure, but all show the same grammar and word choices. Following the authors, what is a sound inference?
options: The students must have different grammar
The essays cannot be compared
Differences in structure may come from priorities and slips, not from different underlying skills
The teacher is at fault
optionExplain: They do not.
They can.
Right: the authors' lesson.
Not implied.
questions.explain: Surface differences need not mean different programs.
questions.teaches: A common program can generate protocols resembling any of the four subjects' by minor variations in priority and in the breadth of inferences drawn.

questions.q: Take a recipe and change one rule: either skip tasting until the end, or taste when two options remain. What happens to different cooks' routines?
options: Different routines can arise from one recipe
The routines must all be identical
The recipe stops working
The cooks swap kitchens
optionExplain: Right: the authors' point.
They differ.
No.
No.
questions.explain: One recipe, many routines. The card shows this for one program.

questions.q: Match each simulated version to the subject it resembles.
pairs: Beta: assign when two alternatives remain
Gamma: beta with an ignored carry
Delta: no inference that E is 9
questions.explain: These are the resemblances the authors note.

questions.q: Which change turns version beta into version gamma?
options: Removing the inference that E is 9 and allowing assignment to any letter at all in the display
Adding trial assignments to any letter
Making no trial assignments
Ignoring a possible carry into column 3 and discarding information from failed branches
optionExplain: That gives delta.
That relates to delta.
That is alpha.
Right: the two degradations.
questions.explain: Gamma is beta with a degraded reasoning.

questions.q: True or false: Version delta resembles S8, but S8 began with R set to 9 and L equal to 4, whereas delta begins with R set to 7 and L equal to 3.
questions.explain: The authors note this difference and also that S8 finally discovered E equal to 9.

questions.q: A simulator of drivers has a rule for lane changes. Switching one rule makes it mimic cautious drivers; degrading its perception makes it mimic confused drivers. What does this show in the authors' terms?
options: Each driver needs a separate program
Individual differences can come from small parameter changes in one program
Simulations cannot show differences
Rules never matter
optionExplain: Opposite.
Right: same logic.
They do.
They do.
questions.explain: Small parameter changes produce a range of behavior.
questions.teaches: In the simulation program, assignments if any are always made for letters in next-column, and when no specific instigator for a new episode exists the program scans right to left to find next-column.

questions.q: Two hikers set out from the same point with boots differing by a few millimetres in tread and end the day in different valleys. What does this show?
options: In a branching terrain small differences can produce very different journeys
The hikers have different goals
One hiker is lost
The boots are the cause of all the difference between the two journeys, and of nothing else
optionExplain: Right: the lesson.
Not shown.
Not shown.
Small causes can start large divergence.
questions.explain: Small starting differences, large divergence. The card states the lesson.

questions.q: In large ____ spaces, small causes can bring about great divergences between search paths.
questions.explain: The lesson is about large combinatorial spaces.

questions.q: Comparing two chess players' move sequences directly shows no overlap. What do the authors warn?
options: The players must have different rules
The sequences are meaningless
One player must have cheated
Direct comparison may exaggerate the underlying differences between their programs
optionExplain: Not implied.
Not implied.
Not implied.
Right: their warning.
questions.explain: Direct comparison of sequences can exaggerate differences.
questions.rule: Do not read paths as programs.

questions.q: True or false: The authors suggest finding commonalities by inducing a family of programs that can vary minorly to yield different paths.
questions.explain: That is their stated route to see commonalities.

questions.q: A company compares two sales reps by their call logs, which look completely different. What is the authors' advice?
options: Conclude that the reps work differently
Look for a common process that small variations could turn into either log
Throw away the logs
Compare only the first call
optionExplain: Premature.
Right: model a family, not each log.
No.
No.
questions.explain: Seek the family of programs that fits both.
questions.teaches: The authors use a simple version of such a program that follows FC whenever any information is produced, so that an episode expands to its maximum limit.

questions.q: A researcher models mechanisms inside one chef's omelet-making and wants to check the model. Which test is most informative?
options: The same omelet again with the same chef in the same kitchen
Asking the chef for an opinion
A different dish that should use the same mechanisms
Counting eggs
optionExplain: Weak for generalization.
Not behavior.
Right: the new-task check.
Irrelevant.
questions.explain: A new task that should use the same mechanisms is a real test. The card says so.

questions.q: S4 solved CROSS+ROADS after a ____-minute break following DONALD+GERALD.
questions.explain: A ten-minute break.

questions.q: Why do the authors say a single task is not as severe a limit as it seems?
options: Because the task is easy
Because many cryptarithmetic tasks are in fact the same task, with different letters standing in for the digits
Because they ran many subjects
They analyze the specific mechanisms behind behavior, not treat the task as an unanalyzed variable
optionExplain: Not their reason.
Not stated.
Few subjects.
Right: mechanism-based analysis.
questions.explain: A mechanism analysis should hold on any cryptarithmetic task.

questions.q: True or false: The authors list intelligence testing and studies of functional fixity as examples of research that treats the task as an unanalyzed variable.
questions.explain: They name these, with the Einstellung effect.

questions.q: A bank tests a fraud model built on a mechanism analysis by running it on a different product line. Which authors' step is this?
options: Replacing the model
Checking that the same mechanisms show up on a new task
Averaging scores
Dropping the old product line and starting again with a new model
optionExplain: Not the step.
Right: the second-task check.
Not the step.
Not the step.
questions.explain: Test on a new task for the same mechanisms.
questions.teaches: S2's main interest is his eye-movement data, which make it possible to ask whether the details of the information processing model are consistent with a second kind of independent evidence.

questions.q: A puzzle starts easily but after two steps has no obvious next inference. What must the solver do?
options: Wait for a hint
Give up
Make a guess and follow its consequences
Repeat the first steps until something new turns up
optionExplain: Not described.
S4 solved it.
Right: conjecture and test.
Nothing new arises.
questions.explain: A stalled puzzle forces a conjecture. The card describes CROSS+ROADS.

questions.q: In CROSS+ROADS, S4 was given R set to 6 as a start, as he had been given D set to ____ in the earlier task.
questions.explain: The hint parallels D set to 5.

questions.q: What is unusual about the three left-hand columns of CROSS+ROADS?
options: They share letters R, O and A, yet give no general information on their own
They contain no letters
They fix every digit directly
They are identical in form to columns 1 and 2 and so yield the same kind of information
optionExplain: Right: coupled but uninformative.
They do.
They do not.
They differ.
questions.explain: Coupled by three repeated letters, they yield nothing general.

questions.q: True or false: In DONALD+GERALD a key step (E equal to 9) unlocks the puzzle, whereas CROSS+ROADS has no such key step.
questions.explain: This is why the authors call the second task somewhat more difficult.

questions.q: A crossword has two easy corners and a hard middle where no clue lets you start. What does this correspond to?
options: A key step that opens everything
A stall after the easy inferences, calling for trial
A puzzle with no solution
A puzzle with no easy start at all, which is hard from the first step
optionExplain: That is the opposite.
Right: like CROSS+ROADS.
Not implied.
It has an easy start.
questions.explain: Easy start, hard middle.
questions.teaches: Even though the left-hand three columns are coupled by three letters that occur more than once, the authors find no way to extract general information from them.

questions.q: A solver can add all column equations of a puzzle together and eliminate the unknown digits. What kind of reasoning is that?
options: Random guessing
Copying a known answer
Checking a final sum by adding the columns of the finished display one at a time
Algebraic reasoning across columns, beyond column-by-column processing
optionExplain: It is deductive.
No answer is copied.
It derives constraints, not checks.
Right: more than local inference.
questions.explain: Combining equations goes beyond local column steps. The card gives the authors' example.

questions.q: From the combined equations the authors show that the combination of carries c5 equal to 0 and c4 equal to ____ is not possible.
questions.explain: c5 = 0 with c4 = 1 is ruled out.

questions.q: Digits cannot exceed 9. If the carry factor were minus 1, the equation would need G plus 21 equal to C plus N. Why is this impossible?
options: Because C plus N is at most 17, less than 21
Because G is always zero
Because carries are negative
Because C equals N
optionExplain: Right: two digits cannot reach 21.
G is not zero.
The factor combines carries; it is not a carry.
Equal letters would not matter.
questions.explain: Two different digits sum to at most 17, so the right side cannot reach 21.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say that the reasoning leading to c5 at least c4 can be carried out by a solver in the augmented space.
questions.explain: They say it is a good example of reasoning that is not possible for someone working in the augmented space.

questions.q: A planner proves that two schedule conflicts cannot both occur by combining three booking equations. A colleague who can only check one booking at a time cannot reproduce it. Which authors' idea is this?
options: Valid reasoning is always local
Reasoning outside a space is invalid, so it cannot be used by anyone solving the puzzle at all
Some valid reasoning lies outside a space whose operators work on one column at a time
The colleague is mistaken
optionExplain: Not so.
It is valid.
Right: like the carry argument.
Not implied.
questions.explain: A space limits what reasoning is available.
questions.teaches: The same conclusion follows more generally from reasoning that R exceeds A, so O plus R exceeds O plus A, hence c4 equal to 1 implies c5 equal to 1.

questions.q: A solver finds that two letters must take the digits 2 and 3 but cannot say which letter takes which. What is this reasoning like?
options: An assignment of one definite digit to one letter in the display
Checking a total
Using an unordered set of digits for two letters
Backing up
optionExplain: Neither letter is fixed.
No total is checked.
Right: the extension.
No backup.
questions.explain: A pair of digits without order is an unordered set. The card names this as S4's extension.

questions.q: S4 derived D equal to ____ almost immediately from R set to 6.
questions.explain: D equals 1 at once.

questions.q: S4's inference that A and O take 2 or 3 combines which two operators?
options: GN and PC
AV and TD
TD and BU
MD and EX
optionExplain: Right: generate available digits and process the column.
Not the combination.
No backup operator.
Those are S6's.
questions.explain: GN supplies the available digits; PC processes the column.

questions.q: True or false: S4's use of unordered sets of digits on CROSS+ROADS is treated by the authors as the sign that he moved to a more sophisticated space than the augmented one.
questions.explain: They call it an additional augmentation but conclude his space is the same one he used on DONALD+GERALD, apart from this.

questions.q: A person lists the two remaining free seats as the pair {A, B} without deciding who sits where. Which part of S4's reasoning is this like?
options: Assigning one definite value to one letter in the display
Testing a digit for reuse
Backing up a step
Treating a pair of digits as an unordered set
optionExplain: No one is assigned.
No test.
No backup.
Right: the same idea.
questions.explain: Order is left open.
questions.teaches: In B58 to B61 S4 reasons that G must equal A plus 4 and the numbers remaining are 2, 3, 4, 5 and 7, so only 3 and 7 fit, treating the two letters without distinguishing their order.

questions.q: A solver tries a pair of values, finds a contradiction at once and moves on. Compared to a solver who makes an error and holds it for long, what is the difference in cost?
options: Both cost the same
Short contradictions cost little; held errors cost much
Held errors cost nothing
Contradictions are always a disaster that wastes the whole attempt
optionExplain: Not so.
Right: S4's contrast with S3 and S5.
They cost much.
Not so.
questions.explain: Quick contradictions are cheap. The card describes S4's case.

questions.q: On CROSS+ROADS about six and a half of S4's ____ episodes arose from errors.
questions.explain: Six and a half out of 21.

questions.q: S4 assigns G and O when S is 8 and the episode ends at once in a contradiction. What does this show about the task?
options: It needs a double assignment before real consequences flow
It has a key step that unlocks it, as DONALD+GERALD did with E equal to 9
It can be solved by parity alone
It cannot be solved
optionExplain: Right: single assignments yield little.
No key step exists.
Not so.
S4 solved it.
questions.explain: The task requires at least a double assignment before consequences.

questions.q: True or false: After finding a contradiction, S4 identified which earlier inference had been wrong and corrected it.
questions.explain: His recovery never involved the discovery that he had made an error, only a set of incompatible assignments.

questions.q: A student on a hard puzzle tries pairs of values, sees clashes at once and moves on without understanding why. Which authors' point is this?
options: Diagnosis of errors is necessary before any recovery can take place at all
The student is wasting time
The puzzle has no key step
Fast recovery from clashes can work without diagnosing errors
optionExplain: S4 shows it is not.
S4 solved it this way.
That is a separate matter.
Right: like S4.
questions.explain: Recovery from incompatibility does not need error diagnosis.
questions.teaches: S4 did not see the more subtle inference that c4 equal to 1 implies c5 equal to 1, which the task's structure would have allowed.

questions.q: A solver after finishing the easy columns turns next to the column whose incoming carry is known. Why is this sensible?
options: It is the largest column in the whole display, so it holds most information
The known carry makes that column's inference possible
It has the fewest letters
It is the most recent
optionExplain: Size is not the reason.
Right: S4's likely reason.
Not the reason.
Not the reason.
questions.explain: A known carry makes inference possible. The card gives this as the authors' conjecture.

questions.q: S4 assigned S as 8 before assigning it as ____, with no cue in the protocol.
questions.explain: He tried 8 first.

questions.q: After columns 1 and 2, S4 turned to column 3. What is the authors' conjecture?
options: He chose the column with the fewest unknown letters in it, as he had in the earlier task
The experimenter told him to
He worked right to left, and knew the carry into column 3 but not into 4 or 5
He picked it at random
optionExplain: Not the stated reason.
Not described.
Right: the stated conjecture.
A reason is offered.
questions.explain: A known carry c3 equal to 1 supports column 3.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say the selection of S as 8 before S as 3 can be explained by a cue in the protocol.
questions.explain: They say there is no cue in the protocol as to why this occurs.

questions.q: A shopper enters the first aisle where the price of one item is already known and works down the list in a direction without telling why. How would the authors treat the unexplained part?
options: As evidence of random behavior that no theory of any kind could be expected to explain
As an error
As proof of a hidden rule
As a choice not explained by the data, left unexplained, with a possible conjecture
optionExplain: They do not claim that.
Not claimed.
Not claimed.
Right: honest reporting.
questions.explain: The authors leave some choices unexplained.
questions.teaches: S4 generated assignments for G from large digits downward but for O and later C upward, a direction difference the authors cannot explain from the protocol.

questions.q: After a solver is shown to use the same method on two puzzles, what level of analysis could be done next?
options: None, since the matter is closed once the model has been confirmed on two tasks
A finer one, on how the steps are linked and how memory and operators work
Only a coarser one
Replace the solver
optionExplain: Finer levels remain.
Right: the authors' next levels.
They go finer.
No.
questions.explain: Finer levels follow once the coarse picture is confirmed. The card says so.

questions.q: On the new task S4 used the same problem space, the ____ space.
questions.explain: S4 used the augmented space again.

questions.q: At the level of production systems, what would analysis concentrate on?
options: The meaning of the letters in the words of the puzzle and the order in which the columns are listed
The final answers
The fine structure of the sequential linkage of behavior and how it is controlled within the space
The eye movements only
optionExplain: No.
No.
Right: control within the space.
Not the production level.
questions.explain: Productions give the fine linkage.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say the episode abstract is too crude an instrument to compare S4's two protocols in detail.
questions.explain: They explain why they did not compare the two protocols in detail.

questions.q: A coach checks that a new drill draws on the same skills as an old one; what follows if so?
options: The coarse model is confirmed, and finer analysis becomes worth doing
The model is refuted
Nothing more can be learned from the drill or from any of the players
The drill is useless
optionExplain: Right: the authors' pattern.
No.
More can be learned.
No.
questions.explain: Confirm the coarse pattern, then refine.
questions.teaches: The authors say that errors of immediate memory were significant in all the protocols, as in S2's failure to recall that E equals 3, which vitiates the remainder of the episodes shown in Figure 7.22.

questions.q: A solver cannot see assignments written down but can ask someone to recall them. What might change in the way the solver works?
options: The puzzle's solution
The operations used to retrieve information
The meaning of the letters in the words of the puzzle
The rules
optionExplain: Same.
Right: external memory changes operations.
Same.
Same.
questions.explain: Where information is stored changes how it is retrieved. The card describes S2's setup.

questions.q: S2 was observed on CROSS+ROADS for the first ____ seconds shown in Figure 7.22.
questions.explain: Only the first 382 seconds are shown.

questions.q: S2 concludes that A cannot be 0 since it would make O equal to G, though neither has a value. Which operator is evidenced?
options: AV
GN
PC
TD, applied more than minimally
optionExplain: No assignment.
No digit set.
No column processing.
Right: a test beyond an elementary check.
questions.explain: He tests an unassigned letter against the exclusion rule.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say S2's display held his assignments in written form like that of earlier subjects.
questions.explain: The display did not hold values; the experimenter held them in memory on call.

questions.q: A shopper keeps no list but asks a friend to remember items on request. Which part of S2's setup is this like?
options: The experimenter holding assignments in memory, called for by S2
A written display
An eye-tracking helmet only, with the assignments written on the display
A shared notebook
optionExplain: Right: external memory on call.
S2 had none.
That is another feature.
No notebook.
questions.explain: Values were held by the experimenter.
questions.teaches: S2 recognized at once that 1 and 2 were unavailable for A, but E6 shows he did not recall that 3 was unavailable as well, since E equals 3.

questions.q: A researcher wants more data to test a model. Which extra data best constrains the model?
options: Data from a much longer session with new events
Data from a different person doing a different task in another laboratory later on
Data gathered at the same time on the same behavior from a second channel
Data made up by the researcher
optionExplain: New events add freedom.
That changes the question.
Right: more points to fit with no extra freedom.
Invented data do not test anything.
questions.explain: A parallel channel adds fit points without adding freedom. The card gives the authors' reason.

questions.q: Gross eye movements increase the number of points the theory must fit without increasing the degrees of ____.
questions.explain: They add data without adding freedom.

questions.q: Which of these belongs to the detailed strategy rather than the broad one?
options: The episode abstracts of several subjects
A survey of many tasks in later chapters
Chapter 6's analysis of a single subject's attempt
A comparison of problem spaces across a number of subjects
optionExplain: Broad.
Broad.
Right: depth for one attempt.
Broad.
questions.explain: Chapter 6 is the detailed, single-attempt kind.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, running a subject for longer sessions is an equivalent way of obtaining more data to test the theory.
questions.explain: Longer sessions let new facts, methods and stimuli enter, adding degrees of freedom.

questions.q: A teacher wants to check a theory of how pupils read. Recording where pupils look while they read aloud offers what advantage?
options: More simultaneous data to match without lengthening the lesson
It replaces the reading altogether
It makes pupils read faster
It allows any theory to fit
optionExplain: Right: the same logic as eye movements with protocols.
It supplements it.
Not the aim.
The opposite.
questions.explain: Parallel records tighten the test.
questions.teaches: Winikoff's study (1967) used four subjects with 15 minutes each and eye-movement data every fifth of a second; three tasks were cryptarithmetic (including S2) and the other was chess.

questions.q: You want people to speak freely while their eyes are recorded. Which equipment tradeoff is reasonable?
options: Clamp the head and ask people to whisper their thoughts while they work
Skip the recording of speech
Record only the first second
Accept somewhat lower accuracy by not clamping the head
optionExplain: That prevents free talking.
Speech is needed.
Too little data.
Right: the authors' choice.
questions.explain: Free speech needed a looser setup. The card gives the authors' reason.

questions.q: Frames were taken at ____-second intervals, so almost no fixations were missed.
questions.explain: Every fifth of a second.

questions.q: Why was the camera mounted on a helmet?
options: To block the subject's view
Because the subject's head moves frequently
To keep the subject silent
To reflect light off the display
optionExplain: No.
Right: the camera moves with the head.
No.
Light is reflected from the cornea.
questions.explain: The head moves, so the camera moves with it.

questions.q: True or false: The timing marks on the audio tape were placed on every tenth frame, so speech and eye movement could be matched only to within about two seconds, and not perfectly.
questions.explain: Time was marked every 2 seconds and a human matched heard time to the word.

questions.q: A study of drivers' eye movements uses a head-mounted camera because drivers turn their heads. What similar trade does it make?
options: Accepting some loss of accuracy to allow natural behavior
Accepting no data
Preventing natural behavior in order to gain the highest accuracy
Making the camera static
optionExplain: Right: same trade as the helmet.
No.
Opposite.
Opposite.
questions.explain: Natural behavior is worth some accuracy.
questions.teaches: Eye movements have been recorded with instrumental arrangements over the last half century, and the arrangement used is in no way exceptional.

questions.q: While you read a line of text, your eyes rest on a word, then jump to the next stop. What are these pauses and jumps called?
options: Blinks and nods
Scans and drifts
Targets and cues
Fixations and saccades
optionExplain: Not the terms.
Not the terms.
Not the terms.
Right: rest and jump.
questions.explain: Rest and jump are fixation and saccade. The card names them.

questions.q: Almost no time is taken by a saccade, and nothing is seen while the eyeball is in ____.
questions.explain: Vision time divides into fixations.

questions.q: An eye spot lies on the D in column 2. What can be said about the neighboring letters?
options: The subject is looking at all of the neighboring letters at once
The subject is probably not looking at them
Nothing can be said
The subject is looking at the whole row
optionExplain: The region is too small.
Right: the region of clarity is about a letter wide.
Something can.
Too wide.
questions.explain: The region of clarity is about one letter wide.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say that if the eye is on a letter, the subject is certainly seeing and thinking about it.
questions.explain: The evidence is only that he is looking at it; whether he sees it is another matter.

questions.q: Pilots scan a dashboard that does not change. What does the authors' point about a static display imply?
options: The pilot misses events whenever he looks away from any one of the dials in turn
The pilot need not look at all
A glance elsewhere does not make the pilot miss newly appearing information
The dashboard becomes a moving display
optionExplain: That is the radar-scope case.
He needs to look to learn.
Right: nothing new arrives.
No.
questions.explain: On a static display nothing is lost by looking elsewhere.
questions.teaches: The authors contrast the cryptarithmetic display with studies such as watching a radar scope, where information missed at a given moment cannot be recovered later.

questions.q: Someone studying a map first stares at one region, then wanders over the whole map, then flicks briefly between regions. Which pattern signals a search?
options: The stare at one region
The brief flicks between regions of the map
None of them
The wandering over the whole map
optionExplain: That is attention.
Those are transitions.
The wandering is a search.
Right: a scan.
questions.explain: Wandering is search. The card gives the units.

questions.q: Match each eye-movement unit to its description.
pairs: Fixations mostly on one task-relevant locale
Brief fixations that leave an attention unit's locale and return
questions.explain: These are Winikoff's four kinds.

questions.q: S2 looks steadily at column 1 while processing it. Which unit is this?
options: A scan unit
An attention unit
A transition unit
An excursion unit
optionExplain: Scans wander widely.
Right: a series of fixations on one locale.
Transitions are brief.
Excursions leave a locale.
questions.explain: Steady looking at a column is an attention unit.

questions.q: True or false: Winikoff treated transition and excursion units as having problem-solving significance equal to attention units.
questions.explain: They are not regarded as having problem-solving significance.

questions.q: A shopper stands before one shelf for 8 seconds, with two brief glances to a nearby price sign, then walks the whole store with quick glances. How would the units be named?
options: A scan unit followed by an attention unit, with a transition between
Two transition units
An attention unit with excursions, followed by a scan unit
A single excursion unit
optionExplain: The order is reversed.
Not transitions.
Right: stay, brief leave-and-return, then wander.
Not an excursion alone.
questions.explain: A stay with brief leave-and-return glances is attention with excursions.
questions.teaches: In Winikoff's study the term transition unit covered both the transitions and the excursions defined here, since the interpretation is the same; the authors separate them to avoid constant reference to within-unit and between-unit transitions.

questions.q: A program groups a list of short events into larger bursts, and then labels leftover gaps as long or short. What justifies treating long gaps as a separate class?
options: A sharp drop in the number of gaps beyond some length
Their being the longest
A smooth tail of lengths that shows no gap anywhere in the distribution
A user's preference
optionExplain: Right: the sign of two distributions.
Length alone does not split classes.
A smooth tail would not justify a cut.
Data are needed.
questions.explain: A sharp drop shows two kinds. The card gives the 1.2-second case.

questions.q: Table 7.3 shows a sharp drop in residual intervals at ____ seconds.
questions.explain: That justifies the cutting point.

questions.q: What happens to a very short misfit fixation inside a run of fixations on one column?
options: It starts a new attention unit
It is absorbed as an excursion
It is deleted from the record
It becomes a scan unit
optionExplain: Too short.
Right: pass 2 handles it.
It is labeled, not deleted.
Too short.
questions.explain: Short misfits are absorbed as excursions.

questions.q: True or false: Winikoff's sensitivity analysis showed the aggregation stays quite stable under small variations in its preset parameters.
questions.explain: This supports the use of the program.

questions.q: An analyst groups taxi trips into shifts using preset break lengths, and checks that small changes to break lengths hardly change the shifts. Which authors' step is this?
options: A calibration of the camera
A coding of verbal reports
A test of statistical chance applied to each comparison of the measures
A sensitivity analysis of the aggregation parameters
optionExplain: Different step.
Different step.
Different step.
Right: Winikoff's check.
questions.explain: Stability to parameter changes is the sensitivity analysis.
questions.teaches: The program builds attention units in a manner analogous to bottom-up grammatical recognition, so large units tend to be made of smaller ones, although the hierarchy does not become very deep.

questions.q: A researcher finds that where people look matches what they say they are doing. Which worry should come first?
options: The match might come from the words they say, not from what they think
The match must be perfect before the method can be counted as useful at all
People never look anywhere
Words are never spoken
optionExplain: Right: the surface-feature problem.
It need not be.
They do.
They are spoken.
questions.explain: Surface features of speech can predict looking by themselves. The card gives the example.

questions.q: Any comparison produces a rate of false ____, so correspondence must be judged against a null model of chance.
questions.explain: False positives are places where a match is asserted but none exists.

questions.q: S2 says S plus S has to equal R and his eyes go to S, S and R. Why is this weak evidence by itself of column processing?
options: Because eyes never follow speech when people are thinking aloud at the display
Because the display is blank
The same eye movements could be predicted from the words spoken
Because the units are too long
optionExplain: They may.
It is not.
Right: surface features suffice.
Not the point.
questions.explain: Surface mention of S, S, R predicts eyes on those letters.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say a perfect correspondence between eye movements and problem solving is what the theory requires.
questions.explain: They expect imperfect correspondence, and see value in eye movements that add information beyond speech.

questions.q: A school compares a test that predicts grades with one that predicts the same grades from attendance. Which authors' idea says the comparison needs a baseline?
options: All comparisons share one chance level, so one baseline is enough
Chance level is irrelevant
Each comparison has its own chance level as a base line
Only perfect matches matter
optionExplain: They do not.
It is essential.
Right: null models differ.
No.
questions.explain: Each comparison has a different chance level.
questions.teaches: Because aggregates are made of fixations, a relation between problem solving and aggregates may owe nothing to the aggregation but only to particular fixations within it, so it might be better not to aggregate at all.

questions.q: If eye-movement aggregates are a better guide to thinking than raw fixations, what pattern would you expect in the data?
options: A closer fit with inferred problem solving for aggregates than for single fixations
No difference between them at all
A better fit for fixations
No fit for either
optionExplain: Right: that is what was found.
Improvement was found.
The reverse.
Fit exceeded chance.
questions.explain: Aggregates fit better. The card gives the results.

questions.q: Order Winikoff's three correspondences from lowest to highest expected fit.
items: Fixations with surface verbalizations
Fixations with inferred problem solving
Aggregates with inferred problem solving
questions.explain: Fit improves almost always along this sequence.

questions.q: Which measure gave better correspondence, according to Winikoff?
options: Numbers of units, rather than duration
Neither differed
Only the first fixation
Total duration, rather than numbers of units
optionExplain: The reverse.
A difference was found.
Not a measure.
Right: duration fit better.
questions.explain: Larger units are likelier to match, statistically and if the relation holds.

questions.q: True or false: In the one chess protocol analyzed, using aggregates and inferred problem solving gave a clear improvement over surface verbalizations.
questions.explain: The problem behavior graph there added little beyond surface verbalizations, so there was no improvement.
questions.rule: No gain in the chess protocol.

questions.q: A bank cross-checks an interview score with a second independent record, and the records corroborate each other most times and add new facts sometimes. Which authors' conclusion does that mirror?
options: The second record replaces the first
An independent measure can supplement the verbal record and not only repeat it
The records must always agree exactly
The first record is invalid
optionExplain: Supplement, not replace.
Right: eye movements supplement protocols.
Not required.
Not implied.
questions.explain: Independent data corroborate and sometimes add.
questions.teaches: The authors add that confirming the information processing models from an independent source of data gives additional assurance that this is an essentially correct way to view human problem solving.

questions.q: When asked what number you wrote at the top of a page, your eyes jump to that spot even before you answer. What does that suggest?
options: The eyes return to where the information was set, as part of recalling it
You have forgotten the number and are looking for it elsewhere on the page
You are reading a new page
You are guessing
optionExplain: Right: the S2 pattern.
Not implied.
Not implied.
Not implied.
questions.explain: Eyes returning to the source signal recall. The card describes S2.

questions.q: The new operator RV recalls the ____ of a variable.
questions.explain: RV recalls the value of a variable.

questions.q: At T128.8 S2 works out that C plus R exceeds 10, so C exceeds 10 minus R, and in getting R (4) goes back to column 1 for 1.8 seconds. What does this show?
options: A scan of the whole display
An excursion without meaning that fell within an attention unit
A random glance
A recall of the value of R by looking at where it was derived
optionExplain: He went to one place.
It matches a recall.
It fits a recall.
Right: RV in action.
questions.explain: Going back to the source of R is the recall.

questions.q: True or false: The authors can determine from the data whether the shift of eyes causes, aids or follows the recall.
questions.explain: They say one cannot determine which; precise timing might help but could not be definitive.

questions.q: A cashier who writes totals on a pad glances at the pad each time the amount is needed, though the cashier does not say so. What does this parallel in S2's protocol?
options: A gap in the cashier's addition that the pad was meant to fill
Eye movements revealing a recall that speech never mentions
An error in the pad
A slip of speech
optionExplain: Not the parallel.
Right: RV is shown by the eyes.
Not the parallel.
Not the parallel.
questions.explain: The eyes show a step the speech omits.
questions.teaches: At production 76 (T167.2), S2 should have moved his eyes to column 5 or 6 to recall D equal to 1; the authors reinterpret the short unit at column 3 and the long 0.8-second transition together as supporting the recall production.

questions.q: Two programs for similar tasks share most rules, but one adds a rule for looking things up. What would you call the added rule's role?
options: A rule for ending the task
A rule for checking the final answer at the end of the work
A rule for recall, which the other program did not need
A rule for generating digits
optionExplain: Not P16.
That is P5, absent in S2's segment.
Right: P16 for S2.
Not P16.
questions.explain: The recall production is S2's new one. The card gives it.

questions.q: As its basic driving mechanism S2 uses ____, which finds the next column in the standard right-to-left sequence.
questions.explain: S3 used FL instead.

questions.q: In responding to a contradiction (P7), what does S2 set up as a goal?
options: Getting a value, as S3 did
Checking the final sum
Recalling a letter
Assigning a new value
optionExplain: That is S3's goal.
No final checking.
That is P16.
Right: S2's version of P7.
questions.explain: S2 goes straight to assigning a new value.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say S2 resembles S5 and S8 more closely than S3 in the way he chooses the next thing to work on.
questions.explain: S2's FNC right-to-left driver matches S5 and S8, while S3 used FL.

questions.q: Two cooks both follow recipes but one picks the next step by finding what is next on the list, while another picks the step needing a missing ingredient. Which is closer to S2?
options: The cook who picks the step by the missing ingredient, like FL
The cook who takes the next step in fixed order, like FNC
A cook who does nothing
A cook who checks only at the end
optionExplain: That is more like FL for S3.
Right: FNC finds the next column.
Not a parallel.
Not the point.
questions.explain: FNC is the next-in-order finder.
questions.teaches: The authors have specified S2's knowledge state more completely than S3's, including the stack of goals as well as the sequence of expressions known at each time.

questions.q: A to-do list with nested items is updated automatically as items are done or fail. Which feature does this match in S2's system?
options: A production that takes time and appears in the eye movements
A new problem space
A goal stack operated by rules and not by productions
A set of assignments
optionExplain: Stack operations take no appreciable time.
Not a space.
Right: automatic bookkeeping.
Not assignments.
questions.explain: Stack operation is automatic. The card says so.

questions.q: Operations on the goal stack are performed in response to the ____ and take precedence over all other actions.
questions.explain: The signal gives the goal's status.

questions.q: A goal has set up a subgoal, and nothing more can be done unless the subgoal yields new information. If the subgoal fails, what do the authors' signals imply?
options: There is no need to return to the original goal
The original goal must be tried again at once, whatever the subgoal did
The whole stack is cleared
The subgoal is pushed again
optionExplain: Right: the conditional fail.
The conditional fail avoids that.
Not stated.
Not stated.
questions.explain: A conditional fail drops the original goal if the subgoal fails.

questions.q: True or false: Stack operations in S2's system are assumed to take appreciable time and to show up in eye movements.
questions.explain: They are assumed automatic, taking no appreciable time and having no implications for eye movements.

questions.q: A manager's checklist is updated by clerks whenever a task is closed. A different design makes the manager return to the earlier task each time before deciding whether anything remains. Which authors' point does this illustrate?
options: Both designs are identical in all of their implications for the eye movements
Alternative stack designs can have different implications for eye movements
Stacks cannot be designed
The first design takes time
optionExplain: They differ in implications.
Right: the always-return design differs.
They can.
Automatic.
questions.explain: The authors choose the design with the eye-movement implications they want.
questions.teaches: In S3's system the operators produced expressions that were then converted into goals by other productions (P6, P10); in S2's the operators produce goals directly and the intermediate products are eliminated.

questions.q: If a person's goal is to add column 2, where should their eyes rest, per a sensible rule?
options: On column 6
Off the display
On the experimenter
On column 2
optionExplain: Not the goal.
Not the goal.
Not the goal.
Right: attention follows the goal.
questions.explain: Attention at the goal's column. The card gives this as rule 1.

questions.q: Under the second observation rule, the subject scans the display when he selects a new column undirected by prior problem solving, that is by ____.
questions.explain: FNC is the undirected selection.

questions.q: A directed search FC fails to find a column. By rule 2, what eye-movement unit is expected?
options: A scan unit
An attention unit at the original column
A transition unit
No movement
optionExplain: Right: a failed directed search leads to scanning.
Not rule 2.
Transitions are discarded by the minimum rules.
A scan is expected.
questions.explain: Rule 2 predicts a scan after a failed FC.

questions.q: True or false: The minimum rules attribute significance to transitions between units, which the maximum rules discard.
questions.explain: The minimum rules discard transitions; the maximum rules give them significance for FC and FNC.

questions.q: A study scores how well a model predicts gaze using a minimum set of rules for matching model to data and a maximum set that credits more transitions and ad hoc interpretations. The authors would say the true state of affairs:
options: Equals the result from the minimum set of rules
Equals the result from the maximum set of rules
Lies somewhere between the two sets of rules
Cannot be said to lie anywhere in particular
optionExplain: The authors do not say the minimum rules give the truth.
The authors do not say the maximum rules give the truth.
Right: the true state of affairs undoubtedly lies somewhere between the two sets of rules.
The authors place it between the minimum and maximum rules.
questions.explain: The authors call the Winikoff rules the minimum rules and their own the maximum rules, and say the true state of affairs undoubtedly lies somewhere between them.
questions.teaches: We can call the rules used in the Winikoff study the minimum rules. The true state of affairs undoubtedly lies somewhere between these two sets of rules for correspondence.

questions.q: A model covers 90 percent of the minutes of someone's behavior but only 70 percent of the separate episodes. Which is likelier?
options: The short episodes are covered best and the long ones less so
Coverage is random
The long episodes are covered well and the short ones less so
Both numbers must match
optionExplain: Then unit coverage would exceed time coverage.
Not stated.
Right: time coverage exceeds unit coverage.
They need not.
questions.explain: Time coverage is higher than unit coverage when long units are covered best. The card states the figures.

questions.q: With the minimum rules the system covers 67.5 percent of units and ____ percent of time.
questions.explain: The minimum-rule figures are 67.5 and 87.5.

questions.q: Which are the maximum-rule coverage figures?
options: 87 percent of units and 94.4 percent of time
67.5 percent of units and 87.5 percent of time
94.4 percent of units and 87 percent of time
100 percent of both
optionExplain: Right: the maximum figures.
These are the minimum figures.
Swapped.
Not reached.
questions.explain: Maximum rules give 87 and 94.4.

questions.q: True or false: Most of the increase from minimum to maximum coverage comes from the additional ad hoc reinterpretations rather than from the systematic ones.
questions.explain: The bulk of the increase comes from the systematic parts of the reinterpretation.

questions.q: A model's accuracy rises from 67 to 87 percent when two general rules are relaxed, while a few special patches add little. What does this suggest?
options: The patches did the work
The model is unscientific
The data are worthless
The improvement reflects general rules, not patching
optionExplain: They added little.
Not implied.
Not implied.
Right: like the S2 result.
questions.explain: General reinterpretation, not ad hoc patches, brought the gain.
questions.teaches: The system's ad hoc operator outputs, those not following from any general rules for the operators, were marked in Appendix 7.6, and they amount to about 10 percent of the total.

questions.q: A model fits a short 200-second excerpt better than a model fits a 1000-second record. What caution applies?
options: The shorter excerpt proves that the model is better than the earlier one
The shorter sample may be easier to fit, so the comparison is not clean
Short excerpts cannot be fitted
Fit has nothing to do with length
optionExplain: Not necessarily.
Right: the authors' caution.
They can.
It may.
questions.explain: Length affects fit. The card notes it.

questions.q: The productions are about half again as dense for S2, 0.47 per second against ____ per second for S3.
questions.explain: 0.47 versus 0.32.

questions.q: Which two reasons do the authors give for the better fit with S2 than with S3?
options: The segment studied is much shorter, and the eye-movement evidence adds fine-grained data
S2 is more intelligent, and the task is easier
The experimenter helped him more often, and the task itself was much shorter than the first
S2 used a new problem space, and a new strategy
optionExplain: Right: both are named.
Not stated.
Not stated.
He used the augmented space.
questions.explain: Shortness and the fine-grained evidence.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say the eye-movement data undermine the reality of the information processing models.
questions.explain: They say the data substantially support the reality of the models.

questions.q: Two independent instruments, a stopwatch and a heart monitor, both fit a model of a runner's pacing. What does this add to confidence in the model?
options: Nothing, since instruments always agree whenever they are measuring the same runner
Proof that pacing is fixed
A new model of pacing
An independent kind of data agreeing with it, as with S2's speech and eyes
optionExplain: They need not agree.
Not implied.
Not implied.
Right: independent confirmation.
questions.explain: Independent agreement raises confidence.
questions.teaches: In the finer production-level analysis, the authors assign meaning to the transitions that Winikoff's study had set aside, though occasionally an apparent excursion turns out to be over-aggregation by the program.

questions.q: A project first studies the task, then one participant in depth, then many participants more coarsely. Why this order?
options: To avoid studying people
Each step supplies the base for the next
Because breadth is always better than depth
Because depth is impossible later
optionExplain: People are studied.
Right: the order in the trilogy.
Not claimed.
Not claimed.
questions.explain: Task, then case, then cases. The card describes the order.

questions.q: Put the contributions of the three chapters in order.
items: Analysis of the task environment and its problem spaces
Detailed study of one subject on DONALD+GERALD
Extension to other subjects and another puzzle
questions.explain: Chapter 5, then Chapter 6, then Chapter 7.

questions.q: Which two tools did Chapter 7 introduce?
options: Problem behavior graphs and production systems, which came in Chapter 6
BNF notation and EPAM
Episoding of behavior and eye-movement analysis with the protocol
Hints and rewards
optionExplain: Introduced earlier.
Earlier chapters.
Right: the two named.
Not tools of the chapter.
questions.explain: Episoding and eye movements.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say the episoding procedure was introduced to avoid having to produce and analyze the full problem behavior graph for every subject.
questions.explain: Episoding treats the data in more summary, less painful ways.

questions.q: A study of a new game first maps the rules, then follows one champion move by move, then compares ten players by phases. Which part of the trilogy does the third step mirror?
options: Chapter 5's task analysis
Chapter 6's detailed case
The next chapter's very different task, proof discovery in a formal system
Chapter 7's broader comparison with episode-level tools
optionExplain: That is the first step.
That is the second step.
That is outside the trilogy.
Right: breadth with coarser tools.
questions.explain: Breadth with coarser tools is Chapter 7.
questions.teaches: The authors say the largest part of Chapter 6 was given to deriving a problem behavior graph from the thinking-aloud protocol and testing the production system against it.

questions.q: A model explains most of a pupil's work as demanded by the task but not the slips that happened. How should it be described?
options: Wrong overall, since it does not predict the particular errors
Good on demanded behavior, silent on the particular errors
Complete
Useless
optionExplain: Most behavior is accounted for.
Right: the authors' assessment.
Errors remain.
Not so.
questions.explain: Strong on demands, silent on slips. The card gives this.

questions.q: Three of the four subjects on DONALD+GERALD worked in essentially the same ____ problem space as S3.
questions.explain: The fourth worked in a simpler space.

questions.q: Which kinds of errors do the authors identify in their subjects?
options: Arithmetic errors and misreading the puzzle
Deliberate misreporting and boredom
Elementary faults of reasoning, such as confusing sufficient with necessary conditions, and lapses of memory
Random keystrokes and fatigue
optionExplain: Not the kinds named.
Not the kinds named.
Right: the two kinds.
Not the kinds named.
questions.explain: Reasoning faults and memory lapses.

questions.q: True or false: The authors claim their theory predicts the errors the subjects made.
questions.explain: They say the errors were themselves not predicted by the theory.

questions.q: A flight simulator model explains most pilot actions as demanded by the situation but not the rare lapses. What would it need to explain the lapses?
options: Detailed data on memory processes, which the logs do not give
More weather data on the days of the flights, collected by the simulator
A bigger aircraft
Nothing more
optionExplain: Right: like the authors' remark.
Not relevant.
Not relevant.
More is needed.
questions.explain: Explaining errors needs data not in the protocols.
questions.teaches: The authors characterize the resulting theory as detailed but particularistic and the chapter as a first cautious step toward generalizing it.

questions.q: After building a theory on one task family, a team plans to test it on a very different kind of task. What does this show?
options: That the theory is finished
A cautious step toward generalizing the theory
That the first task was wasted effort and should be abandoned
That tools must be rebuilt
optionExplain: They call it a first step.
Right: the authors' stated view.
Not implied.
The same tools will be used.
questions.explain: A second task is a generalization step. The card says so.

questions.q: The second task environment is discovering proofs for theorems in a ____ system.
questions.explain: Proof discovery in a formal system.

questions.q: How do the authors describe the state of their tool building at this point?
options: Barely begun
To be redone for each new task
Abandoned
Complete in all essentials, with the same tools used in later chapters
optionExplain: Not stated.
The same tools will be used.
Not stated.
Right: stated at the end.
questions.explain: Tool building is complete in essentials.

questions.q: True or false: The authors describe the theory emerging from the three chapters as a general theory of human problem solving.
questions.explain: They call it a detailed, if particularistic, theory and the extension a first cautious step toward generalizing.

questions.q: A lab finishes tool building on chess and announces it will study medical diagnosis next using the same tools. Which authors' step is parallel?
options: Moving to a second task environment with the same tools
Rebuilding the tools from scratch for the new domain, as in Chapter 5
Dropping the first domain
Studying one subject only
optionExplain: Right: the proof-discovery trilogy.
Opposite.
Not stated.
Not the step.
questions.explain: Same tools, new environment.
questions.teaches: The next trilogy of chapters will devote itself to problem solving in a second task environment, discovering proofs for theorems in a formal system.

questions.q: Volunteers get a sheet of rules and are told to change one string of symbols into another. Which job do they have?
options: Learning the rule sheet by heart and reciting it to a tester
Applying permitted rewrites step by step until the target string appears
Judging whether each written statement is true or false
Translating each symbol into an English word, one by one
optionExplain: Memorizing may help, but the stated job is to transform strings.
Right: the job is a step-by-step transformation toward a stated end string.
Nothing in a recoding task asks for a truth judgment.
No translation is asked for; the symbols are rewritten as symbols.
questions.explain: A recoding task asks for a chain of rule-governed rewrites that ends in a target string. The card next gives the authors' account.
questions.rule: Rewrite by rule until the target appears.

questions.q: The subjects were told to ____ certain strings of symbols into other, specified strings.
questions.explain: The authors report that "recode" was the word used for the transformation the subjects were to carry out.

questions.q: Which activity is most like the logic task as the subjects met it?
options: Deciding whether the claim that all birds fly is true
Writing an essay that explains what a rule sheet means
Reciting the rules of a board game from memory to a friend
Turning COLD into WARM one letter at a time, using a list of allowed swaps
optionExplain: This asks for a truth judgment; the logic subjects made none.
Explaining meaning is not the task; rewriting strings is.
Recall of rules is not the goal; applying them to reach a target is.
Right: given strings, permitted steps and a stated end string.
questions.explain: The word-ladder game has a start string, allowed moves and a target, as the logic task does.

questions.q: True or false: The subjects were told that they were solving problems in a system of symbolic logic.
questions.explain: The authors say the label is misleading: the subjects were told only to recode strings with the given rules.
questions.rule: Subjects knew a recoding job, not logic.
