questions.q: On the rule sheet the expressions use letters joined by four kinds of connector. Which pair of signs is among them?
options: The dot and the wedge
The plus sign and the equals sign
The asterisk and the slash
The ampersand and the question mark
optionExplain: Right: dots, wedges, horseshoes and tildes are the four connectors.
These belong to arithmetic, as in the cryptarithmetic task, not to the logic sheet.
These are not among the connectors the authors list.
Neither appears on the rule sheet.
questions.explain: The sheet joins letters with dots, wedges, horseshoes and tildes. For analysts they stand for and, or, implies and not.
questions.rule: Four connectors: dot, wedge, horseshoe, tilde.
questions.teaches: The connectors are dots, wedges, horseshoes and tildes, which stand for and, or, implies and not.

questions.q: A teacher gives pupils tiles and a card of swap rules and says to reach a given layout, without saying the swaps follow a theory. Which part of the logic setup does this repeat?
options: The analysts and the subjects share one description of the task
The target layout changes after every swap the pupils make
Subjects work toward a target with rules while the theory behind them stays unnamed
Pupils are asked to explain the theory before they begin to swap
optionExplain: In the logic task they do not: the authors' label differs from the subjects' instructions.
In the logic task the desired expression stays fixed.
Right: the logic subjects were told to recode, not that they were doing logic.
Subjects of the logic task were not asked for any explanation of this kind.
questions.explain: The tile game mirrors the setup: a target, permitted moves and no named theory. The analyst's label need not be the subject's.
questions.rule: The analyst's label is not the subject's task.
questions.teaches: The task was developed by O. K. Moore and Scarvia Anderson in 1954, as a recoding task for subjects who were not told its logical nature.

questions.q: A volunteer receives a rule sheet using marks like dots and wedges and is not told what the marks mean. How will they probably use the sheet?
options: By first working out what each mark means and then reasoning in words
By asking which of the expressions is true in everyday life
By matching the shapes in the rules to shapes in the expressions
By refusing to start until the experimenter explains each mark
optionExplain: The authors say subjects do not discover the interpretation.
Truth in daily life is not available for unexplained marks.
Right: with no meaning given, the form of the marks is all there is to use.
The task runs without any such explanation.
questions.explain: Without meanings, form is what remains. The card next names this syntactic handling.
questions.rule: No meaning given, so work by form.

questions.q: The subjects handle the expressions entirely by their ____ properties, without reference to meaning.
questions.explain: Syntactic means having to do with form and arrangement, as opposed to semantic meaning.

questions.q: A board-game card says two blue chips may be swapped for one red chip. A child uses it without knowing what the colors stand for. Which feature of the logic task is this?
options: Following rules by the form of the pieces alone
Discovering the hidden interpretation of the pieces during play
Checking that each position is true before making a swap
Learning the meaning of the pieces from the experimenter first
optionExplain: Right: the swap depends on how pieces look and combine, not on what they mean.
The logic subjects did not discover the interpretation.
Truth plays no part in the rules of the logic task.
The subjects were not given the meaning either.
questions.explain: The child's swaps depend on shape and count only, which is form-based handling.

questions.q: True or false: By the end of the task, subjects typically have not found out that the dot stands for and and the wedge for or.
questions.explain: The authors say the subjects are not told the interpretation and in fact do not discover it.

questions.q: A reader claims that the subjects solved the problems by working out whether each line was true. What is wrong with that claim?
options: Truth cannot be judged for lines containing more than one letter
The subjects judged falsity only, never truth
Truth was judged by the experimenter in place of the subject
The subjects did not know the signs' meanings, so they worked with form
optionExplain: Nothing in the account limits truth judgments by letter count.
The account says nothing about such a split.
The experimenter checks that a rule application is legitimate, not whether a line is true.
Right: without the interpretation, truth judgments were not available.
questions.explain: The claim assumes the subjects held the semantic interpretation. The authors say they did not.
questions.rule: Meaning was not available to use.

questions.q: A new study uses a rule sheet with unexplained marks plus a minus sign. By the authors' remark about the tilde, which mark may subjects read partly through meaning?
options: The unexplained marks, because new shapes draw attention
The minus sign, because it looks like a familiar negative and pairs of them cancel
None of the marks, since form-only handling holds without exception
The longest expression, because it holds the most information
optionExplain: New unexplained shapes give nothing to read meaning from.
Right: the authors say the tilde is a partial exception for just this reason.
The authors call the tilde a partial exception, so exceptions exist.
Length has no bearing on whether a sign resembles a familiar one.
questions.explain: A footnote notes that the tilde is a partial exception: many subjects see that it looks and behaves like a negative or minus sign, and pairs of them cancel.
questions.teaches: The tilde is a partial exception, since many subjects notice that, like negative and minus signs, pairs of tildes cancel.

questions.q: In a puzzle that asks you to turn some given statements into a target statement by rules, what must you be handed at the start?
options: The given statements and the target statement
Only the target statement, with the givens left to you
Only the given statements, with the target left to you
The finished list of rule applications that solve it
optionExplain: Right: the start and the end of the transformation define the problem.
Without the givens there is nothing to transform.
Without a target the solver cannot know when to stop.
That list would be the solution, not the problem.
questions.explain: A transformation problem needs both ends. The card next gives the book's names for them.
questions.rule: Givens and target make the problem.

questions.q: The desired expression of a problem is labelled ____ throughout the chapter.
questions.explain: L0 is the desired expression; the givens are L1 to Ln.

questions.q: A new problem has three given expressions and one desired expression. How does the chapter's notation label them?
options: Givens L0, L1, L2 and desired expression L3
One given L1 and desired expressions L2 and L3
Givens L1, L2, L3 and no label for the desired expression
Givens L1, L2, L3 and desired expression L0
optionExplain: L0 is reserved for the desired expression.
The givens are L1 to Ln; here there are three of them.
The desired expression always has the label L0.
Right: the givens are numbered from L1 and the target is L0.
questions.explain: The desired expression is L0; the givens run L1 to Ln.

questions.q: Sort each item as a given expression or the desired expression.

items.t: An expression handed to the subject at the start
The expression named L0
L2 in a problem with four starting expressions
The expression the subject is asked to obtain

questions.explain: The givens start the problem and the single desired expression ends it.
questions.rule: Start with the givens; end at L0.

questions.q: True or false: In the sixteen regular problems, every problem starts from exactly one given expression.
questions.explain: The regular problems vary the number of givens between one and four.

questions.q: A planner may reach any one of three target seatings in one contest, and must reach all three in another. Which feature of the logic task does this resemble?
options: Problems with several given expressions, as in the sixteen regular problems of the set
Problems with several desired expressions, solved by getting any one or getting all
Practice problems that are easier than the regular ones
Problems whose desired expression is not known at the start
optionExplain: That is the multiple givens case, not multiple targets.
Right: the authors note that such variants can be built and were studied by Anderson.
Practice problems differ in difficulty, not in the number of targets.
The desired expression is always specified in the task.
questions.explain: The authors say it is possible to construct problems with several desired expressions, where the task is to obtain any one of them or to obtain all. Anderson (1957) studied them; this chapter does not.
questions.rule: Several targets: any one, or all.
questions.teaches: Problems with several desired expressions, where the task is to obtain any one or all of them, were studied by Anderson (1957) but are not considered here.

questions.q: A tutor writes each accepted step of a student's solution on a shared board. What does this give both of them?
options: A guarantee that the student will find the shortest route
A way to hide earlier mistakes from view
A visible record that later steps can build on
A replacement for the student's own reasoning
optionExplain: A record shows steps taken; it does not steer toward short routes.
A visible record keeps earlier steps in view.
Right: each new move starts from what is already written.
The record only stores moves; the student still decides them.
questions.explain: An external record lets each step rest on earlier ones. The card next describes the display used in the logic task.

questions.q: The expressions in the lower left quadrant of the blackboard are called ____ expressions.
questions.explain: Derived expressions are the ones produced by rule applications; the problem is solved when one equals L0.

questions.q: Lines 1 to 5 are on the board. The subject asks for a legitimate rule application to line 4. What does the experimenter do?
options: Replaces line 4 by the new expression
Writes the new expression in the upper right quadrant beside the desired expression L0
Renumbers the lines so that the new one becomes line 1
Writes the new expression as line 6, with the rule's name beside it
optionExplain: Earlier lines stay; the record is only extended.
That quadrant holds the desired expression L0.
Numbering continues from the last line.
Right: numbering continues and the rule name goes in the right-hand column.
questions.explain: The board grows downward: each legitimate result is a new numbered line with its rule.

questions.q: Put one cycle of a subject's move in order.
items: The subject asks the experimenter to apply a rule to a line on the board
The experimenter checks that the transformation is legitimate
The new expression is written with the next number and the rule name
The new line is compared with L0 to see if the problem is solved
questions.explain: A request leads to a check, then a record, then the test against L0.

questions.q: Figure 8.3 shows the display for D1 with S4's solution: a numbered column of more than seven derived expressions, each with the rule used beside it. Elsewhere the authors speak of the seven-step proof of D1. Per the authors, how do the two relate?
options: The derivation shown is a different problem with a seven-step proof
The seven-step proof of D1 is embedded in the longer derivation shown
The seven-step proof was found by the experimenter and not by a subject
The longer derivation breaks the rules, which is why it is longer
optionExplain: It is the solution of D1 itself, by subject S4.
Right: the authors call the seven-step proof embedded in Figure 8.3.
The text does not say this; it says the proof is embedded in the figure.
The experimenter accepts only legitimate steps, so all lines obey the rules.
questions.explain: A subject's recorded derivation can contain steps beyond those a shortest proof needs. The shortest, seven-step proof is embedded in it.
questions.rule: A record can hold more than the proof.
questions.teaches: S4's recorded derivation of D1 is longer than the seven-step proof that is embedded in it.

questions.q: A cook may ask an assistant to combine an item already on a numbered list with another item on the list. The assistant adds the result as the next line. Which logic-task detail is this?
options: A rule may be applied only to the desired expression L0
A rule may be applied only to the most recent line
A rule may be applied to a pair of expressions already on the board
A rule may be applied to expressions not yet written down
optionExplain: Rules apply to expressions already on the board, not to the target.
Any expression on the board can be chosen.
Right: the subject can ask for a rule to be applied to an expression, or to a pair of expressions.
The input expressions must already be on the board.
questions.explain: Rules that take two inputs, such as combining two lines, work on a pair of lines already on the board.
questions.rule: Inputs are lines already on the board.
questions.teaches: The subject can ask the experimenter to apply a rule to an expression, or to a pair of expressions, that is already on the blackboard.

questions.q: A researcher can have 64 people solve many puzzles with timing, or 10 people think aloud on a few. What does each design mainly give?
options: Timing data on many people, or rich spoken detail on a few
Spoken detail on many people, or timing data on a few
The same data in both designs, only arranged differently
Neither design gives data about how people solve puzzles
optionExplain: Right: breadth and times from the large group, protocols from the small one.
This reverses the usual trade-off between group size and detail.
The two designs record different kinds of data.
Both record behavior during problem solving.
questions.explain: Large groups suit timing and counts; thinking aloud suits detail. The card next sets out the book's two groups.
questions.rule: Many with times; few with protocols.

questions.q: The ____ group of sixty-four subjects attempted all sixteen regular problems, with fifteen minutes per problem.
questions.explain: Yale: 64 subjects, all sixteen problems, fifteen minutes each. Carnegie: ten subjects, one to six problems, thirty minutes each.

questions.q: The authors want to know how long a typical step took in solving problem D1. Which data can answer this?
options: The Carnegie protocols, which were timed to the second
Either group, since both recorded elapsed time
The Yale records, which include the time elapsed
Neither group, since time data cannot be collected here
optionExplain: Carnegie times were not recorded.
Only one of the two groups has times.
Right: only the Yale experiment recorded times.
The Yale experiment collected them.
questions.explain: Times come from Yale. Carnegie supplies spoken protocols but no times.

questions.q: True or false: If the Carnegie subjects had not been asked to think aloud, their data would still include protocols.
questions.explain: Protocols come from thinking aloud; without it the Carnegie data would hold only the transformations.

questions.q: A critic calls the Yale data unusable because alcohol was part of the experiment. What do the authors say in answer?
options: All subjects and problems received the same alcohol range, and its effects were small
Alcohol was given only to the Carnegie group, so the Yale data are untouched by it
Alcohol had no measurable effect at any dose, so the question does not arise
The alcohol data were removed before any analysis, leaving only the sober trials
optionExplain: Right: the counterbalanced design and small effects justify pooling.
The alcohol study was the Yale group's.
The largest doses cut performance by about 30 percent.
The authors used the data for all subjects on each problem.
questions.explain: Because the design was counterbalanced and effects small, the authors use the data for all subjects throughout. The largest amounts of alcohol did cost about 30 percent in performance.

questions.q: A study of a new puzzle compares two groups: one with scores for 60 people, one with only spoken thoughts from 10. In which ways does this copy the book's logic data?
options: Both groups give times and protocols for every puzzle that they attempted in the study
A large group with step records and times, and a small group giving protocols
The small group gives times and the large group protocols
Both groups give only final answers with no step records
optionExplain: In the book, times belong to Yale and protocols to Carnegie.
Right: this is the Yale and Carnegie arrangement.
This reverses which group supplied which data.
Both book groups gave step-by-step data.
questions.explain: Yale supplied the transformation lists with rule and time; the small Carnegie group thought aloud. The Carnegie subjects first studied the rules and did three easy practice problems, then attempted D1 and C1.
questions.rule: Match the data type to the group.
questions.teaches: The Carnegie subjects studied the rules and solved or were helped to solve practice problems a1 to a3, then attempted D1, followed by C1.

questions.q: A researcher studies how people solve a new kind of puzzle. Which question is mainly about the puzzle rather than about the person?
options: How does this volunteer feel about puzzles in general?
Which solver in the group works the fastest?
How much practice has each volunteer had?
What does the puzzle's structure allow and demand of any solver?
optionExplain: Feelings concern the person, not the puzzle's structure.
Speed compares persons.
Practice is a characteristic of the solver.
Right: it asks about the task environment.
questions.explain: Task structure and person are separate sources of behavior. The card next gives the authors' three questions about them.

questions.q: The authors first analyze the task ____, then examine some human behavior in detail, then take a broader view.
questions.explain: The order mirrors the cryptarithmetic chapters: task environment, detailed behavior, broader view.

questions.q: Which of these is one of the three questions the authors ask again about logic?
options: How many subjects can be recruited to attempt all sixteen problems at Yale?
To what extent is behavior set by the task environment or by the subject's own characteristics?
Which of the twelve rules is the easiest to teach to a subject who knows no logic?
What did the original authors of the task intend it to measure in their subjects?
optionExplain: A logistical matter, not one of the three questions.
Right: this is the third of the three questions.
Teaching ease of rules is not among the three.
Intent of the task's designers is not one of the three.
questions.explain: The three: do humans work in problem spaces, what organizations and heuristics do they show, and task versus person.

questions.q: Put the parts of Chapter 8 in the order the authors announce.
items: The basic problem space in which all behavior occurs
A single program, the General Problem Solver
Sources of problem difficulty in the Yale data
questions.explain: The chapter moves from the space, to GPS in that space, to what makes problems hard for people.

questions.q: True or false: In Chapter 8 the General Problem Solver is used as a model of the subjects' behavior.
questions.explain: Here GPS is considered only as an example of a problem solving IPS for logic; its use as a model of human behavior is left to the next chapter.
questions.rule: GPS as model comes next chapter.

questions.q: A new unit analyzes a different puzzle after the book's cryptarithmetic and logic. Following the authors' practice, how independent is its analysis from the earlier ones?
options: It reuses the earlier problem spaces unchanged
It starts from human behavior and derives the task later
It depends on the earlier cryptarithmetic results to define its problem and its heuristics
It responds to the new task and data, relatively independently of the earlier analysis
optionExplain: The authors respond to each task's own nature.
The order is task first, then behavior.
Independence from the earlier analysis is the stated practice.
Right: the logic analysis was done in this way relative to cryptarithmetic.
questions.explain: The authors say that they will respond directly to the nature of the task and to the data, relatively independently of the cryptarithmetic analysis.
questions.rule: Treat each task on its own terms.
questions.teaches: Throughout the logic analysis the authors respond directly to the task and the data, relatively independently of the earlier cryptarithmetic analysis.

questions.q: A rule card shows a form with a double-headed arrow to another form. How should a solver read it?
options: Either form may be rewritten into the other
The first form may be rewritten, but not the second
Both forms must appear in a line before the rule applies
The rule may be used once only per problem
optionExplain: Right: a double head means both directions are allowed.
That describes a one-headed arrow.
Nothing in the arrow says both forms must be present.
No such limit is attached to an arrow.
questions.explain: Arrow heads show direction. The card next gives the logic sheet's reading.

questions.q: True or false: A transformation marked with a double-headed arrow may be made in either direction.
questions.explain: The authors state this directly for the rule sheet.

questions.q: Rule 8 is shown one-way: from A.B to A, and from A.B to B. A line reads P.Q. Which new line does rule 8 allow?
options: P V Q
P.Q.P
Q
Q ⊃ P
optionExplain: Joining with a wedge is a different rule (rule 9 adds a wedge to a single expression).
Rule 8 shortens a dot expression; it does not lengthen it.
Right: rule 8 keeps either side of the dot.
No rule 8 form produces a horseshoe.
questions.explain: Rule 8 reads one way: A.B yields A or B. Going from A back to A.B is not part of rule 8.
questions.rule: Follow the head of the arrow.

questions.q: Suppose rule 9, A to A V X, were double-headed. What new power would a subject gain? (Our reading)
options: Turning any line A into A.X by adding a dot
Nothing, since rule 9 can already be used on any line
Turning any line A V X into A, discarding the second part
Turning any line A V X into X V A
optionExplain: The rule concerns the wedge, not the dot.
Reversal is a new direction of change, so powers do change.
Right: the reverse direction would let a disjunction be cut to one side.
Swapping sides is rule 1, not a reversal of rule 9.
questions.explain: With a reverse head, the form at the head could be rewritten into the tail. Here that would drop X, which the one-way rule does not allow.

questions.q: Sort each rule form by whether Figure 8.17 shows it as running either way or one way only.

items.t: A V B with ~(~A.~B), rule 5
A V (B.C) with (A V B).(A V C), rule 7
A.B giving A, rule 8
A giving A V X, rule 9

questions.explain: Rules 5 and 7 are double-headed; rules 8 and 9 run one way.

questions.q: A subject holds P V (S ⊃ T) and wants to apply rule 6 (A⊃B with ~A V B) to only the part S ⊃ T. May the subject do so?
options: Yes, giving P V (~S V T), since rules may apply to parts of an expression
No, rules apply only to the whole expression and cannot touch a part inside it
No, because a horseshoe may only change at the leftmost end
Yes, but the result is P V (S ⊃ ~T)
optionExplain: Right: rules can be applied to subexpressions as well as whole expressions.
Many rules can be applied to subexpressions as well.
Position within the expression does not restrict rule 6.
Rule 6 changes the horseshoe into ~S V T; T keeps its sign.
questions.explain: The authors note that many operators can apply to subexpressions as well as to the total expression; their example applies rule 6 inside P V (Q ⊃ R).
questions.rule: A rule may fit a part of a line.
questions.teaches: Many rules can be applied to subexpressions as well as to the total expression.

questions.q: A rule sheet turns A into NOT A. How could it avoid ever writing NOT NOT A?
options: Forbid solvers from using any NOT marks
Require solvers to erase NOT NOT at the end of the problem
Allow NOT NOT but treat it as a different symbol
Build the cancelation into the rule so the sign is removed
optionExplain: That would remove negation from the task.
The sheet avoids the double mark in the first place.
That would add a symbol rather than avoid the pair.
Right: the rule itself changes the sign, so no double mark appears.
questions.explain: Built-in sign changes avoid double marks. The card next shows the logic sheet's version.
questions.rule: Let the rule cancel the sign.

questions.q: The rules make changes in ____ so that multiple negation signs do not arise.
questions.explain: The rule sheet records sign changes so that tildes do not pile up.

questions.q: Rule 2 turns A ⊃ B into ~B ⊃ ~A. Applied to R ⊃ ~S (so A is R and B is ~S), what line results under the task's convention?
options: S ⊃ ~R
~S ⊃ ~R
S ⊃ R
optionExplain: A double tilde never appears; it is removed instead.
Right: ~B becomes S, and ~A becomes ~R.
The sign on S must change because B was already negated.
A is R, so ~A is ~R, not R.
questions.explain: B = ~S, so ~B is S. A = R, so ~A is ~R. The result is S ⊃ ~R.

questions.q: True or false: Applying rule 2 twice in a row to S ⊃ ~R returns the original line S ⊃ ~R.
questions.explain: S ⊃ ~R becomes R ⊃ ~S, and applying rule 2 again gives S ⊃ ~R.

questions.q: Per the authors, applying rule 2 to ~P ⊃ Q (A is ~P, B is Q) gives which line?
options: ~Q ⊃ P
Q ⊃ ~P
~P ⊃ ~Q
optionExplain: Right: the result is written without a double tilde.
The book says the result is ~Q ⊃ P rather than ~Q ⊃ ~~P.
Neither part would be unchanged in sign under rule 2.
This negates only B; rule 2 also trades places.
questions.explain: The authors' example: rule 2 on ~P ⊃ Q yields ~Q ⊃ P, not ~Q ⊃ ~~P.
questions.teaches: Applying rule 2 to ~P ⊃ Q with A = ~P and B = Q yields ~Q ⊃ P rather than ~Q ⊃ ~~P.

questions.q: The sheet notes that rule 2 applies only with a horseshoe, trades the two places, and makes two sign changes. A subject applies it to P ⊃ Q. How many tildes does the result have?
options: None, in Q ⊃ P
One, in ~Q ⊃ P
Four, in ~~Q ⊃ ~~P
Two, in ~Q ⊃ ~P
optionExplain: Two sign changes mean both parts change sign.
Rule 2 changes the sign of both parts, not one.
Under the convention no double tildes appear.
Right: both parts change sign, adding a tilde to each.
questions.explain: Each rule on the sheet notes how many sign changes it makes; rule 2 makes two, one in each part.
questions.teaches: The rule sheet notes beside each rule where it may be used and how many sign changes it makes, for example two for rule 2.

questions.q: Given that the match is off if it rains, and that it rains, what follows in ordinary reasoning?
options: It rains, and so the match is on
The match is off
Nothing follows, because there are two statements
The match is off only if it stops raining
optionExplain: This contradicts the first statement.
Right: given the condition and its cause, the result follows.
Two statements can together yield a third.
The first statement already ties rain to the match being off.
questions.explain: That pattern, from A ⊃ B and A to B, is one of the twelve rules. The card next lists them all.

questions.q: Match each rule to what it does.
pairs: Keeps either side of a dot
Adds a wedge and any expression to a line
Joins two lines with a dot
Chains A ⊃ B and B ⊃ C into A ⊃ C
questions.explain: Rule 8 shortens, rule 9 extends, rule 10 conjoins and rule 12 chains horseshoes.

questions.q: A subject holds the lines P ⊃ Q and Q ⊃ S. Which rule produces P ⊃ S?
options: Rule 11
Rule 10
Rule 12
Rule 2
optionExplain: Rule 11 needs A ⊃ B together with A itself, giving B.
Rule 10 joins two lines with a dot, giving a conjunction.
Right: it chains two horseshoe lines that share the middle term.
Rule 2 turns one horseshoe around; it uses a single line.
questions.explain: Rule 12 takes A ⊃ B and B ⊃ C and gives A ⊃ C; here A is P, B is Q and C is S.

questions.q: Which of these rules take two lines as input?
options: Rule 10
Rule 7
Rule 11
Rule 12
optionExplain: Right: it joins two lines with a dot.
It reshapes a single expression.
Right: it uses A ⊃ B and A.
Right: it uses A ⊃ B and B ⊃ C.
questions.explain: Rules 10, 11 and 12 are the two-line rules; the others change one expression.

questions.q: A subject has the line P V Q and applies rule 8 to obtain P. What is wrong with this step?
options: Rule 8 never shortens a line
Rule 8 needs two lines as input
Rule 8 may be used only on the first line of a problem
Rule 8 works on a dot expression, not on a wedge
optionExplain: Shortening is exactly what rule 8 does for a dot.
Rule 8 is a one-line rule.
No such restriction exists.
Right: rule 8 keeps one side of A.B.
questions.explain: Keeping one side belongs to a dot; for a wedge, other rules apply. Rule 8 is used only with a major dot and a positive total expression.

questions.q: A subject has only the line S and the target S V ~T. Which rule gets there directly?
options: Rule 1, since the wedge sides can be swapped
Rule 9, with ~T in the place of X
Rule 3, since T may be dropped
Rule 8, since one side of the dot is kept
optionExplain: Rule 1 reorders a line that already has a wedge.
Right: X may be any expression, so S V ~T follows from S.
Rule 3 removes repeats; there is none here.
There is no dot, and rule 8 shortens.
questions.explain: Rule 9 may add any coded expression through X, which is why it can create a very large number of new expressions.
questions.teaches: In rule 9 the X may be any coded expression, so rule 9 can create arbitrarily many new expressions.

questions.q: In a puzzle where you start with some statements and may write new ones by permitted rules, what is the state of your work at any moment?
options: Only the newest statement you have written
Only the target statement you are aiming at
All the statements you have, given and derived so far
The count of rules you have used so far
optionExplain: Earlier statements stay available for later moves.
The target is the goal, not the work done so far.
Right: the work so far is the collection of everything on hand.
A count of rule uses leaves out what was produced.
questions.explain: The state of work is the whole collection on hand. The card next calls this the knowledge state.
questions.rule: State is everything derived so far.

questions.q: Match each part of the basic problem space to what it is in the logic task.
pairs: The expression or expressions L1, L2 and so on
questions.explain: The space is built from expressions, rules, the givens and the target.

questions.q: A problem has two given expressions. The subject makes three successful rule applications. How many expressions are in the knowledge state?
options: Five
Three
Two
Six
optionExplain: Right: the two givens plus one new expression per success.
The three derived expressions are joined by the two givens.
The givens are still there, and derived expressions add to them.
Each success adds one expression, not two.
questions.explain: Each successful application adds a new expression to the collection, so 2 + 3 = 5.

questions.q: True or false: When a rule is applied successfully, a new expression is added to the knowledge state and the input expression stays.
questions.explain: The knowledge state is a growing collection: each success adds a new expression, and the input remains available.

questions.q: A student says the desired expression L0 is already in the knowledge state because it is written on the board from the start. What is wrong?
options: L0 belongs to the knowledge state only if it is also one of the given expressions L1 to Ln
L0 can never be produced by a rule application
L0 is the goal; it joins the derived expressions only when a rule application produces it
The knowledge state holds only the last derived expression
optionExplain: Givens and derived expressions form the collection; the goal is separate.
A problem is solved exactly when a rule application yields it.
Right: the problem is solved when a derived expression equals L0.
The state is the whole collection derived so far.
questions.explain: The target is displayed as a goal, not as a derived line. Our reading: the state changes only when a rule produces something.

questions.q: A recipe app holds pantry items, a goal dish and conversion steps; each product is added to the pantry. How would a researcher begin to gauge the size of the search?
options: Assume a simple scheme that applies every step at each point and see how fast the count grows
Wait until a skilled cook has solved the recipe and then time how long the cook took
Count only the steps in the shortest known recipe and treat that number as the size of the space
Assume each step is applicable at most once in the whole problem
optionExplain: Right: the authors begin with simple search schemes like the British Museum algorithm.
Timing an expert says little about the space; the authors estimate the size by counting.
That measures the solution, not the space searched.
That limits the space by assumption instead of estimating it.
questions.explain: Since these are clearly search problems, the authors gain a feel for the size by assuming simple schemes, as in Chapter 4 along the lines of the British Museum algorithm.
questions.rule: Estimate by counting a simple scheme.
questions.teaches: The authors get a feeling for the size of the search by assuming simple search schemes, as in Chapter 4, along the lines of the British Museum algorithm.

questions.q: A lock has 12 buttons and a code takes 3 presses. How many different press sequences are there?
optionExplain: This adds the choices, 12 + 12 + 12, instead of multiplying them.
Right: 12 x 12 x 12.
This counts only two presses.
This is 16 x 16 x 16, not 12 x 12 x 12.
questions.explain: Each press multiplies the possibilities by 12. The card next uses the same multiplication for logic proofs.

questions.q: The simplest estimate of the maze for the seven-step proof of D1 is 12 to the power ____.
questions.explain: Twelve operators at each of seven steps give 12^7, about 4 x 10^7.

questions.q: On the same assumption of twelve operators at each point, how many paths does a five-step proof have?
options: 5^12, which is about 244 million
optionExplain: This is 12 x 5, which adds instead of multiplying.
This counts four steps, not five.
This swaps the base and the exponent.
Right: twelve choices at each of five steps.
questions.explain: With b choices and n steps the count is b^n; 12^5 = 248,832.

questions.q: If a proof needed one more step, how would the simple estimate change?
options: It would grow by twelve paths, one for each of the twelve operators
It would be multiplied by twelve
It would double
It would stay the same
optionExplain: Paths multiply with each step; they do not rise by a fixed amount.
Right: each extra step multiplies the paths by the number of choices.
Doubling would suit two choices per step, not twelve.
More steps give more paths to thread.
questions.explain: Each added step multiplies the maze by twelve, which is why long proofs are so hard to find by blind search.
questions.rule: One more step, twelve times the maze.

questions.q: True or false: The 12^7 figure is only a rough count, since not every operator is applicable to every expression.
questions.explain: The authors say this is only the simplest scheme; not every operator applies to every expression.
questions.rule: The figure is a rough count.

questions.q: A phone menu offers twelve options on each screen, but several are greyed out on most screens. How does that bear on the estimate 12^n for n screens?
options: It makes 12^n too low, since greyed options add paths
It leaves 12^n exact, since the options still exist on the menu even when they are greyed out
It makes 12^n irrelevant
It makes 12^n too high on that account, as the authors note for operators such as R7
optionExplain: Unavailable options remove paths, not add them.
Existing in the list is not the same as being usable.
The estimate stays a rough upper figure; n is known for a given proof.
Right: if an option is rarely available, fewer paths exist than 12^n suggests.
questions.explain: The authors point out that not every operator is applicable to every expression; some, like R7, rarely are. That pushes the count down while other factors push it up.
questions.teaches: Some operators, like R7, are rarely applicable, which works on the side of decreased growth.

questions.q: In a game where you may combine any two items you own into a new item, how does your item count grow compared with rules that use one item at a time?
options: Faster, since the number of pairs grows with the square of the items
The same, since each combination uses up the two items that were combined
More slowly, since pairs are harder to find
Only as fast as the number of single items
optionExplain: Right: pairs multiply much faster than single items.
Combining two items adds an item and does not use up the inputs.
Hard-to-find does not mean fewer; pairs outnumber single items.
Pairs outnumber single items once there are a few of them.
questions.explain: Combining pairs is a squaring effect. The card next names it as one of the factors.

questions.q: Which of these make the logic search space grow faster? Select all that apply.
options: Rules can be applied to subexpressions
Not every operator applies to every expression
Two-input rules add expressions in proportion to the square of those available
R9 can put any expression in place of X
The target expression L0 is fixed
optionExplain: Right: more places to apply a rule.
This works the other way, shrinking growth.
Right: pairs outgrow single items.
Right: arbitrarily many outputs.
A fixed target does not enlarge the space.
questions.explain: Subexpressions, two-input rules and R9 enlarge the space. Limited applicability shrinks it.

questions.q: Ten expressions are available and a two-input rule can pair any two of them. By the authors' squaring rule, how many new expressions does it add?
optionExplain: This doubles the count; two-input growth is not linear.
This is the number of inputs, not the number of pairs.
Right: the square of the number available.
This cubes the number rather than squares it.
questions.explain: Two-input operators add expressions in proportion to the square of the number available: 10 x 10 = 100.

questions.q: If the number of available expressions doubles, the output of a two-input rule such as R10 grows by a factor of ____.
questions.explain: Doubling the count multiplies the pairs by four: 20 x 20 = 400 against 10 x 10 = 100.

questions.q: A student reasons: some operators rarely apply, so the logic space must stay small. What does this overlook?
options: Rare applicability makes the space larger, not smaller
No operator is rarely applicable in the logic task
Three other factors increase growth, so rare applicability is only one opposing effect
Space size does not depend on how often operators apply, only on how many rules there are
optionExplain: Rare applicability reduces growth.
The authors say some operators, like R7, rarely apply.
Right: subexpressions, two-input rules and R9 push the other way.
The count of reachable expressions does depend on it.
questions.explain: The effects oppose each other. The authors list one decreasing factor and three increasing ones.

questions.q: A social app lets any two members be merged into a new group, and any group can be merged again. Which book statement about R10 helps predict its growth?
options: New expressions arise in proportion to the square of those available, exactly the square for R10
New expressions arise one per existing expression, so growth is linear in the number available
New expressions arise only from a fixed list of items, so growth stops once the list is used
New expressions do not arise once pairs are rejected, so a two-input rule adds nothing
optionExplain: Right: pairs of existing items give growth at the square.
That is linear growth, which the authors say two-input rules exceed.
R10 acts on whatever is derived, so the list is not fixed.
R10 does combine any two derived expressions.
questions.explain: R10 combines any two derived expressions into their conjunction, thus assuring growth at exactly the square of the number of previously derived expressions.
questions.teaches: R10 assures growth at exactly the square of the number of previously derived expressions.

questions.q: Each extra part in a design multiplies the number of possible designs by 100. How many more designs have four parts than two?
options: About 200 times as many
About 400 times as many
About 100 times as many
About 10,000 times as many
optionExplain: This adds two hundreds instead of multiplying twice.
This doubles the multiplication in a wrong way.
This counts only one extra part, not two.
Right: two extra parts give 100 x 100.
questions.explain: Two extra parts multiply twice. The card next gives the same rule for expressions.

questions.q: The number of expressions rises by a factor of about ____ for each increase of one in size.
questions.explain: With three distinct letters, each added term multiplies the number of expressions by about 100.

questions.q: A ring of size three holds N expressions. About how many does the ring of size five hold?
options: About 200 N
About 10,000 N
About 100 N
About 1,000 N
optionExplain: This adds 100 twice instead of multiplying.
Right: two extra terms mean two factors of 100.
This counts only one extra term.
This is 10 x 100, which is not two factors of 100.
questions.explain: Size five is two steps beyond size three, and each step multiplies by about 100.

questions.q: Per the picture, a solver starts on D1's four-term L1 and heads for a two-term L0. Compared with the starting ring, which rings does the dashed long-way-around path visit?
options: Larger ones, since complexity is added before it is simplified
Only smaller ones, as in the direct search, since each step simplifies the expression
Only rings of exactly the starting size
No rings, since it leaves the space
optionExplain: Right: the path goes outward before coming back in.
The direct path moves toward smaller rings; the dashed path does not.
The dashed path changes size.
Both paths lie inside the space.
questions.explain: The dashed path makes things more complex before simplifying them, so it passes through larger rings.

questions.q: True or false: On the ring picture, the area of the rings grows as fast as the number of expressions in them.
questions.explain: The authors say the number of expressions rises much faster than the increase in area on the figure indicates.
questions.teaches: The number of expressions rises much faster than the increase in area of the rings in Figure 8.4 would suggest.

questions.q: To reach a town directly across a river, a driver must first drive away from it to find a bridge. In the rings picture, which path is this like, and how likely is a solver to try it first?
options: The solid direct path, the first thing a solver tries
A path through the smallest ring only, tried by every solver
No path, since a detour cannot appear in the space
The dashed long-way-around path, an unlikely direction to search at the start
optionExplain: The solid path is the direct search; the detour is the dashed one.
The detour passes through larger rings.
The authors draw the detour as a possible path.
Right: the authors call the detour an unlikely direction initially.
questions.explain: The authors call the longer path an unlikely direction in which to search initially, and say they will return to problems that require such excursions.
questions.rule: Detours exist but are rarely tried first.
questions.teaches: The long way around, which makes things more complex before simplifying, is an unlikely direction in which to search initially; problems requiring such excursions are discussed later.

questions.q: A tool can be tried at 6 places in a line, but works in only half of them. On average, how many places does it work?
optionExplain: This ignores that the tool works at only half of them.
Right: 6 places times one half.
This doubles instead of halving.
This divides by three instead of two.
questions.explain: Expected successes equal places times the chance of success. The card next applies this to rule R1.
questions.rule: Places times the fraction that fit.

questions.q: In a four-term expression R1 can apply at ____ connective locations, but only where the connective is a wedge or dot.
questions.explain: R1 has three places and works at two of the three cases, so it yields 3 x (2/3) = 2 expressions.
questions.rule: Three places, two out of three.

questions.q: A rule can apply at 4 connective locations and works in 1 case out of 2. How many expressions does it yield on average?
optionExplain: This forgets the half of the cases where it fails.
This multiplies by 2 instead of by one half.
Right: 4 x 1/2.
This takes the fraction alone, not times the places.
questions.explain: Average yield is places times fraction: 4 x 1/2 = 2.

questions.q: True or false: R9, applied to a two-term expression, can contribute a very large number of new four-term expressions, 216 in all.
questions.explain: R9 contributes a total of 216 expressions, which is why not all contributions are below one.

questions.q: R4 regroups chains such as A V (B V C). Which expression can R4 not be applied to?
options: P V (Q V R)
P.(Q.R)
(P V Q) V R
P V ~(Q V R)
optionExplain: Both connectives are wedges and the subpart is positive, so R4 applies.
Both connectives are dots and the subpart is positive, so R4 applies.
Both connectives are wedges, so R4 applies in the reverse direction.
Right: the subpart has a negative sign, and R4 needs a positive subpart.
questions.explain: For each subexpression R4 needs both connectives to be wedges or both dots, and the sign of the subpart to be positive; P V ~(Q V R) fails the sign test.
questions.teaches: R4 requires that its two connectives be both wedges or both dots and that the sign of the subpart be positive, so it does not apply to P V ~(Q V R).

questions.q: A machine has a button that can produce hundreds of different items from any one input. Which statement from the book fits a decision to use it sparingly?
options: Its low productivity is the reason such a rule is used with discretion
Its high productivity is the reason such a rule, like R9, is used with discretion
Its productivity matters only when the machine is idle
Discretion matters only for rules that take two inputs
optionExplain: The reason is high, not low, productivity.
Right: the authors say high productivity is the very reason R9 is used with discretion.
The authors tie discretion to how many outputs it creates.
R9 takes one expression; the authors say R10 is similar.
questions.explain: The authors say this high productivity is the very reason R9, and similarly R10, is used with discretion.
questions.teaches: The high productivity of R9 and, similarly, R10 is the very reason they are to be used with discretion.

questions.q: A pile grows thirty-fold with each step, starting from one item. About how many items after three steps?
optionExplain: This adds 30 three times instead of multiplying.
This is 30 x 30, which is only two steps.
Right: 30 x 30 x 30.
This is 30 to the fourth power, one step too many.
questions.explain: Each step multiplies the pile by 30. The card next gives the book's measured growth rate.

questions.q: With no limit on expression size, the number of expressions grows about ____-fold per step.
questions.explain: The top curve of Figure 8.5 grows about thirty-fold per step.

questions.q: On the lowest curve the growth is about 9 per step from one starting expression. About how many expressions after two steps?
optionExplain: Right: 9 x 9.
This adds 9 twice instead of multiplying.
This is the count after one step only.
This is 9 to the third power, one step too many.
questions.explain: Two steps multiply by 9 twice: 81.
questions.rule: Raise the rate to the number of steps.

questions.q: A solver refuses to generate any expression larger than four terms, the size of L1 in D1. What happens to the growth rate?
options: It falls to nearly zero, so search becomes easy
It stays at about 30 per step
It falls to about 9 per step, still large
It rises, since small expressions multiply faster
optionExplain: Even the lowest curve is large enough to preclude brute-force search.
The size limit lowers the rate.
Right: the lowest curve shows about 9 per step.
Limiting size removes large expressions and lowers the rate.
questions.explain: Rejecting all added complexity lowers growth from about 30 to about 9 per step.
questions.rule: A size limit helps but does not solve it.

questions.q: True or false: With expressions limited to four terms, the search is small enough for a brute-force forward solver.
questions.explain: The authors say even the lower rates are large enough to preclude brute-force forward search.

questions.q: A planner leaves out the one action that would swamp its estimate, though the planner could not afford to use that action often anyway. Which part of the book's calculation is this?
options: Leaving out the contributions of R9 and R10, which it is also plausible to exclude
Keeping all expressions of whatever size, so that no expression is discarded as too large
Taking the starting expression to be of size ten
Plotting the logarithm of the count to make the growth rate look slower than it is
optionExplain: Right: both reasons support excluding them.
That is a separate assumption: all expressions are kept.
The calculation starts with one expression of size four.
The log scale shows exponential growth as a straight line; it does not slow it.
questions.explain: The calculation ignores R9 and R10 since they would swamp it, but excluding them is also plausible, since even a brute-force solver could not afford to use them very often.
questions.rule: Exclude what would swamp the count.
questions.teaches: Excluding R9 and R10 is plausible as well as convenient, since even a brute-force problem solver could not afford to use them very often.

questions.q: A counting model lets a bucket of small items grow without limit, although only 216 distinct small items can exist. What does the model ignore?
options: That small items are cheaper than large ones
That repeated items are not new items
That large items are made from small ones
That buckets cannot hold more than 216 items
optionExplain: Cost does not enter into counting distinct items.
Right: duplicates are not new, so distinct items are limited.
That is a different point; the issue here is repeats.
A bucket can hold repeats; only distinct items are limited.
questions.explain: Distinct items are fewer than items generated. The card next calls this the question of duplicates.

questions.q: Letting each size category grow indefinitely corresponds to a problem solver that does not check for ____.
questions.explain: Without a duplicate check, the same small expression may be generated again and again.

questions.q: With three letters there are six distinct one-term expressions. A solver generates one-term expressions 50 times in all. At most how many are distinct?
options: Fifty
Two hundred sixteen
One
Six
optionExplain: Fifty is the number generated, repeats included.
216 is the number of two-term expressions.
More than one distinct one-term expression is possible.
Right: only six one-term expressions exist.
questions.explain: There are only 6 distinct expressions of size one, however many are generated.
questions.rule: Distinct is at most the number that exist.

questions.q: True or false: Removing duplicates would change the overall growth rate of the estimate by a large amount.
questions.explain: The authors say the effect is too slight to show on the graph, since the limit bites first on the smallest expressions.

questions.q: A student says: since only 216 two-term expressions exist, the logic search must be small. What is wrong?
options: There are in fact many more than 216 two-term expressions, so the limit is far away
The limit bites first at the smallest expressions, which affect total growth little
Two-term expressions are never generated
Duplicates do not occur among small expressions
optionExplain: The authors give 216 with three letters.
Right: large expressions drive the total, and they are not capped so early.
Many small expressions are generated by breaking up large ones.
Duplicates are exactly what the limit concerns.
questions.explain: The total is dominated by larger expressions, so capping small ones changes little.

questions.q: An engineer builds a crude model of a city's streets to see how a naive route-finder would fare before judging a smarter one. Which purpose in the book does this match?
options: Showing that a smarter system is unnecessary
Replacing observation of real solvers
Proving that no procedure can find short routes, whatever heuristics it uses
Giving a feel for the search simple procedures need, as background for a smarter system
optionExplain: The calculations show how much search simple procedures need, motivating GPS.
The models are background; the book still uses human data.
The models make no such claim; GPS finds short paths.
Right: the authors use crude models as a background for GPS.
questions.explain: The authors say simplified models like this provide a feeling for the amount of search required by simple procedures, a background against which to view the mechanisms and heuristics of GPS.
questions.rule: A crude model is a yardstick.
questions.teaches: Simplified models provide a feeling for the amount of search required by simple procedures, a background for viewing the heuristics of a more intelligent system such as GPS.

questions.q: A cooking robot has one part that knows general planning procedures and another part that holds kitchen facts. What benefit comes from keeping them apart?
options: The planning part can be reused with other task knowledge
The robot can cook without any kitchen facts at all
The planning part becomes faster than any alternative
The kitchen facts no longer need to be correct
optionExplain: Right: a clean split lets the same mechanisms serve new tasks.
Without task knowledge the general part has nothing to work on.
Separation is about reuse, not speed.
Wrong facts still give wrong results.
questions.explain: Separating mechanisms from task knowledge makes reuse possible. The card next shows how GPS earned its name this way.

questions.q: GPS grew out of the work on ____ described in Chapter 4.
questions.explain: GPS is the successor of LT; its first task was the Moore-Anderson logic task.

questions.q: Which description fits the word general in the name General Problem Solver?
options: It was able to solve every problem presented to it, whatever the task environment
It was written to run on any computer of the period
A task-independent part is cleanly separated from task-environment knowledge
It contained no knowledge of any task environment at all
optionExplain: The authors do not claim this; the name is about structure.
Nothing in the account concerns machines.
Right: this is the authors' reason for the name.
It holds task knowledge, but in a separate part.
questions.explain: The name records the clean separation of general mechanisms from task knowledge.

questions.q: GPS is moved from the logic task to a new task. Which part must be supplied afresh? (Our reading)
options: The general problem solving mechanisms
Both parts, since they cannot be separated
The part holding knowledge of the new task environment
Neither part, since GPS needs no task knowledge
optionExplain: These are task-independent and carry over.
The design separates them cleanly.
Right: the general mechanisms stay and the task knowledge changes.
GPS needs task knowledge to work in any space.
questions.explain: With a clean split, new tasks need new task knowledge while the mechanisms stay.

questions.q: True or false: GPS received its name because it can solve any problem it is given.
questions.explain: The authors say the name comes from being the first program to separate task-independent mechanisms from task knowledge.

questions.q: How could the claim of generality be supported once GPS had worked on logic?
options: By running the same general part on other tasks with new task knowledge, as was later done
By showing that logic problems are the only ones that matter for a theory of problem solving
By removing the task knowledge from the logic version
By proving that no other program can solve logic problems
optionExplain: Right: GPS has since been applied to a number of tasks, and similar programs to others.
Generality concerns many tasks, not one.
GPS cannot work without task knowledge.
That would not show GPS works elsewhere.
questions.explain: The authors note that GPS has since been applied to a number of different tasks (Ernst and Newell, 1969) and that other programs of essentially similar structure have worked on yet other problems (Quinlan and Hunt, 1968).
questions.teaches: GPS has since been applied to a number of different tasks, and programs of essentially similar structure have worked on other problems.

questions.q: A saw turns logs into boards. In general terms, what is the saw?
options: A feature that logs and boards share
The difference between a log and a board
A goal that the carpenter must evaluate before deciding whether to start cutting
Something that acts on objects to produce different objects
optionExplain: A feature is something an object has; a saw is not part of the log.
A difference is observed between objects, not applied to them.
A goal says what is wanted; a saw is a means of getting it.
Right: it is an operator.
questions.explain: The saw acts on one object to make another. The card next names such things operators.

questions.q: Match each term to the example.
pairs: One board is longer than another
questions.explain: A saw operates on logs; wood is a feature; a length contrast between two boards is a difference.

questions.q: In the logic task, what plays the part of the operators?
options: The given expressions L1 to Ln
The twelve rules
The desired expression L0
The experimenter at the blackboard
optionExplain: The givens are objects.
Right: each rule turns expressions into other expressions.
L0 is a particular object, the goal.
The experimenter only records and checks the moves.
questions.explain: Expressions are the objects; the rules are the operators.

questions.q: True or false: Adding two numbers to produce their sum is an example of an operator that takes several objects as inputs.
questions.explain: The authors use this example for operators with several inputs and one output.

questions.q: Which of these is a kind of problem GPS can formulate with objects and operators?
options: Modifying an object so that a given operator can be applied to it
Deciding whether an operator is morally acceptable
Choosing the best operator without looking at any object
Counting the operators of a task, then stopping
optionExplain: Right: the authors list this among the kinds of problem.
Nothing like this appears in the formulation.
Operators act on objects, so objects matter.
Counting is not a problem of changing an object.
questions.explain: Besides transforming one object into another, problems include modifying an object so that an operator becomes applicable.
questions.teaches: One kind of problem in the objects-and-operators formulation is to modify an object so that a given operator may be applied to it.

questions.q: A tailor must produce any garment with a collar from cloth pieces and sewing steps. Which kind of problem is this in GPS terms?
options: Transforming a given object into one particular other object
Applying one named operator to one named object
Finding the differences between two named objects
Finding an object that possesses a given feature
optionExplain: A transform problem names the object to be reached; here any garment with a collar will do.
No single operator or object is fixed.
Differences are used along the way but are not the problem.
Right: the target is any object with a stated feature, not one particular object.
questions.explain: The authors list finding an object possessing a given feature as another kind of problem formulated in the same vocabulary.
questions.rule: Goals can be features, not only objects.
questions.teaches: Another kind of problem in this vocabulary is to find an object possessing a given feature.

questions.q: Compare two requests: turn this sheet of paper into a boat; fold this sheet in half. How do they differ?
options: The first names a particular action; the second asks for a result by any route
The first asks for a result by any route; the second names a particular action
Both name the action and differ only in difficulty
Both name the result and differ only in difficulty
optionExplain: This reverses the two requests.
Right: one fixes the end, the other fixes the operation.
The boat request does not name a fold.
Folding in half names an action, not a final shape.
questions.explain: One request fixes the end and leaves the means open; the other fixes the means. The card next gives GPS's names for them.

questions.q: True or false: A transform goal asks for a way to turn object 1 into object 2 by applying a sequence of operators.
questions.explain: A transform goal sets an end and leaves the sequence of operators open; an apply goal sets an operator and an object.

questions.q: Sort each logic goal as a transform goal or an apply goal.

items.t: Find L0 from L1
Apply R7 to L1
Get from R.(P V Q) to (P V Q).R
Use R8 on the left part of L2

questions.explain: Goals that name a target are transform goals; goals that name a rule are apply goals.

questions.q: True or false: A transform goal leaves the choice of operators open, while an apply goal names the particular operator to be used.
questions.explain: A transform goal asks for some sequence of operators; only an apply goal names one operator.

questions.q: Where do the principal heuristics of GPS reside?
options: In the executive that runs every goal, which is why the executive is the most complex part
In the description of the task environment alone
In the methods attached to the goal types, so the executive stays quite simple
In the experimenter's moves at the blackboard
optionExplain: The executive is a simple loop.
Task knowledge is held in a separate part.
Right: the heuristics are embedded in the methods.
The experimenter only records legitimate steps.
questions.explain: Each goal type has methods, and the principal heuristics sit in them.
questions.teaches: The principal heuristics of GPS are embedded in the methods, so the executive organization is quite simple.

questions.q: A GPS-style program is given a chess task. Could it pose a transform goal there?
options: No, since transform goals exist only for logic expressions and nothing else
No, since chess positions are not objects of the kind a transform goal needs
Yes, but only after the objects are turned into logic-style expressions
Yes, since a transform goal's objects may be any objects of the task environment
optionExplain: The goal type is general across tasks.
Any object defined in specifying the task environment qualifies.
No conversion is needed.
Right: goal types are task-independent.
questions.explain: The objects of a transform goal may be any objects defined in specifying the task environment.
questions.teaches: The objects of a transform goal may be any objects defined in specifying the task environment.

questions.q: Before starting a large task, a manager asks whether it is worth doing and whether success is likely. What is the manager doing?
options: Selecting a method
Evaluating the goal
Applying a method
Reporting success
optionExplain: A method is chosen after the goal passes evaluation.
Right: judging worth and likelihood comes before choosing an approach.
Applying is the step that follows choosing.
Success is reported only after a method works.
questions.explain: Judging a goal's worth and chances is evaluation. The card next gives GPS's version.

questions.q: Put the steps of the executive in order.
items: Evaluate the goal
Select a method for the goal
Apply the method to the goal
If the method did not succeed, return to evaluation
questions.explain: The loop runs evaluate, select, apply, and repeat on failure of the method.

questions.q: The executive evaluates a goal and rejects it. What does it do?
options: Selects the most promising method anyway
Applies the last method used on any goal
Stops and reports failure
Returns to step 1 and evaluates again
optionExplain: Selection happens only after the goal passes evaluation.
No method is applied to a rejected goal.
Right: a rejected goal ends the attempt.
Re-evaluation does not follow a rejection.
questions.explain: In step 1, a rejected goal means stop and report fail.

questions.q: True or false: If no method can be selected for a goal, the executive stops and reports failure.
questions.explain: Step 2 says: if no method is found, stop and report fail.

questions.q: A reader says that when a method fails the executive returns to the selection step. What does Figure 8.6 show?
options: It returns to step 1, the evaluation of the goal
It returns to step 2 and tries the next method
It stops and reports failure at once
It returns to step 3 and applies the same method again
optionExplain: Right: the loop restarts with evaluation.
The figure sends control to step 1.
Failure of a method repeats the loop; only rejection or no method stops it.
The figure does not repeat the method without re-evaluating.
questions.explain: A failed method sends control back to step 1, so the goal is evaluated afresh before another method is chosen.

questions.q: A project lead's routine is evaluate, choose an approach, carry it out. Some approaches spawn smaller projects that go through the same routine. Which GPS feature is that?
options: The executive is never used for subgoals
Each goal has exactly one method and no subgoals
Methods create subgoals and evoke the executive on them
Evaluation happens only for the first goal
optionExplain: Subgoals are attempted by the same executive.
Methods work by creating subgoals.
Right: the executive does not fully show GPS's control, since methods set up subgoals.
Each goal, including subgoals, is evaluated.
questions.explain: The authors note that the executive does not fully reflect the control structure of GPS, since methods attempt to achieve a goal by creating subgoals and then evoke the executive for them.
questions.teaches: The executive of Figure 8.6 does not fully reflect GPS's control structure, because methods create subgoals and evoke the executive to attempt them.

questions.q: To book a venue you must check the guest list, and to check it you must ask relatives. What structure do these tasks form?
options: Goals nested inside goals
Independent goals with no links
A single goal with no parts
Goals done in parallel by different people
optionExplain: Right: each task depends on a smaller one within it.
Each one here depends on the next.
There are three levels of task.
The tasks are linked in sequence, not parallel.
questions.explain: Nested goals are the mark of a recursive structure. The card next shows it in GPS.

questions.q: Since each method finishes a subgoal before returning, GPS is basically a ____-first problem solver.
questions.explain: Depth-first means everything appropriate to a subgoal is tried before control returns.

questions.q: Put these events in the order depth-first control handles them.
items: The method for goal A creates subgoal B
The method for B creates subgoal C
Subgoal C is attempted completely
Control returns to the method for B
Control returns to the method for A
questions.explain: C is finished first, then control passes back up to B and then to A.

questions.q: Subgoal B ends, in success or failure. Where does control go next?
options: To a fresh goal chosen at random
To the method of the goal that evoked B
To the first goal ever created
To the executive, which discards the creating goal
optionExplain: Control returns to the creator of B.
Right: control returns to the goal that created the subgoal.
Only the creating goal's method regains control.
The creating goal's method continues.
questions.explain: A method resumes when its subgoal has been attempted fully.

questions.q: A reader says: depth-first means the method tries only the first step of each subgoal and then moves on. What is wrong?
options: Depth-first means all subgoals are tried at the same moment
Depth-first means the main goal is dropped once a subgoal is set
Depth-first means every goal has exactly one subgoal
It tries everything appropriate to the subgoal before returning control
optionExplain: That would be a parallel scheme.
The main goal's method resumes later.
A method can create several subgoals in turn.
Right: each subgoal is worked through before control returns.
questions.explain: The authors define the depth-first behavior as exhausting what is appropriate for a subgoal before control returns.

questions.q: A textbook explains a lab's software through a simplified version, saying a fuller version exists elsewhere. How does that match the book's GPS?
options: The authors describe the fullest version of GPS that exists, including all of its later additions
The authors describe a simpler version of GPS, since the Ernst and Newell (1969) version is more elaborate
The authors say that no fuller version of GPS exists beyond the one they describe in this chapter
The authors describe a version of GPS that was never implemented on any computer of the period
optionExplain: The authors say the Ernst and Newell version is more elaborate.
Right: the simpler structure serves the authors' purposes.
A more elaborate version exists.
The planning method was partly unimplemented, but this is a separate matter.
questions.explain: A footnote says the version of GPS in Ernst and Newell (1969) is more elaborate, but the simpler structure described here will serve the authors' purposes.
questions.rule: Use the simplest version that serves.
questions.teaches: The version of GPS in Ernst and Newell (1969) is more elaborate than the simpler structure the authors describe.

questions.q: Your car will not start and you must reach a meeting. What is the most useful first question?
options: Which of all possible actions should I try in turn until one of them works?
Which part of the car looks oldest, and so most likely to have failed?
What did I do the last time this happened, and can I repeat it?
What is the difference between where I am and where I need to be, and what changes it?
optionExplain: Trying everything in turn ignores what you are after.
Age is not tied to the difference you want to remove.
A past event may help but does not name the difference.
Right: name the difference, then look for what removes it.
questions.explain: Naming the difference and what changes it guides the search. The card next calls this means-ends analysis.

questions.q: Put the parent's chain of questions in the order of the book's example.
items: What is the difference between what I have and want? Distance
What changes distance? The automobile
What is needed to make the automobile work? A new battery
What has new batteries? An auto repair shop
questions.explain: The chain runs from the difference, to the means that removes it, to what that means needs, to who supplies it.

questions.q: You want a picture on the wall and have a picture but no hole. In means-ends terms the difference to remove is that the wall has no ____.
questions.explain: Means-ends analysis names the difference, here a missing hole, and then looks for a means that makes one.

questions.q: Which procedure is means-ends analysis?
options: Compare what you have with what you want, then pick actions that change that difference
Apply every available action in turn and keep the one that happens to work
Repeat the last successful action again and again until the time runs out
Choose actions according to how often they were used before in similar tasks
optionExplain: Right: actions are chosen by the differences they remove.
That is blind trying, the kind of search the size estimates warned about.
Repetition ignores the difference to be removed.
Frequency of use does not relate action to difference.
questions.explain: Means-ends analysis connects actions to differences. Blind enumeration does not.
questions.rule: Pick actions by the difference they change.

questions.q: In the book's example, the repair shop does not know a battery is needed. What kind of difficulty does the parent then face, and what addresses it?
options: One of distance, which another automobile removes
One of money, which a bank allows
One of communication, which a telephone allows
One of time, which a clock allows
optionExplain: Distance was the first difference; the shop's ignorance is a new one.
The example does not turn to money.
Right: the chain continues with a new difference and a new means.
Time is not what the example names.
questions.explain: The shop does not know of the need, so the difficulty is one of communication, and a telephone allows communication.
questions.rule: Each means can raise a new difference.
questions.teaches: In the example, the shop's not knowing a battery is needed is a difficulty of communication, and what allows communication is a telephone.

questions.q: A tenant wants a broken heater fixed, but the landlord does not know it is broken. Which step of the car example does this repeat?
options: The original difference of distance is restated
A new battery is bought for the car instead of the heater being fixed, as in the story
A new difficulty of communication arises after the means has been chosen
The chain ends because no means is available
optionExplain: Nothing in the heater case concerns distance.
The heater case has no battery.
Right: the landlord's ignorance is a communication difference to remove.
A means exists: telling the landlord.
questions.explain: The chain of ends and means can open a new difference, here the landlord's ignorance, which communication removes.
questions.teaches: Means-ends analysis can run on past the first means: after the repair shop is chosen, the difficulty of communication leads to the telephone.

questions.q: You have a flat tire and a loose bell and must ride today. Which should you fix first?
options: The flat tire, since it blocks riding
The bell, since it is quicker
Neither until both can be fixed together
Whichever the shop recommends
optionExplain: Right: attack the difficulty that matters most.
Quick fixes do not remove the blocking difficulty.
Fixing the main difficulty first is sensible.
Importance, not a recommendation, decides here.
questions.explain: Some difficulties matter more than others. The card next lists this among the assumptions behind means-ends analysis.

questions.q: Match each assumption to the condition it states.
pairs: A given object that is not the desired one differs from it in noticeable ways
Operators change some features and leave others as they were
Some differences are harder to remove than others
questions.explain: The three listed assumptions are detectable differences, characteristic operators and unequal difficulty.

questions.q: Painting a chair red changes its color and leaves its shape. Which assumption does this show?
options: Differences are always detectable
Hard differences should be removed first
An inapplicable operator may need its input modified so that it fits the object
Operators affect some features and leave others unchanged
optionExplain: This is a separate assumption about detecting differences.
The painting example is not about ranking.
The paint case has no inapplicable operator.
Right: painting is characterized by what it changes.
questions.explain: Painting is described by the change it produces, which is the second assumption.

questions.q: True or false: When GPS ranks difference X as harder than difference Y, it works on Y first.
questions.explain: The assumption favors removing the more difficult difference first, even at the cost of introducing easier ones.

questions.q: A desired operator cannot be applied to the object in hand. According to the assumptions, what may be profitable?
options: Discarding the operator for good
Modifying its inputs so that the operator becomes applicable
Waiting until the operator becomes applicable by itself without any change to the object
Applying it anyway, whatever the input
optionExplain: The assumption keeps the operator and changes its inputs.
Right: change the object until the operator fits.
Operators do not become applicable without a change of input.
An inapplicable operator cannot be applied.
questions.explain: The third assumption: if a desired operator is not applicable, it may be profitable to modify its inputs so it becomes applicable.
questions.rule: Fit the input to the operator.
questions.teaches: If a desired operator is not applicable, it may be profitable to modify its inputs so that it becomes applicable.

questions.q: A mover scuffs a hallway wall slightly to get a piano through the door. Which part of the fourth assumption does this show?
options: Removing a hard difference even at the cost of new, lesser differences
Refusing any new difference, so that each step must leave the object closer in every way
Removing the easy differences first
Leaving every difference in place until a single operator can remove them all together
optionExplain: Right: a minor scuff is accepted to remove the main obstacle.
The assumption accepts minor new differences.
The mover removes the hard obstacle first.
The aim is to remove the hard one.
questions.explain: The assumption says it is profitable to eliminate difficult differences even at the cost of introducing new differences of lesser difficulty, repeating while progress is made.
questions.rule: Trade a hard difference for easier ones.
questions.teaches: It is profitable to eliminate difficult differences even at the cost of introducing new differences of lesser difficulty, as long as progress is made toward eliminating the more difficult ones.

questions.q: To turn a messy desk into a tidy one, what is the first move that follows the idea of finding a difference and removing it?
options: Throw away everything on the desk
Start with whatever is nearest and see what happens, without comparing the desk to the tidy one
Redesign the desk before touching any item
Compare the two and name a main difference, such as papers on the floor
optionExplain: This ignores the difference you want to remove.
Nothing links the action to a difference.
Redesign is not a step toward the tidy state.
Right: find a difference first.
questions.explain: Finding a difference comes first. The card next gives GPS's three steps.
questions.rule: Find a difference, then reduce it.

questions.q: Put the steps of the transform method in order.
items: Match object 1 to object 2 to find a difference
Set up a reduce subgoal for the difference
Obtain the new object from the reduced difference
