Set up a transform goal from the new object to object 2
questions.explain: Match, reduce, take the new object, then transform again.

questions.q: A gardener wants a lawn cut to 5 cm and finds it is 12 cm. After mowing, the gardener checks the lawn again. Which step of the method is the check?
options: Matching object 1 to object 2 for the first time, before any difference is removed
Setting up a transform goal from the new object to the desired one
Selecting a goal type
Abandoning the original goal
optionExplain: The first match found the difference before mowing.
Right: after the reduce, the new object is compared with the target again.
The check is a goal, not a goal type selection.
The original goal is achieved if the new transform goal is achieved.
questions.explain: The new object is again to be transformed into object 2; this recursion repeats the method.

questions.q: True or false: When the reduce subgoal in step 2 fails, the transform method stops and reports failure.
questions.explain: Without the reduced object there is nothing to transform further; step 3 of Figure 8.8 says: if fail, stop and report fail.

questions.q: When the transform method finds no difference between object 1 and object 2, what does it report?
options: That the goal has failed
That a reduce goal must be set up anyway
That the goal is achieved, and it stops
That it must try a different object 2
optionExplain: Nothing remains to do, so the goal is achieved.
A reduce goal needs a difference to reduce.
Right: with no difference, the transform goal is already achieved.
The target is not changed.
questions.explain: In the program of Figure 8.8 step 1, if there is no difference the method stops and reports achieved.
questions.teaches: If matching finds no difference, the transform method stops and reports that the goal is achieved.

questions.q: A proofreader compares a draft with a clean copy and fixes the worst mismatch first, then compares again. Which feature of the transform method does this show?
options: The match ignores all differences except the smallest
The match is made only once for the whole task
The match chooses a difference at random
The match tests for the more important differences first
optionExplain: The method picks important differences first.
The method matches again after each reduce.
The match goes by importance.
Right: the worst mismatch is handled before smaller ones.
questions.explain: The authors say the match in step 1 tests for the more important differences first.
questions.teaches: The match in step 1 of the transform method tests for the more important differences first.

questions.q: A key does not fit because the door is jammed. What sensible approach resembles GPS?
options: Insist on turning the key harder with no change to the door, until it gives way
Remove the difference that blocks the fit, then try the key again
Give up on keys altogether
Replace the door with a new one without trying
optionExplain: Force does not remove the difference.
Right: change the object until the operator fits.
Keys can be used once the blockage is removed.
Replacing everything is far from reducing one difference.
questions.explain: A blocked operator is fixed by removing the difference that blocks it. The card next gives the method.

questions.q: In the apply-operator method, the object is compared with the ____ of the operator, its input form.
questions.explain: The condition of the operator is its input form; the product is its output form.

questions.q: GPS wants to apply rule 8, which needs a dot expression, to P V Q. According to the method, what comes next?
options: Write the output form of rule 8 at once
Report that the goal is achieved
Set up a reduce subgoal for the difference between P V Q and the rule's input form
Delete the rule from the rule sheet
optionExplain: The output is produced only after the operator is applied.
The operator has not been applied yet.
Right: step 2 reduces the difference to the condition.
Rules are never deleted.
questions.explain: The operator's condition is not met, so GPS reduces the difference first.

questions.q: The difference to the condition has been reduced successfully. What does the method do next?
options: Sets up an apply subgoal for the operator and the new object
Returns the old object unchanged and reports that the operator was applied to it
Creates a new operator
Stops and reports failure
optionExplain: Right: step 3 sets up the apply goal on the modified object.
The modified object is the one used.
The operator stays the same.
Success of the reduce leads to a new apply goal.
questions.explain: In step 3 an apply goal is set up on the modified object.

questions.q: True or false: If the operator can be applied immediately, the method first sets up a reduce subgoal.
questions.explain: Step 1 applies the operator at once when it fits; only if it does not fit does a reduce subgoal arise.

questions.q: A recipe step is defined by a program of actions, not by an input form and an output form. How does the book treat such an operator?
options: The same method applies without any change
Such operators cannot be used by GPS
Variants of the method exist for operators defined by a program
Such operators are treated as goals
optionExplain: The method is described for operators with two forms.
The authors note variants of the method for them.
Right: the described method is for two-form operators only.
Operators and goals remain distinct.
questions.explain: The authors say this method suits operators defined by two forms, and that variants exist for operators defined by a program, described iteratively or recursively.
questions.rule: Fit the method to the operator's definition.
questions.teaches: Variants of the apply-operator method exist for operators defined by a program, described iteratively or recursively.

questions.q: To remove a stain, you look for a cleaner suited to that stain. What is that step in means-ends terms?
options: Searching for an operator relevant to the difference
Choosing the cleaner by price
Evaluating whether the stain is worth removing at all before choosing a cleaner
Comparing the stain with a clean shirt
optionExplain: Right: pick the means that bears on this difference.
Price is not relevance to the stain.
Evaluation is the executive's first step.
That is the match that finds the difference.
questions.explain: A relevant operator is one that bears on the difference at hand. The card next gives the reduce method.

questions.q: Match each method to its main steps.
pairs: Match, reduce the difference, then transform the new object
Apply at once, or reduce the difference to its condition and apply again
Find a relevant operator, then set up the apply goal
questions.explain: Each goal type has its method: transform, apply and reduce.

questions.q: GPS sets up the goal reduce difference Ap between L1 and L0. What does the reduce method do first?
options: Applies every rule in turn to L1
Searches for an operator relevant to reducing Ap
Reports that Ap is achieved
Matches L1 to L0 to find another difference before choosing any operator
optionExplain: The method looks for relevant operators, not all of them.
Right: step 1 of the reduce method.
The difference has not yet been reduced.
Matching belongs to the transform method.
questions.explain: The reduce method begins by searching for a relevant operator.

questions.q: True or false: If the reduce method finds no operator relevant to the difference, it reports failure.
questions.explain: Step 1 reads: if fail, stop and report fail.

questions.q: Put the first three goals of the simple example a1 in order.
items: Transform L1 into L0
Reduce a position difference between L1 and L0
Apply rule 1 to L1
questions.explain: The transform goal creates the reduce goal, which creates the apply goal.

questions.q: A plumber tries one tool on a leak, it fails, and the plumber looks for another tool relevant to the same leak. Which step of the reduce method is this?
options: Reporting failure at once
Matching the leak to a clean pipe in order to find a new difference to reduce
Setting up a new transform goal from the leaking pipe to the repaired pipe
Going back to search again for a relevant operator after the apply goal fails
optionExplain: The method continues the search before failing.
That is a match for a new difference.
Transform goals belong to the transform method.
Right: step 3 sends control back to step 1.
questions.explain: In Figure 8.8, step 3 of the reduce method says: if the apply goal fails, go to step 1 and look for another operator.
questions.teaches: In the reduce method, if the apply goal fails, control goes back to step 1 to search for another relevant operator.

questions.q: Comparing the expressions Q and ~Q, what differs?
options: The letter used
The negation sign
The number of letters
The order of the parts
optionExplain: Both use Q.
Right: one is negated and the other is not.
Both contain one letter.
A single letter has no order to compare.
questions.explain: The sign is what differs. The card next names this As.

questions.q: Match each difference to what it compares.
pairs: A variable present in one expression but not the other
A variable occurring a different number of times
questions.explain: At is terms, An is counts, Ac is connective, Ag is grouping and Ap is position.

questions.q: Which difference separates P ⊃ Q from P V Q?
options: As, the sign
Ap, the position of the parts
Ag, the grouping
Ac, the binary connective
optionExplain: Neither expression is negated.
P and Q occupy the same places.
Neither has grouping parentheses.
Right: the horseshoe differs from the wedge.
questions.explain: Both expressions hold P and Q in the same places; only the connective changes.

questions.q: P ⊃ (Q V R) and (Q V R) ⊃ P hold the same parts in different places. The book's two-letter name for this difference is ____.
questions.explain: The same parts sit in different places: this is Ap, the difference of position.

questions.q: A reader calls the difference between P . Q and (P . Q) ⊃ Q a +t difference because Q is needed. What is wrong?
options: Q is already present, so the difference is one of count, +n
The difference is in sign, As
The difference is in position, Ap
There is no difference between the two expressions
optionExplain: Right: another Q is needed, not a new letter.
No sign differs.
Positions are not the issue.
The second contains an extra Q.
questions.explain: At concerns a variable missing altogether. Here the variable exists but must occur once more.
questions.rule: Missing letter is t; extra occurrence is n.

questions.q: Two cups differ in color and also in where they sit, and one difference is in a part of a cup, its handle. Can GPS-style differences be of that kind for logic expressions?
options: No, only one difference may exist for a pair of expressions, and it must be of the whole
No, differences concern only whole expressions, so a part of an expression cannot differ
Yes: several may exist at once, and they apply to parts as well as to whole expressions
Yes, but only differences of sign can occur inside a part of an expression
optionExplain: Several differences may exist simultaneously.
They apply to subexpressions as well.
Right: the authors say both.
All six kinds may occur in parts.
questions.explain: The authors state that the differences apply to subexpressions as well as total expressions, and several may exist simultaneously.
questions.rule: Differences can be many and local.
questions.teaches: The differences apply to subexpressions as well as total expressions, and several differences may exist simultaneously for the same expressions.

questions.q: A repair guide lists, for each symptom, the tools that can affect it. What does that help a repairer do?
options: Rank the symptoms by cost
Predict when a tool will break
Choose a tool relevant to a symptom
Replace the repairer's own judgment
optionExplain: The guide links symptoms and tools; it does not rank costs.
Nothing in it concerns breakage.
Right: it links symptoms to tools.
It is a lookup aid.
questions.explain: A symptom-to-tool lookup is what GPS needs for differences and operators. The card next names it the table of connections.

questions.q: Put these differences in the order of importance GPS uses, most important first.
items: +t, a term to add
-n, a count to reduce
As, a sign
Ac, a connective
Ag, a grouping
Ap, a position
questions.explain: The ranking runs +t, -t, +n, -n, As, Ac, Ag, Ap.
questions.rule: Terms, counts, sign, connective, grouping, position.

questions.q: Which is ranked more important: a term that must be added (+t), or a difference in grouping (Ag)?
options: The term that must be added
The difference in grouping
They are ranked equally
It depends on the expression's length
optionExplain: Right: +t is first in the ranking.
Ag ranks near the bottom.
The ranking is strict.
Length does not enter the ranking.
questions.explain: +t is the most important difference; Ag is among the least.

questions.q: True or false: Trading a +t difference for an Ap difference counts as progress under the ranking.
questions.explain: Ap is ranked below +t, so exchanging the more important difference for a less important one is progress.

questions.q: How do differences inside subexpressions compare in importance with differences between whole expressions?
options: They are more important than whole-expression differences
They are equally important
They are ignored by GPS altogether
Subexpression differences are less important than differences of the whole expressions
optionExplain: The criteria rank them lower.
The criteria make a distinction.
They are considered, but ranked lower.
Right: this is part of the criteria of progress.
questions.explain: The criteria state that all differences in subexpressions are less important than differences in expressions.
questions.teaches: All differences in subexpressions are less important than differences in the whole expressions.

questions.q: A repair guide marks cells with + or - to show whether a tool adds or removes something. What does a + in the first row of the book's table mean?
options: The operator is the most expensive one to apply, so it is tried only when the others fail
The operator affects the first difference by adding a term, +t
The operator is applicable to every expression
The operator is used only once
optionExplain: Cells show effects on differences.
Right: the sign in a row is read as that row's difference with the sign attached.
Cells show effects, not applicability.
No use limit is recorded in the table.
questions.explain: The figure explains that a + in the first row means +t, a - means -t, and so on for the other rows.
questions.rule: Read the sign with the row.
questions.teaches: In the table of connections a + in the first row means +t and a - there means -t, with the same reading for the other rows.

questions.q: You hold R . (~P ⊃ Q) and need (Q V P) . R. What is the most obvious difference?
options: R is at the left end in one and at the right end in the other
The expressions use different letters
One expression is negated as a whole and the other is not, so the signs differ
One expression has more terms
optionExplain: Right: the position of R differs.
Both use P, Q and R.
Neither is negated as a whole.
They have the same number of terms.
questions.explain: A change of place is a position difference. The card next walks through how GPS handles it.

questions.q: Put the rule applications that solve a1 in order.
items: Apply rule 1 to L1
Apply rule 6 to the left part of L2
Apply rule 1 to the left part of L3
L4 matches L0
questions.explain: R moves right, the horseshoe becomes a wedge, and the wedge sides swap.

questions.q: Which rule does the table of connections point to for the position difference Ap between L1 and L0?
options: Rule 8
Rule 9
Rule 12
Rule 1
optionExplain: Rule 8 shortens a dot expression.
Rule 9 adds a wedge part.
Rule 12 chains two horseshoe lines.
Right: rule 1 swaps the two sides of a dot or wedge.
questions.explain: Ap is the difference rule 1 affects; GPS therefore sets up the goal to apply rule 1.

questions.q: If L1 had been (~P ⊃ Q) . R, the step that moves R by applying rule ____ would no longer be needed.
questions.explain: R is already at the right end, so only the left part needs changing.

questions.q: In the trace GPS tried rule 5 on left(L2) and rejected it. Why?
options: Rule 5 produced a wrong expression, which the program then recognized as invalid
The difference to be reduced first was no easier than the one it came from
Rule 5 was not on the rule sheet, so it could not be applied to any line
The experimenter refused the move
optionExplain: The attempt was rejected before it was applied.
Right: the trace notes the attempt was no easier than goal 6.
Rule 5 is on the sheet.
This is the program's own evaluation, not the experimenter's.
questions.explain: Making rule 5 applicable required reducing a connective difference no easier than the goal it was meant to serve, so the goal was rejected.
questions.rule: Reject a subgoal no easier than its parent.
questions.teaches: GPS rejected the goal of making rule 5 applicable to left(L2) because it was no easier than the goal it arose from.

questions.q: A planner's log shows extra bookkeeping goals that the printed program does not create. How do the authors treat the trace of a1?
options: As wrong, since a trace that differs from the printed program should be thrown out
As produced by a human subject, not by GPS, which explains the extra bookkeeping goals
As from a slightly different version that makes a transform goal for the match step
As showing that the printed program is mistaken, so that Figure 8.8 must be corrected
optionExplain: The authors keep it and explain the difference.
It is a GPS trace.
Right: that explains the extra goals 4, 8, 11 and 15.
The note says the version is slightly different.
questions.explain: A note says the trace belongs to a version slightly different from Figure 8.8: it creates a transform goal to carry out the match of step 1 of the apply-operator method, which accounts for goals 4, 8, 11 and 15.
questions.rule: Read traces against the right version.
questions.teaches: The trace of a1 comes from a slightly different version of GPS that creates a transform goal for the match in the apply-operator method, giving goals 4, 8, 11 and 15.

questions.q: You must combine two documents into a third but hold only one. What must you work out?
options: Only which document to throw away
Only how to copy the document in hand
Nothing, since a single document in hand is enough to produce the third one
Which role the document in hand plays, and where to find the other
optionExplain: Nothing needs to be thrown away.
Copying does not supply the second document.
A two-input step needs both inputs.
Right: both the role and the missing partner must be settled.
questions.explain: A two-input step needs a role for the document in hand and a partner. The card next shows how GPS does this.

questions.q: GPS handles the problem of a two-input rule by treating it as another ____ and setting up a reduce goal for it.
questions.explain: No special machinery is added: the missing second input is just another difficulty to be reduced.

questions.q: GPS applies a chosen input of R12 to L3. What is the result?
options: A new expression added to the board as the next numbered line, with the rule named
A partially specified one-input operator, not a new expression
A report that R12 cannot be used
The desired expression L0
optionExplain: The result is an operator, not an expression.
Right: it is an operator waiting for its other input.
The attempt succeeds in producing the operator.
L0 appears only at the end, after more steps.
questions.explain: Because only one of R12's two inputs is supplied, the product is a one-input operator, Q12.
questions.rule: One input fixed, one left open.

questions.q: True or false: Q12 is applied to every one of the nine expressions on the display at once.
questions.explain: The difference of a single expression against a set leads GPS to select one expression from the display, with a similarity test.

questions.q: Why can the selection of an input from nine expressions be done well?
options: Q12 has no information about the input, so any expression is as good as another
The experimenter marks the correct expression
Q12 carries extra information about the needed input, used in a similarity test
Only one of the nine expressions has a horseshoe
optionExplain: It carries more information than a bare rule form.
No such marking exists.
Right: A ⊃ ~R is more specific than A ⊃ B.
The selection rests on similarity to the needed form.
questions.explain: The partially specified operator carries additional information about the expression needed, namely A ⊃ ~R instead of just A ⊃ B, and a similarity test performs a substantial selective function.
questions.teaches: A partially specified operator carries extra information about the expression needed (A ⊃ ~R rather than A ⊃ B), so a similarity test can select well among many expressions.

questions.q: A kitchen program adds a special goal to choose an item from the pantry for any multi-ingredient step. How does this relate to the book?
options: It is like the extra method and goal type in the Ernst and Newell (1969) version of GPS
It is how the book's GPS handles every operator, whatever the number of its inputs
It shows that two-input rules cannot be handled by GPS, which is why they are avoided
It is exactly the scheme the Yale experimenters used to record the subjects' moves
optionExplain: Right: that version handles multiple-input operators with a method and a select-from-set goal type.
The book's GPS uses the reduce-goal scheme instead.
They can; there are several ways.
The experimenters have no such program.
questions.explain: A footnote says the version of GPS in Ernst and Newell (1969) has an additional method for multiple-input operators and an additional goal type to select an element from a set.
questions.rule: There is more than one way.
questions.teaches: The version of GPS in Ernst and Newell (1969) has an additional method for multiple-input operators and an additional goal type to select an element from a set.

questions.q: After the direct ways to remove an unwanted ingredient all fail, what might a cook do?
options: Give up and serve nothing
Repeat the failed ways again in the same order, hoping for a different result
Look over everything on hand for an item already prepared that gets near the dish
Throw away everything on hand and start again from the raw ingredients
optionExplain: The search continues after direct ways fail.
Failed ways are remembered, not repeated.
Right: step back and survey what is already available.
That would remove useful material.
questions.explain: Surveying what is on hand is one way to continue. The card next shows GPS doing this on D1.

questions.q: Put the rules GPS considers, in turn, for eliminating terms in D1 in order.
items: R8
R7
R3
questions.explain: The authors list the rules in this order: R8, R7, R3, R11 and R12.

questions.q: Which are reasons the trace gives for rejecting a path in D1? Select all that apply.
options: The expressions become too complex
GPS remembers the result was already tried and failed or was rejected
The experimenter refuses the rule application
The fifteen-minute time limit runs out
optionExplain: Right: this is one of the two reasons.
Right: remembered failure also ends a path.
The trace concerns GPS's own evaluations.
The GPS trace is not tied to the subjects' time limit.
questions.explain: Complexity and remembered failure are the two stated reasons.

questions.q: True or false: Once every direct way of eliminating the R's has been rejected, GPS gives up on D1.
questions.explain: GPS looks over the whole set of expressions and then selects earlier goals as new starting points, which leads to the solution.
questions.rule: Dead ends lead to new starts.

questions.q: GPS had rejected working on L3 in G46, yet works on L3 in G47. How is that explained?
options: Choosing goals as new starting points is working forward, so GPS ignores its earlier negative evaluation
The experimenter cancelled the rejection of G46, so GPS was free to work on L3 again afterwards
L3 was changed between the two goals, so GPS was in fact working on a different expression
GPS had forgotten that G46 failed
optionExplain: Right: adding terms was judged too difficult, but GPS is prepared to ignore that.
GPS itself decides to revisit.
The same expression is worked on.
The authors say it ignores the evaluation, not that it forgot.
questions.explain: GPS is prepared in G47 to ignore its previous negative evaluation (adding terms is too difficult) and work on L3.
questions.rule: Revisit a rejected line when new starts are needed.
questions.teaches: GPS, when selecting goals as new starting points, is prepared to ignore a previous negative evaluation, such as adding terms is too difficult, and work on the same expression.

questions.q: A mechanic makes a part for one repair and finds it also fits another job. Which point in the D1 trace is this like?
options: A rule is rejected because the result is too complex or has already been tried
An expression generated for another purpose may already be what is needed
The experimenter supplies a missing expression
A goal is dropped because it was tried before
optionExplain: That concerns rejection, not reuse.
Right: expressions made to make an operator applicable can turn out useful.
GPS generated the expression itself.
That concerns remembered failure, not reuse.
questions.explain: The authors note that expressions can be generated for other purposes, such as making an operator applicable, so an interesting expression may already have been generated; this is why GPS looks over the whole display.
questions.rule: Check what is already on hand.
questions.teaches: Expressions can be generated for other purposes, such as making an operator applicable, so an interesting expression may already have been generated.

questions.q: A diagram records only the finished moves of a puzzle solver. What might it fail to show?
options: How many moves were made
Which moves came first
Whether the puzzle was solved by the person at the end of the session
Why those moves were made, that is, the goals behind them
optionExplain: A list of moves does show their number.
Order is shown in a list of moves.
Whether the end was reached can be read from the moves.
Right: reasons and goals are not visible in moves alone.
questions.explain: Moves alone leave out the goals behind them. The card next gives the authors' two ways to show more.

questions.q: In the compact PBG form, only the transform and apply goals are operators, and the ____ are shown as state information in the boxes.
questions.explain: Differences such as -t, +t and Ac appear in the boxes of Figure 8.14.

questions.q: Which PBG form do the authors use for their subjects?
options: The form with rule applications alone as operators, which leaves much of the search unexplained
The form with only transform and apply goals as operators and differences in the boxes
The form with every goal as an operator, including goals that produce no product
A table of times with no graph, listing how long each subject spent on each rule
optionExplain: That is Figure 8.12, which leaves much unexplained.
Right: it is the compact form of Figure 8.14.
That is the fuller fragment of Figure 8.13.
The subjects' graphs are PBGs.
questions.explain: The compact form compresses the horizontal scale and is the one used for subjects.

questions.q: True or false: In the PBG of rule applications alone, an attempt to apply R7 that does not succeed is visible.
questions.explain: Only successful rule applications appear, so the guiding role of R7 is nowhere apparent; this suggests viewing the goals as operators as well.

questions.q: In the fuller form of Figure 8.13, what does an arrowhead on a goal's line signify?
options: The goal failed
The goal was rejected by the evaluation before any method had been selected
The goal was chosen by the experimenter
The goal produces a product, such as a new expression
optionExplain: Failure is not marked by an arrowhead.
Rejection is not what the arrowhead shows.
The experimenter plays no part in GPS goals.
Right: goals that produce a product have an arrowhead.
questions.explain: Goals that produce a product have an arrowhead; goals that do not have none and are held in the goal stack as context.
questions.teaches: In Figure 8.13, goals that produce a product have an arrowhead; a goal without one is stored in the goal stack to provide context.

questions.q: On a manager's board, a task stays open while its subtasks finish and is picked up again afterwards. Which PBG feature is that?
options: A goal in the stack is reapplied when its subgoals finish, drawn as a double line
An arrowhead that marks a product
A box holding a new expression
A dashed line for a path that went the long way round and added complexity first
optionExplain: Right: the goal is taken up again after its subgoals.
That marks products, not a resumed goal.
That is state information.
That belongs to the ring picture in Figure 8.4.
questions.explain: When subgoals are finished, whether successfully or not, the goal in the stack is reapplied; this is indicated by the double line.
questions.rule: A double line marks a resumed goal.
questions.teaches: When subgoals are finished, successfully or not, the stacked goal is reapplied, which is indicated in the PBG by a double line.

questions.q: Walking from town A to town B, you stay near the straight line between them. Why is this efficient?
options: It makes the map itself smaller
It guarantees the shortest path in every kind of terrain, whatever lies between
It confines your exploration to a narrow band and ignores the rest of the map
It makes every path equally long
optionExplain: The map is unchanged; only your exploration is limited.
A river or wall can force a detour.
Right: most of the map becomes irrelevant.
Paths differ in length whatever you do.
questions.explain: Staying near the line shrinks what you explore. The card next gives the book's version.

questions.q: Means-ends search stays within a narrow ____ joining the initial and terminal objects.
questions.explain: The band is the region between start and goal in which the search stays.

questions.q: A space holds a trillion objects, but a given problem's band holds a thousand. On what does the search size mainly depend?
options: The size of the whole space, so that the search is about as large as a trillion objects
The number of rules on the rule sheet
The size of the band, which is small and independent of the whole space
The number of subjects in the experiment
optionExplain: That would be so for undirected search.
The count of rules does not set the band's size.
Right: only the band is searched.
Subjects do not set the size of a search space.
questions.explain: Provided the search stays in the band, its size does not grow with the space.

questions.q: True or false: Means-ends analysis cannot miss a path, because its band covers the whole space.
questions.explain: The band is narrow, and the only path between two small expressions might pass through a very large one; the authors say the method can be wrong.

questions.q: Under what condition would solving be an entirely purposeful activity with no trial and error?
options: Differences split into non-interacting elementary ones, each removed by an operator that adds no new difference
Every operator is applicable to every expression, so that any operator can be used at any point of the search
The goal expression is smaller than the starting expression, so that each step shortens the line
The problem has been solved before by another subject, whose recorded path can then be followed exactly
optionExplain: Right: nothing then interferes.
Applicability is not the condition the authors name.
Size alone does not remove interactions.
Previous solutions are not the condition.
questions.explain: If differences can be factored into elementary ones that do not interact, each with an operator that removes it cleanly, solving needs no trial and error.
questions.teaches: If differences factor into non-interacting elementary differences, each with an elementary operator that removes it without introducing new differences, solving is entirely purposeful with no trial and error.

questions.q: A repair kit has tools that each fix exactly one fault without causing another, while a second kit has tools that fix one fault and create another. Which kit calls for search, per the authors?
options: The first, since single-purpose tools take longer to find and use than general ones
Neither, since a kit needs no search once the faults are known
Both equally, since the faults to be repaired are the same in the two kits
The second, since interactions among differences make some search necessary
optionExplain: Their independence removes the need for search.
Interactions generally make some search necessary.
Interactions, not faults, decide it.
Right: new faults from a fix force trial and error.
questions.explain: Interactions among differences, or the unavailability of operators for individual differences, generally make a certain amount of search necessary (Ernst, 1969).
questions.teaches: Interactions among differences, or the lack of operators to handle individual differences independently, generally make a certain amount of search necessary.

questions.q: In a maze, which information helps most: only the exit's position, or both the entrance and the exit?
options: Only the exit's position
Both, since the relation between them shows which way to go
Neither, since a maze has no direction
Only the entrance, since the exit does not matter
optionExplain: The exit alone says little about the route from where you are.
Right: the relation between the ends gives a direction.
Positions of entrance and exit do suggest a direction.
The goal matters for choosing a direction.
questions.explain: The relation between the two ends is what directs the search. The card next states this for GPS.

questions.q: True or false: GPS works backward from the goal object.
questions.explain: The authors say that in fact GPS works forward, using the relation between start and goal.

questions.q: Sort each description as working backward or as means-ends analysis.

items.t: Start from the goal object and let it anchor the search
Compare the current object with the goal and remove a difference
Choose operators for the differences they remove between current and goal objects
Build the solution from the end toward the givens

questions.explain: Backward methods anchor on the goal; means-ends uses the relation between both ends.
questions.rule: Anchor on the goal, or on the gap.

questions.q: What does using the relation between both terminals give the search?
options: A far more powerful direction than the goal alone
No direction at all
A guarantee of the shortest path
A reversal of the search from goal to start, so that it runs backward
optionExplain: Right: the gap guides every step.
The relation supplies direction.
No such guarantee is claimed.
GPS works forward.
questions.explain: The authors say means-ends analysis imposes a far more powerful directionality on the search.

questions.q: A reader says: GPS uses information about the goal, so it must be a backward searcher. What is wrong?
options: GPS ignores information about the goal and works only from the givens, step by step
Backward searchers do not use the goal object at all, so GPS cannot be one of them
GPS searches in both directions at once and meets in the middle of the space
It uses the relation between goal and current object, and it works forward
optionExplain: It uses a great deal of it.
Backward methods start from the goal.
The authors say it works forward.
Right: information about the goal is used, but the search runs forward.
questions.explain: Using goal information does not make a search backward. GPS works forward with differences.

questions.q: A guidebook says a hiker should compare their position with the summit and choose each step to reduce the gap. Another says to plan the route from the summit down. Which is closer to LT's method, per the authors?
options: The gap-reducing guide, as LT used means-ends analysis
The summit-down plan, a simple working-backward method like LT's
Neither, since LT used no direction
Both, since they are the same method
optionExplain: The authors set GPS's method against LT's.
Right: LT used simple working backward.
LT's method is the backward one they cite.
The authors distinguish the two methods.
questions.explain: The authors say means-ends analysis is to be distinguished from a simple working-backwards method, like that used by LT.
questions.teaches: LT used a simple working-backwards method, which the authors distinguish from the means-ends analysis of GPS.

questions.q: You sketch a road trip on a map without street details, then fill in the streets. Why does that help?
options: The sketch removes the need to travel
Street details do not matter to a trip, so they can be left out altogether
The sketch is a simpler problem, and the fill-in steps are short problems
The sketch makes the map larger, so that more of the route can be seen
optionExplain: The trip still has to be made.
The details are filled in afterwards.
Right: simple first, then small pieces.
Abstraction removes detail, not adds it.
questions.explain: Planning splits a hard problem into a simpler outline and small pieces. The card next gives GPS's version.

questions.q: Put the four steps of the planning method in order.
items: Abstract the objects and operators by omitting details
Form and solve the problem in the abstract space
Use the abstract solution as a plan
Translate the plan back and execute it
questions.explain: Abstract, solve, take the plan, translate back and carry out.

questions.q: Suppose each step offers about 10 choices and exploration grows as 10 to the number of steps. A 12-step problem is split into three 4-step problems. About how do the amounts of search compare?
options: About the same, since the total number of steps is unchanged
Roughly 36 for the whole against 12 for the pieces
Roughly 10^4 for the whole against 10^12 for the pieces
Roughly 10^12 for the whole against about 3 x 10^4 for the pieces
optionExplain: Exponential growth makes short pieces far cheaper.
This treats growth as linear.
This reverses the two amounts.
Right: ten to the twelve against three times ten to the four.
questions.explain: Growth is exponential in steps, so splitting a long problem into short ones saves orders of magnitude. The numbers are an illustration, not the book's.

questions.q: True or false: Replacing a long problem by several shorter ones whose lengths add up to about the same total can reduce difficulty by whole orders of magnitude.
questions.explain: The authors say so, because exploration generally grows exponentially with the number of steps.

questions.q: Did the authors' GPS plan using all twelve rules?
options: Yes, it planned with every rule on the sheet, the two-line rules R10 to R12 included
No, it planned with R1 to R9 but not with the two-line rules R10 to R12
No, it planned with R10 to R12 only
Yes, but only for problem D1
optionExplain: The two-line rules were not used in planning.
Right: a complete planning method was never fully implemented.
The reverse is true.
The limit concerned the rules, not the problem.
questions.explain: A footnote says a complete planning method was never fully implemented: GPS planned with R1 to R9 but not with the two-line input rules.
questions.teaches: A complete planning method was never fully implemented for GPS: it planned with R1 to R9 but not with the two-line rules R10 to R12.

questions.q: An architect solves a layout problem by sketching on a floor plan, a simpler stand-in for the building. Which work do the authors cite as a similar auxiliary space?
options: The Yale experiments, where subjects were given alcohol and their problem solving was compared
Ernst and Newell's table of connections, which links each difference to the operators relevant to it
Gelernter's geometry programs, where the diagram serves as a powerful auxiliary problem space
The Moore-Anderson rule sheet, which the subjects used to recode the logic expressions
optionExplain: Those concern the effect of alcohol.
That is not an auxiliary space.
Right: the geometric diagram works as an auxiliary space.
The rule sheet is the main task, not an auxiliary space.
questions.explain: A footnote cites H. Gelernter's theorem-proving programs for plane geometry, where the diagram provides another example of a very powerful auxiliary problem space, though not one in which planning occurs.
questions.teaches: Gelernter's geometry theorem-proving programs use the diagram as a very powerful auxiliary problem space, though not one in which planning occurs.

questions.q: A map is simplified by ignoring road type and direction of travel. What kind of problem results?
options: A simpler one that records only which places are linked
A harder one with more roads
One that has no solution
The same problem with a new name
optionExplain: Right: links remain and details go.
Ignoring details removes roads' features, it does not add roads.
The simplified problem can still be solved.
Detail has been removed, so the problem is simpler.
questions.explain: Abstraction keeps the structure and drops detail. The card next shows what it drops for logic.

questions.q: The standard abstraction ignores differences among connectives, signs and the ____ of symbols.
questions.explain: These are the Ac, As and Ap differences.

questions.q: Apply the standard abstraction to (S ⊃ ~T) . (~S V U). What do you get?
options: (S~T)(~SU)
(S ⊃ T) . (S V U)
(ST)(SU)
(TS)(US)
optionExplain: The signs are dropped by the standard abstraction.
Connectives are dropped as well.
Right: connectives, signs and order are dropped, leaving the letters grouped as in the original.
The letters stay in their groups; the pairs here are mixed.
questions.explain: Each part keeps its letters: S and T in one group, S and U in the other.

questions.q: Put the abstract solution of D1 in order.
items: Apply R8 to the left part of (PR)(QR)
Apply R8 to the right part
Apply R12 to the two results
The result (PQ) is the abstract goal
questions.explain: Two R8 steps separate the parts and R12 joins them.

questions.q: In the original space, the three parts of the plan are apply goals 5, 7 and 9. How hard are they?
options: The first two are almost trivial and the third needs only five subgoals
All three are as hard as the original problem
The first is hard and the last two are trivial
None can be carried out
optionExplain: Right: carrying out the plan is much easier than the original search.
The plan reduces the difficulty.
The last, with R12, needs the subgoals.
The plan can be carried out in this case.
questions.explain: Goals 5 and 7 are achieved almost trivially, and goal 9 requires only five subgoals; the result, L5, is then transformed into L0.
questions.teaches: Of the three apply goals of the plan, the first two are achieved almost trivially and the third needs only five subgoals.

questions.q: A route planner first picks cities to pass through and then fills in the roads. Which fact does the book give about carrying out a plan from the standard abstraction?
options: Every step of the plan needs a new rule that is not on the original rule sheet
Only operators that become the identity on abstraction are needed to fill in the details
No steps are needed once the plan is made
The connecting steps involve R9 each time
optionExplain: The plan uses the sheet's own rules.
Right: the connecting steps use operators the abstraction ignores.
The plan must be implemented.
R9 and R10 are the productive rules, not the connecting steps.
questions.explain: The authors note that implementing the plan involves only operators that become the identity operator upon abstraction.
questions.rule: Details are filled by ignored operators.
questions.teaches: Implementing the plan involves only operators that become the identity operator upon abstraction.

questions.q: A shortcut you planned on a simplified map turns out to be blocked when you arrive. What does this show?
options: Simplified maps should not be used for planning
The street itself was imaginary, which is why the simplified map did not show it
The trip cannot be completed at all
A plan made from a simplified picture can prove impossible to carry out
optionExplain: They remain useful even when a plan sometimes fails.
The street was real; the map omitted the block.
Another route may work.
Right: simplification can hide what blocks the path.
questions.explain: Details left out may hide a block. The card next gives the authors' name for such a plan.

questions.q: Planning may generate no plan, a single plan, or ____ plans, and any plan found may be illusory.
questions.explain: The authors say planning offers no guarantees: it may generate none, one or several plans, and a plan may prove impossible to carry out.

questions.q: Two plans, P1 and P2, are generated for D1, and P1 turns out to be impossible to carry out when translated back to the concrete task. How do the authors say the effort wasted on P1 should be treated?
options: As a cost that must be counted when evaluating the planning heuristic
As nothing at all, since P1 was never a valid plan to begin with
As a cost charged to the problem space, not to the planning heuristic
As a cost counted only when every plan generated turns out to fail
optionExplain: Right: the time wasted in fruitless efforts to execute invalid plans must be counted in evaluating the planning heuristic.
The authors say the wasted time must be counted, even though the heuristic remains very powerful.
The cost belongs to the planning heuristic being evaluated, not to the space.
The authors count the wasted time whether or not a later plan succeeds.
questions.explain: The authors say a plan may prove illusory, and the time wasted in fruitless efforts to execute invalid plans must be counted in evaluating the planning heuristic.
questions.teaches: The time wasted in fruitless efforts to execute invalid plans must be counted in evaluating the planning heuristic.

questions.q: True or false: If planning generates no plan for a problem, that alone does not show the problem to be unsolvable.
questions.explain: Planning may generate no plan, one plan, or several; failing to produce a plan says nothing about whether a solution exists.

questions.q: A critic says: the cost of carrying out invalid plans can be ignored when judging planning. What do the authors say?
options: The cost is counted, and it shows that planning is useless for problems of this kind
The cost is ignored, because a plan that comes from the abstract space is valid by construction
The cost is counted only for the first plan
The time wasted on invalid plans must be counted, yet the heuristic remains very powerful
optionExplain: They judge it very powerful even so.
Plans can fail.
All wasted effort counts.
Right: they count the cost and still rate it highly.
questions.explain: The authors say the wasted time must be counted but that, allowing for it, the heuristic remains very powerful.

questions.q: A student's essay outline turns out to be impossible to write. Which plan in the book was like that?
options: The first plan generated for D1, R8, R11, R12
The second plan, R8, R8, R12
The plan of applying R1 to L1 in problem a1
The plan of choosing R9 as the last step
optionExplain: Right: it gives no valid derivation in the original space.
That plan can be carried out.
That belongs to the simple example, not to planning.
R9 as a last step is part of the simulation later.
questions.explain: Of the plans for D1, the first, R8, R11, R12, does not provide a basis for a valid derivation when translated back to the concrete task environment.
questions.rule: An illusory plan fails on translation.
questions.teaches: In the D1 example the first plan generated, R8, R11, R12, is illusory: it gives no valid derivation in the original task environment.

questions.q: A form has six yes/no options. How many different combinations of answers are possible?
optionExplain: This adds the choices, 6 + 6, instead of multiplying.
This is 6 x 6, not two choices six times.
Right: two choices six times, 2 to the sixth power.
This counts orderings of six items, not yes/no choices.
questions.explain: Each option doubles the combinations. The card next uses the same count for abstractions.

questions.q: Six differences give 2^6 = ____ possible bases for an abstraction.
questions.explain: Each subset of the six differences is a possible basis.

questions.q: Abstract only from sign (As) in L1 = (R ⊃ ~P) . (~R ⊃ Q). What results?
options: (PR)(QR)
(R V P) . (R V Q)
optionExplain: That is the standard abstraction, which drops more.
That is L1 itself, with the signs kept.
Right: the tildes are removed and everything else stays.
Connectives are kept under a sign-only abstraction.
questions.explain: Ignoring only sign removes the tildes and leaves connectives and order.

questions.q: Under the standard abstraction (As, Ac, Ap), sort each difference as essential or inessential.

items.t: At, terms present
An, number of occurrences
Ag, grouping
As, sign
Ac, connective
Ap, position

questions.explain: The standard abstraction ignores As, Ac and Ap, so those are inessential; the others stay.

questions.q: Why is a graph used to represent (An, Ac, As)?
options: Order, grouping and the identity of terms are kept, which no linear string can show
Graphs are shorter than strings, so the abstraction can be written in fewer symbols
The basis ignores the terms altogether, so only the shape of the expression is left
The experimenters preferred pictures, so the graph was drawn for the readers' benefit
optionExplain: Right: a graph preserves what a string cannot.
Length is not the reason.
The identity of terms is kept.
The reason is structural.
questions.explain: Information about order and grouping, and the identity of terms, is preserved, and no linear representation achieves this.
questions.teaches: Under the abstraction (An, Ac, As), information about order and grouping and the identity of terms is kept, which no linear representation achieves, so a graph structure is used.

questions.q: In a layered map, a rotate tool only changes orientation. If orientation is ignored in the simplified map, what does the tool become?
options: It becomes the most productive tool
It still changes the simplified map
It is replaced by a tool that adds letters
It does nothing, as R1, R2, R5 and R6 do under the standard abstraction
optionExplain: It no longer changes anything.
Its only effect is on what is ignored.
Nothing is added.
Right: an operator whose only effect is on ignored differences becomes the identity.
questions.explain: Under the standard abstraction four operators, R1, R2, R5 and R6, coincide with the identity operator and become irrelevant.
questions.teaches: Under the standard abstraction four of the operators, R1, R2, R5 and R6, coincide with the identity operator and so become irrelevant.

questions.q: A route planner can choose a very rough outline or a detailed one. What is lost with a very rough outline?
options: The outline becomes harder to understand
More outlines look workable but fail when you try to carry them out
The trip cannot start at all
The destination changes
optionExplain: A rough outline is simpler.
Right: roughness admits bogus plans.
A rough outline can still be started.
The destination is the same.
questions.explain: The rougher the outline, the more plans fail later. The card next names this as one of three aspects.

questions.q: Match each aspect of a good abstraction to what it concerns.
pairs: Its size and the difficulty of solving problems in it
How many plans are obtained that do not truly solve the problem
The original space, its size and difficulty
questions.explain: The three aspects are the planning space, spurious solutions and the implementation space.

questions.q: A candidate abstraction yields many plans that cannot be carried out in the original space. Which aspect does it do badly on?
options: The number of spurious solutions
The size of the planning space
The size of the original space
None, since failing plans are expected
optionExplain: Right: plans that fail are spurious solutions. (Our reading of the term.)
The failing plans do not tell us the planning space is large.
The original space is fixed by the task.
The count of such plans is one aspect of quality.
questions.explain: Our reading: spurious solutions are plans found in the planning space that do not work out in the original space.

questions.q: True or false: An abstraction that makes the planning space very small is bound to be good on all three aspects.
questions.explain: A very small planning space may give many spurious solutions and leave a hard implementation space; the aspects trade off.

questions.q: A designer judges an abstraction only by how easy the planning problem is. What is missing?
options: The cost of the experimenter's time, which the three aspects take into account as well
The number of subjects tested
The length of the problem statement, which sets how much detail the planner must keep
The spurious solutions and the difficulty of the implementation problems in the original space
optionExplain: The criteria are about spaces and solutions.
Subjects are not part of the criteria.
That is not one of the three aspects.
Right: the other two aspects.
questions.explain: The three aspects together decide whether an abstraction is good.

questions.q: A trip planner makes the high-level plan very short, so each local leg of the trip is very long. What does the book say about the total depth?
options: The total depth shrinks as the plan shortens, so both problems get easier together
The total depth is fixed, so a shorter plan lengthens the implementation problems
The total depth grows as the plan shortens
The total depth has no connection with the plan, which is judged on its own
optionExplain: The sum of depths stays fixed.
Right: shortening one lengthens the other.
It stays the same.
The sum is invariant under abstraction.
questions.explain: The total depth of the problem, the depth in the planning space plus the depths of all the implementation problems, is fixed. Shortening one lengthens the other, and vice versa.
questions.rule: The sum of depths stays put.
questions.teaches: The total depth of the problem, planning depth plus the depths of all the implementation problems, is fixed; shortening the planning depth lengthens the implementation depth, and vice versa.

questions.q: A ranked list of six items is split into a kept top part and a dropped bottom part, both non-empty. How many ways are there to split it?
options: Six
Sixty-four
Five
Twelve
optionExplain: Six items give five gaps between them, not six.
That counts every subset, not only top and bottom splits.
Right: the cut can fall in any of five gaps.
This counts neither subsets nor cuts.
questions.explain: A cut between ranked items gives one split per gap. The card next shows this for differences.

questions.q: Given the difference order, the possible planning spaces are the ____ divisions of the ordered list into two parts.
questions.explain: The top set is essential, the bottom set inessential.

questions.q: Differences a, b, c, d are ranked from most to least important. Which set of ignored differences fits the ordering?
options: a and d, skipping b and c
a and c
b alone
c and d, the bottom two
optionExplain: It ignores two differences but not those between them.
A higher difference is ignored while lower ones are kept.
A higher difference is ignored while lower ones are kept.
Right: it ignores a bottom block and keeps the top.
questions.explain: Ignored differences must form a block at the bottom of the ranking.

questions.q: True or false: The basis (Ap, At) fits the difference ordering that GPS uses.
questions.explain: It ignores a high and a low difference but not those between, so it violates the ordering, though it fits some other orders.
questions.rule: Do not skip over the middle.

questions.q: Per the authors, which GPS operators become identity operators if only Ap (the difference in position of components) is abstracted, and if all differences are abstracted? R1 is the rule that trades the places of the two parts of a wedge or dot expression, and R9 the rule that adds a disjunct to an expression.
options: Every operator in the first case, only R1 in the second
Only R1 in the first case, and every operator in the second
No operator in either case
Only R9 in both cases
optionExplain: This reverses the cases.
Right: nothing changes when all expressions are indistinguishable.
Abstraction does make operators identity.
R9 is not the operator in question.
questions.explain: Abstracting only from Ap makes only R1 an identity; abstracting from all differences makes all operators identities, since if all expressions are indistinguishable the operators change nothing.
questions.teaches: If only Ap is abstracted, only R1 becomes an identity operator; if all differences are abstracted, all operators do, because indistinguishable expressions cannot be changed.

questions.q: A renovator ranks features by importance and keeps the top ones in a sketch while dropping the rest. A colleague drops the most and the least important but keeps the middle. How does the book's reasoning treat that choice?
options: As the best choice because it is balanced between the most and least important differences
As impossible under any ordering
As inconsistent with the ordering, though it could fit a different ordering
As the same as dropping the bottom block
optionExplain: Skipping the middle violates the ordering.
It might fit another ordering.
Right: the same holds for (Ap, At) in GPS's ordering.
It is not the same.
questions.explain: The basis (Ap, At) is not consistent with the ordering GPS uses, but is consistent with some other difference orders.
questions.teaches: The basis (Ap, At) is not consistent with GPS's difference ordering but is consistent with some other difference orders.

questions.q: When assembling furniture you gather the pieces first and arrange them afterwards. Which differences concern the pieces themselves?
options: Which parts you have, not how they are arranged
How the parts are arranged once they have all been gathered together
The sign on each part
Where the furniture will stand
optionExplain: Right: materials come first.
Arrangement is the second stage.
Signs are part of how pieces are arranged in the expression.
That concerns neither stage.
questions.explain: Materials and arrangement are two stages. The card next uses the same idea for differences.

questions.q: Match each consideration to what it recommends.
pairs: Divide the differences about equally, near the middle
Remove connective differences from the abstract space
Keep the materials, drop the arrangement
questions.explain: The three considerations point to a similar split.

questions.q: Suppose connective differences were kept in the abstract space. What follows?
options: The abstract space would be much easier to search
All plans would be valid in the original space
Tracing plans through would be about as hard as solving in the original space
The planning method would no longer apply
optionExplain: Keeping connectives keeps the difficulty.
Nothing guarantees validity.
Right: the abstraction would save little.
It would apply, but gain little.
questions.explain: Limits on the applicability of operators in the abstract space would prevent plans from being followed through easily.

questions.q: In the material-arrangement analogy, the differences An and ____ determine what materials an expression contains.
questions.explain: An and At fix the letters an expression holds and how often; As, Ac, Ap and Ag fix how they are arranged.

questions.q: The criteria leave open whether Ag is essential. Why do the authors leave the ambiguity unresolved?
options: Only R4 would be handled differently, and it enters rarely into problems C1 and D1
Ag cannot be defined for logic expressions, so it cannot be classed either way
Ag matters for every rule in the same way, so the choice would change nothing
The experimenters ruled it out when they designed the rule sheet for the subjects
optionExplain: Right: the ambiguity has little effect on those problems.
Ag is defined as the grouping difference.
Only R4 is affected.
The authors do not report a ruling.
questions.explain: Only R4 would be handled variously by the two remaining alternatives, and it enters rarely into C1 and D1, so the ambiguity can stay.
questions.rule: Leave it if it does not matter.
questions.teaches: Whether Ag is essential is left open because only R4 would be handled differently by the two alternatives, and R4 enters rarely into problems C1 and D1.

questions.q: Subjects in the logic experiments seem to have used a material-arrangement abstraction. What do the authors suggest about its source?
options: It was taught to them by the experimenters, who explained it before the first problem
It may have come from a familiar everyday distinction, not from the formal features of the task
It came from solving all sixteen problems
It is a fixed property of every logic task, so any solver would find it without help
optionExplain: The subjects were not taught an abstraction.
Right: the analogy may have suggested it.
The suggestion concerns a familiar everyday distinction.
The authors suggest an everyday source.
questions.explain: The authors say the material-arrangement distinction is familiar from everyday situations, so the abstraction the subjects used may have been suggested by this analogy rather than by the formal features of the task.
questions.teaches: Because the material-arrangement distinction is familiar from everyday life, the abstraction the subjects used may have been suggested by that analogy rather than by the formal features of the task.

questions.q: To find which tools in a kit affect which problems, which method needs no outside help?
options: Ask a repairer to rank the tools from the most to the least useful one
Count how often each tool is used
Sort the tools by price
Compare what goes into each tool with what comes out
optionExplain: A ranking would be outside information, not derived from the tools.
Use counts do not say what a tool changes.
Price does not show what a tool changes.
Right: the effect of a tool shows in the change between input and output.
questions.explain: The change a tool makes shows in its input and output. The card next gives this as the way to derive the table.

questions.q: An operator is relevant to the differences it ____.
questions.explain: The table of connections lists, for each difference, the operators that reduce it.

questions.q: Rule 3 turns A V A into A. Matching its output to its input, which difference does the match find?
options: At, a variable missing from one side of the rule, so that it must be added
An, the number of occurrences of a variable
Ac, a change of connective
Ap, a change of position
optionExplain: A is present on both sides, so no variable is missing.
Right: A occurs twice in the input and once in the output.
The output has no connective to compare.
Nothing changes position; one copy of A disappears.
questions.explain: The count of A drops from two to one, which is an An difference.

questions.q: True or false: Matching the output of rule 2, ~B ⊃ ~A, to its input A ⊃ B finds the differences Ap and As.
questions.explain: Rule 2 swaps the parts and negates both, so the match finds a position difference and a sign difference.

questions.q: Why did the authors give GPS the differences and the table directly, instead of having it derive them?
options: Because the differences cannot be derived by any program, however it is built
Because the experimenters supplied the differences to the subjects on the rule sheet
Because the table of connections was unknown when the book was written in 1972
Subjects already hold such structure in long-term memory; otherwise much training is needed
optionExplain: The authors say derivation is possible.
The subjects were not given a table.
It had been derived earlier (Newell, 1962).
Right: the subject brings symbolic structure to the task.
questions.explain: The subject has dealt previously with symbolic parenthesized structures and holds a great deal of structure in long-term memory, ready to transfer to the new task; without it, much training would be required.
questions.teaches: Human subjects bring structure about symbolic parenthesized expressions from long-term memory, which is why giving GPS its differences and table is appropriate; otherwise much training would be needed.

questions.q: To find which kitchen tools change a dish's texture, a cook compares the dish before and after each tool, using the same comparison used to compare the dish with the target. What does the book say about the match used for the table?
options: It is exactly the same match process used elsewhere in GPS
It is a special process used only for deriving tables
It needs a human to judge each difference
It works only for rules with two inputs
optionExplain: Right: no new process is needed.
The authors say it is the same match used elsewhere.
The match is automatic.
It applies to the operators in general.
questions.explain: The relevant differences are found by matching the output expression to the input, with exactly the same match process that is used elsewhere in GPS.
questions.teaches: The relevant differences are found by matching an operator's output to its input with exactly the same match process that GPS uses elsewhere.

questions.q: A to-do list ranks tasks by priority. If every way of finishing the top task re-creates a higher-priority problem, is doing the top task first sensible?
options: Yes, because the top task is always first
Yes, because re-created problems are easy to clear a second time
No, since the higher problems would come back
It makes no difference
optionExplain: Rank alone does not make the order workable.
They return and must be done again.
Right: the effort is undone.
Order matters when fixes undo each other.
questions.explain: A workable order cannot be undone by its own fixes. The card next states this as a test on the table.
questions.rule: Fixes must not undo higher ones.

questions.q: Eavarone's program checks whether the table of connections can be written as a ____ array.
questions.explain: A triangular table means no relevant operator reintroduces a higher difference.

questions.q: Under what condition is working first on a higher difference doomed?
options: Some operator relevant to it produces a lower difference in its output expressions
It is the easiest difference in the list, so there is nothing left to gain from it
Every operator relevant to removing it produces higher differences in its outputs
It appears only in subexpressions, where the operators cannot reach it
optionExplain: A lower difference does no harm.
Ease is not the test.
Right: the higher differences are reintroduced.
Where it appears is not the test.
questions.explain: If every relevant operator brings back higher differences, the higher ones cannot be cleared first.

questions.q: True or false: A program that derives its own differences from primitive perceptual ones would readily use a difference like An, the number of variable places.
questions.explain: The existing schemes work with quite elementary differences and do not use differences like An.

questions.q: Which remaining issue blocks a program from producing its own planning space?
options: A representation for the abstract space that allows problem solving to occur in it
The shortage of operators in the logic task, which leaves too few rules to abstract
The refusal of subjects to use abstractions, which makes any scheme impossible to test
The absence of any difference ordering at all
optionExplain: Right: no general investigation of this has been made.
Operators are plentiful.
Subjects' behavior is not the issue here.
A program can produce an ordering.
questions.explain: Given an ordering, most of the essential-inessential choice is settled, but a representation for the abstract space remains: easy for As, Ac and At by deleting the feature or using a constant value, harder for An.
questions.teaches: Producing a planning space still needs a representation for the abstract space: for As, Ac and At one can delete the feature or use a constant value, but for An matters are not so simple.

questions.q: A scheduling program has several task orders that make its table triangular. What else does Eavarone's program do?
options: It rejects all of them and asks a person to choose the ordering by hand
It picks the first ordering found, in alphabetical order of the difference names
It reports that no ordering exists
It uses additional heuristics to pick one ordering from those that meet the main criterion
optionExplain: The program has heuristics of its own.
The authors say it has additional heuristics.
Several do exist in this case.
Right: the triangular test may leave several orderings.
questions.explain: The program determines whether an ordering exists that gives a triangular array, and has additional heuristics for choosing among several that do.
questions.teaches: Eavarone's program has additional heuristics for choosing a particular ordering when several satisfy the main triangular-array criterion.

questions.q: You can learn a new city's layout from a survey plan, or by walking every street. Which costs more effort per fact?
options: The survey plan, since it covers everything
Walking, since facts come bit by bit
They cost the same
Neither gives any facts
optionExplain: A plan gives many facts at once.
Right: induction from examples is slow.
Gathering by walking takes far more effort.
Both give facts.
questions.explain: Learning from examples is slow but needs no complete model. The card next sets out the comparison.

questions.q: Match each way of obtaining task information to its description.
pairs: Works out the information from a model of the task structure
Builds the information bit by bit from a series of cases
Much greater processing, and more contingent knowledge
questions.explain: Analysis works from a model; induction from cases, at a higher cost.

questions.q: A learner has no complete model of a game's rules but plays many games and notes what works. Which method is this?
options: Induction from a series of examples
Analytic extraction from a full model
Copying the experimenter
Choosing at random
optionExplain: Right: no model is needed.
A full model is what the learner lacks.
No experimenter is involved.
The learner notes what works, which is induction.
questions.explain: Induction does not require a fully formed model of the space.

questions.q: True or false: Induction does not require a fully formed model of the space before it can begin.
questions.explain: That is an advantage of induction, although the knowledge is gained at much greater processing cost.

questions.q: A reader says the authors claim GPS can learn its own planning scheme by induction. What is wrong?
options: The authors say GPS cannot use induction at all
The authors say GPS learned its structures from the subjects, by watching their protocols
The authors say planning is not possible in logic, so no planning scheme could be learned
The authors only show the information is accessible; they do not explore how it is learned
optionExplain: They list advantages of induction.
No such learning is reported.
They present planning for D1.
Right: their purpose was to expose the task environment's structure.
questions.explain: The purpose was to expose the nature of the task environment rather than to explore in detail how its structure might be learned.

questions.q: An astronomer derives a planet's orbit from laws, while another fits it from many nightly sightings. According to the authors, what is the difference between analytic and inductive extraction like?
options: The difference between a fast computer and a slow one
The difference between theory and observation in science
The difference between a subject and an experimenter
The difference between easy and difficult problems
optionExplain: Speed of machines is not the comparison.
Right: the authors draw this comparison.
The comparison is between methods.
The comparison concerns how information is gained.
questions.explain: The authors say the difference between the two is exactly the difference between theory and observation in science.
questions.teaches: The difference between analytic extraction and inductive learning is exactly the difference between theory and observation in science.

questions.q: Fifteen puzzles are ranked by how many of 64 people solved each. What does the count measure?
options: How long each puzzle takes to write
How many rules each puzzle has
How hard each puzzle was for these solvers
How well-liked each puzzle is among the people who tried it
optionExplain: The count says nothing about writing time.
Rule counts are not what the count shows.
Right: fewer solvers means a harder puzzle.
Liking is not measured.
questions.explain: A solver count is a measure of difficulty. The card next gives the book's table.

questions.q: The least difficult problems, D1 and C3, were each solved by ____ of the 64 Yale subjects.
questions.explain: B2 and C1 were solved by only 5 and 6; D1 and C3 by 24 each.

questions.q: Problem X was solved by 6 subjects and problem Y by 24. By the book's measure, which is the more difficult?
options: Y, since more subjects attempted it
They are equally difficult
It depends on the median time only
X, since fewer subjects solved it
optionExplain: All 64 attempted every problem; Y was solved by more.
Different counts mean different difficulty.
Difficulty is measured by solvers, not by time.
Right: difficulty is measured by the number of solvers.
questions.explain: Fewer solvers means more difficult.

questions.q: True or false: A problem with a solution of more than ten steps is likely to be among the harder problems.
questions.explain: All solutions of more than ten steps appear among the seven hardest problems.
questions.rule: Long solutions are in the hard half.

questions.q: How are the median solution time and the number of steps related, according to the authors?
options: The median time is about ten minutes per step
The median time is approximately one minute per step
The median time is independent of the number of steps
The median time drops as steps increase
optionExplain: That would give hours for each problem.
Right: the variation is small.
They are closely linked.
Time rises with steps.
questions.explain: The variation in median solution time is small and, with one exception, times over ten minutes go with solutions of more than ten steps.
questions.teaches: The median solution time is approximately one minute per step.

questions.q: A researcher counts the binary connectives in each proof as a measure of size. What pattern did the authors find between size and difficulty?
options: Large solutions are found only among the easier problems, as the table's last rows show
Size and difficulty are unrelated
Most solutions to the harder problems are large; most to the easier ones are smaller
All solutions have exactly ten connectives, whatever the difficulty of the problem
optionExplain: The pattern is the reverse.
There is some correlation, though not perfect.
Right: only four of the twelve solutions of the seven harder problems have fewer than ten connectives.
The counts vary.
questions.explain: Only four of the twelve solutions for the seven harder problems contain fewer than ten connectives, and only one of the eleven for the nine easier problems contains more than ten.
questions.teaches: Only four of the twelve solutions for the seven harder problems contain fewer than ten connectives, and only one of the eleven solutions for the nine easier problems contains more than ten.

questions.q: To find a parallelogram's area, which move helps most?
options: Drawing perpendiculars so the shape can be turned into a rectangle
Measuring only the longer side again
Coloring the shape in so that its two halves can be told apart at a glance
Naming the corners with new letters
optionExplain: Right: the added lines reveal the rectangle.
Re-measuring a side adds no new structure.
Color does not help find area.
Names do not change the figure.
questions.explain: An added line that is not in the figure can unlock a problem. The card next calls this a construction.

questions.q: A construction adds auxiliary lines or figures that are not contained in the ____ statement.
questions.explain: Constructions go beyond the figures given in the problem statement.

questions.q: Which is a construction in the geometric sense?
options: Measuring a side that is already drawn in the figure to see how long it is
Renaming a vertex of the figure
Drawing a new line that is not in the original figure
Reading the problem statement aloud
optionExplain: The side is already in the figure.
Renaming adds no line.
Right: it adds something not in the problem statement.
Reading adds nothing to the figure.
questions.explain: A construction adds an element that the statement did not contain.
questions.rule: New element, not in the statement.

questions.q: True or false: Allowing constructions enlarges the problem maze, since infinitely many lines could be added and the student must choose among them.
questions.explain: Without constructions the possibilities are few; with them they are immensely more.

questions.q: How does the authors' account explain the difficulty of the Nine Dot Problem?
options: Lines bounded by the dots give few possibilities, none a solution; the question is what else to try
There are too few dots to draw a line through, so nothing can be drawn until more dots are added
The solution needs a formula that most people forget, which has to be recalled before any line is drawn
The lines must be drawn in one fixed order, and few people discover the order by trial
optionExplain: Right: the difficulty is the ill-defined question of what else can be done.
The difficulty lies in the choices, not in too few dots.
No formula is involved.
Order is not the difficulty named.
questions.explain: As long as the subject limits himself to lines bounded by the dots, there are few possibilities and none a solution. The difficulty is the ill-defined question: what can I do that I haven't tried?
questions.rule: The hard question is what else to try.
questions.teaches: In the Nine Dot Problem, lines bounded by the dots give few possibilities and none a solution; the difficulty lies in the ill-defined question of what else can be done.

questions.q: A tiler may place tiles only on a grid, but the answer needs a cut not on the grid. What does a solver need to find it, by the authors' account?
options: A longer time limit alone
Generators and selective heuristics that produce a few possibilities in a larger space
A smaller grid, so that fewer tile positions have to be considered in the search
A second tiler to check the work, so that mistakes in the cuts are caught early
optionExplain: More time does not give a way to choose among many possibilities.
