Right: that is what success on construction problems requires.
The cut lies outside the grid, whatever its size.
Checking does not generate the new possibility.
questions.explain: The authors say such a question is likely to be answered successfully only if the problem solver has an appropriate set of generators and selective heuristics for obtaining a few possibilities in a larger space.
questions.rule: Generate few, in a large space.
questions.teaches: A question like what can I do that I haven't tried is likely to be answered only by a solver with an appropriate set of generators and selective heuristics for obtaining a few possibilities in a larger space.

questions.q: In a puzzle, which step needs the most unusual justification: simplifying what you have, or building something larger for no visible reason?
options: Simplifying what you have
Both need the same justification
Neither needs any justification
Building something larger for no visible reason
optionExplain: Simplifying needs little justification.
Unjustified growth is the unusual one.
A step that adds complexity needs a reason.
Right: added complexity without a reason is the odd move.
questions.explain: Unmotivated growth in complexity is what the authors call a construction.

questions.q: Sort each kind of step as a construction or not a construction.

items.t: A step that makes a larger expression with no direct justification
A simplification of a given expression
A step that reduces a difference with L0
An inessential transformation

questions.explain: A construction needs both added complexity and no direct justification.

questions.q: A rule application makes a more complex expression but directly reduces a difference between a given expression and L0. Is it a construction?
options: Yes, since the output is more complex
No, since the added complexity has a direct justification
Yes, since all rule applications are constructions, whatever their purpose
It cannot be decided without the subject's report
optionExplain: Complexity is only the first condition.
Right: it fails the second condition.
Only some rule applications are.
The definition is in terms of the step itself.
questions.explain: Both conditions must hold; the second is not met here.

questions.q: True or false: A problem that can be solved only by steps that are constructions is predicted to be difficult for subjects.
questions.explain: Subjects can generate what is obtainable without constructions, so problems needing constructions should be difficult.

questions.q: A reader says that simplifications are constructions because they use rules. What is wrong?
options: Simplifications have no direct justification
Simplifications are the only rules that can be constructions
Simplifications are inessential steps
Simplifications do not make a more complex output, so they fail the first condition
optionExplain: Their failure is on the complexity condition.
They are explicitly excluded.
They are a separate class.
Right: they make things smaller.
questions.explain: A construction must increase complexity; simplifications do the reverse.

questions.q: Which comparison does the book draw between a construction in logic and a step in cryptarithmetic?
options: A construction is roughly comparable to a nonobvious step, but the terms are not synonymous
A construction is exactly the same as a nonobvious step, and the two terms are interchangeable
A construction has nothing in common with anything in the cryptarithmetic chapters
A construction is the same as an inessential step
optionExplain: Right: the relation is taken up after episoding.
The authors say the terms are not quite synonymous.
They say the two are roughly comparable.
Inessential steps are excluded from constructions.
questions.explain: The authors say construction is roughly comparable to nonobvious step in the cryptarithmetic chapters, but the two are not quite synonymous, and they postpone the relation until episoding has been taken up.
questions.teaches: Construction is roughly comparable to nonobvious step in the cryptarithmetic chapters, but the terms are not quite synonymous; their relation waits until episoding is taken up.

questions.q: In a drawing, which allows the widest choice: joining two existing corners, or adding a new corner anywhere?
options: Joining two existing corners
Both give the same choice
Adding a new corner
Neither allows any choice
optionExplain: Two given corners leave little choice.
A new point offers far more choice.
Right: a new point can be put in endless places.
A new corner can be put in many places.
questions.explain: New points widen the choice. The card next gives the same contrast for R5, R7, R9 and R10.

questions.q: Match each rule use to how it increases complexity.
pairs: Adds any expression for X, with very wide choice of outputs
Joins any two derived expressions, with wide choice of pairs
R5, adding a tilde to the whole expression
Little choice: only one tilde is added
Little choice: only the existing parts are redistributed
questions.explain: R9 and R10 proliferate outputs, while R5 and R7 enlarge expressions without much choice.

questions.q: In A4 the goal is P V T and no given contains T. GPS gets P and applies R9 to add T. Is this a construction?
options: Yes, since R9 always produces a construction, whatever the goal or the givens may be
Yes, since the output P V T is larger than P
No, since the difference in variables between givens and goal motivates it
No, since R9 is never used in constructions
optionExplain: R9 is a construction only when unmotivated.
Larger is only the first condition.
Right: T is missing and is added directly.
R9 can be used in constructions, as in D4.
questions.explain: The addition is motivated by a difference between given and goal expressions, so it is not a construction.

questions.q: True or false: Every application of R9 is a construction.
questions.explain: R9 is not a construction when it is motivated by a difference in variables, as in problem A4.

questions.q: In problem C1 the last step applies R7 to (P V Q) . (P V R). That input is not on hand. What makes the route a construction?
options: R10 must first join P V Q and P V R, and R10 offers many possible pairs to join
R7 itself is a construction wherever it is used
P V Q cannot be obtained from the givens, so the step cannot be motivated at all
R10 is used after R7 in C1, so the pair is built only after the distribution
optionExplain: Right: the R10 then R7 sequence is a construction.
In A1 R7 fits the form conspicuously and is not one.
The sequence produces P V Q and P V R.
R10 comes first, to build R7's input.
questions.explain: To apply R7 the input must be generated by obtaining P V Q, then P V R, then using R10; working forward, many pairs could be candidates for R10, so R10 followed by R7 is a construction.
questions.teaches: In problem C1 the sequence of R10 followed by R7 is a construction, since working forward a large number of possible pairs might be generated as candidates for R10.

questions.q: A chef adds an ingredient that the finished dish lacks but that two of the starting items contain, so that a later step will work. Which book case is this like?
options: Problem A4, where R9 adds T
Problem a1, where R1 moves R to the right end
Problem A1, where R7 fits the form of a given expression so conspicuously that it is not a construction
Problem D4, where R9 adds Q, absent from the goal but present in two givens, for use in R11
optionExplain: There the goal contains T, which motivates the addition.
That step reduces a position difference.
That fit is conspicuous, so not a construction.
Right: the addition is unmotivated by the goal, so it is a construction.
questions.explain: In D4, R9 produces P V Q from P and the output is used for R11. Q is absent from the goal expression but present in two givens, so adding it is a construction.
questions.teaches: In problem D4, using R9 to produce P V Q from P, with Q absent from the goal but present in two givens, so that the output can be used for R11, is a construction.

questions.q: Of 100 people who try a two-step trick, 50 do step one and all 50 go on to do step two. What does that suggest?
options: Step two is harder than step one
Step two followed readily from step one, or step one was done to enable step two
Step one is unrelated to step two
Half the people did not understand step two, and so stopped before reaching it
optionExplain: Everyone who tried it succeeded.
Right: the steps are linked.
All who did one did the other.
Those who skipped step one never reached step two.
questions.explain: When nearly everyone who does one step does the next, the steps are linked. The card next uses this test.

questions.q: In D4, only half the subjects applied R9, but ____ of those went on to apply R11.
questions.explain: The authors take this as showing R9 and R11 are strongly linked.
questions.rule: All who did R9 did R11.

questions.q: In B3 six subjects applied R10 and all but one of them applied R7. How many of the six applied R7?
options: Five
Six
One
Three
optionExplain: Right: all but one of six is five.
That would be all of them.
One is the number who did not.
Three is the number who solved the problem.
questions.explain: All but one of six means five. Three of the six solved the problem.
questions.rule: All but one of six is five.

questions.q: True or false: The path data show that subjects generally constructed a full plan for the solution before making any transformation.
questions.explain: The data show steady attrition, hastened at difficult steps and slowed between linked steps, not a pattern expected from full plans.

questions.q: In A2, half the subjects regrouped L1 by R4, and four-fifths of those went on to apply R11. What do the authors conjecture?
options: Many applied R11 by chance after R4
Many were told by the experimenter to use R11
Many used R11 before R4
Many worked backward, applying R4 to obtain P . Q as the input for R11
optionExplain: Four-fifths is too high for chance.
No such help is reported.
The order was R4 then R11.
Right: the regrouping was done with R11 in mind.
questions.explain: The authors conjecture that many worked backwards, applying R4 in order to obtain the expression P . Q as input for the R11 application.
questions.rule: A linked step may be done for its sake.
questions.teaches: In problem A2, many subjects probably worked backwards, applying R4 in order to obtain P . Q as the input for R11.

questions.q: In a cooking contest, nearly everyone who made the roux went on to make the sauce, but only half began the roux. What does this pattern resemble in problem C4?
options: All subjects made the R10 step and all of them went on to solve the problem
Ten of the twelve who made the R10 step went on to R7, while half lost the trail earlier
Nobody who made the R10 step went on to R7
Everyone made a full plan before starting, so there was no loss of subjects along the way
optionExplain: Half lost the trail, so not all reached it.
Right: follow-through after the construction, attrition before it.
Most of them did.
The data show attrition, not full plans.
questions.explain: In C4, 10 of 12 subjects who made the R10 transformation made the R7 one; half of the subjects lost the trail while eliminating Q and P . Q.
questions.teaches: In problem C4, 10 of the 12 subjects who made the R10 transformation went on to make the R7 one, while half of the subjects lost the trail while eliminating Q and P . Q.

questions.q: A person keeps a tool for its usual job and does not see another use for it. What is this tendency called?
options: Means-ends analysis
Planning
Functional fixity
Abstraction
optionExplain: That is a method for choosing operators by differences.
Planning solves an abstract version first.
Right: the item is fixed to one function.
Abstraction drops detail from objects and operators.
questions.explain: Seeing an item in only one role is functional fixity. The card next shows it in problem C1.

questions.q: In C1 only about one ____ of the subjects applied R12.
questions.explain: The authors note that the difficulty of C1 was not only the R10-R7 construction.

questions.q: What is special about the way P V Q is used in the solution of C1?
options: It appears only in the goal expression and takes no part in the derivation
It is used only once, as a given expression, and is then discarded from the board
It is not used by any rule in the solution, so it matters only as a distraction
It is put to two uses: building an input to R12 and serving as an input to R10
optionExplain: It appears in the solution's steps.
It is used twice.
It is an input to R10 and used for R12.
Right: it is the only problem where one term has two uses.
questions.explain: C1 is the only problem in which the same term is put to two distinct uses.

questions.q: True or false: A subject who sees that P V Q is a component of L0 may hesitate to use it up through R12.
questions.explain: The authors later present evidence that some subjects were deterred from using up P V Q by R12 because they wanted it as a component of L0.
questions.rule: Reserved terms are not used up.

questions.q: What do the authors say they will present later about C1?
options: Evidence that C1 has no solution that can be found with the rules on the sheet
Evidence that some subjects were deterred from using up P V Q by R12
Evidence that R12 does not apply to C1
Evidence that C1 is the easiest problem
optionExplain: C1 was solved by 6 subjects.
Right: they saw they wanted it as a component of L0.
R12 is used in its solution.
C1 is among the hardest.
questions.explain: The authors say they will later present evidence that some subjects were deterred from using up P V Q by R12 because they could see they wanted it as a component of L0.
questions.rule: A reserved term is a trap.
questions.teaches: The authors say they will later present evidence that some subjects were deterred from using up P V Q by R12 because they wanted that expression as a component of L0.

questions.q: A cook sets one egg aside for garnish, and then a batter that needs an egg goes unmade. Which feature of C1 is this like?
options: A term is wasted on a step that is never needed, leaving the solution unfinished
A term is replaced by a different one in every step, so none remains for later use
A term needed in two places is held back from one because it is wanted in the other
A term is removed by a simplification rule before the solver can use it again
optionExplain: In the story the egg is held back, not wasted.
Nothing is replaced.
Right: the same item is reserved for one use.
The egg is not removed by a simplification.
questions.explain: In C1 the term P V Q is first used to build an input to R12 and later is the left-hand input to R10. A subject who reserves it for L0 is held back from the first use.
questions.teaches: In C1 the term P V Q must first be used to construct an input to R12 and then be used again as the left-hand input to R10.

questions.q: A crude program follows a few rules of thumb and solves easy puzzles but none of the hard ones. What does that suggest?
options: Hard puzzles need moves that the rules of thumb never make
The hard puzzles have no solution, so the program is right to leave them alone
The easy puzzles were solved by luck
The program is too slow
optionExplain: Right: the gap is in the kind of move.
People did solve them.
The program applies fixed rules.
Speed is not the issue.
questions.explain: The missing moves explain the failure. The card next names them constructions.

questions.q: The simulated processor fails on all seven difficult problems because none of its heuristics makes a ____.
questions.explain: Without constructions it can solve only what is reachable by simplification, fit and difference reduction.

questions.q: Which postulate lets the processor deal with L0 = P V T when T occurs in none of the givens?
options: R8 is applied to positive main expressions whose main connective is a dot, to simplify them
R7 is applied when a given has the form (AB)(AC)
R9 is applied as the last step when L0 is A V B and B is not in the givens
R11 and R12 are applied to eliminate letters
optionExplain: R8 shortens dot expressions.
R7 is for conspicuous fit.
Right: the difference in variables motivates it.
T needs to be added, not eliminated.
questions.explain: R9 as the last step is the difference-reducing heuristic for a missing variable.

questions.q: Match each postulate to the kind of heuristic it represents. (R8 simplifies A.B to A; R2 and R5 are the contraposition and wedge-for-horseshoe rules; R7 distributes; R9 adds X to A to give A V X.)
pairs: R2 and R5 to reduce tildes
Inessential rules to make essential rules fit
R7 when a given is of the form (AB)(AC)
R9 as the last step to add a missing letter
questions.explain: The four classes are those that the authors say need no construction.

questions.q: B1 is among the six easiest problems, yet the processor fails it. Why?
options: B1 needs R9 and then R11, a step the processor never takes; the problem's meaning may have helped subjects
B1 is in fact the hardest problem for the subjects, so the processor's failure is expected, as with the hard seven
The processor cannot apply R9 under any of its postulates, so every problem needing it must fail on that account
B1 has no solution within the rules, which is why a processor following the rules cannot find one
optionExplain: Right: R9 comes before R11 here, not as a last step.
B1 is among the easiest.
It applies R9 as a last step in other cases.
B1 is solvable.
questions.explain: To solve B1 the processor would generate P and ~P, add Q V S to one by R9, then cancel the P's with R11. The authors suggest the semantic reading (P and not P) may have helped subjects.
questions.rule: R9 before R11 is out of its reach.
questions.teaches: B1 fails in the simulation because it calls for R9 and then R11; the semantic interpretation, P and not P, may have helped some subjects find the solution.

questions.q: A rule-of-thumb robot discards any item that is not in the target, but one task needs an item it would discard. Which failure in the simulation is this like?
options: C2, where the final R7-R8 sequence is not found
B4, where R appears in L0 and so should not be eliminated, yet R is needed with R11
A2, where R10 forms P . Q after P and Q are found
B1, where R9 and then R11 are needed
optionExplain: That is a failure to find a sequence, not wrongly discarding a letter.
Right: the elimination heuristic discards what the solution needs.
That is a failure to build a conjunction.
That concerns adding a letter, not discarding one.
questions.explain: The three next-hardest problems fail for reasons of their own: in C2 the processor misses the final R7-R8; in B4 it will not use R with R11 since R appears in L0; in A2 it does not use R10 to form P . Q.
questions.rule: Each failure shows a missing heuristic.
questions.teaches: The processor fails the next three problems in order of difficulty for separate reasons: C2 needs a final R7-R8 sequence, B4 needs R used with R11 although R is in L0, and A2 needs R10 to form P . Q.

questions.q: A planner keeps for each goal what is wanted, the methods that could reach it and what has already been tried. What is this record?
options: A table of connections
A problem behavior graph
A planning space
A goal structure
optionExplain: That lists which operators affect which differences.
That draws a search after the fact.
That is a simplified problem space.
Right: the goal holds more than the wanted object.
questions.explain: A goal as a record of wants, methods and history is the first summary idea.

questions.q: Match each summary idea to what it says.
pairs: A goal holds the desired object, methods and past attempts
Choose operators by the differences they remove
Inability to apply an operator sets up a goal of applying it
An IPS constructing its own structures
Differences and connections can come from the task definition
questions.explain: These are the first four of the six summary ideas.

questions.q: GPS cannot apply a rule to the expression in hand and so sets up a goal of making the rule applicable. Which summary idea is this?
options: Goal structures
Difficulties lead to goals to overcome them
Means-ends analysis
An IPS constructing its own structures from the task definition
optionExplain: That idea is about what a goal holds.
Right: the difficulty becomes a subgoal.
That concerns choosing operators by differences.
That concerns deriving differences and connections.
questions.explain: The reaction to being unable to apply an operator is to set up a goal of applying it.

questions.q: Which requirements must be met for means-ends analysis to be effective? Select all that apply.
options: Differences that bridge the objects and the operators
An ordering of the differences
A larger number of operators than expressions
A human experimenter at the blackboard
optionExplain: Right: they link perception and action.
Right: it gives the search additional direction.
No such count is required.
The experimenter is part of the experiment, not of the method.
questions.explain: Differences connect the perceptual world of objects with the action world of operators, and their ordering adds direction.

questions.q: Why do the authors call setting goals to overcome difficulties a rather dangerous heuristic?
options: It stops GPS from ever applying an operator
It makes GPS work backward from the goal, which loses the benefit of using the start
It makes the table of connections impossible to build
It gives up the selectivity of using only applicable operators, so blind paths may go on forever
optionExplain: It sets goals to apply them.
GPS works forward.
The table is built from the operators.
Right: selectivity is lost.
questions.explain: It throws away a source of selectivity, namely working only with operators that are applicable, so it can lead to blind paths without limit unless curbed.
questions.teaches: Setting a goal to overcome every difficulty throws away a source of selectivity, working only with applicable operators, and can follow blind paths forever unless curbed.

questions.q: A game bot keeps, for each goal, a record of what it has already tried so that it does not repeat itself. Which contrast does the book draw?
options: Unlike LT, which gave goal significance to an object, GPS uses a goal holding methods and past attempts
Like LT, GPS gave goal significance to an object, with no record of what had been tried
GPS has no record of past attempts, so it may repeat a failed method without noticing
LT held the history of past attempts, while GPS held only the desired object
optionExplain: Right: the goal is a structure of its own.
The summary says GPS did not simply do so.
The goal holds the history of past attempts.
The contrast runs the other way.
questions.explain: Rather than simply attributing goal significance to an object in the task environment, as in LT, GPS uses a special symbol structure that holds the desired object, the methods of attaining the goal and the history of past attempts.
questions.rule: A goal is a structure, not a flagged object.
questions.teaches: In LT, goal significance was simply attributed to an object in the task environment; in GPS the goal is a symbol structure holding the methods of attaining it and the history of past attempts.

questions.q: Compare a full map with a sketch map. Which is richer in detail?
options: The sketch map
They are equally rich
The full map
Neither has any detail
optionExplain: A sketch drops detail.
The sketch has less detail.
Right: the sketch has less detail.
Both show something.
questions.explain: A sketch is the poorer space. The card next calls a planning space impoverished in this sense.

questions.q: A construction is an operation that increases complexity in the absence of strong ____.
questions.explain: The authors made this concept operational for the logic task.

questions.q: How do the authors understand the relative difficulty of the various logic problems?
options: As a matter of how many letters the problem has, with more letters meaning more difficulty
As a matter of which subject attempted it first
As a combination of the need for a construction and the effect of large search spaces
As a matter of the experimenter's skill in explaining the rules to each subject
optionExplain: Letters alone are not the explanation.
Order of attempts is not the explanation.
Right: the two factors together.
The experimenter plays no part.
questions.explain: Difficulty follows from whether a construction is required, together with the size of the search space.

questions.q: Sort each description as the cryptarithmetic augmented space or the logic planning space.

items.t: Richer than the base space
Consists of less detail than the base space
Serves as a site of the main problem solving
Guides action in the base space

questions.explain: The augmented space adds to the base space; the planning space takes detail away and guides.

questions.q: What happens within a single problem solving attempt that uses a planning space?
options: The attempt oscillates between the two spaces
The attempt stays entirely in the planning space
The attempt stays entirely in the base space
The attempt is split into two separate attempts
optionExplain: Right: it moves between the base space and the planning space.
The plan must be carried out in the base space.
The plan is made in the planning space.
The authors describe a single attempt.
questions.explain: A single problem solving attempt oscillates between the two spaces.
questions.teaches: A single problem solving attempt that uses a planning space oscillates between the planning space and the base space.

questions.q: A reader is told that the authors already hold some evidence that their analysis fits human behavior and are ready to look further. What do they do after Chapter 8?
options: Drop the logic task and return to cryptarithmetic to test the analysis a second time
Replace the Yale data by new data collected with a different set of problems
End the study of logic problems
Examine the application to human behavior more deeply, using GPS as a model
optionExplain: Chapter 9 continues with logic.
The Yale data continue to be used.
Three chapters are devoted to logic.
Right: Chapter 9 takes up GPS and human behavior.
questions.explain: The authors say they already have some evidence that their analysis makes sense for human behavior and are now ready to examine that issue more deeply.
questions.teaches: The authors say they already have some evidence that their information processing analysis makes sense for human behavior and are now ready to examine that issue more deeply.

questions.q: A team has built a program for a task and wants to know whether people solve it the same way. Which test is most convincing?
options: Check that the program solves at least as many problems as people do, whatever steps it takes
Compare the program's steps with detailed records of people on the same problems
Ask experienced teachers whether the program's steps sound sensible
Show that the program needs less time than people do on each problem it is given
optionExplain: Success rates can match even when the processes differ widely.
Detail is what separates a theory of the process from a program that merely succeeds.
Plausibility to teachers is not a comparison with recorded behavior.
Speed says little about which steps were taken.
questions.explain: A process theory is tested against the steps people actually take. The card shows what the authors compare.

questions.q: In the basic problem space of this chapter, the nodes are logic expressions and the operators are the ____ legal rules.
questions.explain: The basic space has logic expressions as nodes and twelve legal rules as operators.

questions.q: A student reads the chapter order (cryptarithmetic first, logic later) and concludes that GPS was written after the cryptarithmetic study. What do the authors say?
options: The student is right: the Logic Theorist came after the cryptarithmetic study and the order is historical
The student is right: GPS was designed from the cryptarithmetic protocols
The student is wrong: the two tasks were studied at the same time, so order is meaningless
The student is wrong: the logic work came first, and the order was reversed for clarity
optionExplain: The Logic Theorist came before GPS, and cryptarithmetic was tackled after logic.
The text says the cryptarithmetic task was tackled after logic.
The authors describe a definite order, with logic first and cryptarithmetic later.
The authors say they reversed the historical sequence because the basic issues are more transparent in cryptarithmetic.
questions.explain: Book order and historical order differ here, and the authors say so.
questions.rule: Do not read book order as history.

questions.q: True or false: If the authors' aim is met, GPS will leave none of the subjects' task behavior unexplained.
questions.explain: The aim is only to leave modest amounts unexplained, and later sections list items that GPS does not explain.

questions.q: How was the Logic Theorist, which came before GPS, compared with human problem solving?
options: Only generally, not in step-by-step detail
In full detail, as GPS was compared later
It was never compared with human behavior at all
Through protocols of seven thinking-aloud subjects
optionExplain: The authors say it was compared only generally, in a 1958 paper.
GPS was the first program developed as a detailed simulation of human symbolic behavior.
The text says it was compared, but only generally.
Detailed protocol comparison belongs to GPS, not to the Logic Theorist.
questions.explain: GPS marks the move from a general comparison to a detailed one.
questions.teaches: GPS was the first program developed as a detailed simulation of human symbolic behavior; the earlier Logic Theorist was compared with people only generally.

questions.q: A lab has built a chess-move program and a checkers-move program. It plans a paper on the process fit. What does this chapter's approach suggest it write first?
options: The program built first, so that the paper follows the history of the lab's projects
The task with the most subjects
The case where the basic issues are most transparent, even if it was built later
The hardest task first, so that the easy one looks trivial by comparison and is skipped
optionExplain: The authors reversed historical order for clarity.
Subject numbers were not the stated reason for the order.
The authors chose cryptarithmetic first because the basic issues were more transparent there.
The authors put the simpler setting first to make the basics visible.
questions.explain: Order of presentation can serve understanding rather than chronology.
questions.teaches: The authors reordered the presentation of their work for clarity: the logic work came first in time but is presented after cryptarithmetic.

questions.q: A model was tuned using some of the very data it is later tested on. What can still make the test meaningful?
options: The model has a large number of adjustable settings that can be tuned to each case
The data come from a single careful person whose records are known to be accurate
The model was fixed by independent principles, so it could still fail to match
The model's author is sure it is correct
optionExplain: More settings make a fit easier, not more meaningful.
Care in collection does not change whether the model could fail.
A fit counts as evidence when a mismatch was possible.
Confidence is not a test.
questions.explain: A fit means something only if failure was possible. The card shows the authors' version of this point.
questions.rule: A fit is meaningful only if it could have failed.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, GPS is defined independently of the subjects' behavior, in terms of the task environment and the theory of Chapter 4.
questions.explain: Methods, heuristics and organization of GPS come from the task environment and the Chapter 4 theory, not from fitting each subject.
questions.rule: Define the model first, then test it.

questions.q: A weather model uses last year's storms to set one constant, then forecasts next week's rain from physical laws. Which reading matches the authors' reasoning?
options: The constant is fitted to data, but a bad forecast is still possible
The forecast is guaranteed to be correct
The forecast is worthless
The forecast proves that the physical laws behind the model are true in every case
optionExplain: Partial adaptation to data allows the model to fail.
A single fitted constant does not guarantee a correct forecast.
The authors grant parameters and still call the test meaningful.
A match supports the model; it does not prove it everywhere.
questions.explain: Parameters taken from data do not remove the chance of failure.
questions.rule: Adapted is not the same as guaranteed.

questions.q: A critic says: GPS was built by studying these protocols, so it has to fit them. What is the flaw, according to the authors?
options: GPS was built from completely different protocols, so no overlap with these data exists
A fit to data that were studied in building the model is the strongest kind of evidence
The critic is right, and the authors concede that the fit proves nothing at all
GPS is set by the task and by Chapter 4, so a subject could fail to match it
optionExplain: The authors admit that GPS was built from some of the same protocols.
The authors make no such claim.
The authors reject that conclusion.
This is the authors' answer: the fit depends on whether subjects really behave this way.
questions.explain: The critic overlooks that GPS is defined independently of subjects' behavior.
questions.rule: Ask whether the fit could have failed.

questions.q: The authors say there is no a ____ reason why humans should behave GPS-like, or why any particular person should.
questions.explain: Without an a priori reason, a match found in one person is not guaranteed for another, so a match is informative.
questions.rule: No a priori reason, so a match is evidence.
questions.teaches: The authors say there is no a priori reason why humans should behave GPS-like, or why any particular person should, even if some other person does.

questions.q: A language-learning app builds its model of learner errors from rules of grammar, then compares it with learners' recorded errors. Following the authors, when is a close match informative?
options: When the model has many tuned weights, so that it can follow each learner closely
When the rules were set without looking at those learners, so a mismatch was possible
When every recorded error is also contained in the app's own training data
When the recorded learners all agree with each other about what they find hard
optionExplain: Many weights allow a fit by construction.
Independence of the model from the data is what gives the match its force.
That makes the match guaranteed, not informative.
Agreement among learners is a separate matter.
questions.explain: The authors defend the fit by pointing to independence in definition, not by denying partial adaptation.
questions.rule: Independence of definition is the safeguard.
questions.teaches: The authors say partial adaptation to the data is true of any model that contains parameters, so adaptation alone does not make the fit tautological.

questions.q: A software package has existed for years under one name, but its internals were rewritten several times. What does a claim about the package need to say?
options: Which version or aspect the claim is about
Nothing extra, because one name means one design
Only the newest version matters, so older ones can be ignored
Only the programming language
optionExplain: One name can cover quite different internals.
A name does not fix the design.
Earlier versions may have produced the results in question.
The language is one difference among several.
questions.explain: A shared name can hide real variation. The card shows how the authors handle this.
questions.rule: A name is not a design.

questions.q: At one time or another GPS has had five basic underlying ____ structures.
questions.explain: Five basic underlying IPS structures, which affect how methods and data structures are represented.

questions.q: True or false: If a later version of GPS changed its table of connections, the authors would still call it GPS.
questions.explain: The variants differ in methods, structures and language, not only in parameters, and they are all called GPS.
questions.rule: Variation is already inside the name.

questions.q: A reader finds that one version of GPS fails to match a subject's step. How should the authors' remark about variants shape the conclusion?
options: Conclude at once that GPS as a theory of problem solving has now been refuted
Ignore the failure, since any variant of the program can be changed to fit
Accept the failure only if the version was written in the same programming language
Ask whether that aspect belongs to the shared organization or to one version
optionExplain: One version's failure need not refute the family.
The authors promise to note where aspects do not fit.
The language is not the criterion.
The authors say they will point out which aspects fit particular forms of GPS.
questions.explain: Version-specific mismatch and shared-organization mismatch lead to different conclusions.

questions.q: How do the authors describe the change of programming language across GPS versions?
options: There were five changes, one for each IPS structure
There has been one change of programming language
No change; all variants were written in one language
There were changes only in the tables of connections
optionExplain: Five is the number of IPS structures, not of language changes.
The text states one change of programming language.
The text records one change.
Tables of connections are one kind of nonnumerical parameter, not the language.
questions.explain: Do not confuse the number of structures with the number of languages.
questions.teaches: GPS has had five basic underlying IPS structures but only one change of programming language.

questions.q: A study says people play chess like Program X, which exists in six versions. Which sentence would the authors prefer?
options: People's play is exactly that of Program X
People's play cannot be compared with the program at all
People's play resembles the program's organization; version 3 fits closely, version 5 less well
Only version 6 matters for the comparison
optionExplain: A name is not a single design.
The authors compare anyway and flag the versions.
This names both the shared organization and where particular versions fit.
Earlier versions can be the ones that fit a given episode.
questions.explain: The authors will mark where behavior fits particular forms of GPS and where it does not.
questions.rule: Name the aspect and the version.
questions.teaches: The authors promise to point out which aspects of the subjects' behavior fit closely to particular existing forms of GPS and which do not.

questions.q: A person solving a puzzle talks aloud in loose everyday words. A program prints formal goal statements. How can the two be compared?
options: Count the words each of them produces and compare the totals for the two
Ask the person to speak in exactly the format that the program prints out
Compare only the final answers that the person and the program reach
Translate each remark into the program's formal terms and match them up
optionExplain: Word counts say nothing about the steps taken.
The authors work with the subject's natural language.
Final answers hide the process.
Mapping loose speech onto formal goals is what makes the comparison possible.
questions.explain: The card shows how the authors bridge speech and program output.

questions.q: True or false: S9's protocol on Problem a1 was taken from the first problem he attempted after studying the twelve rules.
questions.explain: It was a relatively simple training problem, the first one tried after the rules were studied.

questions.q: A subject says, I'm looking at the idea of reversing these two things now. In the comparison, this is read as which kind of program statement?
options: A goal to delete a term from the expression altogether, leaving fewer symbols
A goal to remove the difference in position of corresponding parts of two objects
A report that the problem has been solved and no further rule is needed
A command to the experimenter to write the next transformation on the board
optionExplain: Reversing positions does not remove a term.
The authors give this very reading for such a sentence.
The subject is still planning, not finished.
The remark is about what he is considering, not an instruction.
questions.explain: Reversal of position is a difference in position, so the matching goal addresses position.
questions.rule: Map the remark to the difference it removes.

questions.q: Match each item in the Problem a1 comparison to how the authors describe it.
pairs: Free language, much less stylized than a program's
Produced by a working version of the program
The tree in the earlier paper
questions.explain: The authors note that with a trace there is no need for a PBG of either the protocol or GPS's behavior.
questions.rule: Trace beside protocol; no PBG needed.

questions.q: How does the Figure 9.1 trace differ from the tree in the earlier published paper on the same analysis?
options: The trace uses a different subject and a different problem from the earlier paper
The trace was drawn from memory by the authors after studying the protocol
The trace came from a working version of the program; the earlier tree was hand-simulated
The earlier paper had no trace of any kind, only the protocols of the subjects
optionExplain: The analysis is essentially identical to the earlier one, with the same subject and problem.
The text says it was produced by a working version.
The authors note this single difference in a footnote.
It had a tree, produced by hand simulation.
questions.explain: Running the program, not simulating it by hand, gives the trace weight.
questions.teaches: The Figure 9.1 trace was produced by a working version of GPS, while the tree in the earlier paper (Newell and Simon, 1961c) was hand-simulated.

questions.q: A researcher wants to compare a chef's talk-aloud while cooking with a recipe-planning program. Which first step follows the authors' method?
options: Rewrite the chef's remarks as the program's goals, then compare the two
Wait until the chef cooks silently, then compare the finished dishes with the program
Ask the chef to read the program's trace aloud while cooking and compare the words
Compare only the length of time that each of them takes to finish the dish
optionExplain: The authors translate speech into program terms before comparing.
The method relies on talk-aloud protocols.
The comparison is of the chef's own words.
Time alone cannot show matching steps.
questions.explain: The method depends on a reliable translation of speech into goals.
questions.teaches: The authors say that translating a subject's loose sentences into program goals has been shown in practice to be not too difficult.

questions.q: A computer trace lists rule checks that the person did not mention aloud. What are the possible explanations?
options: The program must be wrong
The program may be wrong, or the person may have thought of them silently
The person must have thought of them
The checks do not matter at all
optionExplain: People do not report everything they think.
Silence in a protocol is ambiguous.
That assumes the answer in advance.
The comparison is about steps, not answers.
questions.explain: The card gives the authors' own view of this ambiguity.
questions.rule: Silence can mean omission or error.

questions.q: True or false: S9 solved Problem a1 mentally and then asked the experimenter to write the transformations on the blackboard.
questions.explain: He worked the problem out in his head before having the steps written down.

questions.q: In the trace, GPS lists R5 and R8 as rules considered, but S9 does not mention them. Which conclusion is justified by the authors' reasoning?
options: The theory is wrong
The theory is right
The comparison is useless
It cannot be told whether the theory is wrong or the subject considered the rules silently
optionExplain: Unspoken thoughts are possible.
The omission could also show an error in the theory.
Many steps do match, as the next sections show.
The authors state exactly this uncertainty.
questions.explain: Absence in a protocol is weak evidence either way.
questions.rule: Do not read silence as proof.

questions.q: If the next version of GPS distinguished covert steps from steps put on the board, what would the trace gain?
options: It could mirror the subject's habit of working in the head, then reporting on the board
It would solve the problem in fewer steps than before, so the trace would be shorter
It would stop considering rules that the subject did not mention in his protocol
It would no longer need the twelve rules
optionExplain: The missing distinction is the cited inadequacy.
The point is fit to the subject, not speed.
That is a separate issue about unspoken items.
The rules remain the operators.
questions.explain: The internal versus external distinction is a gap the authors name.
questions.rule: Add the distinction to fit the habit.

questions.q: GPS and S9 discovered the correct rules in the same sequence, but S9 officially applied them in the ____ order.
questions.explain: The subject worked the problem in his head and then had the experimenter write the steps in reverse order.
questions.rule: Discovery order may differ from report order.
questions.teaches: GPS and S9 discovered the correct rules in the same sequence, but S9 officially applied them in the reverse order.

questions.q: A study compares a pilot's thinking-aloud during a simulated emergency with a planning program. The pilot reports only actions he performs on the controls. What parallel gap would the authors flag?
options: The program has too many rules to be compared with what the pilot says aloud
The pilot should not have been asked to talk while handling the emergency
The program may not separate silent planning from overt action in its trace
The program cannot make decisions in a simulated emergency of any kind
optionExplain: The number of rules is not the gap.
The authors rely on talk-aloud data.
This mirrors the internal versus external gap in GPS's trace.
The gap is about internal versus external steps.
questions.explain: A protocol records only what is voiced or done; the program may include covert steps.
questions.teaches: The authors say the internal versus external distinction has consequences that run throughout a problem, because expressions on the blackboard have very different memory characteristics from expressions generated only in the head.

questions.q: Two solvers see a puzzle with three kinds of difference between where they are and where they want to be. What might show they share a method?
options: They both finish at exactly the same speed on the puzzle
They both say afterwards that they enjoyed working on the puzzle
They pay attention to the same kinds of difference in the same priority
They both begin with the same letter of the alphabet in the first answer
optionExplain: Speed can match without a shared method.
Enjoyment is not evidence of method.
Shared priorities in noticing differences point to a shared method.
Irrelevant to method.
questions.explain: The card gives the three kinds of difference in the logic task and their order.
questions.rule: Match the priorities, not just the answers.

questions.q: Order the differences by how much attention both S9 and GPS give them, most first.
items: Differences in the positions of symbols
Presence or absence of signs
Differences in connectives
questions.explain: Position gets most attention, then signs, then connectives.

questions.q: S9 considers R2 to reorder two terms but drops it. What reason do the authors give for the refusal, shared with GPS?
options: Applying R2 also changes a sign, which creates a new difference
R2 cannot be applied to expressions that contain a horseshoe connective at all
R2 is not on the list of the twelve rules that the subjects were given
R2 changes the main connective, which the subject wants to keep as it is
optionExplain: The authors say both refuse R2 because it also changes a sign.
The text gives no such restriction.
R2 is one of the twelve rules.
The cited side effect is the sign change.
questions.explain: A rule that fixes one difference but adds another is rejected by both.
questions.rule: Reject rules with unwanted side effects.

questions.q: True or false: By the shared priorities, a rule that fixes a position difference but also changes a connective would be refused less readily than R2.
questions.explain: Our reading: connective differences get the least attention, so a connective side effect costs less than the sign change that leads both to refuse R2.

questions.q: The Figure 9.1 version of GPS differs from the Chapter 8 version in its reduce-method. Why must it generate the differences of each rule while looking for one to apply?
options: The twelve rules are unknown to the program until it has generated them for itself
Generating differences lets the program skip the goal expression when choosing a rule
The subject S9 asked that each of the rules be spelled out before he began
A rule applies at the main connective, but the difference lies on the left-hand side
optionExplain: The rules are given; what is generated are their differences.
The goal expression is still used.
The change belongs to the program, not to a request by S9.
The authors give this as the reason the find-relevant-operator step differs.
questions.explain: Matching a rule's input with its output yields the rule's difference, which can be checked against the difference to be removed.
questions.rule: Generate rule differences when the difference sits below the main connective.
questions.teaches: In the Figure 9.1 version of GPS, the reduce-method generates the differences of each rule as it sequences through them, because a rule is applied at the main connective while the relevant difference is on the left-hand side.

questions.q: Two cooks each prepare the same dish and each rejects a shortcut that would fix one problem but ruin another. What does this share with the S9 and GPS refusal of R2?
options: Both avoid any step that takes more than one move to carry out
Both avoid a step whose side effect creates a higher-priority difference
Both pick whichever step is quickest to carry out, whatever its side effects
Both ignore the final goal expression while they are working on the problem
optionExplain: The refusal was about side effects, not length.
That is the logic of refusing R2 for its sign change.
S9 and GPS did not pick the fastest step.
They compare expressions with the goal.
questions.explain: Side effects on higher-priority features can veto a rule.
questions.rule: Look at side effects before applying.
questions.teaches: In S9's case, the path that both the subject and GPS chose from several possible ones was one application of R6 and two applications of R1.

questions.q: A task needs three separate changes, each done in a single move, and the changes can be made in any order. How many different shortest solutions exist?
options: Six
Three
Nine
Eight
optionExplain: Three items can be arranged in 3 x 2 x 1 = 6 orders.
Three counts the changes, not the orders.
Nine would count pairs of changes, not full orders.
Eight is 2 x 2 x 2, which allows each change to be done or not, not to be ordered.
questions.explain: Free ordering of independent steps gives the factorial. The card applies this to the logic problem.
questions.rule: n free steps give n! orders.

questions.q: Because the three changes needed in Problem a1 can be done in any order, there are 3! = ____ shortest solution paths.
questions.explain: Three changes in any order give six permutations, all essentially variants of one path.

questions.q: A cook must do four separate prep jobs (chop, wash, preheat, line the tin), each in one move, in any order. How many shortest sequences are there?
optionExplain: Sixteen is 2 to the fourth power, which does not count orderings.
Twelve would apply if only some orders were allowed.
Four counts the jobs, not the sequences.
Four free steps give 4! = 24 orders, the same reasoning as 3! = 6 for the logic problem.
questions.explain: Independence of the steps is what makes every order work.

questions.q: True or false: In a path for Problem a1 where the connective has already been changed to a wedge, the swap of P and Q would be done by R1 rather than R2.
questions.explain: The authors state that the swap needs R2 if the connective is still a horseshoe but R1 if it has previously been changed to a wedge.

questions.q: How many of the six paths in Figure 9.3 use R2 at all?
options: None, since both subjects avoided R2
Three: those that swap P and Q before changing the connective
All six, since R2 is needed to reverse the whole expression
Two, one for each end of the expression
optionExplain: Avoidance by subjects does not remove R2 from the list of possible paths.
Paths 1, 3 and 4 use R2, each applying it to PQ before R6.
Reversal of the whole expression is done by R1.
The count follows the order of the connective change, not the ends.
questions.explain: The paths that apply R6 before swapping P and Q use R1 for the swap; the others use R2.
questions.rule: R2 appears only when the swap comes first.
questions.teaches: Exactly three of the six paths use R2: the ones that swap P and Q while the connective is still a horseshoe.

questions.q: A planner finds a task that splits into three one-move subproblems whose solutions can each be recognized from the way the result looks. The authors compare Problem a1 to which earlier example?
options: The cryptarithmetic puzzle DONALD + GERALD
The Moore-Anderson problem D1
The clicking safe of Chapter 4
The Logic Theorist's first theorem
optionExplain: Cryptarithmetic is not offered as the comparison.
D1 is the harder problem examined later.
The authors say a1 is, like the clicking safe, factorable into subproblems.
The comparison made is to the clicking safe.
questions.explain: A problem that factors into recognizable one-step pieces can be solved by working each piece in any order.
questions.teaches: The authors liken Problem a1 to the clicking safe of Chapter 4: both are factorable into subproblems whose solution can be recognized from the form of the result.

questions.q: Five people solve the same simple problem and their protocols look alike. What would show the likeness goes beyond what the problem forces?
options: They all reach the same final answer, which the problem itself forces on them
They all use almost the same number of words when they speak aloud
They all solve it in under a minute
They share habits the problem does not require, such as planning aloud first
optionExplain: A single answer is forced by the problem.
Word counts do not bear on process.
Speed alone can be forced by an easy problem.
Shared habits not dictated by the task point to shared processes.
questions.explain: Separating task-forced from process-based likeness is the key move. The card gives the authors' list.
questions.rule: Look for likeness the task does not demand.

questions.q: True or false: All five subjects map out the solution, partly or fully, before asking the experimenter to carry out the official transformations.
questions.explain: This planning before acting is one of the similarities beyond the dictates of the task.

questions.q: A cook plans a sauce. Sort each remark by whether it states a function to be performed or a rule (tool) to apply.

items.t: I need to make it thicker
Use the whisk and a bit of flour
It has to lose some of its saltiness
Put it through the sieve

questions.explain: S9's reversing remark states a function; S15's use R1 remark states a rule. Both kinds of statement occur in the protocols.
questions.rule: Plans are stated as functions or as rules.

questions.q: A sixth subject, much like the first five, begins by describing the plan aloud. Which change is most likely mentioned first?
options: Swapping P and Q inside the left part of the expression before anything else
Reversing the left and right sides of the whole expression
Changing the horseshoe connective to a wedge before looking at anything else
Applying R2 to the left part of the expression, with its change of signs
optionExplain: Three or two subjects mention the part operations only after the reversal.
All five subjects mentioned the whole-expression reversal first.
The connective change follows the reversal in all five protocols.
Only two subjects even mention R2.
questions.explain: Common order in the five protocols supports a prediction for a sixth.

questions.q: Only S10 mentions features of the expression that are not to be changed. What does the authors' interpretation say prompted this?
options: He misread the goal expression and so thought that R4 had to be avoided
He had memorized the rules, so he skipped any comparison with the goal
He compared R4's output with the goal and noticed a new difference it would add
The experimenter told him which features of the expression he had to preserve
optionExplain: The text gives no hint of a misreading.
The remark shows a comparison with the goal.
The authors say he presumably does this after noticing that R4 would alter a feature that is to remain constant.
The remark is his own, not an instruction.
questions.explain: Noticing what must stay constant is a comparison of a rule's product with the goal.
questions.rule: A rule can add a new difference.
questions.teaches: S10 alone mentions features not to be changed; presumably he compares the output of R4 with the goal expression and notices a new difference.

questions.q: A researcher finds that all five testers of a simple app tap the same three buttons in nearly the same order. What does the authors' caution suggest?
options: Some likeness may come from the task itself, so look for likeness beyond what the app forces
The likeness proves that the five testers share a single mental process of the same kind
The likeness is meaningless
The likeness is due only to chance
optionExplain: The authors note that some similarities derive from the shared task environment.
The authors separate task-forced likeness from process likeness.
The authors still draw cautious conclusions from five.
The task explains part of it.
questions.explain: Common structure of the task can produce common behavior without a common process.
questions.teaches: Some of the similarities among the five subjects derive from the fact that all are working in the same task environment, where all paths to the solution are trivial variants on a common theme.

questions.q: Two people compare a messy draft with a clean target. One notes that the paragraphs are in a different order; the other notes swap paragraphs. Which style do the logic subjects mostly use?
options: Description-style: the difference is worded as a plain fact about the pair
Action-style: the difference is worded as the action that would remove it
Neither: they avoid naming differences at all
Numbers only: they count how many symbols differ
optionExplain: Descriptive phrases are conspicuous by their rarity.
Subjects mostly say connective change or change places, not plain description.
They name them often.
The wording is functional, not numeric.
questions.explain: The card shows the pattern. Differences are tied to ways of removing them.
questions.rule: Words for differences name the fix.

questions.q: The differences found by matching are usually expressed in active, ____ terms, that is, in terms of actions to remove them.
questions.explain: Phrases such as connective change and inner grouping change are functional.

questions.q: A subject compares L1 with L0 and sees that the R sits on the left in one and on the right in the other. Which phrasing fits the subjects' habit?
options: The R is in a different order
There are three symbols on each side
The two expressions look alike
Change places
optionExplain: Such descriptive phrases occur rarely in the protocols.
A count is not a difference to remove.
Likeness is not stated as an action.
An action phrase that names the removal of the difference.
questions.explain: Subjects mostly phrase differences as actions.

questions.q: True or false: If a subject proposed turning R into (Q V P), that would match the pattern of all five protocols.
questions.explain: No subject proposes to transform R into (Q V P) or (~P horseshoe Q) into R; they treat the similar subexpressions in different places as alike.

questions.q: In S9's remark 'It's got three parts similar to that ... but there's no switching of order', what is the second half doing?
options: Matching the product of R4 against its condition and finding no switch of order
Matching L1 against L0 to find a difference in the order of the terms
Searching the display for an expression that already meets the rule's conditions
Reviewing his earlier steps to look for an error in what he has done
optionExplain: The authors bracket the second half as matching product(R4) to condition(R4).
The first half matches L1 with the rule's condition; the second compares product with condition.
The remark is about what the rule does.
No review is involved.
questions.explain: Comparing a rule's output with its input shows what the rule does.
questions.teaches: In S9's remark about R4, the first half matches L1 to the condition of R4 and the second half matches the product of R4 to its condition.

questions.q: A mechanic reads a manual and compares what a tool takes in with what it gives out, to learn what the tool does. What do the authors say this kind of matching leads to?
options: Memorizing the twelve rules in numerical order so that each can be recalled in turn
Skipping the goal expression and working only from the start of the problem
Characterizing rules by their functions, independently of the expressions they are applied to
Replacing the rules by pictures that show what each of them does to a line
optionExplain: The point is about function, not order.
Matching with the goal remains.
The authors say comparing rule inputs with outputs yields a function for each rule.
No such replacement is claimed.
questions.explain: Knowing what a rule does lets a solver pick it without a concrete expression in front of him.
questions.rule: Know rules by what they do.
questions.teaches: Using match processes to compare rule inputs with outputs leads to characterizing rules in terms of their functions, independently of the expressions to which they are applied.

questions.q: You need to open a jar and look through a drawer. Which is the search by function rather than by what happens to fit?
options: Trying each item in the drawer to see what it does to the jar
Asking a friend which item they use most
Looking for something that grips the lid
Using the first item you touch
optionExplain: Trying items and checking their results is a search by applicability.
That is a request for advice, not a search type.
Starting from the job to be done is the function search.
This is no search at all.
questions.explain: Two searches differ by starting point: the job or the available tool. The card names both.

questions.q: Match each remark of S9 to the kind of search it shows.
pairs: I'm looking for a way, now, to get rid of that horseshoe
Search for a rule to perform a function
R3 doesn't look any too practical
Search for a rule that is applicable and desirable
Now 4 looks interesting but there's no switching of order
questions.explain: Getting rid of the horseshoe starts from a function; R3 and R4 are judged for applicability and result.

questions.q: One solver tries rules 2 and 6 on a real expression to see whether Q V P results; another asks which rule removes a horseshoe. How do these differ?
options: The first applies rules to a real expression and matches the output; the second compares a rule's input and output
The first is a search by function and the second a search by applicability, as described
Both compare a rule's input and output in the abstract, without any concrete expression
Neither of them involves a rule
optionExplain: S15 and S9 illustrate the two ways, as the authors explain.
It is the other way round for the two ways of finding a relevant rule.
The first applies the rule concretely.
Both involve rules.
questions.explain: A concrete try and an abstract comparison are two routes to a relevant rule.

questions.q: True or false: True or false: In GPS a difference to be reduced and a function to be performed are different things, as they are in the protocols.
questions.explain: The authors say that in GPS the two are synonymous, but not in the protocols.

questions.q: In a case where no applicable rule appears to perform the desired function, what does S9 do next, per the authors?
options: He gives up on the problem and asks the experimenter for help with the next rule
He applies a rule anyway, whether or not it is applicable to the expression he has
He restarts the whole problem from the goal expression and works backward
He searches for a way to remove the difficulty so a rule can be applied
optionExplain: The protocol shows a further search.
He is trying to make a rule applicable.
No restart is described.
S9: 'I'm looking for a way, now, to get rid of that horseshoe'. This matches GPS's find-relevant-operator.
questions.explain: A blocked function leads to a new search for a way to remove the block.
questions.rule: Blocked, so search for the blocker.
questions.teaches: When no applicable rule seems to perform a desired function, S9 searches for a way to remove the difficulty so that a rule can be applied; this corresponds to GPS's find-relevant-operator subprocess.

questions.q: A support agent first settles what the customer is trying to do, picks a tool, then checks that it works on this account. Which order do the authors observe for function-driven searches?
options: Applicability is examined first, and only afterwards is the rule's function determined
Applicability is examined only after the function has been determined
Both are examined together at the same moment, with no separate order between them
Neither of them is ever examined
optionExplain: That is the order for the applicability-driven search.
If the function is already specified, applicability is checked after it.
The authors describe a sequence.
Both are checked in turn.
questions.explain: S9 is an exception: he considers rules 3 and 4 before noticing they do not perform the function.
questions.teaches: If the function has been specified, applicability is not examined until after the rule's function is determined; S9 and the GPS trace modeled on him instead consider rules 3 and 4 before noticing that they do not perform the function.

questions.q: A new employee must find the right form for a task. A veteran knows it by heart. What explains the difference, in the terms of this chapter?
options: The veteran has an association stored in memory; the newcomer must search
The veteran reads the instructions faster than the newcomer does, and so finds the form first
The newcomer does not know what the task requires, while the veteran does know
The veteran avoids the forms altogether and does the task in some other way
optionExplain: A stored link from need to tool replaces searching.
Speed of reading is not the point.
The newcomer knows the need but lacks the stored link.
The veteran still uses forms.
questions.explain: Stored associations versus search are the two routes the card describes.

questions.q: A stored association between a function or difference and a rule is called the GPS table of ____.
questions.explain: The table of connections links differences or functions to rules.

questions.q: True or false: A trainee pilot on a very first day checks each switch one by one to find the right one. The authors would read this as a rule search expected when little table of connections is stored.
questions.explain: The same explanation is given for S9's rule searches: a thin table of connections forces search.

questions.q: A subject who has already solved fifty such problems meets a new one. Compared with S9 on his first problem, what is the subject more likely to show?
options: The same number of rule searches as S9 made on his first problem
More rule searches, since there are by now more rules to compare with one another
No use of functional language at all
Use of stored connections from a function to a rule, with fewer rule searches
optionExplain: Practice stores connections.
Stored associations shorten the search.
Functional language was present from the start.
A fuller table of connections replaces searching.
questions.explain: Fewer searches follow from more stored connections.

questions.q: What do the subjects bring to the task, according to the authors, that is not a stored table of connections?
options: A full list of which rule does which job, built up from the earlier problems
Knowledge of what needs doing, in functional language from algebra and daily life
A complete plan for the whole problem, formed before the subjects begin to work
An exact copy of GPS's methods, which they carry out step by step
optionExplain: They lack that list.
They know what to do in functional terms but not how without trying their tools.
The text describes functions, not a fixed plan.
The subjects are not described as having GPS.
questions.explain: Knowing what versus knowing how.
questions.rule: Know the what, search for the how.
questions.teaches: The subjects already know what needs to be done in the language of functions brought from algebra and everyday life, but they do not yet know how to do it without trying their unfamiliar rules one by one.

questions.q: A second-year student and a first-year student both know they need to reduce a fraction, but only the second goes straight to the right method. In the authors' terms, what differs?
options: The second understands what needs doing in the task, while the first does not
The first is working backward from the goal and the second is working forward
The second has stored a link from the needed function to the method; the first searches
The second ignores the goal and works forward through every method in turn
optionExplain: Both know what needs doing.
The first is searching, not working backward.
Stored connections replace rule searches with practice.
A direct link is not working forward.
questions.explain: Same goal knowledge, different stored connections.
questions.teaches: The authors expect more evidence of a table of connections in the subjects' behavior on later problems, and say they will not be disappointed.

questions.q: A puzzle is rated one of the two easiest in a set of sixteen. Would you expect most newcomers to solve it in 15 minutes?
options: Yes, since the easiest puzzle in a set can be solved by anyone who tries it
No, since nobody solves any puzzle on a first try, however easy the puzzle is
Yes, because puzzles are always built so that they can be solved quickly
Not necessarily: easiest in a hard set can still be hard for a newcomer
optionExplain: Relative ease is not absolute ease.
Some do; the rate is low, not zero.
Nothing guarantees a quick solution.
Rank within a set does not fix absolute difficulty.
questions.explain: The card gives the figures for D1.
questions.rule: Easy in the set is not easy outright.

questions.q: Of the 64 Yale subjects, ____ solved Problem D1 in the fifteen minutes allowed.
questions.explain: Even though D1 was one of the two easiest problems, only 24 of the 64 Yale subjects solved it in fifteen minutes, so it was not easy in an absolute sense.
questions.teaches: Even so, only 24 of 64 Yale subjects solved it in the fifteen minutes allowed.

questions.q: Order the four sessions by the number of subjects (out of sixteen each) who solved D1, fewest first.
items: First session (1)
Second session (4)
Third session (5)
Fourth session (14)
questions.explain: The numbers rose from 1 to 4 to 5 to 14.

questions.q: A new group of subjects meets D1 only after having practised on twelve other such problems. What does the pattern suggest?
options: About the same success rate as in the first session
A much higher success rate than in the first session
A lower rate than in the first session
No solvers at all
optionExplain: The rate rose with practice.
Fourteen of sixteen solved it in the fourth session after earlier problems.
The fourth session had the best result.
Fourteen of sixteen solved it.
questions.explain: Experience with earlier problems made D1 easier.

questions.q: How did the Carnegie thinking-aloud subjects fare on D1?
options: All seven solved it, and each did so within fifteen minutes of starting
None solved it, because talking aloud slows thinking too much to finish
Five of the seven with protocols solved it in the half hour allowed
Two of the seven solved it, about the same share as in the Yale group
optionExplain: They had half an hour and not all solved it.
Five of seven solved it.
Five of seven solved it.
Five of seven solved it.
questions.explain: The Carnegie group had thinking-aloud conditions and a longer limit.
questions.teaches: Five of the seven Carnegie subjects for whom protocols exist solved Problem D1 in the half hour allowed, and they usually met it right after the three training problems.

questions.q: A school tests a new maths exercise on its first-year students in week 1 and finds that few solve it. A teacher says it must be a hard exercise. What does the D1 record caution?
options: A low early rate can reflect lack of practice, as D1 went from 1 of 16 to 14 of 16
A low rate shows that the exercise is beyond what the students can learn to do
Practice has no bearing on success rates, so the first session tells the whole story
Only the first session counts as evidence
optionExplain: The same problem moved from few solvers to nearly all with practice.
D1 was solved by nearly all practised subjects.
The D1 record shows a large effect.
All sessions are evidence.
questions.explain: The authors read the rise across sessions as the effect of practice.
questions.rule: Early failure can mean no practice.
questions.teaches: The 14 of 16 fourth-session solvers had practised, successfully or not, on at least twelve previous problems.

questions.q: A task needs two parts pulled out of one line, one part flipped, the two joined, and a symbol changed twice. How many steps is the shortest plan?
options: Four
Six
Five
Seven
optionExplain: Four skips the two changes of the symbol.
Two pulls, one flip, one join and two changes make six.
Five misses one of the two changes.
Seven adds a step that is not needed.
questions.explain: Counting the moves of a plan gives its length. The card lists the six steps of D1.

questions.q: The shortest solution of Problem D1 from L1 involves ____ steps.
questions.explain: Figure 9.4 shows a six-step path.

questions.q: In the shortest path, which two rules together change the horseshoe in the combined result into a dot?
options: R2 then R12
R8 then R8
R5 then R6
R6 then R5
optionExplain: R2 commutes and R12 combines two lines; neither changes the connective alone.
R8 splits the line into parts.
The order is wedge first (R6), then dot (R5).
The horseshoe is first made a wedge by R6, then a dot by R5.
questions.explain: Two connective changes are needed because the change goes through the wedge.

questions.q: True or false: A subject who applies R2 to L2 rather than L3 will need a further rule to reverse P and Q, so may take seven steps without wasting any.
questions.explain: The authors say such a subject needs a later R1 or R2 to reverse the order of P and Q, giving a seven-step path in which every step is part of the final solution.
questions.rule: A longer route need not contain wasted steps.

questions.q: Order the main moves of the shortest solution, using the functional description.
items: Split L1 into two parts with R8, twice
Commute one part with R2
Combine the two parts with R12, removing the R's
Change horseshoe to wedge with R6, then to dot with R5
questions.explain: The parts must be separated, aligned and combined before the connective is changed.

questions.q: A packer must separate two items from a bundle, turn one around, join them in a new box, and relabel twice. If the turning is done on the other item, an extra turn is needed later. Which statement matches the D1 pattern?
options: The longer route has no wasted move but is not the shortest
The longer route contains wasted moves that are not part of the final solution
The longer route turns out to be shorter than the route first described
Both routes must have exactly the same number of moves when they are carried out
optionExplain: Seven steps without waste still exceeds the shortest path.
In the D1 case every step is part of the final solution.
It adds one step.
The extra reversal makes the second longer.
questions.explain: Length and waste are different measures.
questions.teaches: A subject can take seven steps on D1 without wasting any (that is, taking no step outside his final solution), because other modifications of the path can lengthen it.

questions.q: A puzzle starts with a line containing a symbol that the goal line lacks. What does this comparison suggest a solver should do?
options: Add the symbol to the goal line
Ignore the symbol until the end
Look for ways to remove that symbol
Change the order of all symbols first
optionExplain: The goal is fixed.
It is the key difference.
A symbol present at the start but absent at the goal marks what must be removed.
Order changes do not remove it.
questions.explain: The comparison of start and goal shows where to work.

questions.q: True or false: In Problem D1, matching L1 with L0 shows that R appears in L1 and not in L0, so a step that deletes R is needed.
questions.explain: This is the essential difference the match detects.

questions.q: In the abstract space the original expressions are kept, but their ____, signs and the order of symbols are ignored.
questions.explain: Plans are made on the skeleton of letters, then adjusted by inessential rules.

questions.q: Why are the five plans of Figure 9.5 shown?
options: They are the only five plans that exist for solving the problem from L1
They are the five plans that GPS prefers when it chooses among all the paths
They are the ones needed to analyze the subjects' behavior; more could be generated
They are the five plans that are easiest to carry out from the starting line
optionExplain: The authors say these are not all that could be generated.
Preference is not the reason.
The authors say they serve for the analysis of subjects' behavior on D1.
Only one of them can in fact be carried out.
questions.explain: A selection chosen for analysis rather than for completeness.
questions.teaches: The five plans are not all that could be generated, but they serve for the analysis of the subjects' behavior on D1; each is labeled by the essential rule most characteristic of it.

questions.q: A mechanic compares a broken engine with a working one and finds a missing part. Which idea from the chapter does this match?
options: A match between start and goal reveals an essential difference that suggests plans
