Exhaustive search shows which parts are needed, so no comparison of start and goal is used
An applicable rule is applied because it applies, whatever the goal may be
The goal state is ignored until the last step, when the answer is checked
optionExplain: Comparing current and goal states detects what must be added or removed.
The match avoids exhaustive search.
The mechanic's step is guided by the difference.
The goal is used first.
questions.explain: A start-goal match gives the first clue.
questions.teaches: The authors treat the detection of the need to delete R as an essential difference, in the sense used for planning in Chapter 8.

questions.q: A group makes five plans to remove an unwanted item from a bundle. How can plans that turn out to be unworkable still help a researcher?
options: They do not help at all
They show which of the people is cleverest at choosing plans in advance
They prove that the one workable plan is the best of all possible plans
They may be what people try, so they explain behavior that would look odd
optionExplain: People can still try them.
That is not the researcher's aim.
Failed plans say nothing about optimality.
Unworkable plans still shape what people do.
questions.explain: Unworkable plans can still guide behavior. The card names the five plans.

questions.q: In path.R12, R8 is used to divide the expression L1 into two parts to which the two-line rule, R____, can be applied.
questions.explain: R8 divides L1 and R12 combines the two lines to eliminate the R's.

questions.q: Match each plan to how it eliminates the R's.
pairs: R8 to divide L1, then the two-line rule R12
Successive applications of R8, with the pieces joined by R10
questions.explain: These are the descriptions the authors give.
questions.rule: Name the plan by its characteristic rule.

questions.q: True or false: If R8 could be applied to either half of L1 without any obstacle, path.R10 would eliminate the R's by successive uses of R8.
questions.explain: path.R10 is the plan that removes the R's by successive uses of R8; its success would depend on R8 being applicable again.
questions.rule: A plan stands or falls on its rules' conditions.

questions.q: In path.R9, how is R8 used?
options: To divide L1 into two separate lines to which the two-line rule R12 is applied
To eliminate (RQ), and later again to remove the remaining R
To change the connective of the resulting expression to a dot at the final step
To add Q to the expression, so that the later grouping can be carried out
optionExplain: That is path.R12.
R8 is used twice in this plan.
R8 does not change connectives.
Adding a term belongs to R9, not R8.
questions.explain: R8 is used twice in this plan.
questions.rule: Plan R9 removes one part, then R.
questions.teaches: In path.R9 the rule R8 is used to eliminate (RQ) and later used again to remove the remaining R.

questions.q: A planner draws five routes to a goal. On trying them, only the route that splits the task in two and then joins the halves can be carried out. Which D1 fact does this resemble?
options: Only path.R12 is operative; the other four cannot be carried out
All five plans can be carried out from L1, though they differ in speed
Only path.R7 is operative
Only path.R10 is operative
optionExplain: The authors say the fifth plan alone can actually be done.
Four of them cannot.
path.R7 fails.
Its repeated uses of R8 are blocked.
questions.explain: Which plan works is a fact about the task, not about how neat the plan looks.
questions.teaches: Of the five plans, only the fifth (path.R12) is actually operative; the others cannot be carried out.

questions.q: A machine accepts only positive-sign, dot-joined items. A part cannot be turned into a dot-joined item without becoming negative. Can the machine take it?
options: Yes, because a machine that has conditions can still take items that break them
Yes, because the dot connective is all that matters for the machine
Only if the item is shorter than the items the machine usually takes
No, because the part would no longer meet the machine's conditions
optionExplain: The machine has conditions.
Positive sign is also required.
Length is not a condition.
The conditions fail once the sign turns negative.
questions.explain: Rules have conditions, and conditions can block a plan. The card gives R8's conditions.

questions.q: R8 can be applied only to positive expressions whose main connective is a ____.
questions.explain: R8 needs a positive expression with a dot as the main connective.

questions.q: Which expression could R8 be applied to?
options: A negative expression with a dot as main connective
A positive expression with a dot as main connective
A positive expression with a wedge as main connective
Any expression containing the letter R
optionExplain: A negative expression does not meet the condition.
That is exactly R8's condition.
A wedge main connective does not meet the condition.
The letter is not the condition.
questions.explain: Both sign and main connective matter.

questions.q: True or false: If left(L1) could be changed to a dot connective without making the whole expression negative, R8 could be applied a second time.
questions.explain: The obstacle is that the change to a dot makes the expression negative; remove that and R8's condition would hold.
questions.rule: Remove the blocking condition and the step is allowed.

questions.q: A manager finds that a plan to remove a factor by repeating a step fails after the first use. Which diagnosis fits this chapter's reasoning?
options: The step was applied by the wrong person, so it must be handed to someone else
The step needs more time to work, so a second use is only delayed
After the first use the item no longer meets the step's conditions
The first use was wrong, so the second use is blocked until it is undone
optionExplain: The cause is the step's condition.
Time is not the issue.
R8 cannot be applied again because its conditions fail on the product.
The first use is fine; the second is blocked.
questions.explain: A repeatable-looking step may be blocked by its own conditions.
questions.teaches: Plans that try to extract a single letter from L1 by successive applications of R8 fail, since after the first application the product cannot be given the positive dot form that R8 requires.

questions.q: A shop sells 48 items. They come in groups of six that can be turned into one another by simple swaps, and no swap moves an item out of its group. How many groups?
options: Six
Twelve
Forty-two
Eight
optionExplain: Six is the group size.
Twelve would need groups of four.
That subtracts instead of dividing.
48 divided by 6 is 8.
questions.explain: When groups are of equal size and do not overlap, divide. The card does this for expressions.

questions.q: From any one of the six forms in Figure 9.7, each of the other ____ and only those can be obtained by the four inessential rules.
questions.explain: Six expressions form a class, so each reaches the other five.

questions.q: Count the expressions for two fixed parts A and B: three connectives, two orders, and a plus or minus sign for A, for B and for the whole. What is the total?
optionExplain: That uses only one sign instead of three.
That uses two signs instead of three.
That uses an extra factor of two.
questions.explain: Multiply the independent choices.

questions.q: Which of these changes keeps an expression inside its class (that is, can be done by R1, R2, R5 and R6)? Select all that apply.
options: Swapping the order of the two parts around the main connective
Changing the connective together with the matching signs
Deleting a term from the expression
Adding a new term to the expression
optionExplain: Commutation is done by R1 and R2.
Connective changes are done by R5 and R6.
The inessential rules do not delete terms.
Nor do they add terms.
questions.explain: The four rules permute and re-sign terms; they do not add or delete them.

questions.q: What can be said about two expressions from different classes?
options: They can be obtained from each other by more than one application
They can be obtained from each other if the order is changed
They cannot be obtained from each other by R1, R2, R5 and R6
They can be obtained only if the connective is a dot
optionExplain: Repeated use stays inside a class.
Order change keeps the class.
Only members of the same class can be obtained from one another.
Connective type does not decide it.
questions.explain: The classes partition the 48 expressions.
questions.teaches: Two expressions belonging to the same class can be obtained from each other by R1, R2, R5 and R6, while expressions belonging to different classes cannot.

questions.q: A card game has 48 distinct hands. Allowed swaps connect 6 hands into a set, and no swap leaves its set. A player claims that every hand can be reached from his own. What is wrong?
options: From any hand only 5 others, those in its set, can be reached
Nothing is wrong, since swaps can be repeated until every hand has been reached
Only 3 can be reached, one for each of the three kinds of swap
All 47 others can be reached after enough swaps are made in the right order
optionExplain: The same logic as for classes: reachability stops at the class boundary.
Repeated swaps stay inside the set.
Five can be reached.
Different sets cannot be reached.
questions.explain: Repeating moves inside a class never leaves it.
questions.rule: Reachability is limited to the class.
questions.teaches: With 48 expressions in classes of six, there are exactly 8 classes, and a solver working only with the inessential rules is confined to the six forms of one class.

questions.q: A builder calls some tasks inessential because they do not change the plan's main structure. Can the builder skip them when checking whether the plan is feasible?
options: Yes, since inessential means optional and so can be left out of the check
No: small adjustments can decide whether the parts fit
Yes, if the builder has carried out the same plan on an earlier occasion
Only if there is no budget for the adjustments, which are then left undone
optionExplain: Role in the plan is not the same as optional.
Minor adjustments may still determine feasibility.
Experience does not remove them.
Budget is unrelated.
questions.explain: The card gives the authors' warning about the word.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the inessential rules add no terms, delete no terms and change no grouping of terms.
questions.explain: These rules only permute order and change signs and connectives.

questions.q: Sort each rule by whether it is an inessential (form-preserving) rule or an essential one.

items.t: R6: changes a horseshoe to a wedge
R1: swaps the order of the two parts
R8: discards one side of a dot-joined line
R9: adds a term to the expression

questions.explain: Rules that only permute order and change signs and connectives are inessential; rules that add or delete terms are essential.

questions.q: Why do the authors say form-preserving may be a more descriptive term?
options: The rules preserve the truth value of every problem to which they are applied
The rules cannot be applied in the wrong order, whatever expression is used
The rules were first built for the cryptarithmetic task and carried over
Subjects almost uniformly regard expressions of one class as highly similar
optionExplain: The reason given concerns similarity as seen by subjects.
Order is not the reason.
No link to cryptarithmetic is given.
That is the reason the authors give.
questions.explain: Subjects treat same-class forms as alike.
questions.teaches: Subjects almost uniformly regard the expressions belonging to a single equivalence class as highly similar, which is why the authors say form-preserving would be more descriptive than inessential.

questions.q: A trip planner splits decisions into essential ones (which city, which week) and inessential ones (which hotel on which street). When might the inessential ones still decide feasibility?
options: When every nearby hotel is booked that week, so the plan cannot be fitted together
Never, because inessential decisions can always be changed at will after the plan is made
Only when the trip is short
When the planner has no budget
optionExplain: A minor adjustment can make or break the plan's feasibility.
The authors warn that feasibility can depend on them.
Length is not the condition.
Budget is a different matter.
questions.explain: Adjustments are minor in the plan but can bind it.
questions.teaches: In planning, the essential rules set out the major transformations and the inessential rules provide minor adjustments that fit the segments of the plan together.

questions.q: Two switches are wired so that flipping one setting changes both together. A task needs them set differently. What follows?
options: The task can be done with enough tries
The task is easy if it is done in the right order, one switch at a time
The task cannot be done with those wires, though this may not be easy to see
The task needs a third switch, which would break the link between the two
optionExplain: Tries cannot break a wiring constraint.
Order does not break the link.
Linked settings cannot be set separately.
The block comes from the link, not the number of switches.
questions.explain: A hidden link between features can make a goal impossible. The card shows the logic case.
questions.rule: Linked features cannot be set apart.

questions.q: True or false: In the R7 plan, the two R's would need to have the same sign.
questions.explain: The needed shape has the same sign on both R's (for instance both with tildes, or neither).

questions.q: In expressions with a wedge or dot connective obtained from L1, the sign of R is determined by the ____.
questions.explain: Because sign follows connective, two subexpressions with different R signs must have different connectives.

questions.q: True or false: A subject who tries hard enough with R1, R2, R5 and R6 will eventually put L1 into the shape that R7 needs.
questions.explain: The authors' argument is that the signs of the two R's cannot be changed independently of the connectives, so the shape cannot be reached.
questions.rule: No amount of effort breaks the link.

questions.q: What do the authors say about how obvious this infeasibility is?
options: It is plain to any subject on inspection of the expression L1
It is obvious only to GPS
It is by no means obvious without something like Figure 9.7
It cannot be known by anyone, even with the structure laid out in full
optionExplain: The authors say the result is by no means obvious.
No such claim is made.
The result is not obvious, so a subject may keep trying.
It can be shown, as Figure 9.7 does.
questions.explain: The block is a structural fact that needs analysis.
questions.teaches: A person without Figure 9.7 might not be sure that L1 cannot be put in a form for R7 by the inessential rules, so a subject trying this plan is expected to generate many members of the equivalence class of L1.

questions.q: A puzzle-solver fiddles for twenty minutes trying to set two linked dials apart. In the chapter's terms, which expectation is reasonable?
options: Many tries within the allowed settings before the solver is convinced no route exists
The solver gives up at once
The solver succeeds if given more time
The solver ignores the dials and tries a different task for the time being
optionExplain: Subjects cycled on Figure 9.7's structure until convinced indirect paths were infeasible.
The block is not obvious.
No route exists.
The solver works on them.
questions.explain: Convincing oneself of impossibility takes exploration.
questions.teaches: Subjects cycled on the structure of Figure 9.7 until they became convinced that indirect paths were as infeasible as direct ones for making R7 applicable to derivatives of L1.

questions.q: An object has three parts and each part can be shown in six forms independently. How many whole forms are there?
optionExplain: Eighteen adds the forms instead of multiplying.
Thirty-six counts only two parts.
729 is 9 cubed.
questions.explain: Independent choices multiply. The card does this for L1.

questions.q: Each extended equivalence class of L1 contains 6 x 6 x 6 = ____ expressions.
questions.explain: Three binary expressions, each with six forms.

questions.q: A poster has three panels, and each panel can take any of five layouts independently. How many posters are possible, by the same reasoning?
optionExplain: Fifteen adds instead of multiplying.
Twenty-five counts only two panels.
243 is 3 to the fifth power, which swaps the base and exponent.
questions.explain: Independent panels multiply.

questions.q: True or false: By the same reasoning, an expression made of four binary parts with six forms each would have 6 x 6 x 6 x 6 = 1296 forms.
questions.explain: Our reading of the counting rule: each added independent part multiplies the count by six.

questions.q: The narrower equivalence class of L1 replaces the left and right parts by their six forms each and allows commuting around the main connective, but does not change the main connective. How many members does it have?
optionExplain: That leaves out commuting the whole.
That is the extended class.
That is 6 x 2, which forgets a part.
questions.explain: The main connective is held fixed, so only the two parts and the order vary.
questions.rule: Hold the main connective fixed: 6 x 6 x 2.
questions.teaches: The equivalence class of L1 (which allows commuting around the main connective but not changing the connective) has 72 members, as against 216 in the extended class.

questions.q: A study finds that 42 of the 72 possible forms occur in people's written records. Which reading is cautious?
options: The remaining 30 forms are impossible for subjects to produce under the rules
All 72 must occur if the theory is right, so 30 absences refute it
Forms outside the class were produced instead of the 30 absent ones
Subjects produce a large share of the possible forms, as if searching this class widely
optionExplain: Absence from the records does not show impossibility.
The authors do not expect every form.
The count says nothing about forms outside the class.
42 of 72 is over half; the authors read this as search within the class.
questions.explain: A partial presence in the records is consistent with directed search of the class.
questions.teaches: Of the 72 members of the equivalence class of L1, 42 actually occurred in one or more subjects' records.

questions.q: You can use any of twelve kitchen tools. One tool fits every job. Is the fact that a tool is usable a good reason to pick it?
options: Yes: any tool that can be used is a good choice for the job at hand
No: a tool that always fits tells you nothing about which job it suits
Yes: the more jobs a tool can be used for, the better the choice
Only if the other tools are broken, so that nothing else can be used
optionExplain: Usability alone does not guide.
Universal fit does not discriminate.
A universal tool guides nothing.
The point concerns informativeness.
questions.explain: A clue must separate options. The card applies this to rule R9.

questions.q: It makes no sense to apply R9 only because it is applicable, since R9 is ____ applicable.
questions.explain: R9 can be applied to any expression, so its applicability carries no information.

questions.q: L1 has the shape of two joined parts that share a letter, like the right side of R7. How strong a clue to apply R7 is this resemblance?
options: A decisive one: R7 must then be part of the solution
None: the shape of an expression never matters in choosing a rule
A weak one: it only suggests R7 because the shapes look alike
The strongest one, stronger than the match between the start and the goal
optionExplain: The authors list it among weaker clues.
The authors say it may suggest the rule.
Similarity of input form is a weak clue.
The match with L0 is stronger.
questions.explain: Resemblance to a rule's input can suggest it but proves nothing.

questions.q: True or false: A solver who judges steps by whether the product is simpler than L1 would regard an application of R6 as supported by that clue.
questions.explain: The authors say R6 might be justified because it produces expressions simpler than L1, as well as for the reasons given earlier.

questions.q: How can simplification be used working backward from L0?
options: L0 is positive, so R8 deletes a letter from it to leave a simpler form
L0 is replaced by L1, so that the problem is started over from the other end
L0 is split in two by R12, giving the two lines to be combined later
L0 is negative, so R5 turns it into a positive expression with one tilde within
optionExplain: L0 is a negative expression.
The goal is not replaced by the start.
R12 is used to combine two lines.
Applying R5 to L0 gives (Q V ~P), simpler than L0.
questions.explain: Backward simplification rewrites the goal.
questions.teaches: Working backward from L0, a negative expression, R5 would produce the positive expression (Q V ~P) with only one tilde within.

questions.q: A student replaces a hard exam question with an easier-looking rewritten one, without checking that the rewritten question is easier to answer. What does the authors' remark about the rewritten problem teach?
options: A transformation is justified only if the new problem proves easier to solve
The point is the motivation for the transformation, not whether the problem gets easier
A transformation is never justified by simplification, whatever the expression
The new problem must be harder, or the transformation would not be needed
optionExplain: The authors set that question aside.
The authors say whether the new problem is easier is not their immediate concern.
They count simplification as a clue.
No such claim is made.
questions.explain: Motivation is separate from success.
questions.rule: Ask why the step was suggested.
questions.teaches: If a subject simplified both ends, the original problem would become that of obtaining (Q V ~P) from (R horseshoe ~P) and (~R horseshoe Q); the authors do not ask whether that is easier, only what motivates the transformations.

questions.q: A cook compares a starting dish with the target and finds an ingredient in the dish that the target lacks. Which opening goal follows?
options: Add the missing ingredient to the target
Swap the order of the ingredients
Remove that ingredient
Serve the dish as it is
optionExplain: The target is fixed.
Order is not the difference.
The mismatch names the first goal.
That ignores the difference.
questions.explain: The first move is set by the first difference. The card gives the logic case.

questions.q: After matching L1 with L0, GPS forms a reduce goal that the authors name ____.
questions.explain: R's are present in L1 and absent from L0, so the goal is to delete R.

questions.q: Put GPS's early moves on D1 in order.
items: Match L1 to L0 and find R's only in L1
Find R8 and apply it to produce L2
Reject the goal of adding Q to L2
Return to the Delete goal and try the other form of R8
questions.explain: The trace follows this sequence before moving on to R7.

questions.q: Why does GPS reject the goal of adding Q back into L2?
options: Adding a term is treated as harder than deleting one, so the goal is rejected
L2 already contains Q, so the goal is met and does not need to be pursued
Q cannot be added by any rule of the system, so the goal is impossible
L0 does not contain Q, so the goal would take GPS away from the target
optionExplain: The authors give this evaluation rule.
L2 lacks Q, hence the goal.
R9 can add a term; the issue is relative difficulty.
L0 contains Q.
questions.explain: Evaluation prefers deleting terms to adding them.

questions.q: GPS applies R6 first to remove a connective difference and then again to remove a sign difference. How does the trace treat the second use?
options: As a mistake that the program corrects on a later pass
As the same rule perceived as accomplishing a different function
As an application of R5, which GPS swaps in for the second use
As a rule that GPS has not used before and therefore must learn
optionExplain: No correction is described.
The authors note R6 is used again but for a different function.
The rule is R6 both times.
It was used just before.
questions.explain: A rule can serve more than one function.
questions.teaches: After removing the connective differences with R6, GPS finds a sign difference and applies R6 again; it is the same rule perceived as accomplishing a different function. The resulting expression L6 happens to be identical with L4, though GPS does not notice the identity.

questions.q: A navigation program tries two routes that look different but are the same, and does not notice they are the same. Which feature of the GPS trace does this resemble?
options: GPS rejects R8 because it deletes a letter that L0 needs
GPS chooses the first of two admissible forms of R8 in each cycle
GPS finds R7 by searching the rules for one that removes terms
GPS produces L6 identical to L4 without noticing the identity
optionExplain: That is evaluation, not failure to notice.
That is a choice rule.
That is a rule search.
The program does not detect the repeated expression.
questions.explain: Cycling over equivalent expressions is a feature the program must handle.
questions.teaches: In goal 19 GPS detects the connective difference again and rejects the goal as representing no progress over goal 13.

questions.q: A maze-solving program risks walking in circles. Which safeguard would stop this?
options: Stop when a move undoes something that earlier made progress
Walk faster through the maze so that the loop is finished sooner
Always turn left at each junction, whatever has been seen before
Remove the exit from the maze so that no path can lead back
optionExplain: A progress test halts the loop.
Speed does not break a loop.
A fixed rule can still loop.
That prevents solution.
questions.explain: Cycling needs a stopper. The card gives GPS's.

questions.q: GPS arranges differences in a priority order and removing a connective difference counts as ____.
questions.explain: Reintroducing a connective difference is not progress.

questions.q: GPS has removed the connective difference and now reintroduces it to remove a sign difference. What happens?
options: The sign difference is removed and the search goes on with the next rule
GPS switches to R8, which is the next rule in its list of rules
The progress test fails and the series of transformations halts
GPS restarts from L0 and works the whole problem again from the goal
optionExplain: The test stops the series.
The halt ends this series.
Reintroducing the connective difference is not progress.
No restart is described.
questions.explain: The priority order ranks connectives above signs for this purpose.
questions.rule: Do not re-open a higher-priority difference.

questions.q: Match each method of avoiding cycles to how it works.
pairs: Halts when fixing one difference reintroduces a higher-priority one
Halts when a new expression equals one obtained before
The search may cycle indefinitely over the inessential rules
questions.explain: Two ways of stopping a cycle. They are not equivalent.

questions.q: Why are the two ways of stopping a cycle not equivalent?
options: One of them stops only after the problem is solved
One can be used by humans and the other only by computers
The same expression might be generated in different contexts
One needs a priority order for rules and the other for subjects
optionExplain: Both stop a cycle in progress.
The text gives no such distinction.
Comparing with earlier expressions could halt the search in a context where it would have been useful.
Both concern expressions and differences.
questions.explain: Identical expressions may arise for different reasons.
questions.teaches: The authors say the two means of halting a cycle are not equivalent, since the same expression might be generated in different contexts.

questions.q: A route planner stops a search when a new road leads back to a city already visited. A colleague says the planner should stop only when a trip step undoes progress toward the goal. Which statement follows the authors?
options: The two rules can differ, because the same place can be reached for different purposes
They always give the same result
Only the first can be used
Neither can stop a loop
optionExplain: The same expression may arise in different contexts.
The authors say they are not equivalent.
Either is a possible means.
Both can stop cycling.
questions.explain: Context matters when judging repeats.
questions.teaches: GPS in the version used employs a progress test on a priority order of differences; the alternative of comparing new expressions with those obtained previously would halt on evidence of cycling.

questions.q: Someone says: I can't do that, because it would throw away a letter I need later. Which sequence of steps does the remark imply?
options: Do the step on paper and then undo it once its result has been seen
Ask someone else to judge the step before deciding whether to take it
Skip the goal and choose between the steps at random
Imagine the step, compare the result with the goal, then reject it
optionExplain: The remark describes a step not carried out.
The remark is the person's own judgment.
The remark cites the goal.
A rejection with a reason implies an imagined result and a comparison.
questions.explain: A reasoned rejection reveals hidden steps. The card shows the case from S4.

questions.q: Match each remark of S4 to the part of the GPS trace it corresponds to.
pairs: First we want to eliminate one of the sides by using R8
I will be eliminating either the Q or the P
Covert R8, comparison with L0, rejection
If you apply R6 to both sides ... I'm going to see if I can apply R7
Goals 9 to 14: R7 needs a change of connective by R6
questions.explain: These are the correspondences the authors point to.

questions.q: S4 chooses R6 and not R5 as the rule to change the connectives. What do the authors say this suggests?
options: The subject did not know R5 and therefore turned to R6
The subject, like GPS, made a preliminary feasibility test on the main connective
The subject was guessing, and R6 happened to be the first rule he tried
R5 cannot change connectives, so R6 was the only rule that could be used
optionExplain: The text gives no hint of that.
The choice of R6 over R5 supports the presence of that test.
The authors read it as a test, not a guess.
R5 changes connectives in other contexts.
questions.explain: Selecting the rule that fits the actual connective shows a test of feasibility.

questions.q: True or false: If S4 had used a different mechanism from GPS's, the authors suggest it would be hard to explain why he made the remarks that he did.
questions.explain: The authors say that if the mechanism of the program or something essentially similar were not operating, it would be hard to explain the remarks.

questions.q: S4 views the right-hand R, not the left-hand R, as having the sign difference. What do the authors give as the likely source of this preference?
options: The language habit of working from left to right
A rule of GPS that prefers the right side, which the subject copies
A difference in the typefaces of the two R's on the page
A preference for dot connectives over wedges in the expression
optionExplain: The authors attribute it to this habit, in both the program and presumably the subject.
The authors link it to a language habit, not a rule.
No such cause is given.
The preference is about sides.
questions.explain: A small habit can decide which side the work proceeds on.
questions.teaches: The preference for viewing the right-hand R rather than the left-hand R as having the difference arises from the language habit of working from left to right, and it can affect a whole subsequent stream of events.

questions.q: Two readers of a recipe both start at the top of the page and work down; one ends up with a different dish. What parallel does this have with S4 and GPS?
options: Habits never affect later events
Only programs have such habits
A habit has no effect if the final answer turns out to be the same
A small habit, like working left to right, can fix which side is handled first
optionExplain: The authors say they can.
The authors attribute it to the subject presumably also.
The stream of events still differs.
The authors stress that the preference determines which side is worked on.
questions.explain: Early arbitrary choices can have consequences.
questions.teaches: In the R8 episode the subject apparently worked from left to right and from top to bottom in order to arrive at (Q V P) rather than (P V Q).

questions.q: Two people start a task in different ways, but later they take the same steps again. What does the re-joining suggest?
options: They copied each other's steps from the beginning
A shared mechanism may govern the later steps
They are working at random and happened to meet again
The task is too easy for any path to differ from another
optionExplain: Nothing suggests copying.
Divergent paths seldom merge unless the same process drives them.
Random paths seldom merge.
Ease would not explain the merge.
questions.explain: Re-joining of paths is informative. The card gives the S4 case.

questions.q: True or false: In the last part of the S4 segment, the trace and the protocol come back into good agreement.
questions.explain: Both record futile searches for operators to remove sign and connective differences.

questions.q: The authors read S4's final comment of mild despair as reflecting the impact of several successive ____.
questions.explain: The comment follows repeated futile searches.

questions.q: What is the content of the futile search in the last part of the segment?
options: Looking for a way to delete the Q from the expression he has
Testing R12 on L2 and L3 to see whether the two can be combined
Looking for further operators to remove the sign and connective differences, in vain
Reviewing the rules aloud for the benefit of the experimenter
optionExplain: Deleting Q is rejected earlier.
R12 appears later in the protocol.
The authors describe it as always negative.
No review for E is described here.
questions.explain: Further operators were sought and not found.
questions.teaches: In the last part of the segment the protocol records a futile search for additional operators to remove the differences of sign and connective, always with negative results.

questions.q: A mechanic's remarks and a diagnostic program's trace agree on the last stage of a failed repair although they diverged earlier. How strongly does this support the program, by the authors' reasoning?
options: Not at all, since the trace disagreed with the mechanic's remarks earlier on
Completely, since the paths merged and so the program must be correct
The agreement shows that the mechanic copied the program
Somewhat: divergent paths seldom merge, but agreement on a failing search is not decisive
optionExplain: The authors count the re-agreement.
One merge is not proof.
No such inference is warranted.
Merging is notable; the failing context limits its weight.
questions.explain: Judge the weight of agreement by its context.
questions.teaches: The authors say that paths that begin to diverge do not often merge in the way the trace and protocol do in this segment.

questions.q: A program handles two similar sub-tasks one after the other, while the person handles them together in one thought. What does the comparison suggest to change in the program?
options: Make it slower so that it looks more careful
Let it treat the two as one compound item
Remove one of the two sub-tasks from the task
Let the person use the same words that the program uses
optionExplain: Speed is not the issue.
Grouping similar items matches the person.
Both are part of the task.
The change concerns the program.
questions.explain: Match the grouping. The card gives the S4 case.

questions.q: True or false: S4 applies both forms of R8 together and both applications of R6 together, whereas GPS handles each one separately.
questions.explain: This is the discrepancy the authors call grouping of similar tasks.

questions.q: S4 says he should have used R6 only on the left-hand side and then does so. What does this show that GPS lacks?
options: A way to apply R6 to the right-hand side as well as to the left
A table of connections between the differences and the rules
A mechanism of hindsight about past actions, to correct an earlier step
A rule sheet on which the subject can look up the rules
optionExplain: GPS applied R6 to both sides.
GPS has one.
The authors say it might require a little continuous hindsight.
The rule sheet is a separate matter.
questions.explain: Going back to correct an earlier step is not in the program.

questions.q: Match each discrepancy to how the authors assess it.
pairs: Handling similar items one at a time
Real difference; GPS could be extended to use compound expressions
Serious: implies a mechanism not in GPS
questions.explain: Seriousness depends on whether a new mechanism is implied.

questions.q: Why does the lack of an internal/external distinction matter beyond S4's one remark?
options: Expressions on the board have very different memory characteristics from those in the head
The blackboard is always correct, whereas the head makes errors
The head can hold more expressions than the board can
The experimenter chooses which of the rules the subject applies
optionExplain: The distinction has consequences that run throughout a problem.
That is not claimed.
The memory characteristics differ, not the numbers.
The subject commands the rules.
questions.explain: Where an expression lives affects how well it is remembered.
questions.teaches: The overt-covert distinction has consequences that run throughout a problem, since expressions on the blackboard have very different memory characteristics from expressions generated only in the head.

questions.q: A study of cooks finds they cut vegetables in the head and then call out each cut to an assistant. A program that does not separate planning from calling-out might fail to model which aspect?
options: The cooks' choice of which vegetables to cut first
The different memory properties of things done in the head and things written or done outwardly
The amount of salt that the cooks add to the dish
The speed at which the assistant carries out the calls
optionExplain: That is unrelated to the distinction.
This is the consequence of the overt-covert distinction.
That is unrelated.
That is unrelated.
questions.explain: Models should separate covert and overt acts.
questions.teaches: To explain the S4 remark and I don't see it, the system would need a facsimile of the rule sheet and would have to distinguish search on the sheet from searches in memory.

questions.q: A model fits two different people on two different tasks, with some exceptions. Which conclusion is most reasonable?
options: The model is proved correct in every detail
The model is useless because of the exceptions it fails to explain
The exceptions can be ignored
The main processes have some support, and the exceptions mark what needs work
optionExplain: Exceptions remain.
The fit across cases counts for something.
They show where the model must change.
Approximate fit across cases supports the core and the misses direct revision.
questions.explain: A balanced reading counts both fit and misses. The card shows the authors' reading.

questions.q: The authors say the program explains S4's behavior in the episode with ____ exceptions of varying degrees of seriousness.
questions.explain: Five exceptions: two deficiencies, grouping, a complication comment and the should-have passage.

questions.q: Which of S4's remarks do the authors regard as the one most seriously exposing a missing mechanism?
options: I should have used R6 on only the left-hand side
The early remark that the expression appears too complicated to work with first
The mild remark that he is sort of lost for a second or so
The remark that he will not take that step at the first stage of the work
optionExplain: It implies a mechanism, perhaps a set of them, not in GPS.
They see that as mostly insufficient information.
That agrees with the trace.
That agrees with the trace.
questions.explain: A seriously missing mechanism could add much capability if supplied.
questions.rule: The correction is the serious one.

questions.q: True or false: The authors treat the two versions of GPS (used on a1 and on D1) as different programs, so a fit to S4 gives no confidence in the S9 comparison.
questions.explain: They say the two must surely be regarded as the same program in a basic sense, and the approximate fit to two subjects on two problems gives confidence in the main processes.
questions.rule: Same program in the basic sense.

questions.q: What might adding a mechanism for the should-have passage do for GPS?
options: Reduce the program to a few rules by removing the less used ones
Make the program ignore the experimenter's requests
Significantly increase the total capabilities of the program
Remove the need for the rule sheet in later problems
optionExplain: No reduction is suggested.
The experimenter is not discussed here.
The authors say it could, since it might need a little continuous hindsight about past actions.
The rule sheet is a separate matter.
questions.explain: A missing mechanism is also an opportunity.
questions.rule: Fill the gap to gain power.
questions.teaches: Adding the mechanism required for the should-have passage could significantly increase the total capabilities of the program, perhaps by giving GPS a little continuous hindsight about its past actions.

questions.q: A weather model is checked against two seasons, fits the main features, and misses one pattern that needs a new process. How does the authors' stance apply?
options: Reject the model entirely
Pretend the miss did not occur, so that the fit looks complete
Keep the main processes with some confidence and add a process for the missed pattern
Claim that the model is complete
optionExplain: The authors keep the main processes.
They list it as serious.
That follows the authors' reading of the S4 comparison.
They list five exceptions.
questions.explain: Confidence in the core and work on the gaps.
questions.teaches: The authors say that the early comment about complication is mostly a case of insufficient information, since the program makes numerous comparisons and evaluations that could give rise to comments of that type.

questions.q: A lab has detailed think-aloud records from 7 people and plain outcome records from 64 others. What use can the larger set have?
options: It checks the task analysis, tests the effect of talking and gives a background for the detailed cases
It replaces the detailed records entirely
It shows which of the seven talking subjects is the best problem solver
It has no use
optionExplain: The large silent group serves as a baseline for the small talking group.
Detail comes only from the protocols.
That is not its role.
Their written expressions are data.
questions.explain: A large group can anchor a small one. The card lists the authors' three purposes.

questions.q: Twenty-four of the 64 Yale subjects solved D1. Of the seven Carnegie subjects with protocols, ____ solved it.
questions.explain: Five of seven solved it in their half hour.

questions.q: Thirteen of 24 Yale solvers took six or seven steps, as did two of the five Carnegie solvers. How do the authors read this?
options: The Carnegie group solved the problem in fewer steps than the Yale group did
The Yale group was unable to solve the problem in as few as six steps
The two groups used the same paths and applied the rules in the same order
The distribution of steps looks quite similar for the two groups
optionExplain: The two distributions are similar.
Thirteen did.
Step counts do not show that.
That is the conclusion drawn.
questions.explain: Step counts are a first coarse comparison.

questions.q: True or false: The 64 Yale subjects were asked to think aloud while solving, which is why the authors can compare their written expressions with the protocols.
questions.explain: The Yale subjects wrote expressions on the board without thinking-aloud instructions; the thinking-aloud protocols come from the Carnegie subjects.

questions.q: Which question about thinking-aloud instructions do the aggregate data help answer?
options: Whether subjects can tell the truth about their steps while they are talking
Whether those instructions modify the problem solving process in significant ways
Whether the twelve rules are correctly stated in the instructions to subjects
Whether the experimenter is skilled enough to write the steps on the board
optionExplain: That is not what the data address.
A comparison of silent and talking groups can show that.
Rule statements are not at issue.
Not at issue.
questions.explain: The two kinds of subject can be compared on the same problem.
questions.teaches: The aggregate data throw light on whether thinking-aloud instructions modify the problem solving process in significant ways.

questions.q: A company has interviews with 7 customers and a survey of 64 customers, including those who finished the purchase and those who did not. How does the authors' use of the Yale data compare?
options: They too take a comprehensive view from all 64, solvers and non-solvers, as a background
They use only the solvers
They use only the subjects of the first session, who had no practice at all
They use only the seven talkers, whose protocols are the most detailed
optionExplain: The aggregate view includes all 64 subjects.
The entire group of 64 is used.
All sessions are included.
The talkers are the small group.
questions.explain: A large inclusive group gives the background for the detailed few.
questions.teaches: The comprehensive view of behavior on D1 comes from the entire group of 64 Yale subjects, those who solved the problem and those who did not.

questions.q: A study logs every step of 64 people on one puzzle. How could you test whether their behavior is orderly rather than random?
options: Count how many steps there are in total across all of the people
Ask the people to rate how hard the puzzle was after they finish
Compare the log with a random list of steps and see how the two differ
Predict from the puzzle's structure which kinds of step should be common, then check
optionExplain: A count does not test order.
Ratings do not test the logged steps.
A structural prediction is the sharper test.
Predicting the classes in advance gives a test that could fail.
questions.explain: Structure-based expectation gives a test. The card gives the authors' four classes.

questions.q: The 64 Yale subjects wrote on the board a total of ____ different expressions.
questions.explain: 118 different expressions with 519 occurrences in all.

questions.q: Which of these are among the four classes expected from pursuit of the main paths? Select all that apply.
options: The equivalence class of L1
The equivalence class of L0
The equivalence class of the left part of L1
The class of any expression containing R9
optionExplain: Expected, from the R7 path.
Expected, from the R12 path.
Expected, from R8.
Not one of the four classes.
questions.explain: The four classes are those of L1, left(L1), right(L1) and L0.

questions.q: A subject follows the R7 plan and tries to make R7 applicable. Which class should most of the resulting expressions belong to?
options: The equivalence class of L0
The equivalence class of L1
The class of the right part of L1 only
No class in particular
optionExplain: L0's class arises on the R12 path.
The attempt to apply R7 causes the subject to generate members of the class of L1.
That class arises through R8.
The class is predicted.
questions.explain: Each path leaves a trace in a predicted class.

questions.q: What is the average number of occurrences per expression in the whole record of 64 subjects?
optionExplain: That halves the true average.
That is the average for the four classes only.
519 occurrences over 118 expressions gives 4.4.
That is the average outside the four classes.
questions.explain: The overall average mixes the two groups, which are compared later.
questions.teaches: The 64 subjects' 118 different expressions occurred 519 times in all, an average of 4.4 occurrences per expression.

questions.q: True or false: A researcher logs the pages that 64 readers open on a site, finds that 6 pages account for most visits, and concludes readers are highly idiosyncratic. By the authors' reasoning, this conclusion is poorly supported.
questions.explain: Concentration on a few predicted classes suggests orderly behavior shaped by the structure of the task, not idiosyncrasy.
questions.teaches: The authors ask whether the behavior of the subjects is highly idiosyncratic, or can largely be accounted for in terms of salient characteristics of the task that are easily noticed by the subjects (and by us).

questions.q: A shop sells 118 different items. Sixty of them make up most of the sales, with each sold often, and the other 58 are each sold only once or twice. Roughly what share of sales do the 60 account for?
options: About half of the sales
A small minority of the sales
Exactly 60 percent of the sales
A large majority, because their items sell much more often each
optionExplain: Counting items ignores their frequency.
Those items sell far more often.
The share depends on the frequencies.
Frequency per item matters more than the number of items.
questions.explain: Share of items and share of occurrences differ. The card gives the real numbers.

questions.q: The four classes account for ____ percent of all occurrences of expressions written by the 64 subjects.
questions.explain: 437 of 519 occurrences, which is five-sixths.

questions.q: Using the table, how many occurrences came from expressions outside the four classes?
optionExplain: That is the number of different expressions outside the classes.
That is the count inside the four classes.
That is the number of different expressions inside the classes.
questions.explain: Subtract the in-class occurrences from the total.

questions.q: True or false: The four classes cover a little over half of the different expressions but about five-sixths of all occurrences, because their members occur much more often on average.
questions.explain: They average 7.3 occurrences per expression, compared with 1.4 outside the classes.

questions.q: How many of the 6 members in each class of left(L1), right(L1) and L0 occurred in subjects' records?
options: Four in each class
Only those on the shortest path
All six in each class
Three in each class
optionExplain: All occurred.
All six occurred.
The authors report that all members of these three classes occurred.
All six occurred.
questions.explain: Small classes were fully explored; the larger L1 class only partly.
questions.teaches: All six members of each of the classes of left(L1), right(L1) and L0 occurred in the subjects' records, while only 42 of the 72 members of the class of L1 did.

questions.q: A bakery finds that 60 of its 118 recipes cover 84 percent of orders. A critic says the other 58 recipes prove customers are unpredictable. What reasoning from this chapter replies?
options: Rare items can be many in number yet few in occurrences, so the pattern is mostly orderly
The other 58 recipes are what really matters
The 60 common recipes are chosen at random, so the pattern means nothing
No conclusion can be drawn from counts of recipes, however they are divided
optionExplain: 58 types gave only 82 of 519 occurrences.
They are 16 percent of occurrences.
They are the predicted ones.
The authors rely on counts.
questions.explain: A long tail of rare items is compatible with order.
questions.teaches: Of the other unusual expressions, 26 percent (29 percent of their occurrences) belong to the extended equivalence class of L1, so many apparent oddities are explicable too.

questions.q: Climbers who reach the last camp below a summit almost all finish, and rarely wander around once there. What does that show about the last stretch?
options: It is very hard and often fails, though few climbers try it
It is short and direct, with few wrong turns
It is random, so climbers who reach it are equally likely to take any route
It is unnecessary, since climbers could reach the summit without crossing it
optionExplain: Nearly all who reach it finish.
Little wandering means a direct route.
Direct progress is not random.
Everyone who reached it needed it.
questions.explain: Direct finishing steps leave few extra moves. The card gives the logic data.

questions.q: A solver must use at least ____ expressions of the equivalence class of L0 to change from a horseshoe connective to a dot connective.
questions.explain: Three expressions are the minimum.

questions.q: The 24 solvers produced 84 occurrences in the class of L0, against a minimum of 3 x 24 = 72. What does the excess of 12 show?
options: A large amount of milling about, with each solver adding many extra occurrences
That solvers used fewer expressions of the class than the minimum needed
That 12 of the 24 subjects failed to solve the problem in the end
Very little milling about, about 0.5 extra occurrences per solver
optionExplain: 0.5 each is small.
The total exceeds the minimum.
The 12 counts occurrences, not subjects.
12 extra over 24 solvers is 0.5 each.
questions.explain: Excess over the minimum measures wandering.

questions.q: True or false: If a subject produced an expression in the class of L0, the data say he is very likely to have solved the problem.
questions.explain: Every subject who generated an expression in the class of L0 solved the problem.

questions.q: Of the 32 subjects who generated expressions in both the left(L1) and right(L1) classes, what share solved the problem?
options: 75 percent (24 of 32)
100 percent
50 percent
25 percent
optionExplain: 24 of the 32 solved.
That is the figure for the L0 class.
24 of 32 is 75 percent.
24 of 32 is 75 percent.
questions.explain: Having both halves was a good sign but not a guarantee.
questions.teaches: Of 32 subjects who generated expressions in both the class of left(L1) and the class of right(L1), 24 (75 percent) solved the problem.

questions.q: True or false: A puzzle designer finds that every player who reaches the final board finishes and seldom makes extra moves. The designer should conclude that the last stage is open ended with many possible routes.
questions.explain: Little milling about and universal success point to a short, nearly forced final stage, as the L0 class is.
questions.teaches: Subjects milled about very little once they obtained a member of the equivalence class of L0.

questions.q: A researcher wants to know whether asking people to talk aloud changes how they solve a task. Which comparison is most direct?
options: Ask the talkers afterwards whether talking changed the way that they worked
Time how long the talkers take to talk about each step they perform
Compare what talkers and silent solvers produce on the same task
Compare the talkers with experts who have solved many similar problems
optionExplain: Self-report is weaker than a comparison of products.
Talking time is not a comparison of search.
A matched comparison shows whether the products differ.
Experts are a different comparison.
questions.explain: The card uses the comparison of products. Compare, don't ask.

questions.q: True or false: Only three of the 34 different expressions that the thinking-aloud subjects wrote were not used by the Yale subjects.
questions.explain: Each of the three occurred once; 31 expressions also appeared in the Yale record.

questions.q: The five thinking-aloud solvers produced 19 occurrences of L0-class expressions, where five solutions need a minimum of ____.
questions.explain: Nineteen is only four above the minimum, so few superfluous expressions were generated.

questions.q: True or false: If thinking aloud had distorted the search, the talkers would likely have produced many expressions that the Yale solvers did not write.
questions.explain: Our reading of the authors' test: the absence of such expressions is the evidence that the search was not modified.
questions.rule: Distortion would show as new expressions.

questions.q: What did the two thinking-aloud subjects who failed to solve D1 not produce?
options: Any member of the equivalence class of L1, which was frequent in all records
Any written expression at all
Any member of the classes of left(L1), right(L1) or L0
Any of the 34 different expressions that the seven talkers wrote
optionExplain: L1-class expressions were frequent.
They produced expressions.
The failures stayed out of these classes.
They contributed to the record.
questions.explain: Failure meant never getting beyond the L1 class.
questions.teaches: The two thinking-aloud subjects who failed to solve D1 did not generate any members of the classes left(L1), right(L1) or L0.

questions.q: A teacher finds that students who explain their steps aloud solve a worksheet in the same ways as silent students, with only a few new answers. What does the D1 pattern suggest the teacher can conclude?
options: Talking did not noticeably change the directions of search on that worksheet
Talking aloud leaves search unchanged on every task that students might be given
Talking made the students who talked solve the worksheet less well
Silent students must also have been explaining their steps aloud to themselves
optionExplain: The same reasoning as in the chapter.
The authors restrict their claim.
No such evidence.
Not implied.
questions.explain: The conclusion is limited to the task tested.
questions.teaches: The authors say the finding about thinking aloud is not meant as a general statement about the effects of thinking-aloud instructions on behavior.

questions.q: A review of studies on talking while working finds that most of them required people to explain the reasons for their steps. Do those results settle whether plain thinking aloud changes the work?
options: Yes: any talking has the same effect on problem solving as any other talking
Yes: but only for experts, who can talk and work at the same time
No: because talking while working cannot be studied in a controlled way
No: they test a different condition, so they do not answer that question
optionExplain: The authors separate the two conditions.
Expertise is not the issue.
It can be studied.
Stating reasons is not the same as thinking aloud.
questions.explain: Check that evidence matches the question. The card gives the authors' caution.
questions.rule: Match the evidence to the question.

questions.q: Dansereau and Gregg (1966) found no difference in the times taken by subjects to do mental ____ problems in silent and thinking-aloud conditions.
questions.explain: Mental multiplication problems were their task.

questions.q: A paper shows that telling subjects to state the principles behind their solutions improves learning. How do the authors view its bearing on whether thinking aloud changes problem solving?
options: It settles the question in the affirmative
It has no relevance, since it concerns required verbalization of reasons or principles
It settles the question in the negative
It is the only relevant study
optionExplain: They say it is not relevant.
The authors say such studies do not bear on the question.
It is not relevant either way.
They know of few relevant studies.
questions.explain: Different conditions, different questions.

questions.q: True or false: Because Dansereau and Gregg found no time difference on mental multiplication, the question of thinking aloud in logic problem solving is fully settled.
questions.explain: The authors say they know of no other study that bears directly on the question, so one study on a different task does not settle it.
questions.rule: One task does not settle another.

questions.q: Besides the Dansereau and Gregg study they cite, how many other studies bearing directly on whether thinking aloud changes problem solving do the authors say they know of?
options: None; they say they are not familiar with others
One further study on mental arithmetic
Several dozen studies, most on verbalization
Exactly two further studies on problem solving
optionExplain: Correct: they say they are not familiar with other studies that bear directly on the question.
They name no further study; Dansereau and Gregg is the only one cited as bearing on the question.
The research they mention on verbalization concerns instruction or giving reasons, which they say is irrelevant to the question.
They cite no second or third study bearing directly on the question.
questions.explain: They cite Dansereau and Gregg and say they are not familiar with other studies bearing directly on the question.
questions.teaches: The authors say they are not familiar with other studies that bear directly on the question of whether thinking aloud changes problem solving.

questions.q: A coach finds one small study showing that talking aloud does not slow mental arithmetic. Should the coach assume talking aloud has no effect on any thinking task?
options: Yes: one result is enough
Yes: because arithmetic is the hardest of all thinking tasks to do aloud
No: because thinking aloud always helps and so is certain to matter
No: the authors call for further study of how thinking aloud affects problem solving
optionExplain: The authors ask for more study.
Task difficulty is not the issue.
No such claim.
A single narrow result does not generalize.
questions.explain: Limit claims to the evidence.
questions.rule: Do not generalize from one study.
questions.teaches: Because of the crucial importance of thinking-aloud behavior for understanding problem solving, the authors say the question of whether thinking aloud changes problem solving behavior deserves further study.

questions.q: A chess player records only the moves played, but also imagines moves she rejects. If the rejected moves are of the same types as the played ones, what follows?
options: The played moves are useless as a record
The moves played give a fair picture of her thinking
The rejected moves must be recorded too or nothing is known
She did not think about the rejected moves
optionExplain: They remain informative.
Same types mean the record is representative.
Representativeness is enough.
She did imagine them.
questions.explain: A record is fair if what it omits is similar. The card gives the logic version.
questions.rule: Omitted items similar to recorded ones.

questions.q: True or false: Some expressions that subjects considered were not written on the board, because the subject judged the result undesirable.
questions.explain: Subjects apply a rule mentally, calculate the output and, if it is not desirable, do not ask for it to be written.

questions.q: S4 sees that R8 on L1 would give him a part, but he does not write it, because each part eliminates a letter he needs for ____.
questions.explain: He compares the product with L0 and rejects it.

questions.q: Which of these is working backward from L0 rather than forward from L1?
options: Applying R8 to L1 to see what the rule produces from the first line
Applying R6 to both sides of L1 to prepare for the use of R7
Deriving Q V ~P from the goal expression
Commanding the experimenter to write the next line on the board
optionExplain: A forward step.
A forward step.
A step from L0 toward something simpler.
A command, not a derivation.
questions.explain: Backward work starts from the goal.

questions.q: S4 thinks that with (R V Q) he could apply R7 to derive R*(P V Q). What kind of unwritten consideration is this?
options: A mental application of R8 to a line, followed by its rejection
A command to the experimenter to write the result on the board
A review of the steps that he took earlier in the same protocol
Considering what expression he would need to make a rule applicable
optionExplain: That is another category.
No command is given.
It looks ahead.
He thinks of a required form.
questions.explain: He considers a prerequisite for a rule.
questions.teaches: S4 considers that if he had (R V Q) he could apply R7 to derive R*(P V Q) and then R8 to derive (P V Q); such expressions are considered but not written.

questions.q: True or false: A clerk who writes down only the forms she files, but also considers and drops other forms, gives a record from which her categories of work can still be read if the dropped forms are of the same kinds.
questions.explain: That is the authors' reasoning about unwritten expressions.
questions.teaches: In the protocols examined, the expressions clearly considered by the subjects but not written down fall in the same categories as the written ones, which supports using the written expressions to obtain a general characterization.

questions.q: A group of cooks all preheat the oven, while the cooks who plan to use only the stove do not. What does this pattern show?
options: Preheating the oven is random
Preheating is a preparation for the plan that needs the oven
All cooks prefer ovens, and the stove cooks did not have the time
Oven cooks are more skilled than stove cooks and so prepare more
optionExplain: It follows the plan.
Preparation tracks the plan.
Stove cooks did not preheat.
Skill is not shown.
questions.explain: Preparatory steps follow the plan they serve. The card applies this to R7.

questions.q: To make R7 applicable to L1, three differences must be removed: a tilde on one R and a horseshoe where a ____ is needed in each part.
questions.explain: R7's input form has wedges as the connectives of its two parts.

questions.q: Which two subjects, who made no preparation for R7, produced none of the three expected expressions?
options: S5 and S8
S4 and S11
S9 and S10
S9 and S5
optionExplain: They prepared and produced them.
They produced some of them.
They did not prepare for R7 and generated none.
S5 produced all three.
questions.explain: Absence of preparation fits absence of expressions.
questions.rule: No R7 plan, no R7 prep.

questions.q: True or false: A Yale subject who applies R6 to the left or right part of L1 is, according to the authors' reading, probably preparing to apply R7.
questions.explain: Thirty-five of the 122 rule applications to L1 were R6 to the left or right part, apparently preparatory to R7.
questions.rule: R6 on parts is R7 prep.

questions.q: What do the authors say about odd-looking expressions such as one with a horseshoe in a part and a wedge in the other?
options: They are attempts to reach indirectly what could not be done directly for R7
They are errors with no explanation, so they can be left out of the counts
They show that subjects abandoned the R7 plan and tried something else
They are copies of the problem statement written down by mistake
optionExplain: Subjects cycled on the structure of Figure 9.7 until convinced indirect paths were as infeasible as direct ones.
The authors explain them.
They show persistence with R7.
Not copies.
questions.explain: Strange forms may be indirect attempts.
questions.teaches: Expressions like (P horseshoe R)*(R V Q) are readily explained, as in S5's behavior, as attempts to achieve by various indirect paths what the subject could not do directly by altering the sign of one R and changing both connectives to wedges.

questions.q: A study finds that 35 of 122 steps taken by solvers fit one preparatory purpose, and 95 percent fit one of five known plans. What claim can the researcher fairly make?
options: Every step is explained by that one purpose, which accounts for all the steps
Most steps are explained by a small set of plans; about 30 percent serve one plan
Few steps are explained by any of the plans, so the plans are weak
The plans cannot be tested by counts of the kind that the authors make
optionExplain: Only about 30 percent are.
Roughly 95 percent fit the plans; 35 of 122 are R7 preparation.
95 percent fit.
The authors test them this way.
questions.explain: State what share each explanation covers.
questions.teaches: Of the 122 rule applications to transform L1 in the Yale records, 95 percent fit one or more of the five paths, some 30 percent (35) apparently preparatory to applying R7.

questions.q: A player moves a piece to a square that makes a second capture impossible. How might an analyst read the attempt?
options: As a random move that has no purpose in the game
As an illegal move that the rules of the game do not allow
As a resignation that the player has not yet announced
As an attempt at the second capture that was blocked by a condition
optionExplain: The goal explains the move.
The move was allowed.
No such sign.
The goal is clear though the condition blocks it.
questions.explain: A blocked attempt can still show the goal. The card gives the logic version.

questions.q: In the L0 class, all but ____ of the 63 transformations moved toward the goal expression.
questions.explain: Only two of 63 pointed away from the goal.

questions.q: Subjects change a part of L1 to a dot connective. What do the authors think this usually shows?
options: An attempt to delete the R's by a second use of R8, blocked because the expression cannot be positive
A plan to apply R12 directly to the two parts of the expression
A confusion of dot and wedge, which subjects mix up under pressure
A random change of connective with no purpose behind it
optionExplain: R8 needs a positive dot expression.
R12 uses horseshoe forms.
It is a purposeful attempt.
The authors give a reason.
questions.explain: Dot forms aim at R8.

questions.q: True or false: If subjects had no use for horseshoe forms, no expressions in the classes of left(L1) and right(L1) would serve as inputs to R12.
questions.explain: The authors note 24 cases where horseshoe forms in these classes served as R12 inputs; with no use for them there would be none.

questions.q: How do the authors account for most miscellaneous expressions, such as those of subject 62?
options: They arise from random errors in writing, which no plan can explain
They arise from the shortest solution, which uses R9 and R4
Plans calling for R9 then R4 account for 20 of the 43 miscellaneous expressions
They arise from the instructions that were given to the subjects
optionExplain: The authors find accounts.
They are off the main paths.
That is the account they give for many of them.
Not stated.
questions.explain: Even oddities fall under a plan.
questions.teaches: Plans calling for R9 followed by R4 probably account for 20 of the 43 miscellaneous expressions, and 27 of their 58 occurrences.

questions.q: An analyst can explain 20 of 43 odd entries in a log by a single plan. How should she describe the remaining 23?
options: As explained by the same plan, which accounts for all of the entries
As errors made by the people who recorded the entries in the log
As not yet accounted for by that plan, while stating the share it does explain
As proof that the plan is wrong
optionExplain: That would overstate.
No evidence for errors.
State the share explained and the remainder.
A partial account is not a refutation.
questions.explain: Report coverage honestly.
questions.teaches: Plans calling for R9 followed by R4 probably account for 20 of the 43 miscellaneous expressions; the rest are left unexplained by that plan.

questions.q: A log of 64 people's moves on a puzzle fits a few predicted paths and shows few unpredicted moves. What best explains that?
options: The people follow paths suggested by easily noticed features of the puzzle
The people are acting at random, and the match with the paths is chance
The puzzle has only one path, so every person must follow it
The people all have the same training, which fixes how they work
optionExplain: Salient features guide search.
Random action would not fit predicted paths.
Several paths are predicted.
Training is not needed to explain the fit.
questions.explain: Noticeable task features guide search. The card gives the authors' wording.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say there is little that seems random about the subjects' generation of expressions once the problem structure is understood.
questions.explain: The generation is explained by following paths suggested by noticeable differences.

questions.q: The authors say subjects seek to follow paths suggested by noticeable ____ between L1 and L0.
questions.explain: Noticeable differences, such as R appearing in L1 only, suggest paths.

questions.q: True or false: If the authors' postulate holds, a new group of subjects given D1 would again write most of their expressions in the same few classes.
questions.explain: Our reading: the postulate says expressions follow noticeable features of the task, which a new group would face too.

questions.q: What do the authors mean by explaining the generation parsimoniously?
options: Using many separate rules, one for each subject and each problem
Using no assumptions at all, so the data speak for themselves
Treating every expression that was written as an accident of the moment
Using few assumptions: that subjects follow paths suggested by noticeable differences
optionExplain: Parsimony means few assumptions.
A postulate is still needed.
They find little random.
That is the postulate they state.
questions.explain: Few assumptions cover many cases.
questions.teaches: The authors say the subjects' generation of expressions can be explained parsimoniously by postulating that they seek to follow paths suggested by noticeable differences between L1 and L0 and noticeable features of these expressions.

questions.q: A detective explains many suspects' movements by one idea: each person heads to the exit nearest to a noticeable landmark. Another explains each person separately. Which is the authors' kind of explanation?
options: The second: separate individual stories are preferable
The first: one postulate that covers many cases
Neither: no explanation is possible
Both equally
optionExplain: The authors prefer the parsimonious account.
Parsimony favors the single postulate.
They explain.
They favor the single one.
questions.explain: One postulate over many ad hoc stories.
questions.teaches: Whether the subject is only vocalizing his rule applications or is also thinking aloud has no detectable effect on the paths he follows.

questions.q: A person decides to use a particular tool but finds it does not fit the part in front of her. She then does several small things to make it fit. What would count as one episode?
options: The decision to use the tool, with the small adjustments done to make it usable
Each small adjustment separately
The whole day's work
Only the final use of the tool once it has been made to fit
optionExplain: The decision opens an episode whose body is the adjustments.
Adjustments belong to one aim.
An episode is tied to a goal.
The preparation belongs to the episode.
questions.explain: An episode is anchored by a goal. The card gives the logic definition.

questions.q: True or false: In the logic task, an essential rule is one that deletes or diminishes an R.
questions.explain: The attempts revolve around essential transformations, those that delete or diminish an R.

questions.q: A subject says he must use R7 but R7 does not fit L1. He changes a connective, then a sign, and tries R7 again. Which part is the episode?
options: Only the retry of R7
Only the connective change
Nothing, since R7 was never applied and so no episode began
The whole sequence from the decision to use R7 to the retry
optionExplain: The preparation is part of the episode.
That is one step in the body.
An episode can end without applying the rule.
The decision starts it; the adjustments are its body.
questions.explain: Episodes are tied to essential rules wanted but not yet applicable.
questions.rule: Episode equals pursuit of one rule.

questions.q: Match each task to how obviousness is defined for its episodes.
pairs: Obvious new information gained without positing a new assignment
Obvious steps taken to make a chosen essential rule applicable
A segment of obvious behavior in pursuit of a goal
questions.explain: The abstract notion is made concrete differently for each task.

questions.q: Which is NOT one of the four ways, listed by the authors, in which a subject comes to commit to an inapplicable essential rule?
options: Responding to an essential difference
Copying the experimenter's instruction
Following a general principle such as simplification
Developing a plan of several rules and starting its first rule
optionExplain: This is item 1.
The four are: an essential difference, a general principle, similarity of input form, and a plan of several rules.
This is item 2.
This is item 4.
questions.explain: Four routes lead to a commitment; the experimenter's instruction is not among them.
questions.teaches: A subject comes to want an inapplicable essential rule in four ways: responding to an essential difference, following a general principle such as simplification, applying an operator because its input resembles the current expression, or developing a plan of several rules and starting its first rule.

questions.q: In S4's first segment, the authors see only items 1 and possibly 2 of the list of routes. What is the implication for the other routes?
options: They never occur
They are discussed in the next paragraph
They are examined later, in Chapter 10
They are removed from the analysis
optionExplain: All subjects make such commitments repeatedly.
They are deferred to the next chapter.
The authors defer the other possibilities.
They remain part of the account.
questions.explain: Not every route is shown in a given segment.
questions.teaches: The authors say they will not examine items 3 and 4 of the list until Chapter 10, and that it is not important for present purposes to understand exactly how a commitment to an inapplicable essential rule arises.

questions.q: You are looking for a way to make a key fit a lock by trying small adjustments. Which is harder to decide: that an adjustment works, or that no adjustment will work?
options: That one works, since every key has to be tested against the lock in turn
Neither, since both are equally clear once the adjustments have been tried
That one works, since most adjustments of this kind succeed in the end
That none will work, since it means exhausting all adjustments
optionExplain: Success is recognized when found.
Absence is harder.
Most do not.
Showing absence needs a full search.
questions.explain: Finding is easier than proving absence. The card applies this to episodes.

questions.q: Order the steps of the means-ends cycle inside an episode.
items: A difference is detected
A relevant operator is selected
The operator is applied
The original essential operator is reapplied to judge the result
questions.explain: Detect, select, apply, evaluate by reapplication.

questions.q: A subject remembers at once that R6 removes a horseshoe. Which route to a relevant operator is this?
options: A search of the rule sheet for a rule with the desired function
A direct association from the difference to the operator
A search of the display for an expression that already meets the condition
A suggestion from the experimenter about which rule to apply
optionExplain: That route needs scanning.
A stored link replaces any search.
No expression is sought.
None was given.
questions.explain: Stored links are the table of connections in action.
