questions.q: True or false: A subject whose search finds no way to make the wanted rule applicable will say so sharply and at once.
questions.explain: There is seldom any sharp indication of inapplicability, so subjects may continue for several minutes before acknowledging failure.

questions.q: If the essential operator becomes applicable inside an episode, what may happen?
options: The episode always ends at once
A new episode must start for every essential rule that comes up
It may continue to further essential rules, if it began from a plan or a general principle
The experimenter ends it
optionExplain: It may continue.
The unit is the decision to follow a path.
That is the authors' account.
Not stated.
questions.explain: An episode corresponds to a decision to follow a path, not to each concern with an essential rule.
questions.teaches: A separate episode does not correspond to each concern with an essential rule, but to each decision to follow a path.

questions.q: True or false: A gardener spends several minutes trying small fixes to get a tool to fit a pipe. She cannot easily tell when to give up, because proving that no fix exists means going through all possible fixes. This parallels the authors' point about episode termination.
questions.explain: Failure is not obvious; it requires exhausting the space of inessential transformations.
questions.teaches: Although an available result within an episode is obvious and so obtained with alacrity, it is not obvious that a result is not available, since that involves exhausting the space of inessential transformations.

questions.q: A cook decides to taste every spice on the shelf in order, from left to right. Why is the sequence of her next actions highly predictable?
options: Because she has adopted a method whose steps are known in advance
Because every spice tastes much the same, so the order makes no difference
Because she is tired and so repeats her last action again and again
Because the shelf is short and the spices stand in a fixed row
optionExplain: A method makes the sequence obvious.
The content does not decide it.
Tiredness is not the reason.
Length is not the reason.
questions.explain: Commitment to a method makes later steps obvious. The card applies this to episodes.

questions.q: True or false: Each attempt to solve a1 was a single episode of the direct-goal type, since no essential operators were involved.
questions.explain: Problem a1 needs only changes of sign, order and connective, so no essential rule starts an episode.

questions.q: A subject working forward who has considered R3 will next consider R4, independently of the ____ of the rule.
questions.explain: The sequence follows from the steps of the method, not from what each rule does.
questions.rule: Method makes the next step obvious.

questions.q: True or false: In a plan, the next essential rule starts a new episode each time it comes up.
questions.explain: Given a plan, the next essential rule is obvious and does not start a new episode.

questions.q: How can episodes be arranged relative to one another?
options: They must follow one another in a row, with no overlap between them
They can be hierarchical, one inside another, because they are tied to goals
They can overlap only if two subjects are working on the same problem
They are all of equal length
optionExplain: The authors allow embedding.
Subjects stay with paths for long periods and adopt methods, starting subepisodes.
Not stated.
Lengths vary.
questions.explain: Goals nest, so do episodes.
questions.teaches: Episodes, since they are tied to goals, can be hierarchical, with one episode embedded in another, as when a subject committed to a path adopts a method and so starts subepisodes.

questions.q: A student studying for an exam decides on a method (review one chapter at a time), and within a chapter decides to work every example in order. How does this resemble the authors' picture?
options: Two unrelated episodes with no link between the chapter and the examples
A single flat episode with no structure inside it
No episodes at all
An episode (the chapter) with a subepisode (the examples) inside it
optionExplain: They are linked by goals.
Subepisodes are allowed.
Method adoption also starts episodes.
Nested goals give nested episodes.
questions.explain: Nested goals create nested episodes.
questions.teaches: The adoption of a specific method, not only the decision to apply an essential rule, can start an episode, because the sequence of future actions then becomes predictable.

questions.q: You watch a person at work and want to divide the recording into episodes. What is a sensible clue for where one ends and the next begins?
options: The person changes direction or announces a new aim
Every minute on the clock
Every sentence spoken, since each sentence is a new thought
Every time the person sighs or pauses for longer than usual
optionExplain: Shifts of aim mark boundaries.
Clock time ignores the person's aims.
Sentences can fall inside one aim.
Sighs are not reliable markers.
questions.explain: Boundaries follow aims. The card shows the authors' scheme.

questions.q: S4's behavior on D1 breaks into ____ episodes.
questions.explain: Eleven episodes, one of which has three subepisodes.

questions.q: S4 ends his working-forward episode with: "So 7 seems to be the only one that can help me". What does this remark do?
options: It asks the experimenter for the answer to the problem
It rejects every rule on the sheet and gives up the scan
It closes the scan of the rules by naming the one rule that can help
It starts a new problem after the old one has been dropped
optionExplain: He is stating a conclusion.
He settles on R7.
The scan ends with a conclusion.
The problem continues.
questions.explain: A scan ends with a conclusion about which rule helps.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say their scheme explains why episodes exist and how far they extend, not only where the subject changes direction.
questions.explain: They contrast the present scheme with episoding on the empirical basis of changes of direction.

questions.q: What does the label WF at B99 in S4's PBG signal?
options: A wedge-form expression that he has written on the board
A wrong first step that he later corrects in the protocol
A working-forward episode, in which he looks at each rule in turn to see how it might help
The final stage of the solution, where the answer is checked
optionExplain: WF is a method label.
It labels a method.
WF stands for working forward.
It marks working forward.
questions.explain: PBG notes mark methods.
questions.teaches: The working-forward episode in S4's protocol is initiated at B99, when he says he is looking through the rules one at a time, and terminated at B123 to B124, when he concludes that R7 seems the only one that can help.

questions.q: A manager divides a team's meeting recording into parts wherever the topic shifts. A colleague divides it by the agenda items that set each topic's goal. Which is closer to the authors' preference?
options: The goal-based division, because it explains why the parts exist, though it often matches the other
The topic-shift division, because it never needs interpretation by the analyst
Neither, since meetings do not have parts that can be marked
The clock-based division, because it is objective and easy to apply
optionExplain: The authors' scheme coincides with empirical change-of-direction boundaries in many cases but adds an explanation.
The authors want an explanation.
Episodes exist.
Not the authors' view.
questions.explain: Principled boundaries also explain extent.
questions.teaches: Episoding simply on the empirical basis of boundaries where the subject changes direction or does something different would coincide with the present episoding in many cases, but the present scheme gives a basis for understanding why episodes exist and for explaining their extent.

questions.q: A flowchart of someone's attempts shows some steps joined by arrows and others by plain lines. What might the difference signal?
options: Arrows for easy steps, plain lines for hard steps in the attempt
Arrows for the first half of the attempts, plain lines for the second half
No difference: both kinds of line mean the same thing in the chart
Arrows for completed steps, plain lines for blocked attempts
optionExplain: Difficulty is not the criterion.
Position is not the criterion.
A distinction exists.
A symbol distinction marks success.
questions.explain: Conventions carry meaning. The card gives the PBG's.

questions.q: Match each PBG mark to its meaning.
pairs: Arrowhead on the line between boxes
The operator was not applied; the next box gives the difficulty
A later reapplication of an operator held in the goal stack
questions.explain: These are the authors' conventions.

questions.q: In S4's PBG, a line with no arrowhead is followed by a box describing a problem in applying R7. What does this tell the reader?
options: R7 was applied correctly, so its goal has been met and removed
R7 was not applied and its goal remains in the goal stack
R7 was applied with an error, which the next box describes
R7 was applied by the experimenter on the board, not by the subject
optionExplain: That would carry an arrowhead.
No arrowhead means not applied.
Errors still carry arrowheads.
Who applied it is not shown by the arrowhead.
questions.explain: Blocked goals wait on the stack.

questions.q: True or false: A reader says the arrowhead appears only when a rule is applied correctly and overtly on the blackboard. This agrees with the authors' convention.
questions.explain: An arrowhead marks successful application whether covert or overt, abstract or detailed, accurate or with error.

questions.q: At B158 S4 tries to command the experimenter to change a wedge but corrects himself. What does the authors' note about this say?
options: He named the operator by its function instead of its proper name, R6
He mistook R5 for R6 and then asked for the wrong rule
He asked for R7 by mistake and then changed his request
He refused to command the experimenter to change the wedge at all
optionExplain: Correct: he used the associated function (changing the wedge) instead of the operator's proper name, R6.
The note names R6 as the proper name; it does not describe confusing R5 with R6.
The note mentions R6, not R7, and describes no mistaken request.
The note says he attempts to command the experimenter, then realizes he used a function name.
questions.explain: The note says he named the operator by its associated function rather than its proper name (R6).
questions.teaches: At B158 S4 begins to command the experimenter to change a wedge, then realizes he has named the operator in terms of its associated function rather than by its proper name, R6.

questions.q: A diagram of a cook's attempts shows two uses of R8 that did not occur in the cook's actual behavior but only in a simulation. How do the authors treat such a feature in S4's PBG?
options: They include it, since the program is a good model of the subject
They include it twice for emphasis
They remove the whole R8 episode
They leave it out, as it belongs to the GPS simulation and not to S4's behavior
optionExplain: They separate simulation features from behavior.
Not what they do.
They keep one R8 application.
The PBG does not show two distinct applications of R8.
questions.explain: Keep what the subject did.
questions.teaches: In S4's PBG the authors do not show two distinct applications of R8, since this appears to be a feature of the GPS simulation and not of S4's actual behavior; the PBG from B3 through B26 is the part simulated by GPS.

questions.q: Two people are asked to reduce a long report. One thinks of cutting half of it, the other of splitting it into two files. Which could lead to different actions?
options: No: the same operations follow from either way of putting the task, whatever the words
Yes: the way each represents the task can suggest different operations
Only if their jobs differ
Only if they speak aloud
optionExplain: Different phrasing evokes different paths.
Representation shapes the paths tried.
Jobs are not the issue.
The representation matters regardless.
questions.explain: Wording shapes the plan. The card gives the logic case.

questions.q: Most D1 protocols state the needed change as 'I must ____ the R's', sometimes followed by 'I must group the Q and P'.
questions.explain: The most common statement is that the R's must be eliminated.

questions.q: S9 says he can split the parts up using Rule 8. How is R8 represented for him?
options: As a way to eliminate half of L1, which would lose a letter needed for L0
As a way to change a connective, so that R7 can be applied
As a way to obtain the two subexpressions as separate lines
As a way to add a term to the expression, so that grouping can follow
optionExplain: That is how S4 sees it.
R8 does not change connectives.
He treats R8 as a splitting tool.
That would be R9.
questions.explain: Same rule, different representation.

questions.q: Match each subject to the way he represents R8.
pairs: A means of eliminating half of L1, which would lose Q or P
A means of obtaining the two subexpressions as separate lines
A shift from seeing R8 as a deletion to seeing it as obtaining A and B separately
questions.explain: The shift in S15 shows the influence of viewpoint on which path is tried.

questions.q: What does S15's shift of viewpoint show?
options: He forgot the rules and so lost the way of using R8 that he had planned
He moved from working backward to working forward as his search went on
He abandoned R8 and went on to some other rule for the remainder of the episode
A shift from seeing R8 as removing the R's to using it twice to get A and B separately opens a new path
optionExplain: Not what happens.
The shift concerns how R8 is viewed.
He plans to use R8 twice.
He moves from a view that blocks R8 to one that suggests it.
questions.explain: A change of representation opens a path.
questions.teaches: S15 first says that R8 would get rid of them completely and that he cannot, and later proposes doing R8 twice on L1 to get A and B separately, a shift from one viewpoint to the other that opens the path.

questions.q: A mechanic first thinks of the repair as removing a part, sees it would break the engine, then rethinks it as taking the part out to repair it separately and putting it back. Which feature of this chapter does it show?
options: The use of an irrelevant clue that leads the mechanic to the wrong part
A change in how the task is represented changes which action is tried
A random choice among the repairs that are possible for the engine
A method that fails whenever the parts are taken out and put back
optionExplain: Not what is described.
A shift from deleting to splitting.
A reasoned shift.
The new representation works.
questions.explain: Representation steers the path.
questions.teaches: The authors say that most protocols begin with some characterization of the problem expressions and the differences between L1 and L0, most often I must eliminate the R's, sometimes followed by I must group the Q and P.

questions.q: Five of seven people take the same final route to a goal, but they differ in the detours they try first. Which description fits?
options: No shared structure: each person goes by a different route and ends differently
Identical behavior throughout, from the first step to the last
A shared final route and varied earlier explorations
Random detours and random endings, with no common final route
optionExplain: The final route is shared.
Detours differ.
A common solution path with differing side trips.
Endings are shared.
questions.explain: Look for what is shared and what varies. The card gives the logic data.

questions.q: All the solvers used path.R____ in solving the problem.
questions.explain: All the solvers employ path.R12.

questions.q: Match each subject to a prominent feature of his protocol.
pairs: Extensive time on path.R7 and variants
Only one of seven episodes follows any described path
questions.explain: These are the authors' observations.

questions.q: True or false: The authors expect the path.R12 episodes to be full of comments about differences and possible operators, since they are the key to the solution.
questions.explain: They say the R12 episodes are similar and fairly simple, with few comments beyond instructions to the experimenter; comments cluster where difficulties arise.

questions.q: What would a GPS simulating the R12 episodes have to evoke, according to the authors?
options: The subgoal of obtaining two inputs, then R8 applied twice
A search of the display for an existing expression that already meets the condition
A working-backward step from L0 to an expression that could precede it
A table of connections that leads straight from the difference to R7
optionExplain: That follows the discussion in Chapter 8.
Not the R12 plan.
Not the R12 plan.
R7 is a different plan.
questions.explain: R12 needs two lines, so two uses of R8 are planned.
questions.teaches: A GPS simulating the path.R12 episodes would have to evoke the subgoal of obtaining two inputs, then apply R8 twice, as discussed in Chapter 8.

questions.q: S4 and S8 began path.R12 only after they had applied R8 to L1 for other reasons. What does this suggest a simulation of them must be able to do?
options: Start only from the problem statement, as GPS does at the outset
Start problem solving from any of the displayed expressions
Ignore all displayed expressions and begin again from the starting line
Skip the use of R12
optionExplain: They started from displayed expressions.
They start from an existing expression.
They used them.
They used R12.
questions.explain: Plans can begin from intermediate results.
questions.rule: Start from what is on display.
questions.teaches: A GPS to simulate S4 and S8 on path.R12 would be simpler than one for the other three solvers, but it would have to be able to initiate problem solving from any of the displayed expressions.

questions.q: A person keeps trying small rearrangements to get two linked dials to different settings and ends up back at the start every time. What would explain the effort?
options: He enjoys the repetition of the small steps and sees no need to stop
He does not know what the dials are for and so tries every setting
He believes that there is a fault in the dials, which he hopes to find
He cannot see ahead and must try rearrangements to convince himself none works
optionExplain: No such motive is given.
He knows the dials.
Not stated.
Search can serve as a check of impossibility.
questions.explain: Futile search can be systematic. The card shows S5's case.

questions.q: S5 generated ____ members of the equivalence class of L1, more than any other subject.
questions.explain: He generated 15 members of the class of L1.

questions.q: Order the three subepisodes of S5's attempt (E3.1, E3.2, E3.3) by what he did.
items: E3.1: remove the tilde from the left R, around the right-hand cycle
E3.2: the same goal, around the left-hand cycle
E3.3: add a tilde to the right R, around the right-hand cycle
questions.explain: He moved from one cycle to the other and then changed the target R.
questions.rule: Right cycle, left cycle, new target.

questions.q: True or false: If S5 had a figure like 9.7 showing that every cycle returns to the same expressions, he would likely have cut short his search.
questions.explain: Our reading of the authors' account: he searched extensively because he could not see ahead; the figure shows the structure directly.

questions.q: How does the authors' GPS version fare in reproducing S5's explorations?
options: Its priority order of differences would stop it changing connectives to change a sign, as S5 did
It reproduces them exactly
It cannot apply R6, which is the rule needed to change the connective
It would search even longer than S5
optionExplain: The program would halt where S5 went on.
It does not.
It can.
It would stop earlier.
questions.explain: Changing priorities alone would not fix this.
questions.teaches: The priority ordering of differences in the version of GPS used for S4 would prevent it from following S5's explorations, since it would not change connectives (R6 and R5) in order to achieve a change in sign; to produce such behavior it would have to generate all paths from an expression, using the inessential rules, until it detected a cycle.

questions.q: A reader of a map tries every detour around a closed road in a systematic way before conceding there is no way through. An observer says he is stubborn. How would the authors reply, by analogy with S5?
options: Stubbornness is the only possible explanation of such a long search
The search shows that he is a poor planner in every task he meets
The search is understandable and systematic, given that he cannot see the road structure ahead
The search proves that the road is open and he has not yet found it
optionExplain: The authors propose a structural explanation.
They avoid such generalization.
S5's search is explained by his limited lookahead.
It shows nothing of the sort.
questions.explain: Explain the behavior by task and limits, not by traits.
questions.teaches: S5 said afterwards that he was just horsing around trying to get the expression into the form that would work; the authors nonetheless read his actions as futile but understandable and systematic.

questions.q: A team wants to know if people at a task use a single clever method or try everything. Without building a full program, what could they do?
options: Time how long the task takes each person from start to finish
Ask the people which method they prefer to use on tasks of this kind
Label each step by what prompted it, then count how many fit the clever method
Count the words spoken by each person while working on the task
optionExplain: Time does not separate methods.
Preferences are not steps.
Classifying steps tests the method without simulation.
Words are not steps.
questions.explain: Classification of steps is a lighter test than full simulation. The card shows the authors' version.

questions.q: In S4's PBG the authors count ____ rule applications, including scans that found no rule.
questions.explain: 79 instances of a rule application, ignoring transform goals.

questions.q: At B10, match each operator occurrence to the mechanism that evoked it.
pairs: Means-ends toward the goal object: a difference (group terms) from L0
Means-ends for operator applicability: a connective difference because R7 was inapplicable
A reapplication of the first R7 after the attempt to remedy the difficulty
questions.explain: Each operator is classified by what prompted it.
questions.rule: Cause, not name, sorts the steps.

questions.q: True or false: If subjects relied on exhaustive search, most of their operator occurrences would not be classifiable as means-ends analysis.
questions.explain: Our reading: a high share of means-ends classifications is evidence against exhaustive search as the main mechanism.

questions.q: Which three basic methods do the variants in Table 9.3 fall under?
options: Means-ends analysis, working forward and working backward
Means-ends analysis, exhaustive search and random choice among the rules
Planning, review and command, which are the kinds of repetition
Matching, selecting and applying, which are the steps of GPS itself
optionExplain: These are the three basic methods named.
Exhaustive search and random choice are not the classes.
Those are repetition types.
Those are steps of GPS, not the three methods.
questions.explain: The mechanisms are variants of three methods.
questions.teaches: The mechanisms found in the seven protocols are variants of three basic methods: means-ends analysis, working forward and working backward; the means-ends variants include working toward the goal expression and making an operator applicable.

questions.q: A coach reviews match film by marking every pass as toward open space, toward a teammate under pressure, or back to reset. Which feature of the authors' method does this resemble?
options: Simulating the whole match on a computer and comparing the result
Asking the players how they felt about each pass afterwards
Measuring only the final score of the match and the possession
Classifying each action by the mechanism that evoked it, then counting the classes
optionExplain: The method avoids full simulation.
That is not classification.
That ignores steps.
The tabulation of Table 9.3 does the same for operator occurrences.
questions.explain: Counting classes of action is a middle path between impression and simulation.
questions.teaches: Most of the mechanisms behind S4's 79 operator occurrences can be determined directly from the PBG itself, without further resort to the protocol.

questions.q: You want to peel a tape off a surface but the tape also lifts the paint. Which approach avoids the unwanted effect instead of repairing it afterwards?
options: Pull hard on the tape and repaint the surface afterwards
Warm or prepare the surface first so the tape comes off cleanly
Leave the tape on the surface so the paint is not lifted
Remove the paint first and take off the tape at a later time
optionExplain: That repairs afterward.
Preparing beforehand avoids the damage.
That gives up the goal.
That is not preparation for the same step.
questions.explain: Preparing first differs from repairing later. The card names this method.

questions.q: True or false: A simple GPS-like system would apply the rule and then try to remove the undesirable consequences from the result.
questions.explain: The avoid-consequences method differs by searching beforehand for a rule to apply first.

questions.q: S8 sees that R8 eliminates an R (good) but also drops a P or Q (bad). The rule he wants to apply first, to group P and Q, is R____.
questions.explain: R7 groups P and Q so that R8 would do only the desirable thing.

questions.q: Which of these avoids consequences rather than repairing them?
options: Applying a preparatory rule so that a later rule keeps its good effect only
Applying a rule and then deleting its unwanted result from the expression
Applying every rule in turn to see what each of them produces
Reading the rule sheet from the top to find the first rule that fits
optionExplain: Preparation beforehand is the mark.
That is repair afterwards.
That is working forward.
That is a scan.
questions.explain: The mark is preparation before the rule.

questions.q: S5 wants to change the sign of R with R6 but R6 would change the sign of the P term in (~P V ~R). What does he decide?
options: Apply R6 at once and then fix the sign of the P term afterwards
Give up the plan to apply R7 and turn to some other plan
Apply R8 first, so that one of the two R's is removed
Apply R1 beforehand to bring the sign into the position R6 can affect
optionExplain: That is repair after.
He keeps on with R7.
R8 is not involved.
He prepares the expression for the change of sign.
questions.explain: A preparation for a positive consequence rather than the avoidance of a bad one.
questions.teaches: S5 applies R1 beforehand so that R6 can change the sign of R; this is a form of preparation to obtain a positive consequence, which a standard GPS could not conclude, since R6 has no good and bad pair of consequences but could provide a good one and does not.

questions.q: A baker finds that using the oven for one tray also dries the pastry on the second shelf. She covers the pastry before baking. Which statement is accurate by this chapter's categories?
options: This is repair after the step
This is avoiding consequences, since she acts beforehand to prevent the bad effect
This is working backward from the goal of a finished tray of pastry
This is ordinary means-ends analysis toward the goal object of the bake
optionExplain: She acts before.
Prepare before the step.
No backward reasoning is given.
The act prepares a given step.
questions.explain: Identify the timing of the fix.
questions.teaches: Most examples of avoiding consequences couple a good effect and a bad one that are seemingly independent, as with R8 eliminating an R and also a P or Q.

questions.q: A person stuck on a puzzle tries a move because it differs from everything tried so far. Which kind of search is that?
options: Working backward from the goal, by asking what could produce it
Means-ends analysis toward the goal, by removing a difference with it
Working forward, by doing something different
A review of the past steps, by recalling what has been tried so far
optionExplain: No goal reasoning is involved.
No difference with the goal is used.
No goal comparison guides the choice.
It is a new step.
questions.explain: Choosing a move because it is new is a forward move. The card names three forms.

questions.q: Match each example to the type of working forward.
pairs: S4 looking through the rules one at a time
S11 choosing rules from the three-term form of an expression
S8 applying R5 to try something altogether different
questions.explain: Three forms of working forward.

questions.q: After applying R7 mentally, S11 considers R7 again and then R4, with no comparison against L0. Why do the authors say there is no means-ends analysis here?
options: S11 did not apply any rule, so there was nothing to compare with the goal
The rules were chosen after reading the whole rule sheet in order
S11 had already solved the problem and was only checking his work
The rules were chosen from the form of the expression, with no comparison to the goal
optionExplain: He did apply R7.
He did not consider the rules systematically.
He had not.
Means-ends analysis needs a difference with the goal.
questions.explain: Without a difference to reduce, selection is by form.

questions.q: True or false: On D1, working backward appears frequently, so the chapter illustrates it at length.
questions.explain: The authors say working backward rarely occurs in D1, so they do not illustrate it here and discuss it in Chapter 10.
questions.rule: Working backward is rare in D1.

questions.q: How did S8 justify trying something different?
options: The experimenter told him to try something different at that point
He recalled advice from reading the night before: do not stay in a rut
The goal expression required it
He had a plan that used R5 and was carrying out its first step
optionExplain: It was his own idea.
He quotes it in his protocol.
There was nothing functional about the result.
He could not see its use.
questions.explain: A general maxim can start a forward move.
questions.teaches: S8 applies R5 to L1 after recalling reading last night the advice not to stay in a rut; there is nothing functional about the result he gets.

questions.q: A shopper facing too many options picks the product whose packaging looks most like the one she already likes, without checking what she needs. Which forward type does this resemble?
options: Systematic scan and evaluate, trying every option in turn
Do something different, trying whatever has not yet been tried
Working forward by similarity of input form
Working backward from what the shopper wants to buy
optionExplain: She does not go through all options.
She picks the familiar one.
Choosing by resemblance to a known form.
No goal reasoning.
questions.explain: Similarity of form can pick actions without goal analysis.
questions.teaches: S11's choice of R7 and then R4 is by similarity of input form; the authors note he did not consider the rules systematically, since other rules such as R1 and R5 were also applicable.

questions.q: You try to open a door, find it locked, fetch the key, and then try the door again. What kept the first goal alive during the fetching?
options: A stack of goals, with the door goal waiting while the key is fetched
A fresh start, in which the door goal is dropped and a new goal begun
An experimenter's reminder, which tells the person to return to the door
A change of aim, so that the key becomes the new main goal
optionExplain: The prior goal is held and reevoked.
The goal was not abandoned.
It is the person's own stack.
The aim stays.
questions.explain: Held goals return after subgoals. The card calls this the goal stack.

questions.q: In the PBG, the prior goal of applying an operator is kept in a goal ____ and reevoked after a remedial attempt.
questions.explain: The goal stack explains the reattempts.

questions.q: True or false: In the PBG, an operator with an arrow where no expression appears on the display, followed by a later application of the same operator, is an implementation of an operator first applied covertly.
questions.explain: It was applied and examined first, then applied again, often to put an actual result on the display.

questions.q: Which repetition happens when the subject has thought through a result in detail in his head and asks the experimenter to apply a rule only to get the result on display?
options: A goal-stack reapplication
A command
A review
A noticing
optionExplain: No subgoal was involved.
The special type of implementation labeled command.
A review recapitulates past actions.
A noticing sees something new.
questions.explain: A command serves no function but putting the result on the display.

questions.q: What does a subject using the experimenter's commands usually do, as against the special case of command?
options: Dictates a result already fully known, to have it written on the display
Refuses to give commands and works every rule out alone
Asks for reviews of the whole problem in place of applying rules
Uses the experimenter to calculate consequences, not having thought the result through
optionExplain: That is the special case.
Commands are common.
Reviews are another kind.
Usually the subject has not worked out the result in detail.
questions.explain: Commands often serve as a calculator.
questions.teaches: Usually, when the subject commands the experimenter to apply a rule, he has not thought through the result in detail and thus is using the experimenter to perform a calculation of consequences for him.

questions.q: A cook starts one step, finds a missing item, goes to get it, then returns to the step. A different cook repeats a step she had earlier worked out only in her head, to put the result on paper. Which pair of kinds is this?
options: Goal-stack reapplication for the first, implementation for the second
Implementation for the first and goal-stack reapplication for the second cook
Review for both, since both go back to something done before
Command for both, since each acts to get a result on the display
optionExplain: Held goal returns after a subgoal; a covert result is later implemented.
The reverse of the right pairing.
Neither recapitulates the past.
Commands involve another party.
questions.explain: Hold-and-return versus carry-out-again.
questions.teaches: The authors classify the reapplications by the type of remedial action attempted, and say the reattempt after trying to overcome a difficulty predominates, but all varieties arise from the same basic mechanism, the goal stack.

questions.q: A student rereads their own earlier working to find where they went wrong, and finds the step. What kind of activity is this?
options: A fresh plan for the whole problem, made before looking at the earlier work
A mere copy of the earlier steps, written out again in the same order
A diagnostic review, searching the past for the cause of the trouble
A random check of some earlier step, made without any aim
optionExplain: It looks back.
It looks for a cause.
A recapitulation used to find an error.
It is directed.
questions.explain: Looking back can have a purpose. The card gives the unique case in the protocols.

questions.q: The four main types of mechanism (means-ends analysis, working forward, goal-stack repetition and implementation of plans) account for ____ percent of occurrences.
questions.explain: Together they account for 82 percent.

questions.q: S4, while concerned with how to make R7 apply, thinks of applying R2 to two lines and says it is so he can apply R12. What is this an example of?
options: A review of the whole protocol, to see where he stands
Avoiding consequences, by preparing the expression beforehand
Noticing: seeing something useful while working on something else
A command with no other function than to get a result on the display
optionExplain: He is not reviewing.
No bad effect is avoided.
He sees path.R12 though not looking for it.
He explains his reason.
questions.explain: Noticing is incidental discovery.

questions.q: True or false: The reviews in the protocols are mostly strictly reproductive of past behavior, so they add little new problem solving.
questions.explain: Most of the behavior in reviews is strictly reproductive; the one diagnostic review is the exception.

questions.q: How much of the occurrences do review and commands add to the four main types?
options: 9 percent, being essentially reproductions of past behavior
18 percent
1 percent
They are included in the 82 percent
optionExplain: Reviews and commands add 9 percent.
Not the stated figure.
Not the stated figure.
They are added to it.
questions.explain: 82 plus 9 is 91 percent.
questions.teaches: Review and commands to the experimenter, essentially reproductions of past behavior, add 9 percent to the 82 percent accounted for by the four main types.

questions.q: A reviewer finds that a log of a task is 91 percent explained by four known types plus two reproductive types. What should she say about the remaining items?
options: They disprove the four types, which therefore explain very little
They are errors made by the subjects, which have no explanation
They are the main finding of the tally and the chief interest of the table
They are mainly a few special mechanisms and items with too few data to classify
optionExplain: They are a small remainder.
Not stated.
They are the leftover.
The authors name avoid-consequences, noticings and thin-data items.
questions.explain: Describe the residual honestly.
questions.teaches: S5's diagnostic review at the start of E5 is the only review of its kind in all the protocols: he generates a hypothesis about what he did wrong and works backward from L13 to L12.

questions.q: A report sorts a month of customer calls into issue types and finds a short list of types. What can the report show, and what can it not?
options: How every call unfolds from the first word to the last
That a short list of issues covers the calls, but not how a call unfolds
Nothing at all, since sorting into types removes all information
Why customers call, since the types show their reasons
optionExplain: Counts lose the flow.
Counts show coverage, not the integrated flow.
The counts show coverage.
Counting types does not give reasons.
questions.explain: A tally dissolves the whole into parts. The card gives the authors' analogy.

questions.q: The authors compare the classification of behavior into bits to the results obtained by a ____.
questions.explain: A centrifuge separates a mixture by one property, destroying its integration.

questions.q: Which statement is supported by the tally of mechanisms, according to the authors?
options: No other collection of mechanisms seems required to account for the data
The behavior is fully explained as an integrated whole by the mechanisms
The selection rules are consistent across all the behavior of the subjects
The PBG is a neutral recording that adds nothing of its own
optionExplain: That is what the tally shows.
Integration was destroyed.
Consistency was not examined.
It fills gaps plausibly.
questions.explain: The claim is about sufficiency of mechanism types.

questions.q: True or false: A reader says the PBG gives an unbiased record of the subject's thinking. The authors agree.
questions.explain: They say the PBG overstates the GPS-like character because it fills gaps in a plausible, GPS-like fashion.

questions.q: What do the authors say the tally ignores?
options: The number of operator occurrences in each protocol of the seven
The names of the subjects and the problems on which they worked
The experimenter's commands, which are counted as a separate type
The selective rules used to get operators and the rules used to terminate attempts
optionExplain: Counts are in the table.
Subjects appear in Table 9.4.
Commands are counted.
Both are ignored in the tally.
questions.explain: Selection and termination are not counted.
questions.rule: Selection and ending rules are missing.
questions.teaches: The tabulation ignores the selective rules used to get operators and the rules used to terminate attempts, and so does not test whether such rules are consistent over all the behavior.

questions.q: A study breaks a chess game into single moves, each classified by one property, and finds a small list of move types. Which caution from the chapter applies?
options: The small list proves that the player used no strategy in the game
The breakdown shows what types suffice, but loses the way the moves fit together
The breakdown reproduces the integrated game as well as the moves
The move types must be random
optionExplain: Strategy is integrated behavior the tally loses.
That is the centrifuge caution.
It destroys integration.
A small list is not random.
questions.explain: Parts do not give back the whole.
questions.teaches: Although each instance in isolation possesses a plausible selection or evaluation rule, the consistency of such rules over all the behavior has not been examined.

questions.q: Six people solve a puzzle and the share of each kind of step is almost the same for all six, including two who failed. What does the stability suggest?
options: The people are copying each other as they work
Failure is caused by a lack of any mechanism, as the two failers show
The task's structure and a shared basic mechanism set the mix of steps
The steps are chosen at random, and the mix happens to be the same
optionExplain: No copying is shown.
Failers had the same mix.
Stable shares across people point to shared determinants.
Randomness would vary.
questions.explain: Stability across individuals points to the task and a common mechanism.

questions.q: The two nonsolvers, S11 and S5, do not differ much from the ____ in the mix of mechanisms.
questions.explain: The stability across solvers and nonsolvers suggests the categories are dictated by the task.

questions.q: Which subjects have an almost absent other category in Table 9.4?
options: The nonsolvers S11 and S5, who failed on the problem
S4 and S8 only, whose protocols are the longest of all
All seven subjects equally, with no differences among them
The efficient solvers S10, S9 and S15
optionExplain: The nonsolvers do not differ much from the solvers.
S4 and S8 are longer protocols.
The efficient solvers differ.
They rarely depart from the basic mechanisms.
questions.explain: Good solvers have no occasion to depart from the basics.

questions.q: True or false: As protocols get longer, avoid consequences and review become gradually more frequent in the tally.
questions.explain: Table 9.4 shows a gradual increase of those categories with longer protocols.

questions.q: What do the authors say about within-episode behavior versus episode initiation in the tallies?
options: Initiation is the bulk of the tally, so dropping it would change the results
Within-episode behavior swamps initiation, so dropping initiators would not change the results
The two cannot be separated, so nothing can be said about initiation
Initiation is more GPS-like than the rest of the behavior in the episodes
optionExplain: The reverse.
Initiators are few relative to within-episode applications.
They are not separated in the tables, but their effect is shown to be small.
The rest is, if anything, more consistently GPS-like.
questions.explain: Most operator occurrences occur inside episodes.
questions.teaches: Of the 40 rule applications associated with episode initiation, 50 percent belong to the other category, and these account for 75 percent of all items in that category, so within-episode behavior is, if anything, even more consistently GPS-like than the tables show.

questions.q: True or false: A researcher tallies steps from three experts and three novices and finds the same mix of step types in all six, with the novices who failed no different from the others. By the authors' reading, this supports the idea that the mix is set mainly by the task.
questions.explain: Stability across subjects, including nonsolvers, suggests task structure and basic mechanism determine the mix.
questions.rule: Stability suggests the task sets the mix.
questions.teaches: Of the 176 phrases in S4's protocol, only 19 do not have their primary content reflected in the PBG, and most of these are not relevant to the task, so the PBG comes close to exhausting the total behavior.

questions.q: A person facing a new task could start by comparing the start and goal, by looking for a way to simplify what is in front of them, or by trying whatever tool fits. Which is the most specifically adapted to the task?
options: Looking for a way to simplify what is in front of them
Trying whatever tool fits
Comparing the start and the goal to find differences
All three equally
optionExplain: It is more general.
It is the most general.
It uses the task's specific goal.
They differ in specificity.
questions.explain: Starts differ in how much they use the goal. The card ranks them.

questions.q: Order the three ways of starting an episode from most primitive to least primitive (most specifically adapted to the task).
items: Searching for rules that apply to L1
Finding rules that simplify L1
Matching L0 and L1 to form differences
questions.explain: The authors judge searching for applicable rules the most primitive, then simplifying, then matching L0 and L1.

questions.q: A subject begins with I must eliminate the R's. Which way of starting is this?
options: Matching L0 and L1 to form differences
Finding rules that simplify L1, whatever the goal expression may be
Searching for rules that apply to L1, without any difference in view
Working backward from L0 to an expression that could precede it
optionExplain: A difference between the two expressions is stated.
No simplification is mentioned.
No rule search is mentioned.
No backward step.
questions.explain: The remark names a start-goal difference.

questions.q: True or false: The GPS described in Chapter 8 starts an episode by simplifying L1, and an extended GPS would add the match of L0 and L1.
questions.explain: The GPS described uses only the match of L0 and L1 to start; an extended GPS could add simplifying and rule search, in that order.

questions.q: After one or more episodes, where do searches through rules or earlier expressions occur, and under what condition?
options: Only at the very start of the protocol, before the first match is made
Mainly after episodes have ended, when the subject has no specific goal
Throughout every episode, where they replace the match with the goal
Only when the experimenter asks the subject to look at the rules
optionExplain: At the outset the match is used.
The less primitive initiators take precedence while there is a specific goal.
Within episodes behavior is goal-directed.
Not stated.
questions.explain: Aimless scanning follows termination.
questions.teaches: Except at the outset, searches through the rules or through previously generated expressions occur primarily after episodes have been terminated, when the subject has no specific goals in mind; S4 says of one such scan, I'm just scanning the rules, not in search of anything in particular.

questions.q: A support agent, with no clear lead, starts reading the manual from page one looking for any entry that might fit. A second agent starts by comparing the customer's symptom with the described problem. Which start is more primitive in the authors' sense?
options: The second agent's, because comparison of symptom and problem requires no knowledge
Neither, since both agents are directed toward the customer's problem
Both equally, since each starts without a lead from the customer
The first agent's, because it is less specifically adapted to the particular task
optionExplain: Comparison uses the specific goal.
The first is not goal-directed.
They differ in primitiveness.
Rule search is more primitive than matching start and goal.
questions.explain: Primitive means less task-specific.
questions.teaches: Two of the five solvers (S4 and S8) evoked path.R12, which uses R8 twice to obtain inputs for R12, after having generated one or both of the subexpressions with R8 in the interest of some other goal.

questions.q: Two people try the same dead-end idea. One gives up after two tries; the other tries dozens of variants. Which statement about persistence as a trait is best supported by that alone?
options: Nothing yet: it would take consistency across tasks to call it a trait
The second person is a more effective problem solver on tasks of this kind
The first person is lazy and does not like to work at hard tasks
The second person must have a rigid personality that shows in every task
optionExplain: A single observation cannot establish a trait.
Persistence does not guarantee effectiveness.
That claims a trait without evidence.
That also claims a trait.
questions.explain: Traits need consistency to be testable. The card gives the authors' point.

questions.q: True or false: S4 and S8 each gave up on the R7 attempt after generating only two expressions, whereas S5 went through an elaborate search for indirect routes.
questions.explain: The three differ in when they judge they can think of nothing more.
questions.rule: Two gave up early; S5 persisted.

questions.q: The authors call a label like stereotypy untestable unless the trait is ____ from one problem to another.
questions.explain: Without consistency it is neither testable nor useful for prediction.

questions.q: Suppose S4 had stayed with his first look at R12 as a means of removing the R's (Oh, R12 doesn't apply). According to the authors, what would probably have happened?
options: He would have failed as S5 did, going round and round the same cycles
He would have found a longer solution, using more steps than before
He would have found the solution much sooner
Nothing would have changed
optionExplain: The authors say the reverse.
They say sooner.
The authors say greater persistence there would have helped.
They say persistence could have mattered.
questions.explain: Persistence helps on the right path.

questions.q: What is the lesson about whether persistence reduces problem solving effectiveness?
options: Persistence always reduces effectiveness, as the case of S5 shows
Persistence always increases effectiveness, as the case of S4 shows
Not in general; S4 might have done better with more persistence
Persistence has no relation to the path that is being pursued
optionExplain: S4's case shows otherwise.
S5's case shows otherwise.
Persistence is not necessarily harmful.
It depends on the path.
questions.explain: Judge persistence by the path pursued.
questions.teaches: The authors say one cannot generalize that persistence necessarily reduces a subject's problem solving effectiveness, since greater persistence by S4 on his first look at R12 would have brought the solution much sooner.

questions.q: A manager notes that one analyst drops a failing line of inquiry quickly while another sticks with it for hours, and wants to label the second as stubborn. What would the authors ask before accepting the label?
options: Whether the analyst is consistently so from one problem to another
Whether the analyst is older than the other analysts in the department
Whether the analyst ever succeeds in the end on any of the inquiries
Whether the analyst is liked by the other members of the team
optionExplain: A label needs cross-problem consistency to be testable.
Age is not the condition.
Success is not the test of consistency.
Not the test.
questions.explain: Check consistency before assigning a trait.
questions.teaches: S8, like S4, gives up on path.R7 after generating two expressions, saying Here I am, well, now where am I?

questions.q: A new theory of problem solving is tested on two problems, one very simple and one moderately hard, from one task family, with talk-aloud and silent subjects behaving alike. What can fairly be claimed?
options: Proof that the theory holds for all human thinking on every kind of task
Nothing, because only two problems were tried and so no claim can be made
That talking aloud has no effect on any task that a person is given
Support for the theory in that task family, within the limits of two problems
optionExplain: Two problems cannot show that.
Detailed fits on two problems count.
The claim is limited to this task.
Evidence supports the theory within its range.
questions.explain: Match the conclusion to the evidence. The card gives the authors'.

questions.q: Subjects who talked aloud explored very much the ____ parts of the problem space as subjects who did not.
questions.explain: Both groups explored the same parts.

questions.q: Which of these describe the evidence the authors used to test GPS in this chapter? Select all that apply.
options: Thinking-aloud protocols from their own laboratory
Aggregate data from 64 Yale subjects
Brain scans of subjects
Task analysis based on essential versus inessential steps
optionExplain: Used.
Used.
Not used.
Used.
questions.explain: The chapter combines protocols, aggregate data and a task analysis.

questions.q: True or false: If the same program were tested on a very different task environment, the chapter's evidence alone would show that the program also fits there.
questions.explain: The data in this chapter were restricted to two problems in the Moore-Anderson logic environment.

questions.q: What did the task analysis explain, according to the summary?
options: Why subjects solved D1 faster after practice with earlier problems
Why the subjects' explorations stayed mostly in limited portions of the problem space
Why the experimenter chose to use thinking-aloud instructions with them
Why GPS has twelve rules and not some other number of rules
optionExplain: That is not stated here.
That is the stated use.
Not stated.
Not stated.
questions.explain: Essential versus inessential steps, plus construction and planning, bound the exploration.
questions.teaches: The task analysis based on the distinction between essential and inessential steps, and on the notions of construction and planning introduced in the previous chapter, explained to a considerable extent why the explorations stayed in limited, specified portions of the problem space.

questions.q: A start-up builds one engine of general search methods and plugs in separate knowledge for each domain it is used in. Which feature of GPS does this copy?
options: GPS separates its general problem solving capabilities from task-specific knowledge
GPS stores a separate method for every problem it is asked to solve
GPS uses exhaustive search as its principal heuristic in every task
GPS depends on the experimenter's instructions for its methods in each task
optionExplain: That organization is part of how the summary describes GPS.
The summary says the opposite.
Its principal heuristic is means-ends analysis.
Not stated.
questions.explain: General methods are kept apart from task knowledge.
questions.teaches: In the summary, GPS refers to several variants of the program described in Chapter 8, which employ means-ends analysis as a principal heuristic and are organized to divide their general problem solving capabilities from their knowledge about specific task environments.

questions.q: A study shows that people use the same method within each short stretch of work on a puzzle. What would a careful researcher ask next?
options: Whether the puzzle could be solved faster by a machine than by any person
How the stretches are arranged into the whole attempt, and whether this holds on a harder puzzle
Which of the people found the puzzle most enjoyable to work on
Whether a second puzzle exists that has exactly the same answer
optionExplain: Machine speed does not bear on how people arrange their effort.
The step beyond a single stretch is the overall organization, and a test on more difficult material.
Enjoyment is not part of a process account of problem solving.
The answer to a puzzle says nothing about how the work is organized.
questions.explain: Within-stretch behavior leaves the larger structure open. The card shows what the chapter asks next.
questions.rule: After the parts, ask about the arrangement of the parts.

questions.q: In the earlier chapters the subjects were shown to use goal structures and to set subgoals that reduce ____ between expressions.
questions.explain: The earlier analysis found goal structures and subgoals aimed at reducing differences between expressions and the input forms of operators.
questions.rule: Within episodes: functional analysis, goals, difference reduction.

questions.q: Cooks are first studied one dish at a time, then across a whole dinner service. Which chapter topic does the second step match?
options: The comparison of a single subject's learning over a series of problems
The introduction of working backwards as a new heuristic
The difference between Yale and Carnegie subjects
The arrangement and evocation of episodes, the macrostructure of protocols
optionExplain: Learning over a series concerns change in one person, not the order of episodes.
Working backwards is a particular method, not the arrangement of episodes in general.
That is a comparison of two groups of subjects, not of how episodes are ordered.
Sequencing whole units of work is the macrostructure question.
questions.explain: Macrostructure means how episodes are arranged and brought on, as opposed to what goes on inside one.
questions.rule: Macro: arrangement of episodes. Micro: what happens inside one.

questions.q: True or false: The earlier chapters left unsettled whether subjects used functional analysis and subgoals within episodes, so this chapter settles that first.
questions.explain: The previous analysis had already established the GPS-like character of behavior within episodes; this chapter builds on that.
questions.rule: Build on the established; do not re-prove it.

questions.q: How does the chapter describe problem C1 compared with problem D1, the problem examined in the previous chapter?
options: It is substantially more difficult, with working backwards more prominent in its protocols
It is a close equivalent of D1, chosen to check that the D1 results repeat on a second problem
It is an easy warm-up problem that every subject solved quickly
It comes from a different task, such as cryptarithmetic
optionExplain: The chapter introduces C1 as a harder problem where working backwards is prominent.
The text calls C1 substantially more difficult, not an equivalent.
C1 was solved by only a minority of subjects.
C1 is a logic problem like D1.
questions.explain: C1 serves as a test of the account on a harder problem. Full statement: It is substantially more difficult, and working backwards appears more prominently in its protocols.
questions.rule: A harder problem tests whether the account stretches.
questions.teaches: Problem C1 is substantially more difficult than D1, and the heuristic of working backwards appears more prominently in the C1 protocols than in those examined earlier.

questions.q: A team says driver learning lies outside its main aims but cannot be ignored. Which treatment does the chapter's approach parallel?
options: Leaving it out altogether
Making it the central claim of the whole study
Examining it briefly, as the chapter does for individual differences
Treating it as proof that the main theory holds
optionExplain: The authors say they cannot ignore these topics completely.
The authors call these topics outside the main goals of the undertaking.
The authors call these topics outside their main goals yet too important to leave out, and they examine them.
Examining side topics does not by itself prove the main account.
questions.explain: The authors give a short but real treatment to topics that are not central. Full statement: Examining it briefly, as the chapter does for individual differences and one subject's learning.
questions.rule: Side topics can be examined without becoming the main claim.
questions.teaches: The authors treat individual differences among subjects and the learning of a single subject as lying outside the main goals of the undertaking but too important to ignore completely.

questions.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
questions.q: Which organization of a long task outlines the big steps first, then gives each step its own working session, in order?
options: Always attack whichever problem seems largest at the moment
Do the quickest steps first and leave the hard ones for last
Sketch the outline of key steps, then give each step its own session
Work on all steps a little at a time, rotating among them
optionExplain: Choosing the largest problem each time involves no outline made beforehand.
Ordering by speed is not an outline of the key steps.
Planning first, then carrying out each step, is the organization described.
Rotation among steps involves no prior plan of what the key steps are.
questions.explain: The planning method makes an outline in an abstract space, then executes it. The card shows both routes.
questions.rule: Plan in the abstract, then carry out the steps one episode each.

questions.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
questions.q: In the version of GPS that uses the planning method, each step of the plan is turned into a ____ in the original problem space.
questions.explain: Each step of the abstract solution, an essential operator, becomes a subproblem or goal, and an episode is devoted to each.
questions.rule: Plan step becomes goal; goal gets an episode.

questions.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
questions.q: A repair robot fixes the most serious fault first, with structural faults ranked above cosmetic ones. How will it behave, on the chapter's model?
options: It tackles the worst structural fault, using cosmetic fixes only as preparation, then the next one
It fixes every cosmetic fault first
It writes a full plan of all repairs and checks it with the owner before touching anything
It picks faults at random and gives up on any that fails
optionExplain: This is the pattern the heuristic and the ordering produce.
The ordering ranks cosmetic faults last.
That describes the planning method, not the ranking heuristic.
Random choice is not the ranking the heuristic sets up.
questions.explain: A ranking with essentials first yields essential-goal episodes with inessential preparation, with no plan. Full statement: It goes for the most serious structural fault, using cosmetic fixes only to prepare, then moves to the next structural fault.
questions.rule: Rank essentials first and the episodes follow.

questions.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
questions.q: Order the stages of the planning method as the card describes it.
items: Abstract the problem into a planning space
Find a solution to the abstracted problem
Turn each step (an essential operator) into a goal in the original space
Devote one episode to each of those goals, in order
questions.explain: The plan is made first, in abstraction. The episodes in the original space come afterwards, in the order of the plan.

questions.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
questions.q: According to the authors, what does the second of GPS's two heuristics say about apply-operator goals whose differences are serious?
options: Set up as many reduce-difference subgoals as possible
Postpone them until every inessential difference has gone
Reorder the differences so the serious ones count as inessential
Do not set reduce-difference subgoals for them; abandon the apply-operator goal instead
optionExplain: The heuristic says the opposite: no reduce-difference subgoals for serious differences.
Postponing is not what the heuristic says; it says to abandon the goal.
The heuristic does not alter the ranking; it governs subgoal setting.
This is the second heuristic: serious differences lead to abandoning the goal rather than working on them.
questions.explain: Together with reducing the most serious differences first, this heuristic makes the program skip attempts that would need major repairs.
questions.rule: Serious differences in an apply-operator goal: abandon, do not repair.
questions.teaches: The second heuristic tells GPS not to create reduce-difference subgoals for an apply-operator goal when the differences are serious, but to abandon that apply-operator goal.

questions.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
questions.q: A subject outlines rough steps for one part of a problem and works step by step on the rest. What do the authors' remarks imply?
options: The subject must be mistaken
Real behavior need not match either pure route; a range of possibilities lies between
The subject has shown that planning is never used in this task
The subject has shown the ranking heuristic is unnecessary
optionExplain: The authors allow possibilities between the two routes.
The authors say a whole range of additional possibilities lies between the two answers GPS offers.
Partial planning in one part of a problem is a form of planning.
Nothing in the observation removes the ranking route.
questions.explain: The two GPS routes are endpoints of a range, not the only options. Full statement: Real behavior need not match either pure route, because a whole range of possibilities lies between them.
questions.rule: Treat the two routes as ends of a range.
questions.teaches: The authors say that, besides GPS's two possible answers to how episode goals are chosen, a whole range of additional possibilities lies somewhere between the two.

questions.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
questions.q: A recording of a puzzle solver starts with rough talk, then moves to step-by-step work. What would suggest the rough talk was a plan?
options: The later work follows the order of the rough steps
The rough talk was long and the step-by-step work was short
The person spoke slowly during the rough talk
The step-by-step work was free of mistakes
optionExplain: A plan shows up as the later work being arranged in the plan's order.
The lengths of the two parts say nothing about whether one governs the other.
Speech speed is not evidence about organization.
A plan can be followed with mistakes, and a flawless run needs no plan.
questions.explain: The mark of a plan is that it governs what comes after. The card states the test.
questions.rule: A plan shows in the order of what follows it.

questions.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
questions.q: True or false: If the planning routine organized a protocol, its first portion would contain only abstracted actions in the planning space.
questions.explain: The initial portion would show abstract steps only, with the concrete episodes in the original space coming later.

questions.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
questions.q: A subject spends the opening minutes naming rough operations, then works separate episodes in that order. Which organization fits?
options: Difference ranking alone, since the episodes are in order
Neither, because both routes give random episode order
Difference ranking, because the abstract talk shows that the subject ranks differences by seriousness
The planning routine, since the later episodes follow the earlier abstract sequence
optionExplain: Ranking alone would not give an opening of abstract actions only.
Both routes give a definite order, not a random one.
Abstract talk followed by ordered episodes is the planning signature, not the ranking one.
An abstract opening and ordered later episodes is the planning pattern.
questions.explain: The sequence of a plan, then its carrying out, marks planning.
questions.rule: Look for a plan phase followed by execution in the same order.

questions.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
questions.q: A subject makes a plan, fails at its second step, and makes a new plan. The protocol will show a second ____ phase partway through.
questions.explain: A new plan after failure adds another abstract stretch in the middle of the protocol, before further concrete episodes.
questions.rule: Several plans mean several abstract phases.

questions.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
questions.q: Besides the case of a new plan after a failure, what other complication do the authors mention?
options: The subject may fail to speak aloud during the abstract phase
The experimenter may write the expressions on the board in a different order from the subject's
The subject may evolve several plans before trying to implement any one of them
The subject may solve the problem in only one episode
optionExplain: The text does not name silence as a complication.
That error is mentioned elsewhere for another problem, not as a complication of this test.
The authors name making several plans before trying any as the other complication.
A single episode is not described as a complication here.
questions.explain: More than one plan at a time makes it harder to read off the arrangement.
questions.rule: Several plans before any attempt: another complication.
questions.teaches: Beyond a fresh plan after a failure, the authors note that a subject might evolve several plans before trying to implement any one of them.

questions.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
questions.q: A planner outlines a house build in three steps, does two, then drafts a different third step after trouble. What does her record show?
options: No planning, because the third step changed
Difference ranking, since the steps were ranked by size when she first set them out
Only that she works slowly
Planning with a revised plan, which complicates the pattern without removing it
optionExplain: A change after trouble is among the complications the authors list, not evidence against planning.
Nothing in the description points to ranking of differences.
The description gives no basis for that, and speed is not the test.
Abstract steps, then concrete work in order, then a new plan: planning with a revision.
questions.explain: The test looks for a plan that governs later work, whether or not it survives intact. Full statement: Planning, with a revised plan after trouble, which complicates but does not remove the pattern.
questions.teaches: The authors describe a subject who evolves new plans after failing to execute an earlier one as making things a little more complicated, which is how they treat such protocols.

questions.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
questions.q: Which remark, made before any move, shows a solver planning rather than starting at once?
options: I will try the first thing that comes to mind and see what appears on the page
First something rough, then combine it with the other piece; details later
I wonder whether this problem has a solution at all
Line 5 is now written down, and line 6 will come next in full
optionExplain: Starting at once with a single concrete step shows no sequence of rough steps.
Two rough steps in sequence, with details left open, make up a plan.
Wondering about solvability is not a sequence of steps.
Writing out full lines in order is concrete work, not abstraction.
questions.explain: A plan is a rough sequence worked out ahead of the details. The card gives the authors' test. Full statement: First I will turn this into something rough, then combine that with the other piece, and sort out the details later.
questions.rule: Rough steps in sequence, ahead of the detail.

questions.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
questions.q: Which of these belong to the authors' criterion for planning? Select all that apply.
options: Considering transformations whose input or output is not fully specified
Considering a sequence of at least two such transformations
Writing the complete solution on the board before any step is tried
Telling the experimenter that he is making a plan
optionExplain: Yes: abstracted transformations are the first element.
Yes: a sequence, not a single step, is the second element.
No: a plan need not be complete or worked out in detail.
No: the test is read from the behavior, not from a declaration.
questions.explain: The criterion rests on the form of what the subject considers: abstracted steps, in a sequence of two or more.

questions.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
questions.q: Which traveler's remark meets the first two elements of the criterion?
options: I will take the 9:40 flight to Leeds and then the 12:15 train on to York
I am not sure that I want to travel at all this week
First some flight into the region, then some train onward; times later
I will book the flight and see what turns up afterwards
optionExplain: Every detail is fixed, so nothing is abstracted.
Doubt about whether to travel names no transformations.
Two abstract steps in sequence, with the details left open.
One concrete step with nothing planned beyond it is not a sequence.
questions.explain: The remark leaves times and exact routes open but names an ordered pair of steps. Full statement: First some flight into the region, then some train onward; I will look up the times later.
questions.rule: Two or more rough steps in an order.

questions.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
questions.q: True or false: The authors' criterion for planning asks for a sequence of at least two abstracted transformations.
questions.explain: The criterion asks for a sequence of at least two abstracted transformations.
questions.rule: One rough step is not a plan.

questions.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
questions.q: What third behavior completes the authors' criterion once the sequence has been developed?
options: He carries out the steps of the sequence in a series of episodes in the original space
He reports the sequence aloud to the experimenter in the order in which he will use it
He completes every step of the sequence without a single error
He drops the sequence at the first failure and starts a different problem
optionExplain: Planning is followed by carrying out the steps, one episode at a time, in the original space.
Reporting aloud is not part of the criterion.
Steps may fail; the criterion asks only that he sets about them.
Dropping the plan is not part of the criterion.
questions.explain: Planning has an execution part: the plan is put to work in the original problem space. Full statement: He engages in a series of episodes to carry out the steps of the sequence in the original problem space.
questions.rule: Plan, then episodes that carry it out.
questions.teaches: The criterion's third element is that, after developing the sequence, the subject engages in a series of episodes to carry out its steps in the original problem space.

questions.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
questions.q: A gardener notes: dig a bed, then plant something that likes shade. Why is the second step thought of before the first is done?
options: Because plans are valid only if the first step is guaranteed to succeed in advance
The second step is thought of without detailed knowledge of its input
Because the second step is always the easier one in any plan
Because planning forbids looking at the details at all
optionExplain: The authors say the feasibility of the earlier step need not be known.
That is how the authors describe the second operation in a sequence.
Nothing in the criterion ranks the steps by difficulty.
Details may be examined later; the plan simply does not wait for them.
questions.explain: A plan reaches past what is yet known about the situation after the first step. Full statement: The second operation is contemplated without detailed knowledge of its input or of whether the earlier step can be done.
questions.rule: A plan may run ahead of what it knows.
questions.teaches: In a plan the second operation is contemplated without detailed knowledge of the input to it, and without knowing whether the previous operation can actually be accomplished.

questions.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
questions.q: How do people usually use planning when they work on a tricky problem?
options: Always for the whole problem, before any detailed step is made
Only after every other approach has failed
Only at fixed points, switching between planning and doing on a regular schedule
Often for one part of the problem, moving flexibly between plan and detail
optionExplain: Complete advance planning is a tidy ideal, not the common pattern.
Plans are used from the start in many cases.
A fixed schedule is how a program behaves, not how people do.
Planning is commonly partial, and the move between planning and doing is loose.
questions.explain: People mix and match. The card gives the authors' reading of their protocols. Full statement: Often for one part of the problem, moving flexibly between rough plans and detailed work.
questions.rule: Human planning is partial and flexible.

questions.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
questions.q: The authors say the GPS planning routine was developed ____ , after examining some of the human protocols.
questions.explain: The routine was developed inductively from protocols, then formalized.
questions.rule: The routine came from the protocols, not the reverse.

questions.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
questions.q: One programmer plans a whole task in detail, then codes it. Another outlines only the tricky module and improvises the rest. Which is planning?
options: Both, since planning by the looser criterion may cover only a portion of a problem
Only the first, since a plan must cover the whole task
Only the second, since real planning is always partial
Neither, since neither switched between spaces on a fixed schedule
optionExplain: Partial planning counts under the looser criterion.
The authors say planning may be partial and incomplete.
Complete planning would also count; the point is that partial planning is allowed too.
The authors say no explicit alternation is required.
questions.explain: A complete plan and a partial plan are both plans under the looser criterion.

questions.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
questions.q: True or false: The authors report convincing evidence that subjects changed which differences they counted as essential from one time to another.
questions.explain: The nature of the abstraction could change, they say, but they do not find convincing evidence of any such changes in their protocols.
questions.rule: Possible in principle is not found in the data.

questions.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
questions.q: Which subjects show planning most prominently, according to the authors?
options: The subjects who were slowest to write a first line
The subjects who gave the longest explanations to the experimenter
The more successful subjects and those with experience from previous problems
The subjects who were given thinking-aloud instructions
optionExplain: Slowness is not what the text links with planning.
The text does not connect planning with the amount of talk.
The authors name success and prior experience as the marks of heavy planning.
Thinking aloud was the method for all protocols, not a mark of planners.
questions.explain: Planning goes with skill and practice in this data.
