questions.rule: Planning goes with success and experience.
questions.teaches: Planning is very prominent in the protocols of the more successful subjects and of those who had accumulated experience from previous problems.

questions.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
questions.q: A checklist switches from planning to doing at set points, unlike how expert pilots brief and fly. Which contrast matches the chapter's?
options: The routine is looser than the people, who follow strict schedules at every stage of the work
The routine and the people behave identically, step for step
The routine is stiff and deliberate in moving between spaces; the people are flexible
The routine never plans, while the people plan all the time
optionExplain: The authors say the opposite: the routine is the stiff one.
The authors call the routine formalized and stylized.
The authors contrast GPS's stiff, deliberate movement between problem space and planning space with the subjects' flexibility.
The GPS routine does plan; the contrast is in how.
questions.explain: A formalized model is stiffer than the behavior it describes. Full statement: The routine moves back and forth between spaces with stiffness and deliberateness; the people move flexibly.
questions.teaches: The authors point to a stiffness and deliberateness in GPS's movement back and forth between problem space and planning space that contrasts with the subjects' flexibility.

questions.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
questions.q: A solver faces a goal of the form P or T. Which first idea is a natural way in?
options: Get P alone, since adding T to it is then one easy step
Get T alone, since it is the only letter not in the givens
Remove P from the goal
Rewrite the goal as a horseshoe
optionExplain: Working back from the goal: reach a simple form from which the goal follows in one step.
T appears nowhere in the givens, so it cannot be reached directly.
The goal cannot be altered to suit the solver.
Rewriting the goal does not point to any given line.
questions.explain: S8 begins from the goal. The card shows the whole chain he sets out.
questions.rule: Start with a form that gives the goal in one step.

questions.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
questions.q: S8's plan for A4 is to get P alone and then add the extra letter ____ by applying R9.
questions.explain: L0 is P or T, and T appears in none of the given lines, so adding it to P by R9 is the last step.
questions.rule: Get P alone, then add T.

questions.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
questions.q: Order the steps of S8's plan for A4, from first to last.
items: Combine the second and fourth lines by R12 to cancel the R's
Combine that result with the third line by R11 to cancel the S's
Combine that result with the first line by R11 to cancel the Q's
Apply R9 to P to obtain P or T
questions.explain: The R's go first, then the S's, then the Q's, and R9 adds T to the P that remains.
questions.rule: Cancel R, cancel S, cancel Q, then add T.

questions.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
questions.q: Which statements about S8's plan are supported by the text? Select all that apply.
options: He announced the plan before applying any rule
He knew in advance that R12 could be applied to the second and fourth lines as written
The plan did not fix the exact form of the final result
The plan was a fully worked-out solution in detail
optionExplain: Right: his talk came before any rule application.
Wrong: one line would have to be reversed first, and he did not know the signs would match.
Right: the result might have been not-P instead of P.
Wrong: it left details of every step open.
questions.explain: The plan comes first and is abstract; it fixes the sequence of cancellations but not the detail.

questions.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
questions.q: In basic GPS without planning, what follows a decision to apply a rule?
options: A delay until the whole solution has been found in an abstract space
A check that all other differences have been removed first
A move to a different rule
An apply-operator goal is set up, starting immediate work on its feasibility
optionExplain: That describes the planning method, not basic GPS.
Basic GPS does not wait for that.
Basic GPS does not drop a rule by deciding to apply it.
In basic GPS the decision creates a goal that tests feasibility at once and sets subgoals if it fails.
questions.explain: S8 differs: he decides to use R12 and only describes the result he expects, without testing at once whether it can be done.
questions.rule: Basic GPS tests at once; S8 does not.
questions.teaches: In basic GPS, the decision to apply a rule creates an apply-operator goal and starts immediate activity to test feasibility; S8, by contrast, merely describes some essential features of the result.

questions.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
questions.q: A woodworker plans to glue up a grooved board, then fit the shelf, unchecked. Which feature of S8's plan is shared?
options: A full list of tools needed is drawn up before work begins
A step is chosen before it is known to be possible, its result roughly described
The final product is described in complete detail first
The order of the steps was settled by trial and error at the bench as she worked through them
optionExplain: S8's plan contained no list of tools.
S8 chose R12 without knowing whether it could be applied, and described its result only roughly.
S8 knew only the rough form of intermediate results.
S8's order was set in his talk before any rule was applied.
questions.explain: Plans can include steps whose feasibility has not been tested. Full statement: A step is decided on before it is known to be possible, with its result described only by its main features.
questions.rule: Decide on a step before testing it, describe its result roughly.
questions.teaches: S8 describes the intermediate results of his plan only by the letters they will contain, as in just an S and Q, with no sign that he knows such a result can be obtained.

questions.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
questions.q: A solver outlines a plan aloud and then executes it quickly. What would suggest she was really working out details as she went?
options: Remarks in the middle of the work that show she is deciding the next small step
A confident tone throughout the outline and no hesitation at all while she is working
A very long outline that mentions every step
The absence of any remarks while she works
optionExplain: Spontaneous decisions inside the execution show the details were not settled beforehand.
Confidence says nothing about what was settled.
A long outline would suggest more was settled in advance.
Silence gives no evidence about the details one way or the other.
questions.explain: The evidence for open details lies in the execution phase. The card shows what the authors point to.
questions.rule: Look for decisions made during execution.

questions.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
questions.q: True or false: With only a skeleton plan, S8 would be expected to move between episodes with little hesitation but to search within each episode.
questions.explain: The episodes within the plan involve problem solving; the moves between them are smooth.
questions.rule: Smooth between episodes, active within them.

questions.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
questions.q: Which comment during execution best supports the view that details were being worked out as S8 went?
options: I knew all along that this would come out as P once the plan had been carried out
Everything is exactly as I planned it
I have nothing to add to what I said before
I'm first going to change line 1 to a horseshoe, so apply R6 to it
optionExplain: A claim of foresight would favor the other view.
That suggests the details were all settled beforehand.
Silence offers no evidence about the details.
A decision about a preparatory step made on the spot.
questions.explain: Preparatory moves announced on the spot show that the details were not yet decided.

questions.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
questions.q: A critic says: S8 solved A4 smoothly, so the plan must have contained the whole solution. What is the flaw?
options: S8 did not solve A4 in the end, so there is no smooth run that needs any explanation here
Smoothness is predicted even for a skeleton plan; the evidence is the on-the-spot work
The critic is right because skeleton plans never lead to smooth runs
S8 spoke too little for any inference to be made
optionExplain: S8 reached P or T, so he solved A4.
The authors expect little hesitation between episodes and some problem solving inside each.
The authors predict smooth transitions between episodes of such a plan.
The protocol contains remarks that serve as evidence.
questions.explain: Smoothness between episodes does not distinguish a skeleton from a full solution; remarks inside episodes do. Full statement: Smoothness between episodes is predicted even for a skeleton plan; the telling evidence is the on-the-spot work within episodes.
questions.rule: Check inside the episodes, not just between them.

questions.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
questions.q: To make R12 applicable, S8 first inverted the fourth line by applying R____ to it.
questions.explain: Inverting the fourth line gave a line of the form S implies not-R, which R12 could then combine with the second line.
questions.rule: A preparatory reversal makes the rule applicable.
questions.teaches: To make R12 applicable S8 first inverted the fourth line with R2, obtaining a line of the form S implies not-R, and only then applied R12 to the second line and this new line.

questions.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
questions.q: A tailor plans to cut cloth, then sew seams, and finds mid-cut that the pattern needs flipping. What does this show?
options: The plan was invalid, so it should be abandoned and a new one made from scratch
The tailor must have worked out everything in advance
Planning is impossible when a preparatory step is needed
Details of the plan were being worked out in execution, as with S8's reversal
optionExplain: S8's plan also needed a preparatory step and he did not abandon it.
Finding a step needed in execution suggests it was not worked out in advance.
S8's example shows plans surviving such steps.
A necessary preparatory step arising during execution is just what the authors take as evidence of a skeleton plan.
questions.explain: A plan names the key steps; preparatory steps come out in execution. Full statement: The details of the plan were being worked out in execution, as with S8's reversal of a line.
questions.rule: Skeleton plans leave the preparation to execution.
questions.teaches: The authors cite S8's remarks during execution, which voice surprise that it is going so easily and an expectation of trouble, as substantial evidence that the details had not been worked out beforehand.

questions.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
questions.q: Why might a failed plan tell researchers more than a smooth success about how the plan was made?
options: Failures are more common than successes, so they supply more data
The failure can expose details the planner never thought through
A plan that fails was always badly made in every respect
Planners explain their reasoning more fully after they fail
optionExplain: Frequency is not the reason; what the failure reveals is.
A plan that breaks shows which parts were left open.
A failed plan can be sensible and still miss one detail.
Nothing in the text links failure with fuller explanations.
questions.explain: A plan that works could have been fully worked out; one that fails cannot have been. The card shows the D1 case.
questions.rule: Failure shows what was left open.

questions.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
questions.q: True or false: S8 stated his D1 plan mostly as functions, such as eliminate and add on, not as particular connectives.
questions.explain: Only once, to change a connective to a dot, did he mention a connective at all.
questions.rule: Plans speak of functions, not details.

questions.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
questions.q: A planner says: drop one stop, switch the leg to a train, cut the long section. No train serves the stop. What does this show?
options: She chose the wrong function for every step, so the plan had no chance of working
She had worked out the booking in full beforehand
The plan named functions but not the details that decide feasibility
Plans stated by function cannot ever be carried out
optionExplain: The functions were sensible; one detail was missing.
Then the missing train would have been noticed in advance.
Like S8's plan, hers described what each step should do, and left feasibility details open.
S8's A4 plan was stated by function and carried out.
questions.explain: Feasibility lives in the details a functional plan leaves out. Full statement: Her plan named functions, but not the details that decide whether the steps are possible.
questions.rule: Functional plans leave feasibility to execution.

questions.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
questions.q: Order the steps of S8's D1 plan as the card describes it.
items: Apply R8 to the first line to drop one of its two halves
Change the connective of the remaining half to a dot
Apply R8 again to eliminate R, leaving P or Q
Apply R9 to add the other letter
questions.explain: The two uses of R8 are separated by a change of connective, and R9 comes last.
questions.rule: Drop a half, change the connective, eliminate R, add the other letter.

questions.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
questions.q: What went wrong when S8 tried to carry out his D1 plan?
options: He could not make the connective a dot without negating the expressions, so R8 could not be reused
He applied R8 to the wrong half of the first line, undid it, and then ran out of the time he was allowed
He found that R9 cannot add a letter to a single letter
The experimenter had written the first line down wrongly
optionExplain: The change of connective brought in a tilde that blocked the second use of R8.
He had not even decided which half; the failure was elsewhere.
The plan did not reach R9.
That error belongs to another subject, on C1.
questions.explain: The step that had been mentioned only in passing, the change of connective, proved to be the obstacle. Full statement: He could not turn the connective into a dot without making the expressions negative, so R8 could not be applied a second time to eliminate R.
questions.rule: The unspecified step was the one that failed.
questions.teaches: S8 found that he could not transform the connective into a dot without making the expressions negative, so he could not apply R8 a second time to eliminate R.

questions.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
questions.q: A manager's plan fails at its second step. She tries steps one by one, meets an obstacle, and drops it. Which S8 feature matches?
options: He knew from the start that the plan was infeasible and used it anyway
He found the difficulty by methodically executing the plan, and dropped it when stuck
He persisted with the plan for the rest of the protocol in spite of the obstacle he had met
He asked the experimenter whether the plan was feasible before trying it
optionExplain: He voiced hope at the start; the difficulty came to him in execution.
The difficulty came to light in execution, and the plan was then abandoned.
S8 abandoned this plan; persistence is how the authors describe other subjects.
The text reports no such question.
questions.explain: Execution tests a plan's detail; an obstacle that cannot be overcome ends the plan. Full statement: He discovered the difficulty by methodically executing the plan and abandoned it when he could not overcome it.
questions.rule: Plans are tested in execution and dropped on failure.
questions.teaches: S8 discovered the difficulty by proceeding methodically to execute the plan, and when he could not overcome it he abandoned the plan.

questions.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
questions.q: A solver plans: bring A to form X, bring B to form X, join them, then separate. What is odd about this?
options: Joining the two pieces together is never possible, so the plan could not be completed at all
Separating pieces always destroys the form X
A plan should contain only one step
Success at either of the first two goals would already solve it, so the rest is wasted
optionExplain: Nothing in the plan makes joining impossible.
Separation does not destroy anything by its nature.
Plans may have several steps.
The plan has a redundant stage.
questions.explain: Redundancy can live inside a plan. The card shows how this appears in B2. Full statement: Success at either of the first two goals would already solve the problem, so joining and separating is wasted.
questions.rule: A plan can contain stages that do nothing.

questions.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
questions.q: In S8's B2 plan the two not-Q lines are combined by R10 and then taken apart again by R____.
questions.explain: R10 puts the two lines together as a conjunction of not-Q with itself, and R3 reduces that to a single not-Q.
questions.rule: Combine by R10, separate by R3.

questions.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
questions.q: In C3 S8 planned to cancel the S's between the first two lines. What did he expect to hold afterwards, and what next?
options: The letter R alone, which he would cancel against the third line by another R11
The letter S alone, which he would cancel against the third line by R12
Not-Q directly, so no further step was planned
The letter R, which he would then add to the goal by R9
optionExplain: The S's cancel to leave R, and R then cancels against the horseshoe in line 3.
The S's are what cancel; the letter that remains is R.
The goal is not reached by the first cancellation.
R9 adds a term; the plan removes R by a second R11.
questions.explain: The C3 plan has two cancellations in a row, like the A4 plan.

questions.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
questions.q: True or false: After S8 carried out his C3 plan, the problem was finished with nothing further to do.
questions.explain: He still had to eliminate P from the expression not-(P implies Q), and nothing shows he had planned how to do it.
questions.rule: A plan may stop short of the goal.

questions.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
questions.q: Where did S8 get the idea for his B2 plan?
options: From the experimenter, who hinted at it during the session
From the rule sheet, which lists the order in which rules are used
From a strategy used on a specific earlier problem, which he had not solved
From a problem he had solved earlier in the same session
optionExplain: The text reports no hint.
The rule sheet does not give plans.
He recalled one he had had the other day whose goal was of the form T and T.
The earlier problem was one he had not solved.
questions.explain: Plans can be transported from other problems, whether or not they worked there.
questions.rule: A plan can be borrowed from an earlier problem.
questions.teaches: The B2 plan was generated from a strategy taken from a specific prior problem, one that S8 had not solved.

questions.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
questions.q: A coach borrows a drill that failed for another team and is redundant for hers. How does the account of S8's B2 plan apply?
options: A redundant plan cannot be a real plan, so the coach is only pretending to plan
An infeasible plan is abandoned within seconds
A redundant plan can be real: S8 spent five minutes trying to carry his out
A borrowed plan is always a good plan
optionExplain: The authors take S8's redundant plan as real.
S8 spent five minutes on his.
The authors confirm the redundant plan was his by the five minutes of behavior that followed.
S8's borrowed plan was infeasible.
questions.explain: Whether a plan was real is judged by the behavior that follows it, not by whether it is sensible. Full statement: The plan can still be a real plan: S8 struggled for five minutes to carry it out, though it was infeasible.
questions.rule: Judge a plan by the effort spent on it.
questions.teaches: The authors confirm that the redundant B2 plan was truly S8's by the five minutes of behavior that followed, in which he struggled, unsuccessfully since the plan was infeasible, to execute it.

questions.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
questions.q: When a cook sketches a plan for a stew, which steps are most likely to be named?
options: The major ones that change what the dish is, leaving small adjustments for later
Every small adjustment, so that nothing at all is forgotten when the cooking starts
Only the final step
The order of washing up
optionExplain: Rough plans name the steps that matter and leave routine adjustments for later.
A rough plan does not list the adjustments.
The major steps along the way are named.
Washing up does not change what the dish is.
questions.explain: Plans mention what matters and leave fitting-in work unnamed. The card applies this to S8. Full statement: The major ones that change what the dish is, with small adjustments left to be filled in.
questions.rule: Name the essentials, leave the fitting-in.

questions.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
questions.q: Sort these rules by whether S8's plans named them.

items.t: R9
R1
R2
R5
R6

questions.explain: S8's plans were about R11, R12, R8, R9, R10 and R3, and not at all about R1, R2, R5 or R6.
questions.rule: Plans name R3, R8-R12; not R1, R2, R5, R6.

questions.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
questions.q: An accountant plans: merge the two ledgers, then deduct the loan, leaving re-sorting and relabelling unmentioned. Which part parallels S8's inessential rules?
options: Merging the two ledgers
Deducting the loan, because it removes a part
All of the plan
Re-sorting the columns and relabelling, which fit things for the main steps
optionExplain: Merging combines parts, as R10 or R12 do; it parallels the essential rules.
Removing a part parallels R8, an essential rule.
The plan's two steps are the essential ones.
They are adjustments to details, like changing a connective or reversing an order.
questions.explain: Essential steps change what the structure contains; inessential ones adjust the form.
questions.rule: Essential changes content; inessential adjusts form.

questions.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
questions.q: A subject plans with essential operators only. While carrying out the plan he must supply the ____ operations that make each essential operator applicable.
questions.explain: Reversals and connective changes that the plan left unmentioned are filled in at execution time, as in A4 and D1.

questions.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
questions.q: How widely did the authors find a distinction close to essential and inessential among the subjects on D1?
options: At least five of the other subjects used one on D1
Only S8 used it
Every one of the subjects used it on every problem
None of the others
optionExplain: The evidence is strong that at least five other subjects did.
The authors find it in at least five others.
The authors say at least five, not all.
The authors say the others were examined and five used the distinction.
questions.explain: The distinction is not peculiar to S8.
questions.teaches: The evidence is strong that at least five of the other subjects, on problem D1, used a distinction close to the essential-inessential distinction.

questions.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
questions.q: A student sketches an algebra solution, ignoring signs and brackets until later. Which observation about S8 does this parallel?
options: His plans listed every tilde and connective before he started on any of the work itself
His plans ignored the goal expression altogether
His plans were built only from the inessential rules
His plans left out tildes and connectives, which inessential operations adjust later
optionExplain: His plans left them out.
His plans began from the goal.
They were built from the essential rules.
He abstracted away signs and connective details when planning.
questions.explain: Details of form are the first to be dropped when sketching. Full statement: His plans left out the tildes and connectives, details that inessential operations adjust later.
questions.rule: Sketch the structure, fill in the form.
questions.teaches: The details S8 omits when stating a plan are the tildes and connectives of the expressions that its operations will produce.

questions.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
questions.q: True or false: The authors can show from their data where the subjects' essential-inessential distinction comes from.
questions.explain: They say they can only conjecture, and offer three possibilities. The card lists them.

questions.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
questions.q: Match each conjecture to the observation that supports it.
pairs: Proficient algebra students simplify expressions automatically
Taking an expression apart feels less drastic than deleting a part
Objects that keep identity versus their changeable properties
questions.explain: Each conjecture names a familiar source outside the logic task.
questions.rule: Three sources: other math, objects, perception.

questions.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
questions.q: A child accepts taking a toy apart but not snapping it in half. Which conjecture about the logic subjects does this parallel?
options: Transfer from algebra, where proficient people simplify expressions automatically
Experience with material objects, where disassembling seems less drastic
The perceptual split between identity and changeable properties
None of them, since toys have nothing to do with logic
optionExplain: The child's choice concerns handling objects, not simplifying.
Using R8 to disassemble seems less drastic to subjects than using it to delete.
The child is comparing two ways of handling the object, not types of property.
The parallel is with the conjecture about material objects.
questions.explain: The second conjecture ties the distinction to handling things. Full statement: Experience with material objects, where disassembling seems less drastic than deleting.

questions.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
questions.q: True or false: The authors present the conjectures as established by their protocols.
questions.explain: They call them conjectures; the data do not decide among them.
questions.rule: Do not read a conjecture as a result.

questions.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
questions.q: In the authors' 1959 scheme for trigonometric identities with GPS, which operation counts as essential?
options: Combining a sin x and b sin x into (a + b) sin x
Writing the terms of a sum in alphabetical order
Replacing sin squared plus cos squared by 1
Copying the identity out in a new line
optionExplain: That is the routine algebraic manipulation, the inessential kind.
Nothing in the scheme concerns alphabetical order.
That substitution is an essential trigonometric manipulation.
Copying is not an operation of the scheme.
questions.explain: The scheme shows that GPS-style programs separated essential from routine steps in other fields.
questions.rule: Essential: the identity step. Routine: the algebraic tidy-up.
questions.teaches: In the 1959 scheme for doing trigonometric identities with GPS, replacing sin squared plus cos squared by 1 is an essential manipulation, while combining a sin x and b sin x into (a + b) sin x is a routine algebraic one.

questions.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
questions.q: A potter squeezes a bowl into a vase; another time she turns it on the table. Which is like R7 and which like R1?
options: Turning the bowl is like R7, and squeezing the bowl into a vase is like R1, the reverse
Both are like R7
Both are like R1
Squeezing is like R7, which changes the object; turning is like R1, which rearranges it
optionExplain: The pairing is the wrong way round.
Turning leaves the bowl a bowl, so it matches R1.
Squeezing makes a new shape, so it matches R7.
R7 changes the object into one of a new form, whereas R1 merely rearranges the parts.
questions.explain: Under the perceptual conjecture, some rules change what the object is and others only how it is arranged. Full statement: Squeezing into a vase is like R7, which really changes the object; turning it around is like R1, which only rearranges it.
questions.rule: R7 changes the thing; R1 rearranges it.
questions.teaches: On the perceptual conjecture, R7 really changes an object to one of a new form, while R1 merely rearranges the parts of an object.

questions.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
questions.q: A pupil says: multiply it by 6, add 44 to it, and it comes to 68. What does the repeated word it suggest?
options: The pupil is unsure what the numbers in the problem are meant to stand for
The pupil holds one thing in mind that is changed step by step
The pupil is reading the problem aloud without thinking
The pupil has already solved the equation
optionExplain: Repeated it signals a stable referent, not confusion.
A single referent that is modified while keeping its identity.
Reading aloud need not repeat it for a changing thing.
Nothing here shows a solution.
questions.explain: Pronouns reveal how a thing is represented. The card shows the authors' reading.
questions.rule: Repeated it points to one persisting thing.

questions.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
questions.q: In the second protocol, the subject builds the final equation by assembling a symbolic ____ from parts.
questions.explain: The final equation is assembled as an object out of a set of parts.
questions.rule: Second subject: build the object from parts.

questions.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
questions.q: Cook A: take lettuce, wash it, tear it, dress it. Cook B: put lettuce, tomatoes, dressing in the bowl. Which resembles the first algebra subject?
options: Cook B, who puts the parts together one after another in the bowl as they come
Both cooks, since each ends with a salad
Cook A, who follows one thing as it is changed
Neither cook, since cooking has no equations
optionExplain: Cook B resembles the second subject, who builds from parts.
The two descriptions represent the process differently.
Cook A uses it for one persisting thing, like the first subject.
The contrast concerns how a process is represented, not whether it is mathematics.
questions.explain: One representation follows a thing through changes; the other assembles a whole from parts.
questions.rule: Follow one thing, or build from parts.

questions.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
questions.q: True or false: The second subject's protocol shows a single entity that keeps its identity while being modified.
questions.explain: That description fits the first subject; the second assembles a symbolic object out of a set of parts.

questions.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
questions.q: What does the first subject's repeated use of it show about his representation?
options: An entity, the result so far, modified but keeping its identity
A set of unrelated parts that are put side by side before being combined
An unknown that has not yet been named
A rule that is applied again and again
optionExplain: That is how the authors read the repeated it.
That is the second subject's way.
The first subject does name the number before using it.
It refers to a quantity, not a rule.
questions.explain: The calculation is represented as one persisting thing. Full statement: An entity, the result so far, that is progressively modified but retains its identity.
questions.rule: It stands for the result so far.
questions.teaches: The repeated it in the first protocol shows an entity that could be called the result so far, progressively modified yet keeping its identity.

questions.section: Plans and the Organization of Episodes
questions.q: One planner says: take the draft, trim it, polish it. Another: join intro, body and conclusion. Which contrast between the algebra subjects is this?
options: Solving the problem successfully versus failing to solve it at the first attempt
Operating on one persisting object versus assembling a new object from parts
Writing quickly versus writing slowly
Speaking aloud versus staying silent
optionExplain: Both algebra subjects set up the equation.
The first planner works upon an object; the second builds one from parts.
Speed is not the contrast.
Both subjects spoke aloud.
questions.explain: The contrast in how a process is represented shows up in many domains. Full statement: Operating on one object that persists, versus assembling a new object from parts.
questions.rule: Modify one thing, or build from parts.
questions.teaches: For the second algebra subject, the process is represented much more as assembling a symbolic object, the final equation, out of a set of parts.

questions.q: A teacher notices that exercises needing the pupil to invent a new intermediate form are hardest. What would test this idea?
options: Asking pupils whether they like such exercises
Giving the same exercises again to the same pupils to see whether they improve
Counting how long each exercise is on the page
Predicting a new exercise's difficulty from the invention need, then checking
optionExplain: Liking is not difficulty.
Repeating exercises tests memory, not the idea.
Length may not track the invention requirement.
A prediction on new material is a real test.
questions.explain: An explanation of difficulty is tested on a new problem. The card shows the idea and the test problem. Full statement: Predicting from the invention requirement how hard a new exercise will be, then checking.
questions.rule: Test an explanation on a new case.

questions.q: Earlier analysis tied problem difficulty to the need to make ____ in order to solve a problem.
questions.explain: The need for constructions was the factor linked to difficulty.

questions.q: Two puzzles need equal numbers of moves, but one needs an invented intermediate form not directly obtainable. By the authors' idea, which is harder?
options: The one that needs the invented intermediate form
The one that needs fewer inventions
They are equally hard
The one whose first move is more obvious
optionExplain: A construction is what raises difficulty.
Fewer constructions means less difficulty.
The idea is about constructions, not move counts.
Obviousness of the first move is not the factor.
questions.explain: Construction need, not length, marks difficulty here.

questions.q: True or false: C1 is the difficult problem, and solving it does require a construction.
questions.explain: C1 is the difficult problem, and it does require a construction.
questions.rule: C1 is hard because of a construction.

questions.q: How could difficulty of this kind be reduced, according to the opening of the section?
options: By writing more expressions on the board
By learning the rule sheet by heart
By working backward from the goal, which can avoid some constructions
By starting from a simpler goal expression chosen for the subject by the experimenter
optionExplain: More lines on the board are not said to help.
Memorizing the rules is not the means named.
Working backward from L0 can avoid constructions and so reduce difficulty.
The goal expression is fixed by the problem.
questions.explain: Working backward can sidestep a construction. Full statement: By working backward from the goal expression, which can avoid some constructions.
questions.rule: Work backward to avoid a construction.
questions.teaches: In some problems constructions could be avoided, and the difficulty reduced, by working backward from the goal expression, L0.

questions.q: A chess coach has a theory of why some endgames are hard and wants more data. What do the authors do with C1, by analogy?
options: They replace their ideas with a new theory that is built from C1 and nothing else
They use C1 only to give subjects more practice
They use a new hard problem to test their ideas about sources of difficulty
They use C1 to show the earlier ideas were wrong
optionExplain: C1 is used to test the existing ideas.
C1 is a test problem.
C1 gives additional data for testing those ideas.
The authors do not start from that conclusion.
questions.explain: A harder case provides a stricter test of an explanation. Full statement: They use a new difficult problem to test their ideas about the sources of difficulty.
questions.teaches: Problem C1 gives the authors additional data for testing their ideas about the sources of problem difficulty.

questions.q: People try many expressions on a hard logic problem. Where would most of them lie?
options: Close to the starting expression, reachable by simple changes
Spread evenly across all the forms the rules could produce
Mainly on the route that leads to the solution
Mainly among forms far from both the start and the goal
optionExplain: People tend to explore the neighborhood of what they are given.
Exploration is not spread evenly.
Few of the expressions lie on the solution route.
Remote forms are rare in the data.
questions.explain: Exploration hugs the start. The card gives the figures for C1.

questions.q: About a ____ of the distinct expressions on C1 belong to the classes of L1 and its left and right sides.
questions.explain: Thirty-four of the 121 distinct expressions, about a quarter, fall in the classes of L1 and its two sides.
questions.rule: A quarter lies in L1 and its sides.

questions.q: A log has 120 distinct pages and 480 visits; a home cluster holds 28 percent of the pages. Following C1, what of its visit share?
options: It is lower than 28 percent
Exactly 28 percent, since shares do not change with the way in which one counts
It cannot be said
Higher than 28 percent, since visits are more concentrated than distinct pages
optionExplain: On C1 the opposite held.
On C1 the shares differed by method of counting.
The C1 data show a pattern linking them.
On C1 the classes near L1 hold a bigger share of appearances than of distinct expressions.
questions.explain: Repeated returns to the same few items raise their share of appearances. Full statement: It is higher than 28 percent, since appearances are more concentrated than distinct items.
questions.rule: Appearances are more concentrated than distinct items.

questions.q: True or false: Most of the subjects' distinct expressions on C1 lay in the classes leading to the solution.
questions.explain: Only about 5 percent of the distinct expressions (6 of 121) lay in classes leading to the solution; subjects explored near L1.
questions.rule: Near the start is not on the path.

questions.q: What share of all occurrences on C1 did the Rule 9 classes and the all-other category add up to together?
options: Only about one quarter of the total
About three quarters, since they held most distinct expressions
About one half, shared equally with the L1 classes
More than a third, as for the sides of L1
optionExplain: Together they came to only one quarter of all occurrences.
They held many distinct expressions but few occurrences.
The text gives one quarter, not one half.
More than a third is the figure for the classes of the sides of L1.
questions.explain: Many distinct expressions, few appearances each: the subjects stayed near what simple transformations of L1 give.
questions.rule: Far-flung expressions are many but rarely visited.
questions.teaches: The Rule 9 and all-other categories together add up to only one quarter of the total occurrences, so subjects did not stray far from expressions obtainable from L1 by relatively simple transformations.

questions.q: A shop finds many related-items pages were each viewed about twice, while a few core pages were viewed constantly. Which C1 group do they resemble?
options: The class of L1, few distinct expressions with many appearances each
The classes leading to the solution, a few expressions seen once
The class of L0, the goal, reached by nearly everyone
The Rule 9 classes, many distinct expressions with few appearances each
optionExplain: The core pages resemble the class of L1.
Those classes were small and not the main source of one-time items.
L0 appeared only a few times.
Rule 9 classes made up a third of the distinct expressions but, with all other, only a quarter of appearances.
questions.explain: Operations that add material produce many forms that are seen briefly.
questions.rule: Rule 9 makes many forms, each seen little.
questions.teaches: The Rule 9 classes held about a third of the distinct expressions, yet together with the all-other class they account for only about a quarter of all appearances.

questions.q: Two groups attempt a puzzle, one asked to think aloud and one not. What would show that thinking aloud changed their behavior?
options: The talking group would solve the puzzle faster
The groups would explore quite different parts of the puzzle
The talking group would write fewer lines
The talking group would find the puzzle more interesting than the other group did
optionExplain: Speed is a different measure from where people explore.
A real effect would show as different exploration.
Number of lines is a different measure.
Interest is a different measure.
questions.explain: To test an effect, compare what the groups do. The card gives the authors' result.

questions.q: True or false: On C1 the Carnegie subjects generated somewhat more lines per subject than the Yale subjects.
questions.explain: The Carnegie subjects wrote a few more lines per subject, yet the distribution among classes stayed very similar.

questions.q: Narrating and silent drivers take almost identical shares of three routes, though the narrators make a few more stops. What conclusion matches the chapter's?
options: Narration made the drivers choose different routes
The extra stops prove that narration changed the whole character of the drive itself
Narration did not substantially influence which routes they used
No conclusion is possible without a third group
optionExplain: The shares are almost identical.
A few more stops do not change the distribution.
The same reasoning as for C1: similar distribution means little influence of the instruction.
Comparing two groups is the authors' method.
questions.explain: Close distribution across classes is the evidence of no substantial influence.

questions.q: Had thinking aloud distorted exploration on C1, Table 10.2 would have shown markedly different ____ in the classes for the two groups.
questions.explain: A distortion would show in the shares of appearances across the classes, not in the counts.
questions.rule: A distortion would show in the shares.

questions.q: How do the authors describe the similarity between Yale and Carnegie subjects on the earlier problem D1, compared with C1?
options: Found on D1 but absent on C1
Demonstrated on D1, and shown equally on C1
Found only on C1, never tested on D1, which the authors did not examine at all
Not examined for either problem
optionExplain: The authors say it shows up equally clearly on C1.
The similarity shown for D1 shows up equally clearly on C1.
It had been demonstrated for D1 first.
Both problems were examined.
questions.explain: The result repeats across the two problems. Full statement: Demonstrated on D1, and shown equally clearly on C1.
questions.rule: The result holds on D1 and on C1.
questions.teaches: The similarity between the Yale and Carnegie subjects, first demonstrated on problem D1, shows up equally clearly on problem C1.

questions.q: Talking users click somewhat more per person than silent users, but spread clicks over screens in similar shares. Which C1 result is parallel?
options: The Yale subjects wrote far more lines and explored quite different classes of expressions
Both groups wrote exactly the same number of lines per subject
The Carnegie subjects wrote more lines per subject but spread them alike
The Carnegie subjects explored only classes the Yale subjects never entered
optionExplain: The Yale subjects wrote fewer lines, and the distributions matched.
The groups differed a little in lines per subject.
Volume differed a little; the distribution did not.
The two groups used the same classes.
questions.explain: A difference in amount need not mean a difference in pattern. Full statement: The Carnegie subjects wrote somewhat more lines per subject, yet spread them over the classes in a very similar way.
questions.rule: More lines is not a different pattern.
questions.teaches: The Carnegie subjects generated a few more lines per subject than the Yale subjects (9.8 as against 7.6), yet the appearances distributed themselves among the classes in strikingly similar ways.

questions.section: Sources of Problem Difficulty on C1
questions.q: Six people each try an easy and a hard puzzle. Which pattern of results would best support the hard puzzle being harder?
options: Some solve both, some only the easy one, some neither, and none only the hard one
Everyone solves both puzzles
Some of them solve only the hard puzzle and fail the easy one that they tried first
Nobody solves either puzzle
optionExplain: Solvers of the hard puzzle are a subset of solvers of the easy one.
Then there is no sign of any difference in difficulty.
That would suggest the easy one is not easier.
Then no difficulty difference can be seen.
questions.explain: A harder puzzle is solved by fewer people, and by people who can solve the easier one. The card gives the C1 result. Full statement: Some solve both, some solve only the easy one, some neither, and none solve only the hard one.
questions.rule: Hard solvers are a subset of easy solvers.

questions.section: Sources of Problem Difficulty on C1
questions.q: Of the nine subjects on C1, ____ succeeded and six failed.
questions.explain: Three of the nine subjects solved C1 and six failed.

questions.section: Sources of Problem Difficulty on C1
questions.q: Match each pair of subjects to what happened on D1 and C1.
questions.explain: The six subjects with protocols for both problems fall into these three groups.

questions.section: Sources of Problem Difficulty on C1
questions.q: True or false: Among the six subjects with protocols on both problems, none solved C1 while failing D1.
questions.explain: The three groups are both solved, D1 only solved, and neither solved; there is no C1-only group.

questions.section: Sources of Problem Difficulty on C1
questions.q: How do the authors treat the failure of S2 on C1?
options: As a sign that S2 was the weakest of the nine subjects who were tried on this problem alone
As probably an experimenter's error, making the score four solutions and five failures
As proof that C1 has no solution for some starting lines
As an event they leave out of all counts
optionExplain: The authors attribute S2's failure to an error, not weakness.
A footnote says the failure of S2 was probably an experimenter error.
C1 was solved by others.
They count it but give a corrected score.
questions.explain: The authors give both the raw box score and the corrected one. Full statement: As probably caused by an error of the experimenter, which would make the box score four solutions and five failures.
questions.rule: S2's failure was probably an experimenter error.
questions.teaches: One of the failures, S2's, was probably caused by an experimenter's error, so the box score should probably read four solutions and five failures.

questions.section: Sources of Problem Difficulty on C1
questions.q: A pupil failed a test question because the teacher wrote it on the board wrongly. Which handling parallels the authors' footnote on S2?
options: Drop the pupil from all results without comment
Count the failure as a sign of the pupil's weakness, as with any other failure on the test
Change the test so nobody can fail
Report the raw result, note the probable teacher's error, and give a corrected tally
optionExplain: The authors keep the subject and explain.
The authors suspect an error, not weakness.
The authors do not change the task.
The authors give the raw score and the probable correction.
questions.explain: Be open about a probable error and show its effect. Full statement: Report the raw result and note that the failure was probably caused by the teacher's error, with a corrected tally.
questions.rule: Say what went wrong and give both tallies.
questions.teaches: The experimenter's error was in putting an expression on the blackboard for S2, who then worked from an incorrect expression.

questions.section: Sources of Problem Difficulty on C1
questions.q: A craftsman can reach the final shape only by joining two pieces, one of which he lacks. What is the hard part?
options: Seeing that this particular join is what has to be built
Reshaping the join, which is always the slowest task
Making the piece he already has
Holding the two pieces still while they set
optionExplain: The need for the joint is the discovery.
Reshaping is a routine task once the join is known.
He already has that piece.
Holding pieces is a practical detail, not the key difficulty.
questions.explain: Knowing what to build is the crux. The card shows how this applies to C1.
questions.rule: The hard part is knowing what to build.

questions.section: Sources of Problem Difficulty on C1
questions.q: In C1 the final step applies R7 to (P or Q) and (P or R), after the two are put together by R____.
questions.explain: R10 combines the two components into one conjunction, to which R7 then applies.

questions.section: Sources of Problem Difficulty on C1
questions.q: Order the stages of the solution of C1, from first to last.
items: Split L1 into its two parts by R8
Change the connective of the left part to a horseshoe
Combine the two parts by R12, eliminating the Q's, to leave not-P implies R
Obtain P or R and combine it with P or Q by R10
Apply R7 to reach P or (Q and R)
questions.explain: The right-hand part, P or R, is reached indirectly before the last two steps.
questions.rule: Split, change, combine by R12, join by R10, finish by R7.

questions.section: Sources of Problem Difficulty on C1
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the hardest single step of C1 is the application of R12.
questions.explain: What makes the whole problem hard, on the authors' account, is discovering that P or Q and P or R are wanted.
questions.rule: The difficulty is the discovery, not any one step.

questions.section: Sources of Problem Difficulty on C1
questions.q: How is the left-hand component, (P or Q), obtained in the solution?
options: By R12, combining the two parts of L1
By R7 applied to the whole of L1
Immediately from the left part of L1 by R8
By R9, adding P to Q
optionExplain: R12 is used for the right-hand component.
R7 is not applicable to L1 as it stands.
R8 takes the left conjunct directly.
R9 would add a term, not recover the left part.
questions.explain: One component is immediate; the other is indirect.
questions.rule: Left component: one use of R8.
questions.teaches: The left-hand component, (P or Q), can be obtained at once from the left part of L1 by R8, whereas the right-hand component takes an indirect route.

questions.section: Sources of Problem Difficulty on C1
questions.q: A builder finds each of two sub-assemblies easy, and the hard part is realizing they are the ones needed. Which fact about C1 is parallel?
options: Getting P or R alone is the hardest part of C1, as the authors themselves say
The two sub-assemblies cannot be built from L1 in C1
Getting P or R alone has D1's structure and is not regarded as hard
D1 and C1 share no structure
optionExplain: The authors say it is not hard by itself.
Both can be obtained from L1.
Taken by itself, getting P or R is like D1; the hard part is knowing it is wanted.
The sub-task shares the structure of D1.
questions.explain: A sub-task can be easy while the problem is hard, because the choice of sub-task is the problem. Full statement: Obtaining P or R alone has the same structure as D1 and is not regarded as hard.
questions.rule: The choice of sub-task is the problem.
questions.teaches: Taken by itself, the task of obtaining P or R from (P or Q) and (if Q then R) has the same structure as D1 and would not be regarded as a hard problem.

questions.section: Sources of Problem Difficulty on C1
questions.q: To check whether people's steps relate to plausible routes, researchers first list the routes and what each would produce. Why?
options: Each route then predicts the kinds of steps to look for in the records
So that people can be told which route to take
So that the shortest route can be named as the right one
So that any record can be explained after the event
optionExplain: Predictions make the comparison with records specific.
The routes are for analysis, not for instruction.
Length of route is not the purpose.
Predictions made beforehand are what make the test fair.
questions.explain: A list made beforehand gives predictions that can fail. The card gives the authors' list for C1.
questions.rule: List the routes, derive predictions, then compare.

questions.section: Sources of Problem Difficulty on C1
questions.q: Of the seven paths for C1, only path.R____ is feasible.
questions.explain: Path.R12 is the only one of the seven that yields a solution.

questions.section: Sources of Problem Difficulty on C1
questions.q: Match each path to the expressions it should produce.
pairs: The class of left(L1) and expressions got from these by R9
The class of L1, since R7 does not actually apply
questions.explain: Each path leaves a different trace in the classes of expressions.
questions.rule: Each path predicts its own classes.

questions.section: Sources of Problem Difficulty on C1
questions.q: A subject follows path.R7 on C1. What would you expect him to write?
options: Expressions in the class of not-P implies R, which come from path.R12 alone for it
Expressions equivalent to right(L1) only
The two final expressions of the solution
Expressions in the equivalence class of L1, since R7 is not applicable
optionExplain: That class belongs to path.R12.
That is path.R9'.
Those appear on path.R12.
As in D1, R7 cannot be applied to L1 as it stands.
questions.explain: A path that cannot apply its key rule leaves many forms of the starting expression. Full statement: Expressions in the equivalence class of L1, as R7 is not actually applicable to L1.
questions.rule: R7 cannot be applied; expect forms of L1.

questions.section: Sources of Problem Difficulty on C1
questions.q: Which classes would only a subject following path.R12 be expected to produce?
options: The class of left(L1) and its R9 forms, with the expressions got from them by R9
The class of not-P implies R and the two final expressions
The class of right(L1)
The class of L1 itself
optionExplain: That belongs to path.R9.
Only path.R12 passes through these.
Other paths also pass through right(L1).
Almost every path starts from L1.
questions.explain: These classes are the signature of the one feasible path.
questions.teaches: Only path.R12 should produce the class of (not-P implies R) and the two final expressions, (P or Q) and (P or R) together, and L0.

questions.section: Sources of Problem Difficulty on C1
questions.q: Two suspect routes are each predicted to leave sightings in the same three districts. What can sightings in those districts alone show?
options: They cannot tell the two routes apart
They show that the first route was used
They show that neither route was used
They show that the sightings were mistaken
optionExplain: The chapter expects path.R10 and path.R11 to produce expressions from the same classes.
The same districts fit both routes.
They fit both routes.
Fitting two routes does not make a sighting mistaken.
questions.explain: Routes predicting the same classes cannot be separated by those classes.
questions.teaches: Path.R10 and path.R11 should both produce expressions from the classes of L1, left(L1) and right(L1).

questions.section: Sources of Problem Difficulty on C1
questions.q: Nearly all of the steps recorded fall in the predicted groups; a few do not. What would you expect to explain the few?
options: The predicted groups being wrong for everyone who worked on the problem at all
People guessing at random on those steps
The task being unsolvable for those people
A recording error, or an individual's own unusual plan
optionExplain: Nearly all steps fit them.
Random guessing does not explain a repeated pattern of forms.
Solvability does not explain the exceptions.
Exceptions in a good fit are often errors or idiosyncratic plans.
questions.explain: Exceptions tell you about either the data or a particular person. The card names the two on C1.

questions.section: Sources of Problem Difficulty on C1
questions.q: Subject ____ wrote six expressions derived from an incorrect expression because of an experimenter's error.
questions.explain: S2 worked from the wrongly written expression (P implies not-R).

questions.section: Sources of Problem Difficulty on C1
questions.q: Which of the two exceptions came from the subject's own plan?
options: S2's six expressions derived from the incorrect expression put on the board by mistake
S5's expressions like (P or Q) or P, which he tried to combine
S8's expressions derived by path.R12
The expressions of the Carnegie subjects as a group
optionExplain: Those arose from the experimenter's error.
S5's side path was his own plan.
Path.R12 is one of the seven predicted paths.
The Carnegie group fell within the classes.
questions.explain: One exception was an error from outside, the other a path of the subject's own. Full statement: S5's expressions like (P or Q) or P, which he tried to combine to eliminate (P or Q) by R12.

questions.section: Sources of Problem Difficulty on C1
questions.q: True or false: Two subjects' expressions on C1 fell outside the classes predicted by the seven paths: S2, from an experimenter's error, and S5, from a side path of his own.
questions.explain: There were two exceptions: S2, from an experimenter's error, and S5, from a side path of his own.

questions.section: Sources of Problem Difficulty on C1
questions.q: What was S5 trying to do with his expressions like (P or Q) or P?
options: Add P to the goal expression by R9
Split them into parts by R8
Prove that C1 could not be solved
Combine them so as to eliminate (P or Q) by R12
optionExplain: R9 is not what he applied to them.
The text says he tried to combine them.
Nothing says he tried to show that.
He aimed to cancel (P or Q) by R12, on a path resembling path.R10.
questions.explain: S5 pursued a plan of his own for a long time.
questions.rule: S5 tried to eliminate (P or Q) by R12.
questions.teaches: S5 tried to combine his expressions of the form (P or Q) or P and (P or Q) or (Q and R) so as to eliminate (P or Q) by R12.

questions.section: Sources of Problem Difficulty on C1
questions.q: A customer's odd route resembles a listed route with a detour. How should the analyst treat it, by the chapter's practice?
options: As evidence that the listed routes are useless for predicting where customers go
As a noted exception, explained by its resemblance to a listed route
As an error to be deleted
As the main route of all customers
optionExplain: Two exceptions do not undo a good fit.
The authors note S5's path as resembling path.R10.
S5's expressions are reported.
It is one customer's path.
questions.explain: Report exceptions and relate them to the model where possible. Full statement: As an exception noted separately, and explained by its resemblance to a listed route.
questions.rule: Report the exception and link it to the model.
questions.teaches: S5's exceptional expressions came on a path resembling path.R10.

questions.section: Sources of Problem Difficulty on C1
questions.q: In a puzzle, everyone who made one move solved it, and everyone who solved it made it. What is the most you can safely say?
options: The move causes success in every possible puzzle
The move is easy for anyone to find
The move is closely tied to success, but this does not say why
The move was the only one anyone considered
optionExplain: One puzzle cannot show that.
Nothing here says how easy it is to find.
A tight association does not give the reason.
Others may have considered other moves.
questions.explain: Association is not explanation. The card shows the C1 counts.

questions.section: Sources of Problem Difficulty on C1
questions.q: True or false: Counting S2 as a solver, everyone who applied R12 to get not-P implies R solved C1.
questions.explain: Only the four solvers applied R12 to obtain not-P implies R, and all who applied it solved the problem.
questions.rule: R12 application and solution went together.

questions.section: Sources of Problem Difficulty on C1
questions.q: Five students fail; three had the key idea unused. What does this do to an account placing the difficulty in finding it?
options: It shows discovery alone cannot be the whole difficulty
It confirms that discovery is the whole difficulty
It shows the test was too easy
It shows the other two students were stronger
optionExplain: People who found the idea still failed.
The three discovered it and still failed.
Five failed the test.
The other two failed as well.
questions.explain: A complete explanation must also cover people who found the idea and failed.
questions.rule: Finding the idea is not enough.

questions.section: Sources of Problem Difficulty on C1
questions.q: A critic says S5 and S11 failed D1 too, so they are weak solvers and the anomaly is explained. Which replies are fair? Select all.
options: It names the weakness without explaining its causes
It leaves open why they did not use the R10-R7 idea they had found
It is wrong, because S5 and S11 solved D1
It is wrong, because weak solvers never work backward
optionExplain: Fair: a label is not a mechanism.
Fair: the anomaly is about not using an idea already found.
Wrong: they failed D1.
Wrong: three nonsolvers did work backward.
questions.explain: The critic restates the failure as weakness; the question of why the idea went unused remains.
questions.rule: A label is not an explanation.

questions.section: Sources of Problem Difficulty on C1
questions.q: How did the fourth solver, S8, arrive at not-P implies R?
options: By working backward from L0 in the same way as the other three solvers had done
By copying the expression from the board
By following the experimenter's hint
Without previously noticing that R10-R7 would complete the solution
optionExplain: He is the one who did not.
No board copying is described.
No hint is reported.
S8 derived it by working forward, not by first noticing the R10-R7 route.
questions.explain: S8 reached the key line through forward work.
questions.rule: S8 derived not-P implies R without the backward insight.
questions.teaches: The fourth solver, S8, derived not-P implies R without previously noticing that L0 could be obtained from (P or Q) and (P or R) by R10 and R7.

questions.section: Sources of Problem Difficulty on C1
questions.q: A strong pupil fails a task that weaker peers also fail. In the authors' manner, what is the next move for explaining the failure?
options: Look at the failing protocol for the specific reason; general strength is no answer
Conclude the task is unfair
Conclude the pupil was weak all along
Ignore the case as a statistical accident
optionExplain: S10 solved D1 readily yet failed C1, so the authors examine his protocol.
The authors seek a mechanism, not a verdict.
The pupil solved earlier tasks readily.
The authors treat S10's protocol as instructive.
questions.explain: A subject's earlier success blocks the weakness label, so a specific cause is needed. Full statement: Look at the failing protocol for the specific reason, since the pupil's general strength does not explain it.
questions.rule: Seek the specific cause in the protocol.
questions.teaches: S10 solved D1 readily, so his failure on C1 cannot be put down to general weakness as a problem solver.

questions.q: A solver gets both pieces for the final step but does not finish, partly because of an error in his materials. What remains puzzling?
options: That the materials contained an error at all
That he was able to get the two pieces
That, even allowing for the error, he did not see how to carry on
That his notes were written in pencil
optionExplain: Errors happen; the puzzle is about what follows.
Getting them is what he did achieve.
The error explains some of the failure, but not all of it.
Nothing in the case turns on the writing material.
questions.explain: An error can explain part of a failure but leave a remainder. The card shows S2's case.
questions.rule: Allow for the error, then see what is left.

questions.q: S2 simplified L1 into its two parts with R8, then searched for applicable rules and applied R____.
questions.explain: He found and applied R12 before he noticed that R7 could be used.
questions.rule: Simplify with R8, then apply R12.

questions.q: What, according to the text, stood in S2's way on C1?
options: He never noticed that R7 could be applied
He did not use R8 to split L1
The experimenter wrote an incorrect expression and S2 worked from it
He worked forward only and never considered the goal expression at any stage
optionExplain: He did notice it.
He did split L1 with R8.
The error led him to persistent but failed attempts at R10 and R7.
He is counted among those working backward.
questions.explain: S2 had the idea; the error spoiled the execution. Full statement: The experimenter wrote down an incorrect expression and S2 worked from it, failing with R10 and R7.
questions.rule: The idea was right; the board was wrong.

questions.q: True or false: Even allowing for the experimenter's error, the authors find considerable mystery in why S2 did not see how to go on.
questions.explain: Even allowing for the error, they find considerable mystery in why he did not see how to go on.
questions.rule: A known error may not be the whole cause.

questions.q: What did S2 do after repeated failures to apply R10 and R7?
options: He asked the experimenter to check the board
He applied R12 again to the same expression
He solved the problem by working forward
He abandoned the plan for another
optionExplain: No such check is reported.
R12 had already been applied before he noticed R7.
S2 did not solve it in the end.
He gave up the plan after persistent attempts.
questions.explain: Persistent failure led to a change of plan.
questions.rule: He tried hard, then changed plan.
questions.teaches: After persistent attempts to apply R10 and R7 failed, S2 abandoned the plan for another.

questions.q: A mechanic has made both parts a repair needs, but a misprint in the manual defeats him. What keeps S2's case puzzling?
options: S2 never derived the expression R7 needs
S2 had actually derived both expressions needed as inputs for R10 and R7
S2 did not know that R10 exists
S2 was given no time to try the plan
optionExplain: He did derive the inputs.
Having both inputs, he should have been able to proceed.
Nothing suggests he lacked R10.
He made persistent attempts.
questions.explain: Having the parts is what makes the failure puzzling.
questions.rule: Having the inputs makes the failure strange.
questions.teaches: S2 had actually derived the two expressions, (P or Q) and (P or R), that are required as inputs to R10 and R7.

questions.q: A solver knows that A and B together would finish the job and already holds A. What is the natural next goal?
options: Get B from what is available
Make A itself take the shape of the final result
Throw A away and begin again
Wait until B appears on its own
optionExplain: Obtaining the missing input is the subgoal that follows.
That swaps the missing input for a different task.
A is half of what is needed.
B must be worked for.
questions.explain: Having one of two inputs, the next goal is the other. The card shows what S5 did instead.
questions.rule: Having one input, aim for the other.

questions.q: True or false: S5 noticed early that having (P or R) and (P or Q) would give the answer directly by R7.
questions.explain: He saw this near the beginning of his protocol and already had (P or Q).

questions.q: What did S5 do with the subproblem after seeing what R7 needed?
options: He set out to obtain (P or R) by combining (P or Q) with the horseshoe part
He gave up the problem at once
He asked the experimenter to supply (P or R)
He turned it into the task of applying R7 to L1 itself, which he could not do
optionExplain: That is what he never considered.
He pursued another plan with persistence.
No such request is reported.
He sought to make L1 fit R7, not to build (P or R).
questions.explain: He swapped one subgoal for another that looked simpler and was not.

questions.q: To obtain (P or R), S5 needed to combine (P or Q) with (if Q then R) so that the ____ drop out.
questions.explain: Combining the two lines removes the Q from both, which leaves a line from which (P or R) follows.
questions.rule: Combine two lines to build the missing input.

questions.q: What influenced S5 to turn the subproblem into applying R7 to L1?
options: A hint from the experimenter about R7
A memory of solving D1 with R7
Looking at L1, he was influenced by the two Q's in it
The number of lines already on the board
optionExplain: No hint is reported.
S5 failed D1.
The two Q's in L1 drew him to the idea of getting R7 to apply there.
The count of lines is not given as the reason.
questions.explain: Surface features of L1 drew him off the plan.
questions.teaches: Looking at L1, and influenced by the two Q's in that expression, S5 immediately turned the subproblem into one of applying R7 to L1.

questions.q: A cook needs two sauces, has one. He tries to make it taste like the dish, then follows another recipe persistently. Which S5 fact matches?
options: After failing, he returned to the first plan and then solved it after all by working back
After failing, he quit the task
After failing, he asked for more time
After failing, he followed another plan with great persistence, as on D1
optionExplain: S5 did not solve the problem.
He pursued another plan.
No request for time is reported.
S5 was persistent in infeasible plans on both problems.
questions.explain: Persistence in a poor plan was a mark of S5 on D1 and C1. Full statement: After failing, he went off to another plan that he pursued with great persistence, as he did his infeasible plan on D1.
questions.rule: S5 held on to infeasible plans.
questions.teaches: After the failed attempt to apply R7 to L1, S5 went off to another plan, which he pursued with great persistence, as he had his infeasible plan on D1.

questions.q: One solver explores forward from the givens. Another asks what must be true at the end. Which statement is most reasonable?
options: Only the route that starts from the end can succeed
Both routes can reach a correct solution
Only the route that starts from the givens can succeed
Neither can succeed unless an expert guides them
optionExplain: Forward solving also succeeds.
Different methods can succeed on the same problem.
Backward solving also succeeds.
Neither needs a guide.
questions.explain: More than one route can work. The card shows two on C1.
questions.rule: More than one road leads to a solution.

questions.q: The authors say S8 in effect solved C1 by working ____, using a simplification heuristic and examining the simplified expressions.
questions.explain: S8 derived his expressions forward and examined them for new possibilities, while S9 went backward from L0.

questions.q: Why did S8 set aside path.R7 early on?
options: He had never seen R7 used on D1, so he did not know whether it could apply to L1
He was told by the experimenter that R7 would fail
He recalled from D1 that the signs in L1 cannot be changed to fit R7
He found that R7 needed a horseshoe in L0
optionExplain: He had met the sign problem on D1.
No such statement is reported.
His experience on D1 taught him that R7 cannot be applied to L1.
L0 contains a wedge as its main connective.
questions.explain: Experience on D1 saved S8 the detour.
questions.rule: A lesson from D1 ruled out R7.

questions.q: True or false: S9 knew from D1 that R7 could not be applied to L1 as it stands.
questions.explain: S9 did not struggle with the signs in L1 on D1, so he did not learn this and worked on L1 for R7 for some time.

questions.q: What about L0 suggested a route to S8?
options: Its main connective, a dot, suggested path.R7
Its main connective, a wedge, suggested path.R9 and so R8 and R12
Its two Q's suggested combining L1 by R10
Its length suggested working forward by trial and error until some expression fitted it
optionExplain: L0's main connective is a wedge.
The wedge in L0 pointed him to R9 and then to term-cancelling rules.
L0 contains one Q.
Its length is not given as the reason.
questions.explain: The goal's form told S8 where to look. Full statement: Its main connective, a wedge, suggested path.R9, which led him to rules that cancel terms such as R8 and R12.
questions.rule: L0's wedge pointed to R9, and then to R8 and R12.
questions.teaches: Looking at L0, S8 was led by its main connective, a wedge, to path.R9, and from there to rules like R8 and R12 that cancel terms.

questions.q: A student reasons: the answer needs two parts; I have one; the other is still to be found. Which of S9's remarks does this resemble?
options: His remark that R7 would apply to L1 at once
His remark that the experimenter had made an error in writing an expression on the board
His remark that he did not know where to begin
His statement, once he worked backward, that he had one part and needed the other
optionExplain: He found R7 did not apply to L1 as it stands.
That concerns S2.
He stated the needs clearly.
S9 said he had the first part and still had to get the other.
questions.explain: Backward reasoning names what is still missing. Full statement: His clear statement, once he worked backward, that he had one part but still had to get the other.
questions.rule: Name what you have and what you lack.
questions.teaches: After giving up on putting L1 in shape for R7, S9 went backward from L0 and stated clearly that he had P or Q but still had to get P or R.

questions.q: A person has learned a tool as the one that removes X. A new job needs X kept. What is likely to happen?
options: He rejects the tool, though it could do the job in another way
He uses the tool anyway and X is lost
He uses the tool and tells nobody
He asks for a bigger tool
optionExplain: Tying the tool to one function blocks other uses.
A person who knows X is needed would avoid that.
That is not what the tool's fixed function suggests.
Nothing suggests that.
questions.explain: Seeing a tool by one function can stop its use for another. The card gives the name.
questions.rule: A tool tied to one function resists other uses.

questions.q: The authors call S10's reluctance to use R12 on (P or Q) an example of functional ____ .
questions.explain: The authors apply the term functional fixity (citing Duncker, 1945) because (P or Q) must serve as an input to R10 and R7, so S10 would not let R12 consume it.
questions.rule: The authors cite Duncker (1945) for functional fixity.
questions.teaches: We have here a clear example of functional fixity (Duncker, 1945).

questions.q: Which remark of S10's best shows the reasoning that stopped him?
options: I will use R12 first and keep the P or Q in my head until the next line is written
R12 will not work because there is only one P in L0
We have to keep a P, a Q and an R, so we cannot use R12
R7 is not applicable to L1 so I give up
optionExplain: He did not plan to use R12 at all.
He pointed to a mismatch in P in L1, not to R12 failing.
He rules out R12 for what it eliminates.
He saw that R7 could be used on the pair.
questions.explain: The reasoning rests on what R12 does, to Q's, and what is needed. Full statement: We have to keep a P, a Q and an R, so we cannot use R12, because it eliminates Q's.
questions.rule: R12 eliminates Q's, and Q is needed.

questions.q: Which statements fit the authors' account of S10? Select all that apply.
options: He abandoned path.R12 and never returned to it
He had never used R12 on D1
He thought R12 would remove the (P or Q) he needed for R10 and R7
He failed to see that R7 on the pair gives L0
optionExplain: Yes: he did not come back to it.
No: he used it on D1.
Yes: that is the functional fixity.
No: he saw it.
questions.explain: He saw the finish, then rejected the route that supplies its input.
questions.rule: He saw the end and refused the means.

questions.q: How had S10 used R12 earlier, when he solved D1?
options: To introduce new letters into the expressions, which is how he described its use to us
To check a result against the answer that the experimenter had put on the board for him
To eliminate R's, as he said early that he would
He did not use R12 on D1, which he solved by other means than the cancelling of any letter
optionExplain: R12 was not used to add letters.
No check is reported.
On D1 R12 was his means to eliminate R's.
He did use it.
questions.explain: His successful earlier use fixed R12 as the eliminating rule. Full statement: To eliminate R's, saying early that he would try to eliminate the R's and so would need something like R12.
questions.rule: On D1, R12 meant eliminating R's.
questions.teaches: Early in his D1 protocol S10 said that the thing to do was to eliminate the R's and that he would therefore need something like R12, and so he had used R12 to eliminate R's.

questions.q: A user knows a macro only as the one that clears a column, later needs the column kept, and avoids it. What belief explains this?
options: That an item used in one operation is consumed and unavailable to another
That the macro is slower than doing the same job by hand, so that it is not worth using
That the column must be wrong
That only the first report matters
optionExplain: On the authors' reading, S10 saw (P or Q) as consumed by R12 and so not available to R10 and R7.
Speed is not the issue.
Nothing says the data are wrong.
The person wants both.
questions.explain: The mistaken belief is that using an item in one place uses it up. Full statement: That an item used as an input to one operation is consumed and so is unavailable to another.
questions.rule: Using an input does not consume it.
questions.teaches: The authors say that since (P or Q) is to function as an input for R10 and thence R7, S10 took it that it could not be consumed as an input for R12.

questions.q: Two people hit the same snag: an item wanted for two jobs. One is stopped; the other works through. What can be concluded?
options: The one who got through must be more intelligent than the one who was stopped by it
The one who was stopped did not read the instructions that were given with the task
The two must have misread the task differently
Not much without more evidence, since the snag does not tell who gets past it
optionExplain: Nothing in the snag shows this.
Nothing says so.
Nothing says so.
The same obstacle can stop one person and not another for unknown reasons.
questions.explain: A shared obstacle does not explain different outcomes. The card shows the C1 case. Full statement: Not much without more evidence, since the snag alone does not tell who gets past it.
