questions.rule: Same obstacle, different outcomes, cause unknown.

questions.q: S13 finally overcame the difficulty about the double ____ of (P or Q).
questions.explain: The double role, as input to R10 and R7 and as input to R12, was the difficulty.

questions.q: Which belief of S11's blocked him?
options: That R12 cannot be applied to a horseshoe expression such as the second part of L1
That using (P or Q) in R12 would take out the Q and spoil it for R10
That the goal L0 could not be reached by R7
That the experimenter had made an error
optionExplain: R12 works on horseshoes.
He assumed that (P or Q) would be consumed by R12.
He saw that R7 would give L0.
That concerned S2.
questions.explain: The same consumption belief as S10. Full statement: That using (P or Q) with R12 would take out the Q and so spoil (P or Q) for R10.

questions.q: True or false: The authors have a solid explanation for why S13 got past the double-role difficulty while S10, S11 and S5 did not.
questions.explain: They say there is no very solid ground for speculating why.
questions.rule: The authors do not claim to know.

questions.q: Besides S10, S11 and S5, whom do the authors say did not have trouble with working backward?
options: S4 and S8, who worked backward on both problems
S3 and S13, who solved C1
Every subject except S13
S2 and S9, who applied the working-backwards idea without difficulty
optionExplain: S4 and S8 did not work backward.
S13 had trouble.
Several others were troubled.
These are the two named as having no such trouble.
questions.explain: Trouble was not universal among those who worked backward.
questions.rule: S2 and S9 had no trouble.
questions.teaches: The authors do not know why S10, S11 and S5 were troubled by the double function, while S2 and S9 applied the working-backwards idea without difficulty.

questions.q: A planner notes one report feeds two later jobs, and finds a way to keep it intact. Which of S13's behaviors is parallel?
options: He ignored the double role and went on
He reminded himself of his needs and reworked the expression to bring (P or R) back in
He accepted that he could not break the expression apart and so gave up the attempt on the problem
He switched to working forward
optionExplain: He was troubled by it.
S13 stated his needs repeatedly and aimed to bring the new part back into the expression.
He said he would have to.
He kept working backward.
questions.explain: He met the double role by keeping both uses in view. Full statement: He reminded himself of what he needed, and reworked the expression to get (P or R) back into it.
questions.teaches: S13 said at one point that he wanted to get a P or R from somewhere out of two expressions, and later that he wanted to get that back into the expression, and then that he needed just a P or Q from somewhere.

questions.q: People who reason backward to see exactly which two pieces are needed may hesitate to use a tool that alters one of the pieces. Why?
options: They know the tool is harmful in general
They have never used the tool before
Having named that piece as needed, they want to keep it
They no longer care about the final result
optionExplain: Nothing says so.
That does not follow from reasoning backward.
Knowing what is needed makes them protective of it.
They care about it, which is why they plan backward.
questions.explain: Knowing the need makes the cost of an alteration visible. The card applies this to R12.
questions.rule: A named need protects the item.

questions.q: True or false: S2 and S8 appear to have applied R12 without first working backward from L0 to find that (P or R) was needed.
questions.explain: Both applied it in the course of working forward, in the interest of simplification or the like.
questions.rule: S2 and S8: R12 by forward work.

questions.q: A subject working backward knows (P or R) must be obtained and (P or Q) kept. What does the authors' argument predict about R12?
options: He applies it first
He applies it only to the goal L0
He applies R9 to (P or Q) in its place
He is reluctant to apply it, because it would alter (P or Q)
optionExplain: That ignores his wish to keep (P or Q).
R12 is not applied to the goal.
R9 is not the replacement.
The need to keep (P or Q) deters him from using R12.
questions.explain: The deterrent is the double function of (P or Q).
questions.rule: A kept item deters the rule that alters it.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say the need for R12 was more often discovered by simplifying forward than by working backward.
questions.explain: They say the backward path was the more common route to the need for R12, and that it was the one that deterred its use.
questions.rule: Backward discovery was the common route.

questions.q: Among the Yale subjects, a sizable fraction, ____ percent, of those who applied R12 went on to solve the problem.
questions.explain: The authors give 37.5 percent and link it to the two routes by which R12 came to be applied.
questions.teaches: Among the Yale subjects, a sizable fraction (37.5 percent) of those who applied R12 went on to solve the problem.

questions.q: Staff tracing needs backward hesitate to run a merge that overwrites a column they must keep; others run it casually. What shows in the figures?
options: A rise in the use of the operation by those who reasoned backward from the report's needs
No difference between the two groups
The argument against double functions shows as failure to apply the operation
An error in the experimenter's board
optionExplain: Their reluctance lowers the use.
The argument predicts a difference.
That is how the authors say it shows in the R12 data.
That concerns S2 only.
questions.explain: The deterrent shows as non-use of the operation. Full statement: The argument against double functions shows up as a failure to apply the operation.
questions.teaches: The authors say the argument against double functions would show up as a failure to apply R12.

questions.q: When is it sensible to refuse to use a part for a second job because it has been used for a first?
options: When using the part for the first job consumes it
When the second job is harder than the first and would need the part for longer
When the part is cheap to replace
When someone else owns the part
optionExplain: A consumed part is no longer available.
Difficulty is not the issue.
Cheapness is no reason to refuse.
Ownership is another matter.
questions.explain: The refusal makes sense only for things that are used up. The card applies this to logic and to wood.
questions.rule: Refuse reuse only if the first use consumes.

questions.q: In the logic problems any expression can exist in as many ____ as desired, so a transformation does not destroy it.
questions.explain: Because expressions are copyable, an operation does not use one up.

questions.q: Which case makes the double-function test appropriate?
options: A line of logic used as input to two different rules in the course of one problem
A single plank that could become either the leg or the back of a chair
A number typed into two cells of a spreadsheet
A paragraph quoted in two essays
optionExplain: A line can be reused without being destroyed.
A piece of wood cannot be both.
Numbers can be copied.
A paragraph can be quoted twice.
questions.explain: The test fits things that are consumed, not things that can be copied.

questions.q: Sort each case by whether the double-function test is appropriate.

items.t: A plank cut into a chair leg
A single knight asked to guard two pieces at once
A line of logic used as input to R10 and also to R12
A file copied into two reports
A cashier with one pair of hands serving two tills
A formula that cites the same cell twice

questions.explain: Where a resource is committed, the test is right; where use leaves the original intact, it is wrong.
questions.rule: Used up: test applies. Copyable: it does not.

questions.q: What does the authors' chess example show about overburdened pieces?
options: A knight can guard two pieces at once if the two pieces stand close together on the board
A pawn can be protected only by another pawn, whatever else is happening on the board
A bishop can never be left unguarded
A knight guarding a bishop cannot also protect a pawn under attack
optionExplain: The authors say it can guard either but not both.
That is not what the authors state.
The example is about a knight's duties.
A piece with two duties may fail at both under attack.
questions.explain: The double-function test is often relevant in chess. Full statement: A knight guarding a bishop cannot also protect a pawn against a simultaneous attack, so it can guard either but not both.
questions.rule: A piece cannot do two jobs under attack.
questions.teaches: In chess, a knight guarding a bishop cannot at the same time protect a pawn, and failing to see that a piece is overburdened is a frequent source of blunders.

questions.q: A chess player sees that her opponent's knight is guarding two pieces at once. What does the chapter say her chance is?
options: Exploiting the overburdened piece is a source of combinations for her
None: pieces that guard twice are always safe
Only a draw, since the knight can guard either piece
She must first remove her own overburdened pieces
optionExplain: The overloaded piece gives the attacker a combination.
The authors say a piece cannot do both under attack.
The text gives no such conclusion.
The text does not say this.
questions.explain: The same fact is a blunder for one side and a chance for the other.
questions.rule: One side's overload is the other side's combination.
questions.teaches: For the player who exploits an opponent's overburdened piece, the overburdening is a source of combinations.

questions.q: Two groups attempt a hard puzzle, one working forward and one backward. Would you expect the same source of difficulty for both?
options: Yes, since the puzzle is the same for both
Yes, since difficulty is a property of the puzzle only
Not necessarily: each way of working can meet its own obstacle
No, since the backward group has no obstacles
optionExplain: The same puzzle can present different obstacles to different methods.
Difficulty depends on method too.
Different methods meet different obstacles.
Backward work met a new obstacle on C1.
questions.explain: The obstacle depends on the method. The card gives the authors' two sources.

questions.q: For subjects who worked forward, the ____ construction made C1 difficult.
questions.explain: For forward workers the R10-R7 construction was the obstacle; for backward workers it was functional fixity.

questions.q: A subject working backward rejects a rule because it would use up an expression he needs later. Which source of difficulty is this?
options: The R10-R7 construction that forward workers must find
An error by the experimenter in writing an expression
Functional fixity from the double function of a subexpression
Failure to simplify L1 into its two parts
optionExplain: That is the forward workers' obstacle.
That concerned S2 only.
He treats the expression as consumed by one use and so unavailable for another.
Splitting L1 is not what he declined to do.
questions.explain: Rejecting a rule to protect an expression is the backward workers' obstacle.
questions.rule: Protecting an expression from a rule: double function.

questions.q: True or false: The authors conclude that the source of difficulty on C1 is the same for forward and backward workers.
questions.explain: They name the R10-R7 construction for forward workers and functional fixity from the double function of (P or Q) for backward workers.

questions.q: Besides the R10-R7 construction, which other construction does C1 require?
options: None: the R10-R7 sequence is the only construction required
The R9 addition of the letter R to one of the lines of the solution
The R12 elimination of Q's
The R4 regrouping of L1
optionExplain: The authors say it is the only one.
The authors do not list R9 as a second construction.
R12 is an ordinary rule application, not the construction.
R4 is a path.R4 idea, which does not work.
questions.explain: The anomaly arose because the only construction was seen by subjects who still failed.
questions.teaches: The R10-R7 sequence is the only construction required for C1, which is why the anomaly of subjects who saw it and failed threatened the earlier hypotheses.

questions.q: A drill defeats players: planners will not reuse a player for two roles, and improvisers miss the key play. Which C1 conclusion parts match?
options: Two forward-type obstacles, both of them arising from the construction needed in the solution
Two backward-type obstacles, both of them arising from double functions of expressions
No obstacle of either kind
A backward-type obstacle, the double function, and a forward-type one, the construction
optionExplain: One of the two is a backward-type obstacle.
One of the two is a forward-type obstacle.
Both kinds appear.
It pairs a reluctance to reuse something with a failure to find a needed construction.
questions.explain: Each way of working has its own typical obstacle. Full statement: A backward-type obstacle, the double function, and a forward-type obstacle, the construction.
questions.teaches: Subjects who worked forward could solve C1 only by happening to apply R12 for some reason unconnected with the solution path, as S2 and S8 did.

questions.q: Why would working a logic problem entirely in the head, with the rules memorized, differ from working with a board and a rule sheet?
options: The head cannot hold the rules, however well memorized
The displays hold information, so removing them changes what the solver can use
The board makes the problem logically easier, whatever the solver does
The displays slow the solver, so working in the head is always faster in every case
optionExplain: The comparison grants perfectly memorized rules.
External memories affect performance.
The board does not change the logical problem.
Speed is not the point.
questions.explain: What is on display helps the solver. The card shows how the authors frame it. Full statement: The displays hold information, so working without them changes what the solver can use.
questions.rule: External displays are part of the working situation.

questions.q: The logic task has two displays: the rule sheet, which is static, and the ____, which slowly accumulates information.
questions.explain: The board gathers the expressions the solver writes down as the work goes on.

questions.q: A cook has a recipe book on the shelf and a notepad for tasting notes as she goes. Which pairing matches the logic task's displays?
options: The recipe book is the static display and the notepad the accumulating one
The recipe book is the accumulating display and the notepad the static one in the task
Both are static, since neither changes the dish
Both accumulate, since the cook uses both
optionExplain: The rule sheet is fixed and the board grows.
The pairing is reversed.
The notepad accumulates.
The book does not change.
questions.explain: One display stays fixed and the other grows with the work.
questions.rule: Static: the rules. Growing: the board.

questions.q: True or false: On the authors' view, any information that sits on a display automatically counts as part of the knowledge state.
questions.explain: It counts only if it is available to the solver; they ask whether it is.
questions.rule: On display is not the same as available.

questions.q: When the authors used the problem behavior graph in Chapters 8 and 9, what did they take as the operators?
options: The twelve rules only, with the goals left out of the problem-space element altogether
The expressions on the board only
The experimenter's questions
The goals, not the rules, so the current goal had to be part of the element
optionExplain: That was the basic space; the graph used goals.
Expressions are elements, not operators.
Questions are not operators.
Goals served as operators, and the current goal changes what the solver knows.
questions.explain: The goal supplies much of the information used to choose the next operator. Full statement: The goals, not the rules, so the current goal had to be part of the problem-space element.
questions.rule: With the graph, goals are operators.
questions.teaches: In using the problem behavior graph in Chapters 8 and 9 the authors took the goals, rather than the rules, as the operators, so the current goal had to be included in the problem-space element.

questions.q: A student sits an exam with open notes. Before counting the notes as part of what she knows, what does the chapter's reasoning ask?
options: Whether the notes were written in her own hand
Whether their contents are actually available to her when she needs them
Whether the notes are longer than her memory
Whether the notes were allowed by the examiner
optionExplain: Authorship is not the test.
Knowledge is what is available, which is the opposite of the question goals raise.
Length is not the test.
Permission is not the test.
questions.explain: External memories raise the reverse of the goals' question: all in the knowledge state is available, but is all in the display?
questions.rule: Ask whether the notes are available.
questions.teaches: The issue raised by external memories is exactly the opposite of that raised by goals: all the information in the knowledge state is taken as available, but it is not clear that all the information in the external memories is.

questions.q: After using a reference sheet for a while, which items would you most likely have learned well enough to use without looking?
options: All of them equally
The ones listed last on the sheet
The few you use most often
None of them, since the sheet is always at hand
optionExplain: Learning is uneven.
Position on the sheet is not the key.
Frequent use makes items familiar.
People do learn some entries.
questions.explain: Frequent use makes some entries available without the sheet. The card gives the logic example.

questions.q: Subjects knew R5 and R6 well enough to apply them without the rule sheet, but not R4 or R____.
questions.explain: R4 and R11 were not known well enough to use without checking.
questions.rule: R5 and R6 known; R4 and R11 not.

questions.q: A barista knows the espresso steps by heart but keeps checking the sheet for the seasonal drink. Which finding about the logic subjects matches?
options: The display contents are all available at once
The display plays no role in the barista's work
The barista has changed the task
Some contents of the display are known and others still looked up
optionExplain: The barista's behavior shows the opposite.
She consults it regularly.
Nothing in the case says so.
The same uneven access.
questions.explain: Knowledge of the display is partial.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say the experimental arrangements were not designed to give good information on the use of external memory, though some can be gleaned from the protocols.
questions.explain: They say the arrangements were not designed for this, though some information can be gleaned from the protocols.
questions.rule: No: the design did not target external memory.

questions.q: In the seven protocols on D1, what did the authors find about searches of the board among the 500-odd operator occurrences?
options: There were no searches of the board at all
There were 18 instances of searches of the board, besides many returns
There were more searches of the board than rule applications in all the seven protocols
There were 180 searches of the board
optionExplain: There were 18.
The count of searches was 18.
There were 18 among 500-odd.
The count was 18.
questions.explain: Board searches were few compared with all operator occurrences, and rule-sheet searches were abundant. Full statement: There were 18 instances of searches of the board, besides many returns to earlier expressions.
questions.rule: About 18 board searches among 500-odd operator occurrences.
questions.teaches: Among the 500-odd operator occurrences classified in the seven protocols on D1, there were 18 instances of searches of the board, besides many returns to some earlier expression and abundant evidence of searches of the rule sheet.

questions.q: A researcher wants better information on how people use an external display. Which source comes closest to an exception to the chapter's caution?
options: Protocols from tasks with no external display
Questionnaires given after the task
Eye-movement studies, in which the external memories were entirely static
Studies of the rule sheet by the experimenter alone
optionExplain: These would give no information on displays.
No questionnaires are mentioned.
The eye-movement studies in cryptarithmetic and chess are perhaps exceptions.
No such studies are mentioned.
questions.explain: Eye movements show what is looked at, though the displays there did not change.
questions.rule: Eye movements are the nearest exception.
questions.teaches: The eye-movement studies, one in cryptarithmetic and one to be considered later in connection with chess, are perhaps exceptions to the authors' caution, though in these the external memories were entirely static.

questions.q: True or false: A single external memory must play the same role for a problem solver for the whole task.
questions.explain: The authors allow that a role can change, and different memories can play different roles. The card lists the roles.
questions.rule: A memory's role can differ and change.

questions.q: Match each role to its description.
pairs: A repository for non-current elements reached by recall, not by operators
Searching it counts as an operator like any other
All its relevant information is in fact available at a node
An adjunct with some, but not all, of its information available
questions.explain: These four roles run from a store of old nodes to an extension of the knowledge state.
questions.rule: Four roles: stock, source, part, extension.

questions.q: A mechanic looks up a part in a catalogue as an act in itself and learns new facts. Which role does the catalogue play?
options: An external source of new knowledge, searched like any other operator
A stock of prior nodes
Part of the knowledge state, available at once as though it were in the head
An extended knowledge state
optionExplain: A wholly external memory whose search generates new knowledge.
A catalogue holds facts she has not met, not earlier states of her own work.
Its contents are not all available to her.
The extension role concerns information partly available.
questions.explain: Looking up unfamiliar facts is an information-generating act.
questions.rule: Unknown contents, searched like an operator.

questions.q: Which of the four roles is a genuine elaboration of the problem-space conception rather than a simple assimilation?
options: The stock of prior nodes
The extended knowledge state
The external source of new knowledge
The part of the knowledge state
optionExplain: That role fits the existing conception.
The first three fit the existing conception; the fourth adds to it.
That role fits the existing conception.
That role fits the existing conception.
questions.explain: Only the fourth changes the conception.
questions.rule: Three fit the old view; the extension changes it.

questions.q: True or false: If a problem solver has several external memories, they may play distinct roles.
questions.explain: In logic, the rule sheet and the board need not play the same role.
questions.teaches: If there are several external memories, they may play distinct roles.

questions.q: A new employee searches the manual for each fact; a year later she knows it well. What does the chapter allow about its role?
options: The same external memory may change its role as she becomes familiar with its contents
Its role is fixed once it has been assigned
It stops being an external memory after a year
Its role is whatever the manual's author intended it to be when it was first written down
optionExplain: Acquaintance can change which role a memory plays.
The authors allow change over time.
It stays external; its role changes.
The role is a matter for the solver.
questions.explain: Role depends on how well the solver knows the contents. Full statement: The same external memory may change its role over time as she becomes acquainted with its contents.
questions.teaches: The same external memory may change its role over time, for instance as the problem solver becomes acquainted with its contents.

questions.q: You work a puzzle by writing down your steps and you reach a dead end. Where do you most likely go back to?
options: A step picked at random from anywhere on the page that you have written
The step that took the longest
The previous step, or the very beginning
A step you have not yet written
optionExplain: Retreat is not random.
Duration is not the guide.
Retreat is usually to the latest sound step or to the start.
You return to something already worked.
questions.explain: People retreat to recent or initial states. The card shows the evidence in logic. Full statement: The step just before, or the very beginning.
questions.rule: Retreat to the last step or the start.

questions.q: Subjects fall back to the prior expression or to the ____ expression when the current one is judged undesirable.
questions.explain: The prior one and the initial one are the commonest places to which they fall back.

questions.q: A solver has written lines A, B and C, tries D and rejects it. Where is she most likely to go, on the card's picture?
options: To a line chosen at random from among A, B and C, each with equal chance
To the line with the most letters
Back to the most recent line, C, or all the way to the first line, A
To a new line unrelated to the board
optionExplain: Returns are not random.
Size of line is not the guide.
Prior or initial expression.
She falls back on the board.
questions.explain: Returns concentrate on two lines.
questions.rule: Fall back to C or A, not elsewhere.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say subjects most commonly fall back to the prior expression or the initial one.
questions.explain: Most commonly they fall back to the prior one or the initial one.

questions.q: Why does much of the backing off to the immediately prior expression happen at the covert level?
options: Because subjects avoid entering an expression on the board until it seems to be progress
Because subjects are asked not to write down failures, so that the board stays clean for the experimenter
Because the board erases old lines automatically
Because the experimenter writes only the correct lines onto the board for the subject
optionExplain: Dead-end expressions often never reach the board, so the return is not visible.
No such instruction is reported.
The board keeps its lines.
The experimenter writes what the subject says.
questions.explain: What the board holds is already filtered by the subject's judgment. Full statement: Because subjects avoid entering a new expression on the board until they think it represents progress.
questions.rule: The board holds only what looked like progress.
questions.teaches: Subjects avoid entering a new expression on the display until they think it represents progress, so most backing off to the immediately prior expression occurs at the covert level, a return to the most recent expression entered on the board.

questions.q: After a long fruitless try, a subject says he started back at the beginning, since he was getting nowhere. What kind of move is this?
options: A rise in the number of rules he used
A search of the rule sheet for a new rule
A switch to working from the goal backward
A return to the original expression for the purpose of starting over
optionExplain: Nothing in the remark concerns the number of rules.
He went back to an expression, not to the sheet.
He went back to the start, not to the goal.
The authors cite S4's remark as a clear case.
questions.explain: Starting over is a return to the initial expression.
questions.rule: Starting over means back to the initial expression.
questions.teaches: S4 ended a fruitless attempt, ending at L8, to follow path.R7 on D1 by going back to the original expression for the function of starting over.

questions.q: A solver tries a step to see what it looks like, finds it unhelpful and returns to where she was. What is this move?
options: Scanning the whole record for a new starting point
Backing up one step after an experiment
Giving up the whole problem
Copying the step to another sheet
optionExplain: She returned to where she was.
A trial followed by a return.
She continued from the earlier point.
Copying is not the move.
questions.explain: A short excursion and a return is backup. The card shows S3's case.

questions.q: True or false: Almost all the movement on the display in the logic task is consistent with depth-first search and backup.
questions.explain: Only occasionally is the display searched for a new starting place.

questions.q: Which behavior is a scan of the display rather than a simple backup?
options: Looking over the board for a new expression to start from
Returning to the line written immediately before the present one
Trying a rule on the last expression and rejecting the result at once
Writing the same line a second time
optionExplain: A scan chooses a starting place without regard to genesis.
That is a simple backup.
That is a short trial.
That is duplication, not a scan.
questions.explain: Scanning is choosing a start from the whole record. Full statement: Looking over the board for a new starting expression regardless of how the earlier ones were made.
questions.rule: Scan: choose a start from the whole board.

questions.q: A reader says S8 chose L5 only because it was the most recent expression. What is wrong with this?
options: He chose L5 because it was the first expression written on the board, as his remarks showed
He chose it after being told by the experimenter
He never chose L5 at all
He scanned for a place to eliminate an R inside a subexpression; being latest was chance
optionExplain: L5 was not the first.
No such guidance is reported.
He did choose it.
The authors say there is little doubt about how L5 was selected.
questions.explain: The route to the choice, not the date of the line, shows the scan. Full statement: He reached L5 by scanning for a place where eliminating an R inside a subexpression was possible, and its being latest was a coincidence.
questions.rule: How it was chosen matters, not when it was written.

questions.q: S8 discovered that R8 cannot be applied to a subexpression: it applies only to ____ expressions.
questions.explain: The strategy of eliminating an R inside a subexpression failed because R8 works on whole, main expressions.
questions.teaches: R8 cannot be applied to a subexpression, as S8 soon discovers: it applies only to main expressions.

questions.q: A planner keeps a list of open subproblems and, when stuck, picks the most promising one. Which strategy does this resemble in the chapter?
options: Simple backup to the previous node
Depth-first search without any return to earlier points in the tree of expressions
Search and scan, as artificial problem solvers do with a subproblem list
Random restarts
optionExplain: Backup returns to the latest node, not a list.
Depth-first search involves returns.
The authors mention this as the strategy to which a display scan corresponds.
A choice from the list is not random.
questions.explain: Scanning the whole record corresponds to the subproblem-list strategy of some programs. Full statement: Search and scan, as performed by artificial problem solvers that keep a subproblem list.
questions.rule: Scan: like keeping a subproblem list.
questions.teaches: Occasional scanning of the display for a new starting place corresponds to a search-and-scan strategy as performed by some of the artificial problem solvers that keep a subproblem list.

questions.q: When you look up an unfamiliar fact in a reference book, what kind of act is it in problem-solving terms?
options: A rest from problem solving
A way of changing the problem
A recall of something you already know
An operation that generates new knowledge, like any other
optionExplain: Looking up is part of the work.
The problem is unchanged.
The fact was unknown before the lookup.
Looking up adds to what you know.
questions.explain: A lookup produces knowledge, so it is an operator. The card puts this in the chapter's terms.

questions.q: Searching an external memory unknown to the solver is an operation like any other information-generating ____.
questions.explain: It counts as an operator of the problem space.

questions.q: Which of these is the clearest case of an external memory as a source of new knowledge?
options: A rule sheet the solver has already memorized
A map consulted in a city the traveler has never visited
A notepad of the solver's own earlier steps
A mental picture of a street the traveler knows well
optionExplain: Familiar contents are not a source of new knowledge.
Its contents are not known and must be searched out.
The solver generated those contents.
That is internal.
questions.explain: The mark is that the contents are unknown until found.
questions.rule: Unknown contents: search like an operator.

questions.q: True or false: The rule sheet is a clear case of an external source of new knowledge, since subjects were unfamiliar with it at first.
questions.explain: Subjects become familiar with the rule sheet before the first problem, so searching it soon melds with recollection.
questions.rule: A familiar sheet is recalled, not searched.

questions.q: S8's rule application to left(L5) was blocked because the main expression was negative. What did he do next?
options: He searched the board for an expression with a positive main sign: left(L3)
He looked up another rule on the sheet whose input would fit the negative expression
He asked the experimenter for a new line
He deleted the negative expression
optionExplain: He looked through the board, not the rule sheet.
He searched the board instead.
No such request is reported.
Nothing was deleted.
questions.explain: A search of the display served as a remedy in a means-ends cycle. Full statement: He searched the display for an expression whose main sign was positive and found left(L3).
questions.rule: A display search to fix a blocked rule.
questions.teaches: Blocked by a negative main expression, S8 searched the display for an expression with a positive main sign, found left(L3), tried R8 on it and then rejected it; the authors call this a standard means-ends cycle.

questions.q: A task has operators that search a database and others that infer. A colleague calls the mix unprincipled. What do the authors reply?
options: The mix is a flaw that the twelve logic rules avoid, and a better theory would avoid it too
The operators of cryptarithmetic were also inhomogeneous; operators need not be of one kind
All operators must be search operators
The mix proves the task cannot be modelled
optionExplain: The authors do not call it a flaw.
The authors point to cryptarithmetic as another inhomogeneous case.
That is not stated.
It does not.
questions.explain: Operators of mixed kinds are allowed in the theory. Full statement: The operators of cryptarithmetic were also inhomogeneous; there is no reason for all operators to be of one kind.
questions.teaches: The operators of cryptarithmetic were also inhomogeneous, so there is no reason for all operators to be of one kind, like the twelve rules in logic.

questions.q: How could you tell that a solver does not have a whole board of work in mind?
options: She writes more lines than another solver
She looks at the board before writing each new line of her work
She solves the problem in the end
She writes the same line twice without noticing
optionExplain: The number of lines does not show it.
Looking at it would show the opposite.
Success does not show it.
Missing a duplicate shows the board is not all in mind.
questions.explain: Missing a duplicate is a clue about what is in mind. The card gives the authors' version.
questions.rule: Missed duplicates mark a memory outside the state.

questions.q: The authors' best evidence that a large display is truly external is that subjects fail to detect ____ immediately.
questions.explain: S4 and S5 did not notice repeated expressions at once.
questions.rule: Duplicates missed: the board is external.

questions.q: A shopper buys a third tin of soup, not noticing the cupboard holds two. In the authors' terms, what does this show?
options: The cupboard's contents are not all part of her current knowledge state
The cupboard's contents are entirely part of her knowledge state at that moment
She has no memory at all
Soup tins cannot be copied
optionExplain: She did not have them available when deciding.
Then she would have noticed.
She has memory; it is not complete.
The case does not turn on copying.
questions.explain: Failure to notice a repeat shows the store was not in the current state.

questions.q: True or false: When S4 discovered that L8 repeated L2, it made no difference to what he did next.
questions.explain: The discovery sent him back to start over: it meant he was not making progress.

questions.q: How have the authors treated the rule sheet in their analysis of the logic task?
options: As an outside source that is searched like a reference book each time a rule is needed
As irrelevant to the subjects' choices
As part of the knowledge state, not separating knowing a rule from finding it
As a store of earlier expressions
optionExplain: That is the second role, which they say the rule sheet hardly plays.
They treat it as important.
The treatment proved adequate as a first approximation once subjects were familiar with the rules.
That is the board's first role.
questions.explain: The rule sheet is one sheet, always open to visual search. Full statement: As part of the knowledge state, without separating knowing a rule from finding it on the sheet.
questions.rule: Rule sheet: treated as part of the state.
questions.teaches: The authors tended to treat the rule sheet as part of the knowledge state, not distinguishing whether a subject knows a rule or finds it on the sheet, which proved adequate as a first approximation once the subjects were familiar with the rules.

questions.q: A solver sees her new line copies two earlier lines and says she is back where she started. What next, per S5?
options: She polishes the line and carries on
She writes it a fourth time
She abandons the line
She takes the repeat as a sign of progress
optionExplain: S5 dropped the line.
The duplication sent S5 away.
S5 abandoned L15 after discovering the triplication.
A repeat meant no progress.
questions.explain: Repeated expressions are read as a sign of going in circles.
questions.rule: A repeat is a failure signal.
questions.teaches: S5 on D1 discovered that L15 was a triplication of L11 and L5, remarked that he was back where he started from, and abandoned L15.

questions.q: Some of your notes come to mind when needed; others only if you leaf through the notebook. How would you describe what you know?
options: What is in your head plus what you can get from the notebook by looking
Only what is in your head
Everything in the notebook, as if it were all held in your head at the same time
Only what is written in the notebook
optionExplain: That describes the head and the notebook with its access method.
The notebook is also used.
Not all of it is available at once.
What is in your head also counts.
questions.explain: Knowledge can include what a routine can fetch. The card gives the authors' term. Full statement: What is in your head, plus what you can get from the notebook by a particular way of looking.
questions.rule: Head plus what a routine can fetch.

questions.q: The extended knowledge state is the contents of memory X plus what can be obtained from memory Y by a ____ program.
questions.explain: The retrieval program is the accessing function.

questions.q: Why do the subjects duplicate expressions, on the authors' account?
options: They cannot read the board
They want to check their work by copying each earlier line again onto the board
They have forgotten the rules
They do not search the display each time and rely on noticing a repeat
optionExplain: They can read it.
No such purpose is reported.
Rule knowledge is not the cause.
Duplication follows from relying on noticing.
questions.explain: A search that is not routine misses repeats. Full statement: They do not search the display each time they write a new expression and rely on noticing a repeat.
questions.rule: No routine search, so repeats slip by.

questions.q: True or false: If a deliberate search of the display followed every new expression, most duplications would be caught immediately.
questions.explain: A deliberate scan makes the display's expressions available, so repeats would be noticed.

questions.q: For what routine job was the display reliably available to the subjects?
options: Finding inputs to two-line rules, as GPS scanned the display for a second input
Spotting duplicated expressions on the board at once, without any need to search
Finding the rule sheet
Deciding which goal to adopt next
optionExplain: The protocols show several searches of this kind.
That is where access failed.
The rule sheet is a separate memory.
Goal selection is not given as the job.
questions.explain: The display is available for some functions and not others. Full statement: Finding inputs to two-line rules, as GPS scanned the display for a second input to R12.
questions.rule: Available for inputs, not for duplicates.
questions.teaches: The display is routinely used to find inputs to two-line rules: GPS scanned the display to obtain a second input for R12, and the protocols show several instances of such searches.

questions.q: A cook glances at the pantry only when taking stock; then it is as available as what she has in mind. What does this show?
options: A pantry can never be part of what the cook knows, however carefully and often she looks
Scanning a pantry destroys its contents
The cook has learned the pantry by heart
Contents of an external memory become as available as the knowledge state during a scan
optionExplain: A scan brings its contents into play.
Scanning does not use things up.
She still has to scan.
A deliberate scan makes all expressions as available.
questions.explain: Availability depends on the process of access. Full statement: Contents of an external memory become as available as the immediate knowledge state during a deliberate scan.
questions.teaches: When a subject engages in a deliberate scan of the display, all of its expressions become as available as the information in the immediate knowledge state.

questions.q: You need a tool that cuts, and you face a rack of tools. What do you check first?
options: Which tool is the newest
Which tools cut, and which of those fit the material
Which tool is nearest your hand
Which tool you used last
optionExplain: Newness is not relevant.
Function and feasibility.
Position is not a condition.
Last use is not a condition.
questions.explain: A search by function and fit mirrors the rule sheet search. The card gives the details.

questions.q: When working forward, subjects select rules almost entirely on the basis of the ____ of the expression.
questions.explain: S10 selected R6 and R2 because both given expressions were horseshoes.

questions.q: S10 sees two expressions with horseshoes and names R6 and R2. Which kind of search is this?
options: A search by function alone
A backward search from L0
A forward search by connective
A search of the board for duplicates
optionExplain: He named rules by the connective.
He announced that he was working forward.
The connective determined which rules he named.
That is a different search.
questions.explain: The expression's connective selects the candidate rules.
questions.rule: Horseshoes call up R6 and R2.

questions.q: True or false: When his first search found nothing, S8 searched by function alone, taking rules that delete terms without checking whether they applied.
questions.explain: He took R8, R3 and R11 for their function, dropping the feasibility condition.

questions.q: What happened when S5 on D1 searched for a rule with several requirements at once?
options: R7 satisfied all three and he used it
No rule satisfied all three: change position, keep signs, and apply to a horseshoe
R8 satisfied all three of them, but he missed it because it was low on the rule sheet
The experimenter supplied a rule
optionExplain: He was trying to apply R7.
No rule was found.
No rule satisfies the three.
No such help is reported.
questions.explain: A search with too many conditions finds nothing. Full statement: No rule satisfied the three conditions: change position, keep signs, and apply to a horseshoe.
questions.teaches: S5, trying to apply R7 to L17, wanted to change the order of a term, keep the signs, and do so across a horseshoe, and no rule satisfies those three conditions.

questions.q: A librarian filters by topic only and gets many irrelevant books to look through. Which feature of the rule-sheet searches does this parallel?
options: Searches exclude relevant operators and let nothing irrelevant through, however long the sheet is
Searches rely on many conditions at once
Searches on one functional and one applicability condition let irrelevant operators through
Searches never produce irrelevant operators
optionExplain: They do not exclude relevant ones.
Rarely more than two conditions are used.
The authors say this is a prominent feature.
They often do.
questions.explain: Loose filters pass irrelevant items. Full statement: Searches with one functional and one applicability condition let irrelevant operators through rather than exclude relevant ones.
questions.teaches: Only rarely do subjects search with more than one functional condition and one applicability condition, so the searches let irrelevant operators through, which must then be considered further, rather than excluding relevant ones.

questions.q: A reference sheet lists items in three blocks. A reader checks only the first two for a feature. What may happen?
options: Items in the third block that have the feature are overlooked
The reader finds every matching item anyway
The reader finds only the best match
The reader changes the feature sought
optionExplain: Search follows the layout.
Not if the third block is unread.
Only what was read can be found.
Nothing suggests that.
questions.explain: A search is only as complete as the part of the sheet read. The card gives the logic case.

questions.q: The rule sheet had three sets of rules, marked off by ____.
questions.explain: Lines separated the three sets of rules.

questions.q: Why might S8 have missed R5 in his first search for a dot as major connective?
options: R5 does not involve a dot, so a search for a dot as major connective could not find it
The dot is on the right-hand side of R5, but on the left in rules 1, 3, 4 and 7
He had never heard of R5
R5 belongs to the third set
optionExplain: R5 involves a dot.
He read the left-hand sides.
The text does not say so.
R8 is the one in the third set.
questions.explain: He scanned the side where the dot would be if it were a starting form. Full statement: The dot appears on the right-hand side of R5, while on rules 1, 3, 4 and 7 it appears on the left.
questions.rule: Dot on the right: R5 was passed over.

questions.q: True or false: S8's later remark on first seeing R8 suggests he had considered and silently rejected it at the start of D1.
questions.explain: The remark fits an overlooked rule: it was the first time he saw R8 as a possibility.
questions.rule: A later surprise suggests an earlier miss.

questions.q: Which set of rules did S8 not examine at all in his first search?
options: The third set, which holds R8
The first set, which holds R1
The second set, which holds R5
All three sets
optionExplain: R8 belongs to the third set, which he did not examine.
He examined R1.
R5 is explained by the position of the dot.
He examined rules from the first two.
questions.explain: Overlooking is tied to which parts of the sheet were read.
questions.rule: Third set unread, so R8 missed.
questions.teaches: R8 belongs to the third set of rules on the sheet, which S8 did not examine at all in his first search; the authors judge this from his later remark on first seeing R8.

questions.q: A software menu words each command differently from how users think of the task. Which effect on the logic subjects does this resemble?
options: The wording has no effect on the subjects
The wording determines which problems are solved
The wording used on the sheet affects the functional descriptions subjects use
The wording is changed by the subjects
optionExplain: The authors say it does.
No such claim is made.
The authors say the descriptions subjects use are no doubt affected by the sheet's wording.
The sheet is fixed.
questions.explain: A memory's wording shapes how it is searched.
questions.teaches: The functional descriptions used by the subjects are no doubt affected by the wording used on the rule sheet.

questions.q: A theory ignores the structure of a helper display because the task is dominated by one simple cycle. When is that safe?
options: In every task, on the ground that displays never matter to the solver at all
In no task, since displays always matter
Only to a first approximation, and only for tasks of that kind
Only for tasks done in the head
optionExplain: Displays can matter.
It is safe in some tasks.
It depends on the task.
The logic task used displays.
questions.explain: A simplification holds for tasks where one cycle dominates. The card gives the logic case.
questions.rule: Ignore structure only to first order.

questions.q: True or false: In the logic task the two external memories' structure can be ignored to a first approximation, as the means-ends cycle dominates.
questions.explain: That is the authors' conclusion for logic.
questions.rule: Logic: ignore structure at first order.

questions.q: The authors say all ____ ways of incorporating an external memory show up to some extent in logic.
questions.explain: All four roles are illustrated in the logic protocols, though lightly.
questions.rule: All four roles appear in logic.

questions.q: In a task that is not dominated by the means-ends cycle, can the structure of external memories be ignored?
options: Yes, as in logic, where the structure of the external memories could be ignored in every case
Yes, but only for the rule sheet
Only if the task is easy
Not in general: the authors say that in other tasks this would not be so
optionExplain: They say otherwise.
No such rule is stated.
Difficulty is not the criterion.
The simplification is specific to logic.
questions.explain: A simplification in one task need not carry over. Full statement: Not in general: the authors say that in other tasks this clearly would not be so.

questions.q: How is much of the information in external memories acquired, on the authors' view?
options: Only by long searches between nodes, in which the subject moves through the display
Within the processing at a single node, by a glance or quick scan of a display
Only by recalling it from long-term memory
Only after the problem is solved
optionExplain: Glances and quick scans suffice for much of it.
This is the sense in which the display is part of the node's processing.
It comes from the display.
It is gained during the work.
questions.explain: Quick scans bring much of the display into play at a node. Full statement: Within the processing at a single node, by a glance or a quick scan of a display.
questions.rule: A glance gets much of it.
questions.teaches: Much information in external memories can be acquired within the processing at a single node of the problem space by a glance or quick scan of a display.

questions.q: An engineer asks what a pilot can use at the next step, given displays she may or may not scan. Which concept fits?
options: The extended knowledge state: what information can actually be brought to bear next
The stock of prior nodes, which says where the solver may back up to next
The depth-first search strategy, which says in what order the possible moves are tried
The double-function test, which says whether a part can serve a second purpose
optionExplain: It is the concept for what is actually available.
That is the first role, not the next step.
That is a search strategy.
That concerns reuse of expressions.
questions.explain: The concept is needed because access is not total. Full statement: The extended knowledge state, which says what information can actually be brought to bear at the next step.
questions.rule: Extended state: what can be brought to bear.
questions.teaches: The information in an external memory may not be totally available, owing to characteristics of the problem solver's program for accessing it, and the authors need a way of talking about what can actually be brought to bear at the next step.

questions.q: The authors of a logic-task study compare how several subjects solve the same logic problems. Which is likely to strike them first?
options: Large differences in the kinds of moves allowed
A complete absence of any differences
Differences only between experts and novices
Similarities, with the differences more subtle
optionExplain: The moves are set by the task.
Subtle differences exist.
Differences appear among the subjects generally.
People use the same basic processes.
questions.explain: In a well-defined task, similarity dominates; the authors list where to look for differences, which turn out to be subtle.

questions.q: Which of these are among the six places the authors list for finding individual differences? Select all that apply.
options: The problem spaces in which they work
The operators they apply
Their scores on a separate intelligence test
Their methods
optionExplain: Yes: the first item.
Yes: the second item.
No: this is not in the list.
Yes: the sixth item.
questions.explain: The list is of features of the problem solving process.
questions.rule: Space, operators, differences, order, abstraction, methods.

questions.q: Two chess players use the same kinds of moves and notice the same features, yet one wins more often. Which logic finding does this parallel?
options: Subjects differ greatly in problem space, so performance differs greatly from one subject to the next
Subjects share space, operators and differences, yet subtle differences make some better
Subjects show no difference in performance
Subjects all solve the same number of problems
optionExplain: The logic subjects shared one space.
Subtle differences can separate good from poor performance.
Some were substantially better.
They did not.
questions.explain: Small differences can have large effects. Full statement: Subjects share space, operators and differences, yet subtle differences make some substantially better.

questions.q: True or false: With qualifications for S11, all subjects worked in essentially the same problem space.
questions.explain: The authors say that apart from some qualification for S11, they did.

questions.q: How many of the 24 solutions of D1 by Yale subjects came from the one-fourth with experience of at least twelve other problems?
options: 4 of the 24
6 of the 24
14 of the 24
22 of the 24
optionExplain: The experienced quarter produced most.
The experienced quarter produced most.
The authors give 14 of 24.
The authors give 14.
questions.explain: Experience was linked to success.
questions.teaches: Most of the solutions (14 of 24) of D1 by the Yale subjects were obtained by the one-fourth of the subjects who had already had experience with at least twelve other problems.

questions.q: A coach finds that her swimmers' successful laps increase steadily from the first practice to the fourth. Which published pattern does this resemble?
options: Solutions fell steadily across the four sessions, as the subjects became bored or tired
Solutions were constant across sessions
Solutions jumped only in the last session
The number of solutions rose more or less linearly from the first session to the fourth
optionExplain: They rose.
They rose.
The rise was roughly linear.
The authors cite this study.
questions.explain: Practice improved success steadily in that study. Full statement: Carpenter and colleagues found the number of solutions rose more or less linearly from the first problem session to the fourth.
questions.rule: Practice raised solutions in a roughly straight line.
questions.teaches: Carpenter, Moore, Snyder and Lisansky (1961) showed that the number of solutions obtained by their subjects increased more or less linearly from the first problem session to the fourth.

questions.q: A beginner and an expert at a card game differ in how they use the rule book. What difference is most likely?
options: The expert searches the book more than the beginner does, to be sure of each ruling
The beginner searches the book, the expert recognizes the rule directly
The beginner never opens the book
They differ only in speed
optionExplain: Experts consult less.
Practice replaces searching with recognition.
Beginners use it most.
They differ in method.
questions.explain: Searching gives way to recognition with practice. The card names these methods in logic.

questions.q: Match each aspect of style to the method it reflects.
pairs: Forward search of the rules for ones applicable to an expression
Search of the rules for one that performs a desired function
Find operator to perform function F
Availability of generators and strength of stop rules
questions.explain: Each stylistic aspect shows a method.

questions.q: A subject repeatedly scans the sheet for a rule that would delete a term. Which aspect of style is this?
options: A forward search for rules applicable to an expression
Working backward from L0
A search of the rules for one that performs a desired function
A count of rule applications
optionExplain: He is looking for a function, not for applicability.
He is not working from the goal.
The method Find operator to perform function F.
That is a quantity, not a search.
questions.explain: Searching for a function is a different method from searching for a fit.

questions.q: True or false: The authors expect the two rule-search methods to disappear as the subject replaces them by direct recognition.
questions.explain: They call the methods primitive, used when the forms and functions of the rules are not stored in memory.

questions.q: What does the use of the two rule-search methods imply about the subject?
options: That he has stored every rule perfectly
That he has not stored in memory the forms of the rules or their functions
That he is working backward
That he knows the goal in advance
optionExplain: Then no search would be needed.
He lacks a table of connections.
That is a separate method.
Not implied.
questions.explain: Searches stand in for a missing store.
questions.rule: Search implies a missing table of connections.
questions.teaches: Use of the two rule-search methods implies that the subject has not stored in memory the forms of the rules or their functions, which the authors call a table of connections.

questions.q: A runner's pacing is at first the same in every race, then changes as she learns. What does learning do to a subject's style consistency?
options: It raises it
It leaves it unchanged
It makes style depend on the problem alone
It reduces it
optionExplain: They say learning reduces consistency.
They say it reduces it.
Style still belongs to the subject.
Any learning would reduce the consistency of style of a given subject over a sequence.
questions.explain: Learning shifts style.
questions.teaches: Any kind of learning that occurred would also reduce the consistency of style of a given subject over a sequence of problems.

questions.q: To separate what comes from the task from what comes from the person, which comparison helps?
options: The same person on two tasks, and two people on the same task
Two people on different tasks only
The same person on the same task twice
One person's best and worst days
optionExplain: Persisting traits show across tasks; task effects show across people.
Both factors vary at once.
That shows nothing about the task.
That is a different question.
questions.explain: A two-way comparison separates task from person. The card applies it to S9 and S11.
questions.rule: Compare across tasks and across people.

questions.q: True or false: S9 is reminded of a rule by the form of L0, while S11 matches L1 with L0 symbol by symbol.
questions.explain: The difference is in how they look at the two expressions: S9 abstracts, S11 matches particulars.

questions.q: In an editing session, which remark is typical of S11's style of attack?
options: This reminds me of a headline, so it needs the same key words and about as many
The main problem is how many times each key word occurs
Delete the comma after the third word and make the first article definite
Let me first see what the overall shape of the text is
optionExplain: That is S9's style, reminded of a form and matching letters and counts.
That is S9's style.
It ties particular parts of the draft to particular parts of the target.
That is a general characterization, as S9 gives.
questions.explain: S11 works on particular segments. Full statement: Delete the comma after the third word and change the first article to a definite one.

questions.q: S9 and S11 differ not only in verbal habits but, at a deeper level, in how they ____ L1 with L0.
questions.explain: Their way of comparing the two expressions differs, as well as their wording.

questions.q: How does S9 characterize his central problem in both D1 and C1?
options: Getting the letters in L1, and their numbers of occurrences, to agree with L0
Finding the longest chain of rules that can be applied in turn to get from L1 to L0
Making L1 shorter than L0
Memorizing the rule sheet
optionExplain: That is S9's central problem.
He does not describe it so.
No such goal is described.
That is not what he says.
questions.explain: S9 describes the problem as a mismatch of letters and counts. Full statement: Getting the letters, and the number of occurrences of each, in L1 to agree with L0.
questions.rule: S9: make letters and counts agree.
questions.teaches: S9 characterizes the central problem, in both D1 and C1, as getting the letters and the number of occurrences in L1 to agree with those in L0.

questions.q: One editor changes each word of a draft into a final-text word. Another views the overall shape, then fits details. Which is like S11?
options: The second, who looks at the overall shape of the draft first and then the details
Neither, since editors do not work with symbols
Both, since both end with the same text
The first, who ties particular segments to particular parts of the target
optionExplain: That resembles S9.
The contrast is about method.
The difference is in the route.
S11 transforms particular segments of L1 to particular parts of L0.
questions.explain: S11's attention is on the particulars.
questions.teaches: S11's plans tie locatable segments of L1 to particular parts of L0, as in the changing of the sign on P from a tilde to a dot before it and the taking of the Q out of the first expression.

questions.q: Two people each solve two puzzles. If working style is a stable trait, what would you expect about how much each writes down?
options: Each writes much more on the second puzzle
Each writes about the same amount on both puzzles
Each writes a different amount on the two puzzles, at random
Both write the same amount as each other on each puzzle
optionExplain: That would suggest change, not stability.
Stable style means similar habits on both.
Random variation is not stability.
Stable traits differ between people.
questions.explain: Stable habits repeat. The card gives the authors' count for the logic subjects.

questions.q: S11 worked almost entirely in his head and wrote only ____ expressions on each problem.
questions.explain: S11 wrote three each time, against 17 and 19 for S5.

questions.q: Which subject was inconsistent in the number of expressions written?
options: S4, with 13 expressions on D1 and 6 on C1
S11, with three expressions on each problem
S5, with 17 and 19 expressions
S9, with 8 and 10 expressions
optionExplain: He is the one exception named.
S11 was consistent.
S5 was consistent.
S9 was consistent.
questions.explain: Only S4 broke the pattern.

questions.q: True or false: S5 and S11, the subjects who wrote the most and the fewest expressions, were the best solvers.
questions.explain: Both solved neither problem.

questions.q: Which two subjects did not search the list of rules on either problem?
options: S8 and S9, both of whom solved each problem
S5, a nonsolver, and S9, a solver
S5 and S11, both of them nonsolvers
S4 and S10, both mixed
optionExplain: S8 searched the rules.
The two who did not search were a nonsolver and a solver.
S11 searched the rules.
Both searched the rules.
questions.explain: Searching the rules does not separate solvers from nonsolvers.
questions.teaches: The two subjects who did not search the rules on either problem were a nonsolver, S5, and a solver, S9, so rule searching does not by itself separate solvers from nonsolvers.

questions.q: A student keeps to one infeasible method across problems and does not restate the overall aim. Which subjects in the table does this match?
options: S9 on both problems, who restated the goals often and gave up plans that failed
S4 on D1
S5 on both problems and S10 on C1, who persisted and did not restate the goals
S11 on C1 only
optionExplain: S9 did not persist in an infeasible plan.
S4 solved D1 without being described as persistent.
The authors report persistence for these subjects.
S11 is described differently.
questions.explain: Persistence in an infeasible plan produced most of these subjects' expressions. Full statement: S5 on both problems and S10 on C1, who persisted and did not restate the overall goals.
questions.rule: Persistent subjects: S5, and S10 on C1.
questions.teaches: S5 on both problems, and S10 on C1, showed great persistence in pursuing a particular infeasible plan, which produced most of their expressions, and statements restating the overall problem goals do not recur in their protocols.

questions.q: Which profile more likely belongs to the stronger problem solver: clear general plans, or attention to detail and searching for rules?
options: The one who attends to detail and searches for rules
Neither, since profiles say nothing about strength
Both equally, since each works hard
The one who sets out clear general plans
optionExplain: That is the weakest profile in the chapter.
The authors rank by apparent power.
Effort is not the ranking criterion.
Broad planning goes with strength in this data.
questions.explain: In the data, breadth of planning marks the stronger solvers. The card gives the profiles.

questions.q: Match each subject to his profile.
pairs: Clear general plans, working both backward and forward
Initially less planful, working forward, scanning and reformulating
Concerned with detail, searching for rules without necessarily applying them
questions.explain: The three profiles run from strongest to weakest.

questions.q: A solver writes a line, scans all lines on the board, and reformulates the problem in light of them, repeatedly. Which subject does this resemble?
options: S9, who works from clear general plans
S8
S11, who mostly works in his head
S5, who stays with one plan
optionExplain: S9 plans broadly.
He scans the new expressions and reformulates.
S11 does little scanning of written lines.
S5 persists.
questions.explain: S8 uses the written lines to find new directions.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say S9 executes his general plans with moderate difficulty.
questions.explain: They say he executes them with moderate difficulty.

questions.q: According to the authors' discussion of styles, which habit marked S8 on both D1 and C1?
options: Frequently searching through the expressions he had already written down
Writing only three expressions and working almost entirely in his head
Writing 17 expressions on one problem and 19 on the other
Never searching the board, though he searched the rule list at length
optionExplain: The authors say S8 frequently searched through and scrutinized his earlier expressions on both problems.
That describes S11.
Those counts are S5's.
The authors do not say this of S8.
questions.explain: S8 is the subject who repeatedly goes back over what he has written.
questions.rule: S8 scrutinizes his own written expressions.
questions.teaches: One subject, S8, frequently searched through and scrutinized, in both problems, the expressions he had already written down.

questions.q: A shopper browses many offers and, at the end, buys one only if its use is obvious. Which subject's behavior with rules does this resemble?
options: S9, who works from clear general plans and seldom searches the rule sheet for rules to apply
S11, who searches for rules he can apply but applies them only if the outcome is useful
S8, who scans new lines
S5, who persists in a single plan
optionExplain: S9 plans broadly.
That is the authors' description of S11.
S8 scans written lines.
S5 persists.
questions.explain: S11's search for rules is detailed and tentative. Full statement: S11, who searches for rules he can apply but applies them only if the outcome has an obvious use.
questions.rule: S11 searches for rules but seldom applies them.
questions.teaches: S11 spends much time searching for rules he can apply but does not apply them unless the outcome has an obvious use.

questions.q: A solver pushes one line of attack as far as it goes without returning to alternatives. Which strategy is this?
options: Scan-and-search
Breadth-first
Random search
Depth-first
optionExplain: Scanning compares alternatives.
Breadth-first spreads over alternatives.
The line is not chosen at random.
One line is followed as far as it goes.
questions.explain: Following one line to its end is depth-first. The card applies the term to S5.
questions.rule: Depth-first: one line to its end.

questions.q: Match each subject to his strategy label.
pairs: The clearest alternation between abstraction and concrete detail
questions.explain: The labels connect each subject to a strategy from the earlier classification.
questions.rule: S5 depth-first, S8 scan-and-search, S9 alternation.

questions.q: Why do the authors link S5's failure to his strategy?
options: The depth-first strategy produces stereotypy, so he kept to unproductive plans
He never wrote any expressions
He changed plans too often
He worked backward on every problem
optionExplain: They attribute his inability to solve to that stereotypy.
S5 wrote many.
He persisted in his plans.
No such pattern is reported for S5.
questions.explain: Persistence became a trap.

questions.q: True or false: The authors read S8's repeated reviewing of his earlier expressions as a scan-and-search strategy.
questions.explain: They read it as a scan-and-search strategy: he continues from the expressions that seem most promising.

questions.q: How do most subjects operate in terms of abstraction?
options: Only in terms of the concrete problem space, writing out every expression in full
Only in terms of abstractions
Alternately in terms of abstractions and of the detail of the concrete space
Only when working backward
optionExplain: Most subjects alternate.
Most subjects alternate.
Most subjects alternate.
The alternation is not tied to direction.
questions.explain: Alternation between levels is common. Full statement: Alternately in terms of abstractions and of the detail of the concrete problem space.
questions.teaches: Most of the subjects operate alternately in terms of abstractions and of the detail of the concrete problem space.

questions.q: A designer sketches the whole system abstractly, does most of her thinking there, and drops to detail now and then. Which subject does this resemble?
options: S9, who does most of his problem solving in terms of abstracted expressions
S5, who follows one plan through to its end, whatever the difficulties turn out to be
S11, who works on detail
S8, who reviews written expressions
optionExplain: That is how the authors describe S9.
S5 is depth-first.
S11 attends to detail.
S8 is scan-and-search.
questions.explain: S9 shows alternation most clearly, with most of the work abstract. Full statement: S9, who accomplishes most of his problem solving in terms of abstracted expressions.
questions.teaches: S9's protocols perhaps exhibit the alternation between abstraction and detail most clearly, and he accomplishes most of his problem solving in terms of the abstracted expressions.

questions.q: A person works mostly in the head instead of writing intermediate steps. What cost is likely?
options: More time spent copying
A greater chance of duplicating lines
A wider range of rules tried
A heavy load on short-term memory and no written record to scan
optionExplain: No copying is involved.
Few lines are written.
Not implied.
Without a record, memory carries everything.
questions.explain: Working in the head removes the external record. The card gives the authors' list for S11.

questions.q: S11 told the experimenter to write down very few expressions, in fact only ____.
questions.explain: He had only two written down.

questions.q: Which strategy was closed to S11 by his preference for working in his head?
options: Depth-first search, since he wrote nothing down
Search-and-scan, since he had no written expressions to scan for new goals
Working backward from the goal
Searching the rule sheet
optionExplain: Depth-first search needs only a current expression.
He could not follow it because of the limits on what he can hold in his head.
That does not need written lines.
That does not need written lines.
questions.explain: Scanning needs something to scan.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say S11 does not appear to work in a different problem space from the other subjects.
questions.explain: They say he does not appear to work in a different problem space.

questions.q: How wide is the range of individual differences in the logic problems compared with cryptarithmetic?
options: Narrower
Wider
The same
It was not compared
optionExplain: The range appears narrower.
The text says narrower.
The text says narrower.
The comparison is made.
questions.explain: Logic subjects were more alike than the cryptarithmetic subjects.
questions.teaches: The range of individual differences among subjects in the logic problems appears narrower than the range of differences in the cryptarithmetic problems.

questions.q: A planner will sort the files somehow and does not test whether the somehow works. Which feature of S11's plans does this match?
options: He tested every step before taking it, and so knew each plan was feasible at the start
He wrote out each step on the board
He gave up planning altogether
He would group the terms of L1 somehow, and the somehow was never carefully tested
optionExplain: He did not.
He wrote almost nothing.
He had vaguer plans, not none.
That is the authors' description of S11.
questions.explain: Vague plans were part of his style. Full statement: He would group the terms of L1 somehow, and the feasibility of the somehow was never carefully tested.
questions.teaches: S11 was going to group the terms in L1 somehow, and the feasibility of that somehow was never tested very carefully.

questions.q: A learner reads a formula as a flat string of symbols instead of as nested parts. What mistake is likely?
options: Reading the formula too slowly to hold the nested parts together in the head
Treating symbols of different roles alike and forming wrong subexpressions
Memorizing the formula perfectly
Refusing to read formulas at all
optionExplain: Speed is not the mistake.
Without the structure, roles blur.
Memorizing is not the problem.
Nothing suggests refusal.
questions.explain: Structure tells which symbol governs which. The card gives S11's case.

questions.q: S11 appears unaware of the difference in function between binary connectives and the unary connective, the ____.
questions.explain: The tilde applies to one expression; the horseshoe and dot join two.

questions.q: Which behavior shows S11's preoccupation with tildes?
options: Adding tildes freely to make rules apply to the expressions on the board
Ignoring signs entirely
Trying to avoid introducing tildes into the expressions
Using tildes only in the final line
optionExplain: That is the opposite.
He attends to them heavily.
Other subjects treat tildes as details to adjust later.
No such pattern is described.
questions.explain: He treats a detail as a main issue.

questions.q: Which of these are among the main symptoms of S11's idiosyncrasy? Select all that apply.
options: Less planning and abstraction, with little ability to move from functions to specific rules
Heavy demands on short-term memory from working mostly in his head
Working in a problem space different from the others
Greater importance given to differences in tildes
optionExplain: Yes: the first symptom.
Yes: the second symptom.
No: the authors deny this.
Yes: the third symptom.
questions.explain: The symptoms concern strategy and memory, not a different space.
questions.rule: Symptoms: less planning, memory load, tildes.

questions.q: What do the authors conclude about the source of the differences between S11 and the others?
options: They stem from a different problem space
They stem from a failure to learn the rules, and from a slower pace in using them each time
They cannot be described at all
They seem to stem from subtle differences in strategy and in managing short-term memory
optionExplain: The authors deny this.
That is not the conclusion.
The authors do describe them.
He is regarded as working in the same space as the others.
questions.explain: Differences between people can be subtle, even for the most idiosyncratic one. Full statement: They seem to stem from subtle differences in strategy and in the management of short-term memory.
questions.rule: Same space; differences in strategy and memory.
questions.teaches: Since S11 can be regarded as working in the same space as the others, the authors say that in his case the differences seem to stem from subtle differences in strategy and in the management of short-term memory.

questions.q: A proofreader cannot postpone small fixes and stalls on a page where others would note them for later. Which behavior of S11 resembles this?
options: He ignores details of signs and connectives more than the others, leaving them for later
He does not often ignore details of signs and connectives for a while, as the others do
He plans in more abstract terms than the others
He writes more expressions than the others
optionExplain: He attends to them more.
That is how the authors contrast him with the others.
He plans less abstractly.
He writes the fewest.
questions.explain: Other subjects set details aside until needed. Full statement: He does not often temporarily ignore details of signs and connectives as the other subjects do.
questions.rule: Others postpone detail; S11 does not.
questions.teaches: S11 does not often temporarily ignore details of signs and connectives, as the other subjects do.

questions.q: A learner checks a cheat-sheet constantly at first and then stops. What does the stopping suggest?
options: She has lost interest in the task
