The sheet has become wrong
She has begun to remember what the sheet holds
She has forgotten the task
optionExplain: Nothing suggests that.
Nothing suggests that.
The information has moved into memory.
Nothing suggests that.
questions.explain: Learning shows as less looking up. The card gives S8's case.
questions.rule: Less looking up means more remembered.

questions.q: After problem ____, S8 no longer searches through the rules.
questions.explain: The searches stop after C1.
questions.rule: After C1, no more rule searches.

questions.q: Which of S8's later remarks shows that he knew the functions of the rules directly?
options: As soon as he sees a term it reminds him of a certain rule
He must look through all twelve rules to see which fits
He asks the experimenter which rule applies
He decides to work out the rules from scratch each time
optionExplain: Recognition without search.
That is searching.
No such request is reported.
That is not what he says.
questions.explain: Direct recognition replaces the search.

questions.q: True or false: The authors treat the end of S8's scanning of expressions as certain proof of learning.
questions.explain: They say the change may not reflect learning, since the last problems were easy enough that no searches were needed.

questions.q: Which of S8's six problems did he fail to solve?
options: B2, the difficult problem
A2', a problem of moderate difficulty
C1, the difficult problem of the chapter
A4, an easy problem
optionExplain: He solved B2.
He failed A2' but solved the other five.
He solved C1.
He solved A4.
questions.explain: A2' is a variant of A2 produced by a typographical error.
questions.teaches: Of S8's six problems he failed only A2', which is a variant of A2 produced by a typographical error and is of moderate difficulty; he solved D1, C1, B2, A4 and C3.

questions.q: A language learner says that similar words seemed all mixed up at first and are now getting far apart. Which S8 remark does this parallel?
options: That he had never needed the rule sheet at any stage in the course of his work
That he had forgotten the rules
That the rules had changed
That the rules seemed mixed up in the beginning but are now getting far apart
optionExplain: He did need it early on.
He says he now knows them.
The rules did not change.
S8 said this of the rules in C3.
questions.explain: Learning separates things that first seem alike. Full statement: That the rules seemed close together and all mixed up in the beginning but are now getting far apart.
questions.teaches: S8 said, after solving C3, that the rules had seemed close together and all mixed up in the beginning, but that now they were really getting far apart.

questions.q: Over a series of similar problems, which of these is a solver likely to show?
options: Direct links from features to tools, more planning, and stock sequences
More searching of the instructions each time
Less characterization of the problem at the outset
Fewer links between features and tools
optionExplain: These are the kinds of learning the authors see in S8.
Searching fades.
Characterization increases.
Links increase.
questions.explain: Practice builds links, plans and sequences. The card gives the authors' summary. Full statement: Direct links from features to tools, more planning, and stock sequences of moves.
questions.rule: Practice builds links, plans and sequences.

questions.q: Match each kind of learning to its description.
pairs: Direct links from features and differences to rules
From working forward to abstract characterization and planning
Certain goals reached by fixed sequences of certain operators
questions.explain: These are the three summary points.

questions.q: A cook learns that browning and then deglazing gives a sauce base, and uses the pair without rethinking. Which kind of S8's learning is this?
options: Acquiring a table of connections between features of the problem and rules
Shifting to a working-forward style
Learning that a goal can be reached by a fixed sequence of operators
Learning to restate the goal
optionExplain: That concerns features and rules, not a pair of steps.
S8 shifted away from working forward.
The pair is used as a unit.
That is a characterization of the problem.
questions.explain: A routine sequence is a learned unit.

questions.q: True or false: S8 worked backward from L0 in the first two problems and stopped later.
questions.explain: He worked backward first in A4 and in all later problems.
questions.rule: Backward work came late and stayed.

questions.q: What compound operation did S8 learn toward the end of D1, and what is its side consequence?
options: Changing a dot to a horseshoe by R5 followed by R6, which swaps the two sides
Changing a wedge to a horseshoe by R9, which adds a letter
Changing a horseshoe to a dot by R6 then R5, which adds or removes a tilde
Splitting a dot expression by R8, which drops the tilde
optionExplain: The sequence runs the other way.
That is not the compound.
The sequence has that side effect.
That is not the compound.
questions.explain: S8 used the pair again in A2' and C3. Full statement: Changing a horseshoe to a dot by R6 followed by R5, which puts a tilde before the expression or removes one.
questions.rule: R6 then R5: horseshoe to dot, tilde flips.
questions.teaches: Toward the end of D1, S8 learned that a horseshoe can be changed to a dot by applying R6 followed by R5, a sequence that puts a tilde before the expression or removes one if there is already one, and he used this compound operation again in later problems.

questions.q: At a course's start a student computes at once; by the end she first summarizes and outlines a plan. Which finding about S8 is parallel?
options: He characterized the problem first on the last three problems, and planned on the last two
He characterized the problem at the outset on the first problem only, and on none of the later ones
He outlined a correct plan on every problem
He stopped outlining plans on the last two problems, having outlined them on the first three
optionExplain: S8's shift to characterization and planning.
He did it on the last three.
He did so on the last two.
He outlined plans on the last two.
questions.explain: Characterizing and planning appeared late in the series. Full statement: On the last three problems he characterized the problem at the outset, and on each of the last two outlined a correct plan.
questions.rule: Late in the series he outlined plans.
questions.teaches: On the last three problems S8 characterized the problem at the outset, and on each of the last two he outlined a correct plan for its solution.

questions.q: If a skilled solver's early practice looks like a beginner's, what does it suggest?
options: That the solver is not skilled at all
That practice has no effect
That the practice problems were mis-set
That skill grows with practice, so early work resembles other beginners' work
optionExplain: He later became skilled.
It does.
Nothing says so.
Early behavior is that of a learner.
questions.explain: A skilled solver was once a learner. The card gives S9's early work.

questions.q: True or false: S9's behavior on the practice problems resembled S8's early behavior more closely than S9's own later behavior.
questions.explain: That is the authors' summary, though S9 begins to shift on the third problem.
questions.rule: S9 early looks like S8 early.

questions.q: What did S9 do on the first practice problem to cope with the rules?
options: Memorized the whole sheet in advance
Made notes on the rule sheet about what each rule does
Asked the experimenter to explain what each rule on the sheet does
Ignored the sheet and worked backward
optionExplain: He made notes on it.
The notes were his system for knowing what he could do.
No such request is reported.
He used the sheet.
questions.explain: He built a function index for the rules.
questions.rule: He annotated the sheet by function.

questions.q: S9 failed practice problem a2 because he did not know that expressions can be ____ and the parts used as inputs to two-line rules.
questions.explain: The gap was a kind of move, not a rule: he did not know that parts of an expression can serve as inputs.

questions.q: What new feature did S9 show on the third practice problem?
options: He worked entirely in his head
He stopped using the rule sheet altogether and worked only from memory of what the rules said
He solved the problem on the first line
He characterized the problem fully at the start and made only one extensive rule search
optionExplain: That is S11's style.
He made one extensive search.
No such claim is made.
That is the shift toward his later style.
questions.explain: The third problem shows the start of the later style. Full statement: He characterized the problem fairly completely at the beginning and made only one extensive search through the rules.
questions.rule: Characterization at the start; one rule search.
questions.teaches: On the third practice problem S9 characterized the problem fairly completely at the beginning and conducted only one extensive search through the rules.

questions.q: A violinist knows she is learning scales but not that she has learned to plan her phrasing. Which parallel does the chapter draw for S9?
options: He is aware of learning to plan and to characterize problems, but not of learning the rules
He knows he is learning the rules and their functions, but not that he is learning to plan
He is aware of neither learning task
He is aware of both learning tasks
optionExplain: The reverse of the text.
That is the authors' statement about S9.
He is aware of the first.
He shows no awareness of the second.
questions.explain: A learner may see one thing being learned and miss another. Full statement: He is aware that one of his learning tasks is to learn the rules and their functions, but shows no sign of knowing he is learning to plan and characterize.
questions.rule: Aware of rules learning, not of planning learning.
questions.teaches: S9 is clearly aware that one of his learning tasks is to learn the rules and their functions, but he gives no evidence that he is aware of learning to plan and to characterize the main features of the problems.

questions.q: Explorers who can spot few patterns, draw few consequences and remember few routes explore a landscape. What will their paths reflect?
options: The landscape's true structure, seen in full
Only chance, since their foresight is so limited that structure cannot matter
The landscape's structure as they see it, with limited foresight
Only the explorers' personal tastes
optionExplain: Limited explorers do not see it in full.
Structure still shapes paths.
Paths reflect what the explorers can detect and remember.
Structure matters.
questions.explain: Limits on the explorer shape the paths. The card gives the authors' summary.
questions.rule: Paths reflect structure as seen by limited explorers.

questions.q: The authors say the landscape of logic problems strongly resembled the one met earlier in ____.
questions.explain: The logic territory resembled the cryptarithmetic one.

questions.q: Which is NOT one of the limited capacities of the explorers that the card names?
options: The capacity to detect patterns
The capacity to infer consequences
The capacity to remember paths of exploration
The capacity to read the rule sheet
optionExplain: That is named.
That is named.
That is named.
The card names pattern detection, inference of consequences and memory for paths.
questions.explain: The named limits are about perceiving, inferring and remembering.

questions.q: True or false: The authors found the structure of the logic landscape unlike that of the cryptarithmetic landscape.
questions.explain: They say the landscape resembled strongly what they had met in cryptarithmetic.

questions.q: Besides detecting patterns, inferring consequences and remembering paths, which fourth limited capacity do the authors name?
options: Reading the experimenter's instructions
Learning heuristic generalizations about the character of the landscape
Writing expressions on the board
Searching the rule sheet
optionExplain: Not named.
The fourth capacity is for heuristic generalizations.
Not named.
Not named.
questions.explain: Learning is among the limited capacities.
questions.teaches: The fourth limited capacity the authors name is the capacity to learn heuristic generalizations about the character of the landscape.

questions.q: Hikers differ in memory and learning speed but use the same basic way of exploring. How would the authors summarize the logic subjects by analogy?
options: As behaving in ways that GPS cannot imitate
As behaving like exactly one version of GPS
As behaving very much like a number of variant versions of GPS
As behaving at random on every problem
optionExplain: They say the subjects resembled GPS.
They say variant versions.
That is their conclusion.
They do not say so.
questions.explain: Variants of one scheme fit all the subjects.
questions.teaches: The authors conclude that the subjects behaved, in short, very much like a number of variant versions of GPS.

questions.q: To predict where a group of people will explore on a puzzle, which is the best simple first guess?
options: They will reduce differences from the goal, simplify the givens, and match moves to inputs
They will try every legal move in a fixed order, keeping a record of all expressions reached
They will head straight for the shortest solution
They will avoid any move that changes the givens
optionExplain: Three simple tendencies cover the range.
People do not search exhaustively.
People do not know it in advance.
Simplifying the givens is a tendency.
questions.explain: Three tendencies give a first approximation. The card names them. Full statement: They will compare the start with the goal, simplify what they are given, and use moves that obviously fit what they have.

questions.q: Which of these are among the three bases of the authors' first approximation? Select all that apply.
options: Comparing the start with the goal and reducing differences
Simplifying the initial expressions
Applying operators whose inputs strikingly resemble given expressions
Choosing operators at random until one works
optionExplain: Yes: the first basis.
Yes: the second basis.
Yes: the third basis.
No: randomness is not among them.
questions.explain: The three bases are goal comparison, simplification and resemblance.

questions.q: A mechanic faces an unfamiliar engine. Which behavior matches the third basis?
options: Comparing the engine's state with the working state and fixing differences
Reaching for a tool whose shape strikingly matches a part in front of her
Clearing away clutter so the parts are easier to see
Reading the whole manual before touching anything
optionExplain: That is the first basis.
The input of the operator resembles what is given.
That is the second basis.
That is a plan not described here.
questions.explain: Resemblance of a tool's input to what is at hand drives a choice.
questions.rule: Match the operator's input to the givens.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say the behavior of all of the subjects and all versions of GPS fit the first approximation.
questions.explain: They say the behavior of all of the subjects and all versions of GPS fit it.

questions.q: What do the authors say about the subgoals subjects set up, to varying degrees?
options: They find operators that will modify expressions to fit operators already chosen
They list the rules in the order of the sheet and try each rule in turn on the givens
They restate the goal for the experimenter
They choose operators at random
optionExplain: Subgoals prepare expressions for operators.
Not stated.
Not stated.
Not stated.
questions.explain: Fitting the expression to the operator is the subgoal. Full statement: They find operators that will modify expressions so that the expressions fit operators already chosen.
questions.rule: Subgoals fit expressions to chosen operators.
questions.teaches: To varying degrees, subgoals are set up to find operators that will modify expressions to make them fit operators that have been selected for application.

questions.q: A coach says her players share one basic game plan, and individual differences are details on top. How do the authors treat variations among subjects?
options: As evidence against the first approximation
As noise to be ignored
As second approximations on top of the common first approximation
As first approximations of their own
optionExplain: They do not treat them so.
They analyze them.
That is their term for the variations.
The first approximation is common.
questions.explain: A shared base plus varying details.
questions.teaches: The variations among subjects provide second approximations to the common first approximation.

questions.q: People who share one basic way of solving a puzzle still differ. Which kinds of differences would you expect?
options: In which moves the puzzle allows
In whether they use the same basic processes of searching, planning and recalling
In how they frame the problem, how long they persist, and what they have learned
In whether they understand the puzzle's goal
optionExplain: The allowed moves are set by the puzzle.
The basic processes are shared.
These are the dimensions the authors list.
All understand the goal.
questions.explain: Variation lies in the style of use of shared processes. The card lists the dimensions. Full statement: In how they frame the problem, how long they persist, and how much they have learned.

questions.q: Match each dimension of variation to its description.
pairs: Staying with a subgoal versus returning to the overall problem
Working forward and restructuring versus working backward by a plan
Exploring paths in the head versus writing expressions on the board
Operators tied directly to differences so that no search is needed
questions.explain: Each dimension is a way in which subjects were seen to vary.

questions.q: S5 stays with one infeasible plan and seldom restates the overall goal. In which dimension does he differ from the others?
options: Persistence in a subgoal against readiness to return to the whole problem
Priority given to working backward over working forward in the course of a problem
Extent of mental exploration
Cues used to detect cycling
optionExplain: He sits at the persistent end.
That concerns direction of work.
That concerns where paths are explored.
That concerns detecting lack of progress.
questions.explain: The dimension is persistence. Full statement: Persistence in a subgoal against readiness to return to the overall problem.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say that, to a large extent, differences among subjects can be detected in protocols and used to account for the variety in style.
questions.explain: They say to a large extent these differences can be detected in protocols and used to account for the variety in style.
questions.rule: Differences can be read off protocols.

questions.q: What example of a difference that is not remediable do the authors give?
options: Changing a connective without changing any sign in the rest of the expression
Adding a letter by R9
Splitting an expression by R8
Changing a single sign without changing a connective
optionExplain: That is not their example.
R9 adds a letter, which is a remediable change.
Splitting is a possible move.
That is their example, a signal to end exploration.
questions.explain: Learned knowledge that some differences cannot be removed lets a subject stop a hopeless attempt.
questions.rule: A single sign alone cannot be changed.
questions.teaches: An example of generalized knowledge that a difference is not remediable is that a single sign cannot be changed without changing a connective, so that attempting it should signal the end of that line of exploration.

questions.q: A lab built a problem-solving program and wants to predict which problems people find hard. Which closing claim of the authors supports this aim?
options: Relative problem difficulty is unrelated to any capabilities of the program, and depends only on the number of moves
Difficulty relates to what capabilities a program has; solvability can be estimated from its structure
Solvability can only be known after the subjects have tried
Difficulty is a property of the subjects and not of the problem, and varies with their intelligence
optionExplain: They claim a relation.
These are their closing claims.
They claim it can be estimated from the program's structure.
They relate it to the program's capabilities.
questions.explain: The theory predicts difficulty from what the program can and cannot do. Full statement: Relative problem difficulty is related to the presence or absence of particular capabilities in programs, and solvability can be estimated from the structure of the program.
questions.rule: Difficulty and solvability follow from program structure.
questions.teaches: The authors say they have shown how relative problem difficulty is related to the presence or absence of particular capabilities in programs, and how the solvability of a problem can be estimated from the structure of the program.

questions.q: A team has analyzed two tasks and now takes up a third. Which result of the third study would be most useful to them?
options: It repeats the first two analyses exactly, with no change at all
It confirms or corrects the first two analyses and also exposes some new mechanisms
It shows that the first two analyses apply to no other task
It replaces the earlier methods with a wholly different set of tools and concepts
optionExplain: Exact repetition would add confidence but no new knowledge.
A new task can test old claims and add new phenomena at once.
That would be a limit on the earlier work, not a gain from the third.
Replacing the apparatus is not what comparing tasks aims at.
questions.explain: A further task serves both as a check and as a source of discovery. The card shows how the authors state this.
questions.rule: Use a new task to check and to discover.

questions.q: In the chess part the authors say one function is to ____ or qualify the analyses of the previous parts.
questions.explain: The part is meant to confirm or qualify the earlier analyses as well as to find new phenomena.
questions.rule: Confirm or qualify the earlier work.

questions.q: A researcher finds that chess players use a heuristic not seen in logic or cryptarithmetic. By the authors' test, what should she ask next?
options: Whether it fits the specialized frameworks built for the earlier tasks in logic and cryptarithmetic
Whether it can be removed so chess looks like the earlier tasks
Whether it was already named in a book on chess openings
Whether it can be described with the basic apparatus of information processing systems
optionExplain: The authors say that is not the question.
Removing new phenomena would hide what the new task shows.
Chess literature is not the test used here.
The test is description by the Part I apparatus, not a match with earlier frameworks.
questions.explain: New phenomena are welcome; what matters is whether the basic apparatus can describe them.
questions.rule: Describe new phenomena with the basic apparatus.

questions.q: True or false: If chess turns out to need a mechanism that logic did not, the authors would count this as a failure of their approach.
questions.explain: They expect novelties and ask only whether the basic apparatus can describe them.
questions.rule: Novelty is expected, not a failure.

questions.q: True or false: The authors assume of their readers only some familiarity with a board game such as checkers, tic-tac-toe or Go, not that they are chess players.
questions.explain: They assume only some familiarity with a board game such as checkers, tic-tac-toe or Go.
questions.rule: Aim at readers of problem solving, not of chess.
questions.teaches: The authors do not assume readers are or want to become chess players; they assume familiarity with some board game such as checkers, tic-tac-toe or Go.

questions.q: A cooking study moves from baking to grilling. Which lesson from the authors' move from logic to chess applies?
options: A task can bring out a mechanism more strongly than an earlier one, as logic did
Every later task brings out exactly the same mechanisms as the first
A later task can only repeat what the first task already showed
Mechanisms appear only in the first task and fade in later ones
optionExplain: The authors say logic revealed means-ends analysis and goal structuring more strongly than cryptarithmetic.
The authors expect each task to bring its own quota of new phenomena.
Logic showed more of some mechanisms than cryptarithmetic did.
No such fading is described.
questions.explain: Each task emphasizes different mechanisms, which is why several are studied.
questions.rule: Different tasks bring out different mechanisms.
questions.teaches: Logic revealed means-ends analysis and goal structuring more strongly than cryptarithmetic did, and similar novelties are expected from chess.

questions.q: A lab wants one game for studying how people solve problems. Which feature would make a game most useful for the study?
options: A small number of rules, so that every game ends within a few moves by either side
A random element that makes each result unpredictable
A well-defined goal and a very large record of strong play to compare against
A scoring system that changes from one game to the next, so the goal is unclear
optionExplain: Brevity makes a game easy to play, not rich in problem solving.
Randomness would blur the link between choice and result.
Clear goals and recorded play make behavior and programs comparable.
A changing score would remove the well-defined goal.
questions.explain: A good test task has a clear aim and plenty of comparison data. The card gives the authors' reasons.

questions.q: The authors say a game is attractive because its environment is relatively closed and well defined by its ____.
questions.explain: The rules close and define the environment of a game.

questions.q: A game has two top goals that cannot both be met: winning and drawing. According to the authors, how does this bear on the game's usefulness?
options: It spoils the game
It removes the competitive aspect, so subjects lose their motivation to take part
It is allowed: a well-defined goal may be several incompatible top goals
It means the game has no well-defined rules at all
optionExplain: The authors accept several top goals.
Competition is the source of motivation, and it remains.
The text notes that sometimes several top goals can be incompatible.
Rules and goals are separate matters.
questions.explain: A game's goal can still be well defined when it has several top goals.
questions.rule: Several top goals can still be well defined.

questions.q: True or false: If a person plays chess with no opponent present, the authors expect the competitive aspect to motivate the person anyway.
questions.explain: They say the competitive aspects can be relied upon, in our culture, to produce motivated subjects even when no opponent is present.
questions.rule: Competition motivates even without an opponent.

questions.q: According to the authors, what gives chess some of the flavor of everyday problem solving that theorem proving and puzzles lack?
options: Its irregularity: odd piece moves, castling, and strong effects of the board edges
Its regularity: every piece moves in the same simple way
Its short length: most games end within a few minutes
Its use of chance: dice decide which piece may move
optionExplain: They name these peculiarities as the irregularity of chess.
The authors describe the opposite.
Length is not given as a reason.
Chess has no element of chance in this account.
questions.explain: Irregular structure resembles messy, ordinary problems more than neat puzzles do.
questions.teaches: The authors say the irregularity of chess (odd piece moves, castling, strong boundary effects of the board edges) gives it some of the flavor of everyday problem solving that theorems and puzzles lack.

questions.q: A new game is proposed as a study task: strong players take about ten years to peak, and new ideas still appear after two centuries. What does this support?
options: The claim that the game is easy to program on a small machine of the time
The claim that the game's rules are irregular
The claim that the game has been exhausted by analysis and holds no new ideas
The claim that the game is a difficult task with unlimited depth
optionExplain: Difficulty of play does not mean ease of programming.
That is a separate reason, about structure.
The authors say chess has not become barren or exhausted.
Long mastery and continuing innovation are the authors' evidence of difficulty for chess.
questions.explain: Years to mastery and continuing innovation signal real difficulty.
questions.teaches: The authors say professionals seldom reach their peak with less than ten years' experience, and that after 200 years master play still introduces new tactics, strategy and concepts.

questions.q: In a board game, what would you call the 'operators' that take you from one situation to the next?
options: The players who take turns at the board
The legal moves allowed by the rules
The final results: win, lose or draw
The pieces standing on the board at one time
optionExplain: Players choose among operators; they are not operators.
Operators are the steps the rules permit.
Results mark terminal positions, not steps.
The arrangement of pieces is a position, not a step.
questions.explain: Operators are steps; positions are what they act on. The card gives the authors' wording.
questions.rule: Moves are operators; positions are elements.

questions.q: In the basic problem space of a game, the elements are board configurations, called ____.
questions.explain: The elements of the space are positions, and the legal moves connect them.

questions.q: In tic-tac-toe, which item is a terminal position in the sense used here?
options: A board on which one player has three in a row
The empty board before the first mark is made
A board with two marks on it and the game still open
The rule that players take turns
optionExplain: The rules let us recognize this position as a win or loss, so it ends the game.
That is the starting position.
A position that is not yet decided is not terminal.
A rule is not a position.
questions.explain: Terminal positions are the ones the rules identify as win, lose or draw.
questions.rule: Terminal means decided by the rules.

questions.q: True or false: If a player considers every legal move at every position, the positions and moves together form the game tree.
questions.explain: The game tree is generated by taking all legal moves at each position.
questions.rule: All legal moves at each position make the game tree.

questions.q: Who, according to the authors' note, is credited with first formalizing the game tree, and when?
options: Shannon, in 1949, in his paper on chess-playing programs and their evaluation
Turing, in 1953, in his hand-simulated program
Samuel, in 1959, in his work on checkers
Zermelo, in 1912, though the idea had been used informally much earlier
optionExplain: Shannon's paper comes later and concerns programs.
Turing's program is described later in the chapter.
Samuel is cited for the term ply.
The note gives Zermelo and 1912, and informal use much earlier.
questions.explain: The idea is old in practice and recent in formal terms.
questions.rule: Informal use came long before the formal concept.
questions.teaches: The concept of the game tree was apparently first formalized by Zermelo in 1912, though books on chess and checkers used it informally several hundred years earlier.

questions.q: A player plays a game vicariously but exactly, in her head, move by move. In what space does she move?
options: A space of plans, which the rules of the game do not define and each player must devise
The same basic space of positions and legal moves in which the game itself moves
A space of proofs, as in a logic task
A space of opponents' habits, which she must learn first
optionExplain: The basic space is defined by the rules.
The authors say any problem solver who plays vicariously but exactly also moves in this space.
Proof spaces belong to theorem proving.
The basic space does not depend on the opponent's habits.
questions.explain: Exact mental play is play in the real game space, only without the pieces.
questions.rule: Exact mental play uses the game's own space.
questions.teaches: The game itself moves in the basic problem space, and any problem solver who plays vicariously but exactly also moves in this space.

questions.q: To show that a move wins, what must you be able to do that a proof does not require?
options: Find a single line of play that ends in your victory if the opponent cooperates
Show that the opponent has no legal reply at all
Answer every reply the opponent could make, not only one line of play
Play out the whole game from the start position
optionExplain: One line only shows a win if the opponent cooperates.
Opponents usually have replies; a win handles them.
A win must hold against all replies.
A win is shown from the position at hand.
questions.explain: A proof is one successful path; a win is a strategy against any reply. The card names this the minimax property.
questions.rule: A win must survive every reply.

questions.q: A proof is a definite plan, while a win is a ____ that sets out a tree of paths for all possible moves of the opponent.
questions.explain: A win is a strategy, because it must cover each possible reply.

questions.q: A friend says: I found a line where I win if my opponent plays badly. According to the authors, why does this not yet show a winning move?
options: Because winning lines must contain at least ten moves
Because only the opponent can prove that a move wins
Because a line of play is not a path in the game tree but only a single position
A winning move needs a continuation for each opponent reply, not for one reply
optionExplain: Length is not part of the definition.
Proof by the opponent is not part of this definition.
A line is a path; it just covers one reply.
The subtree must cover every reply for the player to be sure of winning.
questions.explain: One path is a plan; a win needs a tree of paths.
questions.rule: A win needs all replies covered.

questions.q: True or false: In the authors' account, a proof is a single path, whereas a winning strategy is a subtree with the minimax property.
questions.explain: A proof is a single path; a winning strategy is a subtree with the minimax property.
questions.rule: Path for proofs, subtree for wins.

questions.q: According to the authors' footnote, which kind of tree in theorem proving is a closer analogy to game search trees than the trees used in the Logic Theorist?
options: The or trees that the Logic Theorist used
The and-or trees used in some theorem provers
The trees of propositions built by working backwards
The lattices that arise when operators have two inputs
optionExplain: The note says the and-or trees are the closer analogy.
Correct: the footnote names the and-or trees used in some theorem provers as the closer analogy than the or trees of LT.
Those are what LT's tree contains, not a closer analogy.
A lattice differs from a tree and is not the analogy offered.
questions.explain: The footnote says the and-or trees used in some theorem provers are a closer analogy to game search trees than the or trees used in LT.
questions.rule: And-or trees are the closer analogy.
questions.teaches: In theorem proving a closer analogy to game search trees is provided by the and-or trees used in some theorem provers than by the or trees used in the Logic Theorist.

questions.q: A negotiator plans three offers and says she will adapt to whatever the other side replies. Which structure does her plan resemble?
options: A proof, because it is one definite path from start to goal
A single line of play that assumes the best possible replies
A strategy setting out what to do after each possible reply
A terminal position, because the plan has no further steps
optionExplain: She does not fix one path; her plan depends on replies.
She prepares for different replies, not one.
It is a tree of paths for each reply, like a win in a game.
A plan to adapt is not a position.
questions.explain: Planning for replies is the mark of a strategy.
questions.rule: Plans that branch on replies are strategies.
questions.teaches: Because a win is a strategy over all the opponent's replies, the authors say the difference from a proof has important consequences for the nature of game-playing heuristics.

questions.q: In a game of chess, what do the legal moves at a given moment depend on?
options: Only the current position on the board
The current position and a second position held in reserve
The history of every earlier move in the game
The opponent's plan, which is hidden from the player
optionExplain: In chess the legal moves are a function of the current position.
Moves in chess do not take two positions as input.
Legal moves follow from the position, not the history, apart from special rights.
Plans do not define legal moves.
questions.explain: In chess each move is generated from one position. The card contrasts this with logic.
questions.rule: Chess: one position in, one position out.

questions.q: In logic, a rule such as ____ can take more than one expression as input.
questions.explain: Detachment uses two expressions, such as a conditional and its antecedent.

questions.q: A game is defined so that a move combines two pieces on the board into one. Which description of its basic space matches the authors' contrast?
options: Like chess: the legal moves are always a function of one position, so it is a plain tree
Like logic: operators with several inputs make the space more like a web or lattice
Like cryptarithmetic: it is a tree with one input per step
Like no known task: such an operator cannot be defined
optionExplain: Combining two pieces gives two inputs.
The authors tie the web shape to operators that take more than one input.
The text says cryptarithmetic operators have a single input.
Logic has exactly such operators.
questions.explain: Several inputs per operator turn a tree into a web.

questions.q: True or false: If every logic operator took only one expression as input, the space would lose the web-like character that the authors describe.
questions.explain: The web shape comes from operators with more than one input.
questions.rule: One input per operator gives a tree.

questions.q: The authors say that cryptarithmetic differs from logic in this respect. How?
options: Its operators combine several digits into one result, so its space is a web like logic's
Its operators depend on the opponent's last move
Its space is the same as chess, with alternate players making each of the moves
Its operators do not take more than one input, so its space is not a web
optionExplain: That is the logic case.
Cryptarithmetic has no opponent.
Only games have alternate players.
They contrast logic with cryptarithmetic: only logic has operators that depend on more than one expression.
questions.explain: Cryptarithmetic resembles chess in having single-input operators, but it has no opponent.
questions.teaches: The authors say that in logic, though not in cryptarithmetic, the operators can depend on more than one logic expression as input.

questions.q: A planner can schedule a task only after two other tasks are both done. Which basic-space feature does this match?
options: An operator whose inputs are several earlier results, as with detachment
A move whose legality depends on one position only
A terminal position recognized by the rules
An alternation of moves between two opposing players, as in any game tree
optionExplain: Needing two earlier results is the multi-input pattern.
The task has two prerequisites, not one.
The case is about inputs, not endings.
The case has no opponent.
questions.explain: Prerequisites turn a chain into a web.
questions.teaches: Because logic operators can take several inputs, the authors describe the proof space as a web or lattice, in contrast with the tree of chess.

questions.q: A program chooses chess moves. Is it certain that it must search the tree of legal moves to do so?
options: Yes: choosing a move is the same thing as searching the game tree of legal moves
Yes, but only if it plays against a human opponent
No: a program could choose moves by other means, though most do search
No: no real chess program searches the game tree at all and none ever has
optionExplain: The authors say the two are not the same.
The opponent does not change the point.
Searching the game tree is common but not essential.
Most real programs do search it.
questions.explain: Most programs search; none must. The card says what the authors claim.

questions.q: In most game-playing programs of the time, problem solving was a search out along some or all branches of the ____ tree.
questions.explain: The authors say this holds for most extant programs, though it is not essential.

questions.q: True or false: A designer builds a chess program that picks moves by pattern recognition with no search of continuations. The authors would call such a game player wholly conceivable.
questions.explain: They say a game player that does not search in the game tree is wholly conceivable.

questions.q: Which statement about the Logic Theorist's subproblem tree is correct according to the authors?
options: It is a tree of theorems, each one proved from the one above it by a rule of inference
It is the same thing as the tree of legal chess moves
A tree of propositions from which the theorem can be derived, built backwards
It is a tree of the opponent's possible replies
optionExplain: The authors say it is not a tree of theorems.
The three trees are distinct.
It is not a tree of theorems.
LT has no opponent.
questions.explain: LT works back from the goal, so its tree holds propositions that would suffice.

questions.q: Who is cited for the idea of a game player that does not search the game tree at all?
options: Newman and Uhr, 1965
Samuel and Zermelo, 1959
Shannon, 1949
de Groot, 1965
optionExplain: The text cites Newman and Uhr as showing such a player is conceivable.
Zermelo is cited for the game tree.
Shannon described the search approach.
de Groot studied human chess players.
questions.explain: A non-searching player is not just a thought experiment, since it has been proposed.
questions.rule: Non-searching game players have been proposed.
questions.teaches: A game player that does not search in the game tree is wholly conceivable, and the authors cite Newman and Uhr (1965) for this, whereas it is impossible to conceive of a theorem prover that does not discover proofs.

questions.q: A route finder searches a list of landmarks, not the full road map. Which point in the authors' account does this illustrate?
options: The full space of legal steps must always be searched, whatever the program's design
A proof tree and a game tree are the same
A search can find only one path to the goal
The space a program searches can differ from the full space of legal steps
optionExplain: That is the claim the authors deny.
The authors keep them distinct.
That is unrelated to the space searched.
The authors say some schemes work in spaces other than the tree of legal moves.
questions.explain: The search space is a design choice and can differ from the basic space.
questions.rule: Searched space may differ from basic space.
questions.teaches: Some game-playing schemes operate in spaces larger than the tree of legal moves; the search tree is not forced to be the game tree.

questions.q: A prover and a chess player each explore many lines. What is the main difference in what they must finally produce?
options: The prover needs one step; the player needs the whole path
The prover must produce a whole path; the player must produce only a first move
Both must produce a whole path, but the player has less time in which to produce it
Neither needs to commit to anything until the whole search has ended and the game is over
optionExplain: This reverses the roles.
The prover's result is the path; the player's is a move.
A player commits only to a move.
A player's move, once made, is a commitment.
questions.explain: A proof is a full path; a game choice is the first step. The card explains why this matters.
questions.rule: Prover: a path. Player: a first move.

questions.q: In game playing, once a move has been selected and made, it cannot be ____ if it later proves wrong.
questions.explain: Moves are irreversible, which is the source of the first move's special role.

questions.q: A player searches ten plies deep and then makes her first move. After the reply, what may she do, according to the authors?
options: Reconsider her whole future path, since no line beyond the first move binds her
Continue along the line she explored
Take back the first move if the reply was unexpected
Ignore the reply, because the earlier search settled the game
optionExplain: After the opponent replies, the whole future path can be reconsidered.
She is not committed to the explored line.
A move cannot be undone.
The earlier search does not fix the later game.
questions.explain: Only the first move binds; the rest of the explored tree was information.

questions.q: True or false: If a prover explores a long blind alley, the only penalty is the cost of the search time.
questions.explain: In theorem proving there is no penalty for blind alleys other than the cost of search time.

questions.q: How does the authors' account describe the role of later moves in the game tree that a player explores?
options: They are explored in order to select a path to follow through the rest of the game
They are explored to prove that the game can be won
They are explored because rules forbid skipping them
They are explored only for the information they give about the first move
optionExplain: The player is not committed to any path beyond the first move.
A proof is not the aim.
No rule requires this.
Later moves serve to evaluate the initial move.
questions.explain: The tree is a source of evidence about the move, not a plan to be carried out.
questions.teaches: The moves after the first are explored not with the aim of selecting a path or strategy, but solely for the information they may contribute to the evaluation of the initial move.

questions.q: A traveler checks several onward routes before choosing a first road, but can re-plan at every junction. Which part of the authors' account fits this?
options: The traveler must follow the best explored route to the end
Routes beyond the first road are explored only for what they say about the first choice
The first road may be undone at no cost if it proves wrong
Only routes that lead to a proof of the destination are useful
optionExplain: The player is not committed beyond the first move.
The explored paths are information for the first choice only.
The first move is irreversible.
There is no proof of this kind.
questions.explain: Re-planning at each junction mirrors the game player's freedom after each reply.
questions.rule: Explore for the first step only.
questions.teaches: Because the player can reconsider the whole future after each reply, paths in the game tree are incidental to choosing a move, though they may have great informational value.

questions.q: Which standard of success fits a chess player choosing a move better than it fits a theorem prover?
options: Any move at all that does not break the rules
The move that is found first, whatever it is
The move must be the best one, or at least very good compared with the alternatives
The move that the opponent expects least
optionExplain: Legality is not the standard of success.
First found is not the standard, except in a special rule used later.
Games reward relative quality; proofs reward existence.
Surprise is not the standard set here.
questions.explain: A proof is good enough if it exists; a move is judged against others. The card explains the exception.

questions.q: In theorem proving, the task is to find a proof, and ____ one will do.
questions.explain: Any proof will do, whereas a move must be the best or very good.

questions.q: A player finds a move that wins whatever the opponent replies. According to the authors, what should she do about searching further?
options: She must keep searching until she finds the single best move among all the alternatives
She must search further
She must give up the win
She need search no further, unless she prefers one winning line for esthetic reasons
optionExplain: A forced win already settles the question.
A forced win is guaranteed against any reply.
The two are treated alike on this point.
A forced win ends the need for search, except for esthetic preference.
questions.explain: A forced win is the one exception to the need to compare moves.

questions.q: True or false: A move is judged suitable only in relation to an assessment of the other moves available.
questions.explain: Suitability is judged only in relation to an assessment of the other moves available.

questions.q: In what way, according to the authors, are a forced win and a proof treated alike?
options: Both require the solver to search every alternative before stopping, whatever has been found
Neither needs further search, though a taste for elegance may prefer another
Both can be reached only with the help of the opponent
Both are always unique, so there is nothing left to prefer between two solutions
optionExplain: The authors say further search is not needed.
The same esthetic qualification applies to both.
A forced win holds against the opponent's choice.
The text says one may prefer one to another.
questions.explain: Once success is guaranteed, only taste remains to choose among solutions.
questions.rule: Success guaranteed: stop, unless taste differs.
questions.teaches: Even a forced win or a proof may be followed by further search if esthetic criteria lead the solver to prefer one winning strategy (or one proof) to another.

questions.q: A buyer must pick a laptop and cannot be sure which is the best. By the authors' account of a game, what should the buyer aim for?
options: Any laptop that works, as in theorem proving where any proof will do
The first laptop seen, on the principle that the first is best
A very good choice, judged by comparing it with the alternatives
The most expensive laptop
optionExplain: That standard applies to proofs, not to games.
The first-found rule is a later heuristic, not the standard.
Where best cannot be guaranteed, a very good choice is the aim.
Price is not the criterion here.
questions.explain: Comparison against alternatives is what makes a choice good.
questions.teaches: If there is no way of guaranteeing the best move, the task in a game is to find at least a very good move.

questions.q: A program must pick a chess move but cannot reach the end of any game. Which approach is the natural one?
options: Look ahead a limited way, judge the end positions by their features, and pick the best
Wait until the search reaches a position that is certainly won
Copy the opponent's last move whenever that move is legal
Choose the move that leaves the most pieces on the board
optionExplain: Limited look-ahead plus judgment of positions is the scheme the card describes.
Terminal positions cannot be reached from most positions.
Copying uses no analysis of the position.
Counting pieces is one feature, not the whole approach.
questions.explain: Without terminal positions, a program must look ahead and then judge. The card names the steps.

questions.q: Because explorations cannot reach terminal positions, the positions reached are evaluated by the pattern of ____ on the chess board.
questions.explain: The evaluation of end positions uses the pattern of men on the board, called the static evaluation.
questions.rule: Evaluate end positions by their pattern.

questions.q: A program looks three moves ahead, scores each end position by material, and combines scores to pick a move. Which step of the scheme is the combining?
options: Exploring continuations to a certain depth
Minimaxing the static evaluations into an effective value
Evaluating the end positions by the pattern of men on the board
Generating all legal moves of the opponent in the position reached
optionExplain: That is the first step, the look-ahead itself.
Combining static evaluations by minimaxing is the third step of the analysis.
That is the second step, the scoring.
Move generation is part of exploring, not combining.
questions.explain: Explore, evaluate statically, then combine by minimaxing.

questions.q: True or false: A student writes: in Shannon's scheme the hard part is the analysis, not the final choice. The authors would agree.
questions.explain: They say the analysis, not the final choice, is the hard part.

questions.q: The authors use ply as a unit of depth, following Samuel. What does one ply mean?
options: A move together with the opponent's reply
One full search of the game tree from the current position to its end
One piece's journey from its start square to its end square in the game
A single move by one player; a move and its reply are two plies
optionExplain: That is the common use of move, which they avoid.
A ply is a unit of depth, not a whole search.
A ply is counted in moves, not in pieces.
They use ply for a single move, so move and reply are two plies.
questions.explain: Counting plies avoids the ambiguity of the word move.
questions.teaches: The authors count depth in ply, a single move, following Samuel (1959); the word move often means a move together with the opponent's reply, which is two plies.

questions.q: A historian says Shannon's 1949 paper gave the first chess program. Which correction fits the authors' note?
options: The first substantial analysis of chess programs, though it presented no particular program
It was the first working program, which beat strong players
It was a hand-simulation like Turing's, played against a weak opponent
It was a study of the fraudulent chess automata of earlier centuries and of the first computers
optionExplain: The note says this about Shannon's paper.
The paper presented no particular program.
The hand-simulated program is Turing's, of 1953.
The note mentions those automata only as older than the computer.
questions.explain: Shannon supplied the framework; the programs came after.
questions.teaches: Shannon's 1949 paper may be taken as the first substantial analysis of chess-playing programs, even though he presented no particular program there.

questions.q: A solver in a puzzle can wait until the final position appears. Why can a chess player not do the same?
options: Chess has no final position, so a player cannot aim at one
The rules forbid looking at positions beyond the next move
Moves are irreversible, and the final position is not in view when they must be chosen
An opponent hides the final position until it is reached
optionExplain: Chess has terminal positions, but they lie too far ahead to see.
No such rule exists.
A player must commit long before the end can be seen.
The difficulty is distance, not concealment.
questions.explain: Commitment comes before the end is visible; the card shows the consequence.
questions.rule: Commit first, see the end later.

questions.q: In chess programs the ____ acts as a complete surrogate for the ultimate, unforeseeable desired position.
questions.explain: The evaluation stands in for the final position that cannot yet be seen.

questions.q: A program must choose among moves by a simple count of material only. Which of the two new features is this count?
options: The procedure for inferring values from the opponent's choices
The forward search itself, which was already in logic
The evaluation, standing in for a goal that cannot be seen yet
The rule that moves cannot be undone once they have been made on the board
optionExplain: Minimaxing deals with the opponent; a count does not.
Forward search is the old feature.
A material count is a very simple surrogate for the final result.
That is a property of the task, not a program feature.
questions.explain: A count of material is an evaluation of the surrogate kind.
questions.rule: Count of material is an evaluation.

questions.q: True or false: The need for an evaluation comes from the irreversibility of moves, and the need for minimaxing from the two-person character of the game.
questions.explain: Evaluation follows from irreversibility, and minimaxing from the two-person character.

questions.q: According to the authors, what forces the second new feature, the procedure for inferring the effective values of moves?
options: The two-person character of the game
The commitment to irreversible moves
The size of the board
The use of a computer rather than a person
optionExplain: The opponent's choices must be allowed for in valuing a move.
That forces the evaluation, the first feature.
Size is not given as the reason.
The reason lies in the task, not the machine.
questions.explain: An opponent's replies must be allowed for, which is what minimaxing does.
questions.teaches: The complex procedure for inferring effective values is forced by the two-person character of the game.

questions.q: Two friends plan a long trip in stages: stages cannot be revisited, and a rival may take spots first. Which procedure would such a planner need, as chess programs do?
options: A way to undo the stages if they prove poor once the rival's plans are known
A way to ignore the rival
A way to reach the final stage in one step
A way to infer the value of a plan from the choices the rival could make
optionExplain: The stages cannot be undone.
A rival cannot be ignored.
That would remove the need to plan.
A rival forces valuing plans by allowing for the other side's choices.
questions.explain: Irreversibility calls for an evaluation, opposition for value inference.
questions.teaches: The particular procedure used, minimaxing, is basic to all the programs for playing chess.

questions.q: Two players alternate moves and each wants the best result. How should you value a position in which it is the opponent's turn?
options: By the best outcome for you among the opponent's choices, as the opponent is willing to give
By the worst outcome for you among the opponent's choices
By the average outcome over the opponent's choices
By the outcome of the first move the opponent considers
optionExplain: The opponent will not cooperate.
On the opponent's turn the opponent decides, so you take the minimum.
Averaging assumes random choices, not an opponent.
A good opponent does not take the first move that occurs to them.
questions.explain: On the opponent's turn the opponent decides. The card gives the full definition.
questions.rule: Take the minimum on the opponent's turn.

questions.q: In the minimax definition, best means the maximum when the player is to move and the ____ when the opponent is to move.
questions.explain: Best alternates between maximum and minimum, from which the name arises.
questions.rule: Max on own move, min on opponent's.

questions.q: In a small tree it is your move, with two options. Option 1 leads to a position worth 2 or 4, chosen by the opponent. Option 2 leads to one worth 1 or 9, chosen by the opponent. Which do you choose, and what is the value?
options: Option 1, with value 2
Option 2, with value 9
Option 1, with value 4
Option 2, with value 5
optionExplain: The opponent takes the minimum of each (2 and 1); you take the maximum of those, which is 2.
The opponent, not you, chooses between 1 and 9, and will not pick 9.
The opponent will not offer the 4.
No averaging is involved.
questions.explain: Minimum over the opponent's choices, then maximum over yours.
questions.rule: Min at the opponent's node, max at yours.

questions.q: True or false: If a position's values are restated from the opponent's viewpoint instead of the player's, the roles of maximum and minimum are exchanged.
questions.explain: Win, tie, loss and the function best are relative to the player, so the opponent's view swaps maximum and minimum.
questions.rule: Values are relative to the player.

questions.q: According to the authors' footnote, what might have been a better name than minimax, and why was it not used?
options: Backward search, because it works from the end positions toward the root of the tree
Alpha-beta, because it uses two limits
Minimin, because the opponent minimizes twice
Maximin, because it first maximizes then minimizes, but euphony is against it
optionExplain: No such renaming is proposed.
Alpha-beta is a different procedure.
The footnote proposes maximin.
The footnote says it probably should have been called maximin.
questions.explain: The order of the operations gives maximin, but the sound of minimax won.
questions.rule: Maximin in order, minimax in use.
questions.teaches: The authors say minimax probably should have been called maximin, since it is invariably applied in a situation which first maximizes and then minimizes, but euphony is against it.

questions.q: A tic-tac-toe player can see the whole game tree. According to the authors' remark about full trees, what does this make of the game for her?
options: A game that remains hard
A simple game, solved by working back from the end positions
A game with no best move
A game she can only win if she moves first
optionExplain: Minimaxing handles the opponent's best play.
For a player who sees the entire tree, chess (and similar games) becomes simple.
The terminal payoffs are determinate.
That depends on the game, not on the definition.
questions.explain: Full information plus backward values removes the difficulty; the size of the tree is what makes chess hard.
questions.rule: Seeing the whole tree makes the game easy.
questions.teaches: For a player who could view the entire tree and see all the ultimate consequences, chess would become a simple game, and the real difficulty is the size of the tree.

questions.q: You can take a sure draw, or a gamble that wins or loses depending on your opponent's choice. If the opponent plays perfectly, which should you take?
options: The gamble, because the possible win might be realized if the opponent makes an error
Either one, because the two have equal value
The sure draw, because a perfect opponent will turn the gamble into a loss
Neither, because every choice is equally risky
optionExplain: A perfect opponent would not allow it.
The gamble is worth a loss against a perfect opponent.
A skilled opponent picks the loss for you.
The draw carries no risk.
questions.explain: Against a perfect opponent a gamble is a loss. The card works this through.

questions.q: In the example, the value that White imputes to position X is a ____.
questions.explain: The best White can secure is a draw, so X is valued as a tie.

questions.q: Option A gives you a draw whatever happens. Option B gives your opponent the choice of your win or your loss. Option C gives you a loss whatever happens. Rank them, using the authors' reasoning.
options: B, then A, then C
A, then B, then C
A and B equal, then C
A, then B and C equal
optionExplain: This values B by its best case.
B is a loss, not better than C, if the opponent is skilled.
B is not as good as A, since the opponent will choose its worst case.
B is valued as a loss against a skilled opponent, the same as C.
questions.explain: Minimax values B at the opponent's choice, which is the loss.
questions.rule: B is worth your worst case.

questions.q: True or false: A commentator says: White's best move is W3, since it is the only one that offers a chance of winning. The authors would accept this.
questions.explain: With skilled play by Black the win from W3 is a chimera, and W1 is preferred.
questions.rule: A possible win is not a value.

questions.q: How is the value of position X reached in the example?
options: By averaging the six payoffs shown in the figure
By reasoning backwards from the known values of the terminal positions
By taking the value of the first move White considers
By asking which side has more pieces in position X
optionExplain: The figure has six terminal positions, and nothing is averaged.
White works back from the payoffs to the moves and then to X.
The first move considered is not the rule.
The example uses payoffs only.
questions.explain: Values flow backwards from the terminal positions to the root.
questions.rule: Back up values from the end.
questions.teaches: In the example White imputes a value to position X (here, tie) by reasoning backwards from known values, and can then select the best move from the position.

questions.q: A seller may offer a customer a fixed discount, or let the customer pick between a big discount and none, and the customer picks whatever helps the customer. How should the seller value the second offer?
options: As the average of big discount and none
As the big discount
As the no-discount outcome, since the customer picks whichever is worse for the seller
As unknowable, so it cannot be ranked
optionExplain: No average is used.
The seller does not make the choice.
The skilled chooser picks the worse outcome for the seller.
Against a skilled chooser it can be ranked.
questions.explain: When another party chooses, assume the choice is the one worst for you.
questions.rule: The other chooser takes your worst case.
questions.teaches: The authors use the phrase 'chimera' for the possible win of W3: an apparent prize that a skilled opponent will never allow to be realized.

questions.q: A program must choose among candidate moves by comparing their analyzed values. What simple repeated step does the choice need?
options: Compare each new value with the best so far, and replace the best when it is beaten
Sort all moves by name before analyzing any of them, and then take the first in the list
Play each candidate move on the real board in turn
Choose the move that is analyzed last
optionExplain: Comparison and replacement is how the best move emerges.
Sorting by name has no bearing on quality.
Real moves are irreversible.
Position in the order of analysis is not a measure of value.
questions.explain: Keeping the best so far is the core of the loop. The card gives the full outline.

questions.q: In the prototype, a position that passes the depth-termination test gets a ____ value, and analysis stops there.
questions.explain: At the depth limit, the static-value is computed and analysis ends.

questions.q: Put the steps find-move takes for one candidate move in order.
items: Make the base-move to reach the next position
Analyse the next position to get its value
Compare that value with the best value so far
Replace the best-move if the new value is better
Test width-termination to decide whether to continue
questions.explain: Find-move makes the move, has it analysed, compares and replaces if better, then tests whether to go on generating.

questions.q: Which of the prototype's two processes, find-move or analyse, has a depth-termination test, and why?
options: Find-move, because it decides when the game itself ends and who has won the game
Analyse, because it works on positions at various depths below the move
Both, because they are the same process in the prototype and share their tests
Neither, because depth is found by static-value
optionExplain: Find-move works at depth one and uses width-termination.
Analyse tests whether the position is terminal for the search.
They differ: find-move is the top level, analyse is recursive.
Depth-termination and static-value are separate processes.
questions.explain: Find-move handles the first level; analyse handles deeper levels.

questions.q: How many processes does the prototype leave undefined, and what do they include?
options: Two: find-move and analyse
Three: the generators and the minimax rule
Four: material, mobility, development and center control, which are the evaluation terms
Six: base-moves, analysis-moves, the two terminations, static-value and adjusted-value
optionExplain: Those two are defined in the prototype.
The minimax rule is built in.
Those are features of particular evaluation functions.
These six define a particular program.
questions.explain: Fill in the six and the prototype becomes a specific program.
questions.teaches: Six processes are left undefined in the prototype (base-moves, analysis-moves, width-termination, depth-termination, static-value, adjusted-value), and existing chess programs can be specified almost completely by defining them.

questions.q: A designer wants the search to look deeper in lively positions and shallower in quiet ones. Which process of the prototype should she change?
options: Depth-termination, which decides whether to stop at a position
Adjusted-value, which only changes the final reported value of the best move
Base-moves, which are used only at the top level, so the depth is unaffected
Find-move, which does not call any of the six
optionExplain: That test controls how deep the search goes at each position.
Adjusted-value does not decide where the search stops.
Base-moves choose the first-level alternatives.
Find-move calls the undefined processes.
questions.explain: Where to stop is a decision of depth-termination.
questions.teaches: Both the depth of a position in the search tree and the order of generation of its moves (called the width) are used frequently in deciding how to terminate search, and the prototype assumes they are available automatically.

questions.q: Two players are halfway through trading pieces. When is it sensible to count material to judge the position?
options: Right now, since the count is the same at every moment
Only at the start of the game, before any trade
After the trade is carried through, when the count will not change on the next move
After the next trade begins
optionExplain: Mid-exchange the count is about to change.
The count is needed during play.
A count taken mid-trade is misleading.
The count is meaningful only when stable.
questions.explain: A stable position can be judged at once; a changing one cannot. The card names this idea.

questions.q: Turing called a position that is stable enough to be evaluated without further search a ____ position.
questions.explain: A dead position needs no further search before its static evaluation.

questions.q: Turing's program reaches a position where a Queen has been captured and a recapture is possible. Is the position dead?
options: Yes: the capture has been made, so material can now be counted and compared
Yes: all Queen positions are dead by definition
No: the exchange is not carried through, so exploration should continue
No: nothing in chess is ever stable enough to be called dead, so none exists
optionExplain: The recapture will change the count.
Deadness is about stability, not a piece type.
A recapture would change the material, so the position is not dead.
Many positions are dead.
questions.explain: Pending recaptures keep a position live.

questions.q: True or false: If every position reached in the search were dead, Turing's program would explore only the opponent's immediate replies.
questions.explain: Further moves beyond depth one were generated only from positions that were not dead.

questions.q: At depths beyond the first, which kinds of continuation did Turing's program consider?
options: Recaptures, captures of an undefended or higher-valued man, and checkmates
All legal moves, as at the first depth, so that the tree grows without limit
Only moves that advance a pawn toward promotion
Moves chosen at random from those available
optionExplain: These are the analysis-moves for depth greater than one.
At depth one only were all legal moves used.
Pawn advances are not listed.
The continuations are specific, not random.
questions.explain: Only forcing captures and mates keep the exploration going.
questions.rule: Only forcing moves continue the search.
questions.teaches: For depth greater than one, Turing's analysis-moves were only recaptures, captures of an undefended man, captures of a higher-valued man and checkmates, and analysis stopped if none was generated.

questions.q: A photographer calls a scene ready when nothing in it is about to move. Which term do the authors say suits Turing's dead position better?
options: Stationary or frozen, because pieces do not move
Terminal, since the search ends there
Stable-tree, because the whole tree is fixed
Quiet or quiescent, though these are seldom used
optionExplain: Those terms are not suggested.
A terminal position is a different idea: one decided by the rules.
No such term is offered.
The footnote says quiet or quiescent would have been better terms.
questions.explain: The idea is of a quiet position, with no pending changes.
questions.teaches: The authors say quiet or quiescent would have been better terms for a dead position, but they are seldom used.

questions.q: Two moves tie on material. One gives a better position. How should a program that ranks material first treat them?
options: Prefer the move found first
Prefer the better position, since position counts only when material is equal
Add material and position together and prefer the larger sum of the two scores
Reject both moves, since neither is better in material
optionExplain: Position still matters on a tie of material.
Material decides unless it is equal; then position breaks the tie.
That is a weighted sum, not ranking.
A tie is broken, not rejected.
questions.explain: Ranking in order is the lexicographic idea. The card names it.
questions.rule: First component decides; later ones break ties.

questions.q: Turing's evaluations were compared ____: material dominates, and position counts only if material is the same.
questions.explain: The comparison is lexicographic, like alphabetical order.

questions.q: Move A gains one pawn but leaves a poor position. Move B keeps material level and has a splendid position. Under Turing's rule, which is preferred?
options: Move A, since material dominates
Move B, since the position outweighs a single pawn
Neither, since the two trade off against each other
Move B, since it was analyzed later
optionExplain: A single extra pawn outweighs any positional difference in a lexicographic order.
Position counts only when material is equal.
There is no trade-off in the rule.
Order of analysis is not part of the rule.
questions.explain: Material first, position only on equal material.

questions.q: True or false: A reader says Turing's static value was limited to material, with position considered only at depth one. The authors would agree.
questions.explain: The static value was limited to material, with position considered only at depth one.

questions.q: Why did Turing's program let the static value of the position itself act as one more candidate?
options: Because every legal move was analyzed, so the static value served only as a final check
Because material is always worth more than any move
Because the position-value cannot be computed for moves
Because only a subset of moves was usually analyzed, so standing still could be best
optionExplain: When all moves were considered, the best-value was used.
The authors do not say this.
Position-value is computed at depth one.
With a subset, the static value of the position is a candidate for best.
questions.explain: With only some moves tried, the unmoved position may beat all of them.
questions.rule: Static value is one more candidate.
questions.teaches: Turing's adjusted-value is the best dynamic value if all legal moves were considered, and otherwise the better of the static-value and the best-value.

questions.q: In Turing's material values a Knight counts 3 and a Bishop 3.5. If a side swaps its Knight for the opponent's Bishop, what happens to its material component?
options: It rises by half a point
It falls by half a point, because it gives up the piece with the higher value
It stays the same
It falls by two points, as for a Rook
optionExplain: In his scheme the Bishop is worth more.
Giving a 3.5 piece for a 3 loses 0.5.
His values separate the two.
A Rook counts 5, not 3.5 or 3.
questions.explain: The material component adds and subtracts the piece values.
questions.teaches: In Turing's scheme the piece values were P=1, N=3, B=3.5, R=5 and Q=10, so the Queen counted for more than in the NSS program, where it was worth 9.

questions.q: A program built with careful limits on how far it explores is played against a weak but unfamiliar human. What result is most likely?
options: It plays brilliantly because the limits remove all errors from its choices
It cannot make a legal move at all
It plays poorly and loses, though it may put up some resistance
It wins easily, since a program cannot be tired and never makes a blunder
optionExplain: Limits do not remove blunders.
It played legal moves.
That is what happened with Turing's program.
It lost.
questions.explain: A heavily limited search yields weak play. The card gives the authors' verdict.

questions.q: Turing's program lost to a weak human player who ____ know the program.
questions.explain: The opponent was a weak player unfamiliar with the program.

questions.q: A reviewer notes that most of the factors in the program's position-value hardly ever changed its choice. What does this show, in the authors' words?
options: The evaluation was perfect, so no change was ever needed to its choices
The factors were never computed during play
The program had no material count to compare moves, so it chose them blindly
The subtleties of the evaluation function were lost on the program
optionExplain: The program played badly.
They were computed but seldom mattered.
It had a material count that dominated.
Most of the many factors rarely influenced the move chosen.
questions.explain: With material dominating, the finer factors mattered only on ties.

questions.q: True or false: The authors judge that Turing's program reached only the bottom rung of the ladder of human play.
questions.explain: They say it reached only the bottom rung of the ladder of human play.

questions.q: What do the authors say about hand simulation of a program, with Turing's play as an example?
options: It is objectionable in principle
It is not objectionable in principle, but it is almost always inexact for complex programs
It is exact, so Turing's loss shows the program's real strength
It is exact for simple programs and impossible for complex ones
optionExplain: They see no a priori objection.
The footnote reports errors from the human simulator.
They say it was inexact.
They say inexact, not impossible.
questions.explain: A human simulating a program tends to shortcut it.
questions.teaches: Turing's play of his program contains an error: the human simulator, unwilling to consider all alternatives, skipped moves he knew would be eliminated anyway, and once failed to pick the move the program called for.

questions.q: A school tests a new method by having one teacher follow the method by hand. Following the authors' footnote, what is a risk?
options: The method cannot be tested by hand at all
The teacher will follow every step exactly, so errors in the test are impossible
The teacher may shortcut steps she thinks unnecessary, so the test drifts
A hand test always makes the method look better
optionExplain: They see no a priori objection.
Experience shows hand simulation is almost always inexact.
The human simulator in Turing's case did just this.
Nothing of the sort is claimed.
questions.explain: A hand test is only as exact as the person doing it.
