questions.rule: Hand tests drift from the rules.
questions.teaches: Hand simulation of a program is, by experience, almost always inexact for programs of any complexity.

questions.q: A programmer wants the simplest chess program that fits the common scheme. Which design is that?
options: Try every legal move to a fixed depth and judge the end positions by a count
Try a few moves chosen by many special rules, searching without limit
Copy the master's moves from a book of games
Pick the move the opponent made last time
optionExplain: No selectivity and a simple evaluation is the simplest type.
Special rules and variable depth are sophisticated features.
A book of moves is not a search scheme.
That uses no analysis.
questions.explain: The simplest design applies one rule everywhere. The card describes the Los Alamos version.

questions.q: The Los Alamos program explored all continuations to a depth of four ____, two moves for each side.
questions.explain: Four plies is two moves by White and two by Black.

questions.q: Which pair of measures made up the static evaluation of the Los Alamos program?
options: Material and development
Material and mobility
Center control and pawn structure
King safety and area control
optionExplain: Development was a goal of the NSS program.
The sum was of a material measure and a mobility measure.
These were used in other programs.
These were in the Bernstein evaluation.
questions.explain: Material plus mobility was all it used.

questions.q: True or false: The Los Alamos program considered all legal moves at each position; selectivity came in with Bernstein's program.
questions.explain: It considered all legal moves; selectivity came in with Bernstein's program.

questions.q: On what board and machine did the first Los Alamos program run, and what happened to the later 8 by 8 version's details?
options: An 8 by 8 board on MANIAC I; the details of that program were published in 1958
A 6 by 6 board on MANIAC II; the first program was never run on any machine at all
An 8 by 8 board on an IBM 704; the details were published
A 6 by 6 board on MANIAC I; the 8 by 8 version's details were never published
optionExplain: The 8x8 version was for MANIAC II.
The 6x6 program ran on MANIAC I.
The IBM 704 was Bernstein's machine.
The 1956 program used a 6x6 board; the 1958 program for MANIAC II was never fully published.
questions.explain: The reduced board was a concession to the machine of 1956.
questions.rule: 6x6 on MANIAC I, 8x8 on MANIAC II.
questions.teaches: In 1956 the Los Alamos group programmed MANIAC I to play on a 6 by 6 board, and in 1958 a revised program was written for MANIAC II for the regular 8 by 8 board, whose details were never published.

questions.q: A designer of a minimal chess program wants to reward mobility, as the Los Alamos program did. Where is the mobility score added?
options: To the best dynamic value, as an adjustment to the pure minimax value
To the opponent's replies, before any minimaxing is done on the position
To the move list, to decide which moves are generated for the later search
Nowhere: mobility is only used to end the search
optionExplain: That is the Los Alamos adjustment.
The adjustment is made to the best value found.
All moves were generated; none were selected by mobility.
Termination used the depth of four plies.
questions.explain: The adjustment sits at the end of the analysis, not in the move list.
questions.rule: Mobility is added to the best value.
questions.teaches: The Los Alamos adjusted-value is the best dynamic value plus the intermediate mobility score, the program's one departure from pure minimaxing.

questions.q: A position has about 30 legal moves. About how many sequences of four plies start from it?
options: About 120
About 9,000
Close to a million
About a billion continuations
optionExplain: That adds 30 four times instead of multiplying.
That multiplies only three of the four plies.
30 x 30 x 30 x 30 = 810,000, almost a million.
That overstates it by a factor of more than a thousand.
questions.explain: Growth by multiplication is fast. The card gives the authors' figure.

questions.q: On average about ____ legal alternatives are available at each move in chess, according to the authors.
questions.explain: The authors give about 30 legal alternatives per move.

questions.q: At about 810,000 continuations in 600 seconds, roughly how long can the program spend on each continuation?
options: About one second
About ten milliseconds
Less than one millisecond
About a minute for each one
optionExplain: That would take over nine days for the whole move.
That would take over two hours.
600 s divided by 810,000 is about 0.74 ms.
That would take many months.
questions.explain: Divide the time by the count.
questions.rule: Time per item = time divided by count.

questions.q: True or false: If the program were made twice as complicated per position, ten minutes per move would still allow the same depth with the same speed.
questions.explain: A more complicated evaluation costs more time per position, so the budget per continuation would not suffice.
questions.rule: More work per position, less depth.

questions.q: How were the two measures of the evaluation obtained so cheaply?
options: Captures show material changes, and mobility counts the new positions reached
From a stored table of values for every position
From a separate deep analysis of each piece, made before the search
From the opponent's last move alone
optionExplain: Both measures fall out of exploring the continuations.
No table is mentioned.
That would be costly.
The measures use the continuations.
questions.explain: The search itself supplies the data for the evaluation.
questions.teaches: In the Los Alamos program, material changes are noticed if the moves are captures, and the mobility score for a position is the number of new positions to which it leads, computed almost without effort when exploring all continuations.

questions.q: A scanner checks a million items and has ten minutes. Which design principle follows from the authors' Los Alamos arithmetic?
options: Use an elaborate test for each item, to ensure accuracy, and accept a longer total run
Examine only a hundred items and ignore the others
Run the test for ten minutes on a single item
Make the per-item process very simple, so that it barely glances at each item
optionExplain: That would exceed the time budget.
That would be selectivity, which this design lacks.
That would leave the rest unexamined.
The processor barely glances at each position, as the arithmetic requires.
questions.explain: A large count forces a cheap step.
questions.teaches: The MANIAC code for the Los Alamos program was only about 600 instructions long, which the authors present as a consequence of the need to process each position so quickly.

questions.q: A program does very little per position but explores everything. Another explores very little but studies each position. What would you expect of either at the extreme?
options: Both would play at the master level, by different routes
Both would play weakly, perhaps at a beginner's level
The first would play well and the second poorly
Neither could make a legal move
optionExplain: The extremes do not reach master level.
That is the authors' conclusion about the extremes.
Both extremes are weak.
Both made legal moves.
questions.explain: The extremes are anchor points; the card explains what they show.

questions.q: Turing's program minimizes the amount of ____ of continuations, while the Los Alamos program minimizes information per position.
questions.explain: Turing's is the extreme of little exploration.

questions.q: A program explores only three positions but studies each at great length. Which anchor point is it nearer to?
options: Turing's, which minimizes the exploration of continuations
Los Alamos, which minimizes the information used per position
Neither, because the anchor points concern board size
Both equally, because they play at the same level
optionExplain: Little exploration is the Turing extreme.
That extreme studies each position very little.
They concern exploration and information, not size.
Equal level does not mean equal design.
questions.explain: Which resource is minimized tells the extreme.
questions.rule: Match the resource that is minimized.

questions.q: True or false: The authors conclude that a program at either extreme is certain to be unable to play above a beginner's level.
questions.explain: They say the extremes throw doubt on prospects of rising far above that level; they do not claim certainty.

questions.q: What do the authors say about the blunders of the Los Alamos programs?
options: The blunders show that the programs were broken machines, not weak players of chess
The blunders appeared only when the programs played White
Human experts make the same blunders as often
Serious blunders are a common characteristic also of inexperienced human players
optionExplain: They treat the programs as weak players.
Nothing of the sort is said.
The comparison is with inexperienced players.
They compare the programs' blunders to those of human beginners.
questions.explain: Beginner-level play includes beginner-like errors.
questions.teaches: The MANIAC programs were susceptible to serious blunders, a characteristic also common to inexperienced human players.

questions.q: A sports club tries two cheap training plans: practicing one drill endlessly, or watching one video. Both stall at beginner level. What does the authors' conclusion suggest?
options: Either plan will reach the top if it is kept up for long enough
Progress needs effort combined with selectivity rather than either extreme
Selectivity alone is worth nothing without a lot of time
Beginner level is the highest any system can reach
optionExplain: The authors doubt that the extremes can rise far.
The authors say later systems combined power with selectivity.
They present the combination, not one factor alone.
They say only that extremes are unlikely to rise far.
questions.explain: Neither extreme alone suffices; later programs combined the two.
questions.teaches: All systems constructed after Turing's and the Los Alamos programs have attempted to combine computing power, absent from Turing's hand simulation, with appropriate selectivity, absent from the Los Alamos programs.

questions.q: A program may look at only seven of about thirty legal moves. What would be a sensible way to pick the seven?
options: Take the first seven moves in the order the rules list them
Take seven moves at random
Use rules tied to features of the game, most important first, until seven are chosen
Take the seven moves that move the fewest pieces
optionExplain: Rule-list order has no link to the merit of a move.
Random choice ignores what is known of good chess.
That is the plausible-move idea the card describes.
Moving few pieces is not a sign of quality.
questions.explain: Selectivity needs a reason for each move chosen. The card shows the authors' version.

questions.q: Bernstein's program considers at most ____ alternatives at a position, collected by running the generators in priority order.
questions.explain: The generators are run until seven moves are accumulated.

questions.q: In Bernstein's program the King is in check. Which generator should supply moves first?
options: Development, since it is the key aim of the opening and so the first concern
Pawn moves, since they are always legal
Occupancy of open files, to prepare a later attack
King-safety, which is first in the priority order when the King is in check
optionExplain: Development comes after King safety, material and castling.
Pawn moves are among the last generators.
That generator is lower in priority.
The first generator in the figure deals with King safety if the King is in check.
questions.explain: The most urgent feature is served first.

questions.q: Put these four of Bernstein's generators in priority order, most important first.
items: King-safety (if the King is in check)
Material gain, loss or exchange
Castling
Minor piece development
questions.explain: The figure lists King safety first, then material, castling and minor-piece development.

questions.q: True or false: Bernstein's evaluation function was the ratio of two sums, one for White and one for Black, each made of four weighted factors.
questions.explain: The four factors were material, King defense, area control and mobility.
questions.teaches: Bernstein's evaluation function is the ratio of two sums, one for White and one for Black, each of four weighted factors: material, King defense, area control and mobility.

questions.q: A hospital triage nurse checks the most urgent signs first and stops when seven patients are queued for the doctor. Which feature of Bernstein's program does this resemble?
options: Searching every candidate to the end of the game
Running generators in priority order until a fixed number of candidates is collected
Choosing candidates by adding up all factors at once
Replacing the candidates after each result is known, whatever the order of the rules
optionExplain: Bernstein's program searches four plies, not to the end.
Priority order plus a fixed cutoff is the pattern.
The generators are run in sequence, not summed.
The candidate list is fixed by the generators.
questions.explain: Priority and a cutoff are what give selectivity here.
questions.teaches: Bernstein's list of plausible move generators runs from King safety and material through castling, development, key squares and open files to pawn moves and piece moves, in that priority order.

questions.q: A program searches only 1 in 300 of the possible continuations yet still plays passably. What does this most suggest?
options: That most continuations in the game are of equal value, so any selection does as well
That the program must also be searching the others in secret, out of sight of its designers
That its way of selecting continuations picks out many of the useful ones
That the program has solved the game completely
optionExplain: Equal value would make any selection do as well.
The reduction is real.
Tolerable play after a large cut means the selection is effective.
It lost, and has never beaten anyone.
questions.explain: Good play with little search means the selection carries information. The card gives the authors' reading.
questions.rule: Good play on little search shows effective selection.

questions.q: Bernstein's selectivity cut the search by a factor of about ____, from roughly 800,000 continuations to about 2500.
questions.explain: The authors give a reduction in search by a factor of 300.

questions.q: Where does the information that makes the selection effective come from, according to the authors?
options: From the common and tested lore of the chess world, built into the generators
From a search of every continuation done before the game
From the opponent's moves, which the program learns from during play
From random choices that happen to favor good moves
optionExplain: The selections reflect the tested lore.
No such search is described.
The program does not learn.
Randomness is not the source.
questions.explain: The generators encode what chess players have learned.

questions.q: True or false: With such radical selection, the authors expect the program to be prone to overlook moves and consequences that a human would see.
questions.explain: They say such radical selection gives the program a strong proclivity to overlook moves and consequences.

questions.q: In one incomplete game the program kept a Bishop under attack by three successive pawn pushes. What went wrong?
options: The program had too little time and ran out of search depth
The pawn pushes were never proposed as plausible moves, so the program missed them
The Bishop was defended by too many pieces for the pushes to matter
The program gave the Bishop a value of zero in its evaluation
optionExplain: The cause was in the move generators.
The generators never offered those moves, so the threat was overlooked.
The Bishop was repeatedly attacked and forced to retreat.
Nothing of the sort is said.
questions.explain: What the generators do not propose, the program cannot see.
questions.teaches: In a game not shown, Bernstein's program stayed oblivious while a Bishop was attacked by three pawns in turn, retreating one square each time, because the successive pawn pushes were never proposed by the generators.

questions.q: An inspector checks only items that pass a set of expert warning signs. A fault that shows none of the signs is missed. Which point of the authors' account does this illustrate?
options: Selection always improves accuracy
Human inspectors never miss such faults
Search is always preferable to selection, whatever the cost in time and in effort
Radical selection can overlook a threat that none of its generators proposes
optionExplain: The authors show the opposite risk.
Human selection has checks and balances, not perfection.
The authors favor selectivity in the next ideas.
The Bishop-and-pawns case is the same pattern.
questions.explain: A selective procedure sees only what its selectors can express.
questions.teaches: The authors note that human selection on the chess board has checks and balances that the selective mechanisms in Bernstein's program lack.

questions.q: A new method reduces the number of items to examine by 300 times but makes each examination much costlier. What is the likely net effect on total time?
options: The gain may be partly or wholly cancelled by the extra cost per item
A gain of exactly 300 times, regardless of the cost per item
No change in the count of items
A loss of exactly 300 times
optionExplain: Savings in count are offset by cost per item.
The cost per item matters.
The count did fall.
Nothing guarantees a loss.
questions.explain: Total work is count times cost per item. The card gives the authors' estimate.

questions.q: Bernstein's program contains 7000 instructions, against 600 for the ____ program.
questions.explain: The program size is over ten times larger.

questions.q: On the authors' estimate, roughly how long does each of the two programs take per move on an IBM 360/65?
options: Bernstein's about 300 times less than Los Alamos
Los Alamos about ten times less than Bernstein's
About the same, near half a minute
Both in under a millisecond per move
optionExplain: That ignores the extra cost per position.
That compares only the program sizes.
Greater processing per position approximately cancels the saving in positions.
That is the time per continuation for Los Alamos.
questions.explain: Equal time per move is the authors' estimate.

questions.q: True or false: A reader claims that, because Bernstein's program searches 300 times fewer positions, it must play 300 times faster than the Los Alamos program. The authors would agree.
questions.explain: The extra processing per position approximately cancels the gain.
questions.rule: Fewer positions do not mean less time.

questions.q: How do the authors treat the comparison of the two programs' performance?
options: As exact, since each program had played hundreds of games against rated players
As showing that the Los Alamos program is superior
As only crude, since too few games are available to judge them reliably
As unnecessary, since the programs ran on different languages and machines
optionExplain: They say reliable estimates need more games.
The skimpy evidence points the other way.
They say more games are needed and assume rough comparability.
The comparison is made for argument's sake.
questions.explain: The comparison serves to focus on speed versus selectivity.
questions.teaches: The authors can compare the two programs' performance only very crudely, assume them roughly comparable for argument, and note that on the skimpy evidence most chess players would probably assess Bernstein's program as the stronger.

questions.q: A bakery buys a machine that cuts the number of loaves to be hand-checked from 300 to 1, but each check now takes 300 times as long. Which lesson from the authors' comparison applies?
options: The two routes can reach the same overall effort, so total cost decides
The machine must be a loss
The machine must be a gain of 300 times
Neither route can be compared
optionExplain: Two routes achieved the same quality with the same total effort.
A larger cost per check may be offset by fewer checks.
The gain depends on cost per check.
The authors compare them in total effort.
questions.explain: Compare routes by total effort, not by one factor.
questions.rule: Total effort is count times cost.
questions.teaches: The two programs achieve (by assumption) the same quality of performance with the same total effort by two different routes: the Los Alamos program with no selectivity and great speed, Bernstein's with much selectivity and more effort per position.

questions.q: Positions grow exponentially with search depth. To look further ahead, which is the better lever: a machine twice as fast, or a method that discards half the moves at each step?
options: The faster machine, because its speed benefits every step of the search equally well
Neither, because depth cannot be increased by either
They are equal, because both halve the work
Discarding half the moves at each step, because the saving compounds with depth
optionExplain: A constant factor buys only a little extra depth.
Both can add depth, but by different amounts.
Halving the branching at every level does far more than halving the total.
A cut in branching is felt at every level.
questions.explain: A cut that compounds beats a constant factor. The card works through the numbers.

questions.q: In the authors' calculation, going one move deeper multiplies the Los Alamos program's time by about 1000 and Bernstein's by about ____.
questions.explain: Seven squared is 49, about 50.

questions.q: A tree has four branches at every node. A program doubles its speed. About how much deeper, in the unit used, can it look?
options: Twice as deep, from n to 2n
Half a move deeper, from n to n plus a half
One whole move deeper, from n to n plus 1
No deeper, since the tree grows exponentially
optionExplain: That is the result of halving the branches, not doubling speed.
Twice the positions is four to the power of one half more depth.
Twice the positions is only half a level when four branches grow at each level.
It does get a little deeper.
questions.explain: Doubling speed buys log of 2 over log of 4 of a level, which is a half.
questions.rule: Doubling speed buys half a level.

questions.q: True or false: If selectivity is doubled so that only two of four branches are examined at each node, the program can look twice as deep for the same effort.
questions.explain: Two branches at every node to depth 2n gives 2 to the 2n, which equals four to the n.
questions.rule: Halving the branches doubles the depth.

questions.q: Why do the authors say attempts to add selectivity to the Los Alamos program would be costly?
options: It would need diverse information the simple design was built to avoid
Because the program had no way of generating legal moves from a position
Because the board was only six by six and so too small for selection
Because selective programs always lose to exhaustive ones in the long run
optionExplain: Adding it would be extremely costly relative to the cost of more selectivity in Bernstein's program.
It generated all legal moves.
Board size is not given as the reason.
The authors argue the reverse.
questions.explain: A program designed to be simple resists later sophistication.
questions.teaches: The natural way to improve the Los Alamos program is to increase its speed enough to explore three moves deep, but attempts to introduce selectivity into it would be extremely costly relative to adding more selectivity to Bernstein's program.

questions.q: A treasure hunt has three tunnels to try at every junction. Which investment lets the searchers go deepest for the same effort?
options: Walking twice as fast through every tunnel
Hiring one more searcher at the entrance only, to speed up the whole hunt a little
Marking each junction once visited, with no ruling out of any tunnel
Learning to rule out two of the three tunnels at each junction
optionExplain: A constant speed-up buys only a little extra depth.
One extra searcher is a constant factor.
That prevents repeats but does not cut the branching.
Cutting the branching factor compounds with depth.
questions.explain: Pruning branches pays at every level; faster walking does not.
questions.teaches: The authors say it is clear that one could afford to pay an apparently high computing cost per position to achieve selectivity, since heuristics that eliminate branches are so valuable.

questions.q: A chess program is built from separate modules, each concerned with one aspect of the game. Which benefit would the authors expect from such a design?
options: Faster search through the use of a single shared evaluation for all aspects
Flexibility in the considerations on which effort is spent as the game goes on
Guaranteed optimal play, since every aspect is covered by a separate module
Elimination of the need to look ahead at all
optionExplain: The goals bring separate evaluations.
Modules can be called on as the situation needs.
No guarantee follows.
The goals still need analysis of continuations.
questions.explain: Modules allow selection of the relevant ones. The card gives the authors' reason.

questions.q: Each goal in the NSS program has its own base-move generator, its own analysis-move generator and its own ____ process.
questions.explain: These are three of the six processes of the prototype, supplied goal by goal.

questions.q: At the opening position, which goals of the NSS program would be on the current-goal-list, per the authors?
options: King safety, serious threats and pawn promotion
Only material balance, since nothing else applies at the very start of any game
Material balance, center control and development, with the most crucial first
All goals ever written, in alphabetical order
optionExplain: These were goals the program lacked.
All three goals would be evoked at the start.
These are the three goals developed and appropriate to the opening.
Goals are chosen by situation and ordered by priority.
questions.explain: The situation evokes the goals; priority orders them.

questions.q: True or false: The NSS program uses separate width-termination and depth-termination processes for each goal.
questions.explain: Two processes, width-termination and depth-termination, are not specific to particular goals.

questions.q: How are the goals related to one another, according to the authors?
options: They are nested, so removing a goal removes all of those that lie below it in the list
They are identical, differing only in name
They are ordered so that each depends on the one before it in the goal list
They are independent: one can be added or removed without affecting the others
optionExplain: No nesting is described.
Each has its own generators.
The order is of priority, not dependence.
Independence is what makes them modules.
questions.explain: Independence allows goals to be added or dropped.
questions.teaches: The goals form a basic set of modules out of which the program is constructed, and they are independent: they can be added to or removed from the program without affecting the feasibility of the remaining goals.

questions.q: A garden helper has modules for watering, pruning and pest control, and activates only those the season calls for. How does this compare with the NSS program?
options: It differs, since NSS uses every goal at every move
It parallels goals evoked by the situation, such as stalemate denial in some endgames
It differs, since NSS goals are ordered at random
It parallels the Los Alamos program, which has separate modules for each season of play
optionExplain: NSS evokes goals by the situation.
The authors say the stalemate-denial goal is relevant only in certain endgames.
The most crucial goals come first.
Los Alamos has no goal modules.
questions.explain: Situations evoke goals; irrelevant goals are left out.
questions.teaches: The goal of denying stalemate to the opponent is relevant only in certain endgame situations where the opponent is on the defensive and the King is in a constrained position.

questions.q: In a committee, one member suggests actions and a different process then tests each suggestion against all the committee's concerns. What does this design give?
options: Suggestions that need no vetting
Vetting by the member who made the suggestion
Suggestions made for definite reasons, each vetted against every concern
A random choice among the vetted suggestions
optionExplain: A reason for one aim may harm another.
The authors separate the two roles.
Proposal and vetting are separated.
Vetting orders suggestions; it does not randomize them.
questions.explain: A proposer and a judge do different jobs. The card shows how NSS does it.
questions.rule: Propose for reasons, judge against all.

questions.q: In the NSS program the base-move generators find ____ reasons for making moves, while the analysis checks acceptability.
questions.explain: Generators carry the burden of finding positive reasons for doing things.

questions.q: In the opening, which goal's generator alone would propose P-Q4?
options: Center control
Material balance, since pawns are material
Development, since it moves a piece toward the center
King safety, since a pawn move shields the King
optionExplain: Only the center-control generator proposes P-Q4 in the opening.
Material balance proposes moves about exchanges.
P-Q4 is a pawn move, not a piece development move.
King safety was not among the NSS goals built.
questions.explain: Each reason has one owner.
questions.rule: Each proposal has a goal that owns it.

questions.q: True or false: A student says the NSS analysis procedure tries to find positive reasons to make moves. The authors would agree.
questions.explain: That is the job of the generators; analysis only judges acceptability.

questions.q: How do Bernstein's and the Los Alamos programs differ from NSS in their use of generators?
options: They use separate generators for continuations, as NSS does
They use identical generators for base moves and continuations; NSS separates them
They have no generators at all, only evaluation
They use NSS's generators, which came earlier
optionExplain: They use the same generators for both.
In NSS the latter function is performed by a separate set of analysis generators.
Bernstein's program has plausible move generators.
NSS came after both programs.
questions.explain: NSS splits the two tasks that earlier programs combined.
questions.rule: NSS separates base and analysis generators.
questions.teaches: In Bernstein's program, and a fortiori in the Los Alamos program, identical generators are used both to find the base moves and to find the continuations explored in analysis; NSS keeps separate analysis generators.

questions.q: A hiring team lets each department propose candidates for its own reasons, and then lets one process screen every candidate against all departments' needs. Which NSS idea does this match?
options: Goals are removed one by one until a single candidate is left, with no vetting step
Each generator also decides the final choice
The candidates are chosen at random from every department, then checked by a committee
Generators propose for positive reasons; analysis, using all goals, disposes
optionExplain: NSS keeps the goals and evaluates with all of them.
In NSS the analysis does the judging.
NSS proposals are made for definite reasons.
Department proposals are generators; the screening is analysis.
questions.explain: Separate proposing from judging so each does its own job well.
questions.teaches: The center-control generator will propose 2.P-K4 after 1.P-Q4, P-Q4, but the material-balance evaluation rejects it because of the loss of material after 2...PxP; center control never traces those consequences.

questions.q: Two candidate moves are rated on three aspects in a fixed order of importance. The first aspect ties. What decides between them?
options: The second aspect, and the third only if the second also ties
The sum of all three aspects, taken together as one single overall score
The third aspect, because it is the most specific
A coin toss, since the top aspect did not decide
optionExplain: Work down the aspects in order of importance.
Summing is a different, trading-off method.
Importance, not specificity, sets the order.
The remaining aspects can still decide.
questions.explain: Ordered aspects are compared in turn. The card names this lexicographic.

questions.q: NSS compares values ____, so that values on higher-priority components dominate those on lower-priority ones.
questions.explain: The ordering is lexicographic, like looking up words in a dictionary.

questions.q: Value A is (4, 3, 1) and value B is (4, 7, 3), compared in priority order. Which is the larger?
options: A, since its third component is smaller
They are equal, since their first components are equal
B, since the first components tie and 7 is more than 3
A, since its three numbers have the smaller sum
optionExplain: Later components matter only if earlier ones tie.
The tie in the first is broken by the second.
Compare first components (equal), then second components (7 over 3).
No sum is used.
questions.explain: Tie on the first, so look at the second.

questions.q: True or false: Under a lexicographic comparison, the value (5, 0, 0) is preferred to the value (4, 9, 9).
questions.explain: The first component decides, and 5 exceeds 4; no lower component can make up for a loss in a higher one.

questions.q: Besides numbers, what other kind of component value do NSS goals use?
options: Fractions of a second, to record the time of each move
Names of moves, to say which was best
Dichotomous values, only marking the presence or absence of a property such as a doubled pawn
Probabilities of winning, from a table of past games
optionExplain: Time is not a component.
Components describe positions.
Some components are numbers, others only mark presence or absence.
No such probabilities are described.
questions.explain: Not all evaluations are quantities.
questions.rule: Some components are yes or no.
questions.teaches: A component value in NSS is sometimes a number (the material goal uses conventional piece values, such as 9 for a Queen and 5 for a Rook) and sometimes dichotomous, marking only presence or absence of a property like a blocked move or a doubled pawn.

questions.q: A school adds a fourth subject to its ranking of students, placing it last in priority. How does the ordering change for students tied on the first three subjects?
options: They are now separated by the fourth subject, and no other pairs are reordered
All students are re-ranked by the sum of four subjects
Nothing changes, since the fourth subject has the lowest priority
The first subject loses its priority in the new ranking
optionExplain: Adding a last-priority component only breaks ties.
A lexicographic order does not sum.
It does settle ties on the first three.
Higher priorities stay absolute.
questions.explain: A new low-priority goal only refines the order.
questions.rule: Adding a last component only breaks ties.
questions.teaches: The complete ordering must exist independent of variation in the size and composition of the goal list, which is why NSS can use a different set of goals at each move.

questions.q: You must pick a flat. Which strategy is closest to satisficing?
options: View every flat on the market and take the best
Take the first flat you see, whatever its quality
Take the cheapest flat, whether or not it suits you
Set a standard in advance and take the first flat that meets it
optionExplain: That is maximizing over a fixed set.
No standard is applied.
A single criterion with no acceptance level is not satisficing.
Satisficing means accepting the first option that reaches an aspiration level.
questions.explain: A standard plus first-fit is satisficing. The card applies it to chess.

questions.q: In NSS, the level a move must reach to be accepted is called the acceptance level or the ____ level.
questions.explain: The aspiration level is the final criterion for accepting a move.

questions.q: The NSS executive is going down its goal list. Material balance proposes a move that reaches the aspiration level. What happens?
options: The program continues until it has compared all proposals
That move is taken, and the lower-priority generators need not be consulted
The program discards it
The program waits for the opponent's reply before choosing
optionExplain: That would be maximizing.
The first acceptable move is taken.
Priority order puts important moves first.
The choice is made on the move at hand.
questions.explain: First acceptable, in priority order, ends the generation.

questions.q: True or false: If no move reaches the aspiration level, NSS chooses the best move found.
questions.explain: If none reaches that level, the best move found is chosen.

questions.q: On what assumption does the maximum-value rule rest in the other programs, in the authors' view?
options: It rests on the assumption that the alternatives to be considered form a fixed set
Because all those programs generate moves one at a time
Because they are all much faster than NSS
Because the rule was proved by Shannon
optionExplain: Sequential generation removes that assumption.
They generate the whole set first.
Speed is not the reason.
No proof is mentioned.
questions.explain: Maximizing needs the whole set in hand.
questions.teaches: The obviousness of choosing the highest-valued move rests on the assumption that the set of alternatives to be considered is fixed; if base moves are generated sequentially, other procedures such as satisficing become possible.

questions.q: A shopper visits stores in order of how likely each is to carry the item and buys at the first store with an acceptable price. What risk does this approach carry?
options: Spending too long comparing every price in every store
Never finding any store
Buying only from the last store on the route
Committing to an acceptable item before the most promising store has been visited
optionExplain: The approach stops at the first acceptable price.
A standard has been set.
The first acceptable store is chosen.
Taking the first acceptable option can commit before better ones are seen.
questions.explain: First-fit saves effort at the price of possible premature choice.
questions.teaches: The authors say NSS's first-acceptable rule can commit the program to a premature choice before it has considered the most promising moves, yet often the very first move it generated, out of some thirty legal moves, was a strong one.

questions.q: A chess position can be judged on material, on development and on the center. Material is stable but a piece is about to be driven away. Is the position ready to be scored?
options: Yes, since material is stable and material is what matters
Not for every aspect: the aspects that are still in flux should be explored further
Yes, since the position will be scored the same in the end
No aspect can ever be stable in a game with two players
optionExplain: Other aspects are in flux.
Each aspect needs its own stability.
Unstable aspects can change.
Many positions are stable in some respects.
questions.explain: Stability is judged per feature. The card gives the NSS rule.

questions.q: In NSS, a goal's static evaluation is meaningful only if the position is ____ with respect to the feature of that goal.
questions.explain: Dead means no moves are likely to alter the component radically.

questions.q: In NSS a position is dead for material and for center control but not for development. What does the program do?
options: Score the position now, using material and center control only
Stop the whole search and make the first move found
Generate moves from development's analysis-move generator and explore on
Throw out development as a goal for this move
optionExplain: All goals must find it dead.
The search of that branch continues.
A position must be dead with respect to all goals.
Goals are not dropped in mid-search.
questions.explain: One goal's liveness keeps the exploration going.
questions.rule: All goals must call it dead.

questions.q: True or false: In NSS, positions at depth greater than one are cut off by separate width-termination and depth-termination processes.
questions.explain: For analysis there are no separate width or depth terminations; the dead tests decide.

questions.q: Why does the average depth of analysis vary geometrically with the selectivity of the analysis generators?
options: Because the base-move generators operate at every ply
Because the depth is set by the opponent's skill
Because the final choice is made at each ply
Because their selectivity operates at each ply of the exploration, while base-move selection operates once per move
optionExplain: They operate once per move.
The opponent does not set it.
The final choice is made once.
Selection at each ply compounds with depth.
questions.explain: A per-ply effect compounds with depth.
questions.teaches: The selectivity of the analysis generators operates at each ply of the exploration, whereas base-move generators and the final choice procedure operate only once per move, so the average depth varies geometrically with the analysis generators' selectivity.

questions.q: A weather model runs fine detail only where conditions are changing quickly and coarse detail where they are quiet. Which NSS outcome does this resemble?
options: Every position gives a search tree of the same size
Placid situations give search trees with a handful of positions; complicated middle-game positions give much larger ones
Complicated positions give smaller trees than placid ones
Tree size depends only on the number of legal moves
optionExplain: NSS tree size varies with the situation.
The effort of NSS tracks how much is in flux.
The reverse is true.
It depends on how many features are in flux.
questions.explain: Effort follows instability.
questions.rule: Search harder where things are unstable.
questions.teaches: Placid situations produce NSS search trees containing only a handful of positions, while complicated middle-game situations produce much larger ones.

questions.q: A search tree has ended in several finished positions, each scored on three aspects in order of priority. How should the scores be backed up to the root?
options: Add all the scores of the finished positions and divide by their number
Take the score of the first finished position that was found
Choose the best at the levels where the player moves and the worst at the levels where the opponent moves
Take the best score of any finished position, wherever it lies
optionExplain: Averaging ignores who chooses at each level.
The first found is not necessarily the effective value.
That is minimax, with scores compared in priority order.
That would credit the player with the opponent's choices.
questions.explain: Scores flow back by maximum and minimum. The card follows one example.
questions.rule: Back up by max and min.

questions.q: Put these steps of the schematic example in the order they happen.
items: M1 is proposed and leads to P1
P1 is not dead for the third goal, which generates M2 and M3
M2 leads to P2, which is dead for all goals
M3 leads to P3, which needs further moves M4 and M5
questions.explain: The program makes M1, explores P1's unfinished component, evaluates P2 at once and explores deeper from P3.
questions.rule: Propose, find not dead, explore each branch.

questions.q: At a position where White moves, the two reachable values are (3, 9, 9) and (4, 0, 0). Which does NSS choose, and what is the value?
options: The second, (4, 0, 0), since the first component dominates and 4 exceeds 3
The first, (3, 9, 9)
The second, but with the value (4, 9, 9) after combining the two
Either, since their sums are both 12
optionExplain: White maximizes and compares by the first component first.
Lower components cannot outweigh the first.
Values are not combined; one is chosen.
No sums are taken.
questions.explain: Maximize lexicographically on the player's own move.

questions.q: Black, minimizing, must choose between a move leading to (4, 3, 1) and a move leading to (4, 7, 3). Which will Black choose?
options: The move to (4, 7, 3), whose larger second component is better for Black
The move to (4, 3, 1), since the first components tie and 3 is less than 7
Neither, since the first components tie
The move to (4, 7, 3), because the third components are compared before the second
optionExplain: Black wants the smaller value for White, so a larger component is worse for Black.
Black minimizes lexicographically.
A tie on one component is broken by the next.
The second component decides before the third.
questions.explain: The opponent minimizes in the same priority order.

questions.q: In the example, which value becomes the effective value of the proposed move M1, and why?
options: (4, 7, 3), because White's choice at P3 is the highest
(5, 3, 1), a combination of the values found along the way
(2, 8, 1), because it was found first
(4, 3, 1), because Black chooses between M2 and M3 and prefers M2
optionExplain: That is the value of P3, but Black can avoid P3.
Values are not combined.
The first value found does not decide.
Black's minimization picks M2, and its value ends the analysis.
questions.explain: The root's value comes from Black's minimizing choice between P2 and P3.
questions.rule: Black picks the lower of P2 and P3.
questions.teaches: Black, minimizing, chooses M2 (value (4, 3, 1)) rather than M3 (value (4, 7, 3)), so (4, 3, 1) becomes the effective value of the alternative M1, and the analysis ends.

questions.q: True or false: The numeric component values of the schematic example are the real form the NSS program uses.
questions.explain: The authors say numbers are used to keep the picture simple; in reality various sets of ordered symbols are used, depending on the computation.
questions.teaches: The numerical values in the schematic example are used to keep the picture simple; in reality NSS uses various sets of ordered symbols, whose exact structure depends on the nature of the computation.

questions.q: You are checking offers for a flat. You already hold an offer worth 5. Considering a second one, you discover a flaw that caps its value at 3. What should you do?
options: Stop examining the second offer, since it cannot beat the one you hold
Continue examining it fully, in case 3 turns out to be wrong
Reject the first offer, to be fair to both
Average the two offers to decide which to take
optionExplain: It is guaranteed to be worth less than what you have.
The cap is guaranteed.
The first offer is worth more.
Averaging adds nothing here.
questions.explain: A branch capped below your best can be dropped. The card gives the procedure.
questions.rule: Drop what cannot beat your best.

questions.q: In the alpha-beta procedure, a maximizing node keeps alpha, its ____ value found so far.
questions.explain: A maximizing node's alpha is the highest value so far, and a minimizing node's beta is the lowest.

questions.q: A maximizing root has found a first move worth 3. Its second move leads to a minimizing node whose first reply is worth 2. What follows?
options: The second move is kept
The second move is chosen
The second move is abandoned, since its value is at most 2 and the root can already get 3
The root takes the average of the 3 and the 2
optionExplain: The minimizer can only lower the value.
A low reply is bad for the maximizing root.
Beta (2) is below alpha (3), so the node is cut off.
No averaging is used.
questions.explain: A minimizer holding 2 can only go lower, so the node cannot beat 3.

questions.q: True or false: A maximizing root holds alpha 3. A second move reaches a minimizing node whose first reply is worth 5. The node can be abandoned at once.
questions.explain: Beta (5) is not below alpha (3); the minimizer may still find a reply of 3 or less, so exploration continues.
questions.rule: Cut only when beta falls below alpha.

questions.q: From what does the alpha-beta procedure take its name, and whom do the authors credit?
options: From the Greek letters McCarthy used in his chess notation
From the first two programs that used it, Alpha and Beta
From the two limits, called alpha and beta, in the procedure; the name was coined by John McCarthy
From Shannon's two papers, alpha in 1949 and beta in 1950
optionExplain: The name comes from the limits.
No programs by those names are cited.
The note credits McCarthy and the two limits.
The note says McCarthy coined it.
questions.explain: The two limits give the name.
questions.rule: Alpha and beta are the two limits.
questions.teaches: The name alpha-beta was coined by John McCarthy from the two limits used in the procedure, which were called alpha and beta; it is similar to branch and bound procedures in management science.

questions.q: At a minimizing node holding beta, a child maximizing node finds a reply worth more than beta. What is the sense of searching for still higher values there?
options: None, since values above beta will be ignored at the minimizing node
Great, since a higher value always helps the maximizer
Great, since the higher value raises beta
None, since the maximizing node has no further moves
optionExplain: The minimizing node will not choose anything above beta.
The minimizer above will decline it.
Beta can only fall at a minimizing node.
It may have further moves; they are simply useless.
questions.explain: The cutoff works in both directions of the tree.
questions.teaches: The same reasoning works the other way: no move of value greater than beta is worthwhile at a maximizing node below a minimizing one, since it will be ignored in the course of minimaxing.

questions.q: A pruning method discards some branches of a search. Which property would make it safe, giving the same final answer as searching them all?
options: The discarded branches look unpromising to an expert
The discarded branches are the last ones in the move list
The discarded branches have fewer pieces captured
The discarded branches are guaranteed not to affect the final result
optionExplain: A judgment may be wrong.
Position in a list is no guarantee.
That is a feature, not a guarantee.
Safe pruning removes only what cannot matter.
questions.explain: Guarantee, not judgment, makes pruning safe. The card applies it to alpha-beta.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the alpha-beta procedure is not a heuristic.
questions.explain: They state plainly that it is not: the eliminated branches cannot affect the minimax value.

questions.q: A program uses alpha-beta and a rival uses full minimax, both to the same depth. How do their chosen moves compare?
options: They differ often, since alpha-beta is a gamble
They agree, since alpha-beta removes only branches with no effect on the minimax value
They differ only for pieces of high value
They agree only in the opening of the game
optionExplain: It is not a gamble.
The pruned branches could not have changed the result.
Piece value is irrelevant to the guarantee.
The guarantee holds anywhere.
questions.explain: Same value, less work.

questions.q: True or false: A designer says that alpha-beta costs nothing, since pruning has no overhead at all. The authors would agree.
questions.explain: A small cost is incurred in computing and comparing alpha and beta at each node, though the savings far exceed it.

questions.q: In the limit, alpha-beta can reduce the number of nodes examined to the ____ of the number that would be examined without it.
questions.explain: The authors cite Slagle and Dixon (1969) for the square-root reduction in the limit.
questions.teaches: In the limit, alpha-beta can reduce the number of nodes examined to the square root of the number examined without it (Slagle and Dixon, 1969).

questions.q: A program also tries to cut off a branch by predicting that the player will not get a better value from it than one already found. What do the authors say about this extra step?
options: It is a heuristic matter, and no regular algorithms for it have come into use
It is as safe as alpha-beta and widely used as an algorithm
It is impossible in any program
It is the same procedure as alpha-beta under another name
optionExplain: Knowing when a better value cannot be obtained is heuristic.
They say it is heuristic.
They say additional gains are possible.
It is a separate, heuristic step.
questions.explain: Extra pruning beyond the guaranteed kind needs judgment.
questions.teaches: Further gains are possible by carrying forward the best value obtained so far by the player of the position, but knowing when a better value cannot be obtained is a heuristic matter, and no regular algorithms for it have come into use.

questions.q: A search stops at a position whenever it can be valued without looking further. What makes such a search finish sooner?
options: Having a larger memory for storing continuations
Having a longer list of legal moves at each position
Having a slower processor that examines each case with care
Being able to value many kinds of positions directly
optionExplain: Memory does not change how many continuations are needed.
More moves give a larger search.
Speed of the processor does not change the count.
Direct valuation cuts the need for more continuations.
questions.explain: The sooner a position can be judged, the sooner the search ends. The card says how NSS depends on this.

questions.q: The authors say the success of the NSS search depends heavily on the ability to evaluate ____.
questions.explain: Static evaluation without continuations is what terminates the search.

questions.q: A designer adds a rule that lets the program value a common kind of exchange without exploring it. What is the likely effect on the search?
options: It runs longer, since the program must apply one more rule
It terminates sooner, since fewer positions need continuations
No effect, since termination is set by the opponent
It becomes impossible to terminate
optionExplain: The rule saves exploration.
More situations recognized as having a value means faster termination.
The opponent does not set termination.
The rule helps termination.
questions.explain: Recognition replaces exploration.

questions.q: True or false: In a position where many different plausible moves would each change the value, the NSS search is likely to be longer.
questions.explain: The number of plausible moves that affect the value is of consequence for the size of the search.

questions.q: What do the authors say guarantees that the NSS search will converge?
options: The alpha-beta procedure, which prunes the tree to a fixed size
The dead tests, which stop any exploration of live positions
Nothing built in does; only the external limits of space and time
The aspiration level, which stops all search at depth one
optionExplain: Alpha-beta does not give a guarantee.
Dead tests continue exploration while a position is live.
No built-in rule guarantees convergence.
Satisficing applies at depth one only.
questions.explain: Without an external limit the search could go on.
questions.rule: Only external limits guarantee an end.
questions.teaches: There is no built-in rule that guarantees the NSS search will converge, except the external limits of space and time.

questions.q: A fact-checking desk resolves each claim by looking up sources only when it cannot be settled from what the team already knows. When does its work take longest?
options: When every claim can be settled at once from existing knowledge
When there are no claims to check at all
When the sources agree in advance
When few claims can be settled from existing knowledge and many sources bear on each
optionExplain: Then no lookups are needed.
There would be no work.
Agreement shortens, not lengthens, the work.
That mirrors the dependence on static evaluation and relevant moves.
questions.explain: Quick judgment reduces search; its absence enlarges it.
questions.teaches: The authors note that the more numerous the situations that can be recognized as having a certain value without generating continuations, the more rapidly the NSS search will terminate.

questions.q: A chess program has a goal of controlling the center in the opening. What is the most natural first thing for such a goal to propose?
options: Moving a rook to the open file at the edge
Moving a center pawn two squares forward when legal
Capturing the opponent's most valuable piece
Giving up the center pawn at once
optionExplain: That belongs to later development.
Primary center moves are P-Q4 and P-K4.
That belongs to the material goal.
That would lose control.
questions.explain: A center goal begins with the center pawns. The card gives the authors' list.
questions.rule: Primary moves are P-Q4 and P-K4.

questions.q: The center-control generator proposes the primary moves P-Q4 and P-____.
questions.explain: The two primary moves are P-Q4 and P-K4.

questions.q: The primary center moves are blocked by a friendly piece standing in front of the pawn. What does the generator do, in the authors' account?
options: It proposes the pawn move anyway
It gives up the center goal for the rest of the game
It proposes moves for the blocking piece, to prepare its own primary move
It proposes capturing the opponent's blocking pieces only
optionExplain: The pawn cannot move through a blocker.
The goal becomes irrelevant only when center pawns are advanced or gone.
To prepare, it proposes moves for the blocking piece.
Blockers of the opponent are a separate case.
questions.explain: Preparation removes the reason a primary move cannot be made.

questions.q: True or false: A reviewer claims that the center-control evaluation rewards any move that happens to help the center, whichever goal proposed it.
questions.explain: The authors say the evaluation is negative and ignores the possibility that another goal's move contributes to center control.

questions.q: In the authors' account, how does the order of the generator's options affect the program's play?
options: Putting prevention before preparation probably gives more aggressive and slightly better opening play
The order has no effect
Putting preparation first makes the program play more aggressively
The order matters only for the Queen's pawn, not the King's pawn
optionExplain: The style of play depends on this ordering.
The authors say style depends on the order.
The authors say prevention first is more aggressive.
They say the pawn considered first also matters.
questions.explain: Order of consideration shapes style.
questions.teaches: Whether prevention has priority over preparation (as in the authors' description) or the reverse, and whether the Queen's pawn or the King's pawn is considered first, changes the style of play, with prevention first probably giving more aggressive and slightly better opening play.

questions.q: To decide whether preventing an opponent's move is worth trying, the generator tries the opponent's move and evaluates it from the opponent's viewpoint. What does it do next if the move is not rejected?
options: It gives up the goal
It finds moves that bring another attacker to bear on the square or pin a defender of it
It plays the opponent's move itself, to save time
It waits until the next turn without proposing anything
optionExplain: If the move can be made, prevention has a purpose.
Preventive moves then serve some purpose.
The generator does not copy the opponent's move.
It proposes preventive moves at once.
questions.explain: Test whether the opponent's move works; if so, try to stop it.
questions.teaches: To prevent the opponent's primary moves the generator first tries the move and evaluates it from the opponent's viewpoint; if it is not rejected, it proposes moves that add an attacker or pin a defender, normally N-B3 and BP-B4.

questions.q: To judge the material outlook of a chess position, a program lists each capture sequence and works out its profit separately. Which weakness would this method have?
options: It cannot say who wins any single capture sequence
It counts pieces only and cannot see attackers
It cannot be applied unless the whole game tree is known
It may miss how one sequence changes another, such as one piece serving in two
optionExplain: Each sequence is valued.
It lists attackers and defenders.
Exchanges are listed from the position at hand.
Separate valuation ignores interactions.
questions.explain: Separate valuation misses interactions. The card says the same of NSS.

questions.q: In the material-balance goal, each exchange on the list is given a static-____-value.
questions.explain: The static-exchange-value is the approximate worth of an exchange.

questions.q: A Knight attacks a Rook, and the Rook is defended by a Pawn. Which goal handles this exchange, according to the authors?
options: Material-balance, since it is a question of gain or loss of material in the immediate situation
Center control, since the Knight stands near the center
Development, since the Knight is a minor piece
No goal, since pawns and pieces do not exchange
optionExplain: Exchanges on occupied squares are its business.
Center control handles center pawn moves.
Development concerns initial deployment.
Exchanges are the material goal's subject.
questions.explain: Immediate gain or loss of material is its task.

questions.q: True or false: Material-balance also takes care of threats such as pins and forks, where the exchange is still one move away.
questions.explain: Other goals must take care of such threats; material-balance considers only exchanges at hand.

questions.q: What is the static-exchange-value used for, in addition to approximating the true material balance?
options: To decide which side has the move in the position and so who is to play next
To set the aspiration level for the whole program from the first move of the game
To order the exchanges on the list, which orders the moves generated
To tell how many plies to search
optionExplain: The side to move is known from the position.
The aspiration level is separate.
The value orders the specification list.
Search depth is set by deadness.
questions.explain: The most pressing exchanges are dealt with first.
questions.teaches: The static-exchange-value is used primarily to order the exchanges on the specification list, which governs in turn the order in which moves are generated for resolving issues of material balance.

questions.q: A fire crew sends each truck to a different blaze, so that no truck is sent to two. Which NSS design step is a small first step in the same direction?
options: Valuing exchanges together instead of one by one
Searching every exchange to the end of the game, whatever it is worth
Generating defensive moves only for men not already defending
Allowing a man to be used in two exchanges at once, as the earlier programs did
optionExplain: The authors say interactions are not handled.
That is not described.
This avoids overloading one man with several jobs.
That is the weakness, not the remedy.
questions.explain: Avoid giving one resource two jobs.
questions.teaches: A small first step is taken in the move generator to avoid overloading a man with multiple functions: defensive moves are generated only for men who are not already on the list of defenders, a limited but important notion of multiple function.

questions.q: A program stops its search while captures are still pending. Which is better than a plain count of pieces for valuing the position?
options: Playing out the pending exchanges in turn to see what each side gains
Counting pieces again with their values doubled
Ignoring all captures and valuing only pawn structure
Waiting for the opponent to make the next capture
optionExplain: A playoff estimates the outcome of pending captures.
Doubling does not reflect pending captures.
Pending captures matter to material.
The program values its own position now.
questions.explain: Pending exchanges change material. The card shows the NSS playoff.

questions.q: In the NSS playoff of exchanges, the option to take the next exchange passes to the ____ of the player who made the last move.
questions.explain: The option alternates between the sides.
questions.rule: The option passes to the opponent.

questions.q: At a point in the playoff, the side holding the option sees that every remaining exchange would lose material for it. What may it do?
options: Take the least bad exchange
Hand the option back to the opponent without ending
Remove the exchanges from the position
Take none of them and end the playoff
optionExplain: The playoff is not forced.
The option holder may end it.
The position is not altered.
The option holder may choose to terminate the playoff.
questions.explain: Declining all exchanges is always possible, like a defensive move.

questions.q: True or false: A reader says the playoff forces the holder of the option to take an exchange whenever one is on the list. The authors would agree.
questions.explain: The player holding the option could elect to take none, and the playoff was not forced.

questions.q: What does the option to take no exchange correspond to in real play, according to the authors?
options: Resigning the game
Making a defensive move or another attacking move
Offering a draw
Making a capture of a different piece, as in any of the listed exchanges
optionExplain: Nothing so drastic is described.
It corresponds to a defensive or other attacking move.
No draw offers are modeled.
Captures are the exchanges themselves.
questions.explain: Declining the exchanges stands for doing something else useful.
questions.teaches: The option to take none of the exchanges and end the playoff corresponds to making a defensive move or another attacking move, and was considered always possible.

questions.q: A planner estimates what a negotiation will yield by playing out each side's pending offers, but treats each offer separately. What do the authors say is wrong with this kind of estimate?
options: It ignores interactions, such as one resource being used in two offers
It cannot say what the pending offers are without asking the other side
It forces both sides to accept every offer
It values offers by the opponent's moods only
optionExplain: The playoff suffers from this basic simplification.
They are listed in the specification.
The playoff is not forced.
No such values are used.
questions.explain: Independence of offers is the simplification.
questions.teaches: NSS eliminated exchanges whose attackers had all been used up by the time the playoff was evaluated, a small corrective for simple situations of interaction.

questions.q: A piece cannot be developed because another man stands in its way. What are two sensible ways a development goal could respond?
options: Develop a different piece and ignore the blocked one for the rest of the whole game
Capture the blocker with any piece, whatever the cost
Swap the blocked piece with a pawn
Move away its own blocking man, or attack an opposing blocker to drive it off
optionExplain: That leaves the blocked piece undeveloped.
Cost is for other goals to judge, but capture is not the goal's own approach.
No such swap is described.
Clear the way, depending on whose man blocks.
questions.explain: Preparing development means clearing the blocker. The card explains who clears.

questions.q: In the development goal, developing moves with more than ____ blocking men are ignored.
questions.explain: Developing moves with one and two blockers are considered; more than two are ignored.

questions.q: A Bishop cannot reach its good square because the player's own pawn stands in front of it. What does the development generator do?
options: It checks first that the pawn move is safe against capture, then proposes it
It proposes a pawn move that clears the way, and other goals vet it
It rejects the plan
It attacks the pawn with the opponent's pieces
optionExplain: Safety is judged by other goals.
From development's viewpoint, one move is as good as another that clears the way.
It may move its own men away.
That is for opposing blockers.
questions.explain: The goal generates, others judge.

questions.q: True or false: Two positions tie on tempi for the side to move, but in one a piece is wholly blocked. The development goal prefers the position with no wholly blocked piece.
questions.explain: Tempi are compared first, and the count of blocked pieces breaks the tie.

questions.q: What moves does the development goal's analysis-move generator produce?
options: The same preparatory moves as the base-move generator, in exactly the same order of use
All legal moves for the side not on move
Attacks, by men of lower value, on advanced opposing pieces other than pawns
Moves that capture the most valuable pieces
optionExplain: No purpose is served in analysis by preparatory moves.
It is selective.
These can affect the stability of the development.
That is the material goal.
questions.explain: Driving off advanced pieces changes the development balance.
questions.teaches: The development goal's analysis-move generator produces moves that attack advanced pieces (not pawns) with men of lower value, since driving them away can change the stability of the development; a position is dead for development if no pieces are undeveloped or if the development value has changed by more than one.

questions.q: A manager tracks only the number of unfinished tasks for the team currently working, not for the competing team. Which feature of the development goal does this resemble?
options: Counting pieces for both sides to keep the balance
Counting tempi only, ignoring blocks entirely
Counting blocks for the opponent but not for oneself
Counting blocked pieces only for the side on move
optionExplain: The blocked count is for the side on move only.
Blocks form the second component.
The count is for the mover.
The authors give that reason.
questions.explain: Only the mover's blocks matter.
questions.teaches: The count of wholly blocked pieces in the development value is taken only for the side on move, since there seems little reason to include the corresponding measure for the opponent.

questions.q: You want a quick lower bound on how good your position is. Which question helps?
options: What would happen if I took the opponent's best piece?
What would happen if nobody did anything this turn?
What would happen if the board had no pieces?
What would happen if the rules were different?
optionExplain: That is a specific capture, not a bound.
Doing nothing sets a minimum for the value.
That removes the position.
The rules are given.
questions.explain: Doing nothing is a baseline. The card gives its name.
questions.rule: Ask what if I did nothing.

questions.q: NSS assumes that a no-move increases the value of a move for the player who makes it by exactly one ____.
questions.explain: A no-move is assumed to be worth one tempo.

questions.q: A side has many alternatives and each seems about equal. How can no-move curtail the search?
options: By removing all moves except the capture moves, which are the only forcing ones
By ending the game at once with a draw
By giving a minimum value that moves must beat to be worth exploring
By switching the sides of the players
optionExplain: No-move does not filter by type.
It is not a game result.
The value of doing nothing is a floor.
It does not switch sides.
questions.explain: A floor lets the program drop moves that cannot reach it.

questions.q: True or false: No-move is an abstract move that extends the basic problem space of chess beyond the legal moves.
questions.explain: It is an abstract move that extends the space beyond the legal moves.

questions.q: What happened when NSS gave a no-move no tempi?
options: The program misplayed seriously; a standard move should give one tempo
The program played better
The program refused to move
Nothing changed, since tempi are not used in NSS
optionExplain: The authors report serious misplay.
It misplayed.
It continued to play.
Tempi are part of the development value.
questions.explain: The size of the assumed gain mattered.
questions.teaches: The NSS program misplayed seriously when a no-move was assigned no tempi, since one tempo is exactly what a standard move should provide.

questions.q: A budget committee checks whether a proposed cut really hurts by asking what happens if nothing is done. In NSS, where is a similar test used on the material goal?
options: For the opponent's targets, to see whether a capture would be legal in the position
For its own target of an exchange, to see if the attack is in fact damaging
For the center-control goal, to test pawn moves
For the final choice among moves, to break ties
optionExplain: No-move is for the defender's own target.
The material goal tries no-move to test an attack on its own man.
That is not described.
It is used earlier in the generation.
questions.explain: Doing nothing tests whether a threat is real.
questions.teaches: In the material-balance goal, when the target of an exchange is the program's own man, the first move generated is the no-move, to see whether the attack is in fact damaging.

questions.q: A program has rules only for three aspects of a game. How would you expect its play to look when an important fourth aspect arises?
options: Uniformly poor, since one gap in its goals spoils all its play
Uniformly good, since the other three cover the fourth
Unchanged, since a fourth aspect never matters
Uneven: sensible on the aspects it knows, and blind to the fourth
optionExplain: It can play well where its goals apply.
Goals do not substitute for one another.
Missing aspects can be decisive.
Missing considerations leave blind spots.
questions.explain: Play follows the goals available. The card shows this in NSS games.

questions.q: In its game against HAS, NSS played White and had the better of the first ____ moves.
questions.explain: It was better for ten moves, until it ran out of things to do for development and center control.

questions.q: Why did NSS miss the devastating double check on move 14 of its game with a weak player?
options: It had no goal that concerned attacks on the King
It had too little time to search to the required depth
It judged the double check to be an illegal move
It preferred a quiet move, by its aspiration level
optionExplain: The absence of such a goal blinded it.
The cause was in the missing goal.
The check was legal.
A missing goal, not a preference, was the cause.
questions.explain: A move that no goal cares about is not proposed.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say the oversights of NSS are easy to tell apart from those of its human opponents.
questions.explain: They say its oversights are hard to distinguish qualitatively from the human opponent's, as in the Queen pin both missed.

questions.q: What do the authors say about the likeness between NSS's oversights and its opponent's?
options: The program's errors were of a quite different, mechanical kind from the human's
The opponent made no oversights at all
Hard to tell apart; both overlooked the pin of the Queen on the King
The program overlooked only moves involving the Queen, and the human never did
optionExplain: They find little qualitative difference.
The opponent made several.
The pin was missed by both.
No such restriction is stated.
questions.explain: Missing a feature can look like human carelessness.
questions.rule: Program and human both missed the pin.
questions.teaches: The oversights of NSS are hard to distinguish qualitatively from those of the human opponent, such as the oversight by both of them of the pin of a Queen against a King.

questions.q: A tutoring program has rules for spelling and grammar but none for punctuation. How should its performance be described, by analogy with NSS?
options: Equally poor at all three
Equally good at all three
Strong on spelling and grammar, blind to punctuation, sometimes right for wrong reasons
Unpredictable, with no link to its rules
optionExplain: NSS plays well where its goals apply.
Goals do not transfer between aspects.
NSS made strong moves not always for the right reasons.
The authors tie play to the goals.
questions.explain: A goal set predicts where a program is strong and blind.
questions.rule: Strengths and blind spots follow the rules.
questions.teaches: In the game of Table 11.4 the opponent was a weak player, and NSS made several very strong moves (especially 11 and 12), though not always for the right reasons.

questions.q: To see why a program chose a move, a researcher can print everything the program examined. What does this allow her to do?
options: Reconstruct which procedures proposed and which evaluated each move
Prove that the program's move is the best available in the position
Replace the program's evaluation with her own
Predict the opponent's next move exactly
optionExplain: The trace shows the working of generators and evaluations.
A trace shows the process, not the best move.
The trace does not change the evaluation.
The trace concerns the program's reasoning.
questions.explain: A trace exposes the reasoning. The card shows an example.

questions.q: In the example, the center-control generator proposes the move P-____ after 1.P-K4 P-K4.
questions.explain: Center control proposes P-Q4, one of the two primary moves.

questions.q: Put in order the steps by which development comes to reject 2.P-Q4 in the example.
items: Black replies 2...PxP and White recaptures with the Queen
Development finds the exposed Queen and the position not dead
It generates 3...N-QB3, attacking the Queen and developing
White's Queen must move, losing a tempo, so 2.P-Q4 is rejected
questions.explain: The exposed Queen makes the position live for development; the developing attack forces a tempo loss.
questions.rule: Exchange, exposed Queen, developing attack, rejection.

questions.q: If Black's reply to the exposed Queen were 3...B-B4 instead of N-QB3, would development reject 2.P-Q4 on that account?
options: Yes, because any developing reply costs a tempo
Yes, because development rejects every move that exposes the Queen
No, because development cannot see Bishop moves, only moves of the Queen
No, because the Bishop could be taken, so no tempo would be lost
optionExplain: The Bishop could be captured.
It rejects when a tempo is lost.
It sees developing moves; the difference lies in the capture.
The authors say B-B4 would not have caused rejection.
questions.explain: The tempo is lost only if the developing attack cannot be punished.
questions.rule: Check whether the reply loses material.

questions.q: How does the authors' trace of NSS handle a case where the program's move differs from the recorded move?
options: The game is ended
The position is reset to the book move and NSS recalculates its value
The book move is rejected as an error by the program
The program plays on from its own move, ignoring the book
optionExplain: The game continues.
This allowed the book game to continue.
The book move is followed.
The position is reset to the book move.
questions.explain: Resetting keeps the comparison on the book game.
questions.teaches: When NSS's move differs from the move in the recorded game, the position was reset to agree with the book move and NSS recalculated its value, whereupon the game continued.
