questions.q: A teacher grades a student's multi-step solution by comparing each step with the model solution; when a step differs, she substitutes the model step and lets the student carry on. Which part of the NSS method is this?
options: Resetting to the book move after a mismatch, so later steps are compared fairly
Searching all continuations to the end of the game
Giving the student the dead position as a starting point for each new step of work
Removing the goals that the student does not use
optionExplain: That is the NSS comparison method.
The method compares moves in recorded games.
Dead positions are a search idea.
No goals are removed.
questions.explain: Compare move by move, resetting at each difference.
questions.teaches: The rejection of 2.P-Q4 is as it should be: the trace shows that by the end of the exchanges White's Queen is exposed and loses a tempo, a consideration found only by the development goal.

questions.q: A program examines about three of thirty legal moves and thirteen positions per decision. Compared with a program that examines seven moves and 2500 positions, it is more selective by roughly...
options: A factor of 2
A factor of 10
A factor of 60,000
A factor of 200
optionExplain: That compares 7 with 3 only.
That compares moves to legal moves only.
That is the comparison with the Los Alamos program.
2500 divided by 13 is about 200.
questions.explain: Divide the positions. The card gives the authors' figures.

questions.q: In the Morphy game NSS considered on average only about ____ alternative moves in each position.
questions.explain: The average was three, about 10 percent of the roughly thirty legal moves.

questions.q: Using the authors' figures (13 positions for NSS, about 800,000 for the Los Alamos program), the factor of selectivity over Los Alamos is about...
optionExplain: That is ten times too small.
800,000 divided by 13 is about 61,500, which the authors give as 60,000.
That is the comparison with Bernstein's program.
That is nearly the position count itself.
questions.explain: Divide Los Alamos positions by NSS positions.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say this great gain in selectivity came with no apparent loss in playing power.
questions.explain: They say it came with no apparent loss in playing power, and with a gain in the opening part of the game.

questions.q: How often did NSS choose the same move as the Duke and Count in this game?
options: In four of sixteen positions, and always after a long search of many moves
In all sixteen positions
In nine of sixteen positions, seven of them on the first move it considered
In none, since the Duke and Count played badly
optionExplain: It agreed far more often.
It did not always agree.
More than half the time, mostly at the first move considered.
It agreed in nine positions.
questions.explain: Agreement was frequent and cheap.
questions.teaches: In nine of the sixteen positions NSS proposed the same move as the Duke and Count, and in seven of these nine cases it was the first and only move NSS considered.

questions.q: A new method examines far fewer cases than an old one. What partial repayment do the authors note for NSS's great selectivity?
options: None: selectivity comes at no cost whatever
A loss of playing power in the opening
A need for the opponent to cooperate
More effort for each position examined, and some of the gain came from alpha-beta
optionExplain: They note a repayment.
They note a gain there.
No such need is mentioned.
They note both.
questions.explain: Selectivity is paid for by effort per position.
questions.teaches: The great selectivity of NSS is partly repaid by greater effort for each position examined, and the gain also comes from the alpha-beta procedure, which the earlier programs did not use.

questions.q: Two quite different players choose the same move in a position. What is the most cautious conclusion?
options: The move is certainly the best move in the position
The position probably limits the choice, as the players perceived it
The players must have copied one another
The position permits any move, so the agreement is chance
optionExplain: They may share the same mistaken perception.
Agreement points to limits set by the situation, seen through the players' eyes.
Independent agreement is evidence about the situation.
Agreement more than half the time is not chance.
questions.explain: Agreement points to limits but not to correctness. The card states the authors' caution.

questions.q: NSS agreed with the Duke and Count in more than ____ of the positions.
questions.explain: Agreement in nine of sixteen is more than half.

questions.q: Two beginners and a program all make the same plausible but weak move in a position. Following the authors, what does their agreement show?
options: That the move is demanded objectively by the situation, whether or not the players saw it
That the program is as strong as the beginners
How the position's apparent requirements limit choice, not that the move is good
That no better move exists
optionExplain: Perception and objective requirement can differ.
The agreement does not measure strength.
Players meet requirements only as perceived.
A better move may exist but not be perceived.
questions.explain: Perceived requirements are not necessarily real ones.

questions.q: True or false: In the authors' usage, requirements means what the position objectively demands, whether or not the players saw it.
questions.explain: They say the players met the requirements only as they perceived them.

questions.q: Which of Black's moves in the game do the authors call objective, and why?
options: The sixteenth, the only legal move, and the fifteenth, the only one saving the Queen
The second, since both Black players chose the same move at that point in the game, which shows it was forced
The first, since it opens the game
All of them, since the game was lost anyway
optionExplain: These moves were forced by the position.
The authors say the second was not demanded objectively.
No such claim is made.
Most were not objectively demanded.
questions.explain: Forced moves show requirements at their clearest.
questions.teaches: Black's sixteenth move was objective because it was the only legal move, and the fifteenth can also be regarded as objective: no move would avert disaster, but it was the only one that did not lose the Queen immediately.

questions.q: A well-known opening move is played by two strong players of an earlier age but is now thought old-fashioned. What does this show about the move's requirements?
options: It was demanded by the position
It was not objectively demanded: well known, yet the situation required other moves
It is still the only adequate move today
It proves that perception never errs
optionExplain: The authors say it was not.
The authors say this of the second move: well known, old-fashioned, no longer adequate.
It is no longer regarded as adequate.
It shows perception can err.
questions.explain: Fame of a move is not proof of its necessity.
questions.rule: A known move is not a required move.
questions.teaches: The second move chosen by both Black players, well known as Philidor's Defense, was not demanded objectively: it is old-fashioned and no longer regarded as adequate, and the situation required N-QB3 or N-KB3, neither of which NSS considered.

questions.q: A move is condemned by every analyst, yet strong players lose with it for decades. What does this suggest about how its weakness was found?
options: By a single careful analysis done once over the board by a strong player at the time
By the move's name alone
By the rules of the game, which forbid the move
By accumulated experience of results, not easily by analysis during play
optionExplain: Strong players kept playing it, so analysis was not easy.
Names do not prove weakness.
The move is legal.
Condemnation came from history, over many games.
questions.explain: Experience can show what analysis cannot at once. The card gives the authors' reading.

questions.q: In the position after 3.P-Q4 the NSS program examined ten moves and ____ positions.
questions.explain: NSS examined ten moves and 43 positions, many for a program that usually examined few.

questions.q: What does the authors' reading of the phrase 'universally condemned by the analysts' say about the move B-N5?
options: Historical experience among strong players shows it leads to bad consequences
Its weakness can be demonstrated by quick analysis at the board
It loses a piece by force in all variations
It was invented by the Duke and Count
optionExplain: That is how the authors read the phrase.
The authors deny this.
Harrwitz lasted 59 moves.
Harrwitz had played it earlier.
questions.explain: Condemnation rests on results.
questions.rule: Condemned by results, not by quick analysis.

questions.q: True or false: NSS rejected B-KN5 because it correctly saw that the move loses a pawn by force.
questions.explain: NSS rejected it because its analysis erroneously saw the loss of a pawn.

questions.q: Of the other moves NSS considered in this position, which are named in the text?
options: P-KB4, N-QB3 and B-KN5 only, with all other legal moves rejected after analysis
P-KB4, which a modern work rates as best, together with N-QB3 and B-KN5
N-KB3 (chosen), N-Q2 and PxP; twenty-three legal moves never evoked
Only B-KN5, since the other moves were illegal
optionExplain: P-KB4 was not considered by NSS; the named moves also include N-KB3, N-Q2 and PxP.
P-KB4 was not considered by NSS and is rated inferior.
These are the named moves, with 23 legal moves not even evoked by the generators.
NSS considered ten moves.
questions.explain: NSS found some good moves and missed many legal ones.
questions.rule: Some good moves found, many never evoked.
questions.teaches: Besides the move actually chosen, N-KB3, NSS considered N-Q2 (the move now usually played) and PxP, and twenty-three further legal moves were not even evoked by the move generators.

questions.q: A reviewer says that NSS misjudged B-N5 because it did not consider the reply 4.PxP, BxN. Why did it skip that reply?
options: The reply was an illegal move in that position
The program had run out of memory at that point in its analysis of the move at hand
The exchange did not seem to recover the pawn, and its interaction was not seen
The reply was judged too strong to consider
optionExplain: The reply was legal.
No such limit is cited.
The exchange was evaluated alone.
It was not considered at all.
questions.explain: Valuing exchanges separately hid the interaction.
questions.teaches: In its analysis of B-N5 the program failed to consider 4.PxP, BxN, because the exchange of Knight and Bishop did not seem to recover the lost pawn: in evaluating the exchange it did not see its interaction with the Knight's role on its K5.

questions.q: A program takes the first move that meets its standard. Another move that is equally good but generated later is also available. What decides which is played?
options: The order in which the moves are generated
Which move is objectively stronger in the position at the time
Which move the opponent expects
Which move has the longest continuation
optionExplain: First acceptable means the order matters.
Both meet the standard.
The opponent plays no part.
Length plays no part.
questions.explain: Order of generation settles ties among acceptable moves. The card shows its effects.

questions.q: In the Botvinnik-Kmoch game NSS considered on average only ____ moves per position.
questions.explain: The average was two moves and 10.1 positions.

questions.q: At moves 2, 4, 7 and 8, NSS chose differently from Kmoch. How do the authors explain this?
options: Kmoch's moves were illegal in those positions, so NSS could not consider them
NSS valued Kmoch's moves lower after considering them
NSS always picks a move at random in the opening, so its choices vary a good deal
Its choice was sensitive to the order in which moves were generated
optionExplain: They were legal.
It did not consider them; later evaluation gave them values at least as high.
It does not.
That is their account.
questions.explain: A lax standard lets order decide.

questions.q: True or false: A reader says that NSS chose the same move as Kmoch on most of the ten moves of Table 11.6.
questions.explain: It matched Kmoch at three moves (3, 5 and 10), and chose standard book moves at two others.

questions.q: In the authors' example at move 5, what is the search of N-QB3 for?
options: To predict the line that the game will actually follow
To evaluate material balance at a dead position, not to predict the game
To prove that the move wins a pawn
To find a path for the whole game
optionExplain: The authors say the exchanges are not a likely continuation.
The exchanges explored are not a likely continuation.
It is an evaluation of the move.
A game player needs no path.
questions.explain: Search yields information about the first move, not a forecast.
questions.rule: Search informs; it does not forecast.
questions.teaches: At move 5 the NSS analysis of N-QB3 explores sequences of exchanges only to evaluate material balance at a dead position; this is not the likely continuation, since the players will go on developing and struggling for control of the center, which shows the search is for information, not prediction.

questions.q: A hiring screen takes the first applicant who clears a low bar and often misses stronger ones later in the queue. Which fix do the authors name for NSS's similar problem?
options: A higher acceptance standard, or a more complete set of positional goals
A faster processor, so that more applicants are seen
A random order of applicants, so that no one is favored
A rule to accept the last applicant instead of the first
optionExplain: Either would force a more elaborate search before selecting.
Speed does not change the acceptance rule.
Randomizing the order does not remove the sensitivity.
That swaps one order effect for another.
questions.explain: Raise the bar or add criteria.
questions.rule: Raise the standard or add goals.
questions.teaches: Either a higher acceptance standard or a more complete set of positional goals would have forced NSS into a more elaborate search before it selected a move.

questions.q: A program sorts all legal moves by a quick score of the position each produces and then searches only the top few. What is a risk of this design?
options: The program cannot generate legal moves at all
The program searches too many moves at each position
The program cannot use any evaluation
A move scoring poorly on the quick score is never searched, however good it is
optionExplain: It generates all of them.
It limits the number.
It uses the static value for ordering.
The ordering stands in for knowledge.
questions.explain: Ordering by a score picks what the score likes. The card describes the Kotok design.

questions.q: The Kotok program uses a single move generator for both base-moves and ____ moves.
questions.explain: One plausible-move generator serves both.

questions.q: With the typical widths 4, 3, 2, 2, 1, 1, 1, 1 for depths 1 to 8, how many moves does the Kotok program consider at depth 3?
options: Four
Two
Three
One
optionExplain: That is the width at depth 1.
The third entry of the list is 2.
That is the width at depth 2.
Width falls to 1 only from depth 5.
questions.explain: Read the list by depth.

questions.q: True or false: Unlike the Kotok program, Bernstein's program used no fixed width limits.
questions.explain: Bernstein's program also used a fixed set of limits (at most seven); the Kotok limits are tapered.

questions.q: What happened in the game of Table 11.7 between the Kotok program and an expert?
options: The program gave the expert odds of a Queen and lost the game after the opening
The game was drawn after both sides traded Queens
The expert gave the program odds of a Queen and lost
The program lost despite a Queen's advantage, by a mistake in the middle game
optionExplain: The expert gave the odds.
The program won.
The program pressed on to a win after a well-developed game.
The program won.
questions.explain: A sound opening plus an exploited mistake produced the win.
questions.teaches: In the game of Table 11.7 an expert gave the Kotok program odds of a Queen and lost: the program had developed soundly, exchanged pieces whenever possible (it being ahead in material), and took immediate advantage of a mistake on Black's twelfth move.

questions.q: A planner uses factors for early game aims (such as control and development) that are phased out later, and permanent factors such as material. Which Kotok feature is this?
options: A static value that counts only material at all stages, as Turing's program did
A static value that is recomputed by the opponent
A static value that does not change at all during the course of the game
Center control and development are phased out as the game progresses
optionExplain: It has many factors.
No such feature exists.
Some terms are phased out.
These two terms are phased out; material and pawn structure remain.
questions.explain: Opening aims fade as the game goes on.
questions.teaches: In the Kotok program's static value the center-control and development terms are phased out as the game progresses, while material balance and pawn structure stay.

questions.q: A program wins one game and loses eight against rated amateurs. Which description of its strength is most reasonable?
options: Master level, with some bad luck in a few of the games
Weak to middling amateur, with some better play
Unable to play a legal game
Equal to the best amateur in the tournament
optionExplain: Eight losses do not suggest a master.
Mostly losses but one win suggests a low amateur level.
It did play, and won once.
It lost most games.
questions.explain: Results in rated games locate a player. The card gives the authors' numbers.

questions.q: The Greenblatt program was provisionally rated 1239, which is ____ D.
questions.explain: A rating of 1239 falls in class D.

questions.q: The program defeated a player rated 1505. According to the authors' classes, which class was that player?
options: Class D
Class B
Class C
Class A
optionExplain: The 1365 player was class D.
The authors mention class B for the program's possible caliber.
1505 is class C.
HAS was class A in an earlier game.
questions.explain: Match ratings to classes as given.

questions.q: True or false: The authors expect the program's rating to stay exactly the same, since it was fixed at the winter of 1966-67.
questions.explain: The program was under continual revision, so its strength does not remain constant.
questions.rule: A revised program has no fixed rating.

questions.q: What serious weakness do the authors name in the program's play?
options: A blindness about its own King safety
A refusal to exchange pieces when ahead
An inability to play the opening
A habit of resigning too early
optionExplain: They name this weakness.
No such refusal is described.
It played the opening well.
No such habit is described.
questions.explain: Without a goal for King safety, a program can be mated.
questions.rule: King safety was its weak spot.
questions.teaches: Apart from a serious blindness about its own King safety, the Greenblatt program's play may even be of class B caliber.

questions.q: A reviewer says a student's score of 1239 in a rating scale shows nothing, since the student's work changes every month. Which feature of the authors' remark supports this?
options: The program had played only one tournament
The program was under continual revision, so its strength was not constant
The ratings were for class A players, who were much stronger than the program was
The program refused to enter tournaments
optionExplain: It had played at least two.
A rating belongs to one version.
They were for classes D and C.
It competed in at least two.
questions.explain: A rating is a snapshot of one version.
questions.teaches: The Greenblatt program is under continual revision, so its playing strength does not remain constant, and a rating belongs to one version.

questions.q: A program plays the opening by aiming for control of the center and rapid development. What kind of opponent mistake would let it profit most?
options: Developing all its pieces early and castling at once, to get safe quickly
Copying the program's moves exactly
Refusing to make any capture
Wasting time on premature pawn moves, leaving its pieces undeveloped
optionExplain: That is sound play.
That would not give an advantage.
That is not a clear mistake.
Lost time gives the better-developed side an advantage.
questions.explain: Development and time are the opening currency. The card shows the game.
questions.rule: Lost time in the opening is costly.

questions.q: The Greenblatt program won its game with a Queen sacrifice on move ____ followed by checkmate.
questions.explain: The checkmate begins with the Queen sacrifice on move 20.

questions.q: In the won game, why can White's third move, which loses a tempo, hardly be called amateurish?
options: Both players' first three moves match a Mieses-Tarrasch game of 1920
The move is the only legal move available
The move gains a tempo on the following move
The move was chosen at random from the program's list of plausible moves
optionExplain: Master play stands behind the line.
It was not forced.
The authors say it loses one.
No randomness is described.
questions.explain: A move that follows master practice is not an amateur error.

questions.q: True or false: A reviewer says the program's win shows it paid careful attention to its own King safety throughout. The authors would agree.
questions.explain: They say its early success is not unrelated to its ignoring its own King safety after Black's move 11.

questions.q: What do the authors observe about the motive of the final checkmate in the won game?
options: It copies a mating pattern from a game of Mieses and Tarrasch in 1920
It is a standard textbook mate that Morphy never used in any of his games
It is the same motive as Morphy's checkmate of the Duke and Count
It has no connection with any earlier game
optionExplain: That game is cited for the opening moves.
They link it to Morphy.
They point to the same motive as in the Morphy game.
They note the likeness.
questions.explain: The same combination idea recurs a century apart.
questions.teaches: The checkmate beginning with the Queen sacrifice on move 20 employs precisely the same motive as Morphy's checkmate of the Duke of Brunswick and Count Isouard.

questions.q: A chess club notes that a program played the first four moves of a famous line. Following the authors, is that an isolated incident for the programs?
options: Yes: it is the only time any program played a book move
Yes: book moves can only be played from a stored opening book of lines in memory
No: it also won as Black with four book moves; the Kotok program had book lines
No: every program plays only book moves in the opening, and then plays at random
optionExplain: Several book moves are cited.
The programs found them from their own criteria.
The authors say its selection of several book moves is not an isolated incident.
The examples are of three programs' games, not every game.
questions.explain: Book moves recur across programs.
questions.teaches: In its win as Black over H. Dreyfus, the Greenblatt program's first four moves were book, the human opponent being the first to depart from accepted lines; in two published games the Kotok program found book continuations for three and five moves, and in the latter its opponent then left book.

questions.q: A program orders candidate moves by a score of how well they fit general aims, and uses a separate score to judge the positions reached. Why keep the two scores separate?
options: Ordering needs a cheap guide; evaluation must judge positions accurately
Because the same score cannot be computed twice
Because a single score would make the program too accurate to be played in time
Because separate scores are required by the rules of chess for every program
optionExplain: The two jobs call for different information.
Computation is not the issue.
Accuracy is not a drawback.
No rule requires it.
questions.explain: Guiding search and judging positions are different jobs. The card shows the Greenblatt design.

questions.q: In the Greenblatt program the plausibility value mainly reflects material and ____, combined in a system of weights on squares.
questions.explain: Both are combined in weights for squares, scoring how a move changes coverage.

questions.q: In the Greenblatt program, what is a difference from the Kotok program in generating moves?
options: It generates only a few moves, without making all legal moves first, to save time
It has no ordering of moves, only random choice
It searches to a single fixed depth in all positions, whatever happens in them
Its plausibility value is separate from its static value; Kotok's is not
optionExplain: It also makes all legal moves in a subsidiary pass.
It orders by plausibility.
Depth is extended for several reasons.
That is the stated difference.
questions.explain: Both order by a score; they differ in what score.

questions.q: True or false: In the Greenblatt program the width limits at each depth are only base values that several things can increase.
questions.explain: The widths are only base values that several things can increase.

questions.q: Which base widths for depths 1 to 8 are given for the tournament settings?
optionExplain: These are the typical Kotok widths.
These are the tournament base widths in the figure.
A constant width is Bernstein's.
No such setting is given.
questions.explain: The tournament widths are larger than Kotok's but still taper.
questions.teaches: The Greenblatt program's tournament base widths for depths 1 to 8 are 15, 15, 9, 9, 6, 6, 3 and 2, and smaller values are used in casual play.

questions.q: A scout may list at most six possible exits but requires that the list include a variety of different exits, not six uses of the same door. Which Greenblatt feature is this?
options: A diversity requirement, so that a variety of different men take part
A depth extension, adding extra plies for captures and for forced defenses
A secondary search along the principal variation
A static value that is summed over the game
optionExplain: That is the diversity factor.
That concerns depth.
That is a separate feature.
That is the evaluation.
questions.explain: Variety prevents one piece's many moves from filling the list.
questions.teaches: A diversity factor increases the Greenblatt program's width to ensure a suitable variety of pieces take part, which matters when a threatened piece such as the Queen has many retreat squares that would otherwise take all the allowed moves.

questions.q: A search finds a new best move. Before trusting its value, a careful program might spend extra effort on it. Where is extra effort best spent?
options: On the moves that were already rejected
On random side lines unrelated to the move
On the first move in the list, whatever it is, and whatever its value
Deeper along the line that gave the move its value
optionExplain: Rejected moves are not the issue.
Unrelated lines do not test its value.
The new best move is the one in question.
That line determines the value.
questions.explain: A good value may rest on a shallow line. The card names the Greenblatt remedy.
questions.rule: Test the line that carries the value.

questions.q: The path that generated the minimax value of the newly found good move is called the ____ variation.
questions.explain: The principal variation is the path that gave the minimax value.

questions.q: Put the stages of the Greenblatt program's secondary search in order.
items: A depth-one alternative is found to be better than the reigning one
The program travels back out along the principal variation to the boundary of the earlier search
The search is pushed a couple of plies further
The resulting value is assigned to the alternative
questions.explain: The new best move is re-searched deeper along its principal variation, and the deeper value replaces the first one.
questions.rule: Better, back out, push deeper, reassign.

questions.q: True or false: A reader says the secondary search is a change the Greenblatt program shares with all the earlier programs. The authors would agree.
questions.explain: With all other programs the search was one sweep; the secondary search is a substantial departure.

questions.q: What do the search statistics of the 27-move game against an expert show?
options: A median of 30 moves considered and no use of alpha-beta
A median of 1057 moves per move, with alpha-beta used a median of 174 times
A constant 1000 moves at every move of the game
A median of 800,000 moves, as in the Los Alamos program
optionExplain: The numbers are much larger.
These are the figures the authors give.
The numbers varied widely.
That is the Los Alamos count.
questions.explain: The median shows pruning more than made up for the extra work.
questions.teaches: In a 27-move game against an expert, the Greenblatt program considered a median of 1057 moves per move (from 162 at the first move to 16,613 at most), with alpha-beta pruning a median of 174 times; the median being a little over 1000 shows pruning rather more than compensated for the extra moves generated to reach dead positions.

questions.q: A program of modest chess knowledge searches about as selectively as a program of great knowledge, yet plays well. What do the authors conclude from the Greenblatt program?
options: Large amounts of search can never be replaced by chess knowledge of any amount or kind
Speed alone is enough to overcome any lack of knowledge
Small amounts of chess sophistication can substitute for large amounts of search
Selectivity matters only in the opening phase of a game
optionExplain: The authors conclude the opposite.
They stress selectivity over speed.
That is the lesson they draw.
Nothing limits the conclusion to the opening.
questions.explain: Selectivity from knowledge replaces search.
questions.teaches: Only the NSS program is more selective in its search than the Greenblatt program, and the latter's playing strength provides further evidence of the substitutability of small amounts of chess sophistication for large amounts of search.

questions.q: A program chooses each move afresh from the position on the board, with no plan carried over. What follows for forcing it to play a given move?
options: It breaks down, since its plan for the game is spoiled by the forced move
It refuses the move
It restarts the game from the first move
It can accept the forced move easily and carry on from the new position
optionExplain: It has no plan to spoil.
Forcing a move is possible.
It continues from the new position.
With no plan to disturb, the new position is simply a new problem.
questions.explain: No plan, no disruption. The card says this of the six programs.

questions.q: According to the authors, the six programs all choose moves in a chess position rather than ____ a game of chess.
questions.explain: The game is a series of independent move choices.
questions.rule: Choose a move, not play a game.

questions.q: The authors force NSS to make the move played in a recorded game, even when it differs from NSS's own. Why is this possible?
options: NSS keeps a plan for the whole game, which adapts easily
Each move is chosen independently, so no plan exists for the forced move to upset
NSS ignores the position after a forced move
NSS can undo its own move, then redo the forced one
optionExplain: The authors say the programs do not plan.
The game is a series of essentially independent choices.
It works from the new position.
Moves cannot be undone.
questions.explain: Independence of moves allows forced moves.

questions.q: Which of these are shared by all six programs, according to the authors? Pick all that apply.
options: Forward search through a subtree of the legal-move tree
Selection heuristics
Minimaxing of static evaluations
Goal modules like NSS's
optionExplain: A feature of all six.
All six use some.
All six minimax.
Only NSS has goals.
questions.explain: The first three are the common features; goals belong to NSS alone.
questions.rule: Goals are not common to all.

questions.q: Which kinds of chess programs does the authors' count of six leave out?
options: Programs that run on the largest computers available at the time the book was written
Programs that play only the opening
Specialized programs, such as endgame players and the mating program of Chapter 13
Programs whose authors were chess masters
optionExplain: Machine size is not the criterion.
No such group is named.
These are named as exceptions.
Authorship is not the criterion.
questions.explain: The six are the general programs whose structure has been reported.
questions.teaches: The six programs are not all that have been written but all whose structure had been reported in the literature, leaving out specialized programs such as endgame players and the mating combinations program of Chapter 13.

questions.q: A forecaster makes each day's forecast afresh. An official reading is substituted for one of hers. What small thing must she still redo, by analogy with NSS?
options: Recompute a few starting values that depended on her own reading
Rewrite her whole season plan
Replay all earlier forecasts
Nothing at all, since forecasts from different days never share any values
optionExplain: NSS recomputed some initial values of its evaluation for a forced move.
She has no season plan.
No replay is needed.
A very modest connection remains.
questions.explain: Even independent choices share a little set-up.
questions.teaches: NSS did have to recompute some initial values of its evaluation function for a forced move, which the authors call a very modest connection between successive moves.

questions.q: Which design choice would most reduce the number of positions a program examines?
options: Using a faster processor to examine each position in less time than before
Taking the first move that meets its expectations instead of comparing all
Evaluating each position with more factors
Searching every continuation to the same depth
optionExplain: Speed does not reduce the number of positions.
Stopping at the first acceptable move saves search.
More factors do not reduce the count.
Uniform depth gives the largest tree.
questions.explain: Stopping early and separating generation reduce search. The card names both.

questions.q: Rank these programs from the largest tree explored to the smallest, as far as the authors can tell.
items: Los Alamos
Bernstein
Greenblatt
NSS and Turing (very small trees)
questions.explain: The Los Alamos program explores by far the largest tree, then Bernstein, then Greenblatt, with NSS and Turing very small.
questions.rule: Los Alamos, Bernstein, Greenblatt, NSS and Turing.

questions.q: Which two things limit the NSS search so severely, in the authors' account?
options: The use of the alpha-beta procedure and the use of a lexicographic ordering
The small memory of its machine and its use of tapered widths of search at depth
The absence of any evaluation and of any goals
The distinction between move and continuation generation, and satisficing
optionExplain: Alpha-beta is used by other programs too.
Memory and widths are not given as the two sources.
NSS has both evaluation and goals.
These are the two sources.
questions.explain: Two design features limit NSS.

questions.q: True or false: The Greenblatt program explores a smaller tree than Bernstein's.
questions.explain: The Greenblatt program explores a smaller tree than Bernstein's.

questions.q: What is the other side of the coin the authors mention for the NSS first-acceptable approach?
options: Often the very first move generated, of some thirty legal, was strong
The first move generated was always the best move
The first move generated was always rejected by the analysis of the program
The first move generated needed no analysis at all before it was played
optionExplain: They report many such cases.
They say often, not always.
The first move was often strong.
Moves were still analyzed.
questions.explain: A cheap rule also pays off often.
questions.rule: Often the first move is strong.
questions.teaches: The authors note that, besides the cases of premature choice, they have seen many cases where the very first move NSS generated, out of some thirty legal moves, was a strong move, even one of the book moves in the position.

questions.q: A reviewer says that separating the generator of candidate moves from the generator of continuations has a cost. What does the authors' summary say it has already led NSS to do?
options: Fail to generate any legal move
Search a tree larger than Bernstein's
Misevaluate a move, as in the exchange on B-N5
Abandon the alpha-beta procedure altogether when searching
optionExplain: It generated legal moves.
It searches very small trees.
They give cases of misevaluation from this principle.
It uses alpha-beta.
questions.explain: Selectivity from separate generators can hide interactions.
questions.teaches: The authors say they have already seen examples where the sharp separation of move generation from continuation generation leads the NSS program to misevaluate a move.

questions.q: A program can find moves with one process that lists all legal moves and ranks them, or with many processes each looking for moves of one kind. What might the first design protect against?
options: Spending too much time on any single move
Making moves that break the rules of the game in some positions
Overlooking a candidate move that no special process thought of
Using evaluation functions at all
optionExplain: Listing all moves takes time.
Both designs follow the rules.
Listing everything leaves nothing out.
The single generator uses one to order moves.
questions.explain: Completeness versus adaptiveness. The card names the authors' view.

questions.q: The Kotok and Greenblatt programs have a ____ move generator that generates all legal moves and orders them by an evaluation function.
questions.explain: One generator serves them both.

questions.q: Match each program to its way of generating moves.
pairs: Plausible generators tied to features, run in priority order
One generator ordering all legal moves by an evaluation
questions.explain: Bernstein and NSS use many generators; Kotok uses one that orders all legal moves.

questions.q: True or false: Bernstein's program has a single generator that produces all the legal moves and orders them.
questions.explain: Bernstein's program has several plausible move generators, each tied to a feature of the game.

questions.q: What concern does each design express, according to the authors?
options: Many: adaptive response; one generator: candidates not overlooked
Many generators: that no moves be overlooked; one generator: that the response be adaptive
Many generators: speed of play; one generator: depth of search
Both express a concern for the opponent's style
optionExplain: These are the two concerns.
This reverses the concerns.
Neither is given.
Neither concerns the opponent's style.
questions.explain: Adaptiveness versus completeness.
questions.teaches: The many-generator design expresses a concern that the response be specifically adaptive, while the single-generator design expresses a concern that possible candidate moves not be overlooked.

questions.q: A library ranks its whole catalog to choose books to shelve. One library reuses its book-quality score for the ranking; another uses a special ranking score. Which matches the Greenblatt program?
options: The reused quality score, as in the Kotok program's static value
Neither, since no ranking is used
Both, since the two are the same score
The special ranking score, kept separate from the quality score
optionExplain: That is the Kotok design, which orders by the static value.
Both programs order their moves.
They differ.
Its ordering evaluation is a special function, not the static value.
questions.explain: Kotok reuses the static value; Greenblatt uses a special function.
questions.teaches: In the Kotok program the ordering evaluation is simply the static value, while in the Greenblatt program it is a special evaluation function.

questions.q: To choose actions in a complicated situation, a system can try many actions to see which work, or notice features of the situation and try actions that bear on them. Which is closer to NSS?
options: Trying all actions at random until one of them happens to work
Noticing features and trying only moves relevant to them
Trying actions in alphabetical order
Copying the actions of the previous situation
optionExplain: The authors contrast NSS with this.
NSS builds a bridge from features to relevant moves.
Order of this kind has no link to the situation.
NSS works from the present situation.
questions.explain: Features suggest relevant actions. The card shows the authors' account.

questions.q: The authors describe the relation of moves to features in NSS as a relation of means to ____.
questions.explain: Moves are possible means to ends such as gaining material or averting a loss.

questions.q: In NSS an enemy piece is under attack. What does the feature suggest, in means-ends terms?
options: A possibility of gain, with capturing as a means
A possibility of loss, with interposing as a means
A possibility of a draw, with resigning as a means
A source of information only, with no move suggested
optionExplain: An attacked enemy piece is a chance for gain.
That fits one's own piece under attack.
No such link is made.
The feature is tied to relevant moves.
questions.explain: Features define gains and losses; moves are the means.

questions.q: True or false: A program that obtains information only by exploring the specific position would be the Los Alamos program, apart from the knowledge implicit in its static evaluation.
questions.explain: For the Los Alamos program exploration was the sole source, and a major source for Bernstein's program.

questions.q: What does the authors' footnote say about the word theory in the chess literature?
options: It means the same as in the authors' use, general rules and principles
It means a program's evaluation function
It means the rules of chess as set out by the international chess federation
It regrettably means opening book knowledge, that is, chess history
optionExplain: The note points out the difference.
It concerns the chess literature.
The note gives opening knowledge.
The note says the literature uses theory for opening book knowledge.
questions.explain: The same word covers two quite different things.
questions.rule: Theory in chess means opening lore.
questions.teaches: In the chess literature theory regrettably means knowledge of the book moves in the chess openings, that is, knowledge of chess history, whereas the authors use it for general rules or principles.

questions.q: A gardener's rule says to water first, then to prune, then to feed. Which NSS fact does this resemble?
options: Knowledge stored as a table of every game position
Knowledge stored in the order of the goals considered
Knowledge discovered during search and forgotten after each move was made
Knowledge supplied by the opponent after each move
optionExplain: No such table exists.
NSS also stores chess knowledge in the order of its means-ends processes.
The ordering is built in.
The opponent supplies none.
questions.explain: Order itself carries knowledge.
questions.teaches: NSS also stores chess knowledge in the order in which goals are considered, features detected and moves generated: material balance before center control before development, and moves of center pawns, as means toward center control, before preventive or preparatory moves.

questions.q: You can do only one thing this hour, and a pipe is leaking while the shelves need dusting. What does this limit suggest?
options: Dust first, since small jobs are quickest
List every job and do all at once
Deal with the leak first, and dust only if it can be combined with that
Do neither until all the jobs have been ranked in writing by the owner
optionExplain: The pressing matter is the leak.
Capacity for action is limited.
Pressing matters first, with the limited capacity for action in mind.
Delay does not follow from the limit.
questions.explain: Limited action calls for priorities. The card gives the chess version.

questions.q: The authors say that in chess, as in real life, the amount of action that can be accomplished in a given time is ____.
questions.explain: Action is limited, so only the pressing considerations need attention.

questions.q: Which of these are among the three reasons the authors give for the sensible moves of the first-acceptable rule? Pick all that apply.
options: The move is always proposed for a reason, relevant to a goal and specific features
The most pressing problems and important considerations are taken up first
A single move exhausts the program's capacity for action, so less important features need no attention
The program searches every continuation to the end of the game
optionExplain: The first reason.
The second reason.
The third reason.
NSS does not do this.
questions.explain: The first three are the reasons; NSS does not search to the end.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the first-acceptable rule gives sensible moves mainly because NSS searches more positions than other programs.
questions.explain: NSS searches very little; its sensible moves come from reasons, priorities and the limit on action.

questions.q: What do the authors say NSS is aimed at, beyond making good moves?
options: Doing so as fast as possible, whatever the reasons for each of the moves
Doing so by copying the moves of grandmasters
Doing so with the largest possible tree
Doing so for the right reasons, deduced from circumstances noticed
optionExplain: Speed is not the stated aim.
Copying is not the aim.
NSS explores very small trees.
That is their statement of the aim.
questions.explain: The aim concerns the grounds of the move, not only the move.
questions.teaches: The NSS program is aimed not only at making good moves, but at doing so for the right reasons, that is, in the light of consequences deduced from noticing certain circumstances in the situation.

questions.q: A nurse on a busy ward deals with the most urgent patient first and treats no others until that case is handled. Which feature of the NSS rule does this share?
options: Searching all possible treatments to the end
Pressing problems first, with a single action absorbing the capacity
Choosing the first treatment at random
Treating all patients at once
optionExplain: That is not the NSS rule.
Both features appear in the nurse's practice.
The NSS proposals have reasons.
The capacity for action is limited.
questions.explain: Priority plus limited capacity make a simple rule sensible.
questions.teaches: If the Queen is attacked, developing the Rooks becomes a secondary consideration, which is not even worth attending to unless it can be combined with the more important task of saving the Queen.

questions.q: A very fast machine tries to master a game by searching without any ideas about what makes a position good. What do the authors expect?
options: Success, since speed makes up for any concepts that are missing from the program
Success, but only in the opening
Failure to find strong moves or evaluate reliably, for lack of concepts
Failure, but only because the machine tires
optionExplain: The authors deny this.
No such limit is given.
Concepts are needed for strong moves and reliable evaluation.
Tiredness is not at issue.
questions.explain: Speed cannot replace ideas. The card gives the authors' view.

questions.q: Without appropriate ____, even a very fast system cannot explore sufficiently to discover strong moves.
questions.explain: Appropriate concepts are what the fitting of behavior to the situation depends on.

questions.q: A designer wants to give her chess program what the history of chess suggests it needs. What should she supply?
options: A few central concepts that guide what to look for, not only more speed
A faster processor and nothing else
A larger tree of continuations with no evaluation
A random choice among legal moves
optionExplain: Concepts, not speed alone, are what chess history shows.
Speed alone cannot make up for missing concepts.
Without evaluation, search cannot judge.
Random choice has no link to the situation.
questions.explain: Concepts guide search; they are not replaced by it.

questions.q: True or false: A reader says the authors expect a sufficiently fast system to play strong chess even if it has no central concepts.
questions.explain: They say that without appropriate concepts even a very fast system cannot explore sufficiently.

questions.q: Which of these does the authors' passage list among the central concepts that emerged in chess history? Pick all that apply.
options: Piece values
Mobility
Center control
Clock speed
Opening books
optionExplain: Named in the passage.
Named in the passage.
Named in the passage.
A matter of machines, not named.
Not named in the passage.
questions.explain: The passage lists piece values, mobility, development, center control and so on.
questions.rule: Piece values, mobility, development, center control.
questions.teaches: The central concepts whose gradual emergence chess history records include piece values, mobility, development and center control.

questions.q: A company has huge computing power but no concept of what makes a customer likely to buy. What do the authors' remarks suggest about its chance of success by pure computation?
options: Good, since speed will discover the concept in time
Poor, since a concept would not emerge on its own from computation
Good, since concepts are unnecessary in complex tasks
Certain failure, whatever concepts are later added
optionExplain: The authors do not expect this.
Concepts do not simply emerge from computation on other features.
The authors say they are necessary.
Added concepts could help.
questions.explain: Concepts have to be supplied, not just computed.
questions.teaches: One should not expect the equivalent of a central concept simply to emerge from computation in specific positions, where the computation is based on quite other features of the position.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: Which way of choosing a chess move is most plausible for a human player?
options: Examine every legal continuation to great depth, noting one small fact from each
Pick a few plausible moves, judge them, and look deeper only at the most promising
Play the first move that comes to mind, and never look ahead at all, whatever the position
Count the pieces on each side and pick the move that adds the most material
optionExplain: A thorough machine does this, but it needs speed and memory a person lacks.
Right: a short list plus rough and then fine search suits a person's limits. The card names this kind of organization.
People do look ahead; the authors treat search as central.
Material matters, but a single count is not the search the chapter studies.
questions.explain: A person has limited speed and memory, so a short list of plausible moves with rough-cut then fine-cut search is the likelier fit. The card gives the authors' list.
questions.rule: A human is more likely to use a short list of moves than an exhaustive search.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: The authors say a human lacks the speed, memory or ____ of organization to examine 800,000 moves.
questions.explain: They name speed, memory and precision of organization as the three limits.
questions.rule: Speed, memory and precision limit a human search.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: Choosing a hotel, a friend plans to score all 5,000 in the country on ten criteria. Which plan copies the human-fit idea?
options: Score every hotel on all ten criteria, using a larger spreadsheet
Choose the hotel with the best photo and skip any comparison at all
Ask five friends and book whatever the first one names, without checking
Shortlist a handful by quick rules, then compare those few in detail
optionExplain: This is the exhaustive style the authors rule out for a person.
A single glance is no rough-cut then fine-cut search.
This hands the choice over; it does not describe a search organization.
Right: a rough first cut followed by a fine cut on the survivors.
questions.explain: Rough-cut followed by fine-cut search first narrows the field with cheap tests and then spends effort on the few that remain.
questions.rule: Use cheap tests first, effort later.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: True or false: The authors claim that humans must be examining hundreds of thousands of moves because chess programs do.
questions.explain: They say the opposite: the human lacks the speed, memory and precision for such an examination.
questions.rule: A program's feasible method need not be the human's.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: How do the authors rate their chess investigation against the cryptarithmetic and logic tasks?
options: It was far less complete, because chess is a deep task
It was more complete
It was equally complete
It was left out
optionExplain: Right: they call chess a deep task and say the investigation was less complete.
The authors say existing chess programs are far from satisfactory.
Same method, but they say the investigation was far less complete.
The problem space is the basic one; the chapter goes on to study it.
questions.explain: The authors temper expectations: chess is a deep task, and their investigation of it was far less complete than for the other two.
questions.teaches: Chess is called a deep task, unlike cryptarithmetic or elementary logic, and the authors' chess investigation was far less complete than their work on those.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A student reads how a tennis-serving robot is built. By the authors' remark on the previous chapter, what should she expect?
options: To serve better at once
To learn nothing, since an account of a robot cannot explain anything about the task
To understand the robot better, yet be no better at serving herself
To serve better only if she also memorizes the robot's rules by heart
optionExplain: The authors say a reader is probably no better a chess player for reading about the programs, so skill does not follow at once.
Too strong: the account does explain the robot; the authors' point is only that understanding it does not make her a better player.
Right: they say the reader is probably no better a chess player for reading about programs.
The authors make no such claim; they say knowing the programs does not improve play.
questions.explain: The authors expect readers learned something about solving cryptarithmetic or the simple logic problems but are no better at chess for reading the previous chapter. Understanding a program is not the same as gaining skill.
questions.rule: Knowing how a program works is not skill.
questions.teaches: After the earlier chapters the reader probably learned something about solving cryptarithmetic or logic tasks, but the authors say he is no better a chess player for reading the chess task analysis.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A researcher wants to know whether a person's chess thinking can be described as information processing. What first step fits the authors' plan?
options: Count how many games a thousand players win against a program
Ask players afterwards to rate how hard each position felt
Record one player talking aloud while choosing a move, and study it closely
Build the strongest possible program and compare its final score with that of human players
optionExplain: Win counts say little about the thought process behind a move.
Ratings are not a record of the search itself.
Right: they start with a single situation in detail.
Strength is a different question from how a person actually works.
questions.explain: The authors begin as before with a detailed look at a single subject and a single position. The card lists the questions they bring.
questions.rule: Begin with one case studied closely.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: As with other tasks, the authors start by treating a single situation in detail: one subject choosing a ____ in a given position.
questions.explain: The chapter studies one subject choosing White's next move.
questions.rule: One subject, one position, one move.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A researcher studies how a baker decides a loaf is done. Which finding answers the authors' task-versus-psychology question about the process?
options: Any baker must check that the loaf is cooked through, but this baker taps the crust from habit
The baker is a person and therefore a living organism with a brain
The loaf finished in forty minutes, faster than the recipe said
The baker talked a good deal while working, which was pleasant for the observers to hear
optionExplain: Right: the first part is dictated by the task, the second looks personal.
This describes the baker, not which part of the process is task-dictated.
A timing figure does not separate task demands from personal features.
Talk is data; it does not tell task from psychology.
questions.explain: The question splits behavior into what any solver must do because of the task and what comes from the person. The fitting finding names one of each.
questions.rule: Separate what the task forces from what the person adds.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: True or false: The authors treat one position as showing only part of the phenomena of chess.
questions.explain: They say a single position brings out only a part of the phenomena of chess.
questions.rule: One position shows part of chess.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: How does chess compare with logic and cryptarithmetic as a case for the single-position method?
options: A single position shows more of chess
A single position shows the same share in all three tasks
The method is not used for chess; they rely on a large sample of games instead of one
A single position shows even less of chess than one problem showed of those tasks
optionExplain: The authors say the opposite about how much one position shows.
They say chess is even more limited in this respect.
The chapter is a single-subject study.
Right: even more than in logic and cryptarithmetic, one position brings out only part.
questions.explain: The authors note that one position reveals only part of chess, even more than in the other two tasks.
questions.rule: The more varied the task, the less one case shows.
questions.teaches: Even more than in logic and cryptarithmetic, a single chess position brings out only part of the phenomena of chess.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A team studies one commuter's routes in detail, then plans a larger survey. Which part of the authors' plan does this copy?
options: A broad survey first, then one case only if the survey fails
A close study of one case first, with the broader look postponed to a later study
A single case that is meant to settle every question about the topic once and for all
A case study that drops the research questions to remain open-minded
optionExplain: The authors do the reverse order.
Right: they postpone the broader look at chess to the next chapter.
They admit one position shows only part of chess.
They begin with fundamental questions about IPS, task and mechanisms.
questions.explain: The authors treat one subject in detail and put off a broader look to the next chapter.
questions.teaches: The broader look at chess behavior is postponed to the next chapter.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: To capture a chess player's thinking, what would you ask him to do while he analyses a position?
options: Think aloud as he works and record the speech
Stay silent, then write a summary of his reasoning once he has chosen
Answer questions from the researcher after every move he considers
Choose within one minute so that the answer is quick and unstudied
optionExplain: Right: the protocol is taken by talking aloud on tape.
A summary after the fact loses the order of the search.
Interruptions would change the search being recorded.
The setup allows as long as he wants.
questions.explain: The protocol records talk during the analysis, with no time limit. The card gives the details.
questions.rule: Record the talk while the analysis happens.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: S2 was asked to talk ____ while he analysed the position, and his talk was recorded on tape.
questions.explain: Talking aloud produces the protocol the authors analyse.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A researcher wants a protocol from a card player choosing a play. Which setup follows the chess study?
options: Show the hand, allow ten seconds only, and ask for an explanation the next day
Describe the hand by phone, and take notes on the final choice only
Show the hand, allow as long as needed, ask for talk aloud, and tape it
Show the hand with a hint, and watch which play is chosen in silence
optionExplain: This limits time and delays the report.
The route to the choice is the data, not the choice alone.
Right: no time limit, spoken thinking, recorded.
A hint changes the task and silence leaves no protocol.
questions.explain: The study gives the subject the position, no time limit, and a request to talk aloud while a tape records.
questions.rule: Same conditions: free time, spoken thought, tape.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: True or false: S2 was a player of modest ability, active in a college chess club, and not a class A player.
questions.explain: The authors describe him this way: by no means an expert or class A player.
questions.rule: S2 was a modest club player.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: How do the authors compare S2's play with the chess programs of the last chapter?
options: Worse than all of them
Better than all but the Greenblatt program, which is very likely better
Equal to all of them
Better than every program without exception, Greenblatt's included
optionExplain: The authors say his play is undoubtedly better than the programs, with one exception.
Right: the exception is the Greenblatt program.
They rank him above the programs apart from one.
They say the Greenblatt program is very likely the better player.
questions.explain: S2 beats the programs except the Greenblatt program, which the authors think is very likely the better player.
questions.rule: Compare to the programs, but not to the strongest one.
questions.teaches: S2 plays better than the chess programs discussed, except the Greenblatt program, which is very likely the better player.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: Volunteers P1 to P3 are labeled in a memory study and again in a vision study. What does the S2 practice suggest?
options: Treat P2 as the same person in both studies
Ignore all subject labels because they carry no information in reports
Assume the first study's P2 must have been the better performer
Treat the second P2 as possibly a different person; labels are reassigned per task
optionExplain: The authors warn that subject names are reassigned in each task.
The labels identify subjects within a task; they are not meaningless.
Labels say nothing about ranking.
Right: in this book the S2 of chess is not the S2 of cryptarithmetic or logic.
questions.explain: The authors note that names are reassigned to subjects in each task, so S2 here is not the S2 of cryptarithmetic or logic.
questions.teaches: Subject names are reassigned in each task, so S2 in chess is not the same person as S2 in cryptarithmetic or in logic.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: In a position where the opponent's pieces look loosely defended, what decision faces the player to move?
options: Whether to resign, since loose pieces usually mean that the position is already lost
Whether to trade off every piece immediately in order to simplify
Whether to repeat the opponent's last move as a mirror reply
Whether any profitable use can be made of the weaknesses, or a calm move is better
optionExplain: The weaknesses are Black's, not White's.
No such rule is given; the issue is profit from weaknesses.
Mirror play has no place in his analysis.
Right: this is the question de Groot poses.
questions.explain: De Groot frames it as: exploit the weaknesses if possible, otherwise strengthen with a calm move.
questions.rule: Exploit weaknesses if you can; otherwise consolidate.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: Four out of ____ grandmasters who analysed position A for de Groot chose 1. B x N/5.
questions.explain: Four of five grandmasters chose the same move that S2 chose.
questions.rule: Four of five grandmasters chose B x N/5.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A rival firm's key supplier is stretched thin. Which question mirrors de Groot's opening comment on position A?
options: Should we copy the rival's last decision, whatever it was?
Can we profit from this weakness, or should we strengthen our own position?
Should we avoid any action at all until the rival has fixed its supplier problem?
Should we sell our own best assets now to keep cash ready?
optionExplain: Copying is not part of his comment.
Right: exploit the weakness if possible, otherwise make a calm strengthening move.
He asks whether to act on the weakness, not to wait for its repair.
The comment concerns exploiting the other side's weakness.
questions.explain: De Groot's comment is a two-way test: exploit the opponent's weaknesses if profitable, else play calmly.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: True or false: De Groot's analysis found that White has no profitable use of Black's weaknesses, so a calm move is best.
questions.explain: He found that White can get the better of it, with a forced win by 1. B x N/5.
questions.rule: De Groot found a forced win.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: What does the choice of 1. B x N/5 by four of five grandmasters, and by S2, tell us about the move?
options: It is a rare move that all five grandmasters rejected
It is the move only S2 found, which the grandmasters missed
Four of five grandmasters and S2 picked it, so strong players agreed on the move
It is an uncontested move
optionExplain: Four of the five chose it.
Four grandmasters chose it too.
Right: this is the agreement the authors report.
Four of five chose it; one did not.
questions.explain: Four of five grandmasters chose 1. B x N/5, as did S2.
questions.rule: Agreement on the move is reported, not yet explained.
questions.teaches: Four out of five grandmasters who analysed the position for de Groot chose 1. B x N/5, and S2 selected it too.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A student gets the same final answer as the answer key on a hard maths problem. What does the authors' remark about S2's choice warn?
options: A matching answer does not show the working was correct in its details
A matching answer proves the student understood every step of the problem
A matching answer shows the student copied it from a better student
A matching answer is worth less than a wrong answer with good working
optionExplain: Right: the authors say S2 chose the right move yet remained ignorant of essential features.
The authors say this inference cannot be drawn.
Nothing suggests copying.
The authors do not rank them; they only say agreement proves little.
questions.explain: The authors write that one cannot conclude S2's analysis is correct in detail from his choice of the same move. The protocol must be read, not only the answer.
questions.rule: Judge the analysis, not only the answer.
questions.teaches: S2 appears to remain ignorant of several of the essential features of the position even though he chose the same move as the grandmasters.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: Why might a written chess notation need a mark for Black's men even when the piece letters are standard?
options: Because Black's men move differently from White's in this game
Because standard letters exist only for White's pieces
Because spoken phrases often name a man or move without showing whose it is
Because primes show which moves were strong and which were weak in the game
optionExplain: Both sides' men move by the same rules.
Standard letters exist for both sides.
Right: the card gives this as the reason for the prime.
A mark for side does not grade a move.
questions.explain: A prime shows side when the context does not. The card shows the notation.
questions.rule: Mark the side when context does not.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: In the authors' notation, a ____ is used to indicate Black.
questions.explain: A prime (as in N') marks Black's man or move.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: In the authors' notation, what does R x B'/3 mean?
options: The White Rook takes the Black Bishop on the third rank
The Black Rook takes the White Bishop on the third rank
The White Rook takes the Black Bishop on the third file
The White Rook and Black Bishop exchange places on the board
optionExplain: Right: the prime marks the Bishop as Black's, and the number gives the rank.
A prime would then sit on the Rook, not on the Bishop.
The number after the slash is the rank, as in B x N'/5 on the fifth rank.
The x means a capture.
questions.explain: The prime on B shows it is Black's, and /3 gives the rank, as in B x N'/5.
questions.rule: Prime means Black; the slash number is the rank.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: True or false: The authors leave the remark that Black's Kingside is in sad shape without chess notation.
questions.explain: They note chess content only where it is clear. That remark is not objectively true for most definitions of sad shape, and no similar phrase elsewhere helps, so they leave it alone.
questions.rule: No guess when meaning is unclear.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: What does the authors' footnote say about S2's rate of about two words per second?
options: It is unusually fast and shows that chess talk is easier than talk about other tasks
It is also typical of subjects who struggle to express themselves in other tasks
It is unusually slow and shows that S2 was thinking hard
It is recorded only for experts in chess and is not available for others
optionExplain: The footnote says the rate is typical.
Right: counting all words, the rate is similar across tasks.
The footnote calls it typical, not slow.
The footnote compares with subjects in other tasks.
questions.explain: A total flow of about two words per second, counting all words, is typical even when subjects struggle to put things into words.
questions.rule: Word rate alone is a poor sign of fluency.
questions.teaches: The roughly two words per second flow is also typical of subjects in tasks where they have much more difficulty expressing themselves, provided one counts all words.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A chef's talk-aloud while improvising is smooth, without stumbles. By the account of S2, what best explains this?
options: The chef is relaxed, and relaxed people do not hesitate
The chef's task is simple, and simple tasks need little thought before speaking
The recorder removed every pause from the tape afterwards
A well-developed vocabulary for the task, with the right phrases ready to use
optionExplain: The authors point to the task language, not mood.
Chess is a deep task, yet S2's talk is smooth.
Nothing in the account suggests editing.
Right: chess has a developed argot, and the designatory phrases are immediately at S2's service.
questions.explain: The authors say chess has a well-developed argot, and S2 is fluent in it, so phrases like Bishop at Rook 2 are immediately at his service.
questions.rule: Fluent talk follows a well-developed task vocabulary.
questions.teaches: S2's smooth talk is explained by chess's well-developed argot: all the designatory phrases of chess are immediately at his service.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A long recording of one person's problem solving is hard to hold in mind. What is a natural way to organize it?
options: Cut it where attention shifts abruptly, then group neighboring parts by shared aim
Cut it into equal lengths of one minute each and number them
List only the final decision
Sort the sentences alphabetically so patterns become visible
optionExplain: Right: episodes at attention breaks, scenes by common aim.
Equal clock slices ignore what the person was doing.
The authors want the structure of the search.
Sorting destroys the time order that matters.
questions.explain: The authors cut at breaks of attention and group episodes by aim. The card has the terms.
questions.rule: Cut at attention breaks; group by aim.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: S2's 25 episodes are grouped into ____ scenes.
questions.explain: Twenty-five episodes are grouped into seven scenes.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A detective's log: checks alibi A, checks alibi B, checks alibi C, then examines the weapon. Which entries form a scene?
options: The weapon examination alone
Only alibi A, because the first entry starts the case
The whole log, because it is all one case
The three alibi checks, which share one aim
optionExplain: Length does not define a scene.
Order of entry does not define a scene.
The whole log is the problem; scenes are parts of it.
Right: a set of explorations under a common aim.
questions.explain: A scene is a set of explorations under a common aim, as the three alibi checks are.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: Match each term to its meaning in the chapter.
pairs: A stretch of behavior bounded by abrupt discontinuities of attention
A set of explorations under a common aim
Activity within a scene that is not devoted to its main concern
questions.explain: An episode is a unit of behavior, a scene groups explorations by aim, and an interruption is a side step inside a scene.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: What does the first episode, E1, contain?
options: A full exploration of 1. B x N/5, traced down the exchange until the Queen is driven back
A wide search for other White moves such as N x B
An orientation: S2 compares material and lists threats for both sides, exploring no move
The final decision, given as a conditional on Black's reply
optionExplain: That is the second scene.
That comes later, in scene 3.
Right: E1 is the orientation phase and contains no moves.
That is the last scene.
questions.explain: Scene 1 is orientation at 0 seconds: material is even, threats are listed, and no move is explored.
questions.rule: Start by taking stock of the position.
questions.teaches: E1 is an orientation phase: S2 first examines the material situation, then systematically lists Black's threats and then White's, and is aware of the Q' x NP threat.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A student ends each study stretch with a summing-up and a plan for the next. What does this share with episode boundaries?
options: Boundaries are marked only by the clock, such as every thirty minutes
Summing-up statements that end one stretch and proposals that start the next mark boundaries
Boundaries are marked only by a change of room or desk
Boundaries are not observable and must be guessed from the final result of the whole session
optionExplain: The authors mark them by attention shifts and statements.
Right: evaluative and summarizing statements and proposals about what to do next mark episode boundaries.
Physical change is not the sign they describe.
The protocol shows them directly.
questions.explain: The authors say episode boundaries are marked by abrupt shifts and also by evaluative or summarizing statements that end an episode and proposals that start another.
questions.rule: Look for summing-up and next-step statements.
questions.teaches: Episode boundaries are marked not only by discontinuity in the position considered but by evaluative and summarizing statements ending an episode and by proposals about what to do next that begin another.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: After a player finds that his first candidate move seems worth nothing, what is a likely next step?
options: Play the candidate at once
Search for something else, such as a new attacking idea, before settling
Give up the whole position as a draw without any more analysis
Ask the opponent which move he would prefer to see played
optionExplain: S2 kept analysing for many minutes.
Right: S2 tried a mating idea and later returned.
S2 continued to look for a way.
The setup is a lone player's talk-aloud.
questions.explain: S2 followed a poor result with a search for something else. The card sets out the scenes in order.
questions.rule: A doubtful first candidate prompts a search for alternatives.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: Put these stages of S2's analysis in the order they occurred.
items: Explores 1. B x N'/5 for the first time
Searches widely for other moves
Re-examines the B x N'/5 exchange
Tries something else, such as a mating idea
Returns to B x N'/5 and reviews Black's replies
Decides on B x N'
questions.explain: The six stages follow scenes 2 to 7 of Figure 12.2, after the scene 1 orientation.
questions.rule: Explore, search, re-examine, try something else, return, decide.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A traveller who checks five other routes and finds none better matches which scene of S2's analysis?
options: Scene 2, where he first explores the main exchange
Scene 5, where he builds a mating idea around a Bishop and Queen
Scene 7, where he settles on the move and gives it
Scene 3, where he searches widely and finds nothing better
optionExplain: Scene 2 explores the one candidate.
Scene 5 pursues a specific attacking configuration.
Scene 7 is the decision, not a search for alternatives.
Right: scene 3 looks at other moves and each shows nothing.
questions.explain: Scene 3 holds episodes E6 to E10, each exploring another idea and finding nothing.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: True or false: In scene 3, S2 found a stronger alternative to 1. B x N'/5 and switched to it.
questions.explain: Each exploration in scene 3 (N x B', N x BP', N x NP', doubling Rooks, a pawn attack) found nothing; he returned to B x N'/5.
questions.rule: The wide search found nothing better.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
