questions.q: In scene 6, S2 reviews Black's three captures. Which one does he conclude Black must play?
options: Pawn takes Bishop (P' x B)
Bishop takes Bishop (B' x B)
Knight takes Bishop (N' x B)
Queen takes Pawn (Q' x NP)
optionExplain: Right: he rules out the other captures and concludes P' x B.
He concludes the advantage is with White after B' x B.
He decides that 2. N x N' makes this impossible for Black.
That is an earlier counterattack, not one of the three captures.
questions.explain: He argues White's advantage after B' x B, shows N' x B fails to 2. N x N', and concludes Black must play P' x B.
questions.rule: Leave one reply by ruling out the others.
questions.teaches: In scene 6, S2 rules out B' x B and N' x B for Black (the latter because 2. N x N' makes it impossible), concludes Black must play P' x B, and then explores White's gain in terms of a King-side attack.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A hiker finds two of three trails washed out and plans the day on the third. Which part of scene 6 does this share?
options: Searching every trail at once to look for a hidden fourth one
Choosing the trail by the order in which they were first listed on the map
Ruling out the alternatives, then exploring what follows from the one left
Deciding the trail only after the whole day has finished
optionExplain: S2 did not look for a hidden option in scene 6.
S2's elimination was by analysis, not list order.
Right: S2 eliminates two replies and explores the consequences of the third.
S2 decided before moving, using analysis.
questions.explain: In scene 6, S2 shows two of Black's replies fail and then explores White's gain against the remaining one.
questions.teaches: S2 concludes in E24 that Black must play P' x B once the other replies are ruled out, and then explores the gain for White in terms of a King-side attack.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A player remarks that the opponent's Rook is attacking his Pawn. Has he thereby considered capturing with it?
options: Yes: any mention of an attack means that the capture was already examined
Yes, but only if the Pawn is undefended
Not necessarily: he may only be noticing a relation on the board
No, because Rooks cannot capture Pawns in chess
optionExplain: An attack can be noticed without being examined.
The test is what he is processing, not defense.
Right: noticing an attack differs from considering the move.
Rooks can capture Pawns.
questions.explain: A perceived relation is not a considered move. The card sets out the authors' test.
questions.rule: A relation noticed is not a move considered.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: Sort each item as a considered move or a perceived relation, as in the authors' treatment.

items.t: P x N
Q-QB3
Attack
Pin

questions.explain: Moves such as P x N and Q-QB3 are considered; attack and pin are relations on the board.
questions.rule: Moves are examined; relations are seen.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: Which remark in a tic-tac-toe game reports a considered move rather than a perceived relation?
options: 'If I put my O in the middle, he plays X on the edge'
'His two Xs in the row threaten to make three in a row'
'The corner square is open'
'My O in the corner is next to his X'
optionExplain: Right: it traces a move and a reply.
This reports a relation on the board.
This reports a state of the board.
This reports adjacency, a relation.
questions.explain: A considered move is a step in a line of play. The other remarks describe the current board.
questions.rule: Look for a move and a reply.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: True or false: The authors say the move-versus-relation distinction can be read off the board position alone, whoever looks at it.
questions.explain: They base it on characteristics of the information system processing the board, not on features of the board.
questions.rule: The distinction depends on the processor.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: Which example do the authors give of a relation seen without a search in the sense of examining forward moves?
options: The ultimate checkmater of the King in a middle game
A forced win found by tracing an exchange for several moves
A sacrifice that wins a Rook five moves later
An ultimately-promotable pawn in an endgame
optionExplain: They say we know of no way to find this except by searching.
Tracing an exchange is a search.
Finding this takes a search.
Right: some endgames allow it without exploring the forward move tree.
questions.explain: In the endgame one can speak of an ultimately-promotable pawn without searching the forward move tree.
questions.rule: Some remote relations are perceived directly.
questions.teaches: In some endgames one can speak of an ultimately-promotable pawn as a perceived relation without examining the forward move tree in the sense of a search.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A navigator can step a ship forward hourly or see on a chart it is on a collision course. What do the authors imply?
options: Only stepping forward gives real knowledge, while the chart reading is only a guess
Both extract what the present state already implies; only the processor differs
Only the chart reading is valid
They differ because the ship's position changes while the chart does not
optionExplain: The authors say relations could in principle be perceived directly.
Right: searching forward is a way of extracting remote relations contained in the present position.
Stepping forward adds no facts; it extracts implications.
The comparison concerns processing, not change of position.
questions.explain: The authors say considering move sequences is a way of extracting remote relations that are already contained in the present position.
questions.rule: Search extracts what the position already implies.
questions.teaches: Considering move sequences is a way of extracting the remote relations that are already contained in the present position.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: If you put together every move a player considered, what structure do you get?
options: A tree of positions branching from the starting position
A single straight line
A table of moves sorted by their value
A closed loop that returns to the starting position
optionExplain: Right: each line of play branches from the position on the board.
Considered moves branch even though one is played.
Value is not the structure of the considered moves.
The tree grows outward from the start.
questions.explain: Considered moves form a tree growing from the base position.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: The exploration tree contains ____ positions, including the current one.
questions.explain: Figure 12.3 has 64 positions including the current one.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A player examines 40 new positions in 10 minutes. How does that compare with S2's rate of about one new position every fifteen seconds?
options: About twice as fast as S2
About half as fast as S2
About the same rate
Four times as fast as S2
optionExplain: Twice as fast would be one every seven or eight seconds.
Half as fast would be one every thirty seconds.
Right: 10 minutes is 600 seconds, and 600 divided by 40 is fifteen seconds each.
Four times as fast would be one every four seconds.
questions.explain: 40 positions in 600 seconds is one per 15 seconds, S2's rate.
questions.rule: Seconds divided by positions gives the pace.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: True or false: The exploration tree alone shows the order in which S2 generated its positions.
questions.explain: The tree shows which positions were covered, not how it was generated. The problem behavior graph adds the time order.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: In Figure 12.3, what does a branch with no small circle at its tip mean?
options: A position was considered but forgotten before it could be properly evaluated
A move was generated, but the position from it was never considered
A position that S2 considered but whose move he did not say
A node the authors added because the branch was incomplete
optionExplain: The figure does not mark forgetting.
Right: there are eight such moves, for example R-exchange.
That is the dotted line case.
Added nodes are marked by enclosing symbols, four in all.
questions.explain: Eight moves were distinctly generated whose resulting positions were never considered, marked by branches with no small circle.
questions.rule: A branch with no circle was proposed, not examined.
questions.teaches: Eight moves are distinctly generated but the positions from them are never considered; these are shown by branches with no small circle at the tip (for example R-exchange).

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A person says, 'I would do something about the garden fence.' How should a researcher record this, following the authors' treatment of Q-move?
options: As the most likely fix, such as repainting, filled in by the researcher
As nothing, because vague remarks are not moves
As a dotted line
As a fence-move, no more specific than he was
optionExplain: The authors infer no more than he said.
Q-move stays in the tree as a nonspecific move.
Dotted lines mark inferred absence of a proposed move, not vague moves.
Right: nonspecific moves are recorded as stated; the subject was no more specific.
questions.explain: Nonspecific moves such as Q-move are given in the tree as stated because it is inferred that the subject was no more specific.
questions.teaches: Where nonspecific moves such as Q-move are given, the authors infer the subject was no more specific than stated, and the tree records them that way.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A player explores one line of play several moves deep and stops. Where does he most likely begin his next exploration?
options: At the last position he reached in the line
At the position the opponent would like best
At a position chosen at random from the line
At the position on the board in front of him
optionExplain: That would be continuing; S2 returned to the start.
S2 did not pick starts by the opponent's wish.
The returns were to the base position, not random.
Right: S2 returned to the current position after each search.
questions.explain: S2 searched deep, then went back to the base position. The card describes it.
questions.rule: Return to base, then start again.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: Among the 23 starts in S2's PBG there are only ____ distinct initial moves.
questions.explain: Many starts repeat an initial move already analyzed.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A student pushes one proof line deep, wipes the page, restarts from the theorem, and repeats earlier starts. Which PBG feature is this?
options: Wide branching at each step, with all of the branches kept on the page afterwards
Deep searches, each followed by a return to the base, and a repeated earlier start
One long search that never returns to the beginning
A search that stops as soon as one branch fails
optionExplain: S2's PBG has little or no branching.
Right: both the returns and the repeated starts occur in S2's graph.
S2 returns to the base after each search.
The pattern concerns returns, not stopping on failure.
questions.explain: Deep, narrow searches, each followed by a return to the base, and repeated starts are the pattern the authors report.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: True or false: Four of S2's episodes (E18, E20, E24 and E25) pick up at the opponent's first response rather than at the base position.
questions.explain: From E18 onward these four do not go back to the start; the other starts return to the base position.
questions.rule: A few episodes begin one step in.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: What do the exceptions E20, E24 and E25 have in common with E18?
options: Each starts after a move that S2 had never examined before in the protocol
Each ends at the same checkmate position
Each follows a familiar initial move, B x N'/5 or N-K4
Each is an interruption from a different scene altogether
optionExplain: The moves are the most familiar ones.
The authors do not mention a shared checkmate.
Right: they drop back to the position defined by a familiar move.
They are episodes of later scenes; the shared feature is the familiar start.
questions.explain: E20, E24 and E25 begin after B x N'/5, which had already occurred eight times, and E18 after N-K4, which had occurred twice.
questions.teaches: E20, E24 and E25 have B x N'/5 as initial move, which already occurred eight times, and E18 begins with N-K4, which occurred only twice; the subject does not go back to the start in these four cases.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A student reads silently for a minute, then starts trying solutions. Why would a graph of attempts omit that minute?
options: It holds no moves to plot, as E1 does not appear in Figure 12.4
It is too short to count as part of the student's behavior
Silent reading is not thought, so a graph of thought excludes it
The teacher did not time it, so no graph can include it
optionExplain: Right: E1, the orientation phase, contains no moves and so does not show in the PBG.
E1 is counted as an episode but has no moves.
E1 is part of S2's behavior but contains no moves.
The reason is that it contains no moves.
questions.explain: E1 is counted as the first episode, but a graph of moves cannot show a stretch with none.
questions.teaches: E1, the orientation phase, does not show in Figure 12.4 since it contains no moves, even though it is counted among the 25 episodes.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A program reproduces a person's behavior on a task. What does that show about how the person works?
options: That the person must be working the same way
Nothing, because matching behavior can never be informative about method
That the program's method could produce it, though others might as well
That the person's method is more complex than the program's
optionExplain: Matching behavior does not rule out other methods.
A match is informative, though not conclusive.
Right: the program's method is sufficient, not shown necessary.
Nothing in a match compares complexity.
questions.explain: A match shows the method is sufficient. The card gives the authors' wording.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: Showing that a hypothesized organization reproduces the behavior shows it is ____, not that it is necessary.
questions.explain: The authors can show sufficiency, not necessity.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A bread machine bakes a loaf identical to Anna's, but by a different method. What follows by the authors' reasoning?
options: The machine's method suffices for such bread; it does not show how Anna bakes
Anna must be using the machine's method
Anna's loaf must be worse, as the machine is more precise
The machine's method is impossible
optionExplain: Right: sufficiency, not necessity.
A different method is possible, as here.
Nothing compares quality.
Different methods can reach the same result.
questions.explain: An identical result by another method shows only that the method is sufficient.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: Sort each item as part of the search strategy or as information gathered during the search.

items.t: Which position to examine next
What must be kept so the search can be carried out
The value computed for a position when it is reached
What to do with a value once it is found

questions.explain: The strategy covers where to go next and what to keep; computing values and using them belongs to the information side.
questions.rule: Strategy is where to go; information is what is found.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: Which decision shows interaction between the search itself and the information found, yet can be treated inside a fixed strategy?
options: The choice between playing White or Black
The decision to stop searching (depth- or width-termination)
The writing down of each move in standard chess notation as it is spoken
The choice of which tape recorder to use
optionExplain: Side choice does not arise in a fixed position.
Right: the stop decision depends on what has been found.
Notation is a recording matter, not a search matter.
Equipment is not part of the search.
questions.explain: The authors say there may be strong interaction between the search and the information found, as in the decision to stop, but this can often be viewed inside a fixed strategy.
questions.rule: Stopping rules sit inside a strategy.
questions.teaches: The decision to stop searching (depth-termination or width-termination) interacts strongly with the information found, yet can often be treated within a fixed search strategy.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: Researchers find that an alternative organization would produce behavior that conflicts with a person's recorded behavior. What can they conclude?
options: That the person's own method must therefore be the necessary one
Nothing, because only matches carry information
That the behavior was recorded wrongly
That alternative is ruled out as an account of that behavior
optionExplain: Ruling out one rival does not prove another necessary.
A mismatch rules out an alternative.
A mismatch is not evidence of recording error.
Right: some alternative organizations can be shown incompatible.
questions.explain: The authors say that, although necessity cannot be shown, they may be able to show some alternative organizations are incompatible with the behavior.
questions.teaches: Although they cannot show necessity, the authors may be able to show that some alternative organizations are incompatible with the observed behavior.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A program explores a branching set of options. Which search order needs the least memory?
options: Follow one line to its end before turning to the others
Look at every option one step ahead, then every option two steps ahead
Jump among options at random to avoid bias
Rank all options first and discard every one but the best
optionExplain: Right: only a single line needs to be kept.
This keeps every unfinished option in memory.
Random jumps do not reduce what must be remembered.
Ranking needs all options at once.
questions.explain: Depth-first search keeps only a single line in memory. The card sets it out.
questions.rule: Finish a branch before leaving it.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: In depth-first search, all deeper search beyond a position is carried out before that part of the tree is ____.
questions.explain: Everything below a position is searched before the branch is left.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: Which way of listing a folder tree is depth-first?
options: List every folder at the top level, then every folder one level down, then the next level
List the folders in alphabetical order whatever their level
List only the largest folder and ignore all the rest
Go down into a folder's first subfolder, and so on, before returning to the others
optionExplain: This completes a level at a time, which is breadth-first.
Alphabet order says nothing about depth.
Ignoring the rest is not a search order.
Right: finish everything below a folder before leaving it.
questions.explain: Depth-first goes down a branch to its end before backing up.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: True or false: A depth-first chess search must keep in memory every position it has examined so far.
questions.explain: It needs only a single line of positions from the board position up to the position now under study.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: What do chess programs usually store along that single line?
options: The full position at every step, to save recomputation
Only the value of the best position found so far
The moves only, regenerating earlier positions from the current one and the last move
The opponent's expected reply at each step, kept in place of the positions themselves
optionExplain: Usually only the moves are stored.
The line itself must be stored, not a single value.
Right: positions are regenerated rather than stored in full.
The text says moves are kept and positions regenerated.
questions.explain: Usually only the moves are kept, since prior positions are regenerated from the current position and the move that led to it.
questions.teaches: Usually only the moves along the line are kept in memory, not the full positions, since prior positions can be regenerated from the current position and the move that led to it.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A shopper reads each product page and its linked pages fully before the next, visiting each page once. How does this relate to Figure 12.3?
options: It matches S2's actual PBG, which also lists each position once and once only
It matches a depth-first strategy, but differs radically from S2's actual PBG
It cannot be depth-first because pages are not chess positions
It matches breadth-first, because each page is visited once
optionExplain: S2's actual PBG returns repeatedly to the start.
Right: Figure 12.3 would be a depth-first PBG, each node considered once, unlike Figure 12.4.
The structure matches regardless of subject matter.
Visiting once is not what separates breadth-first from depth-first.
questions.explain: Figure 12.3 would also be the PBG generated by depth-first search with the right ordering, since each node is considered once. The authors note that it differs radically from S2's PBG.
questions.teaches: Figure 12.3, the total set of positions S2 covered, would be the PBG of a depth-first strategy if moves are considered in an appropriate order, with each node considered once; this differs radically from S2's actual PBG in Figure 12.4.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A searcher looks at every option one step ahead before looking at any option two steps ahead. What must it keep?
options: Only the single line it is now following
A list of all the positions waiting to be examined
Nothing, because each position is dropped when it is read
Only the best position found so far at each level
optionExplain: That is the depth-first requirement.
Right: all positions are stored until considered.
Positions must be kept until they are examined.
Waiting positions cannot be dropped.
questions.explain: Breadth-first search stores every position that has been generated but not yet examined.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: Breadth-first search completes all positions at one ____ before going on to the next.
questions.explain: It works level by level.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: Which description of exploring an organization chart is breadth-first?
options: Meet one department head, then her manager, then each manager's staff before the next head
Meet people in the order in which they joined the company
Meet only the people who report to nobody
Meet all department heads first, then all their managers, then all their staff
optionExplain: This goes down one branch first, which is depth-first.
Join order is not a level order.
That stops at one level.
Right: complete a level before moving down.
questions.explain: Breadth-first completes each level, top to bottom, before going on.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: True or false: Applied to S2's tree, a breadth-first search would give a PBG of long unbroken lines of play like S2's own.
questions.explain: Finishing levels, not lines, makes the graph highly discontinuous, and up to ten positions wait in storage.
questions.rule: Level order means a jumpy graph.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: What does breadth-first search buy in return for the storage?
options: It avoids going too deep in one part while something obvious waits in another
It gets values for minimaxing faster than depth-first search, with less effort
It needs fewer positions in memory than depth-first search
It always finds the best move first
optionExplain: Right: that is the compensation named by the authors.
The authors say minimaxing is harder with it.
It needs more.
The text claims no such guarantee.
questions.explain: The authors say the storage is compensated by not going too deep in one part when something obvious awaits in an unexamined part at level 1 or 2.
questions.teaches: Breadth-first search avoids looking too deep in one part of the tree when something obvious is awaiting discovery at level 1 or 2 in an unexamined part.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A designer is building a program to play a board game using minimax. Which strategy do the authors' remarks favor, and why?
options: Breadth-first, since it was used successfully by game-playing programs
Breadth-first, since it stores less than depth-first
Depth-first, since breadth-first minimaxing needs more memory, effort and organization
Either one, since minimaxing cannot be done with breadth-first search at all, on any game
optionExplain: They say it has not been used in any game-playing program.
It stores more.
Right: they note breadth-first has not been used in game-playing programs.
They say it can be done, but at greater cost.
questions.explain: Breadth-first search has been used in some theorem-proving programs, but not in game-playing programs; minimaxing with it can be done but needs more memory, effort and organization.
questions.rule: Pick the strategy that suits the inference procedure.
questions.teaches: Breadth-first search has been used in some theorem-proving programs but in no game-playing programs, because minimaxing with it requires more memory, effort and organization than with depth-first search.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A solver follows one line of replies to its end, then restarts from the board. How can repeated visits to one candidate differ?
options: It repeats exactly the same line each time
It forgets the candidate once the first visit ends
It keeps a summary with the candidate to vary the next visit
It plays the candidate immediately after the first visit is over
optionExplain: Repeating one line would add nothing.
The strategy keeps a summary with each base-move.
Right: the summary lets later visits differ.
The loop repeats analyses; it does not decide.
questions.explain: Summary information is kept with each base-move so successive visits can take different lines.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: In simple progressive deepening, the analysis selects only ____ move at each current position.
questions.explain: The analysis is a loop with a single selected move per position.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A writer follows one chain of events per plot idea, returns to the premise, and revisits the first with a twist. Which strategy is this?
options: Simple progressive deepening
Depth-first search with recursion
Breadth-first search
Random sampling
optionExplain: Right: single lines from a base, repeated visits varied by what was learned.
Depth-first completes all alternatives below each node.
Breadth-first completes each level.
The writer is following structured lines, not sampling.
questions.explain: Linear searches from a base, revisited with variation, are the signature of simple progressive deepening.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: True or false: Simple progressive deepening explores all alternatives at a position before going deeper.
questions.explain: It selects a single move at each current position and goes on, so it produces linear searches.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: Why does the strategy lower what Bruner called cognitive strain?
options: The solver stores every position in full so that none is ever lost during the search
The solver never has to evaluate any position
The solver is given the correct move in advance
Only one position is stored, as its difference from the base position under surveillance
optionExplain: Only a single position is stored.
The strategy leaves evaluation open.
Nothing of the kind is stated.
Right: little housekeeping is needed.
questions.explain: No complicated bookkeeping is needed. The current position is held as a difference from the base, which provides a continuing memory of everything that has not changed.
questions.teaches: Only a single position need be stored, in terms of how it differs from the base position under continual surveillance, which gives a continuing memory of everything that has not changed; this lowers cognitive strain.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A hiker loses track on a side path, drops it, and walks back to the trailhead. Which property of the strategy is this?
options: It guarantees the correct path is found on the next try
It is fail-safe: if an exploration goes wrong, it is terminated and the analysis goes on
It requires every exploration to succeed fully before the next one is allowed to begin
It keeps the lost path in memory for later correction
optionExplain: No such guarantee is stated.
Right: the only loss is the effort spent in the abortive exploration.
Failed explorations are terminated, not repaired.
The strategy loses only the effort spent.
questions.explain: If something goes wrong, such as losing track of the current position, the exploration is terminated and the total analysis continues.
questions.rule: A lost line costs only its effort.
questions.teaches: The strategy is fail-safe: if an exploration goes wrong, for example the subject loses track of the current position, the search is terminated and the total analysis continues, losing only the effort spent.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: At each step of a main line, a solver glances at several one-move options before choosing one to continue. What shape does this give?
options: A trunk with small tufts of one-move branches
A wide fan that branches evenly at every level
A single straight line with no side branches
A closed loop returning to the starting move
optionExplain: Right: the skinny Christmas tree.
That would be breadth-first.
That is simple progressive deepening.
The tree grows from the base.
questions.explain: A trunk with one-move tufts is the form the strategy produces.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: The tree of each exploration resembles a skinny ____ tree.
questions.explain: A main trunk with tufts of branches.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A trip planner picks a main route of cities and lists two or three nearby sights at each. Which tree shape is this?
options: A bushy tree that branches fully at every city on the route
A single line with no side branches
A trunk with one-hop tufts, like a skinny Christmas tree
Two separate lines that never meet
optionExplain: The tufts are only one move deep.
Tufts are present at each node.
Right: a main line with short side branches.
The side branches hang off the main line.
questions.explain: A main route with short one-hop sights is a trunk with tufts.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: True or false: Progressive deepening replaces the single selected analysis-move with a set of analysis-moves ordered by plausibility.
questions.explain: Only the analysis changes: a set is generated and ranked, each is considered, and one is selected for continuation. The base-move process is unchanged.
questions.rule: Generate a set, rank, continue one.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: The authors note that this resembles the way which move generators work?
options: The exhaustive generator of the Logic Theorist
The plausible move generators of the Kotok and Greenblatt programs
The recursive generator of a depth-first chess program of the time
The generator of the MATER program
optionExplain: LT is cited for breadth-first search, not for this.
Right: the authors make this comparison.
The modification replaced recursion by a loop.
MATER is mentioned later, in another connection.
questions.explain: Generating a set of moves and considering each before choosing one is similar to the Kotok and Greenblatt plausible move generators.
questions.rule: Plausible-move generation links this to real programs.
questions.teaches: Generating a set of analysis-moves and considering each before selecting one is similar to the way the Kotok and Greenblatt plausible move generators work.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: At each step of a plan, a manager ranks a handful of one-step options and continues with the best. What does this copy?
options: Examining every legal option at each step and scoring them all together
Following a single option at each step without comparison
Completing each level of options before going deeper
Generating plausible moves and ordering them by value before continuing
optionExplain: Only a plausible set is generated, not all moves.
That is the simple version.
That is breadth-first.
Right: a ranked set at each node with continuation along one.
questions.explain: Generating a ranked set at each node and continuing along one is the fuller strategy of Figure 12.8. The authors treat the simple version mainly as a stepping-stone to it; their original paper called the fuller one modified-progressive-deepening.
questions.teaches: The authors use the simple version primarily as a stepping-stone to the progressive-deepening strategy; the original paper named the two progressive-deepening and modified-progressive-deepening, respectively.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A model predicts that most branching will be short side-tufts. In real data, 11 of 15 branchings fit. How should we describe the fit?
options: A perfect fit, since most cases agree
A poor fit, since any exception disproves a model
No evidence either way
A good but imperfect fit, with the other four needing separate explanation
optionExplain: Four exceptions remain.
The authors accept a plausible description with explained exceptions.
Eleven of fifteen is evidence, though limited.
Right: most fit and the exceptions are explained one by one.
questions.explain: Eleven of fifteen is a good fit with four exceptions to explain.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: Of the fifteen instances of multiple branching, ____ are exactly of the single-level tuft form.
questions.explain: Eleven of fifteen are tufts.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: True or false: About three quarters of the multiple-branching instances (11 of 15) fit the tuft form.
questions.explain: Eleven divided by fifteen is about 73 percent, close to three quarters.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: Which episode is NOT among the contrary examples to the tuft form?
options: E2
E5
optionExplain: E2 is a contrary (ambiguous) example.
Right: the contrary examples are E2, E18, E24 and E25.
E18 is a contrary example.
E25 is a contrary example.
questions.explain: The four contrary examples are E2, E18, E24 and E25.
questions.rule: Know which cases do not fit.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: How do the authors read the contrary cases E18 and E24?
options: As evidence that the strategy is wrong
As errors of recording in the protocol that they correct in the figure
As dropping back to the position defined by a familiar move
As additional tufts hidden by silence
optionExplain: They explain them without rejecting it.
They are treated as real behavior.
Right: they appear truly to drop back, not to be tufts.
They are not tufts.
questions.explain: E18 and E24 appear to be truly cases of dropping back to the position defined by a familiar move.
questions.teaches: E18 and E24 appear to be truly cases of dropping back to the position defined by a familiar move, and E25 drops back to the position after 1. B x N'/5 each time.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A thermostat's sensing rate, heating rule and stop rule each depend on the others. Which remark of the authors parallels this?
options: The parts form one system, so each depends on the others and the order begs which comes first
The parts can be designed one at a time, with no effect of any part on the others, in any order
Only the first part matters
Their order of presentation settles which part is the cause
optionExplain: Right: the chickens-and-eggs remark.
The authors say the shape of each part depends on the others.
No part is said to determine all the others.
They say the order begs the question.
questions.explain: The authors write that the processes form a single system, so the shape of each depends on the others, and their order of analysis begs which are chickens and which eggs.
questions.rule: In a system, parts shape each other.
questions.teaches: The additional processes needed for a complete chess player form a single system in which the shape of each depends on the others, so the order of analysis begs the question of which features determine the others.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A subject says aloud what he is trying to do in each stretch of work. How should a researcher treat such statements?
options: As worthless, since people cannot report their aims
As proof of function that needs no checking
As a starting hypothesis about each stretch's function, checked against behavior
As data only for the final decision, and not for any of the earlier stretches of work
optionExplain: The authors use them as evidence.
The authors check against the behavior throughout.
Right: the authors accept the naive hypothesis and check it.
Each episode's statements are used.
questions.explain: The authors take the stated function as the naive hypothesis and test its fit. The card gives the details.
questions.rule: Use stated aims as a checked hypothesis.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: Match each term from Table 12.1 to its meaning.
pairs: Go down the specified path again, for whatever reason
questions.explain: Explore and rework describe the path; result records the outcome for White.
questions.rule: Explore is new; rework is again.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A detective returns to question a witness already interviewed. Which Table 12.1 label fits this stretch?
options: Rework, since it goes down an already specified path again
Explore, since the second meeting is a new event
Result, since it comes after the first interview
Orientation, since the detective is getting reacquainted with the case
optionExplain: Right: a repeat of a path, for whatever reason.
Explore means a new path, not a new occasion.
Result is the outcome, not a type of episode.
Orientation is the opening stock-taking.
questions.explain: Going down the same path again is rework, whatever the reason.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: True or false: The authors infer each episode's function only from the pattern of moves, ignoring what S2 says.
questions.explain: S2's own explicit statements about each episode's function are used, so the function need not be inferred from the move pattern alone.
questions.rule: Use his statements as well as the moves.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: Besides function and result, what else does Table 12.1 record for the episodes?
options: The number of words S2 spoke in each episode, with his average rate of speech per minute
Additional information discovered, such as Q-KB3 found in E2, and notes on rework episodes
The ratings of the moves by the grandmasters
The time at which each episode ended
optionExplain: Word counts are not in the table.
Right: both are noted where relevant.
No such ratings are given.
Times appear in the scene listing, not as a table column.
questions.explain: The table notes information discovered that matters to later episodes and briefly characterizes rework episodes.
questions.rule: The table also tracks what was found.
questions.teaches: Table 12.1 also notes additional information discovered during an episode where relevant to later ones (for example Q-KB3 found in E2) and gives a brief characterization of what happened in each rework episode.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A student's think-aloud comments all fit one another. By the authors' reasoning, should the teacher trust his stated aims?
options: No: stated aims are always unreliable and must be replaced by the teacher's own reading
Yes: but only if the student is an expert
No: any single consistent reading proves every other possible reading to be wrong
Largely yes: interlocking statements make radically different readings hard to produce
optionExplain: The authors accept them.
S2 was not an expert and the authors still accept it.
They say alternative readings are hard to produce, not impossible.
Right: this is why the authors accept the naive hypothesis.
questions.explain: The authors note that the whole set of protocol statements is sufficiently interdependent that radically different interpretations are not easy to manufacture.
questions.rule: Consistent, interlocking statements resist rival readings.
questions.teaches: The whole set of protocol statements is sufficiently interdependent that radically different interpretations of the episodes are not easy to manufacture.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A player analyses three candidate moves. Should what he finds about one change which lines he explores for another?
options: Not in content: each candidate is analysed from its own earlier results
Yes: every finding should shape the analysis of every candidate
Yes: but only findings from the final candidate
No: he should explore all three identically with no use of earlier results
optionExplain: Right: this is R1.
R1 says the opposite for content.
R1 does not single out a final candidate.
Each episode uses the earlier results of its own base-move.
questions.explain: R1 treats each base-move's analysis as independent of the others. The card states it.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: R1 says the analysis of each base-move is ____ of the analysis of other base-moves, except that it can be interrupted.
questions.explain: Independent apart from interruption.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A buyer weighs three used cars. Under an R1-style rule, what shapes her second look at car B?
options: What she found about cars A and C as well
Only what she found on the most recent look at any car
Nothing at all, since each look starts from scratch
Only what she found about car B on earlier looks
optionExplain: R1 excludes content from other base-moves.
The earlier results are those of the same base-move.
Earlier results of the same base-move are used.
Right: each episode is determined by prior episodes of its own base-move.
questions.explain: R1 ties each episode to the earlier results of the same base-move only.
questions.rule: Use results from this candidate only.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: True or false: Under R1, S2's decision to abandon base-move A because B looks better is a way the analyses interact.
questions.explain: R1 allows interaction only through the allocation of effort, including the decision to abandon a base-move because others have proved better.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: How do the authors handle the apparent exception where the move N' recaptures shifts from E13 to E14?
options: As a refutation of R1 that forces them to drop the rule
As a recording error that they quietly correct in the table of episodes
As R5 taking priority, since E13 is part of the analysis of E2 anyway
As a case where R1 and R3 are both violated
optionExplain: They say it could hardly be considered a counterexample.
They treat it as real behavior.
Right: not a counterexample to R1.
They invoke R5 only.
questions.explain: They view the transposition as showing the priority of rule R5, and say it could hardly be a counterexample to R1.
questions.rule: Rules can have priority over one another.
questions.teaches: The apparent exception to R1 (N' recaptures moving from E13 to E14) is viewed as showing the priority of rule R5 (interrupting), not as a counterexample, since E13 is part of the analysis of E2.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A buyer's standards rise or fall according to how all the cars seen so far have fared. Which rule does this conflict with?
options: R1 is untouched, since standards are not part of the analysis of any candidate
R1, since shared standards make one candidate's analysis depend on the others
R3, since standards cannot be changed once set
No rule, because buyers differ from chess players
optionExplain: The authors list this as possible counterevidence.
Right: the authors say setting aspiration levels on all base-moves might be counterevidence to R1.
The conflict named is with R1.
The question concerns the independence rule itself.
questions.explain: The authors note that setting levels of aspiration on the outcome of the episodes of all base-moves might be considered counterevidence to R1, and defer the point to the section on evaluation.
questions.teaches: Setting levels of aspiration, used in evaluating each episode, on the outcomes of the episodes of all base-moves might be considered counterevidence to R1; the authors defer the point to the section on evaluation.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A player is attacked and has several possible replies. Which does he most likely try first?
options: Counterattack on a larger target
Defend the attacked man
Ignore the attack and make some other move
Sacrifice material in exchange for time
optionExplain: A counterattack is a later, more unusual reply.
Right: defending is the normal response.
Ignoring is the most unusual reply.
Loss-making replies come last.
questions.explain: The normal reply to an attack is to defend. The card gives the full order.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: Order the responses to an attack from most normal to most unusual.
items: Defend the attacked man
Counterattack threatening equivalent material
Counterattack threatening less material
Move and ignore the attack
questions.explain: Defense is normal; counterattacks follow in decreasing size; ignoring the attack is the most unusual.
questions.rule: Defend, counter equal, counter less, ignore.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A bakery's rival cuts prices. The owner has tried matching the cut, then a counter-cut of equal size. By R2's order, what comes next?
options: Matching the cut again with exactly the same size as before
Raising prices, as the most normal reply
Cancelling the shop's business
A smaller counter-cut, then later ignoring the rival
optionExplain: Repeating the first step does not move down the order.
The most normal reply, defense, was tried first.
Not a response in the listed order.
Right: the next, more unusual response is a counterattack threatening less.
questions.explain: R2 takes successive visits further down the order: defend, equal counterattack, smaller counterattack, ignore.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: True or false: R2 says successive episodes of the same base-move go from unusual moves to normal ones.
questions.explain: R2 runs from the normal to the unusual: the first episode uses normal moves and later ones increasingly unusual moves.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: When does R2 count a continuation as unusual, besides its position in the list of responses?
options: When it is considered again after earlier analysis showed it bad for its side
When it uses a piece of low value
When it has not been mentioned in the protocol at any earlier point in the analysis
When it is the first move of an episode
optionExplain: Right: as in E4 and E23.
Piece value is not the test.
Novelty alone is not the criterion named.
First-episode moves are the normal ones.
questions.explain: The rule also treats a move as unusual if it is considered again after analysis has shown it bad for the side making it; E4 and E23 extend continuations shown bad for Black.
questions.rule: Re-trying a refuted line is unusual.
questions.teaches: R2 also counts a move as unusual if it is considered again after prior analysis showed the continuation bad for the side making it, as in E4 and E23 where lines bad for Black are extended without choosing other Black moves.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A cook's normal fix for a bland dish is more salt; a colleague's is acid first. What does R2 assume about such orderings?
options: The ordering is computed from the expected chance of success
The ordering is the same for every expert, and so it is always the correct one
A consistent a priori ordering from experience, which need not be correct
The ordering is chosen at random each time
optionExplain: The authors say the subject cannot compute such an expectation before analysis.
They note many good players would call counterattack normal.
Right: the authors say the classification comes from experience and public knowledge and is not necessarily correct.
R2 needs a consistent classification.
questions.explain: The categorization is a priori, from a blend of personal experience and public knowledge of good chess play, and is not necessarily correct; many good players would call a counterattack normal in many situations.
questions.rule: Normal is a habit, not a verdict.
questions.teaches: The normal-unusual classification is a priori, from personal experience and publicly available chess knowledge, requires only an ordering with no numerical expectation, and is not necessarily correct, since many good players would call a counterattack the normal response in many situations.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A player has found a refutation of his candidate move. What does a simple 'stay with a winner' rule predict?
options: He keeps analysing it until he has found three refutations
He plays it anyway since the analysis took long
He drops that candidate and turns to a different one
He starts the whole analysis again from scratch
optionExplain: R3 needs only a single disconfirmation.
Effort spent is not the rule.
Right: one unfavorable result is enough to switch.
He switches base-moves, not restarts.
questions.explain: Stay with a winner, switch off a loser. A single disconfirmation causes the switch.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: R3 says: stay with a ____, switch off a loser.
questions.explain: The rule's short form.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: Setting aside the three priority cases, what share of the remaining relevant cases confirm R3?
options: 16 of 18, about nine in ten
16 of 21, about three in four
18 of 21, about six in seven
2 of 18, about one in nine
optionExplain: Right: 21 minus 3 is 18, and 16 of them confirm.
That counts the three priority cases, which shed no light.
Eighteen is the count that remains, not the confirmations.
Two is the number of negative instances.
questions.explain: 21 relevant cases minus 3 priority cases leaves 18; 16 are confirmatory.
questions.rule: Remove the priority cases before counting.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: True or false: Under R3, a single disconfirmation of a base-move is enough for S2 to switch.
questions.explain: R3 says a single disconfirmation of the soundness of the move is enough to cause the switch.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: What does R3 leave unspecified about the switch?
options: Whether the old base-move is evaluated as unfavorable
Whether a single disconfirmation is enough
Whether the switch happens at all after an episode with an unfavorable result
Whether the new base-move is a new one or an old one, and how it is selected
optionExplain: That is what triggers the switch.
The rule says it is.
The rule says it does.
Right: little can be said about this from the one protocol.
questions.explain: R3 does not specify whether to obtain a new base-move or return to an old one, nor how the new one is chosen.
questions.rule: The rule says when to switch, not to what.
questions.teaches: R3 does not specify whether the switch goes to a new base-move or back to an old one, nor how the new move is selected; the authors say little can be said about this from one protocol.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A cook finds a sauce poor, rereads the recipe, then tries the sauce again. Is that a definite breach of the rule?
options: Yes: any return to a failed attempt is a breach of the rule, however brief
Not necessarily: it turns on whether the rereading is a new trial or a review
No: reviews never count as anything
Yes: because tasting is an evaluation
optionExplain: The authors call the case negative or irrelevant depending on how the review is viewed.
Right: E19 and E20 are the same case, negative or irrelevant according to that reading.
Whether it is a review or a trial is the point.
The question is the status of the review episode.
questions.explain: In E19 S2 reviewed the exchange with discouraging results but went ahead in E20. Whether this is a negative or irrelevant instance depends on whether E19 is viewed as an exploration or only a summary.
questions.rule: Classify the review before judging the rule.
questions.teaches: Whether E20 is a negative instance of R3 or an irrelevant one depends on whether E19 is viewed as an exploration or only as a summary.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: Why might a player test an idea by letting the opponent reply as helpfully as plausible?
options: To see whether any success is possible at all, setting an upper limit
To lull the real opponent into overconfidence
To avoid examining the opponent's strong replies in the final choice of move
To save time by shortening every line to one move
optionExplain: Right: that is the point of R4.
The analysis is private; no opponent sees it.
The bias serves analysis, not the final choice.
Bias is about which replies are considered, not shortening.
questions.explain: A biased test shows the best that could happen. The card explains the rule.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: R4 considers opponent moves favorable to self in order to place an ____ bound on the possibilities.
questions.explain: A favorable bias gives an upper bound.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: An engineer tests a bridge design assuming the best weather, and it still fails. What does this tell her, in R4's spirit?
options: The design is excellent
The weather data must be wrong
Even the favorable case fails, so the design has no chance under any weather
The design is unrelated to weather
optionExplain: Success in the best case would show only possibility.
Nothing suggests data error.
Right: a favorable bias sets an upper bound.
The test is a bound on the design.
questions.explain: A test with favorable assumptions gives an upper bound: failure there means failure generally. Our reading: the authors state the purpose of the bias as placing an upper bound.
questions.rule: Favorable bias bounds the best case.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: True or false: R4 allows the opponent to be assumed to play any foolish move whatever.
questions.explain: That would open the floodgates of foolishness and provide no useful information at all.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: What is the no-move, one of S2's two hints for biasing without foolishness?
options: A move that cannot be made under the rules, so the turn passes to the other side
Ignoring the opponent's move altogether, leaving open what he might do
A reply that the opponent is sure to play
A pass offered to the opponent as a draw
optionExplain: The no-move is a deliberate omission, not an illegal move.
Right: used in E9 and E24.
The no-move skips the reply.
No draw offer is involved.
questions.explain: The no-move skips the opponent's turn so no foolish or helpful reply is imposed; it appears in E9 and E24.
questions.rule: Skip the reply to stay neutral.
questions.teaches: One hint for biasing without foolishness is the no-move: ignore the opponent's move altogether, leaving open what he might do (E9, E24).

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: Rehearsing for an interview, a friend asks questions. Which practice follows the second hint of how to bias?
options: Letting her ask only the easy questions that she picks for you in advance of the session
Letting her ask anything, including nonsense questions
Letting her skip the questions altogether
Letting her pick among plausible questions that a quick look would not call toughest
optionExplain: That is too favorable and foolish.
That opens the floodgates of foolishness.
That is the no-move, the first hint.
Right: the choice comes from normal or almost normal replies that immediate evaluation might not show as best for the opponent.
questions.explain: The second hint permits a choice from the responses that are normal or almost normal, but which immediate evaluation might not indicate offer the best chance for the opponent (E15, E16, E18).
questions.teaches: The second hint is to permit the opponent a choice from responses that are normal or almost normal but which immediate evaluation might not indicate offer the best chance for him (E15, E16, E18).

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: Which goal gives a problem solver more to work with in a chess position?
options: Win the game in some way
Make the position better
Avoid losing material at any point during the whole game, whatever else happens
Get my Bishop to one named square and my Queen to another
optionExplain: This names no differences from the present.
Too general for specific inferences.
A general aim rather than a target state.
Right: a detailed target shows what differs from now.
questions.explain: A specific target exposes differences between now and then. The card shows S2's example.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: S2's mating configuration in E15 puts his Bishop at R6 and his Queen at ____.
questions.explain: The configuration is B at R6 and Q at N7.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: Which plan allows means-ends analysis?
options: Have a good trip
Be at Gate 12 by 9:40, with a boarding pass in hand
End up somewhere nice by the end of the following week
Make the travel day go well
optionExplain: Too vague for specific differences.
Right: a detailed target state with differences from now.
No detailed target state.
No specific inferences can follow.
questions.explain: Means-ends analysis needs a target specific enough to find differences from the present state.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: Sort each goal as specific enough for means-ends analysis or too vague.

items.t: Put the Bishop on R6 and the Queen on N7
Remove the Black Bishop on K2
Obtain a checkmate position
Win the game

questions.explain: Naming squares or a particular difficulty to remove gives something to work on; a bare checkmate or win does not.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: How common is means-ends analysis in existing chess programs, according to the authors?
options: It is the standard method in most of the chess programs described in Chapter 11
It is used in every program that uses minimax
It is not used in most of them, though a modest attempt is discussed later
It is used only by the Greenblatt program
optionExplain: The authors say most do not use it.
Minimax programs search forward.
Right: the authors call it unusual in chess programs.
The authors do not single out Greenblatt for this.
questions.explain: This kind of means-ends analysis is not used in most existing chess programs, although a modest attempt is discussed later.
questions.teaches: Means-ends analysis is not used in most existing chess programs, although the authors discuss a modest attempt later.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: Which allows more means-ends analysis by the authors' condition: building a model from a photo, or exploring a mapless maze?
options: The model, since the finished state can be specified in detail
The maze, since no target restricts the search
Both equally, since both involve moves
Neither, since means-ends analysis is limited to games of the chess kind
optionExplain: Right: the amount depends on whether specific future configurations can be envisioned.
A detailed target is what enables it.
The condition is the detail of the target.
It is the method of GPS, not limited to games.
questions.explain: The amount of means-ends analysis would depend strongly on whether the positions considered permit highly specific future configurations to be envisioned.
questions.rule: More detailed targets, more means-ends analysis.
questions.teaches: The amount of means-ends analysis in chess would depend strongly on whether the positions considered permit highly specific future configurations to be envisioned; a specific goal may trigger constructing continuations even if they are not completely realistic.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: While following one line, a player notices an interesting move that does not belong to it. What does R5 predict?
options: He writes it off since it is unrelated to the line he is following at present
He saves it for the final move only
He explores that new move next, interrupting the current analysis
He asks the opponent whether it is a good move
optionExplain: R5 says it is pursued.
It is explored next, not last.
Right: interruption in favor of a discovered move.
Analysis is private.
questions.explain: R5 gives priority to a promising discovered move. The card has the evidence.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: Under R5, a move discovered and judged promising is explored in the ____ episode.
questions.explain: The discovered move gets priority as the next episode.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: While tasting a stew, a cook sees that a splash of lemon might fix it. What does an R5-style rule predict?
options: She tries the lemon straight away, interrupting what she was doing
She finishes the whole recipe first, then thinks about adding the lemon
She ignores it, since lemon is not in the recipe
She asks a friend to taste it first
optionExplain: Right: the discovered idea is pursued next.
R5 predicts an interruption, not a delay.
R5 covers moves discovered along the way.
No such step is predicted.
questions.explain: R5 interrupts to pursue a discovered idea that seems to have merit.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: True or false: R5 covers discovered moves that seem to have merit for the opponent as well as for the player himself.
questions.explain: The rule says the merit may be either for self or for the opponent.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: How does E17 illustrate an interruption?
options: It terminates the exploration of E16 for good
It sidetracks the exploration, and S2 returns to E16 after it is done
It only takes priority to be the next episode, and then ends the line there
It repeats E1, the orientation
optionExplain: S2 returns to E16.
Right: the interruptive character is shown by the return.
That describes E3 and E14.
E17 is not an orientation.
questions.explain: Interruptions can terminate explorations (E18?), sidetrack them (E17) or only gain priority to be next (E3, E14).
questions.rule: Interrupts can sidetrack or take priority.
questions.teaches: The protocol varies as to whether interruptions terminate explorations (E18, uncertain), sidetrack them (E17), or only obtain priority to be the next episode (E3, E14).

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A researcher tests an R5-style rule on a cook's talk-aloud log. Which excerpt would count against the rule?
options: The cook announces an idea and tries it next
The cook never mentions any new idea
The cook tries an idea that she had not announced beforehand, straight after tasting
The cook announces a promising idea, then works on other stages before trying it
optionExplain: That supports the rule.
No discovery means no test.
The rule concerns announced discoveries.
Right: a discovered, announced move whose exploration is delayed by at least one episode.
questions.explain: No negative instance occurs. To have one would require discovering a move, announcing it in the protocol, and then delaying its exploration for at least one episode.
questions.rule: A counterexample is a delayed discovery.
questions.teaches: A negative instance of R5 would require discovering a move, announcing it in the protocol, and then delaying its exploration for at least one episode; none occurs.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A house-hunter finds a good flat on the first day. What would a look-around heuristic suggest before she signs?
options: Check other flats before committing to this one
Sign at once since a good flat is rare and may be taken
Stop looking at flats altogether
Look only at flats in the same building
optionExplain: Right: looking around when things go well.
R6 says to check alternatives first.
Nothing in R6 suggests that.
R6 is about alternatives generally.
questions.explain: R6 is the check for alternatives made before a final choice. The card has S2's case.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: R6 is the heuristic for looking ____ when things go well.
questions.explain: Before choosing, check for alternatives.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A student finishes a solution that seems right and then scans for other methods before writing it up. Which rule is this?
options: R3, switching away from a losing line
R4, biasing the opponent's choices
R5, interrupting for an idea discovered during the first method
R6, checking for other alternatives before a final choice
optionExplain: Her line was a winner.
No opponent is involved.
She was not interrupted by a discovery.
Right: R6.
questions.explain: Checking alternatives before committing is R6.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: True or false: The authors report many positive instances of R6 in S2's protocol.
questions.explain: There is only one positive instance, though it is clear and important.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: Which of these do the six rules leave undetermined? Select all that apply.
options: When to declare a newly discovered move worth an interrupt
Which side moves first in the game
Whether the protocol was recorded on tape
The notation for Black's men
How to choose a new base-move when switching is called for
When to shift to means-ends analysis
optionExplain: Right: R5 does not fix this.
The rules of chess fix this.
It was recorded on tape.
A prime marks Black's men.
Right: R3 does not say.
Right: not determined.
questions.explain: The rules do not determine how to choose a new base-move, when to shift to means-ends analysis, or when to declare a new move worth an interrupt.
questions.teaches: The six rules do not determine how to choose a new base-move when switching, when to shift to means-ends analysis, or when to declare a newly discovered move worth an interrupt.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A study timetable fixes the order of sessions but says nothing about what happens inside each. Which remark about the six rules does this parallel?
options: They determine every step inside each episode, down to the individual moves made
They set the sequence of episodes but not the internal structure of an episode
They apply only inside the first episode
They cover every base-move choice
optionExplain: The rules are not about behavior within an episode.
Right: the next section takes up that structure.
They govern the sequence across episodes.
Choice of a new base-move is left open.
questions.explain: A program built on R1 to R6 would capture some features of S2's episodic behavior, but not the internal structure of an episode, which is taken up in the next section.
questions.rule: Sequence rules are not step rules.
questions.teaches: The six rules do not determine the internal structure of an episode; that is taken up in the section on move generation.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: When a player re-analyses a line he has already explored, at the repeated positions does he mostly invent new moves or repeat earlier ones?
options: Mostly invent several new alternatives at each of the repeated positions
Mostly repeat the earlier moves, until a variation begins
Repeat for one move, then abandon the line
Choose between old and new moves at each
optionExplain: Nearly all repeat positions offer only the old move.
Right: 20 of 21 repeat positions generate only the repeated move.
No such pattern is reported.
No position poses that choice.
questions.explain: At repeat positions the question is where to start a variation. The card gives the counts.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: Move generation is analysed at ____ positions: 53 where new moves are generated and 21 repeated ones.
questions.explain: 53 plus 21 is 74.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: About what share of the 74 positions generate new moves?
options: About 53 percent
About 28 percent
About 50 percent
About 72 percent
optionExplain: That mistakes the count 53 for a percentage.
That is the share of repeated positions, 21 of 74.
More than half but not exactly half.
Right: 53 divided by 74 is about 0.72.
questions.explain: 53 of 74 is about 72 percent.
questions.rule: Divide the part by the whole.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: True or false: At 20 of the 21 repeat positions, only the repeated move is generated.
questions.explain: Only the lone dissenter in E4 also shows another move.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: How do the authors treat the one repeat position in E4 where another move also appears?
options: As a recollection of the E2 Rook exchange that S2 did not consider seriously
As a serious alternative that S2 compared with the repeated move at length
As a failure of the protocol recording
As evidence that S2 forgot the repeated move
optionExplain: Right: so there is no real choice between new and old moves.
It is clear it was not considered seriously.
It is treated as a recollection.
The repeated move was made.
questions.explain: The lone dissenter in E4 is a recollection of the Rook exchange in E2 (B50), and it is clear the move was not considered seriously.
questions.rule: A stray recollection is not a choice.
questions.teaches: The lone repeat position that also generates another move, in E4, involves a recollection of the Rook exchange in E2 (B50) that was evidently not considered seriously, so no position poses a choice between new and old moves.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A cook repeats earlier steps in a second batch until he decides to vary. What is the main job at a repeat step?
options: Generating a full set of new candidate moves
Evaluating the final outcome of the batch
Diagnosing whether to start a variation here, from prior analysis
Choosing between the old step and each new one, at every repeated step
optionExplain: That is the job at new positions.
Evaluation is not the job at a repeat step.
Right: no move generation is needed to repeat.
No such choice arises.
questions.explain: At repeat positions the decision need not involve move generation, only a diagnosis of the position on the basis of prior analysis and the instructions for variation given to the episode.
questions.rule: Repeat steps call for diagnosis, not generation.
questions.teaches: At repeat positions the decision need not involve move generation at all, but only a diagnosis of the position on the basis of the prior analysis and the instructions for variation given to the episode.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: When a player considers a reply for the opponent, how many alternatives does he typically generate?
options: About five, one for each type of reply
All legal replies
One, with a few exceptions
None: he skips the opponent's turn
optionExplain: No such number is reported.
Legal-move generation is the program style.
Right: 43 of 53 new positions have a single move.
The no-move occurs in plans only.
questions.explain: Single-move generation dominates. The card gives the counts.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: At almost every new-move position the subject generates only a ____ move.
questions.explain: Single moves occur at 43 of 53 positions.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: Of the 53 positions in the set of new-move positions, what share are tufts?
options: About 19 percent (10 of 53)
About 81 percent (43 of 53)
About 6 percent (3 of 53)
About 50 percent
optionExplain: Right: 9 two-move positions plus 1 three-move position is 10.
That is the share of single-move positions, 43 of 53.
Three of 53 would be fewer than the 10 tufts counted.
Tufts are far fewer than half.
questions.explain: 9 plus 1 is 10 tufts, and 10 of 53 is about 19 percent.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: True or false: Most of S2's tufts occur at positions where Black, his opponent, is to move.
questions.explain: Seven of the ten tufts are Black positions.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: By type of position, how do tufts divide between defensive and offensive?
options: 3 defensive and 7 offensive, with the roles of the two types turned round
5 defensive and 5 offensive, an even split between the two types
All 10 defensive, with no offensive tuft at all
7 defensive and 3 offensive (single-move positions: 19 and 24)
optionExplain: Reversed.
Not equal.
Three tufts are offensive.
Right: tufts lean defensive.
questions.explain: Tufts: 7 defensive, 3 offensive (and not all offensive ones are White). Single-move positions: 19 defensive, 24 offensive.
questions.teaches: Of the 10 tufts, 7 are defensive and 3 offensive (the offensive ones not all White), whereas single-move positions are 19 defensive and 24 offensive.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A team under pressure lists several defences, while an attacking team picks one bold play. Which suggestion does this match?
options: Multiple moves are generated only for the stronger side, who can afford to look wider
More moves for the constrained defender; one aggressive move suffices on offense
One move is generated only because S2's working memory is too small for more
Defense and offense generate the same number
optionExplain: No such claim is made.
Right: this is the plausible suggestion the authors set aside.
The authors do not argue this.
The counts differ.
questions.explain: The authors find it plausible that multiple moves are generated for the defensive (constrained) player, whereas a single aggressive move suffices on the offensive, but they take a different tack.
questions.teaches: The authors find it plausible that multiple moves are generated for the player on the defensive, who is constrained, whereas on the offensive a single aggressive move suffices, but they decline to pursue it and take a different tack.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A player says Black must recapture and then names the only way to do it. Which kind of move generation does this suggest?
options: Generation of the moves that serve a stated function
Generation of every legal move followed by scoring of each one
Random choice among the pieces that can move
Copying the last move the opponent made
optionExplain: Right: a function is posed and its moves are generated.
That is the Kotok and Greenblatt style.
The move is chosen to serve the stated need.
Nothing suggests copying.
questions.explain: Posing a function and generating moves for it is generation by function. The card names the alternative.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: Match each approach or example to its description.
pairs: Generate all legal moves, then pick the best by evaluation
Each devoted to a function, selected by higher routines
B46 and B47 of the protocol
A function is posed, then the move meeting it is generated
questions.explain: The first two are the two solutions from Chapter 11; the protocol lines show the second in use.
questions.rule: All legal moves versus moves by function.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: Asked for a book for a diabetic friend, a librarian goes straight to the cookery shelf marked for special diets. Which approach is this?
options: Generating all items and scoring each one
Choosing the first book on the first shelf
Selecting a generator by function, rather than scanning every book
Asking the friend to choose any book at random from the whole library
optionExplain: That would mean scanning every book.
The shelf is picked to fit the need.
Right: the need picks the specific source.
The need steers the choice.
questions.explain: A need that selects a specific source is the functional approach.
questions.rule: Let the need select the source.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: True or false: If there had been several ways of recapturing, the authors would expect all of them to be generated, producing a tuft.
