questions.explain: Presumably all would be generated, and a tuft would have occurred at that position.
questions.rule: Several ways to meet a function give a tuft.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: What do the authors say about combining the products of several separate generators in one position?
options: It happens at nearly every position
Little indication of it: almost everywhere only a single move is generated
It is required before any plausible move can be found at all in a given position
It is the Kotok and Greenblatt method
optionExplain: Single moves dominate.
Right.
They find single generators sufficient.
Those programs generate all legal moves.
questions.explain: Although there is good evidence for generation by function, there is little sign of several generators being combined.
questions.teaches: There is little indication of combining the products of several separate generators; almost everywhere only a single move is generated.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A dispatcher asks for a cab to the airport and three suitable cabs are listed. Which protocol feature does this resemble?
options: A single move generated for a function, as in B47
Generation of all legal moves followed by scoring, as in Kotok's program for chess
A no-move, with the other side's choice ignored
A function with several answers, as in B23, whose branches were all recaptures
optionExplain: Here the function yields several answers.
The list is limited to cabs fitting the need.
Nothing is skipped.
Right: B23 is a tuft of recaptures.
questions.explain: When a function allows several answers, a tuft results. B23 is a tuft whose branches are all recaptures.
questions.rule: A function with several answers gives a tuft.
questions.teaches: B23 is an example where a tuft did occur, with the branches all representing recaptures.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A player sees that his Knight is attacked. What is the first thing he needs before he can choose a move?
options: To list every legal move and score each of them before doing anything else
To remember the last game he played
To count the pieces still on the board at that moment in the game
To classify the situation as an attack and see that a problem exists
optionExplain: That skips the classification step.
Nothing here depends on past games.
Counting is not the first step.
Right: the attack classifies the situation and implies a problem.
questions.explain: The chain starts with classifying the situation. The card gives the rest.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: Put the links of the chain in order, from the situation to the moves.
items: Y attacks Z (situation classified)
A problem is inferred
Defend Z is named as the class of solution
A specific function such as add-defender is chosen
Actual moves for that function are generated
questions.explain: The chain runs from the classified situation to an inferred problem, a class of solution, a specific function, and finally actual moves.
questions.rule: Situation, problem, class of solution, specific function, moves.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A pan catches fire in a kitchen. In the authors' chain, which step is the class description of the solution?
options: Notice the smoke
Put out the fire
Smother it with a lid
Open the nearest window
optionExplain: That is the situation classified, as attack is.
Right: it parallels defend Z.
That is a specific function, like add-defender.
That is an actual action, not a class description.
questions.explain: Put out the fire names the kind of solution; smothering is a specific function, and the actual action follows.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: Sort each item as a situation or class description, or as a specific function.

items.t: Y attacks Z
Defend Z
Capture-attacker
Add-defender

questions.explain: An attack is the classified situation and defend Z the class of solution; capture-attacker and add-defender are specific ways to defend.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: Which of these is also named as a specific function under defend?
options: Sacrifice-the-queen
Repeat-position
Interpose-safe-man
Resign-game
optionExplain: Not named.
Not named.
Right: it is listed with pin-attacker and move-defender.
Not named.
questions.explain: The specific functions under defend include capture-attacker, add-defender, interpose-safe-man, pin-attacker and move-defender.
questions.teaches: The specific functions under defend include capture-attacker, add-defender, interpose-safe-man, pin-attacker and move-defender.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A doctor classes a symptom, names a kind of treatment, narrows it, then prescribes. What does the authors' chain say?
options: It goes from problem to solution through functional steps linking means and ends
It skips the functional level and works from symptoms straight to drugs, with no steps
It works only when every possible treatment is tried first
It applies to chess only, not to medicine
optionExplain: Right: that is the authors' description.
The route has intermediate functions.
The functions avoid trying everything.
The chain is a general pattern.
questions.explain: The authors say we get from problem to solution via a string of functional characterizations, making connections between means and ends at a functional level.
questions.rule: Link means and ends through functions.
questions.teaches: We get from problem to solution via a string of functional characterizations, making connections between means and ends at a functional level.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: Researchers propose a rule to explain a player's move. How could they guard against inventing a rule only to fit that player?
options: Make the rule as detailed as every word that the player spoke in the protocol
Test it on one more move by the same player
Require that the situation and response be common knowledge among players
Keep the rule secret until the study ends
optionExplain: Detail does not prevent invention.
A second move by the same player does not check against ad hoc rules.
Right: that is the authors' check.
Secrecy is no check.
questions.explain: The authors demand that the situations and generators exist in common chess knowledge. The card gives the check.
questions.rule: Rules should be public, not tailor-made.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: On any particular occasion, only ____ generator is evoked.
questions.explain: Several may apply to a situation, but only one is evoked each time.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A researcher proposes a rule explaining a violinist's habit that only she could understand. Does it pass the authors' check?
options: No: situations and generators must exist in common knowledge of the field
Yes: any rule that fits her behavior passes
Yes: but only if she is an expert
No: because rules about music cannot be productions, which belong to chess alone
optionExplain: Right: a private rule is the ad hoc kind.
That is the ad hoc risk the check guards against.
Expertise is not the test.
The check is about commonality, not the field.
questions.explain: The generators must be part of the field's common knowledge, not special to one subject.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: True or false: All the moves produced by one generator serve the same function.
questions.explain: By implication, all the moves a generator produces serve the same function.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: How does an episode that reworks an earlier one proceed through positions already analysed?
options: It starts again from the base position with a new set of rules for the variation
It follows the prior path until a new production applies, then explores as if new
It chooses a new generator at every position along the path it follows
It skips the prior path by using the no-move
optionExplain: It reuses the prior path up to the variation.
Right: after the variation point all later positions are new.
A new production applies only at the variation.
The no-move belongs to plans.
questions.explain: Table 12.2 lists productions in priority order, such as recapture first, then countercapture, then actions with loss. A reworking episode follows the prior path until a new production is applied, and from there is an initial exploration since all subsequent positions are new.
questions.rule: Follow the old path, vary, then explore.
questions.teaches: In a reworking episode the prior path is followed until a new production, next in the priority order of Table 12.2, is applied to generate a variation; from there the search is carried out as an initial exploration, since all subsequent positions are new.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A reviewer wants evidence that a proposed set of situation-response rules is not tailor-made for one chess subject. Which evidence do the authors expect?
options: The subject agrees with the rules when he is asked about them in an interview afterwards
The rules reproduce the subject's moves exactly
Weaker players cannot recognize the situations
Other players of equal or somewhat better caliber recognize the same situations
optionExplain: The test is about other players.
Fitting one subject is what the check guards against.
The comparison is with equal or better players.
Right: that is their stated expectation.
questions.explain: The authors expect other chess players of equal (or perhaps somewhat better) caliber to recognize the same problem situations and know what moves to propose.
questions.rule: Peers should recognize the same situations.
questions.teaches: The authors expect other chess players of equal, or perhaps somewhat better, caliber to recognize the same problem situations and to know what moves should be proposed to solve them.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A rule says: if a man was captured last move, then recapture. How might it be written in short form?
options: As a code: situation left of an arrow, response right
As a list of all board squares
As a single score for the position
As the name of the piece that moves in answer to the situation
optionExplain: Right: x → r is the first example.
The code names a situation and a response.
A production is not a score.
The code includes the situation as well.
questions.explain: A production pairs a situation with a response. The card shows the notation.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: Match each code to its meaning.
pairs: A man is attacked; add a defender
The opponent's pawn is isolated; attack it
An opponent man is pinned; attack it
questions.explain: The letter before the arrow is the situation, and the letter after is the response: capture, attack, isolated pawn, pin.
questions.rule: Read the code left to right.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: Using the legend in which x is capture, c is counterattack and a is attack, what does x → c mean?
options: After a counterattack, respond with a capture
After an attack, capture the attacker
After a capture, attack the opponent's pinned man
After a capture, respond with a counterattack
optionExplain: The arrow points from situation to response.
That would be a → x.
That is not what the letters say.
Right: the situation is a capture and the response a counterattack.
questions.explain: The situation is on the left (x, a capture) and the response on the right (c, counterattack).
questions.rule: Left is situation, right is response.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: Sort each production as usable in actual play too, or only for analysis.

items.t: x → r, recapture after a capture
a → d, add a defender to an attacked man
e → g, go on exchanging in the midst of an exchange
g → g, go on with the plan

questions.explain: The information-gathering productions (go on with the exchange, plan or attack) are for analysis; the defensive and initiative ones are moves one could play.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: Why do the authors urge caution about the production g → g?
options: It is the least familiar production in the whole of the chess literature
It produces moves that are illegal in play
It implies a plan is operating, so the plan must be inferred before it
It always generates several moves at once
optionExplain: All are well known.
Legality is not the issue.
Right.
It generates the plan's moves, usually one.
questions.explain: Before g → g can be inferred, we must infer the plan from which decisions about continuing are derived.
questions.rule: A plan production needs a plan.
questions.teaches: The production g → g implies a plan is operating, from which decisions about continuing the plan are derived, so before it can be inferred the plan itself must be inferred.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A researcher lists a baker's rules using only what happened in one recorded morning. How complete should she say the list is?
options: Complete, since it covers every response the baker made during the whole morning
Far from complete: it holds only the situations that occurred
Complete, since the rules are simple
Meaningless, since one morning proves nothing
optionExplain: A morning covers only some situations.
Right: the same holds for Table 12.2.
Simplicity says nothing about coverage.
It is a partial but useful list.
questions.explain: The list is by no means complete. The subject undoubtedly has available many more response schemes than come to light in this protocol.
questions.rule: A protocol shows part of the repertoire.
questions.teaches: The subject undoubtedly has available many more response schemes than come to light in this particular protocol.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A rule says to list all exits. A person lists two of three, sure the list is complete. Where does the fault lie?
options: In the rule, which must be wrong
In how the rule was applied, rather than in the rule
In the alarm, which should have sounded differently that day
Nowhere, since two exits are enough
optionExplain: The person's belief points to faulty application.
Right: the authors take this view for such cases.
The alarm is not at fault.
The list is objectively incomplete.
questions.explain: Where the subject believed generation complete, the authors blame the application, not the scheme.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: The productions give a reasonably good account at ____ positions, and reason for dissatisfaction at 14.
questions.explain: 39 good, 14 doubtful.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: About what share of the 53 new-move positions does the account explain reasonably well?
options: About half of them (26 of 53)
About nine in ten (about 48 of 53)
About one quarter
About three quarters (39 of 53)
optionExplain: Half would be about 26 positions.
That would be about 48 positions.
That would be about 13 positions.
Right: 39 divided by 53 is about 74 percent.
questions.explain: 39 of 53 is roughly 74 percent.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: True or false: Where S2 believed he had generated all the moves, the authors count that as a failure of the whole scheme.
questions.explain: They argue it is more reasonable to see a faulty application of the particular production.
questions.rule: Blame the application, not the scheme.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: Why do the authors find incomplete generation on the final move of a variation unsurprising?
options: Only a typical move is needed there to provide the evaluation
The last move in the line is always the weakest one S2 considers
S2 forgot the earlier moves in the line
The final move is chosen by the opponent
optionExplain: Right: E6, E8 and E21 are such cases.
No such claim is made.
Memory is not the explanation.
The final position is evaluated from a typical move.
questions.explain: Three cases (E6, E8, E21) occur on the final move, where there is no need to do more than obtain a typical move to provide the evaluation.
questions.rule: A typical move suffices for evaluation.
questions.teaches: Three cases of incomplete generation (E6, E8, E21) occur on the final move, where it is enough to obtain a typical move to provide the evaluation.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A coach drills a team only on best-case plays and does not list every opposing reply. Which finding of the authors parallels this?
options: Four cases where S2 wrongly believed the generation was complete when it was not
Three cases on the final move to supply an evaluation
Two cases of incomplete generation in E15, tied to biasing the search (R4)
The repeat positions where only the old move is generated
optionExplain: Those were mistakes, not deliberate bias.
Those relate to evaluation, not bias.
Right.
Those are not incomplete generation.
questions.explain: Two cases of incompleteness in E15 are intimately tied up with R4 and biasing search in favorable directions.
questions.teaches: Two of the cases of incomplete generation, in E15, are tied up with rule R4 and the biasing of search in favorable directions.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: At a position S2 considers two ways of defending a Bishop. Does this show two generators?
options: Yes: two moves always mean two generators
No: he cannot consider two moves at one position
Not necessarily: both may be ways of realizing one function, defense
Yes: but only if the two moves are made by pieces of two different kinds
optionExplain: A single function can have several realizations.
Tufts exist.
Right: functions form a hierarchy.
The piece is not the test.
questions.explain: Adding a defender and moving away may be equivalent as defense. The card explains the hierarchy.
questions.rule: Equivalent ways to defend need not mean two generators.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: Two of the ____ tufts show some evidence of multiple generators being evoked.
questions.explain: There are ten tufts, and two show the evidence.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A shop's rule is one fix per fault. A lamp gets a new bulb and a new plug. When is this a real breach?
options: When the two fixes answer different faults, not two ways of curing one
Whenever two fixes are made at once, whatever their purpose
Only when the two fixes together cost more than the lamp itself is worth
Never, because shops may do as they like
optionExplain: Right: equivalence at a higher function is not a breach.
Two equivalent fixes may be one function.
Cost is not the test.
The test is about functions.
questions.explain: Two moves count against one-generator-per-position only if they are not equivalent for the subject.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: True or false: In E2, 2...P'xN is a recapture and 2...R'xR is a counterattack.
questions.explain: These are different responses to a capture (x → r and x → c), a case of mixed generators.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: How do the authors handle the E24 pair of moves that are not functionally equivalent?
options: As a second case of two generators at one position, as in E2 and E14
As a recording error to be dropped
As evidence for breadth-first search
They show one production, assuming the negation (→ n), generates both moves
optionExplain: They show one production covers both.
They treat it as real.
It concerns generators, not search order.
Right.
questions.explain: In E24 the pair 2...P'xP and 4...not (P'xP) is not functionally equivalent, yet both come from one production, → n.
questions.rule: One production can yield different moves.
questions.teaches: In E24 a pair of moves that are not functionally equivalent (2...P'xP and 4...not P'xP) are generated by a single production, → n.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A cook adds an ingredient, sees a new option it opens up, and tries that too. What does this parallel in E2?
options: A sign that S2 had run out of productions and was now choosing moves at random
R5 interruption: the counterattack was possible only after the capture
A breach of R1
A plan production g → g
optionExplain: No such claim is made.
Right: S2 tends to attend to possibilities a move uncovers.
The authors point to R5.
E2 is explained as interruption.
questions.explain: The authors suggest the E2 case may be an interruption: the subject tends to attend to the possibilities uncovered by a move, and 2...R'xR is possible only because of 2.NxB'.
questions.rule: New options opened by a move attract attention.
questions.teaches: The mixed case in E2 may be an interruption (R5): S2 tends to attend to the possibilities a move uncovers, as with 2...R'xR, which is possible only because of 2.NxB'.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A move both defends one of your men and threatens an enemy man. How would an information processing account explain how it was found?
options: Generated by one production, then recognized as meeting another's requirement
Generated twice over, by two different productions acting at the very same moment
Chosen at random from the legal moves
Found only by searching the whole tree
optionExplain: Right: the authors' expectation.
Only one generator is evoked at a time.
The account is about productions.
It is generated from a situation.
questions.explain: A double-function move is expected to come from one production and be recognized as serving another.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: Multiple interpretation of a generated move occurs in only ____ cases here.
questions.explain: Two cases, in E2 and E5.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A hardware-store clerk fetches one item that both holds the shelf and fills the gap. Which description follows the authors?
options: Two separate searches ran at once and found the same item
The clerk picked the item by luck, with no particular need in mind at all
One need produced the item, which was then seen to serve the second need
The item is a failure of the rule list
optionExplain: Only one generator is evoked.
The account is need-driven.
Right.
Such cases are not serious deficiencies.
questions.explain: A double-function move comes from one production and is recognized as meeting the other requirement.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: True or false: The authors regard the two multiple-interpretation cases as serious deficiencies in how the scheme accounts for S2's behavior.
questions.explain: They say ambiguous interpretation should not be treated as showing serious deficiencies.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: Which move is connected with a King-side attack but matches no familiar configuration?
options: 4.BxN'
optionExplain: That fits iP → a or p → a.
Right: no production could be assigned.
That fits a → d or c → g.
The base move has no generator proposed.
questions.explain: For two moves no production can be assigned, and for two others the assignment is uncertain; 2.P-B4 is one clear case.
questions.teaches: For two moves no situation-response production can be assigned and for two others the assignment is uncertain; 2.P-B4 is connected with initiating a King-side attack but matches no familiar configuration.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A stuck student tries an alternative for no evident reason, then a step to dislodge a supposed blocker. Which episode is this?
options: E2: a double threat that was generated by two productions at the same position
E5: a move that adds a defender to a Knight in danger
E9: doubling the Rooks as a familiar plan
E20: S2 needs another White move with no evident grounds for 2.N-R4
optionExplain: That concerns multiple interpretation.
That is a fitted case.
That is a plan that fits a production.
Right.
questions.explain: The E20 episode is obscure: S2 needs an alternative White move, his grounds for 2.N-R4 are not evident, and 3.N-B5 is perhaps an attempt to dislodge the defending Bishop since he believes he attacks the Queen.
questions.teaches: The whole of E20 is obscure: S2 needs an alternative White move but his grounds for 2.N-R4 are not evident, and 3.N-B5 is perhaps an attempt to dislodge the defending Bishop since he believes he is attacking the Queen.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: Once a player has a plan, how hard is it to work out the moves?
options: Hard: every move needs a fresh search of all the options at the position
Impossible: plans cannot be turned into moves
Easy only if the plan came from a book
Easy: the plan dictates the next moves, with few alternatives
optionExplain: A plan removes much of the search.
The authors derive moves from plans.
Plans may be built for the occasion.
Right: given a plan, deriving moves is easy.
questions.explain: A plan dictates the moves. The card describes how S2 uses plans.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: The production g → g means go on with the ____.
questions.explain: Moves at eleven positions are accounted for by going on with the plan.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: To show a butler was out at nine, a detective assumes he was in and follows the consequences. Which production is this?
options: Going on with the plan (g → g)
Assuming the negation to test an assertion (→ n)
Countercapture of equal value after a capture (x → c)
Exchanging the attacker (a → e)
optionExplain: A plan is produced by the assumption, but the technique itself is → n.
Right.
That is a chess response to a capture.
That is a move response.
questions.explain: → n demonstrates a fact by assuming its negation and following out the consequences.
questions.rule: Assume the opposite and follow it out.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: True or false: While S2 implements a plan, he rarely generates alternative moves for it.
questions.explain: He operates in an exploratory way and almost never generates alternative moves for implementing a plan.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: When do the positions where the opponent's move is skipped occur?
options: At the base position of every episode
Only in the final episode, E25
All of them during the implementation of plans
Wherever S2 is uncertain which reply to expect
optionExplain: The base position is a different matter.
They occur in plans such as E9 and E24.
Right.
They occur in plan implementation.
questions.explain: All the positions where the opponent's move is skipped (the no-move) occur when S2 is implementing a plan.
questions.teaches: All the positions where the opponent's move is skipped (the no-move) occur while S2 is implementing a plan.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: To test whether an employee is too busy, a manager explores giving her the project. Which of S2's six plans is this?
options: E17, where S2 lets the Queen capture to test whether it is tied down
E9, doubling the Rooks on the QB-file
E15, getting the Bishop to R6 and the Queen to N7 by means-ends analysis
E24, pushing a Pawn on the King side
optionExplain: Right.
That is a familiar plan, not a test of a claim.
That is a means-ends plan.
That is an attack plan.
questions.explain: In E17 S2 explores the consequences of letting the Q' capture the Pawn to determine whether the Q' has been tied down.
questions.rule: Test a claim by exploring its consequences.
questions.teaches: In E17, S2 determines whether the Queen has been tied down by the double attack on the Bishop by exploring the consequences of letting the Queen capture the Pawn.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A chess player sees a piece attacked and at once defends it. What is the simplest account of this?
options: A full search of all legal moves followed by evaluation
A guess made at random
A stored response evoked by recognizing the situation
A plan made earlier in the game
optionExplain: That is the program style.
The account is of fixed responses.
Right: recognition is followed directly by response.
The response answers the situation at hand.
questions.explain: The scheme says behavior directly follows recognition. The card summarizes it.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: Under the scheme, behavior directly follows ____ of the situation.
questions.explain: Recognition triggers the stored response.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A driver sees brake lights ahead and eases off the accelerator without thought. Which scheme feature does this show?
options: A fixed response to a class of situation, evoked by recognition
A full search of alternatives before acting on the situation at all
A plan built for this one occasion
A tuft of several alternative responses
optionExplain: Right.
There is no search.
The response is a familiar one.
A single response is produced.
questions.explain: Recognition of a standard situation evokes a standard response.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: True or false: The authors explain that most tufts are Black and defensive as a derivative characteristic of the generators appropriate to this base position.
questions.explain: They treat it as derived from the generators fitting this particular position, not a basic property.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: What reasoning lies behind the response of defending an attacked man?
options: Defense is a rule of chess etiquette that players are expected to follow
If he is defended, the opponent can no longer make a gain
Defense always wins material
Defense is easy to see on the board
optionExplain: The authors give a logical basis.
Right: each item rests on a small exercise in logic.
No such claim is made.
Visibility is not the basis.
questions.explain: Each item in Table 12.2 rests on a small exercise in logic; defending an attacked man works because the opponent can then no longer gain.
questions.rule: Each production has a logic behind it.
questions.teaches: Each item in Table 12.2 is based on a small exercise in logic; for example, the idea behind defending an attacked man is that if he is defended, the opponent can no longer make a gain.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: Two bakers each fix a sticky dough: one at once, one after long deliberation. By the authors' reasoning, which more likely used a stored production?
options: The one who deliberated
Both equally, since the outcome was the same
Neither, since stored responses are not a recognized idea
The one who acted at once, with no sign of real problem solving
optionExplain: Stored responses appear immediately.
Each instance must be argued on its merits.
The scheme rests on them.
Right.
questions.explain: Preexisting productions seem probable when moves appear immediately upon the situation without evidence of substantial problem solving, but each instance must be argued on its own merits.
questions.rule: Speed of response is a clue to storage.
questions.teaches: One could argue either that the subject has a preexisting production or that he reasons out the same moves by a general problem solving mechanism; productions seem probable when the moves appear immediately, without evidence of substantial problem solving.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A player ends a line of analysis because it leaves the opponent with an isolated pawn. Which style of evaluation is this?
options: Stopping on one decisive feature
Adding weighted scores for many features
Playing out the game to the very end
Asking another player for a verdict
optionExplain: Right: one feature changes the evaluation.
That is the program style.
The line is stopped early.
The evaluation is the subject's own.
questions.explain: S2's evaluations rest on a single feature. The card describes this.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: S2's evaluations involve only a ____ feature of the position at a time.
questions.explain: Single-feature evaluation is the dominant characteristic.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: Which buyer evaluates a used car the way S2 evaluates positions?
options: One who scores forty features and adds up the weighted results into a total
One who buys whichever car is cheapest
One who test-drives every car in the lot
One who rejects it for one decisive fault, without weighing its good points
optionExplain: That resembles a polynomial payoff function.
Price alone is a single feature, but nothing here shows it decides the matter.
That is exhaustive search, not evaluation by one feature.
Right: one feature settles it.
questions.explain: S2 does not trade a pro from one feature against a con from another.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: True or false: S2 balances a pro from one feature against a con from another feature, as polynomial payoff functions do.
questions.explain: There is no such balancing of features. Only balancing of material, such as a piece for a pawn, occurs.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: Which of these appears among the evaluations S2 uses, in Table 12.3?
options: Gain the Bishop pair
Control the center for the endgame
Lose tempo
Improve the whole pawn structure
optionExplain: Not in the list.
Not in the list.
Right: it is one of the listed evaluations.
Not in the list.
questions.explain: Table 12.3 lists terms such as win material, obtain no threat, remove threat, obtain open file, isolate pawn and lose tempo; no evaluation uses more than one term.
questions.teaches: Table 12.3 lists S2's evaluations, such as win material, obtain no threat, remove threat, obtain open file, isolate pawn, double men on file and lose tempo, and no evaluation uses more than one term.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: Two wine judges: one gives a lovely overall impression, the other names a harsh tannin. Which resembles de Groot's subjects, as opposed to S2?
options: The second, whose single named feature suggests a Gestalt-like evaluation
The first, whose global impression suggests a Gestalt-like evaluation
Both, since all judges give global impressions
Neither, since de Groot's subjects gave no evaluations
optionExplain: A single named feature resembles S2.
Right: de Groot's subjects used general evaluations; S2 uses mostly standard terms.
S2's terms are mostly standard and operational.
They gave general ones.
questions.explain: S2 uses few vague terms, such as complications and mess up. De Groot's subjects used general evaluations such as N-K4, take it away, which suggest a global, impressionistic, Gestalt-like evaluation; this is harder to posit for S2.
questions.rule: Standard terms point away from a Gestalt.
questions.teaches: S2 uses mostly standard operational chess terms and only a few vague ones, unlike some of de Groot's subjects, whose general evaluations such as N-K4, take it away, suggest a global, impressionistic, Gestalt-like evaluation.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A job-hunter keeps finding offers that beat her minimum. What would an aspiration mechanism do with the minimum?
options: Lower it
Raise it
Keep it fixed whatever happens
Remove it altogether
optionExplain: Lowering follows scarcity, not success.
Right: continual success raises the level.
An aspiration level adjusts.
The threshold remains.
questions.explain: A level of aspiration rises with abundance and falls with scarcity.
questions.rule: Adjust the bar to what turns up.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: If few positions exceed the threshold, the level of aspiration is ____.
questions.explain: Scarcity lowers the level.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A scout sets a bar for recruits and, after weeks, almost no one clears it. What does an aspiration mechanism do?
options: Raises the bar
Keeps the bar and stops scouting
Removes the scout's judgment
Lowers the bar
optionExplain: Raising follows abundance.
The mechanism adjusts the bar.
The bar is the scout's judgment.
Right.
questions.explain: Few clearing the threshold calls for a lower level.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: True or false: With S2's evaluative procedure, the authors find it difficult to see a level-of-aspiration mechanism at work.
questions.explain: They say it is difficult to see such a mechanism in operation, apart from one striking example.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: What marks the one striking example in E6 to E10?
options: The moves generated are much poorer than elsewhere, such as 1.NxNP'
The moves generated are the best ones of the whole protocol, such as 1.BxN'/5
No moves are generated at all
The same move is repeated five times
optionExplain: Right.
They are much poorer.
Moves are generated, but weak.
Different weak moves are tried.
questions.explain: In E6 to E10 the moves generated are much poorer than the moves appearing elsewhere.
questions.rule: A low bar lets poor moves in.
questions.teaches: In the search-widely scene (E6 to E10) the moves generated are much poorer than those appearing elsewhere, such as 1.NxNP'.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A team stuck for ideas lets in every suggestion, including weak ones. What does this parallel in E6 to E10?
options: The bars were raised to admit only the best
The bars were removed because the evaluation was Gestalt-like in character
The bars were let down in order to gather in all the possibilities
The bars were reset by the opponent
optionExplain: That would reduce the candidates.
The authors do not say this.
Right.
The opponent does not set them.
questions.explain: It appears as if the bars had been let down in order to gather in all the possibilities.
questions.rule: Lower the bar to gather everything.
questions.teaches: In E6 to E10 it appears as if the bars had been let down in order to gather in all the possibilities.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: Why would repeatedly going down the same path in a search need a processor able to symbolize situations?
options: It must store a photograph of the board
It must run many searches at the very same moment as one another
It must keep a stand-in for each situation to return to it
It must never repeat any position
optionExplain: The authors speak of symbolizing, not photographs.
The processor is basically serial.
Right: symbols let the search be repeated.
Repeating paths is the point.
questions.explain: To go down the same path again, the processor must be able to symbolize it. The card explains.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: The behavior is represented as search in the basic problem space augmented by a few ____ moves such as the no-move.
questions.explain: The authors add abstract moves such as no-move and Q-move.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A cook's behavior is modeled as search over cooking steps plus a few vague steps like season-somehow. Which point does this parallel?
options: The basic space augmented by a few abstract moves, like Q-move
A search over every possible kitchen action, with no abstract steps
A model with no problem space at all
A search that needs no symbols
optionExplain: Right.
The space is the basic one plus a few abstract moves.
The authors insist on a precise space.
A symbolic system is required.
questions.explain: The authors keep the basic space of the rules and add a few abstract moves such as no-move, Q-move and B-defense.
questions.rule: Basic space plus few abstract moves.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: True or false: The authors say their analysis reflects only what this task evoked from S2's total repertoire.
questions.explain: They call the parts examined incomplete: they represent what this particular task evoked.
questions.rule: One task shows part of a repertoire.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: Which of these do the authors list as missing from a full chess program built on progressive deepening? Select all that apply.
options: A table of values for each piece
An opening book of known positions
A clock rule for time control
A move generator for basic moves
A criterion for interruption
Criteria for terminating the analysis
optionExplain: Not listed.
Not listed.
Not listed.
Right.
Right.
Right.
questions.explain: The authors list a move generator for basic moves, a criterion for interruption, a criterion for applying a new production when reworking an episode, and criteria for terminating analysis.
questions.teaches: A full program on the progressive-deepening strategy would still need a move generator for basic moves, a criterion for interruption, a criterion for applying a new production when reworking an episode, and criteria for terminating analysis.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A researcher analyses only the single steps of a session with three themed stretches. What does this leave unexamined?
options: The episodes themselves, which were fully modeled in the course of the chapter
The groups of episodes called scenes, and the organizing idea behind each
The notation of the protocol
The identity of the subject
optionExplain: Episodes were examined.
Right: scenes remain unexamined.
Notation was explained.
That is not a gap.
questions.explain: Levels of organization not examined include the scenes; a single organizing idea undoubtedly underlies the search-widely scene, E6 to E10.
questions.teaches: Some levels of organization were not examined, most notably the groups of episodes called scenes; for example, a single organizing idea undoubtedly underlies all of the search-widely scene (E6 to E10).

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: Two equally able players start from the same position with the same goal. How alike will an obvious stretch of their play be?
options: Essentially the same
Entirely different, since players choose freely
Identical down to the word order of their speech
The same only for the stronger player
optionExplain: Right: that is what makes it obvious.
Obvious behavior is shared by equally able solvers.
Only the behavior, not the speech, is the same.
The claim is about equally intelligent solvers.
questions.explain: An episode is behavior that any equally intelligent solver will carry out in much the same way.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: An episode is a stretch of behavior carried out by the problem solver because it is ____.
questions.explain: Obviousness is the defining feature in this notion.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: Two equally skilled cooks given the same pantry must make a roux for a sauce. Which statement matches the authors' notion of an episode?
options: The two cooks must use exactly the same pan and the same timing at every point
The stretch cannot count since cooks differ in taste
The stretch of making the roux runs off in essentially the same way for both
The stretch is an episode only if it is the first step
optionExplain: Details may differ; the essential course is the same.
Taste enters elsewhere.
Right: obvious behavior given the setup.
Position in the sequence is not the test.
questions.explain: An episode runs through essentially the same course for any equally intelligent solver.
questions.rule: Same start, same goal, same episode.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: True or false: If the desired result cannot be obtained, two equally intelligent solvers will run through exactly the same course.
questions.explain: The exact courses can be quite different, but the domain they explore, trying to reach the unobtainable, will be the same.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: Which step does the authors call significantly unobvious, compared with the exploration that follows?
options: Recapturing after a capture
Choosing a base-move at the base position
Defending an attacked man
Ending an episode on a single-feature evaluation
optionExplain: That is an obvious production.
Right: each base-move starts a new exploration.
Also an obvious production.
Evaluation is part of the obvious run.
questions.explain: Each base-move corresponds to a new exploration, and the base-move remains a significantly unobvious step compared with the exploration that follows.
questions.rule: Starting an exploration is the unobvious part.
questions.teaches: The choice of base-move at the base position remains a significantly unobvious step, as compared with the exploration that follows, which is made of immediate action and reaction.

questions.unitTitle: Chess: Behavior of a Single Subject
questions.q: A researcher has one recording of a chef choosing the menu and forty of cooking steps. Which should she model?
options: The cooking steps, since the single menu choice gives little data
The menu choice, since a single event is the most informative thing to study
Neither, since steps can't be modeled
The cooking steps, since the menu choice occurs once and gives little data, as with the base position
optionExplain: A single occurrence gives little data.
Data limits what can be modeled.
The authors modeled the repeated move generation.
Right: the authors proposed no base-move generator for lack of data.
questions.explain: The authors did not try to define a base-move generator for S2: the base position occurs only once whereas the others occur many times, and the base-move is also a significantly unobvious step.
questions.teaches: The authors proposed no base-move generator for S2, partly for lack of data, since the base position occurs only once whereas the other positions occur many times.

questions.q: A researcher has studied one player closely and wants assurance the findings are not peculiar to that player. What is a sensible step?
options: Record a much longer session with the same player again
Compare the findings with independent studies of other players
Drop the findings and look for a different kind of theory
Ask the same player to explain his own thinking after the session ends
optionExplain: More of one player's data cannot show that other players behave the same way.
Right: independent evidence about other players is what tests whether the pattern is general.
One study is a reason to check it, not to abandon it.
A player's own account is another source from the same person.
questions.explain: Independent evidence is what shows a result is not idiosyncratic. The card next shows how the authors do this.
questions.rule: Check a single case against other cases.

questions.q: For cryptarithmetic and logic the authors used naive subjects, but for chess they used ____ subjects.
questions.explain: The chess subjects were experienced players, which is why perception looms larger there.
questions.rule: Experienced chess subjects, naive puzzle subjects.

questions.q: A study tests complete beginners on weeding and veteran growers on pruning. Where does the card's reasoning predict finer noticing?
options: In weeding, because beginners look harder at a plain task
Equally in both tasks
In neither, because noticing is found only in games
In pruning, since veterans have learned features that beginners miss
optionExplain: Effort is not the same as the learned recognition the card describes.
The authors tie noticing to experience, so practice matters.
Nothing in the card limits noticing to games.
Right: long experience builds recognition of subtle features, as with the chess subjects.
questions.explain: The authors link strong perceptual effects to experienced subjects. A novice in chess recognizes very little.

questions.q: True or false: With complete novices as chess subjects, the authors would expect weaker perceptual effects than with experienced players.
questions.explain: A novice in chess recognizes very little, so the perceptual effects come from experience.

questions.q: Which topic does the chapter explore further because it shows strongly in de Groot's analysis but is largely absent in S2?
options: Defining the situation
Selective search in the game tree
Progressive deepening of a move's analysis
Use of the standard chess vocabulary
optionExplain: Right: de Groot shows redefinition often, while S2 largely lacks it.
S2 did search selectively, so this topic is not absent in him.
S2 showed progressive deepening so strongly that the authors named it.
S2 relied on the standard vocabulary like the others.
questions.explain: The authors single out defining the situation as strong in de Groot's analysis and largely absent in S2.
questions.rule: Absent in S2, strong in de Groot.
questions.teaches: Defining the situation shows up strongly in de Groot's analysis but is largely absent in the behavior of S2, so the chapter explores it in more depth.

questions.q: A team wants to learn what a puzzle demands of any solver, apart from one person. Which approach does the chapter use for mating combinations?
options: Interview many grandmasters about their favorite combinations
Time how long one expert takes on each combination
Run a program that performs the task and study the environment with it
Compare a novice's guesses with a random sequence of moves
optionExplain: The authors describe this topic as program-based, not interview-based.
Timing one expert says little about what the task itself demands.
Right: the mating topic is mainly more exploration of the task environment by a program.
Neither a novice nor a random sequence is part of that topic.
questions.explain: The mating-combinations topic is mostly further exploration of the task environment with a program.
questions.rule: A program can map what a task demands.
questions.teaches: The mating-combinations program has some of the flavor of a theorem prover, so that topic adds to understanding how game playing relates to other tasks.

questions.q: One lab tapes a player thinking aloud; another takes hand notes and then reviews them with the player. What is the likely difference?
options: The note-takers get a fuller record
The two records are identical
The tape lets the player correct the record, which notes cannot
The tape gives a fuller record, while note-takers can check with the player
optionExplain: Hand notes are normally less complete than a tape.
The difference is in the recording, so the records are not identical.
It is the immediate review, not the tape, that lets a subject comment.
Right: tapes are more extensive; a review with the subject checks hand notes.
questions.explain: Tape gives more complete protocols; a review gives a check. The card next shows how this applies to de Groot.
questions.rule: Tape is fuller; review is a check.

questions.q: De Groot's subjects ranged from good club players to ____.
questions.explain: His group went up to grandmasters, the best players in the chess world.

questions.q: One coach tapes a tennis pupil; another jots notes and reviews them with the pupil right after. Which advantage is the second coach's?
options: An immediate review of the notes with the pupil, which a tape lacks
A fuller record of every word the pupil said than any tape could hold
A larger group of pupils, covering every ability from beginner to champion
A guarantee that the notes match what the pupil was thinking at the time
optionExplain: Right: de Groot's review of notes with the subject is the advantage the authors did not use.
Hand notes are less extensive than a tape, not more.
Group size has nothing to do with the recording method.
A review helps, but no review guarantees a match with thought.
questions.explain: In the card, the immediate review with the subject belongs to de Groot, while the tape recorder belongs to the authors.
questions.rule: Tape gives extent; review gives a check.

questions.q: Which are real differences between de Groot's procedure and the authors'? Select all that apply.
options: De Groot took notes where the authors used tape recorders
De Groot went over the notes with the subject after each session
De Groot asked subjects to talk aloud, but the authors did not
De Groot gave subjects a different kind of task, not choosing a move
optionExplain: Right: this is the chief difference in observation.
Right: the authors did not do this with S2.
Both studies asked subjects to talk aloud.
Both involved analyzing a position to choose a move.
questions.explain: The task and the thinking-aloud request were the same; the recording and the review differed.
questions.rule: Same task, different recording and review.

questions.q: How does the authors' footnote qualify the claim that grandmasters are incomparably better than S2?
options: S2 and the grandmasters in fact win about equally often
There are no players between them, only one large step
Four to five players, each nearly always beating the one below, fill the gap
The gap is closed by about ten players, each of whom nearly always beats the one below
optionExplain: The footnote does not say S2 holds his own against grandmasters.
It says there is a sequence of players, not a single step.
Right: the footnote says there are four to five such players between S2 and a grandmaster.
The number given is four to five, not ten.
questions.explain: The footnote describes a ladder of players, each nearly always beating the one below and losing to the one above.
questions.rule: A ladder of players links S2 to the grandmasters.
questions.teaches: Between S2 and a grandmaster there are four to five players, each nearly always beating the man below him and nearly always beaten by the man above; perhaps three or four lie between a novice and S2.

questions.q: A study of one mid-level violinist matches famous soloists in many ways. What further point do the authors make about such a match?
options: Soloists are of no use for comparison
The kinship also shows between the human players and the chess programs
The match proves the violinist is as good as the soloists
The match is accidental
optionExplain: The authors use the better players precisely as a check.
Right: the authors add that the basic kinship of human players to chess programs is quite apparent.
Likeness in processing does not mean equal skill.
The authors take the likeness as meaningful, not accidental.
questions.explain: The authors say de Groot's findings show likeness between his subjects and S2, and that the kinship to chess programs is apparent.
questions.rule: Likeness in process need not mean equal skill.
questions.teaches: The authors add that the basic kinship of the human players to chess-playing programs is quite apparent in de Groot's findings.

questions.q: A strong player studies a position for fifteen minutes. About how many different positions does the player consider?
options: No more than about a hundred
Several thousand, about one for every second
Around ten thousand, as a full lookahead would need
Millions, covering every legal continuation
optionExplain: Right: the evidence puts the total at about a hundred at most.
That is far above anything the protocols show.
Ten thousand is the scale of some programs, not of people.
Humans cannot search a space of that size in the time.
questions.explain: Humans search only a small space. The card next shows the evidence.

questions.q: In position A the five grandmasters explicitly considered between 20 and ____ positions.
questions.explain: The range in the protocols of the five grandmasters was 20 to 76 positions.

questions.q: A coach counts 40 distinct positions in a student's ten-minute think-aloud. What does the card suggest this shows?
options: A search far too small to count as real analysis
An exhaustive search that has covered the whole tree
A selective search of a few dozen positions, in line with strong players
A search that shows the student is a grandmaster
optionExplain: The reported counts for grandmasters are of this size.
A whole-tree search would be orders of magnitude larger.
Right: a few dozen positions fits the range reported for strong players.
The count alone does not rank the player; grandmasters in position A differed by a wide range.
questions.explain: Forty positions sits inside the 20 to 76 range found for the grandmasters.

questions.q: True or false: If players often consider positions without mentioning them, the protocol counts understate how many positions they really consider.
questions.explain: Unmentioned positions would make the counts too low, which is why the estimates err on the low side.

questions.q: How far could the true number of positions considered exceed the protocol estimates, according to the authors?
options: The estimates could be ten times too low
The estimates err on the low side, but could not be more than doubled
The estimates err high
The estimates are exact
optionExplain: The authors rule out so large an error.
Right: players may fail to mention positions, but by no stretch could the estimates be more than doubled.
The authors say the bias is toward too low.
The authors say the estimates are uncertain, not exact.
questions.explain: The direction of error is low, and its size is bounded by about a factor of two.
questions.teaches: Protocol estimates of positions considered err on the low side because players may fail to mention positions, yet by no stretch of the uncertainties could they be more than doubled.

questions.q: A program examines tens of thousands of positions per analysis. Which conclusion do the authors draw about its relation to human play?
options: It plays like humans
It must be wrong
It shows humans search many positions but report few
It almost certainly works unlike humans; selective programs are more relevant
optionExplain: Strength is not the issue; the question is how the program works.
The authors do not call it wrong, only unlike humans.
The authors bound the underreporting at a factor of two.
Right: humans both search and search only a small space, which reconfirms the authors' view of such programs.
questions.explain: Players search, but within a small space, so programs with huge searches differ from humans.
questions.rule: Huge search is not human search.
questions.teaches: Because players search only a small space, programs that search thousands or tens of thousands of positions per analysis almost certainly proceed differently from humans, and highly selective programs are more relevant.

questions.q: Why might a short phrase for a board pattern help a skilled player more than a list of its pieces?
options: The phrase tells the player the best move in the position at hand
A knowledgeable player can evoke the whole pattern from it
The phrase is shorter, so it can be remembered by anyone
The phrase removes the need to look at the board
optionExplain: A pattern name describes the board; it does not choose a move.
Right: a name stands for a pattern the player already knows.
Someone who lacks the vocabulary cannot evoke the pattern.
The player still needs the board to know which patterns are present.
questions.explain: A name carries a whole pattern for someone who knows it. The card next defines this as a concept.

questions.q: The phrase fianchettoed short-castled position is enough for a knowledgeable player to evoke a pattern of ____ pieces.
questions.explain: The pattern is made of Black's pawns, a Bishop, a Rook and a King: six pieces.

questions.q: A forecaster says a blocking high sits over the coast. Which feature of the card does this resemble?
options: A search: a tree of consequences looked at in turn
An evaluation: a number placed on the end of a line
A protocol: a spoken record of a person thinking aloud
A concept: one term standing for a whole pattern to an informed listener
optionExplain: Nothing is being searched or looked ahead in the phrase.
The phrase names a pattern; it does not score a result.
The phrase is a term, not a record of thought.
Right: the phrase names a pattern and evokes it for those who know the vocabulary.
questions.explain: Concepts compress a pattern into a name, whatever the field.

questions.q: True or false: Elementary concepts such as pins and open files appear in both human chess play and chess programs.
questions.explain: The same kinds of elementary concepts appear in both, at least superficially.
questions.rule: Both use attacks, pins and open files.

questions.q: Why do the authors say it is to be expected that programs use the same elementary concepts as players?
options: Programs are written by chess-playing programmers who rely on the standard literature
Programs learn the concepts by playing very many games against human opponents over time
Concepts are built into the rules of chess themselves
Both programs and players discover the concepts independently
optionExplain: Right: the programmers bring the vocabulary of the literature into their programs.
The authors do not describe the programs of the day as learning from opponents.
A concept is a classification, not a rule of the game.
The authors point to a common source, not independent discovery.
questions.explain: Overlap in vocabulary has a simple source: the programmers are players and use the literature.
questions.teaches: The same concepts appear in programs and in human play because the programs are written by chess-playing programmers who rely heavily on the standard chess literature.

questions.q: A guide names a pattern as a pinned Knight on the Queen by a Bishop. What does the fianchetto example add about such a name?
options: It stands for any position in which the Bishop is stronger than the Knight there
It stands for a plan, not for a set of men
It stands for a fixed set of men, such as pawns, a Bishop, a Rook and the King
It stands for a single piece and its square
optionExplain: A name for a pattern is about particular men, not for general strength.
The example is a pattern of pieces, not a plan.
Right: the example gives the exact men and squares behind the name.
The example involves six pieces, not one.
questions.explain: A named pattern corresponds to definite men on definite squares: Black pawns on KB2, KN3 and KR2, a Bishop on KN2, a Rook on KB1 and the King on KN1.
questions.rule: A name stands for definite men on squares.
questions.teaches: The fianchettoed short-castled pattern consists of Black pawns on KB2, KN3 and KR2, a Bishop on KN2, a Rook on KB1 and the King on KN1.

questions.q: Two systems both use the term open file. What can you conclude about how they use it?
options: That they treat it the same way
That one copied the other's rules for it
That both use it only to evaluate final positions
Little, until you see how each system uses the term
optionExplain: A common label does not fix the use.
Nothing suggests copying.
A term can be used in conditions or in labels as well as in evaluations.
Right: a shared name leaves extension and use open.
questions.explain: A shared name does not tell you how a concept is used. The card next shows the authors' view.

questions.q: Concepts ____ information that may be used in a variety of ways.
questions.explain: The authors say concepts encapsulate information, which can be put to different uses.

questions.q: A spreadsheet macro and an accountant both flag overdue invoices. What is the safe conclusion in light of the card?
options: They share a word, but the invoices counted and the flag's use may differ
They must flag exactly the same invoices
The macro must be copying the accountant's thinking
The accountant is applying a production system
optionExplain: Right: the word matches, but extension and use are separate questions.
The same word does not guarantee the same extension.
Nothing shows the macro was built from the accountant's reasoning.
Nothing in the case says how the accountant reasons.
questions.explain: Match in name is where the question starts, not where it ends.

questions.q: Sort each chess concept. Elementary concepts name a local feature, as in a production's condition or a move label; global concepts sum up a whole position, as in human protocols.

items.t: Pin
Open file
Isolated pawn
Attack
Control of the center
A won position
A closed position
A weak King's side

questions.explain: Pins, open files, isolated pawns and attacks name local features; the others sum up a whole position.
questions.rule: Elementary names a feature; global sums up the position.

questions.q: Where do the counterparts of global human concepts mostly occur in current chess programs?
options: In the move generators, where they match human concepts closely and directly
In the opening books, where they are stored as complete games
In the static evaluation, where the correspondence does not seem very close
In the search routines, where they decide how deep to look
optionExplain: The authors place them in evaluation, not in generation.
Opening books are not what the authors mention.
Right: the counterparts sit in static evaluation, and the match is loose.
The authors do not tie them to depth of search.
questions.explain: Programs hold crude counterparts of global concepts in their static evaluation; the chess programs of Chapter 11 shed little light on them.
questions.rule: Global concepts have loose program counterparts.
questions.teaches: The counterparts of global human concepts occur mostly in the static-evaluation processes of current programs, and the correspondence does not seem very close.

questions.q: S2 described Black's position as in sad shape. How often did S2 use global descriptions like this?
options: In every episode, as his main way of judging
Only occasionally
Never, since he judged only by search
Only in his opening orientation, never afterwards
optionExplain: He used them rarely, not constantly.
Right: S2 used such general concepts only occasionally.
The example shows that he did use them at times.
The text does not limit them to the orientation.
questions.explain: S2 relied mainly on specific features and search; his global talk was occasional.
questions.rule: S2 used global concepts only now and then.
questions.teaches: Subject 2 used global concepts only occasionally, for example describing Black's position as in sad shape.

questions.q: A person plunged into a complex situation starts by looking it over. What does a chess player do first in analyzing a position?
options: Orients himself to the position before exploring any move
Picks the final move and then finds reasons for it afterwards
Searches the deepest line at once
Compares the position with the last game he played
optionExplain: Right: an initial orientation comes first.
Choosing the move is the end, in the summing up.
A deep search comes after orienting, not before.
The card does not describe a comparison with earlier games.
questions.explain: Orientation comes at the start and a summing up at the end. The card next describes the parts between.

questions.q: De Groot's three major phases are exploration, elaboration and ____.
questions.explain: The third phase is proof; orientation counts as a fourth.

questions.q: A student reads a maths problem, tries several lines, then writes the final answer. Which stages match orientation and summing up?
options: Trying the first line and trying the last line
Writing the answer and then reading the problem
Reading the problem and writing the final answer
Trying several lines and then writing the answer
optionExplain: Those are two of the middle episodes, not the boundaries.
The boundaries are in the opposite order.
Right: the opening look and the final choice are the two boundaries.
Only the final answer is a boundary in that pair; the lines are middle episodes.
questions.explain: Orientation is the opening look and summing up is the closing choice.
questions.rule: Boundaries are orientation and summing up.

questions.q: Put these stages in the order de Groot lists them, with the initial orientation first.
items: Initial orientation
Exploration
Elaboration
Proof
questions.explain: The card lists orientation as a fourth phase, then the three major phases in the order exploration, elaboration, proof.

questions.q: What do the authors say is more important than finding a characteristic phase sequence?
options: Counting the number of episodes in each protocol
Identifying the features of the different types of episodes
Deciding which phase the final move belongs to
Matching each episode to a time on the clock
optionExplain: A count of episodes does not describe their types.
Right: the authors prefer describing episode types to a fixed sequence.
The final move belongs to the summing up, and this is not the authors' point.
The authors do not use clock time to classify episodes.
questions.explain: The authors rank the study of episode types above a search for a fixed phase order.
questions.rule: Study types of episode, not a fixed order.
questions.teaches: The authors hold that identifying the features of different types of episodes considered individually is more important than attempting to find a characteristic phase sequence.

questions.q: Two players analyze one position, one briefly and one for much longer. Which statement fits the card?
options: The longer analysis adds an orientation after every episode
The shorter analysis skips orientation and summing up
Both analyses contain the same number of episodes
Both orient first and sum up last, but the middle varies with the level of analysis
optionExplain: Orientation comes only once, at the start.
The boundaries are present in any analysis, however short.
The number between the boundaries varies.
Right: only the middle varies with depth.
questions.explain: The count of episodes in the middle is variable and depends on how deep the analysis goes.
questions.rule: Depth changes the middle, not the ends.
questions.teaches: The number of episodes between orientation and summing up is variable, depending on the level of analysis.

questions.q: A skilled analyst studies one candidate move. Which habit is more typical?
options: Following one line to the end once and never coming back
Returning to the same move several times, each time more carefully
Looking at every continuation to the same depth in a single pass over the tree
Choosing the move first and never analyzing it
optionExplain: Players do not do one pass and leave it.
Right: repeated reworking of the same ground is typical.
Players search only a few continuations, not all of them.
Players do analyze their candidates.
questions.explain: Humans rework the same ground repeatedly. The card next names this.

questions.q: J. C. Shaw's phrase for the idea is rough cut, ____ cut.
questions.explain: The pair is rough cut, fine cut: a first pass and a closer one.

questions.q: A carpenter shapes a table leg with a saw, then a plane, then sandpaper. Which idea from the card does this resemble?
options: Verification: each pass tests a favorite hypothesis
Redefinition: each pass changes what the job is
Position evaluation: each pass assigns a score
Rough cut, fine cut: each pass reworks the piece more carefully
optionExplain: No hypothesis is being tested here.
The job stays the same through all passes.
No score is being given at each pass.
Right: the same piece is reworked, closer each time.
questions.explain: Successive passes over the same ground, finer each time, is the pattern.

questions.q: True or false: A player who analyzes a move once to the end and does not return to it is showing progressive deepening.
questions.explain: Progressive deepening is defined by repeated returns to old ground, not by a single pass.
questions.rule: Return is the mark of progressive deepening.

questions.q: Which feature of the Kotok and Greenblatt programs comes nearest to rough cut, fine cut?
options: They examine all legal moves statically to pick plausible ones for deeper study
They replay each move to a greater depth after every turn taken by either player
They search only checking moves in each position
They abandon any line that allows the opponent more than four replies
optionExplain: Right: a quick static pass picks the moves to be explored further.
Neither program is described as replaying moves at greater depth in that way.
Checking moves are the basis of the mating program, not of these.
That cutoff belongs to the mating program.
questions.explain: The two programs do a first static look at all legal moves, then go deeper on the plausible ones; the Greenblatt program also uses a single secondary search.
questions.rule: A static first pass selects what to deepen.
questions.teaches: The Kotok and Greenblatt programs examine all legal moves statically to select plausible moves for greater depth, and the Greenblatt program uses a single secondary search.

questions.q: Before a long hike, a planner sketches one rough route to get oriented, then refines it. Which chess habit does this parallel?
options: Verifying a favorite move against all the alternatives available to the player
Redefining the problem after a surprise
Constructing a sample variation to get oriented to the position
Counting the positions already considered
optionExplain: Verification tests a chosen move, which the sketch is not.
The planner has not met a surprise, so nothing is redefined.
Right: some players begin by building a sample variation to orient themselves.
The sketch is not a count of anything.
questions.explain: Some players start with a sample variation to get their bearings before the closer work.
questions.teaches: Some players start by constructing a sample variation to orient themselves to the position.

questions.q: A mechanic suspects a dead battery and tests it. How does this differ from looking around the engine for anything odd?
options: The test seeks new information and the look-around checks an idea
Both do the same job and differ only in length
The look-around is a test and the test is a hunch
The test aims to prove or disprove one idea, while looking around seeks information
optionExplain: The roles are reversed in this option.
Their purposes differ, which can change how they are done.
A look-around is not a test of a stated idea.
Right: one tests a hypothesis, the other explores.
questions.explain: Testing a hypothesis and exploring for information are different jobs. The card next uses these words for chess.

questions.q: Episodes devoted to proving or disproving a hypothesis are devoted to ____.
questions.explain: These are verification episodes; the others explore.

questions.q: A cook tastes soup to see what it needs, adds salt, and tastes again to check the fix. Which taste is verification?
options: The second taste, which tests the idea that salt was needed
The first taste, which tests the idea that the soup was good
Both tastes, because tasting is always testing
Neither taste, because tasting cannot be exploration
optionExplain: Right: the second taste checks a hypothesis already formed.
The first taste gathers information.
The first taste explores; only the second tests.
A taste can well be exploration, as the first one is.
questions.explain: Exploration gathers information; verification checks a chosen idea.
questions.rule: Taste to explore, taste again to verify.

questions.q: True or false: S2's repeated returns to B x N'/5 show that he was trying to prove it his favorite move.
questions.explain: The text finds little reason to see it as a deliberate favorite: it was the only thing of interest he had found.
questions.rule: Repetition is not proof of a favorite.

questions.q: What does the authors' account say a human player gains and loses by handling hypotheses one after another?
options: It keeps all the information and makes the task easier
It uses all the new information and makes the task impossible
It throws away much information but makes the task manageable
It saves time but makes every judgment less reliable in the end
optionExplain: The first half is wrong: much information is discarded.
The authors say the task is made manageable.
Right: the player cannot squeeze all the information out of each observation, but the task becomes manageable.
The authors do not discuss reliability here.
questions.explain: Dealing with hypotheses in sequence, rather than narrowing possibilities deductively, discards information but keeps the task within human limits.
questions.rule: Singular hypotheses: costly in information, cheap in effort.
questions.teaches: Dealing with hypotheses seriatim throws away much information but makes the cognitive task manageable, since the human has no way to squeeze all the information out of each new observation.

questions.q: A detective picks one suspect early and works to confirm the case. Which general tendency in human problem solving does this resemble?
options: Narrowing the possibilities deductively with every clue
Handling a complex world by a sequence of singular hypotheses
Examining every suspect in parallel until one is left
Setting aside all hypotheses until the whole of the evidence is complete
optionExplain: The authors say people do not squeeze each observation that way.
Right: this is the tendency the authors cite from concept attainment studies.
That would be exhaustive, which people are not.
People form hypotheses along the way.
questions.explain: People tend to work through one hypothesis at a time, which is well attested in concept attainment studies.
questions.teaches: The general tendency to deal with a complex world by a sequence of singular hypotheses is well attested in the concept attainment studies of Bruner, Goodnow and Austin (1956).

questions.q: After a long look at a weakness, a player says White must now extract some profit from it. What is the player doing?
options: Restating the problem as a new working assumption
Testing a hypothesis about the weakness
Evaluating a final position of a line
Verifying a favorite move against the alternatives
optionExplain: Right: a summary of earlier analysis taken as the new basis for work.
No testing follows such a statement.
The statement is not the score of a terminal position.
No particular move is being checked.
questions.explain: The statement summarizes earlier analysis and sets the next goal. The card next names it a redefinition.

questions.q: A redefinition is accepted as the new working ____.
questions.explain: The authors say the redefinition is accepted as the new working assumption.
questions.rule: A redefinition is a working assumption.

questions.q: After failing at the ridge, a hiker says: we now need a way around the ridge. Which feature of the card does this show?
