options: A hypothesis whose truth she then sets out to prove
A rough cut that she will later refine
A summary conclusion from earlier attempts, taken as a working assumption
A single advantage mentioned at the end of a line
optionExplain: Nothing is then tested to see whether the restatement is true.
Progressive deepening is about reworking one move, not restating the goal.
Right: the failed attempts are summed up and the goal is restated.
Evaluation of a terminal position is a different job.
questions.explain: A redefinition is a general statement drawn from the prior effort, adopted as the basis for what comes next.
questions.rule: Failed attempts can redefine the goal.

questions.q: True or false: After a player redefines the problem there is normally no episode devoted to proving or disproving the new definition.
questions.explain: Normally no testing activity follows a redefinition, which marks it off from hypothesis formation.
questions.rule: Redefinition is not followed by testing.

questions.q: In position A, which of these contains nothing of the process of redefinition, according to the authors?
options: De Groot's protocols and the protocol of S2
Current computer chess programs and the protocol of S2
Current computer chess programs and de Groot's protocols
De Groot's protocols only
optionExplain: De Groot's protocols are the source of the examples.
Right: redefinition is missing from both programs and S2.
Programs lack it, but de Groot's players do it.
De Groot's protocols are where it is found.
questions.explain: Redefinition is known from de Groot's data and is missing from S2 and the programs.
questions.rule: Found in de Groot, missing in S2 and programs.
questions.teaches: Nothing of the process of redefinition occurs in current computer chess programs or in the protocol of S2.

questions.q: A manager begins working from an assumption without anyone stating a summary. By the authors' contrast, what is this?
options: A redefinition, which always comes with a deliberate summary of the analysis
A verification, since a favorite idea is now being tested
A static evaluation, since the plan is judged at its end
A hypothesis, which can arise without deliberate summarization
optionExplain: A redefinition is a deliberate summary, so this is not one.
Nothing is being tested yet.
The plan is not being scored.
Right: hypotheses can arise without a summarizing step.
questions.explain: Hypotheses can be formed and worked on without a deliberate summary; redefinitions are stated summaries.
questions.rule: Redefinition is stated; a hypothesis need not be.
questions.teaches: Hypotheses can arise, be accepted and be worked on without deliberate summarization, which is one way redefinition differs from hypothesis formation.

questions.q: A buyer compares two houses. Which style of judging is closer to what chess masters do in evaluating a line?
options: Scoring dozens of features and adding the weighted scores
Naming one standout advantage, such as a good garden
Refusing to judge until every feature is measured
Judging each house by price alone
optionExplain: That is the polynomial style of most programs.
Right: players often mention a single advantage.
Players do evaluate, and briefly.
Price is not the single advantage the card has in mind.
questions.explain: Human evaluations tend to be brief and single-featured. The card next sets this against programs.

questions.q: Most chess and checkers programs use elaborate ____ evaluations.
questions.explain: The programs weigh many factors in a polynomial; humans seldom do.

questions.q: A scout writes only: he gains control of the open file. Which style does this show?
options: A polynomial style: many pro and con factors balanced
A style in which no judgment is made
A style that can only be used on final positions of a program
A human style: one named advantage, without a weighed total
optionExplain: No balancing of many factors appears.
A judgment is made, though a brief one.
The note is human, and humans use this style.
Right: a single advantage is the typical human evaluation.
questions.explain: A single advantage is the style described for de Groot's subjects and S2.

questions.q: True or false: A polynomial evaluation weighs many factors, some pro and some con, into one estimate, unlike the single advantages in de Groot's protocols.
questions.explain: That is the contrast the authors draw, without calling it a contradiction.

questions.q: At which positions do human players generally make explicit evaluations?
options: At the terminal positions of each line, not at intermediate ones
At every position along the line, after each move by either side in turn
Only at the starting position, before any search
At intermediate positions, but not at the ends of lines
optionExplain: Right: this matches the static positions of programs, with none at the dynamic ones.
Players make no explicit evaluations at intermediate positions.
The start is not where the evaluation is made.
The pattern is the reverse of this.
questions.explain: Humans evaluate at the ends of lines, which are the static positions of programs; players and programs agree here.
questions.rule: Evaluate at the ends of lines.
questions.teaches: Human players generally make evaluations at the terminal (static) positions of each line of search and make no explicit evaluations at intermediate (dynamic) positions, and in this respect players and programs agree.

questions.q: A grandmaster says only: and it is a won position for White. What does the authors' note on such phrases imply?
options: The evaluation must be the sum of several named factors
The evaluation shows the player has searched to the end
It may not be possible to see which feature leads to the evaluation
The evaluation proves the move is objectively best
optionExplain: Nothing in the phrase lists factors.
It shows nothing about how deep he searched.
Right: very global phrases hide the structure behind the judgment.
A judgment does not prove the move is best.
questions.explain: Some evaluations are so global that their basis cannot be seen in the protocol.
questions.rule: A global phrase hides its basis.
questions.teaches: Sometimes de Groot's subjects used very global phrases such as a won position for White, where it is not possible to see what structure or feature of the position leads to the evaluation.

questions.q: A researcher cannot tell strong chess players from weak ones by counting positions searched. What test might work instead?
options: Counting how many moves the player says aloud while analyzing a position
Asking players to rank themselves
Timing how fast each player moves in a game
Showing a position briefly and asking the player to reproduce it
optionExplain: Statistics of search did not separate them.
Self-ranking is not mentioned as a measure.
Speed is not the measure the card reports.
Right: perceptual reproduction separated the groups.
questions.explain: The brief-exposure test separated players where search counts failed. The card next gives the details.

questions.q: De Groot's players saw each position for only a few seconds, from 3 to ____ seconds.
questions.explain: The exposure ran 3 to 7 seconds.

questions.q: A coach cannot separate good from poor piano students by counting practice notes. Following de Groot's approach, what might she try?
options: A brief look at a short score, then playing it from memory
A longer look at a score, then a written report on what it contains
A count of the notes in the student's pieces
A comparison of how long each student sits at the piano
optionExplain: Right: brief exposure and reproduction mirrors the chess test.
A longer look and a report is not a perceptual reproduction test.
A count is a statistic of activity, like those that failed.
Time at the instrument is also a statistic of activity.
questions.explain: De Groot turned from activity counts to a brief perceptual task.

questions.q: True or false: Because reproduction accuracy fell as ability fell, the brief-exposure test separated strong players from weak ones.
questions.explain: The test worked because performance fell off as chess ability fell off.
questions.rule: A useful test shows a gradient.

questions.q: What do the authors note about the worst of de Groot's players?
options: They had never played in a tournament
They were complete novices at chess who had never entered any contest
They were good enough to play occasionally in local tournaments
They were all club champions of Amsterdam
optionExplain: The card says they did play occasionally in tournaments.
A novice recognizes very little, so these were not novices.
Right: even the weakest were players of some standing.
The text does not describe them as champions.
questions.explain: The group was not made of beginners, which is part of why a simple search count failed to separate them.
questions.rule: The weakest were still tournament players.
questions.teaches: The worst of de Groot's players were good enough to play occasionally in local tournaments in Amsterdam.

questions.q: A scout finds move counts do not separate chess players but memory for positions does. What did de Groot propose from such a result?
options: Search depth is the only factor in very good play
Perceptual abilities and organization matter in very good play
Memory tests measure only how long players practice
Good play comes from reading about the game
optionExplain: The failure of search statistics points the other way.
Right: this was his proposal.
Nothing in the card says reproduction merely tracks practice time.
Reading is not mentioned as the factor.
questions.explain: The test result led de Groot to stress perceptual ability and organization.
questions.teaches: De Groot was led to propose that perceptual abilities and organization were an important factor in very good play.

questions.section: Comparison with de Groot's Protocols on Position A
questions.q: Two players study the same position and look at the same moves. What are the possible sources of the likeness?
options: The demands of the situation, or features players share as human thinkers
Chance alone, with no cause
The players' recorded tapes being copied from one another by the researcher
The players using the same notebook
optionExplain: Right: the task and the shared human processor are the candidate sources.
Likeness in many protocols is unlikely to be chance.
Nothing suggests copying.
Nothing suggests a shared notebook.
questions.explain: The likeness may come from the task or from the people. The card next says how the authors pursue it.

questions.section: Comparison with de Groot's Protocols on Position A
questions.q: The data came from ____ protocols of subjects placed before position A.
questions.explain: De Groot summarized 19 protocols for position A.

questions.section: Comparison with de Groot's Protocols on Position A
questions.q: Two bakers both knead dough for a long time. To tell whether the dough requires it or bakers share a habit, what would you do?
options: Watch one baker for a longer time
Ask the bakers which habit they prefer and which they find more natural
Look at many bakers of different skill and ask what the dough demands
Count the loaves each baker sells
optionExplain: One baker's habits cannot separate the sources.
Preferences do not separate task demands from habit.
Right: many subjects and an analysis of the task separate the two sources.
Sales are unrelated to the source of the habit.
questions.explain: Separating task demands from human habit needs both many subjects and an analysis of the task.

questions.section: Comparison with de Groot's Protocols on Position A
questions.q: True or false: The PBG in Figure 13.1 was drawn from the protocol of S2.
questions.explain: Figure 13.1 shows the PBG of Euwe, one of the fullest of de Groot's protocols, to be compared with S2's.

questions.section: Comparison with de Groot's Protocols on Position A
questions.q: How many of the 19 protocols are reproduced in de Groot's own book?
options: Nineteen, all of them
Sixteen
Nine, one for each master or grandmaster
Five, one for each grandmaster
optionExplain: Three are not reproduced.
Right: sixteen are reproduced.
More than the master and grandmaster protocols are reproduced.
The reproduced set is larger than the grandmasters' set.
questions.explain: Sixteen of the protocols appear in de Groot (1965), so readers can check them.
questions.teaches: Sixteen of the 19 protocols are reproduced in de Groot (pp. 409-421).

questions.section: Comparison with de Groot's Protocols on Position A
questions.q: Two cashiers at different shops both recheck large bills. Which pair of sources would the authors separate in explaining this?
options: The cashiers' pay, and the shops' opening hours
Luck, and the cashiers' hair color
The shop's lighting, and the color of the bills
The demands of the job itself, and common features of human processing
optionExplain: Pay and hours are not the two sources the authors name.
Luck and hair color are not the sources they name.
Lighting and color are not the sources they name.
Right: the two sources the authors name for likenesses between subjects.
questions.explain: The authors want to know what likenesses reflect the objective demands of the task environment and what reveal common characteristics of human information processing systems.
questions.rule: Task demands versus the human processor.
questions.teaches: The detailed comparison is meant to show to what extent communalities reflect the objective demands of the task environment and to what extent common characteristics of human information processing systems.

questions.q: In a position with 56 legal first moves, about how many different first moves would 19 players mention in all?
options: All 56, since every move gets a look from someone
About two dozen at most
About 40, three-quarters of the total
Fewer than 10, the same few for everyone
optionExplain: Most legal moves were mentioned by nobody.
Right: only 22 different moves were mentioned.
The total is far smaller than three-quarters.
The total is more than ten, even though a few moves dominate.
questions.explain: Players ignore most legal moves. The card next gives the exact numbers.

questions.q: Only ____ different initial moves were mentioned by one or more of the 19 subjects.
questions.explain: Twenty-two different initial moves were mentioned.

questions.q: A master mentions 11 different base-moves in position A. How does that compare with the others of master or grandmaster strength?
options: Typical: most masters considered about 11
Unusually few: most masters considered 20 or more
The same as the club players, who also considered 11 on average each
Unusually many: no other master or grandmaster considered over 6
optionExplain: The typical number was under five.
Masters considered few moves, not 20.
Nothing in the account gives club players an average of 11; the average over all subjects was under five.
Right: the master with 11 was an exception.
questions.explain: The average was under five, and 6 was the most for any other master or grandmaster.

questions.q: True or false: If subjects chose among the 56 moves at random, the seven most popular would still account for about two-thirds of mentions.
questions.explain: That concentration is the finding: it reflects agreement among subjects, not chance.

questions.q: How did the moves mentioned most often compare across subjects of different playing strength?
options: The same moves were mentioned most often at every level, from grandmasters to club players
Grandmasters and club players favored completely different moves from one another throughout
Only the grandmasters agreed with one another
Club players agreed with one another but not with masters
optionExplain: Right: the popular moves were the same across levels.
The popular moves overlapped across levels.
Both groups showed agreement.
Both groups agreed, and agreed with each other.
questions.explain: The most popular moves were shared by players of every strength.
questions.rule: Popular moves were shared across levels.
questions.teaches: In almost all cases the moves mentioned most often were the same for subjects of all levels of playing strength, from grandmasters to club players.

questions.q: Weaker players are compared with masters on position A. Which statement fits the data about the seven most popular moves?
options: Masters mentioned all seven and weaker players mentioned none
Weaker players mentioned all seven and masters mentioned only two
Six of the seven drew at least a third of each group
Masters and weaker players had no popular moves in common
optionExplain: Weaker players did mention most of them.
Masters mentioned most of them.
Right: both groups paid attention to six of the same seven.
The overlap is large.
questions.explain: Six of the seven popular moves drew at least a third of each group.
questions.rule: Both groups favored the same six.
questions.teaches: Six of the seven most popular moves were mentioned by at least one-third of the masters and grandmasters, and six of the seven by at least one-third of the other players.

questions.q: Why might a weaker player dismiss, without analysis, a move that gives up a Bishop for a Knight?
options: The rules of chess forbid such an exchange
Such an exchange always loses material at once
A Bishop is worth less than a Knight in every kind of position
A general rule says Bishops are stronger than Knights
optionExplain: Nothing in the rules forbids it.
The move in question was objectively the strongest.
The reverse of the lore is the usual belief.
Right: the general rule can lead to dismissing the exchange.
questions.explain: A rule of thumb can lead to dismissal. The card next shows how the authors treat this.
questions.rule: A rule of thumb can hide a good move.

questions.q: All five grandmasters mentioned 1. BxN'/5, and ____ of them chose it.
questions.explain: Four of the five grandmasters chose it.

questions.q: A club rule says that Bishops beat Knights, so a student refuses every Bishop-for-Knight trade. What do the authors add?
options: The Bishop's edge is mainly in the endgame, so a decision sought earlier may justify a trade
The rule is false, so Knights are always stronger
The rule is right, so trades should always be refused
The rule matters only for beginners
optionExplain: Right: the qualifying phrase is that Bishops are stronger primarily in the endgame.
The authors do not call Knights stronger.
The rule is not to be applied blindly.
The authors do not say the rule matters only for beginners.
questions.explain: The general heuristic has a qualifier that sophisticated players understand.
questions.rule: Bishops: stronger mainly in the endgame.

questions.q: True or false: The authors present their account of why weaker players dismissed 1. BxN'/5 as proved by the protocols.
questions.explain: They say they may speculate; the protocols do not state the reason.

questions.q: How did the move P-KR4 differ from 1. BxN'/5 in who mentioned it?
options: It was mentioned by all five grandmasters and chosen by four of them, as with the other move
It was mentioned by nobody except S2
It was mentioned by two masters but by four weaker players, one of whom chose it
It was chosen by most masters and by no weaker player
optionExplain: That describes 1. BxN'/5.
S2 is not described as the only one.
Right: this move drew more mentions from weaker players.
No such pattern is reported.
questions.explain: P-KR4 was the opposite case, mentioned more by the weaker players.
questions.teaches: The move P-KR4 was mentioned by two masters but by four weaker players, and was chosen by one of the latter.

questions.q: A card player says: the endgame favors my opponent, so I must press the attack now. Which grandmasters' remarks about position A does this echo?
options: Euwe's, that the position was a quiet draw
Flohr's and Fine's, that White must attack since Black's chances are in the endgame
Alekhine's, that White should trade queens
Keres's, that White should avoid the attack and aim for a long and slow endgame win
optionExplain: The text does not give such a remark for Euwe.
Right: Flohr and Fine opened by saying White's chances are in the attack.
The text does not give such a remark for Alekhine.
The text does not give such a remark for Keres.
questions.explain: Two grandmasters commented near the start that White's chances lie in the attack and Black's in the endgame, and that White must play for the attack.
questions.teaches: Flohr commented near the start of his protocol that White's chances are in the attack and Black's in the endgame, and Fine that White has to play for the attack or else has nothing.

questions.q: Nine strong players each analyze the same first move. How alike are the replies they look at likely to be?
options: Largely the same few replies, including the correct one
Completely different replies for each player
Only the first reply that comes to mind, never the others
Every legal reply, in the same order
optionExplain: Right: the consensus continues past the first move.
The data show strong overlap.
Players looked at several replies.
Players did not look at every legal reply.
questions.explain: Agreement extends beyond first moves. The card next gives the numbers.

questions.q: For 1. BxN'/5, ____ replies by Black were mentioned explicitly in the search trees.
questions.explain: Three replies by Black were mentioned explicitly.

questions.q: Nine hiking guides plan one climb: eight discuss the same key fork, and seven the same next step. What does this parallel?
options: A lone expert whose view is copied by the rest of the group of guides
A disagreement about which fork matters
Agreement that continues past the first choice down the tree
A search that has been cut short
optionExplain: Nothing suggests copying a single expert.
The guides agree, not disagree.
Right: eight of nine on the reply and seven on the next move echoes the data.
Nothing suggests the search was cut short.
questions.explain: In the data, eight players explored the same reply and seven the same next move.

questions.q: True or false: Although S2 was far from master strength, the branches the masters explored most account for a large share of his exploration.
questions.explain: They account for a large proportion of S2's exploratory activity.

questions.q: What does the authors' claim say about S2's production system for move generation and the strong players' graphs?
options: It would fit only the graphs of S2 himself
It would fit the graphs of these strong players reasonably well
It would fit none of the strong players' graphs
It would fit only the graphs of the five grandmasters and of nobody else at all
optionExplain: The authors claim a wider fit.
Right: the production system outlined for S2 fits reasonably well.
The authors claim a fit, not a failure.
The text speaks of the strong players as a group.
questions.explain: The production system outlined for S2 would fit the PBGs of these strong players reasonably well.
questions.rule: S2's rules fit the strong players.
questions.teaches: The production system outlined for S2's move generation would fit reasonably well the problem behavior graphs of the strong players.

questions.q: In a poll of nine analysts, eight examine the same reply and most examine one follow-up. Which pattern matches the position A data for follow-ups?
options: Every follow-up examined by exactly the same players
No follow-up examined by more than one player
One follow-up examined by only one player
One follow-up examined by most of the players, and two others by a few
optionExplain: The data show a main follow-up and lesser ones.
The data show shared follow-ups.
The favored move drew seven players.
Right: seven players examined one move and three players each examined two others.
questions.explain: White's next moves drew seven players for one move and three players each for two others.
questions.rule: A main line, two lesser ones.
questions.teaches: After the correct reply, one White move was examined by seven players and two others by three players each.

questions.q: Many players analyzing the same position look at the same moves. What best explains it?
options: A private signal passed between the players
A shared body of beliefs learned from play and books
Each player's independent invention of the very same method of analysis
Nothing but that one move is the best in a vast space
optionExplain: Nothing suggests a signal.
Right: a common culture shapes what players consider.
Independent invention would be unlikely to match so well.
No move is obviously best in a vast search space.
questions.explain: Learning from a shared culture would produce shared choices. The card next gives the authors' account.

questions.q: The sociological account points to a common chess ____ passed on in play, talk and books.
questions.explain: All players belong to a common chess culture.

questions.q: Pastry chefs from different countries all check the oven temperature before baking. Which explanation parallels the authors' first account?
options: A rule of nature that no chef can avoid, whatever country the chef works in
A different private trick found by each chef
A fault in the ovens they use
A trade culture of shared lore taught in kitchens and books
optionExplain: The habit is passed on, not fixed by nature.
Independent invention would not produce the same habit.
A fault in ovens is irrelevant here.
Right: a shared trade culture passes on the habit.
questions.explain: A shared culture transmitted through practice and writing accounts for common behavior.

questions.q: True or false: A reader says the consensus on position A shows culture plays no part, since the position alone fixes the best moves.
questions.explain: The authors say the consensus can be viewed either as culture or as a response to the situation's requirements, and that the requirements are themselves sociologically defined.
questions.rule: Culture and task cannot be cleanly separated.

questions.q: Which fact do the authors cite about the grandmasters in the sample to show how chess knowledge is passed on?
options: Three of them wrote widely read chess books, and a fourth was noted for analyses
All five of them taught in the same school
Each of them had played all the others
Two of them had written the rules of the game
optionExplain: Right: Euwe, Fine and Keres wrote books, and Alekhine was noted for his analyses.
No school is mentioned.
No such claim is made.
The rules are not attributed to them.
questions.explain: The grandmasters are themselves part of the written culture they transmit.
questions.teaches: Three of the grandmasters in the sample (Euwe, Fine and Keres) are authors of widely read books on chess, and a fourth (Alekhine) was noted for his analyses as well as his play.

questions.q: Why did subjects in the cryptarithmetic and logic studies share approaches, compared with the chess players?
options: They had all learned the puzzles from the same books and then taught them to each other in turn
They had played the puzzles together as a group
Their approach came from the tasks' own structure, since they lacked experience with the puzzles
They were all experts in the puzzles themselves
optionExplain: The subjects were not experienced in the puzzles.
No such shared practice is described.
Right: those subjects were not experienced in the puzzles, and their common elements arose mostly from the tasks.
They were naive about the specific puzzles.
questions.explain: In those tasks the common elements came largely from task structure, with only elementary arithmetic or algebra as common culture.
questions.rule: Naive subjects share what the task imposes.
questions.teaches: In cryptarithmetic and logic there was also some common culture, such as elementary arithmetic or algebra, but the subjects were not experienced in the puzzles, so their common elements stemmed largely from the structure and requirements of the tasks.

questions.q: In chess, how should the result of an exchange of pieces be judged?
options: By adding up the piece values at the start of the whole exchange sequence
By choosing the exchange that looks best at first sight
By comparing the colors of the pieces involved
By playing out the exchange step by step to a settled position
optionExplain: A static count at the start would miss what happens in the sequence.
First sight is not an analysis.
Color is irrelevant.
Right: dynamic analysis is needed to evaluate an exchange.
questions.explain: Exchanges need to be played out. The card next shows how the grandmasters did it.

questions.q: After 1. BxN'/5, Black's reply B'xB would lose a ____.
questions.explain: That reply loses a piece.

questions.q: A player considers a Rook trade, an undefended capture of a pawn, and a quiet defensive move. Which are examined dynamically?
options: The Rook trade and the undefended capture, with the quiet move judged statically
Only the quiet defensive move
All three, since every move is examined dynamically
None of them, since all are judged statically
optionExplain: Right: exchanges and undefended captures are examined dynamically.
Quiet moves are generally evaluated statically.
Quiet moves are the ones judged statically.
Exchanges are examined dynamically.
questions.explain: Exchanges and undefended captures call for dynamic analysis; quiet moves are evaluated statically.

questions.q: Order Black's three replies to 1. BxN'/5 from worst to best for Black, as the card describes them.
items: B'xB, losing a piece
N'xB, losing the exchange
P'xB, losing no material
questions.explain: Losing a piece is worse than losing the exchange, and P'xB is the only reply that loses no material.

questions.q: How do the authors read grandmasters who dismissed two of Black's replies without mentioning continuations?
options: They had not analyzed the replies at all
They had analyzed the replies and then hidden the work from the listener
The protocols make it clear that they saw the consequences
They were relying on a rule for dismissing every capture
optionExplain: The authors do not say they skipped the analysis.
Nothing suggests concealment.
Right: the consequences were seen though not stated.
No such rule is described.
questions.explain: Silence in a protocol does not show absence of analysis.
questions.teaches: Three of the five grandmasters dismissed the first two replies without mentioning their continuations, though the protocols make it clear that they saw the consequences.

questions.q: A cook considers only a few small tweaks to a dish, all about its main problem. Which regularity from position A does this resemble?
options: Quiet moves were drawn at random from all legal moves
The few quiet moves considered all bore directly on central features of the position
Quiet moves were preferred whenever pieces were attacked on either side of the board
Quiet moves were never considered by strong players
optionExplain: They were not random.
Right: the quiet moves bore on the pinned Knight, the open King's file and Black's weakened King position.
The analysis did not tie quiet moves to attacks in that way.
Quiet moves were considered, only few.
questions.explain: The small set of quiet moves all related to central features of the position.
questions.teaches: The small set of quiet moves considered, whether initially or after exchanges, all relate directly to central features of the position: the pinned Knight, the potentially open King's file and Black's weakened King's position.

questions.q: Why might a person who cannot write anything down keep going back to the start of a line of thought?
options: Holding branches in mind is costly, so returning to a base is easier
Writing is forbidden in every kind of problem solving
Going back always saves time over going on
The person has forgotten what the problem was
optionExplain: Right: memory limits push toward returning to a base.
Many problem solvers do use written displays.
Returning is not always faster.
The problem is remembered; its branches are what strain memory.
questions.explain: Limits on holding branches in mind favor returning to a base. The card next sets this out.

questions.q: The authors attribute progressive deepening to the burden exploration places on ____ memory.
questions.explain: The burden falls on short-term memory.

questions.q: Two solvers do the same sum: one in the head, one with a notepad. Whose work should show more return to the start?
options: The one with the notepad
Neither, since memory plays no part in sums
The one working in the head, since nothing records steps
Both equally, since the sum is the same
optionExplain: A written record reduces the need to return.
The authors tie organization to memory demands.
Right: without a record, more returning is expected.
The display changes the memory demands.
questions.explain: A written display reduces memory demands; chess gives none.

questions.q: True or false: If players could write tentative moves on a pad, the authors' account predicts less need to return to the base position.
questions.explain: The account ties the returns to short-term memory load, which a written record would reduce.
questions.rule: Reduce the memory load, reduce the returns.

questions.q: What do S2 and Euwe do late in their protocols, after repeating a sequence several times?
options: They begin to branch in many directions at once from the base position
They do not always restart from the very first move of it
They stop analyzing the position altogether
They restart from an entirely new base-move every time
optionExplain: The text does not describe a sudden spread of branching.
Right: once the sequence is fixed in memory they stop restarting from the beginning.
They continue analyzing.
They do not abandon the sequence.
questions.explain: When a sequence has been repeated enough to be fixed in memory, the restart can be shortened.
questions.teaches: After repeating sequences several times, S2 and Euwe do not always restart from the very first move, having had adequate opportunity to fixate them in memory.

questions.q: A hiker tries side trails one at a time, returning to the trailhead after each. What must she still remember, by the card's account?
options: Every fork on every trail she has walked
Nothing, since the trailhead holds the record
Only the trail she is on, forgetting the earlier ones
The main route and result of each trail, so she does not repeat it
optionExplain: Branchings need not be held in mind during a sequence.
Without any record she would repeat trails.
She would repeat earlier trails.
Right: the main sequence and outcome of each episode must be remembered.
questions.explain: Even with progressive deepening, the main sequence and outcome of each episode must be remembered so as not to be repeated.
questions.teaches: Even with progressive deepening, the main sequence and outcome of each episode must be remembered so it is not repeated, but the branchings need not be held in memory while the sequence is followed to its end.

questions.q: A rule built on one subject is tried on five others. What outcome would show the rule is general?
options: The rule holds in none of the five, though it fitted the original subject well
The rule holds in most of the five, with failures that can be explained
The rule holds only for the original subject
The rule is never tested, so cannot fail
optionExplain: Failure in all five would count against it.
Right: broad fit with explainable exceptions supports generality.
Fitting only the original is no generality.
An untestable rule is not supported.
questions.explain: A general rule should fit others, with explainable exceptions. The card next shows the results.

questions.q: Rule R3 says: stay with a good base-move and switch from a ____.
questions.explain: R3 says to stay with a good base-move and switch from a loser.
questions.rule: Stay with a good one, leave a loser.

questions.q: A job-hunter follows leads that go well and drops those that fail. Which rule does this resemble?
options: R1: analyze each base-move independently of the others
R5: predict interruption by a newly discovered move
R6: check alternatives before the final choice
R3: stay with a good base-move, switch from a loser
optionExplain: R1 concerns independence between options, not staying or switching.
R5 concerns interruption by a discovery.
R6 concerns a last check before choosing.
Right: this is staying with good options and leaving losers.
questions.explain: Staying with what works and leaving what fails is R3.

questions.q: Match each rule to what it asserts.
pairs: Stay with a good base-move, switch from a loser
Analysis is interrupted to pursue moves discovered during an episode
Alternative moves are checked before the final choice
questions.explain: R1 independence, R3 stay or switch, R5 interruption, R6 final check.

questions.q: Why does Euwe's protocol fail rule R3?
options: He proceeds more systematically, examining many variations regardless of outcomes
He stays with the first move he examines until the end, whatever its outcome shows
He stops analysis as soon as a move looks bad
He follows the moves he likes best and avoids all others
optionExplain: Right: his order does not depend on how each line turns out.
That would satisfy staying with a good move rather than violate it.
Stopping at a bad move is switching from a loser, which R3 requires.
Favoring good moves is what R3 says.
questions.explain: Euwe works through many variations in a sequence set apart from immediate outcomes, giving about six violations.
questions.teaches: Euwe proceeds in a more systematic manner than the other grandmasters, examining a substantial number of variations in a sequence that seems independent of immediate outcomes, giving some six violations of R3.

questions.q: A guide who has walked a route many times rarely follows an unexpected lead. Which rule's lack of support in the protocols does this parallel?
options: R1, because the guide's choices are independent of each other along the route
R4, because the guide never considers a poor move for opponents
R5, probably because the grandmasters met no surprises
R6, because the guide checks every alternative at the end
optionExplain: R1 was satisfied by all the graphs.
R4 appeared in each grandmaster protocol.
Right: R5 got no support, probably for lack of surprises.
R6 got support only from Alekhine.
questions.explain: R5 needs a surprise to interrupt the analysis, and the grandmasters had none.
questions.teaches: R5 is not supported by any grandmaster protocol, probably because the grandmasters encountered no surprises in their analyses.

questions.q: A player lists the consequences of each candidate move from the board as it stands. Which strategy is this?
options: Means-ends analysis from a stated goal
Redefinition of the problem
Verification of a favorite move
Forward search from the current position
optionExplain: Means-ends analysis starts from a goal and the gap to it.
No restatement of the problem is involved.
No favorite is being tested.
Right: working forward from the position and judging the results.
questions.explain: Working forward from where you stand is forward search. The card next shows how often it appears in position A.

questions.q: In position A the players, strong as well as weak, tended to work ____ from the current position.
questions.explain: They worked forward, evaluating the consequences of moves.

questions.q: A traveler asks what step would bring her closer to the station she must reach. Which strategy is this, in the card's terms?
options: Means-ends analysis, since she picks a step by its fit to a goal
Forward search, since she looks at where she is now and what follows
Static evaluation, since she scores the end of a line
Redefinition, since she restates the whole problem
optionExplain: Right: choosing actions by the gap to a goal.
Forward search weighs consequences of moves from the present.
No end position is being scored.
The problem stays as it was.
questions.explain: Means-ends analysis is driven by the goal and what stands between it and the present.

questions.q: True or false: The two explicit means-ends cases in position A were general goals, such as seeking attack because the endgame favors Black.
questions.explain: These are the two exceptions the authors list.

questions.q: How do the authors account for the working-forward style in position A?
options: Entirely by the weakness of the players
By the absence of any goals in the position
In part by its tactical character, since strategic positions show more of it
By the rule that goals may never be spoken aloud
optionExplain: Strong players worked forward too.
The authors say specific goals could be identified.
Right: de Groot cites many means-ends examples from more strategic positions.
No such rule is mentioned.
questions.explain: De Groot remarks that position A is tactical, which partly explains the analysis, and he cites many means-ends examples in strategic positions.
questions.teaches: De Groot remarks on the tactical character of position A as a partial explanation for the analysis and cites numerous examples of means-ends analysis in protocols from more strategic positions.

questions.q: A checkers player sees a pinned piece and at once thinks of attacking it. By the card, what kind of process is this?
options: A means-ends analysis built on a spoken goal
A feature of the position directly suggesting a response, as in S2's productions
A redefinition drawn from a summary
A terminal evaluation of a finished line
optionExplain: No goal is stated.
Right: a feature suggests a response directly.
No summary is drawn.
The line has not been finished.
questions.explain: In position A certain features suggest directly the kinds of responses to be explored, like S2's productions.
questions.teaches: In the protocols, certain features of the position suggest directly certain kinds of responses that need exploration, as in the productions for S2's move generation.

questions.q: A trained driver corrects a skid without any deliberate thought. What does this suggest about expert responses?
options: A feature of the situation can evoke the response directly
Experts always reason aloud before acting, whatever the situation
Experts have no responses to features
Experts respond only after trying every alternative
optionExplain: Right: overlearned responses fire on recognized features.
Spoken reasoning is not needed for skilled responses.
Experts have learned responses.
Experts do not try everything first.
questions.explain: Learned responses can be evoked directly. The card next shows de Groot's evidence for chess.

questions.q: De Groot says features suggest moves in a highly automatic, ____ way, without verbalized problem solving.
questions.explain: He calls the way highly automatic, overlearned.

questions.q: A nurse sees a pattern on a chart and orders a test at once, without stating a goal. Which idea from the card is this?
options: A redefinition of the problem by a summary drawn from earlier analysis
A polynomial evaluation of a final position
A board feature suggesting a move without verbalized problem solving
A rough cut followed by a fine cut
optionExplain: No summary is formed.
No weighed score is built.
Right: the pattern evokes the action directly.
No reworking passes occur.
questions.explain: Overlearned responses to patterns need no stated goals.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say the forward-working style in position A was forced entirely by the nature of the position.
questions.explain: They say it is not entirely inherent in the position, since specific targets existed.
questions.rule: Targets existed but were not the motive.

questions.q: Which statically identifiable targets did position A offer for means-ends analysis?
options: A Rook on an open file and a fianchettoed King's Bishop on the long diagonal
A hanging Black Bishop and a fork square for Queen and Rook
A checkmate threat and a stalemate trap
A passed pawn and a locked center
optionExplain: These are not the targets the authors name.
Right: these two features figure in the analysis of 1. BxN'/5 and 1. NxN'.
No mate or stalemate is named.
These features are not named.
questions.explain: The Bishop at K7 and the fork square at Q7 could have been targets, but players found them during the dynamic analysis.
questions.teaches: Position A has a hanging Black Bishop at K7, guarded only by the Knight at Q5, and a potential square for forking Queen and Rook at Q7.

questions.q: A nurse's rule fires on low pressure with a fast pulse, without deliberate reasoning. What did de Groot present that resembles such a rule?
options: A table ranking each piece by value
A list of mating patterns in order of beauty
A rule that players must state their goals
A productionlike schema in which features evoke moves
optionExplain: No such table is described.
No such list is described.
The point is that goals need not be stated.
Right: he gave a productionlike schema in a footnote.
questions.explain: De Groot presented a productionlike schema in which features automatically bring up moves.
questions.teaches: De Groot presents a productionlike schema, in a footnote, for how particular board features suggest specific move possibilities.

questions.q: Where would players rethink what they are trying to do more often: a tactical sprint or a long strategic game?
options: In the sprint, which allows no pause
In the long strategic game, which allows more rethinking of aims
Equally in both, since aims never change
In neither, since the aims in a game are fixed by rules and cannot change
optionExplain: A sprint gives less room for rethinking.
Right: strategic situations invite changes of aim.
Aims can change with the situation.
Rules fix the game, not the plan.
questions.explain: Open-ended situations invite redefinition. The card next gives the authors' view.

questions.q: The authors surmise that redefinition was rare in position A because of its ____ character.
questions.explain: Position A is a tactical position.

questions.q: The authors found redefinition rare in the tactical position A and expect it to be more common in strategic positions. A rally driver in a short sprint seldom revises his plan; a sailor on a long crossing often does. Which pairing follows?
options: The sprint is like strategic positions, the crossing like position A
Both are like position A
Neither is like any chess position
The sprint is like position A, the crossing like strategic positions
optionExplain: This reverses the pairing.
Both do not share the character.
Their characters map onto the two kinds.
Right: tactical positions show less redefinition, strategic ones more.
questions.explain: Tactical tasks show fewer redefinitions than strategic ones.

questions.q: True or false: In more strategic positions, the authors would expect redefinition to be more common than in position A.
questions.explain: De Groot shows redefinitions often occur elsewhere in chess, so position A is the quiet case.
questions.rule: Redefinition is common outside tactical cases.

questions.q: Why do the authors leave out the initial orientation phase when they look at redefinitions?
options: Its first act of definition differs substantially from the later ones
It contains no definition at all of the situation, being only an opening look
It is always followed by a redefinition
It is missing from de Groot's protocols
optionExplain: Right: the first definition is a different kind of act.
It is a definition, but a different kind.
No such pattern is claimed.
Orientation is found in the protocols.
questions.explain: The opening orientation is the first act of definition and differs from later redefinitions.
questions.teaches: The initial orientation phase is left out because its first act of definition differs substantially from all the others.

questions.q: A researcher has studied only lookahead in games and turns to how players interpret the board. How does the new topic relate to the old?
options: It is the same process under another name
It is a special case of search through the tree
It is a different kind of processing, in sharp contrast with search
It is a way of counting the positions searched
optionExplain: The authors treat it as distinct from search.
They contrast it with search, not subsume it.
Right: defining the situation contrasts sharply with search.
It does not count anything.
questions.explain: Defining the situation is a different process from searching and had been left aside so far.
questions.teaches: Defining the situation contrasts sharply with search activity, which so far has been the mainstay of the cognitive activity in analyzing a chess position.

questions.q: A builder discovers a hidden pipe halfway through a job and changes the plan. What prompted the change?
options: A wish to make the work longer
A rule that plans must change at the halfway point of any job
A count of the tools used so far
Noticing a feature that had been overlooked
optionExplain: Nothing suggests a wish for length.
No such rule exists.
Tools have nothing to do with it.
Right: the new fact forced a new plan.
questions.explain: Noticing something missed can force a rethink. The card next shows this in chess.
questions.rule: A missed feature forces a rethink.

questions.q: Redefinition may come about because a feature of the situation that was ____ earlier is noticed.
questions.explain: In the first example the subject overlooked a key piece.

questions.q: A shopper hopes a coat will suit her, finds it does not, and settles on a plain one reluctantly. Which cause fits?
options: Initial expectations about the option's value were disappointed
A feature of the situation was noticed that had been overlooked
The option was linked to different outcomes and goals
The shopper made no change of aim at all
optionExplain: Right: her hopes were not borne out.
No new feature appears.
Her aim does not change in that way.
She did change her choice.
questions.explain: Disappointed expectations are the second cause in the card.

questions.q: Match each protocol example to the cause it illustrates.
pairs: A key piece overlooked until line 57
A feature is noticed that was overlooked
A calm move chosen reluctantly at the very last
Expectations about a move are disappointed
The same move played within a different plan
Exploring a move relates it to other goals
questions.explain: Each example shows one of the three causes the authors list.

questions.q: What do the redefinition examples suggest about the dynamic analysis of moves?
options: It is a pure forward search through a branching space
It is a count of the positions that have been searched
It looks more like gathering information than a simple forward search
It is a way of delaying the final choice for as long as the player can
optionExplain: The authors say it is more than that.
It does not count positions.
Right: moves are explored to learn about the situation.
Nothing suggests delay.
questions.explain: Because analysis turns up features and goals that change the definition of the situation, it gathers information.
questions.teaches: In cases of redefinition the dynamic analysis of moves appears more as an information-gathering process than simply a forward search through a branching space.

questions.q: A traveler finds that a route fits two plans and takes it without choosing between them yet. Which chess case does this match?
options: M4 overlooking a key piece until line 57
G5 playing the same move because both plans allow it
M5 choosing a calm move reluctantly, once his hopes had been dashed
S2 returning to B x N'/5 as his favorite
optionExplain: That example is about overlooking a piece.
Right: the move did not change, and a way out of the dilemma was found.
That example is about excessive hopes.
S2 is not in the redefinition examples.
questions.explain: In the third case the subject did not have to choose a plan, because the move was playable in both and spoiled nothing.
questions.rule: A move can serve two plans.
questions.teaches: In the third example the subject finds himself in the happy circumstance of not yet having to choose a plan, because the intended move is playable in both plans and does not spoil anything.

questions.q: Chess players tell novices to check whenever possible, since it may be mate. Why is the advice ironic?
options: Most checking moves are easily refuted and lose time
Checks are forbidden in most positions where the King can still move
Checks always lead to mate
Novices cannot see checks
optionExplain: Right: the advice rarely pays off.
Checks are legal moves.
Checks do not always mate.
Novices can see checks.
questions.explain: The advice is ironic because checks seldom work. The card next says why the topic matters.

questions.q: A mating combination eight moves deep is ____ plies deep.
questions.explain: Each move has two plies, one by each side.

questions.q: A beginner plays a check on every turn and keeps losing time. According to the card, why does this happen?
options: Checks are illegal when the King can move
Checks always lose a piece
Most checking moves are easily refuted
Checks work only for grandmasters
optionExplain: Checks are legal.
Checks do not always lose pieces.
Right: refutation costs the attacker time.
Checks are open to anyone.
questions.explain: Most checks are easily refuted, so the attacker only loses time.

questions.q: True or false: Mating combinations seem to need more search than a human can carry out, which is why they test the limits of search.
questions.explain: That is the authors' reason for interest in them.

questions.q: What do very deep recorded mating combinations feed, according to the authors?
options: The belief that checks always win
Much of the mythology about grandmasters' memory and visualizing powers
The belief that novices cannot learn chess
The belief that programs cannot check
optionExplain: The advice to check is called ironic.
Right: eight-move combinations give rise to such stories.
No such belief is mentioned.
No such belief is mentioned.
questions.explain: Combinations as deep as sixteen plies give rise to the mythology about grandmasters' memory and visualization.
questions.teaches: Some recorded mating combinations are eight or more moves deep, sixteen plies, and give rise to much of the mythology about the mnemonic and visualizing powers of grandmasters.

questions.q: A commentator praises a last-minute goal that ends a patient build-up. Which comparison do the authors use for brilliant mating combinations?
options: A sprint at the start of a race
A slow siege of a walled town that lasts for a whole campaign season
A chess clock running down
The final smashing cavalry charge of an eighteenth-century army
optionExplain: A sprint at the start does not fit.
A siege is not the image they use.
The clock is not the image they use.
Right: the combination is the dramatic finish after the pieces are placed.
questions.explain: The authors liken the brilliancies to the final cavalry charge after the army has moved into position.
questions.teaches: The authors compare mating combinations to the final smashing cavalry charge of an eighteenth-century army that has first moved into position.

questions.q: A program must find forced mates cheaply. Which narrowing of its search is sensible?
options: Consider every legal move equally to be fair
Consider only checking moves, since they force a reply
Consider only quiet moves, which hide the plan from the opponent for longer
Consider only moves that capture pieces
optionExplain: That is the full tree, too large.
Right: checks leave the opponent few replies.
Quiet moves leave the opponent free.
Captures need not restrict the King.
questions.explain: Forcing moves narrow the opponent's options. The card next gives MATER's rules.

questions.q: MATER rejects a move that permits more than ____ legal replies.
questions.explain: It abandons lines that allow more than four replies.

questions.q: After one check the opponent has 2 legal replies; after another check he has 7. Which does MATER explore next?
options: The check that leaves seven replies
Both at once, since they are checks
Neither, since MATER uses only quiet moves
The check that leaves two replies
optionExplain: Seven is above the cutoff of four.
It picks one at a time by fewest replies.
MATER generates only checks.
Right: it takes the move allowing the fewest replies, and drops one with more than four.
questions.explain: MATER takes the unevaluated move with the fewest replies next, and rejects any with more than four.

questions.q: True or false: If an attacked King's adjacent squares were all blocked or attacked, and no reply removed the attack, the King would be checkmated.
questions.explain: That is the condition for checkmate: the King is attacked and immobile.

questions.q: Which checking moves does MATER consider first, and why?
options: Double checks and discovered checks, since they restrict mobility most
Checks that capture a piece
Checks by the Queen
Checks that leave the opponent most replies
optionExplain: Right: they leave the opponent the least freedom.
Material is not the criterion.
No preference for the Queen is mentioned.
That is the reverse of the criterion.
questions.explain: Among checks, those that restrict the opponent most come first.
questions.teaches: MATER considers first the checking moves that restrict the opponent's mobility most severely, namely double checks and discovered checks.

questions.q: Given MATER's rule of following the check that leaves the fewest replies, which sacrifice might it make?
options: None, since sacrifices are never allowed in a mating search of this kind
Only pawns, since they are worth least
A Queen, if it allows the checks to continue
Only a piece the opponent cannot capture
optionExplain: The program is not barred from sacrifices.
It is not limited to pawns.
Right: MATER finds combinations that sacrifice Queens and other major pieces.
A sacrifice is a piece that can be taken.
questions.explain: Because only checks and mobility count, MATER finds combinations with sacrifices of Queens and other major pieces, using modest exploration.
questions.teaches: MATER is remarkably powerful in finding mating combinations, some involving sacrifices of Queens and other major pieces, with very modest amounts of exploration (Baylor and Simon, 1965).

questions.q: A program only needs to know whether it has found a forced win. What values must it assign to positions?
options: A score for every piece and square
A rating of how safe the King feels
A count of moves left in the game
Only two: mate and no-mate
optionExplain: Piece and square scores are for ongoing play.
A safety score is not needed.
Moves left are not needed.
Right: nothing else matters if the search succeeds.
questions.explain: A forced-win search needs only a yes or no. The card next gives MATER's specification.

questions.q: MATER's only static values are mate and ____.
questions.explain: The static values are mate or no-mate.

questions.q: MATER finds a line in which a Queen must be given up to keep checking. What does it do?
options: It attempts the sacrifice unhesitatingly
It rejects the line
It asks another program to decide
It assigns the line a partial score
optionExplain: Right: piece values have no significance for it.
Piece values are not used.
It halts only if it finds no strategy.
It has no partial scores.
questions.explain: Because the game ends if the search succeeds, piece values do not matter to MATER.

questions.q: Put the defender's moves in the order MATER considers them.
items: Captures
King moves
Interpositions
Others
questions.explain: The defender's moves are ordered captures, King moves, interpositions, then others, so that likely refutations come first.

questions.q: What does MATER do when it cannot find a checkmating strategy?
options: It plays the best move by a polynomial evaluation
It searches deeper without limit until it finds one
It halts, leaving some other program to suggest a move
It resigns the game and reports that the position cannot be won
optionExplain: It has no polynomial evaluation.
It halts rather than searching without end.
Right: responsibility is passed to another, unspecified program.
It does not play a whole game.
questions.explain: MATER is specialized: with no mate found, it stops.
questions.teaches: If MATER does not find a checkmating strategy, it simply halts, presumably shifting responsibility to some other, unspecified program to suggest a move.

questions.q: A negotiator's every offer forces an immediate reply, so she sets no limit on how far ahead she thinks. Which MATER feature parallels this?
options: A static value of mate or no-mate
No width or depth limits, because the attacker's moves are forcing
An ordering of the defender's replies
A cutoff at moves with more than four replies, which limits the width
optionExplain: Mate values are about outcomes, not limits.
Right: forcing moves make separate width and depth limits unnecessary.
Ordering concerns the sequence of replies.
The cutoff does limit width.
questions.explain: The forcing character of the attacker's moves removes the need for depth and width termination.
questions.teaches: With the forcing character of the attacker's moves, MATER needs no separate limitations on the width or depth of search.

questions.q: A program can work on the most promising item in a large pile, wherever it is. What does this freedom cost?
options: Extra work to keep track of and rebuild each item's state
Nothing at all, since any order of working is as cheap as another
A loss of every item not yet chosen
A rule that only the first item may be used
optionExplain: Right: jumping around has a housekeeping price.
Rebuilding state is not free.
Items are not lost.
The point is the freedom to choose any.
questions.explain: Jumping to the best item needs bookkeeping. The card next shows the price for MATER.

questions.q: MATER keeps a subproblem list ordered by the number of ____.
questions.explain: The list orders all moves on the tree by number of replies.

questions.q: An emergency nurse picks the most urgent patient from the whole ward each time, though walking there costs time. Which MATER feature?
options: Searching depth-first along one line to its end
Assigning only mate or no-mate
Taking next the move with fewest replies from anywhere on the tree
Rejecting moves with more than four replies
optionExplain: That is the other organization.
That concerns values.
Right: the best node is chosen globally, with a price.
That concerns width.
questions.explain: The subproblem list lets MATER pick the best node wherever it lies.

questions.q: True or false: A depth-first version generating the same moves as MATER would propose exactly the same mating sequence.
questions.explain: Alpha-beta cutoffs might differ, so the final trees might be very different and different, equivalent mates could be proposed.

questions.q: How might the depth-first version end up with a different tree from MATER?
options: The depth-first version uses different checking moves from those of MATER
MATER might establish good cutoffs earlier, so cutoffs differ
The depth-first version ignores all replies
MATER never uses cutoffs of any kind
optionExplain: It generates the same moves in a different order.
Right: order changes which cutoffs arise.
It considers replies.
The difference is about cutoffs, not their absence.
questions.explain: The same moves in a different order can give different cutoffs and so different trees.
questions.teaches: The program of Figure 13.3 is basically depth-first and generates the same moves as MATER in a different order, so owing to alpha-beta cutoffs the final trees might be very different, and alternative mating sequences could be proposed.

questions.q: A person with only a small notepad wants the freedom to return to promising branches. Which strategy do the authors say humans use?
options: A subproblem list over the whole tree
A strict depth-first search that follows one line to its end before any other
A search of every legal move
Progressive deepening, returning to old positions by rebuilding from the base
optionExplain: Humans are said not to use it.
Humans are not depth-first either.
Humans do not search everything.
Right: this approaches the freedom of the list within human limits.
questions.explain: Humans use neither the subproblem list nor depth-first search.
questions.teaches: Humans do not employ MATER's subproblem-list organization, for its processing and memory requirements are too severe, and they do not adopt a depth-first organization either.

questions.q: A coach looks for signs that a mating attack is worth trying. Which signs are most useful?
options: The opponent has more pieces on the board than one has oneself in play
The opponent's King is exposed and one's own pieces are more mobile
The game is in its first five moves
The opponent's clock is running low
optionExplain: More pieces for the opponent is no signal.
Right: exposed King plus superior mobility signals a combination.
Move number alone is not a cue.
The clock is not a cue.
questions.explain: Cues exist in the position. The card next gives the authors' count.

questions.q: Of the 129 positions, checkmate could be forced by checks alone in ____.
questions.explain: Fifty-one positions allowed a forced mate by checks.

questions.q: In a game, your opponent's King is exposed and your pieces are mobile while his are cramped. What should you do?
options: Trade down to an endgame at once
Avoid all checks, which are always refuted by the opponent's best replies
Wait for the opponent to attack first
Look for a checkmating combination, since the cues point to one
optionExplain: Nothing in the cues suggests trading down.
Checks may work when the cues are present.
The cues favor attack.
Right: these are the signals the authors name.
questions.explain: An exposed King and superior mobility signal that a combination may exist.
questions.rule: Exposure plus mobility: look for mate.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, forced mates by checks arise only in composed puzzles and not in tournament games.
questions.explain: They arise quite frequently in tournament games, though relatively rarely between evenly matched grandmasters.

questions.q: Where are forced mates by checks relatively rare nowadays?
options: In games between grandmasters of about equal strength
In games between beginners
In games lasting more than fifty moves
In games played without a clock
optionExplain: Right: strong equal players seldom allow them.
Beginners allow them more often.
Length is not mentioned.
Clocks are not mentioned.
questions.explain: Even players of high and equal strength rarely let the situation arise.
questions.teaches: Positions where checks force mate arise quite frequently in tournament games, although relatively rarely nowadays in games between grandmasters of approximately equal strength.

questions.q: In a heist plan, a guard must be distracted first, and only then does a forced sequence begin. Which of Fine's positions parallel this?
options: The 51 where checks alone force mate
The 73 where the defender can sacrifice material to escape the mate entirely
The five where checks must be preceded by a one-move mating threat
All 129, since each begins with a threat
optionExplain: Those need no preparation.
Those are positions where mate fails or is not forced.
Right: these need a preparatory threat before the checks.
Only five need the preparation.
questions.explain: Five positions require a one-move mating threat before the checking moves begin.
questions.teaches: In five of Fine's positions the checking moves must be preceded by a move of a class known as one-move mating threats.

questions.q: To prove a mating combination, which moves must be shown?
options: Only the attacker's moves
Only the moves the defender is most likely to play in reply to each check
Every legal move for both sides
The attacker's best move at each point and every defender reply
optionExplain: Defender replies must be covered.
Unlikely replies still count.
The attacker needs only his best move.
Right: all replies of the defender must be answered.
questions.explain: A proof must cover all the defender's choices. The card next names this the verification tree.

questions.q: In Figure 13.4 the discovery tree has 14 checks and ____ replies.
questions.explain: That makes the 36 moves of the discovery tree.

questions.q: A trainee lists 36 moves seen and 16 positions examined. Which trees are these?
options: The discovery tree and the exploration tree
The verification tree and the discovery tree
The exploration tree and the verification tree
Two verification trees
optionExplain: Right: moves seen make the discovery tree; positions examined make the exploration tree.
The verification tree is only the proof part.
The verification tree is smaller.
There is one verification tree.
questions.explain: Discovery counts moves seen; exploration counts positions examined.

questions.q: Match each tree to what it contains.
pairs: All moves seen, examined or not
Branches needed to prove the combination
questions.explain: Each tree answers a different question about the search.

questions.q: The verification tree is exactly analogous to what in the Logic Theorist, and why is it a tree in chess?
options: To a theorem's statement; it is a tree because the attacker has many moves
To a subgoal list; it is a tree because it has many theorems
To a proof path; it is a tree because all the defender's alternatives must be tested
To a search path; it is a tree because it is deep
optionExplain: The analogy is to the path to a theorem, not its statement.
It is not a subgoal list.
Right: a proof path becomes a tree when the opponent has choices.
Depth is not the reason.
questions.explain: The tree arises from the defender's alternatives.
questions.rule: The opponent's choices make it a tree.
questions.teaches: The verification tree is exactly analogous to the path leading to a theorem (a proof path) in the Logic Theorist, but it is a tree because all alternatives permitted to the defender must be tested.

questions.q: In a card game, a player's plan must say what to do against each possible reply. In game theory terms, what is a verification tree?
options: A payoff
A strategy
A single move
A bluff
optionExplain: A payoff is a result.
Right: a strategy specifies the answer to every reply.
A single move is only part of it.
A bluff is a tactic of play.
questions.explain: The authors say that in game-theory terms the verification tree is a strategy.
questions.rule: A complete plan is a strategy.
questions.teaches: In game-theory terms, the verification tree is a strategy.

questions.q: If a tree doubles at each step, how large is it after fifteen steps?
options: About 32,000
About 30
About 300
optionExplain: Right: two to the fifteenth power is 32,768.
Thirty is about two times fifteen.
Three hundred is too small.
Three million is too large.
questions.explain: Doubling grows fast. The card next compares this with MATER's trees.

questions.q: MATER found solutions to 43 of the ____ mating positions that met its conditions.
questions.explain: Fifty-one qualified, and 43 were solved.

questions.q: A doubling tree to depth fifteen has about 32,000 moves; MATER's tree for a fifteen-ply mate had 108. About how many times smaller?
options: About 30 times smaller
About 3,000 times smaller
About 300 times smaller
About 3 times smaller
optionExplain: That would give about 1,000 moves.
That would give about 11 moves.
Right: 32,000 divided by 108 is about 300.
That would give about 10,000 moves.
questions.explain: 32,000 / 108 is close to 300, a radical pruning.

questions.q: True or false: If the verification tree in mating positions grew exponentially with depth, deep analysis would be as easy as the table shows.
questions.explain: Linear growth is what makes deep analysis possible in mating situations.

questions.q: Why did MATER fail on the eight qualifying positions it did not solve?
options: All eight failed because they had more than four replies
One was a program bug, and on seven it ran out of memory before finding the verification tree
All eight were beyond a depth of five moves and so could not be reached
All eight needed sacrifices that it forbids
optionExplain: The eight met the four-reply condition.
Right: one bug and seven memory exhaustions.
Depth was not the stated cause.
MATER does not forbid sacrifices.
questions.explain: The bug was a failure to move a pawn that gave a discovered check; the others needed too much search.
questions.teaches: MATER missed one combination entirely by failing to move a pawn that gave a discovered check, and ran out of memory space on the other seven, where too much search was needed.

questions.q: A detective follows about five leads for every one that ends up in the case file. Which MATER ratio does this resemble?
options: The verification tree is about five times the size of the discovery tree
Depth is five times the discovery tree
The exploration tree equals the verification tree
The discovery tree stays near five times the verification tree
optionExplain: The ratio runs the other way.
Depth is a separate quantity.
They are different trees.
Right: the D-size to V-size ratio is around five to one.
questions.explain: The discovery tree keeps a nearly constant ratio of about five moves to one with the verification tree.
questions.rule: About five seen per one proved.
questions.teaches: The discovery tree maintains a nearly constant ratio to the verification tree of around five moves to one.

questions.q: A security guard closes exits so a thief has few ways out, and checks the narrowest passage first. What does this achieve?
options: More escapes for the thief but a faster search for the guard
Fewer escapes for the thief and fewer places for the guard to look
Fewer escapes but a larger search
Nothing, since the order of checking never matters
optionExplain: The opponent's options shrink.
Right: both the opponent's options and the search shrink.
The search also shrinks.
In MATER the order mattered a lot.
questions.explain: A narrow choice for the opponent helps in two ways. The card next gives MATER's version.
questions.rule: Narrow for them, narrow for you.

questions.q: Holding the ____ means acting so forcefully that the opponent must devote all his effort to replying.
questions.explain: That is the authors' definition of holding the initiative.

questions.q: A tennis player hits to alternate corners so the opponent can only run and return. Which idea from the card is this?
options: Fewer branches in a tree
A static evaluation, since the point is scored
A redefinition of the problem after a surprise
Holding the initiative, since the opponent can only reply
optionExplain: There is no tree here.
No end position is scored.
No surprise changes the aim.
Right: the forcing play leaves the opponent no free choice.
questions.explain: Forcing play decides where the struggle is waged.

questions.q: True or false: A reader says the heuristic works only by reducing the opponent's escapes, so the size of the search tree is irrelevant.
questions.explain: It works in two ways at once, and in this task environment their contributions cannot be separated.

questions.q: How did variants that gave the fewest-replies heuristic lower priority perform?
options: Much less successfully, particularly depth-first exploration
About as well, since the order of exploration made no difference
Better, since they explored more of the tree
They were not tested
optionExplain: Right: giving up the heuristic hurt.
The authors report a clear loss.
More exploration did not help.
They were tested.
questions.explain: Depth-first variants did much worse at finding mating combinations.
questions.teaches: Variants of MATER that gave lower priority to the fewest-replies heuristic, in particular depth-first exploration, were much less successful in finding mating combinations.

questions.q: A researcher finds a heuristic works and asks which of its two effects does the work. What do the authors conclude for this heuristic?
options: Only the narrowing of the opponent's options matters
Only the shrinking of the tree matters
In this task the two contributions cannot be disentangled
Neither effect matters
optionExplain: The authors do not credit one alone.
The authors do not credit one alone.
Right: they cannot be separated.
The heuristic is credited as important.
questions.explain: Both effects operate together and cannot be separated here.
questions.teaches: It is not possible in this task environment to disentangle the contributions of the two factors, the opponent's few alternatives and the tree's small branchiness, to the power of the heuristic.

questions.q: A program restricted to checks cannot find a quiet move that prepares a mate. How might it be extended?
options: Let it ignore mate and count material
Let it search every legal move without limit until the mate appears
Let it stop whenever a quiet move appears
Let it find quiet moves that threaten mate, then search from them
optionExplain: Mate is the goal.
That would lose the economy of MATER.
Quiet moves are exactly what it must handle.
Right: threatening moves lead into the constrained checking search.
questions.explain: Quiet threats can lead into forced play. The card next shows how MATER II finds them.

questions.q: MATER II found the checkmates in ____ of the five positions that need an initial mating threat.
questions.explain: It found all five.

questions.q: To test whether a candidate move threatens mate in one, what does MATER II do after making the move?
options: Makes a no-move for the opponent and sees if a mating move exists
Plays the opponent's best reply and then counts material on both sides
Searches every legal reply for the opponent
Rejects the move if it is not a check
optionExplain: Right: pretending the opponent passes shows the threat.
That would test a different thing.
The test uses a no-move, not every reply.
The test is for non-checks.
questions.explain: A no-move for the opponent shows whether the move threatens mate.

questions.q: Put the executive's three parts in order.
items: Search with checks to gather information and keep the tree
Scan the tree for candidate mate-in-one threats and test them
Search again with the threats as base-moves
questions.explain: Gather, test candidates, then search from the threats.

questions.q: What is the second scheme the authors mention for obtaining threatening moves?
options: Counting the pieces each side has left
Copying moves from earlier games in a library
Assessing control of the squares around the King for moves that threaten mate
Playing every legal move once and keeping the winners
optionExplain: Material is not the criterion.
A game library is not mentioned.
Right: control of the King's surroundings is the criterion.
That would be an exhaustive trial.
questions.explain: The second scheme is based on control of the squares surrounding the King.
questions.teaches: In the second scheme for obtaining threatening moves, the control of the squares surrounding the King was assessed, and moves were sought that acquired sufficient control of these squares to present a threat of mate.

questions.q: An inspector tries an action by pretending the other party does nothing, and asks if a decisive follow-up exists. Which MATER II step is this?
options: The first information-gathering search, which keeps the tree
The no-move test of a candidate mate-in-one threat
