The final search, which starts from the threats found
The cutoff of lines allowing more than four replies
optionExplain: The first search comes before any test of candidates.
Right: the move is made, the opponent passes, and a mating move is sought.
The final search comes after the tests are done.
The cutoff limits width and is not a test of threats.
questions.explain: The test is a part of the second step. It cost little: in two of Fine's positions MATER II's eight-ply trees held 37 and 38 moves, so they were about as big as MATER I's.
questions.rule: Test the lead with a pass.
questions.teaches: In two of Fine's positions the eight-ply search trees contained 37 and 38 moves, and only four of 54 and three of 37 legal initial moves were considered, so MATER II's trees were of the same general size as MATER I's.

questions.q: A solver uses search to find answers cheaply. What else must she have if search must be very selective?
options: A way to notice features that tell which branches to take
A way to search every branch at once
A rule never to look at features
A bigger memory so that the same branches can all be held at once
optionExplain: Right: selectivity needs cues from the situation.
That would remove selectivity.
Features are the source of selectivity.
More memory would not make search selective.
questions.explain: Selective search needs cues. The card next says how MATER II gets them.

questions.q: Chess players would call the information-gathering searches of MATER II sample ____.
questions.explain: Sample variations gather information about strong moves that are not checks.

questions.q: A planner sketches a hypothetical plan to see what ideas it turns up, some perhaps not possible in reality. What does this resemble?
options: A verification of a favorite move
A static evaluation of a final position reached at the end of a line
A sample variation, whose moves may not be legal at the start
A redefinition after a surprise
optionExplain: No favorite is being tested.
No end position is scored.
Right: the sketch gathers ideas that must be checked for feasibility.
No surprise has occurred.
questions.explain: Moves found by sample variations are tested for legality and for being one-move mating threats before they are used.
questions.rule: Test what a sample turns up.

questions.q: True or false: Moves found by MATER II's information-gathering search must be tested for legality before they are used.
questions.explain: They may or may not be legal in the initial position, so they are tested for legality and for one-move mating threats.

questions.q: What does MATER II add beyond the basic general search heuristics?
options: A rule that all non-checking moves are to be rejected, whatever the position is
Noticing programs that supply extra selectivity beyond the basic heuristics
A larger search that covers all legal moves
A fixed opening book of mating patterns
optionExplain: MATER II accepts some non-checking moves.
Right: noticing programs provide the extra selectivity.
The search stays small.
No such book is described.
questions.explain: Beyond the basic heuristics, MATER II relies on noticing features to stay selective.
questions.teaches: In MATER II, where the program goes beyond the basic general search heuristics by accepting some nonchecking moves, noticing programs provide the extra selectivity needed to make search successful.

questions.q: A cook learns from one failed sauce which spice clashes, then uses that knowledge on a different dish. Which MATER II feature does this resemble?
options: Rejecting moves with more than four replies
Using only mate and no-mate as values
Searching depth-first along one line
Carrying information from one part of the search tree to another
optionExplain: That is a cutoff rule.
That is a value rule.
That is an organization, not information transfer.
Right: MATER II is one of few programs that do this.
questions.explain: MATER II is one of the few chess programs that carry information from one part of the tree to another.
questions.teaches: MATER II is one of the few chess programs that extract information from one part of the search tree and apply it to another.

questions.q: A program that considers only checks faces a position whose winning move is quiet. What happens?
options: It finds it by trying every legal move in the position in turn
It cannot find that move, since it is not a check
It finds it by counting material
It finds it because quiet moves are checks
optionExplain: It does not try every move.
Right: the move is outside what the program generates.
It does not count material.
A quiet move is not a check.
questions.explain: A checks-only program has a blind spot for quiet moves. The card next shows the case.

questions.q: MATER I would not discover N-N5 because it is not a ____ move.
questions.explain: N-N5 does not give check.

questions.q: A player can choose N-N5 without calculating to the end. What makes this safe?
options: The move wins material at once
The move attacks the King directly
The move blocks all of Black's replies, so that Black has no defense left at all
The move prevents the capture of the Queen and adds an attacker for free
optionExplain: It does not win material at once.
It is not a check.
Black still has replies.
Right: it adds an attacker for free.
questions.explain: The move costs nothing and adds force.
questions.rule: Add an attacker at no cost.

questions.q: Put in order the way MATER II reaches N-N5.
items: Explore the checks Q-N7 and QxRP'
Follow the line that leads to K'xQ and N-N5ch
Find that N-N5 has been discovered
Place N-N5 on a special list to be tested
questions.explain: The move turns up in a line of the check search, and is then listed for testing.
questions.rule: Discover in the checks, then test.

questions.q: Neither of MATER II's first two lines ends in mate. What does MATER II then do with N-N5?
options: It tests whether N-N5 threatens mate in one, then analyzes it
It discards N-N5 since neither line mates
It plays N-N5 without any further test
It repeats the same two lines more deeply
optionExplain: Right: N-N5 does threaten mate in one, so it is analyzed.
Discarding would lose the combination.
It is tested before being used.
The lines are not repeated.
questions.explain: The special list holds the move, which is tested and found to threaten mate by QxRP'.
questions.teaches: The discovered move N-N5 is placed on a special list and tested to see whether it threatens mate in one; it does (N-N5, no-move, then QxRP' mate), so it is analyzed and shown to force a checkmate by a series of checking moves.

questions.q: A detective tests a new lead by asking if it would end the case were the suspect idle. Which MATER II step is this?
options: The first information-gathering search
The cutoff at four replies
The no-move test of a candidate threat
The subproblem list
optionExplain: The first search comes before the test.
The cutoff limits width.
Right: the pretend pass shows the threat.
The list is a MATER I feature.
questions.explain: A candidate is made, the opponent passes, and a mate is sought.
questions.rule: Test the lead with a pass.
questions.teaches: In MATER II's test of a candidate move, the move is made, a no-move is made for the opponent, and the program looks for a move that mates.

questions.q: A builder needs a scaffold to reach a high window and builds one. What is the scaffold in means-ends terms?
options: A hypothesis that is to be tested by further experiment
A random discovery
A redefinition of the aim
A means, found because it supports the action
optionExplain: It is not a hypothesis.
It is chosen for a reason.
The aim stays the same.
Right: it is chosen because it serves a goal.
questions.explain: A means supports a goal. The card next shows N-N5 as such a means.

questions.q: MATER II uses a modified depth-first strategy, while the human graph shows progressive ____.
questions.explain: The human graph shows the usual progressive-deepening strategy.

questions.q: The pawn is defended by the King, so the Queen's attack alone is not enough. How did the human experts reason?
options: They sought a move to support the Queen's attack, and found N-N5
They sacrificed the Queen at once to remove the defending King from the pawn
They gave up the attack as hopeless
They waited for Black to weaken the defense
optionExplain: Right: N-N5 provides the needed support.
Nothing in the card describes a sacrifice.
They found the combination.
They found a way to support the attack.
questions.explain: The support of the attack is the means-ends link.

questions.q: True or false: In MATER II, N-N5 was discovered as a preparation to make the Queen's capture feasible.
questions.explain: MATER II discovered it as a move to continue the attack after the capture; the humans saw it as preparation.

questions.q: In Fine's mating position, N-N5 (a Knight move) is a move that supports the Queen's capture QxRP'. What do the human experts and MATER II have in common once N-N5 has been discovered?
options: They treat it as tied to the Queen's capture QxRP' as its predecessor or successor
They drop it from their searches
They explore it in a new context, as a move that might start a mate
They apply it only as a last move
optionExplain: It is no longer tied to it.
It is not dropped.
Right: it is explored afresh, no longer tied to QxRP'.
It is explored as a possible first move.
questions.explain: Once found, the move is freed from its origin and explored on its own.
questions.rule: A discovered move gets its own context.
questions.teaches: Once discovered, N-N5 is explored in a new context, as a move that might initiate a mating combination, no longer monolithically connected as predecessor or successor with QxRP'.

questions.q: A program searches modified depth-first; a person returns to the base repeatedly. Which pair matches MATER II and the human experts?
options: MATER II: progressive deepening; humans: modified depth-first
MATER II: modified depth-first; humans: progressive deepening
Both: depth-first
Both: progressive deepening
optionExplain: This reverses the pair.
Right: this is the characteristic difference between programs and humans.
The graphs differ.
The graphs differ.
questions.explain: The comparison of the two graphs shows the usual difference between programs and humans.
questions.rule: Programs go depth-first, humans deepen progressively.
questions.teaches: Comparison of the PBGs of MATER II and of the human expert shows the characteristic difference in search strategy: MATER II employs a modified depth-first strategy, while the human graph reveals the usual progressive deepening.

questions.q: A skilled player is shown a new chess position. What does the player appear to do in the first fifteen seconds?
options: Perceive the essential properties of the position
Search long sequences of moves to a considerable depth
Count the number of legal moves available
Choose the final move and then check it
optionExplain: Right: the first moments are spent gathering information, not seeking a solution.
Deep search is not what the first moments show.
Players mention only a few considerable moves, not a count.
The summing up comes at the end.
questions.explain: Early on, perception leads and search follows. The card next gives the authors' evidence.

questions.q: In the first moments with a position a skilled player is gathering ____ about the problem, not seeking a solution.
questions.explain: The player is gathering information about the problem.

questions.q: An experienced doctor glances at a patient on arrival, before ordering any test. Which idea from the card is this?
options: Verifying a favorite diagnosis against others
Searching a tree of consequences to great depth before acting at all
Perceiving essential properties first, which suggest what to do next
Redefining the problem after a surprise
optionExplain: No favorite is being tested yet.
The glance is not a deep search.
Right: perception of key features comes before analysis.
No surprise has occurred.
questions.explain: Skilled people perceive key properties of a situation first, and these suggest actions.

questions.q: True or false: In the first fifteen seconds with a new position, a skilled player appears to be perceiving its essential properties rather than searching.
questions.explain: He appears to be gathering information about the problem, not seeking a solution.

questions.q: What noticing subroutines does MATER use, according to the authors?
options: Counting material, ranking pieces, and scoring the center
Finding the direction between squares, and whether a piece or square is attacked or defended
Remembering past games and replaying them
Timing the opponent's replies and adjusting the clock to match the pace of play in the game
optionExplain: Those are evaluation functions, not noticing routines.
Right: these are direct board-relation routines.
MATER has no such memory routines in the card.
Clocks do not figure.
questions.explain: MATER's move generators and testers rest on subroutines that notice relations directly on the board.
questions.teaches: MATER has subroutines that find the direction between two squares, notice whether a piece lies on the line between them, and notice whether a piece or a square is attacked or defended, all working directly on board relations.

questions.q: A birdwatcher spends her first minute in a new field only looking, without organizing anything. Which de Groot description of a first phase matches?
options: An actively organizing attitude to settle on a plan
A hostile attitude toward unfamiliar patterns of pieces on the board
An attitude of ignoring what is seen
A perceptive and receptive attitude, not an actively organizing one
optionExplain: Active organizing comes later.
No hostility is described.
The player attends to what is seen.
Right: de Groot describes the first phase as perceptive and receptive.
questions.explain: De Groot calls the first phase of problem formation perceptive and receptive.
questions.teaches: De Groot describes the first phase of problem formation as characterized by a perceptive and receptive, rather than actively organizing, attitude on the part of the subject.

questions.q: How fast can a person's eyes move from one square of a board to another?
options: About forty fixations per second
At most about four fixations per second
About one fixation every ten seconds
As fast as the person can think of moves
optionExplain: That is far above the human rate.
Right: about four per second is the maximum.
That is far below the rate observed.
Thinking of moves is not what limits the eyes.
questions.explain: The eyes move in jumps at a limited rate. The card next gives the figures.

questions.q: Eye fixations move between squares at a maximum rate of about ____ per second.
questions.explain: The maximum is about four fixations per second.

questions.q: A researcher says a record shows a player thought hard about one Knight's square. Which limit on eye records does the card warn of?
options: Records show nothing about where the eyes go
Records show exactly what information is processed
Records can be made only with novices
The exact square attended cannot be established with assurance
optionExplain: Records do show fixations.
The card does not say the records show processing exactly.
Novice use is not the limit.
Right: calibration and the eye itself keep the exact square uncertain.
questions.explain: Calibration and the visual apparatus keep the exact square uncertain.

questions.q: True or false: If a player fixates a Bishop, a Rook that defends it, seen in peripheral vision, may be noticed at the same time.
questions.explain: Pieces in peripheral vision bearing a chess relation such as defending are picked up along with the fixated piece.
questions.rule: Relations in the periphery are noticed.

questions.q: Why is peripheral information necessary if eye movements are to be other than random?
options: It is needed to direct the eyes to new fixation points
It tells the player the best move to play in the position
It replaces the fixations altogether
It prevents the eyes from moving
optionExplain: Right: without it the eyes would have no guide.
It gives information about status of squares, not moves.
Fixations still occur.
The eyes still move.
questions.explain: Peripheral vision supplies the information that guides the next fixation.
questions.teaches: Peripheral information about the status of distant squares is necessary to direct the eyes to new fixation points if the eye movements are to be other than random.

questions.q: A camera shows only where a shopper's gaze lands, in order. What can and cannot be concluded about the shopper's thinking, by the card?
options: Exactly what the shopper was thinking at each moment
Nothing at all about where the shopper looked
The order of fixations is known, but not what was processed each moment
The shopper's final choice, from the fixations alone, with no further data
optionExplain: The record does not give thoughts.
The record shows fixations.
Right: records show succession, not content.
The final choice is not given by fixations.
questions.explain: Records of eye movements can only show the succession of fixations.
questions.teaches: Records of eye movements can only show the succession of fixations; they cannot show precisely what information is being processed at each moment.

questions.q: A program must reproduce the order in which a person's eyes visit a board. Which extra assumption does that need beyond knowing what is perceived?
options: A table of all possible boards
A count of the pieces on the board
A rule to look only at empty squares and never at the pieces
A process that produces the perceptions in a definite order
optionExplain: No table of boards is needed.
A count does not set a sequence.
Looking at empty squares would miss the pieces.
Right: a sequence needs a process to generate it.
questions.explain: A simulation of order needs a process that fixes the order. The card next gives PERCEIVER's.

questions.q: PERCEIVER was built from the noticing processes already contained in ____.
questions.explain: Simon and Barenfeld organized the noticing processes of MATER into PERCEIVER.

questions.q: A browser views a page, notices a link to another, and either rereads the first or moves on. Which PERCEIVER assumption is this?
options: Attention: after noticing a relation, attention returns to the first item or moves to the second
Concepts: the relations noticed are attack and defense between two pieces on the board
Fixation: the eyes never leave the first item
Evaluation: each page gets a numerical score
optionExplain: Right: this is the attention assumption.
That assumption lists the relations, not the movement.
Fixation does change when attention does not return.
PERCEIVER does not score pages.
questions.explain: Return to A or move to B is the attention assumption.

questions.q: Sort each relation as one PERCEIVER detects or one it does not.

items.t: A neighbor defends the fixated piece
A neighbor attacks the fixated piece
The fixated piece defends a neighbor
The fixated piece attacks a neighbor
A neighbor is of higher value
A neighbor stands on a dark square
A neighbor moved last
A neighbor is of the same color

questions.explain: The four relations are defend, attack, defended by and attacked by; others could be added but are not among the four.

questions.q: What do the authors say about the extra assumptions needed to fix the detail of PERCEIVER?
options: They decide the whole behavior of the program
They are all taken from MATER unchanged
They include a process to choose the first fixation, but results depend little on detail
They are unnecessary since the two assumptions suffice
optionExplain: Behavior is said to be insensitive to them.
Some are added, such as the starting point.
Right: the starting point needs a process, and details matter little.
Additional assumptions are needed.
questions.explain: A process to specify an initial fixation is among them; the results depend little on detail.
questions.teaches: Additional assumptions are needed to determine the detail of PERCEIVER, including a process to specify an initial point of fixation, but the qualitative behavior of the program is not especially sensitive to variations in the detail of its structure.

questions.q: A modeller says that people perceive relations among objects on a table. To simulate their eye movements, what must she add?
options: A claim that the eyes visit the squares of the board entirely at random
Processes that generate those perceptions in a particular sequence
A list of all objects ever seen
A rule that only one relation can exist
optionExplain: Random visits would not match human data.
Right: perceiving relations is not enough to give an order.
A list is not a sequence.
Several relations exist.
questions.explain: The simulation requires stronger assumptions than simply that subjects perceive relations.
questions.teaches: Carrying out the simulation requires stronger assumptions than simply that the human subjects are perceiving the relations among pieces: it is necessary to posit processes that generate these perceptions in some particular sequence.

questions.q: A simple program follows links between related items and returns often to the best-connected items. Where will its attention go most?
options: To the points where relations are densest
To the items farthest from the others, which have few relations
To a random item each time
To the item first in alphabetical order
optionExplain: Right: following links leads back to the best-connected points.
Isolated items attract little attention.
The path follows links, not chance.
Alphabet plays no part.
questions.explain: A web of relations draws attention to its dense points. The card next shows chess data.

questions.q: In its first five seconds the expert made ____ fixations.
questions.explain: The expert's sequence had 20 fixations; PERCEIVER made 15.

questions.q: A wiki reader follows links from page to page. Which pages will she revisit most, by the card's reasoning?
options: The pages with the fewest links
The pages she has left most recently
The pages where many links meet
The pages whose names begin with the same letter
optionExplain: Sparse pages attract little return.
Returning to the last page is not the pattern.
Right: a train of associations returns to dense points.
Letters do not matter.
questions.explain: Attention following associations returns to the places where relations are densest.

questions.q: True or false: PERCEIVER's fixations would fall on empty squares as often as the expert's did.
questions.explain: By construction, all of PERCEIVER's fixations fell on occupied squares, while six of the expert's fell on empty ones.
questions.rule: The program fixates only on pieces.

questions.q: How do PERCEIVER's fixations differ from the expert's in where they fall?
options: All of the human's fell on occupied squares, but six of PERCEIVER's did not
All of PERCEIVER's fell on occupied squares; six of the human's did not
Both fell only on unoccupied squares
Neither fell on any critical square
optionExplain: This reverses the difference.
Right: this is the one structural difference the authors note.
Both mainly attended to pieces.
Both attended to the critical squares.
questions.explain: The difference is built into the program, yet the objects of attention still match well.
questions.teaches: By construction all of PERCEIVER's fixations fell on squares occupied by pieces, whereas six of the human player's fixations fell on unoccupied squares.

questions.q: A simple rule-follower ends up at the same key spots as an expert. Does this show that it judges importance with subtle evaluations?
options: Yes, since only subtle judgment can find key spots
Yes, since the expert must be using the very same subtle judgments as the program does
No, since key spots cannot be found by any rule
No; attention following relations returns to dense points without such evaluations
optionExplain: The authors say it does not rest on subtle evaluation.
They draw no such conclusion about the expert.
A rule did find them.
Right: the program's attention rests on no subtle evaluation of importance.
questions.explain: PERCEIVER's focus on the key relations does not rest on subtle or complex evaluations of what is important.
questions.teaches: PERCEIVER's focus of attention on these particular relations does not rest on subtle or complex evaluations of what is important on the board.

questions.q: A master and a beginner each see a random scatter of pieces for five seconds. Whose performance suffers more than on a real position?
options: The beginner's
The master's
Both equally
Neither's
optionExplain: The beginner had little advantage to lose.
Right: the master loses the advantage that meaningful structure gave.
They do not suffer equally.
The master's performance drops.
questions.explain: Random placement removes the structure that experts use. The card next gives the results.
questions.rule: Random boards remove the expert's edge.

questions.q: Very weak players can place only about half a ____ pieces correctly after a brief look.
questions.explain: Only half a dozen pieces are placed correctly by very weak players.

questions.q: A typist recalls a ten-word sentence far better than ten random words after a brief look. Which chess finding does this parallel?
options: Weak players do worse on random boards than on game positions
Experts and beginners do equally well on game positions
Random boards help experts more than game positions
Experts reproduce meaningful positions better than random boards
optionExplain: Weak players do not deteriorate on random boards.
Experts do much better than beginners on game positions.
Experts do worse on random boards.
Right: meaningfulness matters most to those who have learned the structure.
questions.explain: Meaningful structure helps the skilled; random material does not.

questions.q: True or false: On random boards, weak players' performance falls even further than on game positions.
questions.explain: The performance of weak players does not deteriorate further on random boards.
questions.rule: Weak players have no structure to lose.

questions.q: Which part of the human performance does PERCEIVER not elucidate?
options: Retaining the information long enough to reproduce the position
Extracting the totality of the information from the board in the first look
Looking at the board for five seconds
Placing the pieces on the board
optionExplain: Right: PERCEIVER does not address retention.
Extraction is what it can model.
Looking is not the problem.
Placing is not the problem.
questions.explain: The two parts of the performance are extracting and retaining; the explanation of the second comes next.
questions.teaches: There are two parts to the human performance: extracting from the chessboard the totality of information about the position, and retaining all of this information long enough to reproduce it, which the PERCEIVER program does not elucidate.

questions.q: A researcher wants to test whether meaning matters for memory. Which design do the chess studies use?
options: Compare two positions the subjects already know well from their own earlier games
Compare short and long exposure times only
Compare unknown positions from games with the same pieces placed at random
Compare players of the same rating
optionExplain: Known positions would confound with prior study.
That varies time, not meaning.
Right: same pieces, with and without game structure.
That removes the proficiency contrast.
questions.explain: The positions from actual games were not known to the subjects, and the random boards used the same pieces.
questions.teaches: Meaningfulness is manipulated by contrasting the reproduction of positions from actual games, not known to the subjects, with that of boards having the same pieces as the game positions but placed at random.

questions.q: Why might an expert hold nine pieces in mind as easily as a novice holds one?
options: The expert has a larger short-term memory
The expert looks at the board for longer
The expert ignores most of the pieces
The expert stores a familiar group of pieces as one unit
optionExplain: Short-term memory holds about the same number of units for everyone.
The exposure is the same for all subjects.
The reproduction is almost without error, so pieces are not ignored.
Right: a recognized group counts as one unit.
questions.explain: A recognized group can count as one unit. The card next defines this as a chunk.

questions.q: Short-term memory holds about seven plus or minus two ____.
questions.explain: The unit of short-term memory is the chunk.

questions.q: A reader recalls the nine letters B B C I T V N H S far better than nine random letters. By the card, why?
options: They fall into three familiar units, so three chunks need holding
They are all capital letters, which memory prefers to lower-case ones
They are shorter than random letters
They are read faster by the eyes
optionExplain: Right: BBC, ITV and NHS are familiar units.
Capitals do not explain it.
Length is not the issue.
Eye speed is not the issue.
questions.explain: Familiar groupings reduce the number of chunks held.

questions.q: True or false: On a randomly arranged board, a grandmaster would find few familiar constellations and do about as poorly as weak players.
questions.explain: Few random configurations are familiar even to grandmasters, so they need too many symbols.

questions.q: In the authors' example, how many chunks describe nine men, and which concepts are used?
options: Nine chunks, one for each man
Two chunks: the White men and the Black men
Four chunks, one for each of four familiar concepts
One chunk for the whole board
optionExplain: That ignores chunking.
No such split is given.
Right: four concepts describe the nine men.
One chunk for the whole board is a more experienced player's way for the nine men.
questions.explain: Four familiar concepts account for nine men, so four chunks.
questions.teaches: In the position of Figure 13.10 four concepts, a Knight pinned on the Queen by a Bishop, a short-castled King, a normally developed King's Knight and a fianchettoed King's Bishop, describe the positions of nine men as four chunks.

questions.q: A more experienced player knows the whole constellation formed by those four concepts together. How many chunks does it cost him?
options: Four chunks, as for a less experienced player
One chunk for the entire constellation of nine men
Nine chunks, one for each man
No chunk, since he need not store it
optionExplain: That is the count for the less experienced player.
Right: a familiar conjunction is a single symbol.
That would be no chunking.
He must still store the symbol.
questions.explain: Greater experience allows bigger chunks.
questions.teaches: A more experienced player familiar with the whole constellation, the conjunction of the four concepts, can designate the entire constellation of nine men by a single symbol, hence as only one chunk in short-term memory.

questions.q: A code uses sequences of seven symbols drawn from a vocabulary of 1,000 symbols. About how many different sequences exist?
optionExplain: That is the number for a vocabulary of about 100 symbols in three places.
That needs ten thousand symbols.
That is far too small.
questions.explain: Raising the vocabulary to the seventh power gives the count. The card next applies this to chess.

questions.q: Simon and Barenfeld suggest the position of Figure 13.10 could be encoded in ____ symbols.
questions.explain: They suggest eight symbols, eight familiar constellations.

questions.q: A vocabulary of \(10^4\) symbols is used in sequences of seven. How many encodings does this allow?
optionExplain: That adds 4 and 7 instead of multiplying.
That is the count for \(10^5\) symbols.
That is the vocabulary, not the number of sequences.
questions.explain: Four times seven gives the exponent 28, and five times seven gives 35.

questions.q: True or false: Different players of comparable skill might organize the same board into different familiar chunks.
questions.explain: The authors say there are different ways to organize the relations on a board and players may characterize it somewhat differently.

questions.q: How does the footnote's more conservative estimate treat the corners of the board?
options: Corner configurations are ignored entirely in the estimate of the number of positions
Corners are stereotyped, perhaps a hundred, and still give about \(10^{23}\) positions
Corner configurations are so varied that no code is possible
Corner configurations add \(10^{40}\) positions
optionExplain: They are counted, as stereotyped.
Right: stereotyped corners reduce the count but leave enough variety.
The conservative estimate still provides sufficient variety.
The estimate is smaller, not larger.
questions.explain: With four stereotyped corner patterns and three others, the product is about \(10^{23}\), still enough.
questions.teaches: A more conservative estimate takes into account that corner configurations are highly stereotyped, perhaps about \(10^2\) in number, giving about \((10^2)^4 (10^5)^3 = 10^{23}\) positions, which still provides sufficient variety.

questions.q: A researcher explains chess experts' memory. Which two mechanisms in sequence do the authors say suffice, with no significant new mechanism needed?
options: Searching the game tree, then evaluating its terminal positions with a score
Redefining the problem, then verifying a favorite move
Reading the opponent's face, then counting material
Noticing relations as PERCEIVER does, then chunking them as EPAM does
optionExplain: Those are search mechanisms, not perception.
Those concern analysis, not first perception.
Nothing like that is claimed.
Right: this is the authors' conclusion about perception.
questions.explain: The information masters extract in a first look is consistent with noticing relations and then chunking them.
questions.teaches: The information known to be extracted by masters and grandmasters in their first perception of positions is consistent, in quantity and quality, with a mechanism that notices relations as PERCEIVER does and then recognizes and chunks configurations of them as earlier memory theories such as EPAM do.

questions.q: An expert says little aloud yet sees a lot. What is a likely explanation?
options: The expert is hiding the analysis from the listener
Familiar features evoke stored analyses, so less search is stated
The expert guesses and happens to be right
The expert searches every position to the end
optionExplain: The card gives no sign of hiding.
Right: stored responses to familiar features cut the need to state steps.
Guessing would not give consistently good analysis.
Exhaustive search is not what experts do.
questions.explain: Stored responses can stand in for explicit steps. The card next gives the authors' account.

questions.q: The symptom-remedy pattern is as automatic as taking aspirin for a ____.
questions.explain: The authors compare it to taking aspirin for a headache.

questions.q: A mechanic hears a rattle and goes straight to the heat shield without reasoning it out. Which idea from the card is this?
options: Progressive deepening: reworking one analysis again and again, more deeply each time
A polynomial evaluation: weighing many factors into a score
Redefinition: restating the whole problem
Symptom-remedy: a means-ends link learned from past experience
optionExplain: No reworking is occurring.
No scoring is occurring.
The problem is not restated.
Right: the symptom evokes the remedy automatically.
questions.explain: A learned symptom-remedy link needs no explicit goal.

questions.q: Which are among the three possible causes the authors give for grandmasters' less explicit protocols? Select all that apply.
options: They search more rapidly than others
They report less
They see consequences with less search
They studied the position beforehand
optionExplain: Right: the first of the three causes.
Right: the second cause.
Right: the third cause, which the authors find most likely.
The text gives no such cause.
questions.explain: The three causes are faster search, less reporting and less search needed.

questions.q: What do the authors say about which of the three explanations is correct?
options: They have no evidence to decide, though the third is the most likely
The evidence proves the first
The evidence proves the second
The evidence rules out the third
optionExplain: Right: they say the evidence does not decide among them.
No proof is claimed.
No proof is claimed.
The third is judged most likely.
questions.explain: The authors are explicit that the evidence does not decide.
questions.teaches: The authors have no evidence to show which of the three explanations is correct; the most likely is that the chessmaster uses his richer vocabulary of concepts to evoke condensed analysis programs.

questions.q: A gardener pulls a weed, sees the gap, and thinks at once of replanting. Which position A pattern does this parallel?
options: A Knight pinned and a search of every legal move
A redefinition after an overlooked piece
A pawn capture opening the King's file and evoking KR-K1
A random choice among quiet moves
optionExplain: No full search is involved.
No overlooked piece is involved.
Right: the change in the position evokes the remedy directly.
The move is evoked, not random.
questions.explain: A pawn capture may change the list of open files and evoke the move that uses the opened file.
questions.teaches: In position A, a capture by a pawn leads the master to see that the King's file is now open and evokes KR-K1, the other prominent positional move the masters considered; any capture involving a pawn may change the list of open files.

questions.q: After studying one subject closely, a researcher checks the findings against other players and extends them to new corners. What is the aim?
options: To replace the first study with a different one that is better and more complete
To show that the first subject was unusual
To avoid drawing any conclusions
To see whether the findings are general and to cover topics left thin
optionExplain: The aim is to support and widen the study.
The chapter finds agreement, not oddness.
Conclusions are drawn.
Right: corroborate and extend.
questions.explain: Corroboration and extension are the two aims. The card next lists what the chapter did.

questions.q: De Groot's general picture of chess thinking ____ the more detailed but narrow analysis of S2.
questions.explain: The authors say de Groot's picture corroborates their analysis of S2.

questions.q: A team studied one cook closely, compared notes with famous chefs, and tested a kitchen robot. Which chess chapter parallel is closest?
options: Comparing with de Groot's grandmasters and testing a mating program
Replacing S2 with a better subject who has far more skill in the game
Dropping the search theory altogether
Studying only the opening position
optionExplain: Right: other players and a program both serve the aims.
S2 is kept as the base.
The search theory is supported.
The chapter ranges over many topics.
questions.explain: Other subjects and a program were used to check and extend.
questions.rule: Check with others and with programs.

questions.q: Match each topic to what the chapter used it for.
pairs: Separating task demands from S2's particulars
A process found in more strategic positions
questions.explain: Each topic served a different corner of the chess situation.

questions.q: What did the mating-combination test show about search, according to the conclusion?
options: Search was insufficient and new mechanisms were needed
Search was irrelevant to the mating task
Search was sufficient, and a few additional search heuristics were found
Search was sufficient with no new heuristics
optionExplain: The authors found that it did suffice.
Search was central.
Right: search sufficed and a few heuristics came to light.
A few additional heuristics were found.
questions.explain: The test asked whether search was sufficient for a task that seemed to need enormous searches; it was.
questions.teaches: The mating-combination task tested whether search of the kind considered in the first two chess chapters was sufficient for a task that appeared to require enormous searches; the authors found that it was, and uncovered a few additional search heuristics along the way.

questions.q: A writer says that agreement among strong players on position A shows the task alone dictates their analysis. How do the conclusion's remarks qualify this?
options: The task has no objective features at all, only the views of players
The task is defined only in comparison with other players' abilities
Strong players never agree with each other
Agreement is due to chance alone
optionExplain: The authors do find objective features.
Right: the explanations had to be tempered by the sociology of chess.
The authors report agreement.
The authors do not attribute agreement to chance.
questions.explain: Explanations by task demands had to be tempered by the role of the sociology of chess.
questions.teaches: Explanations in terms of the particular task environment had to be tempered by the role played by the sociology of chess, whereby the task is really defined only in comparison with other players' abilities to analyze the chess situation.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Two people solve the same puzzle by quite different methods. A psychologist wants one theory covering both. Which stance would the authors resist?
options: Allowing that their methods may differ in structure
Treating the two as the same program with different numerical settings
Describing each as an information processor with its own program
Letting the task's demands shape the account of each person's behavior, whatever the method
optionExplain: The authors accept structural differences between methods.
Right: the authors say subject differences are structural, not only parametric variations.
Describing people as information processors is their starting claim.
Task demands are central to their account.
questions.explain: The authors treat differences between people as differences of program structure, method and content. The card next lists all five propositions.
questions.rule: Differences are structural, not just parametric.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Subject differences are more than ____ variations: they involve program structure, method and content.
questions.explain: A parametric variation would only change a number such as a speed; the authors claim the programs themselves differ.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Two bakers with different habits both produce nearly identical loaves because the recipe leaves little room. Which proposition does this resemble?
options: That subject differences are only a matter of settings
That people cannot be described as information processors
That one subject's behavior cannot be represented in detail by any program of symbols at all
That the task environment largely determines behavior, whatever the solver's inner detail
optionExplain: The authors deny differences are merely settings, and the bakers do not show that.
The scenario says nothing against an IPS description.
The first two propositions claim detailed representation is possible.
Right: tight task demands make behavior similar despite inner differences.
questions.explain: Proposition five says the task and the solver's intelligence largely fix behavior, independently of the detailed structure of the IPS.
questions.rule: Task demands can make different solvers look alike.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: A colleague says: since subject differences are real, the authors must hold that each person needs an entirely separate theory. According to the chapter, this is correct.
questions.explain: The authors ask whether a single theory exists or only a congeries of separate ones, and then propose one theory built on invariants plus a way to determine what varies.
questions.rule: Real differences do not force separate theories.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Which of these is one of the answers to the puzzle that, according to the authors, other psychologists have proposed?
options: Retreating to learning as the only fundamental topic of a scientific psychology
Treating all behavior as innate and unchanging across people
Replacing observation with computer simulation alone as the method of psychology
Holding that problem solving cannot be studied scientifically
optionExplain: Right: the authors list this among the earlier answers.
Nothing in the list says behavior is innate.
The authors list no answer that drops observation.
The listed answers still aim at a scientific psychology.
questions.explain: The authors list several earlier answers, including a representative subject, a purely statistical psychology, and keeping only what is common to all humans.
questions.rule: Earlier answers: representative subject, statistics, common core, no contents, learning.
questions.teaches: The authors list earlier answers to the puzzle: postulating a representative subject, a purely statistical psychology, keeping only what all humans share, abandoning contents, or retreating to learning.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Pilots differ widely, yet landing a plane on a short runway forces similar actions from all of them. What puzzle does this pose for a theory of the pilot's mind?
options: Why pilots never differ in anything they do
Why a theory of the mind is not possible at all once tasks matter
How the mind can matter if the task so strongly shapes behavior
Why runway length is more important than training for a pilot
optionExplain: The scenario says only that the actions are similar here, not that pilots never differ.
The puzzle is about what a theory can say, not whether one exists.
Right: the authors ask what a theory can be when the task makes the internal structure seem almost irrelevant.
Training is not the issue the chapter raises.
questions.explain: The authors pose exactly this: what can a theory of problem solving be when the shaping influence of the task makes the solver's inner specifics seem almost irrelevant?
questions.rule: Strong task shaping makes inner structure hard to see.
questions.teaches: The authors pose the question of what a theory of problem solving can be when the task environment's shaping influence seems to make the problem solver's internal structure almost irrelevant.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A manager wants to predict how a new hire will handle a task. Which chain of influence seems most plausible for an adaptive thinker?
options: Work methods come first and the task adapts to them, whatever the workspace may look like
Personality alone sets both the workspace and the method
The method is free of the workspace, whatever it looks like
Task demands set the possible workspaces, and the workspace limits the possible work methods
optionExplain: Reversing the order makes the task adapt to the method, which is not the theory's claim.
The theory gives the task, not personality, the leading role.
Methods can use only information the workspace holds.
Right: this is the order the card then states for the theory.
questions.explain: The theory chains task, space and program in that order. The card next gives the four propositions.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Order the chain of determination in the theory, from first to last.
items: A few gross IPS characteristics are invariant
These imply the task is represented as a problem space
The task environment's structure limits the possible spaces
The space's structure limits the possible programs
questions.explain: The four propositions run from IPS invariants to the existence of a problem space, then to the task fixing its possible structures, then to the space fixing possible programs.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: In the theory, the structure of the ____ determines the possible structures of the problem space.
questions.explain: Proposition three assigns that role to the structure of the task environment.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Two tasks have very different structures but are given to the same solver. According to propositions two to four, what stays common?
options: That each is represented as a problem space, though the spaces and programs may differ
The exact program, because the solver is the same and carries one program with him to every task given
The exact space, because the IPS is the same
Nothing, because the tasks differ
optionExplain: Right: the existence of a problem space follows from IPS invariants, while its structure follows the task.
The program depends on the space's structure, which differs between tasks.
The IPS fixes that a space exists, not its structure.
The IPS invariants still hold across the tasks.
questions.explain: Proposition two makes the problem space an invariant; propositions three and four let space and program vary with the task.
questions.rule: Space is invariant; its structure and programs vary.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A reader summarizes: propositions three and four tell us exactly which space and which program a person will use. What is wrong?
options: They apply only to computers, not to humans who solve problems, and so say little about people
They say the program is chosen before the space
They speak only of possibilities, so a separate account of actual selection is needed
They are claims about learning, not about problem solving
optionExplain: They are claims about human problem solvers.
The order given is space first, then program.
Right: the chapter says a fifth section must treat the actual determination.
They concern the structure of spaces and programs in problem solving.
questions.explain: The authors state that points three and four concern only possibilities, so a fifth section covers how the actual space and program are determined.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A city planner says: the street grid sets what routes exist, and the routes set which delivery plans are possible. Which part of the theory does this mirror, and what does it leave out?
options: The IPS invariants, leaving out the street grid
The chain from task to space to program, leaving out which plan a driver actually picks
The goal structure, leaving out the routes
The memory sizes, leaving out the plans
optionExplain: The grid and routes play the roles of task and space, not IPS invariants.
Right: possibilities cascade downward, but choice among them is a separate matter.
Goals are a separate invariant, not the chain described.
Memory sizes are not part of this analogy.
questions.explain: As in the theory, each level fixes only the range of the next; picking among possibilities needs further explanation. The authors admit their studies shed little light on that selection.
questions.rule: Each level limits the next; choice remains open.
questions.teaches: The authors say the studies in this book do not shed much light on the mechanisms that select the actual problem space and actual program from the possible ones.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A skilled typist's finger-muscle details hardly show in the text she produces. Why might this be a general pattern in flexible performers?
options: Flexible performers adapt to the task, so most inner detail is hidden by the fit
Inner detail is always identical across people
Only the slowest component ever matters to output
Detail cannot be measured, so it has no effect on the text that the typist produces
optionExplain: Right: adaptation to the task hides most of the machinery.
Inner detail often differs; it simply does not show in the product.
The authors point to gross memory features, not to a single slowest part.
Detail can have effects that are hidden by adaptation, not absent.
questions.explain: The authors argue that adaptive devices shape themselves to the environment. The card next states their argument.
questions.rule: Fit to the environment hides inner detail.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A system that is not flexible enough to meet its environment's demands is not ____.
questions.explain: The authors define adaptiveness by such flexibility, which is why only general features show through.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A gardener adjusts watering to any plant in any soil. Which observer prediction fits the authors' argument?
options: Her results will mirror every habit of her hands
Her results will vary randomly from plant to plant
Her results will reveal little about her particular habits, unless conditions become extreme
Her results will depend only on how fast she walks
optionExplain: Adaptation to conditions masks fine habits.
Random variation is not what adaptation implies.
Right: flexible adaptation hides her particulars except at extremes.
Speed is a gross rate; the argument does not single out walking.
questions.explain: An adaptive agent's behavior mostly reflects the conditions it meets, with its structure showing only in extremes.
questions.rule: Adaptation masks structure except at extremes.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: If the task environment were so extreme that the solver's adaptation broke down, the IPS's structure would show through more.
questions.explain: The authors note that in extreme environments, tautologically the ones where adaptation breaks down, the IPS structure does show through.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: According to the authors, which kind of IPS feature chiefly shows through in task behavior?
options: The particular words in the solver's native language
The kinds of memories available, with their sizes, read and write rates, and access modes
The solver's personality and mood on the day
The exact wiring of nerve cells in the brain
optionExplain: Language specifics are not named as the key features.
Right: memory sizes, rates and accessing modes are the features they name.
Personality variables are not central to the study.
Physiological wiring is not what the argument concerns.
questions.explain: The authors say the features that show through have chiefly to do with memory sizes, rates of reading and writing, and accessing modes, though they cannot yet derive them a priori.
questions.rule: Memory sizes, rates and access modes show through.
questions.teaches: The features of an adaptive IPS that show through concern chiefly the kinds of memories it has: sizes, rates of reading and writing, and accessing modes.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A chess club wants to test a claim about memory limits using its members. Is the argument in this card favorable if the club uses a standard, non-extreme game?
options: No, ordinary games hide every memory limit from view
No, only extreme games let players adapt at all
Yes, because ordinary games reveal fine neural detail
Yes, adaptive players in an ordinary game should show mostly gross memory limits, not fine detail
optionExplain: Gross limits are expected to show; only fine detail is hidden.
Adaptation breaks down in extreme tasks, not ordinary ones.
Neural fine detail is the kind of thing adaptation hides.
Right: non-extreme tasks are where gross features should show without breaking adaptation.
questions.explain: The authors say the studied environments have no extreme characteristics for intelligent, well-educated subjects, so gross features can be read from behavior.
questions.teaches: The authors judge that the tasks of this book are not extreme environments for intelligent, well-educated subjects such as theirs.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A data center manager has three machines whose chip designs differ but whose memory sizes and speeds are the same. What would you expect about their performance on varied programs?
options: Very different, since the chip detail dominates every program
Broadly similar, since memory and access rates largely decide it
Identical to the last digit on every task
Unrelated to memory in any way
optionExplain: Detail is mediated by flexible programs, so it does not dominate.
Right: this is the pattern the authors describe.
Gross similarity does not mean identical results.
Memory features are the ones the authors say count.
questions.explain: The authors note that a few gross features, chiefly memory sizes and access, largely determine computer performance. The card next shows why.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: The flexibility of the ____ mediates between the detailed structure of the computer and the structure of the problems it serves.
questions.explain: A flexible program sits between machine detail and problem structure.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A translation agency switches word processors with different internal designs but the same memory and speed. Which result matches the authors' pattern?
options: A large change from the differing internal designs
A change only in the languages translated
A change that depends on typist's mood alone
Little change in how fast documents are produced
optionExplain: Internal design is mediated by flexible programs.
Language is unrelated to the pattern described.
Mood is not a computer feature in the analogy.
Right: the gross features stay the same, so performance stays similar.
questions.explain: The pattern predicts that equal memory sizes and rates give similar performance whatever the detailed design.
questions.rule: Same memory and rates: similar performance.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: A reader says: since computers show the pattern, the authors have proved the human IPS has exactly a computer's memory features. This is what the authors claim.
questions.explain: The authors use the computer case as supporting analogy; they say which human features show through is not derivable a priori.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: In the authors' account, which machine details does a flexible program keep from showing in performance?
options: The computer's detailed order code and timing
The computer's memory sizes and access rates, which are all hidden by the program
The computer's power supply and cooling
The computer's brand name and case design
optionExplain: Right: the text names order code and timing as the detailed structure the program mediates.
Memory sizes and rates are the features that do show through.
Power and cooling are not mentioned.
Appearance is not mentioned.
questions.explain: The authors say the program's flexibility mediates between the detailed structure of the computer (its order code and timing) and the structure of the problems it serves.
questions.rule: Order code and timing are mediated away.
questions.teaches: Program flexibility mediates between the computer's detailed structure, its order code and timing, and the structure of the practical problems to which it is adapted.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A kitchen's staff change knives and stoves yet the restaurant's output rate stays fixed by the size of the prep counter and how fast things are fetched. Which idea is this?
options: Detailed tools set performance, whatever the size of the counter or the speed of fetching
Flexibility makes performance random
Gross memory-like limits, not detailed tools, set performance in a flexible system
Only the cooks' personalities matter
optionExplain: That reverses the pattern.
Flexibility is what masks detail, not what randomizes output.
Right: the analogy is to storage size and access speed, not tool detail.
Personality is not what the analogy concerns.
questions.explain: The counter and fetching speed play the roles of memory size and access rate in the authors' pattern.
questions.rule: Size and access limits decide output.
questions.teaches: Computer performance, like human problem solving, is largely determined by memory sizes and by the rates and ways of accessing them.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A student claims every careful problem solver must build a map of states and moves. What would be a fair reply?
options: That is true of every conceivable solver whatever its build, memory or speed of processing
That is false since no solver uses states at all
That depends only on the solver's age
That depends on the solver's memory and speed limits, and a different kind of solver might not
optionExplain: They explicitly allow that other IPS's might not use problem spaces.
Their evidence says human solvers do use them.
Age is outside the study's scope.
Right: the authors tie the problem space to human memory and rates.
questions.explain: The authors say a differently built IPS might not use a problem space. The card next gives their argument.
questions.rule: Human limits make the space invariant.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: The particular ____ and processing rates of human beings make the problem space a major invariant.
questions.explain: That is their central claim for the problem space as a major invariant.
questions.rule: Human limits imply a problem space.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A robot has unlimited, instantly writable memory. Which claim fits the authors' argument about it?
options: It might not need a problem space to organize its efforts
It must use exactly the same problem space as humans, whatever its memory
It cannot solve problems of any kind
It has the same memory limits as humans
optionExplain: Right: IPS's with other characteristics might solve problems differently.
The argument rests on human limits the robot lacks.
There is no claim that it cannot solve problems.
The robot is stipulated to differ from humans.
questions.explain: The authors say IPS's with characteristics different from human ones might not employ problem spaces.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: If human long-term memory could be written as fast as it can be read, what happens to the force of the authors' argument?
options: It strengthens, since fast writing forces a solver to build a problem space for each task
It is unchanged, since the argument ignores memory
It weakens, since the argument leans on slow writing and small short-term memory
It disappears, since fast writing means no goals
optionExplain: Fast writing removes a reason for the constraint.
The argument is explicitly about memory.
Right: our reading, the argument depends on those memory limits.
Goals are a separate invariant.
questions.explain: The authors ground the problem space in human memory sizes and rates; changing those removes part of the basis. This is our reading of their argument.
questions.rule: Change the limits, change the argument.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: the authors call their argument for the problem space as an invariant logically conclusive.
questions.explain: They call it not logically conclusive, though it has considerable force.
questions.teaches: The authors call their argument for the problem space as an invariant not logically conclusive but of considerable force.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A study shows people given a puzzle tend to carve it into a sequence of small states, even when told they could think freely. What kind of support is this for the theory?
options: Proof that every possible mind uses states
Evidence that humans prefer the search formulation, not proof that no other formulation can exist
Evidence against any use of memory limits
Irrelevant, since choices cannot be observed
optionExplain: The authors allow other possible formulations.
Right: the authors say the human tends to use the search formulation preferentially.
Memory limits are the explanation, not the opposite.
Observed behavior is the evidence the book uses.
questions.explain: The authors say the evidence from their three tasks indicates a human will preferentially use the search formulation, while leaving other formulations possible.
questions.teaches: The authors state that evidence from their three tasks indicates humans preferentially employ the search formulation, though other formulations are possible.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A chef can only judge a dish using information she has noted about it. What would limit her possible decision rules?
options: The information she has actually recorded about the dish
Only her mood on the day she judges the dish
Only the temperature of the kitchen at the time she judges the dish on the plate
Nothing at all, since rules are free
optionExplain: Right: decisions depend on information available to her.
Mood is not the limiting information.
Temperature is irrelevant to the rules available.
Decision rules need information to act on.
questions.explain: A program can decide only with information in the space, which comes from the task. The card next shows this.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: The question of how the particular problem space is determined is answered largely by the ____.
questions.explain: The authors call the task environment the overwhelming determinant of the problem space.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A solver is given a puzzle with no price information. Which program could not exist for it, per the authors' reasoning?
options: One that chooses moves by trying a legal step
One that tests whether a state is the goal
One that chooses moves by comparing prices
One that retraces to an earlier state
optionExplain: Legal steps are information in the space.
Goal tests are standard parts of a space.
Right: that program would need price information the space lacks.
Backup uses path information, which the space can hold.
questions.explain: Possible programs are categorized by the information available in the space; no price information means no price-based rule.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: If the task environment contains relevant information that does not get encoded in the solver's space, the program cannot use it.
questions.explain: The program can use only information embedded in the space after extraction from the task environment.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: What do the authors say often suffices to predict which problem space a solver will use?
options: His age and his mood on the day, together with the weather in the laboratory
The solver's general intelligence plus his knowledge in the relevant domains
Only the exact wording of the instruction
The speed of his eye movements
optionExplain: Age and mood are not what they name.
Right: this is the authors' statement.
Instructions matter later in the chapter, but this sentence names intelligence and domain knowledge.
Eye movements are not named.
questions.explain: The text says information about the solver's general intelligence and knowledge in relevant domains is often sufficient to predict his space.
questions.rule: Intelligence plus domain knowledge predicts the space.
questions.teaches: Information about a problem solver's general intelligence plus his knowledge in relevant domains is often sufficient to predict which problem space he will use.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: An analyst's model of a billing task leaves out a rule that matters. What does the card's reasoning say about this possibility?
options: It cannot happen, because the task fixes the space completely and leaves out nothing relevant to it
It happens only when the analyst is unintelligent
It makes the analyst's program impossible to run
It can happen, because nothing guarantees all relevant task information is reflected in the space
optionExplain: The task is the main determinant, but the space may still omit information.
Intelligence and knowledge help predict the space, but do not guarantee completeness.
A program can run on what the space does hold; it just cannot use what is missing.
Right: the authors say there is no guarantee that all relevant task information is encoded.
questions.explain: The authors note that, although significant task information must be encoded for effective solving, there is no guarantee that all of it is.
questions.teaches: There can be no guarantee that all the relevant information in the task environment is reflected in the problem space.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A study looks at skilled adults solving half-hour puzzles. Which topic is it least likely to treat centrally?
options: How people choose among moves on a puzzle in a half-hour sitting
How children's thinking develops over years
How long a person stays on one idea
What methods people use to reach a goal
optionExplain: Choice of moves is central to problem solving.
Right: development and age differences are outside this study's focus.
Time on an idea is the kind of data the book uses.
Methods are a main topic.
questions.explain: The authors say they are not concerned with development or age differences. The card next lists the focus.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: The tasks studied are short, about ____ minutes, moderately difficult problems of a symbolic nature.
questions.explain: The authors describe them as half-hour tasks.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A reviewer wants to use the book's evidence to claim something about week-long creative projects. Which comment fits the scope statement?
options: The evidence bears on it most directly
Only perception data is needed
The evidence covers it because all thinking is the same
Long-term activity over days or years received no attention, so the evidence does not directly bear on it
optionExplain: The evidence concerns short tasks.
Perception is not the key limit here.
The scope excludes long activity.
Right: the Chapter 1 statement excludes long-term activity.
questions.explain: The authors list long-term activities extending over days or years among the things that receive no attention.
questions.rule: Long-term activity is out of focus.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: A reader says the authors' scope statement lists learning and development as equal central interests. This is correct.
questions.explain: They say the study is concerned primarily with performance, only a little with learning, and not at all with development.
questions.rule: Performance first, little learning, no development.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Which time scale does the scope statement deemphasize?
options: Elementary reactions of about half a second or less
Tasks lasting around thirty minutes, the main target of the theory
Whole sessions of a problem
Pauses between moves of a few seconds
optionExplain: Right: the scope statement deemphasizes details on that fine time scale.
Half-hour tasks are the focus.
Whole sessions are the focus.
The study uses residence times of seconds.
questions.explain: The text says the integrated activities focus deemphasizes processing detail on the scale of half a second or less.
questions.rule: Neither very fine nor very long scales.
questions.teaches: The study deemphasizes details of processing on the time scale of elementary reactions (half a second or less) and gives no attention to long-term activity over days or years.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A team studies how hospital nurses plan a week of shifts over many days. Using the scope statement, what is the fair description of the book's evidence for them?
options: It covers them fully
It covers them since all work is symbolic
It does not directly cover multi-day activity, so conclusions need further evidence
It is irrelevant because nurses are not adults
optionExplain: Intelligent adults are only one condition of scope.
The tasks are short symbolic tasks, not all work.
Right: long-term activity is outside the focus, though the theory's arguments may be broader.
Nurses are adults, so this is not the issue.
questions.explain: The evidence concerns short symbolic tasks; the authors say the arguments are broader, but the limits are not assessed.
questions.rule: Short-task evidence does not directly cover long tasks.
questions.teaches: The authors say perception, motor skill and personality variables are not central concerns of the study.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A team gets strong results from three kinds of puzzles. What is the most careful way to describe a general claim built on them?
options: Proven for every kind of human activity
Valid only for those three puzzles and nothing else, so no wider claim can be made
Meaningless without further puzzles
General in its arguments, with the limits of its scope not established by these data
optionExplain: The data are too narrow to prove every domain.
The authors say it is broader than the three tasks.
The authors regard the evidence as meaningful.
Right: this matches the authors' stance.
questions.explain: The authors put the theory forward as general without assessing its boundaries. The card next shows why.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: The authors say the arguments from the data are more ____ than the data themselves.
questions.explain: Arguments about the task-organism relation reach beyond the three tasks.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A lab studied only chess but argues from the fit between an adaptive player and its game. Which part of their claim is most likely to travel to other games?
options: The argument about how an adaptive organism relates to its task environment
The specific opening moves used
The exact seconds spent per move
The wording of the instructions
optionExplain: Right: the authors say those arguments are the more general ones.
Opening moves are specific to chess.
Timing details are specific.
Instruction wording is local.
questions.explain: The authors say the arguments about task environment and adaptive organism are the more general ones.
questions.rule: Fit arguments travel; details do not.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: If the authors added data from many other realms, they would be able to state the theory's limits with certainty.
questions.explain: The text says the evidence at hand is ill-suited to define the limits; nothing here promises that more data would make them certain. Our reading: more data could help but is not guaranteed to settle it.
questions.rule: Limits need evidence designed to find them.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Which of these did the authors say they had explored with the same general approach elsewhere?
options: Only chess programs
Only robot motor control
Concept formation, algebra word problems, music and scientific discovery
Only legal reasoning
optionExplain: Chess is one of this book's tasks.
Motor control is not listed.
Right: these appear in the chapter's note.
Legal reasoning is not listed.
questions.explain: A note lists concept formation, algebra word problems, music, verbal learning, creativity, organizational behavior, scientific discovery, emotion and perception.
questions.teaches: Elsewhere the authors have applied the same approach to concept formation, algebra word problems, music, verbal learning, creativity, administrative behavior, scientific discovery, emotion and perception.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A physician proposes a general rule about clinical reasoning from three case studies. What does the authors' stance suggest about how to present it?
options: Present it as proven for all doctors in all settings
State it as general if its arguments are broad, and be open that the cases cannot show where it stops
Withdraw it, since three cases are too few
Say it applies only to those three cases
optionExplain: Narrow data do not prove universal scope.
Right: this follows the authors' own stance.
The authors do not withdraw theories for narrow data.
That would ignore the broader arguments.
questions.explain: The authors say conditions needed for validity can be seen from the arguments, though the limits are not assessed.
questions.rule: Be general in claim, open about limits.
questions.teaches: From the nature of the arguments one can see some conditions that must be present for the theory to be valid, such as the basic memory structures of the adult human IPS.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A designer is asked what stays fixed across all human problem solvers for a theory. Which candidate is most like what the authors choose?
options: How large and fast their memories are and that they process one thing at a time
Which hobbies they have and which hand they use for writing and for the work
How much they enjoy puzzles and which they like
What language they speak and how old they are
optionExplain: Right: memories and serial processing are among the invariants.
Hobbies vary, and are not the invariants.
Enjoyment is a personality variable, outside the focus.
Language and age are not the invariants named.
questions.explain: The authors name memory characteristics, seriality and rates, and a production-like, goal-like program organization. The card next lays them out.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Which pair does the authors' list call invariant aspects of global program organization?
options: Parallel character and random character of the program
Recursive character and memorized character
Production-like character and goal-like character
Visual character and aural character
optionExplain: Seriality is claimed, not parallelism.
Recursion was merely a technique used.
Right: these are the two named aspects.
Modality is not a program organization feature.
questions.explain: The two global aspects are that programs are production-like and goal-like.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Sort each item as an invariant the authors add or not an invariant they add.

items.t: Read and write times of the memories
One elementary process at a time
Goal structures in the program
A particular chess opening repertoire
A solver's preferred method for one puzzle
A solver's mood on the day

questions.explain: Memory parameters, seriality and global program organization are invariants; particular repertoires, methods and moods vary by solver or task.
