questions.rule: Invariants are structural, not content or mood.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: If an invariant of the IPS were found to have little effect on problem solving, the authors would still include it in the list of those that matter for the theory.
questions.explain: They say they concern themselves with characteristics that affect problem solving, although they will also mention invariants that do not seem important for the theory.
questions.rule: Relevance to problem solving is the filter.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Why do the authors not review the experimental literature on these characteristics in detail?
options: The literature disagrees with every invariant listed
Only gross characterizations matter for problem solving, and a serious review would exceed the book's limits
No experiments have ever been done on memory
The review would give away the answers to the book's tasks
optionExplain: They say many invariants are independently validated.
Right: the text gives both reasons.
They say many experiments exist.
No such reason is given.
questions.explain: The authors say the existence of many invariants is independently validated, but only gross characterizations are relevant and much literature detail is too fine.
questions.teaches: The authors do not review the external literature, partly because a serious review would exceed an already long book and partly because only gross characterizations of the IPS matter for problem solving.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: An engineer describes a call-center agent only by speed of speech, memory for scripts and ability to hold one conversation at a time. Which of the authors' invariants has she skipped?
options: Memory sizes and access rates of the agent's memories, which she described in full
Seriality of processing
The rate of elementary processes
The goal-like and production-like organization of the program
optionExplain: Script memory covers memories.
One conversation at a time covers seriality.
Speed of speech touches rates.
Right: she covered memory, seriality and rates but not global program organization.
questions.explain: The list has memories, seriality with rates, and two aspects of program organization; her description omits the last.
questions.rule: Check all three kinds of invariants.
questions.teaches: Related to the memory invariants are the serial character of information processing and the rate at which the elementary information processes can be performed.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A library catalog gives each new book entry a code, and other entries can cite that code. What does this resemble in the authors' picture of memory?
options: Memory is limited to a few entries at once, like the catalog, so codes must be reused often
New structures are named by symbols that other structures can contain
Memory is searched one entry after another
Memory forgets old entries to make room
optionExplain: That describes short-term memory.
Right: new names can be embedded as symbols in other structures.
The authors say LTM reading involves no scanning.
They find no evidence LTM fills up.
questions.explain: The card shows how named structures nest. The authors call this the associativity of the IPS.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: The authors assume LTM has an essentially ____ capacity for symbol structures.
questions.explain: There is no evidence that human LTM can be filled in a lifetime.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A student stores a structure linking a city, its country and its river. Later she stores a trade-route structure that includes the symbol for that city. Which feature is this?
options: Content addressing of stored structures by what they contain, as in a lookup table of contents
A serial scan of all stored cities
Decay of an unrehearsed structure
A newly stored structure's name being embedded in another structure
optionExplain: The authors say content addressing is something the scheme does not provide.
Scanning is ruled out for LTM reading.
Decay is discussed for STM.
Right: embedding a designator in another structure is how association works here.
questions.explain: Association is achieved by structures whose parts include names of other structures.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: A reader says the authors prove human associative memory works exactly as sketched, with no need for content addressing. This is their claim.
questions.explain: They admit lacking operational specifications and say other forms such as content addressing may be needed for tasks with heavy LTM processing.
questions.rule: Adequate here, not proven in general.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: What would content addressing add to the authors' scheme?
options: New structures could designate stored ones without those stored ones having been given addresses beforehand
Structures could be stored faster than they are read
Structures could be kept in short-term memory longer
Structures could be erased on demand
optionExplain: Right: this is the capability the authors describe as possibly missing.
Speed is a different issue.
STM duration is not the point.
Erasure is not content addressing.
questions.explain: The authors define content addressing as letting newly constructed symbol structures designate stored ones without previous address assignment.
questions.rule: Content addressing needs no prior address.
questions.teaches: Content addressing would let newly constructed symbol structures designate stored symbol structures without previous assignment of addresses to the latter.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A study asks people to retrieve facts from long lists using complex cues. Based on the card, why might its results fit the authors' simple scheme poorly?
options: Because LTM has a small capacity
Because LTM is read by scanning in proportion to its size
The tasks may involve heavy LTM processing, which the authors say could call for other forms of association
Because symbols cannot be embedded in structures
optionExplain: They assume unlimited capacity.
They deny scanning.
Right: the authors limit their claim to tasks without extensive LTM processing.
Embedding is part of their scheme.
questions.explain: The authors say their tasks do not involve extensive LTM processing, which might call for other forms of association.
questions.rule: Heavy LTM use may need more.
questions.teaches: The authors say their tasks do not involve extensive processing in long-term memory, which might call for other forms of association.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A novice sees six chessmen as six separate pieces. An expert sees a familiar castled setup at a glance. What explains the difference?
options: The expert's eyes take in more pieces at once than the eyes of the novice can, in one fixation
The novice's memory is smaller by nature
The expert counts the pieces faster
Learning has given the expert a single recognizable unit for the whole pattern
optionExplain: Perception is not the explanation given.
The authors do not attribute it to innate capacity.
Counting is not what happens.
Right: recognition developed by learning makes the pattern one unit.
questions.explain: The authors say chunks arise through learning. The card next defines the term.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A stimulus pattern that has come to be recognized and designated by a symbol is called a ____.
questions.explain: That is the authors' term.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A radio operator hears a familiar three-beep call sign as one unit, while a beginner hears three beeps. How many chunks for the operator?
options: One, since the learned pattern is designated by a single symbol
Three, since there are three separate beeps in the call sign and each is heard apart
None, since sounds cannot be chunks
Seven, since memory holds seven
optionExplain: Right: recognition makes the call sign a single chunk.
That is the beginner's count.
The authors count D and 4 as chunks, and other modalities follow by extension.
Seven is a memory capacity, not a count of this pattern.
questions.explain: A learned, recognized pattern is evoked as a single symbol, whatever the number of parts.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: If a novice studied thousands of chess positions, patterns that once needed several symbols could come to be represented by one.
questions.explain: Chunks develop through learning, so new recognizable patterns reduce the symbols needed.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: According to the authors, how many chessmen make up the fianchettoed short-castled position that an expert represents as one chunk?
options: Two
Twelve
Six
Sixteen
optionExplain: Two is the count for a bishop and a pawn, not the full pattern.
Twelve is an unrelated count.
Right: it is an arrangement of six chessmen.
Sixteen is one side's full set.
questions.explain: The authors give six chessmen as the size of that pattern.
questions.teaches: An experienced chess player's fianchettoed short-castled position is one chunk, though it is an arrangement of six chessmen.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A musician treats a familiar eight-note phrase as one unit. Which statement matches the authors' theory?
options: The phrase is eight chunks held in short-term memory at once
The phrase is a chunk with one stored symbol, which recognition evokes
The phrase is innate and needs no learning, being a musical unit that every listener shares
The phrase cannot be represented in memory at all
optionExplain: That would treat each note as a separate chunk.
Right: recognized patterns evoke their stored designator.
Chunks are not innate.
Recognizable patterns are stored as symbols.
questions.explain: The theory applies in any domain: learned recognition turns a many-part pattern into one designated unit.
questions.teaches: On recognition, chunks evoke their stored designators, which serve as the internal representations of the stimulus patterns.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: How long does a person usually need to name the color of a familiar object on seeing it?
options: Around half a second to a second
Several seconds, since the name must be searched for
About a tenth of a millisecond
Around half a minute
optionExplain: Right: associative reaction times are in this range.
Reactions never take many seconds.
That is far too quick.
That is far too slow.
questions.explain: The card next shows these reaction-time findings.
questions.rule: Recognition plus retrieval: about a second.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Reading a symbol structure from LTM takes of the order of a few hundred ____.
questions.explain: That is the authors' estimate.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A librarian has a ten-times-larger collection in her head than a colleague. If LTM reading involved scanning, what would follow, and what do the authors say?
options: Her reads would be the same; the authors say scanning is required
Her reads would be faster; the authors say size speeds retrieval
Her reads would take ten times longer; the authors say LTM reading does not work this way
Her reads would be impossible; the authors say a large LTM fails once it exceeds a certain size
optionExplain: The authors say scanning is not required.
Size does not speed retrieval.
Right: scanning means time proportional to size, which the authors reject for LTM.
LTM is not limited.
questions.explain: Proportionality to size is the signature of scanning; the authors find no such pattern in LTM reading.
questions.rule: No scan: read time not proportional to size.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: A reader says: since some people take many seconds to recall a name, LTM read times can be many seconds. According to the authors, such behavior is the usual LTM access time.
questions.explain: They note such behavior involves repeated accesses in attempts to remember something not retrieved immediately and does not fit a longer access time in the usual sense.
questions.rule: Repeated retrieval is not slow access.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: What does the card say happens to reaction times as difficulties and retrieval-set size increase?
options: They grow in proportion to the memory size or to the retrieval set, as in a scan of the store
They increase somewhat but never become much longer than a second or so
They shrink because of practice
They jump to tens of seconds
optionExplain: That would be scanning.
Right: the increase is modest.
The text reports no such shrinking.
Reactions never take many seconds.
questions.explain: The authors say times increase somewhat with difficulty and ensemble size but in no case become much longer.
questions.teaches: Associative reaction times increase somewhat with task difficulty and uncertainty and with the size of the retrieval ensemble, but never become much longer than about a second.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Your phone's contact search must return an answer for a list ten times larger. Which description matches the authors' account of human memory but not a scan?
options: The answer time grows tenfold with the size of the list
The answer time shrinks tenfold
The answer cannot be given
The answer time barely changes with list size
optionExplain: That is scanning.
No shrinking is claimed.
Retrieval works.
Right: no scanning means no proportionality to size.
questions.explain: The key signature is independence from memory size.
questions.teaches: Reading LTM does not seem to call for scanning, which would produce read times proportional to the size of memory.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A student must memorize a new nonsense word made of four unfamiliar letter pairs. About how long would the authors expect the storing to take?
options: A fraction of a second
Tens of seconds
A few milliseconds
Several hours
optionExplain: That is the time for reading, not writing.
Right: a few chunks at five to ten seconds each gives tens of seconds.
That is even faster.
That is far too slow.
questions.explain: The card next gives the writing rate. Writing is much slower than reading.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Fixating a structure with K familiar subpatterns takes about 5K to 10K ____ of processing time.
questions.explain: The unit is seconds, not milliseconds.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: By the authors' estimate, how long should it take to fixate a new structure built from 6 familiar subpatterns?
options: About 3 to 6 seconds
About 5 to 10 minutes
About 300 to 600 milliseconds
About 30 to 60 seconds
optionExplain: That would be about half to one second per chunk.
That is ten times too long.
That is a read time.
Right: 6 times 5 to 6 times 10 seconds.
questions.explain: K = 6 gives 5K to 10K seconds, that is 30 to 60 seconds.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A learner has 10 minutes and spends nearly all of it on new information. What does the theory predict about the number of new symbols fixated?
options: Fewer than fifty, since each takes several seconds and other processing needs time too
Several hundred, since reading is quick and each new symbol is fixated almost as soon as it is seen
Several thousand, since LTM is infinite
None, since LTM cannot be written to during a task
optionExplain: Right: even 600 seconds at 5 to 10 s each gives at most 120, and most time goes to other processes.
Reading is quick but writing is not.
Capacity is not the limit; time is.
Some fixation does occur.
questions.explain: The authors say a modest number, almost certainly less than fifty, can be fixated in ten minutes of problem solving.
questions.hint: Divide the available seconds by the cost per chunk.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: A student says: since LTM has unlimited capacity, dozens of new facts can be added in a short problem solving session. This reasoning is sound.
questions.explain: Capacity is not the limit; the slow rate of writing is. Unlimited capacity does not mean fast fixation.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A teacher plans a lesson with 40 brand-new, unrelated terms, each needing a fresh chunk, to be learned in a five-minute activity. Using the card, is it realistic?
options: Yes, because reading and writing times are equal
Yes, because LTM stores whole lists at once
No, because 40 chunks at five to ten seconds each would take over three minutes of pure storing, leaving little for anything else
No, because LTM cannot store any new terms in so short a time
optionExplain: Reading and writing times are not equal; writing a chunk to LTM is much slower than reading one.
LTM does not store whole lists at once; each chunk takes its own five to ten seconds.
Right: 40 times 5 to 10 seconds is 200 to 400 seconds.
LTM can store new terms; it is the number of chunks times the storing time that makes the plan unrealistic.
questions.explain: The arithmetic is 200 to 400 seconds of storing alone, out of 300 seconds, so the plan is unrealistic.
questions.teaches: Storing symbolized representations in LTM takes about five to ten seconds per new chunk, which limits how much can be learned in a short session.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Two researchers measure memorization speed. One finds 10 seconds per unit; the other, using herself as subject, finds 3. What is a reasonable response?
options: Discard the slower result as an error of the first researcher and report only the faster figure
Discard the faster result as an error
Average them and say the matter is closed
Treat both as data and look for conditions that explain the difference
optionExplain: There is no basis for discarding it.
There is no basis for discarding it either.
An average hides the difference.
Right: differences call for finding the conditions.
questions.explain: The authors take a typical value while admitting variation. The card next shows how.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: The authors take about ____ to ten seconds per chunk as a typical fixation time.
questions.explain: Five to ten seconds per chunk, correct within half an order of magnitude.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A study on a pair of nonsense syllables measures 70 seconds for the pair. Using seven chunks per pair, what rate per chunk is that?
options: About 10 seconds
About 3 seconds
About 70 seconds
About 0.1 second
optionExplain: Right: 70 divided by 7.
That would need only 21 seconds.
That ignores the number of chunks.
That is far too small.
questions.explain: Per-chunk time is total time divided by the number of chunks fixated.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: A reader says the authors treat five to ten seconds as precisely established. According to the text, this is correct.
questions.explain: They say much work remains to establish the fixation parameter and the conditions that alter it, and claim only half an order of magnitude.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: What hint do the authors mention about why mnemonic learning can be much faster?
options: Mnemonics make LTM larger
Mnemonics remove the need for recognition
Storing new chunks may take much less time than indexing them for retrieval from a stimulus
Mnemonics turn LTM into short-term memory
optionExplain: Capacity is not the point.
Recognition is still involved.
Right: the authors give this as a hint but little more.
STM is a different store.
questions.explain: The authors say there is at least a hint in the data that actually storing chunks takes much less time than indexing them for retrieval.
questions.teaches: There is at least a hint, but little more, that actually storing new chunks requires much less time than indexing them for retrieval when the appropriate stimulus is presented.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A coach claims a new method teaches each fact in 2 seconds. How should a reader following the authors' caution respond?
options: Reject it, since nothing can be learned in 2 seconds, and the coach must have timed something else
Ask what the facts were, how they are associated with prior knowledge, and who the learners were
Accept it, since it overturns the 5 to 10 second figure
Ignore it, since speeds do not vary
optionExplain: The text itself reports rates of two or three seconds.
Right: the authors note fast rates for meaningful, well-associated items and for experienced subjects.
A single claim does not overturn the estimate; the conditions matter.
Speeds do vary.
questions.explain: Fast rates were seen with experienced subjects and with meaningful words tied to overlearned stimuli.
questions.teaches: Experiments with mnemonic schemes appear to show that familiar meaningful words can be learned in two or three seconds if associated meaningfully with previously overlearned stimuli.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A detective must keep many clues in mind during an hour but cannot write them down. Which constraint is most severe?
options: Storing new items is slow compared with using ones already known
Looking up known facts takes many minutes for each one
Long-term memory is quickly filled by the clues of an hour, leaving no room for more
Every clue is stored automatically
optionExplain: Right: the card next explains why writing is the slow side.
Retrieval of known facts is quick.
No evidence of LTM filling is cited.
Storage takes processing time.
questions.explain: The authors stress the gap between reading and writing. The card next draws the implication.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Writing in LTM takes at least a half order of magnitude longer than ____ it.
questions.explain: Five to ten times longer than reading.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A reading takes 0.5 second and fixating a chunk takes 5 seconds. How many reads equal one write?
optionExplain: That is too small.
That is ten times too many.
Right: 5 divided by 0.5.
That is one hundred times too many.
questions.explain: Ten reads in the time of one write at these figures.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: because writing is slow, a ten-minute problem solving session will add only a modest number of new LTM entries, almost certainly under fifty.
questions.explain: Most processing goes to things other than fixation, and each fixation takes seconds.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Beyond new chunks, what else do the authors assume can be designated by symbols in the IPS's memory with similar read and write times?
options: Only sensory patterns of vision, such as those coming from the eye
Processes and output motor patterns
Only numbers in digit spans
Only goals set by the experimenter
optionExplain: Sensory patterns are one of three.
Right: processes and motor patterns are assumed similar to sensory patterns.
Digits are sensory patterns.
Goals are discussed separately.
questions.explain: The authors assume designations of processes and motor patterns resemble those of sensory patterns, with reading and writing times of the same order of magnitude, though the data are unclear.
questions.rule: Processes and motor patterns are symbolized too.
questions.teaches: Symbols may designate processes of the IPS and output motor patterns as well as sensory patterns, and the authors assume their reading and writing times are of the same order of magnitude.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A coaching plan assumes a player will memorize a hundred new opening lines during one ten-minute warmup. What does the card imply?
options: The plan is sound because LTM is infinite
The plan is unsound because LTM reads slowly
The plan is sound because chunks store instantly
The plan overlooks the slow writing time of LTM, which limits new storing to a modest number
optionExplain: Capacity is not the constraint.
Reading is the fast side.
Chunks take seconds each.
Right: a hundred new entries exceeds the under-fifty bound.
questions.explain: The authors say the large read-write difference has much to do with the strategies available.
questions.teaches: The large difference between reading and writing times in LTM has much to do with the problem solving strategies that are available to a human IPS.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: How many unrelated digits can most adults repeat back correctly after hearing them once?
options: About twenty, as long as they are heard at a normal pace
About five to seven
About two
About fifty
optionExplain: That is far above span.
Right: about five to seven, the span the book reports.
That is below the usual span.
That is far above span.
questions.explain: Simple digit-span experiments, as the book reports, put the capacity at about five to seven.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Short-term memory holds about five to ____ symbols.
questions.explain: The classic range is seven plus or minus two.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A chess master holds a familiar six-piece pattern as one chunk. How much STM does that pattern use?
options: Six slots, one per piece
None, since patterns live in LTM only
Seven slots, the full capacity
One slot, although it designates a large structure
optionExplain: That would be a novice's count.
The symbol itself sits in STM.
One chunk does not fill STM.
Right: one symbol can designate a structure of any size.
questions.explain: Capacity is counted in symbols, and a symbol can stand for a whole structure.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: A person who learns many new chunks will, other things equal, be able to hold more information in a span of five to seven symbols.
questions.explain: Each symbol can designate a larger structure, so more information fits.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A reader says: STM holds seven digits, so it can hold seven whole sentences. What is the fault?
options: Capacity is seven symbols; a sentence needs a single chunk or many symbols depending on how it is known
STM cannot hold any sentences
STM holds seven separate letters only
STM holds more than seven by design
optionExplain: Right: a sentence can fit only if each one is recognized as a single chunk.
STM holds symbols of any structure.
Letters count as symbols, not as a restriction.
Capacity is five to seven.
questions.explain: The span is counted in symbols; whether a sentence is one symbol depends on whether it is a chunk.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A menu board lists nine unrelated items. A server memorizes them by grouping into three themed sets of three. Why does this help, per the card?
options: Groups add capacity to LTM, so that more items can be stored for the evening
Groups slow down forgetting in LTM
Each group can be designated by one symbol, so fewer slots are needed
Groups remove the need for recognition
optionExplain: LTM capacity is already unlimited.
The issue is STM slots, not LTM forgetting.
Right: grouping reduces the number of symbols held.
Recognition is how groups evoke symbols.
questions.explain: Grouping into recognized sets reduces symbols below the span of five to seven.
questions.teaches: STM capacity does not vary much over a wide range of tasks, which is why grouping into fewer chunks is the way to hold more.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: You are asked to remember a phone number while counting backward by threes. What happens to your ability to recall the number?
options: It improves, since counting helps rehearsal
It is unchanged, since counting uses a separate store from the number
It improves, since the number moves to LTM
It drops sharply, since the counting uses the same limited store
optionExplain: Counting prevents rehearsal.
The authors say the tasks compete.
LTM fixation is slow.
Right: the card shows why.
questions.explain: The authors cite exactly this kind of finding. The card next explains it.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: The STM can be defined functionally as the set of ____ available to an IPS process at a given instant.
questions.explain: That is the authors' functional definition.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A cook tracks a timer, a count of eggs, and a mental recipe step while chopping. Why might she lose one item when the chopping gets harder?
options: Harder processing occupies more of STM with its inputs and outputs, leaving less for held items
Chopping erases LTM
STM capacity grows with effort
The timer is stored in EM only
optionExplain: Right: the authors suppose missing capacity is used by processes.
LTM writing is slow, not erasure by activity.
The authors say attention subtracts from capacity.
EM is not the explanation here.
questions.explain: Attention-demanding tasks subtract from effective STM capacity.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: A reader says the authors demonstrate that STM is accessed by serial scanning. The authors make this claim.
questions.explain: They say it is hard to distinguish scanning from direct addressing or content addressing, and that at the problem solving level such details make no difference.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: About how many symbols can be retained when a simple processing task is interposed between presentation and recall?
options: About seven
About twenty, since the interposed task uses no memory
Perhaps not more than two
None at all
optionExplain: That is the uninterrupted span.
That is far too many.
Right: the authors say perhaps not more than two.
Some are retained.
questions.explain: The authors cite the counting-backward-by-threes type of interposed task.
questions.rule: Two symbols with an interposed task.
questions.teaches: Only perhaps two symbols can be retained in STM when even a simple task such as counting backward by threes is interposed between presentation and recall.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A driver on a phone call forgets a turn she was told about a moment earlier. Which part of the card helps explain this?
options: LTM writing is fast but unreliable under distraction
Attention-demanding activity subtracts from STM capacity
STM is a serial-scan store that is full after a few turns
The turn was stored in EM
optionExplain: The authors say LTM writing is slow.
Right: the second task takes up capacity.
Access method does not explain loss.
No external store is given.
questions.explain: Active processing occupies STM with inputs and outputs, so held information is crowded out.
questions.rule: Competing tasks crowd out held items.
questions.teaches: Almost all tasks that require attention subtract from the effective capacity of STM as measured by standard tests.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A craftsperson works slowly enough that she rarely forgets a measurement mid-task. What does this suggest about how much decay affects her results?
options: Little, because her pace is adjusted to avoid it
A lot, since decay limits all output regardless of the pace she keeps
None, because memory never decays
A lot, since slower work is always wrong
optionExplain: Right: self-pacing hides decay.
Decay is avoided by pacing.
Information in STM does decay.
Pace is a way to adapt.
questions.explain: The card next states this reasoning.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Because problem solving is ____, the solver can adjust his rate and style so decay and rehearsal do not appear.
questions.explain: That is the authors' reason.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A tutor lets students take as long as they like on each step and finds few slips of memory. Which part of the card does this fit?
options: STM has no limited capacity, so nothing is ever lost from it
Decay is a feature of LTM only
Self-pacing lets solvers adapt so decay rarely shows
Rehearsal is impossible
optionExplain: Capacity is limited.
Decay is discussed for STM.
Right: self-paced work avoids visible decay.
Rehearsal exists.
questions.explain: Self-pacing makes the effect of decay small.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: A more reliable STM would require the authors to add a new time-constant parameter to the theory.
questions.explain: They say its effect, such as faster work, could be absorbed by the parameters measuring processing speed.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: What example of an STM error with a large effect do the authors give?
options: S2 miscounting the pieces of a chess position
S3 spending a long time on a cryptarithmetic problem because he did not recall that T = 0
S8 forgetting a logic rule at the first step
S5 misreading the letters of a word
optionExplain: Not the example given.
Right: this is the cited example, and it shows the point about rare but costly errors.
Not the example given.
Not the example given.
questions.explain: S3's failure to recall T = 0 meant E could not be 0, costing a long time.
questions.teaches: S3 spent a long time on his cryptarithmetic problem because he did not recall that T = 0, so that E could not be 0; the authors treat this as an STM error.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A sports analyst wants to predict a rare lapse of memory by a pilot. What would the authors say the analyst needs?
options: Nothing beyond the speed parameters of the processor
A model of perception covering how the pilot reads the instruments
A larger LTM model covering everything the pilot has learned
An explicit model of STM decay, since the general processing program limits such errors to low frequencies
optionExplain: Speed parameters absorb typical effects, not rare errors.
Perception is not the issue; the lapse concerns STM decay.
LTM size is not the issue; the lapse concerns STM decay.
Right: predicting these errors rather than treating them as exogenous needs an explicit model of decay.
questions.explain: The argument from adaptivity breaks down here because the program keeps errors rare, so predicting them needs a decay model.
questions.rule: Predicting rare errors needs a decay model.
questions.teaches: The argument from adaptivity breaks down for STM errors precisely because the general processing program limits them to low frequencies; to predict them one would need an explicit model of STM decay.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A reader says people evidently do many things at once, so a serial model must be wrong. What is the best reply?
options: Serial means every thought takes the same time
Serial means one elementary information process at a time, which differs from detecting many stimuli
Serial means memory is searched item by item
Serial means no two events can be near in time
optionExplain: Duration is a separate matter.
Right: the authors separate seriality of processes from awareness of many stimuli.
The authors say serial does not imply scanning.
Near-simultaneity of events does not contradict it.
questions.explain: The authors define seriality narrowly. The card next sets it out.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A serial IPS is one that can execute a single elementary information ____ at one time.
questions.explain: That is the authors' definition.
questions.rule: One elementary process at a time.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A cashier notices three customers waiting while counting change for the fourth. According to the authors, does this show the IPS is not serial?
options: Yes, since she attended to four people at once, her processing cannot be serial in any strict sense
Yes, since counting and noticing overlap
No, since people have only one customer at a time
No, detecting the waiting customers is not the same as executing several processes at once
optionExplain: Awareness is not parallel execution.
Noticing is detection, not processing in parallel.
The scenario is not about customer count.
Right: awareness of many things is compatible with seriality.
questions.explain: The authors specify that seriality does not rule out being aware of many things at once in the sense of detection.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: A student says seriality means LTM must be scanned item by item. The authors endorse this.
questions.explain: They say assuming seriality does not imply memories are accessed by serial scan; LTM clearly does not work that way.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: The authors say the claim asserts more than what?
options: The bare logical necessity that behavior is serial when one process needs another's output
The fact that the brain is a parallel organ
The fact that STM is small
The fact that tasks have goals
optionExplain: Right: dependence between processes forces order but seriality claims more.
Physiology is the source of the misunderstanding, not what the claim exceeds.
STM size is a different invariant.
Goals are another invariant.
questions.explain: The assertion is that even independent processes cannot run simultaneously.
questions.rule: Even independent processes wait their turn.
questions.teaches: The statement that the IPS is serial asserts more than the logical necessity that behavior be serial when one process needs another's output: it says only one elementary process runs at a time.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A computer with one processor switches quickly between several programs. Which feature matches the authors' picture of the human IPS?
options: Many operations execute at once in separate units, one unit for each of the programs being run
Every operation scans all memory
Only one elementary operation executes at an instant, whatever the number of tasks pending
Operations take no time
optionExplain: That is parallel.
Scanning is not implied.
Right: seriality refers to one process at a time.
Elementary processes take time (tens of milliseconds).
questions.explain: A single processor gives the same one-at-a-time structure.
questions.teaches: The authors note that the human IPS can be called serial even though the underlying physiological system is highly parallel.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: You time a friend checking whether each of 1, 2 and 4 words is a noun. Which result would suggest serial processing?
options: Time staying the same for all three, whatever the number of words
Time falling as words are added
Time being random
Time rising in step with the number of words
optionExplain: That marks parallel.
No such pattern is expected.
Not a pattern in the test.
Right: proportional growth marks seriality.
questions.explain: The card next gives the authors' test.
questions.rule: Time grows with K means serial.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: If the time to give K answers is ____ of K, the IPS is parallel with respect to that operation.
questions.explain: Parallel means the time does not depend on K.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Checking one number for divisibility by 7 takes 6 seconds, and checking two takes 12 seconds. What does this suggest?
options: A serial process, since time doubled with K
A parallel process, since time grew
Neither, since K must be larger than 2
A parallel process, since both answers were no
optionExplain: Right: time proportional to K.
Parallel would hold time constant.
Two items already show a doubling.
The answers' values do not matter.
questions.explain: Doubling of time with doubling of K is the serial signature.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: A person able to carry two independent control sequences but not more would show equal times for K of 1 and 2, and rising times beyond that.
questions.explain: The authors say a processor may be parallel for two activities but not for three or four.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: What allowance must be made when comparing the pair with the single number in the divisibility test?
options: The time needed to find a calculator and clear the desk
The time needed to rewrite the numbers
The time needed to state two results rather than one
The time needed to reread the instructions
optionExplain: No calculator is used.
Rewriting is not part of it.
Right: stating two answers takes slightly more than one.
Instructions are given in advance.
questions.explain: A parallel processor might still take a little longer to state two answers than one.
questions.teaches: In the divisibility test, due account must be taken of the time to state two results versus one, even for a parallel processor.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A teacher times students spotting whether each of several sentences contains a spelling error. The time grows in proportion to the number of sentences. What does the authors' test suggest?
options: Spotting errors is parallel
Spotting errors is carried out serially for these students
Spelling cannot be tested
Seriality is disproved
optionExplain: That would need constant time.
Right: time proportional to K.
The test works for any learned yes-or-no operation.
It supports seriality.
questions.explain: The test applies to any well-learned operation with a yes-or-no output.
questions.rule: Apply the test to the operation.
questions.teaches: The test applies to any operation Q that the problem solver has learned well and that yields yes or no on symbols of a given class.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A pianist's two hands play different parts of a piece. Is this a clear counterexample to seriality?
options: Not necessarily, since independent motor systems and automated skill can run in parallel, but central control is serial
Yes, because it proves the mind is parallel
Yes, because the two hands are the same process
No, because the hands do not move at once
optionExplain: Right: the authors allow such cases.
That overstates; central control remains serial.
The hands are different motor systems.
The hands do move at once.
questions.explain: The card next shows the authors' qualification.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Whenever central ____ is involved, seriality reestablishes itself even in motor activity.
questions.explain: Parallel motor activity is limited by central control.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Someone walks while chewing gum. Which description fits the authors' view?
options: Both require the same elementary processes in parallel, inside one central processor
Neither is possible
Physically independent motor systems can proceed together, with little central control
Walking requires scanning memory
optionExplain: That would deny seriality of central processes.
Both are possible.
Right: independent motor systems can run in parallel.
Scanning is not the point.
questions.explain: Motor parallelism is possible when systems are physically independent.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: A reader says the authors claim no parallelism at all can ever occur in human activity. This is correct.
questions.explain: They say the human is serial for almost all operations and note some parallelism in highly automated and independent motor activity.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: What does the authors' text say about parallelism in highly automated activities?
options: None appears under any condition
Some parallelism appears, but with concomitant changes in the task actually being performed
Complete parallelism holds
It appears only in motor tasks
optionExplain: The text reports some parallelism.
Right: the authors qualify their claim this way.
They say uncertainty remains.
It is said of automated activities generally.
questions.explain: The text says there is some uncertainty, since some parallelism does appear, but with changes in the actual task being performed.
questions.teaches: For highly automated activities some parallelism does appear, but with concomitant changes in the actual task being performed.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A trainee driver can only steer or shift gears at first, but after months does both. How would the authors read the change?
options: The IPS became parallel for central operations after months of practice at the two tasks
The IPS lost its seriality
The two tasks were always one process
Possibly through automation, with the task itself changed in the process
optionExplain: Central control stays serial.
Seriality is retained.
Nothing says they were one process.
Right: automation can bring apparent parallelism with a changed task.
questions.explain: This applies the card's qualification to learned skills.
questions.teaches: The head-patting and stomach-rubbing trick illustrates both the extent and the limits of parallelism in motor activity.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A very fast cook has a slow fridge on the far wall. Where does the speed bottleneck lie?
options: In the chopping, since it is the fastest part and so the one that limits the work
In the fetching, since the cook spends most of the time waiting for ingredients
In the recipe length
In the plate size
optionExplain: Chopping is fast.
Right: a processor much faster than its supply is mostly idle.
Length is not the limit.
Plates are irrelevant.
questions.explain: The authors apply the same logic to processing speed. The card next shows the figures.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Elementary processes in STM take times of the order of ____ milliseconds.
questions.explain: Careful experiments give about 40 ms.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A system's processes take 1 microsecond but memory access takes 100 milliseconds. By the authors' reasoning, what fraction of time is the processor doing useful work?
options: Nearly all, since the processing is so fast that it fills the time
Exactly half
It makes no difference
Very little, since it is idle waiting for the next structure
optionExplain: Waiting dominates.
No reason for half.
Balance matters.
Right: such a system would be idle most of the time.
questions.explain: The authors argue against microsecond-level processing on these grounds.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: If elementary processes were far slower than memory access, memory access would remain the main bottleneck.
questions.explain: Then the processes themselves would limit speed. The authors say processes could be slower than access but appear not to be.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: What do the authors say would be the evolutionary objection to a processing time of a microsecond?
options: The system would be idle most of the time waiting for input from LTM or the display, so it is hard to see how it would evolve
It would damage the sensory systems that deliver the input, which evolution would not allow
It would need a far larger LTM to supply the input at that rate
It would stop all learning, because storing in LTM takes seconds
optionExplain: Right: the footnote's argument is that such a system would sit idle waiting for input.
The footnote makes no claim about damage to sensory systems; its point is idleness.
No claim is made about LTM size; the argument is that the system would wait for input.
Learning is not the issue; the argument is that a microsecond system would sit idle waiting for input.
questions.explain: The footnote asks how a mechanism that wastes most of its time could ever evolve.
questions.teaches: The authors argue evolutionarily against a microsecond processing time: the system would be idle most of the time waiting for the next symbol structure from LTM or the visual display.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A courier's van is fast but each parcel takes 10 minutes to load. Using the card's idea of balance, what improves throughput most?
options: Buying a faster van
Painting the van
Speeding up loading, since the van is waiting on it
Lengthening the route
optionExplain: The van is already waiting.
Irrelevant.
Right: balance means matching speeds; speeding the slow step helps.
Worsens.
questions.explain: A balanced system has processing times slightly shorter than access times.
questions.teaches: The authors describe processing times slightly shorter than the unit access time as a satisfactory picture of a balanced system.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: How might a person multiply 37 by 43 quickly?
options: Compute it in one step inside short-term memory, with no memory access or substeps at all
Scan all products until one matches the two numbers given
Guess and check once
Either recall the product from memory or run a sequence of smaller steps
optionExplain: The authors find no evidence of such a process.
LTM reading does not scan.
Guessing is not the account given.
Right: these are the two routes the authors recognize.
questions.explain: The card next sets out these two routes.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: The simplest processes are ____ and replace operations.
questions.explain: Elementary processes are compare and replace.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A clerk knows only single-digit tables. For 37 times 43 she multiplies digit by digit and adds. How does the authors' account classify this?
options: A sequence of subprocesses, that is, a program of elementary steps
A single elementary process
An LTM lookup of the product, found in a single access to a stored table of products
A computation inside STM in one step
optionExplain: Right: complex processes are programs of subprocesses.
It needs many steps.
She does not know the product.
The authors find no such process.
questions.explain: Without the product stored, she must use a sequence of elementary operations.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: A person who has memorized every two-digit product can multiply 37 by 43 in about the time of a simple read from LTM.
questions.explain: The product is read out of LTM, nearly as fast as 7 times 3.
questions.rule: Memorized products are read, not computed.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Why does the authors' note say a computer algorithm that avoids LTM may not be realizable in a human?
options: It needs more seconds of writing
It needs no memory at all
It needs conversion between number bases and substantial STM for intermediate results
It needs an external display
optionExplain: Writing time is not the point.
It needs memory, not none.
Right: the note describes binary conversions and storage for intermediates.
No display required.
questions.explain: The footnote says computer algorithms that avoid LTM use representations such as binary, requiring base conversions and substantial STM.
questions.rule: Binary tricks need STM and conversions.
questions.teaches: Computer algorithms that avoid dependence on LTM use representations such as binary, which require processes for converting between number bases and substantial STM for intermediate results.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A pilot recalls a checklist item at once from memory but works out an unfamiliar fuel calculation in steps. Which two forms of complex processing are these?
options: Two kinds of STM-only computation with no memory access
An LTM access and a sequence of subprocesses
Two LTM writes
Two parallel processes
optionExplain: The authors find no such process.
Right: these are the two routes in the card.
Writing is not involved.
Seriality rules out parallel.
questions.explain: Familiar facts are read; unfamiliar ones are built by programs.
questions.teaches: All more complex processes seem to involve either access to LTM or the subdivision of the process into sequences of subprocesses.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A recipe has five steps taking 2, 3, 1, 4 and 2 minutes. The cook finishes each step before starting the next. How long does the whole recipe take?
options: 12 minutes
4 minutes
2 minutes
48 minutes
optionExplain: Right: with steps done one after another, their times add (2+3+1+4+2).
4 minutes is only the longest step; that total would need the steps to run side by side.
2 minutes is the shortest step and ignores most of the work.
Times of steps in sequence add; multiplying them has no meaning here.
questions.explain: The card next states the same principle for the IPS.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: The authors view the time of a composite algorithm as a ____ of the times of its component processes.
questions.explain: Component times add.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A mental multiplication takes 5 memory transfers at 0.4 s and 6 additions at 0.3 s. Predict the total time by summing.
options: 2.3 seconds
5.5 seconds
3.8 seconds
0.7 seconds
optionExplain: Only the transfers? no, 2.0 plus 0.3.
Doubles something.
Right: 5 times 0.4 plus 6 times 0.3.
Just one of each.
questions.explain: Sum: 2.0 + 1.8 = 3.8 seconds.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: A reader says the authors have firmly confirmed time-additivity for all complex processes. The text supports this.
questions.explain: They call the matter cloudy and the evidence incomplete, with difficulties for complex processes.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: What was the one recent success that the authors mention?
options: A study of chess eye movements
A study of mental multiplication that predicted total time by adding component times
A study of nonsense syllables
A study of the alphabet running time
optionExplain: Not cited here.
Right: Dansereau's study.
Not the success cited.
That is the linear search result.
questions.explain: Dansereau predicted totals by adding times, mostly memory transfer times.
questions.teaches: One recent study of mental multiplication had some success predicting total times by adding up the component times, mostly memory transfer times.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A software team adds the average time of each step in a workflow and gets a poor match with the observed total in a branching process. How does this compare with the authors' findings?
options: It disproves seriality
It is impossible
It shows memory is parallel
It resembles the difficulties found for composite models of complex processes
optionExplain: Seriality is not tested.
Possible.
No link.
Right: complex composites gave trouble in the cited work.
questions.explain: The authors note composite models of complex processes ran into difficulties.
questions.teaches: Simple linear times have been found for linear searches such as running down the alphabet, but composite models of more complex processes have run into difficulties.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A researcher studies how people solve a puzzle displayed on a screen throughout. Does the exact decay time of the retina's brief afterimage matter?
options: Yes, because it limits every move
Probably not, since the display stays in view
Yes, because it determines the solution
Probably not, since vision is irrelevant to puzzles
optionExplain: It would matter if display vanished.
Right: a persistent display makes the buffer irrelevant.
Not what determines the answer.
Vision matters for reading it.
questions.explain: The card next explains why.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: The theory need only postulate that externally written letters are ____ directly and produce internal symbols in STM.
questions.explain: Direct recognition is the summary.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A task flashes a grid for a fraction of a second and then asks for a part of it. Does the authors' simplification still hold?
options: Yes, because buffers never matter in any laboratory task, however brief the display
Yes, because grids are discrete
No, because the display remains visible
Not necessarily, because the visual buffer store would then matter
optionExplain: It matters when displays vanish.
Discreteness does not decide.
The display vanishes in this scenario.
Right: Sperling-type tasks are where the buffer shows.
questions.explain: The authors say the buffer is revealed by tasks where display is removed; their displays stay visible.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: A reader says the authors deny that the visual buffer store exists. The text supports this.
questions.explain: They say it may be present and active but does not significantly affect problem solving at their level of detail.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: About how long does recognizing a letter, digit or chess element take, taken as a primitive?
options: Perhaps forty or fifty milliseconds
About five seconds, as for a hard decision
About half a minute
About a microsecond
optionExplain: Right: this is the estimate.
That is fixation time.
Far too long.
Far too short.
questions.explain: Recognition is a nonproblematic process of perhaps 40 or 50 ms taken as an unanalyzed primitive.
questions.teaches: Recognition of the elements in these tasks, under the experimental illumination and distance, requires perhaps forty or fifty milliseconds and is taken as an unanalyzed primitive process.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A study of reading speed in dim light would likely need what the authors can omit?
options: Nothing about perception
A theory of goals
Detailed sensory processing, since visual detail would matter there
A model of LTM fixation
optionExplain: Perception would matter.
Not the point.
Right: tasks differing from theirs may need the detail.
Not the point.
questions.explain: The authors say such detail might be important for tasks different from those studied.
questions.teaches: Perceptual detail might well be important for tasks different from those studied, or for explaining the processes of reading or writing information externally.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Why would a puzzle of digits in rows and columns be less affected by the details of visual pattern recognition than a photograph of a crowd?
options: Its elements are all identical
Its elements are invisible, so that visual pattern recognition has little to do with solving the puzzle
Its elements are moving
Its elements are discrete and familiar and laid out in conventional ways
optionExplain: Not identical.
They are visible.
They are static.
Right: simple familiar arrangements are recognized immediately.
questions.explain: The card next states this reasoning.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: The chess board is an 8 by 8 square and its men belong to ____ familiar types.
questions.explain: There are six types of man.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: In the logic task, expressions are horizontal strings. How may subjects encode them, according to the authors?
options: As phrase-structure trees, using parenthesis notation
As pictures with no structure of any kind
As random character strings with no grouping of the symbols
As sounds
optionExplain: Right: parentheses let them be encoded as trees.
They are structured.
They are structured.
Visual display.
questions.explain: Parenthesis notation allows encoding as phrase-structure trees.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: If the puzzle letters were in an unfamiliar script, the assurance that pattern recognition does not matter would be weaker.
questions.explain: The authors' assurance rests on familiar discrete elements recognized immediately. This is our reading of their argument.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: How many directions for legal chess moves do the rules encourage subjects to use in encoding patterns?
options: Four
Eight
Sixteen
Sixty-four
optionExplain: Fewer.
Fewer.
Right: sixteen possible directions.
That is the number of squares.
questions.explain: The authors say rules encourage encoding according to the sixteen possible directions for legal moves.
questions.teaches: The rules of chess encourage encoding complex geometric patterns according to the sixteen possible directions for legal chess moves.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A study uses abstract blobs of changing shape as puzzle elements. Why might its authors be unable to make the same assurance?
options: Blobs cannot be seen
Unfamiliar, non-discrete elements may bring pattern-recognition properties into play
Blobs have no memory
Blobs are serial
optionExplain: They can be seen.
Right: the assurance rests on simple discrete familiar elements.
Not relevant.
Not relevant.
questions.explain: The authors' safeguard is the simple discrete displays and cultural expectations.
questions.teaches: In cryptarithmetic, subjects' previous experience with arithmetic conventions encourages encoding the rows and columns in the standard way, and no evidence shows any subject treated the pattern otherwise.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Does the brain need a separate memory mechanism for pictures and for sounds?
options: According to the authors, no: the same central memories hold both, organized differently
Yes, one for each sense
Yes, but only for sounds
No, because there are no memories
optionExplain: Right: modality comes from organization.
That is rejected.
Not stated.
Memories exist.
questions.explain: The card next states this postulate.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Stored information acquires its modality by the way it is ____, not by hardware differences in central structures.
questions.explain: Organization gives modality.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A subject recalls a melody by humming it to find the next note. Which claim of the theory is illustrated?
options: Separate hardware for aural information, kept apart from the central memories that hold the other kinds
LTM cannot store sounds
Information can be organized in an aural way within the same central memories
STM is empty
optionExplain: Rejected.
Not stated.
Right: aural organization within shared memory.
Not stated.
questions.explain: The central memories can be used to organize aural information.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: A reader says the authors claim the IPS cannot tell visual stored information from aural. The text supports this.
questions.explain: They say the IPS can distinguish them; the difference lies in organization.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: What is the authors' evidence for the postulate?
options: The cryptarithmetic protocols of the subjects
The analysis of chess perception in Chapter 13
Digit-span experiments run in the laboratory with adult subjects
Reaction-time studies
optionExplain: Not cited here.
Right: they refer to chess perception.
Not cited here.
Not cited here.
questions.explain: They say what they mean should be clear from the Chapter 13 discussion.
questions.teaches: The authors point to the discussion of chess perception in Chapter 13 as showing that modality arises from how central capabilities are used.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A designer argues that visual and verbal memory must be built on different brain machinery. Which part of the card is the authors' reply?
options: Modality is irrelevant to perception, so that no design of the machinery could ever show the difference
All memory is verbal
All memory is visual
Modality may arise from how a common structure is used to organize information
optionExplain: Not stated.
Not stated.
Not stated.
Right: organization, not hardware.
questions.explain: The theory postulates common central structures.
questions.teaches: In all three tasks the external visual stimulus, continually available, played a major role, so complete programs must include processes for scanning and recognizing its components.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Two words sound alike but are spelled differently. If a person's memory stores them almost identically, which modality is the encoding?
options: Visual, since the spelling of the two words differs
Aural, since similarity of sound is preserved
Neither, since encodings are random
Motor, since words are spoken
optionExplain: Visual would keep spelling similarity.
Right: sound similarity preserved.
Not random.
Not the criterion.
questions.explain: The card next states the criterion.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: The second criterion is relational ____, in which external and internal structures correspond.
questions.explain: Isomorphism of relations.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A subject without a display, in Number Scrabble, tries to complete a triplet from 3 and 9. What does this indicate?
options: He used the magic square, which is the visual form of the game he was asked to play
He forgot the rules
He used a parallel process
His internal representation was not the visual magic square
optionExplain: That would not favor 3 and 9.
Not indicated.
Not indicated.
Right: 3 and 9 do not lie in a line in the square.
questions.explain: A visual encoding would not link 3 and 9 as a winning pair.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: If tout and taut are encoded more alike than taut and taught, the encoding of these words is visual.
questions.explain: Spelling similarity is preserved, which marks a visual encoding.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: In which game did the authors discuss relational isomorphism earlier?
options: Number Scrabble (with tic-tac-toe and the magic square, Chapter 3)
Chess
Cryptarithmetic
Logic
optionExplain: Right: Chapter 3.
Not that.
Not that.
Not that.
questions.explain: It was illustrated by tic-tac-toe, Number Scrabble and the magic square in Chapter 3.
questions.teaches: The earlier discussion of tic-tac-toe, Number Scrabble and the magic square in Chapter 3 illustrates relational isomorphism between external and internal structures.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Two color swatches look similar but their names sound very different. A person's memory treats them as near-identical. Which criterion does this show?
options: Relational isomorphism with an aural modality, from the sounds of the names
No modality
Similarity preserved in a visual modality
Motor modality
optionExplain: Wrong modality.
There is a modality.
Right: similar appearance, similar encoding.
No motor link.
questions.explain: External similarity in the visual domain is mirrored.
questions.teaches: Preservation of modality is a matter of degree: encodings may preserve similarity or relational structure to different extents.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Make a rough estimate: compared with doing it entirely in the head, how much time does multiplying two four-digit numbers with paper and pencil take?
options: About half the time
About nine tenths of the time
The same time
About one hundredth of the time
optionExplain: Far more than that: the authors put the saving at about two orders of magnitude.
Far more than that: the saving is about a hundredfold, not ten percent.
Paper makes a large difference: it saves roughly a hundredfold in time.
Right: the authors estimate about 1 to 100.
questions.explain: The card next gives the authors' estimate.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: The ratio of times to multiply two four-digit numbers with and without paper and pencil is about 1 to ____.
questions.explain: The authors give a ratio of about 1 to 100.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A planner moves from keeping a seating plan in her head to drawing it on paper. Which claim of the card is relevant?
options: The program she uses will depend on the external memory available
Her LTM capacity grows
Her STM decays slower
Her processes become parallel
optionExplain: Right: EM shapes the program.
No.
No.
No.
questions.explain: Programs cannot be specified independently of their EM.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: A reader says the benefit of paper is only that it writes faster than LTM. The authors agree this is the whole story.
questions.explain: They say the matter is deeper: dispensing with the display makes the task much harder even when only scanning is allowed.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: What did the authors note about the difficulty of blindfold chess analysis or cryptarithmetic done in the head?
options: It is easier since there is less clutter
It is equal in difficulty
It is much harder even when writing into EM is not permitted and only scanning is allowed
It requires a faster LTM
optionExplain: Opposite.
Not equal.
Right: dispensing with the display makes the task harder.
Not stated.
questions.explain: Even scanning alone helps.
questions.teaches: Even when writing into EM is not permitted and only scanning it is allowed, dispensing with the external display makes the task much harder.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A new employee is told to run a complex checklist without any written copy. What does the card predict?
options: Identical performance
Slower, more error-prone work and a different procedure from someone with the written list
Faster work
No role for STM
optionExplain: Contradicts.
Right: program depends on EM.
Contradicts.
Not stated.
questions.explain: Applying the card.
questions.teaches: One can predict the problem solving program of an IPS only after characterizing the external memories available to it.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A student solving a puzzle keeps glancing at a number on the page rather than memorizing it. How should we count the number?
options: As part of her working memory for as long as it stays in view
As stored in long-term memory once she has seen it a few times and no longer needs the page
As outside the problem altogether
As taking up no capacity anywhere
optionExplain: Right: the viewed symbol serves as extra short-term store.
Nothing was fixated; writing LTM is slow.
It is used in the task, so it is part of the system.
It extends capacity, so it does matter.
questions.explain: The authors treat it as part of the functional STM. The card next gives their definition.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: The part of the display in foveal view acts as a ____ memory that augments the internal STM.
questions.explain: It can be read but not written.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A cook follows a recipe pinned in front of her, reading each line when needed. What does the card say about her working memory?
options: It excludes the recipe, which is part of long-term memory and so outside her working memory
It must hold the whole recipe internally
It includes the lines in view, which relieve her internal short-term store
It becomes parallel in processing
optionExplain: The recipe is external, not LTM.
Display in view removes that need.
Right: the displayed lines augment the short-term store.
Seriality is unaffected.
questions.explain: The view is merged functionally with STM.
questions.rule: Display in view counts as STM.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: A reader says the authors have shown that every symbol in the display must be re-read into internal STM before it can influence behavior. The text supports this.
questions.explain: They say it is unclear: foveal symbols that stay in view may count as STM without re-reading.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Why do reaction-time experiments fail to settle whether foveal symbols are already part of STM?
options: They never involve vision
They almost always change the external stimulus, so an act of recognition is required anyway
They measure LTM only
They avoid reaction times
optionExplain: They involve vision.
Right: a new stimulus must be recognized, hiding the question.
They include STM tasks.
They record reaction times.
questions.explain: A changed stimulus forces recognition, whatever the merge.
questions.teaches: Reaction-time experiments do not address whether foveal symbols are part of STM, since they almost always involve a change in external stimulus, after which an act of recognition is required.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A chess player keeps the board in view and uses her eyes to recheck an attacked square. Which benefit does this give according to the card?
options: It adds new items to LTM quickly
It speeds up all processes tenfold
It makes the board part of LTM
Fixed information is held externally, relieving internal STM of maintaining it
optionExplain: LTM writing is slow.
No such speed claim.
The board is external memory.
Right: external augmentation relieves STM.
questions.explain: The external augmentation can hold the fixed information that STM would otherwise have to maintain.
questions.teaches: External augmentation of STM can relieve the internal STM of maintaining fixed information, and could affect rehearsal strategies if a region larger than the fovea, reached by saccades, counts.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: How long does writing a symbol on paper take compared with fixating a new chunk in long-term memory?
options: About the same, five to ten seconds for each symbol
Far shorter, about a second for a familiar symbol
Far longer, minutes
Impossible to measure
optionExplain: That is LTM fixation.
Right: external writing is quick for overlearned symbols.
Writing is quick.
It has been measured.
questions.explain: The card next gives the writing times.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Writing an overlearned symbol into EM takes roughly one ____ per symbol.
questions.explain: About a second per symbol.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A student who knows a word aloud but not how to spell or write it tries to note it down. Which part of the card applies?
options: EM writing is always fast
EM is associative
EM has small capacity
Writing slows or fails when internal symbols lack simple external names
optionExplain: Not when mapping is missing.
EM is not associative.
EM is essentially infinite.
Right: easily recorded external symbols are needed.
questions.explain: The Chinese ideogram example makes the point.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: Putting a long, unindexed pile of notes in EM would make later retrieval easy because EM is associative.
questions.explain: EM is not associative; it must be accessed by scanning or from addresses held in STM.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: What does the card say about the time to read from remote EMs such as a distant bookshelf?
options: Access times become larger as more extensive motor behavior and physical distance are involved
They equal LTM reading times
They are always shorter than saccades
They do not depend on distance
optionExplain: Right: distance and motion add time.
Only nearby EM is like LTM.
Saccades are the fastest.
Distance matters.
questions.explain: Remote stores such as work sheets, nearby books and libraries are slower.
questions.teaches: More remote EMs, such as the worksheet on the side of the table or books in the library, have increasingly large access times as motor behavior and distance grow.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A mathematician writes intermediate results on a board during a long proof. Which comparison fits the card?
options: Writing is slower than LTM fixation
Reading takes seconds per symbol
Writing there is quick compared with LTM fixation, and reading it back costs a few hundred milliseconds
Writing takes no time at all
optionExplain: It is far faster.
A few hundred ms.
Right: this is the pattern described.
It takes about a second.
questions.explain: Write about a second, read a few hundred ms, versus 5 to 10 s for LTM.
questions.teaches: Reading from EM, like reading from LTM, takes a few hundred milliseconds, while writing to EM is much faster than writing to LTM.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A chess player may not move pieces while thinking. What strategy might arise to explore a line and come back?
options: Writing down every position reached, which the rules of the game allow at each move
Storing all positions in long-term memory
Skipping search altogether
Re-examining the starting position repeatedly because it stays on the board
optionExplain: Writing was not allowed.
LTM writing is slow.
Search is needed.
Right: the board is a stable record of the start.
questions.explain: The authors link progressive deepening to the absence of external writing in chess.
questions.rule: No writing, return to the start.
