questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: In the chess experiments no ____ was permitted, because the touch-move rule was enforced.
questions.explain: No external writing was allowed.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: In the logic task, new expressions were added to the display without erasing old ones. What does that give the subject?
options: A growing external record of earlier results
A way to erase mistakes from earlier steps of the work
A smaller display
A faster LTM
optionExplain: Right: expressions accumulate in EM.
Nothing was erased.
The display grew.
LTM is unaffected.
questions.explain: Annexing without erasing preserves earlier work.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: If chess subjects had been allowed to write down variations, the authors' reasoning suggests the retracing of the initial position would probably decrease.
questions.explain: Our reading: progressive deepening stands out in chess because no external writing was allowed, so notes would reduce the need to retrace.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: In the cryptarithmetic experiment with eye movements, what did the subject have for storing letter-digit assignments?
options: Unlimited writing on the display, with a page of room for every assignment he made
A pocket notebook
A verbal-auditory external memory, with no writing on the display
No memory at all
optionExplain: No writing was allowed.
Not mentioned.
Right: the subject had to speak them.
A verbal EM was provided.
questions.explain: No writing whatsoever was permitted in that experiment, so a verbal-auditory EM was given.
questions.teaches: In the experiment with eye movements no writing whatsoever was permitted on the display, but the subject was given a verbal-auditory EM for letter-digit assignments.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A manager bans notes in a meeting so people can only listen. Which prediction follows from the card?
options: Participants will remember everything better
Participants will adopt repeated checking and reviewing strategies to compensate
Participants will stop using memory
Participants will become faster
optionExplain: Not predicted.
Right: removing EM changes the program.
Not predicted.
Not predicted.
questions.explain: EM arrangements affect programs profoundly.
questions.teaches: A problem solving program cannot be specified independently of its EM, any more than independently of its internal STM and LTM.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Two programmers can write the same result in different languages. Why might one still care which language a model of the mind uses?
options: Because to describe methods in detail one needs some language, and the choice can affect how easily programs are identified
Because languages differ in what they can compute
Because the brain runs a particular compiler
Because the choice changes the results of experiments
optionExplain: Right: these are the authors' two reasons.
They have about the same power.
Not claimed.
Not claimed.
questions.explain: The card next sets out the reasons.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: The authors say all programming languages have about the same power of ____.
questions.explain: Anything stated in one can be stated in the others.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A team studies how people plan trips and wants to describe each planning method step by step. Which of the authors' reasons applies?
options: Languages differ in what behaviors they can generate
Languages change the subject's behavior while it is being described
A language is needed to speak about the structure of methods
Languages are all equally irrelevant to description
optionExplain: Same power.
Not the case.
Right: without some language, methods cannot be described in detail.
Describing needs one.
questions.explain: The first reason concerns the need to adopt a language.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: A reader says the authors argue that the choice of programming language decides which behaviors a model can produce. This is their view.
questions.explain: They say any reasonable organization could produce the behaviors studied; the choice has only second-order effects.
questions.rule: Choice matters little to what is possible.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: According to the footnote, where do real differences among programming languages lie?
options: In what can be computed
In naming ability, available data structures and basic features such as memory allocation
In how fast humans think
In how many people use them
optionExplain: Computing power is equal.
Right: those are named differences.
Not relevant.
Not relevant.
questions.explain: Given associative LTM and complete-access STM, those differences are irrelevant here.
questions.rule: Differences are in naming, data structures, allocation.
questions.teaches: Differences among programming languages lie mainly in naming ability, data structures and basic system features such as memory allocation, which are irrelevant given associative LTM and completely accessible STM.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Two historians describe the same war in different vocabularies, one of which makes a causal pattern easier to spot. Which of the authors' reasons does this resemble?
options: Equal power makes any choice impossible
The need to adopt no language
Differences in computing power
Second-order effects: a representation can make a program easier to identify or understand
optionExplain: Not what the reason says.
A language is needed.
Power is the same.
Right: a representation can ease identification.
questions.explain: Representations may make it easier to determine in detail what program is used.
questions.teaches: A particular program representation may make it easier to determine in detail what program is being used, or easier to understand how learning and assembly of programs take place.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A trainer teaches a new employee by adding one small rule at a time, such as listen first when a customer is angry. Which kind of program organization does this resemble?
options: A fixed flow diagram with boxes and arrows and a set order of steps
A set of independent condition-action rules
A single long subroutine
A table of memorized numbers
optionExplain: A flow diagram has a fixed structure.
Right: condition-action rules are productions.
Not rule-by-rule.
Not rules.
questions.explain: The card next lists the benefits of this organization.
questions.rule: Rules grow one at a time.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Composition in a production system is simple: manufacture a new production and ____ it to the set.
questions.explain: Productions are independent and just added.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A manual is rewritten from a flowchart into a list of independent if-then lines. Which advantage of the card does this show?
options: The list can express fewer calculations
The list depends on the order of every line
The list cannot grow
Information is encoded homogeneously, with no separate box contents and flow structure
optionExplain: Productions express arbitrary calculations.
Each is independent, with only some ordering information.
It grows by addition.
Right: one format carries all the instructions.
questions.explain: Homogeneity is the second advantage.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: A learner who meets a new situation can add behavior to a production system by creating a new production, without rewriting the existing ones.
questions.explain: Independent fragments make growth easy: the law of composition is to make a new production and add it.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: In what sense do the authors say there remains some division of information between content and structure in a production system?
options: Only to the extent that the ordering of productions carries additional information
None at all, in any sense
Entirely, as in flow charts
Because productions share variables
optionExplain: Right: ordering may carry some structural information.
They say the division mostly does not exist.
Flow charts divide it.
Not stated.
questions.explain: The division largely vanishes, except for what the ordering of productions adds.
questions.teaches: In a production system the division between box content and flow structure does not exist, except to the extent that the ordering of productions carries additional information.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A software team replaces a hand-built decision tree with many independent business rules. Which claim from the card helps explain why updates become simpler?
options: Every rule must be rewritten for each change
The rules share a single flow of control
Each rule is an independent fragment, so a new one can be added without disturbing others
The rules cannot be combined
optionExplain: Not needed.
Flow is not shared.
Right: simple law of composition.
They can be combined.
questions.explain: Independence yields easy growth.
questions.teaches: Production systems are the most homogeneous form of programming organization known, according to the authors.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A rule says: when the light turns red, brake. How is this like and unlike a pure stimulus-response link?
options: Identical in every respect
Unlike it because it has no condition
Like it only because it is learned
Like it in being a response evoked by a condition; unlike it if the condition requires matching and holding values
optionExplain: The authors say identification is overly simple.
A production has a condition.
Learning is not the comparison.
Right: productions add matching, operand identification and subroutines.
questions.explain: The card next states the comparison.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Productions might express the ____ of truth that exists in the stimulus-response position.
questions.explain: The authors' wording is the kernel of truth.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A production says: when a letter has a known value, find another occurrence and use it. Which extra property beyond plain S-R does it show?
options: Matching a condition and identifying the operand to act on
A response with no condition attached to it, fired whenever any letter appears on the page
A purely innate reflex
A memory of the whole history
optionExplain: Right: matching and operand identification.
It has a condition.
Not innate.
Not required.
questions.explain: Productions include matching and operand identification.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: A reader says the authors identify productions fully with S-R units. The text supports this.
questions.explain: They call such identification overly simple.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: What qualification do the authors add to the claim that productions are meaningful components?
options: The productions were found by machine without human choice, so they cannot be questioned
The productions were proven by experiment
They defined them that way as scientists, though the organization still describes the data
The productions are meaningless
optionExplain: The scientists defined them.
Not proven.
Right: this concession is stated.
They say meaningful.
questions.explain: Part of the meaningfulness reflects the authors' own aims.
questions.teaches: The meaningfulness of productions is partly because the scientists sought to define them that way, but the authors say it remains true that such an organization of meaningful pieces describes the data.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A consultant says her checklist rules are meaningful business steps. A skeptic points out she wrote them herself. Which authors' point does the skeptic echo?
options: That rules cannot be meaningful if they are written by anyone
That meaningfulness is partly built in by the definers
That rules are innate
That rules must be ordered
optionExplain: Not claimed.
Right: same concession.
Not claimed.
Not claimed.
questions.explain: The authors acknowledge the same caveat.
questions.teaches: Productions have properties of matching, operand identification and subroutine calling not apparent in the usual S-R formulations, including S-R theory extended to handle internal processing.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A to-do list is a shared notice board: each helper acts only when it sees a note relevant to them, then posts new notes. What plays the role of the board in a production system?
options: Short-term memory
Long-term memory
The program counter
The experimenter
optionExplain: Right: STM is the working memory the productions consult and change.
LTM holds the productions here.
There is no program counter.
Not part of the system.
questions.explain: The card next states the link.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: In a production system the dynamic working memory is the ____.
questions.explain: Productions are contingent on STM contents.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: In cryptarithmetic, FC is followed by PC. How can a one-action-per-production system express this?
options: The first production calls a subroutine stack kept outside STM and returns when it is done
Both run at once in parallel
The first production leaves a linking symbol in STM that evokes the second
The second is hard-wired to the first, with no symbol passed on
optionExplain: The stack would be linking symbols in STM.
Seriality forbids.
Right: linking symbols carry control in STM.
Hard-wiring is the flow-chart way.
questions.explain: The linking symbol identifies the next stage.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: If STM holds linking symbols that act as subroutine pointers, the control apparatus is largely assimilated to the structure of STM.
questions.explain: The authors say almost all the program control apparatus is assimilated to the structure of STM.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: What does 'awareness' mean in the authors' functional definition of STM?
options: That the subject can describe the information aloud
That the subject's immediately subsequent behavior can be a function of the information, not that he can report it
That the information is stored in LTM
That the information is outside STM
optionExplain: Reporting may fail; interruption can lose information.
Right: this is the footnote's meaning.
Not LTM.
It is in STM.
questions.explain: The footnote warns that a subject absorbed in the task may not be aware in a monitoring sense.
questions.teaches: Awareness here means that the subject's immediately subsequent behavior can be a function of the information; interrupting to evoke a reporting program may lose the information from STM.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A flowchart-based program for a task uses unexplained internal variables. Which advantage of production systems does this contrast with?
options: Production systems have no working memory of any kind, which is why they are simple
Flowcharts always use STM
Production systems require unexplained machinery
Production systems tie their working memory to a directly defined construct, STM
optionExplain: Productions have one.
Not so.
Reverse.
Right: other organizations hide unexplained machinery.
questions.explain: Other organizations contain implicitly an unknown amount of machinery needing psychological explanation.
questions.teaches: Other organizations, such as the GPS flow diagram or sequential algebraic programs like that for LT, contain implicitly an unknown amount of machinery that still requires psychological explanation.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A smart assistant stores a fact by adding a rule that links a question to its answer. What is notable about this design?
options: Facts are kept in a separate table from the instructions
Facts and instructions are not kept apart
Rules are discarded after use
It cannot learn anything new
optionExplain: That is the conventional design.
Right: data and program merge.
Rules persist.
It learns by adding rules.
questions.explain: The card next gives the authors' suggestion.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: If LTM were a production system, storing a new item would be equivalent to creating a new ____.
questions.explain: Learning is production creation.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: On this view, what does retrieving a stored fact amount to?
options: Scanning all of LTM
Copying a table entry
Erasing the production
Selecting a production whose condition matches the contents of STM
optionExplain: Scanning is denied.
No separate table.
No erasure.
Right: retrieval is selection.
questions.explain: Retrieval from LTM is just selecting one production.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: A reader says the authors firmly conclude that LTM holds no facts apart from productions. The text supports this.
questions.explain: They call it an intriguing possibility.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: What would the possibility imply about the basic distinction between data and program?
options: That no such basic distinction exists in LTM
That it is sharp and fixed, with data and programs stored apart
That data are held only in STM
That programs are held only in EM
optionExplain: Right: LTM would be one large production system.
It would vanish.
Not implied.
Not implied.
questions.explain: The suggestion erases the data-program distinction in LTM.
questions.teaches: On the possibility that LTM is only a very large production system, there would be no basic distinction between data and program, and taking a new item into LTM would be equivalent to creating a new production.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A start-up stores customer facts as conditional rules rather than rows in a table. Which part of the authors' suggestion does this mirror?
options: Keeping data strictly apart from programs in separate tables, each with its own access rules
Using a serial scan for retrieval
Treating stored knowledge as productions instead of separate data
Storing facts only in the display
optionExplain: Opposite.
Retrieval is selection.
Right: facts as rules.
EM is not mentioned.
questions.explain: This mirrors the suggested view.
questions.teaches: Retrieval from LTM, on this view, is the process of selecting one production from memory, the most obvious way to arrange the memory.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A clerk reacts only to what lands on her desk, while another often acts on her own earlier notes. Which looks more stimulus-bound?
options: The second, whose actions respond to her own earlier notes more than to the desk
Neither, since both use memory
Both identically
The first, whose actions mostly respond to external inputs
optionExplain: Notes are internal.
The difference is in what drives actions.
They differ.
Right: reliance on external input marks stimulus-boundness.
questions.explain: The card next gives this criterion.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: In a production system, all connection between adjacent actions is mediated by the contents of working memory, the ____.
questions.explain: Working memory is STM.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A system's productions mostly have conditions on symbols produced by its own previous productions. How will it look from outside?
options: Not stimulus-bound, since its behavior follows internal symbols
Very stimulus-bound
Unable to act
Entirely random
optionExplain: Right: internal triggers make it look independent.
Opposite.
It acts.
It follows rules.
questions.explain: Internally produced symbols drive the behavior.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: If almost all productions take an external symbol as part of their condition, the system will look very stimulus-bound.
questions.explain: That follows from the authors' criterion.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: What do the authors conclude about the overly focused, nondistractable character some critics attribute to programming models?
options: It is inevitable in any program
It is false of all computers
It is not a structural feature of production organization but depends on the particular productions present
It proves productions cannot model people
optionExplain: Not inevitable.
Not claimed.
Right: it depends on contents.
Not claimed.
questions.explain: The authors cite Reitman and Neisser as having alleged it.
questions.teaches: The nondistractable character alleged for programming models by critics is not a structural feature of a production organization; it depends on the particular productions that the system contains.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A support bot reacts to each message and nothing else; a planner bot mostly follows its own sub-plan notes. How would the authors describe the difference?
options: The bots differ in whether they have working memory
The bots differ in the mix of external and internal symbols in production conditions, not in structure
Only the first is a production system
Only the second can be distracted
optionExplain: Both have it.
Right: same structure, different productions.
Both are.
Distraction depends on conditions.
questions.explain: The same organization can look stimulus-bound or independent.
questions.teaches: STM, as the stimulus for productions, is a combination of the internal short-term store and the foveal parts of the visual field, so the stimulus is per se neither internal nor external.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A switchboard operator decides which line to connect by checking which note on the board fits. What is this like in a production system?
options: Matching production conditions against the contents of STM
Scanning all of long-term memory for the matching note, one item after another in turn
Writing a new fact into EM
Deleting the working memory
optionExplain: Right: discrimination is matching.
LTM retrieval is not by scan.
Not this.
Not this.
questions.explain: The card next describes discrimination as matching.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: In a production system, discriminating is the act of selecting the next ____.
questions.explain: Matching conditions selects it.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: STM first holds (A = 4 new), later (A = 4). Which statement do the authors make?
options: The tag was certainly deleted
A new expression was certainly created
The models cannot tell if the tag was deleted or a new expression was created
STM was cleared
optionExplain: Not certain.
Not certain.
Right: the models are not detailed enough to decide.
Not claimed.
questions.explain: Both schemes fit.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: A reader says a production system needs explicit processes for shuffling information within STM. The authors agree.
questions.explain: They say matching treats STM as a content-addressed memory, so no explicit shuffling is needed.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Which operations does a production system still require beyond matching and placing expressions in STM?
options: Scanning STM serially, one symbol after another, to find a matching condition
Writing in LTM and interfacing with the external world
Rotating productions
Compiling flow charts
optionExplain: STM is content-addressed.
Right: these are the only others.
No rotation.
No flowcharts.
questions.explain: Their exact specification lies outside the data.
questions.teaches: The only other elementary processes a production system requires are processes to write in LTM and to interface with the external world; the book's data do not specify them exactly.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: In an office the filing clerk retrieves a file by recognizing a cue on the desk, with no search of the cabinet. Which part of the authors' picture fits?
options: Retrieval needs a scan of the whole memory, item by item
Retrieval needs explicit shuffling of items in STM to find the file
Retrieval needs EM writing
Retrieval is selecting a production whose condition matches STM
optionExplain: No scan.
No shuffling.
No EM writing.
Right: recognition-triggered selection.
questions.explain: Retrieval from LTM is selection of a production.
questions.teaches: Retrieval from LTM is just the process of selecting one production from memory, at least on the most obvious way to arrange the memory.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A lab adopts one notation for all its models, though evidence for it is only suggestive. What is the honest way to describe this?
options: A proven fact, since the notation has been used throughout the lab for every model of the evidence
A preferred working language chosen without a conclusive case
A temporary accident
A rejected hypothesis
optionExplain: They claim only a judgment.
Right: preference, not proof.
It is deliberate.
It is adopted.
questions.explain: The authors take this stance. The card next states it.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: The authors choose production systems as the ____ language for expressing programs.
questions.explain: They state it as their preference.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A reviewer says the production notation is used throughout, so the authors must claim it is established. What is the fair reply?
options: They say it is proven
They say it is false
They abandon it
They say the case is not conclusive but they prefer it
optionExplain: Not proven.
Not false.
They continue.
Right: preference with candor.
questions.explain: They are explicit about the limits.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: A reader says the authors prove production systems are the correct organization of human programs. The text supports this.
questions.explain: They say a conclusive case cannot yet be made.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: How do the authors suspect the production-system organization will ultimately be verified?
options: By proving relatively satisfactory in many different small ways, none of them decisive
By one crucial experiment that settles the matter for good once it has been run
By a mathematical proof of the organization
By its speed of running on a computer
optionExplain: Right: a cumulative case.
No single test is expected.
Not claimed.
Not claimed.
questions.explain: The authors say no conclusive case can be made yet and suspect that verification may come from many small successes.
questions.teaches: The authors suspect that ultimate verification of the production-system organization may depend on its proving relatively satisfactory in many different small ways, no one of them decisive.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A team adopts a framework because it fits their cases in many small ways, while admitting no single test is decisive. Which authors' stance does this match?
options: Claiming the framework is proven by the cases that it fits
Rejecting the framework
Choosing a preferred language without a conclusive case
Refusing to commit
optionExplain: Not so.
They commit.
Right: same stance.
They commit.
questions.explain: Same judgment.
questions.teaches: The authors say that despite the unresolved difficulties, their judgment stands that production systems should be chosen as the preferred language.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A thermostat keeps a room warm; a rolling ball ends at the lowest point. Does either have a goal in the sense of a stored goal structure?
options: Yes, since both end in a fixed state
Yes, since both test the world
No, since they do not move
Not necessarily, since goal-directed behavior can arise without any stored goal structure
optionExplain: Ending in a state is not enough.
A fixed device is not a stored test.
Motion is not the issue.
Right: apparent direction is not a goal structure.
questions.explain: The authors separate apparent direction from structural goals. The card next states their definition.
questions.rule: Direction is not a goal structure.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A goal carries a ____ to determine when some state of affairs has been attained.
questions.explain: That is the first characteristic.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A to-do app stores an item for sending an invoice, with a check that marks it done when the invoice is sent, and the item triggers reminders. Which two features of a goal does this show?
options: A test for satisfaction and the power to control behavior
A parallel process and a random choice among the reminders
A memory chunk and a decay rate
A display and a saccade
optionExplain: Right: test and control.
Unrelated.
Unrelated.
Unrelated.
questions.explain: The two characteristics are a test and control of behavior.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: A reader says water seeking its own level shows that water has a goal structure in the authors' sense. The authors agree.
questions.explain: They cite such cases to show teleological behavior can be obtained in many ways, so goal-directedness alone does not show a goal structure.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: What do the authors suggest the diversity of goals may mostly concern?
options: The many kinds of memory chips used in the computers
The many languages of the subjects
The many ways of specifying desired situations
The many lengths of the experiments
optionExplain: Not stated.
Not stated.
Right: specification of the desired state.
Not stated.
questions.explain: They have no good empirical information about variety, but suspect it lies in how desired situations are specified.
questions.teaches: Goals may differ mostly in the many ways of specifying desired situations, and the test in a goal may simply be a symbol structure fed to a testing process defined elsewhere.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Two robots reach the charging dock. One stores a goal with a test for reaching it; the other has a fixed route. How would the authors classify them?
options: Both have goals, since both reach the charging dock
Only the first has goals in the structural sense
Neither has goals
Only the second has goals
optionExplain: Same behavior is not enough.
Right: a stored test and control mark a goal.
The first has one.
Reverse.
questions.explain: Equivalent behavior can be encoded into the program in other ways.
questions.rule: Behavior alone does not settle it.
questions.teaches: The important question is whether goals are incorporated in symbolic structures, or whether equivalent behavior occurs because it is encoded into the program in other ways; in the former case only would the system be said to have goals.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A store clerk reorganizes the shelf every time when new stock arrives, without any list of aims. Another clerk keeps a written note naming the aim to restock aisle 3 and acts on it. Which one has a stored goal?
options: The second, because the note is an explicit symbol structure
The first, because he acts consistently on each arrival of stock
Both, because both restock
Neither, because clerks have no goals
optionExplain: Right: an explicit structure is a goal.
Consistent action alone is not enough.
Only one stores it.
People can have goals.
questions.explain: The card next contrasts two productions in this way.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Production P2 uses goals because its 'to get' condition needs an explicit symbol ____ interpretable as a goal.
questions.explain: A goal is a symbol structure.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Two cryptarithmetic productions are P1 (given a new piece of information about a letter, find an occurrence of that letter and try to use the information) and P2 (to get the value of a letter, go to an occurrence of it and process its column). Which description fits how P1 is organized?
options: It sets up a goal structure for the value of a letter and then works on it, producing a goal for each letter
It stores a goal in memory for every letter in the problem
On new information about a letter, a single production finds the letter and uses it, with no goal data structure
It cannot act unless a goal for using the information is already in memory
optionExplain: That describes P2, whose to-get condition needs an explicit goal structure.
P1 stores no goal for any letter; the goal-like behavior comes from one production.
Right: P1 yields goal-like behavior with no goal data structure.
P1 fires on new information alone; the authors say no data structure is the goal.
questions.explain: A single production produces the behavior.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: If no goal for obtaining a letter's value is in STM, production P2 does not fire.
questions.explain: Its to-get condition is satisfied only when such an explicit goal structure exists.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: How does the observer's view of the subject's behavior differ from the program's structure in the P1 case?
options: From outside it looks random, but inside there is a goal
From outside it looks like a goal of using new information, but inside there is no goal data structure
From outside and inside it has a goal
From outside it is serial, inside parallel
optionExplain: Opposite.
Right: appearance versus structure.
Not so.
Not so.
questions.explain: Observation of behavior can suggest a goal that the program does not contain.
questions.teaches: From observation of the subject's behavior, P1 can make it appear that he has the goal of using new information, though no data structure in the program is that goal.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A spreadsheet recalculates a cell whenever an input changes, with no stored aim. A separate planner stores a goal of balancing the budget and picks actions to meet it. Which matches P1 and P2?
options: The spreadsheet matches P2 and the planner matches P1
Both match P1
Both match P2
The spreadsheet matches P1, the planner matches P2
optionExplain: Reversed.
The planner has a goal.
The spreadsheet has no goal.
Right: reaction without goal versus explicit goal.
questions.explain: Stored goals mark P2-type systems.
questions.teaches: A system containing P2 uses goals, because its to-get condition is satisfied only if an explicit symbol structure exists that can be interpreted as the goal.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A project manager keeps a tracked list of objectives with status. What must she also do with the list?
options: Nothing; the list works by itself once it is written
Create, update, check and drop objectives as work proceeds
Memorize the list in long-term memory and then never look at it again during work
Replace it with a display each hour
optionExplain: A list needs upkeep.
Right: goals need processes for managing them.
Not needed.
Not needed.
questions.explain: The card next states the same for the IPS.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A key behavioral feature of goals is that they produce ____ of behavior over long time intervals.
questions.explain: Remembered progress ties distant actions together.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A tourist returns to the same museum hall after lunch and carries on where she stopped. Which feature of goal-directed systems is this?
options: A stimulus-bound reaction to the sight of the hall, evoked afresh by the room itself
A parallel process
A decay of STM
Memory of both having a goal and where she stands in reaching it
optionExplain: She was not triggered by the hall alone.
Seriality is unaffected.
Not decay.
Right: goals store progress.
questions.explain: A symbolized goal remembers that there is a goal and the progress toward it.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: A system that keeps no explicit data about its progress toward a goal will show behavior that is more stimulus-bound than a goal-using system.
questions.explain: The authors say other systems are more stimulus-bound since they retain no such data.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: What general principle does the authors' footnote offer about data types and operations?
options: The data types of a system imply the operations that must be in its repertoire
Operations determine the data types, so any set of operations fixes in advance the structures of a system
Data types are irrelevant to operations
Data types are always numerical
optionExplain: Right: knowing the data types helps predict the order code.
Reversed.
They imply operations.
Not so.
questions.explain: The example given is a computer's addresses, boolean vectors, integers and floating-point numbers predicting its order code.
questions.teaches: The data types of an information processing system imply that the operations proper to those data types must be included in its repertoire, as a computer's data types largely predict its order code.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A smart home agent has 'goal' objects but no way to delete a finished goal. What problem does the card predict?
options: It will have no memory
It will be unable to read
It lacks a needed process for discarding goals and may keep pursuing completed aims
It will become parallel
optionExplain: Not implied.
Not implied.
Right: goal handling needs discarding.
Not implied.
questions.explain: Goal systems need creating, testing, updating, evoking and discarding.
questions.teaches: A program with goals must contain processes for creating goals, testing them, updating them, selecting methods for attempting them, evoking them and discarding them.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A cook is called away mid-recipe, returns, and resumes exactly where she stopped. Which sign of goal-directed behavior is this?
options: Consummation, the stopping of effort once the end is reached
Equifinality
Subgoaling
Interruptibility
optionExplain: That is stopping when done.
That is switching methods.
That is doing a means first.
Right: return to the same point after interruption.
questions.explain: The card next lists six such criteria.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Match each criterion to its description.
pairs: Returns to the same point after distraction
Tries another method toward the same goal after failure
Stops effort once the goal is attained
questions.explain: Each criterion shows a different way the goal's remembered state controls behavior.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A traveler's flight is canceled; she books a train to the same city. Which criterion?
options: Equifinality
Interruptibility
Consummation
Depth-first subgoaling
optionExplain: Right: a different method to the same goal.
No distraction involved.
No ending.
No nested subgoals.
questions.explain: Another method toward the same goal after failure.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A student writing an essay needs a fact; to find it she first needs a library card. She gets the card, finds the fact and returns to the essay. Which criterion, which the authors call particularly conclusive, does this nesting show?
options: Consummation: effort ends once the goal is attained
Equifinality: another method is tried when one fails
Depth-first subgoaling: subgoals nested several levels deep
Avoidance of repetition: memory of attempts prevents repeating them
optionExplain: Nothing here shows effort ending on attainment; the point is the chain of goals the student works through.
She does not try a second method toward the same goal after a failure.
Right: essay, fact and library card are goals nested three deep, and the authors call subgoaling several levels deep particularly conclusive.
The story contains no earlier attempts that she avoids repeating.
questions.explain: The authors call subgoaling to a depth of several goals particularly conclusive.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: What does the authors' criterion of consummation say?
options: Effort continues indefinitely, whether or not the goal situation has been attained
Effort toward a goal ends once the goal situation is attained
Effort doubles after success
Effort moves to another memory
optionExplain: Not so.
Right: terminate when attained.
Not so.
Not so.
questions.explain: When the goal is reached, effort toward that goal stops.
questions.teaches: By the criterion of consummation, if the goal situation is attained, effort is terminated with respect to that goal.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Order a goal episode that shows subgoaling: a repair worker needs a part to fix a leak.
items: Set the goal to fix the leak
Interrupt it to get the part as a subgoal
Obtain the part
Return to the original goal with the part in hand
Stop once the leak is fixed
questions.explain: Subgoaling interrupts the main activity for a means, returns using the result, and consummation ends effort.
questions.teaches: In subgoaling the IPS itself interrupts its activity toward a goal to engage in a means to that goal and then returns, often after considerable time, using the means produced.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A hiker usually takes the downhill path without thinking about it. Is she guided by a goal structure?
options: Not necessarily, since directed activity can be achieved by other means
Yes, all directed activity uses goals, so the downhill path must be guided by one
Yes, since she moves
No, since goals are impossible
optionExplain: Right: direction does not always use goals.
The authors deny this.
Movement is not the evidence.
They accept goals exist.
questions.explain: The card next states the caution.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: The authors conclude that the human IPS ____ has goal structures, though they warn that not all directed activity is achieved through them.
questions.explain: Goal structures are always present in the human IPS, yet the authors caution that much directed behavior can arise without them.
questions.rule: Invariably has goals, but not all direction uses them.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A researcher sees a subject reuse new information every time about a letter and concludes there must be a stored goal of using new information. What would the authors caution?
options: That subjects never use information, so there is no behavior here for a goal to explain at all
That goals do not exist
That a single production without a goal could produce the same behavior
That letters are not symbols
optionExplain: Not claimed.
They exist.
Right: P1-type behavior.
Not relevant.
questions.explain: Behavior can mimic a goal without a goal structure.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: A reader says the authors hold that most directed activity in problem solving is achieved by means of goal structures. The text supports this.
questions.explain: They warn this must not be assumed.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: What do the authors say about the evidence for goal activity in the protocols?
options: It is absent
It is abundant
It is only a few cases
It is only from chess
optionExplain: Not so.
Right: abundant.
Not so.
Not so.
questions.explain: Protocol evidence supports the invariant.
questions.teaches: The evidence for goal activity is abundant in the protocols the authors have studied, which is why they conclude the human IPS invariably has goal structures.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A manager sees staff consistently clear the inbox first thing and infers each has a written aim to do so. What does the card suggest?
options: Every habit needs a stored aim to explain the behavior, however regular the habit
Staff cannot have aims
Clearing the inbox is serial
A habit rule might produce the behavior with no stored aim
optionExplain: Not so.
Not so.
Not the point.
Right: a single rule may suffice.
questions.explain: Applying the caution.
questions.teaches: Directed activity can be produced by a single production, such as P1, without any data structure that is the goal.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Which description best sketches a human information processor as the authors describe it?
options: A parallel processor with a small long-term store
A serial processor with a huge, slow-to-write, quick-to-read long-term store and a tiny short-term store
A serial processor with a huge short-term store
A parallel processor with no long-term store
optionExplain: LTM is unlimited; processing is serial.
Right: this matches the summary.
STM is tiny.
LTM exists.
questions.explain: The card next lists all eight.
questions.rule: Serial; big slow LTM; tiny STM.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Match each memory or process to its approximate figure.
questions.explain: These are the summary's main parameters.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A task has 14 new facts to store, each one chunk. Using the summary's figures, roughly how long will fixation take?
options: About 7 to 14 seconds
About 0.7 to 1.4 seconds
About 700 to 1400 seconds
About 70 to 140 seconds
optionExplain: Ten times too low.
Hundred times too low.
Ten times too high.
Right: 14 times 5 to 10.
questions.explain: 14 times 5 to 10 seconds.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Which pair of items has the closest order of magnitude, according to the summary?
options: Time to read from LTM and to make a saccade
Time to read LTM and to write LTM
Time to write LTM and to write EM
Time to run an elementary process and to fixate a chunk
optionExplain: Right: both are a few hundred milliseconds or about a hundred.
Writing is 10 times slower.
EM writing is far faster.
Elementary processes are far faster.
questions.explain: Reads and saccades are in the hundreds of milliseconds, while LTM writes take seconds.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Although elementary processes take about ____ milliseconds, the overall rate of processing is limited by read rates from LTM and EM.
questions.explain: Reads from LTM and EM, not the elementary processes, set the pace.
questions.teaches: Although elementary processes take about fifty milliseconds, the overall rate of processing is fundamentally limited by read rates from LTM and EM.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A study finds that a task needs access to a store with 10-second read times. Using the summary, how likely is it that humans use that store as part of ongoing thinking?
options: Very likely, since LTM is slow
Certain, since EM reads take ten seconds
Unlikely, since the pace of problem solving depends on reads taking hundreds of milliseconds
Impossible, since reads are parallel
optionExplain: LTM reads are fast.
EM reads are fast.
Right: pace depends on fast reads.
Seriality, not parallel.
questions.explain: Applying the numbers.
questions.teaches: The summary gives EM access times of the order of a hundred milliseconds (a saccade), read times to STM of about fifty milliseconds, and writes of about a second per symbol for overlearned external symbols.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A person receives a puzzle, first works out what it asks and what the pieces are, and then tries one move after another. Which step is search in a problem space?
options: Working out what the puzzle asks
Both steps equally
Neither step
Trying one move after another
optionExplain: Understanding the problem is not itself search in the space.
Understanding precedes the search.
The exploration is search.
Right: the search proper is the move-by-move exploration.
questions.explain: The authors separate understanding and constructing a space from searching in it. The card next gives the claim.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: The authors say a human will preferentially employ the ____ formulation.
questions.explain: Preference for the search formulation, not the set-predicate formulation.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A mechanic first recognizes the symptoms and decides what to treat as the system's parts, then tests fixes in turn. According to the authors, which statement is correct?
options: Recognizing the problem and building the space are not themselves searches in the space
All of these activities are searches in the space, from the first look at the symptoms to the last repair
Only the recognition is search
No part of it uses a space
optionExplain: Right: only the later moves are search.
They state the opposite.
Recognition is not search in the space.
Testing fixes uses one.
questions.explain: Recognizing, constructing and modifying spaces need not be search in a space.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: If a new task were given to the same subjects, the authors would expect the problem solving to be organized as search in some problem space.
questions.explain: Over the range of tasks and individuals studied a problem space is always used, and the argument is that humans do so preferentially.
questions.rule: Expect a space for similar tasks.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A reviewer states: the authors prove every human problem-solving activity is search in a problem space. What is wrong?
options: They say none of it is search in a space
They apply it only to chess
They say they do not know how much of all problem solving uses a space, and recognition and construction are not search
They say search occurs only after the answer is known
optionExplain: They say it holds across the tasks studied.
It covers three tasks.
Right: scope and parts are qualified.
Not stated.
questions.explain: The claim is limited to the studied range and does not cover all relevant behavior.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A theorist proposes that people solve puzzles by recalling a stored set of conditions the answer must meet, and testing candidates against them. Which formulation is this, and how do the authors regard it?
options: The search formulation, which they reject
The set-predicate formulation, which they left open but found humans use less than search
A formulation they have proved impossible
The only formulation humans use
optionExplain: That is the one they favor.
Right: the evidence shows a preference for search.
They did not prove it impossible.
They say search is preferred.
questions.explain: Chapter 3 defined set-predicate and search formulations and left others open.
questions.teaches: Any collection of symbol structures giving information about a task environment, together with interpreters to control the IPS toward achieving some state of affairs, could constitute another problem formulation.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A route planner has places, roads, a starting point and a destination. Which of these corresponds to the operators?
options: The roads that take you from one place to another
The places themselves, where the traveler can stand
The starting point
The destination
optionExplain: Right: operators produce new states from existing ones.
Places are states.
That is the initial state.
That is the goal.
questions.explain: The card next defines the parts of a problem space.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Order the first four elements of the definition as the authors list them.
items: States of knowledge U
Operators Q
Initial state u0
Final desired states G
questions.explain: The authors list elements, operators, initial state and the problem, then add available knowledge.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: In a cryptarithmetic problem space, an element of U can be a partial assignment of digits to letters.
questions.explain: Elements of U are symbol structures representing states of knowledge about the task, and a partial assignment is such a state.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Which pair is correctly matched?
options: Operator: the knowledge the solver starts with in his memory before he begins to work
Operator: an information process producing a new state from an old one
Initial state: a process producing new states from old ones
Problem: the set of all states
optionExplain: That is the initial state.
Right: operators are information processes.
Reversed.
The problem is specifying final states.
questions.explain: The definition separates states, processes, the start and the goal.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: How is the final state of a chess problem space characterized in the authors' example?
options: It is always checkmate of the opposing King, whatever the evaluation of the position
It is the starting position
It is any legal position
It depends on evaluations but is related to checkmate
optionExplain: Not always checkmate.
No.
No.
Right: this is their wording.
questions.explain: Final desired states may depend on evaluation rather than being fixed in advance.
questions.teaches: In chess the final state depends on evaluations but is related to checkmate.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A cook wants a dish that tastes balanced; she has ingredients, can add or remove one at a time, starts with a plain base, and stops when it tastes right. Which part of the definition is the stopping condition?
options: The operator set Q, which says what moves are allowed
The set of desired final states G
The initial state u0
The element set U
optionExplain: Adding or removing are operators.
Right: the goal states.
Plain base is u0.
Dishes at various stages are elements.
questions.explain: The problem is posed by specifying a set of final desired states.
questions.teaches: A problem is posed by specifying a set of final, desired states to be reached by applying operators from Q.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: While solving a puzzle you keep track of which options you already tried at this step. How would you classify that note?
options: Reference information that never changes while the work goes on
Temporary information used only once
Information in another knowledge state
Path information about what was done in this state
optionExplain: It changes as you work.
It persists across the state's visits.
It concerns this state.
Right: tried alternatives are path information.
questions.explain: The card next sorts available knowledge into six kinds.
questions.rule: Path info records what was tried.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Order these from most transient to most stable.
items: Temporary dynamic information within one state
The knowledge state itself
Path information
Reference information constant over the solving
questions.explain: The authors list temporary, state, extended access, path, other states, reference.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: In chess, the conventional value of the pieces is ____ information, constant over the course of solving.
questions.explain: Conventional piece values are in LTM and used in evaluating exchanges; they are reference information.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Which is the difference between the knowledge state and the extended knowledge state?
options: The state is stable; the extended state is transient
The state is in LTM; the extended state is in STM
The state is directly available; the extended state is available only through access information
There is no difference
optionExplain: Reversed.
Not locations.
Right: access information only for the extended state.
They are distinguished.
questions.explain: Direct availability versus access information.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: In the chess example, what is the only other accessible knowledge state besides the current one?
options: Every previously visited position, each available in the display
No other state at all
The final checkmate position
The original position available in the display
optionExplain: Only the original is accessible.
Others are not accessible.
Not accessible.
Right: the original position remains on the board.
questions.explain: The display keeps the original position in EM.
questions.teaches: In the authors' chess example the only other accessible knowledge state is the original position, available in the display.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A bookkeeper makes a trial entry in a ledger, keeps a note of what entries she already tried, and uses the fixed tax rates from a table. Which two layers are the note and the table?
options: Path information and reference information
Temporary information and reference information
Path information and temporary information
Extended state and temporary information
optionExplain: Right: tried entries are path; tax rates are constant reference.
The note persists beyond a single state.
The table is reference.
The table is not temporary.
questions.explain: Applying the layers outside chess.
questions.teaches: Temporary dynamic information is created and used exclusively within a single knowledge state, such as a generator's current position in listing moves that defend a given man.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A cook has a recipe book on the shelf and knows which page covers soups. How should her knowledge of the soup recipe be described?
options: Directly in her working memory
Absent altogether
Accessible, since she holds access information rather than the recipe itself
Irrelevant to the task
optionExplain: She does not have the content in hand.
She can get it.
Right: she knows where to find it.
It is relevant.
questions.explain: The card next makes the same point for knowledge states.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: For other knowledge states, the solver has only ____ information that enables him to recall them.
questions.explain: Without it he could never get to them.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A solver abandons the current line of attack. What must he hold to be able to go back to an earlier state?
options: The whole earlier state in STM, held ready for the return
Access information to that state
Nothing, since states persist
Only reference information
optionExplain: That would use up STM.
Right: access information is the minimum.
He would be unable to return.
Reference facts are not states.
questions.explain: If he did not hold access information he could never get there.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: A reader says the other knowledge states are directly available in the same way as the current state. The authors agree.
questions.explain: Only access information to them is available.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: What does 'available' mean in the authors' definition?
options: The information may be used in decisions or operators and will be forthcoming if called for
The information is held in STM at every moment
The information has been fixated in LTM
The information has been written externally
optionExplain: Right: forthcoming on call.
Availability does not require STM.
Not necessarily LTM.
Not necessarily external.
questions.explain: Availability is functional.
questions.teaches: Available information may be used in decision processes or in applying operators and will be forthcoming if it is called for.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A manager can recall which folder holds last year's contract but not what it says. Is the contract available to her in the authors' sense?
options: Yes, fully in hand
No, she has no knowledge of it
Only via access information; she must retrieve it to use it
Yes, because it is in LTM
optionExplain: She has the pointer only.
She knows where it is.
Right: she has a pointer, not the content.
Availability needs retrieval.
questions.explain: Applying the card.
questions.teaches: The knowledge state itself is directly available, whereas the extended knowledge state offers only access information.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: How many earlier positions can a chess player typically return to, as the authors found?
options: Every position visited
Only one or two
Around fifty
A different one for each move ever considered
optionExplain: People do not keep all.
Right: very few alternative nodes remain available.
Far too many.
Far too many.
questions.explain: The card next lists this among the invariant features.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A knowledge state typically contains a few ____ symbols and at most a few hundred.
questions.explain: More typically a few dozen.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A solver's current knowledge state holds about 40 symbols. Does it fit the invariant?
options: No, since states are limited to seven symbols
No, since states must have thousands of symbols to count
No, since states are empty
Yes, since states typically have a few dozen symbols
optionExplain: Seven is the STM span, not the state's size.
States are moderate.
Not so.
Right: moderate size.
questions.explain: States have at most a few hundred, usually a few dozen.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: That knowledge states are generated from a finite set of objects, relations and properties is what makes the space a closed space of knowledge.
questions.explain: Finite generation of states is the first invariant feature, and it closes the space.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: How do the authors describe the set of operators?
options: Large and growing steadily as the solver gains experience with the task at hand
Infinite and unordered
Equal in number to the states
Small and finite, or at least finitely generated
optionExplain: Not so.
Not so.
Not so.
Right: this is the feature.
questions.explain: Operators are limited.
questions.teaches: The set of operators is small and finite, or at least finitely generated.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A board game has 10 move types and a few dozen board features. Using the invariants, how should we describe its space?
options: A small, closed space of the kind humans have been found to use
An infinite space humans cannot handle with any method
A space with unlimited return points
A space with no operators
optionExplain: Right: matches the invariants.
It is finite.
Return points are few.
It has operators.
questions.explain: Applying the first, second and eighth features.
questions.teaches: The available set of alternative nodes to which the problem solver might return is very small, usually only one or two nodes.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Roughly how long does a problem solver stay at a single knowledge state before making the next move?
options: A few milliseconds
A few minutes
A few seconds
A few hours
optionExplain: Too fast for a move.
Too slow.
Right: residence times are of the order of seconds.
Too slow.
questions.explain: The card next states it.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A solver stays within a given problem space for at least tens of ____.
questions.explain: Tens of minutes at least.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A 30-minute session has states each lasting about 5 seconds. Roughly how many states can be visited?
options: About 36
About 3,600
About 6
About 360
optionExplain: Ten times too few.
Ten times too many.
Far too few.
Right: 1800 divided by 5.
questions.explain: 1800 seconds over 5 seconds per state.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: When a solver backs up to an old state, the dynamic information of the abandoned state is given up, but path information about what was tried may be kept.
questions.explain: Backup abandons knowledge-state information, though not necessarily path information.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: How are moves from one state to the next characterized?
options: Mostly incremental
Mostly random jumps
Always complete re-solutions
Always backward
optionExplain: Right: incremental steps.
Not so.
Not so.
Not so.
questions.explain: Search proceeds step by step.
questions.teaches: The moves from one knowledge state to the next are mostly incremental.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A coach observes an apprentice stay 10 minutes on one move without any intermediate steps. Using the invariants, what would be unusual?
options: A residence time shorter than milliseconds, as for the briefest of elementary steps
Too many return points
A residence time far longer than the seconds typical of the spaces studied
Too small a knowledge state
optionExplain: Not at issue.
Not at issue.
Right: seconds are typical.
Not at issue.
questions.explain: Applying the fourth invariant.
questions.teaches: Search involves backup, that is, return from time to time to old knowledge states and hence abandonment of knowledge-state information, although not necessarily of path information.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A subject takes 600 seconds to make 100 moves. What is the average time per move?
options: 60 seconds
6 seconds
0.6 seconds
600 seconds
optionExplain: Ten times too long.
Right: 600 divided by 100.
Ten times too short.
Not an average.
questions.explain: The authors compute averages this way. The card next gives their values.
questions.rule: Total time over number of nodes.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: The average residence time for S2 on CROSS+ROADS was about ____ seconds.
questions.explain: The lowest average in the table.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A PBG for a logic problem has 40 nodes and the session lasted 300 seconds. How does the average compare with S8's 7.7 seconds?
options: 7.5 seconds, close to S8's
75 seconds, ten times S8's
0.75 seconds, a tenth of S8's
30 seconds, four times S8's
optionExplain: Right: 300 over 40.
Misplaced decimal.
Misplaced decimal.
Wrong division.
questions.explain: 300 divided by 40 is 7.5.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: S2 on chess position A had a longer average residence time than S2 on CROSS+ROADS.
questions.explain: The table gives 6.2 seconds for chess position A and 1.9 seconds for CROSS+ROADS.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Why was the lowest average, from S2 on CROSS+ROADS, different in method?
options: It used no protocol data
It used both protocol and eye-movement data, allowing a more fine-grained analysis
It used a larger sample
It used a computer simulation
optionExplain: It used protocols.
Right: finer analysis.
A few subjects.
Not simulated.
questions.explain: That included recall operators.
questions.teaches: The lowest average came from a PBG based on both protocol and eye-movement data, permitting a more fine-grained analysis, for example one including recall operators.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A researcher times a new puzzle and finds an average 40 seconds per node. How does this compare with the book's data?
options: Within the range reported
Shorter than every task
Equal to the chess task
Much longer than the two to eight seconds found, so worth explaining
optionExplain: Not in the range.
Longer.
Right: outside the range.
questions.explain: Applying the table.
questions.teaches: The average duration is total time divided by the total number of nodes in the PBG, calculated for only a few subjects as an order-of-magnitude estimate.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.section: Residence Times and the Size of the Knowledge State
questions.q: A chef makes a new decision every 5 seconds. Which memory can hold the details of each decision as they accumulate?
options: Entirely long-term memory
Mostly short-term memory, with a little in long-term memory and any notes
Entirely her eyes
No memory
optionExplain: Writing takes about 5 s per symbol.
Right: LTM writing is too slow for much.
Not enough.
Needs memory.
questions.explain: The card next draws this conclusion.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.section: Residence Times and the Size of the Knowledge State
questions.q: Over residence times of several seconds, symbols can also be stored in LTM or ____.
questions.explain: Not only in STM.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.section: Residence Times and the Size of the Knowledge State
questions.q: A subject has 5 seconds in a state. Using 5K seconds to fixate K symbols, how many symbols could be fixated in LTM, at most?
options: About five
About twenty-five
About fifty
About one
optionExplain: Needs 25 s.
Needs 125 s.
Needs 250 s.
Right: 5 seconds per symbol.
questions.explain: K = 1 costs about 5 seconds.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.section: Residence Times and the Size of the Knowledge State
questions.q: True or false: A reader says the authors hold that the whole knowledge state is held in STM alone. The text supports this.
questions.explain: They say it is STM plus a small quantity in LTM plus a variable amount in EM.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.section: Residence Times and the Size of the Knowledge State
questions.q: How much do subjects in these tasks add to EM?
options: Only sporadically, but with a marked effect on their style of problem solving
Continuously throughout
Never
Only at the end
optionExplain: Right: sporadic additions with marked effects.
That fits equation solvers.
They do.
Not only at the end.
questions.explain: Slight changes of task might change this.
questions.teaches: In these tasks subjects add to EM only sporadically, but with a marked effect on their styles of problem solving.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.section: Residence Times and the Size of the Knowledge State
questions.q: A programmer writes code on paper almost continuously. How does this differ from the subjects in the book?
options: Less of it is held in EM
All of it is held in LTM, with none left on the paper
More of the current knowledge is held in EM
None is held in STM
optionExplain: Reversed.
LTM is slow.
Right: continuous writing moves state into EM.
STM still used.
questions.explain: Applying the card.
questions.teaches: A man solving complex equations or writing a computer program generally writes almost continually on scratch paper, putting a significant amount of his current knowledge into EM.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.section: Residence Times and the Size of the Knowledge State
questions.q: A cook has three items on the counter and a large pantry. Which is more immediately usable?
options: The pantry contents, since there are many more of them
Both equally
Neither
The three items on the counter
optionExplain: The pantry needs a trip.
They differ.
Counter items are usable.
Right: what is in view is directly available.
questions.explain: The card next states the difference for knowledge states.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.section: Residence Times and the Size of the Knowledge State
questions.q: The ____ knowledge state is larger than the immediate one and is accessed selectively during residence at a single node.
questions.explain: That is the authors' term.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.section: Residence Times and the Size of the Knowledge State
questions.q: A chess player looks at a part of the board outside foveal view. What must happen before she can use it?
options: A scanning program must bring it into foveal view
Nothing; every part of the board is always available to her
It must be fixated in LTM
It must be written on paper
optionExplain: Right: outside the fovea needs scanning.
Only the fovea part counts as STM.
Slow and not required.
Not needed.
questions.explain: Access to EM depends on specific searches.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.section: Residence Times and the Size of the Knowledge State
questions.q: True or false: If the immediate knowledge state grew very large, the guarantee that all of it is available would weaken.
questions.explain: The requirement of availability keeps the immediate state small; the extended state can grow because it is reached selectively.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.section: Residence Times and the Size of the Knowledge State
questions.q: Which error do the authors cite as located at the interface of LTM retrieval?
options: S2's misreading of CROSS+ROADS in the first minutes
S3's failure to recall that T = 0 in cryptarithmetic
S8's wrong logic rule
S5's miscounting of the letters in the final answer at the end of the session
optionExplain: Not cited here.
Right: a failed retrieval.
Not cited here.
Not cited here.
questions.explain: Retrieval is likely but not assured.
questions.teaches: Some errors that plague problem solvers can be localized at the interface of retrieving LTM information, such as S3's failure to recall that T = 0 in cryptarithmetic.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.section: Residence Times and the Size of the Knowledge State
questions.q: An office worker has a large archive but looks things up only when a specific question arises. Which term fits the archive?
options: Extended knowledge state, reached selectively on specific triggers
Immediate knowledge state, since everything in the archive is in her hands at the moment she looks
Temporary information
Path information
optionExplain: Right: large store, selective access.
Too large to be immediate.
Not transient.
Not route.
questions.explain: Applying the definition.
questions.teaches: The immediate knowledge state is always kept small by the requirement of availability, whereas the extended knowledge state may grow continually provided the solver has appropriate selective accessing programs.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.section: Residence Times and the Size of the Knowledge State
questions.q: A researcher stores hundreds of notes in boxes. What makes retrieving a particular note fast?
options: Having bigger boxes, so that more notes fit in each
Writing faster
Remembering which box each topic is in
Using only one box
optionExplain: Size does not locate.
Writing is not the issue.
Right: an internal index.
A single box is searched.
questions.explain: The card next describes this cooperation.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.section: Residence Times and the Size of the Knowledge State
questions.q: An external memory of more than very modest size is almost useless for problem solving without a complementary internalized ____.
questions.explain: An internal index.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.section: Residence Times and the Size of the Knowledge State
questions.q: A student writes a long set of formulas on a sheet and memorizes only where each type is. Which limits does this strategy work around?
options: EM's slow writing and LTM's search time, which the index avoids
LTM's slow writing and EM's search time
STM's long retention
EM's small capacity
optionExplain: Reversed.
Right: bulk to EM, index to LTM.
Not relevant.
EM is essentially infinite.
questions.explain: Each store covers the other's weakness.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.section: Residence Times and the Size of the Knowledge State
questions.q: True or false: Without a complementary internal index, a very large pile of external notes remains as useful for problem solving as before.
questions.explain: An EM of more than very modest size is almost useless without an internal index, because search time then limits it.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.section: Residence Times and the Size of the Knowledge State
questions.q: What explains the much broader limits on knowledge-state content in internal memory than in EM?
options: Internal memory is faster to write
Recognition is a powerful selective accessing mechanism for internal memory, which EM lacks
EM is smaller
Internal memory has no structure
optionExplain: Internal writing is slow.
Right: this is the footnote.
EM is infinite.
It is structured.
questions.explain: EM has no comparable mechanism.
questions.teaches: Recognition is a powerful selective accessing mechanism to the internal memory, which is why the limits on content of the internal knowledge state are much broader than for EM, which has no corresponding mechanism.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
