questions.q: True or false: A reader says a space whose operator choices are defined only by an arbitrary list is easier to solve than a random space. The authors agree.
questions.explain: They say such a space is no more tractable than a random one.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: What makes the actual problem spaces more manageable than arbitrary lists, according to the authors?
options: They are small enough to list
They have no structure
They are always random
They are approximately factorable and use variables to define functions compactly
optionExplain: Not the reason.
They have structure.
Not random.
Right: two ways.
questions.explain: Factorability and variables are developed next.
questions.teaches: The actual problem spaces are more manageable than arbitrary lists in two ways: they are at least approximately factorable, and the function relating states to operators can be defined compactly by introducing variables.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A game assigns each position an unrelated name and each move another unrelated name. What information could help a player?
options: Only a table pairing each node name with its preferred move
A rule using the meanings of the names given to the positions
A symmetry of the board
A progress test
optionExplain: Right: names carry no structure.
Names have no meaning.
No board.
No distance.
questions.explain: The authors' example of extensional definition.
questions.teaches: In a tic-tac-toe isomorph with arbitrary, noninterpretable names for nodes and branches, useful information could only be a table pairing each node with its preferred branch, a form available even with no regularity in the tree.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A traveler chooses each step by looking only at where she stands. Which strategy is this closest to?
options: Pure working backward
Means-ends analysis
Pure working forward
A fixed priority order
optionExplain: Depends on g only.
Depends on both.
Right: depends only on u.
Depends on neither.
questions.explain: The card next maps strategies to dependencies.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Match each strategy to what the operator choice depends on.
pairs: The difference between current and desired state
questions.explain: The function from U x G to Q may use both, one or neither.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A test measures how far the current state is from the goal. What kind of test is this?
options: A simplicity criterion that depends on the state alone
A progress test, which depends on both u and g
A fixed priority
A working-backward rule
optionExplain: That depends on u only.
Right: distance test.
Not a test.
Not a test.
questions.explain: Progress tests fall in the former category.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: A simplicity criterion that rejects states that are too complex depends only on the current state.
questions.explain: A progress test uses both current and desired states, while a simplicity criterion uses only the current state.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Which program used a fixed priority order of operators, in the authors' example?
options: GPS, which ordered its operators by difference
EPAM
Some versions of the Logic Theorist
The chess mating program
optionExplain: GPS uses differences.
Not stated.
Right: stated.
Not stated.
questions.explain: Priority ordering is a constant function.
questions.teaches: If the operators are always tried in a fixed order of priority, as in some versions of the Logic Theorist, the priority ordering may be regarded as a constant function determining the operator independently of both u and g.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A mechanic tries the cheapest fix first regardless of the symptom. How would the authors classify the dependency?
options: Means-ends analysis
A constant function: the choice depends on neither state nor goal
Working backward
A progress test
optionExplain: Needs a difference.
Right: fixed order.
Needs goal.
A test, not a choice.
questions.explain: Applying the card.
questions.teaches: Means-ends analysis provides an important class of examples where the operator-selection function depends on both the current state and the goal, specifically on their difference.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A technician has a ten-light panel; each lit light calls for its own fix. How many fix rules does she need?
options: 1,024, one per pattern of lights
10, one per light
optionExplain: That is every pattern.
Not the count.
Not the count.
Right: one per feature.
questions.explain: The card next states this saving.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: With n features there are 2 to the n distinguishable states but only ____ feature-operator pairs to learn.
questions.explain: n pairs.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A state has 8 features. How many state-operator pairs would a full listing need, compared with the factored function?
options: 8 against 256
256 against 8
64 against 8
16 against 8
optionExplain: Reversed.
Right: 2 to the 8th is 256.
That is 8 squared.
That is 2 times 8.
questions.explain: 2^8 = 256 states, 8 feature pairs.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: If a space is known to have this feature structure, the mapping can be discovered after searching only a small part of the total space.
questions.explain: Factorability makes the mapping learnable from a small sample.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: How can a weak interdependence among features be reintroduced?
options: By erasing features
By adding goals
By making the mapping random
By ordering the features, so an operator is relevant if its feature is present and no higher one is
optionExplain: Not erasing.
Not goals.
Not random.
Right: ordering.
questions.explain: That keeps most of the economy.
questions.teaches: A weak kind of interdependence can be reintroduced into a factored space by ordering the features, calling an operator relevant if its feature is present and no other feature standing higher in the ordering is present.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A help desk has twelve symptom checkboxes, each tied to a single standard response. Compared with listing all combinations, what is saved?
options: From 4,096 combinations to 12 pairs
From 144 to 12
From 24 to 12
Nothing
optionExplain: Right: 2 to the 12th is 4,096.
That is 12 squared.
That is 2 times 12.
Factoring saves.
questions.explain: Applying the card.
questions.teaches: Simplifying assumptions in the card include that the goal state is invariant over all tasks and that each feature maps to a single operator, though both can be generalized.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A traveler is two cities north and one city east of her goal. She picks actions by these gaps. What method is this?
options: Choosing by the current state alone
Choosing by a fixed list of actions, tried in the same order whatever the gaps between her place and the goal
Choosing operators by the differences between current and desired states
Choosing at random
optionExplain: Goal matters.
Not fixed.
Right: differences.
Not random.
questions.explain: The card next names this means-ends analysis.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: The formal kernel of means-ends analysis is a relevance function from the set of ____ vectors to operators.
questions.explain: From D to Q.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A cook sees: not salty enough, too thick. Which two operators does means-ends analysis suggest?
options: One that cools and one that colors the dish
One chosen at random for each difference
None, since goals are invariant
One that adds salt and one that thins the dish
optionExplain: Unrelated.
Not random.
Goal is used.
Right: each difference selects an operator.
questions.explain: Differences map to operators.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: A reader says means-ends analysis chooses operators from the absolute features of the current state, ignoring the goal. The authors agree.
questions.explain: It depends on the difference between current and desired states.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: What is the claim that means-ends analysis is often powerful equivalent to?
options: That relevance functions from differences to operators can be defined in many task environments
That all spaces are random
That features are unordered
That operators are unlimited
optionExplain: Right: the stated equivalence.
Not so.
Not so.
Not so.
questions.explain: Definability is the condition.
questions.teaches: The assertion that means-ends analysis is a frequently powerful problem solving method is an assertion that relevance functions from difference vectors D to operators Q can be defined in many task environments.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A gardener has a list of garden problems, each mapped to one remedy, independent of the other problems. Which property of the card does this have?
options: Random structure
Spurious structure
Factoring of the state space, since each remedy depends on a single feature
Search-scan
optionExplain: Structured.
Not extra.
Right: factorable.
Not it.
questions.explain: Applying the card.
questions.teaches: Such functions from states to operators factor the state space, because they make the relevance of an operator depend on only a single feature of the state, independently of which other features are present or absent.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A to-do list of independent chores can be done in any order. What does this resemble?
options: A random space where no order of chores matters and no goal can ever be reached
A completely factorable space, where paths are permutable
A space with strict ordering
A space with no goals
optionExplain: Not random.
Right: independence permits any order.
Not strict.
Goals exist.
questions.explain: The card next describes this limiting case.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: In planning spaces the features and operators that are eliminated by abstraction are called ____.
questions.explain: The retained ones are essential.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A planner drops the details of seating and keeps only the main sequence of a day's events. What has she formed?
options: An abstracted planning space keeping the essential features
A completely factorable space, in which every chore of the day can be done in any order
A random space
A model
optionExplain: Right: abstraction.
Not necessarily.
Structured.
Not this.
questions.explain: Planning spaces are abstractions.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: A completely factorable problem space would generally be uninteresting, since the problem is trivial once the function defining its structure is given.
questions.explain: The authors say such spaces are rather uninteresting.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: How does the feature-vector form help represent a goal such as checkmate?
options: A goal must be a single state, so checkmate would have to name one position
A goal cannot be represented
A goal can be a set of features defining a whole class of states
A goal must be an operator
optionExplain: Not single.
It can.
Right: class of arrangements.
Not an operator.
questions.explain: Checkmate is a class of arrangements.
questions.teaches: Representing states as feature vectors facilitates representing task environments where the solution is not a single specific goal state but a set of features defining a whole class of states, as checkmate is a class of arrangements.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A mechanic labels the finer points of a repair as inessential for the first diagnosis and focuses on the main fault. Which concept from the card is this?
options: Complete factorability of the repair into independent parts
Abstraction into a planning space
Backup
Seriality
optionExplain: Not this.
Right: abstraction.
Not this.
Not this.
questions.explain: Applying the card.
questions.teaches: Where a subset of features and operators defines a completely factorable subspace, labeling it inessential creates an abstracted space that retains most of the information important for finding paths in the original.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A formula says: swap the two numbers in any addition. How many specific additions does it cover?
options: Only one
Only those with 5 as one of the two numbers added
None
All of them, with one rule
optionExplain: Not just one.
Not restricted.
Not none.
Right: a variable covers a class.
questions.explain: The card next shows this with the commute operator.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: The commute operator changes A + B into ____, keeping the same values.
questions.explain: Same values, order swapped.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A rule rewrites A(B + C) as AB + AC. Which symbol does the variable notation show to be left invariant?
options: B, which changes places in the output, so the notation marks it as the invariant symbol of the rule
A, which occupies corresponding positions in input and output
The plus sign only
Nothing
optionExplain: B is kept too, but A is the notable one.
Right: A is carried over.
Not the focus.
Something is invariant.
questions.explain: The A positions correspond.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: If the choice of a particular member of a class can be postponed until only one candidate remains, what happens to search?
options: It doubles
It becomes random
It is unchanged, since the same members must be tried in the end
It is avoided entirely
optionExplain: Opposite.
Not random.
Changes.
Right: stated.
questions.explain: Postponing selection avoids search.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: What do operators containing variables allow, by being a form of abstraction?
options: Defining abstract paths from a whole class of states to a class of states, so classes of paths are searched at once
Defining paths only from one single state to another single state, one pair at a time
Defining paths that are free of any goals once the operator contains a variable
Defining paths in which the next state is chosen at random from the class
optionExplain: Right: an operator with variables defines abstract paths for whole classes of states.
Variables allow classes, not single states: one operator covers a whole class of states.
Goals remain in the system; variables only make the paths abstract.
Choice among states is not random; the variable only makes the operator cover a class of states.
questions.explain: Operators with variables allow search over whole classes of paths at once.
questions.teaches: Operators containing variables serve as a form of abstraction, defining abstract paths from a whole class of states to the corresponding members of another class, so that whole classes of paths can be searched simultaneously.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: A spreadsheet formula that totals any column, whatever the numbers, works like an operator with a variable in the authors' sense.
questions.explain: One formula applies to the whole class of columns, binding the variable to each case.
questions.teaches: A variable can specify that an operator which changes specific features of any state in a class guarantees that certain other features remain invariant.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A cook tastes the soup after seasoning and decides whether to start again. Which kind of decision is this?
options: Foresight: picking the next step from the current position
Neither
Hindsight: judging a path from its result
A goal test
optionExplain: That is operator selection.
It is one.
Right: evaluating the outcome.
Not a goal test.
questions.explain: The card next states this contrast.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Operator selection is an application of ____, while state evaluation is an application of hindsight.
questions.explain: Predicting the promise of actions.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A player decides that after her last three moves her position looks worse and she returns to an earlier one. Which decision is this?
options: Selecting an operator in foresight from the current position
Fixing a goal
Recording in EM
Evaluating a state in hindsight and abandoning the path
optionExplain: Not foresight.
Not goal.
Not EM.
Right: hindsight and backup.
questions.explain: Evaluation leads to leaving the path.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: A reader says hindsight information is useful even when a solver has no way of returning to earlier states. The authors agree.
questions.explain: Hindsight can only be used to leave the current path for another, so backup capability is needed.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: What does the evaluation function replace, according to the authors?
options: Prior knowledge of the structure of the problem space
The operators, which the evaluation function makes unnecessary by selecting every move for the player
The memory
The goals
optionExplain: Right: stated.
Not replaced.
Not replaced.
Not replaced.
questions.explain: It computes the value of the action sequence that reached the state.
questions.teaches: The computation of the value of the action sequence that reached the current state takes the place of prior knowledge of the structure of the problem space.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: An investor can either predict from a chart which stock to buy (static) or try small trades and see (dynamic). Which pair of terms from the card fits?
options: Hindsight for the chart and foresight for the trial trades
Both are foresight
Foresight for the chart-based choice and hindsight for the trial-based judgment
Both are hindsight
optionExplain: Reversed.
Trials judge results.
Right: static versus dynamic.
Chart predicts.
questions.explain: Applying the card.
questions.teaches: Foresight takes information that is available statically as part of the current knowledge state, while hindsight makes partial dynamic searches of alternatives to decide which offers greater promise.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A driver knows from the map that a bridge ahead is closed, so skips every route over it. What does this show?
options: Trial driving is always needed
Static information can rule out whole sets of moves without trying them
Maps make routes longer
Bridges are goals
optionExplain: Not always.
Right: static features eliminate options.
Not so.
Not so.
questions.explain: The card next gives the chess version.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A piece so located that moving it would expose another to attack is called a ____ piece.
questions.explain: Pinned against the other piece.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A player sees her Knight is pinned and does not consider any Knight move. What has she done?
options: Used a static feature to eliminate moves without trying them
Made a dynamic search of each Knight move before rejecting it
Selected a backup
Written to LTM
optionExplain: Right: foresight from static features.
That would be trial.
Not backup.
Not LTM.
questions.explain: The pin is read from geometry.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: A forking square is a square from which a piece could attack two or more pieces simultaneously.
questions.explain: That is the definition; a pinned piece is a different notion.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: What is a typical blunder that comes with using static descriptions?
options: Making too many dynamic searches and so running out of time on the board
Failing to see that the opponent's reply wins a tempo
Failing to notice that moving a piece to use one static feature removes another feature that depended on that piece
Overusing backup to earlier positions when the static features no longer match
optionExplain: The blunder arises from relying on static descriptions, which reduce dynamic search, not from doing too much of it.
Missing a tempo is not the blunder the authors tie to static descriptions.
Right: moving a piece for one static feature can remove another that depended on it, leaving a stale description.
Backup is not the typical blunder here; the problem is features that are no longer true after the move.
questions.explain: Static descriptions must be revised as the state changes.
questions.teaches: A typical blunder with static descriptions is moving a piece to exploit one feature, a forking square say, without noticing that another feature dependent on that piece, such as a defended pawn, then disappears.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A planner reads from a schedule that two meetings clash, so rules out a set of arrangements without testing them. After moving one meeting she forgets to recheck. Which risk from the card has she met?
options: A dynamic search that was too long to finish before the meetings were moved
A backup that was too deep to be held in memory
A goal that was satisfied
A static feature that went stale after the change
optionExplain: Not search.
Not backup.
Not a goal.
Right: stale static feature.
questions.explain: Applying the card.
questions.teaches: To the extent that significant properties of a chess position can be described statically, a large dynamic search of a tree of alternative move sequences can be replaced by analysis of the logical implications of static properties, closely related to the distinction between models and descriptions.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A mechanic knows that a certain warning light calls for a certain check. What structure is this?
options: A variable with many values to be filled in later
A feature correlated with a relevant action
An evaluation by hindsight
A planning abstraction
optionExplain: Variables stand for classes.
Right: feature to operator.
Hindsight judges results.
Planning drops detail.
questions.explain: The card next gives chess examples of the same structure.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: In chess, the move of a Rook to a file goes with the feature that the file is ____.
questions.explain: An open file calls for a Rook move.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A player sees an attacked piece and moves a defender to it. Which pairing from the card is this?
options: A difference between initial and goal states, of the kind logic problems supply
A conditional assignment
A branchiness measure
A feature (attack on a piece) correlated with a relevant move (a defender)
optionExplain: That is logic.
That is cryptarithmetic.
That is MATER.
Right: stated pairing.
questions.explain: Features link to relevant moves.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the problem space for MATER best illustrates information about the branchiness of the environment.
questions.explain: They name the chess mating combinations program MATER for this.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Which task gave the clearest examples of planning spaces and the essential-inessential distinction?
options: Logic
Chess
Cryptarithmetic
None of the three
optionExplain: Right: logic.
Chess gives feature-move pairs.
Cryptarithmetic gives hindsight by contradiction.
Logic provided them.
questions.explain: Logic also supplied features as differences and explicit variables.
questions.teaches: The logic task provides the best example of features that take the form of differences between an initial and a goal state, makes explicit provision for variables in its notation, and gives the clearest examples of planning spaces and of the essential-inessential distinction.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A coach tries a play, sees it fail, and then deduces what must be wrong. Which authors' example of dynamic or hindsight information is this like?
options: Choosing a Rook move from an open file
Dropping inessential features in logic
Deriving a contradiction after making a conditional assignment in cryptarithmetic
Measuring branchiness in MATER
optionExplain: That is static feature.
That is abstraction.
Right: learning from the outcome.
That is branching structure.
questions.explain: Hindsight uses results of a tentative step.
questions.teaches: Information acquired by dynamic analysis and hindsight is illustrated by chess evaluation functions and by the contradictions derived after making conditional assignments in cryptarithmetic.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Two search teams are given maps of very different structure. What should we expect about their methods?
options: Their methods will be identical
Their methods will be unrelated to the maps
Their methods cannot be compared
Their methods will differ in ways traceable to the structure of the maps
optionExplain: Different structure, different methods.
Related.
Comparable.
Right: structure shapes method.
questions.explain: The card next states this conclusion.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: To be effective in enormous problem spaces, problem solvers must extract from the environment the information about its ____ that is stored there.
questions.explain: That is the authors' conclusion.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A solver given a huge puzzle has no way of noticing its regularities. What does the card predict?
options: She will be ineffective, since the puzzle's stored structure goes unused
She will be effective by chance
She will be effective since regularities are irrelevant to a solver with enough time
She will change the puzzle
optionExplain: Right: extraction is required.
Chance fails in huge spaces.
They matter.
Not possible.
questions.explain: Effectiveness depends on extracting structure.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: A reader says the authors claim all details of a solver's behavior can be exactly deduced from the task's structure. The text supports this.
questions.explain: They say many characteristics can be inferred at least in broad outline.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: What conditions the possible modes of exploiting structural information?
options: The age of the solver and his years of experience
The length of the experiment
The forms the information takes
The solver's mood
optionExplain: Not stated.
Not stated.
Right: stated.
Not stated.
questions.explain: Forms such as features and differences limit how they can be used.
questions.teaches: The forms that structural information takes in the task environment condition the possible modes of its exploitation.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A library catalog is organized by author only. A student wants books by topic. Which statement from the card applies?
options: Topic search is impossible by definition of the catalog, whatever the student does or knows
The form of the stored information limits how it can be exploited
The student's mood decides
Authors do not matter
optionExplain: Not impossible, just costly.
Right: form limits use.
Not relevant.
They do.
questions.explain: Applying the card.
questions.teaches: A great many of the characteristics of the problem solving systems studied can be inferred, at least in broad outline, from the structure of the environments in which they operate.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A cook has a recipe that suits a certain kind of ingredients and cooking tools. Where does the recipe's form come from?
options: Largely from the structure of what she is working with
Entirely from her mood on the day she cooks and the preferences she brought with her
Entirely from chance
From nothing in particular
optionExplain: Right: structure of the space shapes the method.
Not mood.
Not chance.
There is a source.
questions.explain: The card next states the principle.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: The essential point of the section is that methods are determined by the structure of the ____ space.
questions.explain: Problem space structure.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A researcher wrote a whole production system for S3 with no named methods. How may it be viewed?
options: As no method at all
As an invalid system
In toto, as a single idiosyncratic method
As working forward only
optionExplain: It is a method.
It is valid.
Right: stated.
Not only.
questions.explain: The authors say so of the cryptarithmetic systems.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: If two problem spaces have the same structure, the methods available for them should be much alike.
questions.explain: Methods are determined by problem space structure. This is our reading of the principle.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Which methods does the authors' list name as examples?
options: Seriality, parallelism and hashing, which are the methods the book has named
Working forwards, working backwards, means-ends analysis and planning
Chunking and fixation
Fixation and decay
optionExplain: Not methods.
Right: stated.
Not methods.
Not methods.
questions.explain: These were named methods in the book.
questions.teaches: Many methods used by subjects have been named, including working forwards, working backwards, means-ends analysis and planning.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A manager gives one method to a team for an ordered task and another to a team for an unordered pile. Which principle does this mirror?
options: Methods are independent of the structure of the space
Methods are fixed at birth and then used for every kind of task
Methods are unlearned
Methods follow the structure of the space they act in
optionExplain: Reverse.
Not claimed.
Not claimed.
Right: structure drives method.
questions.explain: Applying the card.
questions.teaches: The authors say the claim that methods are determined by the structure of the problem space is not quite the whole story, so some preliminaries are needed.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A recipe says to chop onions without saying how finely. Is it a complete set of behaviors?
options: Yes, every motion is fixed by the recipe, down to the size of each piece of onion and the speed
No, it leaves details open, so behavior is only partly specified
No, since it is not a recipe
Yes, since onions are fixed
optionExplain: Details are open.
Right: partial specification.
It is one.
Not relevant.
questions.explain: The card next treats methods this way.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: To paraphrase Polya, a method is a ____ that you use twice.
questions.explain: No sharp line between plans and methods.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A chess method says to add a defender when a piece is attacked. Which feature of methods does it illustrate?
options: Complete specification of every move in the method
Absence of any goal in the method
A nonrational plan
Partial specification: which man to use is not fixed
optionExplain: Not complete.
It has a goal.
It is rational.
Right: stated.
questions.explain: The man in question is only partially specified.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: A reader says the authors keep methods and programs as two separate levels of organization. The text agrees.
questions.explain: They identify method and program, allowing functionally specified parts.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: What does rational mean in the authors' sense for a method?
options: If its premises are granted, the method can produce a solution
The method always succeeds, whatever the problem or the premises it starts from
The method is fast
The method is taught in schools
optionExplain: Right: minimal rationality.
Not guaranteed.
Speed not part.
Not part.
questions.explain: It is a functional characterization, with no degrees of chance.
questions.teaches: Rationality of a method means only that, if the premises of the method are granted, it is possible for the method to produce a solution; it is a minimal formulation with no degrees.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A teacher says: a lesson plan used twice is a method. Which authors' remark does this echo?
options: Seriality of processing in the teacher's lesson, with one step following another in turn
The closure of the problem space
Polya's remark that a method is a plan that you use twice
Search-scan
optionExplain: Not this.
Not this.
Right: same remark.
Not this.
questions.explain: Applying the card.
questions.teaches: Including functionally specified subprocesses in programs amounts to an inclusion of goals, or goal-creating processes, in programs, as in the GPS methods of Figure 8.8.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A craft guild has a few general techniques that cover most unfamiliar jobs, and also many specialist formulas. Which set does the authors' modest-variety claim cover?
options: The specialist formulas, which every craftsperson must learn before being given any unfamiliar job
Both equally
Neither
The general techniques used in unfamiliar, problematic jobs
optionExplain: Formulas are programmed.
Only one set.
It covers one.
Right: problematic situations only.
questions.explain: The card next states the qualification.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: The authors say the variety of methods is quite ____, depending primarily on the structure of the problem space.
questions.explain: A small number of common methods.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A mathematician uses the quadratic formula to solve an equation. How do the authors classify the situation?
options: Nonproblematic, since a known method is available
Genuinely problematic, since solving an equation in this way is hard for most people
Impossible
Unrelated to methods
optionExplain: Right: stated.
A known method removes the problem.
Possible.
It uses a method.
questions.explain: When such methods are available the situation is nonproblematic.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: A reader says the authors expect ordinary solvers to frequently discover methods like the simplex algorithm on their own. The text agrees.
questions.explain: Such methods are discovered exceedingly rarely by a problem solver who did not have them.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: What is the second qualification on the claim that methods depend primarily on problem-space structure?
options: The method is independent of everything
The method depends on nothing
The method also depends on aspects of the total situation other than the space's structure
The method depends only on the solver's age
optionExplain: Not independent.
Not nothing.
Right: stated.
Not stated.
questions.explain: These aspects can be specified in detail by analyzing the functions of a method.
questions.teaches: A second qualification is that the method, a production system, does depend on aspects of the total situation beyond the problem-space structure, though these can be specified in detail by analyzing what a method must do.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A start-up is full of staff who each invented personal tricks for rare tasks. Which statement fits the authors' view of the variety of methods in genuinely problematic situations?
options: Every person must have a unique method
A few common methods, shaped by problem-space structure, are more likely than unique ones for each person
No methods are possible
Methods are unrelated to tasks
optionExplain: Not so.
Right: modest variety.
Not so.
Not so.
questions.explain: Applying the card.
questions.teaches: It is theoretically conceivable that a problem solver could consist entirely of methods that are definite algorithms or nothing, but in the light of evolution such a state of affairs could hardly exist for biological organisms.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A project lead decides what to aim for, which tool to use, and whether the result is good enough. Which of these are the controlling decisions?
options: All three: aims, tools and evaluation
Only where to store the files and how to name them
Only whom to inform
None of them
optionExplain: Right: goals, operators, evaluation.
Storage is minor.
Communication is minor.
They control.
questions.explain: The card next lists these decisions.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A method is ultimately a device for generating a coordinated pattern of ____.
questions.explain: Decisions about goals, states and operators.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: In which decision does intelligence usually have least scope?
options: Determining the operator to apply
Evaluating a new state
Selecting an old state to retry
Determining goals
optionExplain: Important.
Important.
Right: usually less scope.
Important.
questions.explain: Saving states and selecting old ones offer less scope.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: The room for intelligence at the decision points is the same in every task environment.
questions.explain: In different task environments they differ in frequency and room for intelligence.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Which three kinds of items do the decisions of a method concern?
options: Memories, rates and capacities
Goals, states and operators
Features, variables and names
Inputs, outputs and cycles
optionExplain: Not those.
Right: stated.
Not those.
Not those.
questions.explain: A small set of decisions determines them.
questions.teaches: Intelligence impinges on problem solving, given the problem space, through a small set of decisions that determine goals, states and operators.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: An editor decides which sections to cut, whether to rewrite a paragraph, and what to leave for later. Which decisions are most like the controlling ones?
options: Choosing the file name and the folder for the finished copy
Choosing the printer
Choosing the paper color
Choosing what to cut and judging a rewrite
optionExplain: Minor.
Minor.
Minor.
Right: operator choice and evaluation.
questions.explain: Applying the card.
questions.teaches: Any two production systems that provide identical translations from problem-space information into patterns of decisions are in an important sense the same method.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Two cooks follow differently written recipes but make the same choices from the same ingredients. Are they using the same method?
options: No, since the writing differs
In an important sense yes, since they make identical decisions from the same information
No, since cooks differ
Yes, since recipes are all alike
optionExplain: Wording does not matter.
Right: same mapping.
Not relevant.
Not all alike.
questions.explain: The card next states this identity.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Any two production systems giving identical patterns of decisions as a function of problem-space information are in some sense the same ____.
questions.explain: Often they end up with a common name.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A production system uses only the symbol structures of the goal, the state and the operators. What does it not have represented directly?
options: The goal
The current state
The operators
The correlations and redundancies that make up the space's structure
optionExplain: Symbolized.
Symbolized.
Symbolized.
Right: assumed by the method.
questions.explain: Structure is assumed, not symbolized.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: A reader says a method receives information about task structure directly from the world, bypassing the problem space. The authors agree.
questions.explain: The only information available is that embedded in the space.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: What does the information actually available to a production system comprise?
options: The symbol structures of goals, states and operators, and its own structure
Only the display
Only the instructions
Only the solution
optionExplain: Right: stated.
Not only.
Not only.
Not available.
questions.explain: Its own structure is part of what it can use.
questions.teaches: The information actually available to a production system comprises the symbol structures of the goals, states and operators and its own structure.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Two software tools take the same inputs and give identical outputs through different internal code. Which authors' notion applies?
options: They are different methods
They are both random
Identical translations of information into decisions make them the same method in an important sense
They are not methods
optionExplain: Same function.
Not random.
Right: functional identity.
They are.
questions.explain: Applying the card.
questions.teaches: The correlations and redundancies that constitute problem-space structure are not symbolized directly but are assumed by the method in the way it uses the information directly available in the symbol structures.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A solver goes one step ahead, finds the result bad, marks it and returns. Which kind of production does the marking?
options: Recognition of the solution
Selection of the operator for the next forward move
Writing in LTM
Evaluation of the new state
optionExplain: That recognizes the goal.
That chooses the step.
Not LTM writing.
Right: reject tag.
questions.explain: The card next lists the four types.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Order the four production types as the authors describe them.
items: Recognize the solution state
Evaluate the present state and tag rejects
Determine how far to back up
Select the operator for the next move
questions.explain: The figure's four types run from recognition to operator selection.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A reject tag is attached to an expression. What does this do to later problem solving?
options: Productions whose conditions do not match rejected expressions will no longer use it, in effect returning to the prior state
It deletes the whole contents of memory so that the search starts again from the initial state
It marks the expression as the solution so that later productions stop searching
It copies the expression into LTM so that it can be recalled in later problems
optionExplain: Right: rejected expressions fail to match the productions' conditions, so search effectively returns to the prior state.
The tag only makes the expression unavailable to productions; nothing else is erased.
A reject tag marks an expression to be avoided, the opposite of a solution.
The tag stays on the expression in the display; nothing is copied into LTM.
questions.explain: The reject tag blocks further use of that expression.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: The recognition method can in principle solve any problem as long as the operator that produces the solution is already available in the solver's LTM.
questions.explain: That is the only condition, as noted in Chapter 4.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Why does operator selection alone not constitute a method?
options: It uses no memory
It has no productions
Evaluative information must be added, unless only a single fixed goal is pursued
It is serial
optionExplain: It uses memory.
It has productions.
Right: stated.
Not the reason.
questions.explain: Without evaluation, operator selection cannot be very adaptive.
questions.teaches: Operator selection alone is not adaptive enough to constitute a method; evaluative information needs to be added unless the system pursues a single fixed goal, in which case the goal state can be built into the production system.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A trainee knows exactly which fix cures each fault but does not check whether the fix worked. What does she lack, in the authors' scheme?
options: The recognition productions that detect a solved state
The evaluation and backup productions
The operator productions
Any productions at all
optionExplain: She may recognize faults.
Right: evaluation and backup.
She selects fixes.
She has some.
questions.explain: Applying the card.
questions.teaches: Working-forward gets its name from using information encoded in the current state to select the operators to be executed next.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A traveler notes a difficulty (no ticket) and keeps working at it until solved. Which production form is this like?
options: Creating a difference goal, which implies continuing effort
Selecting an operator once from the state and the goal, then moving on
Recognizing success
Backing up
optionExplain: Right: goals persist.
That is a one-time act.
That is final success.
That is backup.
questions.explain: The card next distinguishes forms A and B.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: In form B of means-ends analysis, operators are selected solely as a function of ____ created from the current state.
questions.explain: Difference goals encode the state.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A means-ends system picks an operator by comparing state and goal in one step with no record kept. Which form is this?
options: Form B, creating persistent goals that remain in force until the difference is removed
Working forward
Form A, a one-time action leaving no trace beyond its effects
The recognition method
optionExplain: B uses goals.
Working forward ignores goal.
Right: stated.
Not this.
questions.explain: A is a joint function of state and goal.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: A reader says form B is unresponsive to the current state because it selects operators only from goals. The authors agree.
questions.explain: The goals themselves are created as functions of the current state and so encode it.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: What do difference goals describe?
options: Operators to be stored in LTM
Difficulties to be surmounted or gaps in information and specification to be filled
Features of the display
Decay times
optionExplain: Not operators.
Right: stated.
Not display.
Not decay.
questions.explain: They are created from the current state.
questions.teaches: Difference goals describe either difficulties to be surmounted or gaps in information and specification to be filled; they are created as functions of the current state.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A planner who records an open item for budget approval and works until it clears is using which production form?
options: Form A, a one-time action that leaves no trace behind
Search-scan
A progress test
Form B, with a persistent difference goal
optionExplain: A leaves no trace.
Not search-scan.
Not a test.
Right: persistent goal.
questions.explain: Applying the card.
questions.teaches: Working-backward and planning are special cases of the working-forward and means-ends schemes, in that they augment the collection of operators in various ways.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A craftsperson either knows a technique by heart, or looks up each technique in a manual on the bench. Which uses the slower route?
options: Knowing it by heart
Looking up the technique, since each must be found and checked
Both the same
Neither
optionExplain: Fast.
Right: search in external store.
They differ.
One is slower.
questions.explain: The card next describes the same difference for operators.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: In variant D, the operators are stored in ____ and must be searched, with the search controlled by a tag symbol.
questions.explain: They are not in LTM.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A subject has a rule sheet on the table and checks each rule against the expression, one at a time. Which variant is this?
options: A: operators embedded in the selection system itself, known by heart
B: separate production systems in LTM
C: a single operator held in STM and then executed
D: operators stored in EM, searched and evaluated one by one
optionExplain: A is in LTM.
B is in LTM.
C is internal.
Right: external store.
questions.explain: EM operators need scanning.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: STM is large enough to hold the whole set of a solver's operators at one time.
questions.explain: STM is not large enough to hold operators, so C handles one at a time.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Where is the top goal likely to be recorded, in the authors' remark?
options: Possibly in the environment, such as on a blackboard
Only in STM, since the top goal must be held in mind and cannot be recorded anywhere else at all
Only in LTM
Nowhere
optionExplain: Right: stated.
Not only.
Not only.
Recorded somewhere.
questions.explain: The current goal is mostly in STM, higher goals in LTM.
questions.teaches: In the normal arrangement the current goal is in STM with perhaps one or two others in a stack, the more pervasive higher goals are in LTM, and the top goal itself may be recorded in the environment, say on a blackboard.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A worker's task list is posted on a wall, her current step is in mind, and her general mission is something she knows by heart. Map these to the card.
options: List in LTM, current step in EM, mission in STM, with the wall list unused
All in STM
List in EM, current step in STM, mission in LTM
All in EM
optionExplain: Reversed.
Too much for STM.
Right: stated pattern.
Mission is in LTM.
questions.explain: Applying the card.
questions.teaches: Parts of the current state kept in EM give rise to the extended knowledge state, and scanning programs are then required to transfer information to the knowledge state in STM.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A beginner follows a printed recipe line by line; an experienced cook works from memory. Which is interpreting?
options: The experienced cook, who must read the structure of the dish as she works
Both
Neither
The beginner, who works from the written structure
optionExplain: She has assimilated it.
One only.
One interprets.
Right: recipe in EM is interpreted.
questions.explain: The card next defines the contrast.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: When an operation is available as a production system, it is said to be ____.
questions.explain: Interpretation is the other case.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A new operator is added. Which system needs new productions?
options: The assimilated system, which must have a new set built
The interpreter, which must be rewritten for the new operator
Neither
Both identically
optionExplain: Right: stated.
The interpreter handles any operator.
One needs them.
Differ.
questions.explain: Interpreters are general; assimilated ones are particular.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: Everything stored in EM requires interpretation before it can affect behavior, although it is often so immediate that the model need not show it.
questions.explain: The authors say so, citing a 5 written alongside D read as D = 5.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: What structural contrast does the authors suggest this distinction provides a basis for?
options: Serial versus parallel processing of the operators
Model versus description
Meaningful versus rote or mechanical learning
Goal versus subgoal
optionExplain: Not this.
Not this.
Right: stated.
Not this.
questions.explain: The authors say this is not the place to elaborate.
questions.teaches: The distinction between assimilation and interpretation provides a structural basis for distinguishing some varieties of meaningful versus rote or mechanical learning.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Why does the authors' own argument rule out that the productions themselves are run by yet another interpreter on the time scale of the data?
options: Because productions cannot be run by any interpreter at all, however it is built
An interpreter would need about a millisecond or less per operation, even if very fast and parallel, to run productions in 100 milliseconds
Because interpreters never work at the time scale of a single production
Because 100 milliseconds is too slow a time for any interpreter to run productions
optionExplain: Productions are run; the argument concerns the time scale an interpreter would need, not whether they can run.
Right: the authors argue from the millisecond-per-operation limit that productions cannot be run by a further interpreter at the data's time scale.
The argument does not deny that interpreters work; it shows that one on this time scale would have to be implausibly fast.
The 100 milliseconds is the observed time scale of the data, not an obstacle to running productions.
questions.explain: The authors say they cannot know if another mechanism interprets productions, but it would not operate on the time scale of elementary processes.
questions.teaches: The production systems are not themselves interpreted but represent an IPS realized directly; any mechanism that interprets them would need roughly a millisecond per operation or faster, even if parallel.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A chess player first spends a minute looking over the whole board before any analysis. What is this period called in the card?
options: An orientation period that builds up the extended knowledge state
A backup period
A fixation period
A subgoal
optionExplain: Right: stated.
Not backup.
Not fixation.
Not subgoal.
questions.explain: The card next describes such periods.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: In GPS the match yields a ____, a symbol structure that summarizes the comparison and is used to select an operator.
questions.explain: Used to select an operator or reduce goal.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A match of two large logic expressions takes a second or two. What does this show?
options: Feature extraction takes minutes
Feature extraction is instantaneous
Even extracted features need only modest effort, though a separate production system
Feature extraction is impossible
optionExplain: Seconds only.
Not instantaneous.
Right: stated.
Possible.
questions.explain: The authors call it not terribly complex.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: A reader says the authors expect complex feature computations before each move because the solver gathers information at leisure. The text agrees.
questions.explain: They argue computations remain simple because short residence times leave little time and the solver cannot pause solving for information gathering.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: What is the argument for simple feature computations based on?
options: The size of LTM, which sets how many features can be stored
The solver's postulated inability to withhold problem solving in the interests of information gathering
The speed of the display, which sets how fast features arrive
The number of operators, which sets how many features are tested
optionExplain: LTM size is not the basis of the argument; it rests on the solver's postulated inability to withhold problem solving.
Right: the argument rests on the solver's postulated inability to withhold problem solving in the interests of information gathering.
Display speed is not the basis of the argument.
The number of operators is not the basis of the argument.
questions.explain: Where it fails, orientation periods arise.
questions.teaches: The argument for simple feature computations rests on the postulated inability of the problem solver to withhold problem solving simply in the interests of information gathering; when it fails, as in orientation periods, different behavior appears.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A mechanic opens a new job by inspecting everything for ten minutes before touching a tool. Which exception from the card is this?
options: A feature computation inside a move, made while she is already working on the repair with a tool in hand
A backup
A subgoal
An orientation period at the beginning of a new problem solving endeavor
optionExplain: Too long for a move.
Not backup.
Not subgoal.
Right: stated.
questions.explain: Applying the card.
questions.teaches: Orientation periods characterize the beginning of any new problem solving endeavor, with chess the best example; at some point the subject then begins to explore the problem space by selecting and applying operators.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A cook first decides to season, then decides which spice. Which description fits this two-stage choice?
options: Choosing at random among every spice on the shelf, one after another
Choosing a form first and then filling in a detail
Choosing all at once
Making no choice
optionExplain: Not random.
Right: parametrization.
It is staged.
A choice is made.
questions.explain: The card next describes such staged choices.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Operators that select an aspect of the current state as input to the productive operators are called ____ operators.
questions.explain: Productive ones produce new information.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: In cryptarithmetic, FC precedes PC. Which relation is this?
options: A productive operator before another productive one, in a fixed pair of the same kind
Two attentional operators in parallel
A backup before a search
An attentional operator coupled directly before a productive operator
optionExplain: Not that.
Not that.
Not that.
Right: stated.
questions.explain: FC finds the column and PC processes it.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: If gaps in a productive operator's specification are symbolized as difficulties to be removed by other productions, the organization is more flexible than the coupled one.
questions.explain: The authors call it much more flexible and an instance of means-ends analysis.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: How are goals often parametrized, in the authors' remark?
options: As forms such as check(letter)
As numbers only
As operators only, with no variables inside the goals
As time stamps
optionExplain: Right: stated.
Not numbers.
Not operators.
Not time.
questions.explain: Real selection of the variable in a goal was rare in the data.
questions.teaches: Goals are often parametrized as forms such as check(letter), but only rarely does a real act of selecting the variable in a goal appear in the data, which may be an artifact of the tasks.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A technician's work order calls for a part replacement and the part number is left blank until the diagnosis arrives. How does this resemble the card?
options: A fully specified set of productions
A backup
A form with a variable whose value is fixed later, when a determining condition arises
A search-scan
optionExplain: Not fully specified.
Not backup.
Right: delayed binding.
Not search-scan.
questions.explain: Applying the card.
questions.teaches: Parametrization is another way of factoring: dividing the selection of the appropriate operator into parts so that each part can be attended to separately.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Two programs give the same decisions, but one reads its rules from a sheet and the other has them memorized. How do they differ?
options: In function, not in structure
In neither
In both
In structure, not in the function they perform
optionExplain: Same function.
They differ.
Function same.
Right: stated.
questions.explain: The card next states this.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: These variations solve only the ____ problems of effecting a pattern of decisions.
questions.explain: They do not alter the main function.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Which is NOT one of the three structural sources of variation named in the summary?
options: The solver's hobbies
Location of information
Need for interpretation
Parametrization
optionExplain: Right: not named.
Named.
Named.
Named.
questions.explain: The three are location, interpretation and parametrization.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: A reader says location, interpretation and parametrization change what a method is for. The authors agree.
questions.explain: They do not alter the main function of a method.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: What is the main function of a method?
options: To store information about earlier problems in LTM for use on later ones
To increase the capacity of STM so that more goals can be held at once
To effect a pattern of decisions about goals, states and operators from information in the problem structure
To display the problem to the solver in a form that makes it easier to see
optionExplain: Storage in LTM is a memory function, not what a method does.
STM capacity is a fixed parameter; methods work within it.
Right: a method effects a pattern of decisions about goals, states and operators from information in the problem structure.
Displaying the problem is not a method's function.
questions.explain: That function stays the same.
questions.teaches: The main function of a method is to effect a pattern of decisions about goals, states and operators as a function of information embedded in the problem structure.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A company moves its procedures from a binder to an app. Which statement matches the card?
options: The procedure is now a different method in function
The procedure's function is unchanged though its structural form for access has altered
The procedure no longer needs decisions
The procedure is now random
optionExplain: Same function.
Right: same function.
Needs decisions.
Not random.
questions.explain: Applying the card.
questions.teaches: The nature and variety of production systems is not well enough understood to permit a definitive analysis of the structure of methods.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A musician plays mostly classical but sometimes jazz phrases. Which description fits better?
options: A mixture of styles, not a strict choice of one complete style at a time
Only one style at a time
No style
A new style each note
optionExplain: Right: mixing.
Mixing occurs.
Style exists.
Not each note.
questions.explain: The card next compares discrete versus mixed methods.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: The authors suggest named methods may really be ideal ____, with real problem solvers being mixtures of them.
questions.explain: A mixture of types.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: What is wrong with a single production as a unit for building methods?
options: It cannot be written down
It uses too much memory
It leaves the class of all programs, with no useful constraint
It is serial
optionExplain: It can.
Not the reason.
Right: stated.
Not the reason.
questions.explain: Clusters are the candidate units.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: The authors claim the mixture view has been proved to describe all subjects' programs.
questions.explain: They say whether all subjects' programs can be described as mixtures is not determinable here.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: What do the authors say a viable theory of ideal types requires, in their footnote about sociology?
options: More data about culture, gathered in many societies, so that the types may be checked in the field
Explicit laws of composition so that real agents can be described
Fewer types
No types at all
optionExplain: Not data.
Right: stated.
Not fewer.
Types are needed.
questions.explain: Otherwise 'mixtures' is a dodge in the face of complexity.
questions.teaches: A viable theory of ideal types requires explicit laws of composition so that descriptions of actual agents are possible; otherwise calling them mixtures is a dodge in the face of phenomenal complexity.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A school says its teachers use a blend of three named teaching methods in each lesson. What would the authors want to see?
options: Nothing beyond the claim
A larger classroom
A single method
A statement of which clusters of actions belong to which method and how they combine
optionExplain: Not enough.
Irrelevant.
Not required.
Right: units and composition.
questions.explain: Applying the card.
questions.teaches: Almost all multimethod artificial intelligence programs are organized as discrete complete methods with a method-selection mechanism that evokes the appropriate one.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A student uses a direct approach whenever new data come in, and a goal-reducing approach whenever stuck. How would the authors describe her?
options: As using only one method
As a mixture of two methods that take control under different conditions
As having no method
As random
optionExplain: Two methods.
Right: stated.
A method exists.
Not random.
questions.explain: The card next shows this for S3.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: S3's productions P1 and part of P4 realize the working-____ method.
questions.explain: On new information.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: In S3's system, what triggers control by means-ends analysis?
options: Every new piece of information entering the problem
The end of the session
The display
Difficulties arising in the problem
optionExplain: That is working-forward.
Not that.
Not that.
Right: stated.
questions.explain: Working-forward controls on new information.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: Behavior in S3's system oscillates back and forth between working-forward and means-ends analysis.
questions.explain: The authors say so.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: What do the two methods in S3's system share?
options: A common set of evaluation productions, including the final evaluation
The same operators only
The same goal types only
Nothing
optionExplain: Right: P11, P12, P5.
Not only.
Not only.
They share.
questions.explain: P5 is the final evaluation.
questions.teaches: Both methods in S3's system require evaluation, which is achieved in a common set of productions (P11, P12 and P5), the last being the final evaluation of the problem.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: An analyst says their team's workflow decomposes into two methods. What else would the authors ask?
options: Whether the team is large enough to need two methods, and whether its members work in the same room
Whether the room is quiet
Whether the mixing is psychologically real, which is the crucial issue
Whether the methods are named
optionExplain: Not relevant.
Not relevant.
Right: stated.
Not the issue.
questions.explain: The decomposition is parsimonious but its reality is unknown.
questions.teaches: The authors say they cannot determine whether all subjects' programs can be described as mixtures of basic clusters, nor whether all ways of combining clusters make sense, nor the psychological reality of mixing.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Can two solvers with the same task, goals and space still differ in the methods they use?
options: No, never
Yes, without any limits
Only if the task differs
Yes, partly, but within narrow limits
optionExplain: Partly independent.
Circumscribed.
Same task still allows.
Right: stated.
questions.explain: The card next states this.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Which methods a solver uses is partly a measure of his intelligence and ____.
questions.explain: Education and intelligence.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A skilled and an unskilled solver face the same space. How might their methods differ?
options: The skilled one may use better methods from the available range
They must use identical methods
Neither can use methods
The unskilled one uses all methods
optionExplain: Right: stated.
Partly independent.
Both use.
Not all.
questions.explain: A solver need not use all methods or the best ones.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: A reader says the authors treat method as a fully independent variable to be added to the task, goals and space. The text agrees.
questions.explain: They say method is not a completely independent variable; choices are highly circumscribed.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: What does the section's analysis exclude?
options: Working forwards
Means-ends analysis
The highly specific methods of science, mathematics and the practical arts
Planning
optionExplain: Included.
Included.
Right: stated.
Included.
questions.explain: It covers methods in problematic situations.
questions.teaches: The analysis is restricted to the methods available in problematic situations and does not include the highly specific methods of science, mathematics and the practical arts.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: An engineer's special formulas for bridge loads are not covered by the section. Why?
options: They are too simple
They are specific methods of a practical art, outside methods for problematic situations
They are random
They are not methods
optionExplain: Not the reason.
Right: stated.
Not random.
They are.
questions.explain: Applying the card.
questions.teaches: Mixtures of methods reduce the large number of methods to the ideal types, and the functional analysis reduces it further by abstracting from inessential variation.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.section: Determination of Individual Problem Spaces and Programs
questions.q: A new employee is handed a task sheet. Much of how she sets about it was formed earlier. What does this suggest about the evidence?
options: Most of the relevant behavior happened before anyone could record it
All relevant behavior is visible in the first session of work, so nothing earlier matters at all
No past experience matters once the instructions are given
The task sheet fixes every detail
optionExplain: Right: history precedes the record.
Past matters.
Past matters.
Not every detail.
questions.explain: The card next treats this as a limit on the theory.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.section: Determination of Individual Problem Spaces and Programs
questions.q: The program changes little during one problem, so learning must be followed over hours of exposure, not ____.
questions.explain: Learning has a longer time scale than search.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.section: Determination of Individual Problem Spaces and Programs
questions.q: A subject has played chess for years. What does the card predict about her initial performance program?
options: It will be built slowly over the whole session
It will change at every move
It will be assembled very fast and stay relatively stable
It will not exist
optionExplain: Fast.
Stable.
Right: stated.
It exists.
questions.explain: None of the subjects was naive.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.section: Determination of Individual Problem Spaces and Programs
questions.q: True or false: A reader says the authors present a complete, well-tested theory of how spaces and programs are determined. The text supports this.
questions.explain: They call this part of the theory tentative and incomplete.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.section: Determination of Individual Problem Spaces and Programs
questions.q: Why can the invariant structure described so far not by itself explain individual differences among problem solvers?
options: It was worked out for chess alone and does not apply to other tasks
It holds over tasks and persons, while the problem space and program adopted differ by person and occasion
It describes only the sizes of the memories, not the processes that use them
It leaves out the task environment, which is where the differences originate
optionExplain: The invariants are said to hold over tasks, not for chess alone.
Right: invariants are shared by everyone, so differences must lie in the space and program each person adopts.
The invariants include processes as well as memory characteristics.
The task environment is part of the theory; it fixes the class of admissible spaces.
questions.explain: Invariants hold over tasks and persons, so differences must be sought in the space and program a solver adopts.
questions.teaches: So far the theory describes invariants over tasks and over persons, yet large individual differences must be reflected in the actual problem space and program a given problem solver adopts on a given occasion.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.section: Determination of Individual Problem Spaces and Programs
questions.q: A teacher wants to study how pupils learn a new game. Which time scale does the card suggest observing?
options: A few seconds
A single move, the shortest unit of problem solving
The first minute only
Hours of exposure, not minutes
optionExplain: Too short.
Too short.
Too short.
Right: stated.
questions.explain: Applying the card.
questions.teaches: The performance program does not change much in the time it takes to solve a single problem, so studying the development of that program means following behavior over hours of exposure.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A person who has played chess for years is asked whether she would like a game. Where does her program come from?
options: A set of general construction rules applied to the task instructions
Her stored experience with the same task
The course of the first move
A new analogy
optionExplain: Not needed.
Right: stated example.
Not needed.
Not needed.
questions.explain: The card lists this as the second source.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Put these sources in the order the authors list them.
items: Task instructions
Experience with the same task
Experience with analogous tasks
General stored programs
Construction programs
Course of problem solving
questions.explain: This is the list in the text.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A construction program uses the written instructions as its input. How do the sources relate here?
options: They exclude each other
Source six replaces both
Source one is unused
Source five combines with source one, since the instructions serve as data
optionExplain: Not exclusive.
Not replaced.
It is used.
Right: stated.
questions.explain: Sources combine as data and program.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: The instructions tell more explicitly about the problem space than about the program that works in it.
questions.explain: The authors state this.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Which source can change the space or program after work has begun?
options: The course of problem solving itself
The task instructions alone, read at the start
Experience with the same task
A stored general program
optionExplain: Right: source six.
Initial.
Prior.
Prior.
questions.explain: It may augment, modify or radically change either.
questions.teaches: The course of problem solving itself may augment or modify the problem space or program or, on occasion, radically change one or both.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A cook uses a recipe card and also her memory of a similar dish. How many of the six sources are at work at least?
options: None
Only the instructions, since the recipe card is the only source she has and her memory counts for nothing
Two: the instructions and experience with an analogous task
All six necessarily
optionExplain: Some are used.
At least two.
Right: two.
Not necessarily all.
questions.explain: Applying the card.
questions.teaches: The sources are not mutually exclusive: different aspects of a given problem situation can be determined by different sources of information.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
