questions.q: Two groups play the same underlying game, but one is told it is a board game and the other a number game. Which space does each use?
options: The same space for both
A space neither was told
A space chosen at random
The one matching the description each was given
optionExplain: Differ.
Told.
Not random.
Right: stated prediction.
questions.explain: The card next states this prediction.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: The authors call the dual of tic-tac-toe in projective geometry by the name ____.
questions.explain: Lines become points and squares become lines.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A subject is told to play number scrabble. Which objects and operators does she use?
options: Those defined for number scrabble
Those defined for tic-tac-toe, the game she is most used to
None
Those of chess
optionExplain: Right: stated.
Wrong game.
She uses some.
Wrong game.
questions.explain: The space follows the representation.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: A reader says the authors treat the work of fixing a space as the real problem solving and the search as secondary. The text agrees.
questions.explain: They argue instructions contain much information for defining the space and program, and a footnote refutes that view.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: What does the footnote argument say about a sequence of tasks from one environment?
options: Every task is a new problem
No task is a problem
If fixing the space were the real problem, only the first task would be a problem
Tasks are unrelated
optionExplain: Reused space.
They are.
Right: stated.
They are related.
questions.explain: Later tasks reuse the space and program.
questions.teaches: If the real problem solving were the preliminary determination of the space and program, then only the first of several tasks from the same environment would present a problem, since later ones would need no new space or program.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Two firms describe the same job in different vocabularies. What does the card predict about the work plans staff form?
options: Plans will be identical
Plans will follow the vocabulary used in each firm's description
Plans will ignore the description
Plans cannot form
optionExplain: Differ.
Right: representation guides.
Descriptions guide.
They form.
questions.explain: Applying the card.
questions.teaches: Task instructions do more than define the task; they provide a specific representation of it that can serve to define an initial problem space and even parts of an initial program.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A group is taught a puzzle with a worksheet layout. Most solve it using that layout. What is the best explanation?
options: The instructions supplied the representation they adopted
Chance
Prior knowledge of nothing about the puzzle, its layout or any similar puzzle
The solutions were memorized
optionExplain: Right: instructions guide.
Not chance.
Not nothing.
Not memorized.
questions.explain: The card next gives the evidence from two tasks.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: All subjects but S6 in cryptarithmetic worked in the ____ problem space.
questions.explain: It keeps the structure of the basic space.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: What does the augmented space add to the basic space?
options: A new task, a new goal and a new set of subjects, all added to the basic space
A different goal
Relations in the knowledge state with matching operators
A new set of subjects
optionExplain: Not a task.
Goal same.
Right: stated.
Not subjects.
questions.explain: The essential structure stays.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: If logic had been introduced as a formal system with dot and wedge, subjects would be expected to worry over the contradiction in the right side of L1 of A1.
questions.explain: The authors state this prediction.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Which spaces did none of the cryptarithmetic subjects use?
options: The basic space, which no subject of the six used
The algebraic space and the abstract spaces that are possible
The augmented space
A space of any kind
optionExplain: Some used it.
Right: stated.
Most used it.
All used one.
questions.explain: The spaces matched the description.
questions.teaches: None of the cryptarithmetic subjects used the algebraic problem space, nor any of the abstract spaces that are possible.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A class is told a task in everyday words and does not apply the formal model the teacher knows. Which finding does this match?
options: Subjects always find the formal model
Subjects ignore instructions
Subjects invent random spaces
Subjects built spaces matching the instructions, not the available formal alternatives
optionExplain: They do not.
They follow.
Not random.
Right: matches.
questions.explain: Applying the card.
questions.teaches: In logic all subjects built problem spaces that corresponded to the instructions, which would have made their problem solving quite different if the task had been presented as a system of formal logic.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.section: Previous Experience with the Same Task
questions.q: A veteran driver is told to drive to the next town. What do the instructions do?
options: They teach driving from scratch, step by step
They evoke a program already stored in memory
They build a new program from the words of the instructions
They have no effect
optionExplain: Already known.
Right: stored program.
Not new.
They evoke.
questions.explain: The card next treats chess this way.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.section: Previous Experience with the Same Task
questions.q: A process becomes an operator in a space when the subject has much experience and a performance ____ for it.
questions.explain: That is the criterion.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.section: Previous Experience with the Same Task
questions.q: Why do chess protocols tell us little about how subjects learned the game?
options: Subjects refuse to talk about how they learned the game while they are in the laboratory
Chess has no program
The protocols are too short
The instructions evoke a program already learned long before
optionExplain: Not stated.
It has one.
Not the reason.
Right: stated.
questions.explain: Learning took place earlier.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.section: Previous Experience with the Same Task
questions.q: True or false: A reader says the first segment of a chess protocol can tell nothing at all. The text agrees.
questions.explain: It may tell a good deal about how the subject transfers information about a new position to internal memory.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.section: Previous Experience with the Same Task
questions.q: Which component tasks does the card name beyond chess as ones for which subjects hold ready programs?
options: Addition and subtraction in cryptarithmetic and substitution in logic
Searching a library
Writing essays
Playing music
optionExplain: Right: stated.
Not named.
Not named.
Not named.
questions.explain: They act as operators in the spaces.
questions.teaches: The same consideration applies to component tasks such as addition and subtraction in cryptarithmetic and substitution in logic, for which subjects have much experience and a performance program.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.section: Previous Experience with the Same Task
questions.q: An analyst argues that a skill is ready to be treated as one step of a larger plan. What test fits the card?
options: Whether the step is short enough to be done within the span of one minute
Whether the step is named
Whether the person already has much experience and a program for it
Whether the step is easy to explain
optionExplain: Not the test.
Not the test.
Right: stated criterion.
Not the test.
questions.explain: Applying the card.
questions.teaches: A principal criterion for making a process an operator in a problem space is that it represents a task in which the subject already has much experience and for which he has a performance program.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.section: Previous Experience with the Same Task
questions.q: A learner treats a new tool as like an old one and is partly right. What is the likely result?
options: No progress at all
No errors at all
Perfect transfer
Some quick progress and some errors where the tools differ
optionExplain: Some progress.
Errors occur.
Not perfect.
Right: both.
questions.explain: The card next gives logic and cryptarithmetic examples.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.section: Previous Experience with the Same Task
questions.q: Logic subjects tried to use the tilde as if it were the ____ sign of algebra.
questions.explain: This was a dysfunctional analogy.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.section: Previous Experience with the Same Task
questions.q: Subjects who solved cryptarithmetic columns from right to left were using which analogy?
options: Arithmetic addition, which gives a systematic way to break up the task
Chess evaluation
Tic-tac-toe
Planning
optionExplain: Right: stated.
Not chess.
Not tic-tac-toe.
Not planning.
questions.explain: Right-to-left gives an orderly procedure.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.section: Previous Experience with the Same Task
questions.q: True or false: Analogy yields a useful space only if the recognized similarity reflects fundamental isomorphisms between the tasks and the adaptation succeeds.
questions.explain: The authors state both conditions.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.section: Previous Experience with the Same Task
questions.q: Why was working right to left both a flaw and a benefit in cryptarithmetic?
options: It gave no benefit; it only forced the solver to ignore the constrained columns
It was no flaw; it gave information that did not depend on position
Constrained columns give information independently of position, but the order supplies a systematic procedure
It was forced by the display and so was neither a flaw nor a benefit
optionExplain: It did help: the order supplied a systematic procedure.
It was a flaw as well, since the right-to-left order gave up information that constrained columns offer wherever they are.
Right: it is a flaw because constrained columns are used wherever they are, and a benefit because the order is systematic.
The display did not force the order; the authors treat it as a choice with costs and benefits.
questions.explain: The authors weigh both.
questions.teaches: Working right to left is dysfunctional in that information can be extracted from the constrained columns independently of position, but functional at a less sophisticated level since it gives a systematic procedure for decomposing the problem.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.section: Previous Experience with the Same Task
questions.q: A subject separates 'rearranging' a piece from 'removing or adding' material to grasp a rule distinction. Which source of the essential-inessential idea is this?
options: The twelve logic rules alone, read as a formal system
The familiar world of physical objects
The syntax of expressions
The chess board
optionExplain: Formal route.
Right: physical analogy.
Formal route.
Not chess.
questions.explain: Applying the card.
questions.teaches: The essential-inessential distinction in logic may come from the familiar world of physical objects, where manipulating or rearranging material differs from removing or adding material.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A clerk adds numbers for invoices and for inventory. How many addition programs does she most likely have?
options: One, applied to different contexts
One for each context, each written separately for its use
One for each digit
None
optionExplain: Right: a general program.
Not each context.
Not each digit.
She adds.
questions.explain: The card next argues this for arithmetic.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: The relevant input to the addition program is the pair of digits, not their interpretation as pawns or ____ values.
questions.explain: The letter values in DONALD+GERALD.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: In a chess exchange evaluation and a cryptarithmetic column, which is the same?
options: The whole problem space, with its states and its operators
The goal
The general arithmetic program applied to the digits
The table of moves
optionExplain: Not the same.
Differs.
Right: stated.
Differs.
questions.explain: Context differs, the program is shared.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: A reader says the card proves human problem solving programs as a whole are general across tasks. The text agrees.
questions.explain: It says it is not evident how much communality can be extracted for problem solving programs, and it is an empirical issue.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: What is the open empirical issue the card raises?
options: Whether people can add
Whether human subjects actually have general problem solving programs, even if conceivable
Whether digits exist
Whether chess has pawns
optionExplain: Settled.
Right: stated.
Settled.
Settled.
questions.explain: Low-level operations are not in doubt.
questions.teaches: It is not evident how much communality can be extracted from a collection of problem spaces and packaged as a single process, and for human subjects it is an empirical issue whether they actually have such general programs.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A bank uses one routine to compute interest for loans and savings. Which point does this echo?
options: A specific program for each context
A program that cannot be reused
A separate program for each digit
A general subroutine applied in different contexts to different inputs
optionExplain: Opposite.
Opposite.
Not that.
Right: generalized subroutine.
questions.explain: Applying the card.
questions.teaches: The arithmetic operation is employed within a specific context in each case, yet the same general program is being applied, with the particular pair of digits as the relevant input.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A rule says: when you learn a new fact about something, look up where it sits and work out what follows. Is it tied to one task?
options: It is certainly general
It could be general, but it is only known to be used in one task unless there is evidence otherwise
It cannot be used
It is certainly specific
optionExplain: Not certain.
Right: needs evidence.
It can.
Not certain.
questions.explain: The card next treats P1 this way.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: The chess executive can be turned into any chess program by filling open ____, such as base-moves.
questions.explain: Open subprocesses.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Production P1 is evoked in which tasks, according to the evidence?
options: Algebra and cryptarithmetic
Chess and logic
Every task
Cryptarithmetic only
optionExplain: Not algebra.
Not those.
Not every.
Right: stated.
questions.explain: It is specific to cryptarithmetic.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: The chess executive could be used without change to do cryptarithmetic or logic.
questions.explain: The authors say it is specific to chess and certainly could not.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: What would the general form P1* of production P1 say?
options: New information about X leads to finding where X is and deriving consequences there
Select a random operator
Erase the display
Stop searching
optionExplain: Right: stated.
Not that.
Not that.
Not that.
questions.explain: It does not mention columns or digits.
questions.teaches: A general form of the cryptarithmetic production could say that new information about X leads to finding X in some place and deriving the consequences at that place, though there was no empirical ground for asserting that subjects used it.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A guild uses a manual specific to its craft that others cannot use. Which of the card's cases is it like?
options: The arithmetic subroutine that adds in any context
GPS
The chess executive, specific to chess
A general production P1*
optionExplain: General.
General.
Right: task specific.
General.
questions.explain: Applying the card.
questions.teaches: The chess executive, from which all existing chess programs can be written by specifying open subprocesses, is specific to chess and could not be used to do cryptarithmetic or logic.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A word processor works on any text once it knows the language. Which analogy applies to GPS?
options: A separate program for each text, rewritten for each language
No core
No definitions
A general core plus task-specific definitions
optionExplain: Not separate.
A core exists.
Definitions needed.
Right: general core.
questions.explain: The card next describes GPS in these terms.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: GPS describes the world in terms of objects, operators, features and ____.
questions.explain: Four general concepts.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: What must be provided before GPS can attack a new task?
options: Coordinating definitions and task-specific programs for features, differences and operators
Nothing at all
Only the goal
A new method for matching
optionExplain: Right: stated.
Something is needed.
More needed.
Methods are general.
questions.explain: The core is task-free, but linking is not.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: A reader says GPS-2-6 was limited to two tasks. The text agrees.
questions.explain: It handled eleven different tasks.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Which task types did GPS-2-6 cover?
options: Only chess
Only logic
Formal integration, puzzles, sentence parsing and series extrapolation
Only arithmetic
optionExplain: Not only.
Not only.
Right: stated.
Not only.
questions.explain: Eleven tasks in all.
questions.teaches: GPS-2-6 was able to work on eleven different tasks, ranging from formal integration to various puzzles, to parsing a sentence, to series extrapolation.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A spreadsheet engine works for any business once its columns are defined. Which feature of GPS does this resemble?
options: A task-specific program, written afresh for each business and unable to be used for any other business
A general core made to fit a task by coordinating definitions
A random search
A memory limit
optionExplain: Opposite.
Right: general core.
Not this.
Not this.
questions.explain: Applying the card.
questions.teaches: To operate in a specific task environment, GPS requires coordinating definitions identifying object, operator, feature and difference with classes of entities in the task, along with programs specific to the task for detecting features and differences and applying operators.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Two assistants, a new hire and a veteran, are told a task. Which instruction can be skipped for the veteran?
options: Facts the veteran already knows from past experience
Every instruction, since the veteran has seen all of them in earlier work
The goal
The starting state
optionExplain: Right: known facts.
Not every.
Needed.
Needed.
questions.explain: The card compares GPS and a human in this way.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: In the Fathers and Sons instructions, the word sail is declared to be a move ____.
questions.explain: SAIL is an operator.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: The 200 pound boat limit must be stated to both the human and GPS. Why?
options: Because humans cannot read
Because GPS cannot add
It is not universal knowledge, so it is not part of what the human already holds
Because boats have no limits
optionExplain: Not stated.
Not stated.
Right: stated.
Not stated.
questions.explain: Non-universal characteristics are told.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: If the story is rewritten in nonsense words, the extra instructions given to GPS would seem quite essential to a human as well.
questions.explain: The authors say so about the slithy tove version.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: What part of the GPS instructions could be dropped after the later scheme in Chapter 8?
options: The initial state
The ordering of differences
The goal
The operators, which GPS cannot find for itself in the world
optionExplain: Needed.
Right: stated.
Needed.
Needed.
questions.explain: A scheme for deriving the order was developed.
questions.teaches: GPS, unlike the human, was not able to order the differences, but a scheme for deriving the order of differences means that this part of the instructions could now be dispensed with.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A recipe for a stranger must define terms a local cook already knows. Which point does this reflect?
options: Words carry no knowledge
All knowledge must be spelled out for anyone, however familiar the words used may be
Recipes are not instructions
Familiar words evoke stored knowledge that need not be spelled out
optionExplain: They carry.
Not all.
They are.
Right: evoked knowledge.
questions.explain: Applying the card.
questions.teaches: The differences between the instructions to GPS and to a human come from knowledge already accumulated before the experiment, which can be evoked by designating phrases instead of being set forth explicitly.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A builder assembles a shed from stock parts in an hour. What makes this fast?
options: Every part is invented on site, one after another, from raw material
The parts already exist and only their arrangement is chosen
No parts are used
The plan is random
optionExplain: Not invented.
Right: stock parts.
Parts used.
Not random.
questions.explain: The card says the same of spaces.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Order the three things built when a space is constructed, as the card lists them.
items: A representation for the knowledge state
Operators that generate new knowledge
Processes that test applicability and desirability
questions.explain: The text lists these three.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: In S8's typographical space, which part had to be built new?
options: The disjointness test for assignments of digits to letters
The completeness test
The knowledge state
Operators for perceiving letters as digits
optionExplain: Already formed.
Already formed.
Similar to old.
Right: stated.
questions.explain: The other components were available.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: A reader says fast construction implies that far more processing per unit time occurs than the IPS allows. The text agrees.
questions.explain: Construction implies a large selection but need not imply much processing.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Which overlearned items serve as raw components for building spaces?
options: Addition, subtraction, comparison of symbols and simple predicates
Column processors
Digit tests
Complex plans
optionExplain: Right: stated.
Built from them.
Built from them.
Built from them.
questions.explain: These do not by themselves make a column processor.
questions.teaches: The basic components for constructing spaces are overlearned and in the repertoire: addition, subtraction, comparison of symbols and representations for simple predicates, though they do not of themselves constitute column processors or digit tests.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A reader grasps the idea of letters read as digits within seconds of being told. What does this show about operators of that kind?
options: They need hours of work before they can be used
They cannot be built
They can be built rapidly from familiar parts
They need a new memory
optionExplain: Fast.
They can.
Right: rapid construction.
Not needed.
questions.explain: The authors cite the reader's quick response.
questions.teaches: That constructing operators in the vicinity of B82 is not impossible can be seen from the reader's rather rapid response to the written suggestion that such operators exist.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A student learns a test format by studying the sample questions with answers. What does she infer first?
options: The final score of the test, from the sample questions
The author's name
The room size
The form in which answers are to be given
optionExplain: Not inferable.
Irrelevant.
Irrelevant.
Right: form of answer.
questions.explain: The card says EDPS does this.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: EDPS tests a trial performance program against the worked ____ before tackling the test items.
questions.explain: It uses them as a check.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Which answer forms does EDPS determine from the examples?
options: Filling a blank, selecting an item that fits or fails to fit a rule, or stating the rule
Only a number
Only a letter
Only a yes or no
optionExplain: Right: stated.
Wider.
Wider.
Wider.
questions.explain: These are listed in the text.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: The processes EDPS uses to construct a program are themselves problem solving processes.
questions.explain: They involve recognition of salient features with direct selection of components, not problem solving.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Why are compilers not helpful as models for human program construction?
options: They are too slow
They are too small
They work from process descriptions of the programs to be built
They cannot run
optionExplain: Not the reason.
Not the reason.
Right: stated.
Not the reason.
questions.explain: Their inputs are programs in a higher-level language.
questions.teaches: Compilers are synthetic programs that construct programs, but they all work from process descriptions of the programs to be constructed, so they do not appear relevant to how humans build programs from task instructions.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A trainee reads a manual and, instead of its text, learns the task entirely from worked samples. Which program is this like?
options: A compiler
EDPS, which works entirely from the examples
GPS-2-6 with a table of connections and a difference ordering
Waterman's poker program
optionExplain: Not this.
Right: EDPS.
Not this.
Not this.
questions.explain: Applying the card.
questions.teaches: EDPS works entirely from the worked examples, having enough general context to dispense with the written instructions, and builds and tests a trial performance program against those examples.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A manager finds her usual routines run dry and invents a new routine on the spot. How would you describe the change?
options: A modification of her program during the task
No change, since a routine used once is not part of the program
A change of the goal only
A change of the room
optionExplain: Right: program modified.
Change occurred.
Not just the goal.
Irrelevant.
questions.explain: The card next gives S3's case.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: S3's production P3 was the first to execute the ____ operator, assigning L = 1.
questions.explain: AV, the assignment operator.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Why might P3 have been added at that point?
options: The session had ended
S3 was told to add it by the experimenter, who suggested a new way of continuing the problem
The existing production system offered no way to continue
S3 forgot the problem
optionExplain: Not stated.
Not stated.
Right: stated.
Not stated.
questions.explain: The first episode used a pure reasoning system.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: A reader says the authors have a clear account of what adding a production involves in the structure of the IPS. The text agrees.
questions.explain: They say they have no very clear notion of this.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: What did S3 do immediately before P3 was evoked?
options: Solved the problem
Decided to forget the previous line for a minute and try possible solutions
Left the session
Asked for the answer
optionExplain: Not solved.
Right: stated.
Not stated.
Not stated.
questions.explain: It signals a shift of approach.
questions.teaches: S3 had finished his first episode, establishing T = 0 and R odd and failing to establish anything about G, before turning to try different possible solutions by evoking production P3.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Observers see a worker use a procedure for the first time. Why can they not tell whether it was newly learned?
options: They can always tell
Procedures cannot be learned
Procedures are never stored
Use does not distinguish a first evocation of a stored procedure from adding a new one
optionExplain: They cannot.
They can.
They can.
Right: ambiguity.
questions.explain: Applying the card.
questions.teaches: It is possible that P3 was added to the problem solving program at this point instead of being present from the beginning, and nothing in the protocol separates the two.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A student suddenly realizes a general fact and then solves the problem at once. What could have changed in her?
options: Only the weather on the day, which can alter how a student takes in a fact and so what she does next
Her space, her program, or only her current knowledge
Nothing
Only her mood
optionExplain: Irrelevant.
Right: three possibilities.
Something changed.
Not enough.
questions.explain: The card next frames three options.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: S8 derived E = 9 from E = 0 or 9 and T = ____.
questions.explain: Earlier shown T = 0.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Why does the authors' evidence rule out a change in the form of inference?
options: He never used inferences
He used a different form of inference earlier in the session, so it was not new to him
He did not speak
S8 had used inferences of this form several times before
optionExplain: He used them.
Same form.
He spoke.
Right: stated.
questions.explain: It was not new here.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: If S8 had used the carry fact in later problems, the authors could more easily tell whether his space changed.
questions.explain: They say he had no occasion to use it, so cannot be sure.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Why is the generality of S8's statement not a reliable guide to a change of space?
options: Earlier, in E24, he had thoroughly explored carries and concluded they cannot be 2 or more
He never stated anything general
He was silent
The statement was false
optionExplain: Right: stated.
He did state.
He spoke.
Not claimed.
questions.explain: A general statement need not be new.
questions.teaches: Generality of a statement is not a reliable guide, since earlier, some minutes before DONALD+GERALD, S8 had explored the matter of carries and concluded the carry cannot be 2 or more.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A coach cannot tell if an athlete learned a new skill or applied one case. What would help?
options: Asking nothing further, since the athlete's skill is a private matter of the mind
Listening to the crowd
Observing whether the athlete uses it on later occasions
Counting spectators
optionExplain: Need evidence.
Irrelevant.
Right: later use.
Irrelevant.
questions.explain: Applying the card.
questions.teaches: Because S8 had no occasion to use the newly acquired general fact in the rest of his protocol, it cannot be settled whether he changed his problem space or only made a particular inference that added to his knowledge state.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A rule list is checked from the top, and the first matching rule wins. Where should an exception rule go?
options: After the general rule, so that general cases are checked first
Anywhere
Nowhere
Before the general rule
optionExplain: It would be screened.
Position matters.
It is needed.
Right: specialization first.
questions.explain: The card next states this principle.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Waterman's program starts from a null production that makes a ____ bet.
questions.explain: Experience adds productions.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Why does the location of a new production matter in the poker program?
options: Productions near the head of the list screen later ones
Because location is random, so that new productions are placed wherever there is room
Because of memory size
Because of the cards
optionExplain: Right: stated.
Not random.
Not the reason.
Not the reason.
questions.explain: Order shapes behavior.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: A reader says the adding processes in the poker program are more complex than the problem solvers themselves and require special kinds of processes. The text agrees.
questions.explain: They are no more complex than the problem solvers and need no other sorts of symbolic processes.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: What does the authors' footnote say the program provides support for?
options: The claim that STM is large
The claim that EM is useless
The notion that production systems are an appropriate representation of the IPS
The claim that chess is simple
optionExplain: Not claimed.
Not claimed.
Right: stated.
Not claimed.
questions.explain: It reinforces the representation.
questions.teaches: Waterman's program provides strong reinforcement for the notion that production systems provide an appropriate representation for the information processing system of a problem solver.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A help desk adds a special-case rule when the standard script fails. Which program does this resemble?
options: EDPS
Waterman's poker program, which adds productions to remedy failures
A compiler
A subroutine for addition
optionExplain: Not that.
Right: stated.
Not that.
Not that.
questions.explain: Applying the card.
questions.teaches: The processes that add a production to the poker program are diagnostic programs that detect situations in which some specific feature of behavior is unsatisfactory and then fashion a production or cluster to remedy it.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Two tasks are two puzzles that begin and end at different points of the same board. What do they share?
options: The same space
Nothing
Only the solution
Only the date
optionExplain: Right: one space, many tasks.
They share.
Not just that.
Irrelevant.
questions.explain: The card says a space covers a range of tasks.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Studying how performance on one task affects another is the venerable topic of intertask ____.
questions.explain: The authors want the structural means.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: S4 solved DONALD+GERALD and CROSS+ROADS in the same space. What does this show?
options: The two tasks are unrelated
S4 solved neither
Two tasks defined by different end points can share one space
The tasks needed different spaces
optionExplain: Related.
Solved.
Right: stated.
Same space.
questions.explain: Tasks are defined by start and end points.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: Different transfer mechanisms can produce functionally identical programs, so separating them with behavior may prove difficult.
questions.explain: The authors state this.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Which two of the six ways focus mainly on the task at hand?
options: Analogy and general methods, which borrow from other tasks
The task instructions and the course of problem solving
Same-task experience and construction
General methods and construction
optionExplain: Other-task sources.
Right: first and last.
Other-task sources.
Other-task sources.
questions.explain: The four others derive capability from other tasks.
questions.teaches: Only two of the six ways, the instructions and the course of problem solving, focus primarily on the task presently facing the problem solver; the others derive capabilities on the present task from those on other tasks.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: An educator wants to express transfer by correlating test scores. How do the authors' aims differ?
options: They want only correlations between the scores, with no account of structure
They want no explanation
They deny transfer
They want the underlying structural means of transfer
optionExplain: Not only.
They want one.
They accept.
Right: stated.
questions.explain: A footnote states the aim.
questions.teaches: The discussion concerns intertask transfer, but the authors wish to determine the underlying structural means for such transfer, instead of expressing the facts of transfer by correlating performance in different tasks.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A library is organized so that general indexing is fully separate from book contents. What does this assume?
options: That books have no content that the index could use
A clean level of content-free machinery
That indexing is impossible
That all books are alike
optionExplain: Not that.
Right: separate level.
Possible.
Not that.
questions.explain: The card says GPS assumes such a split.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: The authors call GPS a ____ model because it suggests a task-free level of generality.
questions.explain: Other organizations are possible.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: In a GPS-like organization, where would generality across tasks lie?
options: In each space's detail alone
In LTM contents alone
Nowhere
In general mechanisms and the processes that identify a task for them
optionExplain: Not alone.
Not alone.
It lies somewhere.
Right: stated.
questions.explain: Task generality is bound up there.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: A reader says the authors claim a GPS-like separation of general methods from content is the only possible organization. The text agrees.
questions.explain: They say it is possible, as are a number of others.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Which very general concepts do the authors list as having general import because of their content?
options: Causality, time, space, seriation and conservation
Speed, sound and color
Chess, logic and cryptarithmetic, the three tasks of the book
Arithmetic and spelling
optionExplain: Right: Piaget's concepts.
Not those.
Those are tasks.
Not those.
questions.explain: Their content shapes relations between tasks.
questions.teaches: The concepts of causality, time, space, seriation and conservation, whose psychological study was pursued by Piaget, have general import, and their actual content strongly affects the possible relations between tasks.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A school has two ways to organize skills: one general skill layer, or deep knowledge in each subject. What does the card say about choosing between them?
options: Only the general layer is possible
Only subject knowledge is possible
Each form implies a different relation between tasks, and the data do not decide
Neither is possible
optionExplain: Others possible.
Others possible.
Right: stated.
Both possible.
questions.explain: Applying the card.
questions.teaches: Each form of organization of task generality implies a quite different relation between tasks, and the GPS form, with its distinct task-free level, is only one of several.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A workshop sets limits on tool speed and shelf size but not on what is built. What is the best analogy?
options: Limits on content only, with the style left open
No limits
Limits on everything
Limits on style, not on content
optionExplain: Style too.
Some limits.
Not everything.
Right: style.
questions.explain: The card says the same of the IPS.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: The structural limits require only that a person act in a certain style: not too fast and not remembering too ____.
questions.explain: Limits on speed and memory.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Which factor is said to play a large role in the difference between the very young and the mature?
options: Differences in the capacity of STM
Eye color, which differs between the young and the mature
Height
Choice of hobby
optionExplain: Right: STM capacity.
Not named.
Not named.
Not named.
questions.explain: Capacity varies considerably in the population.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: The variation of STM capacity among humans is large compared with the variation among man-made information processors.
questions.explain: The human range is small compared with that across man-made systems.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Which two levels of organizational commonality does the theory state?
options: All humans share one and the same LTM, with the same contents
All humans share one task, which fixes the same behavior for everyone
All humans are IPS's with common organization, and they share a few structural constants such as memory parameters
All humans share one goal, which every solver pursues in the same way
optionExplain: The theory leaves the contents of LTM to individual life history, so LTM is not shared.
Task environments differ; commonality lies in the organization of the IPS, not in a shared task.
Right: the theory states common organization of the IPS and a few shared structural constants such as memory parameters.
No shared goal is claimed; goals vary with the task and the person.
questions.explain: Both are summarized earlier in the chapter.
questions.teaches: The theory describes two levels of organizational commonality: all humans are information processing systems with certain basic organizational features, and all have in common a few universal structural characteristics, such as nearly identical memory parameters.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Two people with the same memory limits behave very differently on the same task. What does the card say about this?
options: It is impossible, since equal limits fix behavior on a task
The structural limits leave many degrees of freedom
Their limits must differ greatly
They did not receive the task
optionExplain: Possible.
Right: stated.
Same limits.
Not needed.
questions.explain: Applying the card.
questions.teaches: Given all the invariant structure, a human IPS is still capable of almost arbitrary behavior in response to a task environment, with the structural limits requiring only a certain style.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Two engineers from the same school give similar answers to a hard problem. Where must the similarity be stored?
options: In the contents of their long-term memories
In the shape of their brains, a common structure of their bodies
In their handwriting
In chance
optionExplain: Right: LTM contents.
Not structure.
Irrelevant.
Not chance.
questions.explain: The card next states this.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: The IPS can be factored into basic structure and the contents of ____.
questions.explain: Programs and data.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Two solvers have strikingly different ways of attacking a task. What does the card predict about their behavior?
options: It must be identical
It must be random
There need be no similarity
It must be impossible
optionExplain: Not identical.
Not random.
Right: stated.
Not impossible.
questions.explain: Similarity depends on shared approach.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: A reader says the commonality imposed by the task is structural, a feature of the IPS hardware. The text agrees.
questions.explain: It is mediated through the IPS but is not structural.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: What do culture, education and class amount to, in the card's terms?
options: Differences in memory parameters
Differences in particular experiences, such as jobs, conversations and books
Differences in sensory structure
Differences in speed of neurons
optionExplain: Not that.
Right: stated.
Not that.
Not that.
questions.explain: They are differences in LTM contents.
questions.teaches: People differ by culture, education or socioeconomic class, which means they differ because of particular experiences they have had, such as jobs they have worked at, people they have talked to and books they have read.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A survey finds that nurses share certain habits. Where does the card place the source?
options: In identical memory sizes, which every nurse is born with to the same degree
In a shared body shape
In coincidence
In similar stored contents acquired through common training
optionExplain: Not the source.
Not the source.
Not coincidence.
Right: LTM contents.
questions.explain: Applying the card.
questions.teaches: Any commonality among problem solvers not attributable directly to basic structure must be represented as an identity or similarity in the contents of the LTM's, in the production systems or other stored memory structures.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Why might a law about human behavior fail to hold across very different cultures?
options: Humans have no memory
Behavior depends on stored knowledge, which varies with the environment
Cultures lack behavior
Laws are impossible
optionExplain: They do.
Right: stored contents vary.
They have behavior.
Not impossible.
questions.explain: The card says this makes laws elusive.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: The authors say man is the ____ of the universe in which he lives.
questions.explain: All that he knows shapes his psychology.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Where does the card place the constraints on possible human behavior?
options: Entirely in psychological mechanisms, with the environment setting no limit on behavior
Nowhere
Only in language
In the environment, as limits on knowledge and on how to obtain it
optionExplain: Not entirely.
Placed somewhere.
Not only.
Right: stated.
questions.explain: It does not limit the ability to use assimilated knowledge.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: A reader says this view is the same as extreme cultural relativism, in which man can be anything he wants. The text agrees.
questions.explain: The authors say the view should not be equated with either.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: What does the universe that man mirrors include besides culture?
options: A lawful physical universe and a biological one, including his own body
Only other people
Only books
Only language
optionExplain: Right: stated.
More than that.
More than that.
More than that.
questions.explain: It is more than his culture.
questions.teaches: The universe that man mirrors is more than his culture; it includes a lawful physical universe and a biological one, of which man's own body is not the least important part.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A psychologist finds that rules she discovered in one town fail in another. How does the card explain this?
options: The human mind has no structure
People lie
Behavior reflects local contents of knowledge, shaped by life history and environment
Rules cannot be tested
optionExplain: It has.
Not claimed.
Right: stated.
Not claimed.
questions.explain: Applying the card.
questions.teaches: The fundamental fact that the human IPS can absorb any specification, with behavior set by the content stored from life history, accounts for the elusiveness of psychological laws.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A tired driver misjudges a distance because of drowsiness. What kind of constraint is this?
options: A task constraint, set by the work the driver is doing on the road and not by her own condition
A cultural constraint
A goal constraint
An internal biological constraint on the information processor
optionExplain: Not the task.
Not culture.
Not goal.
Right: biological.
questions.explain: The card lists drowsiness as one.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: The theory is a first ____, to be refined by adding sensory and other biological limits.
questions.explain: It applies to normal situations.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Which is given as an example of a source of both commonality and individual differences?
options: Visual after-images common to all, and differences in hearing acuity
The task instructions
The size of the paper
The color of the room
optionExplain: Right: stated.
Not named.
Not named.
Not named.
questions.explain: Biological limits can be common or differ.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: The theory is intended to apply to situations in which biological limits are pushed beyond their range.
questions.explain: A normal situation is one in which the limits are not exceeded, and the theory applies to such.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Which states other than sensory limits does the card say affect the IPS?
options: Only hunger
Only age
Emotionality and altered states of awareness such as drowsiness
Only noise
optionExplain: Not only.
Not only.
Right: stated.
Not only.
questions.explain: These are internal.
questions.teaches: Emotionality and altered states of awareness, such as drowsiness, are internal to the person and affect the operation of the information processing system.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A researcher excludes tests run when subjects are ill or exhausted. Which point does this reflect?
options: The theory covers all states
The theory targets normal situations in which biological limits are not exceeded
Illness is irrelevant
Exhaustion improves thought
optionExplain: Not all.
Right: normal situations.
Relevant.
Not stated.
questions.explain: Applying the card.
questions.teaches: A normal situation is precisely one in which biological limits are not exceeded, and it is to such normal situations that the theory of this book applies.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A city must grow its roads while traffic keeps flowing. What does this require of the plan?
options: Changes that the working system can take in without stopping
Stopping all traffic, so that the roads can be changed without disturbing anyone who is using them
No changes
Ignoring traffic
optionExplain: Right: assimilable growth.
Not stopping.
Change needed.
Not ignoring.
questions.explain: The card says the same of the growing IPS.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: The strong proposal is that all increments of knowledge are cast in the form of ____.
questions.explain: Acquisition mechanisms are not specified.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Why does the card say the acquisition mechanisms proposed are not yet adequate?
options: They are too specific
They have been refuted
They are not specific enough to answer the important psychological questions
They are unknown
optionExplain: Opposite.
Not stated.
Right: stated.
Some are proposed.
questions.explain: Waterman's program is an example.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: A reader says the book's data give a full account of how development and learning shape the IPS. The text agrees.
questions.explain: The authors say the data give only glimpses of these aspects.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: What might the need to develop while performing imply?
options: Differences among all systems rather than shared structure
Structural similarities among all human cognitive systems
No structure
Faster neurons
optionExplain: Opposite.
Right: stated.
Not that.
Not that.
questions.explain: It adds to the invariants of the chapter.
questions.teaches: The requirement that the human information processing system grow itself to its adult state while remaining in reasonable working order may imply certain structural similarities among all human cognitive systems.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A child learns new words each day without relearning old ones. Which requirement from the card does this suggest?
options: Learning must stop
Learning must erase old knowledge to make room for the new
Learning cannot occur
Continual learning that the existing system can take in
optionExplain: Not stop.
Not erase.
It occurs.
Right: continual learning.
questions.explain: Applying the card.
questions.teaches: The capacity for learning within the time scales and amounts characteristic of normal humans probably implies additional invariant features common to all human cognitive systems.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Two people have equal amounts of knowledge of different topics. Will they behave alike on a given task?
options: Yes, since amounts are equal, the two will behave alike whatever the topics may be
Not necessarily, since the specific content matters, not the amount
Yes, since the task is the same
No, since knowledge is irrelevant
optionExplain: Not just amount.
Right: specific content.
Not enough.
Knowledge matters.
questions.explain: The conclusion states this.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: The authors say that methods and programs are themselves ____.
questions.explain: They are part of what is stored.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Which feature of content does behavior NOT depend on, according to the card?
options: The specific detail of content held in the memory of the solver
The facts of the task in hand
The semantics of what is said
Only aggregate features such as how much there is
optionExplain: It depends on this.
It depends.
It depends.
Right: stated.
questions.explain: Aggregate features are not enough.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: A model that studied only the syntax of a person's knowledge would, by this conclusion, miss most of the behavior.
questions.explain: Behavior cannot be understood from syntax abstracted from vocabulary and semantics.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: For which sources of information did the authors lack direct human behavioral evidence?
options: Several, so they used synthetic programs to illustrate the mechanisms
All of them
None of them
Only the instructions
optionExplain: Right: stated.
Not all.
Some lacked.
Not only.
questions.explain: Some were shown in subjects' behavior.
questions.teaches: For some of the sources of information in determining spaces and programs the authors had no direct human behavioral evidence and fell back on synthetic programs to illustrate the mechanisms concretely.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A consultant says what matters about a team is the detail of what each member knows. Which conclusion does this match?
options: Behavior depends on amount only
Content is irrelevant
Behavior is a function of specific content, not of how much or how expressed
Only syntax counts
optionExplain: Not just amount.
Relevant.
Right: stated.
Not syntax.
questions.explain: Applying the card.
questions.teaches: The behavior of an information processing system cannot be understood from syntax alone, abstracted from the vocabulary and semantics of what is being said and done.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: To understand how a chess player solves a problem, which three things must one describe?
options: Her height, weight and age, which together with her rating are the facts the authors say must be described
The room, the time and the board color
Her mood, her coach and her ranking
The task setting, the player's representation of it, and the program she uses
optionExplain: Not those.
Not those.
Not those.
Right: three components.
questions.explain: The summary names these three.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: Order the chapter's three elements from the outer world to the solver's inner organization.
items: The task environment
The problem space
The problem solving program
questions.explain: Environment, then the representation, then the program.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: How does the program find solutions despite enormous spaces?
options: By extracting structural information embedded in the environment to search very selectively
By checking every state
By guessing
By copying the answer
optionExplain: Right: stated.
Not exhaustive.
Not guessing.
Not copying.
questions.explain: Selective search guided by structure.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: True or false: A reader says the authors claim to have fully explained how solvers generate a space and program for a new task. The text agrees.
questions.explain: They call their answers sketchy and these areas the largest terra incognita.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: On what did the chapter place its emphasis?
options: The solver's childhood
The costs of experiments
The problem solver's performance program
The history of computers and the programs they run
optionExplain: Not stated.
Not stated.
Right: stated.
Not stated.
questions.explain: Determination was covered in the last section.
questions.teaches: The emphasis in the chapter is on the problem solver's performance program, while the last section brings what evidence there is to bear on how a solver, facing a new task, generates an appropriate space and program.

questions.unitTitle: The Theory of Human Problem Solving
questions.q: A researcher plans future work and asks where the theory is weakest. Which area do the authors name?
options: How STM holds seven items
How spaces and programs arise for new tasks, and how solvers differ
How chess boards look
How fast arithmetic runs
optionExplain: Not the weakest.
Right: terra incognita.
Not the weakest.
Not the weakest.
questions.explain: Applying the card.
questions.teaches: The answers on how the problem solver generates an appropriate space and program for a new task and on commonalities and differences among solvers are sketchy, areas that are the largest and most important terra incognita on the map of the theory.

questions.q: A new instrument arrives in a science. Which is likelier to matter most, over the long run, for how the field theorizes?
options: The instrument's speed, which lets old measurements be repeated faster
The new concepts and precise languages it suggests for describing the field's systems
The prestige it gives the labs that own one, which draws in funding, staff and attention
The way it replaces every earlier method, so that all older data are then set aside
optionExplain: Speed is useful, but it changes the pace of work more than the way the field thinks.
Right: new concepts and descriptive languages change what a field can say, which is the authors' own view of the computer.
Prestige affects who works on a topic, not how the topic is understood.
Tools seldom replace every earlier method; here the old data were reused.
questions.explain: A guess is fair here. The authors weigh the concepts and languages above the hardware, and the card next shows how.

questions.q: The authors say a programmed computer and a human problem solver are both species of the genus ____.
questions.explain: Both belong to the genus of information processing systems (IPS), though they differ at the species level.
questions.rule: Computer and human: one genus, two species.

questions.q: A weather lab buys a powerful computer. Which use fits the authors' account of what computers did for their own work?
options: Taking the machine's raw speed as the chief source of new ideas about weather
Letting the machine's output stand in for observation
Using the machine only as a loose picture, as when clouds are said to 'think'
Simulating a theory in detail, to compare it with data and to draw out predictions
optionExplain: The authors rank concepts and languages above hardware, so speed is not the chief gift.
Simulation is for comparing theory with data, not for replacing the data.
The authors say the computer was more than a metaphor in their work.
Right: simulation allowed detailed comparison between theory and data and many empirical predictions.
questions.explain: The authors name two uses: detailed comparison of theory with data by simulation, and empirical predictions drawn from theory.

questions.q: True or false: The authors hold that a programmed computer and a human problem solver are identical in memory organization, elementary processes and program organization.
questions.explain: They place both in one genus but say the two differ at the species level in exactly these three respects.
questions.rule: Same genus is not the same species.

questions.q: Suppose the authors specify the human IPS directly, with the computer out of sight. What do they still draw from the computing era?
options: Concepts and formalisms for describing an information processing system precisely
Timing measurements of how fast human memory reads and writes, taken from machine hardware
The claim that the human brain is built from the very same parts as a machine
A rule that human problem solving must proceed by numerical calculation, step by step
optionExplain: Right: the book says the computer recedes, while the concepts and languages for describing an IPS remain.
Nothing in the epilogue takes timing from the hardware.
The authors compare genus and species; they do not claim the parts are the same.
They note that numerical uses of computers obscured the symbol-manipulating side, which they stress.
questions.explain: With the hardware set aside, what carries over is the way of describing systems, which is the point of the card.
questions.rule: The language stays when the machine recedes.

questions.q: A kitchen researcher studies only single-step tasks such as salting water and avoids planning a whole meal as too complex. Which earlier habit of psychology does this resemble?
options: Studying behavior only through numerical operations, as early computer uses did
Treating a human and a machine as species of one genus
Passing over complex behavior in favor of behavior that seems simple
Explaining behavior by the physiology of the nervous system alone
optionExplain: That describes computer applications, not psychology's choice of what to study.
That is the authors' own stance, not the habit they describe moving away from.
Right: for a generation psychologists favored behaviors that seemed simple over complex problem solving.
Physiology is named later as a level below the IPS, not as the old habit.
questions.explain: The generation before avoided complex problem solving in the laboratory for behaviors that seemed simple.
questions.teaches: For a whole generation, complex problem solving behaviors were usually avoided in the psychological laboratory in favor of behaviors that seemed to be simple.

questions.q: A chess program and a person solving a logic problem look very different. A theorist wants the simplest account. Which starting point is most promising?
options: Give each activity its own separate machinery
Give the system a very large store of rules for every kind of task
Keep the system simple and let the demands of each task shape what it does
Describe only the hardware
optionExplain: This multiplies machinery; the authors aim to explain different tasks with one simple system.
A huge rule store complicates the system instead of letting the task do the work.
Right: the authors let the environment's demands interact with a simple system.
The authors factor the hardware out from the task environment, not the other way round.
questions.explain: A fair guess either way. The authors keep the system simple and let the task do the shaping; the card next explains how.

questions.q: The authors say that the key to understanding problem solvers is their flexibility, that is, their ____.
questions.explain: Flexibility, or programmability, lets them behave adaptively in a wide range of environments.

questions.q: A traveler plans a train trip. 'All the stations and connections I might pass through' is one layer; 'stepping toward the destination and dropping dead ends' is another. Which layers, in that order?
options: Problem space, then methods
Methods, then problem space
Problem space, then production system
Production system, then methods
optionExplain: Right: the space of possibilities is the problem space, and the stepping and backing out is a method of searching it.
This swaps them: methods are the means of search, not the space searched.
The production system is the program organization realizing the methods, not the stepping itself.
The production system is not the set of stations, and the stepping is a method, not the production system.
questions.explain: The problem space is where solving takes place as search, and methods are the means whereby the search takes place.
questions.rule: Space is searched; methods do the searching.

questions.q: Match each layer to its description.
pairs: Where problem solving takes place as search
The means whereby that search takes place
The program organization that realizes the methods through elementary processes
questions.explain: From the task environment inward: problem space, then methods, then production system, which rests on the IPS's basic characteristics.

questions.q: A student writes: 'The authors say problem solving looks complex because the system itself is complex.' What is wrong with this summary?
options: Nothing; they locate the complexity in a great many elementary processes working together
They say the complexity lies in the hardware, which the book studies in most detail
They say it comes mainly from the task's demands meeting a few basic parameters of a simple system
They say it comes from many small random effects that cancel out across large numbers
optionExplain: This is the very claim the authors reject: the system is very simple.
They factor the hardware out and specify the IPS directly for human behavior.
Right: the apparent complexity is produced by the interaction of environment and a few basic system parameters.
A random-cancelling account is not theirs; they say matters are simple because of adaptation, not averaging.
questions.explain: The simplicity is in the system. The apparent complexity comes from its interaction with a demanding environment.
questions.rule: Complexity sits in the environment's demands.

questions.q: A forecaster wants to predict how a skilled player will tackle an unfamiliar puzzle. By the authors' argument, what does she need?
options: The player's whole production system, written out rule by rule from earlier sessions
The puzzle's demands, the player's general level of intelligence, and the IPS's basic cognitive limits
The player's physiology in the central nervous system, traced down to the cells involved in each move
A statistical profile of how often large groups of players have solved the puzzle before
optionExplain: The authors say the layers are invariant but, for many purposes, can be left out of the explanation.
Right: these three suffice for many purposes of explanation and prediction.
Physiology is a deeper level the authors do not need at the IPS level where they work.
Their theory is not statistical; the link they offer is adaptational.
questions.explain: Because the layers follow from adaptivity and the two boundary conditions, they are for many purposes transparent.
questions.teaches: Because the intermediate layers follow from adaptivity, knowing the environment's demands, the human's general level of intelligence and the IPS's basic cognitive limits suffices for many purposes of explanation and prediction.

questions.q: A forecaster predicts tomorrow's temperature from the seasonal pattern; a colleague traces air currents street by street. Which account gives the gross result, and which the fine detail?
options: The street-level account gives the gross result, and the seasonal pattern supplies the detail
Both give the same gross result, but one of the two is quicker to compute by hand
Only the seasonal pattern is a real theory; the street-level account is noise on top
The seasonal pattern gives the gross result; the street-level account gives the fine detail
optionExplain: This reverses them; tracing street-level currents is the finer-grained account.
The two accounts differ in what they deliver, not merely in speed.
Fine detail is part of a full account; it is not noise.
Right: the coarse pattern gives the main result and the detailed account supplies the fine structure.
questions.explain: A fair guess. The authors use the same split, a coarse account for gross results and a fine account for detail, and the card next shows it.
questions.rule: Gross from the outer, fine from the inner.

questions.q: In the authors' picture, the ____ theory provides the main, gross results.
questions.explain: The outer theory gives the main, gross results; the inner theory gives the fine structure.
questions.rule: Outer is gross, inner is fine.

questions.q: A coach is sure a strong player will solve an endgame puzzle, but cannot say which detours the player will try first. How does this split map onto the authors' theories?
options: Success is the job of the inner theory, and the detours are the job of the outer theory
Success is the outer theory's gross result; the detours belong to the inner theory's fine structure
Both belong to the outer theory
Neither, since only the physiology of the nervous system could explain either one
optionExplain: This reverses them; the detours are the finer detail.
Right: reaching the end point the task demands is the gross result, while wrong explorations are fine structure.
The outer theory gives only the gross results; errors and detours are listed as fine structure.
Physiology lies far below; the authors place errors and wrong explorations within the inner theory at the IPS level.
questions.explain: Only the end points count in the outer theory. Errors, confusions and wrong explorations are among the details the inner theory supplies.

questions.q: Sort each item: is it a gross result of the outer theory, or fine structure from the inner theory?

items.t: That the solver ends up where the task's demands point
The overall result predicted without tracking each step
The broad pattern fixed by the environment's demands
A wrong exploration followed by backing out
A confusion that briefly derails the search
The dynamic details of the steps over time
A lapse from adaptation, such as an error

questions.explain: Outer-theory results concern end points and gross patterns. Dynamic details over time and lapses from adaptation are the inner theory's fine structure.

questions.q: A student restates the authors' analogy with thermodynamics in four lines. Which two lines are wrong?
options: In both pairs the outer theory gives the main, gross results
In both pairs the inner theory provides the fine structure
In both pairs the link between the two theories is statistical
In the authors' case, details cancel out through the law of large numbers
optionExplain: Correct as stated: the authors say the analogy is apt in this respect.
Correct as stated: the inner theory gives the fine structure in both cases.
Wrong: the link in physics is statistical, but the authors' link is adaptational.
Wrong: in their case things line up in a means-ends chain where only end points count, not through averaging.
questions.explain: The authors say the physics link is statistical, but theirs is adaptational, a means-ends chain in which only end points count.

questions.q: A hospital studies why nurses sometimes slip while following a sound protocol. By the authors' remark on fine structure, where might explanations of such lapses lie?
options: Only in the IPS-level program
In the outer theory
At the IPS level, and also in the memories and processes studied in the laboratory, and in physiology
Nowhere, since lapses are only noise that any good theory sets aside as unimportant
optionExplain: The authors say not all such details occur at the IPS level where they work.
The outer theory gives gross results; lapses are named as fine structure.
Right: the authors place such details at the IPS level and also lower down.
The authors count lapses from adaptation as part of the fine structure to be explained.
questions.explain: Errors and confusions are part of the fine structure, which the authors say reaches below their own level.
questions.rule: Fine structure runs deeper than the IPS.
questions.teaches: Details of lapses from adaptation occur not only at the IPS level but also in the underlying structure of memories and processes, as investigated in the psychological laboratory, and further down in the physiology of the central nervous system.

questions.q: A team finishes a long study of three tasks and writes a general theory. How should the report describe the theory's reach?
options: As giving strong clues beyond the tasks, while the limits of the induction stay undefined
As proven for all human thinking
As valid for the three tasks only, with nothing at all to say about anything beyond them
As untestable until at least twenty tasks have been studied
optionExplain: Right: this is how the authors describe their own theory.
A general form does not prove a general reach; three tasks cannot show that.
The authors do claim more than that: they say the theory extends beyond the base.
The authors use the number only to say the gaps are not just a matter of how many tasks.
questions.explain: The authors claim strong clues beyond the base and admit the limits are not defined.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say their present empirical base defines the exact limits of the induction to a general theory.
questions.explain: They say the base gives strong clues to a general theory without defining the limits of the induction.

questions.q: A lab's model of route planning fits three kinds of puzzle. A visitor asks whether it already explains open-ended everyday reasoning. Which reply matches the authors' stance on their own theory?
options: It already does, since everyday reasoning is another kind of puzzle to solve
Not yet shown; success on the puzzles encourages moving toward more complex, open tasks
It cannot, because puzzles are too simple to say anything useful about real reasoning
It has been refuted there
optionExplain: The authors do not claim such coverage; everyday reasoning is named as a task still to be tackled.
Right: the authors say success with their tasks encourages pushing the boundaries of analysis toward everyday reasoning and scientific discovery.
The authors treat their tasks as highly complex by earlier standards and as a base to build on.
A limited base makes a theory untested elsewhere, not refuted.
questions.explain: The authors present everyday reasoning and scientific discovery as the next frontier, to be tackled, not as covered.

questions.q: Sort each gap: is it a gap of extent, or an unexplored aspect of the basic IPS?
groups: Unexplored aspect of the basic IPS

items.t: No analysis yet of everyday reasoning
No study across the stages of child development
No tests yet on scientific discovery
Unknown size of the effective STM when scratch paper is used
Unclear whether the subroutine stack's place keepers reside in STM
Unspecified rules for associative accessing in LTM

questions.explain: The authors say the gaps are not just of extent, as in not having examined many more tasks. Many aspects of the basic IPS have also not been explored in sufficient detail.
questions.rule: Wider tasks and deeper mechanisms are two kinds of gap.

questions.q: A group builds a theory of sauce-making from three recipes and left out some well-studied topics. What does the authors' epilogue model for its closing note?
options: Say the left-out topics are treated as refuted until someone shows otherwise in later work
Say nothing at all
Name the left-out topics as candidates, note work already done, and invite others to extend, amend or refute
Claim the theory covers them already
optionExplain: Omission is not refutation; the authors keep their view open to refutation by others.
The authors do name areas they left out, and say why they matter.
Right: the authors name candidate areas, note existing work, and invite extensions, emendations or refutations.
The authors say they did not go outside the three tasks to show additional coverage.
