questions.explain: The authors name concept attainment and rote memorization as candidates and end by inviting extension, emendation or refutation.
questions.rule: Name the omissions; invite others in.
questions.teaches: Concept attainment and rote memorization were candidates for inclusion, with large experimental literatures and prior information processing work, but the authors kept to their self-imposed set of three tasks.

questions.q: In a closing historical addendum, what kind of account do the authors of this monograph say they are giving?
options: A full-scale history of every development that led to the work, written to be complete
A personal view of their work's antecedents, stressing less obvious links
A neutral survey of the field that avoids saying where their own ideas came from
A list of sources replacing the references they left out of the main text
optionExplain: They say this is not the place for a full-scale history and that they are not the ones to write it.
Yes: they call the notes a somewhat personal view and stress the less obvious connections.
They describe their own antecedents, so the account is not detached from their work.
The main text already holds the references scholarly obligation requires; the addendum adds narrative detail.
questions.explain: The authors describe the addendum themselves. The card shows how they frame it.
questions.rule: Take the authors' own label for their account.

questions.q: The authors treat World War II as a convenient boundary between pre-history and ____.
questions.explain: The pre-history ends and the post-war history begins at the war.
questions.rule: WWII is the authors' dividing line.

questions.q: A founder writes: 'This is not a full company history; it is my view of what led to our product.' Which stance does that match?
options: A neutral audit, which would need records from outside observers
A complete chronicle, which is what the authors say they decline to write
A bibliography, which is what the main text supplies for scholarly obligation
A participant's own account of its roots, shaped by what the writer chose to include
optionExplain: An audit would claim outside neutrality, which the addendum does not.
The authors explicitly say a full-scale history is not what they offer.
References belong to the main text; the addendum is narrative.
The founder gives an insider's partial account, as the authors do for their own antecedents.
questions.explain: Like the authors, the founder disclaims a full history and offers an insider's selective account.
questions.rule: A personal view says it is personal.

questions.q: According to the authors, which two strands make up the pre-history before World War II?
options: One in psychology and one in formal logic
One in physiology and one in physics
One in linguistics and one in electronics
One in economics and one in computer engineering
optionExplain: Yes: the text names one strand in psychology and one in formal logic.
The text does not name physiology or physics as strands of the pre-history.
Linguistics and electronics are not named as pre-history strands; the text names psychology and formal logic.
Economics and computer engineering are not the named strands; the post-war history turns to cybernetics instead.
questions.explain: The opening of the addendum counts two strands: psychology and formal logic.
questions.teaches: The pre-history consists of two main strands, one in psychology and one in formal logic.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say the addendum is a full-scale history of the developments leading up to the work in the book.
questions.explain: They say the opposite: this is not the place for a full-scale history, and they are not the ones to undertake it.
questions.rule: A personal view is not a full-scale history.

questions.q: A historian says: 'I will split my history of printing at one convenient year, and the later period needs attention to one cluster of ideas.' What does this borrow from the addendum?
options: A claim that nothing before the dividing year mattered to the later period
A promise to give equal space to every development on both sides of the year
A convenient dividing line, with the later period centred on cybernetics
A rule that a history must end at the moment its authors began their own work
optionExplain: The authors treat the pre-history as important: it holds two strands that feed the later work.
They do not promise equal space; they give the post-war ideas particular attention.
The authors pick World War II for convenience and single out cybernetics for the later period.
They end their story in 1958, but not because of a rule about when their own work began.
questions.explain: The addendum chooses a line for convenience and then gives the later period particular attention to the ideas called cybernetics.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the addendum is a personal view of antecedents, divided at World War II into pre-history and history.
questions.teaches: After the boundary, the authors say the post-war history requires particular attention to the collection of ideas assembled under the label of cybernetics.

questions.q: Before World War II, which research subjects dominated American cognitive psychology, according to the authors?
options: Gestalt insight tests, thinking-aloud protocols and chess masters
Concept formation, problem solving and the representation of information
Neural networks, information theory and digital computers
Behaviorism, the nonsense syllable and the rat
optionExplain: Those belong mainly to the European side of the story.
Those were the topics left largely unexplored in America in this period.
These tools arrived in or after the war years.
Yes: the authors use these three to sum up the period.
questions.explain: The card names what dominated.
questions.rule: American pre-war work: behaviorism, nonsense syllables, rats.

questions.q: Hull's doctoral thesis of 1920 dealt with concept ____.
questions.explain: It was a notable exception to the gap in American work on higher mental processes.

questions.q: Match each psychologist to the contribution the authors name.
pairs: Organism as goal-seeking and shaped by its environment
How information is represented inside the head
Emphasis on central processes; a debt for the authors and de Groot
questions.explain: Each pairing comes from the authors' account of forerunners.

questions.q: A researcher models a shopper as pursuing a goal while the store layout shapes the path. Whose pre-war stance does that echo?
options: Tolman's: a goal-seeking organism shaped by its environment
Hull's: leaving a hard problem for ones that fit the Zeitgeist better
Bartlett's: treating verbal protocols as unreliable evidence of memory
Skinner's: a system of correlations with nothing in between
optionExplain: Yes: goal-seeking behavior shaped by environmental structure is Tolman's view as the authors put it.
Hull's move was to abandon the problem, not a theory of goal-seeking.
Bartlett is cited for central representations, not for rejecting protocols.
Skinner's empty organism is the view the authors contrast with theirs.
questions.explain: The shopper's goals and the layout fit Tolman's picture.

questions.q: True or false: The authors count Hull's thesis as one of the two real American forerunners of their work.
questions.explain: They say the references to Hull are to his thesis, leaving Brunswik and Tolman as the real forerunners.
questions.rule: The American forerunners are Brunswik and Tolman.

questions.q: A historian wants to know whether a new lab inherits ideas from an older school it did not meet. Which method do the authors use?
options: Counting how many years separate the two schools
Asking whether the older school's members approved
Tracing connections through concepts and citations
Checking whether both used the same experimental apparatus
optionExplain: Time gaps do not show inheritance; the lineages come from ideas that were cited.
The authors say they cannot say whether forerunners would approve, so approval is not their test.
Yes: the authors say that when connections are traced through concepts and citations, the lineages are clear.
Apparatus is not what the authors trace; they follow concepts and citations.
questions.explain: Lineage is shown by concepts and citations.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the American forerunners were Tolman and Brunswik, and the stronger lineage ran from the European work on thought.
questions.teaches: The authors establish lineages by tracing connections through concepts and citations.

questions.q: Which Gestalt-linked writers do the authors say developed the lines the Gestaltists opened?
options: Hull, Tolman, Brunswik and Boring, among others
Maier, Katona, Guetzkow and Luchins, among others
Chomsky, Harris, Miller and Broadbent, among others
Shannon, Wiener, Turing and Lotka, among others
optionExplain: These are American forerunners and a physiological viewpoint, not Gestalt followers.
Yes: the authors list them as developing the lines opened by the Gestaltists.
These belong to linguistics and the post-war psychology streams.
These belong to cybernetics and logic.
questions.explain: Post-war problem-solving work continued Gestalt lines through these names.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the American forerunners were Tolman and Brunswik, and the stronger lineage ran from the European work on thought.
questions.teaches: Maier, Katona, Guetzkow and Luchins are named as developers of the lines opened by the Gestaltists.

questions.q: A psychologist accepts that behavior can in principle be reduced to neural events, yet builds theory at a level above neurons. What is the most likely reason?
options: The reduction is too complex for one step, so layers of theory are needed
Neurons are thought to play no part in producing behavior
Behavior is judged to be caused by stimuli alone, with nothing inside the organism
Intermediate layers make the final reduction unnecessary in principle
optionExplain: Yes: this is the position the authors take, with a physics-and-chemistry parallel.
That would deny reduction altogether, which the authors explicitly do not do.
That is the empty-organism view the authors argue must be filled.
The authors keep the reduction in principle; layers are steps toward it.
questions.explain: The card shows how the authors argue the point.
questions.rule: Layers of theory, not one step.

questions.q: The authors accept the first part of Boring's assumption: the empty organism is to be filled with explanatory ____.
questions.explain: Part one of Boring's assumption is accepted by all except the radical behaviorists, and the authors agree with it.
questions.rule: Fill the organism, but with what?

questions.q: Which part of Boring's two-part assumption do the authors reject?
options: That the empty organism should be filled with anything at all
That stimulus-response correlations are early steps in scientific discovery
That the explanatory mechanisms are to be neurological
That reduction of complex events to physics is possible in principle
optionExplain: They accept this; only radical behaviorists reject it.
The authors have no quarrel with this; Boring says it, and they agree.
Yes: they accept part one and deny part two.
The authors accept reduction in principle; they deny only the one-step version.
questions.explain: Part two is the neurological claim.
questions.rule: Reject part two, keep part one.

questions.q: A team explains a slow website by moving through user clicks, requests, program code and chip behavior in layers, not by jumping to electrons. Which authors' stance does it echo?
options: Denying that the electrons matter in any explanation
Reducing complex events through several successive layers of theory
Treating clicks and chips as a single level of description
Refusing to explain anything above the level of observed correlations
optionExplain: The team does not deny the lower level; it reaches it by steps.
Yes: the authors reduce in several steps with layers between.
The layered approach keeps the levels distinct.
Refusing explanation would be the empty-organism view the authors want filled.
questions.explain: Layers between gross phenomena and the lowest level are the model.
questions.rule: Reduce in steps, layer by layer.

questions.q: True or false: The authors deny that behavior can be reduced to the laws of physics even in principle.
questions.explain: They accept reduction in principle; the denial is only that it can be done in a single step, without layers of theory between.

questions.q: A researcher thanks earlier scholars whose vague ideas she has made precise. Must she claim they would accept her version? According to the authors:
options: Yes: a debt is only acknowledged when the forerunner accepts the new form
Yes: otherwise the earlier scholars are not forerunners at all
No: debts to earlier scholars should not be mentioned
No: acknowledging debts does not require the forerunners' agreement
optionExplain: The authors do not feel called on to say whether forerunners would accept their operationalization.
Forerunner status comes from the line of ideas, not agreement.
The authors give a whole section to naming debts.
Yes: the authors say they are acknowledging debts, not representing their creditors.
questions.explain: Debts can be acknowledged without speaking for the creditors.
questions.rule: According to the authors, mechanisms must fill the empty organism, but they need not be neurological, because the reduction needs layers of theory.
questions.teaches: The authors say they are acknowledging intellectual debts, not representing their creditors, and do not feel called on to say whether forerunners would accept their operationalization of vague concepts.

questions.q: How might the formalization of logic help a science of thought, even if thinking is not logical?
options: By proving that all human thinking follows step-by-step deduction, rule by rule
By showing that symbol manipulation can be described as concrete processes
By showing that ideas are located in the nervous system
By replacing the study of behavior with the study of inference rules
optionExplain: The authors say the opposite: thinking is frequently not rigorous or deductive.
Yes: that is the authors' fundamental contribution of logic.
The point is about ideas as symbols, not locating them in tissue.
Logic gave a language and an example, not a replacement of behavioral study.
questions.explain: The card gives the authors' answer.
questions.rule: Logic showed symbols can be handled as concretely as boards.

questions.q: The authors compare manipulating symbols to working with pine ____ in a carpenter shop.
questions.explain: Symbols can be copied, compared, rearranged and concatenated as definitely as boards can be sawed and planed.
questions.rule: Symbols are as tangible as boards.

questions.q: Why do psychologists say thinking should not be confused with logic?
options: Formal logic cannot be written down with symbols at all
Logicians have shown that valid inference has no standards
Logic belongs to the nervous system, whereas thinking belongs solely to the immaterial mind
Human thinking is often not rigorous and does not follow step-by-step deduction
optionExplain: Logic was formalized with symbols; that was its great advance.
Logicians hold that inference has objective formal standards.
The authors do not tie logic to a physical place; they place its standards in Plato's heaven.
Yes: the authors give this as the psychologist's objection.
questions.explain: Thinking is frequently not logical.

questions.q: A programmer says her editor copies, compares and rearranges text by exact steps, so editing text is as definite as woodworking. Which contribution does that echo?
options: Symbol manipulation can be described as concrete, definite processes
Human thinking follows formal deduction step by step, as logicians do
Ideas can be reduced directly to the tissue of the nervous system
Economic man reasons more perfectly than ordinary people can
optionExplain: Yes: this is the authors' board-and-saw comparison.
The authors say human thinking does not follow deduction.
The point is about symbols, not a direct reduction to tissue.
Economic man is a separate topic, called too rational for psychology.
questions.explain: Text editing, like logic, shows symbols handled by definite processes.

questions.q: True or false: The authors argue that human thinking is the same as formal logic.
questions.explain: They agree with logicians and psychologists that logic and thought should not be confused.

questions.q: A manager wants to steer her team's decisions. Using the premises idea Simon quotes from 1944, what could she specify?
options: The exact emotions each member should feel
The speed at which each decision must be made
The value and factual premises behind its decisions
The final decisions, without telling the team anything else
optionExplain: Emotions are not part of the premises idea Simon states.
Speed is not the premise idea; the idea is that decisions follow from premises.
Yes: Simon says a rational person's behavior can be controlled by specifying value and factual premises.
Specifying only outcomes skips the premises the quote says control behavior.
questions.explain: A decision is a conclusion from premises, so specifying premises shapes it.
questions.rule: According to the authors, logic showed that manipulating symbols can be described as concrete processes, while thinking itself is not logic.
questions.teaches: Simon (1944) used the logic metaphor for administrative decision making: any rational decision may be viewed as a conclusion from premises, so specifying the value and factual premises controls the behavior.

questions.q: Why might psychology have ignored the rational man of economic theory, according to the authors?
options: He was based on experiments with animals only
He ignored decisions and described only emotions
He relied on a mathematics that psychologists did not understand
He was patently too rational by human standards
optionExplain: Economic man came from economic theory, not animal experiments.
He was about reasoning toward courses of action, not emotions.
The authors give his over-rationality, not difficulty of mathematics.
Yes: the authors give this as the reason his relevance was disputed or ignored.
questions.explain: The card shows the authors' reason.

questions.q: Alan Turing described the processor now called the Turing machine in the year ____.
questions.explain: The authors give 1936 and regard it as the culmination of the drive toward formalization.

questions.q: Match each name to what the authors credit it with.
pairs: Described the processor now known as the Turing machine
Elements of Physical Biology (1924), foreshadowing cybernetics
Formalized logical syntax, later a model for formal grammar
questions.explain: Each pairing is in the authors' account of pre-war developments.

questions.q: In 1938 a mathematician models a population with equations, hoping to do for biology what mathematics did for physics. Which strand does this belong to?
options: The belief that mathematics could shape theories of biology, psychology and society
The formalization of the syntax of logic, which later modelled formal grammar in linguistics
The description of a processor that manipulates symbols
The economic theory of a perfectly rational chooser
optionExplain: Yes: Lotka and Rashevsky represent this belief.
That strand concerns the syntax of logic, not population models.
That strand is Turing's machine, not biology.
That strand is economic man, a different topic.
questions.explain: Mathematical biology is the strand of applying mathematics to biology.
questions.rule: Mathematics for biology is its own strand.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say economics recognized its common concerns with psychology at once, because economic man was realistic.
questions.explain: Economic man was too rational, and dealing only with logical, deductive reasoning postponed recognition of the common concerns.

questions.q: A historian asks how statistical decision theory was tied to formal logic. Which link do the authors name?
options: Chemistry, through the laws of quantum physics and atomic structure
Linguistics, through the study of generative grammar and syntax
Philosophy, through probability and the problem of induction
Engineering, through the design of radar systems
optionExplain: Quantum physics appears in the reduction argument, not in the link between statistics and logic.
Generative grammar is a later development.
Yes: the authors say statistics had close historical links with philosophy through those concerns.
Radar belongs to the human factors discussion, not to this link.
questions.explain: Statistics connected to logic through philosophy.
questions.rule: According to the authors, decision theory, the Turing machine and mathematical biology joined logic in a Zeitgeist centred on symbols and their manipulation.
questions.teaches: Statistics had close historical links with philosophy, through the foundations of probability and the classical problem of induction, which tied decision theory to formal logic.

questions.q: Who devised the term cybernetics to embrace information theory, feedback systems and the electronic computer?
options: Claude Shannon
Norbert Wiener
John von Neumann
Alan Turing
optionExplain: Shannon's 1938 thesis is cited as an early publication, not as the source of the term.
Yes: the authors say the term was devised by Wiener.
Von Neumann is cited for logic and game theory, not for the label.
Turing is cited for the Turing machine and the abstract level of the analogy.
questions.explain: The card names the author of the term.
questions.rule: According to the authors, cybernetics joined information theory, feedback and the computer, was tied to logic from the start, and gave the symbolic computer only a muted role at first.

questions.q: Shannon's 1938 master's thesis used ____ algebra to analyze switching circuits.
questions.explain: It is one of the earliest publications showing the tie of cybernetics to formal logic.

questions.q: Sort each element by where the authors place it.
groups: Added by the broader usage behind the Iron Curtain

items.t: Information theory
Feedback systems theory
The electronic computer
Game theory
Management science and operations research
Mathematical economics and statistical decision theory

questions.explain: Wiener's version had three elements; the broader usage added three more.

questions.q: A 1950s European handbook lists game theory and operations research under cybernetics. How do the authors read such broad use?
options: As further evidence that a unified Zeitgeist included logic and decision theory
As proof that the idea of cybernetics was first invented behind the Iron Curtain
As a mistake that wrongly confused cybernetics with management science
As evidence that the war itself produced all of these fields at the same moment
optionExplain: Yes: the authors say the broad use confirms the unity of the Zeitgeist.
They say Wiener devised the term and describe the broader use as an extension.
They treat the broader use as meaningful, not as an error.
They say the war did not produce the developments; it more likely delayed them.
questions.explain: The breadth of the term supports a shared climate of ideas.
questions.rule: Broad use shows a unified Zeitgeist.

questions.q: True or false: the authors say World War II more likely delayed the cybernetic developments slightly than produced them.
questions.explain: They say the war did not produce the developments; it more likely delayed them slightly.

questions.q: A physiologist who studies how the body holds its temperature steady meets feedback theory in 1948. Which older concepts do the authors link cybernetics to?
options: The probability concepts of Brunswik and his lens model of perception
The stimulus-response concepts of Skinner and Hull in the behaviorist tradition
The homeostasis concepts of Claude Bernard, Lotka, Cannon and Henderson
The grammar concepts of Chomsky and Harris
optionExplain: Brunswik is a forerunner on environments, not the link for feedback in physiology.
S-R concepts are what the authors contrast with their view.
Yes: the authors say cybernetics linked strongly back to homeostasis and biological feedback.
Linguistics came later and is not the link for physiology.
questions.explain: Cybernetics had a strong concern with physiology and linked back to homeostasis.
questions.rule: According to the authors, cybernetics joined information theory, feedback and the computer, was tied to logic from the start, and gave the symbolic computer only a muted role at first.
questions.teaches: From the beginning cybernetics had a strong concern with physiology and biological feedback, linking back to the homeostasis concepts of Claude Bernard, Lotka, Cannon and Henderson.

questions.q: In 1955, the Macy Conference summary by McCulloch made a place for logic and Turing machines. What did it not include, per the authors?
options: Feedback, which engineers had not yet studied in continuous systems
Symbolic mechanisms, which awaited further programming development
Information theory, which had been ruled out as irrelevant
Logic, which had been replaced entirely by Boolean algebra
optionExplain: Feedback was one of the main underpinnings of cybernetics.
Yes: symbolic mechanisms were left out until programming developed.
Information theory was the other main underpinning.
Logic and Turing machines were given a place in that summary.
questions.explain: Symbolic mechanisms waited for programming.
questions.rule: According to the authors, cybernetics joined information theory, feedback and the computer, was tied to logic from the start, and gave the symbolic computer only a muted role at first.
questions.teaches: McCulloch's Summary of Points of Agreement at the Macy Conference (1955) made a place for logic and Turing machines but none for symbolic mechanisms, which awaited further programming development.

questions.q: Soon after computers appeared, a brain-computer comparison arose. How did people respond to it, per the authors?
options: It was accepted at once as the basis for all later theory
It was ignored for about a decade before anyone mentioned it
It was welcomed only by logicians and rejected by physiologists
Warnings against taking the analogy seriously soon followed
optionExplain: The authors say the warnings came quickly, not that acceptance was total.
They say it suggested itself almost immediately, not after a decade.
They name physiologically inclined users of feedback, not a logician-physiologist split.
Yes: the metaphor suggested itself almost immediately, with warnings nearly as fast.
questions.explain: The card reports the reaction.
questions.rule: According to the authors, work too far ahead of its Zeitgeist is ignored, and the brain-computer analogy came with warnings from the start.

questions.q: The analogy that first suggested itself compared the brain's neurological organization with the wiring of the ____.
questions.explain: It was this wiring analogy that drew the warnings, including von Neumann's.
questions.rule: The first analogy was brain wiring and computer wiring.

questions.q: At which level did Turing see that the analogy could be pursued more profitably?
options: The level of neurological organization and the wiring of the brain
The more abstract level of information processing
The level of analog versus digital encoding
The level of electrical switching circuits
optionExplain: The wiring level is the analogy against which the warnings were directed.
Yes: the authors say Turing saw this abstract level from the start.
Analog-digital parity was how early cybernetic books treated computers.
Switching circuits were Shannon's Boolean application, not Turing's insight.
questions.explain: Turing's insight was about abstraction, as the Turing machine would suggest.
questions.rule: Pursue the analogy at the information-processing level.

questions.q: A scientist in the 1930s publishes a method far ahead of her field. What does the authors' Zeitgeist idea predict about its reception?
options: It is certain to be recognized at once by logicians
It is recognized at once because novelty draws attention
It is misread but gains influence in the same decade
It is likely to be ignored until its climate arrives
optionExplain: The authors do not claim certainty; they describe a widely held belief.
Novelty alone does not secure recognition in the authors' account.
The examples they give were known to few for a decade or more.
Yes: work too far ahead of its Zeitgeist is ignored, as with early game theory.
questions.explain: Early work waits for its Zeitgeist.

questions.q: True or false: the authors say von Neumann's game theory of the twenties was known to few persons before 1940.
questions.explain: They give it as an example of work too far ahead of its Zeitgeist.
questions.rule: Early game theory was known to few.

questions.q: In 1950 a young researcher hears of colleagues' results before they are printed. Which mechanism did Simon credit for such fast news?
options: An invisible college that spread news among scattered journals and books
A central journal that published every new result within a week of discovery
A government office that circulated all research reports
A single conference that all researchers attended each year
optionExplain: Yes: Simon's footnote says the invisible college operated with efficiency, then as now.
The footnote speaks of widely scattered journals and books, not one journal.
No government office is named.
No single conference is named as the source.
questions.explain: News traveled by informal contact among a scattered community.
questions.rule: According to the authors, work too far ahead of its Zeitgeist is ignored, and the brain-computer analogy came with warnings from the start.
questions.teaches: Simon's footnote says that an invisible college spread news of new contributions, published in scattered journals and books, with great rapidity, so he learned of Shannon, Pitts and McCulloch, von Neumann and Morgenstern and Wiener before publication or within months.

questions.q: Which wartime research area dealt with pilots, gunners and radar personnel as parts of man-machine systems?
options: Concept formation research
Gestalt problem-solving research
Human factors research
Physiological psychology
optionExplain: Concept formation is a related area, but about thinking tasks, not machine operators.
Gestalt work concerned problem solving, not man-machine systems.
Yes: the authors call it human factors research.
Physiological psychology is the viewpoint the authors set aside.
questions.explain: The card names the area.
questions.rule: According to the authors, European thought research, concept formation and human factors all fed psychology's new approach, with human factors and concept formation as the bridge to computer science.

questions.q: Match each work to the year the authors give.
questions.explain: These dates run in order from 1945 to 1956.

questions.q: Why did human factors research lead researchers to see analogies with computers?
options: Their experiments were run on early computers that simulated the subjects' behavior directly
Their subjects were programmers who explained how machines think
Their research was financed by firms that built digital machines
They studied humans in man-machine systems, comparable to servomechanisms and computers
optionExplain: The authors do not say human factors work was run on computers.
The subjects named are pilots, gunners and radar personnel.
Funding is not mentioned.
Yes: the authors give this as the route to the analogy.
questions.explain: The systems themselves showed the analogy.

questions.q: A 1950s lab studies how radar operators hold a few items in mind while watching a screen. To which strand does it belong?
options: Human factors research
Concept formation research
The Wurzburg school
Behaviorism
optionExplain: Yes: attention and short-term memory in man-machine systems are its main emphases.
Concept formation concerns learning categories, not monitoring a screen.
The Wurzburg school stressed central processes in thought tasks.
Behaviorism is the pre-war dominant view, not this strand.
questions.explain: Attention and short-term memory in man-machine systems are human factors topics.

questions.q: True or false: the authors say there was considerable overlap in conceptions, personnel and communication between human factors and concept formation research.
questions.explain: They say the overlap was considerable, which is why the two areas together formed a bridge.

questions.q: A historian asks which two areas gave the main bridge between mainstream psychology and the new field of computer science. Which pair?
options: Gestalt psychology and behaviorism
Linguistics and mechanical translation
Human factors and concept formation
Physiology and homeostasis
optionExplain: Neither is described as the bridge to computer science.
Mechanical translation is placed outside mainstream linguistics.
Yes: the authors say these areas were the bridge.
Homeostasis links cybernetics to physiology, not psychology to computer science.
questions.explain: Human factors and concept formation were the bridge.
questions.rule: According to the authors, European thought research, concept formation and human factors all fed psychology's new approach, with human factors and concept formation as the bridge to computer science.
questions.teaches: The authors say human factors and concept formation provided a bridge between the main stream of psychology and the newly emerging computer science, and a major route by which concepts from computer science became legitimate in psychology.

questions.q: Where do the authors place the efforts in mechanical translation relative to the main stream of linguistics?
options: At its center, as the clearest link between linguistics and computers
Outside it, though one might expect them to tie linguistics to computers
Inside it, led by the same group that wrote Methods in Structural Linguistics
Nowhere; they say mechanical translation was not attempted in this period
optionExplain: That is what one might expect, which is why the authors point out that it was not so.
Yes: the authors say the efforts were made outside the main stream.
Harris's book is cited for formalization, not for mechanical translation.
They cite Locke (1955) for the early history, so such efforts existed.
questions.explain: The card gives their placement.
questions.rule: According to the authors, linguistics was moving from structure toward generative processing, while mechanical translation stayed outside its mainstream.

questions.q: Efforts at mechanical translation were made outside the ____ of linguistics.
questions.explain: The authors say the efforts were outside the main stream.
questions.rule: Mechanical translation was outside the mainstream.

questions.q: Which change does the authors' account attribute to Chomsky's work?
options: A redirection from structure to processing, meaning generative systems
A redirection from formal rules to the study of meaning in everyday context
A redirection from spoken language to the study of written records
A redirection from translation to the study of linguistic history
optionExplain: Yes: the authors describe the shift from structure to processing, that is, generative systems.
Meaning in context is not what they say.
Spoken versus written language is not mentioned.
Translation was outside the main stream; history is not discussed.
questions.explain: Structure to processing is the change named.

questions.q: A field has long catalogued the structure of its objects. A newcomer proposes systems that generate them. Which shift does the authors' account match?
options: From a concern with processing to a concern with structure
From a concern with logic to a concern with machine translation
From a concern with structure to a concern with processing
From a concern with formalization to a rejection of method
optionExplain: That is the reverse of what the authors describe.
Machine translation was outside the mainstream.
Yes: the account describes exactly this shift for linguistics.
Linguistics kept its concern with methodological clarity.
questions.explain: Generating is processing.

questions.q: True or false: the authors say Chomsky's work, begun in 1955, did not have much impact until a few years later.
questions.explain: They date its real impact to 1957 and after.

questions.q: A reviewer says linguists were influenced by logic in this period. What evidence do the authors cite?
options: Harris's book of 1951 adopted the formalism of Principia Mathematica
Some connections with logic are clear, for example in Chomsky (1954)
Mechanical translation programs used the methods of propositional calculus
Locke's history shows linguists building theorem provers
optionExplain: The authors do not say Harris used Principia.
Yes: the authors cite Chomsky (1954) as a clear connection.
Mechanical translation is placed outside the main stream.
Locke is cited only for early history of translation.
questions.explain: Chomsky 1954 is the logic connection.
questions.rule: According to the authors, linguistics was moving from structure toward generative processing, while mechanical translation stayed outside its mainstream.
questions.teaches: The authors say some connections between linguistics and logic are clear, for example in Chomsky (1954), though as outsiders they cannot assess how far linguistics reflected the larger picture.

questions.q: In the early fifties, how were digital computers mostly viewed, according to the authors?
options: As general symbol processors that already seemed to interpret symbols like their users
As analog devices used mainly to build mechanical beasts
As experimental toys with no clear theoretical character
As mathematical machines that work with numbers rather than symbols
optionExplain: The authors say the experience of such a system was not available in the early fifties.
Robots were built separately from computers, and computers were digital.
The authors say their general theoretical character as universal machines was clearly understood.
Yes: the authors say they were viewed as primarily mathematical machines.
questions.explain: The card gives the view.
questions.rule: According to the authors, early-fifties computers were seen as numeric machines, programming was primitive, and robot-building stayed separate from symbolic computer simulation.

questions.q: The first book on programming was published in ____.
questions.explain: Wilkes, Wheeler and Gill published it in 1951.

questions.q: Sort each item by whether it is a mechanical robot effort or a computer program.

items.t: Walter's mechanical beasts of 1953
Ashby's machine of 1952
Boring's 1946 view of mechanisms illustrating theories
The first checker program, coded in 1952
Game-playing schemes described by Bowden in 1953

questions.explain: The authors say the robot efforts were separate from simulation on the computer.
questions.rule: Robots and programs were separate efforts.

questions.q: In 1953 a lab owns a universal machine but has only an assembly language. What does the authors' account say is missing?
options: Any theory that a computer could be a universal machine
A system that seems to interpret symbols as the user does
Any interest in using computers for game playing and puzzles
Any way to build mechanical robots to illustrate theories
optionExplain: The authors say universality was clearly understood.
Yes: that experience was unavailable because programming languages were primitive.
The first checker program was coded in 1952, so game playing existed.
Robot building was a separate effort, not what computers lacked.
questions.explain: Better languages let the machine look like it interprets symbols.

questions.q: True or false: the authors say mechanical robot building was rather separate from computer simulation.
questions.explain: Robot building tended toward mechanical beasts; computer simulation tended toward game playing and other symbolic activities.
questions.rule: Robots and computer simulation were separate.

questions.q: A reviewer in 1952 wants the earliest sophisticated statement of the problem of simulating thought on a machine. Which work do the authors point to?
options: Boring's 1946 article Mind and Mechanism
Wilkes, Wheeler and Gill's 1951 book on programming computers
The 1952 checker program
Turing's 1950 discussion, called justly famous
optionExplain: Boring presents the view on mechanisms but is not called the sophisticated statement.
The programming book is about programming, not simulation of thought.
A program is an instance of simulation, not the statement of the problem.
Yes: the authors say Turing (1950) put the problem of simulation in a highly sophisticated form.
questions.explain: Turing 1950 is the sophisticated statement.
questions.rule: According to the authors, early-fifties computers were seen as numeric machines, programming was primitive, and robot-building stayed separate from symbolic computer simulation.
questions.teaches: Turing (1950), in a justly famous discussion, put the problem of simulation in a highly sophisticated form.

questions.q: At the end of 1954, which task did Newell first aim to program a digital computer to learn?
options: Playing good chess
Proving theorems in logic
Translating between languages
Simulating an air defense radar
optionExplain: Yes: chess was the initial task.
Logic theorem proving was chosen later, after attention shifted.
Mechanical translation was outside the story told here.
The radar simulation was the setting at RAND, not Newell's program.
questions.explain: The card names the first task.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the project began with chess in late 1954 and shifted to theorem proving because that looked simpler for a first effort.

questions.q: By the beginning of 1955, J. C. Shaw and H. A. ____ had joined Newell.
questions.explain: Shaw and Simon associated themselves with Newell by the start of 1955.
questions.rule: Newell, Shaw and Simon formed the core group.

questions.q: Put these steps in the order the authors give.
items: Newell begins the chess effort
Shaw and Simon join him
Attention shifts toward theorem proving
Chess work is resumed toward the end of 1957
questions.explain: The chess effort began in late 1954, Shaw and Simon joined by early 1955, attention then shifted, and chess was resumed late in 1957.
questions.rule: Chess, then theorem proving, then chess again.

questions.q: A team building a program for a hard game finds a simpler task will make a better first target. Which part of the authors' story matches?
options: The decision to drop the air defense radar simulation they ran at RAND
The choice to start with a numeric program, not a symbolic one
The shift from chess to theorem proving for an initial effort
The move of the whole group from RAND to Carnegie in 1957
optionExplain: The radar simulation was the setting, not a dropped target.
The point was to move to non-numerical processing.
Yes: they judged theorem proving somewhat simpler for a first effort.
The setting move is not part of this shift.
questions.explain: Pick a simpler first target.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say the NSS chess program became operational in 1956.
questions.explain: They say the NSS program became operational in 1958.

questions.q: A project borrows satisfactory-solution targets from studies of human decisions to prune an artificial search. What precedent does that follow?
options: Psychology borrowing from physics, and physics borrowing from computing in turn
Programming languages borrowing from logic only, with no return
Artificial intelligence ignoring human behavior to avoid bias
Artificial intelligence borrowing from psychology, and psychology from it
optionExplain: Physics is not part of the stated precedent.
The precedent is two-way, between AI and psychology.
The authors say research was pursued with an eye on psychology.
Yes: the authors say the initial approach established this two-way precedent.
questions.explain: Newell used aspiration values and satisfactory solutions from psychology.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the project began with chess in late 1954 and shifted to theorem proving because that looked simpler for a first effort.
questions.teaches: The authors say Newell's initial approach established the precedent, followed in all later work, that artificial intelligence was to borrow ideas from psychology and psychology from artificial intelligence.

questions.q: Which formal system was chosen as the first target for theorem proving in late October 1955?
options: Propositional calculus, in Whitehead and Russell's system
Euclidean geometry, as treated by Gelernter and Rochester
The natural deduction scheme of Trenchard More
Chess endgames, using de Groot's protocols
optionExplain: Yes: it was the first target.
Geometry was discussed but not chosen as the first target here.
More's scheme was a separate program presented at Dartmouth.
Chess was set aside and resumed later.
questions.explain: The card names the first target.
questions.rule: According to the authors, hand simulation in December 1955 came before the August 1956 machine proof, and the languages were designed for complexity and suited psychology.

questions.q: On December 15, 1955 the first successful hand simulation proved Theorem ____ of Principia Mathematica.
questions.explain: Theorem 2.15 was the one proved in the first successful hand simulation, using essentially the methods and flow diagram later incorporated in the Logic Theorist.
questions.teaches: On December 15, 1955, the first successful hand simulation was carried out of the proof of a theorem in Principia Mathematica (Theorem 2.15).

questions.q: Put these events in the order the authors give.
items: Propositional calculus chosen as first target
First successful hand simulation of a proof
First complete machine proof of a theorem
IPL-I published
questions.explain: The target was chosen in October 1955, the hand simulation came on December 15, 1955, the machine proof on August 9, 1956 and the IPL-I paper in September 1956.
questions.rule: Hand simulation came before machine proof.

questions.q: A designer needs a language for programs whose structures are unpredictable in size. Which cue from psychology guided the authors' languages?
options: The step-by-step deduction used in formal logical proof
The rigid layout of a numeric table
The associative organization of human memory
The single-pass flow of a feedback loop
optionExplain: Deduction is not what they say guided the language design.
Numeric tables were what they moved away from.
Yes: the authors say features of memory, especially associative organization, pointed toward list processing.
Feedback is not cited as the design cue.
questions.explain: Associative memory suggested list processing.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say the first complete machine proof of a Principia theorem came on December 15, 1955.
questions.explain: That date was the first successful hand simulation; the first complete machine proof came on August 9, 1956.

questions.q: Why were the information processing languages suited to writing programs that express psychological theories?
options: They were designed to be as short as possible for numeric work on the early machines at RAND
They were designed first for unpredictable complexity, so the fit was no accident
They were designed to copy the wiring of the brain directly
They were designed after the theories, so they were fitted to them
optionExplain: The point is about complexity, not brevity or numbers.
Yes: the authors say they were designed first and foremost to handle unpredictable complexity.
The authors reject direct brain-wiring analogies.
The languages preceded the psychological theories.
questions.explain: Complexity and memory cues made them suit psychology.
questions.rule: According to the authors, hand simulation in December 1955 came before the August 1956 machine proof, and the languages were designed for complexity and suited psychology.
questions.teaches: The authors say the information processing languages were designed first and foremost to handle unpredictable complexity, which is why their suitability for psychological theories was not entirely accidental.

questions.q: At the 1956 Dartmouth seminar, how many concrete new problem-solving schemes were brought, according to the authors?
options: Two: LT and a natural-deduction scheme
None: it was a meeting for ideas only
One: the Logic Theorist alone
Six: one for each organizer and attendee group
optionExplain: Yes: many ideas were in the air, but two schemes were concrete.
The authors report two concrete schemes, not none.
More's scheme was also brought.
There is no count of six.
questions.explain: The card gives the count.
questions.rule: According to the authors, Dartmouth gathered most active AI workers, but only the Logic Theorist and More's scheme were concrete new programs.

questions.q: The Dartmouth seminar was organized for the month of ____ 1956.
questions.explain: McCarthy, Minsky, Rochester and Shannon organized it for June 1956.

questions.q: Match each name to the role the authors give it in the Dartmouth account.
pairs: Essay Steps Toward Artificial Intelligence, circulated late 1956
Successful work on geometry theorem proving that followed shortly
questions.explain: Each pairing is in the authors' account.

questions.q: At a workshop where many ideas are in the air, one participant brings only a flow diagram she has hand simulated. Which Dartmouth contribution is closest?
options: The Logic Theorist, which was already running as a machine program
Minsky's essay, which was circulated as a technical report
More's natural-deduction scheme, a hand-simulated flow diagram
Gelernter and Rochester's geometry work, completed before the seminar
optionExplain: The LT was exhibited with early debugging outputs, so it was further along.
The essay was a report on pooled knowledge, not a program scheme.
Yes: More's scheme was a flow diagram and hand simulation.
Their work followed the seminar shortly.
questions.explain: A hand-simulated flow diagram is More's case.

questions.q: True or false: the authors say Minsky's Steps Toward Artificial Intelligence was first circulated as a technical report in late 1956 and published several years later.
questions.explain: It reflected the knowledge pooled at Dartmouth and later helped codify it.

questions.q: After a 1956 workshop, which topic discussed there gave impetus to successful work by two attendees soon after?
options: Mechanical translation of languages
Proving theorems in geometry
Playing checkers by machine
Recording thinking-aloud tapes
optionExplain: Translation was outside the main stream and not tied to Dartmouth here.
Yes: geometry was an important topic and gave impetus to Gelernter and Rochester.
Checkers is cited for 1952 earlier, not as a Dartmouth impetus.
Thinking-aloud tapes came later, in 1957.
questions.explain: Geometry became Gelernter and Rochester's successful topic.
questions.rule: According to the authors, Dartmouth gathered most active AI workers, but only the Logic Theorist and More's scheme were concrete new programs.
questions.teaches: Geometry theorem proving was an important topic of conversation at Dartmouth, giving impetus to the successful work of Gelernter and Rochester that followed shortly.

questions.q: What did comparing LT with tape-recorded thinking-aloud sessions show, according to the authors?
options: LT matched human behavior step for step in the detail of each protocol
Humans used no consistent method at all when thinking aloud, answering at random
The tapes were too poor in quality to be compared with any program
LT's organization did not fit the detail, and the means-ends method appeared
optionExplain: The authors say LT did not fit the detail well.
They say the behavior showed evidence of a method.
They used the transcriptions in their analysis.
Yes: it did not fit, and the method that appeared was means-ends.
questions.explain: The card gives the finding.
questions.rule: According to the authors, comparing LT with thinking-aloud protocols showed that LT did not fit, and the means-ends method seen in people led to GPS.

questions.q: The first thinking-aloud tapes were transcribed in the spring of ____.
questions.explain: Transcription began in spring 1957, and analysis followed.

questions.q: Why was the Moore-Anderson task a good basis for comparing humans with LT?
options: It used chess positions that LT could also analyze with its methods
Its formal system was close to that of Whitehead and Russell
It was built by the RAND group for the purpose
It involved no logic, so LT's rules would not matter
optionExplain: The task was logic disguised as decoding, not chess.
Yes: the authors give that closeness as the reason.
It was Moore and Anderson's task at Yale.
It was a logic task, which is why LT could be compared.
questions.explain: The formal systems were close.

questions.q: A team's program matches an expert's reasoning poorly when compared with transcripts of her talking aloud. What does the authors' story suggest?
options: Defend the old program by discarding the transcripts
Recompile the old program with a faster computer
Wait for neurophysiology to explain the mismatch
Let the transcripts shape a new program organization
optionExplain: The authors did not discard the data; they changed the program.
Speed was not the issue; fit was.
The authors reject the demand that mechanisms be neurological.
Yes: the protocol analysis drove the first versions of GPS.
questions.explain: Data from protocols shaped the new program.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say the first thinking-aloud tapes were transcribed in the autumn of 1956.
questions.explain: They say the first tapes were transcribed in the spring of 1957.

questions.q: A lab wants a program to model rote learning of word lists. Which classical source did the authors say mainly gave Feigenbaum the ideas for EPAM?
options: Gibson's 1940 paper on stimulus and response generalization
Hovland's 1952 paper on communication analysis of concept learning
Moore and Anderson's logic exercises
Miller's 1956 paper on the magic number seven
optionExplain: Yes: it was perhaps the most important single source.
Hovland is cited for concept formation.
Moore and Anderson concern theorem proving.
Miller's paper is cited among concept formation work.
questions.explain: Gibson 1940 fed EPAM.
questions.rule: According to the authors, comparing LT with thinking-aloud protocols showed that LT did not fit, and the means-ends method seen in people led to GPS.
questions.teaches: The first memorandum sketching EPAM is dated February 18, 1956, and E. J. Gibson's 1940 paper on stimulus and response generalization was perhaps the most important single source of the ideas Feigenbaum developed into EPAM.

questions.q: What counts as an explanation of observed behavior in the thesis of the 1958 Elements paper?
options: A detailed list of the neural pathways that produce the behavior
A table of correlations between each stimulus and each response
A program of primitive processes that generates the behavior
A statistical average of many subjects' behavior
optionExplain: The authors reject the demand that mechanisms be neurological.
Correlations are the empty-organism view the authors want filled.
Yes: that is the thesis quoted from the paper.
The paper's account is a generating program, not a statistical average.
questions.explain: The card states the thesis.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the Elements paper held that a program of primitive information processes explains behavior, and GPS was first described publicly in May 1958.

questions.q: The Elements paper appeared in the Psychological Review for ____ 1958.
questions.explain: It was published in July 1958, though written over a year earlier.

questions.q: Which feature describes the Elements paper, rather than the later work on GPS?
options: It compared a hand-simulated computer trace with a thinking-aloud protocol line by line
It described the GPS flow diagram in full detail
It was based on tapes transcribed in 1957
It stressed broad resemblances to human problem solving, with no detailed comparisons
optionExplain: That comparison came in the Colorado paper.
The GPS flow diagram dates from late October 1957 and was not described there.
The paper was written more than a year before July 1958, based on LT.
Yes: it was based on LT and avoided detailed behavioral comparisons.
questions.explain: The Elements paper compared in broad terms.

questions.q: A new paper argues that an explanation of a chess player's moves is a program of simple operations that reproduces them. Which position is it stating?
options: The thesis of the Elements paper
The empty-organism view of correlations
The neurological reduction in a single step
The claim that logic is human thinking
optionExplain: Yes: it matches the thesis.
The empty-organism view has nothing inside.
The authors reject a single-step neurological reduction.
The authors say logic is not human thinking.
questions.explain: Behavior explained by a generating program is the thesis.

questions.q: True or false: the authors say the Elements paper did not use the precise phrase information processing psychology.
questions.explain: They call it the first explicit exposition of the position, although that precise phrase was not used.

questions.q: Which paper first set a hand-simulated computer trace beside a human thinking-aloud protocol, even informally?
options: The Elements paper in the Psychological Review of July 1958
The first IPL-I paper, published in September 1956
The paper read at a Colorado symposium on May 14, 1958
The RAND report of May 1956
optionExplain: The Elements paper avoided detailed comparisons.
IPL-I described the language.
Yes: the Colorado paper contained the first fragment of such a comparison.
The RAND report announced LT.
questions.explain: The Colorado paper held the first informal comparison.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the Elements paper held that a program of primitive information processes explains behavior, and GPS was first described publicly in May 1958.
questions.teaches: The Colorado paper read on May 14, 1958 (and again at the RAND seminar, published in 1962) contained the first fragment of informal comparison of a hand-simulated computer trace with a human thinking-aloud protocol.

questions.q: What led to the authors' contact and collaboration with colleagues in Amsterdam?
options: A conference at Dartmouth in the summer of 1956
Finding de Groot's work on the thinking of chess players
The RAND Summer Seminar held in Santa Monica in 1958
The publication of Principia Mathematica by Whitehead and Russell
optionExplain: Dartmouth was in 1956 and is not linked to Amsterdam here.
Yes: the discovery of de Groot's 1946 book led to contact.
The RAND seminar was later and is not linked to de Groot here.
Principia is the system used by LT.
questions.explain: The card gives the link.
questions.rule: According to the authors, chess work was nearly dormant from 1955, resumed late in 1957, and led through de Groot's work to a lasting Amsterdam collaboration.

questions.q: Work on chess was nearly dormant after 1955 and resumed toward the end of ____.
questions.explain: It resumed toward the end of 1957.

questions.q: Which source do the authors name for histories of computer chess programs and the NSS program?
options: Their own 1958 chess paper, and Chapter 11
Minsky's Steps Toward Artificial Intelligence, circulated in 1956
Turing's 1950 discussion of the problem of simulation
Moore and Anderson's 1954 papers on logic problems
optionExplain: Yes: the authors point to these.
Minsky's essay reflects pooled AI knowledge.
Turing's work is cited for the problem of simulation.
Moore and Anderson used logic tasks.
questions.explain: Their own 1958 paper and Chapter 11.
questions.rule: Check the 1958 chess paper and Chapter 11.

questions.q: A lab's game project stalls for two years. A researcher then finds an earlier study of how masters think and starts a collaboration. Which part of the story matches?
options: The shift from chess to theorem proving in geometry or logic
The writing of the Elements paper
Resuming chess work and making contact with de Groot
The Dartmouth seminar's geometry talks
optionExplain: The shift to theorem proving came earlier.
The Elements paper concerned the theory.
Yes: the stall, discovery and collaboration match.
Geometry was a different topic.
questions.explain: Dormancy then discovery then collaboration.
questions.rule: Discovery of earlier work restarts a project.

questions.q: True or false: the authors say work on the chess program had been nearly dormant since 1955.
questions.explain: It was resumed toward the end of 1957.
questions.rule: Chess was nearly dormant in between.

questions.q: Where do the authors send readers who want histories of both psychological research on chess and chess-playing programs?
options: Chapter 3 on the task environment
Chapter 11 of the book
Chapter 6 on cryptarithmetic
Chapter 14 on the theory
optionExplain: Chapter 3 is cited for the environment theme.
Yes: Chapter 11 reviews both histories.
Chapter 6 is cited for cryptarithmetic.
Chapter 14 is where the theory is set out.
questions.explain: Chapter 11 reviews both histories.
questions.rule: According to the authors, chess work was nearly dormant from 1955, resumed late in 1957, and led through de Groot's work to a lasting Amsterdam collaboration.
questions.teaches: Chapter 11 of the book reviews the histories of psychological research on chess as a problem-solving task and of chess-playing computer programs.

questions.q: Who directed the 1958 RAND Summer Seminar on computer simulation?
options: Hovland and Miller
Minsky and McCarthy
Shannon and Wiener
Newell and Simon
optionExplain: Hovland and Miller were on the sponsoring committee and lectured.
Minsky was a lecturer, and the MIT group worked separately.
Shannon and Wiener belong to the cybernetics story.
Yes: it was directed by Newell and Simon.
questions.explain: The card names the directors.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the 1958 RAND seminar taught simulation to psychologists and linked the RAND-Carnegie group to other streams of work.

questions.q: Match each participant to the later work the authors link to the seminar.
pairs: Information processing models of concept formation
questions.explain: Each work is named in the authors' list.

questions.q: What was the aim of the 1958 seminar?
options: To train commercial programmers for industry and for government agencies
To acquaint psychologists and other social scientists with simulation
To present the Logic Theorist to the public for the first time
To settle whether chess or theorem proving was the better first task
optionExplain: The participants were social scientists.
Yes: that was the stated aim.
LT was presented earlier, at Dartmouth.
That choice was made in 1955.
questions.explain: Wider audience, simulation techniques.
questions.rule: The seminar was to spread simulation.

questions.q: A summer school wants to bring simulation methods to researchers in another field. Which features of the RAND seminar would it copy?
options: Lectures only, with every bit of programming instruction left out entirely
Programming instruction with no sample programs to run
A single program chosen by vote of the participants
Lectures plus programming instruction around working programs
optionExplain: It included programming instruction.
It used principal programs as the curriculum.
It used four main programs, not a vote.
Yes: the seminar combined lectures and IPL-IV instruction around LT, GPS, NSS and EPAM.
questions.explain: Teach with programs.
questions.rule: Lectures plus programming around real programs.

questions.q: True or false: the authors say the 1958 RAND summer seminar aimed to acquaint psychologists and other social scientists with computer simulation techniques and their use in studying human behavior.
questions.explain: The authors describe the seminar's aim in just these terms; it taught simulation methods to a wider circle of social scientists.
questions.rule: The RAND seminar spread simulation methods.
questions.teaches: A summer seminar was organized in 1958 at the RAND Corporation with the aim of acquainting a wider circle of social scientists, and particularly psychologists, with computer simulation techniques.

questions.q: Which later product of the seminar's circle had the most influence on psychology, according to the authors?
options: Plans and the Structure of Behavior, by Miller and others
Structure and Direction in Thinking, by Berlyne and others
Methods in Structural Linguistics by Harris
A Study of Thinking by Bruner, Austin and Goodnow
optionExplain: Yes: the authors say it was perhaps the most important in subsequent influence.
Berlyne's book is cited as an example but not as the most influential.
Harris's book was a 1951 linguistics work, before the seminar.
The Bruner book appeared in 1956, before the seminar.
questions.explain: Miller, Galanter and Pribram are named as most important.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the 1958 RAND seminar taught simulation to psychologists and linked the RAND-Carnegie group to other streams of work.
questions.teaches: Miller, Galanter and Pribram's Plans and the Structure of Behavior, written during 1958-59, is called perhaps the most important in subsequent influence, with its references showing the role of the RAND seminar and the RAND-Carnegie work.

questions.q: By 1958, had all the important ingredients of the authors' theory been mixed in, according to the authors?
options: Yes: the theory in Chapter 14 was complete by 1958
No: the theory did not exist before 1962
No: some features, such as production systems, came later
Yes: but the authors chose not to publish the theory until 1972
optionExplain: The authors say a number of features of the theory as it finally shapes up in Chapter 14 postdate the critical years.
They say the basic ideas emerged from late 1954 through 1958, so the theory did not begin in 1962.
Yes: they single out production systems and the environment-organism relation as postdating the critical years.
They note the first drafts of the book go back to 1958; they do not say publication was withheld by choice.
questions.explain: The authors say they do not imply that all important ingredients were mixed in by 1958.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the history stops at 1958 because later work broadened too far, and production systems and the environment-organism relation postdate it.
questions.teaches: By terminating the history here, we do not wish to imply that all of the important ingredients of our theory had been mixed in by 1958.

questions.q: The authors say their attempt at history must stop with ____.
questions.explain: They say even parochial history must stop with 1958.

questions.q: Match each source of production systems to its role in the authors' account.
pairs: Use in symbolic logic; the name is taken from him
Linguistics, where they are called rewrite rules
String manipulation systems that put them to use
questions.explain: These are the lines through which production systems gained currency.
questions.rule: Production systems had a long history.

questions.q: Why were production systems ready to use when the human problem-solving data took the form of problem behavior graphs?
options: They had been invented for the Logic Theorist
They were taken from the physiology of neural networks and brain tissue
They were designed by Newell in 1955 for chess
They had a long history and entered wide use in programming languages
optionExplain: They came from logic, Markov algorithms and linguistics.
They are not described as physiological.
They were first used in the 1965 chess analysis.
Yes: the authors say they were at hand once they entered wide currency in programming languages.
questions.explain: A prepared formalism waited for a mission.
questions.rule: An old formalism became ready through programming languages.

questions.q: Simon wrote that if human rationality had no limits, administrative theory would have a single precept. Substitute psychology; what problem does that state?
options: How the task environment shapes behavior, the concern of Chapter 3
How neurons produce the regularities between stimulus and response in rats
How logic differs from human thinking
How chess programs choose among moves
optionExplain: Yes: the authors say the substitution states the problem of Chapter 3.
That is the neurological question they set aside.
That is the logic-and-thinking discussion.
That is the chess topic.
questions.explain: The task-environment problem is the substitution.
questions.rule: Limits of rationality bring in the environment.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say production systems were first made fully explicit in the chess analysis of 1965.
questions.explain: They say they first used production systems in the chess analysis, but the connection became fully explicit only in the cryptarithmetic work of 1966.

questions.q: A symbol system built as games with arbitrary rules ignores meaning. When it is tied back to the real world, what returns as a central concern?
options: The formal syntax of the rules, which logic had emphasized earlier
The numeric size of the memory
The reference of symbols: semantics and the relation of denoting
The physical wiring of the machine
optionExplain: Syntax was the emphasis inherited from logic.
Size is not discussed here.
Yes: the authors say semantics, the denotative aspect, has reemerged.
Wiring is the analogy they set aside.
questions.explain: Meaning returns when the system meets the real world.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the history stops at 1958 because later work broadened too far, and production systems and the environment-organism relation postdate it.
questions.teaches: Even without external reference, complex processes on complex memory structures need addressing schemes so one symbol can denote another, so semantics, the denotative aspect, has reemerged as a central concern.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A psychologist wants to explain how people solve puzzles. Which kind of theory would these authors favor?
options: Internal mechanisms that, run on the puzzle, would produce the solver's steps
Statistical laws relating the average scores of groups to features of the puzzle
A map of the brain regions that become active during each step of solving
A catalogue of inborn habits that every solver brings to each new puzzle
optionExplain: Right: they posit mechanisms that produce the behavior, and they check it by calculation.
A common style in psychology, but the authors avoid grouped data where they can.
The authors decline to link their processes to places in the brain.
Nothing in the theory says the processes are inborn habits; they are posited mechanisms.
questions.explain: A fair guess either way. The authors posit mechanisms that produce behavior; the card next gives the reasons.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: The authors ask first that a theory's mechanisms be ____ to perform the task, before refining them to fit data.
questions.explain: Sufficiency comes first: a system within human limits that can perform the task, then refinement against specific data.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A robot plans a dinner within a cook's known memory and speed limits. By the authors' order of work, what comes next?
options: Declare that cooks plan their dinners in the same way the robot does
Place the robot's planning rules in a particular region of the cook's brain
Average the robot's menus over many cooks to test how well it fits
Revise the robot toward closer fit with data on how cooks plan
optionExplain: Tempting because the robot works, but being able to do the task is only a first approximation.
The authors decline to assign their processes to brain locations.
Averaging over many cooks is the grouped-data route the authors avoid where they can.
Right: after sufficiency comes a revised system with higher fidelity to specific data.
questions.explain: The robot has met the first requirement. The authors then develop a revised system that fits specific data on human processing better.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A program solves a puzzle only by holding forty items at once in immediate memory. How does it fare against the authors' sufficiency requirement?
options: It passes, because any program that solves the puzzle counts as sufficient
It passes, since memory limits matter only at the later stage of fitting data
It fails, because the system must work within gross human limits such as memory
It fails, since sufficiency requires the program to run as slowly as a person
optionExplain: This drops the condition that the system stay within human limits.
The limits are part of the first approximation, not something added at the fitting stage.
Right: the first-approximation system takes account of gross limits such as processing rate and immediate memory.
Speed matching is not the test; the test is staying within gross limits like those on memory and rate.
questions.explain: The card says the first system must respect gross human limits, immediate memory among them. Our reading: forty items breaks that.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: Because the authors posit mechanisms inside the person, they tie each mechanism to a place in the central nervous system.
questions.explain: They presume the processes exist in the nervous system but decline to speculate on localization; no plausible localizations exist for immediate memory or the symbol.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A school wants a theory of how its pupils learn fractions. Following the authors' approach, how should it begin?
options: Pool all pupils' scores and fit one average curve to the whole group
Model one pupil on one task in detail, then ask what is common
Wait until brain scans can show where fractions are stored in the brain
Build the general theory first and fit individual pupils to it later
optionExplain: Grouped data are what the authors try not to use for testing the theory.
Right: individual first, then the hard task of finding what all share.
The authors do not wait for physiology; they leave localization aside.
This runs the order backward; the authors start from the single individual.
questions.explain: The authors go from one individual to what is general.
questions.teaches: According to the authors, individual differences are not tacked on to the main body of the theory, and grouped data are not used to test it if that can be helped.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Two chess players and a logic student all solve problems by searching. What explanation would these authors give?
options: Each was taught the same search method by the same kind of teacher
General features of the human processor lead any task to be treated as a space to search
Search is a cultural habit that differs a good deal from one group to another
The brain's wiring forces every thought to scan all possible moves in turn
optionExplain: Teaching can matter, but the authors argue for a more general reason.
Right: a few gross processor characteristics suffice to determine that a task is represented as a problem space.
The authors stress invariants over tasks and subjects, not group habits.
The authors say seriality does not mean memories are scanned in turn.
questions.explain: A fair guess either way. The card next sets out the order of the authors' propositions.
questions.rule: Task limits space, space limits program.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Order the layers from the task environment inward, as the authors present them.
items: Task environment
Problem space
Methods
Production system
questions.explain: The environment limits the space, the space limits the methods, and a production system realizes them.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A game designer changes a board game so that three pieces can no longer be captured. By the chain, what is changed first?
options: The set of problem spaces that fit the task
Each player's production system, rule by rule
The size of the players' short-term memories
The brain regions the players use for search
optionExplain: Right: the task environment delimits the possible problem spaces, so a change to the task first changes that set.
A production system is further along the chain and also depends on the solver's history.
Memory parameters are processor traits, which a rule change leaves alone.
The authors make no claims about brain regions.
questions.explain: The task sits first in the chain, so its change first alters which spaces are possible.
questions.rule: Task change shifts the possible spaces.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A student claims the authors say the task environment determines which problem space each person uses. What is wrong with this?
options: It understates: the task limits the possible spaces and also fixes each person's exact program
It is wrong because the authors say the space is chosen before the solver ever sees the task
Nothing is wrong; the authors treat the task as fixing a single space that everyone uses
It overstates: the task limits the possible spaces, and history and instructions pick the actual one
optionExplain: The chain stops at what is possible; it does not fix an exact program.
No such claim is made; the space is tied to the task and to history with it.
A task allows many spaces, and different solvers can use different ones.
Right: propositions three and four give only possibilities.
questions.explain: The propositions speak of what is possible. The actual space and program come from history, instructions and experience.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: The authors claim the chain lets them derive each person's actual space and program from the task alone.
