questions.explain: They call the account of how a particular space and program are chosen tentative and incomplete, and they link it to individual differences.
questions.rule: The chain narrows; it does not finish.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A volunteer arrives to solve a logic puzzle. When do the authors say her working program is mostly set?
options: Gradually, step by step, over the whole of the minutes spent solving the puzzle
Only after her first error, once the puzzle has shown her what is really needed
Before the session and in the first minutes of reading, then it stays fairly stable
Afresh at every move
optionExplain: Change from experience is placed on a scale of hours, not the minutes of one search.
Nothing makes the first error the point where the program is set.
Right: an initial program is assembled rapidly and then stays fairly stable.
The program persists across the states of a search; it is not rebuilt at each move.
questions.explain: Most relevant behavior happens before the laboratory, and the rest in the first minutes or seconds.
questions.teaches: The authors say most behavior relevant to choosing a program occurs before the subject reaches the laboratory and the rest while the instructions are read, so the program changes with experience only on a scale of hours.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Why might a person solving a puzzle keep only one or two earlier positions to return to?
options: The rules of the puzzle forbid returning to more than two earlier positions in a row
Earlier positions are always forgotten within a second or so of leaving them behind
Recording many positions costs time that would slow the search for new information
Returning to old positions is a sign of poor problem solving that good solvers avoid
optionExplain: No rule of the tasks sets this limit; it comes from the processor.
A second is far too short; the limit is about the cost of recording, not instant forgetting.
Right: the authors say recording states costs time, so programs keep few return points.
The authors treat backup as a normal part of search.
questions.explain: A fair guess. The card next ties it to the processor's memory limits.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: The authors give short-term memory a capacity of about five to ____ symbols.
questions.explain: Capacity is about five to seven symbols, and each symbol can stand for a whole structure in long-term memory.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A diner tries to keep a mental list of every dish sampled at a forty-dish buffet. Which limit makes this hard in the authors' model?
options: Reading from long-term memory takes several minutes for each single item
Short-term memory is too small to hold a continually growing state
The processor works on several dishes at once and so mixes them up
External memory cannot be consulted at all while a person is eating
optionExplain: Reading takes a few hundred milliseconds; it is writing that is slow.
Right: STM cannot hold an ever-growing state, which is why states are discrete with limited backup.
The authors describe the processor as serial, one elementary process at a time.
External memory can be read; its use is part of the model, not ruled out.
questions.explain: The growing list would have to sit in short-term memory, which holds only about five to seven symbols.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Suppose writing to long-term memory were as fast as reading it. Which part of the authors' argument for discrete states would weaken?
options: The objection that accumulating knowledge in long-term memory costs too much storing time
The claim that short-term memory is too small to hold a growing state of knowledge
The claim that the processor carries out one elementary process at a time only
The claim that external memory can be consulted while the solver is working
optionExplain: Right: accumulating in LTM is ruled out by its large storing time cost, which this change would remove. Our reading of the argument.
This rests on STM capacity, which faster writing does not change.
Seriality is a separate trait and is unaffected by write speed.
The use of external memory does not depend on the speed of long-term writing.
questions.explain: One support for discrete states is that storing in LTM takes large time. Faster writing would remove that support. Our reading.
questions.rule: Slow writing is one reason knowledge is not simply accumulated.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: The authors claim to prove from memory limits alone that the time spent in each knowledge state must be a few seconds.
questions.explain: They offer a heuristic argument that many small decisions use a serial processor better, and they back it with measured times; it is not a proof.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A person solves a sliding-tile puzzle on a board where each move overwrites the display. How is she expected to return to an earlier position?
options: By reading a stored copy of every earlier position off the board itself
By rescanning all of her long-term memory for the earlier arrangement of tiles
By recording each position in long-term memory as she leaves it behind
By remembering a few recent moves in short-term memory and undoing them
optionExplain: The display holds only the current arrangement; the earlier ones are overwritten.
The authors say retrieval from LTM does not work by scanning memory.
Storing every position in LTM would cost several seconds per chunk, too much for this.
Right: return depends on recalling the last few moves and reversing them.
questions.explain: With a noncumulative display, the past is lost unless a few recent moves are held in short-term memory.
questions.rule: Return is limited to the few most recent moves.
questions.teaches: When each move overwrites the display, as in the 15-puzzle, the authors say a solver can return only as far back as the few recent moves he holds in short-term memory and can undo.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A locksmith faces a four-digit lock with no clues. What could make a search faster than trying 0000, 0001, 0002 and so on?
options: Trying the numbers in a random order instead of in an ordered sequence
Working faster so that many more numbers are tried within each minute
Starting from 9999 and counting downward instead of upward from 0000
Using any information about the lock that guides each next trial
optionExplain: Random order uses no knowledge of the goal and gains nothing in the long run.
Speed helps a little, but the authors place the power in information, not speed.
A different order without information about the lock changes nothing on average.
Right: the authors say gains over random search come from exploiting additional information.
questions.explain: A fair guess. The card next says where search power comes from.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: The authors say gains over random search must come from exploiting additional ____.
questions.explain: A method gains power only from information it actually uses, such as what has been found and what remains.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Looking for a library book, Dana walks only to shelves labeled with the right subject. Which of the authors' three principles is this?
options: Use feedback gathered step by step while the possible solutions are generated
Work with simpler abstractions in place of the full detail of the problem
Generate only elements already guaranteed to have some solution properties
Generate every element in order until one of them passes the final test
optionExplain: That principle needs information learned along the way; this one is fixed in advance.
That would mean working with a coarser description of the books; here the shelves are simply chosen.
Right: the subject label guarantees every shelf visited has one property of the solution.
This describes blind generate-and-test, which the principles replace.
questions.explain: Visiting only the right-subject shelves builds a property of the solution into the generator.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Imagine a task with no structure, where knowing one position tells nothing about any other. What does the authors' account predict?
options: It still becomes selective once the solver is fast enough at the work
It gains little over blind generation, with no redundancy to exploit
It succeeds because abstraction creates structure out of nothing at all
It fails to find any solution, however long the search is allowed to run
optionExplain: Speed is not the source of the power; information is.
Right: with no redundancy, nothing in one place predicts another, so selectivity has nothing to use.
Abstraction simplifies existing structure; it does not create it.
Generate-and-test finds a solution if one exists and it runs long enough.
questions.explain: Structure is redundancy that makes information predictive. Without it, search has little to exploit. Our reading.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: In a game where each move is a threat the opponent must answer, with at most four replies, how does search effort grow with depth?
options: Roughly in proportion to depth, not exponentially
Doubling with every extra move of depth
Staying constant, whatever the depth
Faster than exponentially, since threats multiply branches
optionExplain: Right: in forcing mating situations, the selective heuristics keep the tree growth roughly linear.
Doubling would be exponential growth, which selectivity in forcing positions avoids.
Effort does grow with depth, only slowly.
Forcing moves reduce the replies to consider, so the tree does not explode.
questions.explain: In forcing positions the task environment and selective heuristics keep the tree near linear in depth.
questions.teaches: In the authors' mating program, a fifteen-ply combination needed a discovery tree of only 108 moves, where an exponential tree with two branches per node would hold about 32,000.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: The mating results show that search in all of chess can be kept nearly linear in depth.
questions.explain: The result concerns forcing situations of uninterrupted checks, where the task environment is unusually favorable; it does not show that all chess search is cheap.
questions.rule: A favorable task is not every task.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A researcher fits a program to one volunteer's puzzle attempt. What role can that single fit play for a general theory?
options: It is one data point at which the theory meets particular behavior
It proves the general theory for everyone who ever attempts the puzzle
It is worthless, since one person alone cannot be used to test a theory
It removes any need to study another volunteer on the same puzzle
optionExplain: Right: the authors call each such fit a microtheory and a data point for the general theory.
One fit proves nothing for everyone.
One point tests little, but the authors do not call it worthless.
The authors go on to compare other subjects.
questions.explain: A fair guess. The card next says how the authors use such data points.
questions.rule: One fit is one data point.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Order the three stages the book uses for each task.
items: Task analysis of what spaces and methods the task allows
A program compared with one subject's recorded thinking aloud
A broader view of how far the findings hold across subjects
questions.explain: Each task part runs from task analysis, to one subject's microtheory, to a wider comparison.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A team studying how cooks plan menus has listed which planning methods a menu task allows. By the book's pattern, what comes next?
options: State at once that all cooks plan their menus in the very same way
Average the number of dishes planned across all of the cooks studied
Scan each cook's brain while the cook is busy planning a menu
Compare a program with one cook's recorded thinking aloud
optionExplain: This claims the identical-protocol result the authors expect to fail.
Averages are the grouped-data style the authors avoid.
The authors decline to tie their processes to the brain.
Right: after task analysis comes a microtheory for one attempt.
questions.explain: Task analysis comes first, then a program for one subject's protocol, then a broader view.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A reader says the theory failed because other subjects' protocols were not identical to the first subject's. What is wrong with this?
options: Nothing is wrong; identical protocols are the theory's own stated prediction
The other subjects were too few in number to count as any test at all
The authors expected protocols to differ and ask how and how far they do
The authors dropped the theory as soon as the protocols were seen to differ
optionExplain: Read literally it predicts identical protocols, but the authors say that prediction will fail.
Number of subjects is a fair worry elsewhere, but it is not the error in this claim.
Right: they say at the outset that the prediction will fail; the manner and extent of failure is the test.
They carried the theory forward, comparing it across subjects.
questions.explain: The authors do not treat non-identical protocols as refutation. They study how the behavior departs.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: After one study of how a bakery fills orders, a team wants stronger support. Following the authors, what extra step helps?
options: Add many more questions to the original set of bakery interviews already held
Show that the same mechanisms work on a different task of the same kind
Compare the bakery's scores with national averages for bakeries of its size
Announce that the theory now covers every workplace in the whole country
optionExplain: More of the same task adds depth but not the new-task check.
Right: a mechanism-based theory is tested by showing the same mechanisms on another task.
Task scores plotted against a population are the approach the authors avoid.
Reach beyond the tested tasks is argued, not shown.
questions.explain: Because the authors seek the specific mechanisms behind behavior, they can test whether those mechanisms work the same on another task.
questions.teaches: The authors tried a second cryptarithmetic task, CROSS+ROADS=DANGER, which S4 solved right after a ten-minute break; they call such a check comforting, not conclusive.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: The three-stage pattern across puzzles, logic and chess shows the theory holds for all problem solving.
questions.explain: The pattern shows a theory tested on three tasks; the authors call the book a progress report and mark the reach beyond these tasks as argued, not tested.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A program reproduces a subject's recorded steps closely. What can be concluded?
options: That people must organize their thinking in the same way the program does
That the program's organization is sufficient to produce those steps
That the subject had no other method available for solving the problem
That the program was designed without looking at any of the data at all
optionExplain: This treats a match as proof of uniqueness.
Right: a match shows sufficiency, not necessity.
A match does not show what else the subject could have done.
Some adaptation to data is normal; the question is whether the fit could have failed.
questions.explain: A fair guess. The card next separates sufficiency from necessity.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A program that reproduces behavior shows the organization is ____, not that it is necessary.
questions.explain: Reproducing the behavior shows that the organization is enough to produce it, not that it is the only one.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A weather model reproduces last year's temperatures, and a colleague says that proves its mechanism is how weather works. What is the best reply?
options: The match shows sufficiency for those data; other mechanisms might also fit
Agreed, since matching the data is exactly how a mechanism is proved
The match counts for nothing
The match matters only if the model also predicts next year's weather exactly
optionExplain: Right: a match shows sufficiency, and it still narrows the field of rivals.
This treats sufficiency as necessity.
Fitting does not make a match worthless; it is partly adaptation, and that does not make it trivial.
The standard here is about what a match shows, not exact future prediction.
questions.explain: The reply is the sufficiency point applied to a new case.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Which criticism of GPS does the authors' point that its methods were defined independently of the subjects answer?
options: That thinking aloud changed how subjects searched
That the program was tested on too few kinds of problem
That the program ignored the structure of the task
That the fit to the protocols is circular
optionExplain: That worry is about the data, and the authors address it with separate counts.
Range of problems is a fair concern, but independent definition does not answer it.
GPS is built from the task environment, so this is not the criticism raised.
Right: because GPS is defined from the task and theory, it could have failed to fit, so the fit is not guaranteed.
questions.explain: Independent definition is what makes the fit testable.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Two spam filters score 80 percent on one combined measure; one misses spam, the other wrongly flags good mail. What do the authors suggest?
options: The two filters are equally good, so neither needs any further study of its errors
The filter with fewer misses is better in every respect that could matter to a user
The single score hides different kinds of failure, so each kind needs study
A combined score is the only fair way to compare filters that fail differently
optionExplain: Equal scores can hide very different failures.
Fewer misses may come with more wrong flags, so this does not follow.
Right: the authors call a combined figure not very informative and want both kinds of error understood.
The authors say the opposite: the combined number says little about how to improve.
questions.explain: The authors prefer to understand errors of omission and of commission separately to see why a system could not do better.
questions.teaches: In the book's S3 analysis, 237 of 267 relevant nodes were covered and 23 definite errors of commission were subtracted, giving 80 percent, or 75 percent when questionable errors are counted.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: Because a fit shows only sufficiency, the authors treat it as telling them nothing about the organization.
questions.explain: Sufficiency is still informative: it narrows the field when rival organizations fail to match the behavior.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Two solvers' step sequences on one puzzle differ greatly. What is the most cautious inference?
options: The two must be using entirely different problem-solving programs
One of the two solvers must have made no errors
The programs behind the two paths may be the same or nearly so
Their paths are random and cannot be explained
optionExplain: This treats different paths as proof of different programs, which the authors warn against.
Nothing says either solver was error free; errors are one source of difference.
Right: small differences can produce widely divergent paths from a common program.
The authors explain the paths through priorities and errors.
questions.explain: A fair guess. The card next shows why paths can mislead.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: In large search spaces, ____ causes can bring about great divergences between search paths.
questions.explain: A small difference early on can send the search far from where another solver's search goes.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Two taxi drivers share a map and habits but choose different routes; one slightly prefers highways. Which account fits the authors' reasoning?
options: They must be using two unrelated route-finding programs of their own
A small difference in priority among shared strategies can yield different routes
One of them is not really searching for a route between the two stations
The map must have changed between the first driver's trip and the second
optionExplain: This is the inference the authors caution against.
Right: differences in priority among shared strategies can produce divergent paths.
Both are searching; they simply differ in priority.
Nothing is said to have changed; the difference lies in priority.
questions.explain: Differential priorities among shared strategies account for much of the divergence in paths.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A student claims that, because the four subjects' paths differ, the authors conclude each used a different program. What is wrong?
options: The authors say the component processes and strategies are largely alike in all four
The authors say the four subjects' paths did not in fact differ from one another
The authors say the programs matter much less than the speed of the subjects
Nothing is wrong; the authors treat each path as the work of its own program
optionExplain: Right: differing paths do not imply fundamentally different programs.
The paths did differ; the point is what the difference shows.
Speed is not what the authors point to as the source of the differences.
This is the reading the authors reject.
questions.explain: The differences are accounted for almost entirely by priorities and by particular errors.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Two adults with equal short-term memory spans handle a tax form very differently. Where do the authors locate such a difference?
options: In differing sizes of short-term memory carried from one task to the next
In differing numbers of elementary processes that run at the same time
In differing physiology which the theory describes in careful detail
In differing contents of long-term memory built up over a life history
optionExplain: These two adults are stated to have equal spans, so the cause lies elsewhere.
The theory has the processor serial for everyone, one process at a time.
The theory works at the IPS level; physiology lies below it and is not described in detail.
Right: the theory places differences of content in LTM, which depends on the details of life history.
questions.explain: Equal basic parameters leave the content of LTM open, and the authors place differences of content in what each person has learned over a life history.
questions.teaches: The authors say man mirrors the universe he lives in, so the contents of long-term memory vary as widely as the phenomena from which a person extracts them, and this accounts for the elusiveness of psychological laws.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: The authors claim to offer a complete theory of individual differences.
questions.explain: Chapter 14 says of this part of the theory: "This part of the theory is both tentative and incomplete." The dimensions of variation come from the protocols studied, and the causes of the errors are only rudimentarily indicated.
questions.rule: A list of dimensions is not a theory of differences.
questions.teaches: This part of the theory is both tentative and incomplete.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: One chess player analyzes with the board in view, another plays blindfold. What would these authors expect?
options: No difference, since both players rely on the very same internal memories
The blindfold player is faster
The board only helps by letting the player write moves down on it
The player with the board has an easier problem, as external memory changes the problem
optionExplain: The authors say a processor with only STM and LTM behaves very differently from one that also has external memory.
Nothing in the authors' account favors the blindfold player.
Scanning the display helps even when nothing is written.
Right: with the board in view the problem is much easier.
questions.explain: A fair guess. The card next explains why the board counts as part of the system.
questions.rule: External memory is part of the system.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: The authors define an ____ knowledge state to include what can be fetched from a partly available display.
questions.explain: The extended knowledge state is what is in mind plus what a retrieval process can fetch from the display.
questions.rule: Mind plus what can be fetched.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A pilot cannot recall every item of a printed checklist but can look items up. In the authors' terms, what is her knowledge state?
options: Only the items she is able to recall without looking at the checklist
Everything printed on the checklist, whether or not she can find it when needed
What she holds in mind plus what a retrieval process can fetch from the checklist
Only the checklist, since the printed page is more reliable than her memory
optionExplain: This leaves out the part of the display she can get when needed.
This overstates what is available; contents are available only to the extent they can be obtained.
Right: that is the extended knowledge state.
The knowledge state is defined by what is available for use, in mind and in the display.
questions.explain: A partly available display is treated as an extension of what is in mind.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A solver who has used a display is now given the same task with the display taken away. What do the authors' account predict?
options: The same program works
The solver must adopt a different program, as the program depends on the external memory
The solver gains speed
The solver's long-term memory writes faster to make up for the loss of the display
optionExplain: The authors say the program depends on the external memory as intimately as on the built-in ones.
Right: the program adopted depends on the external memory available.
Nothing in the account links removal of a display to a speed gain.
Write times are a parameter of the processor, not something that adjusts.
questions.explain: Because the program depends on the external memories available, taking one away changes the program that works.
questions.rule: Change the memory, change the program.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: An accountant multiplies two four-digit figures once on paper and once in her head. Roughly what ratio of times do the authors cite?
options: About 1 to 100, paper being far quicker
About 1 to 2, paper being slightly quicker
About 1 to 10, paper being quicker
About 1 to 1, with no difference in time
optionExplain: Right: the authors give the ratio of times as about 1 to 100.
This underestimates the effect; the authors call the evidence the simplest available.
Ten is a reasonable guess but understates the cited ratio.
Equal times would suggest the memory does not matter, which is the reverse of the claim.
questions.explain: The authors give this as the simplest evidence that external memory matters.
questions.teaches: As the simplest evidence that external memory changes the problem, the authors cite that multiplying two four-digit numbers takes about 1 to 100 as long with paper and pencil as without.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: The authors say the benefit of external memory comes only from the slowness of writing to long-term memory.
questions.explain: They say much of the difficulty of mental arithmetic comes from slow writing, but the effect of external memory is not only due to it.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: If a system adapts well to its environment, what will its behavior mostly reveal?
options: The demands of the environment, with only gross features of the system
The detailed inner parts of the system, one by one, as a careful observer sees them
Random variation with no real link to either the system or its surroundings
Only the physical material of which the system happens to be made
optionExplain: Right: an adaptive system shows the environment's demands, with only gross features of itself.
An adaptive system hides most of its inner detail behind its fit.
The authors explain behavior by demands and mechanisms, not by chance.
The authors factor hardware out of the account.
questions.explain: A fair guess. The card next states the outer and inner theory.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: The part of the theory that explains behavior from the environment's demands is called the ____ theory.
questions.explain: The outer theory gives the main, gross results; the inner theory gives the fine structure.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Two drivers reach a town by the shortest route; one then takes a wrong turn going home. Which part of the theory accounts for each?
options: Inner theory for both
Outer theory for both
Inner theory for the shortest route, outer theory for the wrong turn
Outer theory for the shortest route, inner theory for the wrong turn
optionExplain: The inner theory is about fine structure and lapses, not the adapted core.
A wrong turn is a lapse, which the demands alone do not explain.
This reverses the two.
Right: demands explain the shortest route; lapses from adaptation belong to the inner theory.
questions.explain: Adapted behavior follows the task's demands. Errors and wrong explorations are inner fine structure.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: In an extreme environment where adaptation breaks down, what do the authors expect?
options: The environment's demands still explain everything, as before
No system shows any structure, so behavior is unpredictable
The processor's structure shows through in behavior
Behavior becomes simpler, since fewer demands are met
optionExplain: The explanation rests on adaptation, which in this case fails.
The structure shows more, not less, in such cases.
Right: where adaptation breaks down, the IPS structure shows through.
Nothing says behavior gets simpler; it shows the system's own limits.
questions.explain: The argument that only gross features show through depends on adaptation, so in extreme environments more of the structure shows.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: The authors say the fine structure supplied by the inner theory includes lapses from adaptation such as errors, confusions and wrong explorations.
questions.explain: They say the fine structure covers the dynamic details over time and also the lapses from adaptation: errors, confusions and wrong explorations.
questions.teaches: In our case the fine structure relates not only to the dynamic details over time, but also to the lapses from adaptation: errors, confusions, wrong explorations.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Masters of a new board game agree closely on which moves to examine. What two readings of this agreement do the authors' chess discussion suggest?
options: A shared inborn move generator in every player, or a shared fear of losing
A common culture that shapes beliefs, or a common response to the situation's requirements
Luck in the choice of players who were studied, or a flaw in the board's design
A statistical average over many games, or a rule imposed by the tournament
optionExplain: The authors do not argue for an inborn generator.
Right: the authors give both and note the two cannot be fully separated.
Chance and design faults are not what they discuss.
The authors reject averaging as an explanation here.
questions.explain: Because what the task requires is itself defined by the best existing knowledge, culture and requirements are hard to separate.
questions.teaches: In chess the authors note that the task requirement is itself defined sociologically, by the best existing knowledge, so the consensus can be read as common culture or as a common response to the requirements of the situation.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A theory is built from three kinds of puzzle but stated for problem solving in general. What should a careful reader ask?
options: Whether the theory is general
How far the evidence supports reach beyond the three kinds of puzzle
Nothing further, since three kinds of puzzle are enough to prove generality
Which puzzle is best
optionExplain: This rejects generality outright instead of asking how far the evidence goes.
Right: the issue is the distance between the evidence and the claim.
Three tasks give clues, not proof of generality.
The question is about reach, not ranking the puzzles.
questions.explain: A fair guess. The card next gives the authors' own statement of reach.
questions.rule: Ask how far the evidence reaches.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: The authors describe the volume as a ____ report on work that needs to be advanced.
questions.explain: They invite extensions, emendations or even refutations.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A study of six chess players claims its findings hold for all expert business decisions. What is the best response, given the authors' own stance?
options: The claim is argued, not tested, like the authors' own reach beyond three tasks
The claim is proved
The claim is false
The claim is meaningless
optionExplain: Right: the authors treat reach beyond the tested tasks as argued, with undefined limits.
Difficulty of the task does not prove reach.
Falsity is not shown by difference alone; the claim is untested.
Few subjects limit the data but do not make the claim meaningless.
questions.explain: The authors give strong clues but say the limits of the induction are undefined.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A task sends the solver browsing a whole library for ideas. What do the authors suggest about talk of a problem space here?
options: It stays fully meaningful
It becomes more meaningful
It is replaced by a theory of physical movement through the building
It becomes less meaningful, as thinking keeps crossing the boundary of any small space
optionExplain: The authors say a space is meaningful only if thinking seldom crosses its boundary.
A library is a large open source of information, the opposite of a closed space.
Nothing in the account replaces the space by physical movement.
Right: with open-ended search, closure fails, and the concept loses its use.
questions.explain: Closure was the rule in the tasks examined, but a task of browsing a library is a conceivable case where it fails.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: Among unexplored aspects of the processor, the authors name how large the effective short-term memory is when a person uses scratch paper.
questions.explain: They list this and the specifications for associative access in long-term memory as examples of gaps that are not only gaps of extent.
questions.teaches: The authors say the gaps are not only gaps of extent: for example, the effective size of short-term memory with scratch paper and the specifications for associative access in long-term memory remain unexplored.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A researcher applies the theory to a team designing a bridge over many months. Which of the authors' restrictions does this push against?
options: Their focus on children and the young, leaving out the study of adults
Their reliance on statistics, which leaves out the study of single cases
Their focus on short problems, leaving out activity over days or years
Their focus on motor skill, which leaves out purely symbolic tasks
optionExplain: The subjects are adults; development and age differences are not studied.
The book uses little statistics, so this is not its restriction.
Right: the book concentrates on problems of about half an hour and leaves out long-term integrated activity.
Motor skill is not central; the tasks are symbolic.
questions.explain: The book's central focus is short symbolic problems, and it leaves out activity over periods of days or years.
questions.rule: Months of work lie outside the focus.
questions.teaches: The authors say long-term integrated activities extending over days or years receive no attention, and that these restrictions describe a central focus, not a set of boundaries.
